A known theorem ties the Kerr solution to a special spinor field. They turn that tie into concrete conditions on the starting data. The end result states exactly which far-away data grow into a Kerr black hole.
arxiv-2412-03502:
Ankit Chakraborty, Judit Munoz-Matute, Leszek Demkowicz, and Jake Grosek present a new way to model laser pulses traveling through optical waveguides, in this 2024 paper. They propose a modified nonlinear Schrödinger equation tuned to this setting. Depending on the waveguide's parameters, the model splits into a pair of elliptic and hyperbolic equations.

The new form yields a stable first-order system, unlike the standard equation. To solve it, the authors use a space-time discontinuous Petrov-Galerkin finite element method, which treats space and time together on one mesh. They carry out a stability analysis for both kinds of system. Several numerical examples on space-time meshes then show the model behaving stably in practice. The work targets accurate simulation of pulses for photonics design.
arxiv-2412-03702:
Behrad Moniri and Hamed Hassani present a study from twenty twenty-four on linear regression when the input traits lean on each other. Standard theory takes the traits as free of each other and bell curved. Real traits often link in space and time and break that mold. The pair model such traits as processes with a space time spread.

They study ridge regression when both sample count and trait count grow in step. A universality claim shows the long run acts the same if bell curved traits with the same spread stand in. That swap lets random matrix tools pin the error down in a fixed point form. Best penalty picks, overfit, and the double descent curve are read in this linked world.
arxiv-2412-04502:
Jörn Tebbe, Andreas Besginow, and Markus Lange-Hegermann present a new way to steer a linear system toward a target path. Their 2024 paper builds the controller on a Gaussian process, a statistical model whose sample paths obey a set of linear equations. Control inputs come from shaping that model around the setpoints the system should hit.

Soft limits are handled by adding virtual setpoints to the model after data are taken in. The authors show in theory that the plan keeps the open loop system stable for the best control task. A worked numeric case backs the claim. The goal is a control scheme that blends physics based knowledge with a flexible data driven model.
arxiv-2412-05102:
Four researchers present a method for shrinking quantum system models without losing any accuracy, in a 2024 paper. Open quantum systems, those leaking energy to their surroundings, grow too large to simulate directly when many particles interact. Their method builds a smaller model that reproduces exactly the behavior of chosen starting states or measured quantities. It works by exploring the space of operators the dynamics actually visits.

A key proof shows the shrunk model's generator keeps the physically required Lindblad form, so it stays a valid quantum evolution. New kinds of observable-linked symmetries widen where reductions are possible. Benchmarks cover decoherence in central-spin systems, magnetization flow in driven spin chains, and error dynamics in a protected quantum code. The authors aim the tool at both classical simulation and future quantum hardware, where small faithful models save scarce resources.
arxiv-2412-05602:
Lasha Otarashvili, Tamilselvan Subramanian, Jason Holmberg, J. J. Levenson, and Charles Stewart build one system to recognize individual animals across many species in a 2024 study. Ecologists identify animals from photos to track populations, but training a separate model per species is costly and starves rare species of data. Shared looks across species also go unused.

The authors assemble a large community-curated data set spanning many species. A single re-identification model trains on all of it at once. Pooling data should help species with few photos while cutting repeated engineering work. The approach lowers the barrier for conservation groups that need individual tracking.
arxiv-2412-05702:
A muon bound in an atom can convert into an electron without neutrinos, an event that would prove that charged lepton flavor is not conserved. Duarte Fontes and Robert Szafron build a theory framework to predict the exact shape of that signal and of its main background, muon decay in orbit. Experiments will soon sharpen the search limit by four orders of magnitude, so the predictions must be sharp too.

Above the nuclear scale the corrections are manageable, but below it several scales, bound-state effects, and the setup of the detector tangle the math. The authors chain together a series of effective field theories, from heavy quark and non-relativistic theories to soft-collinear ones, and derive a factorization theorem with its renormalization group equations. The framework yields precise rates for both processes and, they report, the most accurate signal shape yet for the coming searches.
arxiv-2412-05802: Sheikh Mannan and Nikhil Krishnaswamy present a real-time system where a human and an AI teach each other a balancing task, in a 2024 paper. The task mimics disorientation during piloting and spaceflight. A visual inverted pendulum display stands in for the balance challenge. A human subject and an autonomous AI model of the user's choice guide each other in staying balanced on that display. The authors show how AI help changes human performance, and how human guidance changes the AI in return, in a two-way learning loop.
arxiv-2412-06002:
Xavier Bekaert, Laura Donnay, and Yannick Herfray build quantum states for an enlarged relativity symmetry in a 2024 paper. The BMS group extends the usual Poincaré symmetries of flat spacetime with extra supertranslation freedom tied to gravity's many vacuum states. Its particle-like states had a known classification but no concrete wavefunctions.

Reworking that classification, the authors split each state's momentum into hard and soft parts in a Lorentz-respecting but nonlinear way. The wavefunctions then emerge naturally. They turn out to describe quantum superpositions of ordinary particles, each riding on a different gravity vacuum. The result gives BMS particles a physical picture that was missing.
arxiv-2412-06102:
Qikang Liu, Yang He, Yanwen Cai, Byeongguk Kwak, and Yuepeng Wang presented a method that writes document database queries from examples in two thousand twenty-four. Document databases store flexible, nested records, which makes their queries hard to write by hand. Their system aims to generate the query automatically.

They first design a small language that expresses a representative set of such queries in algebraic style. Their synthesis method then uses an abstraction of collections to prune the search space with logical deduction. That pruning lets it find the target query fast. On one hundred ten benchmarks from mixed sources, it solved one hundred eight, usually within tens of seconds from a few examples.
arxiv-2412-06302:
Takaaki Nomura and Kei Yagyu explored a rare decay of the Z boson that could reveal new particles in a 2024 paper. In models with a new force, a light scalar and a new Z-like boson can appear together. A Z can then decay through that scalar into three of the new bosons.

Even though the rate is tiny, future Z factories will make so many Z bosons that about one such event could show. That holds when the new force's strength and its mixing with the known Z pass a set floor. The search would sharpen limits on a dark photon measure past present bounds. Benchmark cases also give events with many leptons and jets that the standard model cannot mimic.
arxiv-2412-06802:
Alejandro Nieto Ramos and Elizabeth Cherry ask how roughly a heart model can vary across space and still stay true, in a 2024 paper. Heart cells differ from place to place, and those differences shape the heart's electric waves. Models often wrongly give every cell the same traits. Fine data from light-based heart maps exist, but using every point is costly.

The team let traits vary smoothly over the tissue in a standard heart model. They then rebuilt the full pattern from values known only on a coarse grid. A spacing of about one to one and a half centimetres kept beat-length patterns close to the truth. Flat steps and sloped fills between grid points worked about equally well. The results promise faster models that still honor real heart data.
arxiv-2412-07102:
Shaobing Gao and Yongjie Li train a model of the first visual cortex to test how the brain keeps object colors steady under changed light, in a study from two thousand twenty-four. The model learns to name the light color in natural photos. Its neurons grow fields much like real simple and double-opponent cells.

Double-opponent cells beat simple cells at guessing the light. That flips the usual story, where such cells were said to erase the light's tint. Here they encode it, and the brain can use that read for steady color. The result may guide better machine color tools too. Readers get fresh computational proof on a classic vision puzzle.
arxiv-2412-07402:
Choosing a few people to seed a message so it spreads widest is the influence maximization problem, and real networks refuse to sit still. Yunming Hui and co-authors tackle a harder variant: ties change over time, and people can be activated more than once, not just once as in classic models. They first extend a diffusion model to cover that repeating spread.

Their solver pairs deep reinforcement learning with embeddings that track the network's motion. The agent learns whom to seed while the ground shifts under it. On several real social network datasets, the method beat leading baselines. The authors present it as a step toward influence planning in living networks.
arxiv-2412-07602: Mehrdad Nasernejad and Jonathan Toledo study monomial ideals that meet the copersistence property or the nearly copersistence property. A monomial ideal is built from products of variables, and such ideals form a key test class in commutative algebra. The work asks how the associated primes of an ideal act as the ideal is raised to higher powers. It asks which primes can appear in that sequence, and which ones persist across it.
arxiv-2412-07802:
Xingyi Yang and Xinchao Wang present a 2024 arXiv paper on explaining vision models in words arranged as trees. A picture classifier's reasons are usually hidden in numbers. Their method, LVX, recruits a language model to name layered visual traits, from broad shapes down to fine details, then fetches images that embody each trait.

Those texts and images are mapped into the vision model's own space, growing a tree of concepts it truly uses. The tree is pruned and regrown by asking the language model targeted questions, so stray concepts fall away. Shown a new image, the system explains the model's call as a path through the tree. The team also retrained the vision model against the tree, refining its knowledge. New benchmarks test whether the explanations are plausible, faithful, and stable.
arxiv-2412-07902:
Meyer Scetbon and James Hensman repair shrunken language models in a 2024 paper. Quantization squeezes a trained model to fewer bits per number. Errors creep into both weights and activations. The pair add small full precision matrices to cancel those errors.

Their low rank add ons act on the unquantized activations. A joint optimization tunes the quantized weights and the corrections together. The test case is aggressive four bit compression of both weights and activations. Corrections sized at a tenth of the original cut the accuracy gap by over half. At thirty percent, the gap closed completely. Four recent models, including Llama and Mixtral versions, showed the effect. The method needs only a small calibration data set.
arxiv-2412-08002:
Emily Kerrison, Elaine Sadler, Vanessa Moss, and Elizabeth Mahony study neutral gas in active galactic nuclei in two thousand twenty-four. Their sources were caught in hydrogen absorption in a pilot radio survey. They sort each source by the shape of its broadband spectrum. A link shows up between that shape and the gas signal.

Young radio sources sit at the heart of the puzzle in the title. The link may trace where the neutral gas sits in space. It may also trace how jets push on that gas. Results set up the full survey to come and other broad radio searches.
arxiv-2412-08602:
Imran Latif and co-authors measured power use during training of artificial intelligence models in 2024. Training takes place on costly hardware, often in large data centers. Planners need real numbers, not just rated limits, to size power and cooling.

The team tracked power draw second by second on a node with eight high-end graphics cards. They trained an image model and a large language model. Peak draw was about eighteen percent below the rated limit, even with the cards near full use. For the image model, larger batches cut total energy use by a factor of four. The results can guide data center plans and studies of energy use in computing.
arxiv-2412-08702:
Dying stars shed glowing shells called planetary nebulae, whose brightest members shine at a suspiciously uniform peak across galaxies, making them handy distance markers without any agreed explanation. Lucas Valenzuela and co-authors built PICS, the first method that grows such nebulae inside full cosmological simulations, where stars form and age along realistic histories.

Only with real stellar populations did the simulated brightness ceiling match observations for every galaxy type. The decisive ingredient was letting stellar lifetimes depend on chemical makeup, which alone produced bright nebulae in metal-rich populations. Around a Sun-like setting, the method reproduced the observed brightness distribution down to a millionth of its peak. A fifty-year puzzle gains a working physical account.
arxiv-2412-09002:
Vojtěch Cvrček and co-authors present an astronomy paper, printed in 2024, teaching machines to read the light of stars from a workhorse instrument's full archive. The HARPS spectrograph spent decades hunting planets by measuring stellar spectra with extreme precision. The team trained autoencoder networks on that archive, mixing real and simulated spectra, to predict a star's physical traits and to generate spectra of their own.

The models predicted stellar temperature to within about fifty kelvin and metal content and surface gravity with errors small enough for most astronomy. They also compressed real spectra faithfully. The authors varied training data size, architectures, and learning styles to learn what drives accuracy, aiming at tools for the coming flood of survey spectra.
arxiv-2412-09502:
A drone on a rope never needs to land for charging, but the rope makes it a coupled machine of aircraft and winch. Samuel Folorunsho, Maggie Ni, and William Norris build the full control system for such a tethered drone in a 2024 paper. Onboard controllers steer position and attitude; ground controllers run the winder, paying out line while keeping its hanging curve.

The design uses nonlinear backstepping control, a layer-by-layer method that comes with a stability proof for the combined equilibrium. In simulation the aircraft tracked straight and circular paths accurately across scenarios. The authors publish the code and demonstration videos. Their point is architectural: treating drone, tether, and winder as one system, rather than bolting controllers together, is what makes the stability guarantee possible.
arxiv-2412-09802:
Rita Majumdar, Monojit Chatterjee, and Rahul Marathe study a tiny heat engine in 2024. The engine is a single spin in a magnetic field that changes over time. By timing those changes, the spin can be made to do work like an engine.

The authors derive exact formulas for work, heat, and yield in the long-run limit. They then search for the best field patterns, using both a step-by-step fitting method and a broader math approach. Patterns that settle into flat segments won for yield. Waste heat fell as both power and yield were tuned, which lifted performance.
arxiv-2412-10302:
Zhiyu Wu and co-authors published a research paper in 2024 presenting DeepSeek-VL2, a family of vision-language models built on a mixture-of-experts design. Only a slice of the network wakes for each input, which keeps big models fast. The release improves on an earlier model in both its eyes and its language core.

Pictures are cut into tiles that flex with image shape, so high-resolution pages and charts stay readable. The language side squeezes memory stores into compact vectors for quicker replies. Three sizes are offered, waking one to four and a half billion parameters. Across question answering, text reading, and grounding tests, the models match or beat rivals of like size. Code and weights are public.
arxiv-2412-10402:
Filippo Ziliotto and co-authors let a language model conduct robot skills like an orchestra, with no task training at all, in a 2024 paper. Language models can already stitch vision modules into programs for still images. TANGO extends the trick to embodied agents that move through the world. Its base skills are a point-goal navigator and a memory-guided explorer; the model composes them per task from a few examples in the prompt.

Three hard tests followed: finding named objects, lifelong navigation mixing cues, and answering questions about the surroundings. The composed agent hit state-of-the-art results in zero-shot settings. Training-free composition, the authors argue, scales better than one model per task.
arxiv-2412-11202:
Lucas Hamada wrote a number theory paper in 2024 on elliptic curves. Elliptic curves carry special points that loop back after a set number of steps. Those torsion points form groups whose shapes can be classified. Hamada studies curves over a vast field built by joining all square root extensions of the rationals.

The study limits itself to curves whose j invariant is a rational number, barring two special values. For that family, it lists every torsion group shape that can occur. Such lists are prized because they fence in wild arithmetic behavior. The result extends classic work on curves over smaller fields.
arxiv-2412-11302:
Trishita Tiwari and Edward Suh measure how much of the training text of a large language model can be pulled back out of it. Past measures counted whole texts won back, a blunt yardstick. Their 2024 work scores each text sequence by its own chance of being drawn out. That fine grain lets them retest old claims about what drives leaks.

Tests ran on two known models trained on web crawls. The old measure was found to understate the threat for chance-based models by up to about twofold. Large models and long prompts help on average. Yet for a large share of sequences, small models or short prompts leak more. Partial leaks proved no easier than whole-text leaks under common sampling rules. The team urges the field to adopt the finer measure.
arxiv-2412-11602:
Anton J Heckens, Efstratios Manolakis, Cedric Schuhmann, and Thomas Guhr published a study in 2024 on the joint behavior of stock returns when markets will not sit still. Risk checks need the full pattern of how stocks move together, not just averages. Their earlier work built a random matrix model for such patterns in restless systems, and here they test it on real trading data.

They analyzed minute-by-minute returns for 479 large United States stocks across the twenty fourteen trading year. Extreme moves followed heavy, slow-fading tails, and shifting correlations made those tails heavier still. A formula with few settings captured how the pattern changes with time scale. Better tail estimates mean fewer nasty surprises in risk models.
arxiv-2412-11702:
Mukul Lokhande, Gopal Raut, and Santosh Kumar Vishvakarma built a chip part for AI math that bends to many precisions. Their paper, from twenty twenty-four, deals with processing elements for deep learning and like loads. Models now shift fast, and gear must switch number size and curve shapes on the fly. Past parts do one or the other, not both. Their part, Flex-PE, does both in one cell.

It runs in lanes that split one wide job into many slim ones. It holds the main curve shapes used in neural nets plus the core sum of products step. Throughput scales with how slim the numbers are. Readers who build AI chips get a cell that trades width for speed as the job asks.
arxiv-2412-12302:
Samantha Garza and six co-authors survey gas around galaxies in a paper from twenty twenty-four. The circumgalactic medium holds a galaxy's fuel and waste. Carbon absorption, seen as C IV, traces part of that gas. The team asks how its presence relates to a galaxy's star formation rate.

New Hubble observations anchor their survey, called CIViL. Combined with archival data, they hold forty-six observations of L-star galaxies. Star-forming galaxies showed carbon absorption far more often than passive ones. Detection fractions were roughly seventy percent versus roughly twenty percent. The split is significant at over ninety-nine percent confidence. A similar split was known for oxygen absorption. Readers see the carbon reservoir around galaxies depends strongly on whether the galaxy still forms stars.
arxiv-2412-12402:
Cristian Rodríguez-Camargo and four co-authors predict quantum light effects on molecules in a 2024 paper. Pairs of entangled photons can excite a molecule's vibrations with a selectivity ordinary light cannot match. Full quantum simulations of that process are expensive, limiting exploration.

Using second-order perturbation theory, the team derived a formula for which vibrational levels get populated when a two-atom system absorbs the photon pair. Their formula matches earlier heavy numerical results while running far cheaper. One factor in the expression shows plainly how selectivity grows with the photons' entanglement, the target vibration level, and the molecule's own overlap factors. The authors stress that textbook shortcuts would miss the molecular structure's role. A cheap, insightful formula lets chemists scan conditions and design experiments that use quantum light as a precision tool.
arxiv-2412-13202:
Peter Grindrod, Renaud Lambiotte, and Rohit Sahasrabuddhe map the modules of the fruit fly brain's wiring and find a mirror pattern. Their 2024 report studies the central region of the fly connectome. A flow-based tool groups neurons where signals circulate fast before spreading onward.

The modules stretch across the brain, linking far-apart neurons into single units. Strikingly, they sit in left-right symmetry, in both place and connections. Stacked one level up, the modules form a hierarchy with clear direction to the flow. The authors note the pattern came from wiring alone, with no anatomy fed in. That makes the symmetry a pure product of the network's own structure.
arxiv-2412-13302:
Emile Pangburn, Catherine Pépin, and Anurag Banerjee study unusual charged states in Mott insulators, materials where strong repulsion between electrons blocks normal conduction. They work with a model that adds a magnetic-like term to the standard picture. In this strong regime, electrons can be viewed as pairs of simpler charged pieces.

Using that view, they map out which phases are topological at half filling. They show that both the normal states and special zeros of a key function form protected edge states where two different phases meet. One edge state carries charge, and another carries none. The work may matter for twisted materials with flat bands.
arxiv-2412-13602:
Wenye Lin and colleagues built GAMEBoT in 2024, an arena for testing how well large language models actually reason. Existing reasoning benchmarks are hard to interpret, quickly saturate, or risk leaking into training data. Games offer a cleaner testbed, because strong play demands planning that can be checked step by step against the rules.

GAMEBoT breaks the reasoning inside games into predefined modular subproblems. For each subproblem the designers wrote chain-of-thought prompts that feed the model the relevant domain knowledge before it chooses an action, and rule-based algorithms that compute the correct answer for every subproblem. That makes it possible to grade not only the final moves but the intermediate reasoning itself. The setup also reduces contamination risk, giving a transparent way to compare models' reasoning quality.
arxiv-2412-13702:
Pipatanakul and co-authors release Typhoon 2, a family of open language models built for Thai. Their 2024 paper covers text, image, and audio models in one line. Thai is poorly served by most large models, which train mainly on English and a few big languages.

The text models grow from strong open bases and are trained further on a mix of English and Thai. Sizes run from one to seventy billion parts, in plain and chat-tuned forms. A safety sorter tuned to Thai culture guards the text output. The vision model reads Thai documents while keeping its general sight, and the audio model takes speech in and gives speech out. The team frames the release as open tools for Thai users and builders.
arxiv-2412-13802:
Huiwen Yang, Yu Zhou, and Taolue Chen presented SimADFuzz in 2024, a way to test self-driving systems in simulation. Making test scenes that are varied and that expose faults is the main challenge. Older fuzz testing tools often ignore how scenes change over time and space, and they do not learn much from each run.

SimADFuzz uses feedback from the run, such as speed and heading, to guide its choices. A prediction model scores how likely a scene is to cause a fault, and new scenes are shaped to push cars into closer contact. In tests it found more distinct faults than rival tools, including some real collisions that could be repeated.
arxiv-2412-14002:
Panagiotis Grontas, Anastasios Tsiamis, and John Lygeros build a way that scales for choice tasks with bounds that bulge out, named for Markov. Off the shelf solvers for such tasks work in base rules but scale poor in use. Their first step way rests on a split named for Douglas and Rachford. It splits the move rules of the set from the bounds.

The way swaps steps. One step solves a choice task with a soft add on. The next step casts the result back to the bound set. Both steps are plain to code. The soft add on is built in. It gives last step meet and firm counts with no plain change to the task. When bounds can not all be met, the way spots that fact. It then works out a plan that breaks the bounds by the least sum.
arxiv-2412-14102:
A mechanical resonator that rings long and high is a prize for quantum technology. Yincheng Shi and co-authors design one by computer search. Topology optimization reshapes the device to maximize damping dilution, the effect that stretches out the ring. The new resonators run at higher-order vibration modes rather than the fundamental. That choice lifts both frequency and the quality factor product. Edge bending losses shrink at the same time.

The designs stay compact, which matters for real devices. The authors target quantum information transduction, optomechanical systems, and precision sensing. They present the class as a step past the usual trade between size and performance.
arxiv-2412-14302:
Oleg Lashinin, Denis Krasilnikov, Aleksandr Milogradskii and Marina Ananyeva wrote a 2024 paper on a model that predicts a shopper's next basket. Guessing the next single item is well studied, but baskets hold many items at once. Shoppers also repeat past buys often, which pure deep models underuse. Simple frequency methods still beat many deep ones here.

Their model adds item frequency data into a transformer design. Attention layers read the shop history in order. Frequency signals guide the model toward repeat buys. On several data sets, the model beat all rivals tested. Recall at ten rose by a clear margin over the best baseline.
arxiv-2412-15402:
Water utilities burn large amounts of power moving water, and solar panels could offset much of that bill. Mirhan Ürkmez, Carsten Kallesøe, Jan Dimon Bendtsen, and John Leth ask how many panels a water network should install. Too few waste the chance to save; too many cost more than they earn back. Their procedure hunts for the count that minimizes total cost over the panels' lifetime.

The method samples many possible sunny and cloudy futures from a probability model of solar output. For each future it simulates the network with a pump controller built for solar power, then adds up the cost. A derivative-free search adjusts the panel count until the cost stops falling. For the Danish town of Randers, the best setup cut network costs by about 14.5 percent.
arxiv-2412-15902:
Lorenz Wendlinger and co-authors test large language models on German legal analysis in a 2024 paper. Open models carry some German law knowledge and follow instructions well. Fine style tasks, like sorting parts of a formal legal opinion, trip them up. Full opinions with long context also strain them past simple baselines.

A retrieval method that picks prompt examples by relevance lifts scores where data is rich. On argument mining and essay grading tasks, models fare better. With little or no labeled data, models beat baselines, and step by step prompting helps most there. The study maps where schools can trust such tools and where caution rules.
arxiv-2412-16602:
Chi and co-authors present a computer vision paper, published in 2024, on shrinking a family of image models so they run on small devices. The leading image models are powerful but slow, because their core step grows steeply with image size. A newer family processes images in a line, step by step, which scales far better. On modern chips, though, that line process underuses the hardware and creates a bottleneck.

The team's fix is bold: cut the model's inner width down to a single channel. Their method needs no retraining, so it can be applied to trained models directly. The squeezed model keeps most of its accuracy while running much faster. That trade suits phones, cameras, and other gear with tight power budgets. The paper shows that for these models, a wide inner space is mostly waste.
arxiv-2412-17202:
If space-time coordinates refuse to commute, even plain electromagnetism bends in strange ways. Abla and Neves work out that bending in a 2024 paper. Their stage is a deformed space named for Minkowski with a twist.

They couple point charges to the deformed gauge field cleanly. Field solutions yield a corrected Lorentz force at second order. The correction hints at gravity-like pull born of the deformation. Such effects would shift how particles trace paths. Standard physics assumes smooth commuting space, so any trace matters. The math sets terms for future tests.
arxiv-2412-17402:
Large-scale dynamos build cosmic magnetic fields out of turbulence, and magnetic helicity fluxes decide whether they thrive or choke. Axel Brandenburg and Ethan Vishniac analyze direct simulations of dynamos in rotating, inhomogeneous turbulence, driven without helicity and with or without shear. The forcing peaks mid-domain and fades toward the ends, and an alpha effect of opposite signs in the two hemispheres drives the large-scale field.

With shear, the hemispheric flux of small-scale helicity grows important and can even outweigh the flux the alpha effect passes between scales. That effect had not been seen without shear. The scale-to-scale flux still falls as the magnetic Reynolds number rises, yet the mean field now holds steady instead of declining. The authors argue that shear-driven helicity fluxes relieve the catastrophic quenching that plagues nonshearing dynamos.
arxiv-2412-17502:
Nitin Kumar Chidambaram, Maciej Dolega, and Kento Osuga prove a counting theorem in a 2024 math paper. Hurwitz numbers tally branched coverings of surfaces, a count with many variants. One family, weighted with a parameter and a chosen weight rule, resisted a clean recursive method of computation.

Topological recursion is a machine that builds counting answers step by step from one starting curve. The authors prove the weighted family comes out of that machine in its refined form, on a simple rational curve. Special cases include monotone Hurwitz numbers and counts of maps drawn on surfaces that cannot be oriented. Standard random matrix ensembles fall out as a bonus.
arxiv-2412-17602:
Daniel Graf and Alex Thom introduce a new variant of a flexible method for computing the electronic states of molecules. The base method, non-orthogonal configuration interaction, allows more freedom than the standard approach in how states are built. That freedom creates a problem: no accepted recipe exists for choosing a compact yet accurate set of building blocks. The authors aim to supply one.

Their approach pursues three goals at once. It should be systematic, it should keep the expansion small, and it should treat ground and excited states even-handedly. They develop the method step by step, testing each building block on simple model systems as they go. The tests show the design works as intended. The paper offers the scheme as a step toward making this flexible family of methods routine in quantum chemistry.
arxiv-2412-18402:
Joan Hernández studies when a flaw in a solution to a fractional heat equation can simply be ignored, in a 2024 paper. The equation spreads heat with long-range jumps, unlike the usual case. A solution may go wrong at a few points or along a moving edge. A flaw counts as removable if the solution is in fact fine there.

The work deals with Lipschitz solutions inside domains that change with time. It sets out a capacity, a way to measure how big a bad set is for this equation, and finds the key size below which bad sets cannot matter. Two singular integral operators built from the basic solution are shown to stay bounded on square-integrable functions. Such results tell modelers which flaws in data or shape are harmless.
arxiv-2412-18702:
Yanlin Feng, Simone Papicchio, and Sajjadur Rahman build a benchmark for querying huge knowledge graphs with language models in a paper from 2024. Graphs like Wikidata can feed models private and public facts, but their schemas are too large for a model's context window. Identifiers and tangled relation types add to the problem.

Their fix lays a property graph view over the raw graph, which models can query in the Cypher language. The benchmark holds eleven such graphs across domains, with millions of entities and over ten thousand questions. Building it needed a converter engine and new scoring metrics, both described in the paper.
arxiv-2412-18802:
Zhun Gou and colleagues solved a class of leader-follower games under uncertainty in a 2024 math paper. In a Stackelberg game, a leader commits to a strategy first and a follower replies, here with both sides steering a noisy system over time and costs measured in a linear-quadratic way. Extra affine limits tie the leader's choices to the follower's response, which complicates the contest.

Using stochastic Riccati equations and duality theory, the authors derive feedback forms for both players' best strategies. Under a standard feasibility condition, the leader's problem matches its dual, and a checklist condition helps solve it. A new positivity condition secures a unique answer, and two worked examples with indefinite weights support the theory.
arxiv-2412-19202: Ivanov and Tuzhilin study embeddings into rectilinear space in two thousand twenty-four. Rectilinear space measures distance by the sum of gaps along each axis. They ask when a given finite metric space can be placed inside such a space of set dimension. Their result restates that question in a new form. The test becomes a Gromov-Hausdorff distance between certain special finite metric spaces. That distance gauges how close two spaces sit in shape. The paper is a brief note with a single sharp claim.
arxiv-2412-19402:
Xiong Hu, Xuebing Hao and Baode Li prove endpoint estimates for discrete fractional operators, in their 2024 arXiv paper. Their objects are the discrete fractional maximal operator and the discrete Riesz potential, acting on weighted sequence spaces over the integers. Endpoint cases, where exponents sit at the boundary, are the delicate ones.

They characterize exactly which weights make the operators bounded at the endpoint: a stated weight class is both necessary and sufficient. A second result ties another weight class to an oscillation property of the Riesz potential. A simpler proof of a known boundedness range is also given. More weighted inequalities follow, some new even for the continuous setting.
arxiv-2412-19902:
Popadiuk and ten co-authors gauge spin waves in thin films of the full Heusler mix Co2FeGe. That mix is a pick for gear that uses spin. Films were grown on magnesium oxide bases in not the same heat states. Light spread named for Brillouin and pull wave tests probed how their pull traits shift and move.

A lay down at room heat and then a bake at three hundred degrees for one hour gave the best mix of traits. That plan gave most pull strength and most swap stiffness. It gave least loss of spin moves, just what fast spin gear wants. The team also saw strong mix of spin waves in the Damon-Eshbach shape. Such mix draws staff who build paths that route facts with waves in place of streams of charge.
arxiv-2412-20102:
Counting the ways to split a whole number into prime parts is a classic problem, and Anji Dong, Nicolas Robles, Alexandru Zaharescu, and Dirk Zeindler push it further. They count splits that use only a special family of primes, those from which a fixed root can be drawn a set number of times. Using the Hardy-Littlewood circle method, a classic tool for such counts, they find a formula for how the count grows as the number gets large.

They also prove a twin result built from the von Mangoldt function and the zeros of the Riemann zeta function. To handle the hard parts of the proof, they coin two new notions: strange functions and a relaxed form of smoothness called pseudo-differentiability.
arxiv-2501-00102: Stijn Cambie settles the supply of Šoltés digraphs, directed graphs where removing any single vertex leaves all distances among the rest unchanged. Writing in twenty twenty-four, he proves that infinitely many such digraphs exist, mirroring the known graph result in the directed world. He also gives one example whose only symmetry is the trivial one. The note is short, but it closes an open existence question and hands map makers of directed networks a rare, perfectly balanced family.
arxiv-2501-00302:
Mohamed Belfkir, Mohamed Amin Loualidi, and Salah Nasri build in 2024 a model that unites particle forces and explains particle masses. Their frame joins quarks and leptons in one scheme, a step called Pati-Salam unification. A symmetry with three parts shapes how matter fields may interact.

Three trial models fit sixteen known facts, from mass ratios to mixing angles. Light neutrino masses arise through a seesaw effect built into the frame. All three models favor one order of neutrino masses over the other. Two models predict a signal size that near-term tests could detect. Future tests of rare decays may thus tell the models apart or rule them out.
arxiv-2501-00402:
Giada Basile, Dario Benedetto, Lorenzo Bertini, and Daniel Heydecker analyze the rate function of the Boltzmann equation in two thousand twenty-four. The rate function prices large fluctuations of a gas model over time. Their case is the count of collisions per particle per unit time. Number of particles and time span both grow in the limit.

A phase transition shows in that joint limit, they find. For low collision counts the rate function vanishes outright. That trait traces to special Lu-Wennberg solutions of the equation. Second order checks show such dips are still exponentially rare in particle count. Controllability of the equation is a key step.
arxiv-2501-00502:
Miro Miranda, Marcela Charfuelan, and Andreas Dengel forecast crop losses in a paper whose text is dated 2024. Extreme weather puts harvests and food supply at risk. Classic crop models follow plant physics but often miss the mark. Pure machine learning models score well yet hide their reasoning.

The team blends both paths in a physics informed neural network. Their model estimates water use and water stress at each map pixel. It then solves the standard yield response relation step by step. Inputs came from satellite images, climate records, and field yield data. Accuracy matched or beat strong rival models in their tests. Outputs stayed true to plant physics, so users can read the reasons. Farmers and officials could use such forecasts to plan ahead.
arxiv-2501-00602:
Jiawei Yang and co-authors rebuild moving outdoor scenes in a paper published in 2024. Faithful three-dimensional reconstruction of dynamic streets normally needs dense views and per-scene tuning, which is slow and brittle. Their model instead predicts the scene in one forward pass with a transformer network.

It represents the scene as moving three-dimensional blobs with velocities, using self-supervised flow to gather blobs from all frames into any chosen moment. That yields complete views from arbitrary angles, and moving objects emerge with clean masks from reconstruction loss alone. The method beats prior approaches on public data, rebuilds a scene in a fifth of a second, and renders in real time.
arxiv-2501-00802:
Praveen Kumar reports on energy measurement methods for the DUNE neutrino experiment in a 2025 paper, on behalf of the collaboration. DUNE will use huge tanks of liquid argon that record particle tracks in fine detail. The technology images well and identifies particles, which suits neutrino studies and rare-event hunts alike.

Turning recorded charge into accurate energy is vital and hard, since signals fade and distort as they drift. The paper reviews reconstruction and calibration techniques that correct those effects. It draws on test detectors and simulations run before the main build. Precise energy scales underpin every DUNE result, from neutrino oscillations to supernova watching, so this groundwork carries unusual weight.
arxiv-2501-00902:
Approximating a function by a ratio of two polynomials, a rational function, often beats a plain polynomial by a wide margin. Trefethen tells the story of how new algorithms have turned this old subject into something a laptop can do in milliseconds.

The AAA algorithm, named for adaptive Antoulas-Anderson, computes near-best rational approximations with ease. A companion method, Vandermonde with Arnoldi, does the same service for polynomial fits on regions beyond simple intervals and disks. Rather than teach the algorithms, the article uses six matching figures to display the theory behind the fits, the Walsh and Gonchar picture of where poles gather and errors fall. Examples on the unit disk reach accuracy near one part in a trillion with degree six.
arxiv-2501-01002:
Yusi Wei and co-authors anonymize shared data with optimization in a 2025 paper on privacy for machine learning. Companies increasingly hand datasets to outside analysts, but stripping identifiers badly can gut the data's usefulness, and older anonymization models handle categories poorly and were tested narrowly.

Their model balances two goals at once: lose as little information as possible while leaving as few people exposed to linkage or sameness attacks as possible. Across varied datasets it beat two existing algorithms on information loss and, in several cases, on attack exposure. Machine learning models trained on the protected data are part of the scorecard.
arxiv-2501-01402:
Haixu Liu and co-authors test in 2025 how to train image classifiers when many training labels are wrong. Bad labels come from human slips or faulty collection, and they can drag a model's score down hard. One fix guesses a table of how true labels flip into wrong ones, then corrects for it.

The team improved a known fix with two new variants meant to be steadier. They also built two plain classifiers as yardsticks. Tests used a fashion photo set with known label noise and a harder photo set. The report weighs which route best finds clean labels and best guesses the flip table.
arxiv-2501-01502:
Nadja Willenborg studies, in a 2025 paper, codes built inside the algebra of a special group, the generalized quaternion group. Such codes are sets of group-algebra elements used to store or send data with error control. Her work is limited to the case where the field size does not divide the group order in a certain way, a case with a cleaner structure.

In that case, any code has a single generator element, and the whole algebra splits into simple blocks. Willenborg works out, from that generator, exactly which blocks a given code occupies. She then applies the result to describe the blocks of codes that come from the simpler cyclic group codes, tying the two families together.
arxiv-2501-01802:
Ferhat Ozgur Catak, Murat Kuzlu, and Umit Cali adapt a famous language model design to wireless channel prediction in this 2025 paper. Massive MIMO systems use large antenna arrays to raise capacity and cut energy per bit. Their performance leans on knowing the state of the radio channel, which shifts as users move and signals scatter.

Their model, BERT4MIMO, borrows the BERT architecture built for text and retrains it on channel data. Attention mechanisms let it weigh which parts of the signal history matter for the next state. In experiments the model rebuilt channel information well across varied speeds of movement and channel conditions. The authors report it beat comparison approaches in a range of wireless settings. Reliable channel prediction of this kind can help future networks schedule users and shape beams with less overhead.
arxiv-2501-01902:
Valeria Olivares and co-authors found a tight link between hot gas glow and cool filament glow in galaxy clusters, in a 2025 paper. The biggest galaxies in cooling clusters sit amid hot plasma that rains down in multiphase filaments, from ten-thousand-degree ionized gas to frigid molecules. Black hole jets stir the system, and cooling filaments may feed the black hole back. How the phases connect was unclear.

Across seven X-ray bright clusters, the brightness of the filaments' hydrogen-alpha light tracked the X-ray brightness of the hot gas closely, over a hundredfold range. A similar link appears in stripped galaxy tails. The authors read the match as evidence the phases share an origin in cooling hot gas. The correlation gives modelers a hard number that any filament formation theory must reproduce.
arxiv-2501-02002:
Guhan Sivakumar writes a 2025 paper on forecasting inflation with a blended model. Price growth is hard to predict because economies shift between calm and stormy phases. The approach pairs two tools so that each covers the weakness of the other.

A hidden Markov model first sorts past data into hidden states that stand for distinct economic moods. Those states and their averages are then fed as extra inputs to a memory network that learns long patterns. Tests show the blend forecasts consumer price inflation more closely than the network alone. The blend also coped better with wild swings in the data. A gradient method helps explain which inputs drove each forecast.
arxiv-2501-02102:
Francisco Gonzalez Montoya and Christof Jung track the breakup of a special invariant surface in chaotic systems in a 2025 paper. Normally hyperbolic invariant manifolds organize transport in phase space, acting like highways for trajectories. As perturbation grows, such a surface loses its grip and decays.

The pair follow the decay two ways at once: through the surface's own internal map, and through a time delay function spread over a slice of phase space. Tangential transient effects, trajectories that linger oddly along the surface, leave readable marks in the delay function. Their test system is an electron moving in a perturbed magnetic dipole field. The work shows how indicator functions can betray a hidden structure's decay before it vanishes.
arxiv-2501-02502:
Kroll calculates in 2025 how high-energy light striking a proton can knock out a pion plus an excited Delta state. At wide angles such reactions are too hard for direct quark-level computation, so theory splits them into a hard core and soft form factors. The soft parts encode how quarks share momentum inside the proton and its excited sibling.

Working to a stated accuracy order, the study reuses the hard core from plain pion production. The needed soft inputs are tied to better-known proton distributions through a large-color limit argument. The near parameter-free results land in reasonable agreement with measurements, supporting the handbag picture of the reaction.
arxiv-2501-02602:
Dongwei Chen and Martin Schmoll use transport distances to study probabilistic frames in a 2025 math paper. Frames are flexible stand-ins for bases in signal work: a probabilistic frame spreads that structure over a cloud of points with weights, rather than a fixed list of vectors.

The authors measure gaps between such clouds with Wasserstein distances, the cost of shoveling one pile into the shape of another. Borrowing classic results, they show that clouds sharing the same frame operator can be carried into each other by a best-possible linear push. That bridge lets them carry over recent theorems and prove the clouds form one connected family. They also sort which related transport plans truly come from such pushes.
arxiv-2501-02702:
Binita Saha and co-authors flip question answering around by matching questions to questions, in this 2025 paper. Standard retrieval systems fetch text chunks by likeness to the user's query, which dilutes facts and invites made-up answers. Their system pre-writes likely questions for each chunk.

A user query then meets its closest twin among those pre-written questions, pulling the right chunk with it. The build sits on an open eight-billion-parameter chat model. Test data came from a busy website's five hundred pages, with hand-made answer keys. Scores on two ranking metrics beat classic retrieval setups. The authors target domains where answers must stay exact.
arxiv-2501-03802:
Chiara Castello and colleagues studied a family of error-correcting codes built for network communication in 2025. Cyclic orbit codes live in the geometry of subspaces: a single subspace is rotated by a cyclic group to generate the whole codebook. The paper pursues two questions, how to tell when two such codes are really the same, and how close a code can come to the best possible parameters, the quasi-optimality question.

For the first, the authors connect a code's words to a linear set on the projective line, a translation that yields fresh bounds on code parameters. For the second, they isolate one family of near-optimal codes and prove a general existence theorem for quasi-optimal examples in even-dimensional spaces over finite fields of any characteristic. They finish by describing the chosen family's symmetry groups, both geometric and Galois.
arxiv-2501-03902:
Franco Ruggeri and co-authors present a way to explain AI decisions in a 2025 paper. Agents trained by reinforcement learning choose actions based on value scores that sum up all future rewards at once. That single number hides when good or bad outcomes are expected, which makes the agent hard to understand.

Their method, TPD, breaks the value of an action into a sequence of expected outcomes, one for each future time step. A learning scheme estimates those outcomes for both the best action and weaker ones, so explanations can contrast choices. Tests showed the breakdowns were accurate and clarified the agent's plan. Seeing which rewards arrive when also helps designers tune the reward setup to match human expectations.
arxiv-2501-04102:
Song Wang and six co-authors tackled graph learning under distribution shift in twenty twenty-five. Graph neural networks falter when test graphs differ from training ones. Popular defenses augment the training graphs to create new environments, then extract the subgraph that stays predictive across them. The authors argue both steps can break consistency: augmented graphs may be unrealistic, and hacked-up subgraphs may lose their honest link to the label.

Their framework uses a single modifier to produce both augmented and invariant graphs in a unified way. Augmentation enriches training while preserving label-graph relationships, and a label-consistency mechanism protects supervision inside the invariant graph. Extensive experiments on real-world data sets showed the approach beating state-of-the-art baselines for out-of-distribution graph generalization.
arxiv-2501-04802:
Yongkang Li, Panagiotis Eustratiadis, and Evangelos Kanoulas reproduce and repair a known attack on search engines. Their 2025 paper revisits HotFlip, a method that swaps words by gradient hints to craft passages that poison a retrieval corpus, sneaking hostile text to the top of results. Two flaws dogged the method: it was too slow to build many poisoned passages, and it assumed the attacker knows real user queries.

The team first speeds the gradient work up sharply, making large attacks feasible. They then relax the query knowledge assumption toward what a real attacker could hold. The reproduction doubles as a warning: dense retrieval systems in production inherit these holes unless defended.
arxiv-2501-04902:
Nicolas Rothbacher and five co-authors present a 2025 field study on an AI tool for catching illegal farm waste dumping in Wisconsin. The satellite-based system flags suspect dumping sites for investigation. Both the state natural resources department and an environmental interest group field-tested it in early 2023. The two organizations agreed closely on how accurate the detections were when checked on the ground.

Yet they judged the tool's usefulness very differently. The state agency cared only about clear violations of existing law; dumping by an unpermitted operator, or just before a legal deadline date, counted as irrelevant. The interest group wanted to document environmental risk beyond what the law covers. The authors conclude that AI can target scarce enforcement resources, but the value of the same tool depends on organizational goals. It may also expose gaps in the law itself.
arxiv-2501-05402:
Yinglai Wang, Bryn Davies, and Marc Martí-Sabaté propose a way to build metamaterials with set patterns from the three-gap theorem, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Their paradigm unifies and extends concepts behind edge states that stay local. The model borrows the discretized coupling strengths of the SSH model. A modulation parameter marks how edge modes flow in the spectrum, evoking the Hofstadter butterfly.

A localization factor tied to each eigenmode anchors the analysis. With it, the authors show when localized edge states exist in finite systems. They compare those eigenfrequencies against the spectra of the periodic problem without end. Rich patterns emerge as its settings vary. Edge modes appear, vanish, or delocalize across the parameter space. The frame gives designers a principled route to stock with tunable edge conduct.
arxiv-2501-05502:
Sergei Kudriashov and co-authors tackle a shape problem in language model embeddings in a 2025 paper. Word and sentence vectors from transformer models tend to bunch into a narrow cone, which blurs meaning differences. Spreading them out evenly, called isotropy, improves later task scores, but past fixes cost speed or need much data.

Their method borrows from simplicial geometry, the study of simplex shapes. During fine-tuning it rewards vector sets whose barcodes, a summary from topology, carry high persistent entropy. In plain terms, it shrinks the longest spread directions to even out the space. Tests show better downstream results with lower cone bunching. The gain comes from geometry already present in the data, not from retraining the model.
arxiv-2501-06002:
Kevin Mancini and Islem Rekik control information flow in graph neural networks in a 2025 paper. These networks learn by passing messages between connected nodes. Deep versions blur node identities and squeeze distant signals, two failures called over-smoothing and over-squashing.

Their DeltaGNN scores how information flows across the graph and uses that score to steer messages. The cost stays linear, and theory backs the mechanism. Long-range links, usually the first casualty of depth, survive better under flow control. Graphs from molecules to social networks need such depth, since meaning often sits many hops away.
arxiv-2501-06702:
Sanchari Bhattacharyya and co-authors train machine learning tools to spot ultra-fast particle jets at a planned giant collider. The Future Circular Hadron Collider will smash particles at energies never reached before. Fast jets from heavy particles must be told apart from plain background jets. Their 2025 study tests two learning methods on jets from W bosons and top quarks.

One method builds on boosted decision trees, and the other reads jet images with a neural network. Both were tried in three scenarios that hunt for new heavy particles. The jets fly with huge sideways push, which warps their shape. The authors show both methods can sort the rare jets from background at these extremes. The work feeds design studies for the future machine.
arxiv-2501-06902:
Ghalavand, Klavžar, and Yang present a 2025 graph theory paper on breaking every cycle in grid-like products of trees. The decycling number counts the fewest vertices whose removal leaves a forest. Its twin, the forest number, counts the most vertices a forest can keep. For products of two trees, the pair prove star trees are the easiest case, settling a standing conjecture.

Any tree product needs at least one fewer removals than the first tree's size, and the equality cases are pinned down. For prisms over trees the answer equals the matching number. A general product bound ties the two factors' matching numbers together. Cycle-breaking thus gains exact rules on these networks.
arxiv-2501-07202:
Wassim Kabbani, Kiran Raja, Raghavendra Ramachandra, and Christoph Busch present FaceOracle, a chat helper for face photos on ID cards. Their twenty twenty-five paper starts from a strict need: ID and travel documents demand high-grade face images, and the rules for a good photo are long and detailed.

FaceOracle pairs standard quality checks with a language model that can talk. A user can ask why a photo fails, and get a plain account of the flaw and the rule behind it. The team built a proof of concept for staff at issuing offices. It shows how such a helper could speed their work and make choices clearer to applicants.
arxiv-2501-07302:
Zafar Normatov studies a split form of anti-associative algebras, in a 2025 algebra paper. In an anti-associative algebra, regrouping a product flips its sign rather than leaving it fixed. A dendriform algebra splits one product into two operations whose sum gives the original law. Normatov defines the anti-associative version of that split and develops its basic theory.

The paper uses O-operators, maps between algebras with special properties, to build and interpret the new structures. It also shows that anti-associative algebras carrying a nondegenerate Connes cocycle admit a matching dendriform structure. The results extend a general splitting method, used across many algebraic families, to this setting. The work is pure theory, aimed at readers in abstract algebra.
arxiv-2501-07402:
Pezzotti and co-authors ask whether an inward-drifting planet spun up its star, in this 2025 astronomy paper. The star GJ 504 rotates in just over three days, far faster than a lone star of its age should, and it glows brightly in X-rays. A giant planet sits close by. If that planet spiraled inward, it could have fed angular momentum to the star, winding it up like a top.

New X-ray data from the eROSITA survey tighten the facts the theory must fit. The team weighs the star's spin and glow against models with and without strong star-planet interaction. Sorting true interaction effects from a star's own youth matters for reading exoplanet systems. GJ 504 is one of the best test cases astronomers have.
arxiv-2501-07502:
Mingkang Wu and co-authors build a reinforcement learning method that learns from graded experience, in this 2025 paper. Standard learning treats all attempts alike, guided only by total reward. Humans instead sort tries into levels: a tennis whiff is a worse lesson than a near miss, even at equal reward. The team copies that habit at two levels of information extraction.

At the low level, ratings infer hidden reward values for states and actions. At the high level, the policy is pushed away from poor-level behavior and toward good-level behavior, with weights by level. A new loss term penalizes likeness between the current policy and each experience level. The authors report the joint design improves both reward and policy quality, mimicking human learning from failure.
arxiv-2501-07702:
Vincent Novellino and Dmitriy Anistratov present a multi-level Monte Carlo method for particle transport, in two thousand twenty-five. The method solves how neutral particles stream through a slab of material. It builds on a cheap, low-grade solution and then corrects it step by step across a ladder of grids.

Samples come from a hybrid method based on simpler diffusion equations. The team first draw samples on each grid, then compute the best number to add on each level. For flux totals over the whole slab or a part of it, the correction spread shrank faster than costs grew. Coarse grid work drove both spread and cost, so extra levels should be cheap.
arxiv-2501-07802:
Alejandro Carrasco and five co-authors test vision language models as operator agents for space missions in this 2025 paper. These models read images and text together. The team tried them in two settings. In simulation, the agent watched screenshots of a spaceflight game and flew orbital maneuvers from what it saw. In the lab, the same kind of model drove robots with cameras to inspect and diagnose physical satellite like objects.

The agents produced sensible, context fitting actions from raw views, rivaling traditional methods and text only models in the simulator. Hardware trials showed promise rather than polish. The attraction is generality: one agent that sees can handle tasks no one scripted in advance. Space operations prize that flexibility, since missions meet problems that ground teams never rehearsed. The authors present the work as early evidence.
arxiv-2501-08002:
Marios Aristodemou and co-authors craft a poisoning attack on federated learning in a 2025 security paper. In federated learning, many users train one shared model without sharing raw data. A malicious user can instead send rigged updates that quietly wreck the shared model's trustworthiness.

Their attack, Delphi, aims to maximize the model's output uncertainty. It exploits a link between uncertainty and the weights of the first hidden layer. Two search methods, Bayesian optimization and a trust-region method, tune the poisoned weights. The Bayesian version induced the most uncertainty in tests. The authors also prove the attack's effect on paper. They present the work as a warning: privacy tools alone do not make shared learning safe.
arxiv-2501-08102:
Wentao Xu, Wenlu Fan, Yuqi Zhu, and Bin Wang wrote a study in two thousand twenty-five on how language models handle emotion on social media. The models write text well, but whether they keep a steady emotional tone and clear meaning in online talk was little studied.

The team gave four models posts about climate change from Twitter and Reddit. Each model had to reply to posts and to continue them. Meaning stayed coherent in both human and model text. Emotion differed: the models softened negative feelings. Anger, disgust, fear, and sadness in a post often came back as neutral or even cheerful replies.
arxiv-2501-08302:
Rohit Sahasrabuddhe, Renaud Lambiotte, and Martin Rosvall present a 2025 arXiv paper on network models that remember. Plain network models treat each step in a path as independent, yet real path data often depend on where the flow came from. Full second-order models catch that memory but balloon in size. The team builds networks that sit between the two extremes.

Their method adds state nodes only where second-order effects truly live, guided by a measure that weighs size against accuracy. On synthetic and real data, the compact networks exposed large-scale memory patterns. They matched much of the second-order insight at a fraction of its size.
arxiv-2501-08502:
Melissa Torgbi and co-authors tested speech software on Scottish accents for public services in this 2025 study. Staff who take calls must hear callers clearly, yet speech tools can fail on local speech and harm those who most need help. The team gathered new speech in a service setting from two areas of Scotland.

A leading open speech model made more word errors on the new data than on standard test data. Extra training on speech from one area cut errors there, and it also helped on the other area, which suggests some gains carry across areas. Hand checks of errors showed that a single word error score hides both gains and new flaws, so close reading still matters.
arxiv-2501-08602:
Subwattanachai derives formulas for the generalized Frobenius number of triangular numbers, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. The Frobenius number is the largest integer with limited representations as combinations of given coin values. Here the coin values are three consecutive triangular numbers. Representation counts are capped at a chosen level s in the generalization.

A closed formula covers every non-negative value of s completely. Triangular numbers follow the familiar binomial coefficient pattern in n. The proof also addresses a standing conjecture by Komatsu on the topic. Number theorists gain exact answers for this whole infinite family. Coin problem variants often resist such complete closed formulas entirely.
arxiv-2501-09202: Bryan Johnson and Joseph Rosenblatt wrote a math paper in two thousand twenty-five on series built from averages. They ask when such series converge in the strong senses called absolute and unconditional. The series come from processes in ergodic theory and in harmonic analysis. Cases include Cesaro averages and Lebesgue derivatives. The authors sort out which of these series have the strong forms of convergence. The work is a focused piece on convergence for averaged processes.
arxiv-2501-10102:
Thomas Baruchel presents an algorithm for walking through every ordering of a sequence in a 2025 paper. The method runs on a singly linked list and is indifferent to what the elements are. It uses only constant time elementary operations on recursive lists. No new nodes are ever allocated: the original nodes are rearranged in place from start to finish.

The orderings arrive in an unusual order, yet the steps between consecutive permutations stay smooth. A proof of concept written in Lisp is referenced and discussed. The author offers the algorithm as an elegant take on a classic computing task, with memory thrift as its signature virtue.
arxiv-2501-10302:
Vladimir Pozdnyakov solves the classic gambler's ruin ask for walks whose steps lean on each other, in a study from 2025. A gambler bets till broke or till a goal is hit. Stock math needs free steps, but real runs of luck clump: wins and losses lean on the step before.

His tool is the martingale stop rule, a fair-game math crown. Plain forms come out for ruin odds and mean game span, for steps of one each way and for a three-way step with a stall. A broad trick then serves stalls in the wide case. A last part treats bets on two set patterns, a game where the prize goes to the pattern that shows first. Lean, in his forms, moves the odds in ways free-step math would miss.
arxiv-2501-10802:
Simon Gregersen and co-authors prove the safety of a tool that builds signed data forms on its own. The work dates to 2025. Signed forms let far-off parties run steps and hand back proofs of the result. Such forms are hard to build and easy to get wrong.

The proof rests on a new tie logic for code that uses hash locks. Two sense models of a type frame back the proof. They show how the tool leans on type masks to guard safety and right acts. Speed tweaks to the tool pass the same proof. Hand-built forms can then link with auto code in a sound way.
arxiv-2501-11002:
Federated learning trains one model across many phones or hospitals without moving their data, but one global model fits nobody whose data differ. Yasaman Saadati and two co-authors propose pMixFed in 2025, which blends each client's global and personal models layer by layer, mixing them in the style of the mixup training trick. Which layers stay personal adapts as training proceeds.

The blending eases the drift between local and global models and softens the forgetting that plagues the method. Gradual personalization lets clients settle into their share of the model. Across varied uneven data splits, the authors report faster training and hardier accuracy than rival personalized methods. Personalization, they argue, should be a dial, not a switch.
arxiv-2501-11202:
Lemberg and Indelman help robots plan safely in worlds where what an object is and where it sits are tangled together. A robot's belief about a room mixes discrete labels with continuous poses, and learned models tie the two tightly, making the label space explode. Their 2025 paper plans under that hybrid belief with a partially observable decision framework.

They define safety that respects meaning, not just geometry. The core trick is a reshaped belief that yields fair samples cheaply. Under stated conditions, expected reward and safety odds come out in closed form across all label assignments. Simulations match the accuracy of brute-force sampling over the whole label space, at polynomial rather than exponential cost. The authors target robots in messy real rooms.
arxiv-2501-11302:
Physicists measure how tangled two parts of a quantum system are with a number called entanglement entropy. Xin Jiang, Haitang Yang, and Zilin Zhao compute that number for mixed states in a hot two-dimensional conformal field theory, in a 2025 paper. Mixed states are harder than pure ones, since heat blurs the tangle.

Their method works by subtraction, comparing configurations to peel away the thermal part. With clean values in hand, they test which gravity picture matches each setup in the holographic dual. In one setup built from two copies of the system, the tangle reaches across the horizon that splits them. The results give a firm benchmark for how heat and entanglement trade off in these models.
arxiv-2501-11402:
Thomas Lauprêtre and co-authors probe magnetism in a gas of magnetic atoms held in a light lattice in 2025. The atoms move between sites and interact through dipole forces. The gas sits near full filling and low disorder. A phase shift takes it from a flowing state to a blocked state. The team uses pulse tricks to shield the spins from field noise.

Spin coherence was tracked across the phase shift. In the flowing phase, a metastable magnetic state shows below a set lattice depth. In the blocked phase, the gas warms toward a non magnetic state. That path is driven by a play between site to site and exchange effects. The work tests quantum magnetism in a clean system.
arxiv-2501-11702:
The first galaxies lit up inside a fog of neutral hydrogen, and their spectra still carry the shadow of the fog as a softened break near the Lyman-alpha line. Charlotte Mason and co-authors read that shadow in ninety-nine galaxies seen by the Webb telescope in a 2025 paper. Twelve of the galaxies sit beyond redshift ten, deep in the reionization era.

The team compared the spectra with simulated sightlines through patchy, still-reionizing gas. The break deepens and varies more toward higher redshift, as expected when ionized bubbles shrink and thin out. Beyond redshift nine the gas looks almost fully neutral. A sharpness threshold emerges too: only spectra with strong signal per pixel pin down the neutral fraction reliably. Fits to the best spectra begin the census of cosmic dawn.
arxiv-2501-12002:
Chomez and a large survey team wrote a 2025 paper reporting final results from SHINE, a hunt for planets around other stars. The catalog title carries a long funding note, but the paper itself is the fifth and closing report of the survey. It used a camera on a large telescope in Chile that blocks a star's glare so faint planets can be seen.

The report gathers all the survey's observations and explains how the images were cleaned and searched. It measures how small and faint a planet the survey could have found around each star. It then gives the final count of planets and heavier companions found. Full accounts like this let later teams compare their own haul and plan sharper hunts with the next tools.
arxiv-2501-12502:
Barka and co-authors propose a 2025 way to keep meaning based radio links working under heavy noise. New sixth generation networks aim to send meaning, not just raw bits. In factories, strong radio noise can wreck such links before the meaning gets through.

Their plan spreads each signal out, a classic trick to shrug off noise, then cleans the result with a small neural network. The network is trained apart from the main link, which saves time and cost. Tests gained about a quarter in one word score and a clear lift in meaning match. The plan also lets many users share the link.
arxiv-2501-13202:
David Bryant and co-authors settle when a table of distances can be drawn on a tree using whole subtrees as landmarks. Their 2025 paper studies a softer kind of embedding: each point maps to a subtree, and the distance between two points must equal the shortest path between their subtrees. Such maps suit data where each item spans a range rather than a spot.

A finite version of the characterization was proven in 2006 using the tight span, a canonical space built from distances alone. Extending it to endless sets forced new groundwork: the authors show the tight span of any distance space is hyperconvex, a strong roundness property. They then apply the machinery to diversities, which score whole sets rather than pairs, and characterize when theirs is tree-like.
arxiv-2501-13302:
Akshit Achara and Anshuman Chhabra present a 2025 paper auditing the AI filters that police online content. Moderation classifiers screen social media posts and guard language models against toxic training data. If they flag minority users' speech as unsafe more often, the harm is real, so the authors test four big commercial systems.

The tools came from OpenAI, Google, and Clarifai, plus the Perspective API. Fairness was scored with parity measures across user groups, against both rival filters and a fairness-tuned baseline. Robustness was probed with small, natural edits to the input text. The results expose gaps on both fronts in widely used systems. The authors urge fixes before these filters spread further into platforms and pipelines.
arxiv-2501-13402:
Gyuhyeon Pak and Euntai Kim present a mapping system for large indoor spaces in a 2025 paper. New radiance-field maps look photoreal, but scaling them beyond one room strains tracking and memory. Their system fuses camera depth data with inertial sensors to hold pose while building a Gaussian splatting map of big halls.

An ICP tracker seeded by motion sensor preintegration gives strong pose guesses, which cuts the compute load of splat-based tracking. Results matched leading methods in large indoor tests. Readers get the first proof that splatting maps can run at building scale with inertial help.
arxiv-2501-13602:
Soumya Sankar, Xingkai Cheng, and eight peers catch a shy Hall shift at room heat in thin films of a pull-based seam metal. The work came out in 2025. The odd in-plane Hall shift shows when a pull field lies in the film's own plane. Thought ties the shift to seam-based band states.

Strict flip rules have made a firm catch hard. Most odd Hall work hides in deep cold. The team grew films of the kagome metal Fe3Sn, laid down beam by beam. They gauged the Hall reply of the films. They set that reply next to counts from thought. The proof backs an in-plane shift with seam roots, live at room heat. That counts past mere fun. Pull sense tools, spin-based chips, and heat-to-charge kits all want seam traits that last in plain air.
arxiv-2501-13702:
Xinyu Li and co-authors explore, in a 2025 paper, miniature star-shredding events that could flash near the giant black holes at galaxy centers. In their scenario, a white dwarf orbiting the central giant swings close to a smaller stellar black hole. The smaller hole's gravity can tear the dwarf apart, an event far smaller than the classic disruption of a star by the giant itself. The authors estimate such meetings happen a few times a year across the nearby universe.

Simulations show the outcome depends on how close and how fast the pass is. Near passes leave little bound debris, while grazing ones keep more material in one piece. Captured debris should power a prompt burst of X-rays, and loose debris falling onto the giant could light a fainter, later optical flare. Some bursts seen by a new X-ray probe fit the picture, the authors note.
arxiv-2501-13802:
Mowafak Allaham and three colleagues test whether language models can sort climate misinformation as well as human experts, in a 2025 paper. False climate claims flood social media, and automated help could aid those who police them.

Using an expert-labeled data set and fresh social posts, the team compared commercial and open models against climate-focused tools. Open models lagged far behind commercial ones. Expert-fed specialist tools beat many commercial models, including a leading one. Fine-tuning a commercial model on expert labels lifted it to expert level, matching specialists with decades of experience. The authors argue human oversight is what makes such governance tools trustworthy.
arxiv-2501-13902:
Ömer Tapşın and co-authors send secret keys with single photons from a defect that works on a benchtop, no cooling needed. Their 2025 paper uses a flaw in hexagonal boron nitride as a room-temperature photon source for quantum key distribution. Cold setups have long been the field's burden, adding cost and bulk.

Running the B92 protocol, the team reached a sifted key rate of 17.5 kilobits per second with an error rate near 6.5 percent. A careful finite-key analysis still leaves 7 kilobits per second of secure key, among the best for a warm single-photon source. Comparisons with quantum dot sources and a repeater setup frame where the device wins. The authors also sketch uses for the same defects beyond key exchange.
arxiv-2501-14002:
Zui Chen and co-authors study, in 2025, how problem-solving data can sharpen the math skills of language models. Math-focused models are usually pre-trained on broad math text, then fine-tuned on worked problems. Gains from the first stage have often looked small, and the team asks whether the data type is the reason.

Worked problems during pre-training beat general math text by a clear margin. Among ways to create such data, a tutorship amplification method worked best.
