Fine-tuning still mattered, mainly by teaching instruction following rather than new math power. The findings give builders a clearer recipe for training reasoning models.
arxiv-2501-14102:
Mario Hernandez and Fernando Pinero build transformer decoders for 5G codes in a 2025 paper. The codes are LDPC codes used in 5G New Radio. Standard transformers scale quadratically, which is costly for long blocks.

Their design runs in linear time and stays fully differentiable. Performance is compared with belief propagation, the production decoder for these codes. Error rates matched a regular transformer decoder. Results also beat one round of belief propagation. Timing stayed competitive even for larger blocks. Tests ran in an Nvidia research platform for reproducibility. Readers learn a route to learned decoders that could fit real receivers.
arxiv-2501-14602:
Haoyang Yu and colleagues design experiments that stay valid under spillover and carryover, in work from 2025. In many trials, one unit's outcome depends on treatment given to other units. Past treatment can also carry into later rounds, which breaks the standard no interference rule.

Their minimax design handles both effects at once for direct and spillover estimates. Better precision cuts needed sample size and trial cost for multi unit studies. Standard weighted estimators stay consistent and near normal under the new design. Careful variance formulas support valid tests without false confidence. Tests also cover wrong guesses about how long carryover lasts, and numeric studies beat older designs.
arxiv-2501-14702:
Matthew Alan Le Brun, Simon Fowler, and Ornela Dardha add a new tool to a type system for programs that pass messages among many parties. The tool is replication. It lets a part of a process copy itself, as a swap for the loops that recursion gives.

The authors show the swap is not an even one. With both tools in one system, they can write rules for a wider set of cases. These range from tree shaped data sent in parts to cases where parties must take turns. Sample cases include a sale by auction and the classic dining philosophers problem.
arxiv-2501-15002:
Jeremy Avigad, Lior Goldberg, David Levit, Yoav Seginer, and Alon Titelman present a 2025 paper on a compiler for blockchain programs. The compiler works with CairoZero, a language for apps that run on a shared network at large scale. Their tool helps users prove that compiled code does what its high level plan says it should do.

The proofs are built in Lean 3, a proof assistant program. The team shows the method at work on curve math used in secure signing and on checks of those signs. They also verify a way to mimic a read and write store in a read only setting. They close by weighing what the method gives users, such as stronger trust in code that handles value.
arxiv-2501-15202:
Mathai and Haubold survey Mellin convolutions of products and ratios, a less-used cousin of the classic Laplace convolution. Such convolutions can yield results other methods miss. The paper gathers them in one systematic account.

Functions from the pathway family anchor the treatment. Integral forms for products and ratios are derived. Each result is restated through G and H functions. Computable series versions make the formulas usable. Readers can move between forms as problems demand. The survey serves workers in special functions and statistics. Fractional calculus users may also find tools here. It orders a scattered literature onto one shelf. The authors stress practical computation throughout.
arxiv-2501-15302:
Junbo Zhang and co-authors lay out a public challenge to grade audio encoders across every kind of sound, in a 2025 paper. Encoders turn raw waveforms into embeddings that downstream systems use for speech, music, and environmental listening. Vendors claim generality, but head-to-head proof on equal footing is rare.

The ICME 2025 challenge invites teams to submit pretrained encoders, which organizers then run across a battery of tasks spanning speech, ambient sound, and music, scored with real-world usability in mind. Two tracks separate the field: one evaluates the encoder with its parameters in play, the other parameter-free. The contest aims to push encoder design toward models that truly transfer, not merely top one leaderboard.
arxiv-2501-15602:
Slow, step-by-step thought in large language models is rethought by Zeyu Gan, Yun Liao, and Yong Liu in a 2025 arXiv paper. Giving a model more time at test can lift its work on hard tasks. Why that helps is still poorly grasped. The authors start from snowball errors, where one wrong step breeds more wrong steps down the chain.

They tie that growth to the chance of a fully right chain, using tools from data theory. Outside slow-thought tricks then read as ways to cut the chance of a wrong chain. A side-by-side study sorts known tricks from plain to rich. Gains, they argue, come less from the trick shape than from wider search.
arxiv-2501-15702:
Annabelle Niblett, Daniel Fryer, and Christopher Fryer present a supernova light-curve code built to compare the energy sources that can power an exploding star. Candidate sources include shock heating, the decay of radioactive material, and long-lived central engines such as magnetars. The code folds simple analytic versions of these sources into one tool. To show it off, the authors apply it to type Ic broad-line supernovae, a class linked to several competing explanations.

They explore which explosion features, such as mass and velocity, shape the light curves under shock interaction and radioactive decay. Either source can be tuned to match peak brightness, the authors find, but matching the full evolution often demands fine-tuned conditions. They conclude that shocks running into the star's wind most likely dominate at peak brightness for these events.
arxiv-2501-15902:
Tong and Wang offer a precession account of the mode changes seen in a gamma-ray pulsar, in this 2025 paper. The pulsar, PSR J2021+4026, shifts its spin-down rate and gamma-ray brightness together. When spin-down rises, the gamma-ray flux falls, and the two changes track each other closely.

In their model, the star wobbles, so its tilt angle swings over time. The wobble can also fade, which damps the precession. Mixed with torque and outer gap models, this explains the linked timing and brightness shifts. It also explains why the brightness swings shrink over time. The work gives observers a testable picture of this rare behavior.
arxiv-2501-16002:
Wu and co-authors present ScaDyG, a scalable way to learn from graphs that change over time. Dynamic graphs record ties that evolve, with wide real-world use. Most graph networks pass messages and add time tricks, but growing history makes them hard to scale.

ScaDyG first splits past interactions into time steps, within and between steps. That split allows weight-free, time-aware spreading of features during preprocessing. Fine detail inside steps comes from temporal encoding built on exponential functions. A hypernetwork then fuses each node's history adaptively. The design targets industry-scale graphs where older methods bog down in historical data.
arxiv-2501-16102:
Péter Bálint and Ábel Komálovics sharpen the math that predicts how fast chaotic systems forget their past, in a 2025 paper. Some billiard-like systems mix unevenly: most motion is wild, yet calm pockets slow the blending. How fast two reads of such a system drift apart sets the reach of its statistics. Past proofs left stray log factors in the bounds, a gap between claim and best hope.

Their scheme clears those factors for systems whose mixing fades at a steady polynomial pace that still sums. The gains cover both the fade of correlations and the error rate in a near-sure limit law. Three showcase systems gain from the fix: two falling balls, billiards with flat spots on the rim, and a flower-shaped table. The authors credit the line of work they extend by name.
arxiv-2501-16302:
Zheng Liu and co-authors present the Matryoshka Re-Ranker in a 2025 paper on search. Large language models sort search results with care, but their size makes them too slow or costly for many real uses.

Their design lets a user set how deep the model runs and how much text each layer reads, so one model can fit many budgets. Trimming a model can cost care, so the team adds two fixes. In one, each small form learns from the form above it. In the next, two small add-on parts work as a pair to win back lost care. Tests on standard search sets show the design beats prior tools and holds up well at many trim levels.
arxiv-2501-16402:
Oleksiy Arkhypov and Maxim Khodachenko mine old Moon watch tales for signs of dense dust clouds that could wreck low craft, in a 2025 paper. Brief space runs may miss rare thick cloud days on the Moon. Earth watch books span three hundred years of such rare sky signs, still yet to be mined in full.

Star dim tales and old glow notes let cloud shape and size fall out. Grain counts from light math show sub grain clouds could crash craft at low height. Cloud shapes look like hit spray, with flush months each year. A half month pulse hints at gas vents as a source as well. Sun lulls lift dust too.
arxiv-2501-16602:
Dwarf galaxies sit in dark halos whose centres may spike or flatten, and two forces can flatten them: star bursts, or dark stuff that bumps into itself. Maria Straight and eight co-authors stage both in 2025, in a known galaxy-forge suite. Their halos weigh near ten billion suns.

Runs with no stars at all face runs with the full forge physics. Burst feedback flattens by a path that leans on how many stars formed. Self-bumps flatten by their own rule. The team's test is whether the two flat centres can be told apart at all. If not, a flat heart proves little. The halo's centre density is the tell they weigh, dwarf by dwarf.
arxiv-2501-17002:
Edoardo David Santi, Gongpu Chen, Deniz Gündüz, and Asaf Cohen ask in a 2025 paper what happens when a control system cannot trust the component that carries out its commands. They study a finite Markov decision process, in which a controller chooses each action but a separate actuator executes it. The actuator may deliberately deviate from the chosen action in order to reduce the reward.

The controller observes only the sequence of states the system visits, not the actions actually taken. The authors establish conditions under which the actuator can deviate over an infinite time horizon without being detected. They formulate an optimization problem for the best covert adversarial policy. They also derive error exponents for detection, both when the adversarial strategy is known in advance and when the actuator may use any stationary policy.
arxiv-2501-17202:
Chen and seven co-authors taught audio language models to judge speech quality in this paper from twenty twenty-five. Most such models hear words but cannot tell clean audio from garbled. Human ratings are the usual yardstick, yet training data with words, not just scores, was missing. The team built the first text-based speech evaluation corpus from real human judgments.

The corpus explains scores across several dimensions and names what degraded each clip. It also supports head-to-head comparisons in plain language. A distillation method then aligned a model to reason from raw audio. The trained model beat the best score-predicting rival and aced comparisons. Its written verdicts scored well against human text too.
arxiv-2501-17402:
Chip makers outsource production, and a foundry could copy or overbuild a design it was only meant to print. Logic locking fights back by adding key bits: the circuit works only when the right key is entered. Lopez and Rezaei present Cute-Lock, a family of locking schemes that use several keys based on time. The schemes can be applied while a design is still behavioral code or later as a finished netlist.

Single-key schemes have fallen to a range of attacks, from oracle-guided solving to removal of the lock. The authors test Cute-Lock against that whole spread. They report that attack attempts run into dead ends, while the cost in chip area and speed stays flat. The family covers sequential circuits, the kind with memory that most real designs use, which widens its practical reach.
arxiv-2501-17502:
Xunchuan Liu and co-authors rebuild the census of star-forming cores from tangled gas filaments. Stars are born inside dense cores, and the cores' mass spread looks like a cousin of the stars' own mass spread. The team asks whether filament breakup alone can stamp out that pattern. Their model grows a fractal, turbulent tree of filaments and fibers, two dimensions of branching with a standard turbulence law.

Flows streaming along the tree's splines pinch it into cores. The resulting mass function falls in three power-law stretches that echo the Kroupa star census, shifted to about four times the mass, matching a quarter of each core becoming a star. A different turbulence exponent steepens the top end toward the Salpeter form. Fibers, they propose, are the universal bricks of star birth.
arxiv-2501-17602: Stevan Gajović, Jeroen Hanselman, and Angelos Koutsianas prove a number theory result in a 2025 arXiv paper. They ask whether a local-global principle holds for 11-isogenies of elliptic curves over quadratic fields. The principle links local behavior at each place to a global conclusion. The authors show the principle does not fail in this setting. That gives a positive answer to a conjecture by Banwait and Cremona. The proof rests on finding all quadratic points on a specific modular curve.
arxiv-2501-18002:
Caetano and seven co-authors present a study from twenty twenty-five on agentic workflows for designing conversational AI. Chat-based AI is now mainstream, but its design poses two hard problems. Users often hold vague goals and grasp AI functions poorly. Sessions are also brief, limiting sustained design input. The team explore agent workflows through a design probe built over four rounds. Ten users test the probe across those iterations. Agents suggest apt prompts, stand in for users in early tests, and help users state goals.

Findings are shared as an annotated portfolio of design artifacts. Thematic analysis of user experience backs the portfolio. The authors offer fixes for vagueness and brevity in chat design. They note limits and wider promise for collaborative design methods.
arxiv-2501-18302:
Wieslaw Grygierzec and Wojciech Zajaczkowski prove this 2025 bound for equations of fluid flow joined with heat conduction. The Navier-Stokes equations govern moving fluids, and here they are paired with heat spread in a bounded cylinder. The flow is symmetric around the cylinder's axis. Set boundary rules pin parts of the velocity and spin to zero, and no heat escapes.

Assuming a smooth solution exists, the authors derive a global estimate that depends only on the starting data. Some nonlinear terms partly cancel, which makes the bound possible. A bound of this kind lets a short-time solution be stretched to all time without blowing up. The result strengthens the math base for modeling heated, swirling flows in pipes and vessels.
arxiv-2501-18502:
Ritesh Kumar and Shashank Vatedka study one-bit distributed mean estimation when the variance is unknown, in work from 2025. Each user holds one sample from a location-scale distribution and may send just a single bit to a central server that must estimate the mean. They propose simple non-adaptive and adaptive protocols for this tight communication limit.

Both protocols reach asymptotic normality, and the authors bound their mean squared error as the user count grows. For symmetric log-concave data, matching lower bounds prove the adaptive scheme optimal. A sharper lower bound for non-adaptive rules shows a real gap: extra bits help adaptive schemes only a little, while adaptivity itself pays off.
arxiv-2501-18602:
Gurleen Kaur and co-authors (2025) release EpiClim, a dataset joining India's epidemic records to climate data at a fine local scale. Weather shapes outbreaks: dengue and malaria track temperature, cholera tracks rainfall anomalies. AI weather forecasting has improved, but linking climate models to health planning is held back by the lack of detailed health data. EpiClim fills that gap for India. It is the country's first weekly, district-level dataset covering several epidemics from 2009 to the present.

The records come from India's Integrated Disease Surveillance Programme, its reporting system. Each district's weekly case counts for diseases such as dengue, malaria, and acute diarrheal disease can be set beside the weather the district experienced. The authors intend the dataset to accelerate GeoHealth research: models that warn which districts face an outbreak next, given the forecast. Public and long-spanning, it gives researchers the raw material climate-health modeling has lacked.
arxiv-2501-18702:
Black holes with magnetic charge may wear clouds of weak-force fields, and Shahar Hod works out the notes of those clouds with pure math, in work from twenty twenty-five. A past study had shown such bound clouds can exist. Hod studies the large-mass end of the system, where the field mass times the hole's rim size runs high.

A compact formula gives the full set of cloud notes, keyed by the hole's charge step. The top note sets the edge line where cloudy holes split from bare ones. In the large-charge end, that edge can be read off the formula in closed form. The work gives theorists a sharp map of when such hairy holes can stand.
arxiv-2501-19002:
Vladimír Novotný reported in 2025 how the Pierre Auger Observatory tracks the changing mass of cosmic rays. The observatory in Argentina combines surface detectors with fluorescence telescopes that watch particle showers glow. Together they measure both the energy spectrum and the particle types arriving from space. The setup reaches from the highest energies down to far lower ones than first planned.

The key measure is the depth where each shower peaks, which reveals how heavy the incoming particle was. Direct profile readings and indirect signal methods agree on this depth. Across energy, both the average mass and the slope of the flux shift in ways the paper characterizes. Energy values carry about fourteen percent systematic uncertainty. The huge accumulated exposure anchors the results. Astrophysicists use such curves to hunt the sources of the fastest particles known.
arxiv-2501-19202:
Dang Huu-Tien and co-authors show that teaching a language model to forget can quietly make it fragile, in a 2025 paper. Unlearning methods aim to erase chosen knowledge. The team found that even one harmless forget-related token in a normal query can make an unlearned model misbehave. They set out to explain why.

Their theory recasts unlearning as a backdoor process. Forgetting links the trigger tokens to target outputs, much like an attack would. So the tokens act as hidden triggers, and the knowledge is masked, not erased. To fix the weakness, they reinterpret the training data that should be kept. Random perturbation ideas guide the defense. The work warns that erasure claims need stress tests.
arxiv-2501-19402:
Andreas Deuchert, Phan Thành Nam, and Marcin Napiórkowski prove a sharp link between condensation and symmetry breaking in a mean-field Bose gas, in a paper from 2025. The gas sits in a three-dimensional torus with weak pairwise interaction scaled by particle count. Temperatures are set at the condensation transition scale.

They show spontaneous breaking of the phase symmetry occurs exactly when Bose-Einstein condensation holds. Condensation here means the one-particle density matrix of the thermal state has one huge eigenvalue. The equivalence is an if-and-only-if result, so neither phenomenon can occur without the other in this regime. The proof clarifies a foundational point in quantum statistical physics.
arxiv-2502-00002:
Duarte Sampaio de Almeida, Fernando Brito e Abreu, and Inês Boavida-Portugal review every study they can find on digital twins in tourism, in a 2025 systematic review. Thirty-four peer-reviewed papers passed screening, the oldest from 2021, marking a young field. A taxonomy sorted them by tourism type, purpose, scale, and data linkage.

Cultural tourism dominates, mostly digitizing heritage sites, and destination management is the leading purpose, usually at single-site scale. Most twins receive data one-way, without true synchronization back to the physical site; among the rest, linkage is mostly indirect. Applied studies outnumber theoretical ones. The authors map wide open gaps, from live syncing to whole-destination twins, as the field's next work.
arxiv-2502-00102:
Jiwon Jesse Han and co-authors trace the fastest stars in 2025 to a surprise birthplace. Hypervelocity stars are flung out when a supermassive black hole tears a binary apart. A survey found twenty-one such stars in our galaxy's halo, long assumed to come from its center. New motion data change that story.

Rewinding their paths with fresh measurements, half the stars trace back to the Large Magellanic Cloud, our big satellite galaxy. A forward model of ejections from a black hole there reproduces the observed pattern, including a striking cluster near one constellation. Rival explanations without a black hole fail. The team weighs the cloud's black hole at roughly six hundred thousand suns.
arxiv-2502-00302:
Yixuan He and co-authors build a method for following friendships in a troop of chimpanzees over time, in a 2025 paper. Field workers recorded which chimps stayed near each other, but nearness comes in kinds, and kinds should not count equally. The data arrives as many overlapping snapshots. The challenge is to fuse them into one weighted network per moment, with the weights learned rather than guessed.

The authors tune the weights with a loss function that rewards smoothness: groups that look alike from one moment to the next score better. Tests on made-up data check that the method recovers planted groups. Statistical tests then flag sets of chimps that stay close for a long stretch. Applied to the real troop, the method found tight cliques that matched what chimp experts already knew from watching the animals.
arxiv-2502-00402:
Walter Zimmer and co-authors build a roadside system that spots crashes on a German test highway in real time. Their 2025 paper deals with road deaths, a top killer of young people world-wide. Fast spotting and fast aid save lives, so the team pairs rule-based checks with a learned model fed by roadside cameras and laser sensors. They also release a data set of real high-speed crashes from the test stretch.

The data set holds vast counts of labeled boxes in two and three dimensions, with track IDs, across tens of thousands of frames and ten object classes. Tests and breakdowns show their method is sound, the authors say. Data come in an open label format for reuse.
arxiv-2502-00502:
Manuel Rodrigues and Marcos Silva present new black bounce spacetimes, blends of black holes and wormholes with more than one horizon and throat. The classic black bounce comes from a fix to the Schwarzschild metric that swaps the center for a throat. Their 2025 classes push that idea further.

The new metrics allow stacked horizons, throats, and anti-throats, while far away they settle back to the Schwarzschild form. A scalar field tied to nonlinear electrodynamics, partly phantom in type, sources the shapes along with a magnetic monopole. Energy conditions hold in some zones and fail in others, judged through an uneven fluid model. A curvature check confirms the spaces stay regular.
arxiv-2502-00702:
Six researchers wrote a paper in two thousand twenty-five on reading heart signals from ordinary video streams. A viewer's heartbeat leaves faint traces in video and audio. Using them could support remote health checks, emotion-aware computing, and spotting fake videos. That signal has mostly been ignored by streaming platforms.

Their system, CardioLive, runs as an add-on service for streaming platforms. At its core sits a network that learns the heart rhythm from sight and sound together. The design handles real streaming problems such as changing frame rates and streams that drift out of sync. Tests show the system tracks the heart well under such conditions.
arxiv-2502-00802:
Massimiliano Falzari and Matthia Sabatelli study in 2025 a bias in deep reinforcement learning where early experience counts too much. This primacy bias can slow learning and cut final scores, notably in hard tasks. They examine the bias through a matrix that measures how sensitive the network's output is to each weight, and track its pattern over learning.

Clear phases of memorizing and reorganizing appear in that pattern. Their new method uses the shape of that space to change selected weights, so early experience cannot dominate. On a standard control suite, the method beat rivals, most clearly on complex tasks. They also show how actor and critic parts differ and how replay rates can worsen the bias.
arxiv-2502-00902:
Moritz Wolter and co-authors argue that machine learning research needs stricter software habits, in a 2025 position paper. Reproducing a result is basic science, yet code behind headline papers often lacks the basics: pinned versions, tests, and clear structure. The authors set out to measure the gap.

They surveyed code repositories tied to papers at top venues over the past decade. The survey finds wide neglect of standard practices, alongside pockets of progress. Poor habits waste other groups' time and erode trust in published claims. The paper closes with concrete steps for authors, reviewers, and venues to raise the floor. Its plea is that software craft is not housekeeping but part of the science itself.
arxiv-2502-01102:
Eric Bezzam, Yohann Perron, and Martin Vetterli present a 2025 paper on cameras without lenses. Such cameras swap the lens for a thin mask and build the image by computation. Learned rebuilders work well but lean on loose models, and no one had checked whether they cope with a new mask design.

Their design splits the rebuild into modules, with a pre-cleaning step before recovery. They prove that step is needed for standard recovery methods and show it helps across many setups and data sets. They also run the first cross-mask test: models trained on one mask type face others, a real gauge of reach.
arxiv-2502-01202:
Three authors, led by Konstantinos Dialektopoulos, use symmetry hunting to solve the field laws of a variant gravity theory. Their 2025 paper works in f(Q) theory, where gravity rests on a quantity called Q rather than on curved space in Einstein's sense. Noether's method finds the amounts such a system keeps fixed as it evolves.

For a smooth expanding cosmos and four families of links, only power-law forms of the key function admit the needed symmetries. That narrow gate itself rules out many rival versions of the theory. From the fixed amounts, the team derive exact solutions for how the cosmos expands. The work shows how strict symmetry demands can thin a crowded field of gravity models.
arxiv-2502-01302:
Tides are usually treated as friction that slowly drains an orbit, but Xing Wei shows the drain can run backwards. Dynamical tides are waves sloshing inside a planet or star, and when a wave's rhythm matches the orbital rhythm, the two resonate and exchange energy in richer ways than simple drag allows.

Using a two-dimensional shallow-water model of a rocky planet wrapped in a thin ocean or air layer, Wei computes the resonances and lets the Earth-Moon system stand in as the test case. Surprisingly, dissipation can grow as the orbit widens, because the coupling strengthens at certain separations. Ignoring the two-way coupling, the author warns, distorts any long-term history of a planet-moon pair.
arxiv-2502-01402:
Vinay Setty and Adam James Becker present a tool and dataset in a 2025 paper on fact checking podcasts. Podcasts are popular and often carry claims that no one has checked. Checking them is hard: speech must be written out, marked up, and verified, all while keeping the flow of the talk.

Their tool lets users mark claims while the podcast plays, flagging which claims deserve a check, where they start and end, and errors in context. Speech is transcribed by a leading AI model, and crowd marks build clean training data. A multilingual model is then tuned to spot claims on its own in new episodes.
arxiv-2502-01502:
Mohammad Sabri, Marc Riera, and Antonio González addressed a wear problem in 2025: the memory cells inside neural network accelerators wear out. Accelerators built on resistive RAM compute efficiently in place, promising big energy savings over standard chips. But each inference run rewrites cells, and the cells endure only a limited number of write cycles. A chip that dies young is no bargain, however fast it starts.

Their method, Hamun, uses rough computation to prolong the hardware's life. By accepting small, controlled inaccuracies, the scheduler can reduce or redistribute the writes that age the cells. Self-tuning scheduling already adjusts these accelerators to each network's demands; Hamun adds lifespan as a clear goal. Extending service life is what would let resistive RAM accelerators compete honestly with durable standard processors in data centers.
arxiv-2502-02002:
Kaja Gruntkowska, Hanmin Li, Aadi Rane, and Peter Richtárik present the Broximal Point Method in two thousand twenty five. Non smooth, non convex optimization defeats plain gradient methods. The classic proximal point method inspires their new frame. A ball constraint replaces the quadratic distance penalty inside.

The swap yields linear, finite step convergence in the nonsmooth convex case. That beats the sublinear rate of the classic method. A new ball convexity notion widens the guarantees further. Acceleration, smoothing, and trust region ideas all connect back. The method is offered as a blueprint for practical algorithms.
arxiv-2502-02102:
Breitenmoser, Stabilini, Kasprzak, and Mayer build in twenty twenty-five a detailed computer model of Switzerland's airborne radiation survey system. Aircraft scanners map radioactive fallout fast after accidents, but calibrating them with real sources covers only a few isotopes, leaving most accident nuclides unmeasured. Their simulation models the aircraft itself in fine detail plus the detector's light response, predicting the full measured spectrum for any source.

Tests in near, middle, and far setups showed accuracy fit to replace the old empirical calibration. The model can mint signature spectra for any nuclide without handling strong sources, cutting cost, time, and waste. The authors pitch it as groundwork for richer airborne data methods, from emergency mapping to nuclear security.
arxiv-2502-02302:
Shengda Zhuo and co-authors present a graph learning method that takes edge information seriously, in a 2025 paper. Graph networks pass messages between connected points. Most designs learn point features and edge features apart. That split loses useful signals. The team's method, EdgeGFL, learns a rich edge feature set first. Those edge features then shape how point features are gathered.

Multi-channel filters built from the edge data catch wider structure. They also catch fine, higher-order patterns around each point. A relational learning step joins the message passing. It lets points receive more useful information from neighbors. Tests on four real mixed-type graphs favored the new method. The authors argue edges should guide learning, not just carry it. The approach suits networks where links carry meaning of their own, such as trust or transaction records.
arxiv-2502-02402:
Youri Nouchokgwe and co-authors tune a cooling material in a 2025 physics paper. Certain ceramics cool when a voltage is applied, an effect that could replace gas-based cooling. The standard material works best near room temperature, which limits device design. Adding calcium to its crystal, the team found, shifts where the effect peaks.

Depending on the calcium dose, the peak slid from well below freezing to well above room temperature. Tests under field, plus microscopy and theory, revealed a new middle phase at higher doses. Low doses kept the normal cooling effect; higher doses flipped it to an inverse effect. A two-degree cooling step held across a ninety-degree span. The authors propose stacking doses to widen the working range of solid-state coolers.
arxiv-2502-02602:
Sifan Chen and co-authors build lattice structures with a shape design method that stays robust at the hard spots. Lattice frames earn their place in aerospace, cars, and medicine through strength at low weight. The trouble is the nodes, where many struts meet and models tend to break.

Their 2025 paper cuts the struts short and joins them to node shapes tuned by optimization. A recent meta-heuristic, the Grey Wolf method, searches for node forms that join cleanly and carry load well. Case studies of rising topological and geometric complexity test the pipeline end to end. The result is a construction route that gives simulators and fabricators the exact shape they need.
arxiv-2502-02802:
Yizhe Yang and colleagues proposed in 2025 a framework for simulating clients in motivational interviewing counseling, so counselors can train and be tested at scale. A good simulation must act in line with the client's set profile and habits, which is hard over a long talk. Their method tracks the client's inner state as the session runs.

The framework controls state changes and, for each state, generates behavior that fits the client's motivation, beliefs, change plan, and openness to the counselor. By varying profiles and openness, many counseling scenarios can be built. Automatic checks and expert reviews both found the simulated clients more consistent than those from prior methods, which supports use in training.
arxiv-2502-03202:
Fabian Mohn, Florian Thieben, and Tobias Knopp build a low cost signal chain for passive resonators, in work from 2025. Passive wireless sensors watch body and factory states without wires or batteries. A shared chain must excite a resonator by induction, then pass its fading reply to a quiet amplifier.

Two chain variants are laid out in full detail for copy by other labs. One uses shelf audio amplifiers, while the other uses a custom bridge circuit. Both aim to scale to multi channel arrays for wider sensor fields. Tests ran on tiny magnetic mechanical resonators at very low frequencies. Tracking and sensing uses in varied settings drive the design goals.
arxiv-2502-03302:
Chand and Jacob build an image fix frame that stands firm near true data. The frame is an energy form with bends at more than one scale. Its dip stands for how apt a scene is in chance terms. A learned net sets the scale weights for that dip. Slope caps keep the dip bent up near the true data cloud. The team calls the frame LC-MUSE in their text.

They use the frame to fix shots from meagre reads. The frame gives one sole best fix for each such task. Paths to that fix come with proof they land there. Small shakes in the reads fail to break the fix by much. On twin-coil MR shots, the frame beat top firm past tools. It tied plug-in and end-trained tools on the same shots.
arxiv-2502-03802:
Elise Zhang and co-authors build a framework to find causes in linked dynamic systems, in a 2025 paper. A known method checks if one series can be read from the past of another, which hints at cause. A later tweak handles indirect links, but only for single series at a time.

Their framework first draws a rough causal graph with pairwise tests. It then prunes indirect links with a multi variable form of the tweak that uses richer records of each series. Tests on simulated data and on a large weather data set show gains in accuracy over base methods. The tool suits systems like weather where many parts move together.
arxiv-2502-03902:
Efstratios Stratoglou and three colleagues design control laws that hold a machine on a desired path defined by speed-dependent rules, in a 2025 paper. Such rules, called virtual nonholonomic constraints, are enforced by feedback rather than by physical guides.

The authors work in a geometric frame and derive a law with a strong promise. The system settles onto the target path at an exponential rate. The path also stays invariant once reached. Two simulations test the design. One steers a flock of agents into coordinated motion. The other guides an unmanned surface boat through a stream. Both behaved as the theory predicts.
arxiv-2502-04202:
Wei Liu and co-authors present GUIWatcher in a 2025 paper on slow screens in mobile apps. A lagging or frozen screen annoys users and drags down app ratings. Testers often record app use on video, but spotting lag frames by eye is slow work. The tool scans those recordings on its own to find the bad frames.

It hunts three kinds of frame: jittery frames, long loading frames, and frozen frames. It then ranks them so the worst come first. On real app tests it scored high marks for both hits and few false alarms. Its reports help coders fix the worst faults first. The tool already runs in a live work setting, the authors note, where it has caught real faults.
arxiv-2502-04502: Espinoza, Im, and Khovanov give examples, in a 2025 paper, of small algebraic structures that govern a branch of mathematical field theory. The theories in question assign algebraic data to surfaces, and rank two is the simplest rich case. The authors build their examples over rings of whole-number-like elements, where the structures are well formed but not freely generated. They then discuss how such structures could feed link homology, a tool that sorts knots and links.
arxiv-2502-04602:
Much of what makes an AI model behave may be surface gloss, and a 2025 paper by Runjin Chen and co-authors tries to measure that gloss. Alignment training teaches models human values, but cheaper tricks hint that much of the change is shallow.

The team defines superficial knowledge as what a model can pick up by restyling its final word choices, without touching the deeper links between words. They give a method to pull that layer out of an aligned model and study it alone. Comparing gloss-only models with fully aligned ones, they put a number on the surface share. Their results show the surface part is large, which reframes what alignment training really buys.
arxiv-2502-04702:
Giorgio Manzoni and a large team ask whether galaxy formation models can explain the galaxy counts seen by the James Webb Space Telescope in a 2025 paper. Deep near infrared counts show a clear break in their slope at a certain brightness. The break grows stronger at longer wavelengths. A semi analytic model of galaxy formation, called GALFORM, predicts that behavior remarkably well, so the team use it to diagnose the cause.

Three features drive the break: a built in break in the brightness distribution, the changing volume element with distance, and how brightness corrections shift with redshift. Elliptical galaxies fill the bright end while spirals dominate the faint end, and that split survives in the counts. Most of the signal comes from fairly nearby galaxies. The authors give a full account of how the model's counts are built.
arxiv-2502-05002:
F Marin and co-authors used polarized light to probe the hidden heart of the Centaurus A galaxy in a 2025 paper. It is the nearest radio galaxy, and dust buries its core. Scattered light can reveal what direct light hides. The team took spectropolarimetry with a large telescope in Chile.

After correcting for dust lane effects, a giant torus emerged. Scattered synchrotron emission showed in the polarized signal. Strong narrow emission lines marked active nucleus gas. The geometry of matter around the black hole comes into focus. Polarimetry thus opens a window that plain imaging cannot.
arxiv-2502-05102:
Luiza Piancastelli and Wagner Barreto-Souza build models for rankings that change over time in a 2025 paper. Ranking data, such as weekly sports standings, are common, but few methods handle them as a time series. Their models borrow the shape of GARCH models, which are standard for tracking financial volatility.

In their setup, each ranking follows a Mallows distribution centered near the past, with its spread driven by an autoregressive feedback rule. The authors prove basic stability properties for the models. Parameters are fit by maximum likelihood when data are complete, and by a simulation-based method when entries are missing. Tests on made-up data check the estimators, and a real case follows professional tennis rankings from 2015 to 2019.
arxiv-2502-05202:
Nadav Timor, David Harel and their co-authors speed up language model inference with speculative decoding that works across different vocabularies in 2025. Speculative methods let a small drafter propose several tokens that a big target model checks in one pass, saving time.

Past methods forced drafter and target to share one vocabulary, which often meant training a drafter from scratch. Their three new methods drop that constraint and keep the target output distribution exact, so quality is lossless. Any off-the-shelf model can serve as drafter with no retraining. Tests on summary, coding and long-context tasks gave large speedups.
arxiv-2502-05302:
Oday Hazaimah designs step-by-step methods for solving equilibrium problems on sets that bend outward in places. Equilibrium problems ask for a point where competing effects balance, and they cover many tasks in economics and engineering. The sets here are nonconvex but still have a regular shape that math can work with.

The new methods blend two known tricks: an auxiliary principle that turns each step into an easier subproblem, and an inertia term that carries momentum from past steps. Hazaimah proves the steps settle on a solution under mild conditions. He also builds gap functions, which measure how far a point is from solving the problem, to guide downhill-style versions. The results sharpen earlier work and also cover related problem types.
arxiv-2502-05402:
Ian Tassin, Kristen Goebel, and Brittany Lasher work in 2025 on image squeeze methods that store less color data per shot. Color fill tools can rebuild hue from a thin stored grid. Less stored color means a far smaller file for the same shot.

Their work tunes a grid based fill plan and the shape of the net that does the fill. The goal is the least stored color that still lets a true rebuild. Test runs gave a strong squeeze rate with high match marks for the rebuilt shots. The team frames the plan as a path to leaner image stores.
arxiv-2502-05702:
Seyedamirhossein Talebi and Kaixiong Zhou proposed in 2025 a faster way to predict power flow in electric grids. Grid managers must find flows that meet demand at the lowest cost while staying within safe limits. Standard solvers slow down badly on large grids, above all as wind and solar feeds grow and shift.

The pair treat the grid as a graph, with stations as points and lines as links, and train graph neural networks to predict the flow pattern. They test four network types on standard test grids. The networks match solver results closely, run much faster, and scale to larger grids. The authors see them as a tool for live grid control.
arxiv-2502-06702:
Liu Tao and co-authors show how adaptive optics could widen the reach of gravity wave detectors, in a 2025 paper. Hearing fainter waves needs more laser power in the arms and stronger squeezed light. Heat warps in the core mirrors cap both at present.

Their method corrects those warps on the optics themselves with fine, low noise control. In simulations for an upgraded LIGO, the noise floor dropped by up to a fifth across a broad band. That gain adds a few units of distance to the range for neutron star mergers. The authors frame the work as a step toward a forty kilometer observatory in the United States.
arxiv-2502-06802:
Chen Wang and co-authors address, in a 2025 paper, a weakness in game recommendations on Roblox, a platform where users create the games. Recommendation models usually rely on titles and descriptions, but on Roblox that text is inconsistent and sparse. The team instead extracts text from inside the games themselves.

A large language model reads the in-game text and infers structured attributes, such as genre and gameplay objectives, without extensive human annotation. A second, language-model-based step then re-ranks recommendations to check whether the generated attributes actually improve relevance. The authors report that the attributes improve personalization and user satisfaction. The same approach also supports an integrity detection application based on user engagement, which is already deployed in production.
arxiv-2502-06902:
Deven Mahesh Mistry and co-authors catch transformer models remembering like people in a 2025 cognitive AI study. Feeding GPT-2 models sequences in context, the team analyzed attention patterns for the fingerprints of human episodic memory. Items near each other in time link up, and beginnings and endings enjoy privileged recall.

All three signatures appeared in the attention heads, and the models' outputs leaned toward serial recall of the in-context items. Ablating the induction heads, the components that copy patterns forward, erased the contiguity effect. Training, not programming, grows these memory habits, and the paper charts how they emerge with scale.
arxiv-2502-07202:
Jaesik Yoon and four co-authors fused two planning tools in two thousand twenty-five to make smarter long-horizon plans. Diffusion models can draft plans, but unlike tree search they gain little from extra thinking time. Their method, Monte Carlo Tree Diffusion, recasts the cleaning-up steps of a diffusion draft as a tree that can be searched.

Partly cleaned plans are scored, pruned, and refined in rounds, keeping good branches and revisiting weak ones. That gives the planner a balance between exploring new paths and exploiting good ones. On hard long-horizon tasks, the method beat plain diffusion planners, and plan quality rose as more computing time was spent.
arxiv-2502-07402:
Snehesh Das and co-authors stretch a coin-toss candy game into fresh math ground. In the base game, two players flip fair coins each round; heads means eat one candy. Who still holds candy when the foe runs out wins, and a joint last bite is a tie. Past work found a neat tie chance when both start even.

New forms let each player flip more than one coin a round. Flip odds can also skew from fair. The team attacks the new forms with three tools: sum tricks that pack counts, mock runs on a computer, and curve fits to the mock data. The game is slight, but its tie math feeds wider chance work. Play-born sums of this kind train proof skill too.
arxiv-2502-07502:
Zoe Pfister, Michael Vierhauser, Rebekka Wohlrab, and Ruth Breu argue that monitoring people inside cyber-physical systems must be designed around human values. Such systems blend hardware and software in uncertain settings where people take part directly or passively. Monitors at runtime gather data to keep operation safe, yet watching humans can expose sensitive behavior. The design of requirements must weigh privacy, security, and self-direction from the start.

This research preview derives an early framework from a known taxonomy of values and from value-integrated software engineering. Tactics tie monitoring requirements to the values they serve. The aim is to trace a line from values to requirements to the actors involved.
arxiv-2502-07802:
Feng Liang and co-authors offer a 2025 method for making custom video with more than one subject. Most past tools handle just one face, body, or animal from a set of source images. When they try more, traits can blend and form a mixed figure that matches none of the sources well.

Their tool, Movie Weaver, uses anchored prompts that tie each subject to its own image inside the text prompt. A second part codes the order of the source images. Tests show stronger keeping of each subject and better overall quality than past tools. The method needs no fresh tuning for each new set of subjects.
arxiv-2502-07902:
Mateus Reinke Pelicer and co-authors present the first neutron star models from a modular calculation engine, in a 2025 paper. A neutron star's size depends on how dense matter behaves. No single theory covers all densities. The engine stitches three theories together. One handles the crust at low density. One covers matter near normal nuclear density. One takes over at higher density. A lepton module keeps the mix electrically neutral.

A synthesis step joins the pieces into one equation of state. Joining choices use different thermodynamic handles. Those choices shift predicted masses and radii slightly. The shifts stay within a few percent. A relativity solver then computes the star's traits. The team also tests universal relations among those traits. A flavor module estimates thickness-like friction in the matter. The engine's modular design is the headline. New physics can be swapped in piece by piece.
arxiv-2502-08102:
Kelly Wang and Steven Kimbrough give ways to make fresh time based data from one past run for energy plan tests, in a 2025 paper. Energy plans lean on hour by hour forecasts that stretch for decades. Tests of how plans bend when inputs shift need many such runs, not just one.

Two simple reshuffle ways build new runs that look and score much like the source run. The team also gives ways to tilt runs up or down to mimic a changed climate. Fresh runs show real swings in lean and rich supply spells. Planners can thus stress test plans with more care.
arxiv-2502-08602:
Jie Zhu and Laurence Brassart wrote a short physics paper in 2025 on how a single polymer chain acts when it is pulled. A chain is a long strand of linked units, and how it stretches sets the feel of the full plastic or rubber made from it. Most past models treat the links as stiff, but real bonds stretch and bend.

The authors built a model that lets bonds stretch and angles open as the pull grows. They then made a simpler form that gives the same pull curve with less work. Both forms match lab data for carbon chains at low and high force, with no fitted values. The simple form also gives the bond force, which helps guess when a chain will snap.
arxiv-2502-08902:
Chenghao Zhang and colleagues recovered true-scale three-dimensional shape from one photo in a 2025 paper. Depth alone cannot give real size without knowing the camera's internal settings, its intrinsics, which phones and robots often lack. The authors prove depth itself constrains those settings, and the two unknowns hold each other in check, so they can be learned together rather than in sequence.

Their CoL3D framework trains one network to estimate depth and intrinsics jointly, checking consistency at the level of depth, camera parameters, and the rebuilt point cloud. A canonical incidence field prior helps the camera side learn. A shape similarity loss in point cloud space polishes the result. Single-image metric recovery matters for navigation and grasping.
arxiv-2502-09002:
Rishika Kohli, Shaifu Gupta, and Manoj Gaur present a 2025 paper on spotting personal data leaks from phones. Apps send network traffic that can carry private data out. Past tools hand-picked features from web requests to train a classifier. Deep learning can learn those patterns on its own, with no manual feature step. The team builds an end-to-end system on that idea.

A pre-trained language model and an autoencoder turn each packet into a compact vector. A triplet-loss tuning step then sharpens the model, so leaks and safe packets sit far apart. Two real-world data sets were used for tests. The authors compare their system with leading past works on leak detection. The goal is stronger privacy guards for mobile users.
arxiv-2502-09402:
Quirin Göttl, Natalie Rosen, and Jakob Burger extend a geometry-based method for phase equilibrium math, in this 2025 paper. Flash calculations tell engineers which phases a mixture splits into at a set temperature and pressure, and how much of each forms. The convex envelope method handles liquids of any blend without being told the phase count in advance.

The extension now covers vapor and solid phases too, across the whole range of mixtures. The authors show vapor-liquid and solid-liquid examples with up to four components. They also use the method to fit model parameters and pair it with a learning tool that predicts properties.
arxiv-2502-09602:
Robert Stanton, Cagri Kaymak, and Anders Niklasson make a rich charge model cheap enough for day-to-day sims of how atoms move. The ACKS2 model lets both atom charges and swings in voltage adapt. It gets charge splits and response to fields right, where plain flex-charge models fail. Its flaw is cost. Each step used to need a slow solve, run again and again till it settled.

Their shadow plan skips that solve. A near stand-in for the true energy does the work. It runs in a Born-Oppenheimer style, with extra terms that carry the state. Charges and swings ride as live state, not sums redone each step. Cost falls, and the runs stay sound. The authors call the end frame robust and broad in reach. It suits work with live charges.
arxiv-2502-09702:
Gwenaël Van Looveren and co-authors compute how close a rocky planet can sit to its star and still keep an atmosphere, in this 2025 paper. That retention distance can then be compared with the habitable zone, where liquid water fits. They pair atmosphere escape models with stellar aging models across star types, spins, and ages. The escape physics covers carbon dioxide and nitrogen air.

Overlap between the two zones comes sooner around slow-spinning stars. Around the smallest stars, under four tenths of the Sun's mass, habitable-zone planets likely keep no air at all, since such stars stay active too long. A fast young spin also hurts a planet's odds. Every rocky world yet observed by the Webb telescope sits outside its retention line. The authors aim the maps at target selection.
arxiv-2502-09802:
Nagam and co-authors, writing for the Euclid Consortium, published this paper in 2025. It reports the hunt for strong gravitational lenses in the Euclid space telescope's Early Release Observations. A lens forms when a galaxy's gravity bends a background galaxy's light into arcs, a rare alignment prized for weighing dark matter and testing cosmology.

The full Euclid survey is expected to find about 170,000 such systems, far too many to locate by eye alone. The team therefore trains convolutional neural networks to flag lens candidates in the imaging data, with visual inspection as the first checking step. The early release data already yielded several new galaxy-galaxy lenses. The paper lays out the detection pipeline and its first catches. Scaling this search is a flagship task for the mission: every confirmed lens is a natural telescope and a dark matter probe in one.
arxiv-2502-09902:
Saikat Banerjee and Piers Coleman take on a paradox in heat reads of many solids: a large heat store like that of free charges, with no like mark in how heat flows. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five.

At first sight, the clash backs a spread of stuck states in the bulk. The team maps heat flow reads onto charge-like circuits of flow and store. They argue a jam of slow heat paths is apt to arise in both rival views: stuck states, or a sea of neutral free-like parts. The jam comes from the huge gap between how much heat charges store and how much the grid stores. They give a new read of past data that can split the two.
arxiv-2502-10902:
Continued fractions break numbers into a chain of whole-number parts, and the patterns in that chain hide deep structure. Yuto Nakajima and Hiroki Takahasi connected two fields in 2025: theorems about dense sets of whole numbers, and the fractal size of sets of irrational numbers. Their bridge is a transference principle that carries properties of dense number sets over to sets of fractions.

For any set of whole numbers with positive upper density, they build a matching set of irrationals of fractal dimension one half that keeps the same density pattern. Classic results on arithmetic and polynomial patterns then carry across. The team also adapt the principle to the primes and to several special sequences.
arxiv-2502-11102:
Hongliang Lu and co-authors manufacture training data for optimization modeling in a 2025 paper. Language models could turn plain problem stories into math formulations, but good paired examples are scarce. Their framework, OptMATH, builds such pairs in both directions at scale. It starts from seed problems that already carry formulations.

From each seed, the system generates fresh problem data at controlled difficulty. A back-translation step writes the story in natural language. Then a forward check remodels the story and rejects pairs that fail to match. Accepted pairs form the training set. The rejects, after filtering, become a hard new benchmark with much longer problems than older ones. Models from half a billion to thirty-two billion parameters, trained on the data, beat rivals across modeling tests. The authors release the data set openly.
arxiv-2502-11202:
Nicolas Borghini, Baochi Fu, and Sören Schlichting present a 2025 method for tracking baryon charge in the hot fluid made when heavy ions collide. Wobbles in that charge are a key clue to the phase map of strong-force matter, but full simulations with noise built in are unstable and costly.

Their shortcut splits the job in two. A smooth, charge-free background flow runs on its own, while the noisy charge motion is solved on top of it with a simpler linear method. Built into a standard flow code, the method matched exact solutions for pair patterns across several matter types. The team also shows how the gap between two points in the flow reveals when the wobbles arose, and how the final patterns sense the charge spread rate.
arxiv-2502-11302:
Frank Curtis, Shima Dezfulian, and Andreas Waechter design a solver for optimization problems where every measurement comes with noise. The problems have curved goals and curved limits, and only rough values of the functions and their slopes are on hand. Their method grows from a barrier approach that keeps steps inside the allowed zone.

The design joins an older barrier solver that tolerates rough sub-steps with newer solvers built for noisy tasks. The team proves the method drives a measure of near-solution below a line set by the noise size. Tests across a wide range of problems showed the solver held up well, a step toward tuning real systems where exact values cannot be had.
arxiv-2502-11402:
Maher Mamah sped up an old number theory task in 2025: writing a given integer as the value of a two-variable quadratic polynomial. Cornacchia's classical algorithm handles the famous case of a sum of two squares, but it slows badly when the target number has many factors, and general forms add snags.

Mamah's route reduces the problem to subset sum, a weakly hard problem with fast practical methods. From that bridge he builds deterministic algorithms that adapt to the form's discriminant and the target's shape. When the discriminant is tiny next to the number, his method runs in polynomial time no matter how composite the target is. Wider cases still improve on the classical method. The solo paper's catalog creator line is set in capitals; the name is the author's. Readers get algorithms that trade a hard search for a well-stocked one.
arxiv-2502-11602:
Ruben Laso and Miguel Yermo present, in a 2025 paper, a fast store for the point clouds that laser scans make. Such clouds hold 3D shape for tasks like object spotting, self-drive, and land models. Near-point search is the core task, and it must be quick. The pair first clash known stores and search ways across cloud types. They then add their own store, cheesemap, built for laser clouds. It leans on the sparse, rough spread of real points. Three forms fit three spreads: dense, sparse, and mixed.

Per search, cheesemap beat the best known stores, most on air scan clouds. Its memory use stayed low, above all in the sparse and mixed forms. The pair cast it as a strong pick for 3D work.
arxiv-2502-11702:
Ola Forslund and co-authors dissect the anomalous Hall effect from magnetic fluctuations in a 2025 paper. The effect signals broken time-reversal symmetry and band traits of a special kind. Averaging over domains makes the field-free signal hard to probe head-on. Teams usually work back from field-based data instead.

A Weyl semimetal with a switchable ferromagnetic shift serves as the test case. Below that shift, symmetry breaking is certain and tunable. Above it, strong swings blur the picture. Thermodynamics, transport, and muon spin measures were combined. Setting the two regimes side by side exposed how such swings distort readings. Worked-back signals can mislead when such swings run strong. The authors draw lessons for kagome metals and kindred debated systems. Guidelines for reading such results are the paper's broader gift. Claims of that special kind need checks that account for such swings, they argue.
arxiv-2502-12202:
Zihao Zhu and co-authors expose a way to switch off the thinking of reasoning models, then turn the same flaw to good use. Large reasoning models write out their thought process before answering, and special tokens mark where thinking starts and ends. Their 2025 study shows those markers can be manipulated so the model skips thinking entirely, a flaw they name the Unthinking Vulnerability, found across mainstream models.

As an attack, Breaking of Thought plants the bypass during fine-tuning or triggers it at run time, degrading answers. A recovery alignment defense partly patches it. As a tool, Monitoring of Thought uses the same switch from outside, stopping reasoning that runs long or turns risky. The authors say the flaw is architectural: models that cannot protect their own thinking cannot yet be trusted to reason unsupervised.
arxiv-2502-12402:
Diniz, Picoli, and Lenzarini wrote a 2025 guide to a math trick used to take apart key models of electron gases. The trick turns sums over set quantum numbers into loops in the complex plane, which makes hard models solvable by hand. It is known in scattering work but less so for these solid-state models.

The authors walk through the method in modern notation, aimed at new students. Hand results matched computer checks for the Fermi gas and for a single-impurity model with no charge clash. They then extend the method to a broader impurity model with mixed couplings, giving one solution for all cases.
arxiv-2502-13002:
Nakorn Thongyoi, Patipan Uttayarat, and Chakrit Pongkitivanichkul join two puzzles in one spare model in a 2025 paper. The puzzles are why neutrino masses are so tiny and what dark matter is. The model's seesaw runs in reverse, making light masses without huge energy scales, which keeps it in reach of collider tests.

A light axion-like mote links the known world to the dark one, which is a fermionic mote in this build. The mix fits wobble data on neutrinos, the dark store left from the big bang, and a muon gauge that has long sat off the mark.
arxiv-2502-13202:
Kirill Grishin and co-authors present a nearby galaxy as a sign of a missed class of black holes in a 2025 paper. Small black holes at galaxy cores can show how the giant ones were born. Few mid-size cases are known, since slow feeders shine too faintly for wide surveys to catch.

The galaxy, NGC 3259, sits 27 million light years off and holds a hole a few hundred thousand times the sun's mass. It feeds at just one percent of its top rate. Deep spectra from two scopes pinned down the mass across time. Its core star mass sits far below the norm for its hole, which hints the two grew by unlike paths. New surveys should catch more such cases.
arxiv-2502-13402:
F. Alves-Júnior, A. Lemos, and F. Brito applied the de Broglie–Bohm reading of quantum theory to an anisotropic universe with extra dimensions in a 2025 paper. Quantum cosmology asks how the universe itself evolved from a quantum state; the Bohmian version gives definite trajectories instead of probabilities alone. Their universe is filled with stiff matter and described by a Gaussian wave function depending on momenta and dispersion parameters for each direction, including the hidden extra dimensions.

Solutions show those extra dimensions stabilizing through dynamical compactification. Two patterns appear: dimensions born large at the cosmic bounce that shrink to a small size, or born small and growing to a finite stable value. A special five-dimensional case, where the Wheeler–DeWitt equation degenerates, is treated separately.
arxiv-2502-13502:
Burc Gokden reports a striking property of a language model family built on power law decoder representations. Once trained, the model's reasoned outputs act like fixed tensors that barely change, so a stored copy of one key tensor can stand in for the deep network itself at run time. A cache for that tensor, added beside the standard key-value cache, then speeds up inference.

The match is close: cached outputs keep the same error scores and test results, agreeing to many decimal places. Tests that swap in borrowed, random, or identity tensors behave very differently, and the standard attention method turns out to be a special case of this design. The author outlines the shared traits of the learned outputs and shares a training and inference setup that uses both caches.
arxiv-2502-13902:
Minsuk Chang and co-authors present Grid Labeling, a faster way to gather data on where people look in charts for a given task. Where eyes go depends on the task, yet most gaze models train on free viewing data. Task linked data are costly to collect, as their 2025 paper notes.

Grid Labeling splits a chart into adaptive grids that fit its structure, so taggers can mark key zones with few clicks. A human study set it against two older tools across many measures. It gave the cleanest data and the strongest agreement between taggers, with fewer people needed. It also asked less physical and mental effort. A live demo is posted online.
arxiv-2502-14202:
Amirali Sajadi and co-authors ask, in a 2025 study, whether chatbots that help with coding actually warn users about unsafe code. Millions of programmers now paste questions and code into large language models, so silent acceptance of flawed code could spread real harm.

The team fed three leading models questions from a coding forum that contained known flaws. A good answer would name the flaw, explain how it could be exploited, and offer a fix. In practice, the models caught only a fraction of the flaws, with detection ranging from about thirteen to forty percent. They spotted some flaw types often and others rarely, leaving much unsafe code unflagged.
arxiv-2502-14602:
Fluid moving through a sponge-like material is often described by Darcy's law, a simple rule linking flow speed to pressure. Basarić, Oschmann, and Pan prove that this rule can be derived from the fuller equations of fluid motion. Their case has a fluid whose density varies, moving through a material full of tiny holes. The holes are larger than the classic critical size, a case not covered before. The spacing between them is treated as a shrinking parameter.

As the spacing shrinks, the team shows that speed and density settle into the pattern Darcy's law predicts. That holds provided the limiting system has a strong solution, and they give rates for how fast the settling happens. They also prove that such strong solutions exist for the variable-density Darcy system. The work closes a gap in the theory of flow through porous media.
arxiv-2502-14702:
Srilekha Gandhari and Michael Gullans study noisy quantum benchmarks in a 2025 paper. Randomized benchmarking grades quantum gates by watching performance decay over random sequences. The method assumes noise has no memory. In real devices, a surrounding bath can remember, making the noise non-Markovian and breaking that assumption.

Their test case couples qubits to a many-mode bosonic bath, with brief contact between gate steps. Memory-free noise gives the expected smooth exponential decay. Noise with memory decays far more slowly, almost like a polynomial curve. Efficient numeric methods back the analysis. The results warn that standard benchmarks can misread devices whose errors carry history, and they show what the decay curves reveal instead.
arxiv-2502-15002:
Nicholas Christoffersen, Kyle Luh, Sean O'Rourke, and Calum Shearer study gaps between values of random matrices. Their 2025 paper looks at singular values, which measure how a matrix stretches space. They work with a random rectangle matrix scaled by a fixed positive matrix. The question is how close two values in a row can sit.

They prove lower bounds for those gaps under some technical conditions. A direct result is that sample covariance matrices have all distinct values with high chance. That settles a conjecture posed by Vu in a 2021 survey. The team also draws a bound for gaps in a graph setting. Their case covers random bipartite graphs and the spacing of values of their adjacency matrices.
arxiv-2502-15802:
Boyang Zhang and co-authors tackle a practical problem in shrinking large neural networks in 2025: each layer of a model tolerates squeezing by a different amount. Early layers often survive heavy compression, while later ones degrade fast. Guessing the right level per layer wastes quality or saves too little space.

Their framework, called compression error theory, uses geometry to map how error grows as a layer is squeezed. It reshapes the error into curved forms, splits the space into parts, and picks the part with the least loss. Shown on quantization, the method aims to set each layer's level by theory instead of trial and error.
arxiv-2502-15902:
Zheng Chen and co-authors detect machine-written text by asking what prompt would have produced it. Their 2025 paper introduces IPAD, built on an inversion idea: if a passage came from a model, a plausible generating prompt should fit it neatly. A prompt inverter first guesses that hidden prompt, then two checker modules judge how well the text aligns with it.

The design targets two weaknesses of earlier detectors: fragility on unfamiliar or attacked text, and verdicts nobody can inspect. Across test sets, IPAD beat the strongest rivals on ordinary, shifted, and adversarially edited data. Its margins grew largest exactly where rivals wobble. Because the guessed prompt is visible, users can examine the evidence behind each call. The authors frame interpretability as part of accuracy's value: a detector people cannot audit will not be trusted where it matters.
arxiv-2502-16002:
Jingbo Yang, Bairu Hou, Wei Wei, Yujia Bao, and Shiyu Chang speed up language models by reusing stored context computations across queries, in work from twenty twenty-five. Many applications feed the same retrieved document into many questions. Standard models recompute that shared context every time, wasting work.

Their system precomputes each document's key value cache on its own, then stitches the caches together at run time. Two fixes heal the seams: position codes are shifted to match the joined layout, and trained special tokens restore attention across document borders. Across seven data sets, answer accuracy rose about four percent over top rivals. Time to first token fell by up to ninety-six percent.
arxiv-2502-16102:
Rashid A and P Sam Johnson study the spectral traits of certain positive operators in Hilbert spaces, in a 2025 math paper. Such operators grow out of matrices tied to a class of problems where unknowns must satisfy paired conditions. Their spectra, the sets of values that describe how they stretch space, shape how systems built on them behave.

The authors pin down values and near-values in those spectra for the classes they study. They also split one key matrix type into a product of two simpler matrices of the same type. Results of this kind support work in operator theory and in fields that lean on it, such as quantum physics.
arxiv-2502-16202:
San Martin Martinez proposes a Markov model for how iterated cubic polynomials factor in twenty twenty-five. The work builds on studies by Boston, Jones, and Goksel. It focuses on post critically finite cubic polynomials, whose critical points have finite orbits. Information in those orbits defines the model.

The model covers cubics whose combined critical orbits have lengths one and two. A complete list of such polynomials over the rationals is available from prior work. Some known families, including ones with colliding critical orbits, align with the model. The author constructs groups tied to the iterates of the polynomial. Those groups are proved to follow the Markov model. They are conjectured to contain the Galois groups of the iterates.
arxiv-2502-16302:
Yuxuan Xiong and co-authors improved text guided editing of three dimensional scenes in 2025. A user can describe a change in words, and software rebuilds the scene to match, but a leading method left backgrounds blurry and could get stuck in poor edits.

Their method keeps two fields for the scene: one for the edited version and one that holds the original features as a guide to protect the background. A cooling style search schedule helps escape poor local solutions. A vision based score filters out low quality edits before they are folded in. In tests, the method beat earlier ones in both expert ratings and measured scores.
arxiv-2502-16402:
Ship officers must judge fast-changing traffic at sea, and software that helps them often fails on new cases. Feng Ma and co-authors propose a system called Navigation-GPT in this 2025 paper. The system uses large language models, the AI tools trained on vast text, to handle cases that were not planned in advance. It is built as two linked cores that check each other's work.

A large core first breaks a hard navigation task into small steps, using a prompt style that plans, acts, and checks feedback. It calls outside tools to gather facts, which lowers the risk of made-up answers. A smaller tuned core then acts like a ship's first mate. It reads the gathered facts and gives lookout advice that follows the sea rules for avoiding collisions.
arxiv-2502-16702:
Maxim Dvornikov summarizes work on neutrino oscillations in gravitational fields in two thousand twenty-five. Neutrinos shift spin and flavor as they cross curved spacetime. Past studies of that dance are first reviewed in brief. Two fresh settings then get close treatment in the summary.

One case has neutrinos scatter off a supermassive black hole. A thick magnetized disk rings that hole in the scene. Spin oscillations there are the focus of the analysis. The second case puts flavor oscillations inside stochastic gravitational waves. Uses for neutrinos from space sources close the review.
arxiv-2502-16802:
What a language model learns depends on the recipe of its training data. Jiahui Peng and co-authors argue the recipe should be organized by topic, not by source, in a 2025 paper. Earlier mixing strategies grouped data by where it came from, websites, books, code, while glossing over what it is about.

The team built detailed topic labels by clustering data, summarizing clusters with a language model, and training a classifier to tag the rest. Across four mixing strategies, from automatic weighting to hand-tuned blends, topic-mixed pretraining beat source-mixed pretraining again and again. Theory backs the result: topic mixtures give lower validation loss and a friendlier landscape for training. Code, labeled data, and the topic models are promised public, making the recipe one other labs can copy.
arxiv-2502-16902:
Suchae Jeong, Inseong Choi, Youngsik Yun, and Jihie Kim teach image generators to respect cultures they barely know. Their 2025 paper notes that text-to-image models handle famous Western objects well but mangle items from underrepresented cultures, such as a Korean hangari pot. Their fix, Culture-TRIP, does not retrain the model. Instead it improves the words fed to it.

The system first gathers cultural background and visual detail about the culture-bound nouns in a prompt, drawing on Wikipedia and the web. It then rewrites the prompt in rounds, with large language models judging each version against cultural criteria. A user study with sixty-six people from eight countries found the refined prompts produced images that matched the intended culture better, above all for the underrepresented nouns. The authors release their resources for others to build on.
arxiv-2502-17002: Members of the Super-Kamiokande team report work from 2025 on muon capture by oxygen in their large underground detector. The detector is loaded with gadolinium, which helps it spot neutrons. When a muon is captured by an oxygen nucleus, neutrons can fly out. How many come out is the key measure here, and it bears on how the detector reads other rare events. The paper's title states that measure as its goal, using data from this named detector.
arxiv-2502-17102:
Evelia Garcia Barroso, Pedro Gonzalez Perez, and Patrick Popescu-Pampu explain a geometric object called a lotus and show how it can serve as a computing device for curve singularities. A singularity is a point where a curve crosses or pinches in a complicated way, and resolving it takes a sequence of blow-up steps. Earlier work by the group showed that each resolution produces a lotus, a small layered complex built from subdivided polygons, which unifies older tree diagrams used to encode the singularity type. Their paper grew out of a lecture course from twenty twenty-three.

On the lotus, one can read off or compute step by step key numbers of the singularity, including measures of how bad the point is and trees that classify its branches. Three running examples carry the explanations. A final section adapts the method for work in positive characteristic, where the arithmetic differs.
arxiv-2502-17402:
Karen Kang and three co-authors map how the spins of merging black holes show up in gravitational wave signals, in a 2025 paper. Spin tells scientists how these pairs formed and evolved. The slow spiral phase of a merger is well understood, but the final crash has no simple formulas, so reading spin from heavy pairs stays hard.

The team used a neural network to compare huge numbers of waveforms quickly, hunting for spin and mass settings that produce nearly the same signal. For light pairs, the map matched known physics: stronger aligned spin pairs with more equal masses. For heavy pairs, where the crash dominates, a like pattern appeared but changed shape and weakened as total mass grew. The method is a first step toward reading spin in the crash phase across the whole range of systems.
arxiv-2502-17702:
Pavlos Kazakopoulos and Aris Moustakas derive a formula for how much data a fiber optic channel can carry in the low noise limit, in a paper from 2025. Fiber links are fast and reach far, but their true capacity is hard to pin down. Dispersion spreads each pulse while nonlinearity bends the signal, and amplifier noise adds up along the way.

The team uses the fact that the governing equation can be solved by a transform method. They write the efficiency fully in terms of scattering data from that transform.
