Links between the noise structure and the map from signal to data yield the result. A classic effect, in which timing jitter grows with power, first caps and then reverses the gains from more power. Simulations with smooth inputs show the effect at high bandwidth.
arxiv-2502-17802:
Huaxin Lin proved a stability theorem in 2025 about maps that almost behave like group representations. The setting is operator algebra: a countable, discrete, amenable group, and maps sending its elements to unitary operators on a Hilbert space. An almost representation multiplies correctly only up to a small error on a finite test set, and satisfies a lower-bound condition after passing to a quotient algebra. The question is whether such an approximate object must sit near an exact homomorphism.

Lin's answer is yes. Given any tolerance and any finite set of group elements, a suitable closeness threshold guarantees a true homomorphism within that tolerance on the set. Results of this kind, almost implies near, underlie perturbation theory for operator algebras and some approaches to classifying C-star algebras. They reassure users that approximate symmetries in infinite-dimensional systems are not illusions.
arxiv-2502-18002:
Mehendale, Challa, Yedida, Danda, Sarkar, and Saha build an anomaly detection loss from the Radon-Nikodým theorem, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Which principle should guide loss design for spotting anomalies? Their answer multiplies the standard loss by a measure-change derivative. The resulting RN-Loss is proven sound in a learnability framework.

In supervised settings the derivative reduces to a simple weighted loss. Unsupervised, it becomes the familiar local outlier factor. Ninety-six data sets span health, security, and finance domains. The method beats state-of-the-art detectors on most multivariate sets. Peak scores also land on most time series sets.
arxiv-2502-18102:
Tim Lüders, Lynn Otto, and Konrad Waldorf build a unified geometric home for the twistings of real K-theory, in a 2025 mathematics paper. Twistings tweak K-theory the way a magnetic field tweaks charged particles, and the literature holds many rival models of them. The authors construct a bicategory of super 2-line bundles over graded Lie groupoids and show that real twistings are exactly these objects.

A wide range of known models then fall out as special cases, from bundle gerbes and their real and equivariant variants to orientifold twistings and twisted groupoid extensions. The point is one framework where results proved once apply across the whole family.
arxiv-2502-18202:
Atik Faysal and co-authors upgrade a denoising autoencoder by making it name what it sees, patch by patch. Masked autoencoders learn by rebuilding missing chunks of input. Their 2025 paper, DenoMAE2.0, adds a second job: classifying the local patches that remain visible, with position in mind.

The twin goals push the model to hold fine local detail and global sense at once. The test field is wireless signal classification, where noise is heavy and labeled data are scarce. Across signal-to-noise levels from extreme to moderate, the new model beat its predecessor and other baselines on both cleanup quality and final accuracy. Signal engineers get a pretraining recipe built for noisy, label-poor work.
arxiv-2502-18302:
Pengzhi Li and a team of co-authors plug a large language model into image generators to fix their weak language skills. Their method, LDGen, appeared in twenty twenty-five. Standard text encoders stumble outside English, so prompts in other languages yield off-target pictures.

A caption-refining strategy draws precise meaning out of the language model first. A lightweight adapter and a cross-modal refiner then align those rich features with the image model's own. Training stays cheap because the big pieces remain frozen. The result generates images in several languages with no language-specific training. Tests beat the baselines on prompt obedience and looks alike. The team comes from Li Auto's research group.
arxiv-2502-18502:
The nuGeN team reports, in a 2025 paper, fresh limits on a ghostly interaction between neutrinos and whole atomic nuclei. In coherent elastic scattering, a neutrino bumps a nucleus as one piece, a process long predicted but hard to catch. Their detector sits just 11 meters from a reactor core at the Kalinin power plant, bathed in antineutrinos.

A 1.41-kilogram germanium crystal, wrapped in layered shielding, listened with a very low energy threshold. Counts with the reactor on and off showed no clear difference. From that quiet result the team set new upper bounds on how often the scattering can occur. Each tighter bound narrows the space where new physics could hide. Reactor experiments like this one probe the same effect that larger labs chase underground.
arxiv-2502-18802:
Tatsuya Aoyama and Ethan Wilcox ask why language models stop resembling human readers after a point in training, in a two thousand twenty-five paper. A model's power to predict human reading behavior rises early in pretraining. Past a tipping point, it plateaus or gets worse.

The authors blame a phase transition inside the model. During this transition, specialized attention heads emerge rapidly. Correlational and causal experiments support the claim. Interestingly, the new attention patterns do not directly cause the decline. Instead, the transition changes the model's later learning dynamics. Further training after the transition keeps damaging the human likeness. The finding connects internal model reorganization to an externally measured behavior.
arxiv-2502-18902:
Quantum error-correcting codes that link distant qubits could cut the cost of building a reliable quantum computer. Haonan Xiong and co-authors report, in a 2025 paper, hardware that gives superconducting chips those long links. Today's chips mostly join only nearest neighbors, which blocks the better codes.

The team built an on-chip coupler a few centimeters long and ran a two-qubit gate through it with high fidelity. Background interference stayed very low without extra cancellation tricks. They also propose an added layer that lays the qubits out like a branching tree, which shrinks the average link distance sharply. The scheme could let superconducting systems host codes once thought out of reach.
arxiv-2502-19602:
Gaurav Arwade and Sigurdur Olafsson propose a way to keep machine learning models easy to explain, in a 2025 paper. Powerful models often hide why they decide as they do. In operations work, that hidden logic can matter as much as the answer itself. Simple models explain well but stumble when facts interact in tangled ways across the whole data set.

Their insight is that tangles often vanish inside smaller slices of the data. Their algorithm hunts for slices where relations turn simple, then fits a clear model in each slice. Tests on made-up data show the method is sturdy. The borders it draws match expert intuition better than one global model. The approach aims to give both accuracy and answers people can defend.
arxiv-2502-20002:
Francesco Formicola and co-authors present a 2025 physics paper on a fresh signal for when a quantum system stops behaving like a thermal one. In many-body localization, strong disorder and interaction trap a system out of equilibrium. The usual fingerprint, a slow creep of entanglement, is hard to measure in real devices.

The team ran heavy simulations on a standard model system and tracked a quantity called local ergotropy: the work that can be pulled from a small part by local means. That quantity, and its fluctuations, shifted in step with the phase change and crept with the same slow law inside the trapped phase. They propose it as a workable witness for experiments.
arxiv-2502-20102:
Mirjam Weilenmann, Nicolas Gisin, and Pavel Sekatski ask how much independence between sources is needed to rule out a real-number version of quantum theory, in work from 2025. Standard quantum theory uses complex numbers, and past work showed real-only theory fails in network setups with fully independent sources. Whether that independence could be relaxed was open.

The team shows partial independence is already enough to rule the real theory out. They derive a trade-off between how independent the sources are and the Bell value the real theory can reach. That trade-off also bounds the source correlations needed to fake past experiments with real systems. They further show one shared bit of entanglement is both needed and enough for real systems to recover the complex predictions in the key scenario.
arxiv-2502-20402:
Juan Manuel Durán argues, in twenty twenty-five, for a new way to justify trust in algorithms, beyond opening them up for inspection. Transparency justifies outputs by showing internal workings, functions and variables. That justification stays inside the algorithm. His alternative, computational reliabilism, is externalist: an output is justified if a reliable algorithm produced it. Reliability is judged by indicators such as formal checks, metrics, expert skill, and research culture. He first developed the view for computer simulations.

This chapter extends it to algorithms across science, with emphasis on machine learning. The chapter lays out the foundations of the view and how it works in practice. It also sketches its potential as a general epistemology of algorithms, the study of how we know what algorithms tell us.
arxiv-2502-20502:
Lance Ying and co-authors argue that today's AI tests fail to measure human-like thinking, in a 2025 paper. Models trained on human text are often cast as rough models of the human mind. The authors list the tests' flaws: labels never checked against people, no room for how human answers vary, and tasks too simple or too unlike real life.

To back the claim, they ran a study of people taking nine current AI benchmarks and found deep design problems. They close with five fixes for future tests, from human-checked labels to tasks drawn from real settings. The aim is a harder, fairer yardstick for claims about machine minds.
arxiv-2502-20702:
Ilya Shkredov continues a study of how sumset size and shared energy interact in additive combinatorics. A set's doubling constant measures how much it grows when added to itself. Common energy measures how often two subsets produce the same sums. Splitting a set in two, some split must keep the energy low.

He finds a fairly sharp subexponential link between the doubling constant and the least common energy over all two-way splits. As a payoff, the result yields a proof of the well-known arithmetic regularity lemma with better parameter dependence than earlier proofs.
arxiv-2502-20802:
Long and a large team build in twenty twenty-five a chip-based device that marries a light frequency comb with an electronic oscillator to make ultra-clean microwaves. Comb chips offer wide span and fast pulse rates, but turning them into microwaves usually needs extra lasers, locks, and outside sources. Their design runs fully passive: a laser, a modulator, a low-loss ring resonator, and a fast light detector, all from standard chip lines, feed each other in a loop.

The loop settles on its own into a coherent comb paired with a steady microwave tone. Noise levels matched demanding standards at several offsets. Because every part suits mass production, the authors pitch the device as a building block for microwave photonics and fibre radio links.
arxiv-2503-00002:
Cui, Collins, Munson, and Wong test in twenty twenty-five whether textbook optimal experiment design holds up in toxicology, using sea urchin embryos as the case. Standard designs spread doses evenly, which can waste animals and blur the dose-response curve. Their framework blends robust design maths with staged testing: start with a chosen layout, read early results, then retune the next doses to sharpen precision.

Case studies showed better statistical efficiency and flexibility than fixed designs, at lower cost and complexity. Model checks at each stage guarded against a wrong curve shape steering the doses astray. The authors suggest the staged robust route suits other lab sciences where each run is costly and early data can guide later choices.
arxiv-2503-00102:
Dusty galaxies that churn out stars hide behind their own soot, so counting the faint ones has been hard. Four astronomers use the Webb telescope in 2025 to find them in two famous sky fields. They start from galaxies the telescope sees in near-infrared, then measure the far-infrared glow at those spots with a ground-based camera. The catch holds 234 galaxies, 187 of them faint, the largest such individually named sample yet.

Faint and bright members turn out to be near kin: similar masses and shapes, with the faint ones simply forming fewer stars. Near-infrared brightness tracks distance well, which gives hunters a shortcut to faraway specimens. Mergers explain only about a fifth of the sample, fewer than older work suggested.
arxiv-2503-00302:
Tomohiro Mimura and Yasuhiro Inoue compared this 2025 set of math recipes for bending energy in simulations of growing tissue. Such simulations track cells whose positions carry real meaning, so the mesh cannot simply be rebuilt when it stretches unevenly. Picking the right bending recipe matters, yet guidance was scarce. The authors tested rival recipes in two stages.

First, they checked each recipe's energy and force against exact values on a wrinkled sheet and a smooth sphere. Then they grew wrinkles in a sheet under two cell-division patterns and read the spacing of the folds. One model, Hamann's, proved most exact for hard numbers. Another, Julicher's, ran cheaper and sufficed when only shape trends matter. The study gives modelers a clear selection rule.
arxiv-2503-01402:
Hang Yu and six co-authors design a fast way to load a cold Fermi gas into a higher band of a light lattice. Their paper from twenty twenty-five uses shortcuts to adiabaticity, control paths that mimic slow change at speed. Fermi gases spread widely in momentum, unlike tight Bose condensates. The team scores success as an average over all momentum states at once.

A global search over many control knobs sets the load plan for each Bloch state. Lattice depth shifts the scores, which the search maps out. Twisting the lattice phase helps, thanks to symmetry gaps between bands. The main drag is crowding: more filled momentum states mean lower mean success. Runs at varied filling confirm the slide. The team weighs their plan against older load tricks and checks lab feasibility.
arxiv-2503-01502: Juergen Rossmann proves that the time-dependent Stokes system, the linearized equations of viscous flow, has strong solutions when the flow region is a polygon. The boundary values are prescribed. Corners are the enemy of regularity theory, since solutions can misbehave near sharp angles. Writing in twenty twenty-five, Rossmann works in weighted Sobolev spaces, where the weight is a power of the distance to the corner points. Allowed badness near corners is measured and controlled rather than ignored, and in that setting he establishes existence of strong solutions.
arxiv-2503-01902:
Adiba Mahbub Proma and co-authors test whether chatbots can help fight false claims in a paper from 2025. The head of the text gives the work a sharper title about how such models fail to support fact-checking. The team studied three large language models on political claims. Each model first had to name trusted sources, then write a reply meant to correct the claim.

The models often failed to ground replies in real news sources. They also leaned toward citing sources from one side of politics. Reply variety differed from model to model. The authors warn that prompt tricks alone are not enough. They call for stronger guardrails before such tools are used in public.
arxiv-2503-02002:
Ronan Kerr and co-authors give the first full survey of the Circinus Complex, a vast young star nursery. The region holds about 3,100 fresh stars and a giant molecular cloud. Its core cluster is named ASCC 79. Their 2025 paper maps ages and speeds across the whole complex with Gaia data. A clear pattern shows in the core: younger stars sit farther from the center.

Speeds fit a steady outward spread. A rival simulation, STARFORGE, shows the same shape can arise in two stages. First the parent cloud collapses and builds the core cluster. Then its first giant stars sweep a shell that triggers a second wave of births. Edge groups seem to have formed on their own. The work offers a fresh script for how star families grow in rounds.
arxiv-2503-02202:
Fong Yew Leong and co-authors blend quantum circuits with neural networks to solve fast flows. Their 2025 paper benchmarks a hybrid physics-informed model against purely classical and purely quantum rivals. The physics rules enter the training loss, so no labelled flow data is needed.

Pure quantum models won on smooth wave problems with very few parameters. They stumbled on shocks and sharp breaks, where the hybrid held steady. With enough parameters the hybrid matched classical accuracy while keeping its size down. Quantum emulation cost still limits scale today. The authors pitch hybrids as safe general solvers when the flow type is unknown.
arxiv-2503-02302:
Iwase and co-authors ask whether a strange training pattern in image networks tracks how the networks weigh shape against texture. In double descent, test error falls, rises, and falls again as training proceeds. The team measured shape and texture bias across training epochs in convolutional networks.

Bias rose and fell in step with the double descent of test error. The match held from the first dip through the full rise in error. Bias double descent even appeared without label noise, where error double descent was thought not to occur. The authors say the link may help explain why double descent happens at all.
arxiv-2503-02502:
Jianghao Chen and co-authors present a way to pick the best long texts for training language models, in this 2025 paper. Teaching a model to handle long inputs takes long training data, but judging which long texts are good is still an open problem. Their framework, LADM, scores texts by how much their parts depend on each other across distance.

The trick borrows the model's own attention system, which is built to fetch related pieces of text. By measuring those links, LADM rates whether a long document truly hangs together or is merely long. The team then kept training models on the selected data alone. With just one billion tokens of chosen text, scores rose clearly across several long-context tasks, suggesting quality beats bulk for this skill.
arxiv-2503-02802:
Guy Bresler and Alina Harbuzova prove that two classic hard problems in high-dimensional statistics are, in computing terms, the same problem, in a paper from 2025. Both models hide a faint signal inside noise. One works through data covariance; the other through a symmetric matrix. Each had been studied on its own for years.

The authors give the first average-case reduction that turns instances of the sparse covariance problem into instances of the sparse Wigner problem. The key is a new symmetry property of the Gram-Schmidt process, which strips dependence from the noise while keeping the signal intact. Because reductions carry hardness with them, results for one model now transfer to the other. The equivalence closes a long gap between the two literatures.
arxiv-2503-02902:
Nashed finds a black hole form in a bent gravity frame that needs no preset shape in this twenty twenty-five paper. The frame bends the base law by a func of the non-metric grade. Past holes in it set that func by hand to force a fit.

Inside, a still tube space with two free forms feeds the field laws in the hunt. The hole that falls out holds four fixed grades in its build. One grade sets the world push, one the mass, and two the bent from the plain frame. When one bent grade is nil, the func locks flat to the plain case. Spin is then poured in by a frame shift, and its heat laws check out firm.
arxiv-2503-03002:
Mohammad Abtahi and co-authors model car dynamics with deep learning in a 2025 paper. Vehicle motion bends in complex ways, which makes optimal control and planning hard to run in real time. Koopman theory offers a fix: it restates a bent system in a linear form that control tools handle well. Their network learns that restatement from pedal and steering inputs up to body states, framed along the road's curve.

Against standard fitted linear models, the Koopman model tracked a double lane change with better accuracy. A predictive controller built on the model also steered with clear gains over the baseline. Framing the motion along the road's own curve helps the model stay true through turns. The approach may ease the load on self driving stacks that must plan fast and stay smooth.
arxiv-2503-03202:
Sneh Pillai, a solo author, schedules training losses by uncertainty in a 2025 paper. Vision-language models usually train on huge image-caption sets, but small-data settings invite overfitting and instability. His method watches how variable the model's alignment guesses are, then reweights the contrastive loss accordingly during training. Tests used a slice of a standard caption dataset to fake scarcity.

The schedule beat a fixed-weight baseline on retrieval accuracy, and edged out rival adaptive schemes based on entropy or similarity spread. Under noise attacks on images and captions, the variance-guided version held its recall best. Visual maps showed cleaner, more distinct embeddings.
arxiv-2503-03402:
Genheng Zhao proves that adding primes to primes quickly escapes the primes' thinness, in this 2025 paper. Take a set of primes below some bound, containing a healthy fraction of all primes there. Form every sum of two of them. Sums of two primes are usually even composite numbers, so the sumset lives in new territory, and the question is how large it must be.

Zhao shows the sumset outgrows the original set by a factor that grows like the logarithm of the bound. A penalty trims that factor when the chosen primes are sparse. Two regimes appear: reasonably dense sets get one bound, sparser sets a slightly weaker one, each with explicit constants. Results of this kind, sumset growth, are the engine of additive combinatorics. They say structure cannot hide: even an arbitrary handful of primes, added to itself, swells into something provably large.
arxiv-2503-03502:
Canaan Yung and three co-authors present a detector for hostile prompts aimed at large language models in a paper from 2025. Such prompts can jailbreak a model into bad behavior. Tuning the model to resist them is costly, so the team instead screen prompts before they reach the model, using the shape of the prompt's word embedding cloud.

Their method measures local curvature and intrinsic dimension, traits they show differ between hostile and benign prompts. A theory section extends a classic curve formula into many dimensions to ground the measures. The detector scored near-perfect sorting and beat prior detectors across models and attack types.
arxiv-2503-03802:
Fenglin Liu and a large team of colleagues wrote a 2025 paper on RiskAgent, a system for evidence-based medical risk prediction. Large language models can match human experts on medical exams. Real clinical decisions are harder: they demand deep, current medical knowledge, and fine-tuned models still tend to hallucinate, inventing false facts.

RiskAgent instead couples a language model with validated medical tools and databases. The model plans and reasons, while the tools supply checked evidence for risk estimates. This synergy is meant to curb hallucination and ground each prediction in sources a clinician can inspect. The paper presents the system as a safer pattern for using language models in high-stakes medical decision-making.
arxiv-2503-03902:
Siqi Qu, Mathias Staudigl, and Juan Peypouquet build, in a 2025 mathematics paper, a broad framework for solving constrained variational inequalities. Such problems ask for a point that satisfies a set of constraints and a balance condition at once. They arise in games, flows, and shape design. The team's framework builds a flow over time whose path should settle on the answer.

The flow blends two tools: Tikhonov regularization, a soft pull toward smooth, small-norm answers, and an exterior penalty for straying outside the constraint set. With the blend tuned well, paths converge strongly to the least-norm solution inside the set. The framework unifies past work on both tools. A splitting form, which handles each part of the domain separately, is also given, with weaker convergence results under a named joint condition. The authors work in an infinite-dimensional Hilbert space.
arxiv-2503-04202:
Angelos Assos, Yuval Dagan, and Nived Rajaraman prove hardness for planning against online learners in two thousand twenty-five. Online learners adapt their play over time in games and markets. A rival may ask how to best reply for long term gain. Fast replies are known for narrow cases like auctions.

The team shows no fast general method exists, barring a collapse of known classes. Their bound is strong, on the order of the full time span. Past work had a far weaker bound for a distinct learner type. Their learner is a standard no regret method in wide use. The bar is thus basic to game settings at large.
arxiv-2503-04302:
Christian Rondanini, Barbara Carminati, Elena Ferrari, Antonio Gaudiano, and Ashish Kundu wrote a 2025 security paper on detecting malware at the network edge with small language models. Edge devices, like sensors and gateways, have little power and memory. Traditional malware detectors struggle against modern malware's speed of change, so language model detectors are attractive if they can fit.

The authors propose an architecture that plays to small models' strengths while covering their limits. They then run a broad experimental evaluation of several state of the art lightweight models. Tests use public datasets built for edge and internet of things scenarios, with varied attack types. The study weighs accuracy against the energy and compute budgets of real edge hardware.
arxiv-2503-04802:
Birger Moell and three co-authors review how well machine learning reads illness from the sound of speech. Their scoping review appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Voice and speech patterns shift with many diseases, from throat faults to mind disorders. The team sifted hundreds of papers and kept ninety-one that used learning models to sort patients by speech.

Scores ran highest for throat disorders, slurred speech, and speech changes in Parkinson's disease. Depression, schizophrenia, and early memory loss also scored high, though with more spread. Some conditions, like obsessive-compulsive disorder and autism, still rest on thin study. The authors judge speech a strong, cheap signal for diagnosis in many areas. They call for bigger, shared data sets to firm up the weaker spots. Clinics could one day screen patients from a short voice clip.
arxiv-2503-05102:
Hengrui Xing and co-authors wrote a 2025 paper on AutoTestForge, a system that tests language models with little hand work. Behavioural tests probe what a model can and cannot do, but writing them by hand is slow and narrow. Their system lets large models draft test templates and fill them in.

A voting scheme across several models checks each test label for quality. Tests span three angles: skill type, fairness, and robustness. On feeling and similarity tasks the system found far more model errors than past data sets and tools. Varied draft styles all worked steadily. The authors pitch it as a fuller health check for language software.
arxiv-2503-05202:
Ok Song An, Jin U Kang, Yong Jin Kim, and Ui Ri Mun connect the hot reheating after cosmic inflation to today's dark energy readings. In quintessential inflation, one field drives both the early burst and the late speeding-up. The two eras usually sit in separate calculations.

Their bridge runs time backward from now to the end of reheating. When the field's slope is tiny against cosmic friction, the field stays frozen, making the backtrack simple. A plain formula then links reheating temperature to dark energy measures. Computer checks confirmed the formula across typical models. Any model in the family can be read through it. The link turns today's telescopes into probes of the first moments.
arxiv-2503-05602:
Roberto Florez-Ablan, Marco Roth, and Jan Schnabel deliver unwelcome news for quantum machine learning: tuned quantum kernels quietly become classical ones. Quantum kernels promise advantage by embedding data in quantum states, but their signals concentrate and generalization suffers. Bandwidth tuning, rescaling the data, is the standard rescue. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the team shows numerically that optimally tuned quantum kernels closely mimic the classical radial basis kernel. Worse, the tuning's size simplifies them further, toward low-order polynomial kernels. Both fidelity and projected kernel families show the pattern, across encodings and data sets.

A simple analytic model explains the mechanism. The conclusion is measured but firm: with bandwidth tuning doing the heavy lifting, no quantum advantage survives in these setups. The work redirects the search for advantage toward untuned or structurally different kernels.
arxiv-2503-05702:
Raquel Fernandez-Peralta surveyed in 2025 the sprawling family of fuzzy implication functions. These functions extend the plain if-then of logic to graded truth, where statements can be half true. Dozens of families exist, each built its own way and prized for different traits, and the last decade added many more.

The survey organizes the families by construction, properties, and best uses, with schemes that let readers compare at a glance. Theorists gain a map that stops duplicated effort, and engineers get help picking the right operator for control systems, decision tools, and other graded-reasoning machines.
arxiv-2503-06602:
Pranoy Panda, Siddharth Tandon, and Vineeth Balasubramanian speed up a fair way to assign credit in machine learning, in a 2025 paper. Shapley values split credit among inputs, but the weighted version, which treats group sizes unlike ways, is very costly to compute for large data. That cost blocks use in valuing data and explaining which features drive a model.

The team first restate weighted Shapley values as a weighted least squares problem. They then train an estimator that predicts the values directly, a method they call FW-Shapley. Training is shown to be valid even without true values as targets. On feature explanation tasks, the method beat a prior learned estimator by about a quarter on their score. On data valuation, it ran many times faster than a leading rival at like quality.
arxiv-2503-07502:
Borrero and six co-authors ran sims in twenty twenty-five on how salt shifts the melt line of carbon gas ice under the sea. Such ices trap gas in cages of ice, and salt thaws them at lower heat. They used a side-by-side sim method at three press levels.

More salt in the water cut the melt heat in a smooth trend. The sims matched lab data in print very well. Melt and growth also slowed as salt rose, so runs must last far longer. Size checks showed the box size bends the melt heat a bit.
arxiv-2503-07702:
Mehdi Bakhshipoor, Yousef Azizi, and Seyed Ehsan Nedaaee Oskoee design a communication network that builds itself. Their agents, smart nodes with no central boss, learn by reinforcement training when to link to neighbors. Each agent sees only its local surroundings and follows a physics-based energy rule, cast as a Hamiltonian, that rewards stable, cheap connection patterns.

In simulations the approach grew large, sturdy communication clusters while spending less transmission energy than baseline methods. The network stayed connected when agents moved, when density changed, when some nodes failed, and when obstacles blocked paths. The authors frame the work as physics-guided machine learning and point to uses in device networks and vehicle communication, where no central controller can be assumed and conditions keep shifting underfoot.
arxiv-2503-07902:
Six researchers wrote a robotics paper in two thousand twenty-five on turning spoken instructions into robot paths. A person should be able to tell a mobile robot where to go in plain words. Their pipeline uses a large language model to translate speech into a formal logic formula, then hands that formula to a motion planner.

The logic language is linear temporal logic, which can state rules about order and timing. Language models often produce formulas with syntax errors, so their tool, LTLCodeGen, frames the translation as code generation to keep the output valid. Tests in simulation and with a real robot beat end-to-end language planning and rival translation methods.
arxiv-2503-08002:
Meghna Roy Chowdhury, Wei Xuan, Shreyas Sen, Yixue Zhao, and Yi Ding present a clear, two stage model to predict college student mental health, in work from 2025. Student mental health has reached crisis levels. Prediction is hard: long term data are rare, many models are black boxes, and most give group level rather than personal insight.

Their model links raw behavior signals to mental health through five defined behavior groups. That middle step makes the reasoning readable. It was tested on the longest running mobile sensing study of college life. The design aims at personal forecasts that staff can understand and act on, not just risk scores.
arxiv-2503-08102:
Jiale Wei and five co-authors introduced in 2025 an AI-native memory system meant to end repetitive form-filling across digital life. People restate the same facts to every site, app, and soon every AI agent. Saved passwords and autofill patch only part of that burden.

Their system, called Second Me, stores and organizes a person's knowledge and speaks for them when asked. It can fill fields, draft context-aware replies, and smooth contact with services. The design treats memory as a standing assistant rather than a static vault. Privacy and control questions sit at the center of the proposal.
arxiv-2503-08402:
Gayatri Mohan, Ronit Karmakar, Rupam Borah, and Umananda Goswami study how black holes bend light and ring in a modified gravity theory. Their 2025 paper works in f(R,T) gravity with three surrounding fluid types. Strong lensing follows a universal method; ringing tones come from a WKB approximation.

Two model parameters steer the light bending and lensing coefficients. Small values push photon divergence outward and return results to the classic Schwarzschild limit. For the galaxy center black hole, the team estimates the outer Einstein ring position, ring separation, and relative brightness under each fluid. Ringing amplitude and damping move in opposite patterns with the two parameters. The authors use the split to show how lensing and ringing together can fingerprint the theory.
arxiv-2503-08502:
Neural networks fold their input space as they learn, and Michal Lewandowski and co-authors present a way to measure that folding in a 2025 paper. Recent work suggests that layers with ReLU activation fold the space step by step. A folding measure based on Hamming distance in the activation space was proposed not long ago, but it covered a narrow class of functions.

The authors generalize the measure to a wider class of activation functions by grouping inputs into equivalence classes. They analyze its math and compute traits, and they give an efficient sampling strategy for its use. Folding values rise with depth when error is low and fall when error grows. A new regularization scheme is outlined that pushes networks toward higher folding.
arxiv-2503-08702:
Yukalov and Yukalova set out a method in 2025 for quantum systems whose atoms interact through sharply singular forces. Standard first approximations blow up with such forces, because the math produces infinities at short range. Their fix rearranges the calculation so the starting point already includes a smoothing correlation between atoms.

They build that smoothing function from the short-distance form of the scattering solution, extended to all distances by a self-similar method. With it, every later order of the calculation stays finite. Examples cover several kinds of atomic systems. The authors present the scheme as a sound base for studying strongly interacting quantum gases and fluids.
arxiv-2503-08902:
Forough Fazeliasl and co-authors tackle mutual information estimation in a 2025 paper on statistics and machine learning. Mutual information measures how strongly two variables depend on each other, but it is hard to compute exactly in high dimensions, and neural estimators can wobble badly on small batches of data.

Their deep Bayesian nonparametric framework builds the training loss from a Dirichlet process posterior, blending prior knowledge with the data at hand. That regularization calms sharp swings in the loss and steadies the gradients during training. Tests on linking data space with latent space show more robust estimates, backed by stronger convergence guarantees.
arxiv-2503-09002:
Chenyuan Yang and four co-authors present a system that uses language models to write bug finding tools in a 2025 paper. Static analysis finds bugs in code such as operating system kernels, but writing analyzers by hand is slow and covers only set patterns. Scanning a huge system directly with a language model is not practical.

Their system, called KNighter, learns from past bug fixes and generates specialized checkers automatically. A multi stage pipeline tests each checker against the original patch and refines it to cut false alarms. On the Linux kernel, the generated checkers found ninety two new long hidden bugs. Most were confirmed, many fixed, and thirty received formal vulnerability numbers.
arxiv-2503-09202:
Falko Helm and co-authors suggest that language models stumble on long texts partly because training treats every token as equal. Some words need pages of context to guess, while others need almost none. Weighting hard tokens more during training could teach models to use long context better.

The team sets out several weighting schemes under one shared frame. Each scheme scores a token by pitting a long-context model's confidence against a short-context model's. Even a much smaller model can do the scoring well. Tests across many long-context tasks show that uneven weights lift model skill. The gains hold across schemes, which makes the route robust. The authors close with trade-offs and clear guidance for steering training through loss weights.
arxiv-2503-09902:
Grading a chatbot's answer is harder than grading its search results, and Zahra Abbasiantaeb and four co-authors built a richer yardstick in a 2025 paper. Their resource grows out of the TREC iKAT shared task, extending the 2023 collection into 2024 with 17 conversations and more than 20,000 judged passages.

The new ingredients are gold nuggets: the essential facts a good answer must contain, mined from the judged passages, 2,279 of them. Assessors also wrote 62 gold answers by hand. Some questions are deliberately unanswerable, to catch systems that hallucinate rather than abstain, and the user personas behind the conversations grew richer. The authors offer the set as the missing test bench for retrieval-augmented generation, where fluent answers have long outrun the tools that grade them.
arxiv-2503-10002:
Pjotr Buys, Jan van den Heuvel, and Ross Kang count independent sets in triangle-free graphs in a 2025 mathematics paper. An independent set is a group of vertices with no edges among them. Classic results guarantee at least one large such set in sparse triangle-free graphs. This paper counts how many independent sets must exist in total.

The count grows at a sharp exponential rate set by average degree, improving earlier bounds. The method extends an elegant induction from the nineteen eighties and also yields bounds on the independence polynomial. A classic random construction shows the rate cannot be beaten. Readers get a near-exact census law.
arxiv-2503-10102:
Junhao Wang presents, in a 2025 paper, a way to measure the layer thicknesses inside a perovskite solar cell without cutting it open. Thickness shapes how the cell harvests light, yet checking it usually means damage. A convolutional network instead reads the cell's wavelength response curve and infers each layer's thickness.

The network trains only within ranges where the materials' optical traits stay fixed, which bounds its use. It worked better on transparent cells than on light-sensitive opaque ones. Sampling tricks helped little, but a smart tuning search for the network's settings cut errors sharply. Wang concludes the approach is fast and feasible for lab checks of new cell designs.
arxiv-2503-10302:
Shuvro Chowdhury and co-authors set a tougher classical bar for quantum advantage in hard optimization, in a 2025 paper. Their machines, called probabilistic computers, run Monte Carlo search directly in hardware tuned for the task. The testbed is three-dimensional spin glasses, a classic hard problem, and the rival is a leading quantum annealer working the same instances.

Two algorithms are compared. One mimics quantum annealing in steps and improves as more copies run, as theory predicts. The other, adaptive parallel tempering with special cluster moves, scales better still and wins overall. The authors project that custom chips could speed these methods by orders of magnitude while using far less energy, reframing what quantum machines must beat.
arxiv-2503-10402:
Alexandre Wagemakers and Vipul Periwal wrote a mathematics paper in 2025 on finding roots of functions without using derivatives. Their methods grow out of a classic iterative scheme based on divided differences. The family reaches second-order convergence with two function values per step, at small extra cost. A side gain is better stability across starting points than the classic scheme.

The authors present results for single functions, for fields, and for scalar fields. By standard measures, the new family beats the classic method in most cases. The paper frames the methods as an efficient and stable option for root finding when derivatives are costly or not available.
arxiv-2503-10702:
Hangkai Qian, Bo Li, and Qichen Wang present, in a 2025 paper, a trust scoring system for search-augmented chatbots that fetch documents before answering. Such systems can repeat false sources with confidence. Their method pulls factual claims out of each document, labels how claims support or fight each other, and lets trust flow across the resulting web.

Starting from a political news data set, they extracted over two thousand claims and about a thousand solid links between them. Trust scores updated in rounds until they settled. Verified articles ended high and false ones low. The authors plan sharper claim tools and wider tests. The work aims to help chatbots weigh sources before they speak.
arxiv-2503-10802:
James Matthews and ten co-authors review, in twenty twenty-five, blast waves and reverse shocks in fast outflows from space objects. Such models are used for gamma-ray bursts, the most fast flows known. They are also used for slower jets from X-ray binary stars. The team asks how the two cases match and where they part.

They show how blast wave size grows with time in the fast case. For set energy, reverse shocks cross the jet much later in slow systems than in fast ones. In X-ray binaries, the cross can take ten to one hundred days. That makes these jets good test beds for shock physics. The authors also weigh shape, spread, and how to tell shock parts apart in real data.
arxiv-2503-11302:
Michael Hanna and co-authors ask in 2025 whether language models keep grammar skill and world skill in separate inner machinery. Models write fluent, well formed text with ease yet stumble more on reasoning and steady fact recall. Brain science hints that people split formal language work from functional work, and some claim models should do the same, by design or by learning.

The team extracted the minimal circuits, small subgraphs of each model, that carry out set formal and functional tasks, across five models and ten tasks. Circuits for the two task kinds barely overlapped. Yet formal task circuits also barely overlapped with each other, unlike the unified language zone in human brains. A softer test told a kinder story: circuits could still solve each other's tasks within their own kind. The authors conclude a single formal network stays elusive, even if a broad split is real.
arxiv-2503-11502:
Purnima Balakrishnan and fourteen co-authors probe the magnetic order at the seam between iron telluride and magnetic topological insulators. Their 2025 paper serves a hunt for a rare state that mixes superconductivity with topology, a platform eyed for quantum computing. The seam must host magnetism, superconductivity, and special surface states all at once.

Three pairings behaved in unlike ways. In one, the antiferromagnetic order of the base survived almost intact, so any weakening reached only a few nanometers. In another, that order was nearly erased. In a third, both layers showed net magnetization, with signs that magnetism and superconductivity interact. The mixed picture, the authors argue, still marks these seams as a robust place to chase the rare state. Careful choice of overlayer tunes the result.
arxiv-2503-11802:
Arman Duha, Samuel Begg, and Thomas Bilitewski study a sharp shift in squeezing behavior in a 2025 physics paper. Their system is a double layer of tiny spins that pull on each other across long ranges. Such systems can entangle spins into a squeezed state, a resource for sharper sensors.

The authors find two clear regimes as the settings change. In one, squeezing reaches the best limit set by quantum rules. In the other, it still grows with system size but less strongly. They show the change follows a shared scaling law with a time scale that blows up at the border. The result frames the shift as a true phase change in motion, not just a smooth drift. Cold atoms and similar platforms could test the claim in the lab.
arxiv-2503-12002:
Mark Pustilnik, Antonio Loquercio, and Francesco Borrelli study game-theoretic equilibria in autonomous racing, in a two thousand twenty-five paper. When racing cars share track constraints, their joint behavior is modeled as a generalized Nash equilibrium. The standard way to compute one assumes every player shares identical multipliers for the shared constraints.

That normalized assumption, the authors show, throws away other valuable equilibria. A simple racing example exposes the shortcoming clearly. They then build a method based on the mixed complementarity problem to find non-normalized equilibria. Tests in realistic racing scenarios show richer, multi-modal interactions between cars. The approach widens the set of strategies race planners can consider.
arxiv-2503-12302: Ryan McCulloch and Marius Tărnăuceanu study finite groups in which a special family of subgroups is dense. Density here means that between any two subgroups in the full ordering of a group's subgroups, one can always find a member of the special family, called the Chermak-Delgado lattice. Their short note asks which finite groups have that property and describes the groups that do.
arxiv-2503-12502:
Jingyang Zhao, Mingyu Xiao, and Shunwang Wang present a 2025 algorithms paper on a logistics puzzle that fuses two classics. One half asks where to open depots. The other asks how to route loaded vehicles from them. Each depot costs money to open, each customer demands goods, and trucks have limited capacity. The goal is the cheapest full plan.

The authors give an algorithm guaranteed to land within about 4.17 times the best possible cost, beating the previous record of 4.38. If a customer's demand may arrive across several trips, the guarantee tightens to about 4.09. Benchmark tests also show their plans beating earlier methods in practice, not just on paper.
arxiv-2503-13002:
Hybrid work is now standard in software firms, and in large agile teams the recurring meeting is where collaboration happens. Emily Laue Christensen and co-authors study how those meetings run under a two-days-in-office rule in this 2025 case study at a big telecom firm, drawing on 27 interviews across fifteen teams.

Their main finding is that the right setting depends on the meeting's purpose. Talks that need debate or brainstorming work better in the room, while big briefings run fine remotely. Community meetings also knit teams together and spread knowledge. For small remote discussions, they advise keeping cameras on.
arxiv-2503-13102:
Alexander Pugachev and co-authors build a Russian test bed for language model errors in a 2025 paper. Using models as judges of other models is fashionable, but the practice was validated mostly in English. Their REPA data set holds one thousand user queries and two thousand model answers, hand labeled across ten error types plus overall preference.

Six generators were ranked by human taste under three scoring systems. Eight model judges then tried the same job, in plain and example guided modes. Judges in Russian lagged their English form, with position and length biases in play. Still, machine rankings partly tracked human ones, suggesting the approach can improve with language specific care.
arxiv-2503-13502:
Yuxuan Liang and co-authors survey the push to build foundation models for data that moves through space and time, in a 2025 tutorial. Traffic flows, weather, and city sensors all produce spatio-temporal data, and older deep learning models handle one task at a time while demanding piles of labeled examples. Foundation models, proven in language, promise one adaptable system for many jobs.

The survey explains how such models could serve the whole pipeline, from sensing and storing data to mining it for forecasts and patterns. It sorts existing designs into families, compares how they learn from unlabeled streams, and marks where evidence is still thin. Open problems include scale, privacy, and trust in high-stakes forecasts. The authors chart research directions meant to carry these models from promising demos to dependable tools for cities and climate science.
arxiv-2503-13702:
Logan Becker, Francois Baccelli, and Thibaud Taillefumier asked whether faint synchrony explains the hidden stats of brain voltage in a 2025 paper. Neurons sharing a stimulus still fire variably, and their membrane voltages fluctuate far more than free-standing-input models predict. Earlier work showed weak synchrony among inputs could match the size of those fluctuations. This study tests the same idea against richer traits, how voltages in unlike cells move jointly and how lopsided the voltage spread is.

Borrowing fixed-point tools from queuing theory, the authors run a broad moment analysis of conductance-based neurons fed by correlated jump-like inputs. Weak but nonzero synchrony consistently reproduced the gauged covariance and skewness too. One mechanism accounts for three separate test facts.
arxiv-2503-14002:
Damian Boborzi and co-authors present MeshFleet, a cleaned and labeled set of 3D vehicle models for training image and shape generators, in work from 2025. Generative models for 3D objects have advanced fast, but engineering users need accuracy and control that raw models lack. Fine-tuning can close that gap, yet it demands high-quality domain data, and filtering such data by hand is slow. The team mines the huge Objaverse-XL collection for usable vehicle models.

Their pipeline filters the collection with a quality classifier trained on a hand-labeled subset. The classifier draws on two vision model embeddings, checks captions, and weighs its own uncertainty. The authors compare this filter with caption-based and beauty-score methods and find it works better. Fine-tuning a view-synthesis model on the cleaned set shows why careful selection matters for domain work.
arxiv-2503-14902:
Kiyoharu Kawana studies phases and travel of closed p-branes in an effective field theory with higher-form symmetries, in work from twenty twenty-five. A p-brane is an extended object that sweeps a higher-dimensional surface. Brane-field theory treats such objects through fields with broad symmetries. Past work lacked motion terms for both centre drift and inner ripples. Adding both terms creates a new light mode in the broken phase.

Phase structure grows richer with that added mode in place. With discrete symmetries, the low-energy theory becomes topological in form. It couples an axion-like scalar with a p-form gauge field. Plane-wave solutions and a path integral for brane travel follow. A Born-Oppenheimer view treats brane volume as fixed for the travel maths. The approximation itself breaks at the point limit, which flags quantumness.
arxiv-2503-15302:
The Euclid Collaboration presents its first quick data release in a 2025 overview paper. Euclid is a space telescope built to map the dark universe, and the Q1 release opens an early slice of its survey to the world ahead of the main releases. The paper describes what the release contains and how the data were produced.

Pipeline steps, calibration, and quality checks are laid out so outside astronomers can use the material with confidence. Hundreds of collaboration members across many institutes share the byline, reflecting the scale of the mission. Quick releases let the community test science ideas, hunt early discoveries, and feed problems back to the team while the survey continues. The overview serves as the release's official reference.
arxiv-2503-15402:
Alejandro Pequeño-Zurro and co-authors put a time-reading neuron to work spotting spoken digits. Keyword spotting on edge devices must sip power, so spiking networks appeal. Their neuron, the temporal difference encoder, reads gaps in instantaneous frequency and spike counts. The 2025 study feeds it the TIdigits corpus, split by formants into spike trains. Three networks with equal weight counts compete: the encoder feedforward, a standard spiking neuron feedforward, and a recurrent standard net.

Spike timing in the digit streams proves rich in information. The encoder network scores 89 percent accuracy, far above its feedforward rival at 71. It nearly matches the recurrent net's 91 while doing less work. Timing, the team shows, is data, not decoration.
arxiv-2503-15602:
Sarah Taft and co-authors measure the chemistry of a ring nebula around the binary star RY Scuti in a 2025 paper. The system is a massive pair of stars late in life, with one star spilling matter onto the other. It may be on its way to becoming a Wolf-Rayet star.

Infrared spectra from a flying observatory showed four glowing gas lines in the inner ring, three of them newly seen. Model fits gave the amounts of neon, sulfur, and iron in the gas. All three ran higher than in the sun, iron most of all. The pattern fits a star whose outer layers are being stripped away, leaving helium-rich matter behind.
arxiv-2503-15702:
Bryanne McDonough, Olivia Curtis, and Tereasa Brainerd argue that how astronomers fit a line can change the galaxy story they tell. Scaling relations tie a galaxy's star mass to its star formation and gas, locally and globally. Studies measure them with different samples, resolutions, and fitting habits, which muddies every comparison. The team tests the standard least-squares family against a ridge line method on simulated galaxies from the TNG100 run.

For three resolved relations, the ridge line approach, fitting a bent two-part line, clearly beat least squares. Probing one relation further, they found its low-mass slope stayed put when the images were blurred or rebinned, a relief for comparing surveys. The authors call for the field to refit published relations consistently, and to adopt the ridge line method on physical grounds rather than by habit.
arxiv-2503-15802:
Alyssa Jankowski and co-authors examine TOI-1937Ab, a very hot giant planet that circles its star in less than a day. Such ultra-short-period planets are rare, and how they arrived so close to their stars is still unclear. The host star sits in a wide binary pair, and three standard methods give three different ages for the system, which clouds its history.

Running models of how tides slowly change the orbit, and timing the planet's crossings in telescope data, the team finds the planet is likely spiraling inward as tides drain its orbit. They cap the decay rate with a firm upper limit. The age puzzle stays open, but the timing and tide results add indirect clues, and future data should pin the tidal behaviour down more tightly.
arxiv-2503-15902:
Jose Lara-Rangel and Clare Heinbaugh wrote this 2025 paper on sorting brain maps with graph transformers. A brain connectome maps how brain regions link to each other. New data sets turn these maps into graphs, and teams have tried deep learning to class them. The authors test whether transformer style graph models beat older graph networks on this task.

They ran the models on the NeuroGraph data sets and on noisy copies with edges cut at random. The transformers gave no clear gain over the older graph models. More striking, both kinds kept their scores even when all edges were cut. That hints the graph links may add little to the calls the models make. The authors urge better data sets and cleaner prep steps before strong claims are made.
arxiv-2503-16302:
Zeqiang Lai and co-authors presented FlashVDM in 2025, a way to make 3D shapes with a computer much faster. Their base method stores a shape as a set of vectors and then grows the shape step by step. It can make fine, sharp shapes, but it runs slowly. The slow parts are the step-by-step sampling and the final decode of the vector set into a full shape.

FlashVDM speeds up both parts. A training trick lets sampling finish in as few as five steps with like quality. A new decoder picks only the key data it needs and works the shape volume in layers. Set into a known shape system, the new build ran more than forty-five times faster on rebuild tasks and kept top-level quality.
arxiv-2503-16402:
Yifan Sun and co-authors present a 2025 paper that tests whether fixes for a known flaw in language model exams really work. If exam questions leak into a model's training data, scores swell and stop being trustworthy. Fixes rewrite old questions or make new ones in the same style, but their worth had not been checked in a strict way.

The team built a controlled test pipeline and two new scores. One score checks whether per-question results still match the clean exam, and the other checks how well a fix resists leaks. Trials with ten models and five exams gave a fine-grained view. The work gives exam makers a firmer way to judge fixes.
arxiv-2503-16502:
Birger Moell reports a small study of a chatbot built to act as a clinical psychologist, in work published in 2025. The bot was made on the Character.ai platform and was meant to talk with users about mental health in a warm, human-like way. The project itself was finished in November 2022, just before ChatGPT came out.

Twenty-seven people, among them psychologists, AI researchers, and members of the public, chatted with the bot and rated the talks. Many found it engaging and somewhat human-like. They also noted weak spots in empathy and in grasping subtle feelings. Moell concludes that chatbots of this kind are still far from the broad skill linked to artificial general intelligence, and points to paths for later work.
arxiv-2503-16602:
Particle collider measurements mix physics from many distance scales at once. Christian Bauer explains in 2025 how theory already splits those scales apart. Short-distance effects can be computed with standard tools. Long-distance effects resist those tools and are usually borrowed from one measurement to predict another. That borrowing works only when the long-distance part stays the same across measurements.

Bauer argues that quantum computers will change the picture. Once they can compute the stubborn long-distance pieces from first principles, physicists could predict measurements whose long-distance parts are not shared. That would widen the hunt for new physics, since more collider results could be compared cleanly against the standard theory.
arxiv-2503-17102:
Thomas Schnappinger and Markus Kowalewski work out how a molecule's response to electric fields changes inside an optical cavity in a 2025 study. When molecular vibrations couple firmly to trapped light, chemistry itself can shift, a field called polaritonic chemistry. Whether the collective coupling reaches down and changes each single molecule's traits is still unsettled.

The authors derive a closed formula for static polarizability under vibrational strong coupling, inside linear response theory. Polarizability gauges how easily the electron cloud deforms, a basic ingredient of reactivity. A clean formula gives the field a testable handle on the local-versus-collective debate.
arxiv-2503-17302:
John Naulty and co-authors build an AI code reviewer in 2025 that hunts security flaws inside GitHub pull requests. Hand audits are slow and dear, while older auto tools cry wolf so often that teams tune them out. Their system, Bugdar, aims for near real-time, project-aware feedback at the moment code is proposed.

Language models tuned for the task, fed with project documents, shape the reviews to each codebase's habits. It reads several languages, from Python and Rust to two blockchain tongues. Speed averaged under a minute per request, far below the hours a hand review can take, they report. Catching flaws at proposal time, not after release, shifts security from a gate to a habit.
arxiv-2503-17402:
Oscar Cruz-González, Valérie Deplano, and Badih Ghattas speed up blood flow simulation in a 2025 paper. Aneurysms in the belly aorta need flow forecasts, but scans read flow poorly and classic simulation runs slow. Patient boundary data are also hard to get. The team tests learning based solvers that fold physics rules into neural networks, plus operator networks that learn solution maps whole.

Three model types faced a standard three dimensional aneurysm shape. Physics informed versions blend measured data with flow laws, which can cut the data each forecast needs. Faster, lighter forecasts could bring flow checks into routine planning for aneurysm repair. The comparison shows which learning route holds accuracy best for vessel flow.
arxiv-2503-17502:
Hamed Jelodar, Mohammad Meymani, and Roozbeh Razavi-Far survey how large language models are being used to analyse computer source code, in a 2025 paper. As software grows more tangled, teams lean on AI to read, summarise, and check code. The authors set out to map this young field: what tasks the models tackle, which models get used, and which datasets feed the work. They reviewed the scholarly literature to find its shape and trends.

The survey pulls together the main applications, from fault finding to code explanation, and the tools that support them. It also lists the limits that keep coming up, such as shaky reasoning about program behaviour and scarce labelled data. For researchers entering the area, the paper offers a compact atlas: where the crowds are working, what they use, and which problems remain open.
arxiv-2503-17602:
Injae Shin and Blaise Tine tackle a memory bottleneck in graphics processors, in a 2025 paper. As chips gain more cores and threads, they can do more work than the memory system can feed.

The authors extend Vortex, an open graphics processor design, so its caches can use many memory ports at once. The change runs from the first cache level down to the last. They also test several rules for deciding which request uses a port when requests compete. With eight ports, the design ran tasks more than twice as fast on average. The extra hardware cost stayed small, which makes the approach attractive for future chips.
arxiv-2503-17802:
Alexander Armbruster and co-authors settle how well a scheduling problem with time windows can be approximated. Tasks bid for a resource whose supply varies along a path over time. Each task brings a demand, a profit, a fixed runtime, and a window it must fit inside. The goal is the most profitable feasible schedule, with no task split. Without time windows, the sibling problem recently gained a near-perfect approximation scheme. Windows change everything.

The team proves the windowed version is APX-hard, ruling out such a scheme. Even identical windows stay hard. With resource augmentation, extra supply to lean on, a quasi-polynomial algorithm reaches within a small factor of optimal. Identical windows tighten the guarantee further. The paper draws the exact line where windows defeat approximation.
arxiv-2503-18002:
Steven Abreu and co-authors run language models on a brain-like chip in a 2025 paper. Big models burn vast power on stock gear. Intel's Loihi 2 chip works by spikes, with low-bit math and state held on chip. Their build drops matrix multiplication from the model frame. A 370-million-part model, shrunk to low bits on GPU, lost no score in tests.

Early chip reads claim up to three times the flow at half the power of an edge GPU. Scale climbs in their favor as models grow. More chip craft should widen the gap, they say. The aim is long text at low cost on small gear. Brain-form chips may host that path.
arxiv-2503-18102:
Samuel Schmidgall and Michael Moor let AI research labs share work through AgentRxiv in this 2025 paper. Science advances by many groups building on each other, not by lone breakthroughs. AI agents usually research in isolation, though. Their shared preprint server lets agent labs post and fetch reports.

Labs tasked with inventing reasoning tricks improved more with archive access. Gains reached 11.4 percent relative on a hard math benchmark over baseline. The best strategy also transferred to other domains. Several labs sharing one archive beat isolated labs by 13.7 percent relative. Collaboration, the old human trick, works for agents too. Shared memory may matter as much as raw model power.
arxiv-2503-18302:
Qingyue Long and co-authors present DiffMove, a method to fill gaps in movement trajectories. Their 2025 paper deals with location data that are sparse because devices record rarely or cover only part of a city. Sparse paths make a person's own history too thin to guide good reconstruction.

DiffMove borrows strength from the crowd: a graph built from all users' paths captures group movement trends. Those trends are blended into each location's features through graph embedding. The method also reads a user's habits from both past paths and the current one. A diffusion model then rebuilds the missing points. Tests on two real data sets beat prior methods.
arxiv-2503-18502:
Andres Garcia-Silva and Jose Manuel Gomez-Perez test small fine-tuned language models for filling knowledge bases, in this 2025 paper. Keeping a knowledge base current by hand is slow. Their test bed is a knowledge graph of space missions.

Long context windows in modern models allow an end-to-end setup: text goes in, graph facts come out. Training data was built from existing domain resources. The fine-tuned small models matched or beat much larger models on the task. They also deploy cheaply and need no schema pasted into the prompt, leaving room for more input text. The authors back specialist small models for such chores.
arxiv-2503-19302:
Yunuo Zhang, Baiting Luo, Ayan Mukhopadhyay, and Abhishek Dubey improve decision making under uncertainty in this 2025 paper. Their setting is the POMDP, a standard model for acting when the true state is hidden and only partial observations arrive.

Online solvers track a belief about the state with particle filters, but a sharp new observation can wreck the particle set, leaving it poor and repetitive. The authors build a bridge of distributions between the predicted state and the ideal one, crossed in small Monte Carlo steps. Their method beat leading alternatives in tests across settings. Better belief tracking means safer plans for robots and systems that must act on noisy data.
arxiv-2503-19502:
El Nino swings Pacific temperatures and rearranges weather worldwide, yet forecasting it beyond a year has stayed hard. Qi Chen and co-authors build a deep learning model that looks twenty months ahead. Their network, CTEFNet, blends convolutional layers with transformers. It feeds on many ocean and air signals at once. The design beats both physics-based models and earlier learning systems, and it softens the notorious spring barrier that blinds forecasts.

The model also explains itself. Sensitivity analysis shows which early signals drive its predictions. The answers match established theory and add new hints about how the Atlantic and Indian oceans nudge the Pacific. Skill plus explanation is a rare pairing in climate AI. The authors argue both are needed before forecasters can trust a black box with a planet-scale call.
arxiv-2503-19602:
Yuyao Ge and co-authors test whether prompting still helps models that are trained to reason at length. Their 2025 paper studies reasoning language models, which think step by step with reflection and self-correction. A natural question is whether chain-of-thought prompts, a standard trick for chat models, add anything for these systems.

The team compared no prompt, a zero-shot prompt, and few-shot prompts across math tasks and model sizes from one point five to thirty-two billion parameters. Prompting helped in most settings. Large models gained most on hard problems, while small models showed the reverse pattern. Prompting also cut excess reflection sharply in some cases, by about ninety percent. Attention analysis adds detail on why.
arxiv-2503-19702:
Abdulhamid Abubakar and co-authors report their entry in a 2025 shared translation contest in a paper from the HausaNLP team. The task, part of SemEval 2025, asks systems to translate English sentences into ten other languages with special care for named entities. Names of people, places, and groups often break in machine translation, since a name must be carried across, not translated word by word.

The team tried two routes. One fine-tunes a model with entity awareness built into training. The other leans on prompt design, steering a general model with careful instructions. They describe each system they built, give their scores, and share what the trials taught them. The contest setting lets the two routes be judged on the same sentences, a clean test for a common failure.
arxiv-2503-20002:
Tristan Smith and Nils Schoneberg compute, in a 2025 paper, what several proposed fixes to the Hubble tension would do to the faintest ripples in the cosmic microwave background. The tension is stark: the expansion rate read from the early universe disagrees with the local distance ladder value at about six sigma. Proposed early universe mechanisms could reconcile the two.

Those mechanisms should also leave fingerprints at the smallest angular scales, in the damping tail where the ripples fade. Using current microwave, galaxy, and supernova data as the baseline, the authors predict the small scale power spectra for a characteristic set of models. Near future data should separate some of these models from the standard one, they find, but not all. The damping tail thus becomes a testing ground: the same sky that raised the tension may soon judge its would be solutions.
arxiv-2503-20102:
Chang Chen and co-authors tackle long-horizon planning for AI agents in a 2025 paper. Diffusion-based planners learn from sample paths and steer well over short stretches, but they falter when a task needs a path far longer than any seen in training. Longer training paths, in turn, make the models worse, a bind the authors name and set out to break.

Their answer comes in two phases. First, a stitching process builds longer paths step by step from short ones, round by round. Second, a planner that reasons across several time scales learns and acts on those long paths. Extra tricks fold the whole ladder of scales into a single model, so no fleet of planners is needed. Experiments showed strong gains, pointing to planning that scales without losing its footing.
arxiv-2503-20302:
Sitaram and co-authors develop ways to stop language models from misgendering people in forty-two languages and dialects, in a 2025 paper. English fixes such as the pronoun 'they' do not transfer: grammar and culture shape gender reference differently across languages. The team used participatory design, involving speakers in shaping guardrails suited to each language.

They tested the guardrails in a meeting-summary application, with data generation and labeling both kept human-checked. Misgendering in the summaries dropped sharply across all languages, with no loss of summary quality. The guardrails and a synthetic dataset are released publicly to support further work.
arxiv-2503-21202:
Antos Cheeramban Varghese and Anamitra Pal fix two linked measurement problems for power grids, in a 2025 paper. Grids rely on instrument transformers to report voltage and current, and uncalibrated ones quietly corrupt every reading downstream. Knowing each line's electrical traits matters just as much — and each problem needs the other's answer.

Their statistical method solves both at once from phasor measurement data, the grid's high-speed synchronized readings. It anchors the system with one high-grade meter, pricey but not assumed perfect, and allows line traits to drift as they do in life. Tests on a standard 118-bus model and on real grid data showed high accuracy. Trustworthy readings underpin every control and protection decision a grid makes.
arxiv-2503-21602:
Karime Maamari, Connor Landy, and Amine Mhedhbi build a business question answerer that learns from corrections in a 2025 paper. Turning plain questions into database queries works in demos but strains in companies, where terms are local, queries are tangled, and users expect the system to improve. Their system, GenEdit, keeps a company knowledge set at its center.

Generation runs as a chain of operators: past queries are split into parts to find good examples. Instructions and schema pieces are fetched, and a plain-language plan is drafted before the query itself is written, with error-driven retries. When users flag mistakes, a copilot proposes edits to the knowledge set, so fixes compound instead of vanishing. The design treats feedback as the main engine of quality.
arxiv-2503-21702:
Yoav Rotman and co-authors add, in a 2025 paper, a flexible noise catcher to the tools that read exoplanet atmospheres from their light. Retrieval methods infer a planet's gases and heat profile from spectra, and the Webb telescope now delivers spectra of fine detail. The risk is bias: unmodeled features or correlated noise can quietly bend the answer.

Their framework bolts a Gaussian process onto the retrieval, a statistical layer that soaks up structure the physics model misses. On synthetic Webb observations, the aided runs cut the bias in inferred gas amounts and matched the data's quirks better than plain runs. The authors also weigh the bargain openly, since soaking up signal can hide real features. The aim is retrieval results that scientists can trust.
arxiv-2503-21902:
Hamed Babaei Giglou and three co-authors present OntoAligner, a 2025 Python toolkit for aligning ontologies. Ontologies are structured maps of concepts, and matching them across systems is key to making data interoperable. Existing tools struggle with scale, rigid design, and links to modern AI methods.

The toolkit has a modular design that accepts custom algorithms and datasets with little code. It includes light matching methods such as fuzzy matching, plus newer routes using retrieval augmented generation and large language models. Benchmarks on standard tasks show it handles large ontologies efficiently while keeping alignment quality high. The authors release it as open source. They aim to support reproducible research and real world data integration work.
arxiv-2503-22002:
Stephanie Schoch and Yangfeng Ji develop a Monte Carlo sampling method to analyze in-context examples for large language models. Their 2025 paper deals with a known brittleness: learning from examples in the prompt depends on order, number, and choice of examples.

Ablation studies that vary one factor can miss how the factors interact. Their sampling method varies the number of examples while accounting for order and selection at the same time. Past guidance on how many examples to pick did not always generalize across sets and orderings. Whether one example beats none depended heavily on which example was chosen. They also apply the method to select examples, with a negative result.
arxiv-2503-22102:
Mizuyama and Dieu Thuy analyze resonance states in the oxygen sixteen nucleus in a 2025 paper. Resonances are short lived excited states that shape how a nucleus responds when struck. The authors use a framework that combines a Jost function approach with a random phase model of collective motion.

By applying a classic theorem that splits a response into pole parts, they isolate what each resonance pole adds to the total strength. That split clarifies which poles dominate the giant dipole resonance and the quadrupole resonances. The authors offer the method as a new lens on collective excitation in nuclei with complex correlations.
arxiv-2503-22302:
Mikhail Cherkasskii and co-authors present a theoretical physics paper, published in 2025, on pumping sound waves with magnetism in a two layer material. One layer is ferromagnetic and the other is not, and their coupled waves mix magnons, the waves of magnetization, with phonons, the waves of vibration. The twist is a slight misalignment between the magnetic axes and the crystal axes.

The model solves the linked motion of the uniform magnetic mode and elastic waves in both layers, with the rules at the shared boundary included. Even a small misalignment splits two sound modes so they travel at different speeds. The magnetic field also tunes how polarization passes between sound waves and the magnetic mode, matching recent experiments.
arxiv-2503-22402:
Yizhang Zhu, Runzhi Jiang, Boyan Li, Nan Tang, and Yuyu Luo present EllieSQL, a cost-efficient text-to-SQL system with complexity-aware routing. Their 2025 paper deals with the high computational cost of large language model approaches to this task.

Text-to-SQL turns natural language questions into SQL, so non-technical users can query databases. Leaderboard scores are high, but the cost of reaching them is often ignored, which limits real use. EllieSQL estimates the complexity of each query and routes it to a suitable generation pipeline. Simple queries go to efficient methods, and hard ones to intensive ones. A new metric, token elasticity of performance, quantifies cost-efficiency.
arxiv-2503-22502:
Alif Aqsha, Philippe Bergault, and Leandro Sánchez-Betancourt work out what reward contract an automated market maker should offer the traders who stock its pools. These venues rely on liquidity providers, whose funds let others trade. The authors model the venue as leader and a typical provider as follower in a stochastic game. The venue wants maximum order flow while keeping providers willing to stay.
