They derive near closed-form solutions for the balanced contract and study its shape. Under it, providers add funds only when deeper pools draw in more noise trading on average. The reward depends on the outside market price, the pool's own reference price, and its reserves. The framework offers design guidance for venues balancing flow against provider profit.
arxiv-2503-22902:
Barisha Chowdhury and co-authors study how software projects in the Maven system keep their building blocks up to date, in a paper from 2025. Modern programs reuse many shared libraries, called dependencies. Out of date parts can hurt stability and safety, yet tracking releases across linked libraries is hard work for maintainers.

Using a data set drawn from a large graph database project, the team measured how fresh the parts in each release were. Projects with fewer parts had more missed releases, a result that cuts against first guesses. The newest releases, though, showed parts with good freshness scores. The authors argue that such measures can push teams toward steadier upkeep and a healthier shared software base.
arxiv-2503-23102:
Beibei Li presents a transformer framework to forecast geomagnetic storms in work from 2025. Accurate forecasts of the planetary Kp index matter for protecting satellites and power systems from space weather.

The multimodal model joins satellite measurements, solar images, and past Kp series to predict three and five days ahead. A key idea uses the Wasserstein distance inside the model and its loss to align distributions across data types. Against the standard NOAA model, the system captured both quiet and storm phases well. The author argues machine learning can improve real-time space weather forecasts.
arxiv-2503-23202:
Svitlana Mayboroda and David Spergel present a way in 2025 to measure the fractal dimension of tangled structures from flat images. Many natural patterns are fractal, filling space in a fractional way between a line and a plane. When such a pattern is seen only in projection, like through a telescope, the true dimension is hard to recover.

Their method uses wavelets, small wave packets that sort a picture by scale. Under a fair-view assumption, the wavelet spectrum of the shadow follows a clean power law set by the true dimension, whatever the viewing angle. They applied it to a nearby exploded star. Its layers ranged from dimension near one point seven for cool gas to two point five for hot X-ray gas.
arxiv-2503-23302:
Guang-Wei Mi and co-authors derive an exact formula for true four-party quantum nonlocality and test how black holes warp it. Their 2025 paper starts with a general score for any four-qubit state. Nonlocality of this kind is a core resource for quantum information work.

The team then places the state near a standard black hole and near one wrapped in a universe with dark energy. Hawking heat eats away at the share of nonlocality that outside observers can reach. The hidden share behind the horizon shifts both ways, and for fermion fields the black hole can even create fresh hidden nonlocality. The authors read that as nonlocality passing through the horizon itself.
arxiv-2503-23802:
A team of Indian mathematicians studies a pebbling conjecture on a special graph construction in this 2025 paper. Pebbling is a game of moving tokens on a network's points. A move removes two pebbles from one point and places one next door. The pebbling number is the smallest pile that guarantees delivery to any target. Asking for many pebbles at the target defines a harder version. Herscovici's conjecture concerns that harder version's behavior.

The paper computes these numbers for total graphs. A total graph encodes both points and links of the original as playable spots. It also checks the doubled-target property the conjecture needs. Such results test a general claim on one graph family at a time. The work is pure combinatorics. It adds one more verified family to the conjecture's record.
arxiv-2504-00002:
Xiao Yan and Yi Ding measure how well large language models run on mobile devices, in a study from two thousand twenty-five. Running models on the phone itself would allow new apps without cloud access. But phones have tight limits on memory, power, and speed.

The authors built a simplified app that reads phone sensor data to infer location and activity. They compared phone, edge, and cloud setups for speed and quality. Only small models ran on strong phones, and with weaker output. Compression cut hardware needs but often hurt performance. Phone runs took over thirty seconds for useful output, while cloud took under ten. Edge setups fell in between. The study maps current limits for designers.
arxiv-2504-00202:
Dionysios Kokkinos sets out a route to broad solutions of Einstein equations, in work from 2025. Canonical Killing tensor forms classify spacetimes that hide extra conserved quantities. Past work with those forms yielded vacuum solutions of several special algebraic types.

One family built on two curved two dimensional spaces gets full detail here. A broader solution shares the exact same non zero spin values as that family. A second broad case adds time change and cylinder symmetry under a Lorentz twist. Both cases hold vacuum with a cosmological constant in the field laws. The stated directive invites wider searches on this Killing form recipe.
arxiv-2504-00302:
Pooya Ashtari and six co-authors build a new network for drawing exact borders around organs and tumors in medical scans. Known designs have weak spots: some see only small patches at a time, while others cost too much to run. Their 2025 design, Deconver, puts an old image repair trick at the core of a U-shaped network.

The repair step restores fine detail while it cuts noise, and it swaps out costly focus steps used by rival designs. Tests ran on four scan sets, in both flat and 3D tasks. The network topped rivals on overlap and border scores while using far less compute. The team frames it as a fit for clinics with tight budgets.
arxiv-2504-00502:
Nine authors present ShortV in 2025, a no-train trick that speeds large mixed models. Such models burn cost on size and on swarms of sight tokens in the stack. A new gauge, Layer Contribution, scores how much each layer moves sight and text tokens.

Tests show many layers add near nil to sight token work in the stack. ShortV locks sight token steps in those weak layers and skips the cost. On one big model, flop cost fell by half with top marks kept. Near 60 percent of layers can lock.
arxiv-2504-00602:
Federica Adobbati and Łukasz Mikulski modeled groups of agents that act without a shared clock, in a 2025 paper built on Petri nets. Modeling how parts interact is the first step to checking that a multi-agent system behaves. Earlier work set out two meanings for such systems as state machines.

The pair give a way to build the nets for both meanings, one where agents sync on actions and one where they sync on data. They prove how the joined net matches the global state machine in each case. They also show how to switch a net from one meaning to the other. That switch lets analysts pick the model that fits the trait they want to check. The results tie two lines of theory into one toolkit.
arxiv-2504-00802:
Distant clocks must agree to the picosecond for modern networks. Quantum physics can certify that the timing signal was not faked. Mohammed Alqedra and co-authors sent entangled photon pairs from a quantum dot source through Stockholm's city fiber. The pairs' tight timing correlation synchronized the network with accuracy in the tens of picoseconds.

They also ran full state tomography at the far end, verifying the entanglement itself. Fidelity came out near zero point eight two to the ideal state. Verified entanglement turns a clock signal into a tamper-evident one, a foundation for secure time and key distribution.
arxiv-2504-00902:
A large collaboration presents this 2025 study that ranks 22 exploding stars to find the best one of the set. The ranking uses a playful mix of hard measures and odd ones. It is a light hearted take on how scientists score and compare rare events.

Each star is graded on three points. The first is blast energy, read from light curves and spectra. The second is a beauty score for the star's home galaxy after a picture tool turned it into a human face. The third is the pick of an infant judge, six months old, shown star images many times. The top five stars scored high on energy and on the face test.
arxiv-2504-01102:
Suchitra Narayanan and co-authors measure how a sulfur-bearing molecule behaves in space ice, in this 2025 paper. Methyl mercaptan may carry much of the sulfur between stars and feeds early chemistry. Whether it sits in gas or ice depends on how hard it clings and how it escapes on warming. The team compared its release from pure ice, water ice, and a water and carbon dioxide mix.

Its grip strength in pure and layered forms came out nearly the same, setting a snow line near one hundred five kelvin. Mixed with water, all of it stayed trapped until the water ice cracked open in a volcano-like release. Its presence also trapped carbon dioxide and methanol far better. Being bulkier than methanol, it binds water worse, the authors argue.
arxiv-2504-01202:
Sayera Dhaubhadel and co-authors explain, at global scale, why a cancer report classifier abstains so often. Their 2025 paper studies a deep network that labels pathology reports for national cancer registries across site, subtype, tissue type, side, and behavior at once. The model may refuse hard cases to hold accuracy.

Demanding ninety-seven percent accuracy on tissue type leaves the model keeping only about a fifth of reports. Local explanations for thousands of calls are pooled and compressed. Four error sources emerge: layered class complexity, label noise, thin information, and clashing evidence. Fixes follow, like exclusion rules, targeted re-annotation, and softer penalties for near-miss classes. Training used over a million hand-labeled reports. The method turns abstention from a nuisance into a diagnostic map.
arxiv-2504-01302:
Han Wang and six co-authors build GLaD, a graphics-chip tool that models both the bend of light by a galaxy and the motion of its stars, in one frame. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five.

The lag of light from a lensed quasar gives a clean gauge of how fast the cosmos grows. But a warp in lens models adds doubt to that gauge. Star motion gives a free check on the mass that bends the light. The team joins both in one code that runs on graphics chips. On fake data for a known lensed quasar, fine motion data pin the growth rate to a few parts in a hundred. They test what a giant black hole does to that mark.
arxiv-2504-01402:
Yunfan Zeng, Guangyan Cai, and Shuang Zhao present a 2025 survey of physics based differentiable rendering, a technique now central to computer graphics and vision. Normal rendering turns a scene description into an image. The differentiable kind also reports how the image would change if any scene parameter moved, which lets optimizers work backward from a photo to the scene.

The survey gathers the field's recent progress in one place. It covers new theory for the general problem, better sampling methods for the random ray tracing at its core, and speedups that make the computations practical. Applications in solving inverse rendering tasks run through the review as motivation.
arxiv-2504-01502:
Jeremías Aguilera Damia and co-authors build a dictionary between two distant subjects: variants of supersymmetric gauge theories and classical many-body systems that can be solved exactly. A gauge theory's global variant is fixed by which line-like probes it allows, a choice with real consequences when space includes a circle.

The theories studied are closely tied to Calogero-Moser systems, models of particles pushing on each other with special forces, in a twisted elliptic form. The authors show, on general grounds, how the gauge theory's line data reappears on the particle side, and they define global variants for the particle systems to match. Working through two families of examples, they spell out what the choice does to the pattern of empty states, the symmetries each state displays, and a broken modular symmetry. The paper is theoretical and aimed at mathematical physicists.
arxiv-2504-01902:
Célia Nouri, Jean-Philippe Cointet, and Chloé Clavel work on spotting abuse in social media talk in this 2025 paper. A comment that looks harmless alone can be abusive in context, and most detection tools ignore the thread around it. The authors argue that the shape of a conversation carries much of the signal.

Their method turns each conversation into a graph, with comments as nodes and replies as links. They test several graph layouts and context windows to find the setup that works best. The graph model beat both tools that ignore context and simpler tools that read the thread as a line. Scores rose by a clear margin. The results show that structured context makes abuse detection more reliable.
arxiv-2504-02002:
Davood Momeni and Ratbay Myrzakulov review a family of gravity theories in a 2025 paper. The theories, named for Myrzakulov, change Einstein's picture by letting space twist and stretch in new ways. Supporters hope such changes can explain cosmic puzzles without adding dark matter or dark energy.

The review covers the basic ideas, the main equations, and the leading models in the family. It then turns to uses in cosmology, black holes, and waves in space itself. Tests from cosmic data and wave events are used to limit which versions still fit what we see. The authors place the theories among other changed-gravity ideas and weigh their chance of reshaping basic physics.
arxiv-2504-02402:
Hao Yin and co-authors recover sound without touching the source, using an event camera, in a 2025 paper. Sound waves make objects vibrate, and those tiny vibrations show up as subtle visual changes. Filming them can reconstruct the sound, but older setups trade off speed, range, and field of view.

Event cameras report only changes, pixel by pixel, at very high speed, which suits vibration capture. Their system, EvMic, models space and time jointly to pull clean audio from the event stream. Such recovery could let a camera act as a microphone across a room or through glass. The work also raises clear privacy questions, which the authors' community continues to debate.
arxiv-2504-02702:
Yu Cheng and Shuailiang Ge study axion forces in this two thousand twenty-five physics paper. Axions are light particles proposed as a form of dark matter. They could also carry a faint force between nucleons, the particles in atomic nuclei. The authors ask how a sea of axion dark matter around us changes that force. In empty space the force fades fast with distance.

With the dark matter background in place, they find the force fades far more slowly. Its strength also grows with the number of axion particles nearby. These boosts sharpen the limits that fifth-force tests can set on axion traits. Bench tests like torsion balances may thus probe axions better than once thought. The paper adds a fresh angle to the hunt for dark matter.
arxiv-2504-02802:
Manas Debnath, Lata Thakur, and Najmul Haque compute how a heavy quark pair binds inside a lopsided, colliding quark-gluon plasma. Such plasmas form in heavy ion collisions and squeeze quarkonium states apart. The team built collisions and momentum anisotropy into the medium's dielectric response using kinetic theory. Real and imaginary parts of the potential come from different gluon propagators, one retarded, one symmetric.

Collisions barely moved the real part, so binding energy is safe. Anisotropy alone can blow up the imaginary part through a Weibel pinch, but a strong enough collision rate tames the singularity. In that regime collisions fatten the imaginary part, widening quarkonium decay.
arxiv-2504-02902:
Liangjie Huang, Dawei Li, Huan Liu, and Lu Cheng study confidence in self-improving language models in a 2025 paper. Models can revise their own answers through self-feedback and gain accuracy. That loop may also breed self-bias and inflated confidence in wrong answers.

The team test three self-improvement styles: plain prompting, step-by-step prompting, and tuning-based revision. Across rounds, a standard calibration error grew steadily, showing rising overconfidence. Accuracy at high confidence fell at the same time. The authors then try calibration fixes applied before, after, or during the loop. Their results argue that accuracy gains mean little if a model cannot judge its own certainty.
arxiv-2504-03002:
Feiran Yang speeds up private joint learning in this 2025 paper. In federated learning, many devices train one shared model without handing over their private data. Each device trains locally and sends only updates to a central server. Homomorphic encryption, which lets servers compute on locked data, protects those updates, but it is slow and heavy, above all for large models.

Yang's algorithm encrypts only selected parameters, guided by sensitivity maps showing which values need the most protection, and adds differential privacy noise. He proves the method correct and robust, codes it in C++, and simulates federated training on large models. The result runs three times faster than the best known method while keeping privacy strong.
arxiv-2504-03602:
Kai Lascheit and co-authors fit a digital human body to noisy 3D point clouds with the help of body part labels, in a paper from 2025. Matching a mesh to a scan is key for augmented reality and robots that work near people. Real scans carry noise and clutter, which often throw the fit off.

Their method first labels each point by body part. Those labels guide a two-step fit of the SMPL-X body model, starting from part centers for pose, then refining the whole match. The fitted mesh can then clean up the labels, lifting segmentation scores too. On three messy real data sets, InterCap, EgoBody, and BEHAVE, the method beat prior work on both pose and segmentation.
arxiv-2504-03902:
John Paisley, Ghazal Fazelnia, and Brian Barr published a computing paper in 2025 on tuning a popular learning method called stochastic variational inference. The method can be read as a form of annealing, a slow cooling that helps escape poor answers. Batch size controls the noise: bigger batches give cleaner signals but less escape power. The team wanted both benefits at once.

Their fix sets a real batch size for data accuracy and an effective size that restores the wanted noise level. Theory supports the approach for a broad model family. Tests on a recommendation model, a topic model, and a mixture model show the method works in practice. The authors call it SVI plus.
arxiv-2504-04102:
Dan Li and co-authors simulate the shadows cast by three black holes sitting in balance, in a 2025 paper. A black hole's shadow is the dark patch its gravity stamps on glowing gas behind it. With three holes of equal mass held still, the light paths tangle. The team traced rays across a wide span of spacings to draw the view.

The picture mixes one big main shadow with smaller bent ones shaped like eyebrows. The edges of all of them repeat their pattern at finer and finer scales, a fractal born of photons scattering in chaos. At some spacings, clean rings appear, their width set by the gaps between holes. Draw the holes close, and the shadows merge into one plain disk. A tight trio can thus masquerade as a single giant hole.
arxiv-2504-04202:
Harvey Dam and co-authors report a machine learning study, published in 2025, on training autoencoders to rebuild data more faithfully. Autoencoders squeeze data into a small latent code and then expand it again. Most training uses mean squared error, which checks each point alone and can miss whether nearby points keep their local order.

The team adds a new helper loss called finite-difference sign error, which punishes cases where the rebuilt data rises or falls in the wrong direction next to its neighbors. Across four test tasks, mixing this loss with the usual one cut error by a large margin. Gains were strongest for smooth spatial fields, while the helper loss alone did poorly.
arxiv-2504-04302:
Bellamkonda, Bharani, and Selvam speed up a classic pathfinding algorithm with a custom infinity object, in a 2025 computing paper. Dijkstra's algorithm finds shortest routes through a network and starts every distance at infinity. In Python, that infinity is a float, and repeated float handling costs time. Their object, AbsInf, is a small C extension that stands for infinity directly, skipping float conversion and type checks.

Swapping it in left the algorithm's logic untouched. Runtime fell by up to 17.2 percent, averaging 9.74 percent across synthetic and real-world graphs. Comparisons with the object are constant-time, and arithmetic leaves other values neutral, as infinity should. The authors frame the trick as a case study in shaving hot spots inside interpreted languages.
arxiv-2504-04502:
Jalalzadeh and co-authors wrote a 2025 study of cosmic singularities in a brane gravity frame called Covariant Extrinsic Gravity. Singularities are points where the usual laws break down, at the birth of the universe or perhaps in its future. The work uses a four-dimensional brane set in a wider space.

The authors test whether a still, non-singular start state can hold firm under small shocks of all kinds. For set ranges of the inputs, it does hold, which offers a way past the Big Bang problem. The team then sorts the kinds of future singularities and states the terms under which each one forms or is avoided.
arxiv-2504-04702:
Bo Chen and three co-authors prove a hard limit on how language models learn a basic logic rule. The rule is majority vote: given a string of bits, say which value fills more than half the slots. Models can in form state this rule, since their class can hold such gates. The open point is whether training by gradient steps, the standard method, can teach it from samples.

Tests used a lean form of the transformer model, the base design of most language tools. Sample counts ranged from modest to vast in the input size. Even after a vast count of gradient steps, the error on fresh inputs stayed large and grew fast with input size. The proof pins the flaw on the training path, not the model shape. It warns that fluent speech can hide weak logic skill.
arxiv-2504-04902:
Lorenzo Notaro proves a rigidity result about number-like degrees in a special set theory model, in work from 2025. The model is built by forcing with many copies of one classic forcing side by side. Degrees here rank how hard it is to construct one real number from another.

These degrees form a join structure, where pairs have a least common upper degree. Notaro shows that structure admits no nontrivial symmetries. In other words, its only self-mapping that preserves joins is the identity. The proof works over the constructible universe as the base. Set theorists use such rigidity to map how wild these degree structures can be.
arxiv-2504-05002:
Jiuyang Bu and four co-authors detect vulnerabilities in smart contract bytecode with a BERT enhanced method called SmartBugBert. Contracts on blockchain platforms carry security flaws, yet few Ethereum contracts publish source code. Detection must therefore work at the bytecode level, where meaning is harder to read.

Bytecode is decompiled into optimized opcode sequences, and semantic features come from term weighting. Control flow graphs capture execution logic, and vulnerable graph fragments are isolated for focused analysis. A fine tuned BERT model plus a gradient boosting classifier combine semantic and structural signals. On 6,157 contracts the system reaches about 91 percent F1 across four flaw types, order dependence, access control, self destruct, and timestamp dependence, at 0.14 seconds per contract.
arxiv-2504-05302:
Matthew Burgess and co-authors present a new class of materials called ionomeric extracellular matrices for tissue engineering. Standard engineered tissues often rely on drugs to spur repair. Electric and mechanical signals can also help cells grow, yet today's electroactive polymers lack the biochemical cues of real tissue scaffolds.

The team attached taurine, a sulfonic acid biomolecule, to collagen, a natural matrix protein. The result is a material made fully from matrix matter that can actuate electromechanically, giving controlled electrical and mechanical stimulation while keeping native-like cell contacts. The authors frame it as a base for dynamic, soft robotic devices across many tissue engineering uses.
arxiv-2504-05402:
Fonte Chavez, Esteves, and Hayet filled missing video frames in this paper from twenty twenty-five. Frame interpolation invents the in-between images that make motion smooth. Hand-drawn animation is the hard case, since timing swings far more than in live video. Their method builds on diffusion models that refine an image step by step.

The model takes the target moment as an explicit input and re-estimates it during training. A scheme borrowed from super-resolution work keeps the step count near ten. The random nature of diffusion also yields a per-pixel doubt map for each frame. Tests on animation beat leading models. The authors release the code openly.
arxiv-2504-05502:
Louis Richard and a large team study ion motion in Earth's magnetosheath in a 2025 paper. The magnetosheath is the turbulent zone of plasma behind the bow shock that guards Earth. In still plasma, ion speeds follow a classic bell pattern, but real plasma rarely stays still.

Using data from the Magnetospheric Multiscale mission, the team examined hundreds of thousands of ion distributions. Deviations from the classic pattern were widespread and often large. Turbulence strength and a plasma pressure measure shaped how complex the patterns grew. Curved magnetic fields scattered ions and smoothed the patterns. The work maps how turbulence and particle motion feed each other.
arxiv-2504-05702:
Jonathan Wright and three co-authors grade speech-to-text systems on poetry audio in a 2025 paper. The sound bank PennSound holds the world's largest set of poetry reads and talks, with wild swings in tape grade and voice style. Such range makes it a fair test field for text-from-speech tools.

Near ten hours were drawn at random and typed by trained hands as the truth set. Eight trade and open tools were scored on word slips and speaker splits. The top trade tool edged the field, and the top open one kept close when made-up text was dodged. Gaps were slim all round.
arxiv-2504-05902:
Weijun Li and co-authors propose a defense in 2025 against backdoor attacks on deep neural networks. In such an attack, a foe plants a hidden trigger in a model, so it acts badly only when the trigger shows. End users who get a trained model often lack the data or the knowledge to check it, which makes defense hard.

One cheap defense merges several like models into one, but it fades when few models are at hand. The new defense swaps parts between models to break the hidden shortcut that the trigger uses. The team first checks the idea on small two layer networks, in theory and in tests. They show the swaps push the backdoor's behavior further off course than plain merging does. A defense that works post training, with few spare models, would help users trust models they did not train.
arxiv-2504-06002:
Ioannis Gialamas, Alexandros Karam, Antonio Racioppi, and Martti Raidal ask whether new telescope data have detected quantum corrections to cosmic inflation in a 2025 paper. Inflation models tied to the Higgs field predict values for two key cosmic measures that fit older data well. New results from the Atacama Cosmology Telescope favor a higher value for one measure, creating tension.

The authors add one loop quantum corrections to a Higgs like inflation model without assuming what the inflaton is. The predicted measure shifts upward, easing the tension with the new data. The shift is larger in an alternative gravity formulation with a different field space structure. The work stresses quantum effects in early universe predictions.
arxiv-2504-06102:
Power grids need attack detectors, and detectors need realistic data to train on, which a 2025 arXiv paper by Eric Wagner and co-authors supplies. Their dataset, Sherlock, comes from a co-simulator of grid operations and covers three scenarios where attacks inject false commands or fake measurements into the process.

The need is not abstract: cyberattacks blacked out parts of Ukraine in 2015 and 2016, and Germany logged over 200 energy sector incidents in two recent years. The team ran five recent detection systems on the data and mapped where each one struggles. The dataset and its documentation are public.
arxiv-2504-06702:
Robert de Keijzer and three co-authors present an algorithm for arranging qubits on neutral atom machines in this two thousand twenty-five paper. In these machines, atoms are held by laser tweezers and can be placed in custom patterns. Where atoms sit sets how strongly they interact, which shapes the entanglement a quantum algorithm can use. Good layouts speed up tuning and ease a failure mode called barren plateaus.

Standard gradient methods fail here, because atom interactions blow up at short range. The team instead uses a consensus-based search that samples many layouts and steers the samples toward agreement. The chosen layout is tailored to each algorithm's problem. Their tests show the method finds adapted layouts that work well. The paper serves builders of neutral atom quantum hardware.
arxiv-2504-06902:
Nikolaos Stefanakos and co-authors extend a secure key-sharing method to three users in a 2025 paper. Quantum key distribution is the only proven way to share secret keys with security guaranteed by physics. Their variant is measurement-device independent, meaning the gear that reads the signals need not be trusted. Each of three users encodes bits in the phase of light pulses.

All three send pulses to a central unit of beam splitters and photon detectors. When the pulses arrive together and detection succeeds, at least one pair of users gains a shared key bit. The design grows a known two-user protocol to three. That growth comes at a price: a built-in error appears even when everyone follows the rules honestly. The authors analyze that trade-off in the paper.
arxiv-2504-07102:
Chendi Ge and eight co-authors let a computer design its own graph network for shop advice that crosses fields. A music app, say, may know a user well while a book shop knows the same user not at all. Graph networks can carry that knowledge across, but hand-built designs are slow to tune and often miss the mark. Past work also left which source acts help the target field unweighed.

Their frame searches for the best network shape per field with no retrain at each step. A second part grades how much each source act is worth for the target field, and learns that grade as it goes. Tests on shared sets and on a real ad set beat top past methods. The pair of tricks is claimed as a first for this task.
arxiv-2504-07602:
Heng-Sen Jiao and co-authors test how well future space detectors can read a peaked hum of gravitational waves, in a 2025 paper. The stochastic background from the early universe may carry a peak in the millihertz band, where space antennas will listen. Their framework fits peak-shaped templates to mock data and checks how faithfully the peak's height, place, and slopes come back.

Peak templates beat the standard broken power law at recovering slopes and peak position, by tenfold for a single peak. Plain Fourier data beat spectrogram data. Passing transient glitches, though, wreck the precision, again by about tenfold, worst for two peaks. The work readies analysis plans for the coming observatories.
arxiv-2504-08202:
Yu Fu and co-authors show, in a 2025 paper, that a language model's built-in knowledge quietly steers its answers more as the text it reads grows longer. Models built for very long inputs are prized for using what they are given. What they already know, stored in their weights, got less attention.

The team measured how that stored knowledge shapes output as context stretches. The influence grew with length, they found. Skill at recalling built-in knowledge did not rise alongside skill at retrieving from context. Worse, sharper retrieval could crowd out recall. Their simple remedy aims to restore balance. Long-document tools, from law to research, depend on both sources behaving.
arxiv-2504-08502:
Sebastian Carrillo Santana, a solo author, gives a general method in number theory in 2025. The goal is to show that a set of whole numbers holds endless members free of perfect powers. Past proofs leaned on how evenly such sets spread out.

Santana instead uses bounds on a wave-based transform of the set, plus a mild decay condition. The method then yields endless power-free members with no spread estimates. Uses include endless cube-free palindromes in large bases and square-free numbers whose reverse is also square-free. Missing-digit cases in several bases are covered as well.
arxiv-2504-08602:
Gesina Schwalbe and seven co-authors test whether post-hoc concept methods in computer vision pick up background bias, in work from 2025. Such methods find human concepts inside neural network latent spaces from example sets. Backgrounds are rarely controlled in training, so a method may lean on scene context, such as grass behind wild animals, instead of the animal itself.

Three Net2Vec-based methods were checked against background randomization tools, over more than 50 concepts, two datasets and seven network designs. The methods often captured background bias, with weak results on road scenes as a worrying case. Even cheap setups gave insight and better robustness, the authors report.
arxiv-2504-08802:
Johnson, Krishnaswamy, and Perlmutter improve a tool that reads signals on networks at several scales at once. The tool spreads a signal across a network step by step and records the pattern at each spread length, much like zooming out. Their 2025 paper notes that the spread lengths are usually picked by a fixed rule, doubling each time, with no regard for the data at hand.

The authors propose picking those lengths by how much new information each one adds, using ideas from information theory. The method needs no labeled examples to make the choice. They then plug the new scales into network-based neural models that follow the same zoom-out design. Tests sorting networks into classes show the approach works inside those models.
arxiv-2504-09002:
Shukla and co-authors run a head-to-head comparison of two ways to simulate the edge plasma of a fusion device. Their 2025 study serves divertor design for a planned British pilot plant. Fluid codes are the standard tool, but they assume heavy collisions that future high-power machines may not have.

The fluid code and a gyrokinetic code both ran the same edge setup in two dimensions. In the kinetic runs, ions trapped by mirror forces raised upstream heat sharply. That force, missing from the fluid equations, deepened the voltage drop along field lines. Dirt particles stayed penned near the divertor far better in kinetic runs. The authors warn that fluid tools may overstate core contamination risk.
arxiv-2504-09302:
Junichiro Takahashi and co-authors test a learning method on heart tracings in this 2025 paper. A heart tracing, or ECG, is a cheap, painless test that helps doctors decide who needs deeper checks. The team used tracings from patients at hospitals in Japan, with labels written in Japanese.

Their method learns by matching tracings with the words used to describe them. Most past work used English and far fewer labels. Here the task kept about 98 labels, close to real clinic use. Even with so many labels, their Japanese-based model reached accuracy close to past research. The work extends this kind of tool to non-English clinical settings.
arxiv-2504-09402:
Han and co-authors argue that models fail questions by misreading them, and fix the reading in a 2025 paper. Their study of comprehension failures yields three findings. Step-by-step care helps reading as much as calculation. Repeating question tokens works by pulling attention back, and that pull can be dialed directly.

Backward references, where the end of a question defines its start, remain a core weakness of decoder models. Their Step-by-Step Reading prompts culminate in a version that parses questions finely and re-reads with context until references resolve. The method set new best scores on several reasoning benchmarks without any training.
arxiv-2504-09702:
Yunxiang Zhang and co-authors set word tools a test of true lore craft in a 2025 paper. The test is a suite of lore meets: open tasks where a new way must be coined and built, not a stock sum re-run.

Seven such meets form the bank. A set rule grades the steps: the plan, the build, the mark, each by firm counts, not a peer tool's taste. The best tool tried shut less than a tenth of the gap from base to the best man score. A side read found a split: what a tool judge calls new did not track what won. The bank is built to grow with new meets. The authors give board and code free.
arxiv-2504-10502:
Finding a picture you half-remember defeats most search engines, which tag and index images by machine habits, not human ones. Abraham Weinberg introduces HORSE in 2025, a retrieval system built on how people perceive, store, and recall images. Its neuro-symbolic indexing marries neural pattern-finding with symbolic reasoning, each covering the other's weakness.

By skipping heavy preprocessing pipelines, the system aims at faster, more intuitive search that feels closer to asking a person. Weinberg sketches uses from spotting design errors to managing knowledge, and lays out the design, the implementation, and the metrics still to be sharpened in future work.
arxiv-2504-11402:
Bjarke Frost Nielsen and co-authors explain the long cycles of a pneumonia germ in a 2025 paper. Mycoplasma pneumoniae returns in waves roughly five years apart in Denmark, a rhythm debated for decades. The team fit a dynamical model to Danish records spanning 1958 to 1995 and 2010 to 2025.

The fit points to a simple engine: cycles persist because immunity fades and the pool of susceptible people refills. A noise-free model, though, settles into yearly rhythm and loses the long waves. Random variation in contact rates, plus chance in smaller populations, keeps the long cycles alive. A gap in the records during 1979 to 1985 reads as a random jump between cycle modes. Pandemic-era curbs on contact enter the model as a test of big shocks.
arxiv-2504-11502:
Jatin Nainani, Chia-Tung Ho, Anirudh Dhurka, and Haoxing Ren build an AI agent that debugs chip timing reports the way a veteran engineer would, only faster. Their 2025 paper addresses sign-off timing analysis across many corners and modes, where smaller features have swollen reports beyond comfortable human turnaround. The agent chains several language models through a hierarchical plan-and-solve flow.

Its memory is a Timing Debug Relation Graph, linking report items to the debug traces of experienced engineers. An agentic retrieval method, mixing agents with code, pulls the right precedent for each new failure. On industrial designs the agent passed 98 percent of single-report cases and 90 percent of multi-report ones. The authors pitch it as an apprentice that never sleeps, trained on the firm's own debugging history.
arxiv-2504-11602:
Ferreira and Pinto calculate the mass of a particle in a model with two Higgs fields, in work from 2025. The model has a discrete three fold symmetry, yet a wider continuous symmetry appears by chance in parts of it. When that symmetry breaks, theory expects a massless particle to arise.

The fermion part of the model can tell the two symmetries apart. Loop effects might then give the particle a small mass. Their one loop calculation shows the particle stays massless for all but one tested pattern of couplings. Where a mass does arise, it is strongly suppressed by the spread of fermion masses.
arxiv-2504-11702:
Dorottya Zelenyanszki and three co-authors show how much player behavior can be mined from a blockchain game, in a 2025 paper. Every move in the game Planet IX is written to a public chain, open for anyone to trace. The team built a pipeline that harvests those transactions, rebuilds each player's sequence of actions, and notes how game tokens move through the flows. A graph neural network then embeds each player's flow so clustering algorithms can group similar styles.

Benchmarking several clustering methods, they found clear behavioral clusters with distinct habits. Visualized as graphs, the clusters reveal information an attacker could exploit, and the team sketch a threat model covering several harmed areas. The study is a warning: transparency in decentralized apps cuts both ways. What makes chains trustworthy also makes their users legible.
arxiv-2504-12202:
Light flips molecular switches, and linked switches may flip more cheaply than lone ones. Daniel Siciliano and co-authors measure that saving in a 2025 paper. Their frame treats the flipping process with the tools of quantum thermodynamics, which set cost floors without tracking every detail. Correlations between switches, both quantum and classical, are the variable under study.

The team shows in numbers how shared links raise the efficiency of the flip past the single-switch best. The gain holds across the mix of link types they test. The work also maps how quantum and classical links trade off in the process. Photo-switching sits under many biological light responses. The results hint at design rules for tiny light-driven machines.
arxiv-2504-12402:
Wanchun Shen, writing alone in 2025, studies how two notions of smoothness in algebra relate to each other. One notion, Du Bois singularity, comes from the geometry of singular spaces. The other, K-regularity, tracks how stable certain algebraic groups are under a basic change. Shen builds on the link between them in this work. The payoff is a stronger form of a long-standing conjecture by Vorst. That form covers spaces built as full intersections, in the setting where the ground field has zero characteristic.

The paper also gives tools to build fresh examples in the study of K-regularity. Those examples show distinct behaviors that the theory must allow. The main inputs are theorems that force certain Du Bois groups to vanish. Shen frames the work as a step in a wider program. It is a short note, so the focus stays on the core argument.
arxiv-2504-12502:
Olivier Shelbaya and co-authors present tuning methods in 2025 for a workhorse part of particle accelerators. Long tubes with many gaps push charged beams up to a few percent of light speed and drive nuclear physics labs worldwide. Unlike single-gap parts, these tubes have no neat formula linking settings to the beam that comes out.

The team tracks the beam's spread through the tube's fields using its first two spread measures. A beam-based calibration ties the model to the machine's real radio settings. The method then quickly returns the settings needed for a wanted beam energy and spread. Tests with a sodium ion beam confirmed the method works, giving operators a fast online energy change tool.
arxiv-2504-12802:
Future electron colliders will also act as photon colliders, since the beams shed light particles that can crash into each other. Simone Anedda, Francesco Murgia, and Cristian Pisano propose, in a 2025 paper, using those crashes to study how quarks split into hadrons. Such splitting is described by functions that track sideways motion inside the spray.

Most current knowledge of those functions comes from two other kinds of experiment, which leaves gaps. As a first example, the team studies pairs of light hadrons flying nearly back to back after a photon-photon hit. Patterns in their angles can reveal the splitting functions at work. Similar setups at the LHC and future hadron machines could add more evidence.
arxiv-2504-12902:
Seckin and co-authors chart the rise of Bluesky, the social platform that grew through waves of user migration, in a paper from 2025. The study spans from August 2023 to February 2025. In that window the service moved from invite-only novelty to a stable, active user base.

The authors track how migration waves built the follower network. The result is a dense web with tight clusters and strong hubs. That shape favors fast, viral spread of posts. Engagement levels and network traits look much like those of older, established platforms. The paper offers a data-backed account of how a new network matures when users arrive in floods from a rival service.
arxiv-2504-13002:
Hashini Gunatilake, John Grundy, Rashina Hoda, and Ingo Mueller build a grounded theory of empathy in software engineering, in a study from 2025. Developers constantly work with varied stakeholders, yet empathy is barely studied in their field despite its weight in medicine and education. Interviews supply the raw material.

Twenty-two developers and stakeholders described where empathy arises in their work and what shapes it. Analysis followed a socio-technical grounded theory method step by step. The resulting theory maps contexts, conditions, causes, and consequences of empathy and its absence. It also lists ways to strengthen empathy or clear barriers, with practical advice for teams and researchers.
arxiv-2504-13202:
Timo Aukusti Laine sets out a quantum-inspired model of meaning inside large language models in a 2025 paper. The paper follows an earlier one that sketched the framework. Here Laine states its core assumptions in detail and argues the approach is a valid lens on how these models handle meaning.

Six principles govern how meaning is represented, how parts interact, and how the system changes over time in the model. The tools come from quantum mechanics, used as formal analogies rather than claims about hardware. Laine discusses what the lens reveals about information handling and answer generation. He also sketches how real quantum computing might one day yield stronger, leaner language models built on these ideas.
arxiv-2504-13402:
Vedrana Ivezic and co-authors present a 2025 paper on CytoFM, a foundation model built just for cytology, the study of single cells for cancer checks. Cell samples vary a lot by stain, organ, and lab method, and labelled sets are small. General models trained on other images transfer poorly to this task.

CytoFM learns by itself from a mixed pool of cell images, with parts hidden so it must infer them. On later tasks, like breast cancer sorting and cell type naming, it beat models trained on tissue or on everyday photos in most tests. Its focus maps land on features pathologists care about. The authors say focused pretraining pays off even with modest data.
arxiv-2504-13602:
Kristian Olsen and three co-authors define a new heat function that links textbook partial volumes to the real space each molecule holds. Partial volumes come from how total volume shifts with mix, which is hard to picture. Real space can be carved up in computer sims by neighbor cells.

Their co-molar volume bridges the two views in one clean rule. Sims back the bridge in practice. The new term also ties to a co-moving speed known in two phase flow work. Chemists gain a volume idea they can both compute and picture at once.
arxiv-2504-13802:
Caja-Lopez, Delgadino, Gualdani and Taskovic wrote a 2025 math paper on how solutions of the Landau equation settle toward balance over time. That equation models particle collisions in a plasma. A recent breakthrough showed one key quantity falls steadily along solutions. The team asks whether other useful measures behave the same way.

For the simplest molecule case, a size gap from balance shrinks fast and steadily after some time. They also give a short new proof that a transport-based distance falls over time. For softer interaction laws, that distance contracts under a stated bound. Their route also reproves a known uniqueness result for the equation.
arxiv-2504-13902:
Fahad Alrasheedi and Hesham Ali wrote this research paper, published in 2025. It asks the chicken-and-egg question of electric cars with graph theory: do chargers follow adoption, or does adoption follow chargers, county by county across America?

The team modeled 137 counties in six states as a graph and compared electric vehicle uptake with charging infrastructure growth. They varied the time slicing of the data and split counties into early and late adoption stories. Finer time slices produced tidier, more uniform clusters, and the clusters for cars and chargers did not coincide. Formal causality tests found links running between the two in many counties. Cause appeared more often among early adopters, though it acted more slowly there. The authors say planners cannot assume one lever moves the other everywhere.
arxiv-2504-14102:
Pauline Simon and co-authors test an analog ensemble method for forecasting the solar wind, in work from 2025. The solar wind is a stream of particles from the Sun that can disturb Earth's magnetic shield. The analog method builds a forecast from past episodes that resemble the present one, giving a set of possible futures.

Using spacecraft observations near Earth, the team compared the method with two baselines: persistence, which assumes conditions hold, and climatology, which assumes average conditions. The analog forecasts matched persistence at short lead times and climatology at long ones, and beat both for most samples at a key lead time. A new reduction method preserved small-scale fluctuations that plain averaging erases. The result is a fast baseline for space weather prediction.
arxiv-2504-14202:
Zichuan Liu, Liming Jiang, and colleagues present a way to generate images that keep a person's identity in a 2025 computer vision study. Earlier tools bolted identity features onto a trained model through adapters. Prompts also carry text instructions, and the two signals can pull against each other.

Their encoder, FaceCLIP, learns one shared space for a face, the prompt text, and images. Given a reference face and a prompt, it produces a single combined signal that steers a diffusion model. A training procedure aligns that signal with face, text, and image representations. The built system aims for portraits that look like the person and match the words.
arxiv-2504-14302:
Yogev Kriger and Shai Fine wrote a machine learning paper in two thousand twenty-five on learning to score when true labels are missing. Many tasks sit between labeled and unlabeled data. Here no target labels exist at all, but side information is at hand: facts that correlate with the labels or that constrain the data.

Their model joins three parts: learning a good representation, using the side information, and learning a distance rule. One use is in health care, where symptoms are known but disease stages lack clear criteria. A severity score can still be built. They show the system working on standard data sets and on patient records.
arxiv-2504-14402:
Albert Huber rebuilds in 2025 the mathematics of thin shells, the razor-thin layers of matter that general relativity uses to model surfaces like a collapsing star's skin or a wormhole's throat. The classic formalism manipulates distributions, spiky mathematical objects whose products are not always defined, which breaks exactly the nonlinear calculations shells demand.

Huber switches the foundation to Colombeau's generalized functions, where smoothed versions of steps and spikes can be multiplied safely. The extended formalism then handles shell problems that defeat the conventional one. It is foundational work, the kind that quietly widens what a whole field can compute.
arxiv-2504-14502:
Qiliang Fang, Takashi Moriya, and Keiichi Maeda revisit the red supergiant problem: the puzzling shortage of very bright red supergiant stars among the known parents of type II supernovae. The team reads the masses of fifty exploded stars from their late-time spectra, using an oxygen emission feature whose strength tracks the star's birth mass. A calibrated relation then turns those masses into brightness values.

The resulting brightness spread cuts off at a modest ceiling, and the shortage of bright parents is real at two to three times the level expected from chance. Converted through standard stellar models, the ceiling means no parent above about twenty-one solar masses, in line with limits from direct images and light-curve studies, which all sit below twenty-five. The authors weigh possible physical explanations, from extra mass loss to stars that collapse without exploding.
arxiv-2504-15102:
Nadav Hargittai and co-workers measure cosmic ray muons deep underground at a possible new physics lab in Israel, in a 2025 paper. The site sits in tunnels of a pumped-storage plant under a national park, with thick rock overhead. Low radiation is vital for rare-event physics.

Using stacked detector plates over several days, they compared the muon flow underground with the flow at the surface. The rock cut the flow by a factor of several thousand. The shape of the mountain showed up clearly in the direction data. Radon levels were low. The team concludes the site suits future low-background research.
arxiv-2504-15202:
Jana Hamza and co-authors move a famous encryption scheme onto new mathematical ground. The ElGamal cryptosystem normally lives in the unit group of a number ring, and earlier work had already tried a second such group. Their 2025 paper extends the scheme to the third group of units of the ring of integers modulo n, and argues this setting is more secure than the previous extensions.

The team spells out the arithmetic the new home requires, since every encryption step, from key generation to decryption, must be rebuilt for the new group's operation. Numerical simulations then test the proposal, checking both that the security behaves as claimed and that the scheme runs at a practical speed. The paper belongs to a steady line of work asking how much of classical public-key cryptography survives, and improves, when its algebraic stage is swapped.
arxiv-2504-15302:
Answer-first chatbots that look facts up before replying strain small computers: one graphics card must hold both the model and the knowledge base. Weiping Yu and co-authors built RAGDoll in 2025, a serving system that runs this retrieval-augmented setup on a single card.

Their insight is that lookup and writing make different demands, so running them in a single line wastes both. RAGDoll splits them into parallel pipelines, with joint memory placement and smart batch scheduling. Tests across hardware setups and model sizes showed up to 3.6 times lower average delay than a leading serial system. The design adapts itself as workloads change.
arxiv-2504-15502:
Jose Daniel Castro-Cisneros, Renu Malhotra, and Aaron Rosengren compute how much lunar impact debris reaches Earth, published in 2025. Impacts shuffle material between worlds, shaping meteoroid streams, near-Earth objects, and maybe the delivery of water and organics. The Moon, close and airless, is a natural source to quantify.

A precise numerical integrator followed six thousand test fragments for a hundred thousand years, launched from many lunar locations with speeds drawn from large-crater physics. About a fifth of the ejecta eventually struck Earth, with half of those arrivals inside ten thousand years, following a power-law pattern. Debris from the Moon's trailing face dominated the Earth-bound flow. A small share lingered near Earth, matching recent finds of Earth companions whose spectra look lunar.
arxiv-2504-15602:
Xiaobo Liu and Wanxu Yang study how special surfaces move under mean curvature flow inside hyperbolic spaces, which are spaces of constant negative curvature. Their paper came out in 2025. Mean curvature flow shrinks a surface in the direction that reduces its area fastest, like a soap film settling.

The surfaces here are isoparametric, a highly symmetric family whose curvature quantities follow a rigid pattern. Earlier work covered these flows in flat spaces and spheres, and for single-layer surfaces in hyperbolic space. Liu and Yang treat surfaces of any thickness in hyperbolic space. They show such flows always admit solutions reaching infinitely far into the past. They also describe how those long-lived solutions behave in the limit.
arxiv-2504-15802:
Ellis Owen and co-authors show in 2025 that plain charge free bits in space rays can crack the mag net traps that hold their kin. Space rays are most oft drawn as charged bits bent by fields. Hard hits in gas and light can birth spare free bits from them.

At vast force, those free bits live long by time stretch and fly straight at light speed, un bent by fields. Their leak lets rays trade cross the walls tween hosts, groups, threads, and voids. Swap rates of the high est force bits shift in that frame.
arxiv-2504-15902:
Olivia Curtis and co-authors chart empty regions of the cosmos over time in a 2025 paper. Cosmic voids are vast underdense bubbles between galaxy walls. Their density profiles, from hollow core to raised rim, trace how structure grows.

Eleven snapshots of the TNG300 simulation span most of cosmic history. A watershed method picked out the largest true voids in each era, traced by galaxies and by dark matter. Profiles at all eras look like inverted top hats in broad shape. Yet core depth and rim height evolve, and far more for one tracer than the other. Voids thus record the shifting balance of the universe's growth.
arxiv-2504-16202:
Kfir Blum and co-authors test proposed links between a dense core and the wider halo of dark matter around a galaxy, in a paper from 2025. In theories with very light dark matter, a dense knot forms at the center of each halo. How heavy that knot is shapes what telescopes should see.

Two past proposals can be read as a lower bound and an upper bound on the knot mass, once the energy of the halo is estimated well. The team ran computer simulations of halos to check this picture. Results broadly matched the bounds and matched past work, after care with how halo energy is defined in a finite box. The paper helps narrow what observers can expect.
arxiv-2504-16302:
Lily Agranat-Tamir, Michael Fuchs, Bernhard Gittenberger, and Noah Rosenberg count a family of branching structures in a 2025 paper. The structures are time-consistent galled trees, rooted networks used in the study of evolution. Each tree has leaves at its tips and loops called galls that mark where lineages merged.

Counting such trees helps researchers weigh how likely each shape is. The authors give a fresh derivation, using the symbolic method, for the number of unlabeled trees with a fixed count of leaves and galls. They also derive new generating functions for the labeled version and describe how the counts grow for large trees. The results add exact tools to the math of evolutionary networks.
arxiv-2504-16502:
Marcin Furtak and co-authors present a 2025 system that guides a blind person hand to an object by vibration. A tactile bracelet buzzes directions on the wrist. The new work adds full automation around it. Cameras detect and track the target and its distractors.

Three everyday-style tasks tested the setup. Users grasped varied objects from a table by guidance alone. One task picked a same-class object among lookalikes. Another routed around an obstacle to reach the target. Reliable hand navigation could restore a key daily skill for independent living at home.
arxiv-2504-16702:
Joshua Swaim reports progress on computing electromagnetic corrections to meson masses, in a 2025 paper. Lattice simulations of the strong force now reach fine precision. At that level, small electromagnetic effects can no longer be skipped. Adding them naively brings volume errors that fade only slowly. A newer infinite-volume reconstruction method avoids that trap.

With it, finite-size errors shrink exponentially instead. Leading corrections to meson masses are the target. Bare quark masses receive the same treatment. The work is presented as ongoing progress. Other groups face the same precision wall in lattice studies. Cleaner electromagnetic handling should sharpen quark mass values worldwide. Those values feed tests of the Standard Model itself.
arxiv-2504-16802:
Minghao Guo and co-authors present a zooming method that makes black hole accretion simulations far cheaper in a 2025 paper. Feeding flows span scales from galactic distances down to the hole itself, which ordinary simulations cannot cover at once. Their cyclic zoom repeatedly refines and coarsens the domain while a central mask preserves small-scale physics, especially magnetic behavior.

Tests on classic problems, from spherical inflow to rotating tori around spinning and non-spinning holes, validated the method. It speeds suitable simulations by over a hundred thousand times. Applications show accretion suppressed relative to the simple rate, with feedback power rising sharply with spin, and a torus inflow fading as time to the minus two power. The method opens long-term, galaxy-scale feeding studies.
arxiv-2504-16902:
Idan Habler and co-authors analyze the security of agent-to-agent AI systems in a 2025 paper. Google's A2A protocol lets software agents from different makers discover and task each other. As agents move from simple workflows to real collaboration, weak points in that handshake matter.

The team applies the MAESTRO threat modeling framework, built for AI risks, to A2A deployments. They probe agent cards, task integrity, and authentication for failure modes. Concrete build practices and architecture patterns follow from the findings. Teams adopting multi-agent systems get a checklist grounded in systematic threat analysis rather than after-the-fact patching.
arxiv-2504-17002:
Scherer and co-authors test a new gravity framework in 2025 that generalizes both Newton's theory and a rival known as MoND. Some dwarf galaxies and galaxy clusters have been reported to clash with the rival theory's key prediction.

Their tool is a generalized Poisson equation built on the p-Laplacian, a tool first used in electrodynamics. From it they derive a generalized version of the radial acceleration relation and a formula for the spread of speeds in a simple galaxy model. Each dwarf galaxy and cluster in their data yields its own value of the parameter p. The values stray from the MoND case with strong support, and the speeds they predict match the data well.
arxiv-2504-17102:
Haoyu Li, Xiangru Zhong, Bin Hu, and Huan Zhang tackle a hard control problem, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-five. The problem is finding a proven measure of how fast a nonlinear system settles. Such measures, called contraction metrics, certify stability, robustness, and convergence.

The hard part is that complex systems rarely yield these metrics through older convex methods. Those methods also assume smooth dynamics, while modern controllers built from neural networks switch in steps and are not smooth. The authors instead train a neural network to propose a contraction metric for discrete-time systems. They then add formal checks so the learned metric carries a guarantee, not just a good fit. The work bridges learning and proof for systems steered by network-based controllers. It aims to make such controllers safer to trust.
arxiv-2504-17202:
Kiril Bangachev and Guy Bresler extend a classic idea about random-looking graphs to the job of telling two graph models apart. Quasirandom graphs fake pure randomness so well that a few counts certify the whole graph. Their 2025 paper asks the same for hypothesis testing between a coin-flip random graph and a stochastic block model with hidden communities.

The question becomes which small subgraph counts carry the loudest signal between the models. That signal strength turns into a spin model problem over community labels, which the authors solve in several regimes. Edge rules between and inside groups decide which subgraphs testify best. Network scientists get a principled way to choose the few counts worth computing.
arxiv-2504-17302:
Przybylska and a co-author proved in 2025 that the charged three-body problem cannot be solved in closed form, except in one special case. The catalog lists only the first author, while the head byline names two. Three bodies pulling on each other with inverse-distance forces cover gravity and electric charge alike.

Integrability would mean enough conserved quantities exist to tame the motion. Using a theorem linking integrability to the Galois structure of variational equations, generalised for their setting, the authors rule it out broadly. The single exception comes when two of the three interaction constants vanish, collapsing the problem. The result closes a classical question for this whole force family at three bodies.
arxiv-2504-17502:
Slobodkin and co-authors build a cheap judge for image generators that take a reference photo and a text prompt. Such tools must keep the subject's identity while obeying the words, a double demand. Existing scores check only one side, miss human judgment, or rent costly commercial models. Their metric, RefVNLI, grades both sides in one pass.

Training data came from video-reasoning sets and doctored images, teaching the judge what real mismatches look like. Across benchmarks and subject types, from animals to objects, the metric matches or beats prior scores, gaining up to 6.4 points on text fit and 5.9 on subject keeping. For developers tuning generators, it offers human-like grading without the API bill.
arxiv-2504-17602:
Daniel del-Corral and co-authors trace how the infant universe could have rung with gravitational waves just after inflation ended. As the inflaton field rolled down and swung back and forth, a lopsided well shape could pump up small ripples in space. Those ripples, grown by self-resonance, then fed waves of gravity at second order.

The team studies this chain in alpha-attractor models, a family of inflation setups ruled by one dial, alpha, and looks hardest at small alpha values where the effect peaks. Data from the birth of the first atomic nuclei cap how much wave energy is allowed. That cap sets floor values for alpha in two model variants, and in turn floor values for the tensor-to-scalar ratio.
arxiv-2504-17802:
Paul Frampton offers an exotic reading of a cosmic ray in twenty twenty-five. The Amaterasu particle, announced in twenty twenty-three, is extraordinary. Its arrival direction points back to the Local Void, a region with no galaxies or known sources. Galactic magnetic fields could not have bent its path much, he notes. Together, those facts form a paradox.

Frampton resolves it inside the Electromagnetic Accelerating Universe model. In that model, charged primordial extremely massive black holes drive cosmic acceleration through Coulomb forces. Their structure formation is electromagnetic, not gravitational. Such black holes could therefore sit inside the Local Void where galaxies cannot. He gives an example with an antiproton primary as the cosmic ray. The particle is presented as supporting evidence for the model.
arxiv-2504-18002:
Pariyakorn Maneekul, Zelda Zabinsky, and Giulia Pedrielli sketch a search scheme for hard tuning tasks in a 2025 paper. The tasks are black boxes: you can test a setting but not see inside, and the space of settings is wide. The scheme splits the space into zones and fits a cheap stand-in model in each, then samples where the stand-in looks best.

A timed proof sets the terms under which the scheme can scale to wide spaces. No build will hit that ideal, the team grants, so they try several builds on test tasks. The trials show where the gap between proof and practice sits.
arxiv-2504-18102:
Muhammad Rahim and three co-authors propose a controlled scheme for secure quantum sensing of a remote system. Quantum resources can boost both precision and security in sensing, yet noise in the channel and in state evolution erodes those gains. The team first gives a general scheme with many particles that reaches Heisenberg limited scaling when the channel and encoding are ideal.

For noisy dynamics, local quantum optimal control steps are added to fight dephasing noise. Two cases are analyzed, noisy evolution with a clean channel, and noise in both channel and evolution. The channel is modeled as depolarizing in the second case. Control steps raise both quantum and classical Fisher information under the chosen measurements.
arxiv-2504-18402:
Patrick Ilg, a solo author, solved a hard physics problem in exact form in a 2025 paper. The problem is how tiny magnetic grains respond when a strong magnetic field swings back and forth, a response that is usually found only by heavy computation.

Ilg worked out the full response for one standard model of grain motion, including the higher tones in the reply signal. Those tones shrink in a tidy pattern set by a single combined measure of field strength and speed. The rate at which the tones fade matters for medical scans that use such grains. For modest fields and speeds, the exact results also fit other common models well, which widens their use.
arxiv-2504-18702:
Edward Misback and co-authors built living marginalia for code, in a 2025 paper. Programmers hold rich context in their heads: why a line exists, which edge case bit them, what a failed fix taught. That context evaporates for teammates and for the language models now reading code cold. Codetations stores notes outside the file, pinned to spans by a hybrid of edit tracking and model matching, so the code stays clean while the notes stay put.

Notes can be dynamic and interactive, refreshing their data as the code changes. A worked example shows a well-noted file measurably improving a model's repair work. Developers in the trial prized the persistence and saw wide potential.
arxiv-2504-19102:
Mitra Mansouri and Hadi Salmasian give a pure algebra treatment of a class of functions on groups that mix signs, known as supergroups. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five.

The functions they study stay the same when shifted on both sides by a sub-group. The team builds them as a part of a dual algebra, cut out by a set ideal. For a broad class of paired super structures, they define how to trim such a function down to a core subspace. They prove that trim loses no facts. For one set pair, they compute a base for the ideal and find a link to two famed count lines.
arxiv-2504-19202:
Emelyanov and Kocharovsky build an analytic theory for a surprising effect in turbulent plasma: small magnetic ripples can make much larger ones explode in size. The setting is a plasma whose particles move unevenly by direction, which feeds the Weibel instability and its fine-scale magnetic turbulence. Particles scatter off those small ripples, and the scattering acts like extra collisions. The authors show this effect destabilizes long waves that plain linear theory calls stable.

Under steady conditions, matched to the saturated small-scale turbulence, the long waves grow faster than exponentially, in a burst the authors call explosive. They derive the growth law and estimate when the burst occurs. The analysis stays within a quasilinear approach, setting aside direct clashes between waves. For astrophysicists modeling how magnetic fields arise in space, the work supplies a mechanism by which large-scale fields can appear suddenly from small-scale disorder.
arxiv-2504-19302:
Zhaohua Wu and co-authors settle a basic question about waves moving through shifting media. Textbooks hold that when a wave crosses a flow that varies in space and motion, the conserved quantity is wave action, not wave energy. That claim seemed to dent the law of energy conservation itself, so the team set out to test it.

They prove that wave action conservation is really wave energy conservation in disguise. As a wave travels through such a medium, it deforms, and the deformation hides the energy bookkeeping. Their derivation draws wave action straight from the energy law. The authors say the result holds for every isolated wave system in varying media, from water waves to waves far beyond fluids.
arxiv-2504-19702:
Sharing a secret so that no single holder knows it is a cryptographic staple, but handing out the shares safely usually leans on computational assumptions. Alex Grilo and co-authors present a quantum route in this 2025 paper, built for the Qline, a stripped-down quantum network design meant to cut the cost of quantum links. Their protocol distributes shares of zero with composable security.

The proof sits inside the Abstract Cryptography framework, a strict standard for protocols that must compose with others. Once distributed, the shares support several tasks: standard secret sharing, anonymous veto, and symmetric key setup. The authors aim to give cheap quantum networks a trustworthy primitive for wider cryptography.
arxiv-2504-19802:
Inside a rattling cage of gold and silicon, a cerium atom shivers, and Michelangelo Tagliavini and eight co-authors show its shivering rewrites its magnetism, in a 2025 paper. The compound is a clathrate, a crystal of cages, where heavy-fermion behavior meets low-energy rattling vibrations, a pairing prized for thermoelectrics.

Two measurements refused to agree under any static crystal-field model. Magnetic susceptibility suggested strong mixing between two cerium states; X-ray scattering spectra said the mixing is negligible, with a clean 12 milli-electron-volt gap to the first excited state. The resolution is motion: the rattling couples to the cerium electrons and reshapes the field dynamically. The authors link the effect to phonon-boosted Kondo physics and dynamical distortions, arguing the crystal field in such cages is a moving target, not a fixed landscape.
arxiv-2504-19902:
Maria Galloway-Sprietsma and co-authors map gas surfaces in planet forming discs in a 2025 paper. The exoALMA program studies discs around young stars, where planets take shape. Knowing where gas emits light reveals the thermal and physical structure of a disc, its chemistry, and its motion.

The team located the emitting surfaces for three molecules across the survey sources. One form of carbon monoxide traced the upper disc atmosphere, while a rarer form and a carbon sulfur molecule traced lower layers. The height of the main tracer grew with disc mass, which offers a simple way to infer that mass. They also built two dimensional temperature maps of the discs. Signs of local substructure appeared in some surfaces and radial profiles.
arxiv-2504-20002:
Reyk Borner, Oliver Mehling, Jost von Hardenberg, and Valerio Lucarini map the stability of the Atlantic overturning circulation under rising carbon dioxide, in a paper from 2025. This ocean current system moves warm water north and shapes climate far beyond the Atlantic. It could flip into a weak state, with severe effects, but judging how close that flip sits has been hard.

Using a mid level climate model, the team charted the landscape of stable states at several gas levels. They computed the edge state, a restless in between state that marks the border between strong and weak current basins. Though unstable, that state can rule the climate path for centuries during a flip, driving long swings in the current. The global view goes past the local warning signs that most past work used.
arxiv-2504-20302:
Ben-Benjamin and Cohen study what happens to waves when the source that drives them runs for only a short time, in a 2025 paper. While the source is on, it stirs the medium. Once it stops, the wave settles into a fresh set of standing patterns, called modes, and the paper asks how those later modes relate to the earlier ones.

The authors derive clear formulas linking the two sets of modes, in both the position view and the wave-number view. They work through several special cases to show the method in action. As a payoff, they extend a classic exact solution of the wave equation, due to d'Alembert, to a wider class of wave problems with fixed properties.
arxiv-2504-20402:
Daichi Kozawa and co-authors place single glowing defects inside carbon nanotubes exactly where they want them, in a 2025 paper. Nanotubes fitted with organic color centers can emit single photons, a resource for quantum technology. Forming those centers used to be a matter of chance, with no control over number or position. Their method uses light-driven chemistry watched live as it happens.

Each new center announces itself as a discrete step in the tube's glow. Stopping the reaction at the first step yields exactly one center. Imaging confirmed centers form at chosen positions along the tube. Tests showed the emitted light arrives one photon at a time, proving its quantum character. Atomically defined emitters move closer to practical devices.
arxiv-2504-20602:
Siwei Wang and co-authors put forth PLUSNet in 2025. It is a pipeline for finding small objects in images. Work in the pipeline has three stages. First, features are drawn from the image. Next, training samples are picked. Last, objects are sorted and placed. Past work tried to improve one stage at a time. That held back gains for the whole pipeline.

PLUSNet improves all three stages. A part called the Hierarchical Feature Purifier cleans the features from the first stage in layers. A part called Multiple Criteria Label Assignment picks better training samples in the middle stage. A part called Frequency Decoupled Head uses the data more fully in the last stage. The parts can plug into many detectors. Tests show steady gains across many data sets for small object detection.
arxiv-2504-21002:
Nhat Hoang Le proves a result in the Gan-Gross-Prasad program, a set of conjectures linking two branches of modern number theory. The work concerns pairs of groups built from a vector space and its unitary group, over local fields that are not based on the real numbers. It follows methods developed earlier for related models by Waldspurger and Beuzart-Plessis.

The author sets up two relative trace formulas, tools that compare sums over group data from two sides of a problem. He works out the spectral side of each formula, then gives a partial match between their geometric sides. Putting these pieces together settles the local twisted form of the conjecture for tempered representations. Results of this kind help explain when periods over a smaller group can detect a representation.
arxiv-2504-21202:
Ramon Pires, Roseval Malaquias Junior, and Rodrigo Nogueira build in 2025 a benchmark that grades legal writing by language models using a real bar exam. Legal writing is open-ended and hard to score, so public tests are scarce. The Brazilian Bar Examination offers fresh questions, rubrics, and source texts.

Their set, oab-bench, holds 105 questions across seven law areas from recent exams. Four models take the test, and the best scores 7.93 of 10, passing all 21 exams. The team also asks whether models can grade as human examiners do. Top models track human scores closely on passed exams. That link backs AI help in grading, with care for the subjective core of legal judgment.
arxiv-2504-21402:
Wiparat Worapitpong, Parin Chaipunya, Poom Kumam, and Sakan Termkaew proved fixed point results in twenty twenty-five in Hadamard spaces, curved spaces that generalize flat geometry.
