They study strongly quasi-nonexpansive mappings, transformations that never push points farther from their fixed points. Such maps are the engines behind many iterative algorithms.

The team shows that a product of such mappings, under a demiclosed condition, keeps the same good behavior in an orbital sense. They then prove a convergence theorem for processes chasing a common fixed point of infinitely many such products. Applications include minimizing convex functions, splitting a minimization into finitely many parts, and finding points shared by finitely many sets. The results extend classical Hilbert space theory into curved settings.
arxiv-2504-21502:
Hans Bodlaender, Danny Hermelin, and Erik Jan van Leeuwen studied hard planning tasks in 2025 where some jobs may not run at the same time. A conflict graph marks which job pairs clash. Each job can carry its own length, due date, weight, and release time. The aim is the best schedule that honors all clashes. The same frame covers classic graph coloring tasks.

Even the plainest such tasks are hard in full generality, so the team fixed on graphs with a small tree-like width. There, some tasks can be solved fast with the width as the key measure. Others are shown to be as hard as a known hard class. The split gives a clean line between the two kinds of task.
arxiv-2504-21702:
Antonia Azzini, Ilaria Baroni, and Irene Celino test a chat tool for healthy living in a 2025 arXiv paper. Digital tools are often used to raise awareness and prompt better habits. Their app, a well-being counsellor named Allegra, shares advice and asks questions through a chat screen.

Users tried Allegra in one of three chat styles, then filled in a survey about their experience. The survey probed drive, awareness, and intent to change behavior. The team uses the replies to test their model of how such tools work. Their aim is to show what designers must keep in mind when building chat tools for well-being campaigns.
arxiv-2505-00202:
Kathie Cameron, Chinh Hoang, and Taite LaGrange solve a graph coloring problem in a 2025 mathematics paper. Coloring assigns labels to graph points so that linked points differ, and the difficulty of coloring certain graph families is a known open question. The authors focus on graphs that avoid several small patterns as contained subgraphs.

For one such family, they design an algorithm that colors any member graph in polynomial time. The algorithm rests on a structural theorem that describes what these graphs must look like. That structure breaks the graph into parts that are easy to color and combine. The result settles coloring for this subclass, while the broader problem for the parent family remains open.
arxiv-2505-00302:
Xinlong Zhao and co-authors present a new method for forecasting many linked time series at once, published in 2025. Their model, called TAEGCN, treats each data node as part of a graph. Unlike older methods, it does not assume that the graph stays fixed over time. It also notes that links can look quite different at fast and slow time scales.

Inside, the model learns time patterns with causal filters and a form of self-attention, then builds a changing graph from those patterns. Tests use two public road traffic data sets, METR-LA and PEMS-BAY. The authors report that their method beats prior methods on these tests, which may help with traffic planning and other forecasts.
arxiv-2505-00602:
Jasem Hamoud and Duaa Abdullah introduce a new graph measure in a 2025 paper built from Fibonacci words. Fibonacci words are strings grown by a simple rule tied to the famous number sequence, and trees can be built from them.

Their index adapts a classic measure of how uneven the degrees of linked nodes are. Variants cover total unevenness and a modified form based on squared degree gaps across edges. The authors prove basic bounds that tie these indices to the largest degree in the tree. The work extends known graph invariants into the world of word combinatorics and gives fresh tools for reading the shape of such trees.
arxiv-2505-00702:
Hanwen Jiang and co-authors teach a model 3D awareness from plain photos alone in this 2025 paper. View synthesis tools usually need known camera positions and scene geometry. Their model, RayZer, gets neither. It takes unposed, uncalibrated images, guesses the cameras itself, builds a scene code, and renders new viewpoints.

Training leans only on those self-guessed poses, so ordinary photo sets suffice. Two design choices drive the 3D sense: an encoding that splits camera from scene, and a transformer whose only built-in geometry is the ray linking them. RayZer matched or beat rival methods that cheat with true poses. The authors release it as a step toward 3D learning without labels.
arxiv-2505-01002:
A large team from the NEXT Collaboration describes how to feed very high voltage into a detector hunting one of physics' rarest events. NEXT-100 is an underground chamber of gas that watches for neutrinoless double beta decay, a process that would rewrite our picture of the neutrino. Its electrons must drift over meters, which takes tens of thousands of volts.

The paper covers the cathode feedthrough, the sealed port that carries the voltage in, and the wiring of the field cage that spreads it evenly. The feedthrough held gas at twenty times normal pressure and voltages down to minus 65 kilovolts. The chamber now runs steadily at its design voltages, all within a strict budget for radioactive purity. The authors say the system is ready for the sensitive decay searches ahead.
arxiv-2505-01102:
Surangkhana Rukdee wrote this review in two thousand twenty-five as the sole author. It surveys ground-based gear for high-resolution spectroscopy of rocky exoplanet skies, and what such gear may soon catch.

The mix of gases in a far world's sky can hint at its rocks and at life. High-resolution transmission spectroscopy has read the skies of gas giants and now nears smaller worlds, with many molecules found so far. The review weighs the next round of tools, above all for spotting molecular oxygen in Earth-like skies. Careful time sums show a sharper spectral setting finds the gas with far fewer transits, even through haze.
arxiv-2505-01202:
Reetanshu Pandey and co-authors compute quark traits inside kaons bathed in nuclear matter in this 2025 paper. Kaons are light particles built from two quarks, and dense matter can reshape their inner maps. The team uses a light-cone quark model fed by a second field model for the medium.

They map how the lead quark's sideways and lengthwise motion spreads shift with density. Charge shape and size of the kaons are worked out for both free and in-matter cases. Average motion shares at high density are also charted. The sums match past data and rival models well. Such maps feed plans for heavy-ion crash tests.
arxiv-2505-01502:
Toptun and co-authors use a new X-ray sky survey to weigh galaxy clusters by their heat in a 2025 paper. Galaxy groups and clusters are filled with hot gas, and in the simplest picture a halo's mass and its gas temperature march in lockstep. Real gas physics, cooling and blasts from black holes, can break that step, especially in small groups. The low-mass end of the relation was the least charted.

The team draws on the eROSITA telescope's view, spanning from poor groups to massive clusters. They test where the self-similar prediction holds and where baryonic effects bend it. Getting this relation right matters because cluster counts are a cosmological probe: a biased ruler skews the universe it measures. Groups, being most common, carry much of the signal.
arxiv-2505-01802:
Virtual reality headsets track only a few body points, yet avatars need a full moving body. Georgios Angelis and co-authors proposed in 2025 a lean network that fills in the missing motion without the heavy cost of earlier models.

Their design slices the input stream into short time windows. The current pose is then merged with compressed summaries of those windows, borrowing past context without dragging the whole history along. In experiments, accuracy beat leading methods while computation and memory fell sharply. The authors aim the method at headsets and other small devices where power and memory are tight.
arxiv-2505-01902:
Ali Al-Bustami and Zaid Ghazal built a learning frame in 2025 to forecast winners of World Cup soccer games. Calls in this sport matter to coaches, analysts, and fans. Past tools leant on team totals alone and missed how each player shapes a match. Their frame blends team history with player marks such as goals, assists, pass rates, and tackles. Year-by-year team profiles track how squads change over time.

They trained sorting models with tuned settings and a step that shrinks the input set. On data from the 2022 World Cup, their frame beat a plain base line. The pair say player-level data adds real signal about how teams mesh and clash. They point to graph-style networks as a next step.
arxiv-2505-02102:
Thomas Cohen shows that swings in color charge in a zone are a must in the strong force theory. The work dates to 2025. Still charge in a zone must be zero in all true states, by the field's own law. That fact made the charge seem a weak tool for grasp of bound states.

Cohen proves the square of the zone charge does not read zero in true states. That square gauges how much charge swings from place to place. The read, though drawn from a non-firm term, is itself firm under gauge shifts. A set blend of vacuum and mixed-state swings has a clean far limit as well.
arxiv-2505-02302:
Oleksandr Mokliachuk wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five as the sole author, though the catalog names no creator for it. It builds models that mimic stochastic processes with a set trust level and accuracy, in the Lp space over a time set.

The processes come from a broad class tied to a chosen gauge function, and many split into series with free parts. The author gives ways to build stand-in models that meet the set trust and accuracy marks. Models for processes split into series with near parts are also handled. A Karhunen-Loève model serves as the worked case of the method. The paper is a piece of pure probability theory.
arxiv-2505-02902:
M Fabbrichesi, R Floreanini, and L Marzola sort out where quantum entanglement in top quark pairs is truly nonlocal. Their 2025 paper uses pairs of top quarks made at the Large Hadron Collider, whose spins carry the entanglement signal.

Close to the energy where the pairs are born, they show, the entanglement is local: it can be mimicked by classical hidden variables. A recent collider analysis backs that reading with strong significance. In a boosted central region, though, the entanglement turns nonlocal. The authors also find a zone where the spins are separable yet still hold quantum discord and magic. Top pairs, they argue, form a rare bench for testing how entanglement and locality trade off.
arxiv-2505-03002:
Amirhossein Akbar Tabatabai surveys proof complexity, the study of how long the shortest proof of a claim must be. His 2025 survey centers on feasible interpolation, a method that builds hard theorems whose proofs balloon far past the claim's own length. The tour spans classic and non-classic logics alike.

Readers need only base logic and two complexity classes to follow. New terms are built as they arise. Hard theorems from this method expose the true cost of proof search in each system. Such limits shape what automated provers can hope to do. The survey opens the field to newcomers while keeping the core trick in view.
arxiv-2505-03102:
Huanzhi Pu and co-authors ask how a RISC-V graphics processor should support warp-level features. These features let threads in a graphics program cooperate closely, and modern code relies on them. Should they be built into the chip in hardware, or faked in software? RISC-V graphics chips promise openness, but their usual programming model clashes with warp-level tricks. The team implemented both routes on an open GPU design and measured them.

Hardware support delivered up to four times the instruction throughput on microbenchmarks, measured as a geometric mean. Software emulation still worked and may suit chips where area is tight. The study gives designers a concrete trade-off for bringing modern GPU programming to the RISC-V world.
arxiv-2505-03202:
Xiang-Dong Li carries Perelman's entropy machinery from smooth Ricci flow into the rougher world of metric measure spaces. The W-entropy and the concavity of Shannon entropy power are central tools in geometric analysis. Extending them to super Ricci flows on singular spaces widens where they can be used.

Along the way he proves a Harnack inequality of Li-Yau-Hamilton-Perelman type in the same generality. A headline application shows that, on a class of spaces with synthetic Ricci bounds, volume non-collapsing is equivalent to the W-entropy staying bounded below. The entropy also yields the logarithmic Sobolev inequality with its optimal constant on these flows. The work unifies several strands of modern geometry.
arxiv-2505-03302:
Eneko Osaba, Esther Villar-Rodriguez, and Izaskun Oregi survey early industrial uses of quantum computing, in a 2025 paper. Quantum machines are entering a phase of practical use even though today's devices are noisy and mid-sized. The authors credit three drivers: bigger machines with better-linked qubits, specialized software frameworks, and hybrid schemes that pair quantum steps with classical ones.

The survey gathers recent work that applies these methods to machine learning and optimization problems from real settings. Material simulation stands beside those two as a field where quantum methods may pay off soon. The authors argue that such results could make quantum computing a strong driver of research in the coming years. They present the paper as a map of where industry trials stand now.
arxiv-2505-03602:
Kah Chun Lai, Juan Carlos Algaba Marcos, and Zamri bin Zainal Abidin track changes in a measure of twisted magnetic fields near a distant quasar's jet. Their 2025 paper studies 1633+382, a flat-spectrum radio quasar, across five observation rounds from 2004 to 2008. The measure, Faraday rotation, reveals the magnetized material that radio waves pass through.

Using a continent-wide radio telescope array, they find the core's rotation scales with frequency in a clean power pattern. The sign of the measure flipped between rounds, in both core and jet, on different schedules. They argue a new ejected component likely drives the core changes, while a foreground screen fits the jet poorly.
arxiv-2505-03702:
Srecharan Selvam and co-authors teach a robot arm to grasp leaves gently in farm settings. Their 2025 paper joins classic geometry with neural nets, since leaves bend and vary too much for either alone. A vision model spots each leaf, a stereo method reads depth, and two scoring paths then pick the grasp point.

A trust-weighted blend merges the geometry score with the neural score by how sure each one is. The geometry path also acts as teacher, making training labels on its own. Trials hit eighty-eight percent success in lab terms and near eighty-five in a real greenhouse. Both beat pure geometry and pure neural runs by clear margins.
arxiv-2505-03902:
Vineet Ojha, Xue-Bing Wu, and Luis Ho compare, in a 2025 astronomy paper, what makes the light of Seyfert galaxies flicker. These galaxies host feeding black holes, and their light can vary because of the hot disk around the hole or because of a fast jet of matter.

The team tracked light curves for three matched groups, split by galaxy type and whether gamma rays were seen. The broad-line group with gamma rays varied most, perhaps because its jet points more toward Earth. Galaxies without gamma rays barely varied, pointing to the disk as the source. Color changes over time support the idea that dust around the disk re-emits its light.
arxiv-2505-04002:
Michael Xu and co-authors build a training loop in 2025 that teaches animated characters parkour-style movement. Real motion capture for climbing walls and leaping gaps is scarce and costly, so characters trained on small sets stay clumsy on new ground. Their framework, named PARC in the paper, grows its own training data round by round.

A motion maker first learns core skills, then drafts moves for new terrain. Those drafts often have flaws like wrong contacts, so a physics-based tracker replays them in simulation and fixes them. The cleaned moves rejoin the training set for the next round. Round by round, both parts grow more agile and more versatile on complex ground.
arxiv-2505-04102: Lkhamsuren Altangerel adapts in 2025 a known fix-point scheme to quasi-variational inequality problems in Hilbert spaces, in both continuous and discrete time. The work studies when equilibrium points exist for these problems. It proves convergence for the linked dynamical systems. Linear convergence of the split forms is then checked through examples, illustrations, and special cases.
arxiv-2505-04202:
Nimyi and co-authors published this graphene theory paper in 2025. A single sheet of graphene in crossed fields, a magnetic field through the sheet and an electric field across it, has energy levels no exact formula can give. The team attacked the problem with the WKB method, an approximation from quantum mechanics. Their sheet has a gap, a forbidden energy range that changes the physics. They derived the rule that picks out the allowed energies.

The rule contains a geometric phase, and that phase depends on which of graphene's two valleys the electron occupies. Including it made the approximation match near-exact computer diagonalization across the levels. Only the lowest energy level resisted the match. The authors present the corrected quantization rule as a practical tool. It lets physicists estimate spectra for gapped graphene devices in crossed fields, where brute-force calculation is the only alternative.
arxiv-2505-04602:
Mohit Panwar, Akash Gandhi, and Pankaj Jain propose a simulation method to extract our local velocity from the cosmic dipole, in a 2025 paper. Our motion against the cosmic rest frame creates a lopsided pattern in galaxy counts. Reading velocity from it needs two source parameters, usually handled with averages and assumed curve shapes.

Their simulation uses each source's own spectrum value and avoids assuming the shape of the number count curve near the survey limit. Applied to a large quasar catalog, the method's velocity estimate differed from the standard approach by about one standard deviation. The authors present the shift as a caution for precision cosmology.
arxiv-2505-04702:
Luke Lippstreu, a solo author, studies scattering amplitudes in theories with long range forces in a 2025 paper. Such forces, like the electric force between charges, create infrared divergences that hide basic properties such as causality and crossing symmetry. Lippstreu uses an exactly solvable model: a charged particle moving in a fixed electric background.

In that model he confirms that unitarity and causality still hold after proper quantization. He then works out needed changes to standard formulas that connect theory to scattering results. A key result links the phase divergence from the long range force to real radiation divergences through crossing symmetry. The author argues for solving the full asymptotic theory rather than dressing particles by hand.
arxiv-2505-05202:
Ya-Xin Xiang and co-authors sort two kinds of stuck states in open quantum systems in a 2025 paper. In classic systems, noise flips a system between two stable zones. Quantum systems like qubits show like flips through sudden jumps.

The team split path level flipping from spectrum level slowness. A small gap in the spectrum slows decay, but only for some start states. With flipping on, the start state is soon forgot and rare flips set the pace. Flip rates follow the same heat law seen in classic systems. The split clears up when a stuck state truly slows a quantum device.
arxiv-2505-05402:
Andrew Laack introduces a decision tree algorithm in a 2025 paper that splits data along slanted lines. Standard trees split on one feature at a time, which can force deep, tangled trees. Slanted splits can fit patterns better, but searching all options is costly, so the idea has seen little use.

His method searches a limited set of slanted splits in full at each node. Laack studies the cost of the search and tests accuracy on small data sets. The method matched or beat known tree builders, often with clear gains, while growing shallower and simpler trees. Such trees are easier for people to read, which matters in fields that must explain each call.
arxiv-2505-05502:
Rousseas and co-authors analyze in 2025 how to judge feasibility of constraints in optimization based controllers for autonomous systems. Controllers often compute inputs by solving a constrained optimization problem. When constraints clash, picking a workable subset is both hard and critical.

Their theory gives necessary and sufficient conditions for feasibility of linear constraints. New selection methods grow out of that analysis for control use. Simulations show performance on par with leading methods at better computational efficiency. The frame also offers a general way to assess and handle infeasibility, which extends past the control cases tested.
arxiv-2505-05802:
Yan He and co-authors let artificial intelligence spot a double hypernucleus in nuclear emulsion for the first time. Their 2025 paper enters double-strangeness research, which probes how hyperons bind inside nuclei and what neutron star cores are made of. Emulsion plates record rare events but hide them in vast film.

Generative AI and simulations build training sets; a detection model then finds candidate events. Kinematics and charge checks identify the event as a rare capture forming a double-Lambda nucleus. The binding energy of the two Lambda particles lands near 25.6 mega-electronvolts, with the pair interaction near 2.8. The authors frame the catch as the start of an AI era for strangeness physics, where machines scan what eyes could not finish.
arxiv-2505-06202:
Linda Albanese, Adriano Barra, and Emilio Cirillo published a physics paper in 2025 applying Guerra's interpolation method to spin glass models that freeze in reverse. These disordered magnets melt and freeze in unusual order as temperature changes. The team treats several named models under one broader Hamiltonian with crystal fields and multi-value spins.

They compute free energies under simple and one-step-broken symmetry assumptions, recovering results once reached only by heuristic replica tricks. A stability boundary for the simple solution is derived in this general setting, new even physically. The notes unify a scattered literature and put its claims on firmer ground.
arxiv-2505-06502:
Md Rakibul Hasan and co-authors build in 2025 an image upscaling network for physics simulations that respects the laws behind the data. Generative upscalers make pretty pictures that often break physics, which ruins them for science. Their network adds checks that keep the fine output faithful to the coarse simulation.

It beat standard methods on both sharpness scores they tracked. Strikingly, it needed only about an eighth of the training data to match a leading rival. Sound time stepping schemes are woven into the method, not bolted on. Trustworthy upscaling lets labs run cheap coarse simulations and restore detail later. That trade can cut the huge computing bills of weather, flow, and fusion studies.
arxiv-2505-06802:
Weiqin Sun and seven co-authors ask how much energy electrons in Earth's magnetotail can gain, in a 2025 study. During substorms, the tail frees stored magnetic energy and speeds up particles. A small satellite just saw such electrons reach several million electron-volts, in the relativistic range, which takes a strong accelerator.

The team modeled the tail's electron group with a well-known convection model of the inner magnetosphere. The model matched what was seen. The shape and the energy reach of the spectra matched the satellite data. That match points to the modeled flow and speeding up, as plasma is sent earthward during substorms, as the engine behind the extreme events. The work sets an upper-limit view of how far such speeding up can go in the tail. It also backs the use of such models to read data from satellites in low orbits.
arxiv-2505-07002:
Yuta Inoue, Ken-ichi Kawarabayashi, Atsuyuki Miyashita, Bojan Mohar, and Tomohiro Sonobe prove Grünbaum's conjecture on coloring cubic graphs drawn on a torus. Their paper from twenty twenty-five strengthens a claim from the late nineteen sixties. The graphs in view have three edges per vertex and strong ring links. Apart from one named family, all of them take a three-edge coloring.

The odd family, called Petersen-like, is built by joining copies of the Petersen graph with a dot product. The first members are the Petersen graph and a Blanuša snark. The proof mixes vast computer checks with hand-built extensions of past color arguments. The result reads as a broad lift of the Four Color Theorem. A strong form of the Tutte flow conjecture for torus graphs falls out as well.
arxiv-2505-07202:
Hyouin Liu and Zhikuan Zhang compared training methods for conversational speech synthesis in a 2025 study. Top conversational systems are often closed to the public, raising a question: are open designs weak, or is training the problem? The authors tested two ways to use context in training.

One method trained on single utterances with context supplied, the other on full conversations. Using twenty hours on a high-end graphics card, the utterance method scored higher on listening quality and cut training time by over a third. Full conversation training caused a fault where speaker likeness was hallucinated. The authors give practical guidance favouring the utterance route.
arxiv-2505-07602:
Dong Huang, Qiong Liu, Mark Wyatt, and Grant Kennedy search for dust around nearby stars in a 2025 paper. Dust in the habitable zone of a star, called exozodiacal dust, can blind future missions that hunt for life bearing planets. Knowing which nearby stars carry such dust is therefore essential for choosing targets.

The team searched stars within ten parsecs using infrared data from the WISE satellite. They matched a standard sample of nearby stars to two catalogs and kept 339 targets. Model fits predicted each star infrared glow, and they hunted for excess light in one band. Five candidates emerged, but all were brown dwarfs, whose own atmospheres likely explain the excess. No true cases were found among the main sample, which puts the rate for sun like and smaller stars under one percent.
arxiv-2505-07802:
Robot planners built from generative models can produce smooth motion paths, but they falter when the needed path was never in the training data as one piece. Reece O'Mahoney, Wanming Yu, and Ioannis Havoutis trace the failure to stitching: the models cannot join short known segments into a new long route. They adjust the model's design and training data to fix that.

A new addition to training and inference steadies the stitching further. On a Franka Panda robot arm, in simulation and on real hardware, their method planned around obstacles and met start and end conditions outside the training set. It beat baselines clearly and dodged obstacles up to four times larger. The work targets flexible planning for manipulation tasks.
arxiv-2505-08002:
Ewoud van Dishoeck and a large team of co-authors introduce a space telescope program watching stars being born. Their 2025 paper presents JOYS, a survey of young protostars with the James Webb telescope. The hidden, embedded stage of a star's birth shapes everything after, and mid-infrared light is the key probe of that stage.

Webb's sharpness and sensitivity open details under an arcsecond for the first time. The program's questions span how protostars feed, how their jets and winds launch, the chemistry of their gas and ice, and the disks forming inside the cocoon. Early data on seventeen small and six large protostars already show rich variety. Maps of atomic lines differ by element in ways that trace local shock conditions and depletion.
arxiv-2505-08302:
Oishee Bintey Hoque and co-authors present a mapping system that labels how farms water their fields, using satellite images plus crop knowledge, in a 2025 paper. Knowing the irrigation type matters for saving water and planning food supplies. Models that read images alone often fail here, because farm scenes are complex and labeled examples are scarce.

Their system, KIIM, builds in what is known about farming. It encodes how likely each crop is to use each watering method, marks which land is farmland, and lets image and crop data correct each other. Across five US states it beat image-only baselines, with the biggest gain on drip irrigation, a hard class to spot. A two-step transfer method also lifted results sharply in a state with few labels.
arxiv-2505-08502: Daniel Schmidt and co-authors show a new timing method for X-ray tests that watch crystals change over time. Such tests need both fine time detail and a bright beam, which usually trade off against each other. Their method shapes the X-ray beam into patterned pulse trains with a solid-state picker tool.
arxiv-2505-09002:
Ishraq Tashdid, Tasnuva Farheen, and Sazadur Rahman present SAFE-SiP, a secure authentication framework for chiplet based packages. Modern systems in a package assemble chiplets from many vendors, which raises risks of counterfeiting, overproduction, and unauthorized access. Past fixes assume a trusted integrator or add a dedicated security chiplet, both of which create new attack paths.

SAFE-SiP uses multi party computation to verify chiplet signatures without revealing them to any party. No extra security chiplet is needed, and authentication works even when integration is untrusted. Tests on five RISC-V based designs show low power cost, average area overhead near three percent, and very high computational security. The design scales to larger packages.
arxiv-2505-09302: Castiglioni and Ertola-Biraben give a rough set meaning to a three-valued logic in a 2025 paper. The logic extends a system by Priest and da Costa to first-order form, with three truth values instead of two. Their earlier work on the system used two kinds of negation joined by modalities. Here they build its semantics from rough sets, a tool that sorts objects by rough likeness. The pattern tracks the classic semantics for first-order logic, they note.
arxiv-2505-09502:
Cem Yuce studies subskin modes in a nonlinear non-Hermitian system in this 2025 arXiv paper. Skin modes pile up at a system's edge under the non-Hermitian skin effect. Subskin modes are different: they localize just below the edge, appear only in ones or twos, and normally demand a very specific relation between system size and couplings.

Yuce shows that nonlinear interaction can lift those tight restrictions, letting subskin modes form more freely. The finding widens the conditions under which these unusual localized states exist. The author points to possible practical uses of subskin modes and to new research directions in non-Hermitian physics that the relaxation of constraints may open.
arxiv-2505-09602:
David Khachaturov and Robert Mullins build a defense against jailbreak prompts in this 2025 paper. Large language models can be tricked by adversarial suffixes, odd token strings appended to a request, which remain the strongest known jailbreak and often work without any access to the model inside.

Their pipeline, ASF, sits in front of the model as a preprocessor that spots and strips such suffixes before the prompt is read. It needs no access to the model's internals and adds little cost. In tests against leading suffix attacks, in both black box and white box settings, success rates fell below four percent, while normal use of the model was barely affected.
arxiv-2505-09702:
Yezi Liu and five co-authors catch a fairness flaw in the way graph models forget user data on request. Unlearning scrubs a person's influence from a trained model to protect privacy, and most methods check only that accuracy survives. The team found that after unlearning, a model's predictions lean harder on sensitive traits like group membership, so deletion itself injects bias. Their method, FGU, forgets and debiases in the same pass.

The model is split into shards trained on separate pieces of the graph, so only the touched shard retrains when data must go. Fairness is enforced at two levels: a penalty inside each shard, then an alignment step that pulls all shards toward one global standard. Tests show the method keeps privacy and accuracy while beating rivals on fairness, across many kinds of deletion requests.
arxiv-2505-10102:
Elio Marconi and Laura Spinolo study a traffic model where drivers react to cars beyond their own lane position in this 2025 math paper. The model pairs a law for car density with a moving marker for each driver's desired speed on an empty road. In the nonlocal version, speed depends on a weighted average of density around the car.

The authors prove the model has exactly one well-behaved solution. They then shrink the averaging window to a point and show the model lands on the classic local version. For a common kernel shape, a key estimate makes that limit rigorous. They claim this is the first such limit proof for a two-part system of this kind.
arxiv-2505-10302:
Shao-Feng Ge and co-authors sharpen the hunt for dark photons in a 2025 particle physics paper. A dark photon is a proposed hidden particle that could link normal matter to a dark sector, and labs search for it by watching it vanish into nothing visible.

The team studies an overlooked production route: an electron and positron annihilating while one first radiates a photon. At fixed-target setups like Belle II and NA64, this route can dominate near certain dark photon masses. Including it lifts the reach on the mixing strength by up to about twofold or more in the best spots. A finer split of the Belle II signal shapes the search still further.
arxiv-2505-10802:
Ian Holmes and Min Chi shape rewards for learning agents using a transformer's attention in this 2025 paper. Many real tasks give feedback only rarely, or at the very end. Sparse, delayed rewards make reinforcement learning crawl. Their method, ARES, reads past episodes and their final scores. Attention weights then assign credit to the steps that mattered. That turns one final score into a stream of dense feedback.

ARES trains fully offline, on stored episodes. It works even with small datasets or random-action episodes. Any learning algorithm can plug in the shaped rewards. The team stress-tested the hardest case: reward only at episode end. Trials span varied environments in the full paper. The goal is practical learning where feedback is naturally scarce.
arxiv-2505-11002:
Wei Zhang and Qi Zhou prove a shape result for solutions of a key equation in complex geometry in a 2025 paper. The equation governs how volume spreads in complex space, and whether its solutions bend in a clean power shape is a hard open type question. The authors work on a smooth, strictly convex region in two complex dimensions.

They show the solutions do hold the power convex shape under the stated edge conditions. Their proof rests on a rank theorem that keeps a key matrix from dropping rank, plus a deformation step. To make the rank step work, they refine a helper function from earlier work by other authors.
arxiv-2505-11202:
Guangyuan Huang and co-authors track bubble swarms as they rise through still water, in a 2025 fluids study. How bubbles spread as they climb matters for chemical plants, where gas is blown through liquid in tall columns. The team filmed a column with eight sides in 3D, tracking both bubbles and tracer specks.

Sideways spread in a swarm pulsed up and down near the trend for plain spread, but less than for lone bubbles. Upward spread ran near ten times faster than for lone bubbles, since swarm bubbles jiggle with more force. Tracers shed their first fast phase at times that turned on bubble size and gas share. The split comes from how well wakes mix the water: big bubbles stir a broad churn, small ones leave spread tied to near wakes.
arxiv-2505-11302:
Gabriel Carmona and Giovanni Manzini gave new depth-first layouts for a compact tree data structure in 2025. The structure stores sparse binary matrices well by using both sparseness and clustering of ones. Its standard layout runs level by level, which blocks merging of identical subtrees and slows access to single subtrees.

Their depth-first versions fix both issues. A linear-time algorithm finds and compresses identical subtrees inside the new layouts. On web graph matrices, using identical subtrees improved compression. For some matrices, the depth-first form also ran matrix multiplication faster than the standard form. The authors present the layout as a path worth pursuing for sparse data storage.
arxiv-2505-11602:
Nikola Zubić and Davide Scaramuzza ask when selective state-space models, the family behind Mamba, stay stable. These models process long sequences by letting a token-dependent signal retune their inner coefficients on the fly. That makes the system neither a fixed linear one nor a standard nonlinear one, so classic stability tools do not apply directly. The authors study the continuous-time version using passivity and input-to-state stability, keeping the selection signal separate from the driving input.

They prove four results, covering fast forgetting of old states, a storage function that tolerates abrupt gating changes, and conditions for global stability under any allowed selection pattern. They then turn the theory into a training-time penalty for the real Mamba block. Across seven time-series datasets, the penalty cut stability violations by about 92 percent at almost no cost in accuracy.
arxiv-2505-11702:
Keenan Eikenberry, Lizuo Liu, and Yoonsang Lee show how to bolt invariance onto a trained neural network without retraining it, in a 2025 paper. The goal is a network that ignores rotations or noise yet answers unchanged on plain inputs. They formalize the task through augmented encoders, then propose two training losses built on optimal transport ideas.

A small one-layer adapter, trained with either loss, sits between the frozen network and its classifier. On a standard image set, rotation accuracy jumped from 71 to 94 percent, and noise accuracy from 58 to 86 percent. The base network's weights never moved, which keeps the method cheap.
arxiv-2505-11902:
Jiang You, Xiaozhen Wang, and Arben Cela proposed a learning method in twenty twenty-five for time series whose task keeps changing. In their setup, the same input can demand different outputs under shifting goals, which breaks static models. They built a synthetic data set full of conflicting subtasks to stress-test adaptation under frequent shifts.

Their method splits the model into a trunk and branches. The trunk changes slowly and holds long-term structure. Each branch is reset and retrained for the current task, letting the system adapt at test time without task labels. They prove this design is strictly more expressive than static models and a popular tuning method, and that branch adaptation converges fast under a known condition. Experiments beat strong baselines in clashing-task settings.
arxiv-2505-12402:
Pseudonyms hide who a user is online, but their public posts can still give away private traits. Yuntao Du and co-authors named that risk in 2025 and built a system to measure it. Their AutoProfiler uses four language model agents that work together to gather a user's public activity and pull out personal attributes from it.

Tests on two real datasets and one made-up dataset showed the system was fast and accurate. The traits it found were both sensitive and enough to single out users. The authors review defenses from several angles and urge more public awareness of the risk. The work frames automated profiling as a growing privacy threat.
arxiv-2505-12702:
Finding an object named in words and tracing it through a video is a core skill for editing and robotics. Tianming Liang and six co-authors argue in a 2025 paper that current test sets are too easy: most use clips of a few seconds with the object in plain sight. They built Long-RVOS, a benchmark made of much longer videos.

The set holds more than 2,000 videos that average over 60 seconds each. Objects in them get hidden, vanish and return, and survive cuts between shots. Each object carries three kinds of written description, covering looks, motion, and relations in space and time. The authors add two new scores for steadiness over time. Six leading methods struggled badly on the set. Their own baseline, ReferMo, uses motion cues and a local-to-global design to do better.
arxiv-2505-12802:
Andersen and co-authors weigh newborn stars in a metal-poor cloud to test whether poverty changes their sizes at birth in this 2025 paper. The survey region holds about a third of the Sun's metal content. If metals shape how gas fragments, the mass spectrum of new stars should shift there.

Using the Webb telescope's infrared camera, the team picked out a buried young cluster and measured each member's mass and dust cover. After correcting for how deep the data reach, the mass spectrum peaked near 0.16 suns. Local clusters peak higher, near a quarter of a sun. The gap hints that low metal content does tilt star birth toward smaller stars. The authors warn the answer leans on the cluster's assumed age of one million years; an older age would lift the peak. They call for more metal-poor regions to confirm the shift.
arxiv-2505-13302:
People share news more readily when a picture rides along, and the picture makes even false stories feel truer. Alice Plebe, Timothy Douglas, Diana Riazi, and Maria del Rio-Chanona ask whether vision-language models fall for the same pull. They built a set of fact-checked political stories, true and false, each paired with its image.

A crafted prompting method got four leading models to give sharing decisions instead of refusing. Adding the image raised resharing of false news by about fourteen and a half percent, and of true news by about five. Giving a model a dark, antisocial persona made false sharing worse; a Republican persona made it less sensitive to truth. One smaller model resisted the image effect best. The authors warn that multimodal systems inherit human-like biases.
arxiv-2505-13602:
Evening and morning limbs of an exoplanet atmosphere differ, Matthew Murphy and a large team of co-authors show in a 2025 paper. The planet is WASP-107 b. Limb-resolved transmission spectroscopy can transform understanding of such atmospheres, since the two limbs can be measured apart rather than merged into one average spectrum that hides their contrasts.

Data from several JWST instruments supply a panchromatic characterization, spanning many wavelengths at once. Composition and cloud variations between the limbs are reported. The study also gives insight into stellar contamination, a known nuisance that can mimic or mask atmospheric signals when the host star is active. Readers get a case study in how much detail limb-resolved work can recover for a single planet.
arxiv-2505-13702:
Mariana Fazio and seven co-authors clean up ultrafast diffraction data in twenty twenty-five. MeV ultrafast electron diffraction watches materials change structure in real time. A laser pulse triggers the change and an electron beam probes it. Low signal forces averaging over thousands of shots.

Shot-to-shot beam instabilities distort some patterns in that average. Finding and removing the anomalous patterns improves accuracy. Their method is fully unsupervised, needing no labeled examples. A convolutional autoencoder rebuilds each diffraction pattern. Patterns with high reconstruction error are flagged as anomalous by statistical analysis. Readers in ultrafast science get data hygiene that keeps rare bad shots from blurring fast structural movies.
arxiv-2505-14002:
Wei Zhao and Tao Luo prove when training of neural solvers for physics equations will settle well, in a 2025 paper. Such solvers learn to meet an equation and its edge rules. Users need proof that training will not drift or stall in odd cases.

For straight equations, they grow a past frame to cover a broad class of cases. For curved equations, they prove steps move toward key points with no need for huge networks. Their proof also shows a built in brake that keeps weights from flying off. Test runs on computers back the claims for both solver types.
arxiv-2505-14102:
Shogo Iwazaki, Junpei Komiyama, and Masaaki Imaizumi study decision problems where each choice comes with a rich description. Their work appeared in twenty twenty-five. In contextual bandits, a forecaster picks among arms and learns from rewards, as in ads and recommendations.

Their version uses kernels, which allow flexible links between context and reward. With Gaussian kernels, older methods gave useless bounds once the feature count grew past a slow threshold. The authors add a mild assumption about how contexts are drawn. Under it, learning with almost no regret stays possible even when dimensions grow as fast as the sample count. They also study lenient regret, which tolerates a small loss each round, and derive its rate.
arxiv-2505-14702: A set of maths rules for gauge fields, the Vafa-Witten rules, form a space of answers whose clean shape is key to their use. Bo Dai and Ren Guan nudge those rules in a 2025 study with a small added term. They ask if the nudged space stays smooth for most picks of the nudge size, for two gauge groups.
arxiv-2505-14902:
Junyi Liu and co-authors present RISC-Q, a tool that generates control chips for quantum computers. Such chips must react within a millionth of a second and time signals to a billionth, far past what normal real-time systems do. Past custom systems are hard to scale or adapt, since their tool chains are split and hand-built.

RISC-Q works like a RISC-V setup, so programmers meet a known interface. Built with a hardware design language, it lets users set parameters and swap modules with ease. The team shows it can match the speed of current control chips with far less design effort.
arxiv-2505-15202:
Yu Zhang, Linyu Peng, and Bing-Zhao Li present a study from twenty twenty-five on filling in graph signals that take complex values. A graph signal gives each node a value, like a trait or a reading. In many fields the values are complex, with two parts. Kernel methods can rebuild such signals from samples on a few nodes, but the complex case was near untouched.

Their frame plants the nodes in a high dimensional complex space that hugs a low dimensional shape. Standard kernel tools then stretch to that shape, with tools for its curves and measures. They give both classic kernels and ones built from the graph's own links. Tests on fake and real data beat plain kernel routes.
arxiv-2505-15502:
Christian Röver and Tim Friede examine in 2025 a statistical shortcut that turns earlier study results into a head start for a new trial. Such head starts, called meta-analytic-predictive priors, blend past data into the starting beliefs of an analysis. They also drive shrinkage estimation, where a new result is pulled gently toward what came before, sometimes called dynamic borrowing.

An odd corner case drives the paper: what if the past data are a single study? The math still works, they show, but the analyst's own starting assumptions then carry far more weight and must be chosen with care. The authors lay out the case using the standard normal hierarchical model, the workhorse for pooling study effects. Worked examples from clinical medicine show how to run the method and how to read its output without fooling oneself.
arxiv-2505-15602:
Patrick Cheridito, Jean-Loup Dupret, and Donatien Hainaut brought in 2025 deep learning to control problems where the world moves continuously and jumps without warning. Such stochastic control tasks, finite in horizon, defeat grid methods in high dimensions. Their model-based scheme trains two networks in turns: one plays the controller, the other prices every state.

Training targets come from the classic Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation, in two forms drawn from the continuous-time dynamic programming principle. That keeps the networks honest to the true dynamics, jumps included. Tests on several problems showed accuracy and reach into dimensions older methods cannot touch. The authors present the loop as a general solver. Finance and engineering, where jumps are facts of life, are the natural homes.
arxiv-2505-15802:
Sarah Wessinger and co-authors use deep learning to speed radar weather estimates in a 2025 paper. Near the sea surface, air layers bend radar signals in ways that depend on the weather profile. Standard simulations of that bending are accurate but slow, which limits their use in the field.

The team trained image-to-image networks to predict the propagation factor, a measure of how the environment reshapes a signal. Inputs were maps of the air's bending traits, and outputs were the matching factor maps. One model handled several signal frequencies at once. Results showed the networks can learn the pattern well enough to serve as a fast stand-in for the heavy simulations. The authors frame the work as a step toward quick, practical radar planning tools.
arxiv-2505-16002:
Sasha Boguraev and co-authors prod chat models from inside to test if one shared gear serves a flock of tongue forms. The forms, where a front part waits for its mate past a gap, span asks and kin clauses. Tongue lore holds the flock shares deep traits. Their 2025 study swaps inner states between runs of kin forms and watches the calls bend. Like bends mark like gears.

The models do meet on near-same deep reads of the flock. Three hid wells bend those reads: how oft a form runs, what fills the gap, and what wraps the clause. In-tool proof can thus push tongue lore, not just ape it.
arxiv-2505-16102:
Yash Kumar Atri, Thomas Shin, and Thomas Hartvigsen built this 2025 chatbot helper for weight-loss surgery care. Surgery for severe obesity works best when patients stay engaged with surgeons, dietitians, and others for years. Access barriers keep many from timely, expert-checked answers. Their system pairs a language model with live retrieval of medical evidence.

The tool, bRAGgen, refreshes its answers whenever its confidence dips below shifting thresholds. That self-updating design keeps replies current and lowers the risk of stale advice. The team also built bRAGq, a set of 1,302 surgery questions checked by an expert surgeon, the first large benchmark for this field. In two-stage testing, their system beat leading models on model-scored and surgeon-scored measures alike.
arxiv-2505-16202:
Don Page answers a claim that black holes cannot be made from light alone. A recent paper had argued that quantum effects, as light squeezes itself, bleed off energy fast enough to stop any event horizon from forming. Page's 2025 note grants that such black holes are wildly unlikely in our universe, whether by nature or by any human effort we can foresee.

He argues, though, that the ban is not absolute. In idealized setups, nearly flat pulses of light can be crashed together to form black holes of almost any size, down toward the Planck length. Only a small share of the energy escapes, as scattered light or as electron-positron pairs. The note draws a line between what physics forbids and what practice merely rules out. That line is the heart of the dispute over these light-born black holes, called kugelblitze.
arxiv-2505-16302:
Olivier Besson tackles a classic statistics problem when data are scarce in a 2025 paper. Estimating a covariance matrix, the web of how variables move together, fails when there are fewer samples than variables: the sample version is singular and unusable. Regularization, adding stabilizing structure, is mandatory. Besson builds the fix inside the matrix's Cholesky factor, its triangular square root.

His route starts from Stein's loss, a standard way to score covariance estimates. He derives the best estimator for each data set, then the oracle that is best on average, then a practical scheme that fills the missing part of the factorization. Simulations test it against rival methods, varying how ill-conditioned the true matrix is and how its spectrum is shaped. The method targets radar and signal work, where short data records are the norm.
arxiv-2505-16502:
Wu and co-authors propose RecServe, a framework for serving large language models across device, edge, and cloud tiers. Small devices can only run small models, while sending everything to the cloud overloads it and wastes bandwidth. Cascading systems that pass hard queries upward exist, but they lean on hand-tuned thresholds that lag behind changing networks and task mixes.

RecServe judges each task's difficulty with a confidence score and routes it to a model of matching size, tier by tier. A sliding window tracks recent confidence patterns and adjusts the cut-offs on the fly. Across eight datasets it beat the cascade baseline on both quality and communication efficiency, and it cut the communication load by more than half compared with cloud-only serving. The catalog record is garbled with affiliation notes and lists fewer authors than the text.
arxiv-2505-16802:
Dominique Laurent and Nicolas Spyratos present, in a 2025 paper, a chase-based method for answering warehouse queries truthfully even when the data hold gaps and contradictions. Data warehouses often follow a star schema, one fact table ringed by dimension tables. Missing values and clashes make naive answers unreliable, so the field asks for consistent answers: results true in every repaired version of the data.

Earlier work by the same authors handled plain queries with fast algorithms giving either the exact consistent answer or tight bounds. This paper extends the machinery to analytic queries, those with grouping and aggregation, including the filtering clause that rides on groups. When the selection condition splits cleanly by attribute, their algorithms stay fast, scaling near-linearly with warehouse size. The result is a practical route to answers a warehouse can stand behind, aggregates included.
arxiv-2505-17002:
Abdul Hannan and co-authors matched faces to voices with a new method in two thousand twenty-five. People can often guess a face from a voice roughly. Teaching machines that skill aids search and media tools. Past methods leaned on careful mining of negative pairs. They also hinged on a sensitive margin setting. The new method, PAEFF, aligns the two data types first.

Face and voice embeddings live in unlike spaces. Precise alignment brings them into a shared frame. A gated fusion then blends them with learned weights. Right-angle constraints keep fused codes clean and separate. Tests on a celebrity video dataset showed clear gains. The authors say careful fusion beats brute-force mining. The method may help verify speakers in video calls.
arxiv-2505-17102:
Pramit Bhattacharyya and Arnab Bhattacharya introduce a 2025 language model built for Bangla. Bangla, also called Bengali, has rich word forms that standard tokenizers handle poorly. Their model, BanglaByT5, reads raw bytes instead of tokens. It is the first byte-level encoder-decoder model made just for Bangla, built on a small Google design.

Training used a curated 14-gigabyte corpus of literary and newspaper texts. Tests covered generation and classification tasks, in both zero-shot and supervised modes. The small model beat several multilingual and larger rivals on those tests. The authors say byte-level work suits languages with complex word forms. The tool is light enough for low-resource settings, yet scales as well.
arxiv-2505-17202:
Arnav Verma, Kushin Mukherjee, Christopher Potts, Elisa Kreiss, and Judith Fan test whether AI models read charts the way people do in this 2025 paper. Understanding a data visualization mixes seeing, number sense, and language, and a model that merely answers well might still err in alien ways.

Their human centered protocol puts models and people on the very same items: five known tests of human chart literacy plus one built for models. Eight vision language models scored below people on average, even under lenient grading. Item by item, model rankings loosely echoed human ones, yet every model's error pattern differed reliably from the human pattern. The authors offer the protocol for finding models that could truly stand in for human chart reasoning in science.
arxiv-2505-17302: Marcio Gameiro, Brittany Gelb, and Konstantin Mischaikow addressed a foundational question in twenty twenty-five: what about a dynamical system can be computed from data? Dynamics at the level of invariant sets, the theory's central objects, is known to be not computable in general. The authors recall a coarser description built from order theory and algebraic topology. They prove this characterization can be identified from approximations. That opens a path for machine learning to characterize dynamics with rigor rather than mere fit.
arxiv-2505-17502:
Konstantinos Gkouliaras and co-authors demonstrate quantum key distribution running on a working nuclear reactor, a first step toward quantum-secured control of future reactors. Quantum keys promise security based on physics rather than hard math, valuable for reactors designed to run unattended in remote places. But any add-on to a reactor must respect strict limits on delay, stability, and compatibility.

Their system ran a standard protocol over fiber on Purdue's fully digital research reactor. It encrypted two thousand signals in real time over distances up to well over a hundred kilometers, depending on the cipher. Key rates stayed stable with low error. A reserve key pool covers hours of downtime. Latency stayed minimal.
arxiv-2505-17602:
Muhammad Abdullah and Furqan Shaukat present two related networks for outlining lungs and lung spots in chest CT scans, in a 2025 paper. Finding these spots early matters, since lung cancer kills more people than any other cancer. Drawing the lung borders and the small growths by hand is slow, and the growths vary widely in shape.

Their design adds attention steps and leftover shortcut links to a U-shaped network, so the model can weigh which image features matter. Wider filters let it take in more context at no extra cost. Tested on the large public LUNA16 scan set, the method scored better than recent rivals on standard overlap measures. The team shares its code and prepared data for others to check and reuse.
arxiv-2505-17902:
Ignacio Cabrera Martin and co-authors survey how machine learning can keep learning as its data world keeps changing, in a 2025 paper. Models trained once often fail when the stream of data drifts over time. The survey unifies four core problems: data drift, concept drift, catastrophic forgetting, and skewed learning.

The authors review more than 100 studies and sort methods across supervised, unsupervised, and partly supervised learning. They compare test metrics, benchmark data sets, and real uses, and they offer a taxonomy to organize the field. Fresh tools such as adaptive network shapes, meta-learning, and ensembles get special attention. The survey closes by mapping where current methods fall short.
arxiv-2505-18102:
Takashi Ishida, Thanawat Lodkaew, and Ikko Yamane build an alarm for test set gaming into language model benchmarks in a 2025 paper. Posting a benchmark with its answers invites trouble: builders may train on it or tune to it, and scores stop meaning skill. Keeping tests private only moves the gaming into feedback loops with the hosts.

Their method, CapBencher, hides the true answer key by design. For each item it writes several answers that are all sound, then posts just one as the key. That caps the best score any honest model can reach. A model that beats the cap has almost surely seen the key. Tests across benchmarks and training styles show the alarm trips on overfit runs and stays quiet on clean ones.
arxiv-2505-18302:
Gefei Shen and co-authors wrote a paper from 2025 on training object-finding models with far fewer hand-labeled images. Labeling is the slow, costly part of teaching a model to spot things in photos or video. The team asked whether smart picking of which frames to label could cut that cost. Their work rests on a smoothness premise about how such models behave.

They test two picking plans. One spreads picks evenly yet at random across the range of ways objects can appear and move. The other exploits the sameness of video: it skips frames that barely differ from the last. Both plans built training sets that taught the model well. Yet each needed far fewer labeled frames than full training would. The team frames the plans as a route to cheaper training for video-based detection.
arxiv-2505-18502:
Guodong Du and ten co-authors present GraftLLM in 2025, a method for merging skills into large language models. Moving skills between models is hard when the models differ in size and build. Full retraining can erase old skills, while light tuning often fails to absorb new ones.

Their fix stores each source skill as a compact pack of changes, called a SkillPack. A smart squeezing step shrinks the pack while keeping task know-how. Packs can then be grafted onto a target model without wiping its general skill. Tests across transfer, fusion, and step-by-step learning beat older methods, the authors report.
arxiv-2505-18602:
Hengzhe Zhang and co-authors use in 2025 large language models to design the selection step inside evolutionary search for symbolic regression, where algorithms hunt for formulas that fit data. Past attempts to evolve algorithms with language models lacked meaning aware guidance and produced bloated code. Their frame fixes both faults, with a paired selection method that respects meaning and a control on code growth.

Domain knowledge is folded into the prompt so the model makes apt operators. On standard test sets, the model made operators that beat nine expert designed rivals. The evolved operator also improved a leading symbolic regression system. Results suggest language models can serve as meta designers of search parts.
arxiv-2505-18702:
Xiang-Cun Meng predicts the properties of a kind of binary that has never been observed: an eccentric millisecond pulsar paired with a subdwarf B star. Eccentric pulsar plus helium white dwarf systems have drawn attention, and the rotationally delayed accretion-induced collapse scenario was proposed to explain them. Since subdwarf B stars form through similar channels, such pairs should also exist in the Galaxy.

Within that framework, Meng predicts their orbital parameters: pulsar mass, secondary mass, eccentricity, and period. Two detailed binary population synthesis calculations yield a Galactic birth rate and a conservative upper limit of about fifteen thousand such systems. The most optimistic fraction among all pulsar-subdwarf populations could reach over half. These systems are relatively young, a few hundred million years old, so they should appear in young environments. Most of their pulsars should be comparatively light. The predictions are meant to guide searches.
arxiv-2505-19002:
Jin Zhu and co-authors propose semi-pessimistic learning for decisions from fixed data in a 2025 paper. Offline learning must avoid unseen actions that the data never covered. Many tasks also lack reward labels for most records.

Unlabeled data usually far outweighs labeled data, and the method exploits that surplus. It bounds the reward function from below rather than harder value or transition targets. The simpler goal makes learning easier and fits many model-free and model-based methods. Gains are guaranteed under milder conditions than rivals require. Tests and a brain stimulation case for Parkinson's disease show clear competitiveness.
arxiv-2505-19102:
Sergey Samsonov, Marina Sheshukova, Eric Moulines, and Alexey Naumov derive, in twenty twenty-five, statistical guarantees for a stochastic approximation algorithm driven by Markovian noise. Stochastic approximation powers online learning and control: estimates update step by step from noisy data. Here the noise comes from a Markov chain, so samples are dependent. They study the averaged iterates of the linear version. Berry-Esseen bounds, which cap the distance to a Gaussian limit, are derived without asymptotics.

The convergence rate to the Gaussian is one over n to the quarter power. They also validate a block bootstrap method for building confidence intervals under Markov sampling. It is, they say, the first such non-asymptotic guarantee for this setting. A classical rate for estimating asymptotic variance is also recovered.
arxiv-2505-19402:
Tai-Quan Peng and Xuzhen Yang examine how large language models are reshaping classic quantitative methods in communication research. Content analysis, survey research, and experiments are the core methods at stake. Language models do not simply replace those methods. They add new options for coding text, simulating survey respondents, and creating personalized interactive stimuli.

Validity, bias, and interpretability remain open concerns for each use. The authors revisit the classic Lasswell framework of who says what, in which channel, to whom, with what effect. Language models reconfigure message studies, audience analysis, and effects research by enabling varied interpretation and counterfactual tests. The paper urges rigorous and imaginative use that keeps classic research logic in place.
arxiv-2505-19502:
Guang Yang and co-authors build Code-DiTing, small models that judge whether generated code actually does what a task asks, in a 2025 paper. Checking code today leans on reference answers or runnable tests, both rigid. Letting a big model judge is flexible, but plain judges explain little and reasoning judges cost too much.

Their fix distills a giant reasoning model's judgment into compact graders of one and a half and seven billion parameters. Majority voting across tries steadies the verdicts. The small grader beat every same size rival, matching models five times its size, while the larger one pressed further. Explanations come with each score.
arxiv-2505-19602:
Li, Chen, Yang, and Hwang tackled the memory hunger of a new image generation method in twenty twenty-five. Visual autoregressive models build pictures scale by scale, from coarse to fine. Quality and flexibility are strong, but the stored key-value cache grows explosively during generation, wasting memory.

Their framework, ScaleKV, compresses that cache using two observations: layers differ in how much cache they need, and attention patterns change with scale. Layers split into drafters, which spread attention widely and need more cache, and refiners, which focus locally and need little. ScaleKV sizes the cache per layer and per scale accordingly. On a leading text-to-image model, memory fell to ten percent of the original while picture fidelity stayed at pixel level, the authors report.
arxiv-2505-19802:
Zhiyu Wang, Yang Liu, and Hatice Gunes estimate pain from faces with a graph based method in a 2025 paper. Pain shows in small face moves, called action units, and patients who cannot speak need such tools for care. Older data methods can be hard to read and weak at grading how strong pain is.

Their method maps each action unit as a node and links units that often occur together. A graph network then learns from that map, which makes the steps easier to follow. On a public pain data set, the method reached stated scores for pain grading that beat prior work. The authors frame it as a step toward better digital health checks.
arxiv-2505-19902:
Oikonomou and four co-authors proposed a multiple-access scheme in twenty twenty-five for pinching-antenna systems, a cheap way to deliver millimeter-wave signals indoors. A leaky waveguide carries the signal, and small pinch points along it radiate toward users, keeping a clear line of sight. When many pinches serve many users at once, the channel varies sharply with frequency and symbols smear into each other.

The team models the channel as a finite filter and measures that smearing directly. Their fix uses orthogonal frequency-division access, splitting users across tones. A two-stage scheme assigns tones greedily, then fills power per user to lift the worst user's rate. Indoor simulations beat time-sharing designs by a wide margin and stayed strong when some paths were blocked.
arxiv-2505-20002:
Ondřej Straka and Uwe Hanebeck keep a tracking filter's mixture from exploding in a 2025 paper. Filters that follow nonlinear systems often carry a mixture of Gaussian guesses. The standard moves multiply components at every step, forcing brutal pruning that costs accuracy and time. Pre-digesting the noise into mixtures only worsens the growth.

Their idea is to approximate the transition density itself, the law that carries the state forward, as a tidy axis-aligned Gaussian mixture. Two routes to that approximation are derived. Because the transition is approximated once, the posterior keeps a constant number of components forever, with no explicit reduction step. The design also exposes a clean dial: more components buy estimation quality, fewer buy speed. The authors position the method for tracking problems where mixture filters were previously too heavy to run in real time.
arxiv-2505-20402:
Smarra, Capuano, and Kuntz asked in twenty twenty-five whether pulsar timing arrays could detect scalarized supermassive black holes. In some gravity theories, black holes grow a scalar field coat, breaking the classic no-hair picture. A coupling length sets where deviations from Einstein's theory appear.

Collider-scale tests force that length to be small, seemingly ruling out coats on the biggest black holes. Recent work, though, finds a narrow mass window where supermassive holes could still scalarize. The authors compute how this would change the gravitational wave hum from orbiting black hole pairs, recently heard by pulsar timing arrays. Current data mildly favor a nonzero coupling. They warn that eccentric orbits or gas effects could fake the same signal, so longer observation is needed.
arxiv-2505-20702:
Some metals lose all electrical resistance when cooled, and the magnetism inside them changes in telling ways. Riku Matsubayashi and co-authors study one such material, a compound of lanthanum, ruthenium, and phosphorus, in this 2025 paper. They use nuclear magnetic resonance, which reads the magnetic state at chosen atoms inside the material.

Measurements at two atomic sites, phosphorus and lanthanum, let the team track the spin part of a signal called the Knight shift as the field strength changed. They found that the spin response in the cold, resistance-free state grows in direct proportion to the applied field. It also joins smoothly onto the response seen in the normal state above the change point. The team reads this as a textbook case of pairs breaking through the field's effect on orbits.
arxiv-2505-21002:
Muştu and Ekenel hide faces in photos without wrecking the pictures. Privacy law requires consent to process personal images, which starves vision researchers of good face data. Their pipeline detects each face and reads its features. It then repaints the face region with a modern diffusion inpainting model, guided by a text prompt listing the wanted attributes, such as age, gender, or expression.

Because the generator redraws the whole face from the description, the person becomes unrecognizable while the scene stays natural. The method skips the fragile training of adversarial generators used by older anonymizers. The authors aim it at building data sets that researchers can share and use without exposing anyone.
arxiv-2505-21102:
Leighton Barnes, Alex Dytso, and Vincent Poor study estimation for count data in a 2025 statistics paper. Counts of events often follow a Poisson pattern, set by a single rate. A Bayesian estimator guesses that rate from data plus a prior belief. Under a loss that counts absolute error, the best guess is the middle value of the posterior belief.

The authors ask which priors make that best guess follow a chosen rising rule. They build a new family of priors whose best guesses can be any such rule that meets mild conditions. For straight-line rules, their family differs from the standard gamma priors used for decades. The construction works by matching moment conditions in a limit. It is the first clear account of such priors beyond the classic family.
arxiv-2505-22002:
Zijing Hu, Fengda Zhang, and Kun Kuang improve how image generators learn from human taste, in a 2025 study. Diffusion models often draw pictures that miss the text prompt. A method called direct preference optimization can tune them, but it stumbles when good and bad samples look too unlike. The model then cannot tell which traits made one image better. Their fix, D-Fusion, builds training pairs that stay visually close.

Masks guide a fusion step that blends self-attention so the good image keeps the bad one's look while fixing the prompt fit. The method also keeps the noise path that training needs. Tests across several learning methods showed firmer prompt alignment.
arxiv-2505-22102:
Paul Disberg and Ilya Mandel measure, in a 2025 astronomy paper, how fast newborn neutron stars are kicked by the explosions that birth them. The team gathered motions and distances for young lone pulsars and worked out their true three-dimensional speeds. A bell-shaped curve in log space fits the speeds, peaking near one hundred fifty to two hundred kilometers per second.

An older, higher estimate in the literature turns out to rest on a missing correction for bin widths on a log scale. Claims of two speed families also fade under scrutiny. A second method, reading speeds from the wobble of galactic orbits, agrees with the main fit. The authors say the field's scattered results now reconcile.
arxiv-2505-22202:
Hyeonbin Hwang and nine co-authors ask, in 2025 work, whether language models can reason in whole sentences rather than word bits. Models write one small token at a time, while people think in claims and ideas. The team tests if a trained model can be lifted to work in that higher space.

Their frame predicts the code of the next sentence, step by step, instead of the next token. Two code types are tried: one that keeps surface sense, and one trained to look ahead. Guessing can run by turning each code back to text, or by staying in code space the whole way. The look-ahead codes, run in space, matched step-by-step text reasoning across maths, logic, and planning tests, at about half the computing cost. A lens tool shows the hidden steps as plain sentences.
arxiv-2505-22302:
Triantafyllos Kormpakis, Manuel Linares, and Jordi José connect the eruption clocks of neutron stars and white dwarfs into one relation, in this 2025 paper. Both kinds of remnant steal gas from a companion until the stolen layer ignites in a thermonuclear runaway: X-ray bursts on neutron stars, nova eruptions on white dwarfs. How often eruptions repeat should depend on how fast gas piles up.

The team compiled observed recurrence times and inferred accretion rates across burst sources, millihertz oscillators, and recurrent novae. Models for both object types land near one global, inverse-linear relation between waiting time and accretion rate, the first time the two families have been joined this way. Pure helium burst models matched the ultra-compact binary data. One check: the energy ratio between dwarf and star eruptions matches their surface-area ratio. Ignition, they conclude, cares about the local fueling rate, not the host's nature.
arxiv-2505-22602:
Mahtab Alizadeh Vandchali, Fangshuo Liao, and Anastasios Kyrillidis wrote this 2025 paper on how errors grow in sequential learning. In that approach, a hard task is split into simpler parts that are learned one after another. The authors study the process through low-rank linear regression, where each step learns a rank-1 piece and rests on the steps before it.

The paper builds a framework that breaks the full process into a chain of small estimation problems. It then sets bounds on how errors from tight budgets and limited precision spread through the chain. The results show that these errors build up in ways that can be predicted. That gives designers a clearer guide for keeping such systems stable and accurate.
arxiv-2505-22902:
Freddier Cuenca-Montenegro and co-authors show, in a 2025 paper, how quantum coherence can boost a tiny heat engine. Their engine is a single qubit running an Otto cycle, the quantum cousin of a classic engine loop. The setting is noisy, as real devices are. By spending the coherence stored in noisy quantum states, the engine beats the classical limit on efficiency.

Noise type matters. One kind of damping raised both the work drawn out and the efficiency under partial heat contact. Another raised the work but lowered efficiency. The team also proved the engine's quantum nature by breaking a classic bound on time correlations. They built the whole cycle as a quantum circuit with realistic noise, and propose a way to price the circuit's energy cost.
arxiv-2505-23302:
Tim Hargreaves and five co-authors bring state space models into the Turing.jl ecosystem in two thousand twenty-five. State space models are a strong class for time series in many fields. Past software for them lacks modular build and scale. That gap slows trials and blocks advanced inference.

Two new Julia packages fill the gap. One defines models in a shared, composable way. The other runs inference, from Kalman filters to particle filters and mixes. Code reuse cuts build time and lifts reliability. Memory care and graphics chip speed target large jobs. The work sits inside a known probabilistic programming system.
arxiv-2505-23402:
Lusetti and co-authors take the lowest frequency radio look yet at a famous merging galaxy cluster, in a 2025 paper. The cluster hosts twin shock relics, one nicknamed the sausage, plus other faint radio glows. Waves below one hundred megahertz trace the oldest, weakest cosmic ray electrons, key to how relics shine.

Ten hours with a Dutch low band array gave a sharp, noise limited image. Joined with older data from four other telescopes, the team mapped the spectrum's slope and bend across the relics. Both relics showed the same shock strength estimate, near three times the sound speed. Low frequency views like this pin down how cluster shocks boost particles.
arxiv-2505-23502:
Mingtai Xie and a large team of co-authors study, in a 2025 paper, a magnet built on a triangular lattice that may host an exotic quantum state. The compound KCeSe2 sets its magnetic atoms in triangles. A special bond-dependent interaction, named for Kitaev, is prized because it may yield a quantum spin liquid.

Tests of magnetism, heat, and neutron scattering all pointed the same way. The bond force proved strong and of the attractive sign, next to a competing standard interaction. Together they settle KCeSe2 into a striped magnetic order. A field applied along the special bond direction brought two phase changes.
