Triangular Kitaev materials widen a search long confined to honeycomb lattices.
arxiv-2505-23702:
Six researchers merge neural networks with finite volume solvers in a 2025 paper. Hyperbolic conservation laws govern shocks in fluids and traffic, and their true solutions jump sharply. Classic finite volume methods keep the right physics but lack accuracy and flexibility in hard cases.

Their architecture learns update rules over wider space and time stencils while keeping conservation built in. One variant trains on solution data; the other trains without labels, using a weak form residual loss. Errors fell up to tenfold against the classic Godunov method, beating high order schemes and rivaling heavier solvers. On traffic problems, from equations and real highway data alike, wave shapes were captured with higher fidelity.
arxiv-2505-23802:
Suhana Bedi and co-authors introduce MedHELM in a 2025 paper, a holistic test frame for language models on medical tasks. Exam scores near perfect do not show how models handle the breadth of real clinical work.

MedHELM rests on a clinician-checked taxonomy of five categories, over twenty subcategories, and more than one hundred tasks. Twenty-nine clinicians helped shape that map of real duties. A suite of dozens of benchmarks runs models across the map. The frame is built to grow as new tasks appear. Scores can be split by category to expose weak spots that a single exam hides. Health AI teams get a fairer way to judge readiness for clinic use.
arxiv-2505-23902:
Jeonghoon Lim and co-authors compare disk simulations of planet formation in a 2025 paper. The streaming instability gathers dust grains into dense clumps. Those clumps are the seeds from which planetesimals grow.

Cheap simulations ignore vertical layering of the disk. Expensive ones include gravity-settled dust layers near the midplane. Whether the cheap version captures midplane behavior was unclear. The team ran both kinds across pressure gradient settings. Grain size is fixed at a tenth of the stopping scale. Saturated states of the instability are compared in detail. Readers learn when the shortcut simulation can be trusted for planet birth studies.
arxiv-2505-24002:
Vaishnav Ramesh and co-authors judge in a 2025 study photo quality without a reference image, teaching their model to use scene depth as a guide. Quality models trained on one distortion set often fail on new, natural flaws. Their Depth-CAR module distills depth and texture into a structure-aware signal, bringing object prominence and contrast into the verdict.

A bridge module fuses a transformer's wide view with a convolutional net's local detail, also speeding training and use. The combined model topped synthetic and authentic benchmarks and, more telling, held its lead on unseen data sets and natural flaws like haze and low light.
arxiv-2505-24102:
Mahmood Jasim and Narges Mahyar published this reflection paper in 2025 on visual analytics in civic life. Such systems turn public data into interactive displays that help officials and communities decide. Many work well as research prototypes, then fade once the project ends. The authors draw on their own experience designing, building, and deploying these systems with city partners to explain why.

They argue the barriers are only partly technical. Tight budgets and complex development matter, but so do organizational hierarchies, gaps between what designers assume and what stakeholders need, and plain reluctance to adopt new tools. Their remedies stress deeper integration into daily workflows, fair engagement with all affected groups, and funding models that outlast the pilot. The paper aims to close the gap between civic data research and lasting practice.
arxiv-2505-24202:
Pooja Devi and co-authors link prominence eruptions to coronal mass ejections in a 2025 study of solar cycle 24. Prominences are cool, dense structures in the sun's outer air that can erupt outward. The team used two space instruments to catalog events from May 2010 to December 2019. They found 1225 eruptions and rated how clearly each matched a mass ejection.

About fifty four percent of eruptions matched an ejection at some confidence level. Most matched ejections showed a bright core, suggesting the prominence becomes the core at greater heights. Timing and direction patterns shifted between solar quiet and active phases. Speeds rose from prominence to core to leading edge. Readers see two phenomena as stages of one structure.
arxiv-2505-24302:
Yike Wang, Shangbin Feng, Yulia Tsvetkov, and Hannaneh Hajishirzi present a framework for tracking how language models update their science knowledge in a 2025 paper. Models are now used to support research, but science moves fast and stored facts go stale. Updating a model can also erase old knowledge or fail to take in new claims.

Their framework scores three things: how much old knowledge survives an update, how well new claims are learned, and how well the model projects to future claims. Testing five update methods across ten fields, they found even the best kept only part of the old knowledge and projected poorly. The work sets a clear bar for a hard, neglected problem.
arxiv-2506-00002:
Hao Mark Chen and co-authors tackle the data problems behind using large language models to design computer chips, in a 2025 paper. Design data is scarce, uneven in quality, and often locked inside companies. The team proposes training across those private sources without centralizing them, then personalizing the model at use time for each client.

Their first stage organizes decentralized training in a hierarchy and aggregates models using user-defined quality metrics, so poor data drags less. The second stage speeds up and improves generation for each user, guided by a new efficiency metric they call Trueput. The framework targets practical deployment, where an almost-right circuit is worthless. Results and analysis focus on closing the gap between generated designs and ones engineers can actually ship.
arxiv-2506-00102:
Ema Puljak, Maurizio Pierini, and Artur Garcia-Saez use a tensor network to hunt anomalies in particle collision data in a 2025 paper. Finding new physics at the Large Hadron Collider needs fresh algorithms. Tensor networks sit between classical and quantum learning and can be cheap to run.

Their model is a matrix product state with a feature map that keeps lengths fixed. It reads a compressed picture of simulated events made by an autoencoder. In tests it spotted new phenomena better than established quantum methods. The authors argue such networks could sharpen discovery searches at the collider while staying efficient.
arxiv-2506-00302:
Can Polat and co-authors build a richer dataset for materials science that goes beyond atomic positions in a 2025 paper. Most crystal datasets hold only geometry files, which limits modern multimodal learning. Their framework adds two-dimensional projections and structured text notes, such as lattice measures and coordination data, to each structure.

Experts in the loop helped keep the annotations accurate and uniform. The dataset supports two tasks: predicting properties and summaries from mixed inputs, and generating new crystals under partial supervision. Tests with leading language and vision models exposed large gaps between input types and showed that annotation quality drives generalization. The data and code are shared openly for benchmarking.
arxiv-2506-00402:
Vishwanath Pratap Singh and co-authors use causal discovery to untangle why speech recognition fails children, in a 2025 paper. Children's speech systems lag well behind adult ones. Many factors pile up: small vocal tracts, still-growing pronunciation, limited vocabulary, and background noise. Standard analyses test each factor alone. That misses how the factors drive each other.

The team learned a causal graph among body, mind, and setting factors. Age, for instance, can hurt accuracy directly and also through pronunciation. Causal measures then sized each factor's true effect. The analysis also covered fine-tuned models to see what changes. System builders gain a priority list for fixes. Fairer voice tools for children are the goal.
arxiv-2506-00602:
Karina Arias-Calluari, Theotime Colin, Tanya Latty, Mary Myerscough, and Eduardo Altmann wrote this 2025 study on reading honey bee colony health from hive temperature. Bees hold the nursery zone of the hive at a near-fixed heat, and stress breaks that grip. The team turned that trait into a test of colony strength.

Heat waves in the wild act as ready-made stress tests. By watching how each hive's inner heat answers the outer swings, the method grades how hard the colony must work to hold its line. Twenty-two hives were tracked across the year, three of which later collapsed. Their data showed clear stress signatures before failure. The authors propose a three-step scale, stable, warning, and collapse, readable from a few heat measures, as a cheap, hands-off watch for beekeepers.
arxiv-2506-00702:
The gradient method is the simplest way to solve a system of linear equations, yet it crawls when the matrix is awkward. Ibrahima Dione proposes a stabilized version tied to the normal equation. The classic method needs the matrix to be symmetric and positive, and it leans heavily on a well-chosen step size.

The stabilized algorithm drops both demands. It converges globally as long as the matrix is merely nonsingular, with no structure assumed and no step-size artistry required. Tests cover small and large systems, structured and unstructured matrices, and well- and ill-conditioned cases. The 2025 paper gives a humble method new reach for the linear systems that sit inside countless computations.
arxiv-2506-00802:
Pradhan, Lalnuntluanga, and Giri study how to separate nuclear effects in neutrino interactions using a special frame of reference, in a 2025 paper. Neutrino experiments like DUNE need precise interaction models, but two kinds of nuclear effects blur together: the state of the nucleus before the hit and the interactions of outgoing particles afterward.

The authors use centre-of-momentum variables, an angle and an energy defined in that frame, which respond mainly to the later effects. They apply the idea to eta meson production in the DUNE near detector. The angle, they show, can sharpen models of the outgoing-particle effects, while the energy helps pick out clean events where the neutrino struck a hydrogen nucleus.
arxiv-2506-01002:
Michael Maalouly and co-authors study how drifting pairs spread apart at the ocean surface. Their twenty twenty-five paper uses a global ocean simulation that holds both fast internal waves and slower swirling turbulence. Theory from a simpler turbulence frame predicts that spread laws mirror the energy spectrum shape.

Two regions, the Kuroshio Extension and the Gulf Stream, gave contrasting wave and swirl mixes by season. In winter, spread measures matched the spectrum shape well. In summer, when swirls weaken and high waves gain weight, the match broke down. The split tells modelers when the classic theory can be trusted for search, spill, and drift forecasts.
arxiv-2506-01102:
Julia Lee Romero and co-authors teach computers to spot the key steps inside first-person videos of hands-on tasks. Such recognition helps with training aids and assistive tools, but steps unfold over long spans that strain normal video models. Their framework, GLEVR, turns the task into labeling nodes on a graph, where each clip of the video is one node.

The graphs stay sparse and cheap to run, yet the method beat larger existing models by a wide margin. Training also draws on third-person videos of the same tasks and on automatic captions, added as extra nodes. The team tried several ways to wire the nodes together. On the Ego-Exo4D benchmark, the graph approach clearly outran prior methods for fine-grained step recognition.
arxiv-2506-01302:
Zhengyu Fang, Xiaoge Zhang, Anyin Zhao, and a team of co-authors review how graph neural networks are reshaping computer-aided drug discovery. A molecule is a natural graph, with atoms as dots and bonds as links, and these networks learn patterns directly from that structure.

The review covers three big jobs: dreaming up new candidate molecules, predicting how a molecule will behave, and warning when two drugs would clash in the body. The authors sort the existing models by the kind of input they take and the task they serve, and they gather the standard test datasets in one place. They close by drawing out the trends they see across the field and the directions most likely to matter next.
arxiv-2506-01602:
Kensuke Mitsuzawa, writing alone in a 2025 paper, proposes a way to spot words that are changing meaning. Word senses shift over time, and tracking those shifts helps read old texts and social change. His method borrows a statistics tool, maximum mean discrepancy, which measures how far apart two sets of data sit.

The tool picks out the features that best mark a word's use in each era and scores how much that use has moved. That gives both a flag for shifting words and an account of how the shift unfolded over several periods. The author says this is the first use of the tool for sense change, and tests support the method. Such tools can help dictionary makers and historians date when new senses took hold.
arxiv-2506-01702:
Dominik Macko describes mdok, a detection system for AI written text entered in the PAN shared task at CLEF 2025. Language models now write text in many tongues that people cannot tell from human work, which opens doors to plagiarism, spam, and false news. Automated detection helps, but staying robust on new kinds of data is hard.

The mdok approach fine tunes smaller language models for text sorting rather than using giant ones. It ran in both subtasks of the Voight-Kampff detection contest for 2025. One subtask asks a plain human or machine call, the other sorts varied human AI teamwork cases. The system ranked first in both, the notebook reports.
arxiv-2506-01802:
Heming Zhu and co-authors build clothed human avatars that stay sharp even at very close zoom, by fixing how the surface is tracked. Their 2025 paper names the flaw in past work: depth drift between the avatar's skin and the true surface forces the look model to fake detail. Errors grow glaring at 4K views.

The fix leans on two-dimensional video point trackers, which shrug off shading traps. A latent warp model carries their guidance into three dimensions. A staged training plan anchors point tracks to the rendered avatar, curbing drift and adding depth sense. A new dataset of five long multi-view shoots, shot on forty high-end cameras, tests the method. Gains show in both looks and shape accuracy.
arxiv-2506-01902:
Xinliu Zhong, Kayhan Batmanghelich, and Li Sun teach medical image-text models to notice when a report's meaning has been scrambled. Contrastive pretraining pairs scans with reports, but biomedical language is dense and easy to fake-match. Their 2025 method perturbs reports: same words, broken structure. The model must pick the true report from its scrambled twins for a given image. A parallel track sharpens both senses, contrasting image sub-regions with sub-words under attention weights.

The dual pressure builds representations that carry real semantics, not bag-of-words shortcuts. Wide tests on downstream biomedical tasks beat strong baselines. Robustness improves along with accuracy. The team offers the recipe to labs pretraining on hospital archives, where reports are messy and meaning is everything.
arxiv-2506-02102:
Viuho, Fynbo, and Andersen measure the faint night-sky glow that limits ground astronomy in a 2025 paper. In the near infrared, sky glow between bright air lines sets how faint a target can be. Scattered light from those very lines corrupts most measures. The team used narrow clean bands and a mid-size telescope on La Palma to dodge the scatter.

Zenith glow came out near the values reported for other top sites. Two bands gave only upper bounds, one from scarce clean spectrum and one from weak detector reach at the red end. The authors say careful band choice is the key to honest glow counts for faint-object work.
arxiv-2506-02202:
The authors derived how magnetic fields move in a plasma with Hall currents in a 2025 physics paper. In a plasma threaded by a field, charged bits drift in a sideways pattern between hits, which yields Hall currents. Heat flow across the plasma adds a second twist, called thermal diffusion.

The pair work out the field equations with both effects in play, from standard electrodynamics. They then test the terms on simple models of field shape. One term shows how a seed field can grow from nothing in an unmagnetized plasma, a trick known as the Biermann battery. Such math guides models of stars and fusion devices.
arxiv-2506-02302:
Russell Scheinberg and co-authors teach language models to use grammar rules they already know. Big models can state a rule clearly yet still pick the wrong sentence when judging which of a pair is grammatical. Their trick, grammar prompting, has a large model first write a short note on the rule at play.

That note is fed back as extra context before the judging model answers. The method lifted scores on test sets in English, Chinese, and Russian across many grammar points. Small, cheap models gained the most: the note alone closed about a fifth of their gap to big models. Paired with step-by-step reasoning, it closed over half. The authors offer the cue as a nearly free upgrade for smaller models.
arxiv-2506-02702:
Tibor Kubík and co-authors present ToothForge in 2025, a method that generates new three-dimensional teeth automatically. Dental shape data sets are small, which starves learning models. Their method works in the frequency domain, where a tooth shape becomes a compact spectrum that a model can learn and sample in milliseconds.

Raw spectra are unstable, since each shape's harmonics can twist differently. The team aligns all spectra to a shared basis before training, which removes that bias and frees the method from requiring identical mesh wiring. On real dental crowns, aligned training rebuilt shapes more faithfully than unaligned. The authors also show shape compression and blending, and note uses beyond dentistry.
arxiv-2506-02902:
Marek Kopciuch and Adam Miranowicz compare two ways to model spectral features of atomic vapors, in a paper from 2025. One way uses a Hamiltonian that can lose energy, and the other uses a fuller operator that also tracks quantum jumps. Those jumps refill states and shape real behavior.

For the alkali vapor they study, the simpler model alone often misses key spectral traits. In some cases the two methods place special degeneracy points in different spots, or give them different orders, or one finds points the other lacks. A hybrid method shows how jumps reshape the simpler spectrum into the full one. The authors warn that jump effects must be counted for a sound description.
arxiv-2506-03002:
Alex NieMiera, William Good, and Huey-Wen Lin compute how gluons share momentum inside a kaon with lattice QCD, in work from twenty twenty-five. The kaon is a meson made of quark pairs, and its gluon content is hard to probe in labs. Lattice methods compute it from first principles on a space time grid.

The team took more than a million measurements on a shared lattice ensemble with a light pion mass. They tuned a smoothing step to balance signal quality against long range physics. The gluon momentum share came out near fifty-six parts in a hundred at a set energy scale. They also extracted the full gluon distribution and matched it against equation based forecasts and pion data from the same ensemble.
arxiv-2506-03102:
Sophie Greenwood, Karen Levy, Solon Barocas, Hoda Heidari, and Jon Kleinberg study how to design an AI helper that a person may hand a task to, in a paper from 2025. People judge each case by what they can see, so cases that look the same get treated the same.

The best helper for such handoffs can beat the best lone agent by a wide margin, the authors show. Finding that best helper is hard in the broad case, since the task is a mix puzzle. They still give fast methods for wide sub cases, and tests of a helper tuned over time did well in practice.
arxiv-2506-03702:
Khodabakhshi and two co-authors widen the classic model of a collapsing star to many possible surroundings. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. The Oppenheimer-Snyder model pairs a uniform interior with a Schwarzschild exterior. Real exteriors might carry charge or a cosmological constant. The authors allow any static spherical exterior. Interiors stay of the expanding-universe FLRW type.

Careful coordinates keep the seam between inside and outside smooth. Flat and closed interior cases each get their system. General formulas track apparent and event horizons during collapse. Energy conditions on the matter are checked along the way. Examples cover charged and cosmological black holes. A conjecture on horizon formation time caps the study.
arxiv-2506-03802:
Athanasopoulos and Dimitrakakis teach match markets to learn fair ends from thin feed in this twenty twenty-five paper. Two sides pick mates, then play a foe game with the mate they drew. Pay grades for those games start dim to all hands in the match.

Inside, a match fair point is set where no hand gains by a lone shift. A sway grade counts how far a guess sits from that fair point for the run. Their tool bids by bright-side grades of each pay cell it has yet to test. Proof caps the sway growth in a slow, fair curve class for the tool. Mock runs back the proof with like sway paths in play.
arxiv-2506-03902:
Eleftheria Tsipidi and seven co-authors ask whether the flow of information in a text rises and falls in regular waves. Their 2025 paper starts from a known idea: speakers try to spread information evenly so listeners are neither bored nor swamped. In practice the rate wobbles around an average, and the team test whether the wobble itself has a beat.

Using a wave-fitting method plus a new time-scaling step, they scan texts in six languages, from English and Spanish to Basque. Steady beats show up across the board. Many of the strongest beats line up with discourse structure, such as shifts between topics or sections. The authors read this as a real pressure in language, not noise. Their tools could serve studies of style, teaching, and speech planning.
arxiv-2506-04102:
Thomas Kiely and Cenke Xu published this physics paper in 2025. It asks whether a topological insulator keeps its special status when noise scrambles the phases of its electrons. Such materials conduct on their surface while insulating inside, and their status is captured by a number called a topological index.

Working with a flat Chern insulator and a three-dimensional cousin, the authors define the index through the state's correlation pattern. As the scrambling, called dephasing, grows, the index flips at a sharp threshold from special to ordinary. The flip can be read from the whole system or from one small patch. Even samples perched near the edge of losing their status still need a finite dose of noise to flip. Messy, disordered samples near their own edge showed the same grit. Topology, it seems, is stubborn.
arxiv-2506-04402:
Richard Kessler and co-authors simulate a supernova survey for the Roman Space Telescope. The survey will gather type Ia supernovae to pin down how dark energy behaves. The team built a catalog-level fake run of the strategy a survey panel proposed. Their chain covers light curve fits, photo-based distances, sorting, and bias fixes.

After cuts, the fake sample held ten thousand Roman events. A ground survey adds forty-four hundred more events to the joint fit. The dark energy score from the pair sits well above the mission bar. One caveat is named plain: model training errors for the supernovae were left out. Even so, the study maps the gains the survey design should give.
arxiv-2506-04702:
Shobhan Dev Mandal and Sakuntala Chatterjee present a 2025 paper on how a swimming bacterium hunts food in a moving pattern. Escherichia coli bacteria steer toward higher concentrations of attractant, a behavior called chemotaxis. The authors place a single cell in a sine wave of attractant that travels through space.

Simulations measured the cell's drift across many wave speeds. At slow wave speeds, the drift pointed against the wave's motion. As speed rose, the drift dipped, flipped sign, peaked positive, then died away when the wave outran the cell's response. The team explains the odd pattern through timing. Runs with the wave can surf it and feel no gradient, while runs against it feel a growing one. The imbalance steers the drift.
arxiv-2506-05102:
Mostafa Samy and co-authors compare two flexible antenna designs for millimeter wave networks in a 2025 paper. One design slides small antennas along a guide to sit near the user. The other uses a surface of many tuned elements that reflect signals toward users. Both promise stronger links at high frequencies, where signals fade fast.

Simulations show the surface design needs on the order of ten thousand elements to beat the sliding antennas on data rate. That huge count hurts its energy efficiency badly. The sliding design also held up better against hardware flaws and the severe path loss of high bands. The letter gives network designers a clear early verdict on the trade off.
arxiv-2506-05202:
Daniele Tramontano, Yaroslav Kivva, Saber Salehkaleybar, Mathias Drton, and Negar Kiyavash study causal effect identification in latent variable linear non-Gaussian models. Their 2025 paper uses higher-order cumulants to handle latent confounding.

Two hard setups are addressed. One has a single proxy variable that may itself affect the treatment. The other has fewer instruments than treatments, an underspecified instrumental variable case. They prove that causal effects are identifiable with a single proxy or instrument in these settings, and they give estimation methods. Experiments show accuracy and robustness against existing methods, advancing causal inference for linear systems with hidden confounders.
arxiv-2506-05302:
The Perceive Anything Model is set out by Weifeng Lin and co-authors in a 2025 arXiv paper. The model reads regions in photos and videos and gives back names, glosses, use notes, and full captions, with outlines at the same time. It grows a known segment tool by joining a language model. A part called the Semantic Perceiver turns sight traits into tokens the language side can read.

A data clean and boost pipe made millions of region notes for photos and videos. The model runs faster and leaner than past tools of its kind. Scores stay strong across region tasks.
arxiv-2506-05502:
Ya Jiang and co-authors present a watermark that hides multi-part identity data inside AI-written text without distorting it, in a 2025 paper. Most watermarks either warp the text's natural statistics or carry a single detection bit. Their scheme, StealthInk, keeps the original text distribution intact while embedding provenance details like user ID, timestamp, and model ID. Detection needs neither the model's interface nor the original prompt.

The team derives a lower bound on how many tokens detection requires at a fixed error rate, which guides capacity choices. Experiments across varied tasks show the marks stay hard to notice, easy to detect, and robust to tampering. The authors position the scheme for tracing leaked or misused generated text back to its source. Fast traceability, they argue, is what watermarking has been missing.
arxiv-2506-06002:
Superconducting qubits lose their quantum memory to low-frequency noise, unless they are driven to a sweet spot where the noise cancels. Joachim Lauwens, Kristof Moors, and Bart Sorée study fluxonium qubits driven by two tones at once on the magnetic flux. The two tones tick at whole-number multiples of one base frequency, so their pattern repeats cleanly.

Theory and numerics together hunted for the best drive settings. The second tone widens and raises the peaks of coherence time without badly hurting relaxation. It also enables a cleaner phase gate than a single tone can. Simulations of the gate, noise included, confirmed the gain. Two-tone driving, the authors argue, buys tunability that one tone cannot.
arxiv-2506-06202:
Renato Cordeiro Ferreira and two co-authors report a case study on building a machine learning system for shipping in this two thousand twenty-five paper. The system, Ocean Guard, spots odd patterns in maritime traffic that may signal trouble. It was built as a set of small services, called microservices. That split let several teams work in parallel. The paper tells how the team ran machine learning operations, or MLOps, under this design.

The key device was contracts between services. Separate contracts governed code, models, and data, so each team knew its duties. The authors share the hurdles they hit and the lessons they drew. Software and data teams building large learning systems are the audience. The case shows how contract-based design can keep such projects coherent.
arxiv-2506-06302:
Jia-Mian Li and Bing-Zhao Li tackled a radar problem in 2025: a jamming trick that samples a radar pulse and replays it to fake targets. Older defenses blur when several signals mix, and they fail when the fake signal is nearly as strong as the real one in noisy settings. The pair built a sharper time-and-rate picture of the signal to pull the two apart.

Their picture gives finer detail and tighter energy focus, which lifts the real signal above the noise. They also improved a line-finding method so it locks onto the true signal's track and ignores the jammer's. The result is cleaner target finding under active attack.
arxiv-2506-06402:
Teng Huang and Weiwei Wang prove that a classical splitting of geometric forms survives on spaces that are almost, but not quite, complex, in a 2025 paper. On Kähler manifolds, harmonic forms split by type, and the Hard Lefschetz condition organizes them. Almost Kähler manifolds drop the integrability that makes those proofs work, so whether the structure persists was open.

The authors show when the almost complex structure is not too non-integrable, in a sense they make precise, the harmonic spaces split by type as in the classical case. Two consequences follow: such structures are pure-and-full in the technical sense, and the Hard Lefschetz condition holds for their harmonic forms. They prove a rigidity result for closed four-dimensional almost Kähler manifolds with positive curvature directions. The results extend a cornerstone of Kähler geometry to a broader class of spaces.
arxiv-2506-06602:
Santhosh Kakarla and Gautama Shastry Bulusu Venkata studied composed image search in a 2025 paper. A user starts with a reference photo and a text edit, such as turning a dress blue. Searching with no task training gave weak results on a fashion benchmark.

Fine-tuning a large vision and language model with a small fusion part raised recall sharply across shirts, dresses, and tops. A second route, which tuned only the text side with preference learning, failed almost fully. The authors trace that failure to missing fusion, a poor match of goal to ranking, and weak negative examples. Real fusion, they argue, is the key step.
arxiv-2506-06702:
Zhuo Yu, Qi Wu, and Dian-Yong Chen estimate how often an exotic particle appears in meson decays, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. The particle, Zcs+, is an exotic state with charm and strange quarks. They study its production when a B+ meson decays into charmed meson pairs.

Their model uses a meson loop mechanism, where the decay products exchange a charmed meson and couple to the exotic state plus a light meson. Using an effective Lagrangian approach, they compute branching fractions for several channels. The rates come out at a shared order of magnitude, and their ratios barely depend on model settings. They propose one decay channel as the best place to search, within reach of two major experiments.
arxiv-2506-06802:
Rezaei and co-authors (2025) present a training-free framework that stylizes images while keeping the people in them recognizable. Style transfer often washes out identity, which matters in uses like advertising, and the loss is worst when faces are small or several people share the frame. Their method builds what they call a mosaic restored content image to strengthen identity in complex scenes.

A second piece, a content consistency loss that needs no training, steers the stylization to pay more attention to the original picture, preserving fine detail. In their experiments the approach beat the base model at holding both style quality and identity at once. Because nothing is retrained or fine-tuned, the framework can be dropped onto an existing diffusion model as it stands.
arxiv-2506-07002:
Yunxiao Shi and seven co-authors present a faster way for self-driving systems to map what fills the space around a car, in a research paper from 2025. This task, called 3D occupancy prediction, must capture both fine shapes and object meanings. Dense methods do it well but cost a lot of computing power.

Their system, BePo, blends two views of the scene. A top-down map is cheap but misses small objects. A sparse set of points captures objects of any size but handles flat surfaces poorly. Sharing features between the two branches, then merging them, gave top results on three benchmarks while keeping run time low.
arxiv-2506-07102:
Wei Huo and co-authors show that efficient communication can itself protect privacy in decentralized learning in a 2025 paper. In decentralized optimization, many agents cooperate without a central server, which raises two worries: heavy communication and leaks of private data. Standard privacy methods add noise, which costs accuracy.

Their algorithm activates agents at random and sparsifies the messages they exchange. Using differential privacy analysis, the authors show these two features reduce the noise needed for the same privacy guarantee. Privacy is amplified while accuracy improves, a rare win-win for multi-agent systems such as sensor networks and federated devices.
arxiv-2506-07202:
Ming Liu and Wensheng Zhang propose dynamic evaluation to expose data contamination in multimodal reasoning models. Top benchmark scores may reflect leaked test data, not true skill. Reasoning models tuned from tainted bases inherit that risk.

Instead of altering inputs, their framework alters the task itself. The same image is used across a family of tasks. Questions, captions, question posing, and checks probe distinct skills. Models that overfit one task falter under such shifts. Genuine models hold up across the task family. An automated pipeline scores open answers with a calibrated judge. Paraphrase and corruption sampling steady those scores. The method tests generalization more honestly.
arxiv-2506-07802:
Nicolaj Jensen and co-authors speed up checks of timed multi-player systems in a 2025 paper. Timed alternating-time temporal logic lets verifiers ask what coalitions of players can force over time. Checking such claims on real-time systems is heavy work, since the state space explodes fast.

Their on-the-fly algorithm explores only the states a query truly needs. It builds on an abstract dependency graph frame shared with game and timed logic tools. A widened inclusion check lets the graph shrink while the search runs. A new abstraction then removes the need for that check in this setting. Leaner searches make formal proof of timed systems more practical.
arxiv-2506-08002:
Aadarsh Sahoo and co-authors teach one model to speak of the world in words, pictures, and 3D structure using a single token language. Their 2025 paper builds a unified autoregressive framework where complex 3D objects are tokenized so a language model can reason over scenes the way it reasons over sentences. Designers and robots both need machines that understand space structurally, not just visually.

The team publishes a detailed cookbook of design choices: how to represent the data, which training objectives each modality needs, and where naive unification fails. The model is tested on rendering, recognition, instruction following, and question answering across synthetic and real datasets. It can rebuild complete scenes of complex objects from a single image. The broader claim is that 3D belongs inside the same modeling paradigm as text and images, not in a specialist silo. Token by token, the modalities begin to share one grammar.
arxiv-2506-08302:
Georg Engelhardt, Konstantin Dorfman, and Zhedong Zhang develop in 2025 a fuller theory for quantum sensing with light. Quantum sensors use atoms or molecules to measure fields with extreme care, and spectroscopy is one of their main tools, yet standard theory mostly predicts average readings.

Real sensitivity depends on the random spread of single photon counts, which older semi-classical methods cannot capture well. The authors build a photon-resolved form of Floquet theory that tracks those counts one by one. Their framework aims to predict how sensitive a spectroscopic sensor truly is, not just what it reads on average.
arxiv-2506-08402:
Harley Scammell and Oleg Sushkov propose in 2025 a new route to exciton condensation, a state long predicted but hard to reach. An exciton is a bound pair in a solid, and it condenses when its binding energy matches the band gap. Binding rests on a balance: pull between charges raises it, while motion lowers it, and most materials fall short.

The authors use a sideways electric field as the control knob. That field mixes even and odd parity excitons, and the push apart of their levels in effect raises binding energy. They argue the trick is general and show it in a model of biased bilayer graphene, whose gap can be tuned. A tunneling current with a wavy part offers, they propose, a fresh test for whether condensation has truly formed.
arxiv-2506-08502:
Fei-Fei Wu and co-authors give a single measure that tracks quantized transport of solitons as the strength of their interactions changes, in a 2025 paper. Solitons are self-held wave packets, and slowly cycling a system can pump them by a set amount. Recent work in light guides has put this nonlinear pumping in the spotlight.

When interactions are weak, the bands of the system stay apart, and their measure reduces to a standard count for the filled band. The pumped charge then comes out as a whole number. As interactions grow, the bands tangle, and the measure takes a shared form split across the tangled bands. That shift can make the pumped charge a fraction instead.
arxiv-2506-08702:
Sankalan Pal Chowdhury and co-authors ask teachers to judge AI tutors against human ones, blind, in a study from 2025. Language models now staff homework helpers everywhere. Quality claims usually come from students or from scores. This study turns to the professionals instead.

Grade-school math word problems were taught in text-only chats. Some chats hid a human tutor, others a model. Educators rated both without knowing which was which, on engagement, empathy, scaffolding, and conciseness. The model won all four in their eyes. Empathy showed the widest gap: four of five raters preferred the machine's manner. Text-only tutoring may already favor AI's patience and polish. Classrooms will still decide what that is worth.
arxiv-2506-09102:
Van der Schaar and a large group of industry and academic leaders issue a manifesto in twenty twenty-five. Their subject is the transformation of clinical trials by artificial intelligence. Trials are slow, costly, and often fail to serve patients well. The authors argue two AI technologies can change that.

Those technologies are causal inference and digital twins. Causal methods squeeze more truth from trial and real-world data. Digital twins simulate patients to guide design and personalization. The roadmap stresses integration within existing regulatory frameworks, not around them. The goal is trials that run faster, safer, and more personally. Readers get a collective vision from pharma, consulting, research, and AI leaders for a new gold standard.
arxiv-2506-09302: Sumiya Baasandorj, Simone Di Marino, and Augusto Gerolin prove a smoothness result for a softened form of optimal transport, in a 2025 paper. Optimal transport finds the cheapest way to morph one spread of mass into another. Adding an entropy term smooths the problem and yields a pair of helper functions, the Schrödinger potentials. The team shows those helpers keep a set level of smoothness, with stable bounds, when both spreads live on bounded convex ground with densities bounded above and below.
arxiv-2506-09402:
Nissim Fraija and four co-authors modeled buried magnetic fields in newborn magnetars. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, deals with millisecond magnetars, a would be engine of gamma ray bursts. Right after birth, such a star's field can grow fast. In fall of star debris can then push that field down. A thin crust forms in a fierce feed phase and sinks the field, in what is called magnetic burial.

When the feed stops, the sunk field seeps back through the crust. That delays when the outer field wakes up. Late glow from bursts, as their jets slow in space gas, can bear the mark of that delay. Readers in high energy astronomy get a clock that links crust physics to late light.
arxiv-2506-10102:
Ahmed Elbakary, Chaouki Ben Issaid, and Mehdi Bennis present a federated learning method that lets similar clients teach each other while keeping data local, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Each client holds its own data and its own task, so blind sharing can hurt as much as help. The method aims to pool lessons only where they fit.

Instead of sending whole models to a server, clients send a compact anchor vector that sums up what their data taught them, plus a small shared output layer. A graph links clients by likeness and is updated as their data drift. A community-finding step then groups near-twins, and help flows only inside each group. On two mixed datasets, the method beat leading rivals while using less computation and chatter, and it treated clients more fairly.
arxiv-2506-10802:
Craig Macdonald, Jinyuan Fang, Andrew Parry, and Zaiqiao Meng bring retrieval-augmented generation into a declarative search toolkit in a 2025 demo paper. Search systems are built as pipelines: a fast first pass, then heavier reranking. Generation systems add a final step that writes an answer from retrieved documents.

Their PyTerrier-RAG add-on lets researchers write such set-ups in a compact operator notation. It bundles standard data sets and measures, strong language-model readers, and the wider PyTerrier range of sparse and neural retrievers. The demo shows indexing and question-answering flows on sets like Natural Questions in a few lines. The authors pitch this way of building as the path to generation tests that others can repeat and compare.
arxiv-2506-10902:
Christopher Schafhauser, Aaron Tikuisis, and Stuart White published this 2025 collection of ninety-nine open problems on nuclear C*-algebras. C*-algebras are the operator-algebraic homes of quantum observables, and the nuclear ones form the tractable, classifiable heart of the field. A mature classification program now sorts many of them by computable invariants, which sharpens the question of what remains unknown.

Rather than prove theorems, the authors map the frontier: questions on structure and classification chosen to mark where current methods stop. Such lists serve the community as shared targets, inviting attacks and exposing which obstacles are technical and which are conceptual. The collection follows a classic genre, Hilbert-style, in a field whose recent triumphs make its remaining gaps newly visible. Readers get a guided tour of the problems the experts themselves cannot yet solve.
arxiv-2506-11502:
Mark van der Pas and four co-authors give a reference model and a set of patterns to enrich the event data that plants spew out. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five.

Firms now log vast data as their work runs across many systems. Joined, those logs can bare new facts for watch and study of how work does. That join is most often done by hand, in a slow, ad hoc way. The model gives a standard way to store and draw out such data. It joins a known trade standard with a graph form for event facts. The patterns list the common draw-out tasks and how each can be run by machine.
arxiv-2506-11802:
Diego Blas and co-authors present a 2025 conference summary on using pairs of orbiting bodies as gravitational wave detectors. Most detectors cover limited frequency bands, leaving the very low microhertz band almost untouched. Waves there would shake a binary system in a resonant way when their rhythm matches the orbit.

The summary gathers current efforts to read those tiny orbital effects as wave signals. Binaries could open a fresh window on the universe and, with it, new phenomena. The same setups can also probe dark matter in regions no other method reaches. The authors present the approach as a cheap complement to purpose-built detectors.
arxiv-2506-11902:
Hou and co-authors present a 2025 paper on training language models with tree search inside reinforcement learning. Instead of sampling whole answer chains one by one, a tree search branches at unsure steps and scores paths as they grow. That gives denser feedback during training. Older work often trained a separate reward model, which can drift from the policy and invite gaming.

Their framework, TreeRL, folds on-policy tree search straight into training and needs no separate reward model. Branching from high-uncertainty steps raises search yield for the same token budget. Tests on hard math and code tasks beat chain-based training, the authors report. They released the code in public for other teams.
arxiv-2506-12102:
Franco Bertani and co-authors set out how twin sims can run sun farms in a wire world, in a report from 2025. A twin is a live sim that tracks its true rig step by step. Sun farms face hard calls on yield and care as their fleets grow.

The twin can call faults ere they strike, lift day yield, and back choice with true data reads. Gains span care plans, stock watch, and crew calls on the ground. The team lays out where twins fit in the sun trade and what blocks their spread. Their close frames twins as a shift in how sun farms are run, not a mere tool add.
arxiv-2506-12502:
Julie Bauer, Rishabh Kaushal, Thales Bertaglia, and Adriana Iamnitchi wrote a 2025 paper on how fair hate speech detection tools are when the language is Dutch. Most such work is in English and chases raw accuracy. Fairness toward all groups is a side note at best. This team puts fairness first.

They built a list of Dutch social group terms that fit the local scene of the country. They then made paired texts, alike except for the group named, with the help of language models and set substitution rules. The paired sets were used to fine-tune the detection tools, and the tools were graded on accuracy and on fairness scores. The tuned tools detected hate speech well and scored as fairer than the untuned ones. The team also flags how hard it is to make paired texts that read as natural Dutch.
arxiv-2506-12602:
Yu-xuan Yin and co-authors explore in 2025 whether space-based gravity wave detectors could tie fast radio bursts to merging neutron stars. One idea holds that some repeating bursts come from twin neutron stars whose magnetic fields clash decades before they merge. Those pairs also hum at low frequencies that space detectors can hear.

The team takes the galaxy M81, which hosts a repeating burst source in an old star cluster, as the test case. Current missions fall short on reach, though smarter pointing helps. A detection there would clinch the link at strong significance. Next-generation detectors should hear such pairs easily, in M81 and beyond.
arxiv-2506-12802:
Joon Soo Yoo, Tae Min Ahn, and Ji Won Yoon designed a private biometric login that works both ways in a 2025 paper. Leaked fingerprint or iris templates cannot be changed like passwords, so checking them under strong encryption is attractive. Full encryption schemes, though, ship huge data and strain key handling.

Their framework mixes encryption with transciphering and adds a trusted helper that never colludes. Double encryption guards the trust model, so client data stays private. The design shrinks returned ciphertexts, stops clients from faking a pass, and centers key management for scale. Built with a fast scheme and a stream cipher, it cut transmission size up to 121-fold on iris data against standard setups.
arxiv-2506-12902:
Pantelis Dogoulis, Karim Tit, and Maxime Cordy wrote a paper in two thousand twenty-five on predicting power flow in electric grids with AI. Grid operators need fast, trustworthy forecasts of how power moves. Classic solvers are reliable but slow under stress, while AI is fast yet often breaks the basic laws of circuits.

Their network, KCLNet, builds Kirchhoff's current law in as a hard rule. That law says the currents at any node must balance. A projection step enforces it exactly, so the model reports zero violations. The authors report accuracy on par with rivals, with predictions that always stay physically possible.
arxiv-2506-13002:
Rosa Colyer and Dominik Duda set out a measurement plan in a 2025 particle physics paper. Their target is a subtle property of W and Z bosons made together with a Higgs boson at the Large Hadron Collider. These bosons can spin along their line of travel, a state tied to how the Higgs gives them mass. Catching that state would test our picture of how mass arises.

The authors study which angles and energies best separate the spin states, and they use machine learning to sharpen the split. Their forecasts say a firm discovery is within reach at the high-luminosity upgrade of the collider. With the full data set, rates could be measured to within about ten percent.
arxiv-2506-13102:
Gyutaek Oh and co-authors rethink how to squeeze more thought out of medical AI at answer time, in this 2025 paper. Test-time scaling lets a model spend extra computing while answering, which can sharpen its reasoning. The idea is hot in general AI, but how it plays in medicine, and for models that also read images, was largely untested.

The team ran a broad study across language and vision-language models. They varied model size, the model's built-in traits, and how hard the task was, hunting for which scaling style fits which setting. They also probed how the methods hold up when prompts carry misleading hints planted by users. Their findings distill into practical rules for using the extra answer-time computing safely in clinics, where trust and clear reasoning matter most.
arxiv-2506-13602:
Asai, Iyama, Mousavand, and Paquette introduce brick-splitting torsion pairs and brick-directed algebras, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Torsion pairs sort modules into two complementary classes. A pair is brick-splitting when every brick falls cleanly on one side. Lattice properties, including left modularity, characterize these pairs fully.

Brick-directed algebras forbid cycles of maps between bricks. They generalize representation-directed algebras to a broader class. Tame and wild examples are constructed in abundance. Wall-and-chamber geometry and a Newton polytope also characterize them. A brick-finite algebra is brick-directed exactly when its torsion lattice is left modular.
arxiv-2506-13702:
Bilal Faye and co-authors introduce a 2025 method for tuning language models with simple scores. Each reply to a prompt gets a single reward score, rather than a pair to compare. Older methods in this line must also learn a value model. That extra step adds noise and makes training less steady.

The new method, called RPO in the paper, skips the value model. It scales scores with a rule drawn from the scores for each prompt. The result is a plain training target with no extra models. Tests on several model types beat strong rivals, with replies judged better and less harmful. Stability checks also favored the new method.
arxiv-2506-13902:
Raymond Yu, Paul Han, Josh Myers-Dean, Piper Wolters, and Favyen Bastani present OPTIMUS, in a 2025 preprint, a self-taught method for spotting change in satellite image series. Labeled examples of change are rare, since most of the Earth's surface sits still. The guiding idea is temporal: if a model can tell the order of images in a series, the series must hold durable change to learn from. OPTIMUS trains on that ordering task with no labels at all. Change-point tools then read the trained model's outputs along the series.

Tested at telling changed series from unchanged ones, it lifted the ranking score from near coin-flip for baselines to a high mark. The method needs no annotated change data, the bottleneck. Code and the dataset are public. The authors aim the tool at environmental monitoring, where the changes that matter most are the rarest in the archive.
arxiv-2506-14402:
Wilfried Imrich and co-authors wrote a math paper in 2025 on coloring the nodes of trees. A coloring counts as distinguishing when no symmetry of the tree keeps it in place except doing nothing. The team asks how large node degrees can be while such a two color pattern still exists. They study both finite and endless trees of any size.

For trees with few moved nodes, the authors give a sharp degree bound. They also count how many distinct patterns exist for endless trees. Similar counts hold for a wider class of tree like graphs. The results tie symmetry, degree, and coloring in a clean way.
arxiv-2506-14902:
Adwitiya Sarkar and nine co-authors map magnetic fields in the Pillars of Creation, the famed finger shaped clouds in the M16 nebula where stars form. Dust grains line up with fields, so dust glow polarization can trace them. Their work came out in twenty twenty-five.

Maps came from an airborne observatory's camera at two far infrared bands. A classic method turned the spread in field angles into strength gauges, which fell in a range the authors call typical for clouds of like density. At the finger tips, fields seem too weak to stop collapse yet strong enough to resist star light push. At the bases, fields slow mass inflow.
arxiv-2506-15002:
Kyra Jacobo and Dorian Araya revisit brane world gravity as an explanation for the acceleration of the universe. Their version of the Randall-Sundrum model gives the brane tension an exponential form that shifts with redshift. The scenario assumes no dark energy fluid, so acceleration must come from the modified gravity itself.

Bayesian fits constrain the free parameters with strong lensing, supernova, Hubble, and baryon acoustic data, including new points. Both Planck and Riess priors for the Hubble constant are tried. In both cases the model reproduces late time acceleration in line with observations. The transition redshift agrees interestingly with the standard model. Pathologies remain, including a future divergence of the expansion rate and strong sensitivity to the tension form.
arxiv-2506-15602:
Jun He, Siang Yew Chong and Xin Yao wrote a 2025 paper on timing how long search methods take to hit a goal. A common tool, drift analysis, needs a hand-built function for each case. That craft slows the work. The team offers a way to get the needed bounds from hit chances instead.

Each bound becomes a chance that the search hits a given score level. Paths through the score levels help when the terrain has many peaks. Clear formulas make the hit chances easy to compute. As a demo, they compare two ways to handle rules in a knapsack task. Neither way won across the board.
arxiv-2506-15702:
Peter Belcak and three co-authors introduced in 2025 a gentler way to teach a language model a new domain with little data. Normal fine-tuning on scarce data makes models forget their general skill, and the damage grows as data shrinks. Their method, called minifinetuning, corrects the model against its own answers sample by sample.

Across many models and domains, the method kept two to ten times more general skill per unit of new learning than standard tuning. It held up with as few as five hundred samples and beat parameter-saving methods. It can also stack with those methods for a combined gain.
arxiv-2506-16402:
Xiaoya Lu and co-authors build a test for home robots that run on vision and language models. Their 2025 paper argues that still, one-off tests miss risks that grow step by step as a robot acts. A robot may open a stove, move a pot, or pour water, and each act can create new danger. Their test checks if the robot spots such risks and acts in the right order.

The test holds many hard scenes with hundreds of named risks, all run in a rich simulator. Top chat models did poorly at this kind of safety sense. Careful step-by-step thought helped scores but hurt task success, a trade-off the authors flag.
arxiv-2506-16602:
Viswanath and co-authors propose in 2025 SlepNet, a graph network that represents neural dynamics through spectral subgraphs. Graph networks serve node tasks well but handle signal patterning over graphs poorly. Brain signals are spatio temporal, high dimensional, and hard to decode.

Slepian bases replace Fourier harmonics in their design, since they focus energy on set subgraphs. A learned mask finds the relevant subgraphs automatically, so harmonics concentrate where the brain is active. Representations become canonical and sharply resolved. Tests span three brain imaging datasets on cognitive and visual tasks plus two traffic datasets, against standard graph models and signal processing rivals.
arxiv-2506-16902:
Active galactic nuclei can be classified by how their light varies, Ylenia Maruccia and co-authors show in a 2025 paper. Classification of these nuclei is a standing challenge in astrophysics. Variability features from light curves offer a promising route to distinguish nuclei and their subclasses, above all with the Rubin Observatory's Legacy Survey of Space and Time on the horizon.

The team uses self-organizing maps to classify nuclei based on variability features. They investigate how different subsets of features affect the purity and completeness of the resulting classifications. A set of features, similar to those in previous studies, is derived from light curves and fed to the maps. The distribution of subclasses across the map is explored. Comparative analysis guides which features to keep.
arxiv-2506-17002:
Alex Doak, Karsten Matthies, Jonathan Sewell, and Miles Wheeler constructed large waves for steady Euler flow in two thousand twenty-five. The Euler equations govern ideal fluid motion. Their setting is a two-dimensional channel with rigid walls and two layers of fluid, each with constant vorticity, split by an unknown interface.

Using global bifurcation theory, they build curves of periodic solutions that end in one of two ways. Either flow stagnates on the interface, or the conformal map that flattens a layer breaks down. Numerics suggest the breakdown appears as a corner on the interface or as a layer pinching to near-zero width. Their method handles overhanging profiles and stagnation points together.
arxiv-2506-17302:
Yijun Lin and co-authors teach a machine to map Alaska's soils at a fineness fieldwork never could. Permafrost thaw threatens roads, buildings, and the carbon locked in northern soils, but fine soil maps for the state barely exist. Their model, MISO, fuses a geospatial foundation model for visual features, implicit neural maps for smooth spatial prediction, and contrastive learning to tie images to place.

The target outputs are near-surface permafrost and soil taxonomy across the whole state. Against the random forest standard, spatial cross-validation showed MISO generalizing better to unseen remote regions and catching more of the permafrost that matters. The authors offer the approach as guidance for future sampling and for planning infrastructure on thawing ground.
arxiv-2506-17402:
Domagoj Kuić, Alemka Knapp, and Diana Šaponja-Milutinović published a 2025 physics paper on what happens when a quantum spin chain is disturbed gradually rather than suddenly. In a quench, a system's conditions change and its response is watched. Textbook theory handles the sudden case. Real switches take finite time, and the authors ask how much that difference matters in chains of interacting spins.

Using a field-theory method built for finite-time processes, they compare sudden and gradual switching in two chain models. The difference between the two fades exponentially fast with time, they show, up to small corrections their method tracks. The result holds at every order of their approximation, for a broad family of switching curves. One S-shaped curve serves as the model example. In the limit of fast switching it rejoins the sudden case.
arxiv-2506-17702:
Stefan Mengel gives a 2025 tutorial survey on how hard it is to answer conjunctive queries, a basic kind of database query. The survey gathers known results on the cost of query evaluation across several settings. These range from yes-or-no queries and counting answers to listing answers one by one and reaching answers directly.

A main theme is how recent guesses from complexity theory link to query answering. Under those guesses, many known algorithms for these tasks likely cannot be improved, which tells researchers where the true limits sit. The tutorial is aimed at readers who want a map of what is known, which methods look final, and where the open ground remains in database theory.
arxiv-2506-17802:
Nicolò Scapin and co-authors simulate in this 2025 paper the life cycle of ocean waves bullied by strong wind until they break. Direct simulations of coupled air and water follow a narrow wave train fed by a turbulent wind layer. Growth and breaking trade energy in turns across each cycle.

Pressure from the wind does nearly all the feeding while waves rise; turbulence in the water does nearly all the spending as they crash. The growth rate follows a classic scaling, bent by sheltering at steep slopes, and the breaking loss follows inertial rules tied to slope. Under the foam, sinking turbulence fades with depth in a clean profile. Surf forecasts rest on the same trade.
arxiv-2506-18002:
Mujahidul Islam and co-authors survey quantum generative adversarial networks in a 2025 paper. These models pit two circuits against each other, one forging data and one judging it, in quantum dress. The survey sorts designs by how quantum and classical parts share the work.

Uses range from image synthesis and medical data to channel prediction, software defect spotting, and teaching tools. Tricks like Wasserstein scoring and language model pairings get their own tour. Real runs on light-based and ion-trap hardware are weighed against todays limits. Open problems close the map, from noise to scale, with an eye on practical advantage.
arxiv-2506-18102:
Wang, Li, Zhu, and Jiang built a debate tool in twenty twenty-five that scores and trains large chat models for fair fights of words. Past debate tools chase a reply to one point but skip checks on truth and logic. Their score set rates four felt traits, like clear form and pull on the heart.

It rates two hard traits too: true facts and sound logic. Their score matched expert views far more than past scores did. The full tool adds step thought, a tune step across all traits, and live web facts. In tests it beat base models by a wide gap on debate tasks.
arxiv-2506-18502:
Tao Yu and three co-authors wrote this 2025 arXiv review on a quiet interaction between magnets and superconductors that never touch. Interfaces of these materials are famous for exchange effects, but this review concerns the dipolar route: spin waves in a ferromagnet throw stray magnetic fields that a neighboring superconductor answers by screening. A universal coupling ties the fields' swirl to their direction of travel.

That handshake breeds hybrid particles the authors catalog: magnon-Meissner modes, magnon-cooparons, Josephson plasmonic modes, and photon-linked polaritons. Metallic and superconducting gates can tune the interaction, and with it the magnetization and energy flow through thin films. The review positions this electromagnetic proximity effect as a control knob for magnonics, the effort to compute and communicate with spin waves. For device physicists, non-contact coupling promises influence without the mess of an interface.
arxiv-2506-18602:
R Prashanth compared ways in a study on judging how alike two texts are in meaning, with a focus on narrow fields. Such judgments feed search, question answering, grouping of documents, and translation. The study tested three leading tools, including the BERT model, on two sets of question pairs.

One set came from a private business source and the other from a public Quora set. BERT did much better than the other tools. Fine tuning during its training, which lets it learn patterns from the data at hand, is offered as the reason. The author concludes that BERT is the best choice for field-specific data among the tools tested.
arxiv-2506-18702:
Xiao Ma and Michael Cates explored in 2025 what happens when attraction between phases of a fluid refuses to be mutual. Non-reciprocal interactions, where one component chases another that flees it, are among the simplest ways to push a system out of equilibrium, and they produce patterns equilibrium physics forbids. Their minimal model has three separating phases, two interacting non-reciprocally, with the third acting as a spectator that mimics a boundary.

Simulations revealed three regimes sorted by driving strength. In the mildest, droplets settle into a quasi-static state with well-defined non-equilibrium contact angles where the three phases meet. Stronger driving sets the bulk phases rotating endlessly around the contact line in a limit cycle. Stronger still produces travelling waves with persistent directional motion. Linear stability analysis and a wave speed calculation near equilibrium complete the picture, a starter theory of wetting far from equilibrium.
arxiv-2506-19102:
Five researchers wrote a paper in two thousand twenty-five on how well freight networks withstand attack and climate disruption. Rail and water routes carry global logistics and depend on each other at transfer points. Disasters and failures can cascade through those links, yet robustness under targeted and climate-driven hits is still a key open question.

The team modeled the United States rail and water networks and their interdependence. They simulated deliberate, random, and climate-driven failures, drawing climate detail from several earth system models. Federal data supplied the network layout and tonnage forecasts. The framework measures how much function the system keeps under each kind of blow.
arxiv-2506-19202:
Claire Yang and co-authors ask how much control people want over home help robots, in a 2025 study. Designers often assume assistive robots should do everything alone. Past work hints that users may not agree. A fully autonomous robot can shrink the user's sense of agency, the feeling of being in charge at home.

Participants rated their sense of agency across four levels of robot independence. They also ranked robot styles for varied household tasks. Agency hinged mainly on two things: whether the robot acted alone, and whether an outsider ran it. A robot programmed by the user preserved agency even when acting alone. For risky tasks, like feeding an allergic child, people strongly preferred keeping control.
arxiv-2506-19402:
Samuel Mimram and Émile Oleon build a classic geometric object inside a logic system where proofs act like spaces, in a math paper from 2025. The system is called homotopy type theory. In it, types stand for spaces and proofs must respect their shape.

The object is the hypercubical manifold, first described by Poincaré in 1895. It gives a first step toward a step-by-step model of the quaternion group, a small group of symmetries. The authors define the object as a type and prove it matches the expected form: a three-dimensional sphere divided by that group's action. The proof needs fine counting arguments. They then extend the build to higher dimensions, giving sharper models that approach a full loop space for the group.
arxiv-2506-19502:
Aleksandr Algazinov, Matt Laing, and Paul Laban build a team of AI agents that translates content across senses for disabled users. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Many digital tools ignore wide ranges of user needs. Closed multi-agent systems cannot be customized to fill the gaps. People with disabilities then hit barriers daily. Their system, MATE, converts media to whatever form the user can use.

An image can become a spoken description for someone who cannot see well. Other conversions follow the same pattern. The environment is multimodal and powered by large language models. Healthcare is one of many target domains. Open design lets others adapt the agents. Accessibility gains a flexible, shared toolkit.
arxiv-2506-19902:
Nico Winkel and co-authors traced how a lopsided young star group feeds the black hole in galaxy NGC 4593 in 2025. Giant black holes grow by swallowing gas, lit as active nuclei. Mergers can drive bright feeding bouts, but quiet internal processes may do much of the work over cosmic time.

A single-arm spiral of molecular gas winds from the galaxy's outskirts down to the black hole's doorstep. Star birth in the spiral is feeble, while gas inflow runs a hundred times faster, enough to feed the hole for tens of millions of years. The pull behind the flow is gravity from a young, unevenly spread star component. The case shows a secular engine for steady black hole growth.
arxiv-2506-20002:
Katarina Baucalo and Ana Mitrasinovic test a simple way to sort galaxies by shape in a 2025 study. Galaxy shape links to how a galaxy formed, but detailed sorting takes heavy analysis. The authors ask whether one catalog value, how circular the star orbits are, can stand in for shape in simulated galaxies.

Using data from a major simulation project, they split stars into disk and bulge parts by orbit shape. The split matched a detailed five part split well in a smaller, finer simulation. A disk share above a modest cut marked late type galaxies, and their map of shape versus crowding matched real sky surveys. The cheap proxy could seed training sets for machine sorting.
arxiv-2506-20302:
Abbas Anwar and colleagues combined two fashionable techniques in 2025 to clean up damaged photographs. Images shot in poor conditions arrive noisy, blurred, color-shifted, or veiled by scattered light, and every flaw degrades the detection and classification systems that consume them. Their model, TDiR, pairs a transformer, which reads global structure, with a diffusion process, which rebuilds detail step by step, aiming at restoration rather than mere filtering.

The authors evaluated it on three distinct restoration jobs, underwater enhancement, denoising, and rain removal, spread across five standard benchmark sets. Against eighteen competing state-of-the-art methods scored on four quality metrics, their model came out ahead. They argue the pairing is the point: diffusion supplies the generative power to invent plausible detail, while the transformer keeps that invention faithful to the scene's overall layout.
arxiv-2506-20402:
Computing the gradient of a cost is the engine of machine learning, and one method lets physical hardware compute it by following its own laws. Marc Berneman and Daniel Hexner extend that method, equilibrium propagation, in 2025 to systems that move and lose energy over time.

Earlier versions handled still systems at rest. The new version covers damped motion in the linear range, such as shaking structures and simple RLC circuits. By writing an action whose extreme point matches the motion, the authors derive update rules that stay local to each part. They show the method working in mechanical and electronic setups, even sorting sound signals by pitch, which points toward smart materials that learn from motion itself.
arxiv-2506-20602:
Jay Armas, Akash Jain, and Ruben Lier ask what temperature means inside an active nematic. An active nematic is a fluid of tiny rods that move on their own. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. They use a new flow framework that links the fluid to its surroundings. The work assumes the fluid stays close to heat balance.

In a calm, even state, the team finds that activity does not change how temperature varies from place to place. The fuel use of the rods reacts to force, and that link drives the result. But when the fluid is boxed in and starts to flow on its own, things change. Shearing and twisting build an uneven temperature map. That pattern, they argue, is a heat fingerprint of activity. It could give labs a new way to spot active matter at work.
arxiv-2506-20902:
Marcus Hamilton scales the human niche in a 2025 chapter. The human niche is where biology, ecology, culture, and technology meet to shape how our species lives. Hamilton views it through scaling theory, the study of how traits change with size across species. He seeks the axes along which human strategies have spread and grown.

Four axes get the focus: energy use, thought, social life, and computation. Each follows scaling laws that link people to their surroundings and to each other. Across deep time, human expansion raised energy intake, information handling, and network size together. That path produced today's vast, linked societies. Hamilton argues for a single measured science of human ecology, one that also speaks to sustainability and to expansion beyond Earth.
arxiv-2506-21102:
David Debot, Pietro Barbiero, Gabriele Dominici, and Giuseppe Marra make concept based AI explain its inner steps in a 2025 paper. Such models predict human named concepts first, then answer from them, but the concept calls themselves were black boxes. Their reasoner learns a graph of logic rules linking concepts to simpler ones. An attention step picks which rules to apply for each case, working down the layers.

Accuracy matches leading models, they report. People can step in and fix a wrong concept mid-run, lifting accuracy sharply. Background knowledge fed into the graph also cuts training data needs. Both the concepts and the final answer now come with a readable trail.
arxiv-2506-21202:
Lavakumar Addepalli and Pathak propose a scheme for extra-bright lasing in two modes at once, using two quantum dots inside a patterned crystal cavity. Quantum dots can emit light in step, producing radiance well above independent emission. The cavity here supports two light modes, which opens richer behavior.

Their analysis accounts for how the dots interact with vibrations in the material, using a transformed master equation. They examine a witness of radiance and correlations within and between the modes. Vibration-driven processes that create photon pairs across both modes boost the radiance strongly. Compared with a single-mode cavity, the brighter emission also comes with a narrower spectral line.
arxiv-2506-21802:
Johan Hallberg Szabadváry and co-authors formalize classifiers that may refuse to answer, in a 2025 machine learning paper. Ordinary models always emit a prediction, even when they are probably wrong, which is dangerous in high-stakes use. A reject option lets the model abstain on the shakiest cases.

The authors build the refusal rule from conformal prediction, whose sets carry distribution-free error guarantees. In binary problems the sets can hold one label, both, or none; accepting only singletons yields a classifier with abstention. They prove the resulting error rate and give finite-sample estimates. Worked examples span several conformal setups, from exact to cheaper batch versions.
arxiv-2506-21902:
Chien-Thang Tran, Mikhail Ivanov, Ngoc-Dung Nguyen, and Quang-Chau Vo compute how spin shows itself in rare decays of heavy quark pairs, in a 2025 paper. The charmonium J/ψ and bottomonium Υ(1S) can decay weakly into a lighter meson, a lepton, and a neutrino. Such semileptonic decays are rare windows on the weak force inside bound quark systems.

Working with the helicity amplitude method, the team derive the two-fold angular pattern of the decays. They then predict polarization observables — a forward-backward asymmetry, the lepton's own polarization, and a convexity parameter — using form factors from a covariant confined quark model. Comparing the numbers with the literature tests the model's grip on quark binding.
arxiv-2506-22002:
Sohan Ghosh, a solo author, studies fine Selmer groups over function fields in a 2025 mathematics paper. Selmer groups track deep arithmetic traits of elliptic curves, and their size can vary across infinite tower like extensions of a field. Earlier work by Greenberg and Kleine explored that variation for number fields.

Ghosh adapts those methods to the setting where the base field is a function field in prime characteristic. He relates the invariants of fine Selmer groups across varied extensions of that field. The analysis connects to a conjecture by Coates and Sujatha, restated for this setting. The paper extends a program for understanding how arithmetic invariants shift across towers of fields.
arxiv-2506-22302:
Matthieu Vanhoecke and two co-authors study a Kondo system that leaks particles in pairs, in a 2025 theory paper. The setup pairs a single interacting impurity with a sea of electrons, a classic model of magnetic impurities in metals. Losses that remove two particles at once add a new twist. The team compute the impurity's motion, end state, and spectrum with a self-consistent expansion method, then check the results on small exact chains.

Signs of Kondo physics, the tight screening cloud around the impurity, survive both weak and strong pair losses. Spin calming slows sharply, and the sharp Kondo peak in the spectrum fades, then returns in the strong-loss regime. Pair losses guard the effect better than single losses do. A change of variables yields a cleaner model that explains why. The authors say strong links or strong losses both shield the cloud.
arxiv-2506-22502:
Matvei Anoshin and others stabilize industrial processes by replacing a classic optimizer with two neural networks working as predictor and optimizer. Keeping quantities like temperature steady is a standing problem across industry, and conventional solvers spend heavily on pointwise optimization. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the team reframes the job. An oracle network learns to predict the process, and an optimizer network learns control actions, converting repeated pointwise solving into network training. Once trained, control is read off the networks rather than computed fresh at each step.

On their temperature control tests, the pipeline improved stability about threefold compared with ordinary solvers, while demanding fewer computational resources. The authors present the approach as a general template for steadying time series processes in factories, where both quality and compute cost matter.
arxiv-2506-23402:
Luca Vecchi weighs how a strange quark could contribute to the neutron's electric dipole moment in a 2025 particle physics study. A permanent dipole moment in the neutron would signal new sources of symmetry breaking beyond the standard model.
