Hypothetical electric dipoles on quarks are one possible origin, and the strange quark's share was unclear.

Vecchi lines up several lines of argument, from perturbative theory and large-number expansions to a fresh look at the simple quark model and an effective field theory calculation. All point the same way: the strange contribution should run near a tenth of the up and down quark parts. In many new-physics scenarios that makes it the dominant piece.
arxiv-2506-23502:
Mengxiao Tian, Xinxiao Wu, and Shuo Yang teach a vision-language model to notice actions, not just objects, when matching images with text. Their 2025 paper builds on CLIP, a model that aligns whole images with captions but often misses fine detail like who is doing what to whom. Actions carry much of that missing meaning, since they state how objects relate.

The method draws action knowledge out of a large language model and feeds it in as two kinds of prompts, one for action triples and one for action states. A further module blends this guidance with the image and text features. The authors aim for matches that respect the full scene, including movement and contact, not only the items present.
arxiv-2506-23702:
Hongling Hu and Shangyou Zhang construct a leaner smooth finite element in two thousand twenty-five for rectangular meshes in two and three dimensions. Finite elements split a domain into blocks for solving equations numerically. The classic Bogner-Fox-Schmit element keeps both function and slope continuous across blocks, but it carries many degrees of freedom.

Their Bell-type variant trims the space sharply: on each face the normal slope is a polynomial one degree lower than the function itself. The question was whether accuracy survives the cut. The authors prove the trimmed element keeps the optimal convergence order for degree four and up. Numerical experiments compare the new elements against the originals. The result promises cheaper simulations where smoothness across elements is required.
arxiv-2506-23802:
Konstantinos Bourazas, Savvas Papaioannou, and Panayiotis Kolios build an alarm for shifting dot patterns in a 2025 paper. Many sensors report not tidy tables but clouds of points: radar blips, cell sightings, crowd dots. Spotting when such a cloud turns abnormal, while the normal itself slowly drifts, defeats fixed alarms.

Their framework learns normal behavior live from random finite set data, a math built for clouds of uncertain size. A new discounting scheme lets old lessons fade at the right pace, so drift is absorbed but true anomalies still trip the wire. Heavy simulation, in pictures and numbers, shows the alarm holding its nerve where older detectors cry wolf or sleep.
arxiv-2506-24002:
Felipe da Silva Barbosa and co-authors forecast in 2025 a new test of gravity inside our own galaxy. A Yukawa tweak to Newton's pull would change how stars accelerate along the line of sight. Measuring that drift takes two spectra of the same target a decade apart, then spotting a tiny shift.

With 165 globular clusters as targets, next-generation spectrographs fall short of rivaling rotation curve limits unless precision improves greatly. A far larger target pool, about one hundred thirty thousand RR Lyrae stars, changes the math: at planned precision the acceleration test could match the rotation curve constraints on the added force.
arxiv-2507-00302:
Andrea Gnarini and co-authors collect X-ray polarization results for a class of neutron star binaries in a 2025 paper. These Z-sources trace a Z-shaped path as their brightness and color shift. A space polarimeter has now watched several of them, and the team re-analyzed all such data with one model-free method.

Polarization is strongest on the horizontal branch and fades toward the normal branch, then rises again for some sources on the flaring branch. The polarization also grows with photon energy in most sources. Two sources swing their angle between branches. Readers get a unified map of how these systems polarize light.
arxiv-2507-01002:
Roberto Bruschini introduces SPARSE, a method for solving radial Schrödinger equations that describe particle scattering. The system covers particles with spin in a wave of fixed total angular momentum. From its solutions one can get the quantities that experiments observe.

The method replaces the equations with a finite difference form and applies boundary rules at the center and at a large radius. Standard library routines solve for the wave, and a fit at large distance gives a matrix that yields scattering amplitudes. Poles of the scattering are then found by extending those amplitudes with a rational approximation method known as AAA.
arxiv-2507-01202:
Enes Dilber and Colin Gray propose in 2025 a shrinkage regression for estimating effects of many related treatments from observational data. Practitioners often need to separate effects of overlapping options, like marketing touchpoints or product types. Estimating each effect alone gives noisy results that are hard to act on in practice.

Their customized ridge model moves smoothly between separate and pooled estimates. It cuts error for each sub-treatment effect substantially in theory and simulation. Aggregate treatment effects can be rebuilt easily from the parts. A retail case at Wayfair shows how the method enabled targeted decision making.
arxiv-2507-01402:
Clarissa Astuto and Giovanni Russo build a numerical scheme for a multiscale model of charged particles moving under electric forces in 2025. The setting is a gas bubble anchored in water, surrounded by charged surfactant ions that stick to its surface when they arrive.

Their model treats positive and negative ions together, since the two interact through the shared electric field, where earlier work often handled one species alone. The trap's pull is replaced by a boundary condition derived from conservation and asymptotic analysis. The scheme is asymptotic preserving, meaning it stays accurate when the trap's range is far smaller than the device scale, and validation tests support the approach.
arxiv-2507-01902:
Grier Jones and Hans-Arno Jacobsen present a 2025 paper on splitting quantum chemistry across machines. Distributed quantum computing links small quantum devices to act as one larger system. Chemistry sums are a flagship use case for quantum machines. The team tests five standard electronic structure methods from common packages. Each method is cut with local operations through a known circuit cutting add-on.

Their key finding is blunt: many of these algorithms cannot be split efficiently with local operations alone. Fresh methods are needed before chemistry can run well in the distributed frame. Quantum software teams get a reality check against easy scaling claims. Cutting circuits has a cost, and chemistry circuits pay it heavily. The analysis tells builders where to aim new distribution tricks instead of forcing old ones.
arxiv-2507-02202:
Twagirayezu recasts the quark gluon plasma, the fireball born in heavy ion collisions, as a noisy quantum channel, in this 2025 physics paper. In that language, the plasma does three things to the color entangled quarks passing through it. It drains their energy and scrambles their quantum phases. At the end, as it cools, it forces them into colorless hadrons.

Each effect becomes a standard channel from quantum information theory, stacked into one composite. Tracking entanglement entropy and purity through the stack shows the expected story. Damping alone purifies, while scrambling mixes. The final thermal projection, set by hadron masses and the freeze out temperature, locks in the loss. Simulations decline monotonically, matching the picture of entanglement erased by confinement.
arxiv-2507-02502:
Tao Li and Hao-Song Li compute masses of hidden charm pentaquarks in a 2025 paper. Pentaquarks are rare five quark particles, and a particle collider in Europe has reported several that hide a charm and anticharm pair. Theory that organizes these states by symmetry can predict the masses of partners not yet seen.

Working inside an effective theory for heavy pentaquarks, the authors add quantum corrections up to the next level of precision. They anchor the math on two reported states with a set spin and parity. Two further states then fall out as predictions, with masses near four thousand four hundred eighty and four thousand four hundred ninety units. The numbers guide future searches.
arxiv-2507-02602:
Riccardo Gallon and co-authors wrote a 2025 paper on camera faults in space craft that steer by sight. Faults in the camera can yield wrong outputs or break the whole steering chain, which can put a mission at risk. Smart software can spot such faults, but it needs good training data with faults in it.

The authors map fault cases for cameras used in sight based steering, with causes and effects on image quality. They sort the ways teams now soften those effects. They then build a tool that injects faults into fake images in a set, repeatable way. The data set made this way is meant to train and test fault spotting software. The public link waits for an embargo to end.
arxiv-2507-03202:
Ashot Matevosyan and Armen Allahverdyan study, in a 2025 physics paper, a Brownian particle tied to a bath that spins. Such spin states are wide in nature, yet first-principle work on them is thin. Their bath is a set of harmonic oscillators that rotate as one. The Langevin rule for the particle gains noise with long-range links in time, a mark of the spin. In the plain case, a bath at rest gives the Gibbs state for the particle. Here that state comes back for weak ties alone.

With a steady magnetic field, the end state is not Gibbs at all, even for weak ties. The pair sorts out when a classic claim on magnetism holds for spin states. A round, even well gives a state that acts like balance, and no work can be drawn from cycles that keep the spin symmetry. An uneven well breaks that bar.
arxiv-2507-03602:
Cornet and five co-authors put forth a new model in twenty twenty-five that makes fresh crystal stuffs on a computer. Crystals have set patterns that repeat, and atom spots sit on a loop-like space. That loop shape makes plain spread models hard to fit well.

Their model pairs each atom spot with a helper speed value on flat space. The spread then runs on flat space while still honors the loop and the crystal's own balance. On tests that guess known crystals and that dream up new ones, it scored with the best tools to date. The trick is the flat-space shift, they say.
arxiv-2507-03702:
Almutasem Bellah Enad and four co-authors present a 2025 paper on error rates for data detection in terahertz wireless links. Terahertz bands promise very fast short range links, but their channels fade in complex ways and hardware adds its own distortion. Simple receiver math that assumes tidy, independent noise can mislead design badly.

The team builds an error rate framework for a common linear receiver. They first work out the error rate under the usual independent assumptions. Then they redo it with channel and noise linked, using a coupling method that tracks the dependence. A third case adds distortion noise from flawed hardware. Simulations show the independence shortcut can skew error rates by several decibels.
arxiv-2507-04402:
Judy Ann Donato studies a number-theoretic function built from overpartitions in a 2025 paper. A partition splits a whole number into a decreasing list of parts, and an overpartition allows the first copy of each part to be marked.

The quantity of interest is the minimal excludant, the smallest positive whole number missing from the parts. Earlier work counted it over unmarked parts only. Donato takes up two other versions: marked parts only, and all parts together. For each, she studies the sum of the values across all overpartitions of a number. The paper works out counting formulas, growth behavior, and arithmetic traits of these sums.
arxiv-2507-04502:
Ido Ben-Dayan and Elena Emtsova build forms of gravity where the bend of space itself counts for less than in the standard theory, in a paper from 2025. Two routes are tried. One adds a field that caps the bend term, and the other links a free field to the bend in a matched way. Both routes treat the slicing of space and time as a live field, so the theory stays whole.

The new forms still give the standard worlds for the broad cosmos, black holes, frame drag, and waves. Wave speed shifts next to light speed, a mark tests can hunt. One edge case matches a known low speed gravity with extra symmetry. A single dial sets bend strength, with the standard theory at one set point.
arxiv-2507-04902:
Richard Haburcak wrote this mathematics paper, published in 2025. It sorts out how a family of special loci, the Brill-Noether loci, sit inside one another for algebraic curves of genus up to twelve.

Each locus gathers curves that admit certain kinds of function systems, called linear series. A refined theory asks which systems a typical curve in each locus actually carries. Because these loci can break into several pieces, a first step is to map their relative positions. The author studies bundles on K3 surfaces to tell loci apart and predict how they nest. Combined with older results and hands-on constructions, the paper pins down the relative positions of all Brill-Noether loci in the stated genus range.
arxiv-2507-05002:
Michael Píro and Jaroslav Hamrle study the ground state of tiny round grains in a simple model of matter. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five, though its text head bears a shorter title. The model, called jellium, holds electrons in a smooth field of plus charge. They use a Hartree-Fock method for grains with up to a few hundred electrons.

They check how well local density shortcuts match the fuller method for exchange and motion energy. Large gaps show up, both deep inside the grain and at its skin. They give refined forms for the local energy, tuned by grain size and charge density. They also set these next to gradient-based forms in wide use.
arxiv-2507-05302:
Binjia Zhou and co-authors present a face forgery detector that corrects its own detail claims. Their 2025 framework aims at clear, checkable reasons, not just a fake-or-real label. Visual-only tools give few reasons, while text-paired tools can invent details.

Guided questions push the model to fix wrong detail claims rather than hallucinate fresh ones. A detail-boost module sharpens the visual proof the model works from. A fusion step then merges visual backup and bias checks for hard cases. Tests show top scores against recent rivals. Detail calls stay accurate, and the method holds up on fresh data types. The authors stress trust as much as raw accuracy.
arxiv-2507-05402:
Srikanth Korse, Andreas Walther, and Emanuel Habets fix a timing flaw that smears wireless stereo sound. The catalog creator field is empty, so the head byline governs here. Loudspeakers with independent clocks drift apart by tiny sample rate offsets, and the drift blurs the spatial image that stereo depends on. Network clock protocols exist, but what the offsets do to listeners was unmapped. Their 2025 method works in the audio itself.

Spatial filtering first isolates each speaker's contribution in the room. Comparing those signals with the original playback yields the offset between clocks, which is then compensated before the sound is rendered. Listening tests and objective measures agree: the fix preserves the spatial cues that the drift degrades. The authors offer the scheme for wireless speaker sets that cannot share a wire or a perfect clock.
arxiv-2507-05502:
Arthur Deng, Karsten Householder, Fang Wu, Sebastian Thrun, Christopher Garcia, and Brian Trippe predict how mutations change protein binding, in a 2025 paper. Knowing whether a small change makes two proteins grip tighter or looser guides drug design and basic biology. Learning models trained for the task lag behind costly physics-based estimates, partly because binding data are scarce.

Their trick borrows strength from folding models, which are data-rich. Binding energy is recast as the folding energy of the joined pair minus the folding energies of each partner alone. A pre-trained folding model supplies those energies and scores well with no task training at all. Fine-tuning then sharpens it further, offering a cheaper route to mutation screening.
arxiv-2507-05602:
Vishal Baibhav, Andrei Gruzinov, and Yuri Levin test a proposed rocket effect that might push spinning dead stars through space. A recent claim held that an electromagnetic recoil from pulsars' own beams explains the stretched orbits of wide neutron star pairs found by the Gaia mission. In the cleanest theory of pulsar magnetospheres, the trio proves the beam-aligned recoil is exactly zero.

So something else must stretch those orbits, or the stars must be of the rare weak kind where the clean theory breaks down. They show some birth-kick patterns can do the job without any rocket, given mild assumptions about the stars' past. If rockets do prove necessary, the stars must be old, once fast-spinning, and weakly magnetized.
arxiv-2507-05802:
Gey, Le Gal, and Verhille study how nylon fibres clump in moving fluid in a 2025 arXiv paper. Fibre clumping matters in nature and industry, yet the process is still not well understood. The team built a setup that forms fibre aggregates in turbulent flow.

They mapped which settings produce clumps, building a phase diagram over the setup's parameters. They also measured the size and traits of the clumps that formed. The team then studied how clumps break apart over time. They propose a model for the breakup time and test it against their data.
arxiv-2507-06202:
Seeing a sound can teach a language learner what hearing alone cannot. Charlotte Kiesel and co-authors built an interactive vowel chart that plots tongue position, so learners can watch their own vowels move toward a target. They compared the chart with audio-only practice in a small study.

Learners said the visual feedback gave them a concrete goal, which audio practice lacked. All eight participants practiced more with the chart than without it. The authors conclude that charts work best when the picture maps plainly onto body movement, especially for learners with no phonetics training. Visual feedback also seems to motivate practice itself. The findings guide designers of pronunciation tools.
arxiv-2507-06302:
Effective field theories describe physics with a list of added interaction terms, and basic rules like positivity limit which values those terms may take. Ye, Cao, Wu, and Gu test how solid those limits are when the terms arise only at loop level. Their test bed is scalar QED, a theory of charged particles and light, simpler than the full Standard Model but with the same gauge structure.

They study two scattering processes and build the bounds from the full one-loop results. For one process, the simple tree-level bound can fail, yet the way the coefficient runs with energy tends to restore it at low energy. For the other, the bound survives at one loop. Two example models with a heavy extra particle confirm the pattern. The authors caution that the helpful running looks like a one-loop accident, not a deep law.
arxiv-2507-07102:
Humans recombine ideas effortlessly, but can a vision model name a red cube it never saw paired, after learning red and cube apart? Arnas Uselis and two co-authors test in 2025 whether simply scaling data teaches that trick. They vary dataset size, the variety of concepts, and how many combinations appear.

Variety, not volume, did the teaching. When coverage of combinations grew, models settled into a factored code where concepts add like numbers, and that code let them generalize perfectly from few examples. Famous pretrained models showed the structure only in part. The authors argue dataset builders should chase diversity over bulk. Composition, they conclude, is a data design problem before it is a size problem.
arxiv-2507-07202:
Mohamed Elmoghany and a large team of co-authors survey long-video storytelling generation in a two thousand twenty-five review paper. Today's best video models produce only five to sixteen seconds, and longer clips lose character consistency and scene coherence.

Some methods reach one hundred fifty seconds but with redundant frames and weak temporal variety. The authors study thirty-two papers to find which architectural components and training strategies reliably deliver multi-character narratives with fidelity. They build a taxonomy of existing methods and comparative tables organized by design and performance. The survey maps what cinematic quality, consistency, and length actually require from the next generation of video models.
arxiv-2507-07302: Kumar presents a paper from twenty twenty-five on using large language models as expert planners for multi-agent learning. Exploration is a known weak point in reinforcement learning. Many agents learning together make the problem worse. Expert-guided exploration is one proposed remedy for planning tasks. Kumar tests language models in that expert role. The models supply plans that steer how agents explore. The setting involves multiple agents solving planning-based tasks together. The aim is faster, more efficient learning through guided search.
arxiv-2507-07802:
Zhihui Zhang and co-authors pair fixed and live prompts so sight tools hold up when a sense stream drops, in a study from 2025. Big mix-data models shine when all streams flow. In the field a stream oft fails, and scores fall off a cliff. Prompt tricks help, but stiff prompts can not bend to each loss.

Their frame, SyP, weds two prompt kinds. A live shaper builds prompts that flex with the loss at hand. A set fixed bank holds the base, so no call flies blind. The pair keeps sense shares in tune when a key stream is gone. Gains in the tests were wide, the team reports. Bend plus base, they argue, is the shape a field tool needs.
arxiv-2507-07902:
Jinhong Wang and co-authors fuse data types for medical question answering in this 2025 paper. Language models with vision can aid diagnosis, yet they often state facts that clash with medical knowledge. Fetching outside sources helps, but fetching too much or too little both hurt.

Their framework, MIRA, tunes how much is fetched and how it is fused with images and text. It guards against a subtler flaw: a model that first answers right, then talks itself into error by leaning on fetched text. The design aims for replies that stay true to established knowledge. Safer medical chatbots are the goal.
arxiv-2507-08102:
Ashutosh Singh and co-authors give a full guide to encoding quantum information in the timing of light pulses, in a 2025 review. In time-bin encoding, a qubit rides in whether a photon arrives early or late. The scheme shrugs off shaking, heat drift, and the twists that fiber cables put on light, which makes it a strong pick for long-distance quantum links.

The review walks through the ways labs make and measure these time-bin qubits. Each setup trades off design choices, part fit across optics and electronics, and how the readout is done. The authors weigh the strengths and limits of each route for real communication tasks. Builders of quantum networks can use the guide to pick setups that survive real fiber lines.
arxiv-2507-08202:
Bhowmik, Humble, and Thapliyal design Trojan attacks aimed at quantum neural networks, in a 2025 paper. Such networks are a leading hope for quantum machine learning, yet their security has barely been studied. The team's Quantum Properties Trojans exploit basic quantum traits, using gate behavior to insert noise and Hadamard gates to enable superposition.

The planted Trojans stayed stealthy while dragging down the circuits' performance. The strongest one cut the accuracy of a binary classifier by twenty-three percent in the team's tests. The authors say this is the first Trojan attack on a fully quantum neural network, with no classical part involved.
arxiv-2507-08302:
Xue Dong He, Chen Yang, and Yutian Zhou model arbitrage in twenty twenty-five. Decentralized exchanges use automated market makers, which can leave price gaps against centralized exchanges. Traders who spot a gap can profit, but gas fees and the order of transactions matter. Price gaps are public, so rival arbitrageurs compete for the same chance.

Older models mostly ignored that rivalry. The authors build the first equilibrium model of gas fee competition between two arbitrageurs. They test three settings for how failed trades are reverted. Pure symmetric equilibria do not exist, but unique mixed ones can be described. Data from Binance and Uniswap V2 backed the model's claims about fees, liquidity, and trade size.
arxiv-2507-08702:
Viktoriia Makovska, George Fletcher, and Julia Stoyanovich present ONION, in a 2025 preprint, a layered method for designing data models with the people affected by them. Entity-relationship design is usually done by experts alone, which bakes in their blind spots. ONION runs five stages whose initials give the name: Observe, Nurture, Integrate, Optimize, Normalize. Raw stakeholder input enters at the start. Stage by stage it hardens into a structured diagram. The method draws on design justice and participatory AI ideas.

The team tested ONION in real workshops on social-technical systems in Ukraine. Mixed groups of stakeholders took part. The authors report richer models and better mutual understanding than expert-only design gives. Diversity entered at the earliest stage, where it shapes everything downstream. Scaling the workshops and refining the stages remain open work. The paper offers the framework as a template for inclusive data modeling.
arxiv-2507-08802:
Explaining a neural net as a clean algorithm sounds neat, but the map between them does the heavy lifting. Denis Sutter, Julian Minder, Thomas Hofmann, and Tiago Pimentel stress-test that map in a 2025 paper. They drop the usual rule that maps stay linear.

With free-form maps, any net can be matched to any algorithm, they prove. The match then says nothing about the net itself. Tests back the proof: random, untrained models map perfectly onto a task algorithm. Accuracy hit one hundred percent on the probe task. The trade-off between map power and truth has no set rule. Causal abstraction alone, they argue, cannot open the black box.
arxiv-2507-08902:
Sergio Mares, Ariel Espinoza Weinberger, and Nilah Ioannidis design vaccine candidate peptides with diffusion models in a 2025 paper. Personalized cancer vaccines hinge on peptides that a patient's immune display molecules will present to T cells. Training data come from lab assays with baked-in biases, so truly novel binders may be missed.

The team built the benchmark differently: a diffusion model, guided by the geometry of known crystal structures, generated peptides for twenty priority display types. The designs were new, yet they reproduced the known anchor patterns that binders use, showing the model learned structure rather than copying data by heart. Top sequence predictors then did poorly on these sound designs, revealing blind spots that standard benchmarks hide. The libraries are more diverse than current data sets. Code and data are public, to make training and tests fairer for immunotherapy design.
arxiv-2507-09002:
Karla Varela and co-authors extracted fireball parameters for four gamma-ray burst afterglows in a 2025 paper. The fireball model describes these fading glows well, but pinning down all its parameters without assumptions has succeeded for only a few bursts. The data come from GROND, a seven-channel camera that watched burst afterglows from Chile between 2007 and 2016.

The team combined GROND light curves with public X-ray data and some radio and sub-millimeter observations. All four bursts turned out to have exploded into a wind-shaped environment. The fits also traced how the magnetic field evolved, giving evidence that shocks amplify the field already present around the star.
arxiv-2507-09402:
Anibal Sierra and co-authors report new telescope views of a dust trap that leaks in the planet-forming disk around PDS 70, in a 2025 paper. PDS 70 hosts two young planets still growing inside a ring of dust. Dust traps are thought to pile up the grains that build planets. Whether those traps hold grains of every size was unclear.

Observations at the shortest millimeter wavelengths map the smallest grains. The ring's peak sits at a new radius, between infrared and longer-wave views. A faint outer shoulder also appears only at this wavelength. Small grains seem to slip through the trap. Planet formation models must now explain that leak. The data sharpen the story of how this famous system is assembling.
arxiv-2507-09502:
Sishir Jana and co-authors map the electronic and magnetic phases of a graphene defect in a 2025 paper. Where two graphene crystals meet at a skew boundary, the carbon net forms a ladder of five and seven membered rings.

Using a standard model of electron interaction on that ladder, solved by a mean field method, they chart the phases as two interaction strengths vary. Charge can order partly or fully, with metal or insulator behavior. Magnetism ranges from none to waves of spin and a mixed state where spins cancel overall. One phase carries spin polarization, which suits spin based electronics. The system also shows electric polarization alongside the magnetic order, a pairing called multiferroicity.
arxiv-2507-09902:
Yuanhao Wang, a solo author, wrote a math paper in 2025 on a classic learning rule for games. The rule has each player track what the rival has done so far and reply with a best move. In 1959, Samuel Karlin guessed how fast this rule settles to a balance point in two-player games.

A stronger form of the guess fell in 2014, but only when ties could be broken in a hostile way. Wang shows the plain guess fails too, with no hostile tricks. He gives a ten-by-ten game where the rule settles much more slowly than Karlin claimed. No ties occur in his game after the first step. The result closes a question open for more than sixty years.
arxiv-2507-10002:
Peter Mészáros and Daniel Račko study the young universe just after inflation, when radiation ruled but a trace of solid-like matter may have lingered. Their 2025 paper calls this leftover an anisotropic solid remnant, borrowing from solid inflation models where matter is described by a triplet of fields. Breaking the triplet's inner symmetry makes expansion uneven by direction.

Ripples larger than the horizon behave in new ways in this setting. Wavy patterns of the scalar and vector kinds grow, while the tensor kind, linked to gravitational waves, acts as usual. In one edge case, with very little remnant lasting as long as possible, vector ripples shrink with a fresh scaling law. The authors say the model fits observations of solid inflation better when its nonlinear effects are weak.
arxiv-2507-10602:
Maximilian Stölzle and co-authors show in a 2025 paper how robots can learn rhythmic motion by watching, with stability promised. Learning from demonstration is a lean route to complex behavior, since the robot learns from few examples and moves with force and flow. Tools called dynamic motion primitives come with built-in stability, but they strain to catch rich repeating patterns and to blend between tasks, which shuts out jobs such as walking.

Their frame, Orbitally Stable Motion Primitives, joins a learned encoder that bends shapes smoothly with a supercritical Hopf bifurcation held in a hidden space. That pairing picks up repeating motions with care while it locks in formal stability around the loop. A rhythmic task can thus be reshaped without losing its beat. Readers get blocks made for the repeating world of walking and tool use.
arxiv-2507-11002:
Kim and co-authors improve a hybrid quantum-neural method for finding the lowest energy state of a system. The earlier method let a neural network adjust a quantum circuit's output. Its non-unitary steps broke normalization and made training unstable. Measurement costs also grew steeply with each added qubit. The new version, U-VQNHE, forces the neural part to stay unitary.

That fix removes the normalization problem at its root. Training stays steadier, and far fewer measurements are needed. Accuracy still beats standard variational quantum methods. The authors frame the design as a step toward methods that scale. Ground state estimates matter for chemistry and materials work.
arxiv-2507-11202:
Xinkui Zhao and co-authors present a method from two thousand twenty-five for recognizing emotion when some input channels are missing. Emotion systems often blend face, voice, and text, but sensors fail or privacy rules block a channel. Older methods train all channel blends together, and the training signals for unlike blends can clash.

Their framework adapts a large model with small low-rank updates split by channel blend. One module separates shared information from what each blend holds alone. Another module adjusts how much training each blend gets, based on how clearly its features separate. Tests on several benchmark sets showed clear gains over earlier methods for learning with missing channels.
arxiv-2507-11302:
Jesse Hagenaars and three co-authors flew a quadrotor in 2025 using vision alone, with no inertial sensors at all. Drones normally lean on gyroscopes and accelerometers to stay level; some flying animals manage without any gravity sense. A downward event camera, which reports only changes, fed a small memory-equipped neural network.

The network read tilt and spin from the event stream fast enough to close the control loop in real flight. Tests probed how well it coped with new rooms and lighting. Dropping the inertial unit trims weight, cost, and one whole failure mode.
arxiv-2507-11402:
Robot contests can steer research toward real factory needs, and a 2025 paper by Supun Dissanayaka and co-authors lays out a plan for a new RoboCup league. The old Logistics League focused on moving goods in a smart factory, with tasks built around planning, scheduling, and teams of agents.

The authors argue that the old focus left out much of modern smart manufacturing, which made the contest less relevant over time. Their new Smart Manufacturing League would use several tracks at first, then merge them into one large factory scene. New tracks would cover assembly, robots working beside people, and humanoid robots, while keeping the logistics tasks. The aim is a contest that draws new teams and reflects where factories are heading.
arxiv-2507-11802:
Breanna Shi and five co-authors frame online research mentoring in twenty twenty-five. Research experience matters for computing master's students who aim at academic careers. Online students were long shut out by the physical nature of labs. Their framework, FAIR-CS, is built to open that door.

FAIR-CS pursues research goals, builds research communities, and supports quality mentorship online. It pairs master's researchers with academic mentors in dynamic partnerships. Those partnerships have produced interdisciplinary publications. The paper then describes the framework at work in one group. That group draws students from Georgia Tech's online master's in computer science. Readers in online education get a working model for real research participation at a distance.
arxiv-2507-11902:
Juscimara Avelino, George Cavalcanti, and Rafael Cruz survey ways to fix skewed data in regression in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Many real data sets cluster around common outcomes, leaving rare values thinly covered. Models then predict the rare cases badly. Resampling methods adjust the training data to give rare cases more weight. This fix is well studied for classification, where outcomes are labels. Far less work covers regression, where outcomes are numbers.

The authors ran a broad set of experiments across balancing methods and predictive models. They scored the results with metrics chosen for skewed settings. They also propose a taxonomy that sorts methods by model, learning process, and metric. Their findings show which strategies help which models. The paper guides data scientists who face rare-value prediction.
arxiv-2507-12202:
Anton Klenitskiy and co-authors use sparse autoencoders to open up the black box of models that suggest what a user may want next, based on past picks. Such transformer models work well, but their inner steps are hard to read, which limits trust and control.

A sparse autoencoder learns a set of clean, single sense directions inside the model. Those directions proved easier to read than the raw inner axes. The authors then show a plain way to steer the model by nudging those directions. That gives builders and users a flexible grip on what the system suggests in each setting.
arxiv-2507-12302:
Julius Zeiss and co-authors show, in a 2025 paper, that the value of a small quantum game can be approximated to any set accuracy, fast. The running time grows only modestly as the accuracy tightens. Two-player games assisted by shared entanglement are a test bed for quantum advantage. Older methods for bounding their value blew up exponentially with the demanded precision. The authors change the scaling by proving new symmetry theorems tailored to separability problems.

Their theorems feed a ladder of semidefinite programs that bound the entangled value from outside. Symmetry reduction keeps each program solvable within the claimed time. A rounding scheme then turns those outer bounds into actual entangled strategies with certified quality. Those strategies can also warm-start local search tools. The team expects the methods to serve wider problems in quantum information.
arxiv-2507-12602:
Ohamouddou and four colleagues classify tree species from LiDAR point clouds with a multi-scale graph neural network. Point density varies enormously between trunk and canopy, yet standard graph methods encode edge geometry the same way at every scale. The authors prove this is suboptimal: normalized features suit high signal-to-noise regimes, raw displacements suit low ones.

Their network uses raw vectors locally and hybrid encodings at intermediate scales, with scale-dependent normalization. Ablations confirm each design choice, including robustness under canopy thinning and noise. On a seven-species terrestrial scanning benchmark it reached the highest accuracy among fifty-six models with a compact parameter count. Airborne data results were also competitive.
arxiv-2507-13802:
Europe's food safety checks generate mountains of results that sit scattered across a thousand files. A twelve-author team gathers them into one database in 2025, named CHEFS. It holds 392 million test results from over 15 million samples and more than 4,000 products. The sources are the official monitoring records that member states send to the European Food Safety Authority. Residues of farm chemicals, veterinary drugs, and other contaminants all land in one structured home.

The team then mines the years 2000 to 2024 for trends: what gets tested, what fails, and how countries differ. They present the database as fuel for early warning systems and smarter policy, ready for AI tools that the raw files had kept out.
arxiv-2507-13902:
Learned micro solvers for flow near rough walls are set out by Emanuel Ström, Anna-Karin Tornberg, and Ozan Öktem in a 2025 arXiv paper. Flow past a rough wall is solved at two scales in the classic method, but the small scale runs cost much time. Their net learns those small runs ahead of time. It maps wall shape to the weights for local flow means.

Since the net leans on wall shape alone, it trains apart from edge settings. Proofs tie a bounded training loss to a bounded error in the big flow. Tests match the classic method on skill while the small runs cost far less. Rough scale shifts stay stable.
arxiv-2507-14202:
Pengfei Du presents a way to make large language models safer without the costly step-by-step grading that current methods rely on. The paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Grading each reasoning step needs a separate reward model, which is slow and hard to scale. Du's framework swaps that grader for attack and defense rounds.

Automated red teams probe the model with evolved attacks, team-based plays, and mutated prompts. The weak spots found then guide toughening training, paced like a school course. Extra rules keep the training from drifting too far. Tests across five top models beat the graded approach on safety while cutting costs sharply. Built-in reports and audits let the process improve over time and meet rules. The aim is strong safety for groups with small budgets.
arxiv-2507-14402:
Zamora uses proton scattering to infer the density of nuclear matter in a 2025 paper. When protons bounce off a nucleus at small angles, the pattern reveals the nucleus's matter radius. The method relies on Glauber scattering theory, but its inputs carry uncertainty, including the density profile itself and data on how nucleons scatter off each other.

A joint Bayesian analysis fitted twelve scattering patterns at once, from nickel, zirconium, and lead targets at several energies. The sampling method produced probability ranges for 42 input values. Density values and nucleon scattering values turned out to be moderately linked, and that link affects how the radius is read off. The approach gives a consistent way to extract density from data across energies.
arxiv-2507-14502:
Koley and co-authors, writing for the ALMA-IMF survey team in 2025, measured turbulence inside fifteen massive young star clusters. These protoclusters are dense cradles where many large stars are forming at once. The team used a radio telescope array in Chile to trace a rare form of carbon monoxide gas across each cluster.

The gas motion proved supersonic everywhere, with a spread of speeds that looked similar at every stage of cluster youth. Around the dense cores where individual stars form, the motion calmed to about half the level of the gas around them, as if turbulence drains away at core edges. A size-versus-speed relation came out steeper than the classic law for calm turbulence, which fits squishable gas. The study is among the first to chart turbulence across so many massive cradles at once.
arxiv-2507-14602:
Riyad Hassaine and co-authors present a 2025 set of rates for electron hits on the hydrogen molecular ion and its heavy twin. These ions were among the first species in the early universe and seed the chemistry of space clouds. Low energy electrons can bump them between spin and vibration states or split them apart.

The team used a multichannel quantum defect method to compute fresh cross sections and thermal rates for those paths. The new rates split in a clear way from the values used in past models. When fed into astrochemical models of shock driven, metal free gas, the updates shift the results. The work matters for models of the first stars and early gas cooling.
arxiv-2507-14702:
Partha Sarker, Dipto Dey, and Marium-E-Jannat Mukta study heavy phone use among undergraduates in a 2025 paper. Most tools to curb such use work by locking apps or adding friction, and many users find those tools a pain.

A survey of one hundred nine users found that about one in five would not use a tool that limits apps at all. The team then built an Android app that sends alerts and shows charts of use, a soft push meant to raise self-awareness with no locks. A three-week trial gave early proof that the push can work. The work points to a gentler route for people who reject hard limits.
arxiv-2507-15002:
Xiaokui Yang presents a 2025 mathematics paper, the first in a series, on comparison theorems in Hermitian geometry. That field studies spaces whose local shape mixes complex coordinates with a matching metric. Riemannian geometry, its real cousin, owns famous results of this kind. Those results bound how a space curves by matching its volumes and distances against simple model spaces. Yang builds the analytic groundwork for results of the same kind in the Hermitian case.

The paper develops second variational formulas and index forms. These tools track how curves and surfaces bend under small changes. From that base it proves counterparts of three classics: a Myers-type theorem, Laplacian comparison theorems, and volume comparison theorems. Such results let geometers infer a space's whole shape from local bounds on its curvature. The paper lays track for later parts of the series.
arxiv-2507-15202:
Karim Benharrak, Puyuan Peng, and Amy Pavel built TalkLess in twenty twenty-five, a system for editing recorded speech down to its essentials. Cutting filler and tangents from podcasts and lectures is slow manual work. Pure extraction deletes whole sentences but lacks finesse; re-synthesized summaries lose the speaker's voice and style. TalkLess blends both.

It generates candidate transcript edits, picks the set maximizing compression, coverage, and audio quality, then applies them through a speech editing model. The interface splits wording-level cuts from big content decisions across two panes, keeping creators in control. Against a leading extractive tool, TalkLess kept more content and removed more errors. A study with twelve editors found it significantly lowered effort and mental load.
arxiv-2507-15302:
Kieran Dalton and nine co-authors check whether separate quantum modules really prepare the same states. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Future quantum computers will likely link smaller modules together. Benchmarks must test performance inside and between modules. Cross-platform verification compares state preparation across devices. Communication between modules may be purely classical in cheap protocols.

Their testbed is a six-qubit flip-chip device. Two three-qubit modules share one carrier chip. Links allow entanglement within and across the modules. Resource costs of classical-only protocols grow exponentially with qubit count in the worst case. The experiments show where the protocols stay practical. Modular quantum hardware gains honest scaling data.
arxiv-2507-15602:
Zihui Gao, Jia-Wang Bian, Guosheng Lin, Hao Chen, and Chunhua Shen present a 2025 paper joining two ways of rebuilding 3D scenes from photos. One method, based on signed distance functions, captures clean overall geometry but misses fine detail. The other, Gaussian splatting, renders new views beautifully but can produce incoherent shapes.

Their hybrid, SurfaceSplat, lets each method fix the other. The distance-based model gives the splatting a sound coarse shape. Fresh views rendered by the splatting then sharpen the surface model's detail. On two standard datasets, the pair beat leading methods at both surface reconstruction and new-view rendering from few photos. The authors plan to release their code for other teams to build on.
arxiv-2507-15702:
Brandon Le and co-authors show that the final state of coupled neuron models is often nearly impossible to predict, in a 2025 paper. These multistable systems can settle into chaos or calm, and small differences at the start decide which. The authors propose a mechanism, chance synchronization, that drives the unpredictability.

They test the idea on five simple discrete-time systems, each built from a different neuron model. Basin maps, an uncertainty exponent, and basin entropy all back the claim. The uncertainty is not a side effect of noise or high dimension, they argue. It lives in low-dimensional, fully deterministic models, which matters for how we model the brain and cognition.
arxiv-2507-15802:
Rémi Vaucher and Paul Minchella present a 2025 paper on building hypergraphs from collections of time series. A hypergraph links more than two points in one edge, capturing group relations that plain graphs miss. Earlier work built such structures for a single multi-channel series; real problems often hold many series at once.

The authors extend a topological data analysis method to whole collections. They use signature transforms, which summarize the shape of a path, to add controlled randomness to the construction. That randomness makes the resulting hypergraph sturdier against noise. Tests on synthetic data sets gave promising results. The approach opens the door to studying fleets of sensors or panels of patients as one relational object.
arxiv-2507-16102:
Alyssa Chan and Eva Kanso explain why a fish school remembers: not because it can sit in two stable states, but because noise smears a tipping point. Schools switch between polarized swimming and rotational milling. A standard model, with avoidance, alignment, and attraction rules, shows collective memory. Its patterns depend on the group's history. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the pair combine simulations with bifurcation theory. The switch between milling and schooling turns out to be a transcritical bifurcation, where the two states cross and swap stability. Random noise stretches that crossing into a memory effect.

A simple model of the group's polarization captures the essentials: the bifurcation, the lingering transient milling, and the memory itself. The finding resolves a standing ambiguity about the memory's origin. Noise, usually a nuisance, is here the mechanism.
arxiv-2507-16602:
Antonis Delakouras, Georgios Doultsinos, and David Petrosyan present a 2025 paper on multi-qubit gates between distant neutral atoms. Atoms in arrays store qubits in long-lived ground states. A global laser pulse lifts them to a Rydberg state, where neighbors block each other from exciting together.

Arranged in a star pattern, the atoms excite a number of times set by the input state's parity. Flipping the interaction's sign and pulsing again cancels the dynamical phase while keeping a geometric phase tied to that parity. Combined with single-qubit rotations, the trick yields controlled gates for many atoms at once. The authors extend the scheme to distant qubits linked by a chain of atoms acting as a quantum bus.
arxiv-2507-16702:
Fahad Alharthi and co-authors test a full-chain sim tool for anti-matter beam sources against real runs. The work dates to 2025. Strong sources of such beams drive next-round smash labs. Beam grade shapes how bright the smash light can get.

Source build runs through birth, grab, and haul steps, all tied to each. The tool was checked next to past tools and next to live tests at a Japan source. Key knobs were scanned one by one, from hit spot to field strength to wave phase. The test score was the beam yield at the grab end. Sim and live counts matched well.
arxiv-2507-16802:
Yanjun Zheng and co-authors present a 2025 paper on a family of language models built for finance. General models often falter on money questions that demand careful reasoning, strict trustworthiness, and exact domain terms. Their series comes in two sizes, eight and thirty-two billion parameters, built on an open foundation model.

A label system for financial tasks organizes the training data, and difficulty-aware tuning adjusts the training as it goes. Trust is handled at several layers: curated knowledge, data made by cooperating agents, and strict validation checks. Training runs in two stages. The paper argues that this recipe yields models that reason better on financial problems while staying dependable enough for real deployment.
arxiv-2507-17002:
Sidney Washburn proves that certain Siegel cusp forms are fixed by a small set of their coefficients, in a 2025 paper. These forms are higher-dimensional cousins of classical modular forms. Their expansions carry many coefficients indexed by discriminants. The theorem concerns forms with a level and a character twist. Only coefficients at discriminants coprime to the level are needed, under conditions on the level.

For genus three, the result sharpens further. Coefficients tied to maximal orders in quaternion algebras suffice there. A parallel claim covers Jacobi forms of fundamental index. Their primitive theta components determine them under the same coprimality rule. Results of this kind cut the data needed to pin down a form. That helps both theory and computation in the field.
arxiv-2507-17102:
Misawa and co-authors watch a kagome metal change its shape as it cools. Kagome lattices, named for their woven pattern, host odd electronic states, but many such materials warp from a six-sided form into a less symmetric one at high temperature for reasons little discussed. Using synchrotron X-rays, the team tracks the change in a family of rare-earth ruthenium silicides.

The low-temperature phase pairs up kagome atoms between layers, and a dimer model with one-dimensional disorder reproduces the fuzzy scattering seen mid-transition. The authors argue that molecular orbitals forming between those atoms drive the warp, in line with their calculations. They also propose a simple rule, from atomic size and bonding pull, for judging which kagome metals will keep their symmetry.
arxiv-2507-17202:
Jooyeol Yun and co-authors present DesignLab, a system that designs slides by arguing with itself, in a 2025 paper. Making polished slides is hard for non-experts, who must juggle layout, color, and type choices. Tools that generate a deck in one pass cannot fix their own weak spots, while human designers polish through rounds of review.

DesignLab splits the job between two tuned language models. A reviewer hunts for design flaws in each draft, and a contributor repairs what the reviewer flags. Training data came from drafts spoiled on purpose, so the reviewer learned real error types and the contributor learned real fixes. In experiments the loop beat rival generators, including a commercial tool, ending with slides the authors call professional grade.
arxiv-2507-17402:
Jun Li and co-authors wrote a paper from 2025 on finding the right moments in long videos when a text query covers only part of the footage. Standard spaces for embedding video and text are flat, and flat geometry can warp the tree-like structure inside a video, where scenes hold clips and clips hold frames. That warping dulls how well models match partial content. The team moved the matching into curved hyperbolic space.

Their model, named HLFormer, mixes two attention blocks: one that works in the curved space and one in flat space. A fusion module guided by average features blends the two views on the fly. A new loss term enforces the natural order that a text query sits inside the video's span, using cone constraints in the curved space. On standard benchmarks, the model beat the best past methods for this task.
arxiv-2507-17502:
Three authors study linked quantum states of two charged particles and ask how fast motion changes the link, in a paper from 2025. The pair interact through a pull that is the same in all directions, and the authors judge the link with standard tests for split states. The core claim is proved with full rigor for this setup.

In the fast motion regime the pair stays linked, the authors show. In the slow motion limit of the same setup, the pair can be split with no link at all. The contrast shows that motion itself can create a link that the slow view misses. The result gives a clean case for teaching how quantum links depend on the frame of motion.
arxiv-2507-17602:
A team including Wolfgang Kilian set out a fresh way to read magnetic fields with great care. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, works with free spin precession signals from polarized helium gas. The rate of that spin tells the strength of the field. Old fits use least squares math, which can fail when the signal fades or the rate drifts. Their method uses an extended Kalman smoother to track the signal.

Tests on fake signals with fade and drift showed the new way beats block fits. It adapts on its own with little tuning from the user. Readers who measure fields for physics tests get a sturdier tool. Small errors in field reads can spoil searches for new physics.
arxiv-2507-18202:
Kim, Kim, Jeon, and Lee propose GMTP, a defense that spots poisoned documents planted in the knowledge base of a retrieval-augmented generation system. Such systems fetch outside documents to ground a language model's answers, which lets attackers slip in crafted texts that steer the model toward false or harmful output. GMTP first finds the tokens that most affect how similar the retriever judges a document to be, using gradients of the similarity score.

It then hides those key tokens and asks a masked language model how expected each one is. Tokens planted by attackers look unnatural in context, so their scores stand out as unusually low. In experiments, the method removed over 90 percent of poisoned content while keeping genuine documents, and held up across several data sets and attack styles. The authors offer it as a practical filter for safer retrieval pipelines.
arxiv-2507-18302:
Delong Ran and co-authors show that lightly fine-tuned language models still leak their training data, in a 2025 paper. LoRA fine-tuning adjusts only a small slice of a model's weights, which feels privacy-safe. Membership inference attacks try to guess whether a given text was in the training set. The authors argue that the untouched base model actually helps such attacks.

Their framework, LoRA-Leak, bundles fifteen attacks, including five upgraded ones that use the base model as a reference. Tests on three advanced models across three language tasks show clear vulnerability. Even cautious fine-tuning settings leaked membership signals well above chance. The team also probes which settings raise or lower the risk, and weighs possible defenses.
arxiv-2507-18802:
People rating machine-written text usually face two long passages and a gut call, which blurs exactly the judgments trainers need. Danqing Shi and four co-authors built an interface in 2025 that splits passages into single claims so raters can compare claim by claim.

Their tool, DxHF, shows the claims with their relevance to the conversation marked and look-alike claims linked, letting raters skim to the real differences. Tests showed decomposition raised feedback accuracy, most where raters felt unsure. A 160-person study gained about five percent accuracy at a cost of eighteen extra seconds per judgment. The authors argue interface design itself is a lever on machine alignment quality.
arxiv-2507-18902:
Hongyuan Lu and three co-authors tackle a cost problem in machine translation for the world's low-resource languages. Large language models translate better when handed a dictionary in the prompt, but supplying every one burns tokens and money. Their new task asks a sharper question: which dictionaries are worth including? Their method, SLoW, answers by picking dictionaries for low-frequency words, the rare vocabulary a model is least likely to know alone.

Cleverly, frequencies are estimated from public resources rather than the model's private training data, which is usually secret. No model retraining is needed. Tested on one hundred languages from the FLORES benchmark, the method beat strong baselines while spending fewer tokens. In many languages it even out-translated the full-dictionary approach, proof more help is not always better help. The authors frame smart selection as the flexible middle path between quality and cost.
arxiv-2507-19202:
Nao Tokui and Tom Baker remix sound inside the hidden codes of neural audio models in a 2025 paper. Classic granular synthesis chops audio into tiny grains and replays them in new orders, but the cuts leave clicks and seams.

Their method works one level up. A source recording is encoded into short code segments, forming a grain library. Each grain of a target sound is then swapped for its closest match from that library. Decoding the hybrid keeps the target's timing and shape while borrowing the source's tone. No training is needed, and the decoder smooths over the joins that plague older methods. A public demo lets users try their own sounds.
arxiv-2507-19502:
Chen and Nguyen settle a sum that Euler would have recognized. Euler studied series built from harmonic numbers, the running sums of unit fractions, and found closed forms for simple cases. Here the sum runs over the product of four consecutive harmonic numbers, divided by a matching product of four consecutive integers.

Working with basic methods in Euler's spirit, the pair evaluates the sum exactly in terms of zeta values, the constants Euler himself made famous. The closed form they reach may disprove a conjecture by Furdui and Sîntămărian. They also connect the problem to open questions about whether certain zeta values are irrational or independent over the rationals.
arxiv-2507-19602:
Jaehoon Cha, Tingyao Lu, Matthew Walker, and Keith Butler train in a 2025 paper an autoencoder that sorts spectral features without any labels. New material hunts often stall for want of labeled data or costly simulations. A compact code that mirrors physics could guide the search instead.

Their disentangling model learns from light absorption spectra of candidate solar materials. One latent axis tracks a known peak efficiency gauge closely, though it never saw that label. That axis maps to the switch between direct and indirect band gaps in the spectra. Against two rival methods, the code rebuilds spectra better and uses fewer axes. Guided search then finds top solar candidates in fewer trials than random hunting.
arxiv-2507-20302:
Sangyong Jeon, Alina Czajka, and Juhee Hong study the math behind how a hot, dense form of matter flows, in a 2025 paper. The matter forms when heavy atomic nuclei crash at high speed. Its flow traits, such as thickness under shear, are found through formulas that need response functions for stress and energy. Knowing the exact shape of those functions is a must before the formulas can be trusted.

Using energy-saving laws and results from gravity-based models, the team pins down the shape of all such functions at low rates and long waves. They match those shapes against flow models of second and third order. That match yields new versions of the classic formulas for the case where the rate limit is taken first. The authors also show how the sense of some formulas can shift when higher-order terms enter the flow model.
arxiv-2507-20702:
Andrea Gloppen Johnsen and co-authors write bid rules for hydrogen plants in power markets, in a study from 2025. The plants split water with power to make green hydrogen. Grants in Europe and the United States pay just when each hour's power can be shown to be green, a rule called temporal matching.

That rule makes the grant sum a guess at bid time, since wind and sun swing. The team builds a day-ahead bid curve that weighs odds across scenes of green yield. Math from the best-plan rules gives the curve. In a case study, odds-aware bids raised gain by near four percent. Yet they did not raise the true green match rate. The team flags that gap as a flaw in the grant rule's pull.
arxiv-2507-20802:
Maximilian Reihn and co-authors speed up a simulation method that reveals how molecular systems deform, by running its steps in parallel. Athermal quasistatic deformation stretches a system in small increments, relaxing it after each step to remove thermal noise. The method exposes pure structural response, but its long chain of dependent steps is costly.

Their scheme steps at two levels at once. Large strides first set anchor points along the energy landscape, using multi-threading to guess ahead. Fine steps then fill the path between anchors, checking each guess. The parallel design cuts the computing time to trace the true trajectory, opening larger systems to this kind of analysis.
arxiv-2507-21302:
Christoph Metzner and three co-authors ask whether human-written reasons can teach clinical AI to sort medical texts better. Doctors and coders often jot down why a report points to a given cancer site. Their 2025 study used over ninety-nine thousand such notes as extra training data for transformer models. The models learned to pull the main cancer site from pathology reports. A quality score was also tested as a way to pick the best notes.

Adding the notes helped only when training data was already plentiful, and results were uneven when data was scarce. Models given more plain reports beat the note-trained ones. The authors advise spending labeling effort on more reports if accuracy is the goal, though notes may still help models explain their choices.
arxiv-2507-22102:
Qiaorong Yu and co-authors measured a feature at the edge of dark matter halos in 2025, where matter falling in for the first time piles up. This splashback edge can be described by its depth and width, two measures the team defined for this study.

They used the largest run of a major galaxy formation simulation and stacked halos by mass, age, and other traits. Depth grew steeply with halo mass, following a clean power law. Width tracked most strongly a measure of how rare the halo's peak is. Both measures remembered the halo's long building history more than its recent growth. The authors give fitting formulas in terms of mass, cosmic time, and history.
arxiv-2507-22302:
Elina Sendonaris, Jamison Sloan, Nicholas Rivera, Ido Kaminer, and Marin Soljačić show how tiny optical structures could steer a process that mixes X-rays with light, in a 2025 paper. Nonlinear optics, where materials convert light between colors or split photons into entangled pairs, has mostly worked at optical frequencies and below. A second-order process linking X-ray and optical photons exists, but it is weak and hard to shape because X-ray wavelengths are tiny.

The team develops a quantum theory of that mixing and applies it to crystals patterned at the nanoscale. In their example, a photonic crystal both strengthens the X-ray output, more than doubling the rate for its fill, and directs where the X-rays go. The authors point to uses in purer X-ray sources, ghost imaging of crystal and electron behavior, and measurements past standard quantum limits.
arxiv-2507-22702:
Hendrik Reiter and four co-authors introduce Ecoscape, a benchmark for judging how well self-healing software works at the edge of a network. Edge devices process data close to where it arises, which cuts delay, but they sit in fault-prone places. A remediator is a program that spots trouble and tweaks a service's settings to keep it within its service goals.

Many remediation strategies exist, built for example on Kubernetes, from moving a service to changing its parameters. Until now there was no fair way to compare them. Ecoscape uses chaos engineering to inject realistic faults and scores each strategy on how well it holds service levels. Its goals can be tuned to a given domain. The authors show it at work on edge machine learning inference, where it grades fault tolerance without the need for a physical testbed.
arxiv-2507-23102:
Jin Kunwoo Lee studies a special class of representations of unitary groups, in a solo math paper from two thousand twenty-five. Representations are ways to realize group actions as linear maps. The class at issue sits at a degenerate limit of the discrete series, a family tied to square-summable behavior.

Lee shows one can choose a cohomology group for such a representation that does not vanish. The choice sits at a canonical degree, and the groups obey a duality rule. Twin cases for two group sizes share the same live degree. A linking map for two small cases closes the paper, with a subtle vanishing twist.
arxiv-2507-23202:
Xia and four co-authors built a trick in twenty twenty-five to make fake pics that fool vision-word models while staying close to the true pic. Stock tricks hide their noise in fine detail, where plain filters can wash it out. Their way bakes the fake sense into the maker's noise step.

Since that noise spans all detail bands, the fake sense does too. The end pic blends true pic and noise, so low-pass filters spare the fake part. Tests beat top past tricks on hit rate. The fakes also stood up to more guards, they report.
arxiv-2508-00402:
The authors compute the masses of exotic particles that may be loose unions of two known mesons. Using QCD sum rules, a method that ties particle properties to the vacuum's background fields, they built currents for charm-strange pairs and their heavier bottom cousins, keeping many correction terms.

The predicted masses land right on three known particles, supporting their reading as molecular states. Two bottom pairings come out above their breakup thresholds, so they likely cannot bind. A third bottom pairing falls below its threshold, marking it as a candidate bound molecule worth hunting in experiments.
arxiv-2508-00502:
Jonathan Mannaert, Paolo Santonastaso, and Ferdinando Zullo study a special class of point sets in projective spaces in a 2025 math paper. Linear sets over finite fields link geometry with coding theory. Among them, clubs are sets where one point carries a higher weight and all others carry weight one. Clubs were well studied on a line, but much less in higher spaces.

The authors bound the rank of such clubs by tying them to rank metric codes and using classic identities for codes. They build clubs that reach the top rank in a range of cases and show that unlike builds exist in another range. One special case is fully sorted. Clubs also yield new codes with only three weights.
arxiv-2508-00602:
Francesco Panebianco, Stefano Bonfanti, Francesco Trovò and Michele Carminati present LeakSealer, a semi-supervised defence for large language models against prompt injection and data leakage. Wider use of these models, plus retrieval systems that feed them private text, has opened paths for jailbreaks and leaks of sensitive facts. Their work has two parts, one forensic and one active.

Past chat logs are first mapped by topic, which shows how attack patterns shift over time. The live defence then groups topics, flags odd patterns, and brings a human into the loop. On a public toxic chat set it led on precision and recall for injection spotting. For private data leaks it reached a strong score well above the baselines.
arxiv-2508-00702:
Diego Fernández de la Pradilla and co-authors present a theory paper from 2025 on light and matter at very strong coupling. They ask whether an emitter can reach the ultrastrong coupling regime through photons alone. Photons are treated here as waves of the transverse electromagnetic field in a supporting structure.

The authors argue from basic electromagnetic constraints that emitter-photon coupling has a firm upper limit. On that basis the ultrastrong regime cannot come from photons and must come from Coulomb interactions between charges. A related term for polarization self-energy is also shown to be unneeded. A worked model of an emitter near a metallic nanosphere supports the claim and prompts a fresh look at past work.
arxiv-2508-00802: Connor Jackman studies pairs of contact structures that share a symmetry in a 2025 mathematics paper. A contact structure is a field of planes twisting through a three-dimensional space. Take two that cross transversally, and in general no flow preserves both at once. Jackman asks what such pairs look like when a family of symmetries does exist. He determines local normal forms, standard local shapes, for them. One case involves Anosov flows, which arise globally as the crossing of two oppositely oriented contact structures with maximal local symmetries.
arxiv-2508-01802:
Atom Scott and co-authors release a rich soccer dataset in a 2025 paper. Game study needs two kinds of facts: where each player and the ball are, and what each player does. Past sets gave them apart, or joined them only in broadcast clips that lose players off screen.

Their set joins full-pitch video, long player paths, and linked acts in one trove. Ten college matches give more than nine hundred minutes of wide 4K film. Each frame marks pitch spots, shirt numbers, and who is who, plus ball acts in twelve kinds tied to the actor. Model builders gain a full-field ground truth for game state work.
arxiv-2508-02502:
Shuzhou Yuan, Zhan Qu, Mario Tawfelis, and Michael Färber ask whether big language models shift their mind-like reads when told to be a tongue. Two tasks tap such reads: which made-up word sounds round or sharp, and how warm a word feels. Two big open models were run in English, Dutch, and Chinese. Some runs held one tongue, and some held two at once.

Both models bent their calls by the tongue they were told to wear. One bent more, with sharper splits between Dutch and Chinese reads. Probes of the models' insides found the mind-like signs clearer in the deep layers. Chinese prompts gave the firmest warm-cold reads of the three tongues. Tongue set thus steers both what the models say and how they hold it inside. That fact bears on their use as stand-ins for how folk think in words.
arxiv-2508-02802:
Anton Tselishchev proves a rescaling result for unconditional Schauder frames in Hilbert spaces in a 2025 paper, with a reformulation in terms of completely bounded maps. Frames give flexible ways to rebuild each vector as a series sum.

Suppose every vector can be rebuilt as an unconditionally convergent series from paired sequences. Tselishchev shows nonzero scalars exist that rescale both sequences into true frames. The same claim can be restated for bounded maps from a sequence space into operators. If each basis vector maps to a rank-one operator, the map must be completely bounded. The bridge links frame theory with operator space theory, two fields that rarely meet directly.
arxiv-2508-03102:
Tianjiao Jiang and co-authors untangle image features with a causal twist so few-shot learners adapt from a handful of labels. Their 2025 framework starts from a flaw in standard practice: mixed features force the model to unmix them under scarce supervision. A strong image-text model already unmixes partly, theory says.

An unsupervised separation step pulls clean factors from the model's visual features directly. That skips learning the unmixing and slashes trainable parts. A two-way alignment tune-up then restores the image-text harmony the split disturbed. Outputs from both sides merge for the final call. Across eleven benchmarks, the method beat prior bests and shrugged off distribution shifts, all at lean compute cost.
arxiv-2508-03202:
Faizuddin Ahmed, Ahmad Al-Badawi, and İzzet Sakallı wrote this 2025 physics paper on a quantum-corrected black hole wrapped in dark energy and strings. The black hole is of the quantum Oppenheimer-Snyder type. Around it sit a quintessence field, a form of dark energy, and a cloud of strings, a relic of the early universe.

Because the geometry has a simple mass-function form, the three parts add cleanly in the field equations, with no cross terms. With the state value set at minus two thirds, space does not flatten far away. The horizon rule becomes a fifth-degree equation with three real roots: an inner horizon, the black hole horizon, and an outer dark energy horizon. Inside the static zone, the authors compute the photon sphere, the shadow size, and the paths of light and matter. They also study how small shakes in the system behave.
arxiv-2508-03302:
Kristian Arjas, Grazia Salerno, and Päivi Törmä unify photonics' two topologies, the global kind written across a whole energy band and the local kind carried by vortices in emitted light. Models for the two live in different spaces and meet only through heavy numerics with little intuition. Their framework builds one real-space Hamiltonian that treats the electric field as a vector in near and far fields alike. Band invariants and far-field defects become two readings of the same object.

The Hamiltonian is assembled from the lattice's symmetry representations. It deforms smoothly between localized tight-binding and delocalized photonic limits. Energies of modes with different symmetries at high-symmetry points can be tuned independently. Structures with nearly arbitrary topological properties become designable. The authors note the symmetry recipe applies beyond photonics, to any system with engineered real-space couplings.
arxiv-2508-03402:
Pingchuan Ma and co-authors separate an image's style from its content by learning to merge them reversibly, in work from 2025. Style and content overlap in meaning, and earlier methods that forced them apart hit ambiguity and subjective judgments.

SCFlow instead trains a flow model to combine style and content into one representation, a well-defined task. Because the mapping is invertible, separation falls out naturally when the flow runs backward. A synthetic dataset of 510,000 images, pairing 51 styles with 10,000 contents, taught the system. It also worked zero-shot on standard photo and art collections with competitive results. The authors argue disentanglement can emerge rather than be imposed.
arxiv-2508-03602:
Praveen Kumar Dhankar and five co-authors test Gauss-Bonnet gravity with new survey data in two thousand twenty-five. The theory alters Einstein gravity through a term built from curvature. They check it at the level of the expanding cosmos. Data come from supernovae, cosmic clocks, and baryon acoustic waves from the DESI survey.

Two model forms are fit, a power law and an exponential form. Fits run through Markov chain sampling of the altered expansion laws. Both forms scored better than the standard model on their tests. The exponential form hints at a future shift back to slowing expansion. That trait sets it apart from both rivals.
arxiv-2508-03802:
Joel Steinegger and co-authors wrote a 2025 physics paper on a three-dimensional dimer model, a grid system where pairs of linked sites cover a lattice. Most systems settle to a calm, even state when left alone, a step called thermalization. Some systems dodge that fate, and the team asked whether shape rules alone can cause the dodge here.

They mixed math and computer work to map states that never settle. A whole class of such states shows up in sectors with large winding, where the pattern wraps many times around the grid. An outside field can bring these states out. The results add a clean case of odd settling driven by pure shape, not by disorder or fine tuning.
arxiv-2508-04002:
Zheyuan Zhou and five co-authors build a strict judge for machines that turn words into CAD models, in a 2025 paper. Text-to-CAD tools draft editable 3D parts from a sentence, but grading their output is slow and costly. Rendering each draft takes time, and paying vision models to grade invites gaming that rots quality. The team's judge instead uses the CAD compiler itself as the grader.

A compiler score is fast and hard to fake, and a prospect-based tune pushes drafts toward useful, valid forms. A second compiler pass then reviews finished drafts and sends flaws back for repair, in an agent loop. On hard CAD test sets the system set top marks while staying quick. The authors frame compilers as built-in truth tellers for design AI.
arxiv-2508-04502:
Mahmoud Kalash and co-authors shine a brighter kind of light on squeezed light to prove it is squeezed in sixty places at once. Multimode squeezed states power high-dimensional quantum sensing and communication, but verifying squeezing across many spectral modes at once is hard. Optical parametric amplification offers loss-tolerant, broadband detection, previously shown only for spatial modes.

The team reports the first demonstration in the spectral domain. More than sixty spectral modes of a broadband squeezed vacuum showed squeezing at once, nearly uniform across the band.
