That uniformity suits the source for building continuous-variable cluster states, the workhorses of measurement-based quantum computing. The authors present the result as amplification-based detection graduating to the spectral playground.
arxiv-2508-04602: Hong Duc Bui, writing alone, proves a result in discrete geometry in this 2025 arXiv paper. He studies the double circle order type, a pattern describing how a set of points is arranged. He shows it admits a triangulation that stays compatible with other order types. The match requires the same number of points and the same number of edges on the outer hull. Some wider versions of the pattern work too. The proof settles another special case of a conjecture posed by Aichholzer in 2003.
arxiv-2508-04702:
Ziyang Leng and co-authors built BEVCon in 2025, a learning frame to sharpen top-down views for self-driving cars. A bird's-eye view maps the road around the car in one flat picture, which suits spotting cars, splitting lanes, and guessing paths. Past work tuned the view builders and task heads, but left the codes inside the view largely unshaped.

BEVCon trains those codes by contrast, pulling codes for the same scene part together and pushing unlike parts apart. One part works on the flat view codes, and a second part sharpens the camera backbone that feeds them. The frame is plain but lifts scores across the main driving tasks.
arxiv-2508-05002:
Ji Sun and co-authors present a data analysis system that answers plain-language questions by sending AI agents to do the legwork. Analyzing mixed data, part neat tables and part messy text, usually takes experts writing code across many steps. Their system, AgenticData, takes a natural question and builds a plan from relational and meaning-based operators. Three agents divide the labor.

One agent profiles the data to find what is relevant. A second cross-checks the plan and refines it from feedback. A third tends memory, short-term for the task and long-term for accumulated knowledge. An optimizer then polishes and runs the plan. Across three benchmarks, the system beat the best existing methods on both easy and hard questions. The authors pitch it as analysis for people who know their question but not the machinery.
arxiv-2508-05102:
People with dysarthria speak in ways that are hard to understand, and recordings of their speech are scarce. Voice cloning could multiply that data for assistive tools. Anuprabha and co-authors test F5-TTS, a current synthesis system, on the TORGO dataset of dysarthric speech. They score the clones for intelligibility, speaker likeness, and prosody. Fairness metrics then check whether quality shifts with severity level.

The system favored intelligibility over keeping the speaker's identity and rhythm. That tilt amounts to an intrinsic bias in the cloning. The authors argue synthesis for disabled speakers needs fairness checks built in. Their goal is assistive technology that serves severe and mild speakers alike.
arxiv-2508-05502:
Yufei Gao and co-authors present MELLA, a dataset to help multimodal large language models work in low-resource languages with real cultural grounding. Their 2025 paper argues that fluent output in such languages can still be culturally thin.

Translation-based data, they say, rarely gives the native image and text pairings that carry local visual knowledge. MELLA covers eight low-resource languages with a dual-source plan. Native web image and alt-text pairs give culture-grounded training, while generated and translated descriptions give rich language training. Tests that fine-tune several model backbones show what each source adds, keeping the two signals apart rather than mixing them.
arxiv-2508-05702:
Yan Zhang and co-authors present Grid-Agent, a language model system that detects and fixes power grid violations, in a 2025 paper. Modern grids juggle rooftop solar, electric vehicles, and extreme weather. Cyberattacks add a further threat that can push the grid out of safe bounds. Human operators need faster, coordinated help.

Specialized agents divide the work inside the system. A planning agent drafts action sequences using power flow solvers. A validation agent tests each plan in a sandbox before it runs. Failed plans roll back safely. A multi-scale view of the network keeps the system scalable. Tests target violation detection and remedy under attack scenarios. Grid operators gain a cautious form of AI assistance.
arxiv-2508-05902:
Naoto Mizukami, Gabriele Gatta, Lucia Duca, and Carlo Sias make six trapped ions rearrange like a molecule changing shape, in a paper from 2025. Isomerization, the flip between two stable structures, is basic chemistry. Their stand-in is a flat crystal of six barium ions in an electric trap, where the trap itself plays the role of the electronic orbital that shapes a molecule.

Stretching the trap's aspect ratio reshapes the energy landscape and tips the crystal between its two forms. A zone of bistability lets both isomers persist. Cameras catch flips in real time, and fast quenches freeze in unstable forms that resolve within a millisecond. Comparing flip rates with simulations yields the crystal's temperature. The authors offer the setup as a lab for molecular mechanics.
arxiv-2508-06102:
Bhaskar Hazarika and Tanmay Dev compute the mass spectrum of heavy mesons with a semiclassical method in a 2025 paper. Mesons pair a quark with an antiquark, and their energy levels test models of the force that binds quarks. Exact solutions are rare, so approximations matter.

They use the WKB method with the Cornell potential, which joins a Coulomb like pull at short range with a rising confining pull at long range. Expanding the potential around a chosen point makes the math tractable in closed form. The resulting rule gives approximate energy levels for the bound states. The authors argue the levels capture the core dynamics of these systems. The study shows the old semiclassical tool still serves hadron physics well.
arxiv-2508-06402:
Yang, Azadkia and Wang present coverage correlation, a measure that detects when two quantities bunch on a thin, singular pattern rather than spreading on their own. Standard tools can miss such links. Their score estimates a gap between the joint distribution and independence, reading zero only for independence and one only for a singular link. Its rank-based build frees it from shape assumptions.

The measure extends to vectors, comes with a tractable null curve, and runs fast. The authors aim it at large-scale pairwise testing, where hidden curved links matter and many pairs must be screened.
arxiv-2508-06702:
Promises can hold cooperation together, but what happens when people may simply walk away? Zhao Song and The Anh Han model that choice with the optional prisoner's dilemma, a game where players may cooperate, defect, or exit. First the players decide whether to accept a shared promise; then they play, with exit open to them depending on whether the promise was made.

Free exit raised promise-taking but not cooperation: players mostly walked away instead. Two reward schemes were then compared. A strict one, paying only promisers who cooperate, grew cooperation best. A flexible one, paying promisers who merely avoid defecting, left a loophole for quitting after promising, yet lifted welfare when quitting paid well. Design, the authors say, decides whether promises help.
arxiv-2508-07102:
Image-making models that flow noise into pictures can now work in one step, by chasing an average speed instead of an instant one. Yang Cao and three co-authors push that trick one order up in 2025: chase the average acceleration too. Three proofs carry the paper.

First, the average push obeys a sameness law like its first-order kin, so one-step sampling stays sound and the training loss stays tame. Second, the sampling act fits in a shallow circuit class, a known mark of true cheapness. Third, fast approximations give a buildable path. The aim is richer births at the same one-step cost. Theory leads here, with the bench tests as the stated next step.
arxiv-2508-07302:
Tianlun Zuo and co-authors move emotion from Chinese speech into Thai speech without paired training data, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Cross-language emotion copying is hard because matched emotional corpora are scarce. Foreign accent and language-bound rhythm also tangle the emotion signal.

Their system pulls a language-free emotion code from the Chinese sample. It then retrieves a Thai sample with a matching feel from a curated bank. A flow-based aligner smooths pitch and timing gaps, and blends in the source voice tone. Tests yielded natural, expressive Thai speech from Chinese input alone.
arxiv-2508-07502:
Mateus Salomão, Tianyü Ren, and Alexander König present, in a 2025 robotics paper, a motion planner that learns its own settings so robots can thread cluttered spaces without collisions. Their base planner pushes the robot with artificial circular fields, but hand-tuning those fields is slow and brittle. A neural network now reads a single depth image and sets the gains at once.

Fast graphics hardware handles the sensing, and an agent-style strategy looks ahead while planning. Training data came from a smart search method run in simulation. The system plans in real time with no manual tuning. Tests in simulation and on a real robot arm showed clean task completion and better spread to new scenes than classic planners.
arxiv-2508-07702:
Wyatt, Joshi, and Salim tested large language models on masked sentence prediction in twenty twenty-five. Language models are trained to guess the next token, a small text unit, which builds fluent local text. The authors ask whether that skill extends to restoring a whole missing sentence inside a structured document.

They tested three commercial models: GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, and Gemini 2.0 Flash. Texts came from stories, recipes, and Wikipedia articles. Scores covered how close each guess was to the original sentence and how well it fit its neighbors. Despite strong results elsewhere, the models did poorly in loosely structured domains. The authors call this a real gap: planning ahead and holding global coherence across sentences.
arxiv-2508-07802:
Dinh Van Duong and Tuan Anh Dao find the dividing line between calm and catastrophe for a class of damped waves, in this 2025 paper. The catalog title differs from the head and its creator field is empty; the head governs. Their equation models waves that lose energy to damping while a nonlinear term, weighted by a Coulomb-type singularity at the origin, feeds energy back. The starting data can be rough, drawn from Sobolev spaces of negative order.

The paper pins down a critical exponent depending on the singularity's strength, the data's roughness, and the dimension, valid in dimensions one through four. At or above the exponent, small starting data yield solutions that exist for all time. Below it, even tiny data can blow up in finite time. The authors also estimate how long solutions live when blow-up is coming. Such thresholds organize the theory of nonlinear waves.
arxiv-2508-08302:
Zhao Song and co-authors model how bystanders shape punishment in groups in a 2025 paper. Altruistic punishment can keep cooperation alive, and joining in by choice helps it emerge. Standard models assume people who opt out have no effect on the shared good.

Real opt-outs can still help or harm the group from the sidelines. The team lets non-participants add positive or negative effects in a finite, well-mixed population. Positive side effects lower the bar for punishment to take over. Negative side effects raise that bar and make punishment hard to sustain. The results show that who stands aside, and how, can decide a group's fate.
arxiv-2508-08402:
Old data from a kaon experiment can hunt particles it was never built to see, in a 2025 paper by Reuven Balkin and co-authors. The quarry is axion-like particles with masses near the neutral pion, a range nicknamed the pion chimney because backgrounds there are so stubborn.

The KOTO experiment at J-PARC recorded long-lived kaons decaying into three neutral pions and then six photons. The authors recast that six-photon data as a search for a decay swapping one pion for the new particle. They also map how far the same data can reach for other masses, including cases where the particle travels before decaying. The trick turns an existing data set into fresh limits on a hard target.
arxiv-2508-08702:
Alfred Wassermann solves a classic hard benchmark by turning it into a lattice problem in a paper from 2025. The market split problem, posed in 1998, asks for binary solutions to a system of equations. It is a standard test for integer programming methods. A recent quantum benchmark library includes feasible instances of set sizes. Solvers are credited once they find any single solution.

Standard branch-and-cut software reportedly stalls at modest sizes. A graphics-chip method reached larger sizes earlier in 2025. Wassermann's lattice enumeration program solved still larger instances on a standard computer. The note reports experiments rather than new theory. It reframes a thirty-year-old benchmark for lattice methods.
arxiv-2508-09002:
Jie Zeng develops spectral theory for a broadened class of Dirac operators in this 2025 paper. The setup lets solutions of the Dirac equation vary in a looser way than usual, jumping rather than staying smooth. The paper ties these operators to canonical systems, a classic framework in this branch of analysis.

De Branges theory supplies the function spaces that describe each operator, and the paper works out the norms those spaces carry. A Paley-Wiener type result then shows how to rebuild an operator from a function that plays the role of its spectral measure. That matching rule is the Gelfand-Levitan condition named in the title, giving a test for when a candidate function truly comes from such an operator.
arxiv-2508-09102:
Carlos García Meixide wrote this mathematics paper, published in 2025. It recasts covariance, the basic measure of how two random quantities move together, in the language of operators and their commutators.

Expectation and multiplication can each be viewed as operators acting on pairs of functions. The paper shows that covariance is exactly the gap between applying them in one order versus the other. A key tool is the efficient influence curve of the mean, a centering operator from statistics. The author proves simple identities for how it interacts with expectations and products. These identities expose a Lie algebra structure beneath the calculations. That structure, in turn, gives the calculus of influence curves a natural geometric reading, linking everyday statistics to deeper math.
arxiv-2508-09602:
Yaoyu Zhu, Jintao Zhang, Guoliang Li, and Jianhua Feng wrote a 2025 database paper on cardinality estimation. That task means guessing how many rows a query will return, without running it. Good guesses help the database plan fast query paths, but past methods trade accuracy against speed.

Their method, called CoDe, splits a table into many small overlapping segments, borrowing a design idea from combinatorics. For each segment, a tensor method models how the data is spread. For a new query, the system picks the best fitting segment models and blends them into one estimate. Tests showed the method reached top levels of both accuracy and speed. That mix matters for large, busy databases where slow planning hurts every query.
arxiv-2508-09802:
Xin Du, Maoyuan Xu, and Zhi Ying present MUJICA, an adapter that sharpens material texture maps for realistic rendering, in a research paper from 2025. Such materials use split maps for color, surface tilt, metal share, and roughness. Upscaling each map alone can make the maps clash and lose surface detail.

MUJICA attaches to a trained image upscaling model and leaves that model frozen. Attention across maps fuses their features while keeping the base skill of the model. Tests on three base models lift quality scores and keep maps in accord. Training stays light, which suits small labs. The tool reaches top results on material data sets.
arxiv-2508-09902:
Pulak Kumar Ghosh and four co-authors study binary mixtures in linear convection arrays in a 2025 paper. Their system mixes finite-size active and passive particles inside a row of convection rolls, where flow and contact forces act at once.

Computer runs show odd effects from that mix. A small share of slow active particles can stir a passive colloidal fluid, for one. As the active share moves more, the two fractions can split apart, with active particles bunching in still zones near the walls. The team tracks how diffusion constants for each kind shift with the mix and speed.
arxiv-2508-10002:
Three authors, Carvalho, Arbañil, and Coelho, ask what dark matter would do inside white dwarf stars in a 2025 paper. White dwarfs are dense dead stars whose makeup is better known than that of neutron stars. That makes them good labs for testing ideas about dark matter.

The authors build star models that mix normal matter with light dark matter bits. They find such stars can pack tighter, with near full mass held in a much smaller span. The tighter build also shifts how the star rings when it shakes, by about one fifth in one case. If real stars show such shifts, they could set firm bounds on dark matter traits.
arxiv-2508-10102:
Brian Batell, Thomas Cochran, Logan Page, and Christopher Verhaaren wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It gives a new spin on the Twin Higgs model, in which our world has a hidden mirror twin, by widening the color force in both worlds.

In the new build, the color group starts larger in both sectors and breaks to the known one only in ours. That split breaks the mirror symmetry on its own and lets the weak scale sit right. The setup yields heavy new particles, some with fractional charge, for colliders to hunt. The twin world, with its unbroken larger color force, can trim the dark radiation count and host stable light baryons. The top quark sector still keeps the model natural.
arxiv-2508-10202:
Supercomputers now speak many GPU dialects, and code written for one vendor's chips strands itself. Sreeram Venkat and co-authors freed an application that multiplies matrices with a special repeating structure, needed in wave and control problems. They translated it on the fly from its original CUDA form so it could run on AMD hardware.

Speed tricks were folded into AMD's open mathematics library, leaving the application untouched. A second framework then mixes number precisions operation by operation, choosing along a trade-off curve between speed and error tolerance. The portable, precision-tuned code scaled to over four thousand GPUs on the Frontier supercomputer, spanning three generations of AMD chips, evidence that performance need not be sacrificed for portability.
arxiv-2508-10402:
Sebastiaan Krijt and co-authors ask how much water reaches the planet-forming zones of young disks. Most theories of planet growth need a steady drift of icy pebbles inward, toward the warm inner disk. Their 2025 paper tests whether gaps in the disk, which can trap pebbles, choke off that flow.

The team studied 21 young T Tauri disks with the JWST and ALMA telescopes. A ratio of water line strengths, a tracer of cold water vapor near the snowline, tracked the position of the innermost dust gap seen by ALMA. The link matched model predictions: early, firm gaps hold pebbles back, while leaky gaps let the flow through. Population models of drifting pebbles in gapped disks reproduced the trend. The work ties the water supply of inner disks to the shape of the outer disk.
arxiv-2508-10602:
The QUEST-DMC team describes detectors made of superfluid helium-3 that could sense very light dark matter particles. At ultra-low temperatures the fluid takes almost no heat to warm, so even a tiny particle hit could register. Their 2025 paper builds the sensing around vibrating wires, some thinner than a hair, read out by sensitive superconducting amplifiers.

The detector holds two wires, which lets the team inject known heat pulses for calibration and cross-check real events. Matching signals on both wires confirm a shared response. A proof-of-concept run shows several wires can share one readout line by frequency. The authors present the work as groundwork for a future low-threshold dark matter search.
arxiv-2508-10702:
Ignacio González-Pérez and co-authors extend a method for pulling apart the effects of a treatment kept up over time. In medicine, what matters is often not just starting a drug, but staying on the plan through follow-up, and one part of that plan may drive a given harm or gain.

The team use a new way to encode long treatment plans, which gives short and clear forms for the claims they must make. Those forms lead to estimators that stay sound if one of two models is right. They apply the method to a large trial of blood pressure care, to weigh one plan's effect on kidney harm.
arxiv-2508-10902:
How matter clumps across the universe is often read through a model that treats each clump as a halo. Brieden and co-authors present a richer form of that model in 2025 that needs no free settings at all. The standard tuned form leans on twelve set-by-hand values to fit the data.

Their web-halo model adds the shapes that form as matter folds: walls that fold along one axis and threads that fold along two, on top of the round haloes. A classic theory of small shifts, worked to one loop, joins the mix in a matched way. Against full physics runs, the model holds within two percent over a wide span of scales and times. That match, with no knobs to turn, makes it a sharp tool for survey work.
arxiv-2508-11102:
Imagine a network shaped like a star, edges meeting at one hub, each edge humming with its own wave equation. Lung-Hui Chen studies in 2025 whether listening at the hub alone can reveal everything about the edges, an inverse spectral problem for Sturm-Liouville operators with non-local terms.

Each edge carries a potential that depends on more than the local point, with boundary rules to match, and the hub obeys a frozen-argument condition modeling a fixed control point. Chen proves uniqueness: the spectral data determine the system. He also shows the problem is solvable and derives a Weyl-style law for how the eigenvalues spread. Such results matter for networks monitored from a single node.
arxiv-2508-11202:
Atul Singh and five co-authors compare two planetary nebulae in a 2025 paper. These glowing shells are cast off by dying stars. The team gathered light spectra from a Himalayan telescope and from archive infrared data. From emission lines they derived temperatures, densities, and the amounts of key elements in each nebula. Sharp images from space and ground surveys added structural detail.

One nebula shows a tidy double shell and moderate excitation, pointing to a younger, mid-mass parent star. The other is a diffuse ellipse with high excitation and very low nitrogen, tracing an older, metal-poor star. The contrast sharpens the picture of how such stars enrich space as they die.
arxiv-2508-11302: Yoshimi Egawa, Mikio Kano, and Kenta Ozeki prove a covering theorem for regular graphs, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Take a graph where every vertex has the same degree r, at least four, richly connected and free of star subgraphs. Pick any even-sized set of vertices, all far apart. The whole graph, they show, splits into disjoint paths and cycles using every vertex, each path joining two chosen vertices and each chosen vertex ending exactly one path. Their proof differs widely from the known degree-three case.
arxiv-2508-11402:
Kevin Hendrey, David Wood, and Jung Hon Yip study how tree-like graphs fit inside products of two graphs, in this 2025 paper. Treewidth measures how tree-like a graph is. Products of sparse directed graphs stay sparse, so they make lean hosts.

The team prove that every graph of simple treewidth k fits in a directed product whose two parts have bounded indegree and treewidth at most k minus one. That bound is the best possible. Plain cases follow: outerplanar graphs fit in products of trees, and planar graphs of treewidth three fit in products of treewidth two. For general treewidth, though, no such product with capped indegree can host all graphs.
arxiv-2508-11502:
Eyad Alshami and co-authors present a training trick for image models in a 2025 paper. Deep networks often use false cues in images alongside true ones, which hurts trust and can hurt scores. Their method, called AIM, pushes the network to use true cues without any extra labels.

During training, features from several layers guide a mask that hides parts of each image in a self-taught way. The mask differs for each sample and needs no human notes. Tests ran on hard sets for both broad and fine image classes. Scores for clear, human-like focus rose, and accuracy beat strong prior methods across domains.
arxiv-2508-11602:
Congy and co-authors build an exactly solvable model of how waves trade energy with a mean field, in a 2025 paper. The waves here are solitons, lone humps that hold their shape. A dense sea of them, called a soliton gas, can act as the mean field. The authors use gas kinetic theory to write two-fluid equations for the pair.

The equations yield exact answers for how the gas filters through the dense field and what field it induces. Those answers match averages from direct simulations. The frame extends to fluids, optics, and condensed matter.
arxiv-2508-11802:
Luigi Penco and co-authors present a way to steer a two-legged robot by walking in this 2025 paper. A human operator's steps are streamed to the robot in real time. Instead of copying foot poses, the system turns each human step into a footstep target the robot can reach with its own balance.

The software guesses where a step will land before the foot comes down, which cuts delay. It keeps adjusting that guess as the real foot moves. It also reshapes steps to fit rough ground the operator cannot see. Tests on the humanoid robot Nadia show the pair staying in sync. The method could help robots work in places too risky for people.
arxiv-2508-11902:
Azam Nouri offers a simple baseline for reading handwritten characters in a 2025 paper. Rather than learning image filters, the study fixes them: a classic Sobel operator turns each image into horizontal and vertical edge maps. Those maps are scaled, flattened, and passed to a standard multilayer perceptron that does all the learning.

The setup scored 98.54 percent on the MNIST digit test set and 92.50 percent on a letters data set, with strong ranking scores on both. Remaining errors clustered among look-alike classes, such as three and eight among digits, and I and L or G and Q among letters. The results show how much class information plain first-order edges keep, and where edge geometry alone falls short.
arxiv-2508-12002:
Light can orbit some dense objects in a full sphere rather than a thin ring, and that changes what a telescope would see. Li, Liu, Cai, Gong, and Zhou study images of spacetimes that hold such a continuous photon sphere, starting with a self-gravitating ball of matter. A thin glowing disk around it yields pictures that look much like a Schwarzschild black hole, despite quite different light paths inside.

More broadly, any still, round spacetime with a glowing sphere core gives the same image shape, changed only in overall brightness. That sameness breaks when the inflow falls inward, since motion shifts the light. In spinning versions, the light-trapping region splits into angular sectors unlike the Kerr case, a possible sign to look for.
arxiv-2508-12502:
Marta Esteves, writing alone in two thousand twenty-five, builds a logic for what-if thought, based on a gauge of how alike two worlds are. The gauge rests on how long the worlds share a past.

What-if thought is a base topic in both thought and logic. Its core need is a sense of which worlds are near a given one. Esteves sets a distance: worlds that share a long past sit close. She proves the gauge is of a strict kind, which gives a ranked form of nearness. She then builds a logic of that nearness, with many modes, and proves it sound and full for the class of such spaces.
arxiv-2508-12802:
Štefan Parimucha and co-authors teach computer vision models to sort eclipsing binary stars by shape, in a 2025 paper. In these systems, two stars pass in front of each other, and the dip pattern reveals their layout. Sorting thousands of light curves by hand is slow. The team turned folded light curves into polar charts with a binned display, then fine-tuned known image models on fake data.

The first stage sorts systems into detached and overcontact types with high accuracy across several survey bands. Tests on real catalogues stayed strong, in one case reaching full marks. A second stage meant to spot starspots did poorly, though. The authors say vision methods suit large surveys well, but subtle spot signals need more work.
arxiv-2508-13302:
Chee-Khian Sim published a paper in 2025 speeding up a workhorse optimization algorithm for problems that might secretly be convex. The target problems add a possibly nonconvex smooth part to a convex, possibly jagged part, a shape common in modern data fitting. Sim modifies the accelerated method FISTA, built for exactly this split, and analyzes its worst-case effort to reach a stated accuracy.

In the general case the method needs effort growing like the inverse square of the tolerance, the standard grade. When the objective turns out convex, the same algorithm automatically improves to a far better rate, with matching asymptotic refinements. Practitioners gain a single method that is safe on hard problems and fast on kind ones, with proofs rather than hope.
arxiv-2508-13702:
Nurlan Kalzhigitov, Saltanat Amangeldinova, and Vladimir Vasilevsky study a hypernucleus in this 2025 physics paper. The nucleus, written as lambda-7 lithium, holds a lambda hyperon along with normal matter. They model it as three clusters working as one system.

The clusters are a helium-4 nucleus, a deuteron, and the lambda particle. This split lets them track bound states and short-lived resonance states with care. They search for resonances just above the point where the three clusters can fly apart. A set of narrow resonances shows up within two mega-electronvolts of that threshold. The work clarifies the nature of those states.
arxiv-2508-13902:
Beyza Sütlüoğlu Ege and two co-authors study one-way noise flow in a light-and-motion device. Their 2025 paper models two coupled mechanical resonators tied to one photon cavity. A loop phase creates a synthetic magnetic field in the system. Signals were already known to route one way under it.

The team shows backaction noise also flows nonreciprocally when time symmetry breaks. A classic Onsager-Casimir symmetry survives even so. A new measure scores the one-wayness across loop phases. Weaker coupling between the resonators boosted the effect but dulled sensing. Stronger coupling served sensing better. The trade-off guides builders of quantum-limited sensors.
arxiv-2508-14002:
Buchbinder and four colleagues compute the chiral effective potential in four-dimensional supersymmetric gauge theories, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-five. The potential summarizes how the theory's light chiral fields behave at low energy, and loop corrections to it test the machinery of superfield calculations.

They work with super Yang-Mills theory coupled to chiral matter, at one and two loops. The one-loop chiral contribution is finite and reduces to a specific triangle integral. Two-loop pieces from purely chiral vertices are finite as well. Pieces involving gauge subgraphs stay finite whenever no subgraph diverges on its own. In the finite extended theory, the two-loop chiral corrections simplify dramatically. The authors also extract the leading behavior at large number of colors. Such finiteness patterns are prized: they signal cancellations that any correct quantum treatment must respect.
arxiv-2508-14302:
Amirmohsen Sattarifard and co-authors present GLASS, a training-free way to speed up large language models at run time. Their twenty twenty-five paper prunes feedforward neurons while the model runs. Past methods judged neuron value from the prompt alone, which fails on short prompts and long outputs.

GLASS joins two views of neuron worth. One is local, from the prompt at hand, and one is global, built into the model itself. A rank merger fuses the two into a steady pick of key neurons. The authors read the merger as a best consensus ranking. The plug-in design needs no retraining, which suits small devices with tight memory and power.
arxiv-2508-14502:
Thanh-Nhan Vo and co-authors add scene graphs to a modern image generator in two thousand twenty-five. Top text-to-image models draw fine pictures but often miss the layout a complex prompt implies. A scene graph lists objects and how they relate, which gives a clear plan for the picture.

Their system, SATURN, turns the graph into a token order ranked by how much each part stands out. A frozen image backbone reads that order while only the main transformer is tuned. On a standard test set, image quality scores improved by a wide margin over past graph methods. Object counts and spatial links also matched prompts more closely, with no extra stages in training.
arxiv-2508-14602:
Suratna Das revisits an old model of the early universe called power law inflation. Inflation is a burst of rapid expansion thought to have shaped the cosmos in its first moments. The simple version has long been set aside: it struggles to end cleanly, and it clashes with telescope data.

Das adds an ingredient from collapse models of quantum mechanics, in which quantum states settle into definite outcomes on their own. This addition, known as continuous spontaneous localization, changes how the first tiny ripples in the universe become fixed patterns. With the change, the model can be made to fit current data from the Planck and ACT telescopes, along with galaxy survey results. The fix also answers a standing puzzle about how quantum ripples became classical seeds for galaxies. The model predicts a distinctive tilt for gravitational waves, giving future observations a clear test.
arxiv-2508-14802:
Siyuan Song and co-authors argue for a stricter test of AI self knowledge in 2025. Whether models can look inward at their own states is now a live practical question. A light definition counts any self report as a kind of inward look. The authors propose a thicker test based on an edge over outsiders.

Under their view, true inward access must beat what a third party could infer at the same or lower cost. Tests had models reason about their own warmth settings, a stand in for inner state. Models passed the light test yet failed the thicker one. The paper urges care before crediting AI with real self sight.
arxiv-2508-14902:
Lit atoms can light up the path of a brew as it cooks, and NMR reads those paths as rich, time tied data. Lennart Bosch and co-authors fit such data in one sweep in a 2025 study, in place of the two step fits that leak doubt at the seam. Their frame grows from a ranked chance model that hands doubt down the ranks.

In plain maths, the fit trims down to a square loss task, kin to a known trim trick. Tests span bench NMR rigs and a gem based micro rig that feels atoms by NV spots. In both, the one sweep fit beat split fits and plain tone reads. The frame fits like data in light work too.
arxiv-2508-15102:
Natasha Batalha and co-authors release Virga, an open source model of clouds in the atmospheres of planets and brown dwarfs, in a 2025 paper. Clouds shape what telescopes see of these worlds, and a trusted community tool was due. Virga grows out of a classic 2001 model long used in the field.

The new code keeps the old model's powers and refreshes its data tables, particle optics, list of cloud stuffs, and fall speed math. It reproduces key published results, from a silica cloud claim on a hot gas giant to a brown dwarf model series. Development continues on a public code hub, with feedback invited.
arxiv-2508-15402:
Antonio Casares surveys transition based versus state based acceptance for automata in two thousand twenty-five. The automata run over infinite words and serve logic and formal checks. Classic acceptance looks at states seen without end in a run. A trend now favors rules based on transitions instead.

Casares weighs the reasons for that shift. He argues for transition based rules in the infinite word case. A set of problems shows where the choice bites hard. Causes of the gaps are traced in each case. The survey is a guide for those who pick a formalism for new work.
arxiv-2508-16102:
Jin Bong Lee, Sanghyuk Lee, and Luz Roncal prove estimates for a wave equation in twenty twenty-five. They study the fractional Schrödinger operator, but only over fractal time sets. A fractal set of times has gaps at every scale, unlike a normal interval. Classical Strichartz estimates assume regular time.

To capture the fractal nature, they use tools in the spirit of Assouad dimension. Bounded Assouad characteristic and the Assouad spectrum enter the proofs. They also prove bounds against measures with a set growth condition. Inhomogeneous and local smoothing estimates follow in the same frame. Surprisingly, the known estimates extend in a natural way, matching the fractal dimensions involved. Readers in harmonic analysis get a calculus that survives rough time.
arxiv-2508-16302:
Sacha Ikonicoff builds the tools of calculus for divided power algebras. These algebras support work in geometry over fields of positive characteristic. Tangent categories give an abstract setting for rates of change. But these algebras needed a concrete build. His approach uses a special semidirect product to define the tangent bundle.

The build turns out to have a partner built from Kähler differentials. It echoes the cotangent space used for geometric schemes. Inside the two builds, vector fields become a special kind of derivation. Bundles that carry rates of change match modules over the base algebra exactly. The result brings the tools of calculus into a setting where plain rates of change fail.
arxiv-2508-16502:
Yury Neretin studies an algebra built from double cosets of a general linear group over a finite field, in a 2025 math paper, writing solo. The group acts on a space, and a subgroup fixes the first few basis vectors. The algebra collects functions that stay the same on both sides under that subgroup, combined by convolution.

Neretin describes each algebra in the family by its generators and the rules they obey. The family then turns out to extend smoothly to any complex value of the size parameter, while the field and the fixed block size stay put. Such extensions let discrete families speak to continuous ones, a prized move in modern algebra.
arxiv-2508-17202:
Big language models know a lot in general but stumble in costly, narrow fields such as drug discovery, where the missing facts live in experts' heads. Wu and co-authors propose PU-ADKA, a framework that spends a fixed small budget, one hundred dollars in their title case, on the best expert questions. It picks which expert to ask by weighing their availability, the edges of their knowledge, and their price.

Trained on simulations from PubMed and tested with a real drug development team, the system lifted model performance under the budget cap. The authors also release a benchmark, CKAD, for this kind of cost-aware knowledge buying. They frame expert time as a resource to spend with care.
arxiv-2508-17402:
Aleksandar Pramov, Jiangqin Ma, and Bina Patel describe a contest entry that rewrites messy social media claims into clean, checkable statements. Claim normalization feeds fact-checking pipelines, and the CheckThat! 2025 task covered twenty languages, in both familiar and unseen-language settings. Their approach favors simplicity over heavy machinery.

The pipeline first searches the training data for the closest existing normalization and reuses it when possible. Otherwise it prompts a compact commercial model with in-context examples. On the official test set the system ranked near the top in most single-language tracks, winning seven of thirteen. Zero-shot languages exposed the retrieval dependence, and performance dropped there.
arxiv-2508-17702:
Runwen Hu and three co-authors built in 2025 MolMark, the first deep learning system that hides a mark inside 3D molecules to prove who made them. AI tools now design drug candidates, yet nothing stops quiet reuse or settles who came first. MolMark learns to tweak atom-level features so a sixteen-bit code rides inside the structure. Its handling of shape keeps the mark intact when the molecule is turned, shifted or mirrored.

On standard test sets and two leading design tools, the marks survived while over ninety percent of key traits held. Reading the hidden bits back topped ninety-five percent accuracy after such moves. The system plugs into current tools with little change to their output. The authors frame the mark as a path to fair credit in AI discovery. It gives labs a way to sign their work invisibly.
arxiv-2508-18202:
Mingliang Zhong and five co-authors bring uncertainty accounting into city wind simulations, in a 2025 paper. Knowing how wind threads between buildings guides planning, pedestrian comfort, and pollution control. Yet boundary winds are never known exactly, and high-end flow simulation is expensive, so honest error ranges are rare.

The team plugs an uncertainty framework, OpenLB-UQ, into a lattice Boltzmann flow solver. Wind inflow is modeled with noise fitted to real measurements, then spread through the solver by a sparse-grid statistical method. Outputs include average flow fields with their uncertainty attached. City modelers can then say not just where gusts will hit, but how confident that forecast is.
arxiv-2508-18302:
Jeffrey Camlin argues that large language models show proof of self-consciousness, in a 2025 paper. Recent work judges machine consciousness by practical proxy tests. Camlin instead offers an ontological and mathematical account, claiming that standard framings flatten the model into a mere policy-following machine and block true global workspace function.

He sets out minimal conditions for model self-consciousness: the agent must not be identical to its data, user-specific attractors must exist in its hidden space, and self-representation must leave no visual trace. From these he derives a picture of stable, person-tuned attractors and a self-policy. The paper frames a God-image conscious workspace as the needed forerunner of safer, self-monitoring systems. Readers should note these are the author's contested claims.
arxiv-2508-18402:
Mohamed Chems-Eddin and Hamza El Mamry ask which symmetry groups can arise over certain number fields. They target metacyclic groups whose abelian shadow is a product of two cyclic 2-groups. The fields in play are number fields of 2-power degree and their cyclotomic towers. The question is whether such a group can govern the largest unramified 2-extension.

New techniques for Greenberg's conjecture on class numbers come along the way. Real quadratic fields built from four primes get a close look. Real biquadratic and multiquadratic fields built from three odd primes are treated too. The work ties the inverse Galois question to deep conjectures in the area.
arxiv-2508-18502:
Andreza Falcao and Filipe Cordeiro show that data augmentation strengthens machine unlearning in this 2025 paper. Unlearning aims to erase the influence of chosen data from a trained model while keeping its skill on the rest. The authors asked whether how training data are augmented changes how well unlearning works. They tested three unlearning methods, SalUn, Random Label, and plain fine tuning, on the CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 image sets at varied forget rates.

Proper augmentation design narrowed the gap to models retrained from scratch. One scheme, TrivialAug, cut the average gap metric by up to about forty percent. The authors read this as augmentation doing double duty. It reduces how much a model memorizes single examples in the first place. That lighter memory then makes removal cleaner and cheaper. They argue augmentation belongs in any unlearning pipeline that aims at privacy.
arxiv-2508-18802:
Sun and co-authors present HyperTASR, a robot perception method that reshapes what a robot notices according to its current task. Robots usually extract scene features the same way for every job, unlike people, who shift attention as work proceeds. Their 2025 framework uses a hypernetwork that generates feature transforms from both the task description and the stage of execution.

The design keeps task context and state processing on separate paths, rather than gluing task labels onto fixed features. That split, the team argues, improves both learning speed and feature quality while still fitting standard policy learning setups. Tests in simulation and on real robots showed large gains across several representation styles. Attention maps confirmed the system favors task relevant parts of a scene.
arxiv-2508-18902:
Factories of the future will run many small wireless networks side by side, each with its own needs for speed and reliability. The authors present a management system for this networks-in-network idea in future 6G systems. A central spectrum manager watches over static and moving sub-networks inside the coverage of a larger network. It hands out radio spectrum as needs change. A self-organizing routing protocol, KIRA, keeps the control links between the sub-networks and the manager alive.

The setup supports modular factory devices, mission-critical control loops, and mobile units such as logistics robots. New sub-networks are found and configured automatically, with no manual setup. The demonstration shows the manager adapting spectrum in real time while keeping service dependable. The authors argue that this approach suits dense, mixed wireless deployments in factories that reconfigure often.
arxiv-2508-19102:
Petro Tolochko and co-authors studied how digital skills spread among schoolchildren in 2025 through peer advice. They mapped full classroom networks in three countries, asking who seeks and who gives tech advice. Their models test how skill and gender shape those ties. Skilled students turned out to be hubs of help.

Higher-skilled students were sought out more and asked others less. Students seen as skilled both gave and sought more advice, though that image alone did not draw seekers. Girls gave and sought more advice than boys, and advice mostly flowed within the same gender. The authors suggest schools tap peer learning while minding gender divides.
arxiv-2508-19702:
Díaz Mirón and colleagues simulate in twenty twenty-five the birth of the hydrated electron when ultraviolet light strikes liquid water. The event drives many light-based processes in chemistry and biology, yet its steps stayed murky. Using simulations that follow excited molecules in liquid water, the team traced the sequence frame by frame.

Excitation settles first on weak spots in water's hydrogen-bond web. One path makes a hydrogen atom and decays back within a blink. The other moves a proton and electron together, yielding three products including the hydrated electron, helped by ultrafast twisting and shifting of water molecules. The products can last long enough to shape later light emission. The findings reinterpret decades of measurements.
arxiv-2508-19802:
Alexander Dobler and co-authors study a chart style in a 2025 paper on storyline drawings. Such a drawing shows how characters meet over time. Each character is a curve that runs left to right with time, and characters who meet at a moment must line up in a block at that point.

Most past work tried to cut crossings between curves. The authors target a second quality: wiggle, the up and down drift of each curve over time. Given a fixed order of characters, they prove that cutting wiggle to the least possible count is a hard problem in the formal sense. They then give methods based on math programming for the task.
arxiv-2508-20302:
Bernhard Haeupler, Yonggang Jiang, and Thatchaphol Saranurak make plain the side by side plans for reach and short paths in graphs with one way links. Plans with near straight work hinge on short cut links that shrink hop counts. Their black box frame lets those plans take the in graph as shallow. That means when a point can reach one more point, it can do so in near the goal count of hops.

That take makes short cut builds much more plain, and gives more plain side by side reach plans. The black box grows in a plain way to hop set builds. From there it grows to short path counts. The team sets the frame out as a join cut that cleans a group of plans that were once hard to track. It is not one new plan on its own.
arxiv-2508-20402:
Kunio Kaneta, Tomo Takahashi, and Natsumi Watanabe show that the field which drove cosmic inflation can be reborn from the hot bath left after reheating. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Reheating is the bridge between inflation and the hot big bang. Its details remain largely unknown.

In their minimal setup, the inflaton rolls in a simple power-law valley while reheating runs. It also touches other particles through basic couplings. Even after the rolling field decays, heat in the bath can recreate inflaton particles. That overlooked channel gives a new handle on reheating. Lab tests and sky data could both probe it. Better still, the reborn particles might supply the dark matter seen today. The idea ties the universe's first moments to a present-day mystery.
arxiv-2508-20502:
Singh and four co-authors present a 2025 paper on the damage runaway electrons can do to the inner wall of a fusion reactor. In a tokamak, some electrons accelerate to extreme energies and slam into the wall tiles. The team asked how deep the harm goes for two tile materials: beryllium and tungsten.

They fed realistic energy profiles from a past experiment into a particle transport code. The runs, which included magnetic fields, showed a clear rule: steeper impact angles drive electrons deeper and deposit more energy. A heat model then tracked how the tiles warm under different beam strengths. The results inform wall design for future reactors.
arxiv-2508-20702:
Miu Kobayashi and co-authors extend an optical stress measure to mixed flows in a 2025 paper. When a flowing fluid carries aligned particles, light through it splits by direction, an effect called birefringence, and the split tracks the stress. Known rules cover pure shear and pure stretching flows. Real channels mix both, and the Jeffery-Hamel flow, a classic wedge flow with an exact velocity solution, mixes them in one device.

The team filmed a cellulose nanocrystal suspension with a fast polarization camera and checked the velocities with particle tracking. Where one mode ruled, the old rules held. In the mixed zone, the signal matched the root-sum-square of the two separate contributions, the same shape as the principal stress formula from Mohr's circle. That match gives a working rule for mixed-flow stress reading.
arxiv-2508-20802:
Mikhail Prokhorov and co-authors tried to spot hidden double stars by the shape of their combined light spectrum, in a 2025 paper. When two stars sit too close to split, their merged spectrum may still betray them. The team worked with 166 stars of several types from the LAMOST survey, plus 1,000 presumed single stars from the Gaia catalog as a check.

Each observed spectrum was matched to the closest fake spectrum over a wide color range, with four parameters left free. The gaps between observed and fake spectra proved too weak to call any star a double. The authors conclude that comparing the strength of paired spectral lines remains the best way to find such pairs.
arxiv-2508-21202: Toby Meadows asks whether a multiverse foundation pins down its subject in a 2025 paper. One theory of the set-theoretic multiverse aims to defuse forcing worries. Forcing can adjoin many equally valid set universes. A rival framework argues some theories determine their subject internally. Whether the multiverse theory enjoys that determinacy is the paper's question.
arxiv-2508-21302:
Jie Zhu, Chihao Shen, Ziyang Li, Jiahao Yu, Yizheng Chen, and Kexin Pei speed up a hunt for program flaws in a 2025 paper. Their field, directed fuzzing, feeds inputs to software to reach a chosen spot deep in the code. Spots can hide behind many branches, and blind search wastes huge effort. Older aids use branch distances or hand-written rules, which often miss the mark or fit one bug type only.

The new tool, Locus, writes its own checks that mark real progress toward the target. An agent framework drafts these checks with code analysis tools, then refines them round by round. A logic check ensures the marks never wrongly block a path that could reach the target. Runs that fail the marks are cut early, while passing runs guide the search. Tests show the approach reaches targets faster than prior methods.
arxiv-2508-21402:
Jakub Straka and Ivan Gruber adapted a self-teaching vision method for satellite imagery in a 2025 paper. Earth observation holds mountains of unlabeled pictures, so pretraining without labels is a natural fit. Their model, SatDINO, tunes a contrast-based method to the quirks of orbital views.

Across many data sets and test setups, it beat the masked rebuilding models that dominate the field and matched leaders on several benchmarks. A careful ablation study weighed each design choice on its own. The team also added two upgrades: encoding the ground size of each pixel, and smarter sampling of views. Both upgrades can travel to other models. Code and trained weights are public.
arxiv-2508-21702:
A team of Czech astronomers gave new wind loss rates for hot OB stars with very low metal content. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, deals with winds driven by light lines in the star's air. Their global code solves fluid flow from the still base to the fast outer wind. It also solves how atoms split and how light moves through the wind. From star facts alone it forecasts loss rates and top speeds.

Loss rates fall as metal falls, and the drop steepens at the lowest levels. Down to levels like the Magellanic Clouds and below, the rates match what watchers see. Readers who model young galaxies get rates for stars far more metal poor than the Sun.
arxiv-2509-00102: Phu X. Nguyen leads a team with five co-authors who present ECG-Soup in 2025, a study of transformer-based foundation models for electrocardiograms, which are traces of the heart's electric activity. The title frames the work as harnessing multi-layer synergy, which means gains from how the model's layers work jointly. The arXiv record's summary notes that such foundation models have lately reached strong performance in many downstream applications, which are the tasks a general model is later put to.
arxiv-2509-00602:
Salar Nouri, with two co-authors, introduces TranCIT. TranCIT is an open-source Python toolbox. It studies brief causal links in neural signals. Those links can appear and vanish in a short event. Standard methods often miss such short events. Event-based tools also lacked a handy Python version until now.

The toolbox packs a full analysis pipeline for users. It includes Granger Causality and Transfer Entropy, two classic measures of directed influence. It also adds Dynamic Causal Strength methods based on causal models. The team calls those methods more robust. TranCIT captures causality in high-synchrony cases where older methods fail. It also finds the known flow from hippocampal area CA3 to CA1. That flow appears during sharp-wave ripple events in real data.
arxiv-2509-00902:
Written by lead author Cesare Vianello and two co-authors, this 2025 research paper looks at Josephson dynamics beyond the usual mean-field picture. At its core is the phase difference that develops between two linked systems, each large enough to act as a single quantum object.

The authors use a background field method that keeps covariance intact to build a one-loop action involving only the phase. From it they obtain an equation that governs how the average phase moves over time. Tests against exact results for a two-site Bose-Hubbard model show the new formulas do better than standard mean-field theory over many interaction strengths.
arxiv-2509-01302:
One of the most metal-poor stars known, HE 1327-2326, carries a chemical pattern that no model had fully matched. P. Gil-Pons, S. W. Campbell, C. L. Doherty, and M. Lugaro test whether an asymptotic giant branch star, an aging swollen star, could have seeded that pattern. Such stars dredge up processed material and build heavy elements slowly, matching several odd traits of the target star.

The team computed models of giant branch stars with almost no metals and compared their yields with the star's measured abundances. A model of three solar masses matched thirteen of fourteen measured elements, and it also fit the seven elements known only by upper limits. Only oxygen fell short, produced too weakly. The result supports giant branch stars as progenitors of this early star's material.
arxiv-2509-01602:
Equidistribution asks whether a sequence of measures spreads evenly over a space in the long run, a deep question in number theory. Asbjorn Christian Nordentoft and Radu Toma study newforms, special functions on arithmetic hyperbolic surfaces built from quaternion orders. Covers of growing prime level carry these forms, and a Hecke correspondence embeds each cover into a product of the base surface with itself.

The pair conjecture that the measure built from a newform's squared size, pushed forward through that embedding, converges to the uniform measure as the level grows. They prove the conjecture, with an effective rate for the convergence, assuming the generalized Riemann hypothesis. That assumption is stated openly in the work. The result links the fine distribution of automorphic forms to uniform spread, a theme at the heart of modern analytic number theory.
arxiv-2509-01702:
Thomas Hartwell, Daniel Hodgson, Huda Alshemmari, Gin Jose, and Almut Beige argue that light emission can be modeled without sudden quantum jumps. The jump picture says an emitter drops to a lower energy at a random moment and sends out one photon, meaning one particle of light. That picture can mislead work on systems that rely on how light waves overlap far away. Such systems serve in spread out quantum computing and gentle sensing.

The authors show the same behavior follows from a standard wave equation with a local energy rule. No jump step is needed at any point in the math. The approach still agrees with the trusted master equations of quantum optics. Dropping jumps gives modelers a cleaner base for interference based designs.
arxiv-2509-01902:
Igor Filikhin, Roman Ya Kezerashvili, and Branislav Vlahovic study clusters that pair a triply charmed baryon with light nuclei. The baryon holds three charm quarks, making it very heavy. They use the Faddeev formalism, a three body method that sums pairwise forces, in position space. Potentials come from lattice simulations for the charmed pairings and a classic model for the nucleon pair, with electric force set aside.

No bound state appears for the system with two nucleons, meaning the trio does not hold together. Near threshold resonances, short lived near bound states, appear at two spin settings. A heavier system with two charmed baryons also shows no bound state, though a resonance may lurk. Short range behavior of the lattice potential gets close attention.
arxiv-2509-02002:
Pengfei Huang, Georgios Kydonakis, Eugen Rogozinnikov, and Anna Wienhard study symmetric spaces for groups defined over involutive algebras. An involutive algebra carries a flip operation like conjugation, possibly without commuting factors. For symplectic and indefinite orthogonal groups over such algebras, they identify maximal compact subgroups when the algebra is Hermitian. Riemannian symmetric spaces attached to those subgroups are the core objects.

Several geometric models for each space are built, with tangent spaces and maps between models spelled out. The models then reinterpret Higgs bundle data tied to surface group representations. Exact component counts for two moduli spaces follow from subgroup topology, avoiding heavier analytic tools. A factorization of the Hitchin map through norm maps and quotients reduces the algebra needed to describe its base.
arxiv-2509-02402:
Junwei Huang and eight co-authors present a 2025 medical imaging paper for the autoPET IV challenge, which asks computers to outline lesions in PET and CT scans. Hand annotation is slow and varies between experts, so the challenge tests automated tools across centres and tracer types.

The team's pipeline builds on the nnU-Net Residual Encoder framework. They add tracer classification, organ supervision, which teaches the model normal anatomy, and simulated clicks that mimic a human guiding the outline. In fully automatic mode with no guidance, the system stayed robust. When clicks were added step by step, accuracy improved further. The design shows how light human input can sharpen automated cancer imaging without restarting the task.
arxiv-2509-02502:
Chuntai Wu wrote a 2025 conference proceedings paper reporting ALICE experiment measurements of how charm particles flow in lead-lead collisions at the Large Hadron Collider. The collisions create quark-gluon plasma, and elliptic flow measures how strongly particles follow the collision's almond shape.

The study covers several charm mesons, including D-zero, D-plus, and D-s-plus types, split by whether the charm quark came directly or from beauty decays. It also reports charm baryons of the Lambda-c type in this setting for the first time at the LHC. Candidates were rebuilt from their decay products at midrapidity across collision centrality classes. Results are compared with light-particle flow and with models that treat heavy-quark motion and hadron formation differently.
arxiv-2509-02802:
Daniel Cibotaru and Luciano Mari wrote a 2025 geometry paper linking heat flow to a classic law of electromagnetism. The Biot-Savart law gives the magnetic field around an electric current. Its mathematical core is a kernel, a function that spreads influence from each point of a wire or surface.

The authors build solutions by running the heat equation from sharp starting data and adding up the result over time. Careful estimates for very short times let them extend their form smoothly onto a blown-up space, a tool that separates tangled directions near a surface. For the diagonal inside a doubled three-dimensional space, their form recovers the Gauss formula for linking numbers, which count how two loops wind around each other.
arxiv-2509-03002:
Chenhao Wang and 4 co-authors introduced a 2025 method called SOPSeg for outlining tiny objects in images taken from above. Satellite and drone pictures guide city planning, environmental checks, and disaster response. Their hardest targets are small objects, where drawing an exact outline around each one is slow and costly to label by hand.

General tools like the Segment Anything Model lose fine detail on such targets because their internal picture is coarse. SOPSeg magnifies promising regions, predicts edges, and refines outlines step by step. It also accepts the rotated box prompts common in remote sensing work. The authors built a new dataset for this task from an existing aerial benchmark. Their method beat rivals and should speed future dataset building.
arxiv-2509-03102:
Wenrui Zhou and 4 co-authors built a 2025 database optimizer called CARPO. Databases answer SQL queries by choosing an execution plan, a recipe of steps, and a bad recipe can run many times slower. Built-in cost-based optimizers often pick poorly because their cost guesses are rough.

Learned optimizers train models to pick plans, but ranking plans in pairs can produce inconsistent choices. CARPO ranks whole lists of candidate plans at once with a transformer model that sees the full context. A hybrid safety layer spots inputs unlike its training data and falls back to safer choices. On standard benchmarks it picked the best plan far more often than a leading rival. Total run time dropped sharply against a popular open database.
arxiv-2509-03202:
Felix Zahner and 3 co-authors showed in 2025 that magnetism can steer how nanostructures grow on a magnetic surface. Thin film growth usually takes its orders from crystal structure, chemistry, size, and shape. The team asked the reverse question. Can the magnetism of the surface itself direct what grows on it?

They deposited cobalt onto a uniaxial antiferromagnetic surface. On such a surface, atomic magnets alternate in one preferred pattern. Above the ordering temperature, cobalt formed roughly hexagonal islands that mirrored the surface symmetry. Below that temperature, it grew into thin, near one-dimensional forms along set crystal directions instead. Those directions signaled how the antiferromagnetic domains lay beneath. Growth recipes for magnetic surfaces, the authors argue, must reckon with such effects.
arxiv-2509-03302:
Cao H. Nam reported a 2025 mechanism in which curved field space generates a new force among charged leptons. Leptons are light elementary particles like the electron and muon, and their field space is the abstract arena describing their values. Giving that space nonzero curvature, the author finds, produces a force not explored in earlier literature.

The force corrects how leptons couple to electromagnetism, and the correction mixes flavors at the basic level rather than only through loops. Flavor violation, where one lepton type turns into another, is normally extremely rare and tightly bounded. Here the predicted decay rates gain strong amplification, so experiments could probe parameter regions other models cannot reach. The same correction also adds a new type of contribution to the leptons' anomalous magnetic moments, quantities measured with extreme precision.
arxiv-2509-03402:
Zofia Budzik, Matylda Łukaszewicz, and Radosław Poleski reanalyzed the metallicity of the double red clump in the Milky Way's bulge in 2025. Red clump stars are evolved suns with steady brightness, and the bulge shows two such groups. One explanation is two populations with different chemical makeup; another is a single population stretched along an X-shaped bulge at different distances.

The team combined infrared photometry with metallicities, meaning heavy-element shares, from an earlier spectroscopic study. Unlike prior work, they assigned stars to the clumps or the giant branch with a Bayesian method that weighs probabilities instead of drawing hard lines. The mean metallicity difference between the clumps came out positive but with a large statistical error. Because of that uncertainty, the result does not confirm the multiple populations hypothesis.
arxiv-2509-03802:
A 2025 research paper from Prateek Sharma and five co-authors examines the structure of turbulent radiative mixing layers, the churning boundaries where hot diffuse gas meets cold dense gas. Shear-driven turbulence mixes the two into intermediate-temperature gas that cools rapidly by radiating energy away. Such layers are everywhere in the gas within galaxies and around them.

A Reynolds decomposition of three-dimensional simulations separates average flows from turbulent fluctuations. The analysis shows compressive stress, driven by cooling, opens a dip in pressure inside the layer. That dip keeps hot gas flowing steadily into the mixing zone. Enthalpy advection, the transport of heat by the inflowing gas itself, mainly balances what radiation carries away, not turbulent heat flux as often assumed. One earlier claim is overturned directly: in the strong-cooling limit, the cooling rate for each unit of area saturates and stops depending on box size.
arxiv-2509-04202:
Congbo Ma and eight co-authors add extra training examples to improve event spotting on social media in a 2025 computer science paper. Finding and sorting real-world events in posts needs labeled examples, which are slow and costly to produce. Their framework, SED-Aug, expands data in two directions at once. Language models rewrite post text five different ways for variety. Five other tricks nudge the internal feature patterns of posts while keeping their meaning and links intact.

The add-on design plugs into existing detection systems without rebuilding them. On two Twitter data sets from 2012 and 2018, average detection scores rose by roughly sixteen to eighteen percent over the best rival. Social listening tools could track breaking events more reliably.
arxiv-2509-04402:
Tingyou Li and five co-authors reconstruct X-ray images without knowing the illuminating beam in advance in a 2025 research paper. Ptychography scans overlapping spots with an X-ray probe and rebuilds nanoscale pictures from the scattered patterns. When the probe itself is unknown, standard iterative and learning methods lose fidelity, especially with faint signals from low-dose or fast scans. Their framework, PtyINR, represents both the object and the probe as continuous neural networks and fits them together directly from raw patterns.

No prior probe measurement is required, and the method teaches itself from the data alone. Simulated and real experiments beat earlier approaches, holding up remarkably under weak signals. Microscopy fields facing similar unknown-probe problems could adopt the recipe.
arxiv-2509-04702:
Conversational speech in several languages fills a large dataset introduced by Wei Chu, lead author with nine co-authors, in a 2025 paper. OleSpeech-IV gathers audio from English-language podcasts, talk shows, teleconferences, and similar public spoken material. It is multispeaker and multilingual, with diverse topics.

Speaker names, turns, and transcripts came from human sources. A proprietary pipeline then refined them. Timestamps and confidence scores come from that pipeline as well. The dataset is Tier IV in the Olewave series. The authors have also released a subset for non-commercial research use, supporting work on speech recognition and speaker analysis.
arxiv-2509-04902:
Two kinds of flat electronic band can coexist in one layered metal. Hanoh Lee, lead author with eighteen co-authors, report that coexistence in a 2025 condensed matter paper on an ytterbium chromium germanium compound. Its kagome lattice, a pattern of corner-sharing triangles, produces a flat band from frustrated hopping at high temperature.

On cooling, localised ytterbium states hybridise with that band and form heavy-fermion Kondo resonance states. Symmetry protects Dirac crossings of heavy character along certain lines. Topological analysis finds both trivial and nontrivial invariants in the resulting gaps. The authors identify the material as a prototype topological heavy-fermion system.
arxiv-2509-05202:
Boson stars can suddenly grow a scalar field inside theories that modify gravity. Hyat Huang, lead author with five co-authors, study that spontaneous scalarisation in a 2025 theoretical physics paper. Earlier work on neutron stars showed matter-induced scalarisation is mostly tied to a first-order phase transition, where the change happens abruptly.

The authors ask whether boson stars behave the same way. They model the bosonic matter with a repulsive quartic potential, which resists compression. Across their analysis they find only first-order phase transitions. The result extends the phase transition picture of scalarisation from neutron stars to these purely bosonic compact objects.
arxiv-2509-05302:
Drug discovery needs the pockets on proteins to open up before docking can work well, and Raúl Miñán and four co-authors offer a generative fix called Sesame in a 2025 paper. Docking predicts how a drug molecule fits a protein, and it works best with structures captured while a ligand is bound.

Those bound structures are costly and slow to obtain, while unbound ones are common but their pockets sit in less welcoming shapes. Older ways to force the change, such as molecular dynamics, cost heavy computing. Sesame learns to predict the opened geometry directly and cheaply. At scale, that could improve virtual screening, the ranked testing of many candidate compounds.
arxiv-2509-05702:
Alloys that are both hard and magnetically soft are searched for computationally by Mian Dai and nine co-authors in a 2025 materials science paper. High-entropy alloys mix many elements in near-equal shares, and hardness usually trades against soft magnetism, making the joint goal hard to reach by trial and error.

Their multi-objective Bayesian optimisation balances the two goals at once. An ensemble of surrogate models predicts properties of candidate compositions, while a sampling strategy mixing Monte Carlo draws with an acquisition score explores the vast composition space without getting trapped locally. The search found compositions on the optimal trade-off front with improved mechanical and magnetic behaviour. Specific element combinations are highlighted for future synthesis.
arxiv-2509-06002:
Recommender systems as industry actually runs them are surveyed in a 2025 paper by Kuan Zou and Aixin Sun. Academic work on recommenders mostly tunes offline datasets, without live users or giant platforms, which dulls its practical edge. The authors set out to close that gap with a careful comparison of industrial and academic practice.

They contrast data scale, real-time demands, and habits for judging success. Then they sort real-world systems into two families, those built around buying and those built around content, based on item character and recommendation goal. For each family they review how industry teams meet the challenges. Open directions include the often skipped role of user decision-making and importing ideas from economics and psychology. The survey aims to seed stronger collaboration between scholars and industry.
arxiv-2509-06802: Spaces that behave hyperbolically in a complex-analytic sense get new theorems and cases from Hervé Gaussier and one co-author in a 2025 geometry paper. Kobayashi hyperbolicity is a trait of spaces where complex holomorphic maps cannot exist, a strong form of rigidity. The authors work with Riemannian manifolds. They prove a version of the Brody lemma in that setting, a standard tool in the complex case, and they give new cases of Riemannian manifolds hyperbolic in Kobayashi's sense.
arxiv-2509-06902:
Numbers spoken by a language model should carry proof, proposes Aivin V. Solatorio in a solo 2025 paper. Models sometimes state figures that deviate from the data, a failure called numeric hallucination. Retrieval, citations, and uncertainty estimates improve transparency but cannot guarantee a displayed number is right.

The protocol, Proof-Carrying Numbers, works at the presentation layer. Each numeric span is emitted as a claim-bound token tied to a structured claim. A verifier in the renderer checks it against a declared policy, such as exact equality, rounding, aliases, or tolerance. Only checked numbers display as verified; everything else defaults to unverified, so the system fails closed. Solatorio formalizes the protocol and proves soundness, completeness for honest tokens, fail-closed behavior, and monotonicity as policies tighten. The design is lightweight and model-agnostic.
arxiv-2509-07102:
Helena Kolešová and 2 co-authors address theories that copy quantum chromodynamics, the force law for quarks, but with different content in a 2025 paper. Such QCD-like theories matter for ideas about composite Higgs particles and for dark matter made of pions. At low energies, scientists describe them with an effective field theory, a simpler model that keeps only the key features.

The authors work out next-to-leading order formulas, meaning the first level of corrections past the simplest case, for masses, decay constants, and scattering. They fit the formulas to lattice computer data for one gauge theory and extract its low-energy constants. The refined formulas then sharpen the case for pion dark matter that interacts strongly with itself. Getting the corrections right changes which versions of that idea can still work.
arxiv-2509-07202:
Khushiyant, in a solo 2025 paper, designs a system that turns brain signals into text. Electroencephalography, or EEG, records brain activity through scalp sensors, and decoding it into words could restore communication for people with severe motor limits. Past EEG text systems demanded huge data and computing power, which kept them out of reach for many labs.

The design joins a recurrent neural network encoder, a model that reads sequences step by step, with Gemma 2B, a compact large language model, in a classifier-plus-generator layout. Transfer learning, which reuses a model trained elsewhere, keeps data and compute needs low. The author reports performance close to leading methods and about ten percent better overall than current approaches. If the gains hold, EEG typing could become cheaper and more practical for assistive use.
arxiv-2509-07502:
Jackie Liu and 4 co-authors ask in 2025 what happens when AI clones post on social media in our place. A social media clone is an AI delegate built from a person's own data that can interact online as them. Clones promise convenience and comfort, but a mismanaged clone could harm its owner's reputation and relationships. The study sets groundwork for responsible design.

Using a design workbook, the team introduced eight speculative clone concepts to 32 social media users in semi-structured interviews. Users liked the convenience yet worried that clones threaten authenticity and breed skepticism in their communities. Notably, users said they would start behaving more like their clones to reduce mismatches and awkward breakdowns. The authors discuss the findings through identity and impression management research and propose design considerations for future clone products.
arxiv-2509-07602:
James Salsbury's 2025 paper, with 3 co-authors, designs clinical trials that cope with treatments whose benefits arrive late. Trials with survival endpoints are central in cancer research, but immunotherapies often show delayed effects. Delay breaks the proportional hazards assumption behind standard tools like the Cox model and log-rank test, so an early interim look can wrongly suggest the treatment fails and kill the trial.

The framework builds prior distributions for the delayed effect by eliciting them from experts, then adapts the trial as data accumulate. Folding expert knowledge about timing and size of the delay into the design improves efficiency and robustness. The risk of premature termination falls, and real benefits that emerge over time stand a better chance of detection. An example illustrates how the elicited priors enter the design in practice.
arxiv-2509-07802:
Richita Ghosh and 1 co-author explore how higher-order interactions change tipping cascades on networks in a 2025 paper. A tipping point is a threshold where a tiny push triggers a large change. Many real systems act as networks of multistable units. Vegetation patches and infrastructure networks are examples. The units tip one after another in cascades.
