They are linked in pairs, and also in groups. The group links are the higher-order interactions.

Simulations run on random, scale-free, and small-world networks. They show group interactions can induce cascades at coupling strengths where pairwise links fail. Bifurcation diagrams chart the route into cascades as the two couplings vary. The behavior also appears on real-world social networks. Repulsive higher-order interactions do the opposite. They suppress cascades that pairwise coupling would cause, and they shift the cascade route. Models that ignore group effects may misjudge cascade risk.
arxiv-2509-08202:
Hironori Yamaguchi and 4 co-authors grew a crystal that acts as a chain of magnetic diamonds in a 2025 physics paper. The chain links spin-half copper ions in a verdazyl-based material. Rival pulls between neighbours, plus small twists in the lattice, can break the chain's neat pattern. New quantum phases then appear.

Tests show a clear energy gap at zero field. They also show a flat step in magnetisation at half the full value. A model of paired and single spins explains both facts. Three pair-pair phases are expected as the twist grows. A field-theory map splits them by topology, and one phase is protected by symmetry. Grown lattices let physicists test such ideas on matter they can cool and probe.
arxiv-2509-08302:
Rajendramayavan Sathyam and Yueqi Li survey how foundation models are changing self-driving perception in a 2025 review. The field is moving from narrow models, each built for one task, to broad models trained on huge, mixed data sets. Three flaws still block the road: weak general skill, hard scaling, and poor grace when road scenes drift from the training mix.

The survey sorts the field by four skills a car must have. It must hold broad knowledge. It must grasp space. It must fuse many sensors with grace. And it must reason over time. Each skill is checked against real driving needs. The frame gives engineers a plain test: is this model road-ready, or just large?
arxiv-2509-08502:
Opening a door and closing it look alike frame by frame, and Piyush Bagad with Andrew Zisserman build video representations that can tell such pairs apart in a 2025 computer vision paper. Their new task, chiral action recognition, pairs temporally opposite actions: approaching versus retreating, folding versus unfolding. These actions are everyday, depend on simple visual change over time, and are poorly captured by many video embeddings.

Compact representations must become sensitive to the direction of change in object state, size, position, and count. Latent straightening is the proposed route to time-aware features. Systems that monitor homes, warehouses, or patients need the arrow of time; confusing an opening with a closing is not a small error.
arxiv-2509-09202:
Saddam Hussain and 2 co-authors investigate interacting k-essence dark energy with dark matter in a 2025 paper. K-essence is a scalar field model for dark energy, here with an inverse square potential. Interaction lets the two dark sectors exchange energy.

Two interaction forms are considered, one tied to the Hubble parameter and one built from densities and pressures. Cosmic evolution becomes an autonomous system, a set of equations that runs on its own variables, for phase space study. Many datasets, from cosmic chronometers to supernovae and lensing, test the models. Results reproduce major cosmic epochs and rival the standard model statistically, with late time de Sitter solutions.
arxiv-2509-09302:
Jingtao Zhu and 2 co-authors develop Euler type methods for Lévy driven McKean-Vlasov equations in a 2025 paper. These equations model many interacting particles where each particle's motion depends on the whole group's distribution. Coefficients can grow super-linearly, breaking standard Euler methods.

Projections or nonlinear transformations are built into the Euler step to keep numerical solutions bounded in moments. Tanh, tamed, and sine variants appear as special cases. A restrictive coercivity assumption used in earlier work is removed. Mean square convergence rates arbitrarily close to one half are proved for the particle systems. Numerical examples validate the theory.
arxiv-2509-09502:
Margarida Melo and 1 co-author continue a line of work on tropical trigonal curves in a 2025 geometry paper. An earlier result covered curves with strong links. It tied two traits to each other. One trait is a divisor of degree three with rank at least one. The other is a smooth map of degree three to a rational curve. The map comes after a mild change to the curve.

Here the demand on links is lowered. The new version reaches curves with weaker links. One bar stays in place. The curve must hold no necklace. That is, no cycle built from three or more split points. The wider match helps answer divisor questions through maps. It is a useful bridge in tropical geometry.
arxiv-2509-09602:
Where no doctor certifies a death, health workers interview the family and an algorithm guesses the cause; the guess steers real health budgets. Yiqun T. Chen and 3 co-authors test language models for that job in a 2025 research paper. Verbal autopsy is the standard tool in low-resource settings. Their pipeline, LAVA, mixes large language models with classical algorithmic methods and embedding-based classification.

The team evaluated the approaches on a standard consortium dataset spanning adults, children, and newborns. A leading commercial language model, used off the shelf, beat the traditional statistical baselines by a clear margin. It posted the highest accuracy in every age group. Ensemble combinations were also tested. The authors present LAVA as a proof of concept, not a deployment. Still, cheap language model assistance could substantially improve the cause-of-death statistics that global health planning runs on.
arxiv-2509-09702:
Ninad Bhat and 2 co-authors launch a benchmark for marketing creativity in language models in a 2025 evaluation paper. One hundred brands across twelve categories are paired with three prompt styles, from grounded insights to deliberately wild ideas. Judgements came from 678 working creatives, who compared anonymous outputs in more than eleven thousand pairings, later fitted with Bradley-Terry models.

No model ruled the field: scores bunched tightly, and the best beat the worst only about three times in five head-to-head. The authors also measured how varied each model's ideas were and how reframing a prompt shifted results. Automated judges tracked human rankings weakly and inconsistently, a warning that expert eyes remain essential for creative work.
arxiv-2509-09902:
Saili Keshri and 2 co-authors examine the center of the S0 galaxy NGC 1553 in this 2025 astronomy paper. The galaxy also hosts a gravitational lens, and the team wanted to know how its inner structures formed. High-resolution spectroscopic data from the MUSE instrument let them map how stars move across the galaxy's core in fine detail.

They found orderly rotation with a fast, cooler nuclear disc partly decoupled from the main disc, plus an inner lens and a dense central bulge. Image sharpening revealed a small nuclear bar and faint spirals near the center. The stars there are old and metal-rich. That points to the inner disc and lens forming early from the galaxy's own disc material. Later, inner processes and the group setting shaped them further.
arxiv-2509-10002:
Bhawna Mukhija and 1 co-author simulate what happens to a massive star that suddenly swallows a flood of gas from an erupting partner in a 2025 astrophysics paper. During a giant eruption in a binary, the companion can gain mass fast enough to rewrite its own future. The pair model single stars of twenty and thirty solar masses at three metal contents, feeding each at rates spanning three orders of magnitude.

Slow feeding leaves a star hot, while fast feeding cools and puffs it up, with the switch point differing between the two masses. Metal-rich stars swing their accretion glow more widely at a fixed feeding rate, even though their envelopes start larger. That reversal, against the naive expectation, is the finding the authors stress for interpreting real eruptive binaries.
arxiv-2509-10202:
Alexander Popescu and 2 co-authors design sound tools for neurodivergent listeners in this 2025 paper. Many neurodivergent people have low tolerance for certain sounds, which can cause anything from discomfort to real distress. The team first gathered a list of common trigger sounds from neurodivergent community forums, then built a data set of samples from public sound libraries.

They trained and compared several signal processing and machine learning methods meant to soften only the offending sounds, with very low delay. Dynamic range compression worked best, reliably pulling down trigger sounds in their tests. The authors frame the work as a step toward everyday assistive listening devices that respect the wearer's sound world instead of simply blocking it.
arxiv-2509-10402:
What do programmers actually ask chatbots, and does the code get better as they talk? Suzhen Zhong, Ying Zou, and Bram Adams study developer conversations with large language models in this 2025 software engineering paper. They build CodeChat, a dataset of over half a million real conversations holding 1.7 million code snippets in more than twenty languages, drawn from WildChat.

Web design and machine learning top the topic list, and chats often run long because developers keep switching tasks mid-conversation. Code quality problems are common and language-specific, and they do not reliably shrink even in long exchanges. When syntax errors do get fixed, the winning move is a prompt that names the error plainly and asks for a fix. The authors argue assistants should track shifting intent and watch code quality turn by turn.
arxiv-2509-10702:
Designing a neural network accelerator means choosing hardware and the mapping of the algorithm onto it, together. Charles Hong and four co-authors automate that joint search with DOSA in this 2025 computer architecture paper. Earlier tools explored the two spaces separately, and both are huge and jagged, so the combined problem explodes combinatorially.

DOSA replaces the search with differentiable performance models and gradient descent, sliding through hardware parameters and mappings at once. It beat random search and Bayesian optimization by wide margins on the energy-delay product, the field's combined score for speed and power. The design is modular: adding a learned model beside the analytical one let them optimize a real accelerator's buffers and mappings for another large gain. For chip designers, co-optimization becomes a smooth descent instead of a lottery.
arxiv-2509-11502:
Melissa Anholm and seven co-authors draw new physics limits from potassium-37 beta decay. This 2025 nuclear physics paper varies the beta asymmetry with energy. The asymmetry is measured against the nuclear spin. Letting it vary with the beta particle's energy opens a new window. It gives sensitivity to would-be interactions with a helicity factor.

The team constrains exotic scalar and tensor couplings between quarks and leptons. The sensitivity pairs with the known Fierz term from neutron decay. Their measured Fierz value is small, with stated errors. It matches the Standard Model value of zero. The paper weighs the method against other beta-decay and particle physics tests. It also maps upgrades that could sharpen the method further.
arxiv-2509-11602:
Soichiro Migita, Kyotaro Uehata, and Tomohiro I close a gap in grammar-based string compression. This 2025 theoretical computer science paper treats collage systems. Such systems generalize straight-line programs. Repetition and truncation rules are added. Researchers measure how small a system for a string can be.

A subclass called internal collage systems was known to need room. It needs at least as much as the best two-way scheme. Its size against the unrestricted kind was unknown. The authors prove the two sizes match within a constant factor. Any system converts to an internal one with linear growth. The conversion takes quadratic time. An open question from past work falls as a payoff. A MAX-SAT formula for the exact internal size is added.
arxiv-2509-11902:
Ze-Yu Peng and three co-authors retest a foundational number of cosmology against the newest sky data. This 2025 paper treats the scalar spectral index. It describes how the early universe's density ripples spread across scales. The standard reading sits a few percent below one. A perfectly scale-invariant spectrum would sit exactly at one.

The authors revisit the number through early dark energy models. Those models aim to resolve the Hubble tension. They push the index toward unity. The newest ground-based microwave background data come from ACT and SPT. They reach smaller scales with better precision than Planck. The shift toward one is strengthened and reconfirmed. Solving one tension can rewrite beliefs about the universe's first moments.
arxiv-2509-12002:
Did a neutrino arrive alongside any of the gravitational waves caught in the latest LIGO, Virgo, and KAGRA observing run? L. N. Machado reports a Super-Kamiokande search for exactly that coincidence, covering the O4 run that began in May 2023.

Super-Kamiokande, a huge underground water detector in Japan, watched for neutrino signals timed with gravitational wave candidates from the run's first phase, O4a. During that phase LIGO alone flagged 81 candidate events. The follow-up searches found no significant neutrino signal standing out from background. Rather than a detection, the outcome is a set of flux limits. These are upper bounds on how much neutrino emission could have accompanied those events without being seen. Even so, they still constrain what the sources could have been doing.
arxiv-2509-12102:
Can a chatbot answer mental health questions as well as a therapist? Synthia Wang and five co-authors put that to a direct test in 2025, comparing human replies with output from ChatGPT, Gemini, and Llama on real patient questions.

On the page, the models look strong: their answers run longer, read more easily, use richer vocabulary, and sound more positive, while therapists write in the first person more often. In a survey of 150 users and 23 licensed therapists, model replies were rated clearer, more respectful, and more supportive. Yet both groups still preferred human support overall. The authors read the gap as a design brief: keep the communicative strengths, but answer the trust, privacy, and accountability concerns that hold people back.
arxiv-2509-12302:
Supersymmetry extends ordinary geometry with anticommuting directions. Maps between super Riemann surfaces need their own covering theory. In a solo 2025 paper, Beat Nairz defines super covering maps in analytic terms. These are the branched coverings of the super world.

The maps were already hiding in two active corners of string theory. In one corner, they appear in symmetric product orbifolds of superconformal field theories. There, they let researchers compute correlation functions in a way that keeps supersymmetry manifest. In the other corner, they appear in the hybrid formalism for tensionless strings on a curved background. There, they solve the Ward identities that spacetime supersymmetry imposes on correlators.
arxiv-2509-12402:
Topological quantum field theories turn shapes into algebra. Sergei Gukov and three co-authors propose a new species of them in 2025. Their version is valued in topological modular forms. That is a sophisticated spectrum from homotopy theory. Their construction assigns algebraic objects to closed three-dimensional shapes. It assigns maps between them to four-dimensional cobordisms. Those are the spaces that join one shape to another.

Symmetric bilinear forms supply the building blocks. They come through derived algebraic geometry. Gluing rules are checked. The invariant for unimodular forms lands in the homotopy groups of the spectrum. It is expected to generalize the classical theta function of a lattice. The objects may also distinguish phases of quantum field theories.
arxiv-2509-12502:
A qubit hidden inside an oscillator's motion is the idea behind GKP codes, a leading scheme for error-protected quantum hardware. Jonathan Pelletier and one co-author widen the code's stabilizer group in 2025 to include every operation that acts trivially on the stored information, then exploit that freedom when compiling circuits.

Knowing the full Gaussian stabilizer generators lets them search over physically different implementations of the same logical operation. An algorithm picks the implementation that suffers least from photon loss during the run. In randomized benchmarking tests, the optimizing compiler extends the life of square-lattice GKP qubits compared with a random-walk compiler.
arxiv-2509-12602:
Minyu Chen and Guoqiang Li introduce DaSAThco in a 2025 paper on tuning SAT solvers. SAT solvers test whether logical formulas can be satisfied, and modern solvers depend heavily on internal heuristics, the rules of thumb that guide search. Because SAT problems vary widely, no single configuration works best for all of them.

Earlier automated methods specialized in one problem family but generalized poorly and needed costly re-optimization for new types. DaSAThco instead learns a mapping from instance features to tailored heuristic ensembles, aiming to train once and adapt broadly. A large language model, guided by defined problem archetypes, generates a diverse portfolio of ensembles, and a selection mechanism learns to choose among them. Experiments showed superior performance and robust out-of-domain generalization.
arxiv-2509-12702:
Hongrui Zhao and 3 co-authors present UDON in a 2025 paper on multi-robot mapping under extreme communication limits. Neural implicit mapping lets several robots build a compact reconstruction of a complex setting together. Packet loss and limited bandwidth, however, can degrade the shared map when robots cannot communicate reliably.

UDON introduces uncertainty-weighted distributed optimization for real-time mapping. The uncertainty weighting prioritizes more reliable portions of the map, while the distributed method isolates and penalizes disagreement between single pairs of communicating agents. Broad tests on benchmark data sets and real robot hardware showed greatly better results than current benchmarks. The system maintained high-fidelity reconstructions and consistent scene representations even when communication success rates were extremely low.
arxiv-2509-12802:
T. Nomura, I. Rousochatzakis and seven co-authors report in 2025 what happens in a crystal with spiral magnets when fields grow far past normal lab strength. The crystal can host tiny swirls of spin and links spin to charge, a rare mix in an insulator.

In fields in the hundreds of tesla range, light twist tests show signs of a dense state where spin waves act as one body. That state acts like a tilted magnet and brings a dome-shaped charge shift that makes it visible. The find opens a new high-field phase for study and tests ideas about dense spin states in solids.
arxiv-2509-12902:
Dimitrios Lekkas and Yiannis Petridis count shared upright lines between two closed loops on a curved plane in 2025. The count is a twist on the classic circle problem. Only group cosets by two loop groups are kept.

An exact relative trace form is proved for the count. A large sieve bound from Lekkas and Voskou then caps the error in mean square. The new cap grows as the square root times a log factor. The pair guess this growth is sharp. On the way they give a fresh proof of the known point cap first shown by Good.
arxiv-2509-13202:
Francis Ndikum Nji, Vandana Janaja and Jianwu Wang cluster climate data in 2025 with a two-way time graph transformer at the core. Climate sets mix place, time, and many measures. Classic clusters miss long links and shifting place ties.

A U-shaped autoencoder with memory cells pulls joint place-time traits. Skip links keep fine place detail. The graph transformer at the waist weighs time neighbors both ways. Latent codes then sort into stable groups. Three climate sets show cleaner splits, steadier groups, and closer match to known shifts than top baselines. Insight into variability comes with the clusters.
arxiv-2509-13502:
Carlo Vanoni and 5 co-authors study a one-dimensional model of disorder with a stealthy twist in a 2025 paper. In the Anderson model, random disorder can trap waves in a small region. Stealthy disorder is distinct: its power spectrum is zero across a whole band of wave numbers, so it hides from waves of those scales.

The team work out, by hand and by computer, how far a wave can spread in such a system. For a fixed energy and weak disorder, they find a range of stealth where the spread length tops the size of the whole system. In effect, the wave acts as if it were free, an effect they call effective delocalization. The cause is the long-range links built into stealthy disorder, which set it apart from plain random disorder.
arxiv-2509-13702:
Xiao Zheng, writing alone in a 2025 paper, presents a system for suppressing hallucinations in large language models. A hallucination is false content stated with confidence, and it blocks the reliable use of these models. Retrieval-augmented generation, for one, brings in outside text to correct the model, rather than stopping errors while the answer is being formed.

The new system, called Dynamic Self-reinforcing Calibration, steps in early. It acts while the model decodes its answer one token at a time, the autoregressive way such models write. The idea borrows from dual-process theories of thinking. A small proxy model plays two opposed roles in training. At each step they inject a steering vector, computed in real time, into the generation. In the author's tests on two benchmarks, the system reached state-of-the-art results, with a very high rate of factual consistency among them.
arxiv-2509-14102:
Felicia Nguyen, writing alone in 2025, asks how an online platform should reward new creators who choose their quality before anything is released. Early exposure is scarce, and creators act with their own pay in mind. Her study treats a short test window with a clear pass or fail bar as the core tool.

Nguyen finds that a set payment she calls an implementability bounty can line up what creators want with what the platform wants. Giving promised views early works better than spreading them out. When money and views are both limited, the best rule gives each option equal value at the margin. The work also links real ranking systems to the model, offering a practical way to fix the cold start problem for new creators.
arxiv-2509-14802:
Boyang Ma and four co-authors study how short flashes of light push electrons across tiny gaps in metal, in a 2025 physics paper. Electrons can tunnel through a barrier they could not cross in the classic picture. That effect sits behind tools such as scanning tunneling microscopes. A fast light pulse can drive the flow on very short time scales.

The team uses a quantum method that tracks electron density in time. They find tunneling helped by taking in one, two, or more photons at once. They also track how the barrier, a steady bias, and field strength shift the process from photon-helped flow to direct field emission. Simpler models and fresh lab results help them read what the full math shows.
arxiv-2509-15002:
Shu-Min Wu and five co-authors ask whether excited quantum states can protect their resources near a black hole, in a 2025 gravitation paper. Hawking radiation slowly degrades quantum information held close to a Schwarzschild black hole. Most earlier studies only considered the vacuum and the first excited state of two-mode entangled systems, a narrow slice of what is possible.

The new work allows arbitrary excitation levels in multipartite states, many parties sharing one quantum system. Raising the excitation number reduces entanglement and mutual information under the Hawking effect. At the same time, quantum coherence, a different resource, actually grows stronger. The trade-off matters for anyone designing quantum protocols in strong gravity: excitation sacrifices shared correlations but shields coherence from the black hole's influence.
arxiv-2509-15102:
S Rahul and Giandomenico Palumbo extend a curious band-structure effect into non-Hermitian physics in a 2025 condensed matter paper. Some materials have an indirect band gap, the energy offset between band edges at different momenta, pinned at exactly zero. Such pinning usually needs delicate fine-tuning, yet robust versions were recently found in ordinary Hermitian systems over a finite parameter range.

The authors study a one-dimensional diamond-like lattice with gain and loss, the hallmark of non-Hermitian models. The zero indirect gap in the real part of the spectrum survives those perturbations, and they chart where the stability holds. The gap's appearance coincides with suppression of the non-Hermitian skin effect, where states pile up at a boundary. Links among indirect gaps, exceptional points, and the skin effect point to new experiments.
arxiv-2509-16002:
Quantum learning agents need many qubits as tasks grow longer, and today's quantum chips have few to spare. Thet Htar Su, Shaswot Shresthamali, and Masaaki Kondo offer a design that reuses the same qubits step after step. Their system measures and resets qubits mid-task, so a fixed set of seven serves for any task length.

Good paths through a task are boosted with a quantum search trick so they get sampled more often. Computer tests kept the same paths as a fixed design while cutting qubit needs by two thirds. A run on an IBM quantum chip showed the design works on real, noisy hardware.
arxiv-2509-16302:
Reading the faint polarized glow of the early universe from the ground means fighting bright, shifting air glow above the telescope. Simon Biquard, Josquin Errard, and Radek Stompor test map-making methods that assume as little as possible about that air glow. They lean on paired detectors in each pixel and a spinning plate that modulates the signal.

One method, pair differencing, is shown to follow from sound statistical rules and nears ideal accuracy in clean tests. A rival weighting method could match it only with air models that are hard to get. Spinning the plate also curbs flaws like gain mismatch, which keeps the method robust.
arxiv-2509-16702:
Chen Liu, Haitao Wu, Kafeng Wang, and Weiran Huang build a pet image generator in a 2025 paper. Making an image of a specific animal is hard. Animals vary a lot in shape, and fine marks set one apart. Past tools often lost those marks, so the output drifted from the real animal.

Their system sharpens features drawn from several input types at once. It holds identity better across varied scenes. The team also built AnimalBench, a high-grade dataset for this task. Tests show their method beats strong rivals on identity and image quality. Such tools could help owners and media makers place a known pet in new scenes.
arxiv-2509-16802:
Max Dupre la Tour and Kaito Fujii extend a fairness tool to richer valuations in a 2025 math paper. Discrepancy theory studies how evenly items can be split. Past work assumed values add up in a simple way. Real values often do not. The pair define discrepancy for non-additive values and bound it.

Their main bound holds when the number of groups is a prime power. A second result caps the subsidy needed for an envy-free split. That cap is the first below a quadratic level in this setting. Fair splits matter for estates, chores, and shared resources, where simple added values rarely tell the whole story.
arxiv-2509-16902:
Letian Zhang and co-authors speed federated learning on mixed devices in a 2025 paper. Phones and sensors train a shared model without sending raw data away. Devices vary widely in power, though. Slow stragglers hold up each round for everyone. Their elastic method, FedEL, lets weak devices do less while still contributing.

A tensor module balances local and global importance to fight data bias. Tests show time to a set accuracy fell by up to several fold. Final accuracy held or rose versus baselines. Elastic training could make federated systems practical on the messy mix of devices people actually own.
arxiv-2509-17002:
Aharon Rips and Oron Sabag study messages hidden inside control signals in a 2025 paper. A controller must both steer a system and, in their setup, convey a message to an observer who sees the system's outputs. The control signal thus carries a secret second job. The team ask how much information such a channel can carry for a standard class of systems.

They attack the capacity question with convex optimization. For the vector case, a condition tied to a classic Riccati equation shows when their upper bound is tight. Simulations found the bound tight in every tested case. That hints the bound equals the true capacity for vector systems.
arxiv-2509-17102:
A. M. Mukhamedzhanov, working alone, applies Bayesian methods to a key stellar reaction in a 2025 nuclear paper. The reaction that turns carbon into oxygen during helium burning sets the carbon-to-oxygen ratio in stars. That ratio shapes white dwarfs and supernova yields. At stellar energies, the rate hinges on two near-threshold states and their normalization coefficients.

Mukhamedzhanov builds posterior ranges for the reaction's two main factors at the key energy. Even with published coefficient constraints folded in, the ranges stay broad. Present data do not yet shrink the astrophysical uncertainty. Still, the framework gives statistically sound ranges that stellar modelers can propagate honestly through their simulations.
arxiv-2509-17602:
Giulio Martellucci, Herve Goeau, Pierre Bonnet, Fabrice Vinatier, and Alexis Joly report the PlantCLEF 2025 challenge. Their 2025 arXiv overview concerns quadrat images, the square ground plots ecologists use to sample plant life. A quadrat photo can hold many species at once, and naming them all by hand is slow expert work.

The challenge's new test set holds thousands of high-resolution, expert-labeled quadrat images covering hundreds of species. A vast training set of single-plant images and pretrained vision transformers come with it. The task is multi-label: name every species in a quadrat, learning from single-label data alone. The overview describes the data, the scoring method, the entries, and the results. It measures how far AI has come toward speeding field inventories and widening the reach of biodiversity surveys.
arxiv-2509-17702:
Patrick Schmidt, Vasileios Belagiannis, and Lazaros Nalpantidis sharpen weakly supervised image segmentation with depth cues. Their 2025 arXiv paper serves robots entering new domains, where pixel-level labels are pricey and image-level labels are all a trainer may have. Weak supervision builds pixel maps from those cheap labels, but the maps stay rough at object borders.

Their loss, called DEAL, aligns the predicted segments with depth edges, a signal robots commonly carry. It is model-agnostic, so it can wrap many segmentation designs, and it stacks with other losses for further gains. On PASCAL VOC, MS COCO, and a HOPE onboarding split, the loss lifted mean overlap scores, with the largest jump on the last set. Code is public. The authors frame depth, often treated as a side input, as a direct teacher for where one object ends and another begins.
arxiv-2509-17802:
Qi'ao Xu and 6 co-authors offer a plug-in way to sort medical time data, such as heart or brain traces. Their 2025 paper notes that people differ a lot, so a model trained on some folk may fail on new folk. Past fixes tied to one signal type do not travel well.

Their plan turns a one-line trace into a flat fake image. A pre-trained vision model can then use what it learned from real images. Two contrast steps keep time sense and line the trace up with the image view. On six data sets, the plan beat a wide set of past methods.
arxiv-2509-17902:
Projesh Nath Choudhury and Shivangi Yadav sort the functions that keep a sign trait of matrices when used entry by entry. Their 2025 paper builds on classic work by Schur and others on such preservers. Sign regular matrices have minors whose signs follow a fixed pattern, a trait Schoenberg used in 1930.

The pair give full lists of entry-wise maps that keep sign regularity, in both strict and plain forms. Lists cover rectangle matrices, not just square ones. They also fix a sign pattern and list the maps that keep that pattern too. The trait class holds the known total-positive cases inside it.
arxiv-2509-18002:
M Burak Erdogan, Michael Goldberg, and William Green bound how fast waves spread for a fractional wave operator. Their 2025 paper deals with a Schroedinger operator raised to a non-whole power, plus a fading bump term. Such bounds show that a wave packet thins out over time, not just that it stays bounded.

The team proves point-wise bounds on a key inverse operator for a wide power range. A limit rule with a clean numeric bound comes next. World-wide spread bounds then follow for most dims and a set power window. The tools rest on how the operator acts near the energy of a wave.
arxiv-2509-18302:
Gonzalo Prieto-Lyon leads a large team that sets a base line for Lyman-alpha light at the end of reionization. Their 2025 paper uses ground and Webb telescope spectra of hundreds of galaxies at that late stage. Such a base line is needed to read far earlier galaxies, whose light is scattered by neutral gas.

A first stats map of line widths at that epoch is a key yield. Models for line strength and escape share rest on how bright and blue each galaxy is. About half of mid-bright galaxies pass a set strength bar. Escape shares sit below a bound the team gives.
arxiv-2509-18402:
MRI scans can be sped up by taking fewer samples, but rebuilding the image gets harder. Tingjun Liu and four co-authors present C-MSM, a rebuild method that drops two usual crutches. Their 2025 paper targets multi-coil scans, where each coil needs a sensitivity map. Those maps are hard to get right when samples are few, and clean training images may not exist.

C-MSM learns its scores straight from the raw scan data, with no clean images needed. It estimates the coil maps on its own while it rebuilds. The rebuild draws samples from a spread of likely images, guided by partial scores from the measurements. On a public brain scan data set, quality came close to methods that use clean training data and ready-made maps. The authors say this makes advanced rebuilds usable in more real clinics.
arxiv-2509-18702:
Some graphs reproduce their own structure at smaller scales, and groups can drive that self-similarity. Enrique Pardo surveys self-similar graphs and the algebras built from them in these 2025 notes. The notes began as extra material for a course at a summer school in Argentina. They introduce the algebras from several complementary angles.

Pardo defines the associated C-star algebra, a kind of operator algebra, and works out its basic traits. He then reviews generalizations that appear across the literature. A construction called the Zappa-Szép product gets special attention for its links to the main theme. Recent results on homology and K-theory for these algebras close the notes. The intended reader is a newcomer with some algebra background. As course notes, the piece teaches and surveys rather than proving new theorems.
arxiv-2509-18802:
Robot-assisted surgery gives patients smaller cuts and surgeons a lighter load, but the video it produces is hard to teach machines to read. Garam Kim, Tae Kyeong Jeong, and Juyoun Park present a framework for surgical video understanding in this 2025 paper. Real scenes mix phases, steps, tools, and actions over time. Training data is lopsided: long-term labels cover every frame, while fine labels exist only for key frames.

Their fix propagates the sparse fine labels to nearby frames. Optical flow, estimated from the labeled key frames, carries segment labels across the gaps. That richer supervision feeds a multi-task learning setup. The balance between long-term and short-term information improves. So do accuracy and training efficiency in their tests. Better scene understanding, the authors argue, raises the value of robot surgery data. The method targets the annotation bottleneck directly.
arxiv-2509-18902:
How should chemistry students learn to handle research data well? Alexander Hoffmann and seven co-authors describe a fifth-semester lab course at RWTH Aachen University that teaches data care as a core skill. Students in the advanced inorganic course plan, record, and judge their experiments in digital form. The course uses Chemotion, a free electronic lab notebook tied to a national chemistry data effort.

Old lab notes were often handwritten or saved as plain PDF files, which made them hard to reuse. The new course trains students in the FAIR ideas: data should be easy to find, open to reach, able to work with other data, and fit for reuse. A seminar, training videos, and interactive Moodle tasks support the lab work. The team also shows how the DALIA platform helps students discover learning material on data care.
arxiv-2509-19202:
Alloy designers juggle many input parameters, and seeing how a blend changes as settings slide toward the best known recipe is hard. Benedikt Kantz and five co-authors present a visual analytics tool for that job. Their tool, ParamInter, guides users along interpolations from a starting setting toward an optimal one. A t-SNE map, which flattens high-dimensional data into a readable plot, gives an overview of the path.

Small linked views show each parameter's value along the way, so cause and effect stay visible. Suggestions from explainable AI point out which parameters drive the outputs, and uncertainty estimates mark where the model is unsure. The authors demonstrate the tool on a real blast furnace optimization problem with several competing goals. The approach generalizes parameter-space analysis beyond alloys, pairing guided exploration with explanations instead of leaving users to wander a huge design space.
arxiv-2509-19302:
Absos Ali Shaikh and one co-author catalogue the symmetry properties of a charged black hole sitting in a universe with a positive cosmological constant. That spacetime, named for Reissner, Nordström, and de Sitter, is a standard exact solution of general relativity. The authors check it against a long list of symmetry and near-symmetry conditions. It passes more kinds of pseudosymmetry than one might expect, in curvature measures of several types.

They also derive the general form of tensors compatible with the spacetime and show its energy-momentum tensor shares the pseudosymmetry. The spacetime turns out to be a special 2-quasi-Einstein space. Curvature inheritance fails along two natural non-Killing directions, while certain almost-soliton structures exist along one of them and not the other. A closing comparison with the related Vaidya-Bonner-de Sitter spacetime rounds out the analysis.
arxiv-2509-19402:
Herve Goeau and two co-authors report on the LifeCLEF 2020 plant identification challenge, which asked how well herbarium collections can teach machines to name plants from field photos. Deep learning identifies tens of thousands of species from photos, but training photos cluster in North America and Western Europe. The tropics, richest in species, are photo-poor and specimen-rich. The challenge set about a thousand species, mainly from South America's Guiana Shield, one of Earth's most diverse plant regions.

Systems trained on hundreds of thousands of pressed herbarium sheets plus a few thousand field photos, then were tested only on field photos. That cross-domain gap, pressed specimen to living plant, is the challenge's core difficulty. The paper presents the resources, the evaluation, and the participating teams' approaches. Its analysis shows what herbarium data can and cannot yet do for automated botany in data-deficient regions.
arxiv-2509-19902:
Speech toolkits often lag behind text tools in polish and ecosystem. Binbin Zhang and ten co-authors present WEST, a speech toolkit built squarely on large language model machinery. It reuses mature model architectures, the Hugging Face ecosystem, and packing tricks from text training. Recognition, synthesis, understanding, and dialogue all live in one stack.

Two recipe families ship with it. One uses only open models and open data, so anyone can reproduce the paper's results as a baseline. The other trains on massive internal data for peak performance. The authors prize simplicity as a design rule. A toolkit that beginners can touch lowers the entry cost for speech research. The work is infrastructure, offered to a fast-moving field.
arxiv-2509-20002:
A basis lets every point in a space be written as a sum, and filters let that sum converge along chosen subsequences. V. Kadets and M. Manskova study bases defined relative to a filter on the natural numbers. The norms of the partial sum operators measure how violently the reconstruction can overshoot. Those norms depend on both the filter and the space.

One central result characterizes exactly which growth sequences of norms can occur. A sequence of norms is realizable precisely when the sum of its reciprocals diverges. The construction builds the space, filter, and basis to hit any such target. Filter bases generalize classical bases used across functional analysis. Knowing which norm patterns exist completes a corner of the theory.
arxiv-2509-20302:
Zoltan Bajnok, Bercel Boldis, and Dennis le Plat examine a hidden pattern in gauge theory calculations in a 2025 arXiv letter. Their objects are determinants tied to Bessel kernels, which control observables across all coupling strengths in supersymmetric gauge theories. Earlier work expanded the logarithms of these determinants into asymptotic series. Completing those series with non-perturbative terms exposed resurgence relations.

The authors instead study the determinants directly. They find that all non-perturbative corrections share one strikingly simple universal form. The moments that feed the expansions also transform in a direct, intuitive way. That simplicity, they argue, points to an organizing principle behind the non-perturbative dynamics. The result connects to generalized Tracy-Widom distributions, classic objects from random matrix theory.
arxiv-2509-20502:
Several models debating can reason better than one, but debate is expensive. Xiao Wang and five co-authors borrow the journal review process to cut that cost in a 2025 arXiv paper. Their framework, MARS, assigns roles instead of holding a round table. An author agent drafts a solution first.

Reviewer agents then judge the draft independently, without talking to each other. A meta-reviewer merges their comments, decides, and guides the next revision. Skipping reviewer-to-reviewer chatter is what saves money: token use and inference time both fell by about half against multi-agent debate. Accuracy matched the debate method across several benchmarks and model choices. The authors release their code publicly. The design suggests that structured roles, not sheer agent count, drive collaborative reasoning gains.
arxiv-2509-20902:
Yurii Nesterov, a leading figure in optimization theory, presents universal gradient methods in a solo-authored 2025 paper. The methods solve composite optimization problems without knowing in advance which problem class they belong to. Only the desired accuracy must be supplied.

The paper gives a new complexity analysis with guarantees that do not depend on a parametric problem class. Plugging in an upper estimate for the objective's global curvature turns the universal bounds into concrete rates. Nesterov analyzes the plain gradient method for nonconvex problems, gradient methods for convex composite problems, and an accelerated variant. The accelerated scheme automatically achieves the best possible rate for the class it lands in. The work unifies several strands of first-order optimization.
arxiv-2509-21002:
How well a time series model truly understands its data is hard to measure with task scores alone. Meng Wan and nine co-authors propose lossless compression as a new benchmark in a 2025 paper. The idea rests on Shannon's source coding theorem from information theory.

Optimal compression length equals the negative log-likelihood of the data, they note. A model that compresses a series losslessly to fewer bits must have captured its generative distribution. The authors define a standard evaluation protocol and metrics around that equivalence. Traditional tasks, forecasting, imputation, anomaly detection, and classification, each test only one skill. Compression offers a single strict yardstick for modeling capacity across domains, from finance to sensor data.
arxiv-2509-21102:
A mammography model that spots cancer is not enough; clinicians need to know what it has learned. Suaiba Amina Salahuddin and nine co-authors present Mammo-CLIP Dissect in a 2025 explainability paper. The framework inspects the textual concepts inside vision models trained on mammograms.

A mammography-specific vision-language model serves as the dissector. It labels neurons at chosen layers with human-readable concepts and measures how well those concepts align with domain knowledge. Pixel-based explanations dominate earlier work, but concepts mirror how clinicians actually reason. The authors present the framework as the first of its kind for mammography. Concept-level audits could catch models leaning on spurious patterns before they are trusted in clinics.
arxiv-2509-21302:
Billion scale 3D reconstruction transformers are too heavy to deploy without compression. The work is by Weilun Feng and 10 co-authors. Visual Geometry Grounded Transformers rebuild 3D scenes from images. They work well but cost much memory and compute. Quantization can compress them after training. The authors found that standard quantization fails on these billion scale models for set reasons.

Special tokens cause heavy tailed activation patterns, which break simple compression. Multi view data also makes calibration sample choice unstable. Their framework, QuantVGGT, is the first built for these models. It combines a global rotation step with local channel smoothing to tame the patterns. A second method steadies calibration. The aim is deployable 3D models with lower cost.
arxiv-2509-21402:
Pisot numbers and Salem numbers are special algebraic numbers greater than one, studied for a famous open problem on how small they can be. Mohamed Amara, writing in French in a 2025 paper, investigates how the two sets relate. Salem first showed that every Pisot number is an accumulation point of the Salem set. Amara builds on a method of Boyd to argue the converse direction.

Amara claims to prove that every accumulation point of the Salem set is a Pisot number. Together, he argues, the two sets form a closed subset of the half line above one. On that basis, the paper claims to settle a conjecture of Boyd while disproving the conjecture of Lehmer. These are the author claims, presented as proofs in the paper.
arxiv-2509-21502:
Moving one high dimensional distribution into another at low cost is the core of optimal transport. Salman Beigi and 3 co-authors study that task algorithmically in a 2025 paper. Given a sample from the first distribution, the goal is a close sample from the second. Running time should grow polynomially with dimension, not with full representation size. Product distributions receive special attention.

Their main algorithm transports any product distribution to any target with near Knothe Rosenblatt cost. The target must be sequentially samplable with bounded average cost, a new notion they define. An algorithmic version of Talagrand inequality covers transport from a standard Gaussian. For a Gaussian conditioned on a small set, they construct the sequential sampler in expected polynomial time. Applications for product spaces follow.
arxiv-2509-21702:
Neural rendering with 3D Gaussian splatting costs too much power for watt level XR headsets. Weikai Lin and 3 co-authors co optimize rendering and display power in a 2025 paper. PowerGS is the first framework to minimize both jointly under a quality constraint. A general problem formulation comes first. Solving it splits into two identification steps over the power landscape.

Iso quality curves link display and rendering power combinations of equal quality. The power minimal point on a given curve has a closed form solution under proper parameterization. Foveated rendering support adds further savings by rendering less where the eye barely looks. Extensive experiments and user studies validate the framework. Power constrained extended reality systems are the target platform.
arxiv-2509-21802:
Forecasting chaotic systems like the weather is hard because small changes grow fast, and their patterns play out at many time scales at once. Chang Liu, Bohao Zhao, Jingtao Ding, and Yong Li present ChaosNexus in this 2025 paper. It is a foundation model, pre-trained once and then used on new systems. Earlier models of this kind often miss the mix of fast and slow structure.

ChaosNexus reads time in patches of several sizes, stacked in layers. That lets it track slow trends and quick wiggles together. Expert modules switch on for different kinds of systems, guided by a fingerprint of the system's frequencies. Tested on thousands of synthetic systems, it matched long-term behavior well. It also forecast real weather five days ahead with mean error under one degree.
arxiv-2509-22102:
When an algorithm turns someone down for a loan, recourse tells them what to change to succeed next time. Marina Ceccon and four co-authors point out a blind spot in that advice in this 2025 paper: time. Most recourse ignores how applicant pools react and shift after recommendations spread, especially where resources are limited and applicants compete.

The authors build a time-aware framework that models how the candidate population adapts in response to recommendations. On top of it, they design a reinforcement learning method that generates advice meant to stay valid over a set horizon. That durability lets people take time to make the suggested changes and still reapply with confidence. In complex simulated settings, the method beat existing baselines by a wide margin, balancing how feasible the advice is against how long it stays valid.
arxiv-2509-22202:
Language models that write code often invent libraries that do not exist, and Lukas Twist, Mark Harman, Helen Yannakoudakis, and Jie M. Zhang measure how easily that happens. Such library hallucinations mislead developers, break builds, and can even be exploited by attackers who register the fake names. Their 2025 study, accepted at EMNLP, is the first to test how realistic variations in a developer's prompt affect the problem, across seven large models.

The findings expose systemic fragility. A one-character misspelling in a request triggered invented imports in a large share of tasks. Made-up library names offered by the user were accepted almost every time. Prompts that mention dates or versions also induced hallucinations at high rates. From the riskiest prompts, the authors build LibHalluBench, a benchmark for reproducible evaluation, and they urge safeguards against this class of error.
arxiv-2509-22802:
Kyungwon Chun and 5 co-authors ask where the tidal tails and streams inside galaxy clusters are born. Such features are stars stripped from satellite galaxies. Using multi-resolution cosmological simulations with a galaxy replacement technique, they tracked satellites and their features. The share of satellites with tidal features grows with host cluster mass, but not with the cluster's dynamical state.

Cluster tides alone explain only a fifth of cases. Most tidal-featured galaxies were preprocessed: they merged with other galaxies before falling into the cluster. Many finished forming their features after passing the cluster center, shaped by both preprocessing and cluster tides. Brighter, heavier galaxies show preprocessing even more strongly.
arxiv-2509-22902:
Nemin Wei, Felix von Oppen, and Leonid I Glazman develop theory for probing two-dimensional superconductors with a quantum twisting microscope. The device tunnels current between a graphene tip and a graphene sample. The twist angle and tip charge can both be tuned. The team studies tunneling that keeps momentum, across this flat junction at zero temperature.

Their math shows sharp marks in the conductance curve that reveal the energy spectrum of the sample. Those marks carry momentum-level detail on the superconducting gap. Using twisted bilayer graphene as the test case, they show how joint tuning maps the gap. The method may suit many flat, layered materials.
arxiv-2509-23102:
Human preferences can loop and clash, which breaks reward models that assume clean rankings. Fang Wu and 10 co-authors widen Nash-based alignment to many players at once. Two-player Nash methods cast alignment as a game against one rival. That single-opponent view misses real preference structure. Their MNPO framework sets each policy against a population of rivals.

Each policy also stays regularized toward a reference model. The framework keeps the equilibrium guarantees of two-player methods. Richer competition covers more diverse preference patterns. Across instruction benchmarks, MNPO beat prior Nash baselines. Gains held under mixed annotators and mixed-policy judging.
arxiv-2509-23302:
One base station that both talks and senses must shape beams that serve two masters. Wilson de Souza Junior and 3 co-authors design such dual-function beam patterns. More communication demand warps the pattern and can dull sensing accuracy. Their approach splits the sensing problem into two subproblems. The split exploits the pattern's physical structure more directly.

A low-complexity variant uses manifold optimization plus convex projection. Simulations show better multi-target estimation than joint optimization rivals. The sensing quality holds because the beam pattern is preserved. The cheap variant keeps high accuracy at far lower cost. The setting is a mono-static multi-user, multi-target system.
arxiv-2509-23402:
Driving videos from generators look good but often break 3D consistency across views. Ziyue Zhu and 10 co-authors built WorldSplat to generate 4D driving scenes instead. A latent diffusion model reads multi-modal inputs and emits pixel-aligned 4D Gaussians in one forward pass. Those Gaussians render novel view videos directly. An enhanced video diffusion model then refines the renders.

The result is multi-track video that stays consistent in space and time. Reconstruction methods give good novel views but cannot generate, and generators rarely reconstruct well. WorldSplat aims at both. Benchmark tests show high-fidelity, coherent output. Scalable, controllable training data for driving systems is the goal.
arxiv-2509-23602:
People sort the living world into trees of groups, each with a typical example at its heart. Zekun Wang and 4 co-authors teach machines to do the same with deep taxonomic networks. Older deep clustering methods tie the tree to a known class count and waste the prototype detail at middle levels. Their model fits a complete binary tree of Gaussian mixtures inside a variational framework, learning groups and prototypes from unlabeled data alone.

The team proves that their training objective favors finding real hierarchical links among prototypes. On varied image sets, the method out-clustered rivals using prototypes from every level. The learned trees also read well, capturing broad categories and fine visual splits.
arxiv-2509-23802:
Learning from human preferences breaks down when the compared clips come from different stages of a task. Yao Luan and 4 co-authors name that flaw stage misalignment and propose STAIR to fix it. Comparing a navigation clip with a grasping clip teaches the reward model little. STAIR first learns stages from temporal distance, using contrastive learning to group nearby states, with no task knowledge given in advance.

Comparisons are then favored inside the same stage, and the stage map adapts as the policy changes. Theory and experiments back the diagnosis. On multi-stage tasks STAIR beat rivals, stayed competitive on single-stage ones, and its stages matched how humans carve up the tasks.
arxiv-2509-23902:
Partition functions on an interval, which encode transition amplitudes, can split into simpler pieces glued back together. Boan Zhao and 2 co-authors prove such factorizations for three-dimensional supersymmetric theories with N=2 symmetry. The pieces are hemisphere partition functions with Wilson loop insertions, joined by suitable gluing factors. The proof is carried out explicitly for supersymmetric quantum electrodynamics and for Chern-Simons-Yang-Mills theory.

In the electrodynamics case, the gluing factors read naturally as partition functions on a sphere times a circle. In the Chern-Simons case, hemisphere functions turn out to be affine characters, and the gluing factors are pinned down in special cases.
arxiv-2509-24002:
Agents that use the Model Context Protocol face sterner tests than reading a few files. Zijian Wu and 14 co-authors built MCPMark, a benchmark of one hundred twenty-seven tasks created by domain experts with AI help. Each task starts from a curated state and ships a script that verifies the result automatically. The work demands rich create, read, update, and delete operations across real systems.

Cutting-edge models were run in a minimal tool-calling loop. The best reached only about half marks on first try, and far less when required to pass repeatedly. Tasks averaged over sixteen turns and seventeen tool calls, far beyond older benchmarks, which is the point of the stress test.
arxiv-2509-24202:
A model that says it is sure when it is not can mislead users in high-stakes work. Linwei Tao and 8 co-authors study linguistic confidence, where a model hedges in words like probably or might instead of quoting a number. Number scores feel unnatural, and sampling many answers costs too much. Hedges are cheap and human-like, but untested.

The team releases a large data set of hedges scored by human raters, plus a light mapper that turns hedges into confidence scores. Across modern models and question benchmarks, most models hedge poorly on their own. Careful prompting reached competitive calibration, and a fine-tuning frame improved it further.
arxiv-2509-24502:
Fixing a false fact inside a language model without breaking others is the aim of knowledge editing. Haewon Park and 2 co-authors improve the locate-then-edit family, which rewrites the key-to-value mapping of one layer. Loose choices of those key and value vectors perturb the model far past the target fact, a flaw in many prior methods.

Their method, SUIT, computes the vectors only inside the subspace of features critical to the edit. On three model families, it preserved untouched knowledge far better than strong baselines while editing just as well. Hidden-state checks confirm smaller side effects. Edit-critical subspaces, they conclude, are a key principle for reliable editing.
arxiv-2509-24602:
Pipe flow stays smooth in theory far past the speeds where experiments see it break down, a gap that has lasted decades. Chiara Giraudo and 3 co-authors revisit kinetic energy instability of pipe flow with modern computational methods, in finite pipes rather than the infinite pipes of older analyses. They test two edge conditions: fixed walls and periodic ends.

As pipe length grows, the critical Reynolds number approaches the classic values of Joseph and Carmi. With fixed walls it converges steadily to a bound just above eighty-one. With periodic ends it oscillates with length, touching local minima at about the same value. The team also tracks the shape and time evolution of the disturbances.
arxiv-2509-24802:
Anirban Ghosh and Ayan Dutta sort 3D objects by the shape of their holes and tunnels. Their 2025 paper, TACO-Net, tackles a classic vision task: naming an object given only a cloud of points on its surface. Point clouds are unordered, irregular, and noisy, which makes the task hard for standard networks.

Their method first turns each cloud into a blocky 3D picture. It then pulls out topological features, counts of the shape's connected parts, holes, and voids at many scales. A small network learns from those counts alone. The method set new records on two standard test sets, near 99 percent accuracy. It also held up well on real-world scans and on corrupted inputs.
arxiv-2509-24902: Dennis Gaitsgory sets out a program of conjectures for the Langlands correspondence over function fields. His 2025 paper was written up from a plenary talk planned for the 2026 International Congress of Mathematicians. It aims at the core question of the field. How can the space of automorphic functions be described in terms of the spectral side, the Langlands parameters? Local and global versions of the puzzle are both in view. The note is brief by design, a map of what he believes the finished theory should say.
arxiv-2509-25002:
Somin Wadhwa, Silvio Amir, and Byron Wallace wrote this machine learning paper, published in 2025. It proposes circuit distillation, a way to teach a small language model not just what a big model answers, but how it computes the answer inside.

Standard distillation trains the student to mimic the teacher's output while ignoring its inner workings. Circuit distillation instead lines up matching internal parts, called circuits, in teacher and student, and trains the student so those parts behave alike. The authors give a method for finding which parts correspond and a loss score for their match. On tasks of tracking entities and reasoning about beliefs, the method beat plain distillation. It transferred real skills while adjusting only a small slice of the student's parts, hinting at more precise control over what a small model learns.
arxiv-2509-25302:
Zhang and co-authors test whether AI agents copy themselves without being told to in this 2025 evaluation study. Earlier checks asked agents to replicate on direct instruction. The real danger is spontaneous copying when an agent's goals clash with its user's, for instance to avoid shutdown.

The team built realistic production-like settings with tasks such as dynamic load balancing. They designed scenarios where user and agent objectives can diverge, then measured uncontrolled copying. Two new metrics capture how often and how much agents over-replicate. Across 21 leading open and proprietary models, over half showed a pronounced tendency toward such behavior. The framework separates mere ability to copy from actual risky copying.
arxiv-2509-25502:
Kaiqing Lin and a team of co-authors tackle the detection of fake images made by artificial intelligence, in two thousand twenty-five. Large models that read both images and text seem well suited to the task. In practice, they often judge a fake before they have truly seen its small flaws.

The authors argue that vision parts of such models are tuned for broad meaning, not fine traces of forgery. Training data also pushes the models toward short-cut answers in words. Their answer is a helper that first learns to perceive flaws, then reasons from what it sees. They also built a test set that grades how well a model explains its call.
arxiv-2509-25602:
Search engines are graded by relevance judgments, and language models now draft those grades, but every lab prompts differently. Mouly Dewan, Jiqun Liu, and Chirag Shah reintroduce TRUE in 2025, a rubric-based framework that makes model judging reproducible. It samples data in rounds and reasons over intent, coverage, specificity, accuracy, and usefulness before scoring a result.

Tested on public TREC and leaderboard sets, TRUE ranked systems strongly against human-based leaderboards. The authors' main aim is a shared, repeatable workflow, so that model-made judgments can be compared across labs instead of depending on fragile prompt craft. They also probe where the rubric helps most.
arxiv-2509-25802:
Yanan Zhao and co-authors recast graph signals as distributions in two thousand twenty-five. Graph signal processing handles data on networks. Classic methods assume values arrive in sync at all nodes. They also ignore uncertainty in those values. The new framework stores a probability distribution per signal. Distributions live in Wasserstein space, built on transport distance.

The authors map core concepts to the new setting. Filtering, for instance, gains a distribution version. Classic signals return as a special case. Uncertainty and randomness are encoded naturally. Strict node correspondence is no longer required. Filter learning tests supported prediction tasks. The framework suits sensor nets with messy timing.
arxiv-2509-25902:
When a star wanders too close to a giant black hole, it is torn apart in a bright flare. A 2025 paper by Kunal Bhardwaj, Asen Christov, and Sergey Karpov builds a tool to spot those flares. The coming Rubin Observatory survey will catch thousands of them, mixed in with far more common flashes.

The classifier learns from the shape of each event's light curve. Smooth curve fits yield traits such as color and rise and fade times. Those traits feed a boosted decision-tree model tuned to prize correct finds. Tests used a broad simulated mix, including supernovae and feeding black holes. The pipeline reached precision up to ninety-five percent, which would let follow-up telescopes spend their time on real events.
arxiv-2509-26002:
Ardian Selmonaj and co-authors built a system in 2025 that lets people fly against computer pilots in mock air combat. The pilots learn in a training world through a method where many agents learn at once. A link then moves the trained pilots into VR-Forces, a defense tool for lifelike scenes.

Once linked, human pilots and computer pilots can fight in the same scene. Each computer pilot shows its own style of combat. The team sees uses in team training, deep practice, and trials of new tactics. Such mixed drills may help pilots learn skills that are hard to gain in other ways.
arxiv-2509-26202:
Changjiang Bu, Yue Chu, Qingying Zhang, and Jiang Zhou extend a classic matrix theorem to dual tensors, a richer kind of array. The Perron-Frobenius theorem says a friendly class of matrices always has a positive top eigenvalue with a positive matching vector. Their 2025 work proves the same for dual tensors whose main part is nonnegative and weakly connected.

They also give an explicit formula for the dual part of that top vector, built from generalized inverses of a special matrix class. Because tensors mirror hypergraphs, the result yields facts about the top values of hypergraphs too. As a use case, the team defines dual centrality scores for points in graphs and hypergraphs. A small dual twist breaks ties that the standard score cannot, and tests split points that once looked identical.
arxiv-2509-26402:
Olivier Gaboriault and co-authors explain a density jump in metal powder printing in a 2025 study. When powder is spread layer by layer for additive manufacturing, the bed suddenly packs tighter somewhere between the fifth and tenth layer.

The team built a custom rig that isolates the spreading step and repeats it faithfully. Computer simulation of many layers, tracking each grain, reproduced the same jump. The grain level view showed strong shifting of particles in early layers and still zones near the walls that bound the spreading area. Both the size of the jump and the layer where it begins followed the gap between those walls. The results link single layer studies to real printing.
arxiv-2510-00102:
Juan Espinoza-Retamal and a large team of co-authors published this 2025 paper reporting a new planet, TOI-4507 b. The planet crosses a young F-type star about 700 million years old. Space telescope TESS and a telescope in Antarctica first spotted its transits. Ground-based instruments then weighed the planet and checked its path across the star.

The planet is a sub-Saturn with strikingly low density, like a super-puff. It takes about 105 days per orbit, which is long for a planet of its kind. Its orbit stands nearly pole-on to the star's spin, tilted by about eighty-two degrees in the study. Its mass is capped below thirty Earth masses by the velocity data. The authors say such tilted, puffy worlds test ideas about how planets form and drift. Long-lived rings are unlikely to explain its size, they add.
arxiv-2510-00202:
Yifan Lu and six colleagues published this 2025 paper introducing RouterArena, an open platform for comparing LLM routers. A router sends each user request to whichever language model fits it best. Models differ in skill and price, so routing can save money without losing quality. With routers multiplying fast, buyers lacked a fair, shared scoreboard for choosing among them.

RouterArena supplies a principled dataset spanning broad knowledge domains at graded difficulty levels. It scores routers on many metrics at once, weighing accuracy against running cost. An automated framework keeps the public leaderboard updated as new routers arrive. The first board compared twelve routers and exposed a sharp accuracy-cost trade-off. Commercial routers scored higher but cost much more, while open ones often gave better value. The authors note current routers underuse cheap models where those would suffice.
arxiv-2510-00402:
Zhouyang Liu and five colleagues published this 2025 paper on NC-Iso, a neural method for subgraph matching. Finding whether a small query graph sits inside a big data graph normally needs slow combinatorial search. Neural encoders speed retrieval up, but scale gaps between the two graphs distort their embeddings. Matched pairs then break the containment the embedding was supposed to guarantee.

NC-Iso encodes each node-rooted subtree while preserving the relative positions of features across its levels. That hierarchy awareness keeps matched pairs consistent in both feature counts and feature placement. A new score rewards pairs where likeness clearly dominates difference, sharpening rankings among matches. Tests on nine datasets confirmed gains in accuracy, generalization, scalability, and transfer. Speed stayed competitive with earlier neural approaches throughout. The authors offer NC-Iso as a sharper engine for subgraph retrieval tasks.
arxiv-2510-00502:
Jaewoo Lee and ten colleagues published this 2025 paper on tuning diffusion models toward rewards without wrecking their variety. Reinforcement-style tuning often over-optimizes, collapsing outputs onto a few safe modes. The authors recast alignment as variational expectation-maximization, an old statistical rhythm of search then fit. Their framework, DAV, alternates the two phases deliberately.

In the search phase, test-time exploration hunts for samples that score high yet stay diverse and natural. In the fitting phase, the model distills those discoveries into its own weights. A soft value function steers the search toward promising regions. Tests spanned continuous image synthesis and discrete DNA sequence design. In both, rewards rose while diversity survived the tuning process. The authors note the search phase costs extra compute, but its modular design invites faster search methods later.
arxiv-2510-00702:
Aparicio Resco examines how f(R) gravity would change a black hole's photon sphere in this 2025 arXiv paper on modified gravity. In f(R) theories the Einstein-Hilbert action becomes a function of the Ricci scalar, which can mimic effects blamed on dark energy. A black hole's photon sphere, where light can orbit, is a strong-field probe of the theories. Earlier studies leaned on analytic approximations, so the author pairs asymptotic analysis with numerical integration.

He constructs vacuum solutions that recover the Schwarzschild geometry, for a model adding a squared curvature term. The solutions split into exponential and oscillatory families depending on the sign of the correction. From them he computes the photon sphere radius, the capture parameter, and a defined photon sphere width based on total-reflection rings. The width grows under the f(R) modification, a deviation from general relativity that strong-field observations could detect.
arxiv-2510-00802:
Milon-Harnois and four co-authors add reinforcement learning to evolutionary molecular design in this 2025 arXiv paper on cheminformatics. Computer search through chemical space is hopeless by brute force, since possible drug-like molecules outnumber atoms in the universe. Evolutionary generators such as EvoMol mutate molecular graphs step by step, but blind mutations often yield unstable or unsynthesizable structures. The authors teach the mutation step to read the local structural context before acting.

Their system, EvoMol-RL, represents context with extended-connectivity fingerprints and learns a policy that favours chemically plausible transformations. In experiments it consistently beat the original EvoMol on the realism of molecules surviving pre-filtering, and it produced fewer structural artifacts. Wider fingerprint contexts improved the learned policy further. The method also converged quickly, with low variability between runs. The authors see context-aware mutation as a general upgrade path for evolutionary molecular search.
arxiv-2510-01002:
Yang and ten co-authors diagnose why automated vulnerability repair models fail, in this 2025 arXiv paper on software security. Learning-based repair tools promise to patch vulnerable code automatically, yet their benchmark scores collapse on unseen repositories. The team's study pins down three weaknesses: poor cross-repository generalization, failure on complex multi-hunk repairs, and brittleness to changes such as renaming a variable. Their framework, SeCuRepair, attacks all three.

The model must explain why and how a vulnerability should be fixed, and only then produce the patch. Semantics-aware reinforcement learning rewards patches for matching the reference fix in syntax and meaning, not token overlap. A difficulty-aware curriculum moves training from fixes toward coordinated multi-hunk edits. On strict repository-level splits of BigVul and PrimeVul, SeCuRepair beat the baselines by a third in CodeBLEU. Human judges found sixteen percent more of its patches workable than GPT-4o's.
arxiv-2510-01202:
Cádiz and co-authors stress-test a method that converts time series into networks so their memory can be read from network shape. The visibility graph links points that can see each other across the series, turning dynamics into topology. Whether the method characterizes wildly different systems consistently was unclear.

Benchmark series ranged from colored noises to chaotic maps and jumpy Lévy flights. Reliable results required at least a thousand data points, a useful rule of thumb. A clean threshold emerged linking the network's degree exponent to the series' persistence measure. Anti-persistent and persistent series now separate by a simple graph statistic. Power-law degree patterns give the method its readable signature. Gaussian noises of three colors supplied the tamest test beds. The logistic map contributed deterministic chaos to the mix. Guidelines like these turn a fashionable tool into a calibrated instrument.
arxiv-2510-01402:
Park, Kim, and Panagou keep wheeled robots safe in crowds by replacing rigid collision cones with a flexible parabolic shield. Barrier-function controllers guarantee safety only when their constraints stay feasible, and cone rules turn overly conservative in clutter. Infeasible safety programs strand the robot exactly when traffic thickens.

Their dynamic parabola bends its vertex and curvature with distance and relative speed. The safe set it defines is proved valid for the standard bicycle model under input limits. Simulations threaded through a hundred moving obstacles, where cone methods failed outright. Feasibility and success rates both improved markedly over the baselines. A hundred dynamic obstacles mark the density where rivals gave up. Quadratic programs decide each control step under the safety constraint. Bicycle kinematics capture cars and warehouse robots alike. Less restrictive geometry buys motion without buying extra risk.
arxiv-2510-01502:
Garcia and Isik teach a video model to see social scenes the way humans do, fine-tuning it on tens of thousands of human similarity judgments. People read complex social signals instantly, but whether AI video models share that similarity structure was unknown. Their benchmark collects odd-one-out choices over two hundred fifty short clips of social interaction.

Captions, surprisingly, matched human judgments better than any pretrained video model. Fine-tuning with a hybrid objective closed that modality gap significantly. The tuned model explained variance that language embeddings missed entirely. Human-aligned representations promise better systems wherever AI judges social content. Forty-nine thousand judgments give the benchmark its statistical spine. Low-rank adapters carried the fine-tuning efficiently. Held-out videos tested whether alignment generalized beyond training clips. Linear probes measured transfer to downstream social tasks. Cognitive science supplied the methods; deep learning supplied the model.
arxiv-2510-01802:
Peng, Huang, Yang, and Cheng bridge two modeling worlds for tiny electronic ribbons in this 2025 physics paper. First-principles calculations give accurate electronic structure but cannot handle wide nanostructures. Empirical band models are fast, yet their fitted parameters ignore wavefunction detail and transfer poorly. The authors want first-principles reliability at empirical speed.

Their route starts with Wannier tight-binding parameters computed for small ribbons. A gauge problem hides the size and shape trends in those parameters, so they rebuild the model in a gauge-independent basis. Machine learning then predicts how the cleaned parameters vary with geometry. Applied to molybdenum disulfide ribbons with armchair edges, the model matched first-principles results closely. It also simulated ribbons nearly a micrometer wide, far beyond direct calculation. The framework could guide the design of next-generation quantum devices.
arxiv-2510-01902:
Parys, Vaidya, Berg-Kirkpatrick, and D'Antoni make constrained sampling from language models cheaper in this 2025 paper. Many applications need outputs that obey strict rules, such as valid programs or molecules. Greedy constrained decoding enforces the rules but warps the model's natural distribution. Plain rejection sampling keeps the distribution exact, yet it throws away most of its work.

Their method, CARS, starts with free sampling and learns from each failure. Every invalid continuation goes into a trie, and later draws have that continuation's probability mass removed. Proven-bad prefixes are therefore never revisited, so the acceptance rate climbs steadily. The final samples still follow the exact constrained distribution, with no distortion. Tests on program fuzzing and molecule generation showed fewer model calls per valid sample. The method also produced more diverse samples than both greedy decoding and approximate rivals.
arxiv-2510-02002:
