Kratz, Zschaler, Kosiol, and Taentzer argue that reoptimization problems should be generated, not hand-written, in this 2025 vision paper. Solved plans often need repair when context shifts, as in crew rescheduling, nurse rerostering, or aircraft recovery. Re-solving is not solving again: changes should stay minimal, frozen parts of the old plan must not move, and a change script must link old and new solutions.

The authors propose deriving those modified problems automatically with model-driven engineering. Declarative modeling languages and model transformations would turn an original problem specification into its reoptimization variant. They offer an initial categorization of how problems change and which derivation strategy fits each case. A proof of concept builds on the GIPS tool for graph-based integer programming specifications. The running example allocates teaching assistants to teaching sessions. The paper frames a research agenda, betting that systematic derivation beats ad-hoc edits.
arxiv-2510-02202:
Reyna and thirteen co-authors announce a community challenge to detect Chagas disease from heart tracings in this 2025 paper. Chagas is a parasitic infection endemic across the Americas, and its chronic form damages the heart and gut. Blood testing capacity is limited where the disease is common. The cardiomyopathy it causes leaves fingerprints in electrocardiograms, though.

The George B. Moody PhysioNet Challenge 2025 invites teams to build algorithms that read those fingerprints. A good detector would prioritize patients for scarce confirmatory testing and treatment. The paper lays out the challenge's data, rules, and evaluation design. It stresses clinically meaningful scoring over leaderboard vanity metrics. Past PhysioNet challenges have repeatedly produced methods that migrate into practice. This one targets a neglected tropical disease with a cheap, ubiquitous sensor. The ECG is already recorded worldwide; teaching computers to mine it for Chagas costs almost nothing per patient.
arxiv-2510-02402:
Rigas characterizes new probability distributions over a key family of quantum error correcting codes. His 2025 paper studies CSS codes, named for Calderbank, Shor, and Steane. These codes protect quantum information from noise. They also underpin quantum key distribution protocols. Two-universal hashing secures those key exchanges. Rigas connects hashing security to functions of parity check matrices. Those functions relate to marginals of a measure over random matrices. He introduces real, simulator, and ideal isometries for the analysis. Collision bounds between hashing functions then drive the security result.

The protocol ends up slightly less secure than ideal claims suggest. A strictly positive loss factor appears in the exponent. Its size grows with the cost of two key functions. Conditional security statements prove easier to formalize honestly. Quantum cryptography gains a more careful accounting. Near term quantum applications depend on such accounting.
arxiv-2510-02802:
Mitchell reports a new sighting in high-energy astronomy. The H.E.S.S. telescope array in Namibia recorded very energetic gamma rays around a pulsar. The pulsar is named PSR B1055-52. It is a middle-aged, spinning remnant of an exploded star. The glow around it spreads over about two degrees of sky. That spread marks it as a pulsar halo. A halo forms when fast particles leak out and light up the space nearby.

This halo is only the third one ever confirmed. It is the first found in the southern sky. The team measured how fast particles spread through the halo. The spread is much slower than in normal interstellar space. The Geminga halo showed the same slow spread. Two cases now suggest that slow spread is a shared trait of halos. Each new halo helps scientists trace how pulsars feed particles into the galaxy.
arxiv-2510-03102:
Pearson, Adnan, and Abdallah score how alike two radiology reports really are. A junior doctor drafts a scan report first. A senior doctor edits that draft into the final version. The gap between drafts reveals what the junior still must learn. Language models can comment on reports but grade them loosely. Entity recognition alone misses the sense of the text. Their hybrid, Llama-EntScore, weds the two approaches. Llama 3.1 supplies the reading, and a medical entity tagger grounds it.

Weights in the score can stress or soften each difference type. The output gives a number plus a plain explanation of it. Radiologists supplied the ground truth scores for testing. The hybrid hit the exact score in two thirds of cases. Nearly all scores landed within one point of the truth. Both parts alone scored worse on every metric tried. Training programs could still use it to track growth.
arxiv-2510-03202:
Ebrahimi, Wiemerslage, and von der Wense rank which language a model should learn from before tackling a new one. Cross-lingual transfer borrows labeled data from a source language. Choosing that source well can make or break the transfer. Older rankers judge languages by fixed lexical or family traits. Their NN-Rank algorithm reads the model's own hidden states instead. Unlabeled target text supplies the other half of the signal.

Two multilingual models and two tasks tested the idea. Part-of-speech tagging and entity recognition were the tasks. Fifty-one source languages faced dozens of target languages. NN-Rank beat the feature-based state of the art clearly. In-domain data produced the largest ranking gains. Even Bible text alone, a widely available fallback, stayed competitive. Tiny target samples already ranked nearly as well as full ones. Twenty-five examples captured most of the achievable quality.
arxiv-2510-03402:
Chrimes and colleagues present a 2025 arXiv paper on the origin of luminous fast blue optical transients, cosmic flashes of unknown cause. These events rival the brightest supernovae yet fade with speed. Rival ideas blame shredded white dwarfs, merging black holes, or failed supernovae. The authors test whether the collapse of massive stars could explain the flashes. Such collapses would form black holes and might match clues that point in two directions.

Population models gave a formation rate for black holes close to the observed flash rate. The parent stars leaned toward low metal content and had lost most of their hydrogen and helium. Dense gas around the stars also matched radio clues from events. Long lived glow from a feeding disc, seen in the event AT 2018cow, fit the picture too. Some host galaxies stay hard to explain, but the authors call massive star collapse a plausible source.
arxiv-2510-03802:
Recupito and colleagues present a 2025 arXiv paper tracing the lifecycle of technical debt that developers write into systems. Self admitted debt lives in comments where programmers confess a shortcut or a flaw. The team mined forty machine learning projects and tracked one hundred eighty five specific debt instances through commit histories. They recorded when debt appears, when it is acknowledged, and how long it survives. Training code and hardware configuration emerged as the longest lived debt sites.

Most debt was introduced in the early and middle stages and persisted. Feature work was the common occasion for adding it, ahead of bug fixes. Debt tied to training pipelines and hardware setups lingered longest before cleanup. Those are the components whose flaws degrade model quality. Where debt pools tells maintainers where review checklists pay off. The authors call for debt management strategies built for code rather than borrowed from software.
arxiv-2510-03902:
Khan and colleagues present this 2025 arXiv paper on using language models to write cloud infrastructure code that deploys. Infrastructure-as-Code tools like Terraform describe servers and networks in files that must obey strict rules. A single model writing in one pass often produces syntax errors, policy breaches, and designs that do not scale. The authors split the job among a team of specialized software agents instead.

Their system, MACOG, assigns agents to architecture, engineering, review, security, cost, and operations roles. The agents share a workspace and follow a finite-state orchestrator that keeps work ordered. Finished configurations are checked with Terraform's planning tool and a policy engine before acceptance. On the IaC-Eval benchmark, MACOG lifted every model tested, with one frontier model's score rising from about fifty-five to about seventy-four. The design shows validation, not just generation, makes AI infrastructure trustworthy.
arxiv-2510-04102:
Dakhmouche and Gorji present this 2025 arXiv paper asking why neural networks fail to extrapolate while physical laws succeed. Time-series foundation models excel at short-range forecasting yet lose to simple baselines on long horizons. A network trained on laminar flow data predicts turbulent flow badly, while the Navier-Stokes equations cover both regimes. The authors seek the precise structural property separating the two kinds of model.

They formalize a property that characterizes when a statistical learner can improve outside its training domain. Their analysis shows common network architectures structurally flatten toward constants beyond the training range. Appendix results prove perceptron outputs converge exponentially fast to fixed values outside the training interval. Empirical tests on current architectures confirm the predicted deterioration in extrapolation settings. The work gives designers a target: build forecasting models whose functional form stays alive outside the data.
arxiv-2510-04802:
Han Zhang and eleven coauthors wrote this 2025 paper on replaying surgery from the viewpoint of team members. Operating rooms have wall cameras, but fixed views cannot show what the surgeon actually saw. Those person views guide decisions, yet they vanish from the record. The authors built EgoSurg, a system that rebuilds egocentric video from ambient room sensors. It needs no wearables and does not disturb the workflow.

Geometry driven rendering supplies the three dimensional structure of the scene. A diffusion stage then polishes the synthesized views for realism. The system can render the view of a staff member at a moment. It renders viewpoints that no camera ever held. Tests spanned surgical cases at sites plus controlled studies. Reconstructions kept visual quality and fidelity to the views. A record of the room changes how teams review and teach operations. Trainees could stand inside a surgery from the lead surgeon view.
arxiv-2510-04902:
Johannes Liebenow, Thorsten Peinemann, and Esfandiar Mohammadi wrote this 2025 paper on tuning shared model settings without leaking private data. In distributed learning, clients must agree on one set of hyperparameters, like the learning rate. Tuning on sensitive data risks privacy, and heavy cryptography slows everything down. Their algorithm, DP Hype, lets each client test candidate settings locally. Clients then vote, and the shared choice follows the majority taste.

The vote is wrapped in differential privacy at the client level, the strong standard. Remarkably, the privacy cost does not grow with the number of hyperparameters tested. The authors prove utility bounds: the chance of reaching a compromise stays high. They built the method inside an open framework for distributed learning. Tests covered both uniform and skewed data splits across clients. Even under tight privacy budgets, the chosen settings performed well. Compromise matters because one client ideal setting can fail the rest.
arxiv-2510-05102:
Cheng Xin and four co-authors make graph neural networks explain themselves in this 2025 arXiv paper. These models predict properties of molecules and other graph-shaped data. Users in science and medicine need to know which substructure drove a prediction. Existing explainers falter when the true rationale subgraphs vary widely in shape.

Their framework, TopInG, uses persistent homology, a tool from topology, to find stable rationale subgraphs. A learned filtration grows the rationale step by step. A self-adjusting constraint, topological discrepancy, forces a clear gap between rationale and irrelevant parts. Theory shows the training loss is uniquely minimized by the true rationale under stated conditions. Experiments beat prior methods on both accuracy and interpretation quality, even with spurious correlations present.
arxiv-2510-05202:
C. I. Chousein-Basia and three co-authors compile the first population statistics for exploded stars' remains in this 2025 arXiv paper. Over 300 supernova remnants are known in our galaxy. Only 64 have published optical measurements of shock velocity and electron density. The team gathered those values through an exhaustive literature survey.

They handled limits and rough values with a Monte Carlo scheme that respects each measurement's uncertainty. Across the population, electron density follows a log-normal distribution. Shock velocity follows a skewed version of the same shape. Younger remnants showed larger internal scatter, reflecting the uneven medium around each explosion site. Trends of velocity and density with age matched theoretical models well. The catalog now anchors population-level studies of remnant evolution.
arxiv-2510-05402:
Ahmad Alsheikh and Andreas Fischer teach two models to design steel heat treatments backwards in this 2025 arXiv paper. Many different recipes of temperature, duration, and composition yield the same final hardness. That many-to-one ambiguity makes the inverse question hard: which inputs produce a desired hardness? Engineers need that answer to hit target properties reliably.

A Teacher model first learns the forward map from 13 metallurgical features to hardness. A Student model then proposes input configurations for a target hardness value. The Teacher grades each proposal, and the Student improves through that feedback loop. On a public tempered steel dataset, the pair achieved the lowest error of all models tested. It also converged fastest, beating random forests, plain networks, and a reinforcement learning agent.
arxiv-2510-05502:
Xiao and Liu study a hybrid device where electrons and light interact closely. Such electron-photon systems are promising interfaces for quantum networks and computers. They usually run far from equilibrium, so electric and light currents flow together. The 2025 paper asks how the random fluctuations of those two currents behave jointly.

The test system pairs a double quantum dot with an optical cavity. The authors extend the standard master equation with counters for both kinds of particle. Earlier studies tracked electrons or photons alone, never the pair together. They find that current ratios and spreads break the expected quadratic pattern at strong coupling. They also show that the usual treatment of photon loss breaks a basic fluctuation symmetry. Fixing that treatment restores the symmetry that the fluctuation theorem demands. The results should help engineers judge and design better light-matter interfaces.
arxiv-2510-05902:
Mahendran and colleagues design subsampling that survives model misspecification. Subsampling analyzes a chosen subset instead of a huge dataset. Informative subsets are usually picked using probabilities from an assumed model. Their 2025 approach derives those probabilities while admitting the model may be wrong.

The probabilities minimize mean squared error of predictions from the imperfect model. A misspecification vector captures the gap between model means and data means. Estimating that vector at large-data scale is the novel technical piece. Simulations span several misspecification forms for generalized linear models. Two real large datasets benchmark the method against current practice. Competing criteria based on standard optimality notions lose consistently. Analysts' queries, not just model fit, should guide subset choice. The misspecification-aware approach outperforms existing methods across all scenarios tested. Linear, logistic, and Poisson regressions all fall within the framework.
arxiv-2510-06002:
Hudson de Martim sets out a 2025 design for legal software agents that must give answers a court could audit. Standard retrieval systems search flat text and ignore how laws change over time. De Martim instead builds on a temporal knowledge graph that stores legal norms, their versions, and the events that changed them.

The core proposal is a library of small, fixed operations, called canonical primitives, that an agent combines into a visible plan. These operations support point-in-time version lookup, tracing the causal lineage of a rule, and hybrid search that mixes text with structured filters. Because every step is deterministic and logged, another reviewer can replay the search and check it. The design offers a blueprint for legal AI tools that stay verifiable in high-stakes work. Use cases in the paper walk through example legal questions.
arxiv-2510-06102:
Mathur and Tale sharpen the complexity map of a labeled graph problem in a 2025 theoretical computer science paper. Labeled Contractibility asks whether one labeled graph becomes another by contracting edges. A 2025 study opened the parameterized analysis, with hardness in contraction count and nonconstructive tractability in treewidth.

The new work supplies an explicit algorithm running in time exponential in treewidth squared, times a polynomial factor. A matching lower bound bars any faster treewidth dependence unless the Exponential Time Hypothesis fails. The problem also stays NP-complete even when both graphs have bounded maximum degree. For contractions plus degeneracy, the authors rule out subexponential algorithms and improve the known tractable one. The obvious brute-force search is optimal too. Few problems enjoy such a complete set of matching bounds.
arxiv-2510-06402:
Keeney and three co-authors design optical composites from multihyperuniform particle patterns modeled on bird retinas in a 2025 materials science paper. Such materials suppress large-scale density swings, giving them optical behavior unlike crystals or random media. Almost all earlier work, though, studied single-species patterns.

Avian photoreceptor mosaics contain several cone types laid out in a disordered but hyperuniform mosaic. The authors model multispecies particle mixes, varying species count, size ratios, and interaction competition. Such mixes reach robust, stealthy hyperuniform order even in highly disordered states. These patterns map onto multifunctional composites with tailored optical responses. Shown options include isotropic structural coloration and enhanced absorption. Dielectric properties can also aid transmission while cutting scattering. The broader lesson is that multihyperuniformity generalizes, rather than being a single-species accident. Disordered photonic materials built on this principle could be tunable, scalable, and simple to build.
arxiv-2510-06502:
Trinh, Menghani, and Vee introduce GUIDE, a distillation method making students match teachers in parameter space, in a 2025 machine learning paper. Standard distillation forces students to imitate teacher outputs only. Teachers are expensive to train, so their internal knowledge deserves fuller extraction.

GUIDE initializes and guides student embeddings toward the teacher's embedding parameters. Students inherit representational structure, not just final answers. On large students trained on roughly twenty billion tokens, GUIDE cut the quality gap by about a quarter. The experiments used student models between four hundred million and one billion parameters. Analysis shows GUIDE combines with ordinary knowledge distillation. Their improvements stack nearly additively. GUIDE alone beat knowledge distillation alone. The method adds no training or inference overhead whatsoever. Quality gains arrive virtually free, making GUIDE an easy pipeline default.
arxiv-2510-06602:
Fynn Otto and four co-authors work where quantum information meets quantum gravity. Their 2025 paper studies tensor networks that mimic a famous duality called AdS/CFT. That duality links a gravity theory in a volume to a quantum theory on its boundary. Adding a local symmetry ties the networks to spin network states from loop quantum gravity.

The authors ask which such networks can exist, and where the limits lie. They show that key parts of the duality appear in genuine loop gravity states. That gives earlier model proposals a foundation from first principles. They also prove no-go results that rule out some stronger network types. In particular, the symmetry blocks certain perfectly entangled building blocks. Weaker networks built from shared Bell pairs still capture the holographic behavior. They even give access to geometric quantities like curve lengths and surface areas.
arxiv-2510-06702:
Ivana Miháliková, Joseph Carlson, Duff Neill, and Ionel Stetcu study how to prepare quantum states on quantum computers. Their 2025 paper uses the Variational Quantum Eigensolver, a leading method for finding low-energy states. Success depends heavily on respecting the symmetries of the target system. The authors test that claim on two spin problems.

One problem mimics neutrino flavor swings inside a supernova, with random couplings between all spins. The other is the standard Heisenberg model on a small lattice. In both cases, keeping every symmetry in the trial state changed the outcome dramatically. Nearly exact answers appeared where standard methods without symmetry constraints failed. Symmetry-respecting steps also allow richer correlations during optimization. That speeds convergence beyond what projection methods alone achieve. The lesson is practical for near-term quantum hardware. Building the right symmetries into a trial state can rescue a failing calculation.
arxiv-2510-07302:
Alam, Islam, Woo, and Muhammad present SpecGuard, an image watermarking method built to survive heavy editing. Their 2025 paper embeds hidden messages in the frequency pattern of an image rather than its pixels. Frequency content is reached through wavelet and Fourier tools, and a strength setting hardens the mark. The decoder leans on a classic energy theorem to learn and recover the pattern. The aim is a mark that stays invisible yet readable after distortion, regeneration, or deliberate attack.

In experiments, SpecGuard recovered its bits with near-perfect accuracy while keeping image quality high. It beat leading watermarking methods on reliability and imperceptibility together. Regeneration attacks, where a model re-synthesizes an image, erase many marks, so surviving them matters for proving ownership. The authors frame it as a new benchmark for watermarking under real-world abuse.
arxiv-2510-07602:
Gandikota, Grigorescu, Jha, and Venkitesh extend quantum decoding guarantees to the realistic case where the error report itself is noisy. Their 2025 paper studies hypergraph product codes, a flagship family of quantum low-density parity-check codes with near-optimal properties. Decoding means inferring errors from a syndrome, the pattern of parity checks that fired. Recently, Golowich and Guruswami reduced quantum decoding to classical syndrome decoding for a broad class of codes. Real hardware, though, measures syndromes imperfectly, and the earlier reduction assumed a perfect report.

The result holds for a general family where a code and its dual are simultaneously well-behaved, admitting good syndrome decoding with similar structure on both sides. Expander codes, Reed-Solomon codes, and their variants qualify. The noisy reduction means decoders for this whole family can be designed and analyzed through the classical syndrome problem, even under faulty measurements.
arxiv-2510-07802:
Zhang and ten coauthors wrote this 2025 quantum physics paper on using AI to control many-body quantum systems. Good control pulses are essential for quantum technology. State spaces grow exponentially, and lab conditions defeat tidy theory. The authors built a learning framework that designs pulse sequences directly. It combines tree search, neural network filtering, and simulation guidance, and it runs on desktop-level computing with little lab input.

The objective was preserving coherence in spin systems, a basic need for quantum information work. The search found over nine hundred high-performing sequences with structures that defy standard design rules. Established optimizers largely failed to find such solutions. In a diamond spin ensemble, the best AI sequence more than doubled coherence time over leading baselines. The result approached the limit set by temperature itself. Changing the objective should extend the approach across spin-based quantum devices.
arxiv-2510-07902:
Li and six coauthors wrote this 2025 energy systems paper on running battery swapping stations for electric vehicles. A swapping station trades a flat battery for a charged one in minutes. Operators can profit by charging when power is cheap and selling flexibility back. Aggressive trading, though, wears batteries out faster. Existing control schemes use crude aging models or fixed rules, leaving money on the table.

Their controller, BSS-MPC, plans ahead with model predictive control and a physics-informed aging model. The model tracks both fast charge changes and slow capacity fade. The joint problem mixes energy arbitrage, swap logistics, and battery health in one optimization. Algorithms solve it in real time. In simulations, the controller beat rule-based and low-fidelity rivals on energy cost and capacity fade. It also met every swapping demand. The authors suggest faster surrogate models as the next step.
arxiv-2510-08602:
Cong Zeng and co-authors flip AI text detection on its head in a 2025 arXiv paper: human writing is the outlier. Detectors usually train a binary classifier between human and machine text. That assumes human writing forms one coherent distribution, which it does not. Limited samples make classifiers memorize quirks of seen human text and fail on new writers.

The team reframes detection as out-of-distribution detection, treating machine text as in-distribution and human text as outliers. Their framework uses one-class learning methods, including DeepSVDD and HRN, plus energy-based scoring. One-class methods learn the boundary of a single class rather than separating two classes. Extensive experiments across domains and generator models tested the approach. The reframing aims at robust, generalizable detection as AI text floods digital communication. Binary classifiers' poor cross-domain generalization motivated the whole redesign.
arxiv-2510-08802:
Rafiuddin presents a system for reading students' emotions during online lessons, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Feelings such as confusion, curiosity, boredom, and frustration signal how well learning is going, but online platforms give teachers no live read on them. Camera, microphone, and text channels each carry clues, yet any one channel can turn noisy or drop out in real homes. Static blends of the three fail exactly when they are needed most.

The framework, Edu-EmotionNet, lets the channels inform each other through an attention step that aligns them moment by moment. A separate estimator scores how trustworthy each channel is at each instant and weights it accordingly. A feedback loop carries past judgments forward so the emotion track stays smooth over time. On re-labeled education data from two public corpora, the system set new best scores and stayed robust when channels went missing or noisy.
arxiv-2510-08902:
Lv and a large team unify the task of spotting medical terms in text using large language models, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Biomedical named entity recognition picks out things like diseases, genes, and drugs in records and papers. The task is snarled by entities nested inside other entities, fuzzy boundaries, and sharp differences between languages. Earlier tools handled each snarl separately, if at all.

The framework recasts extraction as text generation, with a symbolic tagging scheme that marks flat and nested entities and their exact boundaries in one pass. Joint fine-tuning on Chinese and English datasets builds cross-language strength. A contrastive selector then re-checks each candidate, trained on near-miss examples that sharpen boundary judgment, and discards the spurious ones. The method set new best scores on four benchmark sets and kept working on two corpora it had never seen, in both languages.
arxiv-2510-09002:
Hershkowitz and Huang design an algorithm for building cheap networks that respect a strict reach limit, in this 2025 arXiv paper on theoretical computer science. The problem asks for the lightest spanning tree, the cheapest way to connect every node, such that no node sits farther than a set distance from a chosen root. Each edge carries both a cost and a length, and the two pull against each other. On flat, planar graphs like road maps, they find a fast algorithm with guarantees.

Their method returns a tree near optimal in cost, while letting distances overshoot the limit by only a small fraction. The engine inside is a new length-aware version of the classic planar separator, a way of splitting flat graphs along small seams. It also solves the Steiner variant, where extra junction nodes may help. A hardness result for general graphs shows the planar advantage is real.
arxiv-2510-09202:
Jensen proves that a wave governed by a hyperbolic Schrödinger equation cannot hide at two moments in time unless it never existed, in this 2025 arXiv paper. The Schrödinger equation describes quantum waves and related wave packets in water, plasma, and optics. Its hyperbolic variant mixes the sign of the spatial derivatives, as happens for deep-water wave envelopes. Hardy's uncertainty principle says a function and its transform cannot both be extremely concentrated.

The theorem is a unique continuation result: if a solution decays like a Gaussian at two different times, it must be identically zero. Jensen proves this for the nonlinear hyperbolic equation and for the equation with a potential, under suitable conditions on each. The work extends a celebrated 2008 result for the classical equation by Escauriaza, Kenig, Ponce, and Vega. The proofs rest on Carleman estimates, rigorously justified for the hyperbolic setting.
arxiv-2510-09702:
Sara Behnamian and Fatemeh Fogh study grapevine timing with survival statistics in a 2025 arXiv paper. The European grapevine is a perennial plant, sensitive to climate, whose flowering and ripening dates govern yield and wine quality. Watch programmes record those events only at uneven visits, so the true transition dates are known only within intervals, a problem called interval censoring.

The authors build a repeatable workflow that treats each phenological event as a time-to-event outcome. Citizen-science records from the national phenology network become interval bounds, linked to daily NASA weather data. Parametric accelerated failure time models then relate the timing to weather summarised over fixed pre-season windows, avoiding bias from pooling weather up to the event itself. Warmer pre-season conditions were linked to earlier ripening. Flowering responses were modest and uncertain in these data, and rainfall played at most a minor role.
arxiv-2510-09802:
Gracyn Jewett and twelve co-authors survey the heaviest pulsating white dwarfs in a 2025 arXiv paper. ZZ Ceti stars are white dwarfs that ring with pulsations while sitting in a narrow temperature band called the instability strip. The team took time-series photometry of thirty-one massive examples, most never before monitored this way, drawn from a catalogue of white dwarfs within one hundred parsecs.

Sixteen of the thirty-one are confirmed pulsating. Among them is J0959-1828, at about one point three solar masses the most massive pulsating white dwarf known. Across the sample, average pulsation periods grow as the stars cool, shrink as mass rises, and amplitudes fade at the strip's red edge, all as theory predicts. At high masses the strip may not be pure, though: apparently non-variable stars inside it may be weakly magnetic, their fields suppressing pulsations below detection.
arxiv-2510-10002:
Sachdeva and Tom van Nuenen study values in language model debates in this 2025 arXiv paper on AI alignment. Models now give moral guidance, personal advice, and mental health support. Most tests of their values use single-turn prompts, one question and one answer.

The authors ask whether those findings hold in multi-turn debate, where values surface through dialogue, revision, and consensus. In a debate, a model must defend, adjust, or abandon positions under pressure from another speaker. That process can reveal values that static prompts miss, or expose values that shift too easily. The study frames deliberation itself as the test setting, closer to how people actually reason through moral questions together.
arxiv-2510-10102:
Li and co-authors present PANTHER in this 2025 arXiv paper on user behavior modeling. Language models showed that generative pretraining can pack vast knowledge into compact tokens. But user behavior is a different modality: each action carries attributes like time, context, and transaction type, forming a behavioral token.

PANTHER pretrains generatively on sequences of such tokens, learning the patterns of how people act over time. The model aims to capture behavioral knowledge that text-trained models miss entirely. Sequential behavior underlies recommendation, fraud detection, and product analytics. A pretrained behavior model could transfer across those tasks the way language models transfer across text tasks, instead of each team training from scratch.
arxiv-2510-10502:
Rong Huang and Jungong Xue present a method for computing the SVD of a product of nonnegative bidiagonal matrices, in this 2025 arXiv paper. The SVD is a core factorization in numerical computing. Zero singular values are a notorious source of trouble in such computations. The method handles factors of any rank, whether square or rectangular, full rank or rank deficient.

Its key feature is exact deflation: it removes all zero singular values exactly, at favorable cost, whatever the rank or conditioning. The nonzero values, however tiny, are then computed with high relative accuracy. The method can also pull out accurate SVDs of submatrices from the factorization of the whole product. The authors back the claims with error analysis and numerical tests. Such care matters where small singular values carry real physical or statistical meaning.
arxiv-2510-10602:
Zhuoheng Gao and seven co-authors build a grasping system that skips the point clouds most robots rely on, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Standard grasp detectors convert sensor data into explicit 3D point clouds before planning a grip. Brains do no such step. Their framework, SpikeGrasp, processes raw events from stereo spike cameras, which mimic retinas, and infers six degree of freedom grasp poses directly.

The model fuses the two spike streams and uses a recurrent spiking neural network to refine grasp hypotheses step by step. To test the approach, the team built a large scale synthetic benchmark dataset. SpikeGrasp beat traditional point cloud baselines, especially in cluttered and textureless scenes where depth reconstruction struggles. It also showed strong data efficiency, learning from fewer examples. The authors present this as evidence that a neuro-inspired pipeline can support fluid manipulation, including for moving objects.
arxiv-2510-10702:
Usman Gani Joy, Shahadat Kabir, and Tasnim Niger build a forecasting model for Bangladesh's temperature and rainfall, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Bangladesh is highly exposed to climate change, and accurate forecasts matter for farming and planning. Older models often miss long range patterns in climate data. The team's model pairs a Long Short-Term Memory network, a design suited to sequences, with an attention mechanism that weighs which past periods matter most.

They trained on data from 1901 to 2023, drawn from NASA's POWER Project and the Humanitarian Data Exchange. The model beat XGBoost, plain LSTM, and GRU baselines on monthly forecasts. For temperature it reached an R-squared of 0.9834 in their tests, with similarly strong scores for rainfall. Under simulated climate trends, its error grew by only 20 percent, while baseline errors more than doubled. The authors argue the model can support climate sensitive sectors in Bangladesh.
arxiv-2510-10802:
Md Abdullah Al Mazid, Liangdong Deng, and Naphtali Rishe build a network that outlines clouds in satellite images, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Clouds block optical satellite views and limit environmental and climate analysis. Cloud types vary strongly in spectrum and scale, which makes segmentation hard. Their model, MSCloudCAM, is a multi scale context adapter with convolution based cross attention, designed for multispectral, multi sensor data.

Its key idea is to model several complementary context extractors explicitly. Instead of stacking their outputs, it pairs one extractor's fine detail features with another's global context, enabling dynamic, scale aware feature selection. A cross attention adapter fuses the local detail with the broader context. The model sits on a hierarchical vision backbone with channel and spatial attention. On the CloudSEN12 and L8Biome benchmarks, it achieved superior overall segmentation and competitive per class accuracy against recent state of the art models, at comparable complexity.
arxiv-2510-10902:
Sleem Abdelghafar, Maryam Aliakbarpour, and Christopher Jermaine audit how much a trained model reveals about each of its training examples, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Their approach is attack agnostic: it uses mutual information to measure what the final model discloses about whether a point was in training. They show this disclosure is bounded by per iteration gradient disclosures, which grow with a quantity they call gradient uniqueness, how distinct one point's gradient is from the batch's.

Computing it naively is infeasible at model scale. Their algorithm, BS-Ghost, computes it during training for every point with minimal overhead, working in batch space with ghost kernels. Experiments show the score predicts membership inference vulnerability with no shadow models, and predicts reconstruction attack success. Removing high scoring points and retraining reduced disclosure causally. For attribution, their filtering handled 1,000 points in 17 seconds, roughly seventy times faster than baselines.
arxiv-2510-11202:
Machine learning detectors can flag a whole function of code as vulnerable, but programmers need to know which lines are actually at fault. Marco Pintore and co-authors evaluate whether detectors really localize flaws in this 2025 arXiv software security paper. They worry that reported performance rests on spurious correlations and biases in the data rather than on the vulnerable lines themselves.

Their procedure, Detection Alignment, compares the code lines that most influence a model's prediction against the ground-truth location of the vulnerability. The measure is model-agnostic and adaptable to other detection tasks beyond this use case. Applying it to multiple learning-based vulnerability detectors and datasets, they show that predictions are consistently biased by non-vulnerable lines. The results highlight how strongly biases and spurious correlations shape what these detectors appear to achieve, and why finer localization claims need this kind of check.
arxiv-2510-11302:
Training an object detector costs thousands of dollars in annotation, while vision-language models can detect objects from text prompts with no training at all. Samer Al-Hamadani compares these two routes economically in this 2025 arXiv study. He evaluates supervised YOLO detectors against zero-shot Gemini Flash 2.5 and GPT-4 on thousands of benchmark and product images, with total cost of ownership modeling.

Supervised YOLO reached 91.2 percent accuracy against 68.5 percent for Gemini and 71.3 percent for GPT-4 on standard categories, but that advantage cost 10,800 dollars of annotation for a 100-category system and only pays off beyond 55 million inferences. On diverse product categories, the zero-shot models still detected about half the objects while YOLO scored zero on classes it was never trained on. Cost per correct detection favored the zero-shot models at moderate volumes, and the paper turns the numbers into decision rules.
arxiv-2510-11402:
Recommender systems face a cold-start problem for new items: with no interaction history, models trained to imitate a collaborative filter must guess from content alone. Gregor Meehan and Johan Pauwels show that this imitation imports an unfairness along with the accuracy in this 2025 arXiv recommender systems paper. Popularity bias, the tendency of collaborative filters to over-recommend already popular items, is inherited by cold-start models trained on their outputs.

On three multimedia datasets, the authors found the inherited bias is worse than the original. Unable to see interaction data, cold models estimate popularity from content features. They heavily over-predict cold items whose content resembles popular warm items, even when their true popularity is low. They propose a post-processing fix that uses embedding magnitude as a proxy for predicted popularity. Correcting with that proxy produced more balanced recommendations while doing limited harm to cold-start accuracy.
arxiv-2510-11502:
A good tutor must understand not just the right answer but the wrong reasoning behind a student's mistake. Alexis Ross and Jacob Andreas build models that reason incorrectly in this 2025 arXiv paper. Their method, called MISTAKE, targets the latent misconceptions, such as treating fractions as two whole numbers, that generate predictable student errors.

MISTAKE first constructs synthetic examples of reasoning errors by exploiting cycle consistency between wrong answers and the misconceptions that could produce them: a proposed misconception must regenerate the observed error. The generated data then train models for three educational tasks. Evaluations showed higher accuracy simulating misconception-based wrong answers, better inference of latent misconceptions, and closer alignment with expert-written distractor answers when generating wrong options for tests. Such simulators can give classroom feedback and let trainee teachers practice against realistic errors.
arxiv-2510-11602:
Attention is credited with the success of transformer language models, but it bundles several design principles at once, and which ones matter was untested. Huiyin Xue, Nafise Sadat Moosavi, and Nikolaos Aletras take the mechanism apart in this 2025 arXiv machine learning paper. They isolate four principles: mixing information across positions, input-dependent attention weights, the dot-product-plus-softmax mathematical form, and the coupling of queries and keys to the evolving hidden states.

The team built controlled variants that relax one principle at a time, both in every layer and in hybrid models where only some layers keep standard attention. Token mixing proved indispensable: removing it collapsed models to near-random behavior. The exact form and sequence dependence could be relaxed, especially if standard attention survived in some layers. Surprisingly, variants that failed on their own performed robustly when interleaved with standard attention layers, a cooperative effect.
arxiv-2510-11702:
T. Emil Rivera-Thorsen leads a large team studying how ionizing light escapes from a distant galaxy. Their 2025 arXiv paper uses the JWST space telescope to observe the Sunburst Arc. This galaxy is stretched and magnified by gravitational lensing, which bends its light around a nearer cluster. That magnification makes it the best available target for watching Lyman-continuum light leak out. Similar leaks once reionized the early universe.

The team mapped the galaxy's gas motions, dust layout, ionization, and chemical makeup. They found a galaxy that rotates yet is dominated by turbulence, a sign of a recent or ongoing collision with another galaxy. One star cluster leaks the ionizing light. That cluster stands out for its very high ionization, not for unusual dust or motion. The authors suggest the collision stripped away neutral gas around the cluster, letting its own light clear the remaining path out.
arxiv-2510-12202:
Shahoseini surveys the Taylor Wiles patching method and the deformation theory behind it, in a 2025 arXiv chapter on number theory. Galois representations encode symmetries of number fields, and deformation theory studies how such a representation can vary in families. The patching method is a central tool for proving that these families match families coming from modular forms, a link at the heart of modern number theory.

The chapter first recalls Mazur's deformation theory and sets up local and global deformation problems. It then introduces Taylor Wiles primes and explains the role they play on both the Galois side and the modular side. Finally it assembles the patching argument and proves the equality of the two rings, known as R equals T, in the minimal and non minimal cases alike. For the modular side the chapter sticks to the rational numbers to avoid the harder theory of Hilbert modular forms.
arxiv-2510-12302:
Chen and Pfenning report work in progress on running logic programs inside a framework that can express infinite proofs, in a 2025 arXiv paper. Logical frameworks such as LF were designed to specify deductive systems and give generic proof checkers. Programming in them follows a computation as proof construction paradigm, realized in languages based on backward or forward chaining.

Those earlier frameworks could not directly express infinitary objects or proofs, which the newer CoLF framework can. The authors sketch an approach for its first order fragment that already includes such infinite objects and proofs. Their key idea treats logic variables as channels and computation as message passing between processes. A concrete compiler realizes this, translating the framework into Sax, a parallel language based on proof reduction within the semi axiomatic sequent calculus. The report presents the design as a route to proof exploration where programs and infinite proofs interact.
arxiv-2510-12502:
Buffenoir revives the quantum logic program of Birkhoff and von Neumann by reversing its usual assumptions, in a 2025 arXiv paper. The 1936 program tried to found quantum theory on a logic of experimental propositions, but it stalled on no-go theorems. The elementary logics resisted combining into composite systems, and entangled states seemed impossible to represent.

Buffenoir instead takes two structures as the only prerequisites. One is a tensor product for combining systems. The other is a star involution, an operation like complex conjugation. State spaces are then defined from these alone. Surprisingly, the resulting quantum logics connect closely with irreducible Hilbert geometries, although no such structure was imposed at the start. Within the framework he proves basic quantum like properties: contextuality, the no broadcasting theorem, and Bell nonlocality. The paper argues this rebuilt program can achieve the founders' ambition of grounding quantum theory in logic.
arxiv-2510-12702:
Richter and Wehrheim ask language models to write full formal contracts for software functions, not just the usual postconditions, in a 2025 arXiv paper. Automatic verifiers can check code against formal specifications, but real code rarely has any. Models can infer postconditions, statements about outputs, from names and comments, yet verifiers fed only postconditions suggest invalid inputs that turn out false alarms.

The authors define the NL2Contract task: translate informal natural language into a functional contract with both preconditions, the assumptions on inputs, and postconditions. They introduce metrics for soundness, for whether contracts separate buggy from correct behavior, and for usability in automatic verification. Evaluating several language models, they find the generated contracts are usually sound for all inputs. They are expressive enough to separate bugs from correct code. Verifiers given full contracts produced fewer false alarms than with postconditions alone, and the inferred preconditions usually matched developer intentions.
arxiv-2510-12802:
Towell explores a foundational puzzle of cryptography in this 2025 arXiv paper: how can two hundred fifty-six bits pretend to be endless randomness? Cryptographic theory often assumes a random oracle, an imaginary function answering every possible input with perfectly random output, yet no real computer could store such a thing. The paper asks what systems actually do instead.

Towell first builds a true oracle in Python and shows it failing through memory exhaustion and an inability to persist or be shared. That amounts to a constructive proof of impossibility. He then presents a lazy alternative that generates answers on demand from a small seed of entropy. The resulting sequence is not truly random and must eventually repeat. Yet no computationally limited observer can tell it apart from genuine randomness. He frames this as hardness wearing randomness as a disguise.
arxiv-2510-12902:
Shahgholian tells the story of creating a course on mathematics and sustainability in this 2025 arXiv note. He teaches at KTH in Sweden. He was asked to build an applied mathematics course with sustainability woven in, and he calls the journey rough. The note is openly personal. It reflects on the hard parts of course design rather than reporting a research result.

The lectures linked big ideas with hands-on work. They combined math modeling with critical discussion and case studies of real sustainability problems. Most student work happened in group sessions and short projects. In them, students used numbers and reasoning to guide green choices. His aim was twofold: teach technical tools, and build respect for math as a way to read complex problems in society. He offers these reflections to inspire similar efforts elsewhere.
arxiv-2510-13602:
Huang, Xiao, Han, and Liu present NOSA, a sparse attention design that can offload its memory cache off-chip. Their 2025 arXiv paper attacks the decoding bottleneck of long-context language models. Trainable sparse attention already cuts memory accesses during generation. Yet the key-value cache stays full size, limiting batch sizes and throughput.

The authors show that token choices barely change between neighbouring decoding steps. That locality should let the cache live partly on the CPU, but transfers still dominate the cost. NOSA tightens locality by splitting token selection into query-aware and query-agnostic parts. The split reduces transfers while keeping the attention computation itself unchanged. A one-billion-parameter model pretrained with NOSA kept near-lossless task performance. It also delivered up to 2.3 times the decoding throughput of the baseline in their benchmarks, a gain they attribute to cheaper cache movement.
arxiv-2510-13702:
Shin and co-authors define a new task, multi-view customization, and build MVCustom to solve it. Their 2025 arXiv paper joins two skills that generative models usually keep apart. Multi-view generators control camera poses but cannot personalize a subject. Customization models personalize subjects but offer no viewpoint control at all.

MVCustom learns a subject's identity and geometry in a feature-field form during training. A text-to-video diffusion backbone with dense space-time attention keeps views consistent with each other. At generation time, depth-aware feature rendering enforces geometric consistency across the views. A latent completion step then aligns the subject and its new surroundings in perspective. Training data for customization is scarce, which is why rival generators generalize poorly here. Experiments show MVCustom is the only framework hitting both goals faithfully at once, the authors report.
arxiv-2510-14102:
Nicolò Pinciroli Vago, Juan Rafael Martínez-Galarza, and Roberta Amato teach a network to compress X-ray spectra from the Chandra telescope into a compact code, in this 2025 arXiv paper. X-ray surveys produce more spectra than humans can inspect, and automatic methods had not been applied to an archive as large as the Chandra Source Catalog.

Their transformer-based autoencoder squeezes each spectrum into an eight-dimensional code and rebuilds it, proving information survives. Clustering sources in this space classified eight source classes. Balanced accuracy was around forty percent. It rose to about sixty-nine percent when restricted to active galactic nuclei and stellar-mass compact objects. Latent features correlated with quantities such as hardness ratios and hydrogen densities, and with time-domain properties. The code thus captures physics about as effectively as hand-crafted features that cost computation. It shows promise for spotting transient events.
arxiv-2510-14202:
Edgar Vidal, Alexander Gagliano, and Carolina Cuesta-Lazaro build a machine-learning system that works out what powers a supernova and how, from its light curve alone, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Coming surveys will discover millions of transient events yearly, far too many for costly likelihood-based analysis, which tends to assume a single energy source.

Their hierarchical simulation-based inference model identifies which energy sources power an event, then infers the properties of each component, and flags anomalies in its embedding space. The architecture couples a transformer that summarizes light curves with a flow-matching regression module and a categorical classifier. Trained and tested on roughly one hundred fifty thousand synthetic light curves, the network identified energy sources with ninety percent accuracy. It produced well-calibrated probability estimates for every active component. It also detected rare anomalies such as tidal disruption events through the latent space.
arxiv-2510-14402:
Sean Cowan and Ron Noomen automate the design of gravity-assist trajectories for spacecraft with electric propulsion, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Mission designers must choose a sequence of planetary flybys that slingshot the craft toward its target, and the combinatorial possibilities explode, so optimization takes experts days of simulation.

Their Recursive Target Body Approach builds the optimal sequence step by step. It recursively evaluates which next gravity-assist target is best. It uses a hodographic-shaping representation for the low-thrust arcs between planets, plus tree-search methods. Parallelization based on the Generalized Island Model, where searches exchange candidates, adds robustness and speeds convergence through figures of merit. On an Earth-to-Jupiter problem allowing up to three assists, the method spent about a day of computation. It identified an Earth-Mars-Jupiter transfer with a fuel cost as optimal. Extensive tuning then improved trajectory quality.
arxiv-2510-14502:
Maier, Fottner, Greven, and Stöcker, writing on arXiv in 2025, work on a statistics problem. How can researchers model a whole distribution that shifts with measured factors, when they only see samples from it? Their answer is an additive density regression method. The model is built in a special space that keeps densities valid, so they stay nonnegative and sum to one.

The authors prove that their estimator exists and is unique. They also show it behaves well in large samples and give confidence regions for the estimated densities. For computation, they turn the problem into a penalized regression that standard software can handle. They then apply the method to German survey data. The study asks how a woman's share of a couple's labor income varies with the year, the place of residence, and the youngest child's age.
arxiv-2510-14602:
Koncki and Rimányi, in a 2025 arXiv paper, study universal formulas describing where a map between manifolds can go wrong in complicated ways. A map's source and target split into layers by the kinds of singularities that occur. The formulas at issue, called higher Thom polynomials, compute a geometric class for the locus of each multisingularity, each combination of singular behaviors.

The authors prove a structure theorem that reduces every such polynomial to data from a linear series attached to the singularity type. One series, tied to the empty multisingularity, plays a master role for all the others. They also prove an interpolation theorem, which makes the polynomials computable by an algorithm within a known range of dimensions. As an application, they derive an explicit formula for the image Milnor number of a class of map germs, settling one side of the Mond conjecture, computable up to the theoretical bound.
arxiv-2510-14702:
Zhai and a large team of co-authors tackle, in a 2025 arXiv paper, predicting where a person will go next, a core location-based service task. Language models are promising here because they can generate the next destination directly. But they are trained on plain text, so they lack a feel for geography and for how people move through places in sequence. They also ignore context shaping trips: seasons, weather, holidays, and a user's habits.

The authors' framework, CoAST, uses natural language as the interface for all of that knowledge. It works in two stages. First, continued pretraining on enriched, privacy-protected trajectory data teaches the model spatial and temporal movement patterns. Second, a cognitive alignment stage, using supervised fine-tuning and then reinforcement learning, aligns its judgments with human preferences. The design aims at industrial-scale prediction that is more accurate and more in tune with how people decide.
arxiv-2510-14802:
Herath and co-authors present, in a 2025 arXiv paper, a way to aim very large antenna arrays without paying the usual cubic computing cost. The MVDR beamforming technique steers an array to hear a desired signal while suppressing interference. Its standard cost grows with the cube of the number of antennas, which makes massive arrays impractical to run in real time.

The authors' method targets cases where the wanted signal sits below the noise floor, as with GPS. It combines the Sherman-Morrison formula, a shortcut for updating matrix inverses, with low-rank approximations from the singular value decomposition, plus careful algebraic rearrangement. The result scales only linearly with the number of antennas. In simulations, the method cut computational load dramatically while keeping beamforming accuracy close to the conventional approach. The authors point to radar, sonar, and wireless systems, where arrays keep growing, as natural beneficiaries.
arxiv-2510-15002:
Binnendyk settles, in a 2025 arXiv paper, the computational difficulty of a geometric recognition problem. A unit distance graph places points in the plane so that edges connect exactly the pairs one unit apart. Ask whether a graph can be realized this way, with every point on integer coordinates. The question turns out to be as hard as computer science's canonical hard problems.

The author proves NP-completeness by building the decision into a graph. He implements the logic engine of Eades and Whitesides, a gadget construction that encodes Boolean logic into constraints, within this setting. The construction yields a graph that is realizable as a unit distance graph on integer coordinates if and only if a formula in NA3SAT, a satisfiability problem, is satisfiable. So any efficient algorithm for the geometric question would crack satisfiability, and none is expected to exist.
arxiv-2510-15102:
Y. S. Abylkairov and co-authors from several countries ask how far away scientists could read the physics of dense matter from an exploding star. Their 2025 arXiv paper studies gravitational waves, tiny ripples in space, emitted when massive stars collapse. The brief bounce signal at collapse carries clues about the nuclear equation of state, the rules governing matter squeezed to extreme densities.

Using a support vector machine, a standard classification algorithm, the team sorted simulated signals from eighteen competing equations of state. For a supernova ideally oriented toward Earth, the upgraded Advanced LIGO detector could likely identify the right model for events inside our own galaxy. Signals from randomly oriented or more distant explosions would need next-generation observatories such as the Einstein Telescope. The authors caution that their distance estimates rest on simplifying assumptions, so they mark the practical upper limits.
arxiv-2510-15702:
Noncommutative geometry smooths the singularity inside black holes, changing how particles orbit them. Zihan Xi, Chen Wu, and Wenjun Guo map those orbits for Nicolini's noncommutative black hole in a 2025 arXiv paper. They compute the metric's effective potential and draw its curve for test particles and light. From the potential they classify the possible orbit types in this spacetime. Dynamical equations then give the actual time-like and null geodesic paths.

The team varies total mass and angular momentum to see how orbits respond. Both increases reduce the perihelion precession rate of the orbit. The mass effect turns out nonlinear, while the angular momentum effect is linear.
arxiv-2510-15802:
Tommaso Bonato and a large team present Uno in a 2025 paper. Uno is one system for congestion control. It also guarantees reliable delivery. It handles traffic inside a datacenter. It also handles traffic between datacenters. The two kinds differ hugely in round-trip time. When they share links, trouble follows. Local flows respond fast and react first. Slower long-distance flows get starved. This creates unfairness.

Uno unifies control across both scopes. It replaces separate mechanisms that fight each other. The design targets cloud computing and AI workloads. Their communication demands keep rising. Fair, predictable throughput matters within sites. It matters just as much across sites.
arxiv-2510-16002:
Alejandro González del Pino, Manuel Jesús Castro Díaz, and Jorge Macías Sánchez build numerical schemes that respect geostrophic balance on a rotating sphere. Large-scale air and ocean flow is governed mainly by the balance between the Coriolis force and the pressure gradient. Schemes that break that balance corrupt forecasts, above all as the Rossby number shrinks toward zero.

Their finite-volume methods solve the two-dimensional rotating shallow-water equations in spherical coordinates at second and third order. By construction the schemes preserve geostrophic equilibrium in the small-Rossby limit, a property called asymptotic well-balancing. The end use is forecasting meteotsunamis, long ocean waves raised by air pressure disturbances that grow as they near the coast. Tests on analytic and real cases underscore how much long-run balance matters, the three authors report.
arxiv-2510-16102:
Michael LaHaye and five co-authors build math to read the history of extreme mass-ratio inspirals, or EMRIs. In an EMRI, a small body slowly spirals around a huge black hole, singing gravitational waves as it goes. If the big hole's spacetime is slightly bumpy, the spiral's rhythm drifts over time.

The team adapts the Teukolsky formalism, the standard tool for waves from orbiting masses, to holes that are not perfectly round. The drift in rhythm changes the wave flow in ways that can reveal the bump. They test the method on a bumpy Schwarzschild hole, the simplest non-spinning kind, as a proof of principle. The groundwork points toward describing EMRIs around spinning, perturbed holes in later work.
arxiv-2510-16202:
Sophie Rosu and six co-authors untangle Tau Canis Majoris, a crowded star system watched for over a century. What looks like one bright point is four stars. Two evolved giant O stars circle each other over about three hundred fifty years. One of them also has a close companion on a one hundred fifty-five day orbit.

The team used sharp images and spectra to find which star hosts a known eclipsing pair. That pair circles in just over a day. The evidence points to a pair of B stars tucked inside the brighter giant's companion. Long records also show slow drift in one orbit. The wide pair's pull explains it best, not a slowly turning oval orbit. The verdict stays tentative until more data lands, but the system's family tree is now far clearer.
arxiv-2510-16402:
Bernd Finkbeiner and Julian Siber take up a logic puzzle in their 2025 paper. Smart systems must not just act, but be able to say why. The pair ask how to state that need in exact terms. They treat it as a hyperproperty, a trait that links many runs of a system at once.

They blend three forms of logic to state when an agent knows why a thing took place. The blend can state a range of such needs for whole systems. They then show the logic fits inside a known hyperlogic. Best of all, checks in this logic can be solved by machine. That opens the door to auto checks of why-needs in real systems.
arxiv-2510-16502:
Sebastián Pizard leads four co-authors in a 2025 study on AI help for review work. Reviews that pool past studies need a step called qualitative synthesis. That step sums up themes across studies in words, not numbers. It is done in varied ways and often told poorly. The team asks what goes wrong when language models do this step.

They ran two trials as a joint self-study of their own work. Each trial was judged for rigour and for real use. They then read the results through a lens of how such models are built. Their lens flags known flaws, like smooth text that hides weak proof. The study warns that weak steps can get worse, not better, with AI help.
arxiv-2510-16702:
Huy Minh Nhat Nguyen and three co-authors present SDPA plus plus, a self-supervised method for cleaning noisy eye scans. The scans come from optical coherence tomography, a non-invasive imaging method that shows detailed three-dimensional views of the retina. Clean training pairs are hard to collect because real scans carry speckle noise.

The method learns from noisy scans alone. It first builds cleaner target images by fusing and denoising the scans themselves. Those targets then train a group of denoising models that work patch by patch. The team checks image quality with contrast and texture measures. The goal is clearer retinal images for earlier and more accurate diagnosis of eye disease.
arxiv-2510-17002:
Chang Liu and Danial Chitnis automate drawing analog circuit diagrams in a 2025 paper. A schematic is the drawing engineers use to check a circuit. Text lists of connections, called netlists, hide the visual layout. Designers still need clear diagrams for review and discussion.

Their agent, EEschematic, uses a multimodal language model. Multimodal means it reads text, images, and symbols together. Six example substructures teach it typical placements. A visual step-by-step strategy refines placement and wiring repeatedly. The output stays in a format humans can edit afterward. Tests covered an inverter and two amplifier designs. The generated diagrams showed high visual quality and correct structure. The tool could speed a tedious step in chip design.
arxiv-2510-17602:
Chinese tort cases, where one party seeks compensation for harm, require a careful chain of legal reasoning that generic logic templates capture poorly. Huiyuan Xie and six co-authors build LexChain, a framework that spells out that chain in three modules, each broken into finer steps drawn from how tort analysis is actually done. Most earlier computational work on legal reasoning aimed at criminal cases, leaving civil reasoning of this kind largely unmodelled.

The team turns the framework into a benchmark task and tests current large language models on it. Xie and her co-authors find that the models still mishandle crucial elements of tort reasoning. Adding LexChain style steps, through prompting or extra training, lifted performance clearly and transferred to related legal tasks, which supports explicit reasoning chains as a design principle.
arxiv-2510-17802:
Rui Pan and four co-authors fix a bias problem in memory-saving training for large models. Gradient low-rank projection stores only compressed optimizer states during training. GaLore is a well-known method of that kind. Many such methods lack convergence guarantees because projection skews the updates.

The team adds a layerwise sampling step to remove that skew. Their method, called GUM, pairs GaLore's mechanism with the Muon optimizer. They prove GUM matches Muon's convergence guarantees on paper. It keeps the memory savings of low-rank training at the same time. Experiments on fine-tuning and pretraining backed the theory.
arxiv-2510-18102:
V A Bobkov, with two co-authors, checks a shortcut used to model thin stacks of a superconductor against a magnet. The shortcut replaces the stack with one even material under a steady exchange field. The team tests how well that stand-in works for clean thin films with metal and insulating magnets, including newer altermagnets.

For insulating partners, the proximity effect creates a clear spin splitting in the superconductor, and the simple model fits well. Other pairings behave less neatly. The comparison tells theorists when the easy model can be trusted and when the layered structure must be kept in full.
arxiv-2510-18402:
Matthias Lorenzen, joined by Teodoro Alamo, Martina Mammarella, and Fabrizio Dabbene, studies motion planning for mobile robots that cannot move sideways, such as wheeled vehicles. Model predictive control, which repeatedly plans a short stretch of motion and then replans, is popular for this job. Most theory behind it, though, quietly assumes the robot can move in any direction and that the allowed region is convex, meaning free of dents and blocked pockets.

Real spaces break both assumptions, so proofs that a robot will always reach its target have been scarce. The authors present a new formulation of the control method built for non-holonomic robots in non-convex spaces. Under stated conditions that can be checked in realistic settings, their version guarantees the robot converges to the desired target, closing a gap between daily practice and formal proof.
arxiv-2510-18602:
Rachele Sciotto and Karsten Albe study the defect chemistry of barium indate, a ceramic considered for the electrolyte inside solid oxide fuel cells. How well such a material carries ions and electrons depends on its defects: missing atoms, extra atoms wedged in, and paired combinations of both. Using quantum-mechanical calculations, checked at key points with a more exact method, they computed how costly each defect is to form and how that changes with oxygen pressure.

Oxygen vacancies and oxygen interstitials dominate the material's inner defect landscape. Among the interstitials, the authors found a stable dumbbell form, where two oxygen atoms share one site, which stays electrically neutral across the whole energy gap. Other interstitial forms carry charge and become the main balancing defects at high oxygen pressure. The work sets up later studies of how oxygen actually moves through the material.
arxiv-2510-18802:
Vik Pant and Eric Yu lay computational foundations for coopetition, the business pattern where rivals cooperate to grow a market while competing to divide it. Rich modeling languages can draw the dependencies between actors but cannot quantify their trade-offs, while classical game theory is rigorous but strips away context. This technical report tries to join the two.

Interdependence is grounded in dependency analysis from the i-star modeling language, translating who depends on whom, and for what, into numeric coefficients. Complementarity is formalized through the Added Value idea from business strategy, capturing synergistic gains, and bargaining power enters the sharing of created value. A game-theoretic version then lets Nash equilibrium reflect structural dependence. Validation ran more than twenty-two thousand trials across value function choices, checking that the framework's behavior is robust rather than an artifact of one formula.
arxiv-2510-19102:
John Worley and seven co-authors report X-ray observations of Nova Scorpii 2023, a stellar explosion that became a bright supersoft X-ray source about three months after its outburst. Monitoring came from Swift and the NICER instrument on the space station, with long Chandra exposures at several points after the optical peak.

The supersoft glow lasted more than two months and flickered unevenly, at one point rising nearly threefold over a few months. When observations resumed after the nova passed near the Sun, the source was fading fast, which limits how long its steady bright phase could have lasted.
arxiv-2510-19302:
Simone Celora and five co-authors build patient-specific computer models of the heart and circulation to study hypertension, aiming toward digital twins of individual patients. Their framework is grounded in the physiology of the disease, so a model can be tuned to one person's measurements and then used to test what changes would help.

Two model levels are offered: a circuit-like whole-circulation model, with and without capillaries. A richer model couples a three-dimensional left ventricle to the same circulation code. It also reports muscle deformation and stress. Sensitivity analysis on the simpler model shows which parameters drive its predictions most.
arxiv-2510-19502:
Anvarbek Meirmanov and Akbota Senkebayeva argue that standard models of two liquids filtering together through rock miss the physics that matters. Such models drive simulators of oil displacement, a core task in petroleum production. The widely used Buckley-Leverett model, they note, treats the flow as a set of axioms and ignores the boundary where the two liquids meet.

The processes that decide how the liquids interact happen at pore scale, tens of micrometers across, while reservoirs span hundreds of meters, so direct simulation would take years. The authors build correct models from classical Newtonian continuum mechanics at the microscopic level. They then use homogenization, a method traced to Keller and Sánchez-Palencia, to bridge the two scales.
arxiv-2510-19702:
Daniela Calvetti and Erkki Somersalo test a Bayesian dictionary learning algorithm for mapping which brain regions are active during a task, using magnetoencephalography data. MEG records the brain's electromagnetic activity directly and with excellent time resolution, an advantage over blood-flow-based imaging. The hard part is the inverse problem: working back from sensor signals to the active regions.

The brain's source space is split into the one hundred forty-eight regions of the Destrieux atlas, giving the algorithm its subdictionaries. In simulations, a small random patch in each region is activated and the method must find it, first compressing the dictionary and then coding with a deflated version. A probabilistic reading of the confusion matrix scores how well the regions are identified.
arxiv-2510-19802:
Xiaozhen Qiao and six co-authors present CPL-NC, a lightweight method for adapting vision-language models at test time when the deployment data drift from training conditions. Test-time adaptation updates the model on unlabeled target data, but two problems bite: prototypes for rare classes degrade in long-tailed data, and similar classes get confused. Their framework attacks both.

A class-aware prototype cache adjusts how much it stores per class based on how often that class appears, and revives inactive classes so rare categories are not forgotten. A negative contrastive mechanism pins down hard look-alike examples to keep classes separable, while only text prototypes are updated against stable visual features. Across fifteen benchmarks and two backbone networks, the method consistently beat earlier adaptation approaches.
arxiv-2510-19902:
Matthew Blakeney and four co-authors connect two areas of mathematical physics: fusion categories, algebraic structures describing exotic particle fusion rules, and integrable spin chains. They show that any fusion category containing a non-invertible, self-dual object yields an integrable chain of anyons whose interaction satisfies the Temperley-Lieb algebra. The chain comes from projecting the fusion of the object with itself onto the identity channel.

The construction relates to Pasquier's ADE lattice models. Arguing from the Temperley-Lieb structure, the authors conclude these chains are gapped when the object's quantum dimension exceeds two. For categories with dimension close to two, like the Fibonacci-squared and Haagerup categories, finite-size effects are large enough to obscure numerical checks of the gap.
arxiv-2510-20302:
Yuhang Wang builds InvDec, a net for forecasts of many time series at once. It keeps time traits and cross-series traits in split parts. PatchTST is strong on time traits but skips links from one series to the next. iTransformer flips that flaw. InvDec pairs a patch-based time coder with a flipped decoder that attends across the series side.

Late series tags enrich each series code only after time work is done. That guard keeps time traits clean. A tuned mix step weighs time facts and series facts for each set. On seven test sets, the PatchTST form cuts error by near 21 percent on a 321-series power set. Gains hold on most sets, and the edge grows as series count grows.
arxiv-2510-20602:
Zitong Lan, Yiduo Hao, and Mingmin Zhao name a task called resounding: to gauge room echo traits at new source spots from a few gauged spots. Rich sound in a fake world needs source spots that can roam free. The task plays the part that relighting plays for sight. Their way, Versa, leans on the swap law of sound: trade source and ear spots to make true new samples.

Gain shapes of source and ear units block a plain swap, so a self-taught step is built to mend that. Marks show Versa lifts sound field learning on fake and real sets by a lot. User tests with ears in the loop show a much more deep, wrapped sound feel.
arxiv-2510-20802:
Sandra Kiefer and one co-author classify graphs that force the colour refinement algorithm to run for the longest possible number of rounds. Colour refinement detects graph symmetry by repeatedly recolouring vertices from local information, and it underpins many graph matching tests.

Whether graphs attaining the theoretical maximum round count exist at all was open for a long time, following exhaustive searches on small graphs. The classification pins down the long refinement graphs in structural terms, clarifying the worst case behavior of the method and its Weisfeiler Leman generalization. Knowing the extremal shapes helps designers judge when refinement will be slow and when stronger tools are needed.
arxiv-2510-21102:
K Godbey leads eighteen co-authors on a summary of the FRIB Theory Alliance topical program on paths to superheavy nuclei, held in June twenty twenty four. Superheavy elements test nuclear theory at its limits and guide costly experiments at rare isotope facilities.

The report assesses the current state of theory, surveys production mechanisms and models, and marks the developments most needed next. Links with neighboring fields are detailed so experimental programs can choose fruitful routes.
