The document is a community roadmap rather than a single result, setting priorities for the hunt for new elements.
arxiv-2510-21402:
Whie Jung, Dong Hoon Lee, and Seunghoon Hong teach vision models to split a scene into separate factors, such as object identity and style, a task called disentangled representation learning. Older methods hard-wire a special goal or network shape for each factor, so a new kind of factor forces a costly redesign.

Their fix is a modular bias that lives outside both the goals and the network. The key observation is that factors recombine by different rules: a face has one nose, so global traits exclude each other, while objects can appear in any combination. They shuffle the model's inner codes by factor-specific rules and train it so every shuffle still decodes into a believable image that matches its code. Changing only the shuffling rules separates traits, objects, or both at once.
arxiv-2510-21902:
Timothé Boulet, Xavier Hinaut, and Clément Moulin-Frier test whether software engineering agents, programs that write and fix code on their own, can build controllers for embodied tasks in a grid-world game. Such agents shine on ordinary coding jobs with readable codebases, but jobs where the agent must first figure out how an environment works are largely untested.

Adapting a compact agent framework, the team set it loose on twenty varied tasks from the Minigrid environment. Conditions changed what the agent could inspect: sometimes the environment's source code, sometimes only live interaction, in different mixes. The study measures how each kind of access changes success, weighing reading code against learning by trial. It sets baseline numbers for a testbed the authors offer to future work on efficient reasoning systems.
arxiv-2510-22202:
Christoph Wiederkehr, Christian Heumann, and Michael Schomaker stress-test a respected causal method against two real-world messes. The first mess is missing data. The second is near-failure of the positivity assumption. That assumption demands that every kind of patient could receive either treatment. The method under test is targeted maximum likelihood estimation. It is prized for estimating treatment effects with machine learning inside.

Simulations walk through five missing-data diagrams common in epidemiology. Some cases lose values for reasons tied to the unobserved values themselves. A design-based simulation uses a real water-and-sanitation trial dataset from Bangladesh. Eight missing-data strategies are compared. Plain complete-case analysis paired with a model for outcome missingness showed lower bias. Fancier imputation options did worse. The authors report the result against the usual instinct to impute.
arxiv-2510-22302:
Naveed Ahmed Azam and Seemab Hayat count family trees for molecules. Their objects are tree-like multigraphs, branching structures that allow two extra freedoms ordinary trees forbid: a vertex may carry a loop to itself. Two vertices may be joined by several parallel edges, both of which real chemistry and polymer science produce.

Older counting tools, from Pólya's theorem to branching algorithms, strain on the symmetries and sheer combinatorics involved, especially with loops and multiple edges handled together rather than separately. The pair's unified dynamic programming framework counts the non-isomorphic structures exactly, for fixed numbers of vertices, loops. Multiple edges, by building canonical rooted forms and recursing over subgraphs so duplicates never arise. Recurrence relations and analytical bounds describe how the counts grow, giving the enumeration a theoretical backbone instead of a brute-force table.
arxiv-2510-22502:
Stephen Scully and Guangzhao Zhu study rational cycles on products of quadrics, a topic in algebraic geometry, in a 2025 mathematics paper. Quadrics are shapes defined by degree two equations, and the work is set in characteristic two, a setting where ordinary rules for such forms can fail.

Building on earlier work by Karpenko and others, the pair extend results about cycles counted modulo two to arbitrary products of generically smooth quadrics. Their aim is tools for comparing general quadrics, including smooth and non smooth cases. They apply the theory to degenerate quadratic forms in characteristic two and list open problems in that area.
arxiv-2510-22602:
Daily health guidance, rather than care only during illness, is the vision behind the Personal Care Utility proposed by Mahyar Abbasian and Ramesh Jain in 2025. The system is imagined as a global, artificial intelligence powered utility supporting people across their whole lives.

It would combine personal sensing, personal knowledge, and population data through agents that track events and context. Three core services are trusted tailored information, proactive navigation and behavior guidance, and ongoing reading of recovery after medical events. The paper describes architecture, design principles, and implementation challenges for such an ambient companion, and argues it could also support public health and research.
arxiv-2510-22702:
Tracking how cities grow from satellite images is clouded by weather, seasons, and atmospheric noise. Mithul Chander, Sai Pragnya Ranga, and Prathamesh Mayekar introduce the Atlas Urban Index in 2025, a development score computed with vision language models from Sentinel-2 satellite imagery.

For each region, a time series is cleaned to pick the least cloudy image in each time window. The vision model scores that image against curated reference images showing different urbanization levels. The most recent past image is also supplied, anchoring scores over time and reducing cloud related noise. The design aims for more stable large scale monitoring than older built up indices.
arxiv-2510-22902:
Galaxies in groups may lose atomic gas to their surroundings. Shulan Yan leads a team with five co-authors. In 2025 they measure hydrogen gas in group galaxies. Data come from the FAST All Sky HI Survey. FAST is a large radio telescope in China. HI means neutral atomic hydrogen.

Their sample holds two hundred thirty group galaxies. A matched control sample covers isolated systems. Censored data modeling includes non detections. At fixed mass and color, group medians differ little from controls. Satellites are gas poor, while centrals are not. Galaxies near group centers show stronger deficits. Outskirts galaxies match controls closely.
arxiv-2510-23002:
Pravin Kumar studies congruence subgroups of small Artin and Coxeter groups, a topic in pure algebra. Small Coxeter groups are those whose Tits representation takes whole-number values, which makes their subgroups of finite index worth mapping. He uses a matrix representation over Laurent polynomials that unifies the Tits and braid group pictures.

Kumar defines small Artin groups by when that representation stays integral at chosen values. He then examines the congruence subgroups that arise. The work clarifies structure in groups that encode braids and reflections, with results other algebraists can use to test finiteness and related properties.
arxiv-2510-23102:
Alberto Bonicelli expands the Feller semigroup of a one-dimensional Ito diffusion as a power series in time, using trees borrowed from numerical analysis. Earlier work labeled expansion terms with exotic trees, but the combinatorial factors were not fully explicit. Bonicelli derives those factors, giving an exotic Butcher series form.

A key step extends tree factorials and the Connes-Moscovici weight to this richer family of rooted trees. The explicit formula is well suited for comparison with the MSR path integral picture of diffusion statistics. Probabilists gain a bridge between semigroup expansions and field-style methods.
arxiv-2510-23302:
Bhavik Kumar and Daniel Malz propose a simple protocol to measure the applied potential at each site of a cold atom lattice simulator. Atoms in optical lattices realize Hubbard models with site-resolved readout, and arbitrary site potentials can in principle be applied. In practice the tight spacing sits below the diffraction limit, so calibrating potentials is hard.

Their protocol measures any potential with high precision using an efficient experimental sequence. Accurate knowledge of the potential is essential before simulator results can be trusted as physics. The method should help labs verify the landscapes they think they imposed.
arxiv-2510-23402:
Thinh Hoang and Daniel Delahaye address air traffic flow management when many rules interact and cascade. Rising demand and staff shortages have increased the use of flow regulations. When several regulations influence each other, their compounding, nonlinear effects can undermine the operator ability to protect sectors reliably.

Their RegulationZero framework plans in sequence to handle interacting regulations and flow programs. Anticipating cascades, rather than reacting to them, should reduce delays and overloads. The work targets a growing pain point for crowded airspace systems worldwide. Readers can follow the full argument and data in the paper itself.
arxiv-2510-23802:
Nathan Paek and three co-authors make the inner workings of AI music generators readable, using sparse autoencoders to pull interpretable features out of audio latent spaces. Sparse autoencoders have exposed clean concepts inside language models, but audio is denser and harder to compress without losing meaning. Naming what each feature means also remains a manual chore.

Their framework trains sparse autoencoders on the latents of audio autoencoders, then learns straight-line maps from the found features to simple acoustic traits. The traits are pitch, loudness, and timbre, each split into bins. That setup allows both control — turning a trait up or down — and analysis of how traits emerge while music is synthesized. They validate the method on one continuous and two discrete audio latent spaces, then dissect a leading text-to-music model. The same recipe should extend to image generation models, the authors note.
arxiv-2510-23902:
Jans Solano and a co-author build a navigation system for a cheap wheeled quadruped robot that can stand up after falling and keep going. Wheels give efficiency and legs give obstacle handling, but most platforms use costly motors and sensors, and fall recovery is rarely built in — almost never for wheeled-legged designs. Their system pairs a depth camera with deep reinforcement learning policies for both locomotion and self-recovery.

In simulation, the robot moves over rough ground despite low-torque actuators. It recovers from pushes and from failures it causes itself. The team shows goal-directed navigation through indoor spaces using only the low-cost perception. The point of the work is economic as much as technical: robust, recovery-aware navigation should not require a research-grade budget. That lowers the barrier for labs and hobbyists to deploy legged robots that can survive their own mistakes.
arxiv-2510-24102:
Yihan Wang and four co-authors introduce Squrve, a framework that turns research methods for text to SQL into a usable system. Text to SQL lets a user ask a question in plain words and get a database query back. Many methods score well in studies, yet firms lack good tools to combine and deploy them in real products.

Squrve sets a shared way to call each method and breaks the work into seven small actor parts that can be teamed in workflows. Tests on common benchmarks show team workflows beat the single methods they came from. The authors release the code and argue this path helps with complex real world queries.
arxiv-2510-24602:
Federica Ferretti, Mehran Kardar, and Arvind Murugan ask how living groups learn to cope with new stress. In their study, each member of a group meets a slightly unlike set of tests over time. That mix, they argue, can push the group toward broad, safe traits.

Their math shows the mix adds a noise term that punishes traits that work in just one test. Tests in code back up the claim and show when the effect holds. The idea may help in work on drug proof pests, farm strain, and shots that must hold up as germs change.
arxiv-2510-25102:
Junta Igarashi leads a team with eleven co-authors who flip the magnet state of a memory part with a lone laser pulse. The part is a tunnel stack used in a known spin based memory, but built with no rare earth stuff. Such parts hold bits as like or cross magnet states.

By tune of a cap layer's depth, they set how the part takes in laser heat. Past a set cap depth, one pulse flipped the state from like to cross. They read the flip in a micro sized part by a change in its flow block. Fast spin moves or field pulls may drive the flip; the true cause is not yet sure.
arxiv-2510-25302:
Ryuki Hyodo and Shigeru Ida ask why inner planets lack rings. Their 2025 astronomy paper compares ringed and ringless worlds. Giant outer planets all host rings today. Some small distant bodies also host rings. No inner Solar System object shows rings. The pair seek a dynamical cause for that split.

They model Poynting-Robertson drag over billions of years. That drag comes from sunlight acting on small particles. Their model was checked with numeric work. It tracks particle size and distance from the Sun. Without extra effects, drag alone explains the pattern. Outer bodies can keep rings for the Solar System age. Inner planet rings vanish far more quickly. Lifetime grows steeply with distance from the Sun. They predict surveys will find more distant ringed bodies.
arxiv-2510-25502:
Vladyslav Moroshan led four co-authors in presenting TempoPFN. Julien Siems, Arber Zela, and Timur Carstensen helped. Frank Hutter closes the five-author team. Their 2025 paper pretrains forecasting models on synthetic data. Foundation models forecast time series with zero-shot use. Long-horizon prediction and reproducibility remain challenging there. Current synthetic-only methods underperform on hard benchmarks.

TempoPFN is a univariate time series foundation model. It builds on linear recurrent neural networks. A GatedDeltaProduct architecture with state-weaving enables parallel training. Training stays parallelizable across all sequence lengths. Robust time state tracking is maintained throughout. Their synthetic pipeline unifies diverse generator types. Audio synthesis generators also appear. Zero-shot tests used Gift-Eval and other benchmarks. TempoPFN reached top-tier competitive results in tests. It outperformed all current synthetic-only methods tested. Most real-data trained models were also surpassed.
arxiv-2510-25702:
Feng Wang and Xiangyu Hu improve open-edge flows in particle runs. Their 2025 paper implements a bidirectional buffer quickly. Particle-based approaches struggle with strong backflow settings. Multiple open edges complicate flow runs further. Three enhancements improve consistency, independence, and quality. Buffer-based open edge settings are their target.

Strong backflow can otherwise add too many particles. Complex open-edge flows benefit from that separation. Third, pressure edge settings gain first-order consistency. A mirror edge treatment corrects the matrix there. Implementation uses a validated smoothed particle hydrodynamics method. Reynolds-averaged turbulence modeling couples with the solver. Four test cases validate the proposed improvements. Channel flows, plane jets, and micro-mixers were simulated. Turbulent jets simulated successfully in compact domains. Minor code modifications yield great results gains.
arxiv-2510-25802:
Jayant Biradar, Smit Shah, and Tanmay Naik build a hybrid intrusion finder. Their 2025 paper mixes graph and recurrent networks with an attention step. Finding intrusions needs stronger tools in complex networks. Graph networks capture spatial dependencies in network form. Recurrent networks study time changes of events sequentially.

Multi-head attention gives interpretability and feature choice benefits. Analysts can focus resources on high-impact security events. The UNSW-NB15 dataset supplies diverse network traffic patterns. Extensive testing compares against classic machine learning methods. Standalone deep learning models are also compared. Their hybrid model reaches superior results across metrics. Quality, precision, recall, and F1-score all improve. Mainly strong results appears on sophisticated attack patterns. Advanced persistent threats and denial-of-service attacks are detected. Zero-day exploits are also detected strongly, they report. next-gen cybersecurity uses may use such hybrids. Real-time finding in complex environments is critical.
arxiv-2510-25902:
Shashi B. Mishra and Elena R. Margine examine a high pressure superconductor whose behavior needs corrections beyond the standard theory. The material is H3S, hydrogen sulfide squeezed to extreme pressure, and its heavy twin D3S made with deuterium. Superconductivity there comes from fast lattice vibrations coupled to a sharp peak in electronic states near the Fermi level, the energy surface that separates filled and empty states.

Mishra and Margine include anharmonic vibration, meaning the lattice does not vibrate in a simple spring pattern, plus vertex corrections that go past the usual Migdal approximation. Both effects weaken the coupling and lower the predicted transition temperature. Their full calculation matches measured values well for D3S at two pressures and for H3S at the higher pressure.
arxiv-2510-26002:
Sergey G. Bobkov and Devraj Duggal study inequalities that bound how far apart two probability measures can be. A probability measure assigns chances to events, and total variation distance is a standard way to measure the gap between two such assignments. Their weighted version gives some outcomes more importance than others, and they relate it to powers of Renyi divergence, a family of measures of difference between distributions.

Bobkov and Duggal consider Pinsker type inequalities, which are classic bounds of distance by divergence, in this weighted setting. They then apply the bounds to derive transport entropy inequalities, which link the cost of moving mass to an entropy gap, under moment type conditions on the distributions involved.
arxiv-2510-26102:
Lisha Shuai leads seven co-authors in a defense for local differential privacy against poisoning attacks. Local differential privacy lets each device add noise to its own data before sharing, a model widely used in the Internet of Things for its light, decentralized design. Attackers can poison the perturbed data, and prior defenses cost too much or need domain knowledge in advance.

Their framework, PEEL, is a post processing module that re encodes the perturbed data by sparsifying, normalizing, and projecting to low rank form. Poisoning then shows up as structural inconsistencies in the rebuilt space, for both output and rule attacks. Theory shows the method keeps estimates unbiased and accurate when paired with the privacy mechanism, and evaluations support the claim.
arxiv-2510-26302:
Ziliang Chen, Tianang Xiao, Jusheng Zhang, Yongsen Zheng, and Xipeng Chen explain, from a causal angle, why image text models fail at composition. CLIP aligns images and text in a shared space and generalizes well, yet it often behaves like a bag of words matcher, missing which attribute belongs to which object. Prior causal accounts treat a text prompt as one vector, which hides token level structure and leaves prompt sensitivity unexplained.

Their token aware causal framework models text as a sequence of tokens in a structural causal model. They prove the contrastive objective can recover the shared latent variable at sentence and token levels, then show a sharper problem at token level: composition nonidentifiability. Some encoders align perfectly yet stay provably blind to swaps and replacements in the prompt.
arxiv-2510-26402:
Vikrant Sahu, with Gagan Raj Gupta, Raghav Borikar, and Nitin Mane, wrote a 2025 paper on grading code for class. Their tool, Autograder+, uses a large language model, a computer program trained on text, to give feedback. Old graders often said only pass or fail.

It was trained on student code and notes from teachers, then tested on six hundred student submissions. It also groups like solutions in clusters, or sets with a shared style, so teachers can see trends. Maps of the clusters help teachers spot shared errors fast. Teachers can pick prompts to guide tone and focus. The aim is less grading work and clearer help for students.
arxiv-2510-26502:
Dinesh Kumar Keshari, Avijit Pal, and Bhaskar Paul work in operator theory, the study of linear maps on spaces of functions. Their objects are tuples of commuting bounded operators, groups of maps that can be applied in any order. Two families of such tuples are named by the sets that control them, sets written with the letter Gamma and long subscripts.

Keshari and his two co-authors establish the basic operators tied to each family and show they are unique. They give a representation, of Beurling-Lax-Halmos type, for the invariant subspaces of the pure cases. They also build a conditional dilation, a way to lift the tuple to a nicer one on a bigger space, plus an explicit model for a subclass. Last, every such tuple splits uniquely into a unitary part and a fully non-unitary part.
arxiv-2510-26602:
Tanmay Mishra, Dakota Hamilton, and Mads R Almassalkhi help hybrid energy systems earn money in power markets. A hybrid system mixes controllable generators, flexible loads, and batteries at one site. Such systems can offer frequency regulation, quick adjustments that keep the grid's rhythm steady, but wind and solar uncertainty makes bidding risky.

Mishra and his two co-authors build a two-level framework. The upper level picks capacity bids with a chance-constrained optimisation based on past regulation signals. The lower level splits the called power among the site's resources in real time. They benchmark that split against an offline optimum. The study also tests overbidding, bidding more than a site can surely give, and finds the points where weak performance starts to draw penalties. Uneven mixes of resource sizes are compared too.
arxiv-2510-27002:
Mihir Mahajan, Alfred Nguyen, Franz Srambical, and Stefan Bauer release Jasmine, an open codebase for training world models. A world model learns to predict how an environment changes, which can ease data scarcity in fields like robotics. Training tools for such models are still young, so the team built a fast, reusable base in the JAX framework.

Jasmine scales from one machine to hundreds of accelerators with little code change. Speed work across data loading, training, and checkpointing reproduces a standard CoinRun case about ten times faster than prior open code. Training stays fully reproducible and supports many sharding layouts. Paired with curated datasets, it gives researchers shared ground for fair model comparisons.
arxiv-2510-27202:
Krishan Kumar, P. Danumjaya, Anil Kumar, and Amiya Pani analyze strongly damped wave equations with careful error and decay estimates. Such equations model waves losing energy through two damping channels with separate strengths. The team first proves exponential decay for the continuous problem, with explicit rates tied to model parameters and the principal eigenvalue of a linked elliptic operator across all damping combinations.

For a semi-discrete finite element scheme they derive optimal error estimates that preserve the decay behavior. A fully discrete scheme adding finite differences in time again keeps exponential decay, with constants that stay controlled as either damping vanishes. Extensions cover forcing terms and varying damping, plus spectral approximations. Numerical experiments confirm uniform decay rates and stability predictions.
arxiv-2510-27302:
Kirill A. Chertoganov and Valery I. Shipalov sharpen a classic solver for hard equations in this 2025 paper. The equations are integral equations, where the unknown sits inside an integral sign. The solver is the Newton-Kantorovich method, an update scheme that homes in on the answer step by step. Rounding error can spoil it when the equation reacts sharply to small changes.

Their fix is to do the math with many more digits than usual, using a Python library built for that. Careful high-precision sums over the equation's kernel, its inner rule, steady the process. In their tests, the approach beat standard low-precision runs, above all for strongly curved kernels and stiff cases. That widens where the old method can be trusted in science and engineering work.
arxiv-2511-00102:
Vivan Doshi offers a hybrid approach that finds conservation laws on its own from noisy path data. Conserved amounts are pillars of physics, but finding them in observed data is hard, mainly with noise. A neural usual differential formula first learns a steady model of the system's motion from the paths.

A transformer then creates symbolic candidate invariants based on that learned vector field, and a symbolic-numeric verifier confirms the candidates with a strong numeric check. Scientific machine learning readers get a full find-and-verify loop. Verification is the crucial stage: a guessed invariant is only a conservation law once it passes independent checking.
arxiv-2511-00202:
Jacqueline Mitchell and Yasser Shaaban argue that vibe coding, building software by chatting with a language model, needs formal checking as its reasoning partner. Developers report tech debt, security issues, and code churn from the practice. Their finding: models cannot reconcile piling up human-imposed constraints, and they favor the latest user command over consistency of the code base, while coders miss the conflicts.

Because models respond well to checking-based feedback, formal methods can catch those conflicts and soften the pitfalls. Software engineering readers get a position with a process, not just a complaint. Verified feedback loops could make chat-based coding lasting for real systems.
arxiv-2511-00302:
Andreia Chapouto, Justin Forlano, and Thierry Laurens settle when a family of nonlinear Schrödinger equations on the real line has well-behaved solutions. Well-posedness means solutions exist, are unique, and depend smoothly on the starting data. The family includes the continuum Calogero-Moser models, and earlier work needed fairly smooth starting data, a regularity level above one half.

The authors lower that bar to above one quarter, with no extra Hardy space restriction on the start. A gauge transformation exploits the nonlinearity's structure, and refined bilinear estimates recover derivative losses. A splitting of solutions reveals a nonlinear smoothing effect away from Hardy spaces. They also find a new Lax pair for the equation family, and use it to prove global well-posedness for small starting data.
arxiv-2511-00502:
Peng Zhang, Vitaly Petrov, and Emil Björnson revisit a boundary that terahertz links cannot ignore. Terahertz waves are so short that the radiative near field stretches far, and inside it the usual far-field rules fail. Standard formulas for that boundary, the Fraunhofer distance, assume antenna arrays face each other perfectly. Real deployments suffer misalignment from motion and mechanical flaws.

The authors derive exact expressions, plus simpler approximations, for the near-field boundary when linear or planar arrays are offset from ideal alignment. Simulations confirm the theory and measure how misalignment reshapes the near-field region. For engineers placing terahertz links in realistic, imperfect settings, the results supply guidelines that the ideal formulas could not.
arxiv-2511-00602:
Wai-Chung Kwan, Joshua Ong Jun Leang, Pavlos Vougiouklis, Jeff Pan, Marco Valentino, and Pasquale Minervini let a language model teach itself. Reinforcement learning for reasoning usually needs annotated problems with checkable answers, a leash that can cap the model at human level. Self-play removes the leash but earlier attempts generated only familiar problems, yielding marginal or negative gains on already trained models.

Their reasoner, OpenSIR, alternates one model between teacher and student roles, starting from a single seed problem with no external verifier. Diversity rewards push toward unfamiliar concepts, and difficulty calibration keeps problems learnable. Across seven math benchmarks it improved every model tested, even beating a baseline trained on thousands of annotated examples. Skills learned on self-made math also transferred to general reasoning.
arxiv-2511-00702:
Alberto Di Biase borrows a medical imaging technique and turns it into a paintbrush. Doctors use diffusion tensor imaging and tractography to trace fibrous tissue by following local orientation through the body. Painterly rendering faces the same geometry problem: strokes should follow the forms inside an image, the way an artist's hand does. Di Biase maps one field onto the other, explicitly and in tractography's own language.

A tractography algorithm lays down brush strokes that mimic a painting process. For local direction, the structural tensor of the image replaces the gradient, giving richer orientation information. Portraits and general images demonstrate the method, and the paper discusses the parallels between fiber tracking and stroke placement at length. Code is public, inviting artists and researchers to experiment with the crossover.
arxiv-2511-01102:
Pablo Rocha revisits his own earlier estimates for the Riesz potential, a central operator in harmonic analysis, acting between weighted Hardy spaces whose exponent varies from point to point. Two earlier papers proved the operator is bounded between these spaces under two assumptions on the weight and the exponents.

In this note he re-establishes the same boundedness without the second assumption, a condition comparing the sizes of cubes in the two weighted norms. Dropping it widens the results to more weights, and he reports the new proofs are simpler than the previous ones. Short corrective notes like this matter in analysis, where a theorem's value depends heavily on how few hypotheses it needs.
arxiv-2511-01402:
Massimo Bianchi, Donato Bini, and Giorgio Di Russo examine the W-soliton, a recently found solution in gravitational theory, in its neutral form. They work with both the genuine five-dimensional version and its reduction to four dimensions, comparing what the two share and where they part ways.

Much of the study follows particles moving through this background. The authors reconstruct the scattering angle for massless and massive particles, using exact formulas where possible and expansions they show how to sum up neatly. They then send a test scalar field through the soliton, compute its quasi-normal mode spectrum, and derive a fully analytic result for the radiated energy in a post-Newtonian expansion.
arxiv-2511-01702:
Sadek Al Harbat classifies the elements of affine Coxeter groups of types A, B, and D, infinite symmetry groups that extend the classical finite reflection groups. To classify them he assigns every group element a canonical reduced expression. That is one chosen shortest spelling of the element as a product of simple reflections. It is built using tools including affine length.

The canonical form pays off immediately. It yields a description of what left multiplication by a simple reflection does. It yields a study of each element's right descent set. And it yields a proof that affine length is preserved along the tower of type-A affine Coxeter groups. That preservation implies the corresponding tower of affine Hecke algebras is faithful regardless of the ground ring. Parallel canonical expressions are given for the affine groups of types B and D.
arxiv-2511-01902:
Alexander Bakumenko, Aaron Masino, and Janine Hoelscher offer a pre-clinical guide for health AI. It covers what must be built and checked before a system ever meets patients. Their core is a pair of linked principles. One is user Understandability. The other is clinician Operability. Together they turn explainable-AI ideas, such as contestability and calibration, into concrete product duties and test steps.

The authors ground both principles in known explainability work. They map them to documented clinician needs. They show the fit with new governance rules. That gives researchers, clinicians, and regulators a shared vocabulary. The aim is to ensure AI meets human needs before it reaches the clinic.
arxiv-2511-02002:
Xiangru Jian, Zhengyuan Dong, and M. Tamer Özsu make SPARQL, the query language of the semantic web, usable by people who do not already know it. SPARQL's complex syntax and its demand that users understand intricate data schemas shut out non-experts. Their system, InteracSPARQL, explains each query in natural language so users can see what it asks and fix it.

The explanations are built in two passes: a rule-based method extracts a structured explanation directly from the query's abstract syntax tree, then a language model polishes the wording. Users refine queries through direct feedback, or let the model self-refine, correcting ambiguous or wrong components in real time. On standard benchmarks the system significantly improved query accuracy, explanation clarity, and user satisfaction over baselines, supporting the combination of rules and language models for accessible data interfaces.
arxiv-2511-02602:
Ferhat Özgur Catak, Jungwon Seo, and Umit Cali draw a roadmap for trusting quantum machine learning before it is deployed where it matters. Quantum models promise power against problems that strain classical AI, but today's NISQ devices are noisy and hybrid pipelines open new failure and attack surfaces. The roadmap organises trustworthiness into three pillars: knowing the model's uncertainty, resisting adversarial attack, and preserving privacy.

For each pillar the authors define quantum-specific metrics grounded in quantum information theory, from a variance-based split of predictive uncertainty to trace-distance bounds on robustness and differential privacy for hybrid learning channels. An assessment pipeline, tested on parameterised quantum classifiers running on current hardware, uncovered links between uncertainty and prediction risk. It also found an asymmetry between classical and quantum perturbations under attack, and privacy costs driven by measurement shot noise. Trust, they argue, must be a design objective from the start.
arxiv-2511-02702:
Free boundary problems ask where a region ends when the edge itself is part of the answer. Shiouhe Wang, Fang Shen, Yi Yang, and Xueshang Feng revisit one such problem, the Bernoulli problem, in a 2025 comment paper. An earlier attempt proved that a best shape exists by using an energy-gap cost, but one step of that proof had a gap of its own.

The flawed step tried to bound solutions with the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality, which does not carry the weight placed on it. The authors fix the proof using the Poincare-Friedrichs inequality instead. The repair matters because shape optimization methods lean on that existence result: without it, a search for the best shape might chase a target that is not really there.
arxiv-2511-03202:
Zeqi Ye, Qijie Zhu, Molei Tao, and Minshuo Chen prove a split between copying and creating in diffusion image models. Those models sometimes repeat training pictures instead of making new ones, which cuts creative value and risks privacy. Hands-on fixes exist, yet the theory behind the copying has stayed thin until now.

From a statistics view, the true cleaning rule does not best fit the training loss, and that gap pushes models toward copying. From a size view, copying demands networks that grow with the data set, while the true rule stays compact. Guided by both splits, the team offers a pruning method that trims copying while keeping output quality. The result gives builders a principled lever against memorization.
arxiv-2511-03302:
Xiaoyun Wang and colleagues sketch a next step for mobile radio networks as sixth generation systems take shape. Their plan grows from an older design that prized central, joint, cloud-based, and clean operation. The new version adds shared sensing and shared artificial intelligence to shared communication, and leans toward service-focused design.

Cooperation, in their telling, should run through the whole chain of gathering, sending, and handling information. That spread aims to raise both quality and thrift across varied uses, from dense cities to sensing-heavy sites. The article lays out the architecture and the gains each layer of sharing should bring. It offers network planners a frame for building more aware and flexible radio access.
arxiv-2511-03402:
Dennis Belotserkovskiy and Joe P Chen pin down the second eigenspace of a particle-swapping process on any connected weighted graph. A known theorem says its second eigenvalue matches that of a simple random walk on the same graph. The new work asks which functions actually fill that eigenspace.

Except for one special case, an even four-cycle with equal weights, the whole space lives inside copies of the standard representation. It is spanned by lifts of the random walk's own second eigenspace. A refined induction argument isolates the only summand that could support equality. Results of this kind clarify how fast swapping mixes, a question with echoes in sampling and statistical physics.
arxiv-2511-03802:
Kenneth J Duncan, writing alone, tackles redshift estimation for galaxies in deep James Webb Space Telescope surveys that use only about six filters. Template fitting, the usual tool, can give confident but wrong redshifts for the distant galaxies these pure parallel surveys most want to find.

Duncan tests two machine learning methods, Gaussian processes and nearest neighbours, against template fitting. Simple nearest-neighbour estimates proved more accurate out to high redshift and cut catastrophic outliers by a factor of about two to three. Hybrid estimates that combine both approaches improved reliability further. The added computing cost is small, so the method can raise the value of wide-area survey data.
arxiv-2511-04302:
Nicolas Angelini and Ursula Molter build a two-scale Frostman measure framework linking classical Hausdorff dimension with the intermediate dimensions introduced by Falconer, Fraser, and Kempton. These middle dimensions probe how a set's size behaves between the finest and box-counting scales, and Frostman measures are the standard tool for certifying dimension from below.

A new geometric value is defined for a set. Under mild assumptions, a family of measures on the set meets two decay conditions at once, one matching Hausdorff and one matching intermediate Frostman inequalities. Those two-scale measures then pin down the set's dimension across both regimes in a single construction, joining tools that were used apart before.
arxiv-2511-04902:
Shuvendu Roy leads four authors testing label-free reinforcement learning on weak base models. Unsupervised methods promise better reasoning with no external labels at all. Whether they help small models with little reasoning to start from was untested.

The team sweeps model sizes from half a billion to seven billion parameters. Label-free training leans hard on reasoning the base model already has. For weaker models, scores often fall below the starting baseline instead of rising. Small models also fail to produce long enough reasoning traces to learn from. The title states the moral: reasoning training needs reasoning to build on.
arxiv-2511-05302:
Qianru Meng and co-authors ask when added retrieval hurts code review generation, the task of writing reviewer-style notes on a code change. Pure generation can be vague, while pure retrieval fits new cases poorly, so a blend seems natural.

They frame the blend as in-context learning: past reviews are placed in the prompt as guides. Their RARe framework picks those examples in a set way. Results show more retrieved text is not always better; poor picks can pull the review off point. The lesson guides how much past text a review tool should show.
arxiv-2511-05802:
Bo Xue and co-authors unite two goals for decision systems that rank their objectives in a strict order. In lexicographic bandits, each choice pays off on several objectives, and the learner must serve the top objective first, then the next. Past work chased either low regret over time or quick identification of the best arm.

Two elimination algorithms are proposed. One prunes arms layer by layer in priority order, matching the best single-objective rates. The other reads all objectives each round and shares information across them. Strikingly, it beats the known lower bound for single-objective bandits, showing the bonus that cross-objective sharing brings. Tests confirmed both beat baselines, and the theory ties the two classic goals together.
arxiv-2511-05902:
Tianyu Jiang and co-authors estimate fast-changing radio channels for millimeter-wave MIMO systems, where many antennas send and receive at once. The channel matrix is both low-rank and sparse, facts the team exploits to rebuild it from few observations. Mobility makes the rank jump suddenly, which breaks static methods.

Their two-phase method first completes part of the matrix with a robust rank-one completion routine. A time-series model tracks how rank correlates across moments, adapting the completion as users move. A second phase then recovers the sparse channel with a rank-aware pursuit method at low cost. A tailored measurement design sharpens angle estimates. Simulations showed better accuracy than benchmarks with far less computation and training overhead.
arxiv-2511-06202:
Shahram Najam Syed and co-authors help robot vision-language-action models specialize for one workplace instead of staying general. Broad models like OpenVLA handle many tasks passably but can stumble where one site needs steady high performance. Their method, ExpReS-VLA, adapts a pretrained model on the device itself, quickly and without forgetting earlier skills.

Adaptation stores compact embeddings instead of raw image and action pairs, cutting storage by ninety-seven percent. Similar past experiences are retrieved to enrich each training round, and a new loss learns from failed attempts as well as successes. Scores rose sharply on the LIBERO benchmark, and a real robot hit ninety-eight percent success after adapting in about half a minute.
arxiv-2511-06402:
Lionel Wang and co-authors detect social media posts tied to sugar dating, arrangements that trade intimacy for money or gifts. Such content spreads on mainstream platforms and raises social and regulatory worries. Detection is hard because posters hide behind euphemisms and vague wording, and genuine cases are rare next to ordinary posts.

Their system, SugarTextNet, layers a pretrained transformer with an attention-based cue extractor and a phrase encoder that reads context. A new training loss weights hard, rare cases by their surrounding context to fight the imbalance. On a hand-labeled set of about three thousand Weibo posts, the system beat classical models, deep baselines, and large language models.
arxiv-2511-06502:
Vasileios Aravantinos-Sotiropoulos works in enriched category theory, building exact completions for categories whose arrows carry an order structure. The ambient world is Pos, the partially ordered sets and their maps, and the starting categories are weakly lex. Exact completion freely adds the exactness properties such categories may lack.

A basic construction does the job, and a description in terms of projective objects mirrors the classical unenriched theory. Applied to Eilenberg-Moore algebra categories for monads on Pos, the theory shows every variety of ordered algebras arises as such a completion of a smaller one built from free algebras. That answers a question posed by Kurz and Velebil.
arxiv-2511-06602:
Kasra Jalaldoust and Erfan Zabeh ask what it would take to prove that brain waves cause behavior rather than merely mirror neuron spikes. Neuroscience tracks both single-cell spikes and population waves, and both predict behavior, yet correlation cannot separate cause from echo. The Causal Hierarchy Theorem says observation alone, however vast, can never settle such a question.

Their framework defines epiphenomenality precisely inside structural causal models, as sameness of outcomes under intervention. From Pearl's do-calculus they derive a certificate stating when a variable can be dropped from a model with no causal loss. The goal is reframing: not which signal matters most, but when any signal can be shown to matter at all.
arxiv-2511-07002:
Giuseppe Birardi and Gonçalo Paulo propose a way to interpret the internal circuits of a large language model without hand-labeling thousands of parts. Sparse attribution graphs built from cross-layer transcoders capture much of a model's computation, but even short prompts yield graphs with thousands of nodes. Current automated labels come from corpus activations and are rarely checked by intervening on the model.

Their pipeline, probe prompting, groups features into concept-aligned supernodes using their responses to a small set of concept-targeted prompts, summarized as cross-prompt activation signatures. On Gemma-2-2B with a public transcoder dictionary, across four factual domains and more than forty-five thousand entity-swap actions, every labeled supernode showed the predicted steering behavior. Code, data, and an interactive demo accompany the paper.
arxiv-2511-07102:
Dawei Chen and Guillaume Tahar prove a non-existence theorem in the geometry of meromorphic differentials. Strata of such differentials group surfaces by the prescribed orders of zeros and poles of a differential defined on them. The question is whether these strata, once projectivized, can contain complete subvarieties of positive dimension, which would be entire classes sitting wholly inside the stratum.

The authors construct a globally defined, strictly plurisubharmonic function on the projectivized strata of strictly meromorphic differentials. The existence of such a function rules out positive-dimensional complete subvarieties, giving a proof rooted in flat geometry rather than algebraic methods. Beyond that result, the construction supplies a concrete analytic tool for studying the global geometry of these strata.
arxiv-2511-07202:
Praveen Kumar Donta, Alfreds Lapkovskis, Enzo Mingozzi, and Schahram Dustdar design self-healing for the distributed computing continuum, the layered world running from tiny IoT sensors through edge nodes to high-performance clusters. Failures there are normal, yet AI workloads still need real-time, coordinated reliability. Their work-in-progress agent, PAIR-Agent, applies active inference, a system in which an agent maintains beliefs about its system and acts to keep them consistent.

The agent performs three operations: it builds a causal fault graph from device logs, identifies faults while tracking certainty and uncertainty using Markov blankets and the free energy principle. Then heals problems autonomously by reconfiguring the system. Continuous monitoring keeps services running under diverse failure conditions, and theoretical validations support the system's reliability.
arxiv-2511-07302:
Benjamin Brindle works on q-analogues of multiple zeta values, number patterns that extend classic constants in number theory. In 2015 Bachmann conjectured that the formal version of these values is spanned by one very specific set. Brindle tests that claim on a controlled part of the space.

For words meeting conditions on zeros and depth, the conjecture is proved true. The proof uses linear relations among the formal values that follow from duality, a symmetry linking different expressions. Brindle also lays out an explicit route toward the full conjecture. Specialists get both a partial theorem and a concrete plan for finishing the job.
arxiv-2511-07502:
Galina Weinstein writes an essay linking two famous divides in how knowledge works. Matrix mechanics builds answers step by step, while wave mechanics lets one recognize a solution as a whole. Though the two quantum theories agree formally, Weinstein reads them as different styles of knowing.

That contrast mirrors the P versus NP question, which separates finding solutions efficiently from checking them efficiently. Weinstein treats the parallel as philosophy, not as a claimed proof of either side. The essay traces the math history behind both divides. Readers interested in foundations get a lens connecting physics, computation, and cognition without overstating what analogy can show.
arxiv-2511-07902:
Mohammad Ali Afshar and Javad Sadeghi track how orbits precess near charged black holes pushed toward extremality. The periapsis shift, the slow rotation of an orbit closest approach, encodes spacetime shape. Stable photon spheres outside the horizon add an Aschenbach-like twist previously spotted in rotating cases.

Across representative charged models, the shift stays well defined as extremality nears and keeps mirroring geometry changes. Solutions admitting stable photon spheres show the interplay most sharply. Precession is observable in principle through stars and pulsars near real black holes, so clean theory for extreme cases prepares interpretation of future measurements.
arxiv-2511-08002:
Wejdan Beida and colleagues implement a DFT plus U plus V method inside the all electron FLAPW code FLEUR. Standard density functional theory struggles with localized electrons, so onsite corrections help, yet interactions between neighboring sites also matter in many solids. Adding an intersite term promises better treatment of charge order, charge transfer, and related effects.

The correction values come from first principles through a constrained random phase method, using two different basis choices. Tests cover graphene, silicon, germanium, and nickel oxide. Results improve selected properties across these bonding types and agree better with experiments, earlier calculations, and the authors own many body reference results.
arxiv-2511-08102:
Shohei Okawa and Yuji Omura use leptonic meson decays to set new bounds on neutrino portal dark matter. In this model a neutral fermion and a scalar couple mainly to neutrinos, opening hidden interactions. Ordinary two body meson decays into a charged lepton and an antineutrino can reveal those particles in two distinct ways.

A new three body decay lets the antineutrino split into the hidden pair, escaping the usual helicity suppression. Loop corrections also shift the decay width up or down without changing the lepton spectrum. Comparing modified branching ratios with pion and kaon data beats existing limits across much of the parameter space.
arxiv-2511-08202:
Jiyuan Lyu gives an exact mean field solution for the Mesa Boltzmann wealth model, a standard agent based example of money exchange. The paper replaces simulation with exact analysis for a model that is usually studied only on a computer. Instead of local trades, the mean field version uses global random matching with synchronous updates.

A master equation for the wealth distribution, solved through probability generating functions, yields the steady state in closed form. Variance, the Gini inequality coefficient, and tail behavior follow directly from that solution. Simulations of the matching agent model agree closely with the formulas, giving an analytical benchmark for checking related simulations.
arxiv-2511-08302:
Arshyn Altybay and Michael Ruzhansky attack the inverse problem of recovering a time dependent potential coefficient inside a one dimensional diffusion equation. Only edge data plus a nonlocal integral measure, reflecting spatial averages, can be used to spot the unknown coefficient. The authors first prove the forward problem is well posed and derive an estimate giving uniqueness and stable dependence on data for the inverse problem.

Three numeric routes are then tested: an integration based scheme, a Newton Raphson iterative solver, and a physics informed neural network. Tests with exact and noisy data show how exact, robust, and lean each method is. The comparison guides practitioners choosing a solver for similar coefficient recovery tasks.
arxiv-2511-08502:
Ruya Karagulle, Cristian-Ioan Vasile, and Necmiye Ozay learn autonomous system behavior from human preferences while keeping formal safety guarantees. Feedback arrives as comparisons, rankings, or demonstrations, and many methods adapt behavior without proving the result stays safe in critical domains. Their approach expresses preferences in weighted signal temporal logic, a language for timed requirements with adjustable importance across goals.

A naive setup creates multi linear constraints in the weights to learn. Structural pruning and a log transform shrink the problem and recast it as a mixed integer linear program, preserving the safety guarantees. Experiments on robotic navigation and real Formula 1 data show the method captures nuanced preferences and complex task objectives.
arxiv-2511-08602:
Tatsuru Kikuchi builds a single framework that joins two ways financial crises spread: across bank networks and across space. The test case is the 2008 crisis, using bilateral exposure data for one hundred fifty-six institutions in twenty-eight countries from 2007 to 2023.

Three findings stand out. First, consolidation backfired: bank counts fell by nearly half while a network fragility measure more than tripled, so tighter links mattered more than fewer banks. Second, contagion crossed the globe with almost no distance decay, unlike technology diffusion, which fades within tens of kilometers. Third, standard difference-in-differences estimates overstate crisis damage by almost three quarters when network structure is ignored. Kikuchi argues risk policy must model both geography and network shape together.
arxiv-2511-08702:
David Sanchez Jr. and three co-authors argue that fair and private machine learning cannot be fully automated, because fairness is a human judgment about context. Privacy tools can quietly worsen group disparities, and fairness fixes often need the very sensitive data that privacy rules lock away.

Their framework, FAIRPLAI, puts people inside the loop in three ways. It draws privacy-fairness frontiers so trade-offs among accuracy, privacy, and group outcomes stay visible. It lets stakeholders pick fairness criteria and operating points interactively. And it adds a differentially private auditing loop where reviewers inspect explanations and edge cases without exposing individual records. On benchmark datasets the approach keeps strong privacy while cutting fairness gaps versus automated baselines.
arxiv-2511-09002:
Hongru Zhao, Jinwen Fu, and Tuan Pham analyze a feedback loop now built into generative AI: models retrained round after round on a mix of real data and their own earlier outputs. Earlier work studied such self-consuming models with uniform human curation; here the human curators have heterogeneous preferences, generalizing that model.

The long-run behavior of the retraining dynamics is worked out across four regimes, with tools that include nonlinear Perron-Frobenius theory. The analysis improves on the earlier results and proves convergence in settings where the standard Banach contraction argument fails outright. Stability and instability results for the dynamics round out the picture. The stakes are practical: as synthetic data floods training pipelines, knowing when the loop settles and when it spirals decides how much curation the process needs.
arxiv-2511-09202:
Itshak Lapidot, Yann Sepulcre, and Tom Trigano present a stochastic version of mean-shift clustering, a classic way to group data points around density peaks. In their version, a randomly chosen sequence of points moves by partial gradient ascent steps. Only some points move at each step, unlike the standard algorithm's full updates.

The authors prove convergence results for the stochastic scheme. On synthetic two-dimensional data from Gaussian mixtures, it beats standard mean-shift in most comparisons against state-of-the-art methods. They also test it on a practical task, clustering speakers from audio. The stochastic twist keeps the method's spirit while improving its performance in these trials.
arxiv-2511-09502:
Jerrin Bright, Yuhao Chen, and John S. Zelek estimate three-dimensional human poses from video using a diffusion model that imagines motion. Most pose systems read each frame's geometry alone, so ambiguous movements confuse them and sequences jitter. Humans instead anticipate how a motion unfolds, and the authors borrow that strategy.

DreamPose3D conditions its denoising on action prompts extracted from the two-dimensional pose sequence, capturing intent. A representation encoder folds kinematic joint relationships into the attention mechanism. A hallucinative decoder, used in training, predicts coherent future pose sequences to resolve ambiguity. The system reports state-of-the-art results on the Human3.6M and MPI-INF-3DHP benchmarks, and stays strong on noisy broadcast baseball footage.
arxiv-2511-09702:
Katie Matton and nine co-authors build the first automatic method for grading phonotrauma severity from images of the vocal folds. Phonotrauma is tissue damage from the forces of voicing, and its severity, running mild to severe, guides treatment choices. Today grading rests on clinician judgment, which is costly and varies in reliability between experts.

Because severity labels are ordered, the authors adopt ordinal regression rather than plain classification. Their novelty is a loss modification that trains on soft labels. Those labels encode the whole distribution of annotator ratings, embracing uncertainty instead of hiding it. The method approaches medical experts' predictive performance while producing well-calibrated uncertainty estimates, they report. Automated grading could enable large-scale phonotrauma studies.
arxiv-2511-09802:
Parinaz Binandeh Dehaghani, Danilo Pena, and A. Pedro Aguiar study how to classify environmental sounds with small, cheap neural networks. The work compares ways of shrinking the data, including a sparse salient region pooling method and two variants of it, against the standard principal component approach. Experiments run on the ESC-50 dataset of environmental recordings.

The Top-K variant of sparse pooling reached accuracy up to about eighty-one percent, well above the plain network baseline near sixty-seven percent. Principal component reduction performed poorly by comparison, near thirty-eight percent. The authors conclude that a carefully tuned sparse pooling strategy gives a robust and efficient option for sound classification when computing resources are tight.
arxiv-2511-10202:
Athanasios L. Konstantinidis, Charis Papadopoulos, and Georgios Velissaris study Hedge Cluster Deletion, a grouped version of the classic cluster deletion problem. In a hedge graph, edges come partitioned into hedges, and the task is to remove the fewest hedges so the remaining graph splits into disjoint cliques. Deleting whole groups at once models settings where edges fail or are removed together.

They show the problem is NP-complete, pin down polynomial cases tied to disjoint three-vertex paths, and prove a strong inapproximability result. The problem is fixed-parameter tractable in the solution size but admits no polynomial kernel under standard assumptions. Positive results include a constant-factor approximation when each triangle is covered by at most two hedges, and a polynomial algorithm when the hedge intersection graph is acyclic.
arxiv-2511-10302:
Karim Nasreddine, Christo Kurisummoottil Thomas, and Walid Saad give semantic communication systems a shared memory, so old concepts can be reused instead of retransmitted. Learned semantic codecs usually freeze their representations, wasting bandwidth when content drifts gradually. Their framework stores semantic concepts in modern Hopfield networks held by both transmitter and receiver, and retrieves matches through soft attention.

Soft retrieval adjusts stored prototype weights smoothly as data evolves, avoiding the constant memory updates that hard quantization schemes suffer. The team optimizes encoder, decoder, and retrieval jointly for a reasoning capacity metric combining reuse rate and compression, and proves a rate-distortion-reuse trade-off. Video simulations saved about fourteen percent of bits on average, and up to seventy percent under gradual change.
arxiv-2511-10502:
Vincenzo Carletti and four co-authors examine a privacy risk in federated learning, a method that trains models across many devices without moving private data to a central server. Attackers who control the server can tamper with the shared model so that the updates clients send back reveal their local data, a strategy called an active gradient inversion attack.

Recent attacks claim to be too stealthy for clients to notice. Carletti's team gives the first broad check of those claims, studying four state-of-the-art attacks and proposing lightweight client-side detectors. Their detectors look for statistically improbable weight patterns and odd loss and gradient behavior. Across many test settings, the detectors caught the attacks reliably, without requiring any change to the training protocol.
arxiv-2511-10602:
Ioana A. Stelea leads a 23-author team reporting the first localized detections of the cold neutral medium in IC10, a small starburst galaxy with only about a quarter of the Sun's metal content. Because conditions there resemble the early universe, its gas offers a window into how interstellar material heated and cooled long ago.

Using the Local Group L-band Survey's sharp radio resolution, the team searched for hydrogen absorption against nine background sources and found it along three sightlines inside the galaxy. The cold gas has spin temperatures of roughly 30 to 55 kelvin and makes up about a fifth to a third of the atomic gas along those paths. Molecular emission appears at the same velocities, showing the cold atomic and molecular gas are well mixed and more tightly coupled than in the Milky Way.
arxiv-2511-10802:
Renan da Silva Souza, Youjiang Xu, and Walter Hofstetter simulate a gas of ultracold fermions living in a square optical lattice and coupled to an optical cavity. In the right regime the system's steady state follows an extended Hubbard model in which the cavity mediates long-range interactions between the atoms.

Using real-space dynamical mean-field theory, they focus on the paramagnetic phases at quarter and half filling. At quarter filling, warming the system can paradoxically drive it from a uniform Fermi liquid into an ordered density wave, because the ordered phase carries more entropy. At half filling they map the competition among Fermi liquid, Mott insulator, and density wave phases, finding a coexistence region and settling which phase wins by comparing energies.
arxiv-2511-11302:
Junqing Cai, Guanghui Wang, and their colleagues pin down the exact degree threshold that forces an antidirected Hamilton cycle in an oriented graph. An antidirected cycle visits every vertex once while never letting two consecutive edges point the same way along the cycle. Degree conditions of Ore type, which sum out-degree and in-degree over non-adjacent pairs, are classic tools for forcing such spanning cycles.

Woodall's classic result forced a directed spanning cycle under a strong degree sum, and a recent result covered oriented graphs at a lower bound. The authors prove the sharp threshold for the antidirected case in large oriented graphs and show the bound cannot be improved.
arxiv-2511-11702:
Lian He and five co-authors introduce TASA, a framework that finds where an embodied agent can act in a three-dimensional scene, given a plain-language instruction. Knowing that a handle affords pulling, in the right place, is what separates a robot that watches from one that helps.

Earlier methods handled single objects or simply lifted flat image predictions into 3D, wasting the geometry inside point clouds and paying high computing costs. TASA works coarse to fine, pairing task-aware two-dimensional detection with geometric refinement in 3D. The combination aims at scene-level affordance segmentation that is both semantically aware and spatially precise enough for real interaction.
arxiv-2511-12102:
Abhisha Garg and five co-authors design a method to estimate terahertz wireless channels for many users at once. Terahertz links can carry huge data rates. Their channels are wide in both space and frequency. They suffer losses from absorption and reflection. They must also be read with low-grade converters to save power.

The team models those effects, then linearizes the quantized signals and applies a Bayesian group-sparse method that learns the channel across subcarriers at once. They also derive a bound on the estimation error to judge performance. Simulations show gains over other sparse methods in error measures for these dual-wideband systems.
arxiv-2511-12502:
Yu Liang and six co-authors propose an online training algorithm for binary spiking neural networks, which promise efficiency on resource-limited hardware. Training such networks usually stores latent weights and processes many time steps, so memory cost is high. That burden blocks training on the small devices where the networks are meant to run.

Their algorithm, BSO, updates weights directly through flip signals raised when the product of momentum and weight passes a threshold, with no latent weights kept. A temporal variant uses gradient information across time steps to adapt that threshold. Theory gives convergence guarantees and regret bounds for both versions, and experiments show stronger optimization than existing training methods.
arxiv-2511-12602:
Ria Shekhawat and four co-authors propose a detector for face morphing attacks. In such an attack a synthetic image blends biometric features from several people. It can fool recognition systems at borders and in security checks. Their approach works from a single image, with no reference photo needed. A teacher-student design carries the method.

A convolutional teacher refines a vision transformer student through knowledge distillation. Low-rank adaptation tunes the student cheaply, cutting computing cost while keeping detection accuracy. Experiments use a morphing dataset built from three public face sets and ten morphing algorithms, and compare against six leading single-image detectors. The authors report better detection performance and efficiency than those baselines.
arxiv-2511-12702:
Safaeid Hossain Arib and four co-authors address counting objects that are partly hidden. Counters for visible objects fail under occlusion, because their image features describe the covering surface instead of the target behind it. Their framework, CountOCC, rebuilds the missing features. It combines spatial context from visible fragments with meaning-based cues from text and image embeddings, filling in feature maps at hidden locations across several scales of the image pyramid.

A second objective keeps attention maps consistent between hidden and unobstructed views of the same scene. To test the idea, the team built occlusion versions of two counting benchmarks. CountOCC cut counting error sharply on both, and also set a new best result on a real-world capture dataset. The gains were large, around half the prior error on one benchmark. The work targets open-world counting, where objects of any kind may be blocked from view.
arxiv-2511-12802:
John M. Mango and Ronald Katende study when one small linear sketch can preserve the extreme singular values of every low-rank matrix. Sketches compress matrices for fast computation, but classical results do not control the extreme singular values. The authors state a conjecture: a sketch with only modestly more rows than the rank should suffice for that stronger preservation task.

On the constructive side, they pair a sparse sketch with a balancing map and show the sketched singular values collapse to a common scale when the input is well conditioned and incoherent. On the negative side, they prove sharper accuracy demands force much larger sketches. Experiments on structured matrix families show balancing improves conditioning and speeds iterative solvers, while coherent or nearly rank-deficient inputs fail as predicted. The paper mixes a conjecture, partial progress, and evidence about its limits.
arxiv-2511-12902:
Jose Pinedo Soto's doctoral thesis, completed at the University of Alberta under Valeri P. Frolov, builds black hole models without singularities. General relativity predicts points of infinite curvature inside black holes like the Schwarzschild and Kerr solutions, where the theory stops making sense. The thesis studies modified gravity theories that keep the event horizon but remove the singularity.

Throughout, the models are held to physical standards: each must reduce to ordinary general relativity in the right limits and keep its curvature quantities well behaved. The collected results argue that regular black holes are viable within modified gravity. Offering a semiclassical picture of black holes that does not need a full quantum theory of gravity to erase the singularity. The thesis runs to one hundred seventy-three pages and speaks to relativists weighing how much of classical black hole theory can survive.
arxiv-2511-13302:
Paul Bratch and 4 co-authors build a formal theory of cyclically ordered graphs, objects that sit between plain graphs and graphs drawn on surfaces. In such a graph, the edges at each vertex carry a cyclic order. The objects appear in topological graph theory, knot theory, and mathematical biology.

The authors set out several ways to present these graphs and show how each view helps build invariants, meaning numbers or polynomials that do not change under allowed moves. They adapt the matching, transition, and Yamada polynomials to this setting. The result gives workers in several fields a shared language and a tested set of tools.
arxiv-2511-13602:
Jungwoo Ho, Sangun Park, and Soyeong Oh propose a training-free estimator for multivariate joint entropy based on partitioned sample spacing. Entropy gauges uncertainty, and spacing methods infer it from gaps between sorted samples. Their method extends the one-dimensional idea by cutting space into local cells and pooling within-cell gap statistics.

Under mild conditions the estimator is strongly consistent, meaning it settles on the true value as data grow. Benchmarks across varied distributions beat nearest-neighbor estimators and rivaled recent flow-based methods, all without training or a fitted density model. It scaled well into moderately high dimensions and stayed robust when data were correlated or skewed, suiting information-theoretic machine learning tasks.
arxiv-2511-13702:
Luyao Niu and Nuoxian Huang present ST-ProC, a semi-supervised framework that identifies travel modes from GPS traces when labels are scarce. Naming whether a trip used walking, cycling, or transit powers urban planning, yet hand labeling traces is costly. Standard semi-supervised methods suffer confirmation bias here, teaching themselves their own early mistakes, and ignore the shape of the data.

ST-ProC joins a graph-prototypical core, which anchors classes and rejects noisy pseudo-labels by a margin rule, with contrastive and teacher-student support losses. Graph smoothing exploits the data manifold to steady learning. In sparse-label tests it beat every baseline by a wide margin, gaining over twenty percent against strong methods such as FixMatch.
arxiv-2511-13802:
Filippo Cenacchi and 3 co-authors screen for dementia passively from short talking-head videos by reading tiny facial movements over time. Most tools lean on speech or scripted interviews, which ties them to clinics and to language. Their method needs no words at all: blink patterns, small mouth and jaw motion, gaze shifts, and subtle head adjustments carry the signal.

Stabilized facial streams are summarized per short window by how motion is shared across channels, which makes each channel's role transparent. A new dataset of three hundred public videos, half self-reported dementia and half controls, benchmarks the approach. Shallow classifiers scored strongly on the standard ranking measures, with gaze instability and mouth dynamics the most telling cues.
arxiv-2511-13902:
Sara Jensen and Mark L. Lewis classify certain finite groups using the degrees of their characters, which are numbers tied to a group's representations. For a group whose largest character degree is d, the group order can be written using a gap value e. Earlier work bounded the group order when e exceeds one, and the extreme case is where the order reaches a specific quartic bound in e.

The authors settle that extreme case when e is a prime, and also when e equals four, nine, or twenty-five. Along the way they uncover a new nonsolvable Camina pair, a special configuration of conjugacy classes. The result narrows exactly which groups can attain the maximal character degree bound.
arxiv-2511-14002:
Chengpeng Li, Farnaz Behrang, August Shi, and one co-author present FlakyGuard, a tool that automatically repairs flaky software tests at industry scale. Flaky tests pass or fail unpredictably and waste developer time. Language models can fix them, but earlier tools starved the model of needed code or flooded it with irrelevant code.

FlakyGuard treats the codebase as a graph and explores it selectively to gather only the most relevant context. On real flaky tests from industrial repositories, it repaired nearly half of the reproducible cases, and developers accepted about half of its fixes. It beat prior methods by at least twenty-two percent in repair success, and every surveyed developer found its root-cause explanations useful.
arxiv-2511-14402:
Nicola Gambino, Richard Garner, and Christina Vasilakopoulou give one common account of several tensor products in category theory. Such products describe how two structured systems combine. Past work treated enriched categories, operads, and related structures as separate cases. Each case had its own definitions and proofs.

The three authors show that all these products come from one construction for double categories of monads. They then extend the product to bimodules, which link such structures. As a main build they form a double category for symmetric multicategories with a matching monoidal structure. The unified view should make future transfers between fields much simpler.
arxiv-2511-14702:
Farheen Ramzan, Yusuf Kiberu, and seven co-authors present a method for outlining heart muscle scars in enhanced MRI scans. Scar maps help doctors judge how much heart tissue is still alive, but uneven contrast and image flaws make the maps hard to draw. Heart tracing signals, or ECGs, offer extra clues, since faulty conduction often points to scarred regions.

Their framework blends ECG information with a standard atlas of heart segments to keep results true to the body. A fusion step weighs the two sources by the time gap between the tests, since they are not taken together. On clinical data the method beat prior approaches by a wide margin.
arxiv-2511-15002:
Fatemeh Lotfi, Hossein Rajoli, and Fatemeh Afghah improve resource management for open radio access networks, the modular design behind next-generation mobile service. A controller layer is meant to shift spectrum and computing resources as demand moves, and reinforcement learning agents are a popular way to run it. Those agents, though, often fail to generalize when conditions change.

The authors strengthen a leading actor-critic method with sharpness-aware training, applied through several cooperating agents. The extra regularization is switched on selectively, driven by how much each agent's learning signal fluctuates, so only agents facing complex conditions pay its cost. The targeted design aims at steadier performance with less wasted training effort.
arxiv-2511-15202:
Yinsheng Wang and three co-authors present SOLID, an approach that synergizes mathematical optimization with large language models for choice making. Optimizers excel at structured constraints, while language models add contextual judgment. SOLID lets the two agents collaborate iteratively through dual prices and deviation penalties. That exchange raises choice quality while keeping modules split and data private.

Under convexity assumptions the approach retains convergence guarantees. Those guarantees also inform prompt design for the language model agent. A stock mix case uses historical prices and financial news as inputs. Results show convergence across scenarios and higher annualized returns than an optimizer only baseline. The case validates the claimed synergy in a concrete financial setting.
arxiv-2511-15302:
Radek Machulka, Václav Michálek, and two co-authors calibrate cameras that count single photons using a glow-in-the-dark style light source. Knowing a camera's quantum efficiency, the share of incoming photons it actually registers, is basic to trusting its measurements. The gold standard uses pairs of photons born together, but that setup is demanding.

The team tests radioluminescent emitters, materials that glow steadily from internal radioactivity, as a simpler calibration light. They compare the glow-based method against the correlated-pair gold standard. They also propose using the emitters to transfer an absolute calibration from a reference camera to others. A cheap, stable transfer standard would ease precision photon counting in optics labs.
arxiv-2511-15602:
Midhuna V Ajith, Peter J Cameron, Mainak Ghosh, and Aparna Lakshmanan S build graphs whose points are the elements of a finite group. In the endomorphism graph, an arrow runs from one element to another when some structure-preserving map of the group to itself sends the first to the second. Dropping the arrows gives a simpler undirected version, and using only reversible maps gives the automorphism graph.

The authors study basic graph properties such as size, planarity, and shortest cycle length. They determine for which kinds of groups these graphs are complete, split into pieces, trees, or two-sided, and they compute the graphs for some special groups. Closing examples show the behavior is not always simple.
arxiv-2511-15802:
C. Weeks, P. Strange, P. Drmota, and J. Quintanilla study quantum advantage in a one-step graph domination game played on cycle graphs. In a domination game, players place pieces so every vertex is covered by a chosen vertex or its neighbor, and quantum strategies can use superposition to coordinate choices. Prior work found upper bounds for small graphs, leaving open how far the advantage extends.

The authors give explicit strategies that reach those bounds for small cycles and generalize them to larger cycles. They test the ideas three ways: numerically, analytically, and on noisy intermediate-scale quantum processors available today. The hardware runs realized the predicted quantum advantages with high accuracy, confirming the theory in practice.
arxiv-2511-16202:
Pei Yang, Ke Zhang, and six co-authors present a collaborative reward model for reinforcement learning from human feedback. A single black-box reward model must balance clashing preference dimensions, such as factuality, helpfulness, and safety. It also cannot explain its scores.
