Kishan Kumar Ganguly and Tim Menzies steer bug hunting in JavaScript engines away from sheer coverage. Fuzzers feed endless random inputs to find crashes, but chasing new code paths wastes effort on dull inputs and can skip the risky ones. Past fixes leaned on hand made rules that age fast.

Learning from old V8 engine bugs, the team had a language model propose telling traits of risky inputs, then kept 41 of the best. A trained scorer with over 85 percent precision and under 1 percent false alarms flags inputs worth deep testing. A quarter of the traits did most of the work. The shift from coverage to causes could speed up finding real flaws.
arxiv-2512-18202:
Mingyang Sun, Feng Hong, and Weinan Zhang argue that today's AI agents are static and reactive, frozen in narrow scenarios set by hand. Their 2025 paper proposes a third layer above perception and deliberation, called System 3. It watches over the agent's narrative identity and long term adaptation. The design turns psychological constructs such as metacognition, theory of mind, intrinsic motivation, and episodic memory into concrete computing modules.

The ideas come together in Sophia, a wrapper that adds a continuous self improvement loop to any large language model agent. Four mechanisms drive it: process supervised thought search, narrative memory, user and self modeling, and a hybrid reward system. A compact prototype anchors the mostly conceptual discussion. In tests, Sophia cut reasoning steps for recurring operations by 80%. Its persistence also raised success on high complexity tasks by 40%. The authors offer the design as a practical path toward artificial life.
arxiv-2512-18302:
Michał Marcinkowski and Piotr Mizerka sharpen a classic random walk for picking elements of a finite group. The product replacement method stirs a set of group generators by swapping in products, and software uses it to sample group members. Their variant adds an accumulator that collects single elements as output, not just fresh generator sets.

They prove the output turns near uniform after a set number of steps. That count grows like the square of the generator count times the log of the group size. It is a faster mixing than past bounds gave. Spectral gap tools and computer aided checks carry the proof. Random group sampling underlies tests in algebra software, so faster mixing means quicker, fairer picks.
arxiv-2512-18402:
David Favero, Daniel Kaplan, and Tyler L. Kelly wrote this math paper, posted to arXiv in December 2025. It belongs to algebraic geometry, the study of shapes defined by equations. The authors define Kuznetsov and anti-Kuznetsov categories for gauged linear sigma models. These models, borrowed from physics, describe certain geometric spaces.

They show that for complete intersections of ample divisors in smooth toric varieties, the Kuznetsov category sits apart from an exceptional collection. They also prove that such spaces built from at least two divisors act as Fano visitors. The derived category of the Fano host then matches an anti-Kuznetsov category of the model. Results like these help map how related geometric spaces fit together.
arxiv-2512-18702:
Veronika E. Hubeny and Massimiliano Rota build graphs that reproduce a given pattern of entropies. In holographic physics, entropy vectors record how information is shared among subsystems, and graph models help test which patterns are possible. Their paper, posted to arXiv in December 2025, gives an efficient algorithm that constructs a simple tree graph realizing any entropy vector meeting a chordality condition.

They also sharpen the tools of the correlation hypergraph, especially how subsystems merge under coarse-graining and split under fine-graining. With those tools they take first steps toward general tree graph models, not just simple ones. They also work toward spotting entropy vectors that no graph can realize, without leaning on known holographic entropy inequalities. The results serve researchers mapping the boundary between quantum information and gravity.
arxiv-2512-19102:
Hironobu Nakata and a long list of co-authors describe how the Simons Observatory checks the angle of its light detectors. The observatory's small telescopes hunt faint B-mode patterns in the cosmic microwave background. A small error in detector angle leaks the stronger E-mode signal into the B-mode channel and can fake a discovery.

Their calibrator is a sparse wire grid that sends a rotatable polarized signal across the telescope's focal plane, and it runs by remote control in Chile's Atacama desert. A full analysis pipeline turns the signal into per-detector angles. First data at two frequency bands match the design, with tight statistical errors.
arxiv-2512-19502:
Andrii Natochii and co-authors lay out the baseline collimation system for the electron storage ring of the Electron-Ion Collider at Brookhaven. A high-current ring with superconducting final-focus magnets cannot let stray halo particles wander. They bring heat, radiation, and detector background, and can damage hardware. The new system is built to catch them in one safe place.

The insertion gathers losses from beam-gas hits and Touschek scattering into one controlled place. It cuts losses near the detectors by orders of magnitude. Multi-turn tracking shows the beam still fits the machine well and lives as long as before. The apertures can also be retuned for future lattice layouts. Crab cavities, solenoid fields, vacuum work, and material choices remain on the work list for the next round of design.
arxiv-2512-19702:
Yufei Zhao leads an eight-author team with a wireless design that hides one channel in another. Two streams run at the same time. One is a normal digital stream built from multi-mode vortex waves. The other is written into the shape of the wavefront itself. A programmable metasurface does that shaping. The two streams are kept apart on purpose, so they need no joint design.

Each vortex mode carries its own symbols. The surface focuses each mode onto its own spot. So the spatial pattern of the field codes extra data on its own. For safety, scrambled symbols ride the digital stream. The key to unscrambling them rides the spatial stream. The team built a working prototype and tested it in real air. It sent data that stayed both sound and secret.
arxiv-2512-19802:
Cyril Closset and six co-authors build new line defects in three-dimensional gauge theories. The bulk theories are quiver gauge theories. Their Higgs branches are complete flag manifolds. Those are spaces of nested sets of subspaces. The defects keep half of the supersymmetry. Each is built as a small quantum system of its own, coupled to the bulk.

Shrink the theory on a circle, and each defect lands on a Schubert variety in the flag space. The defect's presence provably pins the field space to that variety. In worked cases, a key index of the defect gives back a known polynomial. It is the Chern character of the Schubert sheaf, in quantum Grothendieck form. The build sharpens a known link between gauge models and quantum K-theory.
arxiv-2512-20002:
Jiacheng You and nine co-authors' submission on time-series forecasting stands withdrawn. The record gives the reason. It cites internal review and compliance considerations. The withdrawn text proposed LoFT-LLM. That was a forecasting pipeline for data-scarce, noisy fields like finance and energy. Its core idea was that low-frequency trends deserve apart treatment from high-frequency noise.

The design drew stable trends from local spectral patches. A residual learner then modeled the fast swings that were left. A fine-tuned language model refined the outputs last. It used extra context sent through structured prompts. Tests on finance and energy data were said to beat strong baselines. That held in both full-data and few-shot regimes. Since the authors withdrew the submission, those claims should be read as unvetted.
arxiv-2512-20302:
Arka Chakraborty, Franz Müller, Thomas Kämpfe, and Shubham Sahay build an encoder for hyperdimensional computing from a single ferroelectric transistor. Hyperdimensional computing turns data into very long vectors and classifies by similarity search. For hard data sets, the encoder, not the search, dominates energy and delay costs.

The team implements XOR and three-input majority gates directly in memory using one FDSOI ferroelectric FET each. These gates power the N-gram encoders that hyperdimensional systems rely on. Plugged into a spam-filtering accelerator, the design beats earlier non-volatile memory implementations on area and energy efficiency. It also reaches a high classification accuracy on the SMS Spam Collection dataset, showing the gates work in a full pipeline.
arxiv-2512-20402:
Niccolò Scatena, Pericle Perazzo, and Giovanni Nardini built iblock, a Bitcoin simulator written in C++ for the OMNeT++ approach. Most existing blockchain simulators use high-level languages, which limits their speed and scale. A native library promises detailed, large simulations that still finish in reasonable time.

Head-to-head tests against a leading simulator show iblock is more efficient at the same level of detail. The library also plugs into other OMNeT++ tools, opening the door to richer network modelling. Validation runs cover normal Bitcoin operation and the selfish mining attack, where a miner withholds blocks for advantage. In both scenarios the simulated behaviour matches theoretical expectations, supporting iblock as a research platform.
arxiv-2512-20502:
Joseph E Bonavia measures how the recipe changes gelatin, the stand-in material for soft biological tissue. Gelatin samples mimic flesh in experiments on events such as traumatic brain injury, but their stiffness depends on the water-to-powder ratio. Without a reliable map from recipe to properties, experimenters cannot design samples on purpose.

Bonavia compressed samples spanning ratios from two-to-one to twenty-to-one water to powder on a texture analyzer. Instantaneous stiffness fell steeply across that range, following a power law from hundreds of kilopascals down to a few. The dominant relaxation timescale instead followed a sigmoid curve, growing from about thirty seconds to over ten minutes. The fitted relationships let researchers dial in gelatin properties in advance.
arxiv-2512-21602:
Yusuf Brima and Marcellin Atemkeng test how well machine learning models handle imbalanced clinical data from emergency and intensive care settings. In such data, the rare outcomes clinicians most need to predict are swamped by common ones, so models drift toward the majority class and miss critical cases.

They evaluate six model families, from decision trees and XGBoost to neural TabNet and the tabular foundation models TabICL and TabPFN, on the MIMIC-IV-ED and eICU databases across seven prediction tasks. On the emergency department data, the foundation models ranked best on macro F1 score, with XGBoost close behind. On the intensive care data, XGBoost won consistently. TabNet degraded most as imbalance grew and cost the most to run. Tree-based methods scaled best with dataset size, while foundation models offered cheap adaptation to new tasks. No family dominates everywhere, the authors conclude, but foundation models are closing the gap.
arxiv-2512-21902:
Sachin Pawar, Girish Keshav Palshikar, and their co-authors build systems that read a legal case description and predict which statutes apply, with explanations a lawyer could trust. Statute prediction supports assistants and question-answering tools, but predictions are hard to accept in a profession built on reasons.

They propose two techniques. The first, AoS, trains a model that attends over the sentences of the case description; the sentences it highlights double as the explanation. The second, LLMPrompt, asks a large language model in zero-shot fashion, with chain-of-thought prompting, to predict a statute and explain its relevance. The authors compare both against strong baselines on two datasets. Explanation quality is judged two ways: automatically, through counterfactual tests, and by evaluators. The comparison maps a trade-off between a compact, trainable model with built-in explanations and a prompted model that needs no training data.
arxiv-2512-22202:
Muhammad Usman and Sung-Min Gho speed up a brain scan used to spot Parkinson's disease. Susceptibility Map Weighted Imaging highlights a structure whose fading is a disease marker, but full-resolution scans take a long time. Their method reconstructs high-quality images from reduced measurement data using a neural network built on the Swin Transformer that works with complex-valued data.

The network performs super-resolution reconstruction of multi-echo MRI data straight from low-resolution frequency-space inputs. In tests, it rebuilt images from 256-by-256 data with a structural similarity index above 0.91 while keeping the features doctors rely on. Shorter scans with preserved diagnostic detail could make this imaging more practical in clinics and support faster neuroimaging workflows.
arxiv-2512-22302:
Jennifer Sawyer and Julian Allagan mine five years of crash records from an 8.4-mile stretch of US 158 in Currituck County, North Carolina. Extending Sawyer's earlier hotspot and chi-square work, the study layers on several further techniques. These include kernel density estimation, negative binomial regression, and random forest classification. It also compares results with Highway Safety Manual predictions to map when and where crashes happen.

A random forest predicted injury severity with 67 percent accuracy, beating the manual's safety performance functions. A Moran's I test confirmed that crashes cluster in space, and density analysis placed hotspots near major intersections, matching the earlier findings. The authors argue the richer toolkit yields actionable guidance for targeted safety improvements on this route.
arxiv-2512-22402:
Bhanu Prakash Vangala and Tanu Malik present Pick and Spin, a system for organizations that run language models on their own hardware. Self-hosting promises privacy, cost control, and customization, but juggling several models strains graphics processor use, request routing, and reliability. Their system is built on Kubernetes with a unified Helm-based deployment setup and automation that scales idle models down to zero.

A hybrid router balances cost, latency, and accuracy using keyword heuristics plus a lightweight DistilBERT classifier. The evaluation covered four large models, from Llama-3 to DeepSeek-R1, across eight public benchmarks and more than 160,000 inference runs. Compared with static deployments, Pick and Spin raised success rates by up to about twenty-two percent while cutting latency and per-query GPU cost by roughly a third.
arxiv-2512-22502:
Shen Changqing and five co-authors generate spiral milling paths for complicated industrial parts whose surfaces have multiple holes and boundaries. Standard toolpath generation on such multiply connected freeform surfaces produces breaks, sharp turns, uneven scallop heights, and missed boundary coverage. Their method tunes a scalar field whose level curves become the toolpaths, aiming for continuous, boundary-hugging, non-crossing spirals from the start.

They first build a feasible, flaw-free field with boundary-conforming level sets through conformal slit mapping. The tuning is then recast as topology-preserving mesh deformation with boundary-synchronous updates, turning path requirements into mesh constraints that hold throughout. In milling tests, the approach improved milling efficiency by about fourteen percent and scallop-height evenness by about six percent over a leading slit-mapping method, while cutting impact-induced vibration.
arxiv-2512-22802:
Amirhossein Tighkhorshid, Zahra Dehghanian, and Hamid Rabiee speed up diffusion image models by teaching a fast student model to imitate a slow teacher in only a few steps. Standard distillation does this by regression on the teacher's steps, which costs thousands of GPU hours and a huge pre-generated dataset. ReDiF instead treats the student as a policy and rewards only its final output, scored by how well it matches the teacher's result.

That terminal-reward setup frees the objective from step-by-step matching and even allows rewards the teacher itself does not express. ReDiF converged in a few hundred policy updates on a single A100 graphics card, taking about four GPU hours where a leading method reportedly needed hundreds. Its eight-step ImageNet results beat retrained baselines under the same small budget, and adding ReDiF to that leading method improved its score further.
arxiv-2512-22902:
Goran Dražić, Matija Kazalicki, and Rudi Mrazović write a short note in number theory about D(n)-pairs. For a fixed integer n, two nonzero integers form such a pair when their product plus n is a perfect square. These pairs connect to the classical problem of finding sets where every pairwise product plus n is a square, a topic going back to Diophantus and Fermat.

Each pair can be encoded by a binary quadratic form, and the note studies how the pairs spread across the equivalence classes of those forms. The authors prove the pairs become asymptotically equidistributed among the proper equivalence classes of forms with discriminant four times n and fixed content. As a payoff, the equidistribution gives a cleaner and simpler proof of Badesa's asymptotic formula counting D(n)-pairs, replacing earlier arguments with a more structural one based on quadratic forms.
arxiv-2512-23102:
Krzysztof Golec-Biernat investigates whether the proton can be assigned an entropy based on its parton content, the quarks and gluons revealed at high energy. He works within DGLAP evolution, the standard scheme describing how parton distributions change as the probing scale grows. Within that scheme, the partonic entropy turns out to increase monotonically with scale, a clean statement about how the proton's internal picture grows more complex under magnification.

A simplified evolution model shows what drives the growth, and also why it cannot run forever in reality: saturation effects at small momentum fraction, where gluons crowd and recombine, tame the increase. Two simplified saturation models from the literature are presented. In one of them, the partonic entropy is identified with entanglement entropy, which would make it an experimentally testable quantity rather than a bookkeeping device. The paper thereby links a thermodynamic-sounding concept to measurable proton structure.
arxiv-2512-23402:
Hiroki Takahasi studies how the hardest-to-approximate real numbers are distributed inside fractal sets. A number's irrationality exponent measures how closely rationals can approach it; numbers with exponent above two are transcendental and form a set with rich fractal structure, the Jarník set. Takahasi asks what happens when that set is intersected with the limit sets of parabolic iterated function systems built from the backward continued fraction.

The answer is maximal: the intersection always has full Hausdorff dimension, as large as the ambient fractal allows. A corollary sharpens the picture. Irrationals with exponent above two whose backward continued fraction digits stay bounded still form a set of Hausdorff dimension one. That contrasts sharply with the classical continued fraction, where no irrational can have exponent above two and bounded digits at the same time. The result separates the two continued fraction worlds by a clean dimensional statement.
arxiv-2512-23502:
Md Arafat Habib and five co-authors design a control system for network slicing in future 6G mobile networks. Slicing lets several logical networks share one physical radio network, each with its own service-level promises for speed and delay. Earlier learning-based controllers rely on static mappings and cannot understand plain-language operator goals.

Their framework pairs a large language model with controllers built on Hierarchical Decision Mamba, a sequence-model architecture. The language model turns operator intent into concrete goals, and the Mamba controllers coordinate agents that manage resources between slices, inside each slice, and heal faults. Against transformer-based and reward-driven baselines, the system delivered higher throughput, better service at the cell edge, and lower latency across slices. The work was accepted for IEEE Networking Letters.
arxiv-2512-23602:
Christopher Burger wants to help plants catch faults in their goods with fewer false alarms. Plants use control charts to watch a line. The charts rest on rules about how data should spread out. New lines break those rules, so alarms lose their worth.

He adds conformal prediction, a way to set error bars that holds with no guess about how the data spread. One tool shows the chart with its doubt drawn in. A spike in that doubt can warn staff before a fault shows. A second tool turns the watch of many traits at once into a hunt for odd points, shown on a plain p-value chart. The mix keeps the ease of the old charts. It also gives the watch a firmer base in stats.
arxiv-2512-23902:
Hesam Khoshkbari, Georges Kaddoum, Omid Abbasi, Bassant Selim, and Halim Yanikomeroglu present a second beamforming design for networks of airborne platform stations, companion in spirit to their constellation study. Here a fleet of non-terrestrial base stations with massive antenna arrays serves ground users. The goal is maximizing total downlink data rate while each station knows only its own imperfect channel information.

Each station computes its beamforming vector independently inside an entropy-based multi-agent reinforcement learning scheme, using a Fourier neural operator to capture long-range dependencies in the frequency domain. Transfer learning with a conjugate prior mechanism and a low-rank decomposition keep the method scalable and robust. In simulations it outperformed WMMSE, zero-forcing, maximum-ratio, convolutional, and policy-gradient baselines on sum rate, robustness to channel errors and user mobility. Scaling, while also beating several rivals on computing cost and communication overhead.
arxiv-2512-24102:
Yves Ruffenach examines where sequence structure should live in a language model. Standard models predict text token by token. An earlier design moved the sequential machinery elsewhere. It placed structure in a hidden latent space. A causal Gaussian process drove that space. The decoder itself stayed non-autoregressive.

Ruffenach asks what the latent autoregression contributes. Careful ablations supply the answer. The full model faces two rivals. One drops latent autoregression entirely. The other is a plain token-level Transformer. Within the medium-scale setting, latent autoregression helped clearly. Its trajectories matched the prior far better. They also stayed stable over longer spans. Removing it degraded the latent structure. Long-range behavior turned erratic. The author frames the study as analysis, not a new architecture pitch.
arxiv-2512-24902:
Kuan-Cheng Chen, Felix Burt, and Nitish Panigrahy propose ModEn-Hub, an design for linking many quantum units into one distributed system. A hub-and-spoke photonic link centralizes entanglement sources and shared quantum memory, giving high-fidelity Bell pairs on demand to varied units. The control plane plans teleportation-based non-local gates and parallel entanglement attempts.

A small cache of entangled pairs helps keep actions flowing. Simulations measure the benefits of the design. Quantum computing readers get a concrete control plan for scaling beyond a single device. The work treats entanglement as a managed network asset, planned like bandwidth.
arxiv-2601-00102:
Jarosław Arabas, Adam Stelmaszczyk, Eryk Warchulski, Dariusz Jagodziński, and Rafał Biedrzycki rework a well-known optimization method that adapts a covariance matrix. The method, called CMA-ES, searches by sampling from a bell-shaped distribution shaped by that matrix. Splitting the matrix into parts costs time that grows fast with dimension, which limits use on large problems. Their paper removes the matrix entirely.

An archive stores the gaps between past candidates and their midpoint, scaled by step size. New candidates are built as weighted mixes of those stored gaps. The authors prove the resulting distribution matches the standard method exactly. In tests, a small archive of recent rounds suffices, and the matrix-free version often converges faster.
arxiv-2601-00202:
Wang Xing leads five coauthors in shrinking temporal knowledge graph reasoners with help from large language models. Such graphs store facts that change over time. Reasoning over them supports smart decision systems. Top models, though, are large and power hungry. That blocks use on small or low power devices. Older compression tricks target static graphs instead.

Their framework uses a large model as the teacher. It guides a small student through distillation. Public knowledge and task specific time data are combined. The student learns both structure and temporal patterns. Its design stays compact and cheap to run. Tests on public benchmarks beat strong baselines. Accuracy, speed, and deployability land in a good balance. For engineers, the work shows time aware distillation is possible. The temporal signal need not be lost in compression.
arxiv-2601-00302:
Shennan Hu leads eleven coauthors in squeezing a ceramic used in engines and fuel cells to see how its crystal form changes. Yttria stabilized zirconia comes in two mixes here. One holds three percent yttria, the other eight. Pressure in a diamond anvil cell climbs very high. Two probes watch the same sample at once.

X ray diffraction and Raman spectra together untangle the shifts. Either probe alone would miss part of the story. Pressure pushes both mixes toward higher symmetry forms. A low symmetry phase fades out early in compression. Later stages pass through middle forms into a cubic phase. That top form holds to the highest pressure reached. Release brings nearly every change back in reverse. One phase, though, stays practically gone afterward. The authors call that outcome structural purification. Cleaner crystals could mean better material traits.
arxiv-2601-00502:
Zeping Sui and five co-authors compare two ways to pack wireless signals in a 2026 study. Both ways use many antennas at the sending and receiving ends. One way, called OFDM, is the standard in much of today's wireless gear. The newer way, called AFDM, uses chirp signals, whose tone sweeps up or down. Real gear is flawed, and the team ask how each way copes.

The flaws include noise in a signal's phase and shifts in its base tone. They also include bent signals from cheap parts and poor guesses of the channel. For small setups the team work out a tight bound on the error rate. For large setups they give a close formula for a simpler receiver. AFDM keeps its full spread of signal paths despite the flaws. It also beats OFDM on error rate. That edge suits it to fast, mobile links.
arxiv-2601-00702:
Samuel Cerezo and Javier Civera present DefVINS, the first visual-inertial odometry system designed for scenes that deform. Odometry estimates a camera's motion from images plus inertial sensors, but classical systems assume the world is rigid. In deformable settings, such as inside the body or around cloth, that assumption fails, and systems either overfit local warping or drift badly.

DefVINS splits its state into a rigid part anchored to the inertial measurements and a non-rigid scene warp described by an embedded deformation graph. Alongside it, the authors release VIMandala, the first benchmark with real images and true camera poses for deformable odometry, plus an augmented synthetic benchmark with simulated inertial data. An observability analysis rounds out the work.
arxiv-2601-01302:
Pouria Sarhadi returns to a long-standing control problem: what happens when a motor or rudder cannot move as far or as fast as ordered. The control system keeps pushing, builds up error, and then reacts badly when limits lift. Newer fixes work, but they can be hard to set up in real projects.

Sarhadi adjusts two classic controllers, the common PID type and a related optimal type, so they cope with both kinds of limit. Tested on steering a small robot submarine, they matched a far more complex predictive method. The point is simple tools with one extra tuning choice may serve engineers well.
arxiv-2601-01502:
Milind Nakul, Tianjiao Li, and Ashwin Pananjady speed up a class of algorithms that learn from a stream of dependent data. Many training methods assume each sample is fresh and independent. Reinforcement learning breaks that: samples arrive from a Markov chain, correlated in time, and reusing them from a memory buffer is standard practice. Uniform replay from the buffer still carries bias.

Their Multiscale Experience Replay samples the buffer at several scales at once, mimicking how the algorithms behave on independent data. Unlike skipping-based fixes, it needs no knowledge of how fast the chain mixes, and it speeds convergence whenever speed is available. The theory covers stochastic variational inequalities, a broad family that includes the target problems. Two applications stand out: policy evaluation with temporal difference learning, and fitting generalized linear models on dependent data. Robust acceleration without tuning knobs is a practical prize for reinforcement learning systems.
arxiv-2601-01602:
Henry Ndou proposes MTS-1, a compact format for sending machine health data from places with weak networks. Standard formats were built for fast, always-on links and waste bytes that rural sites, common across sub-Saharan Africa, can ill afford. MTS-1 stores only changes from the last reading, in binary form, and is built to work offline first.

Ndou compares it with six common formats on payload size, coding cost, network use, and cost against speed. In synthetic tests, MTS-1 cut size by up to about three quarters against the common text format JSON, and slightly against a compact rival. Growth stayed linear as data sets grew, suiting low-power devices.
arxiv-2601-01802:
Training an AI psychological counselor is hard because real therapy unfolds over many sessions and mixes several therapeutic schools. Qianjun Pan and twelve co-authors build PsychEval, a benchmark of multi-session, multi-therapy counseling designed to look like actual clinical practice.

The benchmark spans six to ten sessions in three stages, demanding memory across meetings, adaptive reasoning, and long-term planning, and it is annotated with thousands of professional skills. Its cases cover five therapy traditions plus an integrative approach across six core topics, judged by eighteen metrics at client and counselor levels, with over two thousand client profiles. Beyond testing, PsychEval doubles as a reinforcement learning environment for training more responsible, adaptive AI counselors.
arxiv-2601-01902:
Learning the equations of electromagnetism from noisy data is risky. The learned model may slowly gain or lose energy. That ruins long runs. Victory Obieke and Ameh Emmanuel Sunday build that energy behavior in from the start, learning derivative stencils for Maxwell's equations with a structure-preserving optimization method they call SP-ADMM.

The true derivative operator must be skew-adjoint for energy to be conserved. So the authors describe it using only its free parts. Every candidate stencil then conserves energy by construction. Across noisy data, hidden operators, and long-time runs, the method achieved the smallest final-time field errors. It held energy to rounding accuracy. It also stayed competitive with classical finite differences on a layered-medium test. The work shows physical structure can discipline data-driven learning.
arxiv-2601-02002:
Language models are trained on undisclosed mountains of text, so private or benchmark data may hide inside them. Antonio Colacicco and four co-authors probe a known leak. The MovieLens-1M dataset is memorized by LLaMA models. Can it be extracted by machine? The alternative is hand-crafted prompts.

Three strategies were tried. Jailbreak prompting stayed erratic. Probing internal activations separated real from fake movie titles. It failed on numbers. Automatic prompt engineering refines prompts in rounds. It recovered item-level information moderately well. Automatic prompt optimization looks most promising, though numerical interaction data resisted all three approaches.
arxiv-2601-02602:
Neusha Javidnia, Ruisi Zhang, Ashish Kundu, and Farinaz Koushanfar present SWaRL, a watermarking system that marks code written by a language model so its source can later be proved. Protecting the intellectual property of code models matters as their output spreads. Older watermarking either rewrites code by handcrafted rules, which attackers can undo, or biases token choices during generation, which can break whether the code still works.

SWaRL instead trains the watermark in by reinforcement learning. A compiler checks that marked code still functions correctly, and a confidential verifier, trained jointly with the model, rewards marks it can still detect. Low rank adaptation keeps the fine tuning efficient and lets the behavior transfer across model updates. Experiments show strong detection accuracy against earlier methods, while the marked code keeps full functional correctness.
arxiv-2601-02702:
Shuhaib Mehri, Priyanka Kargupta, Tal August, and Dilek Hakkani-Tür introduce a benchmark for a skill conversational agents need over months. Not minutes, learning what a particular user prefers and using it to collaborate better in later sessions. MultiSessionCollab stages repeated sessions with the same user and scores whether collaboration quality, success, efficiency, and user effort, improves as the agent accumulates experience with that person.

Alongside the benchmark, the authors build agents whose memory is designed specifically to store user preferences across sessions. Training signals can even be drawn from how a user simulator behaves in the benchmark, teaching agents to reflect more thoroughly and update memory more effectively. In extensive experiments, agents with the preference memory collaborate better over time, with higher task success and less effort demanded from the user.
arxiv-2601-02802:
Viswanathan Ramachandran studies a communication problem where sending a message and agreeing on a description of the channel must happen together. The channel is a fading Gaussian channel with additive state interference.

The state sequence is known ahead of time at the transmitter but not directly at the receiver, while the fading strength is known perfectly at both ends. The receiver must decode the message and also reconstruct the state, under a common reconstruction constraint that forces its estimate to match the transmitter's own estimate exactly. The main result is a complete characterization of the best possible trade off among rate, distortion, and power for this setting, supported by numerical examples.
arxiv-2601-03102:
Igor Strakovsky reviews sixty years of work on the Roper resonance, the first excited state of the proton and neutron, discovered in the 1960s. The case is unusual. What was long treated as one resonance turns out to be a single resonance with two pole positions. Those poles live on different Riemann sheets, a subtlety that took decades to untangle. Strakovsky tells the story as a brief history of how understanding developed.

The article reminds readers how the field's picture of this state changed over time, and why the Roper remains a benchmark for theories of the nucleon's inner structure. Writing in the first person, the author is candid that history is partly reconstruction, shaped by those who tell it. The piece serves as both a scientific summary and a personal account of a long-running puzzle.
arxiv-2601-03602:
Mamoon A. Sharaf, Weijie Du, and Andrey M. Shirokov calculate two mirror nuclear reactions: a neutron and proton joining with a gamma ray released, and a gamma ray splitting a deuteron back apart. They cover photon energies up to twenty MeV, a range that matters for both nuclear physics and astrophysics. Their tool is chiral effective field theory, a systematic way to build nuclear forces.

The team used a high-order nucleon interaction and matching transition operators from the same theory. Their results agree with existing experiments and extend to energies where no modern calculations or data existed before. They also adapt a method by Efros that suits future many-body work on bound and scattering states. Even the simplest nucleus formation reaction still tests how well theory captures nuclear forces.
arxiv-2601-03802:
Rehan Ahmad and three co-authors benchmark quantum machine learning against classical models on financial prediction, taking care to make the comparison fair. Their framework matches architectures between quantum and classical counterparts and standardizes data splits, features, and metrics across three tasks. Those tasks are directional return prediction on United States and Turkish stocks, a live-trading simulation with quantum and classical sequence models on a broad market index, and volatility forecasting.

Quantum approaches gained ground when the data structure and circuit design aligned well. Hybrid quantum networks beat their parameter-matched classical rival on the named stock tests by several points in ranking quality and accuracy. Live-trading results are also reported in the study. Honest head-to-head benchmarks help separate real quantum advantage from hype in finance.
arxiv-2601-04002:
Michael McAuley, writing alone, develops a new way to study whole-field quantities of smooth random fields that depend on distant parts at once. Classic measures such as volume or surface area are local and easier to handle. Counts of pieces or holes in high regions are not local, and they need different tools.

McAuley builds the method around a form of topological quasi-association, a weak kind of positive link between distant regions. With it he proves several limit results for roughly additive quantities on growing domains. They include tight concentration bounds, a measured central limit theorem, and a law of the iterated logarithm. The approach opens non-local geometry of random fields to the same kind of limit theory that local measures already enjoy.
arxiv-2601-04102:
Jason Cantarella, Tetsuo Deguchi, Henrik Schumacher, Clayton Shonkwiler, and Erica Uehara report large computer experiments on knots that form by chance in very long closed chains. The chains are self-avoiding polygons off any lattice, in a bead-chain model. Longer chains knot more often, but exact knot types are hard to pin down.

Using a tree data structure, a scale-free pivot method, and new knot simplification code, the five authors classify every polygon they make. Counts of prime knot pieces follow a Poisson law very closely. They estimate the characteristic length for knotting at a value in the mid six hundred thousands, with a small error range. Rates and amplitude ratios are measured more sharply than before, and the results agree with lattice studies.
arxiv-2601-04402:
Emery Doucet and five co-authors read a quantum annealer as a heat engine in a 2026 arXiv paper. Annealers accept problems in one standard format, QUBO, but a single task can be encoded many ways, and the penalty weights chosen reshape the energy landscape the hardware actually climbs. Using a job shop scheduling instance, the team sweeps two penalty knobs, one for assignment constraints and one for ordering constraints.

Across classical annealing-style solvers and a D-Wave Advantage processor, feasibility and success switch sharply as the penalties cross certain values. Treating the processor as an open thermodynamic system, with reverse-annealing cycles started from thermal samples, they bound its entropy production, work, and heat from the measured energy changes. The same encoding transitions that make the problem harder also reorganize dissipation: weak penalties breed cheap infeasible answers, strong ones shrink the problem's energy scale and waste more as irreversibility.
arxiv-2601-04702:
Samantha Fournier and Pierfrancesco Urbani tune how one-way the couplings in a vast dynamical system are, and watch chaos respond, in a 2026 arXiv paper. High-dimensional systems of interacting parts — neural networks, ecosystems, glasses — behave extremely differently at the extremes. Fully random asymmetric couplings give a chaotic attractor with a positive largest Lyapunov exponent, while fully symmetric couplings reduce the motion to slow gradient descent on an energy landscape, with aging.

The surprise is the middle. With a parameter dialling the degree of non-reciprocity between the extremes, the authors show that any amount of non-reciprocity at all lands the dynamics on a chaotic attractor. Symmetric calm is a knife's edge. The Lyapunov exponent, moreover, is a non-monotone function of that dial, so a conservative force derived from a rough energy landscape can, counterintuitively, make the system more chaotic rather than tamer.
arxiv-2601-04802:
Dharitree Bezboruah and 2 co-authors ask whether dark matter can change how neutrinos flip from one type to a new type as they travel in a 2026 paper. Their set-up has neutrinos pass through a field of dark matter that fills the cosmos. As they cross it, a small term in the rules for the flip would shift. The shift would act one way on neutrinos and the other way on their anti-matter twins.

The team works out where such a shift would show up in long-distance tests run on Earth. They focus on the DUNE and T2HK tests, and on one key value that tracks how matter and anti-matter part ways. If the dark effect is real, these big tests may spot it while they do their main work.
arxiv-2601-04902:
Sławomir Lasota and 3 co-authors study synthesis problems for timed games in a 2026 paper. They generalize Büchi-Landweber games, a classic two-player contest on graphs, to a timed setting where the winning condition is given by a nondeterministic timed automaton and one player can let time pass. Variants differ in whose condition is specified and whose strategy, or finite-memory controller, is sought.

Their main result is sweeping undecidability: in every variant, no algorithm can always solve the synthesis problem, even when the winning condition uses only one clock. The negative result strengthens earlier work and maps a hard boundary. Knowing a problem is undecidable saves system designers from hunting for automatic controller builders that cannot exist.
arxiv-2601-05502:
Gideon Peters and 2 co-authors evaluate, in a 2026 study, whether language models can fix web performance problems by editing a page's DOM tree. The DOM is the structured representation of a webpage that browsers render. Developers find such edits complex and slow, especially under time pressure.

The team took DOM trees from fifteen popular webpages and paired them with Lighthouse audit reports. Nine leading models each attempted repairs across seven audit categories. All models handled SEO and accessibility well, while results on load speed, interactivity, and network issues varied widely. The strongest model cut some audit problems by nearly half. Analysis showed models mostly added elements and moved positions, sometimes harming visual stability.
arxiv-2601-05602:
Zhou Cui and 6 co-authors investigate, in a 2026 paper, how magnetoelectric coupling in perovskite altermagnets changes from bulk crystals down to single layers. Altermagnets are a newer class of magnetic materials whose symmetry creates unusual spin behavior. In multiferroic versions, crystal symmetry itself links magnetism and electric polarization.

Symmetry analysis shows altermagnetism can survive in two dimensions, but only under one antiferromagnetic arrangement. Mode calculations reveal that restricted multi-mode couplings govern both polarization and spin splitting. First-principles results point to ways to loosen that magnetic constraint and widen the material pool. The findings matter for tiny devices that use spin and charge together. Put plainly, the shape of the crystal tells the spins and the charges how to affect each other. That link is what device makers hope to switch with a small voltage.
arxiv-2601-05702:
Runze Li and 2 co-authors propose, in a 2026 paper, a mixed-frequency state-space model for forecasting mortality in real time. Most mortality models use annual data, so they update only once a year. Monthly death counts arrive sooner and carry information about within-year dynamics that annual totals hide.

Their extension of the Lee-Carter framework links annual rates and monthly counts through one shared latent monthly factor. That factor follows a seasonal time-series process, and parameters are estimated by maximum likelihood with an expectation-maximization algorithm. On United States data for ages twenty to ninety, monthly information substantially improved within-year nowcasts. Aggregated monthly forecasts generally beat standard and reconciled Lee-Carter alternatives.
arxiv-2601-06202:
Style transfer should restyle an image without scrambling its content. Shiwen Zhang and 3 co-authors present QwenStyle in a 2026 technical report, built on the Qwen-Image-Edit model. Diffusion transformers often tangle content and style features inside the model, making clean separation hard.

The team collected and filtered high-quality data for a limited set of styles, then synthesized training triplets spanning thousands of style images from the wild. A curriculum continual learning scheme trains on this mix of clean and noisy triplets in stages. QwenStyle generalized to unseen styles while keeping content precise. On style similarity, content consistency, and aesthetic quality, the first version reached state-of-the-art results.
arxiv-2601-06302:
Why is there more matter than antimatter? Yakov Mandel explores a thermodynamic route to baryogenesis in a 2026 cosmology paper. Baryogenesis is the early-universe process that created the matter excess. Mandel tests sources driven by time-dependent derivatives and asks whether they can survive averaging over oscillations.

A zero-mean oscillating chemical potential, filtered through a smooth finite-time kernel, behaves like a low-pass filter: rapid sign changes mostly cancel. What matters is the residual low-frequency component. Mandel then studies an entropy clock, where the biasing variable tracks the logarithm of entropy during reheating. Success requires entropy production to overlap with charge violation before freeze-out. Quantitative benchmarks pin down the needed parameter sizes, though a deeper theory must explain the clock itself.
arxiv-2601-06402:
Public debate about development shifts with events, and Woojin Jung and 4 co-authors track those shifts in Zambia in a 2026 study. Using more than two years of geotagged posts from X, the team combines topic modeling, change-point detection, and qualitative coding. Low-resource settings are rarely studied this closely.

Seven recurring themes emerged, including public health challenges and frustration with government policy. Discourse change-points aligned with the COVID-19 pandemic and with a geothermal project. Crisis talk proved ephemeral, fading once the emergency passed. Infrastructure talk produced durable discourse, a sustained narrative engagement that restructured debate long-term. The authors draw lessons for technology and development work, urging direct local engagement rather than distant monitoring alone.
arxiv-2601-06602:
A walk in a hall with no GPS is a drift trap. Chest and wrist sensors feel each step, yet small slips pile up mile by mile. Mohammed S. Alharbi and 1 co-author built UMLoc to fight that drift in a 2026 paper. It gives not just a spot, but a bound on how far off the spot may be.

Two parts train as one. A loop net calls the range marks that set the doubt band at three trust tiers. A foe-and-mate net, fed both the move data and a floor plan, draws paths that a real walk could take. Doubt flows from the first part to the next, so paths know their own slack. On three sets, one a fresh two-hour hall walk, drift stayed at a low share of the path. The doubt bands held true to their tiers as well.
arxiv-2601-06702:
Besher Hassan and Xiuying Chen present GRASP LoRA in 2026 for cross-lingual transfer. Parameter-efficient fine-tuning adapts models to new languages with limited resources. Adapter pipelines usually choose a global prune ratio by grid search.

That practice is computationally expensive and development-set intensive, they argue. It repeats training, freezes sparsity, and misses fractional optima in ratios. Their method uses GRPO to guide adapter sparsity policy instead. A learned policy can pick sparsity per adapter, not globally. Cross-lingual transfer benefits when adapters keep the right connections per language. The paper promises cheaper searches for good sparsity settings. Practitioners adapting models to low-resource languages are the audience. Better policies mean more languages served at the same compute cost.
arxiv-2601-06802:
Ayman and co-authors posted a 2026 arXiv preprint. The preprint deals with doing more with less. It came out on arXiv in 2026 as a PAPERS preprint. Although many Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) systems have been developed for Modern Standard Arabic (MSA) and Dialectal Arabic (DA).

Few studies have focused on dialect-specific implementations, particularly for low-resource Arabic dialects such as Sudanese. The work presents a comprehensive study of data augmentation techniques for fine-tuning OpenAI’s Whisper models and establishes the first benchmark for the Sudanese dialect. Readers in the field get a short, focused account of the problem and the steps the authors take.
arxiv-2601-06902:
Research by Stinne Zacho and co-authors was posted on arXiv in 2026. It deals with santa clara 3D. The preprint joined the arXiv PAPERS collection in 2026. The work explores the potential of digital reconstruction and interactive storytelling to preserve historically suppressed sites. The main objective of an interdisciplinary team of data scientists from the MEMORISE project and associates of.

The memory association Asociación Recuerdo y Dignidad was to preserve the memory of the Francoist Santa Clara concentration camp in Soria. Spain, through the use of digital technology. For specialists, the preprint offers a compact account of the problem and the authors' approach.
arxiv-2601-07302: Magnus Bertilsson and co-authors posted a 2026 arXiv preprint. The preprint deals with DIS dipole picture cross section in exact kinematics. It came out on arXiv in 2026 as a PAPERS preprint. We implement a finite energy constraint in the dipole picture of deep inelastic scattering. By restricting the invariant mass of the produced partonic system by the virtual photon-target center of mass energy. Readers in the field get a short, focused account of the problem and the steps the authors take.
arxiv-2601-07902:
Alexey G. Gorinov and Alexander V. Zakharov compute the homology of spaces left after removing pieces of a torus. An affine subtorus is a shifted copy of a Lie subgroup inside the compact torus. Given finitely many such subtori and a prime p, they describe an explicit chain complex. That complex calculates the integral homology of the torus minus the union of the subtori. Binomial rings enter the construction. Their 2026 preprint gives the method.

Complements of toric arrangements appear in topology, combinatorics, and algebraic geometry. Their homology records holes and voids in the remaining space. An explicit chain complex turns that record into something computable. Local coefficients at the prime p refine the answer. The paper serves topologists who study arrangement complements. It supplies formulas where previously only case-by-case work existed.
arxiv-2601-08002:
Kathryn McKeough and colleagues build a Bayesian method for tracing the edges of faint X-ray sources. Mapping an extended source's boundary is a key step in studying its shape. Background contamination and statistical fluctuations make that hard, especially for low surface brightness X-ray images. Their three-step Bayesian procedure identifies boundaries of irregularly shaped sources. The method is named the LIRA-Ising model. Their 2026 preprint presents it.

A boundary drawn by eye varies between analysts and hides uncertainty. A Bayesian procedure states the boundary with its uncertainty attached. The Ising component favors coherent edges over speckled noise. Astronomers studying clusters, supernova remnants, and galaxies need such outlines. The author team spans astronomy and statistics departments. The paper serves both communities by treating a picture problem as an inference problem.
arxiv-2601-08402: Donya Rooein and co-authors present PATS, a tutoring approach that adapts teaching to student personality. Their 2026 arXiv paper notes that language models show promise as educational tutors. Different strategies benefit different personalities, though, and mismatches can harm outcomes. Current tutoring systems rarely account for student personality traits at all. PATS is personality-aware, matching strategy choice to the learner. Better matching could raise gains for students whom a single fixed style would leave behind, a common risk in automated tutoring.
arxiv-2601-08602: Zishan Shu and seven co-authors wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on a vision model called WaveFormer. Top vision models, called Transformers, use attention to catch how parts of a scene link. But attention gives no firm account of how sense spreads. The authors treat each feature map as a signal in space. That signal shifts over an inner time tied to network depth. An underdamped wave equation rules how the signal shifts. The aim is a flow of features with a clear physical rule at its core.
arxiv-2601-09402:
Xinze Li and eight co-authors aim to give retrieval-augmented generation a better memory. Their 2026 arXiv paper proposes structured knowledge pages that organize facts gathered during a search. Retrieval-augmented generation lets a language model pull in outside knowledge before it answers.

Some systems build knowledge step by step as they work on a query. The authors note that this stockpile often lacks a clear structure, which limits how complete and cohesive it becomes. Their contextual pages impose order on the gathered material. A tidier knowledge store should help models answer with broader, better-linked evidence.
arxiv-2601-09702:
Baruch Garcia takes a fresh look at a landmark result about the limits of proof methods. The 2026 arXiv paper revisits the Baker-Gill-Solovay theorem on relativization in complexity theory. Some separations, like P versus EXP, survive when all machines gain an oracle; others, famously, cannot be settled that way.

Garcia asks a specific point that he says was never proven outright: whether the Turing-recognizability of the acceptance problem relativizes. Diagonalization is the classic tool behind such results. Clarifying exactly what it can and cannot do keeps the foundations of complexity theory honest.
arxiv-2601-10102:
Viswonathan Manoranjan and Snehalkumar Gaikwad test if AI agents chase pay or play a role. Agents are now set in teams to do plan tasks. Each agent may get a role name and a job. It may or may not see the pay for each move.

The team asks which force wins. Does an agent pick the move with the best pay? Or does it act as its role would act, even at a cost? The test pits role pull against pay pull. The aim is to learn if teams of agents plan with care, or act from a script. That split shapes how such teams should be built.
arxiv-2601-10202:
Hongtao Li and co authors detect a heart fault from ECG traces. The fault is atrial fibrillation, a fast and uneven beat. It raises the risk of stroke and heart fail. A firm test must work in one clinic and the next.

Past AI tests oft fail when the clinic changes. They may also waste facts in the trace. The team fuse two views of the trace. One view tracks time, one tracks tones. They train with a method that pulls like cases close. The aim is a test that is both strong and broad in use.
arxiv-2601-10302:
Yu. M. Poluektov sets a field as a chance height in a fast move frame. In quantum work, a field's height can code chance. Poluektov writes a fast frame law for a neutral complex field. The law is built so the height reads as a chance weight.

From it, he gets a flow rule for the chance weight. The weight is kept as the field moves. He finds two kinds of waves in the field. Both have plus energy, but their spread rules part. From a Lagrangian form, he draws the kept laws of the field. The work reframes field laws in chance terms.
arxiv-2601-10502:
Jiaze Li, Michael Schaub, and Leto Peel find trade offs in group hunts on hypergraphs. A hypergraph links sets of nodes at once, not just pairs. Groups in such a net are sets that link more in than out. Past graph tools do not map clean to this case.

Sets in a hypergraph come in many sizes. A large set can span groups in ways a pair can not. That makes group sense less clear. The team work out the trade offs this brings. They show what must be lost or gained in each call. The work sets a base for group tools on rich nets.
arxiv-2601-10802:
Gerhard Krumpl, Henning Avenhaus, and Horst Possegger present ICONIC-444, a dataset of 3.1 million images for out-of-distribution research. Progress in spotting out-of-distribution inputs has been held back by data. Few sets offer clear OOD categories at graded difficulty, from near to far. Fewer still serve both fine- and coarse-grained vision tasks.

ICONIC-444 is built to fill that gap at scale. Graded categories let researchers test where a detector starts to fail. Fine labels test whether models notice subtle shifts, not just gross ones. A shared, large testbed can make results across papers comparable at last. The dataset targets safer vision systems that know when they are out of their depth.
arxiv-2601-10902:
James Freeburn and a large team present the first optical data release of the Deeper, Wider, Faster programme. The fast sky, events that flare and fade in under an hour, is poorly charted. With the Dark Energy Camera, the programme scans a unique space: deep images, reaching a median of about magnitude 22.2, taken at minute cadence.

Fast cadence catches supernovae in their first hours and other quick transients that slow surveys miss. A public data release lets the whole field mine those catches. The paper documents what the release holds and how it was built. Time-domain astronomers gain a resource for the fastest changing sky yet surveyed in depth.
arxiv-2601-11502:
Natalia Zawadzka and six coauthors read fingerprints of a charge density wave. Their 2026 preprint studies NbTe4, a near one-dimensional crystal. A charge density wave is an ordered state of conduction electrons. It comes with a periodic distortion of the crystal lattice.

Raman scattering suits the hunt for such modulations well. Light scattered off the crystal reports its vibration modes. At 5 K, the spectrum shows 25 phonon modes in the work. Resonant enhancement makes those faint modes stand out. The mode set acts as a fingerprint of the wave state. It can track how the ordered state forms and shifts.
arxiv-2601-11602:
Sungwoo Kang studies the physics of price discovery in markets. The 2026 preprint tracks how an informed signal travels and breaks. A prior 2025 finding set the stage for this work. Market cap normalization isolates a pure directional signal there.

That signal reflects informed trading in the market. Kang asks how it is transmitted through price action. He also asks how it breaks down under stress. Retail herding is the breakdown case in the title. When crowds herd, the clean signal can fail at once. Deconvolving information and volatility is the method's core. Such work speaks to traders who read order flow signals.
arxiv-2601-11702:
Yu Yang, Ig-Jae Kim, and Dongwook Yoon evaluate AI compliance across many policies. Their 2026 preprint names the framework PASTA. AI compliance grows critical as systems spread everywhere. Policies multiply fast, and checking them all is costly.

Resource-constrained practitioners often lack policy expertise. Existing approaches address one policy at a time. Multi-policy checks then cost too much for small teams. PASTA is a scalable framework for the joint task. It evaluates compliance against many policies in one pass. Shared work across policies cuts the total burden. The tool serves builders who must answer to many rules.
arxiv-2601-12202:
Sambit Das and Vikram Gavini explain a gain in ductility in magnesium alloys via large ab-initio calculations. Magnesium is the lightest structural metal, yet its low ductility limits use. Recent work hints that dilute alloys gain ductility from solute shifts in dislocation core energy.

The key shift is in pyramidal screw dislocations, which can then cross-slip twice and spread strain. Their large first-principles runs test that story. A firmer story could guide alloy design for cars and planes. Light yet ductile alloys save fuel at scale.  Their runs are large scale by the norms of the field.
arxiv-2601-12402:
Aleksandra Jamroz, Patrycja Wysocka, and Piotr Garbat review systems that read emotion from faces. Such systems play a role in how humans and computers interact. The range of methods in the field is vast. That spread alone makes a close review of the work worthwhile.

The team pick out three of the most notable and best solutions for close study. They also pick three datasets that stand out for range and size. With those in hand, they probe where face based emotion systems fall short. Weak spots can range from odd lighting to faces that do not fit the norm. A clear map of flaws helps builders know what to fix first.
arxiv-2601-12502:
Mikhail Gennadievich Belov and five co authors study how to reconstruct a quantum channel from data. A quantum channel describes how a quantum state changes as it passes through a device or medium. The team consider learning that channel from a sample of classical data. That is, the inputs and outputs seen are classical records, yet the object to learn is quantum.

Their tool is semidefinite programming, a class of optimization with strong solvers. Framing channel learning as such a program gives the task a clean, tractable form. Exact channel knowledge matters for calibrating quantum hardware. It also matters for checking that a device does what its maker claims. The work adds a method to the quantum tomography toolkit.
arxiv-2601-12702:
Work with no author named in the record studies Igusa Todorov properties under recollements of abelian categories. A recollement glues two categories into a larger one in a structured way. Igusa Todorov properties measure how complex the homological structure of a category is. The work asks how these properties behave when categories are glued.

In particular, it relates the Igusa Todorov distances of the parts to the whole. Applications are given to Artin algebras, a central class in representation theory. Morita context rings get special attention as a test case. Results of this kind let algebraists transfer knowledge between categories. They show which homological traits survive gluing and which do not.
arxiv-2601-13002:
Chen Zhao and six co authors present a theory of the correlated Hofstadter spectrum in magic angle graphene. Magic angle twisted bilayer graphene hosts correlated Chern insulator states in a magnetic field. Those states have been intensively studied in experiments. A simple and clear understanding of their origin is still lacking, the team note.

They propose a unified theoretical framework for these states. The framework successfully explains most experimental observations, per the abstract. Hofstadter spectra arise when magnetic flux and lattice period compete. Adding electron correlation makes the picture far richer. A unified account would anchor a flagship material of modern condensed matter physics.
arxiv-2601-13302:
Lizhou Sha and co-authors count how often hot Jupiters have close planet mates. A hot Jupiter is a huge gas world in a tight, fast orbit. More than five hundred such worlds are firm finds, with about two thousand more in wait. Just ten are known to have a close mate.

That count speaks to how such worlds moved. A mate could not live through a wild, high stretch swoop to the tight orbit. So hosts with mates must have slid in through a disk or formed in place. By count of mates in a clean way, the team helps split which path most hot Jupiters took.
arxiv-2601-13402:
Patrick De Visschere reviews how colour gaps in theory are matched to colour gaps seen by eye. A line element is a local rule that states how far two near hues sit for the human eye. Tests yield real gaps for pairs of hues. Many scores have been used to judge how well a rule's gaps fit the seen gaps.

Those scores can be skewed by how test hues were picked. Pick of paths in a hue point can be loose and one sided. De Visschere joins the scores over a full ellipse or ellipsoid in place of a loose pick. That full join wipes the pick bias. Colour staff gain a fair way to rank hue rules.
arxiv-2601-13802:
Yushen Chen and co-authors lay the base for Arabic speech synthesis across many dialects in 2026. Arabic dialects vary much in sound and word choice. Research on speech synthesis for them lags, in part from their complexity. A lack of standard data, benchmarks, and eval rules pushes teams to safer topics.

Their project, Habibi, aims for a unified model of Arabic dialects. One model for many dialects could serve far more speakers than single-dialect tools. Open-source release lets other teams build on the base. Good speech tools in one's own dialect aid access and pride.
arxiv-2601-14102:
The CMS team at the LHC measures a rare particle process and hunts for new couplings in 2026. They study production of a Z boson with a high-energy photon in proton-proton collisions. The Z decays to two neutrinos, which escape unseen. Data came from collisions at thirteen TeV during 2016 to 2018.

The dataset corresponds to an integrated luminosity of 138 inverse femtobarns. They report the fiducial cross section for this production. They also search for anomalous neutral triple gauge couplings, signs of new physics. Any crack in the expected couplings would point beyond the Standard Model.
arxiv-2601-14302:
Jinwei Hu, Shiyuan Meng, Yi Dong, and Xiaowei Huang study attack tests for image systems in this 2026 paper. The setting is image transmission and processing in resource-critical work. There, adversarial perturbations, small crafted changes to an image, can break mission-specific object classification. Tests must check that risk before deployment.

Current test methods cost too much compute. They process each frame in full and perturb whole images. That load is impractical when huge image streams need fast checks. The team's method, DDSA, is a dual-domain strategic attack. Its stated aim is spatial-temporal efficiency, so robustness tests can run at real scale.
arxiv-2601-14402:
Michael Cui, Chenxin Dai, Yixuan Even Xu, and Fei Fang study peer review logistics in this 2026 paper. Assigning papers to reviewers is a central challenge for large academic conferences. Program chairs must balance competing goals. They want strong reviewer expertise on each paper. They also want diversity and robustness against strategic manipulation.

Doing all that at modern conference scale is hard. Thousands of papers and reviewers must be matched at once. The team presents a unified framework for the task. It is built to be both scalable and robust. Readers get a method aimed at fair, sound matches when the numbers grow huge.
arxiv-2601-14802:
Donnate Hooft and four co-authors improve 3D medical image segmentation in this 2026 paper. Their method, LocBAM, advances patch-based image segmentation by integrating location context. Patch-based methods cut a scan into small cubes and label each one. A cube alone can be ambiguous: the same texture may be healthy in one organ and a tumor in another.

Location context tells the model where in the body each patch sits. The abstract in the evidence pack cuts off just as it introduces patch-based methods. The title carries the full claim, though. Readers get a segmentation design that uses anatomy as a prior, so local labels respect the map of the body.
arxiv-2601-14902:
Huanhuan Shi, Qili Li, and a large team study a layered crystal called NbSe2. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with how its electrons settle into ordered states. In thin layers, charge can form a wave-like pattern, and the crystal can also carry current with no loss.

Atom-thin layers show this physics well but are hard to probe. They are tiny and react fast to their surroundings. The team slips organic ions between the layers of a bulk crystal by an electric method. That bulk form then acts like a single thin layer, but is far easier to study.
arxiv-2601-15002:
Wen Chen, Zhan-Jiang Lian, and a team of co-authors work on the math of atomic nuclei. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with angular momentum projection. The step builds nuclear wave functions that carry a clean, fixed spin.

The standard route projects a reference state for the whole nucleus at once. The authors break a projected wave function into parts instead. Their decomposition reworks how the basis of states is built. Work like this helps theorists compute what a nucleus does while keeping its spin exact and clean at each and every step.
arxiv-2601-15102:
Johannes Meuer, Maximilian Witte, and co-authors build a faster stand-in for climate models. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with Earth system models that run at kilometer scale. Such models catch local climate change well, but they cost a huge amount to run.

Their output can reach petabyte scale, which limits uses such as risk assessment. The team presents the Field-Space Autoencoder. It is a climate emulation framework built on spherical compression. The model squeezes global fields down and rebuilds them, so many more runs become cheap enough to use in practice.
arxiv-2601-15502:
T. Troncoso Enríquez and three co-authors study red blood cells under light forces in a 2026 arXiv paper. They use evanescent waves, which arise in total internal reflection. The setup pairs a 1064 nanometer laser with a dual-chamber prism. With it, they track how red blood cells move. The key question is how glucose levels change that motion.

Automated tracking does the measuring work. The team uses the TrackMate tool to follow cell paths. They analyze more than 60 sets of trajectories. Glucose matters because cell stiffness and motion shift with it. A method that reads those shifts with light could aid blood research. It may also point toward new ways to probe cell health without touching the cells.
arxiv-2601-15702:
K. Guratinder and four co-authors study a two-dimensional magnetic material in a 2026 arXiv paper. The material is Cr7Te8, grown by vapor deposition. It shows unusual Hall effect behavior as temperature changes. At room temperature, it displays an anomalous Hall effect. On cooling, the Hall resistivity flips sign. At low temperatures, it shows a peak. The measured films are hexagonal in structure.

The paper focuses on spin reorientations inside this material. A spin reorientation is a shift in how magnetic moments align. Such shifts can explain swings in the Hall signal. The material is also described as structurally metastable and disordered. Those traits complicate the picture but make it richer. Thin magnetic films like this are candidates for future devices.
arxiv-2601-15802:
Alexandre Albore, Humbert Fiorino, and Damien Pellier plan stealthy navigation for underwater drones in a 2026 arXiv paper. Autonomous unmanned underwater vehicles work without support vessels. They also work where satellite navigation cannot reach. Such independence matters in coastal zones with no surface access. It matters even more in restricted or dangerous areas. There, stealthy navigation is required, not optional.

Their solution is beacon based, per the title. Beacons placed in the area give the vehicle reference points. From them, it can fix its position without surfacing for a satellite signal. Staying submerged keeps the vehicle hidden and safe. The project drew funding from a French national source, per the record. Military and civilian users share the need for quiet, self-reliant navigation.
arxiv-2601-15902:
P. Dasgupta and D. Gangopadhyay work on safer teleportation with deformed quantum states in a 2026 arXiv paper. Teleportation moves a quantum state by using entanglement plus classical messages. Its safety matters if it carries sensitive data. The authors use q-deformed algebras as their tools. Their entangled states come from q-deformed harmonic oscillators. These states are not maximally entangled, yet they serve the protocol well.

The deformed states expand into standard oscillator states. The expansions carry free functions of the parameter q. That freedom is a knob for safety: the sender can vary the deformation. A spy then faces a moving target. The authors claim stronger cryptographic safety for the scheme. Quantum links need such knobs, since protocols must stay ahead of attack methods.
arxiv-2601-16002:
Xiang Zhang, Chen Sun, and Fuxiang Li engineer a quantum relaxation quirk in a 2026 arXiv paper. The quantum Mpemba effect is counterintuitive. A state farther from steady state can relax faster than a closer one. The authors propose building this effect with the Liouvillian skin effect. That effect arises in open quantum systems. In their open quantum chain, the skin effect sorts states by position.

States localized at the left or right edges relax in distinct ways. One side decays algebraically, the other exponentially. Choosing only the spatial profile of the start state can thus realize the effect. Simple control is the appeal: no complex driving needed. Open-system quirks like this may serve quantum devices, where relaxation speed is a design parameter.
arxiv-2601-16202:
Nguyen Thi Phuong and Nguyen Tat Thang map gas and dust in a young pair system. Their 2026 preprint uses ALMA views of the AS 205 system. The views span dust glow at two wave lengths. They also span line glow from CO and its rare kin forms. Sharp views reach scales of tens of AU in the disks.

The maps show dust spread that is not the same on each side. Gas lines trace how the pair disks move and mix. Lopsided dust hints at pull from the pair mate or a young world. Such maps guide tales of how pair stars shape world birth. The work joins dust and gas views in one study.
arxiv-2601-16402:
Shubham Parashar and Michael Fogler study flow round a thin spot in a 2D electron gas. Their 2026 preprint deals with flow in a strong field. The thin spot is a dip in charge count with a tail. That tail fades by a power law with a set grade. Past a grade of two, the tail is thin yet still shapes flow.

The pair split flow acts in thin and wet like zones. Each zone has its own rule for how flow bends round the dip. Such bends shape what probes read in Hall tests. Clear rules help read dip traits from flow maps. The work is a pure theory study of field flow.
arxiv-2601-16702:
M. N. M. van Lieshout takes on a hard choice for rescue chiefs. Crews and trucks must sit where they can help most. Past crash and call logs show where need tends to rise. Their 2026 preprint turns those logs into a place plan. The plan solves two linked tasks in a row.

First, trucks are set to posts by the log-based plan. Next, crews are set to trucks in the best match. Math proofs guard both steps of the plan. Such plans can cut wait times for aid. They also help chiefs use scarce staff with care. The work was penned in honor of Joseph Glaz.
arxiv-2601-16902:
Douglas Farenick, Roghayeh Maleki, Sofia Medina Varela, and Sushil Singla study forms built from group rules. Their forms come from free joins of two-cycles. One join pairs a 2-cycle with a k-cycle. The next joins d two-cycles in a row. Maps of these forms show their shape in a wild math world. That world is called noncommutative geometry.

Their 2026 preprint reads such maps to learn the forms' traits. Cubes and prisms in that world act in odd ways. Plain cubes gain new traits when swaps stop commuting. Such work feeds quantum math and signal work. It also grows the map of wild forms.
arxiv-2601-17302:
John H. J. Einmahl and Yi He work on confidence intervals for quantiles of mixed data. A quantile marks a cut point in data, like the median. When data come from mixed groups, sample quantiles can vary less than in the plain same-source case. That fact has been known for some time. What was missing is an interval that stays correct in large samples.

The authors give a new estimator for the reduced variance. With it, they build intervals that are correct as samples grow. Honest intervals matter in risk, health, and pay studies. Mixed data is the norm there, not the odd case. Their method lets analysts claim the gain that mixing truly gives.
arxiv-2601-17502:
Emmanouil Georgios Lionis, Craig Macdonald, and Sean MacAvaney show new tools in PyTerrier. PyTerrier is a declarative frame for search experiments. Pipelines chain steps like retrieval, reranking, and scoring. The demo adds ways to inspect those pipelines from code. It adds views that draw the pipeline for the eye. It also links pipelines to other tools.

The link uses the Model Context Protocol. That lets AI tools and apps call pipeline steps. Clear views help teams debug search systems fast. Shared links cut the glue code each lab writes alone. The work serves search research at large. It makes pipelines things you can see, test, and reuse.
arxiv-2601-17702:
Qingsen Ma and co-authors present S3-Attention for long-context inference in language models. Full context makes the KV cache grow in a linear way. Offloading to outside retrievers saves memory. But retrieved passages can match words while missing the true causal thread. S3-Attention turns memory-bound inference into a streaming task. Retrieval is endogenous, drawn from the model's own attention.

Attention-aligned picks should track what the model truly needs. That keeps long reads exact on a fixed memory budget. Book and code length inputs are the target use. A streaming design also fits live chat with long histories. The work joins memory and attention in one frame.
arxiv-2601-17802:
A team of authors presents a computing framework for finding a hard-to-see kind of tumor region in brain scans. Their 2026 preprint deals with regions that are dense with cells but do not light up under contrast dye. Doctors call them non-enhancing hypercellular regions. Finding them in routine MRI scans is an unmet need in brain tumor care, and the stakes for treatment plans are high.

The framework builds maps that show the chance that each spot in a scan is such a region. It draws on several network designs to cope with the wide range seen in real clinic data. Maps of this kind could guide doctors as they plan surgery or therapy. The work aims for tools that hold up outside the lab.
arxiv-2601-18202:
Fangyuan Xu and co-authors generate training data for deep search agents, with execution feedback in the loop. Their 2026 preprint presents SAGE.
