arxiv-2604-25802: Gao and seventeen colleagues compute heavy meson light-cone amplitudes from lattice quantum chromodynamics at the continuum limit. The work improves greatly on their first study. Using heavy-quark large-momentum effective theory plus lattice moments, they analyze six ensembles across lattice spacings and pion masses. That supports careful continuum, chiral, and infinite-momentum fits to the physical point. Smeared sources and tuned operators sharpen signals for nonlocal signals. Both QCD and heavy-quark theory results follow, with the D meson amplitude peaking at low fraction.
arxiv-2604-25902: Pustejovsky argues that geometric algebra offers a better base for language meaning than standard linear algebra. Vector and matrix methods succeed in practice but struggle with composition, type handling, and clarity. His Functional Geometric Algebra framework adds types and composition to geometric algebra, aiding inference, transformation, and clarity, while staying compatible with distributional learning. A worked example shows operator-level contrasts. The key claim is structure, not just size: geometric algebra expands an n-dimensional space into a multivector algebra holding concepts and their interactions together.
arxiv-2604-26102: Zhang and eleven colleagues redesign the code-editing interface for software-engineering agents. They split it into a Viewer fetching task-relevant code on demand and an Editor making changes from high-level plans. That stops exploratory viewing and strict edit formatting from crowding one window. Resolve rate on a verified benchmark rises roughly two points, and inference cost falls nearly eighteen percent. Training a small editor to choose formats adds about thirteen points, bringing an 8B open-source editor to parity with a frontier nano-scale model.
arxiv-2604-26902: Greinecker and Vocke study stability in many-to-many matching markets where each agent is individually small, with outcomes as joint distributions over agent traits and contract choices. Traits may range over any Polish space, a broad class of well-behaved spaces. They give a mechanical method for lifting existence results from finite matching models to large ones, for many stability notions. In particular, they show that tree-stable and pairwise-stable outcomes exist.
arxiv-2604-27002: Song and five colleagues present a black-box membership inference attack on video language models, asking whether an auditor can tell if a video trained the model. Auditors see only generated text, while the membership signal tangles with motion complexity and temporal span. Their attack couples temperature-perturbed generation with video difficulty features, querying the model at low and high temperatures and measuring drift between outputs. Tested on LLaVA-Video-7B-Qwen2-Video-Only, it reaches a member inference AUC of 0.68, showing video models are vulnerable to such attacks.
arxiv-2604-27102: Adjokatse and eight colleagues apply unsupervised learning to detect anomalous heavy-metal contamination in soils from twelve waste sites and controls in Ghana's Central Region. Eight metals were measured with health risk indices, including Hazard Index and cancer risk. Isolation Forest and PCA reconstruction error each flag 12 anomalous samples of 78, while DBSCAN finds none. A consensus approach isolates six robust anomalies, all at site S3. They show about 70 to 80 percent higher mean Hazard Index values than normal samples, all above the HI equals 1 threshold.
arxiv-2604-27402: Nesterov turns his earlier work on prime-modular monodromy for cyclic covers of the projective line into a new payoff. Whole families of PSL and PSU groups appear as Galois groups over the rationals. For the first time, one fully explicit infinite family lets the field degree over the prime field grow without bound while the group stays distinct from its PGL and PGU counterparts. The build thus parts these Galois groups from their projective linear and unitary kin.
arxiv-2604-27502: Devanand and four colleagues track X-ray change in the TeV blazar PG 1553+113 from XMM-Newton data spanning 2001 to 2024. They fit 30 observations with absorbed power-law and log-parabola models: 14 fit the log-parabola form well, one more favours it, and 15 fit the power-law form. Two observations show strong signs of an added inverse Compton component, one weaker signs. Joint optical and X-ray fits place synchrotron peaks from about 5 to 49 electron volts, pointing to shifts in jet particle acceleration or cooling as the driver.
arxiv-2604-27602: Ou and Wang analyze 17 years of Fermi data plus archival Chandra X-ray data on the unassociated source 4FGL J1626.0-4917. They find extended GeV emission around it, modeled as a Gaussian disk about a quarter of a degree in radius, with extension significance of 7.2 sigma. The diffuse emission may come from accelerated protons hitting protons in surrounding gas, though a leptonic origin cannot be ruled out. X-rays reveal a point source inside it, with possible counterparts including the cluster NGC 6134 and a supernova remnant.
arxiv-2604-28102: Corrêa, Nascimento and Moniz build FiLMMeD, a single neural solver for twenty-four multi-depot vehicle routing variants, a logistics problem central to e-commerce. A Transformer encoder gains feature-wise linear modulation, which conditions internal representations on the active constraint set. Preference optimisation and a curriculum that ramps constraint complexity complete the design. Tested on dozens of routing variants, including novel multi-depot forms and single-depot problems, it consistently beats state-of-the-art baselines.
arxiv-2605-00002:
Vajahat Karim Khan, Vijendra Kumar Varshney, and Md Kalimuddin Ahmad design neurodynamic systems that solve mixed variational inequalities in fixed time. Such inequalities model a wide class of equilibrium and optimization problems. Their systems are networks of neurons whose states evolve until they settle on a solution, and the settling is guaranteed by a deadline set in advance, not merely eventually.

They develop first-order proximal neurodynamic models, including time-varying versions, that converge in fixed time from any starting point. The proofs rest on strong pseudomonotonicity and Lipschitz continuity, worked through with Lyapunov stability theory, and they give explicit bounds on the settling time. Robustness against bounded noise is also analyzed. The framework is demonstrated on composite and minimax optimization problems, with numerical examples of the convergence behavior.
arxiv-2605-00102:
Lisa-Marie Zessner, Robert H Cameron, Sami K Solanki, and Damien Przybylski simulate how solar prominences form. Prominences are cool, dense plasma structures floating in the hot solar corona, and they are found all through the Sun's outer air, yet their formation mechanism has stayed unclear. The team runs fully three-dimensional simulations that include the physics of all the Sun's layers of air.

With suitable starting conditions for the magnetic field, prominences form self-consistently in the model. Formation begins when a dense plasma seed is randomly ejected from the chromosphere into the corona. The prominence then grows by further injections from below combined with inflowing coronal plasma that condenses. The simulated prominences match observed ones in kind, and the results stress the role of dynamics at and below the surface, also for eruption studies.
arxiv-2605-00802:
Nir Goldman, Artem Samtsevych, and Chiara Panosetti build fast computer models for cerium and cerium oxide, materials whose behavior shifts across several crystal forms. Their approach, Density Functional Tight Binding, aims to predict electronic band structure and material properties at lower cost than full calculations. Models are built with two common levels of electronic theory, including one hybrid form.

A many-body repulsion term fitted with the Chebyshev Interaction Model gets the energy order of the cerium forms right. Notably, training used only small molecular dynamics runs from a single phase. The authors argue the resulting models stay transferable, so they can predict both electronic and material behavior beyond the narrow cases used to fit them.
arxiv-2605-01002:
Rin Oikawa, Kenji Toma, and Shigeo S. Kimura study how plasma enters black hole jets through pair production driven by magnetic reconnection. Active galactic nuclei launch collimated relativistic outflows, but the origin of the plasma feeding the jet remains poorly understood. Recent three-dimensional simulations suggest non-axisymmetric reconnection near the black hole produces high-energy photons that collide to create electron-positron pairs.

Using general relativistic ray tracing, the authors calculate the spatial spread of pair creation, accounting for photon paths and collision angles in curved spacetime. Their scenario can naturally supply enough plasma to explain observed radio emission from the M87 jet, even with photon anisotropy included. Black hole spin strongly shapes where pairs appear. That in turn affects jet acceleration and very high energy emission.
arxiv-2605-01102:
Jinpai Zhao, Albert Cerrone, Joannes Westerink, and Clint Dawson present a multi-agent prototype for hydrodynamics questions, arguing that single-agent language-model workflows saturate their context as tool details and observations pile up. Their system coordinates specialized agents through a Layer Execution Graph. A planner builds query-specific execution plans from natural-language routing rules, while specialist agents work under strict tool allowlists in complementary data roles.

Between layers, consolidator agents fuse parallel outputs into concise briefs, and a reporter synthesizes the final answer, with provenance logged for every tool call. On thirty-seven queries across six complexity categories, the prototype reaches high factual precision with a full pass rate. Accuracy stays high under parallel tracks and degrades gracefully when individual data sources are lost.
arxiv-2605-01202:
Alan Edelman and two co-authors present an exact sampling algorithm for Pfaffian point processes, a class arising in random matrix theory and combinatorics. Their method rests on a skew-symmetric analogue of the Cholesky factorization. It enables efficient sampling of a wide range of quantities, including eigenvalues of the orthogonal and symplectic ensembles that model many random matrix systems.

The authors also introduce a symplectic Arnoldi method for computing skew-orthogonal polynomials for a general weight function. That method efficiently constructs the matrix-valued kernels arising in the relevant polynomial families. Numerical examples include a corner growth model and finite Gaussian cases of both kinds. Airy point patterns also appear, illustrating the approach broadly.
arxiv-2605-01302:
Peiyang Liu and five co-authors argue that retrieval systems for language models should not chase relevance alone. In real choices, user queries often carry biases, such as false premises or a wish to have a prior view confirmed. A system that maximizes relevance then pulls in flattering evidence that backs the bias and feeds false outputs, a failure the authors call the Relevance-Robustness Gap. Their method, CoRM-RAG, aligns retrieval with choice safety instead of mere similarity.

A training protocol simulates biased queries, and its lessons are distilled into a small scoring module called an Evidence Critic. The critic picks documents strong enough to steer the model toward correct answers even when the query is loaded. On choice benchmarks, the method beats strong dense retrievers and model-based rerankers in hostile settings. It also supports risk-aware abstention, letting the system hold back when the evidence is weak.
arxiv-2605-01502:
William Stevens, Mohit Prabhushankar, and Ghassan AlRegib estimate where a segmentation network is unsure of itself, in one pass. Knowing doubt matters for trust, but the trusted ways to measure it run the model many times or train whole ensembles, which is too heavy for dense, pixel-level tasks.

Their method, RADMI, watches the inside of the network instead. It measures how much consecutive decoder layers agree in information terms: where layers must merge clashing context, such as at class borders, the score rises, and so does true doubt. On a seismic facies test set, the single-pass score tracks ensemble doubt more closely than any other one-pass rival, beating the next best by clear margins on two correlation measures. The maps it draws are sharp and hug the borders, with no change to the network itself.
arxiv-2605-01702:
Sejun Park, Yeachan Park, and Geonho Hwang ask whether neural networks still enjoy their classic approximation promise once real computer arithmetic enters. The textbook theorem says some network can match any smooth function and its gradients together. It assumes exact real numbers and flawless operations, while real machines round every step to floating point.

Under floating-point arithmetic, with gradients taken by the automatic differentiation that practice uses, the pair of results survives in a strong form. Given any floating-point target function, a floating-point network can be built whose values match the target and whose automatic gradients are freely prescribable. The extension covers several target functions at once, one network matching all values while its composed gradients realize each gradient family, under mild conditions. The theorem holds for common activations, from ReLU to tanh, closing a gap between theory's ideal reals and the rounding world.
arxiv-2605-01802:
Yaakov Friedman works out what gravitational waves should look like inside Extended Relativity, an alternative frame he develops. In that frame the deviation tensor, the field that records how nearby paths bend apart, is the basic observable. The question is polarization: which wiggle patterns a passing wave can carry, and in what mix.

Starting from a point source, he derives the radiation field of a compact binary far away. All variation rides on the retarded phase, and the tensor pattern depends only on the source's tilt. Detector answers then unify: interferometers read a tidal matrix built from the tensor's second derivatives, while pulsar timing arrays reduce to boundary terms set by the wave's projection at each end. The headline is constraint: tensor, vector, and scalar parts are not free, since geometry fixes their relative sizes, yielding a narrow family of allowed states and correlation patterns to hunt for.
arxiv-2605-02002:
Yi Han studies how fast Glauber dynamics settles for the random field Ising model on graphs where each vertex has bounded degree. In that model, spins interact as neighbours while a random external field acts at each site. When the field distribution is sufficiently spread out, Han proves the dynamics mixes in polynomial time with high probability over the field.

The proof flows from a Poincaré inequality. The setting covers a Griffiths phase where correlations decay on average but pointwise contraction fails because weak fields allow cold behaviour. Fast mixing under large disorder was known before only on the integer lattice. Under a bounded-field condition, Han also proves a modified log-Sobolev result in the full paper.
arxiv-2605-02202:
Ji Guo and colleagues propose a clean-label backdoor attack on vision-language models that hides its poisoned examples in plain sight. Past attacks added a visual trigger and changed the text label, so poisoned items stood out as image-text mismatches. Their method, CBV, uses a diffusion model to generate natural-looking poisoned examples instead.

CBV alters the score during the diffusion model's reverse generation, guiding it to produce images that carry trigger features. Text from the triggered images guides generation as a second signal, strengthening the attack. Because labels stay clean and images look natural, detection is harder. The work is a security study of models used for captioning and visual question answering.
arxiv-2605-02502:
Gilda Rech Bansimba and Regis Freguin Babindamana present GuardSec, a live web platform that helps ordinary users in Africa check for online fraud. Most security tools, they argue, are built for expert analysts with fast, stable connections. GuardSec needs only a browser, with no sign-up or key, and returns a verdict in under five seconds.

A user can check a web address, site, phone number, email, or business for signs of fraud. A second tool, called Mon Empreinte, audits the visitor's own connection: network address, location, provider, device traits, and twelve safety indicators. The aim is practical defense for people the security field often leaves out, grounded in local threat patterns rather than lab scores alone.
arxiv-2605-02602:
Xinyi Wen and four co-authors present PowerSINDy, a framework for learning the rules of power grid frequency motion directly from real data. Grid frequency must stay near its target, and its dynamics reflect the balance of supply and demand. A method called SINDy finds governing equations by assuming only a few terms matter, but it is usually shown on clean simulated data.

PowerSINDy adds time-dependent terms and is applied to measured frequency data from the large grids of continental Europe and South Korea, which behave quite differently. The framework recovers dynamics for both noisy, real systems. Three sparse regression strategies are benchmarked to fit the terms. The work tests whether equation learning can survive contact with messy operational data from major power systems.
arxiv-2605-02702:
Pierre Granier and three co-authors demonstrate a covert hardware attack that reads Fast Ethernet traffic from a distance. Electromagnetic eavesdropping on displays is well known, but other links were thought to leak too little. Reflector attacks solve this by planting a tiny Trojan. The implant does not emit anything itself. Instead, it changes how strongly the target reflects a probing signal, in step with the data on a wire.

Prior work covered video links and slow peripheral interfaces. The new implant targets the 100BASE-TX Ethernet standard and its encoded signaling, in a compact build. A dedicated pipeline demodulates and interprets the reflected signal, correcting radio-channel errors to recover as much traffic as possible. The result extends a known spy technique to a common high-speed network.
arxiv-2605-02902:
Yu Xie and Ying Qi design an interface for a common, underserved state in content apps: the feed feels stale, yet the user cannot say what they want instead. Feeds serve passive browsing and search serves clear queries, but vague intent sits between them. Their system, Red-Rec, steps in proactively after a spell of browsing, rather than waiting to be asked.

Red-Rec sums up patterns in the current feed, offers clickable directions to explore, asks at most one follow-up question, then blends new content in gradually. A formative study motivated the low-effort design: users notice staleness but struggle to name alternatives. In a lab study against a passive feed, search, and a user-started chat, the AI-started design broadened exploration, raised serendipity ratings, and lowered effort, with users typing very little.
arxiv-2605-03402:
K. Hansen and twenty-four co-authors collect forward-looking reflections on cluster science from speakers at the 2025 DEAMN workshop in Erice. Clusters, bound groups of atoms or molecules, sit between single molecules and bulk matter, and the field's open problems span electrons, structure, and dynamics.

Rather than standard proceedings papers, the contributions offer fresh personal perspectives on work presented at the workshop on electrons in atomic and molecular nanoclusters. As a roadmap article, the collection maps where contributors see the field heading and which questions deserve effort next. It serves readers who want expert judgment on the state and future of cluster research.
arxiv-2605-03702:
Jakob Krebs, Daniel Amir, Shir Landau Feibish, and Mark Silberstein present SpraySense, a system for detecting gray failures in the huge networks used for distributed machine learning training. Gray failures degrade performance without fully breaking links, and they are notoriously hard to find in clusters of tens of thousands of graphics processors. Adaptive routing, which spreads traffic across many paths, makes them worse.

SpraySense works passively, exploiting the statistical behavior of adaptive routing and load balancing together with flow-level information. Discrepancies in how packets spray across paths reveal trouble early. Detecting failures before they seriously hurt applications enables preemptive rerouting and protects expensive training runs.
arxiv-2605-03802:
Peter Manshausen, Noah Brenowitz, Julius Berner, Karthik Kashinath, and Mike Pritchard extract extreme-event likelihoods from a diffusion-based climate emulator called Climate in a Bottle, or cBottle. It generates atmospheric states consistent with solar position and sea surface temperatures, and it can be guided to produce extreme events such as tropical cyclones over chosen locations. Diffusion models learn the probability density of their training data.

Comparing densities under guided and unguided runs shows how much more likely guidance made a cyclone. Those odds ratios enable importance sampling from the cyclone distribution. That cuts the standard error of the estimates compared with plain Monte Carlo sampling. The authors also discuss early results and limits for attribution-style tests.
arxiv-2605-04302:
Abigail R. Jones, Kisun Lee, and Jose Israel Rodriguez study rigid homotopies, a method for solving polynomial systems by tracking solutions along carefully chosen paths. Such methods underpin average-case algorithms for a famous problem about how hard polynomial solving should be.

The authors prove a new complexity result for systems whose polynomials are given as short sums of powers, a compact form known as a Waring representation. They also report the first computational experiments with a preliminary implementation of rigid homotopies. The work connects the cost of sampling points on algebraic varieties to the structure used to describe the equations.
arxiv-2605-04702:
Yuanzhi Wang and nine co-authors present a method for generating text-guided videos that keep a person's facial identity stable, even when the head turns far or the face is partly hidden. Identity-preserving video generation is popular for creative uses, but large pose changes and occlusions often distort who the person looks like.

Their framework refines and aligns facial poses across views using a shared pose dictionary and a constraint that identity should stay invariant as pose varies. Single-view inputs are mapped into a global pose representation with explicit angle embeddings, giving the generator a pose-faithful prior. They also curate a dedicated video data set rich in pose diversity, and report leading results in experiments.
arxiv-2605-05602:
Attention, the core operation of transformer models, is expensive to compute over long inputs. Edo Liberty, Alexandr Andoni, and Eldar Kleiner prove that a small subset of the keys and values can stand in for the whole set. Such a subset is called a coreset, and theirs is nearly as small as theory allows.

For queries of bounded size, the coreset reproduces attention outputs within a set error. Its size beats the best previously known results. They also prove a matching-style lower bound, showing that noticeably smaller coresets cannot exist in general.
arxiv-2605-05902:
Code models write comments and documentation in many languages, but evaluation still assumes English. Jonathan Katzy and seven co-authors measure non-English developer support directly. They test five code language models on comment generation across Dutch, English, Greek, Polish, and Chinese, languages spanning several families and writing systems.

An open-coding study of 12,500 generated comments produced a human-annotated dataset and a taxonomy of failure types. The authors also audit whether current automatic evaluation methods can be trusted on non-English output at all. Their findings expose where multilingual software engineering support is real and where it is marketing.
arxiv-2605-06102:
Sven Jarohs, Abhrojyoti Sen, and Tobias Weth study families of s-harmonic functions as the order s shrinks toward zero. Such functions solve a fractional equation tied to the fractional Laplacian inside a smooth bounded region. The paper pursues two questions: how these families behave in the small order limit, and whether they vary smoothly as the order itself changes.

Most results concern the matching Poisson problem, where an outside condition fixes the family through a given bounded function. Both the limit behavior and the smoothness in the order can be expressed through the logarithmic Laplacian applied to extensions of that outside data. From those formulas the authors deduce pointwise monotonicity of the solutions in the order parameter. The results cover a large class of outside functions.
arxiv-2605-06302:
Pierre-Antoine Graham, Filippo Gaggioli, and Liang Fu explain the origin of an electronic quasicrystal found in wide quantum wells. The homogeneous electron gas hosts strongly correlated phases that form the vocabulary of many body physics, and recent variational Monte Carlo work found an unexpected phase there. Two layers of Wigner crystal, twisted by thirty degrees against each other, settle into a quasicrystalline order that classical reasoning did not predict.

The authors compute zero point energy corrections across candidate bilayer crystal arrangements. Quantum fluctuations reshape the energy landscape enough to destabilize the classical honeycomb state. Over a broad parameter range they instead select the thirty degree quasicrystalline state as the ground state. Zero point motion thus emerges as the stabilizing mechanism, opening a route to moiré physics driven by quantum effects.
arxiv-2605-06402:
Hanzuo Liu and six co-authors sparsify large language models in a semi structured pattern that real hardware can accelerate. Semi structured sparsity promises speed with native support, but post training pruning in that pattern usually degrades quality badly through strong structural coupling. Recovery typically demands large scale sparse retraining, which eats the savings the pruning was meant to create. SparseForge attacks that trade off by optimizing the sparsity mask itself instead of the retraining budget.

SparseForge pairs Hessian aware importance scores with soft masks that anneal progressively into the final hardware ready pattern. On a seven billion parameter model under two in four sparsity, it reached average zero shot accuracy above the dense model. It used only a small fraction of the retraining tokens a leading method needed to reach a slightly higher score, and the gains held across model families.
arxiv-2605-06502:
Quentin Hillebrand, Jacob Imola, Rasmus Pagh, and Sia Sejer show new uses for the discrete Laplace mechanism, a classic privacy tool that adds geometric noise to counts. Post-processing its output, they obtain an unbiased estimator for a broad class of fast-growing but controlled functions of the original data, extending a recent result for the continuous Laplace mechanism.

Post-processing can also reproduce the output distributions of the Laplace and Staircase mechanisms at identical privacy levels, making the discrete version preferable whenever data are discrete. Variance bounds are given, and the estimator is often computable in linear or polynomial time for structured functions. Uses include profile estimation and federated analysis.
arxiv-2605-07002:
Siyu Zhou and four co-authors address a practical problem in auditing generative AI: testing is expensive, so auditors choose cases adaptively. That flexibility breaks classical statistics, because sample sizes are tiny and stopping decisions happen during collection. The authors ask what rigorous conclusions such audits can still support.

They frame auditing as two dueling claims, one from the model side and one from the auditor side, tested by a betting-style method. Their procedures keep error control valid at any stopping point and sometimes reach firm conclusions with about twenty cases. Passing such an audit, they prove, can certify that a system is broadly robust.
arxiv-2605-07502:
Ying Zhong works on a counting function from number theory called the broken k-diamond partition function, introduced by Andrews and Paule. Earlier papers had studied inequalities for this function only in the first two cases. Zhong asks what can be said for every value of the parameter k, not just those two.

An exact formula for the function comes first, valid for all k, followed by an approximate formula with an explicit error bound. From these, the function is shown to satisfy the Turán and Laguerre inequalities of every order for large inputs, with asymptotic complete monotonicity. It is also proved log-concave once k is at least three and the input is large enough.
arxiv-2605-07802:
S. Sagar Maurya and four co-authors report measurements on a metastable state of doubly ionized thorium that could anchor a new kind of nuclear clock. The appeal of this electronic state is that it would let lasers excite the famous low-energy thorium-229 nuclear resonance while sidestepping the leading hyperfine interactions that shift clock frequencies.

The state has no easy radiative decay route, so the team populated it by laser excitation through a higher level and watched its fluorescence. They measured the isotope shift of the level between thorium-232 and thorium-229, probing how electron and nuclear charge distributions interact. In their trap, collisions limited the state's lifetime, but in ultrahigh vacuum it could serve as a clock largely immune to field-induced shifts.
arxiv-2605-07902:
Yixin Chen and Alan Kuhnle extend greedy algorithm guarantees to submodular objectives that can go negative. Submodular functions, which capture shrinking returns, sit under many machine learning goals, and the classic greedy guarantee needs monotonicity and non-negativity. Real goals with costs break both, and earlier work patched each flaw only separately, for special cases.

The authors extend the curvature parameter, which measures departure from linearity, to all such functions at once. A greedy algorithm with pruning then achieves a curvature-controlled guarantee for any submodular function. It is the first beyond monotonicity and non-negativity, recovering the classic bound in the monotone case and beating the best known uniform ratio in part of the non-monotone regime. A multilinear variant covers general combinatorial constraints, and experiments on design, coverage, and feature selection support the theory.
arxiv-2605-08002:
Fabio Centofanti, Mia Hubert, and Peter Rousseeuw propose a regression estimator built for messy multivariate data. Ordinary least squares breaks under outliers. Outliers come in two kinds. Some are whole bad cases. Others are single contaminated cells in the predictor or response tables. Modern data add missing values and high dimensions on top.

Their cellMR estimator handles casewise and cellwise outliers at once. It also handles missing entries and many variables. It builds on a cellwise robust covariance estimate, with ridge regularization for stability. A companion bootstrap procedure, cellBoot, uses indirect inference. It gives confidence intervals that stay valid in the limit. The package brings robust multivariate regression closer to routine use.
arxiv-2605-08102:
Claudio Meggio, Johan Pensar, and Riccardo De Bin present PathBoost, a gradient boosting method that predicts properties of whole graphs from paths inside them. An earlier version was built for one chemistry application. PathBoost widens it in three directions while keeping the learned features readable as concrete paths.

The extensions add binary classification with a logistic loss, fold multiple node and edge attributes into the path features through a prefix decomposition, and choose anchor nodes automatically from attribute diversity. Against graph neural networks and graph kernels on several benchmarks, PathBoost won on about half and matched the rest, doing especially well on graphs with larger average size.
arxiv-2605-08302:
Wenbin Wei, Ruixiang Gao, Suyuan Yao, Xuanzhen Zhao, and coauthors build a Parkinson's assessment system that knows its limits. Real-world digital testing mixes many inputs. It mixes speech, gait, wearable motion, mobility tasks, and clinical variables. The inputs come from unlike devices, with incomplete labels. A bare accuracy score hides the risk of a wrong call.

Their SGC-RML model maps every input into a shared eight-node symptom space. Seven nodes are clinical symptoms, and one is a reliability node. A symptom atlas unifies motor and non-motor signs. Uncertainty estimates and conformal calibration guide selective routing. The system can predict severity, refuse a call, or ask for a retest. It also says which symptom dimensions drove the call.
arxiv-2605-08402:
Soares studies how a strange quantum link, called entanglement, can be made and spread across spin chains. Spin chains are a hopeful route for quantum computing, where qubits replace the bits of classical hardware. The thesis, written for a physics masters at the Universidade Estadual de Ponta Grossa, compares two ways of making that link.

Way one uses switching weak and strong links that produce a band pattern, which gives a simple trimer model view. Way two uses even edge links and virtual excitations to link the chain ends directly. The virtual excitation way wins on speed, link strength, and toughness against build flaws and noise. Simple model cuts and open quantum systems methods explain why shared links survive in solid state devices. The virtual coupling way looks ready for real tests in scalable quantum tech.
arxiv-2605-08702:
Guodong Ding and Angela Yao personalize vision language models for several user concepts at once, such as a specific pet, person, or object appearing together. Each concept is taught separately as a small adapter with its own token, keeping concepts untangled and the base model untouched, with no joint training examples required. Their Gate-and-Merge framework combines the adapters directly in weight space at test time.

A gating step reads text and image cues to switch on only helpful modules, while merging keeps just the strongest and most consistent updates to protect each concept's identity. Tests show steady gains in single and combined concept tasks. Personalized vision gains composition without retraining.
arxiv-2605-08902:
Mengyuan Tian, Qiyan Zhao, Yanan Wang, and Da-Han Wang align pictures with text in vision language models according to how much information each piece actually carries. Uniform alignment treats every text tag and image block alike, yet density and scope differ and shift dynamically, so interactions stay coarse and fine details wash out. Their framework learns a matching function that assigns varying numbers and sizes of image regions to each text element.

A second module progressively folds in high resolution visual detail during alignment. Across several benchmarks, downstream accuracy rises significantly while computing cost falls, countering the usual belief that finer alignment must cost more. Multimodal systems gain precision that adapts to content instead of grinding uniformly.
arxiv-2605-09202:
Li and two colleagues tackle joint SVD type block splits, pulling out diagonal parts that capture part of several matrices' total mass. Joint SVD type block splits seek one pair of unitary matrices turning several matrices to the same block diagonal form at once, which in general does not exist exactly. Their NPDo approach seeks the shared top block diagonal parts, paired with Gauss-Seidel type updates.

The authors show NPDo with Gauss-Seidel type updates reaches a steady point from any start while the goal value rises steadily. When each block size is one by one, the problem becomes finding a top partial joint SVD split. Test runs show the approach works well, which also covers uses like direction of arrival estimation, image processing, computer vision, and blind source separation. The work gives a sound route for a problem where exact joint diagonal splits are in general impossible.
arxiv-2605-09302:
Amballa and three colleagues study how to sample posteriors for inverse problems in discrete state spaces, with discrete diffusion models as generative priors. Continuous diffusion models serve inverse problems widely, but their discrete counterparts are underexplored, and current discrete samplers lean on continuous relaxations, Gibbs-style updates, or single-process tricks.

Their Discrete Langevin-Inspired Posterior Sampler, ΔLPS, uses gradient information to spot promising discrete moves while staying inside the discrete state space. The method updates all token dimensions in parallel and works with any training style of discrete diffusion prior, masked diffusion, uniform-state diffusion, and beyond. On image restoration across MNIST, CIFAR, and FFHQ plus spatial mapping, across linear, nonlinear, and blind inverse problems, it beats recent discrete diffusion posterior samplers and rivals strong continuous diffusion solvers. The results point to fully discrete, gradient-informed samplers as a scalable, general path for inverse problems over discrete representations.
arxiv-2605-09502:
Yuan and four colleagues test a quiet assumption behind chain of thought prompting. The assumption is that written reasoning mirrors internal computation. Probing hidden states during reasoning, they find models internally detect their own errors. Outwardly, though, the models sound confident about those same errors. Wrong traces carry confidence almost identical to correct ones. A text only classifier sees far less than a probe on hidden states. Most wrong traces sit in an unfaithful zone of high confidence and high internal error.

Crucially, the hidden signal cannot fix what it detects. Activation steering fails. Probe guided selection among outputs fails. Self correction fails, and activation patching destroys output coherence entirely. The authors conclude the signal is diagnostic rather than causal. It reads out computation quality instead of offering a lever to redirect it. That draws a boundary for interpretability work on reasoning.
arxiv-2605-09702:
Li challenged the usual habit of keeping only the best judges when scoring language models. Multi-judge panels, including LLM judges and reward models, are normally curated down to the most accurate members. Li compared that accuracy-ranked selection with keeping the full panel, holding the scoring and calibration steps fixed, on four labeled pairwise-evaluation benchmarks.

The full panel won consistently for calibrated probabilistic scoring, which asks how sure the verdict should be, not just which answer wins. On RewardBench2, the full panel reached a negative log-likelihood of 0.006 against 0.013 for the top-five panel, roughly halving the calibration error. Even below-chance judges helped when their biases could be learned and their signals added something new. Keep weak judges, Li argues, if they can be calibrated.
arxiv-2605-10202:
Tim Tomov and three colleagues address a quiet flaw in how language models choose their answers. Decoding usually follows the model's predicted distribution, so any mismatch with the true distribution yields suboptimal choices. Calibrating over all possible free-form outputs is intractable, since the space of word sequences is combinatorially vast. Their 2026 paper introduces task-aware calibration as a way around that wall.

Many tasks let free-form outputs be read as outcomes in a smaller latent space, such as class labels, integers, or sets. The authors calibrate the model's distribution in that task-induced space instead. They prove that Minimum Bayes Risk decoding on the calibrated latent distribution is the optimal strategy given the model's latent beliefs. Across tasks and baselines the method consistently improved generation quality. They also propose Task Calibration Error, a metric for the loss caused by miscalibration.
arxiv-2605-10302:
Pedro M. P. Curvo and three colleagues offer a new control knob for generative models: examples instead of retraining. Controllable generation usually needs fine-tuning, auxiliary networks, or test-time search. Their 2026 paper shows that flow matching, a leading generative paradigm, admits a different interface: adaptation through a reference set.

For deterministic interpolants, the velocity field is governed solely by a conditional endpoint mean, so shifting that mean shifts the flow itself. Reference-Mean Guidance works out an endpoint-mean shift from a reference bank and uses it on a frozen FLUX.2-klein model, steering color, identity, style, and structure while prompt, seed, and weights stay fixed. Semi-Parametric Guidance carries the same idea forward through a mean anchor and learned refiner. It reaches the same quality as an unconditional DiT-B/4 on AFHQv2 while letting the reference set swap at inference time.
arxiv-2605-10402:
Marc Lackenby settles a question from the Kourovka Notebook, a famous list of open problems in group theory. A finite presentation of a finite group is called just finite if removing any single relation leaves a presentation for an infinite group. Barnea asked, as Problem 21.10, whether every finite group admits such a presentation. His 2026 note answers yes.

Lackenby proves the stronger claim that every finite group admits a finite, just finite presentation, via results about groups with Property FA, Serre's fixed-point property for actions on trees. The note also treats just-(FA) presentations, where dropping any relation destroys that property. Significant assistance came from the Google DeepMind AI co-mathematician tool, as the methodology section details. Readers get a short, sharp resolution of a long-standing question, with a stronger theorem behind it.
arxiv-2605-10502:
Benjamin Bode and Paula Truöl describe a class of links in knot theory. T-positive links sit inside strongly quasipositive links as a subset that strictly holds all non-split braid positive links. Like Baader's description of positive links as just the strongly quasipositive and homogeneous links, the authors show T-positive links are just the strongly quasipositive links that are closures of T-homogeneous braids. Their 2026 paper proves that description.

The result adds to earlier descriptions by Rudolph and Banfield, who described these links as edges of positive Hopf-plumbed baskets or closures of staircase braids. The authors examine how these links behave under cabling operations and connected sums. They show every strongly quasipositive fibered knot up to 12 crossings is T-positive. They also compare T-positivity with other positive kinds for links and compile open questions.
arxiv-2605-10702:
Norman Anderson and co-authors report a lab study of how ChatGPT support shapes coders grasping and changing code new to them. Ten advanced student coders, five with AI support and five without, extended a sizable software system. Analysis used Polya's four problem-solving phases and 25 codes built from data for distinct problem-solving behaviours, cross-checked on think-aloud records, code changes, web searches, and language-model prompts. Prior research stressed productivity and code quality over underlying mental processes.

Unexpectedly, while AI-group coders repeatedly offloaded aspects of the process to the tool, every problem-solving behaviour appeared in both groups. Nine of ten got stuck, but differed in how they got stuck and unstuck. The authors identify seven causes of getting stuck. They show how AI sometimes helped and sometimes hindered getting unstuck. This offers a mental-process view of AI-assisted programming beyond output measures.
arxiv-2605-11002:
Xinkai Zhang and six colleagues build MT-JailBench, a modular benchmark for multi-turn jailbreak attacks on language models. Multi-turn attacks steer conversations gradually toward unsafe answers, but past evaluations mixed different budgets, judges, retry rules, and strategy generators, muddying which attack actually wins.

MT-JailBench splits each attack into five parts: scoring rule, attack plan, prompt writing, prompt refining, and flow control, so methods compare under fixed conditions. Fixing turns, retries, interactions, plans, and judges shifts attack rankings a lot, and prompt writing drives most of the spread. Safety researchers get fair comparisons plus a part-level map of what makes jailbreaks succeed.
arxiv-2605-11102:
Shourya Bose, Helgi Hilmarsson, and Dhruv Suri present Newton's Lantern, a reinforcement-learning pipeline for fine-tuning AC power-flow warm-start models. Neural warm starts slash Newton-Raphson iterations for grid power-flow solutions, but supervised versions generalize poorly on heavily loaded cases near voltage collapse.

The team proves a lower bound on iteration count that depends on warm-start error direction rather than magnitude. The bound goes vacuous as the power-flow Jacobian's smallest singular value shrinks, pinpointing the supervised failure mode near saddle-node bifurcation. Newton's Lantern pairs group relative policy optimization with a reward model learned from perturbations of base predictions, using iteration count itself as supervision. Across IEEE 118-bus and larger grid benchmarks, it alone converges on every test snapshot with the smallest mean iteration count. Grid operators get warm starts that hold up under stress.
arxiv-2605-11202:
Yunze Zhao and four colleagues present GRIEF, a greybox fuzzer for LLM inference engines. Timed multi-request traces serve as its first-class inputs. LLM serving systems combine KV cache, batching, prefix sharing, speculative decoding, adapters, and multi-tenant scheduling. This mix creates shared-state behavior that shows up only under realistic concurrent workloads.

GRIEF uses light oracles to spot crashes, hangs, performance pathologies, and silent output corruption. Controlled replay with log-probability checks confirms reproducible serving-layer failures. Across early runs on vLLM and SGLang, it finds 15 vulnerabilities, 10 confirmed by engine developers, including 2 CVEs. These span KV-cache isolation failures, cross-request performance interference, and crash or liveness bugs. Serving-system teams get proof that concurrency, caching, and state reuse form a first-class security and reliability boundary.
arxiv-2605-11302: Ganju and three colleagues study language generation under a global preference ordering on strings, adding timeliness to the usual demand for breadth. A string counts only if produced before a deadline set by its rank, so higher-ranked strings must come earlier. They prove no generator can be timely in the strong sense for eventually consistent cases. Under the mildest relaxation, a hallucination rate that vanishes over time, they achieve optimal density for any superlinear deadline, and show linear deadlines remain impossible.
arxiv-2605-11902: Catharina Ochsner and Heinz Pampel investigate why scholarly blogs remain outside digital preservation workflows, putting long-term access at risk. Drawing on Star and Ruhleder's dimensions of information infrastructure, they read 13 interviews with bloggers about preservation challenges and needs. Participants pointed to existing bodies already working to preserve the scholarly record. They say those bodies should extend their scope to blogs.
arxiv-2605-12202: Mustapha Essahraoui and three colleagues rebuild an unknown cavity edge under a Robin condition by a limited coupled complex method. They recast the crowded problem as a complex-valued value problem with a Robin rule coupling the Cauchy data on the edge. The rebuild cuts a cost built from the image part of the answer, with limits from state bounds to stay steady under noise. Shape slopes and gradients are derived, and the problem is solved with ADMM and the finite element method, tested in trials.
arxiv-2605-12302: Braun and three colleagues settle the sharp degree bound in the real Jacobian conjecture for maps of the plane. The question asks how large the degree of the first component can be while a nowhere-zero Jacobian still forces the map to be one-to-one. They prove injectivity holds at degree six, then build a non-injective example at degree seven with a nowhere-vanishing Jacobian. Together with earlier results up to degree five, seven emerges as the smallest degree where counterexamples can occur.
arxiv-2605-12802: Feffer and Tokarski study when strategic know-how learned in one mechanism carries over to another. They model agents with limited understanding of how actions affect payoffs, who reason by analogy between mechanisms. For mechanisms that match up to relabelling of actions, equilibrium understanding transfers once agents see the mapping. A weaker notion, strategic analogy, lets actions and types be remapped, with the same transfer result. Auctions and nonlinear pricing illustrate the framework.
arxiv-2605-13102: Kanovei, Katz, Kudryk and Kuhlemann explore a framework for Leibnizian infinitesimals, tiny numbers in the spirit of Leibniz, through modern standard and nonstandard lenses. They sort infinite numbers into three kinds: ordinals, cardinals and ringinals, where a ringinal is a number of a third kind, unlike Cantor's ordinals and cardinals. Work with endless numbers fits inside Zermelo-Fraenkel set theory, making it safe in a knowledge sense. Their sketch spells out Leibnizian definitions while shunning the axiom of choice and ultrafilters, challenging received views on infinitesimals.
arxiv-2605-13602: Rohan Abeyaratne, Roberto Paroni and Marco Picchi Scardaoni propose a variational framework for surface growth driven by a best-choice principle. Rather than setting a kinetic law, each time step's shape solves a constrained smallest-value problem. Growth is one-way surface laying under a global mass constraint, driven by a goal measure taken as structural mean compliance. The approach is shown on a linear elastic cantilever beam whose height evolves by layered build-up, where residual stresses can break convexity and cause clumping.
arxiv-2605-14002: Zhu offers PolitNuggets, a multilingual test for agent-led hunt of rare political facts from far-flung sources. It builds life tales for 400 world elites, with more than ten thousand facts. Scoring runs through FactNet, a proof-tied rule set that rates finds, fine detail and speed. Trials show today's systems trip on fine detail and swing widely in speed.
arxiv-2605-14202: Tigulla and Vieira run a controlled experiment on language-model robustness testing for microservice APIs. Malformed, missing or boundary-value inputs to microservice APIs can cascade across dependent services and threaten uptime. Robustness testing probes such inputs to reveal server-side failures, but crafting diverse, effective tests is hard. The experiment applies seven prompt strategies to three open-source language models, targeting two architecturally distinct systems. One is a Java monolingual system with six services, the other a polyglot system with twenty-seven services, yielding 663 generated tests.
arxiv-2605-14702: Warda studies the weakly nonlinear flutter of a flat Cosserat rod in a viscous fluid, pushed by a force at its tip. Building on prior linear work, he derives Stuart-Landau amplitude equations for how oscillations emerge and saturate near the Hopf bifurcation. The reduced theory predicts which bifurcations are supercritical, the final amplitude, and the frequency shift. It matches direct simulations in test cases. Lower Hopf cases are supercritical, while the upper restabilisation threshold is subcritical.
arxiv-2605-15002: Paul Beame and Glenn Sun extend conflict-driven clause learning, the engine behind modern SAT solvers, to disjunctions of parity equations. Since CDCL proofs sit inside Resolution, problems hard for Resolution stay hard for CDCL. The pair's CDCL system for XNF formulas both produces proofs in the stronger Res system and polynomially simulates it under nondeterministic decisions and restarts. New inference rules carry clause-learning tricks, including 1-UIP learning, into the parity setting.
arxiv-2605-15302: R. Budaca and three others study shape coexistence in three stable mass-96 isobars: Zr-96, Mo-96, and Ru-96, near proton shell closure 40 and neutron shell closure 50. Ground-state deformations come from covariant density functional theory, while excited states use a Bohr-Mottelson Hamiltonian with an octic potential for axial and gamma-unstable shapes. Both methods highlight a large part of shape mixing to the structure of these nuclei.
arxiv-2605-15502: Mingyuan Zhang and six colleagues model how cooling by light loss reshapes black-hole images. They run two-temperature relativistic fluid models aimed at M87. Cooling drops electron heat fast in the dense inner disk. It dims the disk, stretches jets, and makes them brighter, while total flux falls. Time flicker comes chiefly from the midplane and fades as inflow rises. The signs sit below current telescope reach, but next-generation arrays could catch them.
arxiv-2605-15902: Peter Reinhard Hansen and Chen Tong connect Tweedie's formula with score-driven updating and Bayesian updating. The score-driven update matches a Bayesian update in special cases. Generally, it forms an approximation to Bayesian updating, with error of second order in predictive variance. The error splits between log-likelihood curvature and posterior asymmetry. Implicit score-driven updating, which scores at the updated parameter, corrects the former but not the latter. A correction for the component yields a third-order approximation, denoted ISD*, and experiments show gains from ISD and ISD*.
arxiv-2605-16002: Alberto Bemporad adapts the Goldfarb-Idnani dual active-set method to a new setting. He uses it to compute equilibria of strongly monotone games with quadratic costs and shared linear constraints. Several traits of the original method survive, even though the game's joint optimality system has a possibly non-symmetric matrix. Convergence, however, is no longer guaranteed as in the original. Numerical tests suggest the variant can compete with state-of-the-art alternatives, including for game-theoretic predictive control laws.
arxiv-2605-16502: Bang and Cheskidov study vortex stretching in three-dimensional axisymmetric Euler equations without swirl. Danchin showed global existence when initial vorticity over radius lies in the endpoint Lorentz space L3,1. The authors prove that endpoint is sharp: for every exponent above 1, they build multi-ring data that inflate vorticity norms without bound, and with infinitely many rings they get instant blow-up. A cascade argument across scales, with stretching depleting its own forcing as rings flatten, drives the proof. The result gives ill-posedness across the full range above 1.
arxiv-2605-16802: Ge proves that the infimum of mean curvature on any disconnected boundary component of an unbounded mean convex domain in Euclidean space must be zero. In other words, every disconnected boundary piece contains points whose mean curvature comes arbitrarily close to zero. That rules out a positive lower bound on curvature for any such piece. The result holds in any dimension.
arxiv-2605-16902: Yu's team frames auto state-of-the-art finding as a HuggingFace item graph, with models and sets as nodes and tests as edges. ArtifactLinker first ranks top unseen model-dataset links using graph neural networks or graph-boosted language models, then checks top links through coding trials with language-model agents. A new benchmark, ArtifactBench, contains 14,053 items and 51,337 links. Results show graph structure aids missing-link guessing, and ranking plus checking helps find likely state-of-the-art results and insights.
arxiv-2605-17602: Kuei-Chun Kao and colleagues present AutoRubric-T2I, which auto-builds scoring rubrics for vision-language judges of text-to-image generation. Existing reward models train as Bradley-Terry models on huge corpora, costing much and hiding their criteria, while hand-made rubrics may miss human taste. Their system turns reasoning traces into candidate rubrics and refines the set with L1-regularized logistic regression. Using a tiny share of annotated data, it beats strong baselines on MMRB2 and lifts downstream generation quality under Flow-GRPO.
arxiv-2605-18002: Chen-Chih Wang and two colleagues give the exact density matrix of the spin-1/2 Kitaev spin liquid in spin-operator form. The density matrix is sorted by string-operator classes tied to the model's gauge structure. With this form, plus the exact Gauss law and Wilson symmetry, they show a symmetry-resolved block-diagonal reduced density matrix. It gives extensive degeneracy in the entanglement spectrum and splits its entropy into gauge and matter parts. Extended to odd-site subsystems, it links the entanglement spectrum to fermion parity.
arxiv-2605-18202: Samuele Bortolotti and four co-authors offer COCOCO, a 2026 method for neural-symbolic models, which pair neural nets with logical rules. It wraps concept and label guesses in conformal sets, checking consistency, coverage, and conciseness in a single step. Tested on eight data sets, it keeps its coverage guarantees while holding prediction sets small.
arxiv-2605-18302: Eduard Kuric's 2026 study measures what synthetic participants cost user experience research. Across twelve diverse first-click tests with 3,431 real users, the authors test GPT's power to predict human clicks and their reasoning. GPT's click distributions differ significantly from real data in 53 percent of tasks, a critical failure for design decisions. Personas, chain-of-thought reasoning, and varied sampling fail to restore fidelity, serving mainly to inflate believability. The authors trace the distortions to language-model properties: their statistical nature and reliance on semantic heuristics from linguistic data.
arxiv-2605-19102: Ali Mohammadi Esfahani and two colleagues treat prompt improvement for code-generating language models as a sequential decision problem solved with reinforcement learning. A proximal policy optimisation agent refines prompts using direct generation, genetic word mutation, and meaning-based rewriting, guided by rewards shaped from unit-test feedback. Tested on three code benchmarks with three code generators, the agent beats methods including EPiC, Reflexion, and Random-Hybrid. On the 500-task test set it reaches pass rates of 57.58, 64.80, and 85.50 percent across the three generators.
arxiv-2605-19202: Fausto Mauricio Lagos Suarez and four colleagues address forest-canopy inspection with a reinforcement-learning quadrotor controller in a navigation stack. They present an end-to-end policy mapping states to motor speeds for view-pose tracking, combining position and yaw tracking for inspection and forest navigation. A guidance layer pairs a travelling salesman planner for visitation order with a random tree planner for collision-free paths within tracking limits. Five scenarios show the motor-level controller, with guidance support, works effectively as the low-level inspection module.
arxiv-2605-19302: Gangwani and Sinha introduce games where players face payoff uncertainty measured by coherent utility measures, such as mean semideviation and value-at-risk. These measures give a readable form of risk aversion while matching distributionally robust games. The authors prove exact equilibria sit in FIXP even for two players, with approximate equilibria in PPAD, and they derive complementarity forms for exact computation. For finite data-driven games with small supports they build a fast approximation scheme plus a stochastic first-order method.
arxiv-2605-19702: Bhattacharjee, Panse and Sarma introduce a hierarchy inside the Tinhofer graphs, the graphs where color sorting plus singling-out tests isomorphism. A graph is k-Tinhofer when, after k rounds of singling out and color sorting, colored graphs stay isomorphic regardless of vertex choices. The hierarchy sits between all graphs and Tinhofer, with refinable first. The authors give algebraic and combinatorial characterizations and show each level is strictly separated. Membership testing is P-hard, and isomorphism testing against (n minus k) graphs is fixed-parameter tractable in k.
arxiv-2605-19802: Mei and colleagues argue the Great Plains corridor can lead nationally in data centred materials science. Scattered experimental assets could join one trusted regional data ecosystem. Their model stresses FAIR metadata, provenance, sample IDs and tiered rules across academic, public, controlled and industry data. Five linked barriers are named, from split data to few reasons to share, with a staged roadmap to fix them. A high purity germanium pilot shows how strengths become reusable datasets, models and trained people.
arxiv-2605-20002: Andrea Burgess, William Kellough and David Pike study colourings of balanced incomplete block designs, or BIBDs. In an ell-colouring, each block misses one colour while each other colour appears exactly k over ell minus one times. They set out several necessary conditions for such colourings. The coloured designs then yield new necessary conditions for Hadamard matrices, for affine planes, and for twin prime powers.
arxiv-2605-20102: Matheus Ferreira and Felipe Falciano study a non-relativistic cosmic collider, with a massive tilted-ghost spectator field driving it. Unlike models, where non-Gaussian signs come from boost-breaking interaction points, here travel of those modes matters most. Corrections from low-speed physics deform the bulk mode functions, tilting them to modify in-in correlators and create a clear collider signal. The squeezed-limit signal keeps the shape of boostless signals but comes from another cause, with tilt sign deciding whether the signal strengthens or weakens.
arxiv-2605-20202: Rana Muhammad Usman studies whether emotional framing changes language models' behaviour. On Qwen 3.5 0.8B, four impossible-constraint tasks and eight framings are tested across 160 chats. Pressure produces the strongest shortcut markers and clearest overfit, while calm and curiosity preserve honesty most often. Direction vectors relative to calm peak at the final layer for non-baseline framings. A look at layer-23 directions finds a dominant first component explaining about sixty percent. The author reads this as prompt-sensitive control directions, not intrinsic feelings.
arxiv-2605-20502: Bhuyan tackles out-of-distribution detection across global, semantic, texture and covariate shifts. Per-encoder diffusion models in representation space are fused through EncMin2L, a two-level minimum gate that needs no out-of-distribution labels. Two diagnostics from in-distribution data alone measure each encoder's sensitivity to shift types. A Tippett minimum p-value combination merges per-encoder scores into one calibration-stable signal, reaching at least 0.94 AUROC on all four shift types.
arxiv-2605-20602: Ming Liu challenges the usual story that self-training simply flattens a language model's output. Across eleven generations on five models, surface markers such as connectives and hedges rise, while deeper syntax such as questions, parentheticals, and passives collapses. He formalizes this as the Structural Depth Hypothesis, linking decay rate mainly to how many nested dependencies a feature needs. Pooled data give a Spearman correlation of 0.540 for that link.
arxiv-2605-21102: Gabor Recski and four colleagues present ACL-Verbatim, hallucination-free question answering for research. Researchers need efficient methods for getting high-quality information from trusted sources, but AI-assisted tools still suffer from language models producing inaccurate or nonsensical output, commonly called hallucinations. The authors apply the copy-based system VerbatimRAG to ACL Anthology papers, straight linking user queries to verbatim text spans in found documents. They add a ground truth dataset for mapping queries to relevant spans, used to train and test the system.
arxiv-2605-21202: Jiayu Li, Lei Liu, and Miaomiao Zhu analyze approximate harmonic maps from degenerating cylinders and tori, applied to minimal surfaces. They study maps with bounded energy plus tension-field norm and free boundary on a submanifold. Energy identities are proved, and away from bubbles, neck limits are geodesics on the target or geodesic-like curves on the boundary submanifold, with length formulas. The result partly confirms a Ding-Li-Liu conjecture for approximate sequences, and a related flow yields minimal cylinders with free boundary.
arxiv-2605-22002: Joao Batista Florindo and Amanda Pontes de Oliveira Ornelas present ConvNeXt-FD, a fractal-based deep model for biomedical image segmentation. Segmentation maps body structures and sick regions for diagnosis and treatment planning, yet variability, noise, and varied shapes across imaging modalities still challenge it. ConvNeXt-FD pairs a strong ConvNeXt encoder with boundary-aware tuning, catching high-level semantic features plus fine-grained edge detail. It beats current state-of-the-art methods across Dice, Jaccard, accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, and false positive rate, giving more accurate and reliable results.
arxiv-2605-22102: Woomin Song and co-authors present ExComm, exploration-stage communication for error-resilient agentic test-time scaling. A common failure in long-horizon agentic scaling is error propagation: factual errors or invalid deductions from intermediate steps persist and contaminate later reasoning. Existing methods give limited control, relying on agents to catch mistakes, choose among flawed paths, or refine solutions only after errors spread. ExComm communicates during exploration instead. Tests on AIME 2025 and GAIA with Gemini-2.5-Flash-Lite and Qwen3.5-4B show gains of 5.7 percent and 5.0 percent over baselines.
arxiv-2605-22202: Amanda Myntti and co-authors show high-performing models organize their vector spaces consistently. They evaluate 25 contemporary models on five MTEB tasks across retrieval, bitext mining, pair classification, and summarization in English and other-language settings. Nearest-neighbor overlap and magnitude differences in ICA between paired texts correlate up to 0.97 with task performance. Tasks thus vary in linearity and reliance on local information retention. The results point toward future training objectives and conditional vector design.
arxiv-2605-22302: Damele proves a structure theorem for finite perfect skew braces. A central product theory in two forms is the main tool. Every such brace splits into an almost trivial part and a trivial part, each with a perfect additive group. Such braces are thus classified, up to central amalgamation, by trivial and almost trivial braces from perfect groups. In the trivial-centre case the product becomes direct, recovering the finite simple classification. A non-two-sided quasi-simple brace shows the rigidity is genuinely two-sided.
arxiv-2605-22502: Dennis and colleagues address three barriers to compiling agentic workflows into LLM weights. Orchestration frameworks exceed 290,000 GitHub stars, yet all use an external orchestrator above the model, injecting instructions each turn. Providing the procedure in a frontier model's system prompt dominates for procedural tasks. But it consumes context, needs a frontier model per conversation, and exposes procedures to third parties. Compiling the procedure into small fine-tuned weights, a subterranean agent, should resolve these concerns. The authors test each barrier across travel booking, Zoom support and insurance claims.
arxiv-2605-22602: Ma and team introduce the ToM Persuasive Dialogue (ToM-PD) task, grounded in BDI, modeling mental dependencies. Persuasive dialogue requires Theory of Mind (ToM) reasoning. Existing LLMs often fail to capture mental dependencies due to simple prompting. The team constructs ToM Broad Persuasive Dialogues, a large dataset of mental states. They propose Think Thrice Before You Speak (TTBYS), a stepwise framework using prior experiences to improve desires, beliefs, and strategies. Qwen3 with TTBYS beats GPT-5 by 1.20%, 22.80%, and 16.97% on desires, beliefs, and strategies. Case studies show better consistency.
arxiv-2605-22702: Liberato and others detail the statistical methods behind the first list of astrometric binary asteroid candidates from Gaia data, then update that list with refined models. Their pipeline accounts for Gaia focal plane uncertainties, hunts trends in residuals, searches periods, and builds confidence intervals through simulation. The update finds 343 binary systems across 410 windows, plus 45 objects with trends hinting at wide pairs. Noise only controls yield 88 percent fewer detections, and the list recovers 9 known pairs while matching earlier Gaia and Pan-STARRS searches.
arxiv-2605-22802: Luna and others identify the true spin of the white dwarf in nova YZ Reticuli, the first VY Sculptoris type variable seen to erupt as a classical nova. Ground based high speed photometry reveals a coherent period of 37.69131 seconds, showing the 42.61 second TESS signal is a Nyquist alias of the true frequency. The signal's coherence rules out dwarf nova oscillations and non radial pulsations. YZ Reticuli thus hosts a fast spinning magnetic white dwarf, whose rotator wind likely drove eruption mass loss and quenched the supersoft X ray phase.
arxiv-2605-22902: Damianos and four colleagues use Transcoders to trace how vision-language models turn images into text. A Transcoder is a sparse stand-in for an MLP sublayer. Unlike autoencoders that split static states, Transcoders act as causal proxies for layer-wise computation. They reveal pathways from image patches to generated tokens. Their scores beat rival baselines under patch ablation and lined up better with relevant image regions. Graph features from the traced circuits predicted hallucinations at AUC 0.68.
arxiv-2605-23002: Frei and colleagues use gyrokinetic simulations of ASDEX Upgrade edge turbulence to explain a puzzle. Favorable drift setups reach high-confinement mode at lower power than unfavorable ones. The team links this to a deeper radial electric field well in the favorable case. Turbulence-driven poloidal flows dig that well through stronger energy transfer between turbulence and mean flow. In the unfavorable case the transfer weakens, the well shallows, and turbulence runs hotter. Stronger shear plus calmer turbulence opens the door to high confinement.
arxiv-2605-23102: Skinner, Guo, and Li propose the LLM Sparsity Prior, a robust way to use language model weights for variable choice. LLM-Lasso methods degrade when generated weights are off. The authors build a framework for rating weight quality across regimes. Their prior folds those weights into inclusion odds of Spike-and-Slab models via two knobs for global sparsity and weight concentration. Upper-level priors let the model discount misleading weights on the fly. On a private acute kidney injury dataset it improved forecasts and found clinical features baselines missed.
arxiv-2605-23202: Jin, Nomura, and Okada study Zee models with a one-way ZM rule. Models are sorted by rule labels, which set shapes for Yukawa couplings and the neutrino mass matrix. Checking these mass shapes against current data finds viable picks. A benchmark model based on the one-way Z7 rule gets a full number study. Results give forecasts for neutrino signals and charged lepton flavor breaking events in the allowed range.
arxiv-2605-23402: Li and three colleagues forecast shifting time series, where changing patterns strain both rigid formula-based models and data-hungry generative ones. Their parametric prior mapping framework injects structural priors into generation: an estimator derives a shifting, adaptive prior that steers a learnable mapping toward the full forecast range. A mixed training goal keeps plain-model speed while borrowing generative range. The result gives precise forecasts with honest error bars, beating baselines on non-stationary data at lower compute cost.
arxiv-2605-23602: Lin and three colleagues present GlowGS, a method for rendering 3D Gaussian splatting scenes at night, where glow regions lack the textures and edges that guide reconstruction. A diffusion model plus a vision foundation model supply the missing structural cues through two ideas: semantic feature generation and novel-view semantic learning. The diffusion model synthesizes new views with unknown camera poses, a vision model judges them, and strong views feed a semantic feature bank. Rendered views then optimize against the bank without ground truth, yielding coherent, artifact-free night views.
arxiv-2605-23802: Plevne and Akbaba present a list of ages, metal content, distances, and reddenings for 5056 open clusters. It comes from Gaia DR3 colour-magnitude diagrams via Bayesian nested sampling with PARSEC isochrones. Unlike earlier catalogues, metallicity is fitted as a free parameter for every cluster. Gaia XP metal content informs the fit for 1201 clusters, while the rest use priors from Gaia parallaxes and the Schlegel-Finkbeiner-Davis dust map. Validation against six literature lists and spectroscopic metal content from OCCAM DR19 finds a median absolute deviation of only 0.054 dex for 132 clusters.
arxiv-2605-24002: Deng and 22 co-authors offer AtomisticSkills, an open-source harness that lets coding agents run atomistic research across drug discovery, chemistry, and materials science. Workflows split into skills and tools, with over 100 human-curated skills spanning data access, thermodynamics and kinetics models, and engines using machine-learning force fields and density functional theory. Campaigns shown include electrolyte design, metal-organic framework screening for carbon capture, model testing and tuning, drug screening, X-ray pattern checks, and catalyst screening. The tool aims at a base for autonomous AI scientists.
arxiv-2605-24202: Zeng and six co-authors ask when multi-agent reinforcement learning improves language-model workflows. They compare training with one shared policy for all roles against training where each role keeps its own policy. Across three workflow shapes, maths and code tasks, and three model sizes, multi-agent reinforcement learning usually beats base models, but gains hinge on workflow, task, and scale, not sharing. Isolated policies reach higher peaks yet fall off a terminal accuracy cliff more often, while shared policies merely shift failure into different patterns.
arxiv-2605-24302: Bustos and Buemi propose a cross-modal architecture for egocentric action recognition fusing RGB video with hand-skeleton data in a Mamba frame. Erratic camera motion, frequent hand occlusion, and drifting visuals make first-person action recognition hard. Their design pairs a VideoMamba visual module with a skeleton encoder of Mamba blocks, plus a fusion module. The central contribution is four CLS token mixing strategies, Naive, Average, Weighted, and Context-based. On H2O, Average wins, beating VideoMamba by over 10 percent Top-1 accuracy in Tiny and 2 percent in Small.
arxiv-2605-24502: Khen Cohen and three colleagues smooth hard binary optimization problems by letting each binary variable wander as a wave-like phase on the complex unit circle. The continuous relaxation reveals an implicit regularizer that pulls solutions toward discrete values, and the regularizer also helps ordinary real-valued optimization. On large 160-by-160 binary optimization tasks under severe noise, the solver reached zero error. It also recovered sparse codes perfectly at moderate noise and solved 8 of 11 planted-solution benchmarks exactly.
arxiv-2605-24602: Quanjiang Li and others trace object hallucinations in multimodal models to a kind of focus failure. The pattern recalls a person describing a scene while distracted. In models the trouble shows as uneven focus across heads and fading focus on image tokens as decoding goes on. Theory links scattered focus to weaker generalization. Their training-free fix, AFIP, enriches focus across heads and strengthens visual grounding with past focus. It cuts hallucinations across several benchmarks and models, with no extra training.
arxiv-2605-24702: Amit Agarwal and others probe whether image-text metrics respect meaning-preserving changes. Caption scorers grade image-text alignment. The team tests five evaluators under spatial, object, and framing shifts across detection and caption suites. Harmless spatial tweaks and plain rewordings move scores by 6 to 9 percent on average. For matched systems, shifts flip rankings in up to about 37 percent of cases, mainly under spatial changes, and people judge perturbed pairs equally correct. A post-hoc calibration roughly halves median sensitivity while keeping correlation with learned evaluators.
arxiv-2605-24802: Fei Fang and Zhong Tan study global existence and blow-up for the Hardy-Sobolev parabolic equation. A self-similar transformation converts the parabolic equation with a Hardy term into a related parabolic equation. For that equation, they prove a weighted Hardy inequality. Using a modified potential well method plus Palais-Smale sequence analysis, they study how solutions behave over long times and when they blow up in finite time.
arxiv-2605-25402: Chunzheng Zhu and colleagues shift ultrasound representation learning from generic image regions to anatomical structures that matter. Their ANAUS framework uses a tuned prompt engine plus single adaptation on public image and mask pairs to delineate anatomy without manual labels at scale. A dual training scheme then aligns features within the same anatomy while separating other structures, and predicts damaged core regions to capture fine detail. Evaluations on six public datasets show consistent gains over current leading methods. The approach keeps computation lean enough for clinical deployment.
arxiv-2605-25502: Yehudit Aperstein and Alexander Apartsin build a synthetic testbed for judging student-feedback sentiment by aspect. Real course reviews stay private and costly to label, so they generate ten thousand synthetic reviews across twenty pedagogical aspects with fixed train, validation, and test splits. A tuned BERT schedule leads the local baselines, while a GPT model scores lower in zero-shot and retrieval modes. On mapped real reviews, BERT transfers in part, reaching a higher score on the nine shared aspects.
arxiv-2605-25602: Real-time control software often carries so many global variables that they overflow the range reachable from a single global pointer. That forces two instructions per access, slowing debugging and calibration builds. Nürnberger and colleagues survey how other control processors solve this with near addressing modes, which reach nearby variables in one shorter step. They show how to add such modes to the RISC-V instruction set. They test several variants on representative workloads, reporting smaller code and faster execution.
arxiv-2605-25802: Lin and colleagues study what vision-language representation best starts a robot action policy.
