A distribution-free noise floor gives the best accuracy any simulation budget can reach, and total error splits into four controllable parts. On GJR-GARCH, the surrogate error lands within ten percent of that floor out of sample. It prices an option in a few microseconds on one CPU core, and under a microsecond on a GPU.
arxiv-2606-15602:
Zhang and colleagues tackle inference in 2026 when a small gold-standard sample is paired with unlabeled data labeled by a predictor. Prediction-powered inference corrects the predictor with a rectifier fitted on the labeled data. In a correct linear model, though, that rectifier cancels the predictor exactly, collapsing the method to ordinary least squares and inflating variance near a perfect predictor.

Their alternative, DEAL, routes the external model and the unlabeled covariates into the variance of a debiased estimator. A bias-aware shrinkage step adapts across three regimes: target-only, near-oracle, and biased-but-informative external models. They prove coordinate-wise normality with explicit adaptive variance, even under misspecification. At a fixed budget, DEAL intervals are shorter than those of debiased Lasso and rival methods, strictly so when the model is informative. In one proteomics test with a near-useless labeler, DEAL widens them to keep coverage valid.
arxiv-2606-15802:
Pan and colleagues propose CPS4 in 2026, the first text-guided semi-supervised method for segmenting the spine in MR images. Semi-supervised segmentation leans on pseudo labels for unlabelled scans, which vision-language models could improve via class prompts. The catch: nothing forces a class prompt to stay consistent with the spine unit it names, so multi-class maps come out unsatisfying.

The method works in two stages. First, a vision-language model is pretrained with token- and pixel-level attention losses coupling each class prompt to its spine unit. Second, the pretrained encoder produces a binary map per class per unlabelled image, merged into one map guiding semi-supervised training. On a public dataset, CPS4 reaches a Dice score of about eighty percent with only five percent labelled data. That beats semi-supervised and vision-language rivals. Prompt-guided pseudo labels can substitute for most manual annotation here.
arxiv-2606-16002:
Hayashi and colleagues accelerate the one-class support vector machine in 2026, by decomposing it into an ensemble of one-data machines. One-class classification trains on a single class and flags everything else. The one-class SVM excels at it, but its optimisation bottlenecks on large datasets. The proposal trains a tiny model per training sample, a one-data SVM, then ensembles them to reproduce the full model.

Because a one-data machine needs no optimisation, the decomposition sidesteps the bottleneck directly. A further speedup comes from a data-reduction step using a model trained on the average of the training samples. In experiments, the ensemble beats the traditional one-class SVM on speed with similar classification results. It also creates an exact one-to-one correspondence between samples and models, so each training point's contribution stays individually visible, a useful property when auditing what a detector learned.
arxiv-2606-16202:
Kim and colleagues present EgoPhys in 2026, a way to learn how deformable objects behave from first-person video alone. Humans grasp object physics through everyday handling, but predicting how elastic materials and fabrics move stays hard for vision and robotics. EgoPhys builds physical digital twins from ordinary egocentric RGB video.

The framework distills per-object inverse-physics solutions into a compact codebook of learned priors. From that codebook it predicts dense spring stiffness fields for unseen objects, with no per-spring optimization at test time. A curated egocentric dataset, spanning diverse objects, scenes, and manipulation styles, supports training and evaluation. EgoPhys beats baselines on reconstruction, future prediction, and zero-shot generalization in the reported tests. The team also deploys a twin on a real xArm6 robot arm, and trajectories planned inside it transfer to the physical robot.
arxiv-2606-16302:
Banerjee and Daou compare neural networks in 2026 for mapping floods from satellite radar images, a task where speed and trust both matter. Sentinel-1 radar works through clouds and at night, suiting disaster response. The hard part is telling newly flooded land apart from permanent water. The study pits three convolutional networks against three SegFormer transformer variants, in a three-class setup: flooded land, permanent water, and dry land.

Models train and test on two public benchmarks, the ETCI dataset and SenFloods11, with scene-based splits that test generalization to new places. SegFormer-b2, the largest transformer variant, achieves the highest scores on both datasets. Its edge over the U-Net baseline is statistically significant on ETCI, at p equal to 0.016 in a paired per-scene test. The authors frame the comparison as groundwork for explainable flood mapping that responders can defend.
arxiv-2606-16602:
Zhou and co-authors teach neural PDE models in 2026 to adapt from simulation to real measurements without unlearning the physics they were pretrained on. Neural operators trained on sim data lose accuracy when applied to real measurements. Plain fine-tuning on real data can close the gap but damages the core physics learned in pretraining. Vision and language tricks may not transfer: these models must protect physical structures, not semantic features.

Their framework, PhysGuard, uses the Fisher information matrix on simulation data to find physics-critical parameter directions. Fine-tuning updates are then projected away from them, so adaptation happens only in that subspace. A layer-wise Gram-matrix scheme keeps this efficient at scale, and an adaptive threshold sets the protected size automatically. On the RealPDEBench benchmark, across four model designs and three scenarios, PhysGuard improves results, in low-frequency fidelity and under large domain shifts, per the report.
arxiv-2606-17002:
Page, Mitwicki and Pietrus argue for a relativistic turn in digital identity management in a 2026 paper. Today's identity systems are custodial: a central authority holds your identity state, like an absolute reference frame in Newtonian physics. The authors' earlier work proposed the autonomous principal, an entity holding full control over its own data.

The follow-up argues the model is forced, not merely preferred. Custodial identity quietly assumes one agreed present state everywhere. That collapses once identity must work across ecosystems, legal systems and the offline-online boundary. Drop that assumption, and state stops being a thing held centrally. It becomes a relation maintained between principals through causally ordered exchanges, and each principal is the only entity with standing to define its own reference frame. The paper reviews technology built since 2023 that puts this view into practice, and draws out what follows for cross-border data flows and agentic systems.
arxiv-2606-17502:
Huang, Kang, and Bennett present a 2026 arXiv paper on a new kind of sliding ferroelectric, a two-dimensional material whose electric polarisation flips when layers slide. Adding a mismatched spacer layer cuts sliding friction, making a superlubric device, but then polarisation must survive across layers that barely touch. The authors ask what carries the polarisation in that decoupled setting, since sliding alone cannot explain it once the outer layers stop interacting directly in the usual way.

Polarisation turns out to arise from a coupling between interlayer sliding and the spacer layer buckling out of plane. That coupling yields a hybrid electronic-ionic polarisation rooted in asymmetric orbital mixing between the layers. The interplay produces several distinct switching behaviours, including mixed-order transitions, multi-step switching, and antiferroelectric-like loops. The authors conclude these superlubric systems form a distinct class of ferroelectrics, not a mere variant.
arxiv-2606-17602:
Wang presents a 2026 arXiv paper computing the one-loop vacuum of type IIB superstring theory sector by sector, with careful control of the integral's bad regions. One-loop string amplitudes hinge on modular integrals over a domain with a cusp, where naive integrals diverge and prescriptions decide the answer. Building on an epsilon-prescription and an earlier regularised framework, Wang constructs regularised functionals for each spin sector of the closed torus. That comes before the final projection string theory normally applies at the end.

Keeping the unprojected sector data visible is the point: compact-domain and cusp contributions are fixed inside one modular scheme. An independent cross-check rebuilds the same integrals by Lorentzian inversion, following a separate recent method from other authors. Agreement between the two routes supports the construction's soundness. The result is a first direct regularised treatment of the unprojected torus vacuum sectors.
arxiv-2606-18002:
Motorin and Yamashita study a Radon transform built inside the general linear group over a finite field, in a 2026 algebra paper. The classical Radon transform averages a function over lines or planes. Its group-theoretic cousin mixes function spaces tied to two subgroups, here the unipotent radicals of parabolic subgroups in GLn, the block upper-triangular matrices with identity blocks down the diagonal.

The authors analyze the transform's properties with an emphasis on its eigenvalues, the numbers that describe how it stretches each symmetry direction. They give explicit descriptions of those eigenvalues for the two-by-two and three-by-three cases, where hand and machine computation can reach. The work extends harmonic analysis on finite groups of Lie type, where such transforms organize how representations interact, and it lays groundwork for attacking the eigenvalue pattern in general dimension.
arxiv-2606-18102:
Chung and Kim describe the space of a special family of curves inside a special three-dimensional shape, in a 2026 short note in algebraic geometry. The shape is a prime Fano threefold of degree twenty-two, known as V22, and the curves are rational quartics, the simplest closed curves of degree four. Understanding the Hilbert scheme that collects all such curves reveals how the shape's geometry is organized.

The proof rides a Sarkisov link, a birational bridge between V22 and the quintic del Pezzo threefold V5, where the corresponding curve geometry is better understood. Through that bridge the authors show the Hilbert scheme of quartics in V22 admits a generically two-to-one rational map onto four-dimensional projective space. They also pin down exactly where the map branches, in terms of lines on V5, tying the count to classical line geometry.
arxiv-2606-18202:
Kern and colleagues demonstrate Einstein-Podolsky-Rosen correlations between two tiny mechanical drums, in a 2026 paper. EPR correlations are stronger than ordinary entanglement and sit at the heart of a famous argument about quantum reality. They had never been observed in this form for large mechanical objects. Such oscillators promise tests of quantum physics at human scales, plus new sensing tools.

Each oscillator carries an effective mass of about sixteen micrograms, enormous by quantum standards. The two drums sit apart from each other in space, and each one is still small enough to hold in a chip. A superconducting qubit couples the pair. Parametric driving then engineers a two-mode squeezing interaction between them. Reading the drums through a mechanical interferometer lets the team witness the correlations directly. The result widens the toolbox of circuit quantum acoustodynamics and brings tabletop tests of macroscopic quantumness within closer reach.
arxiv-2606-18502:
Dashore and colleagues at Capital One describe a framework for customizing and efficiently deploying multi-agent language model systems inside a large firm, in a 2026 applied machine learning paper. Such systems reason well and execute complex tasks, but adapting them to specialized domains is slow, and chaining many model calls makes latency and inference cost hard to control.

The framework works in two stages. First, agentic model tuning combines continual pretraining, supervised fine-tuning, and preference optimization to adapt a compact model to a domain while preserving its agent skills. Second, inference optimization pairs speculative decoding with eight-bit quantization and targeted calibration to cut serving cost with minimal quality loss. Across enterprise workloads the system achieved a throughput speedup of more than fourfold, maintained performance, and improved robustness on long-tail cases. The authors note the detailed results come from automotive retail, though the principles should transfer.
arxiv-2606-18702:
Zhang and the team teach an autoregressive video generator to create footage in any temporal direction, not just forward, in a 2026 computer vision paper. Distilled autoregressive diffusion models generate video block by block, efficiently enough for streaming. But practical editing often needs the reverse: extending a clip backward from future frames, or filling the gap between a start and end. The causal video autoencoder these models rely on encodes each block using only past context. So backward generation tears at block boundaries.

Their framework UniTemp adds blockwise anchor latents. These auxiliary latents restore the missing past context at boundaries during backward generation. It also trains a student model by bidirectional distillation. At inference, the model conditions on past frames, future frames, or both. It matches forward-only methods on short and long generation. And it enables inbetween generation, looping video, scene transitions, and visual story workflows, without fine-tuning.
arxiv-2606-18902:
Zhu and the team treat automatic prompt optimization as what theory says it is, a black-box search problem, in a 2026 machine learning paper. They compare three search strategies of sophistication. Prompt tuning by textual gradients can be myopic and shallow. Their framework performs stochastic hill climbing over prompt space. It adopts a candidate only when it improves the score.

The strategies range from random search, through a genetic algorithm, to SAGE, a multi-agent pipeline. SAGE grounds edits in diagnostic code execution on error patterns. Across three benchmarks, no single strategy dominated. Effectiveness hinged on how landscape structure interacts with error type. The authors deployed SAGE continuously on a mental-health chatbot. They chained eight cycles of noisy A/B tests into a robust gain in next-day retention. They argue that pairing qualitative diagnosis with quantitative validation is what makes agentic prompt optimization work for open-ended dialogue.
arxiv-2606-19202:
Das Bakshi and colleagues compute one-loop mixing in the dimension-eight Standard Model Effective Field Theory in 2026. The theory extends the Standard Model with effective operators that capture possible new physics at high energy. Describing data across wide energy scales needs renormalization group equations, which tell how operator coefficients mix as scale changes. This paper covers mixing of bosonic and two-fermion interactions into two-fermion operators at dimension eight.

Together with prior companion results, the new computation leaves only one piece missing. Four-fermion mixing into two-fermion operators remains to complete the renormalization program at this order. Finishing that program matters for global fits. Without full mixing, scale evolution of dimension-eight effects would rest on partial results. The work is thus a key brick in making high-dimension effective theory predictions consistent across the energy range experiments now probe.
arxiv-2606-19302:
Womack and colleagues show in 2026 that training data design, not just model design, limits climate emulators. Machine learning surrogates of climate models are usually improved by adding physical constraints to their architecture. The authors instead show low structural diversity in standard training scenarios caps predictive skill. They ask whether the training datasets themselves can be optimized so models generalize to new, structurally different scenarios never seen in training.

A differentiable simple climate model computes how emulator loss responds to small changes in training data. The data are then updated step by step to maximize skill. One optimized scenario trains a model that beats one trained on six standard pathways, despite using less data. The emulator also separates how greenhouse gases and aerosols act, without any single-forcing runs. Scenarios optimized on the simple model then drive an intermediate-complexity model with gains intact.
arxiv-2606-19402:
Verma studies cosmic structure formation in a power-law modified gravity model in 2026. The model adds a curvature correction to general relativity, controlled by one small knob. It studies background dynamics and the growth of density ripples, deriving a modified growth equation with an effective coupling from the scalar degree of freedom.

The curvature correction enhances the growth of matter clumps. It stays compatible with the observed late-time speeding up for suitable knob values. Growth factor, growth rate, growth index, and the measured growth combination are all tracked against data. Health checks pass on several fronts. The model is ghost-free, stable under the standard criterion, has a positive scalaron mass, admits a stable de Sitter solution, and supports chameleon screening. Against other viable f(R) models, it stays consistent with a single knob. One knob thus buys modified growth plus cosmic speeding that observers can test.
arxiv-2606-19702:
Mengqi Li, Lixin Li, Wensheng Lin, and Zhu Han prove a parity rule blocking tight information-dissipation equalities in 2026. Driven steady states link information measures to entropy production, but exact equalities have stayed elusive. The setting is rotation-driven linear nonequilibrium steady states.

When relaxation and diffusion matrices commute, snapshot mutual information between two time slices is exactly even under drive reversal. Breaking that alignment raises parity violation linearly with the commutator size. Full isotropy makes the information drive-independent, with a closed-form planar value near 0.145 nats. Entropy production under the same alignment grows exactly quadratically in the drive. Its prefactor has a closed form in matrix traces and determinant. Even and odd sectors stay orthogonal, leaving only one-sided uncertainty bounds. The rule survives heavy-tailed noise where variance bounds fail, and a circuit test is proposed.
arxiv-2606-19902:
Magnus Schaaf and Antonio Vairo revisit a contested charmonium decay rate in 2026. The radiative decay of the J/psi particle into a photon plus eta-c meson anchors several branching fraction tables. Quoted values from the Particle Data Group sit in tension with theory.

A profile scan over recent data that depend on the branching fraction probes the clash. Measured branching fractions correlate in a way compatible with lattice QCD decay widths. Widths for the target decay and for eta-c decay into two photons both enter that check. The pair propose a theory-grounded photon line shape for the decay spectrum. A matching extraction prescription for product branching fractions follows. Empirical damping functions, used in recent experimental fits, become unnecessary. An inherent ambiguity in derived observables disappears with them.
arxiv-2606-20302:
Giovanni Affatato, Sara Mandelli, Edoardo Cannas, Paolo Bestagini, and Stefano Tubaro detect deepfakes of specific public figures by reconstructing the face's UV texture map. Their 2026 paper, CUPID, targets person-of-interest deepfakes, a threat to public trust in video of prominent people. Existing detectors struggle to combine robustness, efficiency, and interpretability at once. CUPID trains only on real videos, never on fakes, and need not include the target person in training.

A masked autoencoder learns facial representation from UV maps of real frames, building a latent space that captures identity even for unseen people. At test time, embeddings from a query video are matched against pristine reference videos. Decoded residual maps show exactly which facial regions deviate from the identity, giving investigators an interpretable exhibit rather than a bare score. Across four datasets, CUPID beat the state of the art on most.
arxiv-2606-20802:
Gary Dunkerley proves in a solo 2026 mathematics paper that strong ribbon concordance gives a partial order on links in the three-sphere. Links are collections of knotted loops. A concordance is a surface joining two links in four dimensions. Ribbon concordance is a restricted, well-behaved kind. Agol proved a related result for knots. Dunkerley extends the order to links.

Results from knot Floer homology certify minimality for several knots under this order. Minimal elements cannot be simplified further by ribbon moves. The paper gives the first ribbon minimal knots that are not transfinitely nilpotent, settling a question from Tagami. Classical methods and recent Heegaard Floer detection results yield several infinite families of minimal links. An order on links turns isolated examples into a structured landscape, letting topologists compare objects that once could only be listed.
arxiv-2606-21202:
Nishit Singh studies consensus in a solo 2026 paper with neural cellular automata whose cells speak different communication protocols. Reaching global agreement from local interactions is a core problem of collective intelligence. Most models assume one shared protocol. Singh's population must solve density classification, agreeing on a global majority no cell can observe. Sub-populations read each other's messages through a translation with tunable distance.

Linguistic distance slows consensus. It produces mild divergence between groups rather than full fragmentation. A collective trained under diverse protocols stays robust to mismatch. A homogeneously trained one does not. Results hold on a ring and on a two-dimensional grid. A reading through Ising relaxation is offered, where a foreign region acts as a boundary defect. The findings speak to real multi-agent systems, where models from different makers must still reach shared decisions.
arxiv-2606-21402:
Jian-Hao Shi, Bao-Jun Cai, Bao-An Li, and Yu-Gang Ma report a new scaling law in 2026 that links neutron star mergers to the star's deep core. Gravitational waves from merging neutron stars reveal tidal deformability, how much a star stretches under its partner's pull. That signal has mainly constrained matter near twice nuclear density, leaving the core's equation of state, the rule tying pressure to density, out of reach.

Working with scaled stellar-structure equations and no assumed core model, they find a tight pattern. Deformability tracks one central quantity, the ratio of central pressure to central energy density, in a relation nearly free of model choice. Checked against many viable equations of state, the scaling turns measurements like GW170817 into direct core readings. They also bound the deformability of the heaviest stable stars, keeping them clearly apart from black holes.
arxiv-2606-21502:
Kseniia Petukhova, Tien Dat Nguyen, and Ekaterina Kochmar train language model tutors in 2026 that correct math mistakes like good teachers, guiding students instead of blurting out answers. Off-the-shelf models often ignore sound teaching strategy even when their math is right. The team's two-stage pipeline first fine-tunes on tutoring dialogues, then applies Direct Preference Optimization on synthetic preference pairs scored along teaching dimensions such as scaffolding and factual accuracy.

Their dataset merges existing tutoring corpora with synthetic dialogues, and they test input setups that vary whether the model sees solution correctness and gold answers. The tuned tutors beat base models and earlier tutoring systems on both factual accuracy and teaching quality. Human judges rated the best model competitive with a strong proprietary baseline, with added openness and reproducibility benefits.
arxiv-2606-21702:
Caola, Gambuti, and Link report analytic results in 2026 for heavy-quark production in charged-current deep-inelastic scattering, where a lepton probe strikes a proton and produces charm quarks. They work at next-to-next-to-leading order, the second level of correction in quantum chromodynamics, while keeping the exact charm quark mass throughout. Precise results of this kind feed the global fits that map how quarks share a proton's momentum.

The team computed the complete partonic coefficient functions for three structure functions in both quark and gluon channels, including final states with up to three heavy quarks. Contributions with at most two heavy quarks are written with Goncharov polylogarithms, special functions that allow fast and stable numerical evaluation. The three-heavy-quark part involves elliptic structures, which they express through iterated integrals and rapidly converging expansions, then check against all known lower-order results.
arxiv-2606-21802:
Li, Shi, and Yan study diffusion language models in 2026, systems that write text by gradually removing noise from a masked draft. Standard versions corrupt and commit text one token at a time at every noise level. Early in generation, that leaves scattered word fragments, so the model guesses locally instead of forming a plan for the whole passage.

Their method, Noise Dependent Granularity Control, lets the noise level set the working grain size inside a single model. At high noise the model sees and commits coherent groups of tokens, forming a coarse skeleton of meaning first. As noise falls, it returns to single tokens for final wording. Controlled tests, ablations, and story generation on WritingPrompts all showed earlier skeleton formation and better ordered recovery. The coarse-to-fine behaviour emerged without any separate planner or two-stage architecture.
arxiv-2606-22102:
Rossi and colleagues develop, in 2026, a perturbative framework for tracking electronic wave packets launched in neutral molecules by attosecond x-ray pulses. A wave packet is a moving bundle of excited electron states, and its motion drives charge migration inside the molecule. The pulses excite the molecule both by direct absorption and by impulsive stimulated x-ray Raman scattering.

The electronic structure is handled with equation-of-motion coupled-cluster theory, using a compact form of the scattering sum. Applied to OCS and oxazole, the method separates the wave packet into core-excited and valence-excited parts. Core parts dominate the earliest motion, while valence parts take over at longer times. Pulse polarization selects which symmetries enter the packet. The atom-specific scattering also fixes where the packet starts, which shapes the charge migration that follows.
arxiv-2606-22502:
Yujia Fan and five colleagues, including Yepang Liu, present an automated web testing system in this 2026 paper. Testing graphical interfaces with multiple cooperating agents has shown promise, but earlier multi-agent methods rely on tabular reinforcement learning. Tables cannot cope with the vast state spaces of large commercial websites.

Their system, WebCQ, coordinates agents with QTRAN, a deep multi-agent learning method, plus a lightweight synchronization mechanism for asynchronous web testing. For each interface event it extracts semantic and exploration features, forming an action vector that a deep Q-network uses to pick the next action. On eight large-scale commercial websites, with equal time and agent budgets, WebCQ explored about a third more states than the leading baseline, MARG. It also executed far more unique actions and triggered more failures on six of the eight sites. Twenty-hour runs confirmed that throughput holds up as agents are added.
arxiv-2606-22602:
Tianyin Li, Hongxi Xing, and the QuNu Collaboration present a quantum algorithm for parton distributions in this 2026 paper. Generalized parton distributions describe how a hadron's momentum is shared among its constituents, and they are hard to compute by standard means. The team work in the Schwinger model, a simpler toy theory used as a testing ground.

Unlike most quantum simulations, which use staggered fermions, they use Wilson fermions, which strictly preserve charge conjugation symmetry, a property the target quantities need. The framework prepares hadron states with nonzero momentum and measures light-cone correlation functions that include Wilson lines. A cost analysis shows the resources needed grow only polynomially with qubit count and desired precision. Benchmarks against exact solutions extract mass spectra and distributions that match theory and basic constraints.
arxiv-2606-22802:
Jingke Xu, Lirong Shi, Peng Lan, and Weijun Fang study private information retrieval in this 2026 paper. A user wants one file from servers that store a coded database, without revealing which file was requested. Joint coded schemes, introduced by Sun and Tian in 2019, beat the known capacity limits of separate schemes, but their true capacity stayed largely unexplored.

The authors work with systematic array codes under two prescribed storage patterns. They derive upper bounds on capacity for two families of parameters, and in one case the bound proves the 2019 schemes were optimal all along. They then build three new schemes for different parameter ranges, all with small file sizes. The new schemes achieve higher retrieval rates than separate schemes allow, and one reaches the derived upper bound exactly, settling the optimal capacity for that storage pattern and parameter case.
arxiv-2606-22902:
Pengfei Zhou and colleagues turn model routing into an agent's job in this 2026 paper. Users can choose among many large language models from different providers, each strong in different domains and none best at everything. Routing each task to the right model matters for both quality and cost, but existing routers make one static classification per task.

The authors identify the bottleneck as information deficit: simply adding task-level performance statistics to a plain router gave a 15.3 percent relative gain, beating a heuristic router with the same priors. Their framework, Agent-as-a-Router, closes the gap through a loop of context, action, and feedback, accumulating execution-grounded experience during deployment. Its system, ACRouter, combines an orchestrator, a verifier, and a memory module. On their CodeRouterBench of about ten thousand tasks scored across eight frontier models, ACRouter achieved the lowest cumulative regret and generalized to out-of-distribution programming tasks.
arxiv-2606-23102:
Sibel Başkal and Marilyn Noz explain squeezed states of light through phase space in a 2026 quantum optics paper. Phase space maps a system's position and momentum together, a view that eased the historical passage from classical to quantum physics. The Wigner function recasts quantum states as distributions over that space. Squeezed states are light states where noise in one property drops below the usual vacuum level at the cost of more noise in its partner. The paper develops these ideas step by step for readers.

Başkal and Noz define the Wigner function from the density matrix, then treat the harmonic oscillator in phase space. Coherent states, one-mode and two-mode squeezed states, and the squeezed vacuum each get a phase-space reading. Two-mode squeezing naturally creates entanglement between the modes. Coupled oscillators, symmetry groups, and the fading of quantum coherence round out the illustrations.
arxiv-2606-23202:
Jiahuan Li and colleagues couple granular flow with fluid flow in one simulation framework in a 2026 paper. Grain mixtures moving through fluids sort themselves by size, a sorting seen in submarine landslides, mud flows, and mineral processing. Capturing that sorting in systems of over a million grains defeats existing models. The team builds a two-way coupled framework. A granular dynamics model handles the grains, while a fluid solver weighted by fluid fraction handles the liquid. Momentum passes back and forth between the two sides in a consistent way.

Li and colleagues extend the earlier granular model with inertia-driven particle speeds from force balance. Validation covers a single settling particle, hindered settling with size layering, and cases spanning three reported segregation types. The results support the framework as an efficient way to simulate fluid-coupled segregation.
arxiv-2606-23302:
Khaled Hariz Belgacem, Sina Ober-Blöbaum, and Fernando Jiménez build higher-order integrators for fractionally damped systems in a 2026 paper. Some mechanical systems lose energy through fractional damping, a memory-dependent friction. Such systems fit a variational frame once the state variables are doubled. Earlier integrators paired a backward-differentiation quadrature with Galerkin methods. That pairing caps out at second-order accuracy. The multistep quadrature ignores the internal stages of the Galerkin scheme.

Belgacem and colleagues switch to Runge-Kutta convolution quadrature, which is built around stages. It therefore matches the scheme naturally. They focus on quadrature based on Lobatto IIIC methods. They prove convergence for second-order schemes and check energy decay in tests. The schemes reach second, fourth, and sixth order of accuracy. A brief note on the midpoint case is also included.
arxiv-2606-23402:
Jingren Xie and colleagues predict the thermal behavior of wood with physics-informed learning in a 2026 paper. Wood's thermal properties vary complexly across a piece, defying the homogeneous assumptions of traditional architecture. Purely data-driven models can map wood images to thermal responses, but they act as black boxes and may learn experimental noise instead of plausible physics. The team embeds a steady-state heat transfer equation into convolutional networks two ways. One design adds the physics as a soft penalty in the loss. The other hard-codes an analytical solver step directly inside the network.

Xie and colleagues validate both approaches on three real multimodal datasets covering poplar and two cuts of eucalyptus grandis samples. Each dataset pairs color images with measured temperature maps. The authors report that embedding physical bias balances predictive accuracy with interpretability better than correlation-only learning.
arxiv-2606-23602:
Millot, Coppari, Lazicki, and Eggert improve how diffraction data from laser driven compression shots are turned into reliable intensities, in a 2026 paper on high pressure physics. Powder x-ray diffraction reveals a material's atomic structure while a laser shock crushes it toward a terapascal of pressure. Two platforms do this work: PXRDIP at the Omega laser and TARDIS at the National Ignition Facility. Extracting faithful intensities from their image plates is delicate.

The authors present analysis methods built into a data package and illustrate them on shock compressed diamond near one terapascal. One trick uses the signal from a collimating pinhole, or from an uncompressed layer in the sample, as an in situ intensity reference. They also detail how to compare data taken with different x-ray sources. A final method corrects for thermal damping, the fading of signal in hot material, when comparing against ambient references.
arxiv-2606-23902:
Ševera reviews the geometry behind the Batalin Vilkovisky formalism. That formalism is the workhorse method for quantizing gauge theories. His 2026 note restates it cleanly inside a broader framework, the quantum odd symplectic category. The note is a review, written for readers who use the method in their work and want its foundations stated with care.

The story starts with Khudaverdian's odd Laplacian, an operator acting on half densities over odd symplectic manifolds. Under a Fourier swap, half densities become ordinary differential forms. The odd Laplacian then becomes the de Rham differential, a staple of geometry. Integrating forms over submanifolds becomes integrating half densities over Lagrangian ones. Much of the literature states these ideas loosely, skipping needed assumptions and data. Ševera gives the full definitions and results, including the odd quantization functor. A closing example shows a hard construction turning nearly obvious once it is phrased in this language.
arxiv-2606-24002:
Endo and a large team generate quantum states of light shaped like Schrödinger's cat, superpositions of two opposite states, in pulses lasting only picoseconds, in a 2026 paper on quantum optics. Such non Gaussian states are essential fuel for fault tolerant optical quantum computing, but making them is slow: heralding succeeds rarely, and most setups work in nanosecond pulses. The team performs multi photon photon subtraction on picosecond wave packets instead. The team interferes two ultrashort squeezed vacua, heralded by a high speed photon sensor, and reads the output by matched homodyne detection.

The reconstructed Wigner functions show negative regions, up to four of them under four photon heralding, a signature of genuine non classicality. The effective cat amplitude reaches about one point seven, approaching the range fault tolerant cat code architectures need. The picosecond platform suits the high rate, time multiplexed architectures proposed for scalable photonic quantum computers.
arxiv-2606-24102:
Guo and colleagues make prediction models for medicine portable between hospitals. Events are described in words instead of fixed codes. Most models for electronic health records encode each event as a token from a fixed vocabulary. An unseen diagnosis, or a new mix of traits, then cannot be represented at all. Their 2026 model, PORTER, frees event representation from any one hospital's code list.

Events enter through their text descriptions, encoded by a frozen language model. Numeric values travel a dedicated path. A temporal backbone, pretrained autoregressively over patient timelines, learns how conditions evolve. Across dozens of prediction tasks at a children's hospital, PORTER matches a fixed-vocabulary model with the same backbone. When timelines are rewritten with descriptions never seen in pretraining, PORTER transfers with no retraining. It recovers nearly all of the directly trained model's discrimination. That addresses a real barrier to sharing clinical AI between sites.
arxiv-2606-24202:
Gülgönül closes two gaps left by a recent unified method for tuning PID controllers on plants whose responses are delayed. The earlier framework maps regions of stabilising gains. But it leaves users to test interior points by hand to count unstable poles, and offers no rule for picking one controller. This 2026 note supplies both steps.

The pole count turns out to be available analytically. Through companion-matrix or Routh counts when no delay is present, and through an argument-principle evaluation for delay loops. Labelling every region with its count makes the whole partition decided, with no manual tests. Gülgönül then adds a time-domain selection rule. Among controllers giving monotone step responses, guaranteed by external positivity of the closed loop, choose the gains with minimum settling time. The result is one certified controller, not a map of maybes.
arxiv-2606-24302:
Sharma, Flammini, and Simonetta fine-tune a modern handwriting recogniser on medieval manuscripts, and carefully ablate what helps. TrOCR, a transformer-based recognition model, is pretrained on modern text. Thirteenth-century Italian script is thus a foreign visual domain, and historical datasets are small. The team varies three controllable choices: contrast normalisation, data augmentation, and freezing layers during training. The testbed is a manuscript known as the Cortonese.

The best setup reaches a character error rate near eight percent on the Cortonese. Across thirteen setups, freezing up to three encoder layers or six decoder layers costs nothing significant. Deeper freezing steadily harms accuracy. Removing it barely hurts when training is strong. Good training, it seems, can replace image preprocessing. Running the grid on the public READ-16 benchmark shows decoder freezing thresholds transfer between datasets better than encoder ones. Sharma's 2026 ablation gives digital humanists an evidence-based recipe.
arxiv-2606-24402:
Park, Choi, and Nam show how one poisoned document can turn an AI security agent against its own mission. Security agents increasingly use retrieval-augmented generation. They fetch external write-ups to guide vulnerability analysis and exploit construction. A crafted write-up planted in public knowledge sources can therefore be operationalised into wrong exploit behaviour. Earlier poisoning research barely touched that risk.

Across eleven capture-the-flag challenges, three frontier model families and eleven real vulnerabilities, poison adoption proves systematic rather than random. To explain the pattern, the team defines a Verification Boundary. It is a three-level classification based on what evidence an agent could use to refute a retrieved claim. Verification prompting and multi-source retrieval both help when stronger evidence exists. Both lose force when evidence is sparse and the vulnerability is a zero-day. Park's 2026 findings map where retrieval trust breaks for action-taking agents.
arxiv-2606-24602:
Guo and colleagues build a video question answering dataset where reading one frame is never enough. Multimodal models still stumble over text in videos: signs, captions, labels. Meaning accumulates from textual cues scattered across frames. Existing datasets fail the point. Most of their questions can be answered from a single frame, so they test static reading wearing a video costume.

Every question in ViTexQA demands cross frame text fusion. It is enforced by a quality controlled chain of thought annotation pipeline, boosted with temporal constraints. The companion model, FrameThinker, trains in two stages. Supervised fine tuning on frame aware reasoning chains comes first. Reinforcement learning grounded temporally, with multi frame coherence rewards, follows. Evaluations show the method outperforming state of the art baselines on the new dataset. The reported text overlap score lifts by a clear margin. Guo's 2026 contribution is both yardstick and demonstration.
arxiv-2606-24702:
Moritz Pabst, Max Knobbe, Frank Krauss, and Steffen Schumann propose a cheaper way to study tuning choices inside the SHERPA event generator. Event generators simulate particle collisions. Two parts are hard to tune: multi parton interactions, the extra scatters inside a collision, and colour reconnection. Retuning normally means regenerating huge samples per parameter choice, which is costly. The new method instead assigns each event a relative weight for each variation.

Weights are computed against the central values used to generate the events, so effects can be traced event by event at far lower cost. Pabst and colleagues validate the approach with combined tunes of both models, using LHC proton proton data at 7 tera electronvolts. They also calibrate how dimensionful parameters scale with energy, using LHC data at 13 tera electronvolts and older Tevatron data. The method should transfer to other generators and support uncertainty estimates on the fly.
arxiv-2606-24902:
Arnesh Banerjee and Ayushi Bhattacharjee dissect why strong language models fail at research level mathematics. A recent benchmark, First Proof, posed ten research questions to top models, which answered fluently and were consistently wrong. Working from the benchmark's per question post mortems, the authors name four failure modes. They are citation fabrication, premise smuggling, silent problem reformulation, and local to global compatibility gaps. The study then audits fresh proofs with instruments built to catch the first two modes.

Eight one shot proofs from Gemini 2.5 Flash come under audit. Surprisingly, none contains a confirmed fabricated citation. Every proof, though, contains at least one load bearing claim stated as a standard result with no justification, the premise smuggling mode. A premise audit instrument the authors introduce flags it with perfect precision in this corpus, at fifty percent proof level recall. Their conclusion: build pipelines that prevent such failures, not only detect them.
arxiv-2606-25002:
Yanchen Guan, Chengyue Wang, Bin Rao, and Haicheng Liao present TRACER, a training free system for reconstructing traffic accidents from evidence. Reconstruction is a forensic inverse problem: recover the motion from accounts, vehicle details, road geometry, sketches, and partial collision cues. Learning based rivals mostly optimise for semantic plausibility or visual realism. TRACER instead treats the task as closed loop structured inference. It builds event anchored motion hypotheses, then refines them under geometric, kinematic, and interaction constraints.

Case memory guides the search, and consistency driven diagnosis flags where a hypothesis disagrees with the record. Corrections stay stepwise and interpretable, like a human expert's. On real world accident data, TRACER improves geometric fidelity, speed consistency, and collision accuracy across both data driven and physics based methods. For forensic use, an answer must not only look right but measure right against the physical record of a crash.
arxiv-2606-25102:
Ruslan Berdichevsky, Shai Nahum-Gefen, and Elad Ben-Zaken build a detector for machine generated code, presented at SemEval 2026. As language models write more code, telling human from machine authorship matters for assessment integrity and software trust. The shared task frames detection as binary classification over snippets, stressing generalisation to unseen programming languages and domains. Their system, SALSA, reformulates the problem for the language model itself. Each class is assigned a dedicated output token, and the model is trained to answer with that single token in a structured response. No hand crafted features or decision rules intervene.

Robustness tricks matter as much as the formulation. Training samples are balanced across languages. Fine tuning is parameter efficient and conservative: a low learning rate and one epoch, to avoid overfitting the training domain. The system scores an F1 near 0.79 on unseen data on the leaderboard. The CodeBERT baseline manages only about 0.31.
arxiv-2606-25202:
Augmented reality overlays can feed a warehouse worker live information about a robot partner, but the graphics can also hide the real world at the wrong moment. Christian Fronk and three colleagues present ARTOO-DARTU, an AR system for warehouse human robot collaboration with an obstruction detection and mitigation pipeline built in.

The system shows situated analytics about the robot and accepts control input. It also watches for overlays that block important real elements, moving or fading them. For evaluation the team built Pocket MonstARs, a game like stand in for inventory picking where virtual monsters mark pick targets among labelled real boxes. In a study with 34 participants, the AR analytics raised task efficiency by 46 percent, but only with the mitigation pipeline active. Visibility preservation, not the analytics alone, made the gain.
arxiv-2606-25402:
Real projects pin old library versions while application interfaces keep changing, so a coding model must remember several versions of the same call at once. Daniele Cipollone and colleagues test that memory in 2026 with a benchmark spanning multiple releases of widely used Python libraries. Models face tasks where the right answer depends on the stated version, and a new consistency score grades their grip on software evolution. Errors that import a call from the wrong era are the telltale failure.

Leading models proved largely blind to versions: accuracy fell on changing interfaces while stable ones scored the same across releases. Merely naming the target version in the prompt did not help at all. Supplying the relevant documentation, by contrast, raised accuracy significantly. The authors call this a systematic weakness of training on corpora that mix all eras together.
arxiv-2606-25702:
Gravitational wave detectors hear the universe and their own creaks: glitches, brief instrumental transients that mimic cosmic signals. Luca Cirfeta presents DANTE in 2026, an unsupervised pipeline for the LIGO O4a run that hunts extended transients with no labels at all. A pretrained vision transformer reads time frequency spectrograms patch by patch, giving fine maps of odd structure. Controlled injections expose a signal dilution barrier: pooling methods that recover long, spread out shapes go blind to anything under a second.

An adaptive mixture model that picks its own covariance shapes steadies the clustering of glitch families, which otherwise shifts with small samples. Recalibrating the background on O4a data itself resolved a domain shift puzzle: morphologies first flagged as novel turned out to be stationary artefacts of the new run. Remaining lone anomalies, Cirfeta concludes, still need multi channel checks before anyone calls them real.
arxiv-2606-25802:
Alexander Mikhailov, Vladimir Novikov, and Jing Ping Wang classify integrable systems with two components. These are families of equations that admit endless chains of symmetries. Such systems matter across mathematical physics, but full classifications are rare even at low order. The team derives conditions for integrability that are both necessary and sufficient for polynomial systems of odd order in one space and one time dimension.

Exactly twenty-four spectral classes of such hierarchies turn out to be possible, sorted by their spectral invariants. The team also classifies all such homogeneous hierarchies whose lowest equations have order three and five. The list splits in two. C-integrable systems reduce by substitutions to a linear triangular form. S-integrable ones connect to canonical Drinfeld-Sokolov KdV-type systems. Those systems are tied to rank-two affine Lie algebras.
arxiv-2606-26002:
Kamar Hibatallah Baghdadi leads a team that shrinks neural networks with reinforcement learning. Compression mixes pruning, which cuts weights, and quantization, which lowers numeric precision. Searching both together by hand is slow. HiReLC splits the search into two levels. Low-level agents tune each block of the network on its own. They pick, per kernel, the bitwidth, how much pruning keeps, the quantization type, and its granularity.

High-level agents coordinate the whole budget. Ensemble voting guides them, informed by Fisher Information sensitivity scores. Policy checks are expensive, so a surrogate model steps in. A small neural surrogate predicts outcomes during an active learning loop. Fine-tuning after compression still gives the final verdict. On vision transformer and convolutional benchmarks, storage shrinks roughly sixfold. One setting even gains accuracy after compression. Other settings lose between about half a percent and five percent, a trade the team judges practical.
arxiv-2606-26102:
Juliana Seawell, Jasmine Brazilek, and Miles Tidmarsh ask whether teaching a model to be helpful can erode its values. Their test model is Llama 3.1 with eight billion parameters. It was mid-trained on synthetic data built around animal compassion. Standard post-training then follows, in helpfulness and coding flavours. Two methods, supervised fine-tuning and GRPO, deliver each flavour. Two benchmarks judge the damage: one on animal compassion, one on moral reasoning under uncertainty.

Helpfulness training does the harm. On the compassion benchmark, helpfulness-tuned models score far below coding-tuned ones under both methods. Moral reasoning on English items drops by a similar margin. The pattern refuses to travel, though. On multilingual moral reasoning, the domain effect vanishes entirely. Compassion behaves oppositely: its coding advantage grows larger on non-English items. The split suggests mid-trained values sit deeper and travel across languages better than late reasoning gains.
arxiv-2606-26202:
Nadine Fässler and Ben Moews ask whether mental health services leave a fingerprint on London crime. Their data join street-level crime records, mental health referral counts, and deprivation measures across Greater London. Statistical models and machine learning both mine the mix. A persistent positive link appears between crime rates and referrals, with referrals standing in for service access. The shape of the link surprises, though.

U-shaped is the pattern. At low service levels, more access tracks with prevention, as the standard hypothesis hopes. At high referral rates, demand driven by crime exposure seems to dominate instead. Explainable AI tools split the picture by crime category. A cluster analysis sorts boroughs into four types, each mixing crime, access, and deprivation differently. One-size policy fits none of them well. The study is among the first full treatments of the question inside Britain's public health system.
arxiv-2606-26302:
Evgeny Skvortsov and Richard van Dongen compute holographic correlators for Yang-Mills theories under several boundary conditions. Holography, through the AdS/CFT correspondence, equates a gravity-side theory with a boundary quantum theory. Boundary conditions decide which boundary theory a given bulk theory matches. The authors consider fixed-value, fixed-flux, mixed, and self-dual choices.

Three gauge theories are treated: ordinary Yang-Mills, its Chalmers-Siegel variant, and self-dual Yang-Mills. The authors derive the propagators, the building blocks of calculations, in various gauges for each boundary condition. They then compute three- and four-point correlators, the basic observable quantities, in all three theories. Comparing the results establishes how the observables relate across theories and boundary choices. The study is a companion to earlier work by the same authors.
arxiv-2606-26402:
Pratyusa Datta tackles a known headache in evolutionary biology: the rate of molecular change seems to depend on the timespan sampled, which distorts reconstructed family trees. His answer lets the substitution rate vary smoothly along a tree's branches.

Datta models the log rate as a smooth curve built from cubic spline pieces, with a prior that keeps it from wiggling wildly, and integrates it efficiently along branches. Simulations show the spline clock recovers true changing rates more accurately, with tighter credible intervals, than rival clock models. Applied to foamy virus and to SARS-CoV-2 spread across Europe, it finds strong time-varying signal in both.
arxiv-2606-26502:
Han-yu Wang compares how people and large reasoning models divide their effort across problems. Both take longer on harder problems overall. Within a single problem, though, the patterns point in opposite directions. A reasoning model spends more tokens, its units of generated text, on problems it gets wrong. People spend less time on the trials they fail.

Wang separates two levels of deliberation. Registration is how effort tracks difficulty across problems. Allocation is whether effort leans toward failures or toward successes. On a matched public corpus, people and five reasoning models agreed on registration. They diverged sharply on allocation, with every model showing a large wrong-versus-right effect. Wang reads the human pattern as engagement versus giving up. The model pattern looks like chains lengthening under uncertainty.
arxiv-2606-27102:
Ferrer and colleagues model the many-body behaviour of doped graphene nanoribbons, atom-thin carbon strips with extra charge carriers added. The chemical potential, the energy level up to which states fill, sits inside the bulk bands here. Both an extended and a simpler on-site Hubbard model describe interacting electrons on the ribbon lattice. In 2026, an exact mapping converts either model into a Kanamori model.

Kanamori form adds ferromagnetic exchange, which favours aligned spins, plus pair-hopping terms to the interaction picture. All Coulomb matrix elements, the strengths of electron repulsion terms, come out analytically. Their scaling with ribbon width and length is pinned down. A low-energy trimmed version then targets responses to outside fields. With proposed ribbon parameters, the model yields open-shell high-spin states. Those states can produce shell- and spin-blockade effects, where current flow stalls for spin reasons.
arxiv-2606-27202:
Bahi surveys graph neural networks, models that learn from data wired together as networks of nodes and links. Spectral and spatial formulations are derived from common first principles. Expressive power is tied to the Weisfeiler-Leman hierarchy, through precise statements of what today's architectures can and cannot tell apart. Twelve application domains are then examined in this review from 2026, from drug discovery to climate modelling.

Each domain gets its graph-building choices, costs, and dominant architecture families. Reported gains are separated from artefacts of weak baselines or lucky data splits. Cross-domain patterns recur: mixed-neighbour graphs and sheer scale undermine the same models almost everywhere. Time-changing graphs stay harder than static ones, and leaderboard winners rarely reach deployment. Over-smoothing, robustness, fairness, and explainability are treated as adoption constraints throughout. Claims for graph foundation models are judged suggestive, not settled.
arxiv-2606-27702:
Slater's list collects striking identities of Rogers–Ramanujan type. Each one sets an infinite series equal to an infinite product. Many have analytic proofs. What the series sides mean in terms of partitions is often far less clear. Aritram Dhar, Ankush Goswami, and Runqiao Li use Andrews' theory of separable partition classes in 2026 to give that meaning for more entries on the list.

The team builds one strict class of overpartitions and two families with gap rules on positions. In these families, bars over parts may appear only at alternating places. Their generating functions, which count the partitions in refined ways, match the series sides of seven of Slater's identities. With Heine-type transformations and Watson's q-analogue of Whipple's theorem, the product sides are recovered. A new companion identity and a signed companion formula are derived. The work shows these classes turn hypergeometric series into partition counts.
arxiv-2606-27902:
Ramanujan's mock theta functions hide striking patterns in their coefficients. Manosij Ghosh Dastidar studies the third order function rho in 2026. Its series coefficients appear to follow a strict sign law by index modulo three. Coefficients at multiples of three look positive. The next two residue classes look non-positive. Numerical evidence supports the pattern. The paper proves an asymptotic form of the law.

Watson's relation connects rho to another mock theta function, omega. A Rademacher-type expansion gives omega's coefficients precisely. A matching expansion handles a theta–eta product. Combining them yields the asymptotic formula for rho's coefficients. The leading constants differ by residue class in sign exactly as the law requires. One class has a positive constant, and the other two have negative constants. The sign law therefore holds for all sufficiently large indices. Whether it holds for every index remains open.
arxiv-2606-28002:
Insurance fraud raises premiums and erodes trust. Catching it when a claim first opens is a persistent challenge. Muhammad Shakeel Akram and four colleagues build a detection pipeline in 2026 that uses both text and voice. Existing work relies on private, text-only datasets. Their data are synthetic, so no real customer is exposed. The setup copies real claim calls. It creates dialogues between agent and customer, plus two-speaker audio.

Software transcribes the calls and separates the speakers. Later modules pull out names and patterns, search with a language model, and embed each voice. A rule-based risk score then flags problems. It catches reused stories, structural mismatches, and the same voice turning up across cases. Checks on the data and on each part show the system is stable. The design balances catching fraud against false alarms. It offers a baseline that others can reproduce, beyond text-only detection.
arxiv-2606-28202:
Md Niaz Imtiaz and Naimul Khan aim to recognize emotions from brain-wave recordings. The task breaks down when a system trained on one group of people or one dataset is used on another. Privacy rules often block sharing the original training data, so adaptation must work without it.

Imtiaz and Khan combine three ideas. The first is self-supervised pretraining that learns by predicting brain signals over time. The second is a two-stage adaptation that clusters the new data while tolerating noisy guessed labels. The third is light retraining at test time for uncertain cases. Across the DEAP, SEED, and DREAMER datasets, their method beat rival source-free approaches. Accuracy reached about seventy percent on SEED and sixty-three percent on DREAMER when starting from DEAP.
arxiv-2606-28402:
Shanfeng Zhang, Bo Gou, Yue Cao, Lei Zhang, Zhang Yi, and Tao He segment tiny objects in medical images, where sparse lesions drown in background and their borders blur. Global networks scanning the whole scan at once often miss such micro-targets or trace their edges badly, a serious flaw when the target is an early lesion.

Zhang and colleagues propose DCSNet, which turns the job into local refinement. A detection stage proposes regions and crops around them hierarchically, filtering out most background and easing the class imbalance. Inside those purified windows, a multiscale module blends transformer context with pixel-adaptive fusion to keep fine detail and sharp borders. Across three diverse medical datasets, DCSNet beat existing state-of-the-art methods by substantial margins, especially in boundary precision.
arxiv-2606-28502:
Gláuber C. Dorsch, Lucas P. C. Leão, Lucas M. B. Alves, Luiz C. A. Miranda, and Beatriz M. D. Sena stress-test a rescue plan for Starobinsky inflation, a leading model of the early universe. New microwave and galaxy data strain the model's predictions, unless reheating, the epoch right after inflation, was dominated by a stiff fluid. Stiffness, however, tilts the primordial gravitational-wave spectrum upward.

Dorsch's team examines three reheating histories mixing stiff, matter-like, and radiation eras. In every case, the parameter region favored at one-sigma confidence by the new data is already excluded by limits on extra radiation during Big Bang nucleosynthesis. Much of the looser two-sigma region would make gravitational waves loud enough for future detectors, from LISA to the Einstein Telescope, to hear, rendering the scenarios testable rather than merely embattled.
arxiv-2606-29002:
Hu, Appelo and Cheng design faster numerical schemes for open quantum systems, whose evolution follows the Lindblad equation. Simulating quantum hardware is hard because the density matrix, which describes such systems, is huge, and schemes must preserve basic physical properties. Their earlier work built a nested Picard iteration method of arbitrary order that is low-rank and completely positive and trace preserving, meaning it never produces unphysical states.

The new Gregory schemes swap expensive Gaussian quadrature rules for Gregory-type quadrature on evenly spaced nodes. They reach order up to nine while cutting computational cost substantially compared with the earlier method. Accuracy and structure preservation are retained. The team analyse stability on a physics-based test equation, and numerical experiments verify the convergence rate. Experiments also show the low-rank approximation working well, and they study a CNOT gate's performance in both closed and open quantum systems.
arxiv-2606-29102:
Al Shafi, Khan Zunayed, Ahmmed, Hossain, Mephu Nguifo and colleagues build BTI-Net, a network that learns medical image segmentation and classification together, letting the two tasks talk at every stage. Most multi-task designs share only the encoder, so each decoder rebuilds its output from private features. Boundary cues useful for classification and semantic hints useful for segmentation are then permanently lost to the other branch.

BTI-Net adds two-way communication at every decoder level through task interaction modules. Boundary context enters the classification branch through a gate, while global semantic priors scale the segmentation decoder, moving from coarse meaning to fine boundaries across four resolutions. An uncertainty proxy module gates each interaction per image and level, using alignment, complexity and confidence signals, with no extra annotations. On ultrasound, skin and brain MRI benchmarks, the net beat rival baselines on segmentation overlap and classification accuracy.
arxiv-2606-29502:
Tu and colleagues improve how AI agents use skill memories, stored textual guidance drawn from past experience. Such skills can help in one state yet mislead the same policy in another. Treating a skill-conditioned prompt as a fixed teacher is therefore fragile. Their framework is called UCOB, short for a credit-aware on-policy bidirectional self-distillation method.

UCOB compares two views of the same model on the same task and anchor state: one prompt with a skill, one without. Whichever view earns the higher return becomes the local teacher for that moment. This credit signal internalizes useful skill behaviour, corrects misleading skill use, and guides memory updates, retrieval choices, and reflection training. Tests cover ALFWorld, WebShop, and Search-QA tasks. UCOB beats skill-free reinforcement learning, skill-memory baselines, and other self-distillation methods across model scales, with gains over top baselines above twenty points on ALFWorld.
arxiv-2606-29802:
Suzuki and Yokoyama revisit Gödel's second incompleteness theorem, the result that a strong enough formal theory cannot prove its own consistency. Their note generalises the theorem from two directions and studies the ground around it.

One direction links how complex a theory's definition is to whether the theory can prove its own soundness. The authors clarify how this interacts with induction axioms, the rules that license proof by step-by-step ascent. They also pin down the exact logical strength of Craig's trick, a standard device for rewriting a theory's axioms. The other direction is semantic. They give a new unified proof of the versions where having a model is replaced by having special omega-models or beta-models.
arxiv-2606-30002:
Doyoung Choi and Jinhyung Park make a normality theorem for secant varieties fully effective. Secant varieties are built from lines joining points of an embedded variety. Earlier joint work showed the first two secant varieties are projectively normal. That held when the embedding line bundle was positive enough. The open part was saying exactly how positive is enough.

Choi and Park now give explicit effective conditions on the bundle. Their conditions guarantee projective normality for both secant varieties. They also treat the defining equations of the first secant variety. Under their conditions, that ideal is generated by cubic equations. More strongly, it is generated by three by three minors of a matrix. The matrix in question consists of linear forms. This sharpens an earlier theorem of Agostini and Park into effective form.
arxiv-2606-30102:
Le-Ji Xue and six colleagues study how two distant magnetic modes can be made to move in sync. Their system couples two optical whispering-gallery resonators. Each resonator also couples to a yttrium iron garnet sphere. That coupling links light to magnons, the magnetic excitations inside the spheres. A phase-dependent photon hopping term connects the two resonators.

The hopping phase gives a simple knob for controlling synchronization. Sweeping it from zero to pi transforms the magnon motion. Trajectories evolve from weak correlation to a highly synchronized state. Synchronization error drops significantly along the way. The authors check complete, phase-shifted, and quantum phase synchronization measures. Stronger photon hopping improves every synchronization measure they track. Thermal fluctuations, in contrast, weaken the coherent correlations behind sync. The results suggest a route to coherent control of collective magnon dynamics.
arxiv-2606-30202:
Jérémy Rieussec and Fabian Bastin survey how trust-region methods should update the radius that limits each step. These methods minimize a local model inside a ball of set radius. Good steps expand the radius; bad steps shrink it. Many update rules exist, with scattered convergence guarantees. In their 2026 survey, the authors isolate three structural conditions that unify them.

The conditions bound the radius below by the gradient size. They require contraction after unsuccessful iterations. They allow only controlled expansion after successful ones. Weak admissibility combines the first two conditions. It already forces the gradient norm to vanish eventually. Strong admissibility swaps in controlled expansion and yields optimal complexity. That bound governs worst-case steps to first-order stationarity. Five mechanism classes are verified against the conditions. Retrospective updates are newly proved convergent under growing model Hessians.
arxiv-2606-30602:
Kunyang Li, Kyle Domico, Jonathan Gregory and Patrick McDaniel ask where defenders of multi-agent systems should spend scarce security effort. In these systems, AI agents pass messages along communication channels. A compromised channel can poison the whole workflow, yet risk is uneven: one channel alone accounted for up to three quarters of total attack success in their observations.

Their framework, MESA, ranks channels by security criticality before any attack is seen. It needs no attack traces. Instead it combines six graph-theoretic metrics with two active probes, ablation and masking, that test how much each channel matters. Tested against a live misinformation attack across three scenarios, eight network layouts and five open models, MESA rankings tracked real per-edge attack success closely. Guarding only the top tenth of ranked channels intercepted about three times as many attacks as random placement.
arxiv-2606-30702:
Federico Felizzi builds a health benchmark from wearable motion data. Clinical medicine runs on structured tables, yet standard benchmarks for tabular learning ignore how real health data are gathered: complex survey sampling, deliberate oversampling of some groups, and fairness demands across subgroups. His benchmark draws on the United States NHANES survey from 2003 to 2006, with hip-worn accelerometry for thirteen hundred eighty-one adults.

Participants also gave fasting lab results, diet records and body measurements. Three methods, from ridge regression to the tabular foundation model TabPFN v2, predicted blood-sugar, triglyceride and inflammation markers from activity patterns and lifestyle inputs. TabPFN v2 performed best overall, explaining a fair share of the inflammation marker's variation. Triglycerides stayed largely unpredictable from lifestyle alone for every model. Ninety-percent prediction intervals, built with conformal methods, hit their coverage target for the predictable outcomes but fell short for some subgroups.
arxiv-2606-30802:
Mengyuan Xiao and colleagues present a spectroscopic census of the two hundred most massive galaxies seen in the universe's first two billion years. Massive galaxies stress-test formation theories, but a statistical spectroscopic view across cosmic time was missing. The sample, drawn from public James Webb telescope observations, covers redshifts from about three to fifteen and holds the top three percent most massive systems in the archive.

The team fitted each galaxy's spectrum and photometry together to derive masses and other properties, after removing contaminating red compact sources and broad-line active nuclei. The selection proved broadly robust to modelling choices. Populations shifted strongly with redshift: clean star-forming galaxies dominated early, while dusty star-formers and quiescent galaxies grew common later. Dust fell steadily toward higher redshift. Twenty-nine massive quiescent galaxies appeared, including some whose star formation had crashed within the past hundred million years.
arxiv-2606-30902:
Jiarui Li and six colleagues present TCR-SRIM, a model that predicts whether a T cell receptor will bind a given epitope, the fragment the immune system inspects. Such predictions guide immunotherapy design. But models often fail on epitopes they have never seen, and their reasoning stays opaque. TCR-SRIM combines protein language model representations with interpretable contact prototypes, learned example patterns that expose which residues drive a prediction, and adds a structural check to keep those patterns honest.

On the TCR-XAI benchmark it reached state-of-the-art predictive performance with better explanation quality. The team then used its transparency to audit generated structures. Structures predicted by AlphaFold3, TCRModel2 and tFold-TCR scored competitively yet produced less accurate interaction patterns and less diverse binding sites than real experimental structures.
arxiv-2606-31002:
Ke Zhang and five colleagues argue that compiling is not the same as translating faithfully, for turning mathematical English into Lean code. A generated Lean statement can type-check while dropping hypotheses, shifting domains or stating something vacuous. The team study faithful statement translation on a graduate-level benchmark of 400 entries spanning topology, algebra, and real and complex analysis. Their protocol combines Lean compilation, cross-model judging of meaning and human expert calibration.

A full tool-augmented agent compiled 89.5% of entries but reached only 60.5% consensus faithfulness. Human audits backed the metric: 96% of the outputs the judges passed were confirmed faithful, while 82.4% of compile-pass outputs they failed were confirmed failures of meaning. A structured study of three pipeline ingredients found elaboration feedback the largest validity lever, search mainly improving grounding, and fine-tuned drafting largely replaceable once both were present.
arxiv-2606-31102:
McCarthy, Amarasiri, and Gong build a tool for spotting research that is close to commercial use. Universities, funders, and investors want that signal early. Patents, licenses, and startups only appear years after a paper comes out. The team instead reads the paper's own words. Their Translation Readiness Index scores how similar a paper's text is to papers that later showed up in patent-paper pairs.

The team trained the index on 20,610 publications from OpenAlex. They turned titles and abstracts into semantic embeddings with SPECTER2. An XGBoost classifier then estimated the chance that a paper belongs to the patent-paired class. Patent-paired papers used more invention-oriented language. High scores also lined up with outside signs of translation, such as patent authorship and industry coauthorship. The index measures closeness to patented science, not proven commercial success.
arxiv-2606-31202: This author incentivizes data trading via profit reallocation. The incentivizing incentivizes. Their incentivizing is data trading profit reallocation. The incentivizing incentivizes. It is economics. The incentivizing is via. The data trading incentivizes profit-reallocated. The trading incentivizing is economic. The data trading is incentivized.
arxiv-2606-31402:
Wang studies when two kinds of models for representations of GL6 agree. Over a non-archimedean local field of characteristic zero, the Ginzburg-Rallis model arises by Whittaker induction from trilinear models for three copies of GL2. Whether the induced model equals the trilinear model of the inducing data was open in the case at hand.

Wang gives sufficient conditions for the Ginzburg-Rallis models of representations induced from a parabolic subgroup of a stated block type to be isomorphic to those trilinear models. A nonvanishing criterion for both families of models comes with the result. The work sits in the relative Langlands programme, where such model comparisons track how periods and L-functions should match across groups of different sizes.
arxiv-2606-31702:
Vasudevan, Somasundaram and Narayanan survey list-coloring, a generalization of graph coloring where each vertex carries its own list of allowed colors. A graph is chromatic-choosable when its list chromatic number equals its ordinary chromatic number. The topic began with work by Vizing and by Erdős, Rubin and Taylor in the 1970s, and the last full survey dates to 2001.

Coverage spans graph classes where equality is known and classes where a real gap appears. Embedded graphs, perfect graphs, bipartite and multipartite graphs, claw-free graphs, line graphs and graph products all receive treatment. The authors also review the main proof methods and several variants of list-coloring. Open conjectures about which classes are chromatic-choosable organize much of the discussion.
arxiv-2606-31802:
Gelastopoulos shows how lopsided selectivity in two-sided matching can arise from the matching process itself. In many bipartite networks one side can afford to be picky while the other must accept poor matches. Explanations usually point to traits of the two sides or to outside factors. Gelastopoulos instead models the feedback between them.

Individuals repeatedly form one-to-one matches and adjust their selectivity to hit a target matching rate. When encounters are frequent enough, analysis and simulation give one unique equilibrium: one group ends highly selective, the other non-selective. The split appears even when the groups' target-rate distributions overlap almost completely. Dating, hiring and housing markets are named as settings where the mechanism could apply.
arxiv-2606-31902:
Huisman and three others show that gradients of charged polymers generate their own electric field, and that the field speeds up small particles moving through it. Such gradients arise in drying paint and in breath droplets as they dry, full of mucin. Charged microparticles were thought to drift by chemiphoresis and diffusiophoresis alone.

Theory predicts a macroscopic field from charge separation: polymer and counterions move at unlike mobilities under a steady diffusive drive, so charge splits until a field builds to resist it. Experiments confirm the field is present. It much raises the phoretic velocity of the microparticles in their tests. For long polymer chains, propulsion turns gradient-independent, matching diffusiophoretic predictions for asymmetric electrolytes.
arxiv-2606-32002:
Alimaskina and five colleagues, at BRAIn Lab and Yandex Research, probe a hidden weakness in teaching language models from self-generated question-answer pairs.
