Nestin is a cytoskeletal protein first found in neural stem cells. Evidence now shows nestin-positive cells in many other tissues. Bone marrow stands out among them. These cells hold progenitor or regulatory roles there.

The review covers nestin's part in self-renewal, differentiation, and migration. It surveys in vivo models used to study these cells and their progeny. Their nature in the nervous system and bone marrow stays elusive, the authors note. Better models and detection methods are needed. The cells may one day serve as therapy targets.
europmc-pmc5954002:
Slart sets out joint rules for FDG-PET/CT scans in large vessel swelling and polymyalgia rheumatica. The rules were published in the European Journal of Nuclear Medicine and Molecular Imaging. A set of medical bodies from many lands backed them. The swelling hits the large blood vessels of the body. Its two main forms harm the arteries in distinct ways. One form often comes with muscle pain and stiffness.

The scans can aid diagnosis and track how active the disease is, the paper notes. Yet no shared scan standard was in place till now. The rules cover how to prep the patient step by step. They also cover how scans are taken and read. The goal is one world standard for reports.
europmc-pmc5981902:
Chlebicz and Śliżewska review four zoonotic foodborne diseases and the bacteria behind them. Their review appeared in the International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. Zoonoses pass from animals to humans, often through food. WHO counted 600 million cases of food-caused illness in 2010. Pathogenic bacteria caused almost 350 million of them. Campylobacter, Salmonella, Yersinia, and Listeria dwell in livestock.

Animals often carry these pathogens without symptoms, the authors note. They shed them in faeces into the environment. Bacteria can then reach crops or form biofilms in food plants. Symptoms range from mild, flu-like illness to fatal complications. The paper sums up each disease and its virulence factors.
europmc-pmc6001902:
Junttila gives an update on two kin signals, IL-4 and IL-13, and the cell parts that catch them. His review was published in Frontiers in Immunology. The two signals are close kin that steer allergy swelling. They act on blood cells, clean-up cells, and other tissue. IL-4 drives young T cells toward the Th2 type. It also makes B cells switch to two antibody kinds. Both signals push clean-up cells into a calmer state.

The review sets out how the catch parts are built and joined. Grip speed and part counts vary by cell type. Those facts set how strongly signals pass in the cell. Drugs that aim at this path now treat allergy ills.
europmc-pmc6013902:
Chen and co-authors present a simulation study in BMC Medical Research Methodology. It compares two common ways to estimate risk ratios for binary outcomes. One is the log-binomial model. The other is the robust Poisson model. Both often give similar results when a model is correct. The authors ask what happens when the model is wrong.

They ran each scenario 1,000 times in SAS. They varied the link function and cut off response chances at the high end. They also changed sample size and the true risk ratio. They tracked bias, standard error, and mean square error. The authors report that log-binomial estimates grew biased under these errors. The bias grew as more cases were cut off. Robust Poisson estimates stayed near the true value. They advise favoring robust Poisson when a model may be wrong.
europmc-pmc6080902:
Nakajima and co-authors show how IgA antibodies steer friendly gut bacteria. Their research article appeared in the Journal of Experimental Medicine. IgA coats many resident microbes in the gut. The team made a sugar-rich monoclonal IgA for tests. It bound the common symbiont Bacteroides thetaiotaomicron.

Coating switched on a set of bacterial genes. Those genes help the bacterium colonize mucus. They also support teamwork with other commensal species. Mice carrying it gained protection against chemical gut inflammation. Human colon samples showed the same gene pattern. Readers get a mechanism for antibody-guided gut balance. It reframes IgA as a gardener, not just a guard.
europmc-pmc6163202:
Burdușel and co-authors wrote an up-to-date overview in Nanomaterials on silver nanoparticles in biomedicine. Silver particles at the nanoscale have drawn intense study in recent years. Their traits suit many medical uses. Interest is strong in care tailored to the individual patient.

The overview covers their use as antimicrobial agents that fight germs. It also covers drug-delivery formulas and platforms for detection and diagnosis. Coatings for biomaterials and medical devices feature as well. So do materials for restoring and regrowing tissue. The authors weigh the promise against the challenges that remain. Readers get a broad survey of where nanosilver may fit in future healthcare.
europmc-pmc6211502:
Yang and co-authors review reactive oxygen species in cancer chemotherapy. Most cancer drugs raise these reactive molecules in cells. The rise can injure cancer cells and help kill them. Yet new treatments that target these levels give mixed results. The review appeared in the Journal of Experimental and Clinical Cancer Research.

The authors set out what is known about these molecules in cancer. They cover their role in tumour growth and in drug action. They review methods to measure the levels in cells. Such levels shift fast and are hard to track in patients. Math models may help predict levels during treatment. The authors suggest paths for better drugs based on this science.
europmc-pmc6233802:
Troeger and co-authors measured the world burden of rotavirus diarrhoea in young children. Their analysis appeared in JAMA Pediatrics. It draws on the Global Burden of Disease Study. Rotavirus is a leading cause of severe diarrhoea in children under five. The team tracked cases and deaths across countries and years. They also asked how much vaccine use had changed the picture.

Diarrhoea killed nearly half a million young children in 2015. The authors note that rotavirus caused close to three in ten of those deaths. Health groups have urged all countries to add rotavirus vaccine to child schedules since 2009. Uptake support comes from Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance. The authors argue that wider vaccine use and better care can still prevent many deaths.
europmc-pmc6364502:
Gao and co-authors present a research article in Advanced Science on a nanoparticle treatment for tumors. The team built tiny silica particles loaded with gold and iron oxide. Each metal mimics an enzyme, and together they run a two-step chemical cascade inside tumors.

The gold particles turn glucose into hydrogen peroxide, like glucose oxidase does. The iron oxide then converts that peroxide into hydroxyl radicals, which kill tumor cells. Tests in cells and in animals showed strong tumor suppression, reported at about 69 percent. The authors present the design as effective and safe. It needs no laser, ultrasound, or other outside trigger.
europmc-pmc6443602:
Willemink and Noël trace how CT scanners learned to build sharper images from less radiation, from filtered back projection to AI. The first scanners of the early 1970s already toyed with looping methods, but weak computers shelved them. Filtered back projection ruled for decades, and step-by-step reconstruction reached the market only in 2009.

Vendors then raced through mixed and model-based versions, cutting dose and sharpening images, and paper counts soared. The authors argue that advanced rebuilding is now a must, and key for coming hardware such as photon-counting CT. Networks trained to clean up low-dose scans point to the next jump, with AI set to lift image quality further.
europmc-pmc6476302:
Yao and co-authors review macrophage polarization at the maternal-fetal interface. There these immune cells make up 20 to 30 percent of all white blood cells and help the mother tolerate a half-foreign fetus. Macrophages swing between the inflammatory M1 style and the calming M2 style as pregnancy demands, supporting invasion of the placenta and spiral artery remodeling.

Normal pregnancy leans M2, while miscarriage, preeclampsia, and preterm birth show M1 excess in the wrong places and times. Signaling routes such as Notch can force the M1 turn during infection-driven preterm labor in mice. Because the cells stay plastic, re-polarizing them is an attractive therapy idea still awaiting definition.
europmc-pmc6527602:
Ivetic, Hoskins Green and Hart review L-selectin in leukocyte adhesion and movement. Their review appeared in Frontiers in Immunology. L-selectin, also called CD62L, sits on most circulating white blood cells. It was first found in 1983. It is best known as a tethering and rolling receptor.

Newer work gives it a wider role. It guides monocyte protrusion as cells cross vessel walls. Its lectin head binds many glycans, among them sialyl Lewis X. Its short tail, just 17 amino acids long, links to ERM proteins. Shedding of its outer part helps set cell polarity. The review details each domain and its signals.
europmc-pmc6559702:
Heslehurst and co-authors pool the evidence on how a mother's weight before pregnancy shapes her child's obesity risk, writing in PLOS Medicine. Childhood obesity tracks into adult disease, and prevention keeps starting too late. The team asked whether the risk is already set before conception, and how it grows with maternal body mass index.

Seventy-nine studies from 59 cohorts met their criteria. The link was strong and nonlinear. Children of mothers with obesity had odds of obesity raised by 264% — well over triple — in the pooled analysis of nearly 89,000 children. Maternal overweight nearly doubled the odds. Effects grew steadily across the BMI range. The authors argue support for women's weight must begin before pregnancy to break the intergenerational cycle.
europmc-pmc6566902:
Malaguarnera reviews how resveratrol, the red-wine polyphenol, steers the immune system, writing in Nutrients. Found in grapes, peanuts and rhubarb, resveratrol touches many switches at once: it activates the longevity-linked enzyme Sirt1, damps the master inflammatory signal NF-κB, and mops up reactive oxygen species.

The review walks cell type by cell type. Macrophages make less TNF and IL-12 under its influence, T-cell growth and interferon output fall, and natural killer and B cells shift their behavior as well. Dose flips the effect, stimulating immunity at low levels and suppressing it at high ones. A standing caveat closes the survey: the body metabolizes resveratrol so fast that oral bioavailability stays very low, which tempers the test-tube results.
europmc-pmc6591002:
Pandolfini and co-authors uncover a hidden chemical mark inside microRNAs, writing in Molecular Cell. The mark, m7G, was known at messenger RNA caps and inside transfer RNAs, but spotting it in scarce microRNAs needed a new trick. Their chemical assay, BoRed-seq, found m7G in a subset of microRNAs that restrain cell migration.

The writer is METTL1, an enzyme previously assigned to transfer RNAs. In the let-7 family, mass spectrometry pinned the mark to a single guanosine. That one methyl group breaks a knot in the precursor's structure that otherwise blocks processing, so more mature let-7 gets made. Tuning METTL1's activity shifted how cells migrate, tying this small mark to a cancer-relevant behavior.
europmc-pmc6602502:
Greiner, Lehwark, and Bock present version 1.3.1 of OrganellarGenomeDRAW. Their article appears in Nucleic Acids Research. The tool draws graphical maps of plastid and mitochondrial genomes. Such genomes help resolve family relationships between species. Sequencing has made them abundant, so map drawing must keep pace.

The new version has a rebuilt front end as a single-page app. Settings now cache, so users can compare outputs with less effort. The server holds a local copy of the NCBI RefSeq organelle database. Batch processing handles many GenBank files at once. Whole taxonomic groups can thus be drawn in one run. The server draws about 120 maps per day.
europmc-pmc6678302:
Doyle and Wang overview extracellular vesicles, with a focus on exosome isolation and analysis. Their review appears in Cells. Vesicles come in three main subtypes. Microvesicles, exosomes, and apoptotic bodies differ in origin and size. Their cargo spans lipids, nucleic acids, and proteins. Exosomes form inside endosomes and measure 30 to 150 nanometres. They appear in nearly every body fluid tested. Marker proteins like CD63 and CD9 aid detection. No marker cleanly separates the subtypes, though.

Isolation methods shape the proteome researchers see. That dependence blocks clinical translation for now. The review compares current separation and analysis options. Standardisation is the authors' central demand. Only then can biomarker use move into clinics.
europmc-pmc6713402:
Grohskopf and co-authors present the U.S. flu vaccine advice for the 2019-20 season. The report updates guidance from the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices. Annual flu vaccination is urged for everyone aged 6 months and older without a medical reason against it. Several vaccine types were set to be offered that season.

The report lists inactivated, recombinant, and live nasal spray options. Most standard shots that year covered four flu strains. High-dose and boosted shots for older adults covered three. It also names the exact virus strains picked for the season's shots. Clinics use the report to plan orders and advise patients.
europmc-pmc6715802:
Shen and co-authors built a deep learning system to spot breast cancer on screening mammograms. Reading these X-ray images is hard, and expert labels for each lesion are rare. Their method trains in stages, so later stages need only a whole-image cancer label. That makes far more images usable for training.

On film mammograms from a public database, averaging four models reached an AUC of 0.91 across the full test set. On digital images from a second database, the averaged score rose to 0.98 with strong accuracy. AUC here gauges how well the system ranks cancer cases above non-cancer ones. The results rival earlier methods.
europmc-pmc6721602:
Demine and co-authors reviewed mitochondrial uncoupling and its wide effects in the body. Mitochondria make ATP, the cell's energy currency, using a voltage across their inner membrane. Uncoupling lets that voltage leak away without making ATP. Once seen as a defect, the process is now known to be run by dedicated proteins such as UCP-1.

The review compares uncoupling proteins and chemicals, noting their side effects. It then links uncoupling to cell cleanup, oxygen byproduct control, cell death, exercise, and fat tissue change. The authors close with medical prospects. Controlled uncoupling might one day treat obesity, heart disease, or brain disorders.
europmc-pmc6889302:
Sahin and co-authors review checkpoint drugs for a distinct bowel cancer type, in the British Journal of Cancer. Some colorectal cancers cannot repair DNA mismatches. Their tumours carry many mutations and draw in immune cells. Such MSI-high cancers respond to immune checkpoint inhibitors in a lasting way for many patients. Response rates, though, sit between 30 and 50 percent.

The rest resist from the start, and some responders later relapse. The review covers the trials that proved the benefit, then dissects resistance. Tumours can lose the machinery that displays antigens, including through faults in the beta-2 microglobulin gene. Broken interferon signalling through Janus kinases is another escape. The authors map trials now testing combinations.
europmc-pmc6895602:
Palmqvist and co-authors chart Alzheimer's biomarkers in EMBO Molecular Medicine. Failed drug trials have pushed the field to read the disease earlier and more precisely. Proteins in spinal fluid and blood shift as amyloid, the disease's signature protein, builds up in the brain. When each marker moves, relative to that build-up, was the question.

The team studied 377 participants in the BioFINDER study, testing seven spinal fluid and six blood markers against amyloid PET scans. In spinal fluid, the Aβ42 measure changed first, with tau markers close behind. Markers of nerve damage and inflammation rose only after scans turned positive. Assays from five makers told the same story, which strengthens the sequence.
europmc-pmc6906302:
Duong and co-authors review bacteria as cancer therapy, in Experimental and Molecular Medicine. New cancer treatments still struggle with harm to healthy tissue, poor reach into deep tumours, and drug resistance. Certain bacteria naturally gather inside tumours, where oxygen is low and immunity is weak. There they multiply and can stir an immune attack. That behaviour makes them a living drug platform.

Engineers can programme such bacteria to make and release anti-cancer agents on site. Control systems time the release: some answer outside signals, others the bacteria's own density. The review covers the main species in use and the safety switches built into them. Keeping the bacteria out of healthy tissue remains the central design problem.
europmc-pmc6916202:
Mukund and Subramaniam map skeletal muscle at the molecular level. Their review appeared in Wiley Interdisciplinary Reviews: Systems Biology and Medicine. Muscle is built to contract, make force, and move the body. It joins nerves, blood vessels, and metabolic machinery.

The pair start with muscle formation and satellite cells. They explain how injured muscle regenerates. They then work through each structural part in turn. Sections cover the neuromuscular junction and the sarcomere. Others cover the cytoskeleton, matrix, and blood supply. The authors flag faulty pathways with clinical relevance. They stress how inflammation and oxidative stress drive atrophy, excess growth, and fibrosis.
europmc-pmc6945602:
Yang and co-authors show how sticky webs cast by immune cells help liver cancer spread. Their study appeared in the Journal of Hematology and Oncology. Neutrophils, the most common immune cells, can throw out webs of DNA called extracellular traps, or NETs. Such traps form in many inflamed tissues.

Blood neutrophils from liver cancer patients formed more NETs, above all in patients whose cancer had spread. The webs caught tumour cells, then made them harder to kill and more invasive. Trapped cells swallowed parts of the web, switching on a TLR4/9 and COX2 signalling route. Blocking that route erased the boost to spread. In mice, shredding NETs with an enzyme, plus anti-inflammatory drugs, cut metastasis sharply.
europmc-pmc6981202:
Pillon and co-authors pool gene data to map how muscle answers exercise and idleness. Their study appeared in Nature Communications. Exercise prevents and treats metabolic disease, yet the molecular steps behind its benefits stay murky. Inactivity alone raises disease risk and death.

The team built MetaMEx, a meta-analysis of 66 published data sets on human muscle. It covers aerobic and resistance training, single bouts and long programs, plus inactivity. Distinct pathways switched on for each pattern. One gene, NR4A3, ranked among the most responsive to both exercise and inactivity. Lab tests confirmed it helps mediate metabolic responses to exercise-like signals. People with metabolic impairments answered exercise differently. The database is open online for others to query.
europmc-pmc7015702:
Hailes and co-authors present an umbrella review in The Lancet Psychiatry. They gather and grade the many meta-analyses on the long-term effects of childhood sexual abuse. The outcomes span mental illness, social and behavioural problems, and physical health in adult life.

The team searched four databases through the end of 2018. They found 19 meta-analyses covering 559 primary studies and 28 outcomes, with over four million participants in total. Abuse was linked to 26 of the 28 outcomes. The strongest links were for conversion disorder, borderline personality disorder, anxiety, and depression. Only three reviews met high quality standards, though. The authors call for better meta-analyses and more work on how harm develops over time.
europmc-pmc7017302:
Teng and co-authors report a cell study in the journal Cancers. They test polyphyllin VI, a saponin from the traditional Chinese medicine plant Trillium tschonoskii, against non-small cell lung cancer. Earlier work showed the compound slows these cancer cells through apoptosis and autophagy. The team now examines a second death route, pyroptosis.

Working with A549 and H1299 lung cancer cells, and with tumour-bearing mice, the authors show that polyphyllin VI switches cells from apoptosis toward pyroptosis. The compound raises reactive oxygen species, which activate a chain through NF-kappaB, the NLRP3 inflammasome, caspase-1, and gasdermin D. That chain drives the inflammatory cell death. The findings support polyphyllin VI as a candidate drug for this lung cancer.
europmc-pmc7041302:
Sterling and co-authors present updated United States guidelines for treating latent tuberculosis infection in MMWR Recommendations and Reports. People with latent infection carry the tuberculosis bacterium without illness, but it can activate later. Comprehensive guidance was last published in 2000, and several new regimens have since been tested. The National Tuberculosis Controllers Association and the CDC convened a committee to revise the advice.

The committee ran a systematic review of clinical trials and graded the evidence with the GRADE method. A network meta-analysis compared regimens never tested head to head. Effectiveness meant preventing tuberculosis disease; toxicity meant liver damage. The resulting recommendations favour the most effective and least toxic courses for people living in the United States. Wider use of shorter, safer treatment should help move the country toward eliminating tuberculosis.
europmc-pmc7064602:
Chong and co-authors improve the hunt for unusual tumour antigens in Nature Communications. Immune therapy works when T cells spot peptides shown on a cancer cell's HLA molecules. Recent work suggests some targets come from genome regions once marked as non-coding. Finding those odd peptides in a trustworthy way takes mass spectrometry joined with deep sequencing.

The team's method combines whole exome sequencing, bulk and single-cell RNA data, ribosome profiling, and two mass spectrometry search tools. Together they identify hundreds of shared and tumour-specific non-canonical peptides with confidence. One standout is an immunogenic peptide from a reading frame downstream of ABCB5, a melanoma stem cell marker gene. Predicted peptides of this kind vastly outnumber classic neoantigens. The authors argue the wider set could supply fresh targets for cancer vaccines and cell therapies, as long as identification stays this strict.
europmc-pmc7069202:
Abasalizadeh and co-authors review alginate hydrogels in the Journal of Biological Engineering. Hydrogels are water-absorbing networks of crosslinked polymers that swell without dissolving. Among the materials used to make them, polysaccharides win special attention in medicine. Sodium alginate, drawn from seaweed, is non-toxic, biocompatible, and biodegradable, with traits well suited to carrying drugs.

Alginate gels form when the polymer meets multivalent cations in a gentle gelation process. Their stiffness, swelling, breakdown, and cell attachment can all be tuned by chemical or physical changes, as can the release of the molecules they carry. The review explains the gels' properties, then covers three uses: delivering cancer drugs, dressing wounds, and serving as a printable material for three-dimensional bioprinting of tissues. High water content and a softness like natural tissue make the gels at home in the body, which underlies all three uses.
europmc-pmc7181102:
Dietz and co-authors present guidance on breast cancer care during the COVID-19 pandemic. Their article appeared in Breast Cancer Research and Treatment. Experts from several cancer care groups wrote the guidance together. Hospitals faced shrinking staff and resources as the virus spread. Some patients needed care at once, while others could wait safely. The guidance sorts patients by how urgent their care is.

The authors define three priority levels, labeled A, B, and C. Level A covers life-threatening or severe cases that need urgent treatment. Level B covers cases that should start treatment before the pandemic ends. Level C covers cases that can wait until it is over. For each level, the article gives treatment advice by specialty. The authors stress that local virus spread and hospital capacity must shape each choice. Delay risks must be weighed against infection risks.
europmc-pmc7186402:
Song and Long review the links between Nrf2 and ferroptosis in brain disease. Their article appeared in Frontiers in Neuroscience. Ferroptosis is a form of cell death driven by iron and fat oxidation. It differs from other known cell death types. Nrf2 is a protein that directs the cell's defense against oxidative stress. Its activity falls with age. The authors ask how these two processes interact.

The review sets out how ferroptosis is controlled in cells. A key guard is the enzyme GPX4, backed by glutathione. The authors then trace how Nrf2 and its target genes limit this death route. Ferroptosis seems to speed up diseases like Parkinson's and Alzheimer's, they note. Yet direct proof of the Nrf2 link in brain disease is still thin. The authors frame the link as a promising line for new research and treatment ideas.
europmc-pmc7205802:
Popov updates the science of mitochondrial biogenesis, the process by which cells build new mitochondria. The review appeared in the Journal of Cellular and Molecular Medicine. Cells launch this renewal when energy demand rises or stress hits. New mitochondria grow out of existing ones. Recent work has uncovered many of the proteins and genes involved.

Popov focuses on how the main players work together inside the cell. One theme is keeping mitochondrial mass and function in balance. Another covers the signals that switch biogenesis on or off. A third weighs medical uses of this knowledge. Cancer research features, since some tumors lean heavily on new mitochondria. Drugs that raise or block a master regulator called PGC-1 alpha appear throughout. Readers get a current map of the field.
europmc-pmc7206502:
Li and co-authors examine whether SARS-CoV-2 appears in the semen of men with COVID-19. Their cohort study appeared in JAMA Network Open. The virus had already been found in stool, saliva, and urine. Whether it reaches semen mattered for transmission questions. The team described the men's clinical features alongside their test results.

Some patients' semen tested positive for the virus. It could still be detected in men who were recovering. The authors suggest imperfect barriers around the testes may let the virus in. Systemic inflammation could help it cross. Whether semen can transmit infection remained unproven. The findings argue for caution and further study. They widened the list of body fluids checked for the virus.
europmc-pmc7213702:
Alqahtani and co-authors review how COPD and smoking relate to COVID-19 severity and death. Their rapid meta-analysis appeared in PLoS ONE. They searched databases up to March 24, 2020. No earlier review had summed up the risk for lung patients. Two reviewers extracted data independently using standard guidelines.

Across the pooled studies, only 2 percent of confirmed patients had COPD. Yet those patients faced worse severity and higher mortality. Smoking data came from eight studies covering 193 current smokers. Results again pointed to added risk. Numbers were still small in this early evidence. The authors call for vigilance around patients with chronic lung disease. Their review set an early benchmark for later, larger studies.
europmc-pmc7237502:
Kang and co-authors show that web-like traps released by neutrophils hinder brain repair after stroke. Their study appeared in Nature Communications. New vessel growth and remodeling are vital for recovery. Neutrophils gather around the stroke site at every stage. Their extracellular traps, strands of DNA and proteins, peaked at 3 to 5 days after stroke.

Removing neutrophils reduced blood-brain barrier damage. It also boosted new vessel growth by day 14. An enzyme called PAD4, needed to make the traps, rose in the injured brain. Forcing more PAD4 meant more traps, fewer new vessels, and worse barrier damage. Blocking the pathway improved behavior in mice. The study names the traps as a brake on stroke recovery worth targeting.
europmc-pmc7395502:
Escobar and co-authors test whether the tuberculosis vaccine BCG softens COVID-19, in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. BCG is known to confer broad protection beyond tuberculosis, training the immune system generally. Countries differ in BCG policy, which offered a natural comparison early in the pandemic.

Raw links between BCG use and COVID-19 deaths are tangled with social, economic, and demographic differences between countries. After adjusting for many such confounders, several significant associations with reduced deaths remained. The authors are careful: an ecological pattern is not proof of protection. They call for studies of the mechanism and for clinical trials of BCG against severe COVID-19. Readers get a disciplined look at a tempting shortcut.
europmc-pmc7410202:
Zhang and co-authors measure hip fracture in urban China in PLoS Medicine, using national insurance databases covering about 480 million residents. Hip fracture brings disability, excess deaths, and high costs, and China has the world's largest older population. Their data span 2012 to 2016 and about 102.56 million people aged 55 and over.

They identified 190,560 new hip fractures, with patients averaging about 77 years old and 63.99 percent female. Age-adjusted incidence did not rise despite rapid aging; for women it eased from 180.72 to 177.13 per 100,000, and for men it fell more clearly. Yet because the older population grew, the absolute number of fractures in those 55 and older rose about 4-fold. Prevention is working per person, the numbers say, while the total burden still climbs.
europmc-pmc7422602:
Young and a large expert group set out shared guidance on ADHD in girls and women. The group met under the United Kingdom ADHD Partnership. Their aim was to help doctors spot and treat a condition that is often missed in females.

The group notes that girls and women often show quieter, more inward signs than boys and men. Bias, other health problems, and coping tricks can hide the signs. The guidance covers symptom patterns, when to refer, how to assess, and how to treat. It stresses care across the whole life span, since needs shift with age and life stage. Schools, health teams, and other services should work as one team. Good care, the group argues, lifts long-term health and daily life.
europmc-pmc7425302:
Bai and co-authors review why cancers resist immunotherapy, treatment that frees the immune system to attack tumors. Checkpoint drugs give lasting gains for some patients. Yet most patients gain little, respond in only some tumors, or relapse after a first response.

The review splits resistance into primary resistance, where tumors never respond, and acquired resistance after early success. Causes inside the tumor include gene changes, altered metabolism, and inflammation. Causes outside it include poor blood vessel growth. The authors show how these forces combine in one patient. Knowing the exact cause in each case could guide care that fits the patient, not just the cancer type.
europmc-pmc7427302:
Singanayagam and co-authors study how long people with COVID-19 stay infectious in England. They link lab virus growth to RT-PCR cycle threshold values. The work covers cases from January to May 2020.

Viral load in the upper airways peaked near the start of symptoms. Live virus persisted for 10 days in mild to moderate disease, based on 324 samples. Higher cycle threshold values meant less chance of growing live virus. The chance fell to 8% when values passed 35, and to 6% after 10 days. People without symptoms could still carry live virus. The results help set isolation periods on firm ground.
europmc-pmc7457002:
Ku and Cheng review ATF3, a stress-linked transcription factor, as a master control of metabolism and cancer. ATF3 switches on under cell stress. Signals such as ER stress, cytokines, and bacterial products all feed into it.

ATF3 can both start and block gene activity. It shapes glucose control and fat tissue function. It also guides immune defense and keeps host protection in balance. In cancer, it plays roles in prostate, breast, colon, lung, and liver tumors. Those roles can help or hinder tumor growth by context. The review maps ATF3 signals across these fields. The authors propose ATF3 as a target for treating metabolic, immune, and cancer disorders.
europmc-pmc7590402:
Simons, Shahab, Brown and Perski present a living review of smoking status and COVID-19 risk. They track infection, hospital care, severity and death by smoking group. The review is updated as new studies appear.

Version 7 drew on searches to August 25 in that year. It included 233 studies in total. Meta-analyses used 32 good or fair quality studies. Current smokers had lower infection risk than never smokers. Their relative risk was 0.74 in the pooled result. Former smokers faced higher hospital and death risk. Their severity risk ratio was 1.52 overall. Current smoker results for severe outcomes stayed inconclusive in the data.
europmc-pmc7693302:
Zhang and co-authors dissect a spike change that swept the SARS-CoV-2 world. The change, called D614G, swaps one amino acid in the spike protein. Viruses with this change came to dominate worldwide. The team compared fake viruses bearing the old and new spike forms.

Viruses with the new spike entered target cells more readily. They shed less of the spike's outer part and packed more spike into each particle. Binding to the ACE2 receptor did not change. Neither did sensitivity to antibodies. The authors say the change likely raises infectivity by loading more working spikes onto each virion.
europmc-pmc7791602:
Leung and co-authors assess how fast the new N501Y mutant strains of SARS-CoV-2 spread in the United Kingdom. Two lineages carrying the N501Y spike mutation rose quickly in late 2020. The team compared their growth with the older 501N lineage. Data covered October to November 2020.

The earlier 501Y lineage lacked the Δ69/Δ70 deletion. It spread mainly from early September to mid-November. The authors estimate it was 10% more transmissible than the 501N lineage. The range given was 6–13%. A second 501Y lineage carried the deletion. Early estimates like this one guided the first public health response to the variants.
europmc-pmc7811002:
Ko and co-authors present a fourth-generation neural network model for atomistic simulation. Machine learning models now guide simulations in chemistry and materials science. Most older models read only local surroundings. They miss global shifts in electron structure. Long-range charge transfer is one such shift.

The new model adds a charge balancing scheme. Atomic pull on electrons depends on each atom's setting. Atomic energies stay accurate at the same time. Global charge patterns come out right in varied systems. Test cases that fool older methods matched reference calculations well. The authors say this widens what machine learning models can safely simulate.
europmc-pmc7840502:
Hartmann and co-authors present BiofilmQ, a tool for measuring microbial communities in images. Biofilms are a hugely common form of microbe life. Their members differ across space and over time. Microscopy is the main way to watch them. Numbers must be pulled from those images with care.

BiofilmQ turns microscope images into hard data. It splits images into cells or patches for measurement. Traits can then be tracked across the whole community. Growth patterns and local differences become numbers. The tool serves labs that study biofilm structure. It is built for shared, repeatable analysis. Such numbers help explain how biofilms work and resist treatment.
europmc-pmc7845802:
Rosenow writes on focal infection spreading from oral sepsis. The article gathers extracts from a longer paper. Hidden pockets of infection drew blame for body-wide disease. Such pockets often cause no local symptoms. The author marshals the facts of his day.

Clinical studies found such foci in a high share of the sick. Children were among them. Removing the foci often improved general health. The author argues that germs settle in chosen sites. This idea was called elective localization. Mouth infection is treated as a prime source. The piece is a period statement of the focal infection theory. It helped drive an era of tooth removal as treatment.
europmc-pmc7907602:
Zheng and co-authors present a review of how bacteria first stick to surfaces and start biofilms. Biofilms are layered cell communities that cling to surfaces in hospitals and industry. Once mature, they resist killing and removal. Stopping the first contact is the best defence. The review examines what shapes that first contact.

Surface charge, wetting, roughness, shape, and stiffness all sway whether bacteria settle. The authors gather recent work on each trait and on their combinations. Two often-missed factors get special attention: how bacteria swim, and the flow of fluid over the surface. Both can change the outcome of contact. The review closes with nanotechnology-based antifouling designs. These aim to keep surfaces clean by blocking sensing and adhesion at the start.
europmc-pmc7920402:
Skjefte and co-authors report a survey of COVID-19 vaccine acceptance among pregnant women and mothers in 16 countries. Vaccines only cut deaths if people take them. Pregnant women and mothers shape uptake for themselves and their children. The team surveyed these groups online in late 2020, before wide rollout.

The survey drew 17,871 responses. Given a vaccine with 90% efficacy, 52.0% of pregnant women said they would take it. Among non-pregnant women, 73.4% said the same. Most women, 69.2%, planned to vaccinate their children. Acceptance ran highest in India, the Philippines, and Latin America. It ran lowest in Russia, the United States, and Australia. Trust in health agencies and worry about the disease were strong predictors. The authors urge campaigns shaped to each country.
europmc-pmc7977302:
Marin-Acevedo and co-authors present a review of the next generation of immune checkpoint inhibitors. The immune system is the core defence against cancer. Tumours escape it in part by pressing the brakes built into immune checkpoints. Blocking those brakes has become standard care for many cancers. Yet only a small share of patients gain real benefit. The hunt is on for new brakes to block.

The best-known targets are CTLA-4, PD-1, and PD-L1. The review moves past them to fresh pathways and molecules. Each candidate is weighed for its promise and its problems. Some may widen the group of patients who respond. Others may pair with current drugs for a stronger effect. The authors set out the logic of each design in turn. The field's aim is plain: more patients, deeper responses.
europmc-pmc8093302:
Kim reviews how short-chain fatty acids from gut bacteria steer lymphocyte behavior. Dietary fiber feeds gut bacteria, which ferment it into these acids. Acetate, propionate, and butyrate are the big three products. Fiber was once classed as a nonessential nutrient. That view has flipped: the acids it yields help balance the whole immune system.

The review walks through the lymphocyte families one by one. Innate lymphoid cells come first, then helper and killer T cells. B cells and their antibody work close the survey. The acids act through several routes at once. They block histone deacetylases, ring G-protein-coupled receptors, and feed cell metabolism. The net effect can raise defense or calm it, as context demands. Allergy and inflammation outcomes trace back to those settings. Diet, through bacteria, becomes an immune lever.
europmc-pmc8151502:
Mathew-Steiner, Roy, and Sen examine the role of collagen in wound healing. Healing moves through inflammation, growth of new tissue, and remodelling. Collagen, a key part of the extracellular matrix, guides each phase.

The review covers collagen types in skin and how the body processes them. It shows how chronic wounds break this pattern, with lasting inflammation and heavy enzyme damage. Collagen has also been used as an added therapy to aid healing. The authors review collagen formats and clinical study results. Aging effects on collagen close the survey. The survey ties basic collagen science to bedside choices.
europmc-pmc8356302:
Papakonstantinou and co-authors present CINeMA, software for judging confidence in network meta-analysis. Network methods compare many treatments through linked trials. They mix direct and indirect evidence into one ranking.

Decision makers lacked a friendly way to grade that evidence. CINeMA fills that gap as a web application. It scores six domains that affect confidence. The frame builds on work by Salanti and others. This tutorial walks users through the app step by step. Ratings come out in a form guideline panels can use. Treatment rankings gain an honesty label. The six domains structure every rating the app produces.
europmc-pmc8363502:
Solís and co-authors measure COVID-19 vaccine acceptance across low- and middle-income countries. Ending the pandemic needs wide vaccine uptake. Attitudes in poorer countries were little studied as rollout began.

Fifteen survey samples covered 10 such countries, plus Russia and the United States. In all, 44,260 people took part. Willingness averaged 80.3% in the poorer-country samples. The United States averaged 64.6%. The spread within the group reached about 30 percentage points. Acceptance ran higher where rollout was just starting. The data calm fears that hesitancy would block global coverage. Russia, an upper-middle-income case, sat below the poorer-country mean.
europmc-pmc8512302:
Adepu and Ramakrishna review controlled drug delivery systems, their status now and their future paths. Plain tablets, capsules, and syrups suffer from poor uptake and swinging drug levels. They cannot release a drug at a steady rate. Without sound delivery, a good drug can fail.

Controlled systems aim to release at a set rate, at the right site. The review starts with drug movement basics and the flaws of old systems. It then sorts controlled designs and their build rules. Nano-scale delivery and smart materials that answer cues get full treatment. Targeted systems close the survey. The field has moved from macro devices to intelligent delivery.
europmc-pmc8515002:
Norori and co-authors call for open science to fight bias in health AI and big data. Artificial intelligence could aid clinical choices and reshape care. But algorithms learn from data that often miss or distort whole groups of people. Skewed training data can lock bias in.

The results can be fatal errors, missed diagnoses, and tools that fail on new groups. The authors set out the challenges of making algorithms fairer. They propose concrete steps drawn from open science practice. Shared data standards and joint work with the public feature in the plan. Their point is plain: fair AI needs open, shared science from the start.
europmc-pmc8516002:
Jean-Baptiste and co-authors track gene expression in single root cells of Arabidopsis thaliana. Root traits trace back to special cell lines and their parent cells. Older methods cut tissue apart or sorted cells by markers. Both were slow and rough, and marker lines exist for few plants.

Single-cell RNA profiling offers a cleaner path. It can map growth paths cell by cell. It can also catch cell-type shifts during heat shock at single-cell detail. The team applied the method to root cells of this model plant. Their work shows how single-cell data replace labor-heavy approaches. The result is a fine map of root cell identity and change.
europmc-pmc8522202:
Salari and co-authors pool world studies to fix the global prevalence of osteoporosis. This bone-thinning disease touches patients, families, and health budgets alike. A clear world picture helps policy makers plan care and spending. Past counts varied by region and method.

The systematic review followed PRISMA rules and searched six databases to August 2020. In all, 86 studies entered the meta-analysis. Together they covered over 103 million people aged 15 to 105 years. The pooled world prevalence came out under one in five people. The authors checked study spread and publication bias as well. Their count gives planners a shared base figure.
europmc-pmc8837802:
Ling, Wang, and Kuzyakov take stock of the bacteria living around plant roots. This zone, the rhizosphere, is a microbial hotspot fed by roots. The team pooled 557 pairs of published sequence datasets. Each pair compared root-zone soil with bulk soil. Sites spanned ecosystems around the world. The goal was general rules, not one field's story.

Root zones held fewer kinds of bacteria than bulk soil. Plants appear to select a seed bank from the soil pool. Fast-growing groups such as Bacteroidetes and Proteobacteria were enriched. Bacterial networks there were modular but unstable. Dormancy rested on toxin-antitoxin systems rather than spores. Genes for nitrogen fixation and denitrification were enriched. Genes for nitrification were depleted. The study frames the rhizosphere as a plant-shaped community.
europmc-pmc8840702:
Zhang and co-authors review ferroptosis as a way to break cancer drug resistance. Ferroptosis is a form of cell death driven by iron. It differs from apoptosis, necrosis, and autophagy. It also helps suppress tumors. Resistant cancers, though, often dodge standard treatments. Forcing ferroptosis may corner them again. The review tests that idea therapy by therapy.

The authors first explain how ferroptosis works inside the cell. They describe the redox imbalance at its core. They name GPX4 as a central guard against it. They then review chemotherapy and targeted therapy cases. Immunotherapy resistance gets its own treatment. In each case, triggering ferroptosis restored drug effect in studies cited. The authors close with prospects and challenges. Clinical use, they note, is still ahead.
europmc-pmc8863502:
Feikin and co-authors ask how long COVID-19 vaccine protection lasts. The answer shapes booster policy. They ran a systematic review with meta-regression. The search screened 13,744 studies. Full review narrowed those to 18 studies. All predated wide Omicron spread. The team measured how efficacy changed from month 1 to month 6 after full vaccination.

Protection against infection fell by 21.0 percentage points on average. The fall was similar in older adults. Protection against symptomatic disease fell by 24.9 points. Protection against severe disease held up better, the data showed. Four vaccines contributed most evaluations. Bias risk varied across the studies. The authors give policy makers a clear waning curve. Boosters, the pattern suggests, have a real role.
europmc-pmc8870502:
Bunge and co-authors review how human monkeypox has changed since 1970. The virus causes a smallpox-like illness. First found in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, it spread across parts of Africa. Cases outside Africa have appeared in recent years. The team ran a systematic review of journal and grey literature. They tracked case counts, ages, deaths, and spread. Forty-eight articles and 18 grey sources fed the analysis.

Cases have climbed, above all in the Congo. The median age at illness rose from 4 years in the 1970s to 21 years in 2010–2019. The overall fatality rate was 8.7%. The Central African clade killed more often than the West African one. Travel-linked outbreaks reached beyond Africa after 2003. The authors blame waning smallpox vaccine protection in part. They call for stronger surveillance.
europmc-pmc9139602:
Shiravand and co-authors review immune checkpoint inhibitors in cancer therapy. Drugs that block PD-1, PD-L1, or CTLA-4 have changed care for several cancers. They have helped patients with melanoma, kidney, head and neck, and lung cancers. Yet only some patients respond well to them.

The review updates what is known about each approved drug class. It then turns to markers that may predict who will benefit. Those markers include tumor mutation burden, PD-L1 levels, the microbiome, and interferon-gamma. Tumor surroundings also shape outcomes. The authors stress that better markers are a pressing need. Readers get a broad update on a therapy class and the search to aim it well.
europmc-pmc9352102:
Frescura and co-authors lay out the path to the 95-95-95 HIV targets for 2025. The goals: 95% of people with HIV know their status, 95% of those diagnosed get steady treatment, and 95% of those treated reach viral suppression. UN member states adopted them in June 2021. They replace the earlier 90-90-90 goals.

The paper reviews proof behind raising each bar. The older goals put 27.5 million people on treatment by the end of 2020. Gains were uneven, with men and young people lagging in status knowledge. The new targets stress every subgroup, age band, and region. Prevention goals and social enablers sit beside the treatment cascade. The aim is to end AIDS as a public health threat by 2030.
europmc-pmc9417302:
Gui and co-authors report that STING, a key immune adaptor, also switches on autophagy. The cGAS pathway spots stray DNA in the cell and raises an alarm. That alarm was known to drive interferons and cytokines. A second, older job now comes to light.

Once STING binds its signal, it moves to a membrane zone near the Golgi. That zone feeds membrane into new autophagosomes, the cell's cleanup sacs. The path needs WIPI2 and ATG5 but not the usual starter kinases. This cleanup helps clear DNA and viruses from the cell. STING from a sea anemone drove autophagy but not interferons. The authors take that as a sign autophagy came first in evolution.
europmc-pmc9452302:
Deng and co-authors describe spatial-ATAC-seq, a method that maps open chromatin in place inside tissue. Gene activity depends on the local tissue setting. Spatial methods can map gene expression across a slice. No tool could yet map epigenetic state at genome scale in place.

The method pairs Tn5 chemistry done in the tissue with microfluidic barcoding. Each spot in the slice gets its own code before sequencing. Maps of mouse embryos showed region-specific epigenetic patterns. Gene regulators for nervous system growth stood out. Brain maps in mouse and human showed fine area borders. Tonsil maps split immune cell types by zone. The tool adds an epigenetic layer to spatial biology. It can help link cell fate choices to their gene control base.
europmc-pmc9465902:
Shahid and co-authors study how low health literacy affects outcomes for hospital patients. Health literacy is the skill to read, grasp, and use health information. The team recruited patients on general medicine units at two urban hospitals. Literacy was scored with a standard adult test.

Half the patients had adequate health literacy. Another 32% scored inadequate and 18% scored marginal. Patients with inadequate scores were far more likely to revisit the emergency department within 90 days. The odds ratio was 3.0 against the adequate group. Oddly, low literacy with high schooling gave the highest revisit odds. No clear link showed for length of stay or readmission. The authors flag literacy checks as a way to spot risk early.
europmc-pmc9489702:
Tong and co-authors take stock of osteoarthritis pathogenesis and new ways to study it. The disease is the most common degenerative joint disease. It harms the whole joint, not just cartilage. Its molecular drivers are still not known.

The review opens with epigenetic control of the disease. DNA methylation, histone changes, and microRNAs are covered in turn. Key mediators of joint pain come next. New lab tools then take the stage. CRISPR, single-cell RNA sequencing, and lineage tracing all feature. Cell death paths get a full section, from pyroptosis to ferroptosis and autophagy. The last theme is the synovial lymphatic system and its role in joint drains. The authors say sharper mechanism maps should yield more precise drugs. No drug yet modifies the disease itself.
fbi-vault-9-11-commission-report-9-11-ch:
Part 2 of 2 of a working chronology from the Federal Bureau of Investigation forms a dated grid of moves by the September 11 hijackers and the men around them. Staff built the tables for the commission that studied the attacks. Each row ties an act to a date and to the case paper that backs it.

Entries for May 29, 2001, show flight training checks, a car hire, and cash taken from bank accounts. Rows for August 2001 note a gym sign-up, laundry, and a cell phone used as a contact number. Bank, phone, and travel records give the grid its facts. The text layer is rough, with codes and short forms in most rows, but the shape of the last months before the attacks comes through.
fossey-magie-assyrienne-1902:
Charles Fossey published his study of Assyrian magic in French in 1902. He gathered magical texts copied from ancient clay tablets. Transcription, translation, and commentary accompany each text in his edition.

The spells show priests battling demons with ritual formulas and sacred names. Illness, nightmares, and misfortune all had demonic causes in this world. Fossey explained the language and the rites for fellow scholars carefully. His study became a foundation stone of Mesopotamian religious studies. French Assyriology led the field in this period, and Fossey's book shows why. Anyone tracing magic's oldest written roots passes through his work.
frus-1861-d102:
Lord Lyons wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 23 October 1861. The letter is document 102 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

By late October the Lyons correspondence had a rhythm of its own: claim, answer, claim. Each round tested the other's patience and law. This note is one more move in that slow game, played for stakes that included the life of the Union. Lyons judged the Union likely to last, a view that shaped his counsel to London. His counsel to London carried weight because it was so seldom wrong.
frus-1861-d202:
On 12 August 1861, William H. Seward wrote to Cassius Clay in a graver tone after Bull Run. The letter is document 202 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Seward's mid August letter to Russia shares the grave tone of that month's orders. Defeat at home called for plain words everywhere. His note to Clay kept the one friendly great court close, without taking its favor for granted. Favor not taken for granted stayed favor, a lesson Seward taught by letter after letter. Favor kept by care is the theme the Russian file sounds from start to end.
frus-1861-d302:
A letter home from Mr. Thayer, dated 20 July 1861, landed on Seward's desk. It was printed as Document 302 in the foreign affairs papers sent to the two houses of Congress. It belongs to the first summer of the Civil War, when keeping Europe out of the war was a core task for Washington.

Such reports fed the facts and rumors together into one desk in Washington, week by week. For students of the war, the value lies in the sequence: one dated step in a long exchange. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1862-d102:
In a report dated 17 July 1862, Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London wrote home to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It was printed as Document 102 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs for 1862. The letter comes from the summer of 1862, the war's second year, a time when each foreign capital watched the war with care.

Such reports fed the facts and rumors together into one desk in Washington, week by week. Read in order with its neighbors, it shows diplomacy as daily work rather than grand speeches. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1862-d202:
Lord Lyons wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 9 January 1862, in a letter printed as Document 202 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Lyons had represented Britain in Washington since 1859 and knew the capital well.

A minister's letters to a secretary of state carried his government's questions, protests, and replies in formal form. Lyons used the channel briskly in early January as the Trent settlement closed. His note belongs to the file that documents how the two governments, having nearly fought, settled back into wary daily dealings. Each note was numbered and docketed by clerks, which is why the file reads so evenly.
frus-1862-d302:
On 9 August 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward sent William L. Dayton a dispatch printed as Document 302 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Dayton was the American minister to France, posted in Paris.

Seward wrote the day Cedar Mountain was fought in Virginia, though the result was not yet clear in Washington. His Paris letters that month worked to offset the gloom of a bad summer. For Dayton, each dispatch was both instruction and ammunition. Words he could use with French officials who read Union defeats as reasons to favor the South. France's Mexican venture shared the court's attention with the American war all year.
frus-1862-d402:
Horace J. Perry in Madrid received this dispatch from Secretary of State William H. Seward on 29 May 1862. It appears as Document 402 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, issued with the President's annual message.

Late May 1862 found Union forces before Corinth and Richmond, and foreign courts watched to see if the rebellion would crack. Spain's court, ruling Cuba across a narrow sea from Florida, heard Confederate pleas often. An instruction like this one armed Perry with Washington's view of the war and its aims. The case for the Union was thus put in Madrid in Seward's own chosen words.
frus-1862-d502:
James Shepherd Pike received this instruction from Secretary of State William H. Seward on 21 May 1862. It is Document 502 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the State Department's printed record.

Late May 1862 was a confident moment in Washington, with Richmond threatened and Corinth about to fall. Seward's orders abroad struck a firm note on neutral duties and on the hopeless state of the rebellion, as he saw it. Pike at The Hague was to carry that note to the Dutch government in his plain style. The dispatch belongs to the spring sequence in which the Union, for a few weeks, argued from strength in every capital in Europe.
frus-1862-d602:
Headed Despatch 10 and dated 15 April 1862, this paper concerns the extraordinary diplomatic mission of Spain in Mexico. It is Document 602 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, among the translated Spanish papers.

Mid-April 1862 was the hinge of the Mexican affair: the allies quarreled openly, and Spain and Britain moved to withdraw while France advanced alone. A Spanish paper of that date, numbered in its own series, belongs to the diplomacy of that breakup. The State Department printed such documents because the United States, absorbed in civil war, was managing Mexico by record and protest. The despatch is evidence in that record, in Spain's own hand.
frus-1862-d702:
Charles N. Riotte, the American minister in Costa Rica, wrote this dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 15 May 1862. Riotte was a German-born lawyer whom Lincoln had sent to Central America. The letter is document 702 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862.

Central America drew Washington's eye because any canal or transit route across the isthmus would run through it. Riotte's reports covered the small republics' politics and the safety of American trade and travel there. This dispatch is part of that watch. It is the ground-level record of a post that rarely made the news but sat on a route the whole world wanted.
frus-1863p1-d102:
William H. Seward sent this letter to Charles Francis Adams on 2 March 1863, the sixth of twelve dated that day in the file. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 102 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

Halfway through the batch, the shape of the day is clear: Seward worked down the London file point by point, one sheet each. The claims at stake were the war's claims — fair dealing, no aid to the South, no warships from British yards. This letter is the sixth stroke of that work. It takes its meaning from its place in the row, a brief rebuilt in a day.
frus-1863p1-d202:
On 18 May 1863, orders left Washington for London: Secretary of State William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. The paper is document 202 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. The document comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States, the government's own published record of Civil War diplomacy. It was one of 3 letters between the same men dated that day.

The CSS Alabama, built near Liverpool, had slipped away in 1862 and was raiding Union trade. Washington pressed London to stop such ships and answer for the losses. Historians still mine this correspondence for the inside story of Anglo-American relations during the war.
frus-1863p1-d302:
Reporting on 1 October 1863, Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, wrote home to Secretary of State William H. Seward. The report is document 302 in the 1863 diplomatic papers. The letter is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, the official series that publishes American diplomatic papers.

Union wins at Gettysburg and Vicksburg in early July 1863 weakened the case for aiding the South. British leaders grew more careful, and Adams's post grew a little less tense. Alone it settles little; in the run of the volume it helps explain why Britain stayed out of the American war.
frus-1863p1-d402:
On 24 February 1863, Secretary of State William H. Seward put the American position in writing to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington. This note is document 402 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. The text is preserved in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume, which gathered the year's diplomatic mail for Congress and the public.

Read together, these letters trace a slow cooling of the crisis mood of 1861 and 1862. Recognition of the South grew less likely with each month the channel stayed open. Historians still mine this correspondence for the inside story of Anglo-American relations during the war.
frus-1863p1-d502:
In the flow of wartime mail, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Lord Lyons, Britain's envoy in Washington on 8 May 1863. America was then in the third year of its Civil War, and every letter to or from London carried weight. The letter is one piece of the steady stream of notes that passed between the two governments in the spring of 1863.

Letters like this one were the tools of a quiet contest. The Union meant to keep Britain out of the war, and it made that case note by note. The letter also shows the craft of the period: a few stiff phrases could carry a warning, and both sides knew how to read them. Alone it is one note among hundreds. In place, it is part of how a war stayed between the two sides that started it.
frus-1863p1-d602:
From Secretary William H. Seward to Britain's minister in Washington, Lord Lyons: a letter dated 4 August 1863. The letter was later printed in the 1863 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, issued with the President's annual message. The State Department later published the letter in its 1863 foreign affairs volume, laid before Congress with the President's message.

The real subject under all the polite wording was British neutrality. Washington wanted it kept strict, and London wanted no quarrel it could avoid. Single letters rarely settle anything here. Their worth is in the chain they form, which lets a reader watch a dispute rise, cool, and fade in real time. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it helps the full story of wartime diplomacy stay traceable, letter by letter.
frus-1875v02:
Haiti opens Volume II of the 1875 papers. Bassett writes from Port au Prince through the year. Italy, Japan, and Liberia follow. Mexico takes a long section. Russia's file carries a debate on the laws of war. It praises the Brussels conference for shielding the wounded. Prisoners and civilians, it argues, need defined rights.

Spain and the Virginius return near the end. A separate run prints the steamer's later correspondence. Sweden, Switzerland, and the Turkish Empire follow. Egypt gets its own sub-file under the Porte. Uruguay and Venezuela close the volume. The mix is typical of the series at rest. Old crises echo while new posts report. Bassett's steady letters give the book its spine.
frus-1902:
Cuba frames the 1902 volume's circulars. American military occupation there has ceased, Washington announces. United States consuls will now guard Cuban interests abroad. Passport rules fill the opening pages. Austria-Hungary's legations rise to embassies in another file. Both capitals agree to the new rank. A mid-volume letter extends the consular web further. Hay asks London to charge its Sofia agent with American interests. Bulgaria has no American post of its own.

Argentina settles a difficulty with Chile in its section. Telegraph operators there refuse a military service exemption. Manchuria appears in a Russo-Chinese agreement. The volume records an empire quietly ending. New republics and new embassies take its place.
frus-1914-20v02:
Volume II of the Lansing Papers covers American belligerency. War aims and peace negotiations lead the files. Cooperation with the Allies fills the longest run. General Bliss reports from the Supreme War Council. His single report earns its own heading. Russia's collapse takes a large section. The Far East follows, with Lansing-Ishii at its center. Shantung gets two documents of its own.

Latin America closes the volume. A Pan-American treaty is proposed and debated. The Danish West Indies pass by purchase. Mexico fills the last country file. The mid-volume assessment looks to 1918. Allied officers judge that full victory needs maximum effort. Unforeseen chances might still open success. The volume records a secretary managing a world war.
frus-1917Supp02v02:
Volume II of Supplement 2 builds America's trade control system. Export control grows step by step in these papers. Britain and France withdraw their black lists of American firms. The Espionage Act of June 15 authorizes an embargo. An Exports Council forms on June 22. Wilson states the policy on June 26. A July proclamation restricts exports in law.

Officers abroad must now report on neutral trade. Information flows between Washington and the Allies. A Swedish letter begs support against economic ruin. Brun warns of disaster if arrangements lag. Neutrals feel the squeeze from both sides. The volume documents a blockade turned inward. America's own commerce becomes a weapon. Licensing replaces the old neutral rights.
frus-1918Russiav02:
Russia Volume II treats disintegration and foreign intervention. Siberia and Manchuria fill its chapters. Japan debates sending troops as local governments form. America declares against intervention on March 5, 1918. Japanese forces land at Vladivostok a month later. British troops land beside them. Semenov advances, then falls back. The Czecho-Slovaks appear and clash with Soviet forces. Consuls offer good offices between the fighters.

A mid-volume report fears Japan's deeper design. Her moves, it says, contradict her official statements. Allies fear she exploits the Allied focus elsewhere. Horvat and the railway boards crowd the pages. Every power backs a different Russian future. The volume documents intervention's confused birth. No capital controls the story it starts.
frus-1918Supp01v02:
Volume II of the 1918 supplement runs the blockade as a belligerent. Export and import controls tighten through the year. America presses Britain to drop navicerts and Halifax exams. Bunker license rules issue in January. An executive order seizes control of foreign finance. February proclamations license every export and import. The Allied Blockade Committee forms in London in March. Trade committees follow in neutral capitals.

Sweden and the Netherlands win eased terms for nonessentials. Denmark follows in the relaxation. Certificates of interest now guard neutral shipments. The mid-volume agreement delivers chartered steamers to America. Ships pass at their charter's end port, by Shipping Board choice. The volume shows economic war administered. Forms and licenses do the fighting.
frus-1918Supp02:
This 1918 supplement deals with men and goods caught by the war. The first part treats prisoners held by each side. It sets pay for officers in enemy hands. It weighs a plan to send health staff back home. A Berne meeting with Germany ends in a pact. That pact bears the date of the armistice day itself.

The next part sorts enemy aliens by birth and ties. Men from Alsace and Lorraine get kind terms in the files. Czechs, Slovaks, and Poles win the same kind care. The last part takes charge of enemy goods and rights. Patents and trade marks fall under state control. German banks in Brazil draw notes of advice. German cacao farms in Ecuador earn two short files. German firms in Honduras fill a much longer run.
frus-1919Parisv02:
Volume II of the Paris papers turns to defeated and newborn states. Germany's armistice terms open the book. Conventions prolong it in December and January. The former Kaiser's status gets its own file. The Dresel mission reports from inside Germany. Austria's Coolidge mission follows. Jugoslavia takes the longest territorial run. Montenegro, Albania, and Czechoslovakia follow. Poland and Roumania fill solid files.

Reparations and finance come after territory. Food relief outweighs both in bulk. The blockade's regulation closes the volume. A mid-volume dispatch despairs of Austria's liquidation. Nothing is left undone, it says, yet normality lags. German Austria protests its goodwill all the while. The volume maps a continent in pieces. Relief ships matter as much as borders.
frus-1919v02:
Volume II of 1919 works the hemisphere and the new states. Cuba asks General Crowder to help rewrite election law. Liberals there beg for American supervision. Czechoslovakia gains an American minister in April. Danzig gains an American commissioner in October. The Dominican Republic lives under military rule. Its customs and tariff pass through American hands. Ecuador's railway bonds draw steady pressure. A modus vivendi settles that quarrel in April.

A mid-volume wire presses Japan on Tientsin. Polk wants Tokyo's answer to an American memorandum. Press comment, he notes, makes delay costly. Such nudges fill the year's diplomacy. The volume ranges from Prague to Santo Domingo. New flags and old debts share its pages. Washington manages both with telegrams.
frus-1920v02:
Cuba dominates Volume II of 1920. Its election law passes with Conservative backing. Menocal promises the people a fair vote in October. Crowder sails on a special mission as results lag. Money panic follows the sugar crash. Banks face heavy withdrawals; a moratorium follows. Rathbone advises Cuba on a rescue loan. Cable companies win concessions in the same files. Rice imports spark a trade quarrel. Havana restricts them; Washington protests twice.

A mid-volume note guards the Reparation Commission's honor. Its rulings, America insists, must rest on free judgment. Great powers must not bend it to their interests. The volume pairs island crisis with allied finance. Sugar, ballots, and bonds fill its pages. The Caribbean comes first in bulk.
frus-1921v02:
Volume II of 1921 settles the war's leftovers with Germany. A treaty signed August 25 restores friendly relations. Berlin asks America to mediate on reparations. A German-built airship for America wins assent. Britain then fills the middle files. London protests charges of unfair oil rivalry. America refuses British claims for the Turkish Petroleum Company. Standard Oil meets limits in Palestine. Canal tolls for coastwise ships stay in place.

A mid-volume letter moves warships off Mexico. The Sacramento sails from Galveston to Tampico. A second ship comes up from the Canal Zone. Oil ports needed watching that season. The volume joins treaties to tankers. Its diplomacy smells of petroleum throughout. The postwar order ran on oil rights.
frus-1922v02:
Volume II of 1922 ranges from Greenland to Egypt. America denies any third power a first claim on Greenland. Denmark's rights there stand untouched in the file. The Dominican Republic plans the military government's end. A ten-million-dollar bond issue wins consent. Egypt's independence gains American recognition. Ethiopia's firearms imports draw a British request. France's mandates in Syria and Africa need treaties. Germany's reparations draw American help again.

A mid-volume wire drafts Haiti's loan law. Hughes promises a counter-draft by mail. It would give force to the protocol's terms. Haiti's own draft of December sits beside it. The volume shows the era's two faces. New nations win recognition; old protectorates persist. Both fill the same diplomatic pouch.
frus-1923v02:
France leads Volume II of 1923. Talks resume on American rights in Syria and the Lebanon. Togoland and the Cameroons win conventions in February. An old arbitration pact gains more years in July. America protests French scholars' sole rights in two lands. Albania and Afghanistan both barred rival diggers. Germany then signs a broad trade treaty in December. Reparations help fills a long file after it. The occupation army's costs win a five-power deal. That army then sails home for good.

Ruhr exports draw protests over unfair rules. A mid-volume case defends an American protégé in Morocco. Ben Said's file shows the charges shifting ground. Shifting grounds, the note says, prove nothing. The volume is mandates and their discontents.
frus-1924v02:
Germany's Dawes Plan claim opens Volume II of 1924. America insists on its share of reparation payments. An American becomes the plan's Agent General. Belgium pays toward the occupation army's costs. Tank ships of a German oil firm draw compromise talks. The airship ZR-3 crosses to American hands. Hughes urges the Senate to ratify the German trade pact. Britain's files follow the German ones. Central African mandate rights need a treaty. Palestine's old court rights are guarded meanwhile. A Palestine convention signs in December.

Iraq's oil door must stay open, Washington argues. New Zealand's Samoa trade rules draw protest too. A mid-volume rule specifies passport paper. It must be stout, distinct, and signed by few hands. The volume joins reparations to travel papers.
frus-1925v02:
Cuba opens Volume II of 1925 with an island's title. The Isle of Pines treaty of 1904 is ratified at last. Consular, extradition, and smuggling pacts follow. Czechoslovakia signs an extradition treaty in July. Private loans to Prague wait on its war debt. The Dominican convention of 1924 is explained in notes. Ecuador owes a bank for its cacao growers. Its rebel government wins no recognition. Estonia signs two trade deals within the year. Finland signs two of its own.

A mid-volume article frees state property from taxes. Consuls may hang their arms above the office door. Such clauses fill the trade pacts' texts. The volume is the year's treaty harvest. Small print binds the hemisphere and Europe. Each pact here took effect in ink.
frus-1926v02:
Volume II of 1926 opens in Colombia. A trade treaty is drafted but stalls. The Colon fire claims will not be arbitrated, Bogotá says. Border disputes crowd the early list. Colombia faces Peru; Costa Rica faces Panama. Cuba then signs a cluster of pacts. Liquor smuggling wins two conventions in March. Consular and extradition deals follow within weeks. The Dominican Republic floats a new bond issue. Egypt's files guard American diggers' rights. Consular courts there judge British seamen, London protests.

A mid-volume file traces a Japanese firm's debts. Takata bought American electrical goods on credit. Much of it served Japanese government contracts. New York banks now hold the paper. The volume joins customs houses to courtrooms. Trade's failures fill its back pages.
frus-1927v02:
China fills all of Volume II for 1927. Civil war rages as the Nationalists purge their Communists. American lives and property need guarding throughout. Nationalist troops attack foreigners at Nanking in March. The powers demand amends in a long file. Citizens flee danger towns across the spring. That evacuation file runs longest of all. Peking's legation guards take over the Russian sector. Arms shipments to China stay banned. A wireless set on a Yangtze warship stays too.

Treaty revision talks close the volume. Tariff control and foreign courts are the stakes. A mid-volume note tracks a diplomats' joint statement. Japan's minister first balked, then withdrew his block. The volume is a treaty system collapsing. Gunboats guard its last years.
frus-1928v02:
Canada shares this 1928 volume with Chile's opening file. Shipping profits escape double tax by arrangement. Halibut and sockeye fisheries need new pacts. Missisquoi Bay's fish win no joint study. Lakes diversion calls for works to offset it. The Roseau River's drainage goes to the Joint Commission. St. Lawrence improvement returns for another round. Trail's smelter fumes damage Washington farms. That claim fills the Canadian file's longest run. Border officers' bullets stray into Canada, Ottawa protests.

Peaches and milk face embargoes both ways. A mid-volume note from Kellogg weighs China. Action there, he concludes, costs more than it gains. The volume is neighborly friction in full. Fish, fumes, and farms fill its diplomacy.
frus-1929v02:
Belgium opens Volume II of 1929 with peace machinery. Arbitration and conciliation treaties sign in March. Battle monuments win a site agreement in October. The Chaco quarrel between Bolivia and Paraguay follows. Bulgaria signs its own pair of treaties in January. Canada then fills the volume's heart. The rum-runner I'm Alone goes to arbitration. Salmon of the Fraser River lack a sealed pact. Halibut rules await replacement as well. Missisquoi Bay at last wins its commission. Niagara's beauty gets an unperfected convention in January.

A mid-volume case guards a citizen's status. Mr. Char's file warns against a precedent. China must not gain sway over Americans of Chinese birth. Proof was demanded; none satisfied the court men. The volume joins scenery to sovereignty. Falls, fish, and citizenship fill it.
frus-1930v02:
China takes all of Volume II for 1930. Civil war ends as Manchuria backs Nanking. The north's rival regime loses by autumn. Guarding Americans fills the longest file by far. Customs and salt funds face seizure up north. Trade taxes judged unfair draw steady protest. A Shansi tobacco monopoly is fought in turn. Russia and China clash over their shared railway. An arbitration pact signs in June. Shanghai's settlement gains Chinese courts by deal in February.
