Giving up foreign courts dominates the tail. China insists the powers relinquish them. Jurisdiction over Americans fills file after file. A mid-volume talk parses favored-nation clauses. Wu probes the American reading; Hornbeck holds it firm. China might plead the conditional reading instead. The volume is the treaty order negotiating its end.
frus-1931-41v02:
The second Japan volume covers the slide to war. Tension grows through 1939, 1940, and 1941 in turn. Tokyo's Axis ties take their own file. America kills the old trade treaty of 1911. Economic squeezes follow in a long run. Japan pushes south into Asia and the Pacific. Then come the talks of 1941 in full. A summary heads hundreds of conversation records. Hull and Nomura circle the same hard ground for months.

A mid-volume draft lists what must be cleared. War in Europe, the China affair, sea power, trade. Each side's whole outlook is item one. The papers end with the year itself. Readers know what December brought. The volume is diplomacy's last act, kept entire. Its failure needs no narrator.
frus-1931v02:
Colombia's oil laws open Volume II of 1931. The Barco dispute settles in the same file. Bankers and Bogotá reconcile with Washington's help. Cuba's unrest fills the next run. Santo Domingo cannot borrow and halts debt payments. Ecuador shakes with its own unrest. Egypt's mixed courts must share seats fairly. The Salem claim goes to arbitration by pact. El Salvador's revolution takes the largest space. Its legation in Washington suffers a burglary too.

Ethiopia weighs a new basic treaty with the powers. France's premier Laval visits in the later files. A mid-volume note drafts Haiti's financial truce. The adviser's visa on payments is the sticking point. A fair formula is offered as the last concession. The volume is the Depression abroad. Loans fail from Havana to Addis Ababa.
frus-1932v02:
The British Commonwealth and Europe share the 1932 second volume. Kuwait's sheikh is courted for an oil grant. Palestinian goods must not win favor in Britain's ports. Four American destroyers, rebuilt for trade, draw protest. Bahama rum-running draws a request for facts. War inventions' claims go to a joint board. Turtle fisheries link Borneo and the Philippines. Canada then takes its long turn. A St. Lawrence treaty signs in July, unperfected. The seized Josephine K brings a Canadian protest.

Radio waves are shared by notes in May. Warplanes gain blanket leave to cross in September. A mid-volume note counts Greece's refugee loan. Six million of it was raised in America. A fresh Greek loan deal signs in May. The volume mixes empire, dominions, and debts.
frus-1933v02:
The British Commonwealth opens the 1933 second volume. Canadian grain shipped through America poses a tariff puzzle. Property pacts and citizenship cases fill small files. An arbitration treaty is shelved without a date. Canada then bargains over trade in earnest. Trail's smelter claim grinds on in its file. Canadian officers seize four American salmon boats. Their names head a protest file. An American's prison treatment in Canada draws visits' demands. The St. Clair's shoals are dredged by joint deal. River water is shared by another.

Memoranda fill the mid-volume pages. Phillips records talks as the year turns. A British chargé reads his instructions aloud in one. Such minutes are this volume's texture. Empire business runs on paper courtesies. The volume ends before Ottawa's deal.
frus-1934v02:
Austria's agony opens the 1934 Europe volume. Socialists rise; Nazis plot; Dollfuss is murdered. Those papers run longest at the front. An Austrian trade mission then visits America. Vacuum Oil seeks a bigger crude quota there. Belgium bargains over trade in short files. Bulgaria's soldiers seize power in a coup. Czech papers report on the German minority's mood. Mormon missionaries face expulsion in their file. Denmark talks trade and air rules.

A mid-volume letter proposes opening trade talks. Obstacles on both sides are frankly owned. Direct talks, the writer urges, deserve a path cleared. Such letters fill the year's commerce drive. The volume pairs a chancellor's murder with tariff drafts. Europe's crisis and its paperwork share one binding.
frus-1935v02:
Britain leads the 1935 second volume on trade. Talks toward a pact open the contents. Air rules and pilot licenses are swapped in spring. London questions America's anti-smuggling reach at sea. Australia opens its own trade talks. Canada then signs the year's big deal in November. Trail's smelter wins a tribunal by April pact. Lakes cargo and a border lake's level follow. Consuls gain the right to visit jailed nationals.

A mid-volume cartoon shows the Nazi mood. Hitler Youth's paper draws a broom sweeping firms. Radical youth, the report warns, still press their fight. Germany's domestic storm fills such enclosures. The volume joins dominion trade to Reich politics. Tariff schedules and cartoons share its pouch. Ottawa's signature is its high point.
frus-1936v02:
Europe's trade drive fills the 1936 second volume. Albania first wins regret for a newsreel insult. The March of Time film drew Tirana's complaint. Austria and Belgium talk trade without closure. An old naturalization pact needs joint reading. Belgian shipping escapes double tax in January. Czech trade bias against Americans draws protests. Estonia seeks to recast its 1925 pact. Finland signs a full trade deal in May. Its seized ships' claims ride along. France signs its trade deal on May 6. Tax talks with Paris run on beside it.

A mid-volume decree shows Poland's grip. All exchange deals pass through its state bank. Permits guard every transfer abroad. The volume is commerce under control. Each capital now rations its currency. Trade deals multiply as freedom shrinks.
frus-1937v02:
Trade with Britain leads the 1937 second volume. London's talks fill the first long run. Australia and New Zealand ponder British-only shipping. A seized motor vessel draws London's protest. Pacific islands are claimed by both flags. Their air age value drives the quarrel. Australia's trade curbs ease in its file. Canada talks a new trade deal in turn. The St. Lawrence plan and tax pact follow. A British steamer's halibut voyage draws joint protest.

An Alaska highway is sought in earnest talk. Halibut rules sign in January that year. Radio license news is swapped by agreement. A mid-volume draft article frees state land from taxes. Consuls' premises win the same shield in the text. Such clauses recur in the era's treaties. The volume is dominion business, well papered.
frus-1938v02:
Trade deals crown the 1938 second volume. Britain signs its pact on November 17. Canada signs its own the same day. Pacific islands still split the two flags. Air routes make those atolls precious. Australia talks trade without a deal. The St. Lawrence plan gets two papers. Rainy Lake's level wins an emergency pact in September. Patent practice, pilot licenses, and air rules follow. Each swaps by notes through the year. Radio traffic with Alaska is regulated too.

A mid-volume text lists Italy's new race creed. A pure Italian race exists, it declares. Jews stand outside it by the manifesto's logic. The points were cabled home as warning. The volume joins tariffs to racial laws. Commerce proceeds while Europe darkens. Its two November signatures close an era.
frus-1939v02:
Odd corners of the world fill the 1939 second volume. America reserves its rights in the Antarctic first. A new Antarctic Service is then created for science. Cotton exporters meet in Washington in September. Wheat and whaling rules draw London meetings. Flying fuel's taxes are lifted by a pact. War debts from the first war sit unpaid. The League wins thanks for wider non-political work. Refugees from Germany take the longest file. Committees labor to place those forced to flee. Japan's fishing off Alaska draws sharp notes last.

A mid-volume wire reports a Prague rebuff. Britain's envoy sought a consul's papers there alone. Berlin's men refused the request outright, Kirk cables. Consulates became front lines that year. The volume ranges from ice to exile.
frus-1940v02:
Neutral rights fill the 1940 second volume's front. America's policy is stated, then defended in protests. Allied controls pinch trade with neutrals in files. Wood pulp shipments draw joint protests with two neutrals. Bringing Americans home takes the largest space. Ships and trains move thousands from the war zone. Aliens seek release from the belligerents too. Refugee aid continues with the Evian committee. Defense stockpiles then take over the contents. Rubber and tin are bargained from world cartels. Copper is bought from sister republics for arms.

A mid-volume letter mourns France's fall. Bullitt praises her soldiers' last stands. They charged with bayonets when shells ran out. Her upper classes failed wholly, he writes. The volume joins rescue to rearmament. Its mood shifts from rights to readiness.
frus-1941v02:
Europe's squeezed states fill the 1941 second volume. Belgian tankers shift flags to Panama in protest files. London's Czech government wins recognition in its turn. Greenland's defense is pledged by Denmark's envoy. His captive government's acts are disowned meanwhile. Danish ships in American ports are seized for use. France then dominates the middle contents. Collaboration with Berlin alarms Washington in files. Food and drugs for the unoccupied zone are weighed. North Africa becomes the volume's second half. The Murphy-Weygand deal signs in February.

Aid to that region halts, then resumes in summer. Observers watch where the goods go. A mid-volume talk weighs a Free French landing. St. Pierre's seizure might set a bad precedent, Moffat warns. Darlan could seize on it, he fears. The volume is empire in suspense.
frus-1942v02:
Europe's exiles and victims fill the 1942 second volume. Belgium signs mutual aid on June 16. Its Congo trade needs a three-power deal. War with Hungary, Bulgaria, and Rumania is owned. Czechs sign mutual aid in July. Finland's file runs longest by far. Washington begs Helsinki to quit Hitler's war. France then takes the volume's center. Vichy's help for the Axis ends relations. The Dunkerque's move to Toulon draws protest. Trapped French warships at Alexandria follow.

North Africa's aid restarts amid resistance plotting. A mid-volume statement hails French liberation's start. Africa begins it, Hull declares to the press. All Frenchmen resisting the Axis win welcome. The volume is a continent half enemy, half ally. Its files sort them week by week.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d102: Roosevelt wrote to Stalin on November 8, 1943, in one of the last letters sent before his journey. It is Document 102 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Twenty days later the two men would shake hands at Tehran, ending two years of writing to a stranger. The record names the date and the leaders only. The letter rests in the Foreign Relations series, at the edge of the voyage papers.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d202:
Acting Secretary of State Edward Stettinius cabled Ambassador Averell Harriman in Moscow on 9 November 1943, in telegram 1180, marked secret and personal. Roosevelt had handed him Harriman's message 6100, sent by Navy channels three days earlier, about the Allied agreement on Turkey.

Stettinius gives the answer Harriman needed. He is authorized to grant Molotov's request that his letter carrying the President's message on Turkey be made part of the secret military record of the Moscow conference. The short cable is the final Washington approval in that small chain of messages, which had begun with Harriman's own request from Moscow.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d302:
Civil affairs in France are the subject of a long secret telegram Secretary of State Cordell Hull sent President Roosevelt from Washington on 24 November 1943. A paper on the subject, approved by Roosevelt, the War Department, and the British, had been sent to the Moscow conference and referred to the European Commission.

London now proposes a different approach. The French resistance is strongly represented on the French Committee at Algiers. Britain therefore argues that French cooperation in planning civil rule for liberated France can be won only one way. The matter must first be cleared with the Committee at government level. The British also expect the Soviets to raise the Committee's status at Tehran, and want an Anglo-American line agreed before that happens. A planners' note sketches a French director of civil affairs under the Allied commander.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d402:
Prime Minister Churchill wrote President Roosevelt a short personal letter at Tehran on 1 December 1943, his sixty-ninth birthday weekend, thanking him for a present. The gift, sent with a signed message of affection, was a beautiful bowl.

Churchill says he was indeed touched by the present. He will always treasure the bowl as a reminder of their sunlit days in Tehran. It also recalls the most memorable of his birthdays. He cannot thank Roosevelt enough, he adds, for all his friendship and support in the years they have worked together. He is glad of the occasion to send a message of sincere affection and gratitude. The letter is signed, as his letters to Roosevelt often were, yours always, Winston S. Churchill.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d502:
Laurence Steinhardt, the American ambassador to Turkey, was temporarily at Cairo when he wrote to Harry Hopkins on December 6, 1943. Turkey was the Second Cairo Conference's special business: Roosevelt and Churchill had just met President İnönü to urge Turkey toward the war. The State Department printed Steinhardt's message in its Cairo-Tehran volume.

Steinhardt, posted in Ankara, was Washington's expert on the Turkish question, and Hopkins was the man to reach at the President's side. Their exchange ties the embassy in Turkey directly to the summit's central negotiation. For readers, it shows specialized knowledge moving from the man on the spot to the center of power in a single step.
frus-1943v02:
Europe fills Volume II of the 1943 Diplomatic Papers, issued in the Foreign Relations of the United States series. Country by country, it tracks ties with states under occupation, in exile, or still neutral. France takes the most space, from the split between Giraud and de Gaulle to rule in North Africa.

Italy stands out, with the fall of Mussolini, surrender, and co-belligerent status. Other chapters cover Spain, Portugal, Poland, and the Low Countries, plus aid and legal accords. Embassy cables and policy memos show Washington weighing military needs against the politics of each capital.
frus-1944-quebec-d102:
Hull wrote to President Roosevelt on August 30, 1944. The State Department printed the letter in its Quebec 1944 volume. It belongs to the final run of papers before the conference. Hull advised the President on all foreign affairs.

End-of-August letters from Hull carried the department's settled views. Roosevelt would host Churchill at Quebec within two weeks. Germany's future dominated the coming talks between them. Aid to Britain and the Pacific war also awaited decisions. For readers, the letter shows the Secretary of State briefing his President. He wrote in the last stretch of summit preparation.
frus-1944-quebec-d202:
At tea on September 15, 1944, Roosevelt received Empress Zita of Austria and her sons, the Archdukes Otto and Felix. No American record of the talk was found. The editors print a State Department translation of Otto's own memorandum, which reports the president's remarks on Austria, Hungary, and Russia in unusual detail.

Austria and Hungary, Roosevelt said, would undergo the least territorial change of any countries; only Transylvania was unclear. The main concern was keeping the Communists out of both, especially Hungary. If Hungary surrendered unconditionally to the Americans and British alone, she could be saved from communism and expect mild terms. Roosevelt liked Stalin personally, Otto recorded, but called him untrustworthy and deceitful.
frus-1944-quebec-d302: Editors of the Foreign Relations series supplied this short note, dated 19 September 1944, as document 302 of the Quebec volume. Editorial notes in the series explain gaps, point readers to related papers, or record facts the documents themselves leave unclear. The note is brief, but it forms part of the apparatus the Office of the Historian built around the conference record.
frus-1944v02:
Economic and social matters fill Volume II of the 1944 Diplomatic Papers. Postwar trade and money lead off, with the Bretton Woods meeting at the core. Relief for freed lands, UNRRA work, and the Safehaven hunt for hidden Axis funds come next.

Long sections cover civil aviation talks at Chicago and joint shipping plans. Coal, transport, whaling, rubber, and sugar each get papers, as does uranium control with Britain and Belgium. The volume shows experts laying the rules for world trade and aid. Much of that order lasted for decades. The wartime alliance's strain shows in nearly every exchange here.
frus-1945-50-intel-d102:
Magruder, writing as the SSU's director to Secretary of War Patterson on 4 February 1946, addressed the head of his department directly. The central intelligence settlement was then two weeks old. The text comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States volume that looks back at American intelligence work from 1945 to 1950.

A unit chief writing to his cabinet secretary marks a question that has outgrown the staff channels. The SSU's future under the new Central Intelligence Group was exactly such a question. Its secret operations were the richest prize the new body could inherit. Readers should place this paper at the start of the transfer story. What the CIG became in 1946, it became largely by absorbing the people and stations whose fate papers like this one decided.
frus-1945-50-intel-d202: A draft memorandum from the Central Intelligence Group bears the date 2 December 1946. It is document 202 in the Foreign Relations volume on intelligence for 1945 to 1950. A draft shows wording still open to change, before a final text went out. The Group was the working arm of the new central intelligence system that year.
frus-1945-50-intel-d302:
Dated 8 October 1948, this memorandum runs from Acting Director of Central Intelligence Wright to the Executive Secretary of the National Security Council (Souers). It is document 302 in the Foreign Relations of the United States volume on intelligence for 1945 to 1950. It was a season of stock-taking: the CIA was a year old, and its friends and critics were both writing things down.

The memo form let a staff officer speak straight to a chief: here is the point, here are the facts, here is what is asked. Kept in sequence, such memos form the true diary of the office that sent them. Kept with its neighbors in the volume, it shows the new system being built one dated paper at a time.
frus-1945-50-intel-d402:
Fisher Howe, deputy in the State Department's intelligence office, wrote to Sheppard, a special assistant to the Secretary of State, on 17 October 1949. The memo is document 402 in the Foreign Relations volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

A note from the intelligence bureau to the Secretary's own front office carried weight out of size. It shows the bureau working to place its views where they would be read at once. For readers, the memo is a small lesson in how access and timing shape power inside a department. The paper's path through the building tells as much as its text about how State was run.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d102:
Archibald MacLeish wrote to Under Secretary Grew on 24 January 1945 with a reminder and a warning. MacLeish, an assistant secretary of state, asks Grew to raise one topic with the Secretary the next day. His top secret note is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume.

The topic is provisional governments in freed areas, Yugoslavia being the case in point. MacLeish wants the coming talks to seek a public pledge: such governments rest on the promise of free elections once elections are possible. Recognition should depend on those elections truly being held. Without such safeguards, he warns, the recent wave of disillusion will grow, and talk of Atlantic Charter principles will ring hollow.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d202:
Admiral Leahy passed a draft message up to the President on 5 December 1944. His short note, printed in the Malta and Yalta volume, carries a text Stettinius suggested sending to Churchill that day. It concerns Stalin's two messages about de Gaulle.

The draft tells the prime minister that the President has received Stalin's messages of 2 and 3 December about his talks with the French leader. Stalin, the draft notes, sent Churchill identical messages of his own. Before answering Stalin, Roosevelt would like to have Churchill's views. The editors record that the message was in fact sent, as number 667. It is a small gear in the three-cornered exchange that ran ahead of the Big Three meeting.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d302:
Grew kept the traveling Secretary fed with world news in this roundup of 31 January 1945. His top secret excerpts, printed in the Malta and Yalta volume, gather the day's general information from Washington. Each item runs a line or two, and together they map the war's loose ends.

Winant is to act with his Soviet colleague in the European Advisory Commission to approve the French claims to equality on German matters. Under extreme Soviet pressure, the Czechoslovak cabinet has decided to recognize the Lublin Committee. Subasic waits in London until Tito recognizes the King's regency council. Greece is settling, with EAM accepting the government's plan for the peace talks. Bohlen, Grew adds, holds a long memorandum from Mikolajczyk proposing a settlement of the Soviet-Polish quarrel.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d402:
Five Latin American states get a quiet push in Stettinius's cable to Grew of February 8, 1945. The five associated nations that had not yet declared war should be urged to do so at once. They should also adhere to the United Nations Declaration. The cable calls this absolutely essential by the end of the month.

Only if they acted in time would their step count for their interests — a seat at the founding conference. Knowledge of the message was limited to five named men in Washington. Stettinius signed off relying on Grew to renew the Department's recommendations. The wire shows the guest list being filled by pressure, in secret.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d502:
Germany must pay in kind. The protocol on reparations, agreed by the three heads of government at the Crimea Conference, opens with that rule. Payment would go first to the countries that bore the main burden of the war, suffered the heaviest losses, and organised victory over the enemy.

Reparation in kind would be exacted in three forms. The first was removals within two years of Germany's surrender, drawn from German national wealth at home and abroad. Equipment, machine tools, ships, and rolling stock are all named. The protocol fixed the principle and the forms. The famous sum — twenty billion, half to Moscow — stayed in the discussion record, not in this signed text.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d102:
General Deane sounded hopeful in a second telegram to General Bradley on June 26, 1945. The message is document 102 in the Foreign Relations volume on Potsdam. He had taken up the signal crews, the Zehlendorf scouting, and the air route once more, this time with Lieutenant General Slavin, who stood in for Antonov.

Deane hopes the communications men will be allowed in at once, with official approval possibly coming by telephone that night. Slavin asked how many men the signal work needed. Rather than lose time cabling Frankfurt, Deane answered 90. He judged that to be enough until July 1, when the Americans could move freely into their Berlin sector. He also hopes for answers on the Zehlendorf survey and on switching the air route from Stendal to Halle.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d202:
Ambassador Winant reported Eden's approval of the American agenda in a telegram from London on July 8, 1945. The personal message to Secretary Byrnes is document 202 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. Washington's topic list had been delivered to the Foreign Office the day before.

In a brief talk over his private wire, Eden volunteered that he was very much pleased with the agenda as forwarded. Eden was about to come to London to act as Prime Minister while Churchill vacationed in France before the conference. Winant planned to dine alone with him on Tuesday and send a fuller account of the British reaction afterward. No report of that dinner has been found, a note in the volume adds.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d302:
Ambassador Harriman cabled from Moscow at midnight on June 30, 1945, about reshaping Hungary's Allied Control Commission for the armistice's second period. He deferred to General Key in Budapest on which points belonged in new statutes. Key, he said, sat closer to the problem than the Moscow embassy did.

Harriman reported no answer from Molotov to his June 1 letter urging real three-power authority. He doubted Moscow would accept any plan letting British or American members block commission acts. Pressing too hard now, he advised, might do more harm than good. His caution captures the weak hand Washington held in Hungary.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d402:
French aims on the Rhine are summarized in extracts from a briefing book paper on France dated June 23, 1945. Paris had put forward no concrete proposals, the summary says, but the views of French officials could be stated. France disclaimed any design to annex German territory outright.

Instead, France wanted the Rhineland and Westphalia, including the Ruhr, separated from Germany. The two would be kept apart from each other, under distinct regimes. Ruhr-Westphalia would sit under an international regime. The Rhineland, from the Swiss frontier to beyond Cologne, would sit under permanent French military and economic control. That area takes in the Saar and bridgeheads on the right bank. Luxembourg, Belgium, and the Netherlands might share in the control.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d502:
Delivery of the recognition texts in Moscow is reported in Harriman's cable of July 5, 1945. That evening he delivered to the Polish ambassador the texts of the President's message to Osóbka-Morawski and of the public statement on recognition of the Polish Provisional Government of National Unity. The ambassador expressed his appreciation for being provided with the texts.

He stated that he would transmit them to his government immediately. The announcement of recognition, he added, would appear in the next morning's papers in Poland. Harriman notes that the British ambassador was also sending a communication to the Polish ambassador that same evening, keeping the two recognitions in step.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d602:
A planning date for the end of Japan's organized resistance is set in a U.S. Chiefs of Staff memo of July 7, 1945. It is document 602 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. The date was meant for staff talks with the British at the conference.

The chiefs propose November 15, 1946, as the planning date. It would guide factory output and the assignment of manpower, and it could be adjusted as the war went on. They also ask that the phrase end of the war be avoided in this context. Some U.S. laws lapse at set times after the end of a war. Those laws, the chiefs note, should stay in force through the occupation of Japan. The Combined Chiefs took up the paper at Potsdam on July 19.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d702:
Acting Secretary Grew recorded a courtesy call by Turkey's ambassador in a memo dated July 7, 1945. It is document 702 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. Ambassador Baydur came with his secretary, who served as interpreter.

After talk of the San Francisco Conference's success, Baydur passed on his foreign minister's regrets. An early sailing from Boston had kept the minister from a hoped-for stop in Washington. Grew replied that he fully understood the reasons. Baydur then turned to the Moscow talks of three weeks before. He restated Molotov's three stated demands on Turkey. They were a rectification of the Turkish-Soviet frontier, bases on the Dardanelles, and a two-sided revision of the Montreux Treaty. The memo shows Ankara working Washington directly as the summit neared.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1002:
American members of the Economic Subcommittee reported to the Secretary of State on August 1, 1945. The printed text is an extract of their report. One section covers German external assets, where the Americans and British had pushed a new clause for the Economic Principles.

The clause would have the Control Council take control and power of disposal over German-owned external assets abroad. It covers assets not already held by Allied nations that fought Germany. The pair also wanted the matter named in the conference communiqué. Soviet members showed little interest and reserved their stand pending study. The attached third report records plainly that no decision was reached.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1102:
Another working paper from the American team at Potsdam carries the date 25 July 1945. Like the papers drafted around it, it was staff work, written behind closed doors. Its job was to give United States negotiators a clear, agreed stand to carry into the talks.

By the second week the summit had moved past opening speeches into close bargaining over details. Papers of this sort were drafted, revised, and sometimes dropped as the talks shifted. This one holds a snapshot of the American team's thinking on a single day. Read with its companion papers, it shows a large staff machine at work.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1202:
London's team tabled this proposal on 19 July 1945, the summit's third day. British papers at this stage set out what the government wanted from the peace. Each gave the Americans and Soviets a clear British stand to answer.

The government behind this paper was itself days from falling. Churchill's team wrote the stand; another team would have to defend or drop it. That odd fact hangs over the British papers of the first week. This proposal is the formal British bid from the opening round, kept in the American files for later readers to weigh.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1302:
The Acting Secretary of State wrote to Ambassador Baruch in Portugal on 1 August 1945. The message reached Lisbon on the summit's last full day. Washington kept even its neutral posts in step as the conference closed.

Guidance to Lisbon mattered because Portugal's stand touched trade and the Atlantic routes. A cable at the end of the talks could align the post with the new lines the peace had drawn. This one shows the home office closing the circuit with a quiet embassy. It is the Potsdam web at its widest reach, touching a capital far from the German table.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1402:
Ambassador Caffery reported to the acting secretary of state from Paris on 6 August 1945. After a week of writing to Bidault, Caffery here writes home, summing up for Washington. The text comes from the second Potsdam volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official history series.

Reports home after a bout of local talks are where ambassadors explain what they have done and what it means. Caffery had spent the turn of the month in close exchange with the French foreign minister. Readers can set this report beside the letters themselves and judge how faithfully the ambassador described his own work. That double view, act and account, is one of the pleasures of the Foreign Relations series.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-102: Printed among the unnumbered pieces after document 710, this editorial note is part of the second Potsdam volume's working frame. The historians behind Foreign Relations of the United States used such notes to mark sources and links. A reader gains bearings from it: what kind of paper sits nearby, and where its story continues. It is brief by design, a guide rail rather than a document.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d802:
Melbourne reported from Rumania on July 19, 1945, in document 802. The acting representative in Bucharest wrote to the Acting Secretary of State. His post sat inside a Soviet-chaired control commission. The report entered the second Potsdam volume of the official record.

Reports from Bucharest carried a distinctive strain. Melbourne had to work with partners who often shut him out. Readers feel that strain between the lines of a formal report. The document shows the alliance's eastern edge fraying in real time. It also honors the officers who kept reporting clearly while their influence waned.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d902:
The Economic Sub-Committee sent this extract of its report to the foreign secretaries at Potsdam on July 20, 1945. The full report also appears earlier in the volume. This extract covers the reparations section of the talks. It records agreement on seven basic principles from the Allied Commission on Reparations.

One clause stayed disputed. It would have paid for approved imports before reparation deliveries, while leaving Germans enough to live on. The sub-committee could not agree on it. Talks on defining reparations, restitution, and war booty were put off at Soviet request. The Americans held that definitions and sharing formulas had to be settled together.
frus-1945Berlinv02:
Proceedings fill Volume II for the Potsdam Conference, held near Berlin in the summer of 1945. A log of President Truman's trip opens the record. Minutes then follow each day, from staff meetings to plenary sessions with Churchill and Stalin.

Readers can track talks on Germany, reparations, Poland, and the war against Japan as they unfolded. Foreign ministers' sessions and side talks fill out the days. The volume pairs formal minutes with memos written at the table. It is the fullest day-by-day account of how the victors divided the postwar world.
frus-1945v02:
General political and economic matters make up Volume II of the 1945 Diplomatic Papers. Atomic bomb materials and early bids to control atomic energy open the record. The London and Moscow foreign ministers' meetings follow, with their minutes and cables.

Relief dominates the middle, from UNRRA work to aid for freed lands and help for displaced persons. German population transfers, the Safehaven program, and art salvage also appear. Trade talks, coal, and inland transport close the volume. The papers show the victors trying to feed Europe while they argued over its future.
frus-1946v02:
Volume II for 1946 belongs to the Council of Foreign Ministers. Deputies met in London and Paris to set up the second session. That session then sat in Paris in two parts, in spring and early summer.

Minutes and cables track the drafting of peace treaties clause by clause. A third session in New York closed the year, with early work on German and Austrian treaties. The record is dense and day by day. It shows the wartime allies turning into rivals at the table, while the texts they argued over still shaped Europe.
frus-1947v02:
Volume II for 1947 joins the Council of Foreign Ministers with Germany and Austria. Deputies met in London first, then the council sat in Moscow in the spring. Minutes, reports, and tabled drafts track the German peace question without a settlement.

A London session late in the year failed the same way. Back in Germany, the record turns to bizonal teamwork, coal, and the level of industry plan. Food crisis papers and reparations fill long runs. The Austrian treaty commission worked apart. Readers watch four-power rule give way to two blocs.
frus-1949v02:
Volume II for 1949 pairs the United Nations with the Western Hemisphere. At the UN, the Essentials of Peace debate and China's charge against Soviet treaty breaches set the East-West tone. Chinese representation appears as the mainland war neared its end.

Headquarters work, elections, and voting rules fill shorter runs. Canada follows, with trade and air talks. The hemisphere block then works on the Bogotá accords and Caribbean tensions. Delegation cables show one agenda in New York and another in the Americas, with the same rivalry behind both. Law work on genocide and treaties also appears.
frus-1950v02:
Volume II for 1950 pairs the United Nations with the Western Hemisphere. China's seat leads the UN record, as the mainland regime claimed its place. The Uniting for Peace plan follows, built to act when the Security Council stalls.

Headquarters issues, trusteeship, and South-West Africa fill shorter runs. Human rights drafts and refugee questions also appear. Canada comes next, with defense teamwork. The hemisphere block then covers OAS approval, Caribbean disputes, and arms aid. The papers show two stages where one rivalry played out. Genocide and treaty law work appears in shorter files.
frus-1951v02:
Volume II for 1951 pairs the United Nations with the Western Hemisphere. China's seat again dominates the UN record, with hundreds of papers. New members and Italy's case as a special plea follow.

Soviet peace drives and Yugoslavia's charge of hostile acts mark the rivalry's tone. Trusteeship fights, the Ewe question, and South West Africa fill the colonial block. Canada and the republics close the volume. Delegation reports show procedure and power mixed in each vote, as blocs hardened and new states pressed for a voice. Refugee and rights drafts fill the human rights block.
frus-1955-57v02:
Volume II of the 1955–1957 set is the Taiwan Strait crisis of early 1955. Policy toward both Chinas runs from January to July. The Formosa Resolution, the Tachen pullout with American help, and the Quemoy-Matsu question drive the record.

Bids to free American prisoners in the People's Republic fill later files. Those bids led to the Geneva ambassadorial talks. A mid-sample talk record shows President Eisenhower calling Quemoy-Matsu a liability he could not shed. The volume catches a superpower at the brink, then stepping back to a table. Each move was weighed against the risk of a wider war.
frus-1958-60v02:
The United Nations and general international matters fill Volume II of the 1958–1960 set. UN debates, votes, and membership fights lead the record. Outer space and the law of the sea take long blocks.

Antarctica's treaty also appears in these files. General questions, from disarmament forums to colonial issues, fill the rest. The papers show world bodies used as arenas. Each vote was counted in advance, and each speech was drafted for home as much as for the hall. Space law and sea law were new fields, argued from first rules in these pages.
frus-1961-63v02:
Vietnam, 1962 fills Volume II of the 1961–1963 set. The Taylor plan moves from paper to ground. Advisers, helicopters, and new commands fill the early files, as the effort takes fixed shape.

Strategic hamlets spread through the middle record. Saigon's rule and its costs draw steady study. The Diem government's grip, and its price, run through the cables. Reports of gains sit beside reports of rot. The volume reads as deepening. By its close, exit talk has left the files, and the war's logic runs on its own. Adviser counts climb through the middle files here.
frus-1964-68v02:
Vietnam, January–June 1965 fills Volume II of the 1964–1968 set. Saigon's coups and chaos lead, with reprisal strikes after attacks on American posts. The bombing of the North takes fixed form in February.

Ground combat troops land from March, and grow through the spring. A May bombing pause fills the next block, weighed and ended in the files. Saigon's government changes again in June. The record shows a war crossing its line in steps. Each paper adds a mission or a battalion, and no paper takes one back. The pause's end is argued in the closing files.
frus-1969-76v10-d202:
Minutes of a Washington Special Actions Group meeting, held April 2, 1975, record the U.S. response to collapse in Indochina. The record is document 202 in Volume X of the 1969-1976 Foreign Relations series. Kissinger chaired the meeting. Colby briefed that few South Vietnamese units were still fighting. The group agreed to start moving U.S. dependents out of South Vietnam at once. It also asked Embassy Saigon for a ranked list of Vietnamese to evacuate.

The talk turns to stretching the Cambodia airlift to April 17. Schlesinger presses for fast removal of staff who are not essential. The minutes catch a government shifting from war support to rescue.
frus-1969-76ve02:
Arms control and nonproliferation from 1969 to 1972 fill Volume E-2 of the 1969-1976 series. The first section covers the Non-Proliferation Treaty and its safeguard system. The second covers the Geneva disarmament talks and the Seabed Arms Control Treaty. The longest section treats chemical and biological warfare. It runs through the Geneva Protocol to the Biological Weapons Convention. Later sections cover test ban issues and the Latin American nuclear free zone.

Talk records show Kissinger probing why toxins mattered if research was for defense only. The papers trace the U.S. choice to give up biological weapons. The volume pairs treaty texts with the fights behind them.
frus-1977-80v02:
Human rights and humanitarian affairs fill Volume II of the 1977-1980 Foreign Relations series. The first and longest section covers human rights policy itself. Later sections treat world hunger and food policy, then health, population growth, and women's issues. An internal paper urges a major speech by a top official to set out the policy's gains and setbacks. It also urges naming a human rights advocate inside the White House.

The records show the Carter team building a policy and then defending it. Country reports, demarches, and aid choices fill the pages. Food aid is treated as both relief and leverage. The volume is the core record of a signature Carter theme.
gao-gaoreports-b-295502:
On March 14, 2005, GAO issued its ruling in file B-295502, the protest of Liberty Power Corporation. The General Services Administration had awarded Pepco Energy Services and Constellation NewEnergy contracts to supply electric power to federal and other facilities. Liberty, a small disadvantaged business, said it was denied a price evaluation adjustment it had been led to expect. GAO sustained the protest. The agency's own exchanges had led the firm to price its offer on the faith of that preference.

Having shaped the firm's price, the agency could not then deny the preference as unauthorized. If it thought the adjustment barred, GAO held, it had to amend the solicitation and let offers be repriced.
gao-gaoreports-b-296602:
Encompass Group protested the terms of two Veterans Affairs calls for linens and blankets in GAO decision B-296602, dated August 10, 2005. Both calls were set aside for small firms. The firm said no small firm made bulk cloth. Thus, it said, no small firm could supply the goods.

GAO denied the protests. Market checks found two or more small firms for the work. Those firms could give goods made by small firms. Prices were fair as well. A set-aside needs proof that small firms can do the work at fair prices. That proof was made here. The set-asides thus stood.
gao-gaoreports-b-296902:
Delphinus Engineering protested its loss in a Navy contest for ship repair support in GAO decision B-296902, dated September 20, 2005. The work backed ship living spaces. The firm was in the 8(a) small firm program. It said it was the sole fit 8(a) bidder with a fair price. It thus claimed a deal was due.

GAO denied the protest. The call was open to all firms. It said deals would go to the most strong bids on tech and cost. No right to a deal came from 8(a) rank alone. Marks on a test task were also sound. Work not named in the bid need not be weighed.
gao-gaoreports-b-297702:
Draughn and Associates protested Agriculture orders for probe work in GAO decision B-297702, dated February 15, 2006. Three rival firms won the orders. The work was equal job chance probes. The buy used schedule firms. The firm's quote was not weighed. It said that cut was wrong. The call asked firms to show how they would meet the work.

GAO denied the protest. The quote failed to show how the work would be met. That sketch was required by the call in plain terms. A quote that skips a required sketch can be cut. The agency need not guess how a firm would do the work. The sketch must be in the quote itself.
gao-gaoreports-b-298102:
GC Services protested Treasury task orders for debt chase work in GAO decision B-298102, dated June 14, 2006. Three firms won the orders. The buyer was the Internal Revenue Service. The work was private debt collection. The firm hit marks on its quote and on a rival quote. It also hit a fitness call for a rival.

GAO denied the protest in part and cut part. Tech marks on the firm's quote fit the call terms. They were also sound on the record. Debt chase work is scored on the plan shown in the quote. A firm must show its plan well to earn top marks. No flaw that would shift the orders was shown.
gao-gaoreports-b-298502:
MD Helicopters, Inc. and AgustaWestland, Inc. protested an Army award for Light Utility Helicopters. The contract went to EADS North America Defense Company. The new fleet was to replace aging aircraft in support roles. GAO decided B-298502 and its joined cases on October 23, 2006.

Each firm attacked the best-value call from a distinct side. One held a lower score and a higher price. The other held a higher score but cost far more. GAO found the scoring deep and well kept. The top firm's edge was not worth an added $800 million over the $3.9 billion winning bid. GAO denied both protests.
gao-gaoreports-b-299702:
A National Archives delivery order to Alon drew a protest from Data Management Services Joint Venture. The order covered support staff for an electronic records archives office. The buy ran through a federal supply schedule deal. GAO decided B-299702 and B-299702.2 on July 24, 2007.

One claim faulted how past work was judged for relevance. The terms set a scope test for like work. The panel bent that test for some past jobs. GAO found a fair base for the bend and no harm to the firm. A second claim alleged a bait and switch on staff. Swaps for like or better staff do not prove that wrong. GAO denied the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-305402:
Cash from an insurance change raised a deposit question in this GAO decision, B-305402, dated January 3, 2006. Caltech runs a NASA lab under a long pact. Caltech held Prudential Life policies for lab staff. When Prudential changed its form, Caltech got stock as compensation. The stock was later sold for cash.

GAO held that NASA may not keep the sale cash. The cash was not a repayment to NASA. No law lets NASA credit it to its own funds. NASA must put the cash in the Treasury as miscellaneous receipts. GAO also faulted the wait to deposit it. Staff had told Caltech to hold the cash in a money market fund. That broke the prompt deposit rule.
gao-gaoreports-b-310502:
Bottled water for field crews is cleared, with terms, in this GAO decision, B-310502, dated February 4, 2008. The Army Corps of Engineers runs work sites in its Savannah District. Some far sites have no safe water at hand. Law and Corps rules call for safe water for staff at work. A pay officer asked if funds could buy bottled water for those crews.

GAO raised no bar to the buy. The Corps may pick the best way to get safe water to a site. Jugs and coolers are one path. Bottled water is a fair path too. The Corps must first judge, site by site, that bottles are the best fit.
gao-gaoreports-b-310902:
Ceres Environmental Services, Inc. lost its protest. GAO decided B-310902 on March 3, 2008. The Army Corps of Engineers sought a firm to build a drain canal. The canal is the last leg of a flood plan for southeast Louisiana. The Corps used talks-based bids, not sealed bids. Ceres said sealed bids were the right path for build work of this kind.

GAO denied the protest. The Corps judged that speed of build was key here. That need made non-price points count in the pick. Sealed bids weigh price with scant room for such points. A rush need can back the talks path.
gao-gaoreports-b-311002:
LEADS Corporation lost its protest; the GAO decision is B-311002, dated March 26, 2008. The Patent and Trademark Office sought program aid services. The order went to Enterprise Information Services, Inc. LEADS held the past deal for the work. Its quote scored high on know-how and shift plans. The winner's quote scored low on those points and cost less in price.

GAO denied the protest. The agency weighed the score gap against the price gap. It found the high marks did not earn the high price. That trade call was fair on the facts. A past holder's edge in know-how can be outweighed by cost.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-202:
Homeland Security, GAO-05-202 of February 23, 2005, reviews the spend plan for a vast border check system. The US-VISIT program tracks set foreign guests as they enter and leave the United States. It holds facts and body marks, such as finger scans, on each guest. Congress told the department to send its spend plan for GAO review first.

GAO tests the plan next to each rule Congress set for it. It adds notes on how the build is run day to day. Some gains stand, the title grants. Many hard tests still wait, from data flow to cost control across the program's long life.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-702:
A blueprint for the Pentagon's back office has consumed years and money, GAO-05-702 reports on July 22, 2005. After almost 4 years and about $318 million, the defense department still lacks a working business enterprise architecture to guide its system buys. The governing board set up in 2001 holds too little power. No program plan sets measurable goals, tasks, or dates. No one has mapped the staff skills the work needs.

Draft products are patchy, at odds with each other, and unapproved. A law-set deadline lands in September 2005. GAO repeats its standing advice and scores the department against each past recommendation.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-802:
The national archives' digital records project is tracked in GAO-05-802, released July 15, 2005. Work began in 2001 to build a system for electronic records. Two design contracts were let in August 2004. One design was to be picked in August 2005. Congress told GAO to report on cost, schedule, and performance. GAO also checked status on its past recommendations.

GAO found the program is meeting its cost, schedule, and performance aims so far. All major milestones were met on or ahead of time. Three big deliverables met the set standards. Risks were named, though no single schedule ties all related agency work together. One past recommendation is fully done. Others are partly done. New security flaws were found, including the lack of a tested disaster recovery plan.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-102:
Truck crash data quality is graded in GAO-06-102, a report dated November 18, 2005. Big trucks are 3 percent of registered vehicles. They were in 11 percent of fatal crashes in 2003. States gather crash data and send it to a federal safety agency. That data must be complete, timely, accurate, and consistent to be useful. GAO asked what is known about its quality and what states do to lift it.

Headings state the pattern. States still have data quality problems, but they pursue many fix efforts. Meeting the standards remains a challenge. Faults often start at the scene, where officers misread criteria on report forms. Processing backlogs add more. The federal agency's grant program has supported state work with real gains. Its data quality map spurred states to improve, GAO found. But the map's limits curb its further use.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-202:
Livestock price reporting and the trust it needs are reviewed in GAO-06-202. The report is dated December 9, 2005. Ranchers earned $63 billion in gross income in 2004. They lean on the Agriculture Department's daily, weekly, and monthly market news to price cattle, hogs, and lamb. Packers use the same averages to pay many growers under contract. A 1999 law forced packers to report far more of their deals. GAO judged the department's quality checks as Congress debated renewing that law.

The department took real steps to guard report quality, GAO found. Yet its reporters left some packer deals out of the reports they built. That habit clouds how open the reports are. GAO urged the department to make the reports clearer and to audit packer data more closely. It also weighed how two department arms share the job of guarding competition. The department broadly agreed and said work on the advice had begun.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-402:
Once a drug is on sale, watching for harm is a second, vital job. GAO's March 31, 2006 report, GAO-06-402, reviews the Food and Drug Administration's postmarket drug safety work. High-profile cases in 2004 raised doubt about the agency's skill. In some cases, staff inside the agency disagreed on how to act.

GAO describes the agency's structure and process for safety choices. It grades how well that process works. It also checks steps the agency is taking to improve. Case studies cover four drugs: Arava, Baycol, Bextra, and Propulsid. GAO called for improvement in decision making and oversight. Readers see how disputes can slow safety action.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-502:
Tobacco settlement money flows to states each year, and this report tracks where it went. GAO's April 11, 2006 report, GAO-06-502, is the fifth and final in a yearly series. In 1998, four large tobacco companies signed a Master Settlement Agreement. They agreed to pay 46 states each year, without end. The payments repay states for past tobacco-related health care costs. A 2002 farm law requires these yearly GAO reports through fiscal year 2006.

GAO surveyed all 46 states. It reports payments received in fiscal year 2005 and expected in fiscal year 2006. It shows how states split the funds among program types. Changes from prior years are included.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-802:
Joint war training is the subject of GAO-06-802, which GAO issued on August 11, 2006. The Defense Department built its Training Transformation Program so forces arrive in theater ready to fight jointly. The centerpiece is the Joint National Training Capability, a web of linked ranges and simulations. It accounts for 84 percent of the $2 billion the department plans to invest by 2011. GAO checked whether the effort is improving joint training.

GAO found that the department does not know how far the initiative has improved joint training. It had not yet assessed the program's impact. GAO's review of five enhanced training events found some signs of potential gains. But the first department assessment was still pending. GAO urged management actions to prove the value of the investment. Training claims, GAO implied, need evidence like any other program.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1102:
Patent backlogs will not shrink on hiring alone, GAO finds in report GAO-07-1102, dated September 4, 2007. More, and more complex, patent bids have stretched the time the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office takes to work them. A growing pile of unexamined bids waits.

GAO traced 5 years of hiring. It asked how the office sets its yearly hiring aims, and how those aims link to the pile. It weighed how far new hires are offset by staff who leave, and why they leave. It checked if efforts to keep staff match why staff stay. GAO polled 1,420 examiners, with an 80 percent reply rate.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-202:
The federal long-term care insurance program sells coverage to federal workers and retirees. GAO compared its design with private rivals in GAO-07-202, dated December 29, 2006. Long-term care spending ran about $193 billion in 2004 and is set to rise. This is the second of two reports the 2000 law required. GAO studied the program's profit setup and its marketing. It also updated the picture on claims.

The program pays its manager under a set profit formula, GAO found. Three yearly payments stand apart from program costs. Two rest on premiums and one on program assets. Some of those profits are guaranteed, unlike in private plans. Marketing hit a snag: the program lacked home addresses for nearly all active workers. It had to rely on less direct outreach. Claims also ran below forecasts. The program had paid 44 percent of the expected claim dollars per enrollee.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-102:
Federal support for electricity is cataloged in GAO report GAO-08-102 (October 26, 2007). Electricity comes mostly from coal, other fossil fuels, and nuclear power, with hydropower and renewables behind. The federal government aids the sector in many ways. It funds research, grants tax breaks, and runs other support programs.

GAO estimates that research funds for the sector came to $11.5 billion from fiscal year 2002 through fiscal year 2007. That sum grew 35 percent across the period. Nuclear programs took the largest share, at $6.2 billion. The report sorts support by fuel type and by kind. It gives Congress a single tally of what the government spends to back power production.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-402:
Nanotechnology risk research reporting is examined in GAO report GAO-08-402, released March 31, 2008. The National Nanotechnology Initiative links 25 federal agencies that fund work at the scale of a nanometer. GAO checked how five agencies reported their fiscal year 2006 research on environmental, health, and safety risks.

The initiative said agencies spent $37.7 million on such risk research in fiscal year 2006, 3 percent of the $1.3 billion total for nanotechnology. GAO found that 22 of 119 projects counted as risk research were not truly aimed at measuring risk; many used nanotechnology to clean up hazards instead. Weak reporting rules and a lack of guidance caused the mix-up. GAO recommended clearer guidance from the Office of Science and Technology Policy, which generally agreed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-502:
Defense base facilities come up in GAO report GAO-08-502, issued April 24, 2008. The Defense Department runs about 577,000 structures worldwide, valued at about $712 billion. It plans to spend over $55 billion in fiscal year 2008 to support these facilities and run its bases.

A sustainment model used since 2003 gives a steady way to estimate yearly upkeep needs, but two of its inputs are shaky. Services have not verified property records as rules require, and an outside study found only 13 of 45 cost factors sound. Services also missed department funding goals for upkeep, citing tight funds and higher priorities. The Army, Navy, and Air Force each report repair backlogs over $50 billion. GAO recommended fixing the model inputs and the deferred work. The department generally agreed.
gibbs-elementary-statistical-mechanics-1:
Elementary Principles in Statistical Mechanics, from 1902, was the one book J. Willard Gibbs shaped as a whole. In it he founds statistical mechanics, the study of how vast groups of particles act. Rather than track each particle, Gibbs studies whole ensembles of possible systems. From those ensembles he derives the behavior of heat and energy.

The canonical distribution, his central tool, states how energy spreads among a system's states. Entropy gains a clear statistical meaning in his hands. The book's math is dense, yet its plan is clean. Physicists treat it as a founding text. It gave physics its statistical soul, as one summary puts it.
gorky-lower-depths-1902:
The Lower Depths, Maxim Gorky's play of 1902, reached English in Jenny Covan's translation of 1922. The scene is a night lodging house in a Russian city, run by a hard landlord and his wife. Thieves, ruined nobles, sick women, and a former actor fill its bunks and argue through the night.

An old pilgrim named Luka comforts each lodger with kind, useful lies. When he vanishes, hope collapses and the actor hangs himself offstage. The Moscow Art Theatre made the play a triumph under Stanislavsky in 1902. Gorky asks whether truth or mercy serves the desperate better. The question, never settled, keeps the play alive.
govdocs-archive_org-ProjectSCANATECIARDP:
Project SCANATE was an early CIA effort to test remote viewing, the claimed ability to describe distant places using only the mind. The declassified file preserves the agency's own paperwork on that research, approved for public release in 2003.

Inside are the records of a program that treated psychic perception as a possible tool for gathering intelligence during the Cold War. The papers show officials taking the idea seriously enough to fund and file formal studies of it. For readers, the file is direct evidence of how far intelligence agencies were willing to go in the 1970s.

Filed under the CIA's own name, a second copy of the Project SCANATE document holds the agency's early study of remote viewing. The research centered on Ingo Swann at SRI, who reported that he could view far-off locations without leaving the room.

The papers record how the agency set up and judged those tests, and they were approved for release in 2003. Keeping this duplicate matters because releases can differ in small ways, and researchers compare copies line by line. Together with its twin file, it documents the first step in the government's long remote-viewing program.
govdocs-archive_org-ks_-_cia_vault_8_201:
On November 9, 2017, WikiLeaks published Vault 8, source code and technical analysis from the CIA's Hive project. The release belonged to the long Vault 7 series of CIA hacking documents that WikiLeaks issued through 2017. It was the eighth installment in that series.

Hive was the agency's system for controlling implanted malware on target computers while hiding the CIA's hand in the operation. Vault 8 went past description to the code itself, together with analysis meant for technically minded readers. It is kept complete for researchers of cyber history and of the leak era, when secret tools became public documents.
govdocs-archive_org-ting_environment_201: WikiLeaks released the CIA's Vault 8 material on HIVE, a piece of agency hacking infrastructure. The HIVE operating environment papers describe the environment in which that system ran. Vault releases show the tools behind public headlines about state hacking. Technical readers can study how the environment was organized in 2012. The release is held as a United States government document taken from the archive's holdings.
guy-mannering-or-the-astrologer-volume-0:
Sir Walter Scott's Guy Mannering, volume two, resumes the novel at chapter thirty-two with Gilbert Glossin in possession of Ellangowan. Glossin, the low-born lawyer who engineered the Bertram ruin, finds the county cold to him. Gentry exclude him from their clubs, and common people refuse him the name of Ellangowan. The shooting of young Charles Hazlewood draws his anxious exertions.

The second volume carries the exposure: the lost heir Harry Bertram returns from India, and the smuggler Dirk Hatteraick's confession nears. Meg Merrilies, the gypsy prophetess, drives the reckoning she foretold at Harry's birth. Dominie Sampson, Colonel Mannering, and Julia's romance fill the social frame. Glossin's guilt ripens toward the doom the first volume promised. Scott's second novel ends as romance and justice in one knot. This hosted volume completes the tale from its midpoint, the astrology of the opening fulfilled in gypsy vengeance.
hale-modest-enquiry-witchcraft-1702:
John Hale was pastor at Beverly, near Salem, and at first he backed the witch trials of 1692. A Modest Enquiry into the Nature of Witchcraft, printed at Boston in 1702, is his second look at that hard year. He wrote it after doubt had time to grow.

Hale asks what witchcraft is, how a guilty person can be proved, and how the innocent can be kept safe. He casts doubt on spectral proof, claims based on visions only the accusers could see. Scripture and hard experience guide his argument on both sides. The book is the first clear critique of Salem from a man inside it.
harold-the-last-of-the-saxon-kings-volum:
Book Two of Lytton's Harold is titled Lanfranc the Scholar, and the hero of its early pages is the Norman churchman who would one day be Archbishop of Canterbury. Its first chapter dwells, though, on Saxon appetites: four meals a day, from earl to ceorl, were not thought too lavish an reading of the daily bread. Happy times, the narrator sighs, for the ceorl, yet never sweet is the food of servitude.

Drink, the vice of the warlike nations of the North, is traced to the example of the Danes. Around the feasting, Lytton weaves the scholar Lanfranc's rise at the Norman court and the tightening web between England and Normandy. The part is more chronicle than romance in stretches. It shows Lytton's method at full stretch: history first, with the tale carried along on a strong current of learning.
hastings-dictionary-bible-vol4-1902:
Volume Four of Hastings's Dictionary of the Bible, published in 1902, completes the main alphabet, from Pleroma to Zuzim. James Hastings had driven the huge project for a decade. The final alphabetical volume was long awaited by subscribers.

Long articles on prophecy, the Psalms, Rome, sacrifice, and the Temple anchor this volume. Writers sum up the scholarship of the 1890s on the Bible's history and teaching. The set's balance of faith and learning made it a fixture in seminaries. Readers today use it to see how the best scholars of 1900 understood the scriptures. Sets were sold volume by volume to ministers across the English-speaking world.
hilbert-foundations-geometry-townsend-19:
David Hilbert rebuilt geometry on strict axioms in The Foundations of Geometry, Englished by E. J. Townsend in 1902. The text here is the second edition of Hilbert's German work. He starts from undefined terms and a short list of axioms. Every theorem must follow from those axioms alone, with no help from pictures.

Hilbert tests his axioms for consistency and for freedom from hidden overlap. He shows which theorems fall if a given axiom is dropped. The rigor of the method set a new standard for all mathematics. Teachers call the book the axiomatic method's manifesto. Readers need patience, and gain precision. Its influence spread to every exact science.
history-of-friedrich-ii-of-prussia-volum:
Thomas Carlyle's History of Friedrich the Second, in twenty-one volumes, reaches its second here, containing Book Two, Of Brandenburg and the Hohenzollerns, from 928 to 1417. Carlyle warns that Brandenburg before the Hohenzollerns has little history worth remembering, though much has been written. Henry the Fowler and the town of Brannibor open the story.

He traces Saxon emperors, margraves, and the empire's loose German politics, with Richard of Cornwall buying gleams of authority in the Rhenish provinces before quitting Germany in 1263. Pytheas of Marseilles, sailing past two thousand years before, gets the book's first backward glance. This deep background prepares the elector family from whom Prussia, and finally Frederick, will come.
history-of-the-revolt-of-the-netherlands:
The second book of Friedrich Schiller's History of the Revolt of the Netherlands centres on Cardinal Granvella, born Anthony Perenot at Besançon in 1516. Perenot's father, a blacksmith's son, rose by merit to serve Margaret of Savoy and then Charles the Fifth, becoming privy counsellor and keeper of the king's seal.

Schiller shows how the son inherited his father's honours, influence and political knowledge, and how, as Archbishop of Malines and minister in the Netherlands, he became the target of his contemporaries' hatred. The book follows Granvella's career through the councils and intrigues that made him the symbol of Spanish rule. Readers will find Schiller's portrait both hostile to its subject's policies and fair to his formidable ability.
hobson-imperialism-1902:
John Atkinson Hobson was a British journalist and economist who reported from South Africa before writing Imperialism: A Study in 1902. He asked why rich nations were racing to seize colonies across Africa and Asia. His answer pointed home, to the flow of money itself.

Hobson argues that the rich save more than they can spend at home, a fault he calls underconsumption. Surplus capital then hunts for profit abroad, and flags and armies follow the investments. Lenin read the book closely and named it as a source for his own theory of imperialism. Hobson wrote with direct sight of the South African war and its costs.
homo-sum-volume-02:
Volume 2 of Homo Sum, by Georg Ebers, stays through one night watch beside a sick old hermit. Ebers shows Paulus sitting motionless by Stephanus, holding back even a cough so the light sleep will not break. A senator's potion has done its work, and past midnight the old man wakes with his deepest worry ready to speak in this volume.

Chapter V gives Stephanus a long, honest confession about his son Hermas. He admits that love, not duty alone, kept the boy beside him on the Holy Mountain. Hermas's mother fled with a lover and never asked for the child. The father hoped desert life would spare his son the world's sorrow. Now the young man has come back from Alexandria unable to laugh, and the old plan looks like a kind mistake.
in-the-blue-pike-volume-02:
Volume 2 of In the Blue Pike, by Georg Ebers, gives the rope dancer Kuni a task worth more than applause. Ebers writes that she has been nursing a sick mother and her babies, working with all her strength for strangers. The man who promised the woman a cart ride to her home village of Schweinfurt has quietly withdrawn his help in this volume.

Chapter IV explains his reason without cruelty. He keeps himself and his family alive by trained poodles performing in taverns, under village lindens, and at fairs, where children clap heartily and often pay nothing. Feeding a mother and twins is more than his tricks can carry. Kuni, herself near the roadside's edge, takes the burden up. Finding someone needier than herself lifts her out of her own despair, and service becomes the one success left to a failing performer.
iraq-wmd-nie-2002:
In October 2002 the American intelligence agencies issued a National Intelligence Estimate on Iraq's weapons programs. Congress had demanded the summary judgment before voting on whether to allow war against Saddam Hussein. The declassified excerpts released to the public stated the agencies' key claims in strong terms.

The estimate said with high confidence that Iraq held chemical and biological weapons and was rebuilding its nuclear program. After the 2003 invasion, search teams found no such stockpiles and no active nuclear effort. Reviews later found that weak evidence had been stated as near certainty and that doubts inside the agencies were buried. The episode became a standard case of intelligence failure, since the estimate had served as the public basis for war.
jacobs-lady-of-the-barge-1902:
W. W. Jacobs mixed sea tales and dark tales in The Lady of the Barge and Others, his set from 1902. Most tales are brisk and wry. Sailors spin yarns, con men scheme, and small folk meet odd turns of luck in port towns.

One tale towers past the rest. In it, a paw plucked from a mummy grants three wishes, and each wish turns to grief. That tale is now the most famed short fright tale in the tongue. It taught hosts of scribes how dread can grow from one small, plain choice. Jacobs, a clerk turned scribe, had a keen ear for dock side talk. That ear makes both the jokes and the dread feel true to life.
jesuit-relations-thwaites-vol-02:
Acadia in 1612 to 1614 is the ground of Volume 2, printed in 1896. Thwaites placed these reports second in his vast edition of the Jesuit Relations. The French missions on the Atlantic shore were still small and weak.

English raids, bitter winters, and thin supplies test the priests at every turn. Their letters home mix faith, fear, and plain facts about the land. They note Mi'kmaq customs, trade goods, and the mood of each camp. Step by step, the volume preserves the first French foothold in North America. Few records of those years are as close or as frank.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aaron-of-york-f:
Aaron of York was a Jewish financier and chief rabbi of England, born in York before 1190. He died after 1253. He was probably the son of Josce of York, the leading figure in the York massacre of 1190. In 1237 he was made presbyter, or chief rabbi, of the Jews of England.

Aaron told Matthew Paris he had paid the king no less than 30,000 marks in silver and 200 in gold in all. In 1250 he was fined 14,000 marks of silver and ten of gold on a charge of falsifying a deed. A number of Hebrew deeds from his dealings still exist, one wholly in his own hand.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abdima-b-hamdur: Abdima ben Hamdure was an amora of the third century. The entry is short, and its one claim is a matter of identity. He is most likely, it says, the same man as Mar Bar Hamdure. That man was a disciple of Samuel, the Babylonian master. Four Talmudic passages are cited in support of the link, from Shabbat, Yoma, Sukkah, and Menaḥot. No ruling, saying, birthplace, or date of Abdima ben Hamdure is given in this notice beyond that match of names.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abner-of-burgos:
Abner of Burgos, later Alfonso of Valladolid, was born in 1270 and died in 1348 or a little later. Trained in Bible, Talmud, philosophy, and astrology, he qualified as a physician at twenty-five. At about sixty he converted to Christianity.

Contemporaries held that gain, not belief, drove his conversion. He won a sacristan post at Valladolid. In his Epistle on Fate he blamed the planets for his choice and denied free will. He then wrote many works against Judaism. In 1336 he pressed charges that led to a royal ban on an old prayer formula.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abraham-ben-ben:
Polish Talmudist Abraham ben Benjamin Aaron died at Brest, Lithuania, in 1642. He served as rabbi at Tarnopol in 1636 and in other Polish towns. That year Brest, then Poland's largest Jewish community, called him to its rabbinate, and he stayed there until his death.

Leading rabbis such as Joel Sirkes, Meir Kohen-Zedek, and Rabbi Heschel of Cracow treated him with the greatest respect in their writings. His responsa survive inside their works. He also left notes on the Tur Orah Hayyim, added to his father's book. His father, Benjamin Aaron, who died in 1620, wrote the responsa collection Masat Binyamin.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abraham-ha-levi: Abraham ha-Levi was a tosafist who is not yet fully identified. A Piske Tosafot quote names an Abraham ha-Levi known in no other way. He was probably one of the many German or French tosafists named Abraham, with ha-Levi dropped for ease. He may be Abraham ben Baruch, brother of Meir of Rothenburg. That man flourished about 1225-93 and wrote a work still in manuscript. The entry leaves the puzzle open, resting on Zunz's study of the sources.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abraham-of-troy:
Abraham of Troyes headed the community of Troyes, France, about the middle of the twelfth century. He was a contemporary of Rabbenu Tam. The sway he held at Troyes gave rise to a curious legal incident, told in some detail.

Eleazar ha-Nadib, sued by Abraham, refused to face the rabbinical court at Troyes. Backed by Isaac ben Samuel of Dampierre, he got his case sent to another court. Eleazar's son later did the same and won backing from Judah Sire Leon of Paris. In a linked case, kin of Simson of Troyes also feared the local court's bent and objected to trial there.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abumai-702: Abumai was Gaon in Sura from 811 to 819. He was a brother of Rabbi Mordecai. He seems to have been the father of Cohen-Ẓedeḳ. That son also became Gaon of Sura. He won fame for his many calls on ritual and court questions. The hosted text is very short. It gives the office, the years, and the two family links. It points the reader to the entry on the Geonim for more, and it adds no facts about Abumai's own acts or works.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-adibe-jacob-802: Jacob Adibe was a Jew cast out from Portugal in 1496. He lived at Azamor, in the province of Duccala, Morocco. In 1512 that town's ruler had bowed to Portugal, then broke faith. King Manuel sent a fleet under his nephew Don Jaime, duke of Bragança. A day of hard fight gave no clear win. At dawn Adibe came to the duke with news. The city had been left empty. He asked cover for his family and his fellow Jews, and got it.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-agobard-902:
Agobard was archbishop of Lyons, born in 779. He died on June 6, 840. He ranks as a chief foe of Judaism in the ninth century. Jews of Lyons lived in a set quarter at the foot of Fourvière hill. King Louis the Debonair gave them a court shield, a master of the Jews named Eberard. That grant roused Agobard's wrath.

He set his case in four letters to the king, court priests, and bishops. He told the faithful to shun trade and meals with Jews. He charged that Jews boasted of court favor and fine gifts. He charged them with building new synagogues against law. Last, he charged them with stealing Christian children for sale as slaves. His push failed. In 834 he lost his post and fled to Italy.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ahot-ketannah-t:
Ahot Ketannah, "The Little Sister," is a ritual poem of eight stanzas. Its title comes from a verse in the Song of Songs. The stanzas carry the acrostic of Abraham Hazan. In the Sephardic ritual it is sung before the New-year's evening prayer. Its refrain asks that the year end with her woes. The last stanza changes the line to a hope for blessings.

Abraham Hazan was a cantor born in Salonica in 1533. He probably composed the melody as well as the words. The tune is in the hypo-dorian mode. The entry compares it with airs from the Greek islands of the same age. Italian Jews altered its coloring, it says. Dutch, English, and West Indian Sephardim kept older traits of the tune.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aldabi-meir-ibn:
Meir ibn Aldabi was a writer of the fourteenth century. He was a son of Isaac Aldabi, called the Pious. He was also a grandson of Asher ben Jehiel, and he traced descent from the exiles of Jerusalem. His name is fixed by an acrostic poem in his chief book, where its letters spell Aldabi.

In 1360 he wrote "Shebile Emunah," the Paths of Faith. It is a wide treatise on philosophy, science, and theology. Its ten chapters run from the being of God to the world to come. They cover creation, the spheres and stars, the body and its health, the soul, reward and punishment, and Israel's redemption. The book stayed a favorite with the educated for centuries, in many editions. Later study showed it to be a gathering from older writers, chiefly Gerson of Arles.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-america-the-dis:
Discovery of America is tied to Jews at more than one point. Star books by Jewish hands helped Columbus sail. One tool for reading the stars was a Jewish find. Levi ben Gerson first set out the Jacob's Staff. Abraham Zacuto fit that tool to sea use. His tables served Columbus on the voyage. Once, the entry says, they saved the whole crew.

Luis de Santangel took a chief part on land. He was a Marano close to King Ferdinand. He won Queen Isabella to the plan. He then lent the cash to fit out the ships. Columbus sent his first full report to Santangel. That letter was dated Feb. 15, 1493.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-amittai-1402: Amittai was the father of the prophet Jonah. Two verses name him as Jonah's father. Rabbinic sources place him in the tribe of Zebulon.
