Tewkesbury's plain and the Tower of London close the plan. Reading the list alone shows the play's shape: council, battlefield, council, battlefield, until one house stands. It is the most battle-filled of Shakespeare's histories.
kipling-just-so-stories-1902:
Rudyard Kipling published Just So Stories in 1902, a book of tales he first told his own children. Each story explains, in playful fashion, how an animal got its trait. The whale gets its throat, the camel its hump, and the leopard its spots. The tales begin in the high and far-off times.

Kipling mixes prose with poems and speaks straight to the reader as Best Beloved. The stories draw on India, Africa, and the sea. Their rhythm begs to be read aloud. Generations of families have kept the book in print. It shows Kipling at his warmest and most inventive.
kropotkin-mutual-aid-1902:
Peter Kropotkin published Mutual Aid: A Factor of Evolution in 1902. Kropotkin, a Russian prince turned rebel and a trained geographer, had watched animal life in Siberia. He argued that working together, not just struggle, drives the change of species and helps them survive hard times.

Chapters survey help among animals, early human clans, medieval towns, and modern workers. Kropotkin answered Darwin's followers who stressed struggle alone, using field reports and past records as proof. The book became the base text for his free, shared way of life without rulers. It also shaped later study of how living things help each other thrive.
leadbeater-man-visible-invisible-1902:
C. W. Leadbeater said he could see the fine forms that clothe each soul. His Man Visible and Invisible came out in 1902. It claims to show men as they look to trained clairvoyant sight. Bright plates in the book paint auras and thought forms round the head.

Leadbeater sorts men by the hues and forms his sight found in them. Saints glow in calm tints, while base moods cloud the form. The book set the look of the aura for the whole New Age field. Few theosophy books have been copied so much in art and print.
life-of-edward-earl-of-clarendon-volume-:
Sir Henry Craik's second volume follows Clarendon into power. Edward Hyde, Earl of Clarendon, served as Lord High Chancellor. Volume Two opens with the Restoration of Charles II. A miniature portrait of John Hampden fronts the contents.

Chapters weigh Scotland, Ireland, marriage treaties, and religious settlement. The Dutch War and administrative friction strain the restored monarchy. Clarendon's influence decays as bitterness among his foes grows. The volume closes with the triumph of faction against him. Scottish administration and Ireland's problems occupy early chapters here. Domestic dissension and foreign complications precede the Dutch War chapters.
lucretia-volume-02:
Volume 2 of Lucretia carries on Bulwer Lytton's tale of the children of night. It opens with conferences in the great house of Sir Miles. He keeps his rooms in King James's chamber, off the picture gallery. Mr. Vernon represents the newer, easier school of manners against him.

Old formality and new freedom meet in these drawing-room scenes. Behind the talk, the novel's dark design keeps working. People formed by bad early influence move toward their fates. Lytton builds his tragedy slowly, through talk and character. The contrast of generations sharpens every scene here. This volume deepens the shadow over the house and its heirs.
lybeaus-desconus-weston-1902:
Jessie Weston turned the English Fair Unknown romance into plain modern prose in 1902. Sir Libeaus Desconus renders the medieval poem of the knight who did not know his own name. Weston's clear prose was made for readers new to such tales.

Libeaus comes to Arthur's court a raw youth, is mocked for his looks, and rides out to prove himself. Fights, rescues, and a lady freed from sorcery mark his road to honor. The tale is the English twin of the French Bel Inconnu. Weston's version keeps the story whole while dropping the hard old verse.
maeterlinck-plays-1902:
Maurice Maeterlinck, a Belgian writer who worked in French, wrote the plays translated here in the 1890s. The English book appeared in 1902. Alladine and Palomides is a brief tale of doomed love in a castle. Pelleas and Melisande tells of a love that leads to death in a dark kingdom.

The Death of Tintagiles shows a child prince threatened by unseen powers. Maeterlinck was a leader of Symbolist drama, which favors mood and suggestion over action. His figures speak softly and often seem to wait for fate. These plays shaped modern theatre and also inspired famous music, including an opera by Debussy.
margery-gred-a-tale-of-old-nuremberg-vol:
Volume two of Margery finds summer wearing away over Nuremberg. Chapter six opens with oats garnered and the vintage begun. Margery pauses to praise forest life in spring and autumn alike. The fir tree, she says, lights brighter tips to its boughs.

Her voice, warm and fanciful, colors every scene she tells. Family matters and young love advance beneath the seasons. Georg Ebers lets his heroine narrate in her own old-fashioned way. Clara Bell's translation keeps the speech quaint but clear. The forest festivals of her youth glow in these pages. This volume deepens the portrait of Gred and her kin.
maupassant-necklace-stories-1902:
Guy de Maupassant's The Necklace and Other Short Stories gathers thirteen of his sharpest tales dress. The title tale, The Necklace, is the most famous product of the master of the ironic short story. Maupassant wrote some three hundred tales in ten years, and this set shows his range at its height.

Mathilde Loisel borrows a necklace for a ball, loses it, and spends ten years in poverty replacing it. The close, the original was paste, lands with the quiet cruelty that became Maupassant's signature in the tale. Other pieces here turn on peasants' cunning, soldiers' lust, and the small revenges of the slighted and the poor. His prose wastes no word, and each ending reframes all that came before it in the story. School readers meet him here first, and few forget the snap of his endings.
memoirs-of-napoleon-bonaparte-volume-02:
Volume two of Bourrienne's memoirs holds chapters five to fourteen. The year in view is 1798, by the contents page. Bourrienne joins Bonaparte at Leoben on April 19 in this part.

Peace terms had just been signed when he arrived at that town. He no longer spoke to Bonaparte as an equal from that day. He took his place at the head of the general's cabinet at once. Milan and Montebello host the court of the rising man that season. The fall of Venice frames the peace signed in those days. Woe to small states, he writes, caught between two great empires.
monsieur-madame-and-be-be-volume-02: Volume Two continues Gustave Droz's Monsieur, Madame, et Bébé in English. Its Project Gutenberg header ranks it eleventh in the French Immortals series. The sketches follow the young household as marriage settles in and the baby grows. The hosted sample, however, preserves no readable content from the volume itself. It holds only the Gutenberg header, naming title, author, and release data. Readers learn what the volume is, but the sample shows none of its pages.
my-novel-volume-02:
Edward Bulwer-Lytton's second book of My Novel opens with a family debate. Mr. Caxton insists each part needs an opening chapter, as Fielding used. Pisistratus asks for Fielding's reasons and gets a comic answer. One gain, says Caxton, is skipping the first pages.

Behind the joke sits the Caxton family circle at Hazeldean. Pisistratus narrates his own tale while his elders judge it. The talk defends long, wandering novels with wit. Readers meet the book's method as much as its plot. This volume carries the family story forward into wider English life, with love and ambition ahead.
mysteries-of-paris-volume-02:
Eugene Sue's second volume of the Paris mysteries opens at chapter thirty-eight. The chapter is called The Execution. Two hard men enter a poor lapidary's garret. Malicorne is tall and thin, with a vulture-like throat.

His mate Bourdin wears cheap finery and a long gold chain. Both men sneer at the stink of misery and death. Sue builds his Paris from such dens and garrets. Prince Rodolphe moves through this underworld on a secret mission. V1 says new villains rise and old secrets surface here. The serial's mix of crime and pity held all France spellbound.
nider-formicarius-latin-1602:
Johannes Nider, a Dominican reformer, wrote the Formicarius, the Ant-hill, around 1437. This text follows the Douai edition of 1602. Five books compare the church's enemies and its saints to the orders of an anthill, and the work became the first great demonological treatise of the witch-hunt era.

Nider collects tales of witches, heretics, and wonders from the Alpine world he knew. Heinrich Kramer quarried the Formicarius heavily when building the Malleus Maleficarum. Much of the Hammer's matter flows from Nider's hill. The dialogue form keeps the heavy doctrine readable. Anyone tracing the witch stereotype to its sources must pass through this book.
novalis-disciples-at-sais-1802:
Una Birch translated The Disciples at Saïs into English in 1903, in her Methuen edition of Novalis. The fragment, left unfinished at Novalis's death in 1801, gathers young seekers at the temple of Isis in Egypt. They debate how nature hides her secrets and how the heart may learn them.

Some trust study, some trust love, and a fairy tale within the fragment gives its own answer. Birch's volume adds Novalis's famous fragments on poetry, faith, and the world. Together they state the Romantic creed in its purest form: nature and spirit are one book. The prose is dense yet luminous, meant for slow reading. It remains a source text for students of Romantic thought.
novalis-henry-ofterdingen-1802:
Henry of Ofterdingen, Novalis's unfinished novel, appeared in 1802, after his early death, and in English in 1842. Henry, a young poet of medieval Germany, dreams of a blue flower and sets out to seek its meaning. His road leads through merchants, miners, crusaders, and hermits, each teaching him part of poetry's secret.

Tales within the tale, songs, and visions carry Henry further than any map could. The blue flower became the central emblem of German Romantic longing. Novalis meant the novel as an answer to Goethe's Wilhelm Meister, exalting poetry over prose life. His friend Tieck published the fragment, and its spell has never lifted. Few unfinished books have shaped a movement so deeply.
ocean-of-story-kathasaritsagara-tawney-1:
Volume two of The Ocean of Story, in Penzer's edition of Tawney's translation from 1924, continues Somadeva's Kathasaritsagara. The frame hero, Naravahanadatta, gathers the tales that will attend his rise as king of the Vidyadharas. Each book adds fresh streams of story to the ocean Somadeva promised.

Merchants sail to golden islands, fools outwit kings, and faithful wives undo curses in these middle reaches. Penzer's footnotes trace motifs from India to Iceland, tale by tale. Tawney translated the whole vast cycle while serving in India, a feat of stamina in itself. The edition's ten volumes restore a work English readers once knew only in extracts. Volume two keeps the current strong.
on-english-homophones-society-for-pure-e:
Robert Bridges wrote this tract on English homophones in 1919. It is tract number two for the Society for Pure English. Homophones are words that sound alike but differ in meaning. They may also differ in spelling, Bridges notes. Spoken without context, such words leave meaning unclear.

Bridges explains the Greek sense of the word homophone. He gives pairs such as son and heir as examples. The tract lists and sorts same-sounding English words. Phonetic symbols in the text mark exact sounds. The work helped the society push for clearer English. It suits readers curious about sound and spelling.
openalex-w2019294202:
Fernando Bozza, Jorge Salluh, Andre Japiassu and colleagues tested blood markers of sepsis severity. Their paper appeared in Critical Care in 2007. Sepsis is a severe whole-body response to infection. Doctors lacked good markers to sort patients by severity. Such sorting helps research and treatment choices.

The team ran a study in four large hospitals. They enrolled sixty patients with severe sepsis. Blood samples were tested for seventeen cytokines at once. Cytokines are small proteins that guide immune responses. The team linked cytokine levels to illness patterns. They checked how levels related to organ problems and outcomes. A combined profile may sort patients better than single markers.
openalex-w2048145302:
Renata Sousa, Cleusa Ferri, Daisy Acosta and colleagues studied dependence among older people in poorer countries. Their survey appeared in BMC Geriatrics in 2010. Older populations are growing fast worldwide. Chronic diseases drive disability and the need for care. Dependence itself had rarely been measured directly.

The team surveyed over fifteen thousand people aged sixty-five and up. Sites covered seven countries in Latin America, China and India. Dependence rose with age at every site. Dementia made the largest single contribution to dependence. Limb problems, stroke and depression also contributed strongly. Rates were lower than in the United States. The authors warn that dependent numbers will grow fast.
openalex-w2090813402:
Jayme Garcia Arnal Barbedo surveyed computer methods that spot plant diseases from photos. His paper appeared in SpringerPlus in 2013. Disease signs show on leaves and stems as spots and patches. Image software can detect and measure them. Such tools could speed field diagnosis.

The survey sorts methods by their main goal. Some methods only detect disease presence. Others measure how severe the damage is. A third group classifies which disease it is. Each group is split by the technique used. The paper limits itself to visible-spectrum images. It aims to serve both plant pathologists and computing researchers. The overview maps a fast-growing research field.
openalex-w2117403402:
Capucine Picard, Waleed Al-Herz, Aziz Bousfiha and colleagues updated the classification of inherited immune deficiencies. Their paper appeared in Journal of Clinical Immunology in 2015. An expert committee maintains the list for the field. New gene defects are found every year. Doctors need a current, organised reference.

Thirty-four new gene defects joined the list in two years. Each disorder entry gives its key clinical features. Laboratory features are listed as well. The update shows growing overlap between categories. Immune deficiency now blurs into immune dysregulation. Shared classification helps doctors reach diagnoses faster. It also guides genetic testing choices. Researchers use it to compare cases worldwide.
openalex-w2126526402:
S. Chatrchyan and colleagues in the CMS Collaboration published this search in Physical Review Letters in 2011. They hunted for supersymmetry, a proposed partner for every known particle, in events at the Large Hadron Collider. The telltale sign would be sprays of particles called jets plus missing sideways energy from unseen particles escaping.

The team studied proton collisions recorded by the CMS detector. They used a special motion measure to pick out events that stand apart from ordinary background. The search was not tuned to one single model, so it could catch other new physics with the same sign. Results were read against a standard constrained supersymmetry model with five main settings.
openalex-w2132886902:
Rosa Figueroa, Qing Zeng-Treitler, Sasikiran Kandula, and Long Ngo published this study in BMC Medical Informatics and Decision Making in 2012. They address a planning problem in machine learning: labeled training data are scarce and costly. Researchers need to know how many labeled examples a classifier needs before they pay for the labeling.

The authors fit an inverse power law curve to early points on a learning curve. Their fitting weights points by their reliability, then predicts scores for larger sample sizes. They tested the method on clinical text and waveform tasks, fitting hundreds of models. The weighted method beat a plain unweighted fit, giving researchers a practical planning tool.
openalex-w2136201502:
K. E. Giller, Jens Andersson, Marc Corbeels, and colleagues published this review in Frontiers in Plant Science in 2015. They examine conservation agriculture, a farming approach promoted as a path to growing more food with less environmental harm. Its three rules are minimal soil disturbance, constant soil cover, and crop rotation.

The authors trace the approach back to the Dust Bowl era and the rise of no-till farming. They note that farmers practiced parts of the system long before the label existed. Strict judges count a farm as true conservation agriculture only when all three rules are followed closely. The review weighs that strict ideal against the mixed practices farmers actually use.
openalex-w2340594102:
Shaiza Janif, Patrick Nunn, and Paul Geraghty led this 2016 study in Ecology and Society. They asked if the old oral stories of rural Fiji could help villages face climate change. Plans from outside often fail to engage island villages. Elders' tales hold a long watch over the land and sea.

The team held talks and watched life in twenty-seven villages. Most of those they spoke with were elders aged seventy to seventy-nine. People widely saw the old tales as at risk of being lost, and felt sad about it. No tales of past disasters that no one alive had seen were found. Yet five villages held tales of past moves forced by changes in their land. The authors weigh what these tales can still offer planners.
openalex-w2550337802:
Reindert J. Haarsma, Malcolm John Roberts, and Pier Luigi Vidale led this 2016 paper in Geoscientific Model Development. It sets out HighResMIP, a coordinated project inside CMIP6, the world climate model comparison effort. The project asks whether sharper model resolution improves how climate processes are represented. High-resolution runs are costly, so only a few centers had tried them, without coordination.

HighResMIP defines a shared set of experiments for many modeling centers to run. The target resolution is at least fifty kilometers in the atmosphere and a quarter degree in the ocean. Early results suggest finer grids can change large-scale circulation and improve extremes and small-scale processes. Running the same experiments across models shows which changes are robust. The design links closely to the core CMIP6 experiments used for climate projections.
openalex-w2551500002:
Germán Baldi and José María Paruelo studied land-use change in South America's temperate grasslands for this 2008 Ecology and Society paper. Their focus is the Río de la Plata grasslands, a vast farming region. Technology shifts and new market conditions had reshaped agriculture there over the previous two decades. The authors mapped how the landscape changed between the late 1980s and the early 2000s.

They built land cover maps for eight pilot areas covering about a third of the region. Grassland share fell from about sixty-seven percent to about sixty-one percent between the two periods. Annual crops took its place, mainly soybean, sunflower, wheat, and maize. Some subregions, like the Flat Inland Pampa, switched from grass to crops much faster than others. The study gives a regional baseline for judging what farming expansion costs these grasslands.
openalex-w2624885502:
Andrew David Beale, Mário Pedrazzoli, and Bruno da Silva Brandão Gonçalves compared sleep in two Mozambican communities, with colleagues. Their study appeared in Scientific Reports in 2017. One site is the town of Milange; the other is the nearby village of Tengua. Urbanization is still at an early stage in the region. Researchers wondered whether town life already shifts sleep, as electricity lets people stay up later.

Town residents went to bed about an hour later than villagers. They also saw more light in the evening and less during the day. Yet total sleep time was nearly identical, around seven and a quarter hours in both places. That contrasts with earlier reports blaming electricity for shorter sleep. Town sleep was not poorer either; rural sleep was actually more restless. Mats on floors, shared rooms, and heavy daytime labor may explain that restlessness.
openalex-w2912652602:
Guido España, Cosmina Hogea, Adrienne Guignard, and colleagues published this simulation study in PLoS ONE in 2019. It asks whether uneven exposure to dengue can distort how well a dengue vaccine seems to work in large phase three trials. Such trials guide decisions about which vaccines reach the public.

Using a city-wide model built from field data collected in Iquitos, Peru, the team simulated a vaccine of known strength across many trial runs. Standard methods understated true efficacy by as much as about one fifth when exposure varied between people. Counting each person's exposures removed the bias, while a statistical term that lets exposure vary by person reduced it in part.
openalex-w3035895802:
Luis García wrote this review in Frontiers in Immunology in 2020, working alone. It covers the immune response, inflammation, and the range of illness seen in COVID-19. The disease, caused by the SARS-CoV-2 virus, began in Wuhan, China, in December 2019 and spread across the world.

The World Health Organization declared a global health emergency at the end of January 2020. Research moved at rare speed, clarifying how the virus spreads, whom it hits hardest, and how it is built. García gathers the immunology of that picture: how the body's defenses meet the virus, and how inflammation can turn a mild infection severe. The review explains why one infection can leave one patient well and another fighting for breath.
openalex-w3092560102:
Javad Sharifi-Rad, Youssef El Rayess, Alain Abi-Rizk, and colleagues wrote this review in Frontiers in Pharmacology in 2020. It covers turmeric and its main active compound, curcumin, and their effects on health. The Curcuma genus holds about one hundred twenty species, with turmeric the best known.

Turmeric's underground stems are the part most used, as spice and as medicine. They carry curcumin and related compounds plus fragrant oils. Traditional and lab claims credit the plant with a long list of actions, from calming inflammation to fighting microbes and lowering blood sugar. The review weighs the evidence for those bioactive effects and sets out safety profiles for uses in food, drugs, biotechnology, and medicine.
openalex-w4394029502:
Adame, Aguilar, Steven Ahlen, and the DESI collaboration measure the cosmic expansion rate from quasar light. Their paper appeared in the Journal of Cosmology and Astroparticle Physics in 2025. Distant quasars shine through clouds of hydrogen gas, which leave a forest of absorption lines in their spectra. Patterns in that Lyman-alpha forest reveal how fast the universe expanded when the light passed through. The team used the first-year data of the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument.

Their sample held more than four hundred twenty thousand forest spectra, matched with over seven hundred thousand quasars. The analysis was blinded and stress-tested on synthetic data before the real values were revealed. They measured the expansion rate at a lookback time near the universe's youth with about two percent precision. Companion papers combine such results to test theories of dark energy.
openalex-w4403443402:
Makoto Shimizu and Youichi Yanase calculate how pressure changes the electronic structure of the compound UTe2. Their paper appeared in the Journal of the Physical Society of Japan in 2025. UTe2 is a leading candidate for an unusual form of superconductivity. Its behaviour under pressure is rich but poorly understood.

Using density functional theory, the authors find that the low-energy band structure barely changes under pressure in some settings. When heavy f-electrons sit at the Fermi level, pressure does matter. The density of states there rises, driven by squeezing along one crystal direction. Knowing this baseline helps physicists explain the material's magnetic and superconducting phases.
openalex-w7204486002:
João Paulo Gonçalves de Freitas led a Portuguese-language experimental study, in Brazil in 2026, on artisanal gummy candies. The recipe uses agar as the gelling agent, commercial vitamins as the active ingredient, and powdered ginger as a natural sweetener and flavoring. The goal was a healthier, animal-free alternative to gelatin gummies, and the team assessed whether the formulation works, mainly how the agar gelled and how adding vitamins affected texture and stability.

The vitamins and the agar's gelling point created tech limits, the authors report honestly: the candies did not reach the expected texture or uniformity. Adjustments to the agar proportion, heat, and the method of adding the vitamins are needed. Even so, the experiment clarified the variables involved in producing gummy candies.
openalex-w7208726502:
Francisco de Sousa Junior and four colleagues read how women show up in the pics of a Brazil sums book set. The set has four books. It won a place in the state's book plan for 2024, for the last years of grade school. The team sorted pics and draws by who leads the scene, the place, the mix of race and class, and how each pic ties to the sums on the page.

Women do show in scenes of labs and sport, Black women among them. Yet they stay scant in the parts on the past of sums. Most pics serve to show or tell, not to build sums skill in their own right. Such reads, the team holds, bare both the strong and the weak sides. Staff can hone the books with tasks that join sums to asks of sex and race.
openalex-w7208804902:
Everaldo da Silva Santana and Rosa Severina de Souza Oliveira reflect on teacher training in literacy, and on the difference between learning the code and living the written word. In Brazilian scholarship, alfabetizacao names the skill of reading and writing itself, while letramento names using reading and writing in real social life. Training teachers, they argue, must hold the two together with more consistency than it often does.

A teacher formed this way teaches children to decode, but also to use written language for real purposes and to follow each student's individual growth. The introduction places the stakes widely: in a fast-changing, connected world, command of written culture is how a person gains and produces knowledge and takes a full place as a citizen. The article gives literacy teachers a conceptual grounding for that wider task.
openalex-w7212603302:
Dirchely Samara de Lima Farel reads a 1963 tale of the Madeira-Mamore rail line in Brazil's far west. The line was cut through the rain woods to haul goods past river falls. Its build cost the lives and health of crowds of hands. Farel reads the tale with three guides from the study of lands once ruled from abroad.

The tale, he finds, sings the praise of new ways and gloss. The white man's world stands high; the folk of the land stand low. Yet the facts the tale holds cut the other way: harsh use of the hands and pain on the build. Read so, the tale turns from a hymn to rule into proof of its cost.
openalex-w7213930402:
Rafaella Ferreira Rocha Santana, as named in the sample, leads a review of ECG findings in young athletes. Their 2026 integrative review concerns heart conditions linked to sudden death in child and adolescent athletes. It works in six stages, searching PubMed and a health library with screening terms.

Sport brings health benefits, yet intense exercise can trigger grave events in young people with hidden heart disease, the authors note. Normal athletic changes were frequent, including slow resting heart rate, early repolarization, and partial right bundle branch block. How often each pattern appears, and how it should be read, varied by age, sex, racial traits, and sport. Screening judgement must fit the athlete.
openalex-w7213987302:
Jaqueline Mendonça Torres and colleagues analyse walkability around metro stations in Brasília's Plano Piloto. Their 2026 article reanalyses georeferenced data, field observation, and photographs from an earlier study, processed in mapping software. Three parts are read separately: sidewalks, crossings, and shade and shelter.

Shade and shelter were widely available, thanks to trees and architectural elements. Sidewalk irregularities and broken crossings persisted at the same time. When the parts are merged into one score, the picture turns favourable and specific weaknesses vanish, they show. Summary indices suit territorial comparison, the authors conclude. Planning real interventions, though, needs the disaggregated reading, above all where access and safety fail.
openalex-w7214617902:
Paulo Henrique Azevedo Lima led an eight-author 2026 field study of glyphosate, a widely used weedkiller, on farms around the village of Iguaíba in Maranhão, Brazil. The team identified the farm chemicals local growers use and tested the soil, measuring texture, organic matter, acidity, moisture, and nutrients, along with how strongly the soil holds onto glyphosate.

Local soils were mostly clay-rich, with high organic matter and moderate acidity, while nutrient levels varied with farm management and season. Glyphosate was only weakly held by the soil, leaving more of it dissolved in soil water. That raises the risk it will wash downward and contaminate the wider environment. The authors conclude that repeated glyphosate use can favor its movement through soil, and that soil traits themselves shape how available and mobile the chemical stays.
openalex-w7215082602:
Luis Carlos de Souza Braga led a seven-author 2026 library review on the mental effects of unplanned retirement for athletes. Leaving competitive sport is a critical transition, and it turns harsher when injury, deselection, or chance ends a career all at once and without support. The review gathers national and international studies on the whole person after sport: body, money, mind, and contracts.

Physical effects include lost conditioning, functional limits, and trouble settling into a new way of life. On money, poor planning brings shaky finances, badly used resources, and debt. In the mind, athletes face loss of sporting identity, anxiety, depression, and a sense of emptiness, while legal and contract problems surface without guidance during the career. The results point toward public policies and multi-field follow-up programs as the missing protection, so that the end of a career does not become the start of a crisis.
original-short-stories-volume-02:
Volume two of Guy de Maupassant's Original Short Stories, in the English translation by Albert M. C. McMaster, A. E. Henderson, and others, holds eleven tales. Its contents include Mother Sauvage, Madame Baptiste, The Blind Man, and Beside Schopenhauer's Corpse, a spread that runs from Norman peasant life to Parisian drawing rooms.

The first story, The Colonel's Ideas, is a comic monologue. Old Colonel Laporte is gouty, and his legs are stiff as wood. Yet he swears a pretty woman could make him jump through the eye of a needle. France, he insists, still breeds knights of love and fortune, and he will die one. Maupassant lets the old beau hang himself with his own gallantry.
ostrogorski-democracy-parties-vol-1-1902:
M. Ostrogorski's study of party machines, Volume 1, appears in Frederick Clarke's translation of 1902. The full title covers the way parties are run, with England as this volume's case. Ostrogorski lays bare the caucus system: the machine of local bosses, whips, and wire-pullers. He shows how machines capture the free choice of voters.

The book is the first close study of party machines in the modern age. Ostrogorski feared parties would replace voters as the real actors in public life. His cure was short-lived leagues for one cause in place of fixed parties. Few took the cure, yet all cite his findings. Clarke's version made the work a classic.
paul-clifford-volume-02:
Volume 2 of Paul Clifford resumes the tale at chapter seven, with Paul in prison. Waking thirsty among fellow prisoners, he spies a familiar frieze coat and narrow shoulders across the floor. A gentle kick wakes an old acquaintance, who stares and cries out in thieves' cant at seeing little Paul.

Lytton tells the scene with comic learning, quoting scholars and poets over a jail floor. Paul's boyhood among criminals, and the company that formed him, stay at the centre. The volume keeps building the author's case that prisons school the young in the very crimes they punish.
paulus-aegineta-seven-books-adams-vol-02:
The second volume of Francis Adams's English Paul of Aegina appeared in 1846. Paul, a Greek physician of the seventh century, wrote the Seven Books as a complete guide to the healing art. This middle volume carries on his survey of disease and cure through the body.

The books treat fevers in their kinds, then the ills of the head, the eyes, the chest, and the gut, with the drugs and diets for each. Paul writes as a working doctor, short and sure. His handbook ruled medicine from Baghdad to Paris for a thousand years. Adams, a Scottish country doctor himself, notes where his own practice matched the ancient text.
pelham-volume-02:
Volume 2 of Pelham takes the hero to Paris, and chapter nineteen finds him in the gambling houses of the Palais Royal. At a rouge et noir table he watches a sallow stranger play with painful intensity. Across the room stands a man in a rough greatcoat, gazing at the gambler with a fixed look of blended evil passions.

The watcher neither plays nor speaks, and Pelham never forgets his face. The novel's darker thread, of crime and pursuit behind the fashionable surface, thickens in these Paris scenes. Lytton keeps the polish of the salon and the menace of the gaming room in one frame.
plaw-107-109-2002:
Drugs approved for adults but used in children draw Congress's attention in the Best Pharmaceuticals for Children Act, Public Law 107-109, approved January 4, 2002. The act amends the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act to improve the safety and efficacy of pharmaceuticals for children.

One set of changes revises the rules for pediatric studies of already-marketed drugs. The Secretary may press for a study when information about a drug's use in the pediatric population may produce health benefits there. An older list-based route is struck. The act also writes a program for pediatric studies of drugs into the Public Health Service Act. It begins with a list of drugs for which such studies are needed. And it renumbers duplicated research sections to clear the way.
plaw-107-110-2002:
Few federal laws reshaped American schools like the No Child Left Behind Act of 2001, Public Law 107-110, approved January 8, 2002. Its stated aim is to close the achievement gap with accountability, flexibility, and choice, so that no child is left behind. The act works by rewriting the Elementary and Secondary Education Act of 1965, the main federal school law.

Title I takes up improving the academic achievement of the disadvantaged. Title II creates a teacher and principal training and recruiting fund, for preparing, training, and recruiting high quality teachers and principals. Title III covers language instruction for limited English proficient children and immigrant children and youth, and Title IV is headed 21st Century Schools. Early sections set out references, transition rules, and the effective date.
plaw-107-111-2002: African elephants keep their federal support under Public Law 107-111, the African Elephant Conservation Reauthorization Act of 2001, signed January 8, 2002. It extends the funding authority in that act through the years 2001 to 2007. Of the money in hand each year, the Secretary may spend not more than three percent, or 80,000 dollars, whichever is greater, on office costs. A new section lets the Secretary call together an advice group of people from public and private groups working to save African elephants.
plaw-107-112-2002: Rhinoceros and tiger conservation won more years of funding from Public Law 107-112, signed January 8, 2002, which reauthorizes the Rhinoceros and Tiger Conservation Act of 1994 through 2007. Office spending by the Secretary is capped at three percent of amounts in hand each year, or 80,000 dollars, whichever is greater. The Secretary may also call together an advice group of groups working to conserve rhinoceroses and tigers.
plaw-107-113-2002: Federal police help for the District of Columbia widens under Public Law 107-113, the District of Columbia Police Coordination Amendment Act of 2001, approved January 8, 2002. It amends the National Capital Revitalization and Self-Government Improvement Act of 1997. It adds one entry to the list of agencies that may sign cooperative agreements with the Metropolitan Police Department. The entry is any other federal law enforcement agency that the Department's Chief and the United States Attorney for the District deem appropriate.
plaw-107-114-2002:
Family cases in the District of Columbia courts gain a dedicated bench under the District of Columbia Family Court Act of 2001, Public Law 107-114, approved January 8, 2002. The act amends title 11 of the District of Columbia Code and redesignates the Family Division of the Superior Court as the Family Court of the Superior Court.

The rewritten organization section lists the Superior Court's parts as the Civil Division, the Criminal Division, the Family Court, the Probate Division, and the Tax Division, each divisible into branches by rule. The chief judge designates one Family Court judge as its presiding judge. Beyond the name, the act aims to recruit and retain trained and experienced judges for the Family Court. It also aims to promote consistency and efficiency in assigning judges and handling family actions and proceedings.
plaw-107-115-2002:
American aid and export support abroad are funded by the Foreign Operations, Export Financing, and Related Programs Appropriations Act, 2002, Public Law 107-115, approved January 10, 2002. It appropriates sums for foreign operations, export financing, and related programs for the fiscal year ending September 30, 2002.

Title I, Export and Investment Assistance, opens with the Export-Import Bank of the United States, which may make expenditures, contracts, and commitments within its available funds and borrowing authority. A subsidy appropriation of about 727 million dollars covers the cost of direct loans, loan guarantees, insurance, and tied-aid grants, available until September 30, 2005, with loan disbursements running until 2020. One proviso bars using the year's funds for exporting nuclear equipment, fuel, or technology to any country outside the nuclear-weapon states. The bar applies where the country has detonated a nuclear explosive after enactment.
plaw-107-116-2002:
Jobs, health, and schools draw their money from one large act, Public Law 107-116, approved January 10, 2002. It is the Departments of Labor, Health and Human Services, and Education, and Related Agencies Appropriations Act, 2002, covering the fiscal year ending September 30, 2002.

Title I funds the Department of Labor, opening with Training and Employment Services at about 3.17 billion dollars, plus reimbursements. Most of that account runs on staggered schedules into 2003 and beyond: about 1.13 billion dollars carries out chapter 4 of the Workforce Investment Act, roughly 225 million dollars carries out its section 169, about 80.8 million dollars carries out section 167, and about 30.4 million dollars is set aside for construction, rehabilitation, and acquisition of Job Corps centers.
plaw-107-117-2002:
Public Law 107-117, approved January 10, 2002, is the defense spending act for the year of the September 11 response. Its Division A is the Department of Defense Appropriations Act, 2002. The wider act is styled for defense and emergency supplemental appropriations for recovery from and response to terrorist attacks on the United States.

The act appropriates sums for military functions administered by the Department of Defense for the fiscal year ending September 30, 2002. Title I pays military personnel: the Army account provides about 23.75 billion dollars for members on active duty, cadets, and aviation cadets, spanning pay, allowances, clothing, subsistence, permanent change of station travel, and payments to the Department of Defense Military Retirement Fund. The Navy account follows on the same terms.
plaw-107-118-2002:
Polluted industrial land gets a second chance under the Small Business Liability Relief and Brownfields Revitalization Act, Public Law 107-118, signed January 11, 2002. The act amends the Comprehensive Environmental Response, Compensation, and Liability Act of 1980, the federal cleanup statute, and it speaks to both relief and reuse.

Title I, the Small Business Liability Protection Act, adds exemptions to the cleanup law's liability section. Under the de micromis exemption, a person is not liable for response costs at a National Priorities List facility. That holds when liability rests only on having arranged disposal or transport of a very small amount of material containing hazardous substances. The remaining titles promote the cleanup and reuse of brownfields, provide funding for brownfields renewal, and enhance state response programs.
plaw-107-119-2002: The federal ethics watchdog keeps its funding authority under Public Law 107-119, the Office of Government Ethics Authorization Act of 2001, approved January 15, 2002. One amendment to section 405 of the Ethics in Government Act of 1978 does the work. The words 1997 through 1999 are struck, and 2002 through 2006 are inserted. The change extends the funding authority for the Office of Government Ethics through fiscal year 2006. The measure passed the Senate in November 2001 and the House the following month.
plaw-107-120-2002: A plaque in a Kentucky post office is the whole work of Public Law 107-120, approved January 15, 2002. The Postmaster General shall install it in the Williamsburg, Kentucky Post Office Building to honor Dr. James Harvey Early. The text, fixed by the act, records that Early was born June 14, 1808, in Knox County. He became postmaster of the town's first post office in 1829 and served in the Kentucky Legislature in 1844. He died at Rockhold on May 24, 1885, aged 77.
plaw-107-121-2002: A clarification for Native American cancer patients is made by Public Law 107-121, the Native American Breast and Cervical Cancer Treatment Technical Amendment Act of 2001, approved January 15, 2002. It amends title XIX of the Social Security Act to clarify one point. Indian women with breast or cervical cancer eligible for care through the Indian Health Service or a tribal program are included in the optional Medicaid category created in 2000 for such patients. Related clauses repair doubled subsection labels from overlapping amendments.
plaw-107-122-2002:
Students caught in the emergency after September 11 receive protection under the Higher Education Relief Opportunities for Students Act of 2001, Public Law 107-122, approved January 15, 2002. The act gives the Secretary of Education specific waiver authority to respond to the national emergency declared by the President on September 14, 2001.

The Secretary may waive or modify any statute or rule of the student aid programs under title IV of the Higher Education Act of 1965 as the emergency requires. The authorized waivers aim to keep affected federal student loan borrowers from ending up in a worse financial position because of their status. They aim to ease administrative requirements so borrowers avoid technical slip-ups or defaults. And they aim to adjust how family income is figured when need for aid is set.
plaw-107-123-2002:
Wall Street transaction fees fall under the Investor and Capital Markets Fee Relief Act, Public Law 107-123, approved January 16, 2002. The act amends the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 to reduce fees collected by the Securities and Exchange Commission.

Section 2 cuts the section 31 transaction fee at once. It strikes one three-hundredth of one percent and inserts fifteen dollars per million dollars. It also extends the fee language to options on securities indexes, except narrow-based ones. A related charge drops from two cents to nine-tenths of one cent. The new rates apply pro rata to amounts and balances under a million dollars, and the next section revises the transaction fee provisions for additional fee reductions.
plaw-107-124-2002: Spouses of treaty traders and treaty investors may work in the United States under Public Law 107-124, signed January 16, 2002. The act adds a single paragraph to section 214(e) of the Immigration and Nationality Act. The case covered is a spouse admitted under the treaty trader and investor category, accompanying or following to join the principal alien. For that spouse, the Attorney General shall authorize employment in the United States and provide a work endorsement or other proper work permit.
plaw-107-125-2002:
Public Law 107-125, approved January 16, 2002, helps the households of employees transferred to the United States by their companies. It amends the Immigration and Nationality Act in two ways, both touching the intracompany transferee category.

First, a spouse admitted alongside an intracompany transferee, accompanying or following to join that worker, must be allowed by the Attorney General to work in the United States. The spouse gets an employment endorsement or other proper work permit. Second, the one-year period of steady work otherwise required of certain transferees counts as a six-month period. That is so when the importing employer has filed a blanket petition and met the requirements for expedited processing of those it covers.
plaw-107-126-2002: Judicial officers keep a privacy shield under Public Law 107-126, signed January 16, 2002. The act extends for four years, through December 31, 2005, the authority to redact financial disclosure statements of judicial employees and judicial officers. It does so through one edit to the Ethics in Government Act of 1978: striking 2001 each place it appears in the redaction provision and inserting 2005 in its place.
plaw-107-127-2002:
Congress honors its senior soldier in the General Shelton Congressional Gold Medal Act, Public Law 107-127, approved January 16, 2002. It authorizes the President to award a gold medal on behalf of Congress to General Henry H. Shelton and provides for bronze duplicates to be produced and sold to the public.

The findings describe Shelton as Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, the principal military adviser to the President, the National Security Council, and the Secretary of Defense. They credit his leadership in Operation Allied Force. The air campaign he helped plan won a decisive victory in Kosovo in 1999 without a single allied combat casualty, against the forces of Slobodan Milosevic. Earlier service ran from Green Beret duty in Vietnam to helicopter forces in Operation Desert Storm and command of the Special Operations Command and the 18th Airborne Corps at Fort Bragg.
plaw-107-128-2002: The employment eligibility check pilot runs longer under the Basic Pilot Extension Act of 2001, Public Law 107-128, approved January 16, 2002. One edit does it, to section 401(b) of the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act of 1996. The basic pilot program for employment eligibility verification is stretched from a four-year period to a six-year period. The amendment takes effect on the date the act is enacted.
plaw-107-129-2002: Public Law 107-129, approved January 16, 2002, names a New Jersey post office building for Todd Beamer. Beamer was a passenger killed in the September 11 attacks. The United States Postal Service facility at 65 North Main Street in Cranbury, New Jersey, shall be known and designated as the Todd Beamer Post Office Building. Any reference to the facility in a law, map, regulation, document, or other record of the United States is deemed a reference to the Todd Beamer Post Office Building.
plaw-107-130-2002: Public Law 107-130, approved January 16, 2002, names the headquarters and visitors center at Humboldt Bay National Wildlife Refuge in California. The building at 1020 Ranch Road in Loleta is designated the Richard J. Guadagno Headquarters and Visitors Center. Any reference in a law, map, regulation, document, or other record of the United States to that building is deemed to be a reference to the Richard J. Guadagno Headquarters and Visitors Center.
plaw-107-131-2002:
College tuition paperwork gets simpler under Public Law 107-131, signed January 16, 2002. It amends the Internal Revenue Code of 1986 to simplify the reporting rules on higher education tuition and related costs.

The act rewrites who must make the return under section 6050S: an eligible educational institution that enrolls any student for any term. It then reworks the form and manner of the returns. The returns report the name, address, and taxpayer identification number of enrolled individuals. They report the total amount of payments received, or the total amount billed, for qualified tuition and related expenses during the calendar year. Redundant subparagraphs are struck and the remaining ones redesignated.
plaw-107-132-2002: The nation's school for diplomats takes the name of a former secretary of state in Public Law 107-132, approved January 16, 2002. The act designates the National Foreign Affairs Training Center as the George P. Shultz National Foreign Affairs Training Center, working through an amendment to the Foreign Service Act of 1980. Any reference in law to the training center, or to the Foreign Service Institute, is considered a reference to the Shultz center, and conforming amendments carry the new name into other statutes.
plaw-107-133-2002:
Child welfare programs are renewed and widened by the Promoting Safe and Stable Families Amendments of 2001, Public Law 107-133, approved January 17, 2002. The act extends and amends the program called Promoting Safe and Stable Families under subpart 2 of title IV-B of the Social Security Act.

Title I covers grants to states for promoting safe and stable families. It takes up the definition of family support services, reallotments, payments to states, evaluations, and research. It takes up technical assistance and improvements to state courts as well. A separate subtitle authorizes a program for mentoring children of incarcerated parents. The act also amends the Foster Care Independent Living program under title IV-E of the Social Security Act to provide educational and training vouchers for youths aging out of foster care.
plaw-107-134-2002:
Tax bills shrink for families of the September 11 victims under the Victims of Terrorism Tax Relief Act of 2001, Public Law 107-134, approved January 23, 2002. The act amends the Internal Revenue Code of 1986 to provide tax relief for victims of the terrorist attacks against the United States.

Title I, in its relief subtitle, addresses the income taxes of victims of terrorist attacks, excludes certain death benefits, reduces estate taxes, and treats payments by charitable organizations as exempt payments. It also excludes certain cancellations of indebtedness. A second subtitle excludes disaster relief payments. It authorizes postponement of certain tax deadlines and required actions. It applies some provisions to terroristic or military actions. It clarifies the due date for airline excise tax deposits. And it sets the treatment of certain structured settlement payments.
plaw-107-135-2002:
Nurses for veterans' hospitals are the first concern of the Department of Veterans Affairs Health Care Programs Enhancement Act of 2001, Public Law 107-135, approved January 23, 2002. The act amends title 38 of the United States Code to enhance the authority of the Secretary of Veterans Affairs to recruit and retain qualified nurses for the Veterans Health Administration.

Title I enhances the employee incentive scholarship program and the education debt reduction program. It also requires a report on requests to waive pay reductions for reemployed annuitants who fill nurse positions. Its retention subtitle provides additional pay for Saturday tours of duty for more health care professionals. It counts unused sick leave in annuity computations. The act also supplies an additional basis for establishing that a veteran cannot defray the expenses of necessary medical care, and enhances other department health care programs.
plaw-107-136-2002:
A veterans' cemetery takes the name of the congressman who fought to create it in Public Law 107-136, approved January 24, 2002. It names the national cemetery in Saratoga, New York, the Gerald B.H. Solomon Saratoga National Cemetery.

The findings sketch Solomon's life. Born in Okeechobee, Florida, he grew up during the Great Depression, moved to New York in 1945. He enlisted in the Marine Corps at the onset of the Korean War. He worked as a Glens Falls businessman before his election to the House in 1978. Across ten terms he gained a reputation as outspoken and tenacious. He served as ranking Republican on the Committee on Veterans' Affairs. He spearheaded the effort to create the cabinet-level Department of Veterans Affairs. And he led a 15-year drive to establish the Saratoga cemetery, where he is now interred.
plaw-107-137-2002:
The Ronald Reagan Boyhood Home National Historic Site in Illinois is authorized by Public Law 107-137, signed February 6, 2002. The act directs the Secretary of the Interior to set up the site once the land has been bought.

The Secretary must buy the land as soon as practicable, at fair market value and from a willing owner only. The purchase uses donated or appropriated funds. It takes fee simple, unencumbered title, together with related personal property the Secretary finds fitting. After the purchase, the Secretary names the land as the historic site. The Secretary runs it under a pact with the Ronald Reagan Boyhood Home Foundation, on terms that preserve its historic meaning. A general plan, prepared after talks with the Foundation, is due within two years of enactment.
plaw-107-138-2002:
Bringing together Pueblo of Acoma land in New Mexico is the aim of Public Law 107-138, signed February 6, 2002, under the heading Pueblo of Acoma Land and Mineral Consolidation. It concerns nontribal interest ownership of subsurface rights, including mineral rights, within the boundaries of the Acoma Indian Reservation.

Within six months of enactment, the Secretary of the Interior shall determine the extent and value of that nontribal ownership. The Secretary then negotiates exchanges with willing sellers. The trades swap interests in nontribal land inside the reservation for federal land in New Mexico that the Bureau of Land Management has identified as available for disposal, at roughly equal value. As an alternative, the Secretary may buy the interests outright, paying fair market value in cash or issuing Certificates of Bidding Rights under the mineral leasing laws.
plaw-107-139-2002:
Student loan interest becomes a set of fixed numbers under Public Law 107-139, approved February 8, 2002, which amends the Higher Education Act of 1965. The act establishes fixed interest rates for student and parent borrowers and extends the existing law on special allowances for lenders.

For most loans under the federal family education loan program whose first disbursement falls on or after July 1, 2006, the applicable rate is 6.8 percent on the unpaid principal balance. PLUS loans, for parents, carry 7.9 percent. A consolidation loan bears the lesser of the weighted average of the interest rates on the loans consolidated, rounded to the nearest higher one-eighth of one percent, or 8.25 percent. These fixed rates apply in place of the rates the prior subsection would have produced.
plaw-107-140-2002: One wrong section number is corrected by Public Law 107-140, approved February 8, 2002. The act amends title 18 of the United States Code to correct a technical error in the codification of title 36. In section 2320(e)(1)(B), the citation reading section 220706 of title 36 is struck. Section 220506 of title 36 is inserted instead. Nothing else in either title changes.
plaw-107-141-2002: Asian elephants receive renewed federal backing from Public Law 107-141, the Asian Elephant Conservation Reauthorization Act of 2002, signed February 12, 2002. It renews the Asian Elephant Conservation Act of 1997, extending its funding across the years 2001 through 2007. Office spending is capped at three percent of available funds, or 80,000 dollars, whichever is greater. A new section lets the Secretary call together an advice group of public and private groups working to save Asian elephants.
plaw-107-142-2002:
Three tribal water studies in the State of Washington are authorized by the Pacific Northwest Feasibility Studies Act of 2002, Public Law 107-142, approved February 12, 2002. The act authorizes the Secretary of the Interior to engage in feasibility studies of water resource projects in the state.

The Tulalip Tribes study seeks ways to meet future domestic and commercial water distribution needs of the Tulalip Indian Reservation on the eastern shore of Puget Sound. The Lower Elwha Klallam study looks for additional rural water supply sources for that tribe's reservation on the Olympic Peninsula. The Makah study addresses present and future water supply and distribution needs of the Makah Indian Tribe, likewise on the Olympic Peninsula. The Secretary must make each study's results available to the public on request and publish notice of their availability in the Federal Register.
plaw-107-143-2002: For the second straight year, Congress marked Ronald Reagan's birthday by resolution. Public Law 107-143, approved February 14, 2002, recognizes his 91st birthday. It notes that he is the first former President ever to attain the age of 91. The recitals honor his two overwhelming election victories and the restored roar of American progress and optimism. They honor leadership that united a Cold War-divided world, and Nancy Reagan's crusade against illegal drugs. And they send the country's thoughts and prayers to Reagan in his battle with Alzheimer's disease.
plaw-107-144-2002: Yerington, Nevada's post office gains a name from Public Law 107-144, approved February 14, 2002. The United States Postal Service facility at 811 South Main Street is designated the Joseph E. Dini, Jr. Post Office. All references to the facility in federal laws, maps, regulations, documents, and records are deemed references to the Joseph E. Dini, Jr. Post Office.
plaw-107-145-2002: Public Law 107-145, approved February 14, 2002, designates a postal facility in Maine. The United States Postal Service facility at 39 Tremont Street, Paris Hill, is designated as the Horatio King Post Office Building. Under the act, any reference in a federal law, map, regulation, or other record to that facility is deemed a reference to the Horatio King Post Office Building.
plaw-107-146-2002: Long Branch, New Jersey, receives a named post office through Public Law 107-146, approved February 14, 2002. The United States Post Office located at 60 Third Avenue shall be known and designated as the Pat King Post Office Building. From enactment onward, any reference in a federal law, map, regulation, or other record to that post office is deemed a reference to the Pat King Post Office Building.
plaw-107-147-2002:
An economic stimulus follows the 2001 downturn in the Job Creation and Worker Assistance Act of 2002, Public Law 107-147, signed March 9, 2002. The act's stated purpose is to provide tax incentives for economic recovery, and its amendments run to the Internal Revenue Code of 1986.

Title I, Business Provisions, grants a special depreciation allowance for certain property acquired after September 10, 2001, and before September 11, 2004. It allows carryback of certain net operating losses for five years. And it suspends, for a time, the 90 percent alternative minimum tax limit. Title II builds unemployment assistance on federal-state agreements. It sets up a temporary extended unemployment compensation account and payments to states that sign agreements. It adds financing provisions and fraud and overpayment rules, along with a special Reed Act transfer in fiscal year 2002.
plaw-107-148-2002:
American broadcasting reaches into wartime Afghanistan through the Radio Free Afghanistan Act, Public Law 107-148, signed March 11, 2002. The act authorizes Radio Free Afghanistan, a surrogate broadcasting service aimed at Afghan listeners.

Not later than 15 days after enactment, RFE/RL, Incorporated must submit a detailed plan to the Broadcasting Board of Governors for providing broadcasting in the Dari and Pashto languages to Afghanistan. Once that report is in, the Board is authorized to make grants supporting Radio Free Afghanistan. Fiscal year 2002 grants may be made without regard to an existing limit on total annual grant amounts. The act also makes the general authorities of United States international broadcasting law available for the service, which must follow the same standards of skill and accountability.
plaw-107-149-2002:
Appalachia's growth program is renewed by the Appalachian Regional Development Act Amendments of 2002, Public Law 107-149, approved March 12, 2002. The act reauthorizes the Appalachian Regional Development Act of 1965 and adjusts its aims and workings.

One stated purpose is to ensure that the people and businesses of the Appalachian region have the knowledge and skills they need. They must also have access to telecom and technology services to compete in the knowledge-based economy of the United States. The amendments write eco-industrial development into the 1965 act's goals. They describe it as growth that lifts jobs and the economy together with saving natural resources. They also name eco-industrial development tools among the region's tools. Later sections amend the functions of the Appalachian Regional Commission.
plaw-107-150-2002:
A family's immigration case need not end with its sponsor under the Family Sponsor Immigration Act of 2002, Public Law 107-150, approved March 13, 2002. The act amends the Immigration and Nationality Act to allow acceptance of an affidavit of support from another eligible sponsor when the original sponsor has died.

The substitution works only where the Attorney General has determined, for humanitarian reasons, that the dead petitioner's classification petition should not be revoked. The alternative sponsor must be a close relative of the sponsored alien. The list covers a spouse, parent, parent-in-law, sibling, adult child, son- or daughter-in-law, sibling-in-law, grandparent, or grandchild. The alien's legal guardian also qualifies. The substitute accepts joint and several liability, signs an affidavit of support, and must show the means to maintain an annual income of at least 125 percent of the federal poverty line.
plaw-107-151-2002: One homeless shelter's grant is capped by Public Law 107-151, approved March 13, 2002. The Secretary of Housing and Urban Development shall not award a grant to Liberty Center for the Homeless Incorporated in excess of 459,600 dollars. That cap holds notwithstanding the fiscal year 2001 funding notice for Continuum of Care Homeless Assistance Programs. If a larger award was already made, the Secretary shall modify it. The excess goes to other applicants from the Jacksonville, Florida, Continuum of Care, in the order of their application's project priority chart.
plaw-107-152-2002:
West Point turns two hundred in Public Law 107-152, a joint resolution approved March 14, 2002. It congratulates the United States Military Academy on its bicentennial anniversary and commends its outstanding contributions to the nation.

The recitals recall that Congress passed legislation on March 16, 1802, to establish the academy at West Point, New York. George Washington called the site the key to the continent. President Thomas Jefferson signed the law. Sylvanus Thayer, superintendent from 1817 to 1833, founded its strong academic program, strict discipline, and emphasis on moral and ethical conduct; Douglas MacArthur modernized the academy as superintendent from 1919 to 1922. It was the first school in America to teach engineering. It produced the builders of early railroads, bridges, roads, and canals, and of the Panama Canal. It also produced leaders of the Manhattan Project, along with 74 Medal of Honor recipients and Presidents Grant and Eisenhower.
plaw-107-153-2002: Tribal trust claims get time to settle under Public Law 107-153, approved March 19, 2002, an act to encourage the negotiated settlement of tribal claims. For limitations purposes, a reconciliation report given to an Indian tribe under the American Indian Trust Fund Management Reform Act of 1994 is deemed received on December 31, 1999. Its stated purpose is to let tribes postpone filing claims, or dismiss them voluntarily, so settlement talks with the United States can proceed.
plaw-107-154-2002: Workers who lost jobs in the September 11 attacks keep unemployment help longer under Public Law 107-154, approved March 25, 2002. The period set in section 410(a) of the Robert T. Stafford Disaster Relief and Emergency Assistance Act does not control here. Under this act, the President shall make unemployment assistance available for 39 weeks after the major disaster is declared. That holds for any individual eligible for that assistance as a result of the terrorist attacks of September 11, 2001.
plaw-107-155-2002:
Campaign money rules change in the Bipartisan Campaign Reform Act of 2002, Public Law 107-155, signed March 27, 2002. The act amends the Federal Election Campaign Act of 1971 to provide campaign reform from both parties.

Title I, Reduction of Special Interest Influence, takes up the soft money of political parties, raises the contribution limit for state party committees, and sets reporting rules. Title II governs campaign spending by noncandidates. Its electioneering communications subtitle requires disclosure of such ads. It treats coordinated ads as contributions. And it bars corporate and labor spending for electioneering communications, with rules for targeted ones. A second subtitle defines outside spending on one's own and draws the line between independent and coordinated spending.
plaw-107-156-2002: The Export-Import Bank keeps its authority a few weeks longer under Public Law 107-156, approved March 31, 2002. The Export-Import Bank of the United States shall continue to exercise its functions, in connection with and in furtherance of its objects and purposes, through April 30, 2002. That holds notwithstanding the dates specified in section 7 of the Export-Import Bank Act of 1945 and in Public Law 103-428.
plaw-107-157-2002:
More District of Columbia students qualify for tuition help under the District of Columbia College Access Improvement Act of 2002, Public Law 107-157, approved April 4, 2002. It amends the District of Columbia College Access Act of 1999, and it also opens the program to students at private historically black colleges and universities nationwide.

The rewritten eligibility rules cover an individual who begins an undergraduate course of study within three calendar years of graduating from a secondary school. Periods of active duty in the armed forces, Peace Corps service, or national community service do not count. The student must have been domiciled in the District for at least the 12 months before the freshman year. They also reach individuals who graduated before January 1, 1998, and are currently enrolled at an eligible institution, including those who enroll more than three years after graduating.
plaw-107-158-2002:
Taiwan's push for a voice at the World Health Assembly gains a dated American plan in Public Law 107-158, approved April 4, 2002. The act amends Public Law 107-10, the 2001 law on Taiwan's participation in the World Health Organization. It authorizes a United States plan to endorse and obtain observer status for Taiwan at the Assembly's annual summit in May 2002 in Geneva, Switzerland.

Added findings quote President Bush's letter of May 11, 2001, to Senator Murkowski. The letter says the United States should find opportunities for Taiwan's voice to be heard in international organizations even if membership is not possible. The findings also record that Secretary of Health and Human Services Tommy Thompson announced the administration's support at Geneva on May 16, 2001. The operative amendment is a single date, changing the plan's target from May 2001 to May 2002.
plaw-107-159-2002: Disputes on one Arizona reservation may go to arbitrators under Public Law 107-159, approved April 4, 2002. It amends the 1955 act authorizing long-term leases of restricted Indian lands. A lease, or a contract under section 2103 of the Revised Statutes, affecting land within the Gila River Indian Community Reservation may contain a provision for binding arbitration of disputes. Such agreements count as commerce under title 9, and refusing arbitration under one is deemed a civil action arising under federal law.
plaw-107-160-2002: Public Law 107-160, approved April 18, 2002, designates the United States Postal Service facility at 3698 Inner Perimeter Road in Valdosta, Georgia, as the Major Lyn McIntosh Post Office Building. Any reference to the facility in a law, map, regulation, or other record of the United States is deemed a reference to that building. The measure passed the House in December 2001 and cleared the Senate the following March.
plaw-107-161-2002: Richmond, Virginia, gets a named post office from Public Law 107-161, approved April 18, 2002. The United States Postal Service facility at 805 Glen Burnie Road shall be known and designated as the Tom Bliley Post Office Building. References to it in federal records are deemed references to that name. The bill passed the House on February 12, 2002, and the Senate on March 22.
plaw-107-162-2002: Public Law 107-162, approved April 18, 2002, designates the postal facility at 685 Turnberry Road in Newport News, Virginia, as the Herbert H. Bateman Post Office Building. The references section deems any mention of the facility in a law, map, regulation, document, or other record of the United States to be a reference to the Herbert H. Bateman Post Office Building. The House passed the bill in October 2001; the Senate followed in March 2002.
plaw-107-163-2002: A Michigan post office is renamed by Public Law 107-163, approved April 18, 2002. The United States Postal Service facility at 310 South State Street in St. Ignace, Michigan, shall be known and designated as the Bob Davis Post Office Building. References to the facility in United States laws, maps, regulations, and records are deemed references to the Bob Davis Post Office Building. The House acted in February 2002 and the Senate in March.
plaw-107-164-2002: Public Law 107-164, approved April 18, 2002, designates the postal facility at 216 2nd Street, S.W., in Harlem, Montana, as the Francis Bardanouve United States Post Office Building. Any reference in a law, map, regulation, document, or other record of the United States to that post office is deemed a reference to the Francis Bardanouve United States Post Office Building. The measure had passed the House the previous October.
plaw-107-165-2002: Petersburg, Virginia, receives a postal namesake in Public Law 107-165, approved April 18, 2002. The United States Postal Service facility at 3131 South Crater Road is designated the Norman Sisisky Post Office Building. Under the references clause, any mention of the facility in a federal law, map, regulation, or other record counts as a reference to the Norman Sisisky Post Office Building. The bill passed the House in October 2001 and the Senate in March 2002.
plaw-107-166-2002: Public Law 107-166, approved April 18, 2002, puts a local name on the post office at 125 Main Street in Forest City, North Carolina: the Vernon Tarlton Post Office Building. Every reference to the facility in a law, map, regulation, document, or other record of the United States is deemed a reference to the Vernon Tarlton Post Office Building. The House passed the bill in December 2001, the Senate in March 2002.
plaw-107-167-2002: Deer Park, New York, gains the Raymond M. Downey Post Office Building under Public Law 107-167, approved April 18, 2002. The law designates the United States Postal Service facility at 375 Carlls Path with that name. Its references section deems any reference to the facility in federal laws, maps, regulations, documents, or other records to be a reference to the Raymond M. Downey Post Office Building. Passage came in December 2001 in the House and March 2002 in the Senate.
plaw-107-168-2002: One more month of life for the Export-Import Bank comes from Public Law 107-168, approved May 1, 2002. In nearly the same words as the extension signed at the end of March, the bank shall continue to exercise its functions through May 31, 2002. That holds notwithstanding the dates specified in the Export-Import Bank Act of 1945 and in Public Law 103-428.
plaw-107-169-2002: Punctuation and margins occupy Public Law 107-169, signed May 7, 2002, which makes technical amendments to section 10 of title 9 of the United States Code, the arbitration provision on vacating awards. The paragraphs of subsection (a) are indented two ems. The capital Where at their heads becomes lowercase where. Periods at the ends of three paragraphs become semicolons with an or added. And one paragraph is recast as a new subsection (b), with subsection (b) redesignated as (c). No substance of arbitration law changes.
plaw-107-170-2002: The family farmer bankruptcy chapter is extended once more by Public Law 107-170, approved May 7, 2002, this time for eight additional months. It amends the reenactment provision shaped by Public Laws 106-5, 106-70, 107-8, and 107-17. It strikes October 1, 2001, each place it appears, and inserts June 1, 2002. Two subordinate dates shift by half a year to match. Although signed in May 2002, the amendments are given effect as of October 1, 2001.
plaw-107-171-2002:
American farm policy through the middle of the decade is written in the Farm Security and Rural Investment Act of 2002, Public Law 107-171, approved May 13, 2002. The act provides for the continuation of agricultural programs through fiscal year 2007.

Title I covers commodity programs. Its direct and counter-cyclical payments subtitle builds the new payment system on base acres and payment acres established for each farm. Payment yields are set. A producer agreement is required before payments flow, and farmers get planting flexibility. A second subtitle makes nonrecourse marketing assistance loans and loan deficiency payments available for loan commodities. Definitions open the title, and a period of effectiveness provision bounds the system.
plaw-107-172-2002:
Blood cancers receive a dedicated federal push from the Hematological Cancer Research Investment and Education Act of 2002, Public Law 107-172, approved May 14, 2002. The act amends the Public Health Service Act to provide for research, information, and education with respect to blood cancer.

Congress found that an estimated 109,500 people in the United States would be diagnosed with leukemia, lymphoma, or multiple myeloma in 2001, that such cases were 8.6 percent of new cancers yet would kill an estimated 60,300 people, and that less than five percent of federal cancer research funds went to diseases causing eleven percent of cancer deaths. The act writes a new section into the Public Health Service Act. It begins with a Joe Moakley Research Excellence Program, under which the Director of the National Institutes of Health shall expand blood cancer research.
plaw-107-173-2002:
Border screening hardens after September 11 in the Enhanced Border Security and Visa Entry Reform Act of 2002, Public Law 107-173, approved May 14, 2002. It is an act to enhance the border security of the United States.

Title I authorizes appropriations for hiring and training government personnel and for improvements in technology and infrastructure, and it sets machine-readable visa fees. Title II orders interagency information sharing. It gives interim access to law enforcement information. It sets up an interoperable law enforcement and intelligence data system with name-matching capacity, called the Chimera system. It adds a commission on interoperable data sharing, and special personnel authorities for building it. Title III reforms visa issuance, requiring electronic provision of visa files, an integrated entry and exit data system, and machine-readable, tamper-resistant entry and exit documents.
plaw-107-174-2002:
Federal workers gain stronger protection in the Notification and Federal Employee Antidiscrimination and Retaliation Act of 2002, Public Law 107-174, signed May 15, 2002. The act makes federal agencies answer for breaking antidiscrimination and whistleblower protection laws.

Title II makes agencies pay back judgment funds. It adds notice and reporting rules, guidelines, and a clarification of remedies. It also orders General Accounting Office studies on exhaustion of remedies and Department of Justice costs. Title III covers complaint data disclosure. Each agency must post, four times a year on its public website, data about the federal sector equal employment opportunity complaints filed with it.
plaw-107-175-2002: St. Thomas gains a named federal building from Public Law 107-175, approved May 17, 2002. The federal building located in Charlotte Amalie, St. Thomas, United States Virgin Islands, shall be known and designated as the Ron de Lugo Federal Building. Any reference in a law, map, regulation, document, or other record of the United States to that building is deemed to be a reference to the Ron de Lugo Federal Building.
plaw-107-176-2002: Public Law 107-176, approved May 17, 2002, designates the federal building at 143 West Liberty Street in Medina, Ohio, as the Donald J. Pease Federal Building. Any reference in a law, map, regulation, or other record of the United States to that building is deemed a reference to the Donald J. Pease Federal Building. The House passed the bill in June 2001 and the Senate in April 2002.
plaw-107-177-2002: Alton, Illinois, gains a double-named courthouse from Public Law 107-177, approved May 17, 2002. The federal building and United States courthouse at 501 Bell Street shall be known and designated as the William L. Beatty Federal Building and United States Courthouse. Federal references to the building are deemed references to that full name. The measure cleared the House in November 2001 and the Senate on April 30, 2002.
plaw-107-178-2002: Public Law 107-178, approved May 17, 2002, names the federal building and United States courthouse at 400 North Main Street in Butte, Montana, for a Montana statesman. It is designated the Mike Mansfield Federal Building and United States Courthouse. Any reference to the building in a federal law, map, regulation, or record is deemed a reference to that name. The House acted in December 2001, the Senate in April 2002.
plaw-107-179-2002: A report deadline jumps fifteen years in Public Law 107-179, approved May 20, 2002, an act to require a report on the operations of the State Justice Institute.
