The act amends section 213 of the State Justice Institute Act of 1984. It strikes the words On October 1, 1987. It inserts Not later than October 1, 2002. That moves the date by which the report on the Institute is to be made.
plaw-107-180-2002:
Washington's criminal justice table gains federal seats under the Criminal Justice Coordinating Council Restructuring Act of 2002, Public Law 107-180, approved May 20, 2002. The act authorizes certain federal officials with responsibility for administering the District of Columbia's criminal justice system to serve on, and take part in, the District of Columbia Criminal Justice Coordinating Council.

The officials named include the Director of the Court Services and Offender Supervision Agency and the Director of the District of Columbia Pretrial Services Agency. They include the United States Attorney for the District of Columbia and the Director of the Bureau of Prisons. They also include the chair of the United States Parole Commission and the Director of the United States Marshals Service. A further section requires the Council to prepare an annual report, due within 60 days after each calendar year ends, for the President, Congress, and District and federal entities.
plaw-107-181-2002:
Ministers' housing allowances are tied to rental value by the Clergy Housing Allowance Clarification Act of 2002, Public Law 107-181, approved May 20, 2002. The act amends the Internal Revenue Code of 1986 to clarify that the parsonage allowance exclusion is limited to the fair rental value of the property.

The amendment inserts that limit into section 107. The exclusion holds only to the extent the allowance does not exceed the fair rental value of the home. That value includes furnishings and appurtenances such as a garage, plus the cost of utilities. It applies to taxable years beginning after December 31, 2001. For earlier years it reaches taxpayers who had already limited the exclusion on a return. It provides that no one else faces the new limit for a pre-2002 year, whatever earlier Internal Revenue Service guidance said.
plaw-107-182-2002: Chicago's Job Corps site is renamed by Public Law 107-182, approved May 21, 2002. The federal building at 3348 South Kedzie Avenue, until then known as the Chicago Job Corps Center, is redesignated the Paul Simon Chicago Job Corps Center. References to the building in any law, map, regulation, document, or other record of the United States are deemed references to the Paul Simon Chicago Job Corps Center.
plaw-107-183-2002: Public Law 107-183, approved May 29, 2002, names the chapel in the national cemetery in Los Angeles, California, the Bob Hope Veterans Chapel. The designation is made notwithstanding section 531 of title 38 of the United States Code. After enactment, any reference in a law, map, regulation, document, or other record of the United States to that chapel is deemed a reference to the Bob Hope Veterans Chapel. The bill passed both chambers in the same week of May 2002.
plaw-107-184-2002: Wichita's veterans center takes a Kansan's name under Public Law 107-184, approved May 29, 2002. The Department of Veterans Affairs Medical and Regional Office Center in Wichita, Kansas, shall be known and designated as the Robert J. Dole Department of Veterans Affairs Medical and Regional Office Center. References to the center in federal laws, maps, regulations, and records are deemed references to the Dole center.
plaw-107-185-2002:
Adult children of former Vietnamese re-education camp prisoners keep a path to the United States under Public Law 107-185, approved May 30, 2002. The act extends eligibility for refugee status of unmarried sons and daughters of certain Vietnamese refugees.

For in-country refugee processing in Vietnam during fiscal years 2002 and 2003, a covered person is considered a refugee of special humanitarian concern. The person shall be admitted for resettlement if admissible as an immigrant. The person must be the son or daughter of a qualified national, be at least 21 years old, and have been unmarried when the parent was accepted for resettlement. A qualified national was formerly interned in a re-education camp in Vietnam by its government, or is the widow or widower of such a person. The national qualified under the Orderly Departure Program or through the United States Consulate General in Ho Chi Minh City.
plaw-107-186-2002: The Export-Import Bank receives two more weeks from Public Law 107-186, approved May 30, 2002, the third short extension of that spring. Notwithstanding the dates in the Export-Import Bank Act of 1945 and Public Law 103-428, the bank shall continue to exercise its functions through June 14, 2002. The bill moved quickly, passing the House on May 21 and the Senate on May 22, 2002.
plaw-107-187-2002:
NATO's door should stay open, Congress declares in the Gerald B. H. Solomon Freedom Consolidation Act of 2002, Public Law 107-187, approved June 10, 2002. The act endorses the vision of further enlargement of the NATO Alliance articulated by President George W. Bush on June 15, 2001, and by former President William J. Clinton on October 22, 1996.

The findings walk through a decade of enlargement law. The NATO Participation Act of 1994 declared that ready Partnership for Peace participants should be invited to full membership at an early date. The NATO Enlargement Facilitation Act of 1996 called for prompt admission of Poland, Hungary, the Czech Republic, and Slovenia. It named Slovakia, Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, Romania, Bulgaria, Albania, Moldova, and Ukraine as further candidates. The European Security Act of 1998 added that Poland, Hungary, and the Czech Republic should not be the last invited.
plaw-107-188-2002:
Preparing for germ attacks becomes national policy in the Public Health Security and Bioterrorism Preparedness and Response Act of 2002, Public Law 107-188, signed June 12, 2002. The act's purpose is to improve the ability of the United States to prevent, prepare for, and respond to bioterrorism and other public health emergencies.

Title I covers national readiness and response planning, coordinating, and reporting. It sets up an Assistant Secretary for Public Health Emergency Preparedness and the National Disaster Medical System, and for improving the ability of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Companion sections address advice panels and messaging. They cover education and training of health care personnel, including pediatric issues. They cover grants for shortages of health professionals. They cover an emergency system for signing up health professions volunteers in advance, and antimicrobial resistance.
plaw-107-189-2002:
After a spring of short extensions, the Export-Import Bank receives a full reauthorization in the Export-Import Bank Reauthorization Act of 2002, Public Law 107-189, signed June 14, 2002. The act reauthorizes the bank and extends its authority. It clarifies that its purposes include United States employment. It increases its overall loan, guarantee, and insurance authority.

The twenty sections listed run from office expenses to work relating to Africa, small business, technology, and renewable energy sources. The act expands authority to use the Tied Aid Credit Fund. It requires an annual competitiveness report and an annual report. It also requires a General Accounting Office report on the reserve practices of export credit agencies and private banks. Other sections address human rights, authorize denying applications where any party engaged in fraud or corruption, and require weighing a foreign country's helpfulness against terrorism.
plaw-107-190-2002: Public Law 107-190, approved June 18, 2002, designates the United States Post Office building at 3101 West Sunflower Avenue in Santa Ana, California, as the Hector G. Godinez Post Office Building. Any reference in a law, regulation, map, document, or other record of the United States to that building is deemed a reference to the Hector G. Godinez Post Office Building. The House passed the bill in April 2002 and the Senate in June.
plaw-107-191-2002: Lake Linden, Michigan, receives a named post office through Public Law 107-191, approved June 18, 2002. The United States Postal Service facility at 600 Calumet Street shall be known and designated as the Philip E. Ruppe Post Office Building. References to the facility in federal laws, maps, regulations, and records are deemed references to that building. The bill cleared the House in April 2002 and the Senate on June 3.
plaw-107-192-2002: Public Law 107-192, approved June 18, 2002, designates the postal facility at 2829 Commercial Way in Rock Springs, Wyoming, as the Teno Roncalio Post Office Building. Any reference in a law, map, regulation, document, or other record of the United States to the facility is deemed to be a reference to the Teno Roncalio Post Office Building. The House passed the measure in March 2002, the Senate in June.
plaw-107-193-2002: A Florida panhandle post office is renamed by Public Law 107-193, approved June 18, 2002. The United States Postal Service facility at 3719 Highway 4 in Jay, Florida, shall be known and designated as the Joseph W. Westmoreland Post Office Building. Federal references to the facility are deemed references to that name. The bill passed the House on April 16, 2002, and the Senate on June 3.
plaw-107-194-2002: Public Law 107-194, approved June 18, 2002, designates the United States Postal Service facility at 1590 East Joyce Boulevard in Fayetteville, Arkansas, as the Clarence B. Craft Post Office Building. The references section deems any mention of the facility in a law, map, regulation, or other record of the United States to be a reference to the Clarence B. Craft Post Office Building. The House acted in May 2002, the Senate on June 3.
plaw-107-195-2002:
Deadlines for selling television spectrum vanish in the Auction Reform Act of 2002, Public Law 107-195, signed June 19, 2002. The act ends the deadlines for spectrum auctions of spectrum previously allocated to television broadcasting.

Congress found that circumstances in the telecommunications market had changed dramatically since auctioning spectrum in the 700 megahertz band was mandated in 1997. That raised doubts whether the original or revised deadlines fit sound policy. No comprehensive plan yet existed for allocating additional spectrum for third-generation wireless and other advanced services. A study of whether the Department of Defense could share or relinquish spectrum would not finish until after the June 19 auction date. That created uncertainty about the frequencies' best use. The findings also point to interference problems in the 800 megahertz band, especially for public safety.
plaw-107-196-2002:
Chaplains killed in the line of duty gain death benefits under the Mychal Judge Police and Fire Chaplains Public Safety Officers' Benefit Act of 2002, Public Law 107-196, approved June 24, 2002. The act amends the Omnibus Crime Control and Safe Streets Act of 1968 to ensure such chaplains receive public safety officer death benefits.

The act writes a definition of chaplain into the benefits law. A chaplain is an officially recognized or designated member of a legally organized volunteer fire department or police department. A chaplain may also be an officially recognized public employee of such a department. Either way, the person was responding to a fire, rescue, or police emergency. The phrase as a chaplain joins the list of covered service. The act also adds an eligible beneficiary: where no spouse or child survives, the individual the officer designated as beneficiary under the officer's most recent life insurance policy.
plaw-107-197-2002:
Two anti-terrorism treaties enter American criminal law through Public Law 107-197, signed June 25, 2002. The act carries out the International Convention for the Suppression of Terrorist Bombings and the International Convention for the Suppression of the Financing of Terrorism. Its aim is to combat terrorism and defend the nation against terrorist acts.

Title I, the Terrorist Bombings Convention Implementation Act of 2002, adds section 2332f to chapter 113B of title 18. The new statute punishes whoever unlawfully delivers, places, discharges, or detonates an explosive or other lethal device in, into, or against a place of public use. It covers a state or government facility, a public transportation system, or an infrastructure facility. The act must intend to cause death or serious bodily injury, or extensive destruction likely to bring major economic loss. Attempts and conspiracies are covered on the same terms.
plaw-107-198-2002:
Small firms get help with federal forms from the Small Business Paperwork Relief Act of 2002, Public Law 107-198, approved June 28, 2002. The act amends chapter 35 of title 44 of the United States Code, the Paperwork Reduction Act framework, to facilitate compliance by small business concerns with certain federal paperwork requirements.

The Director of the Office of Management and Budget must publish an annual list of the compliance assistance resources available to small businesses. The list appears in the Federal Register and on the Internet, in consultation with the Small Business Administration. The first list is due within one year of enactment. Each agency must also establish one point of contact to act as a liaison between the agency and small business concerns on information collection and paperwork. The act establishes a task force to examine information collection and dissemination as well.
plaw-107-199-2002: The national borrowing cap rises in Public Law 107-199, approved June 28, 2002, which amends title 31 of the United States Code to increase the public debt limit. In section 3101(b), the figure of about 5.95 trillion dollars is struck and about 6.4 trillion dollars is inserted in its place. The Senate passed the bill on June 11, 2002, and the House followed on June 27.
plaw-107-200-2002:
Nevada's objection to a nuclear waste repository is overridden by Public Law 107-200, a joint resolution approved July 23, 2002. Pursuant to the Nuclear Waste Policy Act of 1982, the resolution approves the site at Yucca Mountain, Nevada. The site is for a repository to dispose of high-level radioactive waste and spent nuclear fuel.

The approval covers a site for which the Governor of Nevada had submitted a notice of disapproval on April 8, 2002. That notice is the state objection the 1982 act provides for, and Congress may set it aside. The House passed the resolution on May 8, 2002, and the Senate on July 9, after energy committee reports in both chambers.
plaw-107-201-2002:
The Mint's silver supply is secured by the Support of American Eagle Silver Bullion Program Act, Public Law 107-201, approved July 23, 2002. The act authorizes the Secretary of the Treasury to purchase silver on the open market, to be used to mint coins, when the silver stockpile is depleted.

Congress found that the American Eagle Silver Bullion coin leads the global market and that the program, established in 1986, is the most successful silver bullion program in the world. From fiscal year 1995 through fiscal year 2001 it generated revenues of about 264 million dollars and profits that helped reduce the national debt. With silver reserves in the Defense Logistics Agency's strategic stockpile running out, the Treasury needed another source so the Mint could keep the program going profitably. The findings add that silver was commercially produced in twelve states in 2001.
plaw-107-202-2002:
Benjamin Franklin's 300th birthday gets its planning body in Public Law 107-202, approved July 24, 2002, which establishes the Benjamin Franklin Tercentenary Commission.

The findings call Franklin one of the most extraordinary men of the founding generation and, around the world, one of the best-known Americans who ever lived. They cite his literary work, the philanthropic and educational institutions he created, and his scientific explorations. They cite his service as a statesman and diplomat. And they note that he was the only American to sign all five enabling documents of the United States. Since January 17, 2006, would be the 300th anniversary of his birth, the act creates a commission to study and recommend to Congress fitting activities to celebrate it.
plaw-107-203-2002:
When a Forest Service firefighter dies on the fire line, an outside investigator must find out why, under Public Law 107-203, approved July 24, 2002. The act provides for an independent investigation of Forest Service firefighter deaths that are caused by wildfire entrapment or burnover.

In the case of each such fatality, the Inspector General of the Department of Agriculture shall conduct an investigation. The investigation shall not rely on, and shall be completely independent of, any investigation of the fatality conducted by the Forest Service itself. As soon as possible after completing it, the Inspector General submits a report of the results to Congress and to the Secretary of Agriculture.
plaw-107-204-2002:
Corporate accounting is remade by the Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002, Public Law 107-204, signed July 30, 2002. Its stated purpose is to protect investors. It aims to make corporate disclosures more accurate and more reliable under the securities laws.

Title I creates the Public Company Accounting Oversight Board. Accounting firms register with the Board. The Board sets auditing, quality control, and independence standards. It inspects registered firms, and it runs investigations and discipline cases. All of this sits under oversight by the Securities and Exchange Commission, with standards and funding addressed as well. Title II guards auditor independence. It covers services outside the scope of practice of auditors, preapproval requirements, audit partner rotation, and auditor reports to audit committees. It covers conflicts of interest. And it orders a study of mandatory rotation of such firms.
plaw-107-205-2002:
Nursing's workforce shortage is addressed by the Nurse Reinvestment Act, Public Law 107-205, approved July 30, 2002. The act amends the Public Health Service Act with respect to health professions programs regarding the field of nursing.

Title I, Nurse Recruitment, provides for public service announcements regarding the nursing profession and establishes a National Nurse Service Corps. Title II, Nurse Retention, takes up building career ladders and retaining quality nurses, comprehensive geriatric education, and a nurse faculty loan program, with reports by the General Accounting Office. The act works by amending the nursing title of the Public Health Service Act, beginning with added definitions such as ambulatory surgical center and federally qualified health center.
plaw-107-206-2002:
More recovery money following the September 11 attacks is appropriated by Public Law 107-206, approved August 2, 2002. The act is the 2002 Supplemental Appropriations Act for Further Recovery From and Response To Terrorist Attacks on the United States. It covers the fiscal year ending September 30, 2002.

Title I, Supplemental Appropriations, opens with the Department of Agriculture. An additional 18 million dollars goes to the Office of the Secretary, to remain available until expended. The Secretary shall transfer the funds among four services: the Agricultural Research Service, the Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service, the Agricultural Marketing Service, and the Food Safety and Inspection Service. The entire amount is designated by Congress as an emergency requirement under the Balanced Budget and Emergency Deficit Control Act of 1985. It is available only to the extent the President transmits a budget request designating it as such.
plaw-107-207-2002:
A definition with wide legal reach is set by the Born-Alive Infants Protection Act of 2002, Public Law 107-207, approved August 5, 2002. The act adds a new section 8 to chapter 1 of title 1 of the United States Code, the definitions chapter of federal law.

The section provides that, in reading any act of Congress or federal regulation or interpretation, the words person, human being, child, and individual include every infant member of the species homo sapiens. The infant must be born alive at any stage of development. Born alive means the expulsion or extraction from the mother of an infant who afterward breathes, or has a beating heart, pulsation of the umbilical cord, or definite movement of voluntary muscles. This holds regardless of whether the cord was cut and however the birth occurred. A closing clause says the section neither expands nor contracts any legal status before that point.
plaw-107-208-2002:
Immigrant children who turn 21 while a petition waits gain protection from the Child Status Protection Act, Public Law 107-208, approved August 6, 2002. The act amends the Immigration and Nationality Act. It judges whether an alien is a child, for classification as an immediate relative, by the alien's age on the date the classification petition is filed.

The new rules added to section 201 make that filing-date age the general test. If a petition filed for a child of a lawful permanent resident later converts to an immediate relative petition because the parent naturalizes, a different date controls. The age used is the child's age on the date of the parent's naturalization. A third rule, for a petition first filed for a married son or daughter, uses the age on the date the marriage ends. Each rule freezes the age at a fixed moment rather than the day the case is finally decided.
plaw-107-209-2002:
Honorary American citizenship, conferred only four times before in more than two hundred years, is granted again by Public Law 107-209, a joint resolution approved August 6, 2002. It proclaims Marie Joseph Paul Yves Roche Gilbert du Motier, the Marquis de Lafayette, posthumously to be an honorary citizen of the United States of America.

The recitals remember a Frenchman who put forth his own money and risked his life for American freedom. Congress voted him to the rank of major general, and he was wounded at the Battle of Brandywine. Lafayette secured the help of France against Great Britain, was honored by Virginia and Maryland, and in 1824 became the first foreign dignitary to address Congress. At his death both chambers draped themselves in black. An American flag has flown over his grave in France ever since, unremoved even during the Nazi occupation of World War II.
plaw-107-210-2002:
Trade policy for the decade is bundled into the Trade Act of 2002, Public Law 107-210, signed August 6, 2002. The act extends the Andean Trade Preference Act, grants added trade benefits under that act, and organizes itself into five parts.

Division A is Trade Adjustment Assistance. It reauthorizes the help program for workers. It speeds petitions with rapid response help and quick review by the Secretary of Labor. It also sets group eligibility rules and qualifying rules for trade readjustment allowances. Division B grants Bipartisan Trade Promotion Authority. Division C carries the Andean Trade Preference Act rules. Division D extends certain other preferential trade treatment. Division E gathers miscellaneous rules.
plaw-107-211-2002: A Colorado county gains years to sell land under Public Law 107-211, approved August 21, 2002. The act amends the Clear Creek County, Colorado, Public Lands Transfer Act of 1993. It gives the county more time to dispose of certain lands transferred to it under that act. In section 5(c)(2), the wording fixing the deadline at ten years after the 1993 act's enactment is struck and May 19, 2015, is inserted in its place.
plaw-107-212-2002: Foreign investors in Guam gain treaty-rate withholding under the Guam Foreign Investment Equity Act, Public Law 107-212, approved August 21, 2002. Amending the Organic Act of Guam, it sets the withholding rate on Guam-source income under listed Internal Revenue Code sections, for Guam income tax purposes. The rate is the one that would apply if Guam were treated as part of the United States for treaty purposes. The rule does not apply to income from a Guam payor whose taxes were rebated under Guam law.
plaw-107-213-2002:
A large Idaho monument changes character in Public Law 107-213, approved August 21, 2002. The roughly 410,000 acres added to the Craters of the Moon National Monument by Presidential Proclamation 7373 of November 9, 2000 are redesignated as the Craters of the Moon National Preserve. The acres are those identified on the proclamation's map for administration by the National Park Service.

Except as the act provides, the preserve is administered under that proclamation, the Antiquities Act of 1906, and the laws generally applicable to units of the National Park System. One exception is hunting. The Secretary of the Interior shall permit hunting in the preserve under the laws of the United States and the State of Idaho. Zones and seasons may be closed for public safety, protection of resources, administration, or public enjoyment, ordinarily only after consulting the state.
plaw-107-214-2002:
The Long Walk National Historic Trail Study Act, Public Law 107-214, approved August 21, 2002, marks a forced march of Native peoples for study. The act amends the National Trails System Act. It designates the route in Arizona and New Mexico that the Navajo and Mescalero Apache tribes were forced to walk in 1863 and 1864. The route is designated for study toward addition to the National Trails System.

Congress found that, from the fall of 1863 into the winter of 1864, the Government forced thousands of Navajos and Mescalero Apaches from their lands to Fort Sumner, New Mexico. There they were held captive, virtually as prisoners of war, for over four years. Thousands died at Fort Sumner from starvation, malnutrition, disease, exposure, or conflicts with military personnel. The study route runs through Canyon de Chelly, Arizona, and Albuquerque, Canyon Blanco, Anton Chico, Canyon Piedra Pintado, and Fort Sumner, New Mexico.
plaw-107-215-2002: Fifteen acres join a Virginia monument under the Booker T. Washington National Monument Boundary Adjustment Act of 2002, Public Law 107-215, signed August 21, 2002. The boundary of the monument is changed to include the roughly 15 acres shown on a February 2001 boundary map for Franklin County, Virginia. The Secretary of the Interior may acquire the added land from willing owners by donation, purchase with donated or appropriated funds, or exchange. Land so added is run as part of the monument.
plaw-107-216-2002:
Colorado gains new protected high country in the James Peak Wilderness and Protection Area Act, Public Law 107-216, approved August 21, 2002. The act designates the James Peak Wilderness and Protection Area in the Arapaho and Roosevelt National Forests in Colorado.

About 14,000 acres of those forests, as shown on a September 2001 map, are added to the Colorado Wilderness Act system as the James Peak Wilderness. Two further parcels enlarge the Indian Peaks Wilderness Area: the Ranch Creek addition of roughly 2,232 acres and the Fourth of July addition of roughly 963 acres, each mapped in September 2001. The Secretary of Agriculture must file the maps and legal boundary descriptions with the House Committee on Resources and the Senate Committee on Energy and Natural Resources.
plaw-107-217-2002:
A whole title of the United States Code is rebuilt by Public Law 107-217, signed August 21, 2002. The act revises, codifies, and enacts without real change certain general and lasting laws related to public buildings, property, and works, as title 40 of the Code, Public Buildings, Property, and Works.

The codified title is arranged in five subtitles: Federal Property and Administrative Services, Public Buildings and Works, Information Technology Management, Appalachian Regional Development, and Miscellaneous. Subtitle I opens with chapters on the organization of the General Services Administration, property management, foreign excess property, urban land use, selection of architects and engineers, and public property. As a codification, the act's gift is arrangement and settled wording: it gathers scattered statutes into a single title rather than making new policy.
plaw-107-218-2002:
An Arizona mission park grows under the Tumacacori National Historical Park Boundary Revision Act of 2002, Public Law 107-218, signed August 21, 2002. It revises the boundary of the park in southern Arizona.

The findings recall that Tumacacori Mission was declared a national monument in 1908 in recognition of its significance as one of the oldest mission ruins in the Southwest. The historical park established in 1990 joined the mission with the ruins of Los Santos Angeles de Guevavi and the Calabazas site. The park was set up to protect and interpret places tied to Spanish missionaries and explorers of the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries. The act's purposes are to add roughly 310 acres of adjacent land to the park. The added land protects and interprets the mission's resources. It also enhances the visitor experience by developing access to those resources.
plaw-107-219-2002:
Wolf Trap sheds the word Farm in Public Law 107-219, approved August 21, 2002, which renames Wolf Trap Farm Park as Wolf Trap National Park for the Performing Arts.

The renaming strikes the old name from the Wolf Trap Farm Park Act wherever it appears and inserts the new one. A guard clause provides that laws, rules, or regulations applying solely to National Park System units designated as a National Park do not apply here. They do not govern Wolf Trap. A new references section requires the Secretary of the Interior, other federal employees, and the Wolf Trap Foundation to use the new name in maps, publications, signs, and official communications. It also reads older references in federal law and records as references to the Wolf Trap National Park for the Performing Arts.
plaw-107-220-2002: A Louisiana disease center is renamed by Public Law 107-220, approved August 21, 2002, which amends the Public Health Service Act to redesignate the Gillis W. Long Hansen's Disease Center as the National Hansen's Disease Programs Center. The new name replaces the old one in section 320(a)(1) of that act and in section 211 of Public Law 105-78. It also replaces it in deeds, agreements, and other documents under that section. And it replaces it in any other law, map, regulation, document, paper, or record of the United States.
plaw-107-221-2002:
Lewis and Clark's winter camp may grow under the Fort Clatsop National Memorial Expansion Act of 2002, Public Law 107-221, approved August 21, 2002. The act authorizes the acquisition of additional lands for the memorial in Oregon, whose size Congress had limited by statute to 130 acres.

The findings call Fort Clatsop the only unit of the National Park System solely dedicated to the Lewis and Clark Expedition. In 1805 the expedition's members built Fort Clatsop near the mouth of the Columbia River and spent 106 days there waiting out winter before the journey home. Congress established the memorial in 1958 to commemorate that encampment. The 1995 general management plan recommends expanding it to include the trail the expedition used to reach the Pacific Ocean and the shore and forest lands around them. Congress adds that expansion is timely ahead of the expedition's bicentennial, planned for 2004 through 2006.
plaw-107-222-2002:
Cleanup money for thorium sites is raised by Public Law 107-222, signed August 21, 2002. It amends title X of the Energy Policy Act of 1992, on reimbursement of licensees, and related provisions.

The cap on payments to licensees rises from 140 million to 365 million dollars. Yearly ceilings are 90 million dollars in fiscal year 2002 and 55 million dollars in fiscal year 2003. The ceiling is 20 million dollars in each year from fiscal 2004 through fiscal 2007. Amounts authorized for one year but not paid may be paid in later years. The authorization climbs from 490 million to 715 million dollars, and a deposit figure in the Atomic Energy Act of 1954 rises to about 518 million dollars. The act also authorizes the Secretary to spend what is necessary to maintain enrichment capability at the Portsmouth, Ohio, facility on cold standby.
plaw-107-223-2002:
Gas pipelines may cross a famous park under permits authorized by Public Law 107-223, signed August 21, 2002. The act empowers the Secretary of the Interior to issue right-of-way permits for natural gas pipelines within the boundary of Great Smoky Mountains National Park.

Section 1 covers pipelines that exist as of September 1, 2001. Section 2 covers proposed pipelines, but only where they would cross three named park corridors: the Foothills Parkway, the Foothills Parkway Spur between Pigeon Forge and Gatlinburg, and the Gatlinburg Bypass. A permit must be issued consistently with the laws and regulations generally applicable to utility rights-of-way within National Park System units. It is subject to whatever terms and conditions the Secretary deems necessary. These include provisions for the protection and restoration of park resources disturbed by pipeline work.
plaw-107-224-2002:
A plaza beside Washington's performing arts center is authorized by the John F. Kennedy Center Plaza Authorization Act of 2002, Public Law 107-224, approved September 18, 2002. Amending the John F. Kennedy Center Act, it authorizes the Secretary of Transportation to carry out a project for construction of a plaza adjacent to the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts.

The new section 12 defines its terms. The plaza means improvements to the area surrounding the center building. It is comprised of transportation elements, including roadways, sidewalks, and bicycle lanes. It also has non-transportation elements, including landscaping, green space, open public space, and water, sewer, and utility connections. Air rights means real property interests conveyed by deed, lease, or permit for the use of space between streets and alleys within the project's boundaries. Green spaces are areas within or affected by the project that are covered by grass, trees, or other vegetation.
plaw-107-225-2002: Washington's Brentwood mail plant is renamed by Public Law 107-225, approved September 24, 2002. The facility of the United States Postal Service located at 900 Brentwood Road, NE, in Washington, D.C., and known as the Brentwood Processing and Distribution Center, shall be known and designated as the Joseph Curseen, Jr. and Thomas Morris, Jr. Processing and Distribution Center. Federal references to the facility are deemed references to the new name. The bill passed the House on September 4, 2002, and the Senate on September 5.
plaw-107-226-2002:
The Flight 93 crash site becomes a national memorial under the Flight 93 National Memorial Act, Public Law 107-226, approved September 24, 2002. The act authorizes a national memorial to commemorate the passengers and crew of Flight 93. On September 11, 2001, they courageously gave their lives, thereby thwarting a planned attack on the nation's capital.

Congress found that thousands had since visited the Flight 93 site, drawn by the heroic action and sacrifice of the passengers and crew. Many worried about the site's future, including grieving families, the region's people, its current stewards, and citizens across the country; many were forming the Flight 93 Task Force to voice those concerns. The findings call the site a profound symbol of American patriotism and spontaneous leadership of citizen-heroes. They conclude the crash site should be designated a unit of the National Park System.
plaw-107-227-2002: A Minnesota post office is named by Public Law 107-227, approved September 24, 2002. The facility of the United States Postal Service located at 6101 West Old Shakopee Road in Bloomington, Minnesota, shall be known and designated as the Thomas E. Burnett, Jr. Post Office Building. Federal references to that facility are deemed references to that name. The House passed the bill on September 4, 2002, and the Senate on September 5.
plaw-107-228-2002:
American diplomacy and security aid are authorized for a year by the Foreign Relations Authorization Act, Fiscal Year 2003, Public Law 107-228, approved September 30, 2002. The act authorizes appropriations for the Department of State for fiscal year 2003. It also authorizes funds under the Arms Export Control Act and the Foreign Assistance Act of 1961 for security assistance for the same year.

The act is organized into two divisions. Division A is the Department of State Authorization Act, Fiscal Year 2003, whose first title of authorizations covers the administration of foreign affairs and United States educational, cultural, and public diplomacy programs. Division B is the Security Assistance Act of 2002, carrying the arms export and foreign assistance side of the package. Opening sections give the act its short title, lay out the division structure and a long table of contents, and set definitions for the terms used across both divisions.
plaw-107-229-2002: Fiscal year 2003 begins on borrowed time under Public Law 107-229, a joint resolution approved September 30, 2002, making continuing appropriations for the year. Until regular bills are enacted, it appropriates such amounts as may be necessary to continue fiscal 2002 projects and activities. The rate may not exceed the current rate. The spending follows the authority and conditions of the fiscal 2002 appropriations acts. Section 101 lists those acts, from Agriculture through Defense, Foreign Operations, Interior, and Labor, Health and Human Services, and Education.
plaw-107-230-2002:
New York's transportation planners, their offices and resources destroyed by acts of terrorism, get breathing room from Public Law 107-230, approved October 1, 2002. The act provides a temporary waiver from certain transportation conformity requirements and metropolitan transportation planning requirements under the Clean Air Act and other laws for certain areas in New York.

Until September 30, 2005, the conformity provisions of section 176(c) of the Clean Air Act do not apply to transportation projects, programs, and plans in the New York City area counties. The covered counties are New York, Queens, Kings, Bronx, Richmond, Nassau, Suffolk, Westchester, Rockland, and Putnam, plus seven named Orange County towns. Interagency consultation procedures remain in force, though. By January 1, 2004, the Governor of New York must submit an interim progress report to the House and Senate committees, the EPA Administrator, and the Secretary of Transportation. The report details steps taken toward compliance, steps remaining, and a regional emissions analysis.
plaw-107-231-2002:
Building failures gain a federal investigative team under the National Construction Safety Team Act, Public Law 107-231, signed October 1, 2002. The act creates investigative teams to assess building performance and emergency response and evacuation procedures after building failures. The failure must have caused heavy loss of life, or posed a serious potential of it.

The Director of the National Institute of Standards and Technology may establish a National Construction Safety Team for such an event. To the maximum extent practicable, the team deploys within 48 hours. Notice of the team is published in the Federal Register. The purpose of a team's work is to improve the safety and structural integrity of buildings nationwide. Its duties: establish the likely technical cause of the failure, judge the technical aspects of escape and emergency response. It must recommend improvements to building standards, codes, and practices. It must also recommend research to improve structural safety.
plaw-107-232-2002: Growing suburbs keep transit flexibility under Public Law 107-232, approved October 1, 2002, amending section 5307 of title 49. A special rule for fiscal year 2003 lets the Secretary make urbanized area formula grants to finance operating costs of mass transportation equipment and facilities. The grants go to areas that first exceeded 200,000 people in the 2000 census after falling below that mark in 1990, or not being designated at all. Amounts are capped at the area's fiscal year 2002 apportionment, or, for newly designated areas, its fiscal year 2003 apportionment.
plaw-107-233-2002: An orbiting deadline moves in Public Law 107-233, approved October 1, 2002, which amends the Communications Satellite Act of 1962 to extend the deadline for the INTELSAT initial public offering. In section 621(5)(A)(i) of that act, October 1, 2001, is struck and December 31, 2003, inserted, and December 31, 2002, is struck and June 30, 2004, inserted. The Senate passed the bill on July 26, 2002, and the House on September 10.
plaw-107-234-2002: An exchange program tied to Northern Ireland runs longer under Public Law 107-234, approved October 4, 2002, which extends the Irish Peace Process Cultural and Training Program. The act amends the Irish Peace Process Cultural and Training Program Act of 1998 in four places. Two figures of 3 are struck and 4 inserted, in the program's duration provisions. And two references to 2005 become 2006, in its closing dates. The House passed the bill on July 22, 2002, and the Senate on September 18.
plaw-107-235-2002: The stopgap stretches by days in Public Law 107-235, a joint resolution approved October 4, 2002, making further continuing appropriations for the fiscal year 2003. Its single sentence amends Public Law 107-229 by striking the date specified in section 107(c) of that resolution and inserting in lieu thereof October 11, 2002. The House and Senate both considered and passed the resolution on October 3, 2002, one day before it was approved.
plaw-107-236-2002: A California recreation area gets a new map in the Santa Monica Mountains National Recreation Area Boundary Adjustment Act, Public Law 107-236, signed October 9, 2002. It amends the National Parks and Recreation Act of 1978. It replaces the boundary map named there, dated May 1978, with a boundary map numbered 80,047-C and dated August 2001. Lands within the Wildlife Corridor Expansion Zone may be acquired only by donation or with donated funds, and a closing section makes technical corrections to the 1978 statute.
plaw-107-237-2002: Four Oregon river basins may be studied for better water use under Public Law 107-237, signed October 11, 2002. The law is the Burnt, Malheur, Owyhee, and Powder River Basin Water Optimization Feasibility Study Act of 2002. The act authorizes the Secretary of the Interior to conduct feasibility studies on water optimization in four basins. They are the Burnt River basin, Malheur River basin, Owyhee River basin, and Powder River basin, all in Oregon. It also authorizes to be appropriated such sums as are necessary to carry out the act.
plaw-107-238-2002: A headquarters property joins a Mississippi battlefield park under the Vicksburg National Military Park Boundary Modification Act of 2002, Public Law 107-238, approved October 11, 2002. The boundary of the park is modified to include the property known as Pemberton's Headquarters, as shown on an August 2001 map on file with the National Park Service. The Secretary of the Interior may acquire the property, and up to one acre nearby for parking, only with each owner's consent, by purchase, donation, or exchange. The Secretary administers it as part of the park.
plaw-107-239-2002:
Public Law 107-239, approved October 11, 2002, ratifies an agreement between The Aleut Corporation and the United States. The agreement exchanges land rights received under the Alaska Native Claims Settlement Act for certain land interests on Adak Island.

The findings describe Adak as an island 1,200 miles southwest of Anchorage, between the Pacific Ocean and the Bering Sea, with a deep-water harbor and abundant wildlife. Reserved as a preserve in 1913, portions were withdrawn for military purposes from 1901 onward, culminating in the 1959 withdrawal of about half the island for the Navy. By 1990 the base supported a community of 6,000 residents, but the Adak Naval Complex has since closed under the 1990 base closure act. The Aleut Corporation is the Alaska Native regional corporation for the Aleutian Islands' indigenous people, and none of Adak had been available for it to select under the settlement act.
plaw-107-240-2002:
A third stopgap for fiscal 2003 arrives as Public Law 107-240, approved October 11, 2002, headed Third Continuing Appropriations, Fiscal Year 2003. It works by amending Public Law 107-229, striking the date in section 107(c) and inserting October 18, 2002.

The resolution does more than move the date. Section 2 trims a clause from the original's section 101(2). Section 3 strikes a subsection of the 21st Century Department of Justice Appropriations Authorization Act. The strike is effective as if included in that act at enactment. Section 4 rewrites section 117 around government printing. It finds the law requires government printing, binding, and blankbook work to be done at the Government Printing Office. It bars any funds from implementing a May 2002 Office of Management and Budget memorandum on procuring printing elsewhere. It also bars funds from paying to print the federal budget anywhere else.
plaw-107-241-2002: A veterans group modernizes its charter in Public Law 107-241, approved October 16, 2002, amending the AMVETS charter in title 36. The name AMVETS (American Veterans of World War II, Korea, and Vietnam) becomes AMVETS (American Veterans), in the chapter heading as well. The governing body is recast. Seven national vice commanders and the officers listed after them give way to two national vice commanders, a finance officer, and a judge advocate. A chaplain and six national district commanders complete the body. Headquarters moves from the District of Columbia to Maryland.
plaw-107-242-2002: More service members can join the VFW under Public Law 107-242, approved October 16, 2002, which amends the charter of the Veterans of Foreign Wars of the United States organization. It adds a membership category to section 230103 of title 36. The new category covers an individual who served in an area entitling the individual to special pay for duty subject to hostile fire or imminent danger under section 310 of title 37. The act also clarifies the corporation's purposes, inserting the word charitable before educational in the purposes section of the charter.
plaw-107-243-2002:
Public Law 107-243 is the Authorization for Use of Military Force Against Iraq Resolution of 2002, passed by the 107th Congress and approved on October 16, 2002. It gave the President legal authority to use the United States Armed Forces against Iraq.

The resolution builds its case in a long set of findings. It says Iraq kept weapons of mass destruction, broke the cease-fire that ended the 1991 Gulf War, blocked weapons inspectors, and supported terrorism. On that basis it authorizes the President to use force to defend United States security and enforce United Nations resolutions on Iraq. It became the legal basis for the 2003 invasion.
plaw-107-244-2002: Approved on October 18, 2002, Public Law 107-244 is a short joint resolution that kept the federal government funded early in fiscal year 2003. It does only one thing: it amends the earlier continuing appropriations law, Public Law 107-229, by moving the deadline in section 107(c) to November 22, 2002. Measures like this buy Congress time to finish regular spending bills without a shutdown.
plaw-107-245-2002:
The Sudan Peace Act, Public Law 107-245, was approved on October 21, 2002, during the long civil war between Sudan's government and the south. Congress wrote it to push for a negotiated end to the war and to support famine relief across the country.

Its findings say the war had cost more than two million lives and displaced more than four million people. The act backs an internationally sponsored peace process, stronger humanitarian relief, and continued United States leadership. It also says areas outside the government's control need real civil institutions if peace is to last and people are to support themselves.
plaw-107-246-2002:
Passed by the 107th Congress in 2002, the Russian Democracy Act (Public Law 107-246) made Foreign Assistance Act money available to support democracy inside the Russian Federation. Its stated goals were good governance, anti-corruption programs, civil society, and independent media in that country.

The findings note that after the Soviet Union fell, Russia's leaders promised democratic institutions, human rights, press freedom, and a market economy under the rule of law. The act treats United States aid as a way to help that change along. It channels support toward the programs building those institutions on the ground.
plaw-107-247-2002:
Public Law 107-247, the Veterans' Compensation Cost-of-Living Adjustment Act of 2002, raised the monthly payments the government makes to veterans hurt in service. It also raised dependency and indemnity compensation, the payments made to survivors of certain disabled veterans.

The amounts come from sections of title 38 of the United States Code, the title covering veterans' benefits. The increase took effect on December 1, 2002. The Secretary of Veterans Affairs was directed to raise the set dollar amounts for disability compensation, extra amounts for dependents, and the clothing allowance. Laws like this one are passed most years to keep veterans' benefits in step with rising prices.
plaw-107-248-2002:
The Department of Defense Appropriations Act, 2003 (Public Law 107-248) is the law that funded the United States military for the fiscal year ending September 30, 2003. Congress approved it on October 23, 2002, while the armed forces were fighting in Afghanistan.

Title I covers military personnel, paying for the pay, allowances, clothing, food, and travel of soldiers, sailors, airmen, and Marines. For Army personnel alone the act provides nearly twenty-seven billion dollars, with separate sums for each service and for the military retirement fund. Later titles fund operations, weapons buying, and research across the department.
plaw-107-249-2002:
Public Law 107-249, the Military Construction Appropriation Act, 2003, paid for building work at military bases for the fiscal year ending September 30, 2003. It also covered family housing for service members and the costs of closing or realigning bases.

For Army construction the act provides more than one and a half billion dollars, covering new buildings, facilities, and real property, with money set aside for planning and design. It also takes back about forty-nine million dollars left over from earlier construction acts. Similar sections fund Navy and other Defense Department building projects.
plaw-107-250-2002:
The Medical Device User Fee and Modernization Act of 2002 (Public Law 107-250) changed how the federal government regulates medical devices. It amends the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act, the main law behind Food and Drug Administration oversight of devices.

Title I sets up a user fee program, so device makers help pay for the review of their products, with yearly reports and checks on devices after they reach the market. Title II lets trained outside experts inspect factories and review some devices. It also covers combined drug-and-device products, electronic labels, and electronic registration.
plaw-107-251-2002:
Public Law 107-251, the Health Care Safety Net Amendments of 2002, renewed and strengthened the community health centers program and the National Health Service Corps. Both programs bring basic medical care to places and people that private practice often misses.

The act also creates the Healthy Communities Access Program to help coordinate care for people with no insurance or too little of it. Its titles support rural health networks, telehealth grants that link distant patients to doctors, mental health services by telehealth, and training and equipment for rural emergency medical services. Together they form much of what health workers call the safety net.
plaw-107-252-2002:
The Help America Vote Act of 2002 (Public Law 107-252) was Congress's answer to the troubled 2000 presidential election. It set out to fix how federal elections are run in every state, from the machines voters use to the officials who oversee them.

The act pays states to replace punch card and lever voting machines and to improve election administration. It creates the Election Assistance Commission to help with federal elections and sets minimum standards that states and local governments must meet. It remains the main federal election reform law of that era.
plaw-107-253-2002:
Public Law 107-253, the Inland Flood Forecasting and Warning System Act of 2002, told the nation's weather agency to get better at predicting floods away from the coast. It works through the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration and its United States Weather Research Program.

The law calls for better flood research and computer models, and a new flood warning index that tells the public and emergency managers more clearly how dangerous an expected flood is. It also requires training for forecasters and emergency officials, plus study of long-term flood trends and how climate and building change a region's risk.
plaw-107-254-2002: Public Law 107-254 is a one-section fix from October 2002 about the Navy-Marine Corps Intranet, the two services' big shared computer network contract. Normally such a base contract could run no more than five years. This law lets that one contract run longer than five years but no more than seven, by amending the defense authorization law that first set the limit.
plaw-107-255-2002:
Public Law 107-255 is a joint resolution from October 2002 honoring Patsy Takemoto Mink, the longtime congresswoman from Hawaii. Congress passed it soon after her death to recognize what she had done for women's rights, civil rights, and working families.

The resolution notes that Mink, elected in 1964, was one of the first women of color to win national office. It credits her work on women's health, children, students, and working families. Its one legal act renames Title IX, the 1972 law against sex discrimination in education, as the Patsy Takemoto Mink Equal Opportunity in Education Act.
plaw-107-256-2002: The Niagara Falls National Heritage Area Study Act (Public Law 107-256) ordered a study, not a park. It directed the Secretary of the Interior to examine lands in Niagara County, New York, along the Niagara River. It asks whether a Niagara Falls National Heritage Area would be suitable and workable. The study weighs the area's natural, historic, scenic, and cultural resources and whether local partnerships could manage them.
plaw-107-257-2002: Public Law 107-257 gives a name to a federal courthouse that had not been built yet. It says the United States courthouse to be built at 8th Avenue and Mill Street in Eugene, Oregon, will be known as the Wayne Lyman Morse United States Courthouse. Morse was Oregon's longtime United States senator. Any official reference to that courthouse now means the name this law gave it.
plaw-107-258-2002:
The Persian Gulf War POW/MIA Accountability Act of 2002 (Public Law 107-258) deals with American service members still missing from the 1991 Gulf War. It amends the Bring Them Home Alive Act of 2000, an earlier law about bringing missing Americans home.

The act creates an asylum program with a clear bargain. A citizen of Iraq or another Middle East country who personally delivers a living American Gulf War prisoner or missing service member into United States custody gets refugee status here. The rescuer's parents, spouse, and children qualify too, though terrorists and persecutors are shut out.
plaw-107-259-2002: Public Law 107-259 writes specific highways into the Ports-to-Plains Corridor, a high priority route on the National Highway System. The added stretches run through Texas, Oklahoma, Colorado, and New Mexico, following United States Routes 287 and 87. They include the run from Dumas, Texas, toward the Oklahoma and New Mexico borders, then north through Oklahoma and Colorado to Limon. Corridor status matters when federal highway money is handed out.
plaw-107-260-2002:
The Benign Brain Tumor Cancer Registries Amendment Act (Public Law 107-260) changed what the national cancer registry program counts. Until then, the statewide registries run under the Public Health Service Act focused on cancer itself, collecting data state by state.

The amendment adds benign, meaning noncancerous, brain-related tumors as a category of data the registries must collect, alongside each form of invasive cancer. Tracking tumors that are not cancer still matters, because growths in the brain can harm people even when they never spread. The change gives researchers and doctors a fuller picture of brain tumor cases nationwide.
plaw-107-261-2002: One of several postal namings approved on October 30, 2002, Public Law 107-261 renames the Postal Service facility at 127 Social Street in Woonsocket, Rhode Island. From then on it is the Alphonse F. Auclair Post Office Building, and every federal law, map, and record must use that name for the building. The act has two sections, one for the name and one for later references.
plaw-107-262-2002: Public Law 107-262 does a single thing: it names the United States Postal Service facility at 7 Commercial Street in Newport, Rhode Island, the Bruce F. Cotta Post Office Building. Congress approved it in October 2002, and all official federal references to that facility now use the Cotta name instead. It runs to two sections in all.
plaw-107-263-2002: With Public Law 107-263, Congress gave the post office at 89 River Street in Hoboken, New Jersey, a famous local name: the Frank Sinatra Post Office Building. Sinatra was born in Hoboken, and the redesignation took effect in October 2002. Federal maps and records now refer to the building by the singer's name.
plaw-107-264-2002: Public Law 107-264 names the Postal Service facility at 1299 North 7th Street in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, the Herbert Arlene Post Office Building. It was approved on October 30, 2002. Under the law, any mention of that facility in a federal law, map, regulation, or record counts as a mention of the Herbert Arlene building.
plaw-107-265-2002: Approved October 30, 2002, Public Law 107-265 designates the post office at 6150 North Broad Street in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, as the Rev. Leon Sullivan Post Office Building. Sullivan was a Philadelphia pastor and civil rights leader. The law orders that every official federal reference to the facility use his name. The whole act runs to just two short sections.
plaw-107-266-2002: Public Law 107-266 names the Postal Service facility at 925 Dickinson Street in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, the William A. Cibotti Post Office Building. Approved on October 30, 2002, it directs that every reference to that facility in federal laws, maps, and records use the Cibotti name. Naming laws like this change no postal operations; they only fix the name a community knows its post office by.
plaw-107-267-2002: In Fallon, Nevada, the post office at 120 North Maine Street became the Rollan D. Melton Post Office Building under Public Law 107-267. Congress approved the naming in October 2002, and federal records must call the facility by that name from then on. The act runs to just two sections, one making the designation and one covering later references to it.
plaw-107-268-2002: Public Law 107-268 designates the Postal Service facility at 1199 Pasadena Boulevard in Pasadena, Texas, as the Jim Fonteno Post Office Building. The law, approved in October 2002, makes the Fonteno name the one used in all official federal references to the building. It is a two-section law: the first sets the designation, the second makes the name stick in later records.
plaw-107-269-2002: For the facility at 204 South Broad Street in Lancaster, Ohio, Public Law 107-269 sets the official name: the Clarence Miller Post Office Building. The designation was approved on October 30, 2002, and it binds how federal laws, maps, and records refer to that post office. Nothing about mail service changes under the law; only the facility's official name is new.
plaw-107-270-2002: Oceanside, California's post office at 1895 Avenida Del Oro took a new name under Public Law 107-270: the Ronald C. Packard Post Office Building. Packard had represented the area in Congress. The October 2002 law makes his name the facility's official one in federal records. The short act contains only the designation itself and a rule that later references mean the new name.
plaw-107-271-2002:
Public Law 107-271 redesignates the post office at 265 South Western Avenue in Los Angeles, California, as the Nat King Cole Post Office. Before the naming section, Congress filled the act with findings about Cole's life, which is unusual for a postal law.

The findings say Cole was born Nathaniel Adams Coles in Montgomery, Alabama, raised in poverty on Chicago's south side, and met racism through his career, including a 1956 stage attack in Birmingham. They call him the best selling African-American recording artist of his generation and recall that his television show was the first hosted by an African-American artist.
plaw-107-272-2002: Under Public Law 107-272, the post office at 6910 South Yorktown Avenue in Tulsa, Oklahoma, was redesignated the Robert Wayne Jenkins Station. Congress approved the change in October 2002. From then on, laws, maps, and other federal records refer to the facility by the Jenkins name. The law itself is brief, holding only the redesignation and a references section to make it stick.
plaw-107-273-2002:
Public Law 107-273, the 21st Century Department of Justice Appropriations Authorization Act, set the approved funding levels for the Department of Justice for fiscal years 2002 and 2003. Authorization laws like this one set policy and spending ceilings; separate spending laws hand over the actual money.

Beyond the sums, the act authorizes more assistant United States attorneys, including some for Project Safe Neighborhoods, a program aimed at gun crime. It also makes some Justice Department authorities permanent and adds oversight aimed at waste, fraud, and abuse inside the department. Its opening division pairs the funding tables with those lasting changes.
plaw-107-274-2002:
The Border Commuter Student Act of 2002 (Public Law 107-274) created a new kind of student status in immigration law. It was written for Canadians and Mexicans who live at home across the border but study at schools in the United States.

The act adds a commuter category to both the academic student class and the vocational student class in the Immigration and Nationality Act. A commuter student must keep an actual home in Canada or Mexico and travel to an American school, and unlike regular foreign students may study part time. Before this law, border students had no category that fit daily commuting.
plaw-107-275-2002: Black lung benefits for coal miners were once split between two agencies. Public Law 107-275 has a long name: the Black Lung Consolidation of Administrative Responsibility Act. It moved the Part B benefit duties under the Black Lung Benefits Act. They went from the Commissioner of Social Security to the Secretary of Labor. One official now runs the whole program, which is the point of the act's long name.
plaw-107-276-2002: Public Law 107-276 trims paperwork for state and local political groups under section 527 of the tax code. It frees state and local party committees and candidate committees from having to notify the tax authorities that they exist as section 527 organizations. It also stops committees from reporting the same information twice when state law already requires them to report it publicly.
plaw-107-277-2002:
The Enterprise Integration Act of 2002 (Public Law 107-277) put the National Institute of Standards and Technology to work with American manufacturers on shared electronic standards. The goal was supply chains that connect by computer, from small parts shops to the big companies they supply.

Congress found that more than ninety percent of United States companies in manufacturing are small or medium sized, and most make parts that end up in large companies' products. It also found Europe and Asia investing heavily in the same standards, which could leave American firms behind. The act authorizes the standards institute to lead a national effort to close that gap.
plaw-107-278-2002: Public Law 107-278 is a single short section with a narrow job. It amends the International Organizations Immunities Act so that law can be extended to the European Central Bank, the central bank for Europe's shared currency. The bank can now receive the same privileges and immunities the law gives to other international organizations the United States deals with.
plaw-107-279-2002:
Public Law 107-279, the Education Sciences Reform Act of 2002, rebuilt how the federal government studies education. It covers federal research, statistics, evaluation, and the sharing of results, all meant to rest on stronger evidence than before.

The centerpiece is a new Institute of Education Sciences inside the Education Department, led by a director and advised by a National Board for Education Sciences. The act also sets up national centers for education research and for education statistics, each with its own commissioner. Research funded under the act must meet set standards for how studies are run and judged.
plaw-107-280-2002:
The Rare Diseases Act of 2002 (Public Law 107-280) set up an Office of Rare Diseases at the National Institutes of Health. Rare diseases are those affecting fewer than two hundred thousand people in the United States each, so single conditions can be easy to overlook.

Congress found more than six thousand such diseases, together affecting about twenty-five million Americans, including Huntington's disease, Lou Gehrig's disease, and cystic fibrosis. Because each patient group is small, drug companies long ignored these conditions and their medicines were called orphan drugs. The new office was meant to focus federal research attention on them.
plaw-107-281-2002:
Public Law 107-281, the Rare Diseases Orphan Product Development Act of 2002, is the companion to the Rare Diseases Act passed the same day. It amends the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act to push development of products for rare diseases.

Its findings repeat the problem. More than six thousand rare diseases affect about twenty-five million Americans. Yet drug makers rarely profit from medicines for such small groups. So treatments stayed unmade, and they earned the name orphan drugs. Where its sister act built a research office, this one works through the food and drug law to spur companies to develop treatments.
plaw-107-282-2002:
The Clark County Conservation of Public Land and Natural Resources Act of 2002 (Public Law 107-282) is a wide-ranging lands law for Clark County, Nevada. It tries to protect wild country in the county while still leaving room for careful, high quality development there.

Title I redraws the boundary of the Red Rock Canyon National Conservation Area and sets up a land exchange there. Title II adds land to the National Wilderness Preservation System, the strongest protection federal land can get. The act pairs those protections with rules for managing nearby land and for military flights overhead.
plaw-107-283-2002: Public Law 107-283 names the Postal Service facility at 301 South Howes Street in Fort Collins, Colorado, the Barney Apodaca Post Office. Approved on November 6, 2002, the law requires federal laws, maps, and records to call that facility by the Apodaca name. The act has the standard two parts: a designation section and a references section covering later mentions.
plaw-107-284-2002: The post office at 4 East Central Street in Worcester, Massachusetts, became the Joseph D. Early Post Office Building under Public Law 107-284. Early was a longtime Massachusetts congressman. The designation, approved on November 6, 2002, fixes the name for all official federal uses. As with the other namings of that session, the law changes the name only, not the service inside.
plaw-107-285-2002: Public Law 107-285 designates the facility at 380 Main Street in Farmingdale, New York, as the Peter J. Ganci, Jr. Post Office Building. Ganci was the New York City fire department's chief of department, killed in the September 11, 2001 attacks. The naming was approved on November 6, 2002. The act follows the usual pattern, pairing the designation with a rule for later federal references.
plaw-107-286-2002: In Encino, California, Public Law 107-286 names the post office at 5805 White Oak Avenue the Francis Dayle 'Chick' Hearn Post Office. Hearn was the beloved longtime broadcaster of the Los Angeles Lakers. Congress approved the honor on November 6, 2002, months after his death. The two-section act pairs the designation with a references rule so the name holds everywhere.
plaw-107-287-2002:
The Department of Veterans Affairs Emergency Preparedness Act of 2002 (Public Law 107-287) made the veterans' hospital system part of the country's emergency planning. It was passed a year after the September 2001 attacks, when preparing for mass-casualty events had become urgent.

The act orders the Secretary to open four medical emergency preparedness centers at VA medical centers, staffed by department employees and watched over by the Under Secretary for Health. The centers' work is judged on an ongoing basis. The wider aim is that VA hospitals, spread across the country, can help in a national emergency.
plaw-107-288-2002:
The Jobs for Veterans Act (Public Law 107-288) revised the job help the federal government gives to veterans. It amends title 38, the veterans' benefits title, to improve employment, training, and placement services for people who have left military service.

Its best-known rule is priority of service: veterans come first in Department of Labor job training programs. The priority also reaches certain spouses, including widows and widowers of veterans who died of service-connected disabilities. The act spells out who counts as a covered person and rewrites the chapter of law on veterans' employment programs.
plaw-107-289-2002:
The Accountability of Tax Dollars Act of 2002 (Public Law 107-289) widened which federal agencies must produce audited financial statements each year. It amends title 31 of the United States Code, the title covering money and finance.

Before this law, only a listed set of large executive agencies faced the audit requirement. The act swaps in a broader class of covered executive agencies, so more of the government must open its books to outside auditors. The budget director may excuse a small agency, one with no more than twenty-five million dollars in budget authority, when an audit is not warranted by the risks of its work.
plaw-107-290-2002: Public Law 107-290 is a narrow fix for retired Washington, D.C. police officers. Federal benefit payments to certain Metropolitan Police retirees include a service longevity part that is hard to compute exactly for people who retired between 1972 and 2001. The act lets the Secretary of the Treasury use estimated amounts for that part instead, and pay benefits based on the estimates.
plaw-107-291-2002: Public Law 107-291 designates the post office at 206 South Main Street in Glennville, Georgia, as the Michael Lee Woodcock Post Office. The naming was approved on November 7, 2002. Like the other postal laws of that fall, it pairs the designation with a rule that later federal references use the new name. The act itself is brief.
plaw-107-292-2002:
Public Law 107-292 is the Native American Housing Assistance and Self-Determination Reauthorization Act of 2002. It kept the 1996 housing law for Native American communities running for more years, extending its programs through fiscal year 2007.

Section by section, the act extends the dates for Indian housing block grants, federal guarantees for housing finance, and training and technical assistance. It does the same for the Indian housing loan guarantee fund. The pattern matters: tribes plan housing years ahead, and the reauthorization gave those programs a firm horizon instead of a looming cutoff. The 1996 act it renews is known by its initials, NAHASDA.
plaw-107-293-2002:
Public Law 107-293, passed in November 2002, reaffirms the words one Nation under God in the Pledge of Allegiance. Congress acted months after a federal appeals court had ruled the phrase unconstitutional in public schools, a decision that set off a national argument.

Most of the act is findings, a march through American history meant to show faith's place in public life. It quotes the Mayflower Compact, the Declaration of Independence, Jefferson's Notes on the State of Virginia, and Washington at the Constitutional Convention. The findings build Congress's case that the phrase belongs in the pledge.
plaw-107-294-2002: Public Law 107-294 is another stopgap: a joint resolution keeping the government funded into fiscal year 2003. It moves the deadline in the earlier continuing appropriations law to January 11, 2003. It also lets the new Secretary of Homeland Security shift up to five hundred million dollars inside the young department. The money must go to higher priority needs, with notice to Congress. The budget office may also move money to pay the department's startup costs.
plaw-107-295-2002:
The Maritime Transportation Security Act of 2002 (Public Law 107-295) was the seaport answer to the September 2001 attacks. It amends the Merchant Marine Act of 1936 to build a security program for United States ports and shipping.

Its first title covers port security, identification for international seafarers, and Coast Guard personnel assigned as sea marshals. It extends the Coast Guard's seaward reach, lifts limits on Coast Guard strength, and sets performance standards for security work. It also orders reports, including one on foreign-flag vessels calling at American ports each year. The act was the ports' counterpart to the airport security law of the year before.
plaw-107-296-2002:
The Homeland Security Act of 2002 (Public Law 107-296) created the Department of Homeland Security, the largest new federal department in decades. Congress passed it in November 2002, a little over a year after the September 2001 terrorist attacks.

Title I establishes the department, its mission, and its secretary. Title II builds a directorate for information analysis and infrastructure protection, with rules for handling sensitive information that companies share voluntarily. The act pulled many existing agencies and duties under one roof so that intelligence, border, transport, and emergency work could be coordinated. The new department began work in the spring of 2003.
plaw-107-297-2002:
Public Law 107-297, the Terrorism Risk Insurance Act of 2002, was written to keep terrorism insurance available after the September 2001 attacks. Insurers, facing losses they could not predict, had begun dropping terrorism coverage from commercial policies.

Title I creates a federal Terrorism Insurance Program that shares the cost of insured losses from a certified terrorist act. The act wipes out some policy exclusions written before it passed and manages the lawsuits that follow an attack. Other titles let victims satisfy court judgments from blocked terrorist assets and adjust Federal Reserve authority. Its table of contents even lists the program's termination, since the help was meant to be temporary.
plaw-107-298-2002: Public Law 107-298, the Real Interstate Driver Equity Act of 2002, stops states from double-charging interstate limousine and car services. It bars any state or local government from demanding a license or fee just because a vehicle provides pre-arranged ground transportation across state lines. The protection covers carriers that meet federal registration requirements and the rules of their home state. In practice it shields airport and business car services booked ahead of time.
plaw-107-299-2002: Public Law 107-299 reauthorizes the National Sea Grant College Program, the network that pairs universities with the federal oceans agency for coastal research and outreach. The amendments require a strategic plan at least every four years, built with the sea grant colleges and institutes. They also stress strong collaboration between government scientists and university scientists, and tie the program's plans to those of the Commerce Department.
plaw-107-300-2002:
The Improper Payments Information Act of 2002 (Public Law 107-300) attacked a quiet problem: federal agencies paying out money wrongly, to the wrong people or in the wrong amounts. It requires every agency to measure the problem instead of guessing at it.

Agency heads must review all their programs each year, flag the ones open to significant improper payments, and estimate how much money goes out wrongly. They report those estimates to Congress by March 31, using one shared method set by the budget office. They must also report what they are doing to bring the error rate down.
plaw-107-301-2002: Public Law 107-301 cleared the way for a Boys and Girls Club in Springfield, Missouri. In 1955 the United States gave part of the former O'Reilly General Hospital land to Missouri but kept a reversionary interest, a right to take the land back. This act orders the General Services Administrator to release that interest for free, so the local club can use the property without the old string attached.
plaw-107-302-2002: Public Law 107-302 lets Washington, D.C.'s Court Services and Offender Supervision Agency arrange supervision across state lines. The agency can arrange for D.C. offenders on parole, probation, or supervised release who want to live elsewhere to be supervised there. It can also arrange supervision inside the District for offenders from other jurisdictions who want to live in Washington.
plaw-107-303-2002:
The Great Lakes and Lake Champlain Act of 2002 (Public Law 107-303) amends the federal clean water law to attack polluted mud at the bottom of the Great Lakes. It authorizes the Environmental Protection Agency to run cleanup projects and research in the lakes' areas of concern.

Title I orders reports on remedial action plans and funds the cleanup of contaminated sediment, alongside a research program. Title II covers the Lake Champlain Basin Program, for the lake between New York and Vermont. A final title handles storm water rules and other water business, including a freight project study for New York harbor.
plaw-107-304-2002: Public Law 107-304 does two unrelated jobs. First, it lets federal workers age fifty or over make extra catch-up contributions to the Thrift Savings Plan, the government's retirement savings plan, beyond the normal limits. Second, it reauthorizes two watchdog offices: the Merit Systems Protection Board, which hears federal employee appeals, and the Office of Special Counsel, which protects whistleblowers.
plaw-107-305-2002:
The Cyber Security Research and Development Act (Public Law 107-305) authorized federal money for computer and network security research. Congress passed it in November 2002, as government and business systems were knitting together into one vast network.

The findings warn that power grids, pipelines, banks, water systems, and emergency services now ride on connected computers, so a failure can spread fast.
