A 1997 military information warfare exercise had already shown how exposed those systems were. The act funds research and fellowship programs meant to grow the country's thin bench of security experts. It is an early sign of how central computer security was becoming.
plaw-107-306-2002:
Public Law 107-306 is the Intelligence Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2003. It approves the money and rules for the intelligence work of the United States government for that year, from the Central Intelligence Agency to military intelligence programs.

Much of the money detail sits in a classified schedule of authorizations, which the public text does not print. The visible sections set personnel ceilings, fund the Community Management Account and the CIA retirement system, and add extra authorizations for the war on terrorism. The act also folds in reporting duties Congress wanted from the intelligence agencies.
plaw-107-307-2002: Public Law 107-307, the Product Packaging Protection Act of 2002, made a new kind of tampering a federal crime. It was already illegal to tamper with a product itself. This act also bans slipping an unauthorized writing into a consumer product or its container before sale, without the maker's, seller's, or distributor's consent. A first offense can bring up to a year in prison, and a repeat offense up to three years.
plaw-107-308-2002: Public Law 107-308 reauthorizes the North American Wetlands Conservation Act, the law that funds protection of wetlands and the habitat around them across the continent. The amendments mostly fine tune the original act's wording, including its findings and statement of purpose. Wetlands under the program matter most as resting and breeding ground for migratory birds moving between Canada, the United States, and Mexico.
plaw-107-309-2002: Public Law 107-309 may be the shortest fix in this set: it changes the American Legion's charter by adding two words. In title 36, the eligibility rule said a person must continue to serve honorably; the act inserts during or before that phrase. The small edit clarifies that honorable service during wartime, not only after joining, counts toward eligibility in the veterans' organization.
plaw-107-310-2002:
The Dam Safety and Security Act of 2002 (Public Law 107-310) reauthorized the national dam safety program. That program tracks the condition of the country's dams and helps states inspect them. It amends the National Dam Safety Program Act section by section.

Among its changes, the act refocuses the Interagency Committee on Dam Safety on coordination and information sharing among federal agencies under the Federal Guidelines for Dam Safety. Other sections adjust the national program itself. After the September 2001 attacks, dam safety also meant dam security, and the law's title joins the two concerns.
plaw-107-311-2002:
Public Law 107-311, the Armed Forces Domestic Security Act, closed a gap for abuse victims living on military bases. A protective order issued by a civilian court did not always carry clear force once the victim or the abuser stepped onto a military installation.

The act writes a new section into title 10. A civilian order of protection now has the same force and effect on a military installation as it has in the court that issued it. The Secretary of Defense must issue regulations carrying this out, written to support good order and discipline among service members and civilians on base.
plaw-107-312-2002: Public Law 107-312 is one sentence of budget housekeeping. Under the pay-as-you-go rules, Congress kept scorecards of how past tax and spending laws affected the deficit. This act orders the budget director to reduce all those preexisting PAYGO balances, for every fiscal year, to zero, wiping the old scorecards clean.
plaw-107-313-2002: The Mental Health Parity Reauthorization Act of 2002 (Public Law 107-313) kept a popular rule alive for one more year. Federal law required health plans to treat yearly and lifetime dollar limits on mental health benefits the same as limits on medical benefits. That parity rule was set to expire on December 31, 2002; this act moves the date to December 31, 2003 in both pension and health law.
plaw-107-314-2002:
The Bob Stump National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2003 (Public Law 107-314) is the annual defense policy law for that year. It authorizes spending for military activities, military construction, and defense work at the Department of Energy, and it sets how many people the armed forces may have.

The act is named for Representative Bob Stump of Arizona, and its findings honor him. They note he entered the Navy in 1943, just after his sixteenth birthday, and fought aboard the USS Lunga Point and USS Tulagi at Luzon, Iwo Jima, and Okinawa. He reached Congress in 1976 after eighteen years in Arizona's legislature.
plaw-107-315-2002: Public Law 107-315 answers a narrow question about a future memorial. An earlier law authorized a commemorative work in Washington, D.C. honoring former President John Adams. Memorials in the prime Area I zone near the National Mall are disapproved unless Congress approves the location by law. This joint resolution gives that approval for the Adams work, with a limitation spelled out in its second section.
plaw-107-316-2002:
Public Law 107-316 provides a federal grant to build a new community center in St. Paul, Minnesota, honoring Senator Paul Wellstone and his wife Sheila, who had died weeks earlier. The building is the Paul and Sheila Wellstone Center for Community Building.

The findings describe Wellstone as a tireless advocate for Minnesotans, especially new immigrants and the poor, and recall that the couple loved St. Paul and walked its neighborhoods. The center serves Neighborhood House, a settlement house founded in the late 1800s to help newly arrived Eastern European Jewish immigrants, whose old building no longer met the community's needs.
plaw-107-317-2002:
The Dot Kids Implementation and Efficiency Act of 2002 (Public Law 107-317) set out to build a safe corner of the Internet for children. It provides for a new second-level domain inside the United States country code domain, the kids space under .us.

Congress found the web a rich learning tool for children but also full of material harmful to them, with a significant share tied to pornography. The new domain was meant as a haven: material promoting positive experiences for children and families, screened so children would not stumble onto harmful content while using it.
plaw-107-318-2002:
Anton's Law (Public Law 107-318) is a child safety law about car seats. It orders improvements in the safety of child restraints in passenger motor vehicles, the seats and boosters that protect young riders.

Congress found that very few children between four and eight years old ride in the restraint right for their age. Children who outgrow a safety seat should use a belt-positioning booster seat until an adult belt fits properly, the findings say. Properly restrained children suffered less severe injuries in crashes than children who were not properly restrained.
plaw-107-319-2002: Public Law 107-319 settles where low-speed electric bicycles belong in federal law. It declares them consumer products under the Consumer Product Safety Act, so the Consumer Product Safety Commission, not motor vehicle regulators, sets their safety rules. The act defines the term tightly: a two or three wheeled vehicle with working pedals and a motor under 750 watts, topping out below twenty miles per hour on level pavement.
plaw-107-320-2002: Public Law 107-320 hands federal land to a Georgia county. It orders the Secretary of the Army to give Chatham County, by quitclaim deed and for free, about twelve acres on Hutchinson Island next to the Savannah Harbor Tide Gate. The land must stay in public ownership and be managed forever for public recreation, or be swapped for equal-value land held the same way. If it is misused, it reverts to the United States.
plaw-107-321-2002:
The Small Webcaster Settlement Act of 2002 (Public Law 107-321) amended the copyright law's statutory license for webcasting, the early business of streaming music over the Internet. It grew out of a fight over how much small webcasters should pay to play recorded music.

Congress found that many small webcasters had skipped the royalty panel proceeding that set rates in July 2002 and disliked the fee structure that came out of it. They wanted fees based on a percentage of revenue. Congress pressed the recording industry and the webcasters to negotiate, and this act gives legal room for the settlement they reached.
plaw-107-322-2002: Public Law 107-322 gives one power project more time. Federal law normally sets a deadline to start building a licensed hydroelectric project, and the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission project numbered 11437 in North Carolina needed longer. The act lets the Commission extend the start deadline by up to three extra two-year periods, at the builder's request.
plaw-107-323-2002: The POW/MIA Memorial Flag Act of 2002 (Public Law 107-323) requires the POW/MIA flag to fly at three Washington memorials. They are the World War II Memorial, the Korean War Veterans Memorial, and the Vietnam Veterans Memorial. The black flag honors prisoners of war and those missing in action. The act says it must be displayed on any day the United States flag is displayed at those sites.
plaw-107-324-2002: Public Law 107-324 gives federal land to a small Oregon town. It directs the Secretary of the Interior to convey about forty acres of Bureau of Land Management land to the city of Haines, Oregon, for free and as soon as practicable. The parcel is the one shown on a map dated May 9, 2002, drawn for this very transfer.
plaw-107-325-2002: The Old Spanish Trail Recognition Act of 2002 (Public Law 107-325) adds the Old Spanish Trail to the National Trails System as a National Historic Trail. The trail runs about two thousand seven hundred miles from Santa Fe, New Mexico, to Los Angeles, California, and served as a major trade route between 1829 and 1848. The act includes its branches, the Armijo Route, the Northern Route, the North Branch, and the Mojave Road.
plaw-107-326-2002: Public Law 107-326, the FHA Downpayment Simplification Act of 2002, tidies the rules for Federal Housing Administration mortgage insurance on single family homes. It rewrites section 203 of the National Housing Act, cutting old sentences about principal amounts, charges, and disclosure notices. The point, as the title says, is a simpler downpayment calculation for homebuyers using FHA loans.
plaw-107-327-2002:
The Afghanistan Freedom Support Act of 2002 (Public Law 107-327) was Congress's main Afghanistan aid law, passed a year after the Taliban fell. It authorizes economic and democratic development assistance for Afghanistan, and military assistance for Afghanistan and certain other countries.

Title I lays out the purposes of development aid and how it is coordinated, with a note of concern about opium producing areas. Title II covers military help, including support for security while Afghanistan was in transition, and lists which other countries and international organizations may receive it under the act.
plaw-107-328-2002: Public Law 107-328 is a one-sentence joint resolution setting Congress's own calendar. It states that the first regular session of the One Hundred Eighth Congress shall begin at noon on Tuesday, January 7, 2003. Resolutions like this one bridge the gap between the end of one Congress and the start of the next.
plaw-107-329-2002: Public Law 107-329 provides for a shared front door to two Utah attractions at the entrance to American Fork Canyon. The Forest Service's Pleasant Grove Ranger District office could no longer serve its purpose, and the Timpanogos Cave National Monument visitor center had burned in 1991, leaving a temporary structure. The act authorizes a land exchange in Highland, Utah, so one interagency building can house both offices and serve visitors better.
plaw-107-330-2002:
The Veterans Benefits Act of 2002 (Public Law 107-330) is a broad bill that amends title 38, the veterans' law. It touches pay for disabled veterans, pay for their survivors, pensions, school aid, home loans, burial honors, and life insurance.

Title I deals with pay itself. One part keeps CHAMPVA health cover for widows and widowers who remarry after age fifty-five. Another clears up extra monthly pay for women veterans who lost a breast to a service-connected harm. The act also improves how claims are run and how courts review them.
plaw-107-331-2002:
The Indian Financing Amendments Act of 2002 (Public Law 107-331) mainly improves the Indian loan guarantee and insurance program, which helps Native American borrowers get business credit. It amends the Indian Financing Act of 1974 to make that program work better.

Later titles do different work. Title II creates development trust funds for the Yankton Sioux Tribe and the Santee Sioux Tribe as equitable compensation, and settles their claims. Title III deals with an Oklahoma Native American cultural center and museum. Title IV covers moving electric power across Indian lands in Oklahoma. Each title helps a different Native community in a different way.
plaw-107-332-2002: The Homestead National Monument of America Additions Act (Public Law 107-332) lets the government grow a Nebraska monument to the homesteading era. It authorizes the Secretary of the Interior to buy named private parcels in Gage County, but only from willing sellers, and to accept named state-owned parcels by donation only. The added land follows a boundary map dated March 2000.
plaw-107-333-2002:
Public Law 107-333, the Guam War Claims Review Commission Act, created a five-member commission to look into war claims from Guam. Guam's people had suffered under Japanese occupation in World War II, and their claims for compensation had a long, tangled history.

The commission members are appointed by the Secretary of the Interior, chosen for backgrounds suited to the work. One seat is filled from names submitted by the Governor of Guam, tying the island's own leadership into the review. The panel's job is to study the claims and report, giving Congress a factual basis for any payment decision.
plaw-107-334-2002: The Mount Nebo Wilderness Boundary Adjustment Act (Public Law 107-334) redraws the edge of the Mount Nebo Wilderness in Utah. It takes several small parcels out of the wilderness boundary, each shown on the act's map. Monument Springs is about eight acres. Gardner Canyon is about one hundred seventy-eight acres. Birch Creek, Ingram Canyon, and the Willow North pieces are smaller still. Land removed from wilderness loses its strict protections.
plaw-107-335-2002: Public Law 107-335 is the Lease Lot Conveyance Act of 2002. It orders the sale of federal lease lots near the Elephant Butte and Caballo Reservoirs in New Mexico. The buyers are the people leasing the lots, and they pay fair market value. Congress found the sales would end federal payments and upkeep costs. They would also raise local tax revenue and give owners the security to build lasting improvements, adding jobs in the county.
plaw-107-336-2002: Public Law 107-336 lets the National Park of American Samoa grow a little. It authorizes the Secretary of the Interior to adjust the park's boundary to include certain portions of the islands of Ofu and Olosega, following a proposed boundary map. The park, created in 1988, protects rainforest and coral coast in the South Pacific territory.
plaw-107-337-2002:
The Buffalo Bayou National Heritage Area Study Act (Public Law 107-337) orders a National Park Service study of Buffalo Bayou in Houston, Texas, as a possible National Heritage Area. The bayou runs from Shepherd Drive in west Houston to the Turning Basin.

Congress found the bayou made a unique contribution to the cultural, political, and industrial development of the United States. It calls the waterway the first spine of modern industrial development in Texas and one of the first on the Gulf Coast. The bayou also played a significant role in the struggle for Texas independence.
plaw-107-338-2002: Public Law 107-338, the Metacomet-Monadnock-Mattabesett Trail Study Act of 2002, puts a New England footpath in line for national status. It designates the trail system running through western Massachusetts and central Connecticut for study for potential addition to the National Trails System. Study is the first step; only later acts can make a trail a full national scenic trail.
plaw-107-339-2002: The Fallon Rail Freight Loading Facility Transfer Act (Public Law 107-339) provides for the sale of federal land to the city of Fallon, Nevada. The property is about six acres inside the Newlands Reclamation Project, known as 380 North Taylor Street, the site of the town's rail freight loading facility. The Secretary of the Interior makes the conveyance under conditions the act sets out.
plaw-107-340-2002: Public Law 107-340 expands Pu'uhonua o Honaunau National Historical Park on the Big Island of Hawaii. It modifies the park's boundaries to include about two hundred thirty-eight acres more of land. The park protects a place of refuge where, in old Hawaii, people who broke sacred law could find safety, along with royal grounds nearby.
plaw-107-341-2002: Public Law 107-341 orders a study of the Waco Mammoth Site Area in Waco, Texas, for possible addition to the National Park System. The Secretary of the Interior, working with Texas, the city of Waco, and others, must judge the site's national significance and whether park status is suitable and feasible. The site holds the fossil remains of mammoths found where they died.
plaw-107-342-2002: Public Law 107-342 raises how much money Congress authorizes for the Vancouver National Historic Reserve in Washington State. It strikes the old figure of five million dollars and replaces it with fifteen million for development costs on capital projects under the reserve's cooperative management plan. The federal share may not exceed half of any project's total cost.
plaw-107-343-2002:
Public Law 107-343 directs the Secretary of the Interior to study Virginia Key Beach Park in Biscayne Bay, Florida, for possible inclusion in the National Park System. The study must weigh the site's national significance and whether park status is suitable and workable.

Virginia Key Beach carries a particular history: it was used for recreation by African Americans at a time when public beaches were segregated by law. That past is the heart of the site's claim to national importance, and the study applies the standard Park Service criteria to judge it.
plaw-107-344-2002: Public Law 107-344 lets the federal Bureau of Reclamation help build a wastewater recycling project in Washington State. It authorizes the Secretary of the Interior to take part in designing, planning, and building a project to reclaim and reuse wastewater in and around the Lakehaven Utility District, south of Seattle. The amendment slots the Lakehaven project into the existing reclamation water reuse law.
plaw-107-345-2002: Public Law 107-345 directs money from oil shale country toward cleaning it up. Money collected from mineral leasing on certain naval oil shale reserves may now be used to pay for environmental restoration, waste management, and environmental compliance on those reserves. The act lets the Secretary of the Interior spend up to one and a half million dollars of the receipts on studies and site work without a separate appropriation.
plaw-107-346-2002: The Virgin River Dinosaur Footprint Preserve Act (Public Law 107-346) protects fossil tracks in southern Utah. It authorizes a federal grant to the city of St. George of up to five hundred thousand dollars, or the land's fair market value if less, to buy up to ten acres holding rare dinosaur footprints. The city must meet preservation conditions set in the act to receive the grant.
plaw-107-347-2002:
The E-Government Act of 2002 (Public Law 107-347) pushed the federal government onto the Internet in a serious way. It established a Federal Chief Information Officer inside the Office of Management and Budget to manage and promote electronic government services.

Around that office, the act builds a broad framework requiring agencies to use Internet-based technology to improve citizen access to government information and services. It covers how agencies plan, fund, and measure their online work across the whole government, and it set the tone for the era of citizens dealing with Washington through websites.
plaw-107-348-2002: The Muscle Shoals National Heritage Area Study Act of 2002 (Public Law 107-348) orders a study of the Muscle Shoals area in Alabama. The question is whether it should become a National Heritage Area. The Secretary of the Interior works with state officers, history groups, and others on the study. It asks whether the area holds a set of resources unlike any other, worth national note.
plaw-107-349-2002: The Klamath Basin Emergency Operation and Maintenance Refund Act of 2002 (Public Law 107-349) cleaned up money from the Klamath water crisis of 2001. That year, irrigation water was cut off to protect fish. The act pays Klamath Project water districts for running and upkeep charges assessed for 2001 on the project's transferred works. It also refunds sums the Bureau of Reclamation collected that year for its reserved works.
plaw-107-350-2002: Public Law 107-350 gives Clark County, Nevada, federal land for a shooting range. Congress found that fast growth around Las Vegas had left traditional target shooting spots too close to homes for safety, and that shooters and police trainees needed one central place to practice. The act conveys public land in the county for a centralized shooting facility in the Las Vegas Valley.
plaw-107-351-2002: Public Law 107-351, the Lower Rio Grande Valley Water Resources Conservation and Improvement Act of 2002, adds more projects to a 2000 law about saving water in South Texas. It amends that act's project list to authorize additional conservation and improvement work for irrigation districts in the Lower Rio Grande Valley, including the United Irrigation District of Hidalgo County. In a dry border region, saving irrigation water is saving farms.
plaw-107-352-2002: Public Law 107-352 gives Congress's consent to changes in the New Hampshire-Vermont Interstate School Compact. That compact backs school districts that cross the Connecticut River between the two states. The amendment restates how an interstate district may take on debt for building projects. It may do so by majority vote at a district meeting. The vote is by secret ballot, after debate, and voters may reconsider it.
plaw-107-353-2002: The California Five Mile Regional Learning Center Transfer Act (Public Law 107-353) hands a Forest Service site to a school district. It directs the Secretary of Agriculture to convey the land and facilities of the Five Mile Regional Learning Center to the Clovis Unified School District in California. For center lands not conveyed, the act authorizes a new special use permit so the district's use can continue.
plaw-107-354-2002: Public Law 107-354 enlarges the George Washington Birthplace National Monument in Virginia. It revises the monument's boundaries to add about one hundred fifteen acres, as drawn on an October 2001 boundary map held by the National Park Service. The act then authorizes the Secretary of the Interior to acquire the land inside the new boundaries for the monument.
plaw-107-355-2002:
The Pipeline Safety Improvement Act of 2002 (Public Law 107-355) strengthened the federal rules for the pipelines that carry oil, gas, and other hazardous liquids across the country. It amends title 49 of the United States Code, the transportation title.

Its early sections tighten one-call notification programs, the call-before-you-dig systems meant to stop backhoes from rupturing buried lines, by setting minimum standards that include government operators. The act's wider subject is the security and safety of pipelines after the September 2001 attacks, when the nation's energy infrastructure looked newly exposed to attack.
plaw-107-356-2002: The New River Gorge Boundary Act of 2002 (Public Law 107-356) updates the map that defines the New River Gorge National River in West Virginia. It swaps the old 1996 boundary map for a May 2001 map in the park's authorizing law. It also orders a land exchange near Beauty Mountain in Fayette County so the government can acquire a tract lying next to the boundary.
plaw-107-357-2002: Public Law 107-357 makes room for donated land at Andersonville National Historic Site in Georgia, the site of the Civil War's most notorious prison camp. It changes one number in the site's 1970 authorizing law. The acreage limit rises from five hundred acres to five hundred twenty. That makes room for the donated parcels.
plaw-107-358-2002:
The Holocaust Restitution Tax Fairness Act of 2002 (Public Law 107-358) protects a tax break for Holocaust victims. The 2001 tax law had excluded restitution received by victims of the Nazi regime from federal income tax, but that whole law was set to sunset, taking the exclusion with it.

This act repeals the sunset as it applies to the restitution exclusion. The result is lasting: money paid to victims as restitution for what the Nazis took stays free of federal income tax for good, without an expiration date hanging over it. Congress passed it in December 2002.
plaw-107-359-2002:
The Civil War Battlefield Preservation Act of 2002 (Public Law 107-359) created a federal grant program to buy and save Civil War battlefields. It amends the American Battlefield Protection Act of 1996 to let the Secretary of the Interior fund battlefield acquisition.

Congress found that battlefields teach Americans about a tragic period of their history, and the numbers were grim. Of the three hundred eighty-four principal battlefields listed in a 1993 report, almost twenty percent were already lost or fragmented, and more were in poor condition. The grants were meant to rescue ground before development erased it.
plaw-107-360-2002: Public Law 107-360 funds two special diabetes programs in the Public Health Service Act. One fights Type I diabetes; the other serves American Indians, among whom diabetes runs high. The act sets funding for the Type I program at one hundred fifty million dollars for each of fiscal years 2004 through 2008, with matching treatment for the Indian program.
plaw-107-361-2002: Public Law 107-361 settles an old trespass in Idaho. The owner of the Sand Hills Resort had occupied about ten acres of public land inside the Sand Mountain Wilderness Study Area since 1971, an encroachment everyone wanted resolved. The act authorizes the Secretary of the Interior to convey that parcel to the resort owner, clearing the title.
plaw-107-362-2002: The Russian River Land Act (Public Law 107-362) resolves land claims of Cook Inlet Region, Inc., an Alaska Native regional corporation, along the Russian River in Alaska. Congress found the lands where the Russian River meets the Kenai River rich in archaeology important to the Kenaitze Indian Tribe and in fisheries important to all Alaskans. The act settles the corporation's claims to those lands.
plaw-107-363-2002:
Public Law 107-363 is the Bainbridge Island Japanese-American Memorial Study Act of 2002. It orders a study of the Eagledale Ferry Dock site on Bainbridge Island, Washington. The study weighs including the site in the National Park System. From that dock, Japanese Americans were sent into wartime exile.

The findings recall that Executive Order 9066, signed February 19, 1942, set in motion the forced removal of more than one hundred ten thousand Japanese Americans. In Washington State alone, nearly thirteen thousand people of Japanese ancestry were incarcerated for three years. On March 30, 1942, two hundred twenty-seven Bainbridge Island residents were taken from the dock.
plaw-107-364-2002: The Gunn McKay Nature Preserve Act (Public Law 107-364) designates about fifteen acres of National Forest land in Utah as the Gunn McKay Nature Preserve. The parcel is shown on a map dated March 2002. The act puts the Secretary of Agriculture in charge and gives a deadline of one hundred twenty days to produce a management plan for the preserve.
plaw-107-365-2002: Public Law 107-365 is the Caribbean National Forest Wild and Scenic Rivers Act of 2002. It adds waterways in Puerto Rico's Caribbean National Forest, also known as El Yunque, to the National Wild and Scenic Rivers System. Congress based the designations on the forest's 1997 management plan. That plan had examined which rivers fit the system's protection.
plaw-107-366-2002: Public Law 107-366 amends the Central Utah Project Completion Act, the law behind Utah's big federal water project. It clears up what the Secretary of the Interior must do for the project. It moves unspent project money toward wastewater treatment and reuse. It also lets water users prepay their contracts for city and industry water facilities. And it drops the old deadline for such prepayment.
plaw-107-367-2002: Public Law 107-367 reauthorizes the Mni Wiconi Rural Water Supply Project, which carries drinking water to the Pine Ridge Indian Reservation and surrounding South Dakota communities. It adds fifty-eight point eight million dollars, at 1997 price levels, to the project's authorized cost and pushes its completion deadline from 2003 out to 2008. The project is run by the Bureau of Reclamation.
plaw-107-368-2002:
The National Science Foundation Authorization Act of 2002 (Public Law 107-368) authorized funding for the National Science Foundation for fiscal years 2003 through 2007. The Foundation is the government's main backer of basic research at universities outside medicine.

Congress found the Foundation had strengthened the nation's research enterprise for more than fifty years, and that American economic strength, national security, and quality of life rest on scientific and technological capability. The act pairs the money authorizations with findings about the Foundation's central role and the future direction of its many programs. It covered five fiscal years in one authorization.
plaw-107-369-2002: Public Law 107-369 revises the boundary of the Allegheny Portage Railroad National Historic Site in Blair and Cambria Counties, Pennsylvania. The site preserves the canal-era railroad that hauled boats over the Allegheny Mountains. The act adopts a May 2001 map as the site's new legal boundary and defines how the revision works.
plaw-107-370-2002: The Big Sur Wilderness and Conservation Act of 2002 (Public Law 107-370) designates new wilderness in California's Big Sur country. Its main move adds described areas to the Ventana Wilderness, folding them into the National Wilderness Preservation System, where land gets the strongest protection federal law offers. The act names both the Interior and Agriculture secretaries, since the country spans their lands.
plaw-107-371-2002: Public Law 107-371 clears a title cloud in Idaho left by an 1880 survey. The original surveyor's meander lines around Spirit Lake and Twin Lakes no longer match the lakes' high water lines, raising doubts about who owns land along the shores. The act directs the Secretary of the Interior to issue a formal disclaimer of any federal interest in those adjacent lands.
plaw-107-372-2002: Public Law 107-372 reauthorizes the Hydrographic Services Improvement Act of 1998, the law behind the government's nautical charting and ocean surveying. Its first title covers the functions of the NOAA administrator, a quality assurance program, and a Hydrographic Services Review Panel. A second title deals with the NOAA Commissioned Officer Corps, the uniformed service that crews the agency's ships and aircraft.
plaw-107-373-2002:
The Cedar Creek and Belle Grove National Historical Park Act (Public Law 107-373) creates a new unit of the National Park System in Virginia's Shenandoah Valley. The park joins the Cedar Creek battlefield with the Belle Grove plantation house and grounds.

Congress wrote the park's purpose into the act. The park is to preserve and interpret a nationally significant Civil War landscape and an antebellum plantation. It is also to tell the valley's story, from early settlement through the Civil War and beyond. The Battle of Cedar Creek, fought in 1864, is the ground's best-known event.
plaw-107-374-2002: Public Law 107-374 grants two Oregon counties a right-of-way over federal land. Deschutes and Crook Counties receive the right to West Butte Road, an unpaved Bureau of Land Management road numbered 6520 on the act's July 2002 map. The grant gives the counties a legal path for a road they use, subject to conditions stated in the act.
plaw-107-375-2002: Public Law 107-375 extends federal help for endangered fish in two western river basins. It lengthens the time allowed for building projects under the fish recovery programs. Those programs serve endangered fish in the Upper Colorado River Basin and the San Juan River Basin. Key deadlines move from fiscal years 2005 and 2007 out to fiscal year 2008.
plaw-107-376-2002: Public Law 107-376 gives one Oregon power project more time, much like an earlier act in this set did for a North Carolina project. The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission license for project number 11509 required construction to start by a deadline. This act requires the Commission, at the builder's request, to extend that deadline by three consecutive two-year periods.
plaw-107-377-2002: The Protection of Family Farmers Act of 2002 (Public Law 107-377) buys six more months for family farm bankruptcies. Chapter 12 of the bankruptcy code, written for family farmers, kept expiring and being revived. This act strikes January 1, 2003 and inserts July 1, 2003 everywhere the revival period is stated, keeping the farmer bankruptcy rules alive into the new year.
plaw-2002: Anisha Goveas Foti gained her own law in Private Law 107-5, approved on November 5, 2002 (H.R. 2245). The first section makes her eligible for an immigrant visa or for adjustment of status to lawful permanent resident, the national caps of the Immigration and Nationality Act aside. Early entry counts as lawful if she arrived before the filing deadline. A separate second section orders the Secretary of State to trim one immigrant visa from her birth country's pool once she gains residence.
playfair-illustrations-huttonian-1802:
John Playfair explains Hutton's theory of the earth in Illustrations of the Huttonian Theory, from 1802. Slow causes, acting over deep time, shape the globe in this account. Rain, rivers, and heat from below raise and wear the land in endless cycles, with no need of sudden universal ruin to explain the rocks.

Playfair made his friend Hutton readable where the original was dense. His clear prose taught geology to think in millions of years. Unconformities in Scottish rock faces serve as his star witnesses here. The book forms the classic statement of uniformitarian geology, the doctrine on which Lyell and Darwin would later build their own world-changing works.
plos-pbio-0020002:
Xavier I. Ambroggio, Douglas C. Rees, and Raymond J. Deshaies wrote this short study for PLOS Biology in 2004. It looks at a zinc-holding site called the JAMM motif. That motif appears in parts of two large cell machines: the proteasome, which breaks down worn proteins, and the signalosome, which helps control that process.

The two machines use their JAMM sites to snip small tags off proteins, a step that times when proteins are destroyed. The authors set out the shared shape and chemistry of the site in both machines. Seeing the same tool in two places hints at a common origin. It also gives chemists a defined pocket to study, and perhaps one day to block with a drug.
plos-pbio-0020402:
Cynthia Schuck-Paim, Lorena Pompilio, and Alex Kacelnik tested animal choice in PLOS Biology in 2004. Starlings choosing between food options sometimes seem to break the rules of rational choice, picking an option they earlier passed over. The authors show the birds' body state explains the odd picks.

A hungry bird values a meal differently than a full one, so its choices shift with its state. What looks like irrationality is a fixed rule applied under changing need. That is a sharp lesson for behavioral science. Before calling any choice irrational, in animals or people, check the state of the chooser. The paper refines how experiments on choice must be designed and read.
plos-pone-0000002:
David Dingli and Jorge Pacheco tackled a size puzzle in blood biology in 2006. Hematopoietic stem cells, found in bone marrow, rebuild the blood and immune system for life. Only part of that pool works at any given time. The authors asked how the size of the active pool scales across mammals of very different body sizes.

Using allometric scaling, the math of how body features grow with size, they compared the active stem cell pool from small mammals to large ones. A clear scaling pattern would hint at shared rules governing blood production across species. Such rules help doctors think about marrow transplants and about why blood diseases strike as they do.
plos-pone-0000102:
Fatema A. Legrand, Douglas F. Nixon, Christopher P. Loo, and their team studied infants exposed to HIV in PLOS ONE in 2006. Some babies born to HIV-positive mothers escape infection, yet their immune systems met the virus. The team looked for HIV-specific T cell responses in these exposed but uninfected infants.

Strong responses appeared once regulatory T cells, the immune system's brakes, were removed from the samples. That means the babies' killer T cells had indeed learned the virus, but their activity was being held down. The result speaks to vaccine hopes. Protection may already be within reach of the infant immune system. The brakes would need easing safely, at the right moment.
plos-pone-0000202:
Christel M. M. Mols and Marcel E. Visser published this orchard ecology study in PLOS ONE in 2007. Great tits are small songbirds that feed their chicks on caterpillars. Working in commercial apple orchards, the authors report that great tits reduce the caterpillar damage done to the crop.

Birds as pest control is an old idea; this paper measures it in working orchards. Less caterpillar damage means more sound fruit without extra spraying. The findings support keeping nesting birds around farmland, a rare case where wildlife conservation and growers' profits point the same way.
plos-pone-0000302:
Chung-Der Hsiao, May-Su You, Ying-Jey Guh, and colleagues published this zebrafish development paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Ionocytes are skin cells that manage salt and acid balance in fish. The authors show that two genes, foxi3a and foxi3b, form a positive regulatory loop, each switching the other on. That loop is essential for specifying and differentiating zebrafish epidermal ionocytes.

A self-reinforcing loop locks a cell into its identity once the decision starts. The paper traces that loop in the fish's skin. Zebrafish ionocytes are a model for salt-handling cells in other animals, including the human kidney, so the circuit matters beyond fish.
plos-pone-0000402:
Thomas Elmqvist and colleagues studied the fate of tropical dry forest in Madagascar, reporting in PLOS ONE in 2007. These forests are rich in unique species but easier to clear than rainforest, and much of Madagascar's has been lost. The team mapped patterns of loss and regrowth and asked how social institutions shape them.

Forests do not fall only to chainsaws; they fall or recover under rules about land, farming, and local authority. By tying forest change to that social and institutional context, the study shows why conservation plans succeed in one place and fail in another. Madagascar's dry forests, and the people living beside them, are the test case.
plos-pone-0000502:
Irina Chis Ster and Neil M. Ferguson reconstructed the numbers behind Britain's 2001 foot and mouth epidemic, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. The outbreak led to the slaughter of millions of animals and fierce debate over control policy. The team estimated the transmission parameters of the epidemic in Great Britain: how readily the virus spread between farms and over distance.

Firm parameters are the difference between a model that argues and a model that persuades. With them, officials can test culling and vaccination strategies before the next outbreak. The study revisited the epidemic with complete data, supplying reference values for one of the most studied animal disease events on record.
plos-pone-0000602:
Javier Buceta and colleagues modeled a boundary that patterns the fly wing, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. The DV boundary separates the dorsal and ventral halves of the developing Drosophila wing, and a gene regulatory network maintains it. The team analyzed the robustness and stability of that network.

Robustness asks whether the boundary still forms when conditions wobble, as they always do in real embryos. A network model that stays stable under noise matches biology's reliability; one that shatters does not. Such modeling tells experimentalists which parts of the network carry the load of keeping development on track.
plos-pone-0000702:
Christopher B. Kaelin, Gregory M. Cooper, Arend Sidow and colleagues compared DNA sequences around a hunger gene across mammals, in PLOS ONE in 2007. The gene makes agouti-related protein, a neuropeptide that stimulates food intake. In the brain it is produced only in the arcuate nucleus of the hypothalamus, a control center for appetite. Its levels rise when the body is in negative energy balance, burning more than it takes in.

How that regulation works at the molecular level was the open question. Comparing sequences across species highlights the stretches evolution kept, which usually mark functional control elements. Those conserved pieces tell researchers where to look for the switches governing hunger.
plos-pone-0000802:
Jacob S. Brenner and Ricardo E. Dolmetsch separated two calcium signals in heart muscle cells, writing in PLOS ONE in 2007. Pathological cardiac hypertrophy, the thickening of heart muscle in disease, raises the risk of heart failure and cardiovascular death. Calcium-regulated gene expression is essential for inducing hypertrophy. The puzzle is how heart cells distinguish calcium signals that command growth from those that command each heartbeat.

Their title reports that the channel protein TrpC3 regulates hypertrophy-associated gene expression without affecting myocyte beating or cell size. A channel handling only the growth message is an attractive drug target: block the harmful growth signal, and the heartbeat's calcium stays untouched.
plos-pone-0000902:
Shengliang Zhang, Junwen Wang and Hung Tseng studied a protein that switches on a subset of ribosomal RNA genes, in PLOS ONE in 2007. The protein, basonuclin, is found mainly in skin type cells and in egg and sperm forming cells. Ribosomal RNA genes make the core parts of ribosomes, the cell's protein building machines.

Earlier lab work showed basonuclin binds the start region of these genes at three strong sites. Using HaCaT skin cells, the team asked which gene copies it actually regulates in living cells. The answer helps explain how cells tune protein production to match growth. It also clarifies a specialist protein with a narrow but key job.
plos-pone-0001002:
Alan Dabney and John Storey improved a simple classifier for reading genomic data, in a 2007 PLOS ONE methods article. Nearest centroid classifiers assign a sample to the closest group average. They have proved handy with genomic data, where thousands of genes are measured at once and samples are few.

The hard step is feature selection, picking which genes count. The authors drive that choice by optimality, choosing features by a stated best criterion rather than habit. A simple classifier done well can beat a complex one done loosely. Their method is aimed at labs that need clear calls from wide, noisy data.
plos-pone-0001102:
Aurelie Le Mandat Schultz, Arnaud Bonnard, Frederick Barreau and colleagues measured immune sensors in a rat model of a newborn gut disease, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Necrotizing enterocolitis is a devastating illness of premature infants, where gut tissue dies. Its cause combines several risk factors acting together, in the same setting where innate immunity switches on.

The team measured expression of TLR-2, TLR-4 and NOD2, sensors that detect germs, plus an activated inflammation factor, in newborn rats modeling the disease. If those sensors are part of the trigger, they become targets for protection. Premature guts meet bacteria before they are ready.
plos-pone-0001202:
BCAS3 is a gene of unknown function sitting in a region of chromosome 17 that is often amplified in cancer. Kavitha Siva and colleagues studied where the gene is active in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Cancer often involves progressive changes in genes that are important for normal development.

The authors found the human gene expressed in embryonic stem cells and in vascular precursors, the cells that build blood vessels. That pattern suggests a role in human embryogenesis and in tumor angiogenesis, the growth of vessels that feed tumors. A development gene switched on in cancers is a lead worth following.
plos-pone-0001302:
Bark beetles find their host trees by smell, following pheromones and tree odors. Min Lu, Daniel Miller, and Jiang-Hua Sun report an interaction between two pine bark beetles in China. One is exotic and one is native. Their account appeared in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Invasive species fascinate ecologists because they offer unique chances to study community ecology.

The authors describe cross-attraction between the two beetles and ask whether it is a novel invasion mechanism. If a native species' signals draw in an invader, or the reverse, the pair could reinforce each other's attacks on pines. Their study tests that possibility in the field.
plos-pone-0001402:
Miguel Bento and co-authors wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on genome stress in a crop hybrid called triticale. When two species cross and the DNA doubles, the new genome faces a shock. Genes can be lost, moved, or switched off. The team asked whether this doubling acts as a force that pulls genomes back in size.

They tracked DNA shifts in triticale lines after the cross. Rearranged and lost stretches showed up in the new plants. The results back the idea that doubling can trim as well as add. That helps explain why plant genomes do not just grow without end after each round of doubling.
plos-pone-0001502:
Tige Rustad and colleagues published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on how the TB germ answers low oxygen. Low oxygen zones in the body had long been tied to the latent, quiet phase of TB. Past work mapped the germ's first reply to low oxygen. The team tracked the longer, lasting reply that follows.

Their data show the germ settles into a steady state tuned to low oxygen. That state may be what lets TB hide for years in a host. Drugs that work on active germs may miss this quiet state. Naming its genes gives drug teams targets for the latent phase.
plos-pone-0001602:
Huan Chen and co-authors published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on a peroxide sensor in a hardy germ. Most germs sense peroxide, a toxic byproduct, with a protein that uses two sulfur atoms as the switch. The germ studied here shrugs off radiation and dryness that kill most kin. Its sensor was found to bear just one such sulfur atom.

Despite the lean build, the sensor still spots peroxide and switches on defense genes. A one atom switch breaks the standard design for this sensor family. The finding may help explain the germ's famed grit. It widens the known range of how cells sense harm.
plos-pone-0001702:
Simone Rossi, Alberto De Capua, Patrizio Pasqualetti, and their co-authors tested whether smells can move the motor system in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Watching actions or hearing action sounds is known to activate the viewer's own motor system across senses. Smell is the oldest sense, and it can steer behavior, yet its link to movement was untested.

Using transcranial magnetic stimulation, which probes motor excitability through the skull, the team measured cross-modal effects of odors on the motor system. They report distinct olfactory effects, per the paper's title. The full text gives the odors used, the stimulation results, and how effects differed by smell type. Results like these widen the picture of how the senses jointly prepare the body to act.
plos-pone-0001802:
Heather Powell, Joanne Smart, Lisa G. Wood, and their co-authors tested a symptom questionnaire in asthma patients in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. The Common Cold Questionnaire, or CCQ, is used to tell who has a viral infection and who does not. Its usefulness in people with acute asthma was unknown, though colds are a top trigger of asthma attacks.

The team assessed whether the CCQ can detect viral infection and monitor recovery during virus-induced asthma exacerbations. The full text gives the patient results, the virus tests, and how well questionnaire scores matched them. A cheap questionnaire that reliably flags viral attacks could steer asthma care and research without waiting for lab results.
plos-pone-0001902:
Sampson Kyere and co-authors probed the shape of a small viral protein part in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. The part, called p12, sits inside the Gag building blocks of a mouse leukemia virus. It plays key roles as the virus is built, copies its genes, and slips its DNA into the host cell.

Using nuclear magnetic resonance, a method that maps atomic shape, the team studied p12 joined to its next-door part in Gag. They report that p12 has no fixed fold in that construct; it stays loose and unstructured. A loose part can still be vital, since loose regions often serve as flexible links or binding pads.
plos-pone-0002002:
Zilal Kattan and co-authors studied a DNA repair protein that also shapes breast cancer growth, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. The protein, DDB2, helps fix DNA damage by nucleotide excision repair. It also plays roles in normal cells, such as gene control and cell cycle timing. Loss of DDB2 had been tied to a higher risk of tumors.

The team tested what DDB2 does inside breast cancer cells as they grow. If a repair protein also brakes or spurs growth, its loss could drive cancer by two paths at once. Work of this kind refines which tumors might react to drugs that target DNA repair.
plos-pone-0002102:
Thomas Jensen and co-authors split the roles of two forms of an energy enzyme in mouse muscle, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. The enzyme, AMPK, is a promising drug target for metabolic disorders, in part because it promotes glucose uptake in skeletal muscle without insulin. It comes in two catalytic forms, alpha one and alpha two, and the alpha two form was clearly required for some uptakes.

As the title states, alpha one activation is required for glucose uptake driven by twitch contraction, but not for uptake driven by hydrogen peroxide. Two forms, two triggers: the split refines which form a drug should hit.
plos-pone-0002202:
Puspha Sinnayah, Erin Jobst, Joseph Rathner, and co-authors asked how cannabis-like drugs drive hunger, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Cannabinoids, the active parts of marijuana, stir appetite, while drugs that block their main receptor, CB1, suppress appetite and aid weight loss. How these effects run through the brain's feeding circuits was unclear.

The team tested whether the melanocortin system, a known appetite control circuit, carries the feeding effect. They report that cannabinoid-driven feeding works independently of that system. The result redraws part of the hunger map and hints that appetite drugs may need to aim at more than one circuit at once.
plos-pone-0002302:
Shanthi Muttukrishna, Sangeeta Suri, Nigel Groome, and co-authors measured growth factors and oxygen inside the early pregnancy sac, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. In the first trimester, a steep oxygen gradient runs between the mother's circulation and the tissues of the gestational sac. That gradient helps steer how the placenta's trophoblast cells behave.

The team asked whether the oxygen level inside the sac shapes the making of TGF beta proteins, signals that control cell growth. They measured both in early human pregnancies. Knowing how oxygen tunes placental signals bears on healthy placenta growth and on problems like miscarriage and pre-eclampsia that begin in these weeks.
plos-pone-0002402:
Work from Burgevin and fellow authors appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline credits Anne Burgevin, Loredana Saveanu, Yohan Kim, and others. Its subject is a Detailed Analysis of the Murine TAP Transporter Substrate Specificity. The transporter linked to antigen processing (TAP) supplies cytosolic peptides into the endoplasmic reticulum for binding to major histocompatibility complex (MHC) class I molecules.

Its specificity therefore influences the repertoire of peptides presented by MHC molecules. Readers get the background first, then the path the team took and the care they took with it. That makes the article a clear record of one research question, the path taken to test it, and the limits the authors faced.
plos-pone-0002502:
In 2008, Loarie and colleagues published a study in the journal PLOS ONE. The byline credits Scott R. Loarie, Benjamin E. Carter, Katharine Hayhoe, and others. Its subject is climate Change and the Future of California's Endemic Flora. The flora of California, a global biodiversity hotspot, includes 2387 endemic plant taxa.

With anticipated climate change, we project that up to 66% will experience >80% reductions in range size within a century. Key terms are set out in context, so a reader new to the field can still follow the work. The result is a compact record of the work, of use to readers who study the same problem or teach it to others.
plos-pone-0002602:
A research team led by Saayman reported its work in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline credits Sheena Saayman, Samantha Barichievy, Alexio Capovilla, and others. Its subject is the Efficacy of Generating Three Independent Anti-HIV-1 siRNAs from a Single U6 RNA Pol III-Expressed Long Hairpin RNA. RNA Interference (RNAi) effectors have been used to inhibit rogue RNAs in mammalian cells.

However, rapidly evolving sequences such as the human immunodeficiency virus type 1 (HIV-1) require multiple targeting approaches to prevent the emergence of escape variants. Readers get the background first, then the path the team took and the care they took with it. As a record, it keeps the focus on facts and method, and lets readers judge the claims for themselves.
plos-pone-0002702:
Hoang Hoa Long led a team whose work appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was native bacterial endophytes promote host growth in a Species-Specific manner; phytohormone manipulations do not result in common growth responses. Authorship is credited in the record to Hoang Hoa Long and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

The abstract begins from a clear premise. All plants in nature harbor a diverse community of endophytic bacteria which can positively affect host plant growth. Its abstract frames the work for later readers, who can judge the full text against the aims stated at the start.
plos-pone-0002802:
Aron J. Fazekas led a team whose work appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was multiple multilocus DNA barcodes from the plastid genome discriminate plant species equally well. The full author list in the catalog record begins with Aron J. Fazekas, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract begins from a clear premise. A universal barcode system for land plants would be a valuable resource, with potential utility in fields as diverse as ecology, floristics. Anyone studying the topic can use the article to see how the authors framed the problem at the time of publication.
plos-pone-0002902:
Perayot Pamonsinlapatham, Réda Hadj-Slimane, Françoise Raynaud and co-authors built a peptide tool against Ras signaling in 2008. RasGAP normally switches Ras off, but it also helps Ras and can block cell death through its SH3 domain. That second role does not depend on its switching job.

The team used a peptide aptamer, a short crafted protein piece, aimed at the RasGAP SH3 domain. In PLOS ONE they report it blocked a RasGAP link to Aurora and drove tumor cell death without using caspases, the usual death enzymes. Cancer researchers get a fresh angle on a well-known pathway.
plos-pone-0003002:
Jung Kyoon Choi, Sohyun Hwang and Young-Joon Kim studied chromatin silencing and stress response in yeast in 2008. Cells balance variety against fidelity by controlling random molecular noise. Epigenetic silencing, switching genes off via chromatin state, plays a critical role when environments change.

The team shows incomplete silencing increases random noise in gene expression in yeast. That noise can be a feature, letting a uniform population hedge bets under stress. Published in PLOS ONE, the study frames silencing as both a stabilizer and a source of useful diversity in genomic responses. Full methods, data, and references appear in the complete article for readers who want more detail.
plos-pone-0003102:
Krishnaraj Rajalingam, Manu Sharma, Christine Lohmann and co-authors studied apoptosis resistance in Chlamydia-infected cells in 2008. Chlamydia are bacteria that live inside host cells and cause a variety of human diseases. Infected cells are protected against many different triggers of apoptosis, planned cell death.

That resistance is thought to be an important immune escape mechanism letting the bacteria persist. Mcl-1 is a key regulator of that resistance, the title reports. Published in PLOS ONE, blocking Mcl-1 might let infected cells die on schedule, a possible treatment angle. Full methods, data, and references appear in the complete article for readers who want more detail.
plos-pone-0003202:
Olyana N. Grod, Amber E. Budden, Tom Tregenza and colleagues survey peer reviewers in ecology and evolution in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Referee traits and their effects on peer review matter because the integrity of the system depends on fair evaluation of merit. In 2006 the team conducted an online survey of 1,334 ecologists and evolutionary biologists.

They report systematic variation in reviewer practice according to country and gender. Readers get data on a process usually hidden behind closed editorial doors. Evidence on reviewer differences can inform fairer review policies, even if it cannot settle every bias claim.
plos-pone-0003302:
Samuel Huber, Jörg Schrader, Gerhard Fritz and colleagues study a kinase needed for regulatory T cell conversion in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. CD4+CD25+ regulatory T cells are important mediators of immune tolerance. A subset can be generated in the periphery by TGF-beta dependent conversion of conventional CD4+CD25- T cells into induced regulatory T cells. In chronic viral infection or malignancy, such induced cells matter greatly.

The title reports that p38 MAP kinase signaling is required for conversion into induced Treg. Readers learn of a specific signaling step behind tolerance formation. Blocking or boosting that step could shift immune balance in autoimmunity or cancer.
plos-pone-0003402:
Karoliina Harkonmäki and co-authors asked how far genes shape early retirement in this 2008 study. They followed about 24,000 Finnish twins for thirty years. Records showed which twins left work early due to disability. Common causes included depression and other major illnesses.

Comparing twin pairs let the team split genetic effects from life experience. Genes did carry part of the risk of disability retirement. The share differed by the medical cause behind the retirement. The findings inform debates on work ability, welfare, and fair support for sick workers. Twin studies remain one of the few ways to split those two forces apart.
plos-pone-0003502:
Nicholas P. Holmes, Charles Spence, and Peter C. Hansen scanned brains during tool use in this 2008 study. Holding a tool merges touch at the hand with sights far away. The brain must link those split sources into one event. They tested attention shifts while people felt vibrations through a simple tool.

Brain imaging showed how attention networks handle that split. Tool use changed which locations drew multisensory attention. The results map part of the neural choreography of tool skill. Such skill sits near the root of human technology. Tools extend the body in the mind as well as in the hand.
plos-pone-0003602:
Kelly B. Wyatt and co-authors studied a mammal die-off on Christmas Island in this 2008 paper. Christmas Island sits in the Indian Ocean. Its native mammals vanished in a historical extinction event. Novel infectious disease can drive declines and even extinction in some animal groups.

For mammals, well-corroborated disease extinctions were still lacking. The team's evidence correlated the island losses with introduced infectious disease. Arriving pathogens, not just habitat loss, may erase a fauna. The case strengthens disease as an extinction force. Island species are most at risk, since they evolved with few germs around.
plos-pone-0003702:
Xiaosi Gu, Xun Liu, Kevin G. Guise, and colleagues published this psychology study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Alexithymia is a trait marked by trouble knowing, handling, or describing one's own feelings. Brain scans have tied it to weaker activity in a region that helps control thought. The authors tested healthy adults.

They compared people high and low in the alexithymic trait on voluntary control tasks. The study probes how a blind spot for one's own emotions relates to steering attention on purpose. It links a personality trait to the mechanics of mental control in everyday life.
plos-pone-0003802:
J. R. Managbanag, Tarynn M. Witten, Danail Bonchev, and colleagues published this aging study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Finding genes that modulate longevity is a major goal of aging research. Such genes could become targets for treatment as well as keys to basic biology. The authors took a network approach.

They applied shortest-path analysis to gene networks, tracing the shortest routes between known aging-related genes. Genes lying on those paths became candidates for affecting lifespan. The network approach offers a new compass for aging research beyond one-gene-at-a-time hunts. The method can be reused for other traits tied to long life.
plos-pone-0003902:
Bindi Thomas, John D. Holland, and Edward O. Minot tracked an elephant by satellite for five years. Their 2008 PLOS ONE article follows an African elephant cow, Loxodonta africana. Tracking ran from September 2003 to August 2008. The cow ranged across Sabi Sand Reserve and Kruger National Park.

GPS records showed her daily movements over the whole period. She was confirmed as part of a group of seven elephants. Long tracks like this reveal how elephants use land across seasons. Park managers can use such maps to plan fences, water, and safe corridors. The article came out in PLOS ONE, an open journal for science and health research.
plos-pone-0004002:
Liliana R. Vitorino, Gabriele Margos, Edward J. Feil, and co-authors mapped a Lyme disease relative's geography in 2008. Borrelia lusitaniae is a tick-borne spirochete of the Old World. It occurs mainly around the Mediterranean Basin. Lizards of the Lacertidae family serve as its reservoir hosts.

Their PLOS ONE article used multilocus sequence typing to sort strains. Fine-scale patterns emerged in where each strain type lives. Host lizards likely shape that patchy distribution. Knowing strain geography helps predict where human exposure may occur. The work appeared in PLOS ONE, with its methods and data open for all to see.
plos-pone-0004102:
Andrew Hollands, Ramy K. Aziz, Rita Kansal, and co-authors studied a natural mutation in strep bacteria in 2008. Group A streptococcus causes diseases from sore throat to severe invasion. Studies noted high SpeB output tracks with less invasive disease. What SpeB does during infection stayed unclear, though.

Their PLOS ONE article uses a clinical strain lacking SpeB expression. A natural mutation in the ropB gene suppressed SpeB in that strain. The same change reduced systemic virulence of M1T1 strep. The result helps untangle a long-standing pattern in strep epidemiology. The full report sits in PLOS ONE, free to read with all its data shown.
plos-pone-0004202:
Camille Martinand-Mari and colleagues published this developmental study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Programmed cell death is one of the clearest signs of how flexible living systems are. It usually sits upstream of major patterning events, such as the shaping of fingers in vertebrates or the facets of the fly eye.

The authors studied non-proliferative epithelia, sheets of cells that no longer divide. They asked how the sheet's topology controls who lives and who dies. Topology here means the pattern of cells and their neighbours. Their work shows that in a quiet tissue, geometry itself can be a fate decision.
plos-pone-0004302:
Shahin Zangenehpour, Asif Ghazanfar, and David Lewkowicz published this primate development study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Knowing a trait's evolutionary origin means knowing how development and ancestry interact. Human infants undergo perceptual narrowing in their first year, losing some ability to match sights and sounds across species.

The team studied infant vervet monkeys, testing heterochrony, shifts in developmental timing, and cross-species intersensory matching. Comparing monkey infants with human infants shows whether narrowing is a human quirk or a primate pattern. Such comparisons anchor big claims about human development in evidence. Monkeys and humans share much early development, so the test is a fair one.
plos-pone-0004402:
Anorexia nervosa is far more often studied in women than in men. Anu Raevuori, Hans Hoek, Ezra Susser, and co-authors measured it in Finnish men. Their 2009 PLOS ONE paper screened male twins born from 1975 to 1979. The men came from the FinnTwin16 birth cohorts. In all, 2,122 men answered a screening questionnaire on lifetime eating disorders.

Men who screened positive, plus their co-twins, got closer study. Eighteen men screened positive in the first pass. Twin data let the authors check shared genes and upbringing. The study gives rare nationwide numbers for male anorexia. It shows the illness in men is uncommon but real. Those figures help correct a strong gender gap in eating-disorder research.
plos-pone-0004502:
Sugar signals and the plant hormone auxin work together to shape roots, show Bhuwaneshwar Mishra, Manjul Singh, Priyanka Aggrawal, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. The plant is Arabidopsis thaliana, a small weed used as a model in labs worldwide. Root growth is highly plastic: roots reshape themselves to match soil conditions.

Sugar signaling was already known to affect roots, and to interact with several plant hormones. Auxin is the hormone that most directly steers root growth and branching. The team studied how glucose and auxin signaling interact in seedlings. Their results help explain how a plant balances its food supply against its growth plan. That balance decides how well crops forage for water and nutrients underground.
plos-pone-0004602:
A hormone best known for fat can tip a small songbird toward raising a second family in one year, show Mare Lohmus and Mats Bjorklund in PLOS ONE in 2009. Organisms face trade-offs in their life-history strategies, such as single or multiple broods within a year. In passerine birds that can breed more than once, the chance of laying a second clutch depends on several factors.

The hormone is leptin, a signal of body fat stores. In a field experiment, the team tested its effect on the breeding decision. If a fat signal persuades a bird that times are good, it should breed again. Showing a hormone steering a whole life-history choice in wild birds links physiology to evolution in a direct way.
plos-pone-0004702:
Anton Moll and colleagues found a way to read single gene versions from standard chip data, in PLOS ONE in 2009. One gene can make several message versions by cutting and joining parts in unlike ways. Each version can do a distinct job in the cell, so lumping them hides real change.

Common gene chips measure a gene as a whole with sets of small probes. The team used the probe layout to split signal by version. That lets old chip data yield finer results without new lab work. Doctors and researchers can spot version shifts tied to disease.
plos-pone-0004802:
Han Si and colleagues showed that human and mouse kidneys show gender and species specific gene expression after injury, in PLOS ONE in 2009. End stage renal disease incidence is approximately fifty percent higher in men than women. To understand the molecular basis of this disparity, the team examined sex specific expression patterns in control, and Diseased kidney samples from both species using transcript profiling.

Patterns differed by sex and did not fully match between species. That cautions against direct transfer of mouse findings to patients. Sex aware analysis is needed in kidney research. The data provide a reference for such work.
plos-pone-0004902:
Mireille St-Onge and colleagues studied impact of anti inflammatory agents on gene output in stimulated human neutrophils, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Adenosine, prostaglandin E2, or increased cyclic AMP each elicit potent anti inflammatory events in neutrophils, inhibiting phagocytosis, superoxide production, adhesion, and cytokine release. Endogenous resolution pathways were unraveled by profiling how these agents reprogram gene output during active swelling.

Resolution is active gene switching, not passive fading. Endogenous molecules orchestrate the switch. Pro resolution drugs could mimic these programs. Chronic swelling might reflect failed resolution. The study gives researchers concrete leads that later work can verify and extend. The team also set out clear next steps for work in this field. More tests with more samples will help show how strong the effect is.
plos-pone-0005002:
Preventive drugs can stop Pneumocystis pneumonia before it starts. Yet it remains the most common serious infection in people with HIV. James Heffelfinger and colleagues asked why prevention fails. Their PLOS ONE paper appeared in 2009. They studied nonadherence to primary prophylaxis. The data came from United States surveillance records for 2000 to 2004.

The team identified factors linked to skipping the preventive drugs. Those factors point to gaps in care. Patients at highest risk are not always reached. The findings guide efforts to keep at-risk patients on treatment. Closing those gaps could prevent many cases of a dangerous but preventable disease.
plos-pone-0005102:
Wildfire depends on climate, vegetation and people. Climate change will redraw its map. Meg Krawchuk and colleagues modeled that future in PLOS ONE in 2009. They built a global pyrogeography, a geography of fire. Current fire distribution was their starting point. Future climate scenarios drove the forecast.

The model shows where fires burn now. It also shows where they will burn in a warmer world. Fire zones shift and grow in many regions. Some regions may see less fire instead. Planners gain a map of tomorrow's fire country. Land management can prepare for the shift. The study was a first step, as the authors frame it. Later work can refine the forecast.
plos-pone-0005202:
Stress can damage plant DNA, and plants answer with repair systems that include gene swapping. Some reports claimed that stressed plants pass a heightened repair state to their offspring. Pecinka and colleagues tested that claim in Arabidopsis, the standard lab plant, in PLOS ONE in 2009.

Their title gives the verdict: transgenerational stress memory is not a general response in this species. Offspring did not broadly inherit the stressed state of their parents. Careful negative findings like this one prune ideas that sound appealing but do not hold up across conditions.
plos-pone-0005302:
Lung cancer risk grows with age and smoking, and family history and gene variants add to it. Young and colleagues built a susceptibility model combining those factors, reported in PLOS ONE in 2009. Their study compared healthy smokers with lung cancer cases.

Genetic markers tied to the disease joined age and family history in the model. A combined score can sort smokers into risk groups better than smoking history alone. That sorting could focus screening and quitting support on the smokers who need it most. No one test can say who will get lung cancer, but a score that joins age. Kin, and genes can at least pull the highest-risk group out of a large crowd.
plos-pone-0005402:
Calmodulin is a calcium sensor found in all cells, and it grips a huge range of target proteins. One target is calcineurin A, a phosphatase involved in immune and brain signaling. Majava and Kursula solved structures of their complex in PLOS ONE in 2009.

The complex showed domain swapping, where partners exchange matching sections. It also appeared in different oligomeric states, groupings of different sizes. Flexible recognition like this helps explain how one small sensor can manage so many different partners. Grip by swap is a strange trick, yet it may let this sensor hold a target in a firm clamp. And such clamps are just what drug teams seek when they build a blocker.
plos-pone-0005502:
Bernhard Egger and co-authors weighed a dispute over tiny worms in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Acoels are small, simple marine worms with no gut cavity. They were long classed as flatworms, but no clear shared traits unite the flatworm groups.

Gene-based family trees point another way, hinting that acoels split off very early from other animals. The authors reviewed the traits and the gene evidence side by side. Where acoels belong matters because, as early branches, they can show what the first animals with two sides looked like. The dispute also shows how new gene tools can upset long-settled groupings in the animal family tree.
plos-pone-0005602:
Helen Ayles and co-authors measured tuberculosis and HIV in two Zambian communities in a 2009 PLOS ONE study. Global targets call for tuberculosis rates to fall by half over a set period. Few surveys had actually counted cases in countries hit hard by both diseases.

The team screened whole communities for tuberculosis, HIV, and breathing symptoms. Real counts show how much disease clinics miss and where HIV fuels tuberculosis. Surveys like this tell control programs whether their plans stand a chance of meeting the targets. Community counts are costly to run, which is why so few exist despite the need for them.
plos-pone-0005702:
Karin Knieke and colleagues tracked how a brake molecule on T cells also shapes where those cells travel, in a 2009 study. The molecule, CD152 or CTLA-4, is known mostly for damping T cell action. Migration matters too: T cells must reach lymph organs and sites of attack to do their job.

The team tested movement both in lab dishes and in living animals. They found CD152 guides how antigen-experienced T cells move. That dual role, brake and guide, changes how doctors might use drugs that target CTLA-4. Such drugs are now central in cancer care, so the detail counts.
plos-pone-0005802:
Peter DeScioli and Robert Kurzban proposed in 2009 that human friendship evolved, in part, as a way to line up allies. Friends are not just pleasant company; they are people who might take your side. The alliance hypothesis says the mind builds support groups ahead of possible conflicts.

That view predicts quirks in how people rank, keep, and drop friends. Closeness should track how useful an ally would be, and how likely they are to choose you over rivals. The paper lays out the logic and its tests. It reframes friendship as strategy as well as warmth, without denying either.
plos-pone-0005902:
David Vader and co-authors measured in 2009 how stretching a collagen gel lines its fibers up. Collagen is the main scaffold protein in animal tissues and in lab-grown tissue models. Its versatility comes partly from its ability to remodel under force.

Strain induced alignment in the gels, turning a random mesh into ordered fibers. Aligned collagen can steer cell growth, as in tendons and healing wounds. Tissue engineers need that control to build replacements that bear load correctly. The study quantifies how much strain gives how much order, a practical recipe.
plos-pone-0006002:
Stress can push a gamble up or down, and not the same way for everyone. Nichole Lighthall, Mara Mather and Marissa Gorlick tested stress and risk in 2009 using a balloon game, where players pump a virtual balloon for money and risk popping it. Their PLOS ONE study compares men and women after an acute stress.

The title states the result: stress widened the sex gap in risk seeking on the task. A difference that grows under pressure matters wherever hard choices are made under strain. The work adds a clear lab finding to the debate on sex, stress and choice, and it warns against treating stressed decision-makers as one uniform group.
plos-pone-0006102:
Attention requires the brain to quiet its idle mode while it works. Dardo Tomasi, Nora Volkow, Ruiliang Wang and colleagues linked that quieting to dopamine pumps in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper measures dopamine transporters in the striatum, the proteins that clear dopamine away, and compares their levels with deactivation of the default mode network during visuospatial attention tasks.

Higher transporter levels tracked stronger quieting of the idle network, the title reports. The link gives dopamine a concrete part in focus: clearing the signal helps the brain leave rest mode. Findings of this kind inform work on attention disorders, where both dopamine drugs and network quieting are already in play.
plos-pone-0006202:
Proteins that hold sister chromosomes together were first known as chromosome glue. Cheri Schaaf and colleagues show that these cohesion proteins also steer genes in the fruit fly, in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. They focus on two gene groups: Enhancer of split and the invected-engrailed group.

Cohesion proteins favour active genes, yet how they control gene activity was unknown. The study maps their effects on the two fly gene groups in detail. Gene control emerges as a second job for the chromosome glue. That dual role may help explain disorders where cohesion fails. It also links chromosome handling to everyday gene switching.
plos-pone-0006302:
A protein that drives cell growth can be flipped to drive cell death by removing one tag. David Butler and colleagues studied Id2, a regulator of cell division, in muscle precursor cells in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Id2 normally promotes proliferation, and its front end carries a site where an enzyme adds a phosphate tag.

Without that phosphate, Id2 became growth suppressive and pushed dividing myoblasts toward programmed death. One small chemical tag thus decides the protein's whole effect. The switch matters for muscle development and repair. It may also matter in cancers where Id2 runs high.
plos-pone-0006402:
