Meselech Assegid Roro and colleagues audited 1,050 pregnancy records at three public hospitals in Addis Ababa to see whether screening for gestational diabetes follows the guidelines that recommend testing every pregnant woman. Their 2026 retrospective review recorded who was tested, when, by what method, and what the testing found.

Only about one woman in eight was screened at all, and almost all screening was triggered by risk factors rather than offered universally. Most tests came late, well past the recommended window in the middle of pregnancy, leaving little time to act. Among those tested, a striking four in ten actually had the condition. The authors conclude Ethiopia's hospitals are finding diabetes in pregnancy largely by luck and late, and urge universal, on-time testing.
plos-pone-0357202:
Subir Biswas, Yida Yang, and colleagues propose routing network data the way physics moves particles through a force field. Their 2026 paper introduces Particle Dynamics-based Routing. A network is treated as a landscape of gentle pushes. Each packet is launched with starting settings that steer it to its destination. It carries no directions in its header.

Because intermediate nodes need no destination tables, and headers never grow with network size, the scheme suits tiny Internet-of-Things devices with little memory. Simulations show forwarding stays light while trajectories remain controllable. Destinations stay hidden from nodes along the path. The authors frame the gravity-based version as a first proof that trajectory thinking can reshape routing design.
plos-pone-0357402:
Kathryn Biernacki and colleagues published a 2026 protocol in PLOS ONE for VICTORY, a clinical trial testing whether magnetic brain stimulation can reduce opioid craving. People on buprenorphine, the standard medication for opioid use disorder, still drop out and relapse often. The trial will enroll up to one hundred twenty such patients and randomly assign them to real or sham stimulation aimed at a left frontal brain region involved in control and craving.

Treatment runs weekly for eight weeks, two short sessions per visit, with craving, use, and retention checked before, during, and after. Some volunteers will also have brain scans to test whether stimulation rewires connections between the target region and the brain's reward circuits, and whether those changes track with craving. Running at an academic center and a private clinic should show whether the approach works beyond a university hospital.
plos-pone-0357602:
Yufeng Chen, Hongyang Bian, and Yuye Li published a 2026 methods paper in PLOS ONE on spotting kidney injury early in sepsis patients. Sepsis often damages the kidneys quickly, but early signs are vague and outcomes are poor. The team built a dataset from two centers, an American public intensive care database and a Chinese hospital's records, extracting dozens of risk factors per patient as both text and numbers.

Their model reads those two streams with separate networks, one tuned for medical language and one for numerical patterns, then fuses them to classify risk. It performed steadily at the first center and carried over well to the second hospital, and the combined model beat versions using text or numbers alone. Training on two centers made it more adaptable to local patients. It is offered as decision support for earlier intervention, not a replacement for clinical judgment.
plos-pone-0357902:
Sitthatka Jaratsaeng and three colleagues test whether a phone selfie video can help assess Parkinson's disease, in PLOS ONE in 2026. The illness stiffens facial expression as well as movement, and clinic visits capture only snapshots. The team recorded forty participants with a standard smartphone front camera across several facial movement tasks, engineered measurements from the footage, and trained models to flag the disease and estimate its severity.

Smiling videos carried the most signal. The best classifier sorted patients from controls with accuracy near seventy-seven percent, and a companion model estimated standard motor scores, though with wide error margins. An explainability analysis showed the system leaned most on movements of the lips and mouth corners, which matches what clinicians watch. The authors present phone video as a low cost screening aid for remote follow up, not a stand alone diagnosis.
plos-pone-0360002:
Zuzanna Gurzyńska and five colleagues published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It examines academic stress among students. The authors focus on two resources students draw on: coping strategies, the ways they handle pressure, and psychological resilience, the capacity to recover from setbacks.

The study asks how these two resources shape the level of stress students report. If certain coping styles clearly soften stress, universities can teach them rather than only treating stress after it harms grades or health. Counselors and student support services are the readers who would turn such findings into workshops and advising.
pmc-10200802:
Chen, Saeed, Liu and co-authors reviewed the roles of macrophages in controlling immunity and in treatment, in a 2023 article. Macrophages live in most tissues, body cavities and mucosal surfaces. They form a core part of the innate immune system, eating germs and shaping later immune responses.

The review gathers what is known about how these cells switch between attack and repair states, and how that switching affects disease. It also surveys treatments that aim to steer macrophages in cancer, infection and chronic inflammation. Such steering is a growing drug strategy.
pmc-10652702:
The EFSA Panel on Food Additives and Flavourings checked the safety of Smoke Concentrate 809045, a beech wood smoke product sold as SF-003. The opinion supports a ruling on whether to renew its licence as a food flavouring in the European Union.

The panel found the product description sound and estimated dietary exposure at up to about 5 mg per kilogram of body weight per day for heavy users. However, eleven components raised possible genotoxicity concerns, as did part of the unknown mixture. Two of them showed genotoxic effects in living animals at levels above the safety threshold. The panel therefore found that the product raises concern with respect to gene damage.
pmc-10654502:
Yanan Hu and co-authors test whether daily melatonin, taken before any crisis, can shield the brain when the heart stops. Brain damage after cardiac arrest decides most survivors' fate, yet preventive drugs for high-risk patients stay unexplored. Melatonin is a cheap supplement with cell-guarding traits.

Rats got daily melatonin shots for two weeks before a staged arrest and resuscitation. Treated rats survived at about twice the rate of untreated ones a day later. Their hippocampus, the memory hub, showed less cell death and fewer death-path proteins. Power plants inside cells kept their shape, charge, and breathing better under melatonin. The hormone lifted a repair protein and calmed swelling switches, while cell cleanup flows steadied. The authors frame supplements as buying time for the brain.
pmc-10655402:
Su-Fei Huang, Bow-Yin Wang, and Jung-Yu Liao explore how nurses and aides care for dementia residents with sundown syndrome. Sundowning brings growing confusion and unrest late in the day. The study uses a person-centered care model, which treats each resident as an individual.

The team ran focus groups with twenty-nine staff in four accredited dementia care units in Taiwan. Six themes emerged, grouped under one core idea: commitment. Practices included preparing oneself, not suppressing the resident, diverting attention, calming, keeping contact steady, and working as a team. The authors offer these habits as training material for long-term care homes that want better dementia care.
pmc-10656402:
Mitja Rupreht and co-authors issued a correction in 2023 to a survey on radiology training in Europe. The survey covered how subspecialty training in imaging is approved across countries. The correction fixes two faults in the first version. One fault left out a key endorsement that should have been declared.

The notice states that a European board diploma in interventional radiology had backing from the European Society of Radiology. Counts tied to that backing rise by one in the results and in a key table. The chart based on that table is updated as well. Corrections like this keep the published record clear and honest.
pmc-10656502:
Le-Cheng Wang and three co-authors forge gamma-amino acid building blocks in a single step. Their 2023 paper uses cobalt catalysis on simple starting parts. Gamma-amino acids appear in drugs and natural products alike. They also resist breakdown better than their alpha cousins.

The recipe mixes amides, alkenes, and carbon monoxide gas. A radical relay under cobalt joins them into complex products at once. The products carry varied useful groups for later chemistry. The same trick can decorate advanced molecules late in a synthesis. Peptide-like products are within reach of the method. One pot replaces what once took many steps.
pmc-10657002:
Li and a team including Li study shared drug targets in artery disease and lung cancer in twenty twenty-three. Heart disease and cancer share some risk factors and are top causes of death. Atorvastatin, a drug for atherosclerosis, may also have anti tumor effects. The team used network pharmacology to predict shared targets.

They gathered disease genes from large cancer and expression databases. Fifteen genes were common to both diseases. Four genes stood out as key targets for the drug in both conditions. Lab tests showed the drug slowed migration of lung cancer cells. It also lowered levels of those four genes in the cells. Tissue from treated patients showed the same pattern. The authors propose the four genes as shared targets.
pmc-10658902:
Lucy Davies and co-authors look inside the walls of a house to map the microbes that live hidden in its frame, in a study from 2023. Most indoor microbe studies sample surfaces or dust. The space inside a wall, called the building envelope, can also host fungi and bacteria, shaped by heat and damp that vary across a building.

The team drilled small holes across the walls and caught microbes on air filters for gene sequencing. Where a sample sat changed what they found. Height above the floor and the compass direction the wall faced both shifted the mix of species. The work warns that where you sample inside a building can bias what a study claims to find.
pmc-10669802:
Anila Duni and colleagues tracked a tiny RNA marker in dialysis patients in two thousand twenty-three. Heart events strike this group notoriously often. Risk prediction in them remains challenging. The RNA fragment regulates fat and sugar metabolism. It was recently linked to heart disease development. Several centers joined this forward-looking pilot study.

Patients showed lower marker levels than healthy controls. Liver enzymes and heart measures predicted its levels. Inflammation markers pulled in the opposite direction. Over two years, many patients hit the combined bad outcome. Those patients started with higher marker levels. Baseline levels predicted events significantly afterward. A simple blood measure may sharpen dialysis risk checks.
pmc-10671402:
David García-García and co-authors studied how health knowledge relates to healthy living among primary care patients in the Madrid region of Spain, in a 2023 study. The team measured general health literacy, digital health literacy, and lifestyle with three standard questionnaires given to adults who needed nursing care at a local center. The head byline names three authors, while the catalog record lists a fourth, so the description uses team framing.

Only some parts of the two knowledge scales tied to a healthy lifestyle, and most ties were weak. Two dimensions stood out as positive predictors: one about actively managing health, and one about using digital tools with confidence. The authors say the findings help show which kinds of knowledge most support daily healthy habits, guiding where clinics should focus teaching effort.
pmc-10671902:
Jiayu He and eight co-authors test a medical ceramic made by microwave heating instead of the usual furnace methods. Silicon nitride is a hard ceramic that resists germs and suits bone implants. Their 2023 study checks whether the microwave route keeps those virtues while improving strength.

Under the microscope, the microwave-made ceramic showed a porous structure. Strength tests favored it over standard versions. Cells grown on it stayed healthy and spread well, with no toxic effects in lab assays. It also fought two common bacteria, Staphylococcus aureus and Escherichia coli, about as well as ceramic made the standard way. The authors see strong implant potential in the cheaper, faster method, though more work is needed.
pmc-10672602:
Zhichao Cheng, Ji-Chuan Kang, and five co-authors study soil fungi in a northern forest after fire. Their paper, from twenty twenty-three, uses plots burned at light, medium, and heavy levels ten years before. One plot never burned and serves as the base case. Fungi matter here because they rot dead matter and feed trees.

The team read fungal DNA from the soil to name who lives there. Total variety held steady, but the mix shifted with burn strength. Two groups, Cortinarius and Tomentella, grew dominant after fire. Soil traits changed by fire help explain the new mix. The work shows fire leaves a long mark under the forest floor.
pmc-10672802:
Emilie Benson and co-authors used light to watch the brain during heart bypass surgery in newborn pigs, in a 2023 study. Bypass machines keep blood and oxygen moving during heart repair, but their effect on the newborn brain is unclear. Two light-based tools tracked blood flow, oxygen use, and metabolism in the brain. The team also sampled brain fluid markers of stress and injury.

Twenty-seven young pigs were watched before, during, and for a day after bypass. A correction for changes in blood thickness proved vital: without it, oxygen use seemed to jump in ways that cannot be real. With the fix, flow and metabolism fell as bypass wore on, and injury markers rose for hours. The trends cleared by the next day, and the correction sharpened the whole picture.
pmc-10673202:
Huan Meng and co-authors show how a protease from the COVID virus damps a key alarm system inside immune cells, in work from 2023. The NLRP3 inflammasome triggers a fiery cell death that releases alarm signals. In late COVID it can drive a harmful cytokine storm, yet early in infection the virus benefits from muting it.

Gene checks in blood cells from patients showed eight alarm related genes turned down. Lab work traced the effect to the viral papain like protease. It cut the clumping and tagging of ASC, a core adapter of the alarm complex. With that step blocked, alarm output and the fiery death both fell. The finding maps one route of immune evasion.
pmc-10674402:
Kailang Sun and co-authors turn a common clay into a layered support for palladium catalysts, in a materials paper from 2023. The clay, montmorillonite, was propped open with pillars of mixed aluminum and manganese oxides. Chains of one of two nitrogen-rich polymers were then slipped between the layers.

The treated clay gained wide layer gaps, high surface area, and large pore volume, all tunable by recipe. Palladium particles loaded onto it drove coupling reactions between ring compounds and carbon chains. The version with the natural polymer chitosan beat the synthetic polymer version overall. The authors credit its larger area, stronger grip on the metal, and better resistance to solvents. The work offers a cheap, sturdy base for metal catalysts.
pmc-10674602:
Yanan Wang and co-authors hunt for the genes behind drying sensitivity in Panax notoginseng seeds in a 2023 paper. This plant, long used in East Asian medicine for blood and heart conditions, makes recalcitrant seeds that die when dried and cannot be stored for long. Little was known about the genes that drive that weakness.

The team built gene libraries from fresh seeds and drying seeds and read them with Illumina sequencing. The data yielded over fifty-five thousand assembled genes, and more than twelve thousand genes changed activity during drying. Many sat in core metabolism, hormone signaling, fatty acid handling, and protective pathways. The dataset gives seed biologists a rich resource for understanding, and perhaps easing, storage losses.
pmc-10675702:
Francisco Llorente and co-authors show that the choice of antibody test skews COVID-19 exposure surveys in a 2023 study. The team followed essential workers in Madrid who were exposed in the first wave. Eleven detection methods were compared on blood taken in April 2020.

Most enzyme-based tests and one automated method performed well, while a rapid test and one automated method lagged. Of the workers positive in April, samples at two and seven months were retested with five methods. Some tests kept finding the antibodies months later, while one lost sensitivity as antibodies matured. Recalibrating its cutoff restored much of the loss. The authors warn that survey estimates of past infection depend on the kit and its settings.
pmc-10684302:
Reenika Aggarwal and co-authors use full geriatric review to surface care goals in a frailty clinic. Their 2023 study covers more than three hundred community-dwelling older adults sent to a Canadian clinic over four years. Many older adults never help shape their own care plans, though doing so brings clear gains. The review spans health, function, mind, and social ground, letting patients name what matters most.

Mobility topped the worry list, named by most patients. Services and pain came next, then self-care at home. Top actions were doctor follow-up, a falls clinic referral, and drug changes. The authors back team-based review to fit care to each frail patient.
pmc-10686002:
Anneke van Houwelingen, Theo Wubbels, and three co-authors turn drug kinetics lessons into an escape room. Their study, from twenty twenty-three, builds the game for bachelor students. Puzzles encode how the body absorbs and clears drugs. Forty-one students joined, and twenty-eight finished both before and after surveys.

A standard inventory measured the room's motivational climate. Situational interest rose with a solid effect size. Open answers echoed that gain in engagement. Students, though, doubted the room's worth as a test of knowledge. The authors suggest adding a control group next time. They also urge study of real grade effects.
pmc-10686602:
Lingling Zhu and co-authors review nano-scale strategies that reshape the tumor immune environment to fight lung cancer spread, published in 2023. Lung cancer kills largely through metastasis, a dynamic, multi-step process with no effective preventive therapy in the clinic. Immunotherapy can reverse the suppressive network around tumors, but resistance arises from poor delivery and uncontrolled immune activation.

Nanocarriers can improve how drugs dissolve, penetrate, and persist, and can deliver them steadily and on target. That helps overcome resistance while sparing healthy organs from inflammation. The review sorts strategies by the stage of spread they attack: escape of cells from the primary tumor, travel through the blood, and preparation of distant sites for colonization. The authors see targeted nanomedicine immunotherapy as a promising route against metastasis.
pmc-10687202:
Philipp Maier and four co-authors bounce helium atoms off a layered crystal to read its surface, in a 2023 study. The crystal, 1T-TaS2, hosts a charge-density wave, a frozen ripple of electrons that shapes its behavior.

Helium scattering is gentle enough to touch only the topmost atoms. It measured how strongly electrons and lattice vibrations trade energy, a coupling at the heart of superconductivity. The value in the wave phase, about 0.59, dwarfed a comparison material's 0.09. Diffraction patterns gave the surface's thermal expansion, step heights, and the shape of the atom-surface potential. The surface's electronic waviness resembled that of semimetals. Such numbers anchor theories of the material's phases.
pmc-10687902:
Yang Nan and colleagues show a steppe grass shrugging off low calcium in its roots, in work from 2023. Leymus chinensis rules Inner Mongolian steppe, where soils can run low on calcium. Model plants wilt under calcium shortage, with membranes leaking and growth stalling fast.

The grass seedlings grew unmoved, with root uptake and membrane selectivity intact under shortage. Its membrane fat ratio, a stability gauge, ran five times the model plant level. No major fat class shifted under shortage, unlike the model plant pattern. Damage marks fell and defence enzymes rose, the mirror image of model replies. A unique membrane recipe may underwrite the grass's wide range.
pmc-10690802:
Maria Chrysina and co-authors present a 2023 study on the water-splitting heart of photosynthesis. A manganese cluster in Photosystem II cycles through five states as it strips electrons from water. The last stable state before oxygen release is disputed: is the stored charge on the metals or on oxygen? Crystal studies have been read both ways.

The team used a sharp X-ray method on clean samples of every state. Quantum chemistry helped assign each spectral feature to a structure. The verdict: no peroxo or oxyl group sits in the key state. All stored charge rests on the manganese ions through every watched step. Oxygen-oxygen bonding must wait for the final flash of light. The result narrows how the enzyme's last act can run.
pmc-10691702:
Genes that switch on together across the body may share control systems, and comparing those patterns between tissues can expose them. Madison Russell and four co-authors built a multi-layer gene network in 2023 from four exocrine gland tissues to hunt for such groups.

Each layer of the network held one tissue's co-expression map, and the team wrote methods to find communities that span layers or sit in just one. They found five groups shared across tissues and two confined to a single tissue. Some groups' genes also sat physically close on chromosomes one and eleven, more than chance allows. That clustering hints at shared regulatory machinery written into the genome's layout.
pmc-10692102:
Eve-Line Bancel and co-authors published a physics paper in 2023 demonstrating an all-fiber light source that emits three frequency combs at once. Triple-comb methods can watch complex systems change almost in real time, but laser-based setups are rigid and hard to synchronize. Their source broadens three modulator-made combs inside a three-core fiber, locking them together through the fiber itself.

Stability checks and paired-comb tests confirmed the combs stay mutually coherent. A two-dimensional pump-probe experiment mixing four waves proved the point in practice. The design frees comb spacing from laser limits and drops complex electronics. The authors see wide use for precise, fast spectroscopy of changing systems.
pmc-10693302: Lili Tian, Maochen Li, and Huahao Fan report a short finding from 2023 on how flu viruses slip past a human defense. A protein in human cells, BTN3A3, can block influenza A viruses from copying themselves. The team shows that a single change at one spot in the virus's nucleoprotein, or matching changes at a nearby spot, lets the virus escape that block. Such escape changes matter because they may help animal flu viruses infect people.
pmc-10693602:
Mingze He and co-authors (2023) show how to tune waves of light and vibration that travel inside layered materials. These waves, called hyperbolic phonon polaritons, squeeze long-wavelength light into tiny spaces. Their behavior depends on the material beneath the layer, but metal and glass supports offer little control. The team instead placed boron nitride on doped semiconductors such as indium arsenide and cadmium oxide. The doping level sets how the support responds, which shifts the waves.

Near-field imaging showed tuning as large as eightfold as the support changed. Shining light on the indium arsenide injected extra carriers and shifted the wave pattern by about twenty percent on the spot. That gives a live control knob, not just a fixed design choice. The authors present the platform as a route to adjustable infrared devices, sensors, and other systems built on these confined waves.
pmc-10693702:
Sijie Yu, Yuhan Zhang, Chongkai Shen, and Fei Shao review drug treatments for bulimia nervosa in this 2023 analysis. The illness involves cycles of binge eating and purging, and several drug types have been tried against it. The team pooled results from randomized trials found in major medical databases.

Thirty-three studies covering eleven drugs were included, spanning older antidepressants, newer ones, mood drugs, and seizure drugs. As a group, the drugs reduced binge eating and vomiting episodes more than placebo. Weight and low mood also improved slightly. Dropouts from side effects did not differ clearly. The authors note that each drug helps different symptoms, and overall effects were modest.
pmc-10693902:
Tong and coauthors ask if high body weight dulls response to COVID infection. Severe obesity is known to blunt vaccine response a lot. What mid-range weight does to infection response stayed unclear. The team took blood from adults who had recovered from infection.

Samples came at about 3 months and 13 months after illness. No one in that span had new exposure or a vaccine. A next group gave blood five months after dose two. Antibody levels were gauged in all samples. High weight tracked with weaker antibody response in the sets. The work may shape vaccine plans for adults with high weight.
pmc-10694302:
Maartje Hereijgers and a large team asked whether tests already done before a heart procedure can reveal hidden lung problems, in a study from twenty twenty-three. The patients had an irregular heartbeat condition and were set for a catheter treatment. Limited airflow from the lungs can worsen outcomes, yet these patients are not routinely checked for it.

Handheld breathing tests found limited airflow in a quarter of the patients, and most of those cases were new. Heart scans already on file often showed lung damage or thickened airways in these patients. A clean scan, in turn, made normal lung function likely. Other heart and sleep tests added little. The authors suggest using the scans to flag who needs full lung checks.
pmc-10695502:
Baricitinib, a drug that damps inflammation, was a candidate for the worst cases of COVID-19, and Wenxin Song and co-authors pool the trial evidence. They searched the literature through the end of 2022 for studies comparing the drug with standard care in severe disease, then combined the results with a fixed-effects model.

Patients on baricitinib died less often and needed mechanical ventilation less often than controls. Hospital stays were no shorter, and serious side effects were no more common. The authors conclude the drug earns a place in treating severe COVID-19, balancing a real survival benefit against a safety record that matched standard care. Their review is a meta-analysis, so its strength rests on the trials beneath it, which varied in design and setting.
pmc-10695902:
Lupus can strike skin, joints, kidneys, and more, from childhood through old age, and care guidance has not kept pace. Md Yusof and a large guideline team set out the scope of a new British Society for Rheumatology guideline covering the whole life course. It updates the 2017 adult guideline and adds children and teenagers, organ-specific treatment, and daily management, with patients among its target readers.

The document explains what the finished guideline will cover, from diagnosis and monitoring to drug and non-drug care, including newer approved therapies. It also names the strict process the team will follow. The scope itself is the plan, published ahead of the full recommendations.
pmc-10696002:
Yasa Baig and co-authors use neural nets to squeeze germ growth paths into few-score forms. The study appeared in 2023. Growth paths of germ mixes are rich and hard to sum in few terms. A net that codes and then rebuilds its input can learn such a squeeze on its own.

The squeezed forms rebuilt the raw growth paths with high faith. On tasks such as strain ID and drug fight calls, they did as well as the raw data or beat it. They also called how mixes would grow next. Key growth facts fit in far fewer scores than past hand-built models need.
pmc-10696802:
Kidneys recover unevenly after a blood-flow cutoff, and males fare worse than females. Riyaz Mohamed and Jennifer Sullivan test whether an enzyme called 12/15 lipoxygenase drives that gap. They injured the kidneys of hypertensive rats for half an hour, then tracked a week of recovery in both sexes.

Males recovered slowly, with the enzyme switched on, its fat product raised, and more cell stress, death, and inflammation. Females showed far less of all of it. A drug blocking the enzyme lowered the fat product in males and sped their recovery toward the female pattern. The 2023 study names sustained enzyme activity as a male-specific brake on healing.
pmc-10699602:
Nongluck Jaito and co-authors hunt through DNA from natural environments for new fat-cutting enzymes shaped like a famous industrial one, in a 2023 study. The template enzyme, from the yeast Candida antarctica, is a workhorse catalyst, and cousins with the same shape might bring fresh traits. The team screened metagenomic data by sequence and by predicted structure.

Two bacterial enzymes matched the template's shape while sharing under 40 percent of its sequence. After partial purification, one behaved much like the template, working best at pH 8 and 50 degrees. The second liked it hotter, peaking at 55 degrees, and kept working at 70 degrees or pH 9 where the template faded. The authors say fuller tests should follow.
pmc-10700502:
A large team of German researchers compared babies and mothers seen at a clinic before and after the first COVID-19 lockdown, in a study published in 2023. Lockdowns brought illness fears and isolation that may have strained mothers and their bond with infants. The team reviewed interviews on the mental health of mothers and children, plus ratings of how each pair interacted. Both groups came from the same clinical population.

Sleep problems in infants stood out more in the group seen after lockdown began. Panic and anxiety also rose among mothers in that later group. A mother's panic linked to her child's sleep trouble in the pooled results. Before lockdown, a mother's warmth seemed to guard children against such problems, but that guard looked weaker afterward. The authors say the findings show how a crisis can ripple through the youngest children in a family.
pmc-10701302:
Chang Woo Chae, Young Hyun Jung, and Ho Jae Han review how a gene switch in lysosomes shapes stem cell fate under stress. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-three. Stem cells need much energy to copy themselves and to turn into many cell types. When food or energy runs low, that stress can push them to rest, renew, or mature.

Lysosomes are the cell's bins, where worn parts are broken down and reused. A switch called TFEB, with its kin TFE3, turns on the genes that run those bins. The review sums up how the switch is ruled, and how its work in the bins steers stem cell fate when metabolism is stressed.
pmc-10704102:
Abdulla Kamashki and co-authors report a liver mass that turned out to be anaplastic thyroid cancer in a 2023 case paper. This cancer is harsh and fast, and it most often shows up in the neck, not far organs.

A woman in her late sixties came in with jaundice and breath trouble, with scans showing spread to liver, lungs, glands, kidneys, and brain. A guided liver biopsy gave the first firm diagnosis. Stain tests fit a sarcoma-like form of anaplastic thyroid cancer. She died within days of the diagnosis. The case shows that wide-spread disease can still be named exactly when biopsy, cell study, and stain patterns are read together with care.
pmc-10704702:
Mario Della Mura and co-authors report a breast tumor of a rare kind that also carried a growth gene fault, in a 2023 case report. The tumor type mimics a salivary gland cancer and is almost always negative for the usual hormone markers. Only sixty-four cases had been written up.

A fifty-eight year old woman returned twenty years after breast cancer treatment with a new growth in the same breast. Microscope study of the removed tumor showed the type's three cell kinds, yet gene tests found the growth receptor doubled, a first for this cancer. Gene fusion checks were negative. She went on to receive drug therapy aimed at that receptor.
pmc-10704802:
Mulu Lemlem and co-authors survey, in a 2023 study, drug-resistant gut bacteria on chicken farms in Malaysia. The bacteria, Escherichia coli, were tested for resistance to colistin, a last-resort antibiotic long used in farm animals. Heavy farm use has driven resistance up, and the team wanted the molecular picture in broiler chickens and their surroundings.

They collected 453 samples from six farms and isolated the bacteria from most of them. About one in ten isolates carried one or more colistin resistance genes, and just over half of those resisted the drug in lab tests too. Every gene-carrying isolate resisted several drug classes. The most common resistance gene was mcr-1, with six other mcr types also found. The authors frame the results as a warning for farm drug use and food safety.
pmc-10705802:
Marta Liliane de Vasconcelos and co-authors test whether a stack of daily stresses cuts milk output in goats in this 2023 study. Heat, handling, and weather each nudge a dairy animal, but their combined drag was unclear in a warming climate. Thirty lactating Saanen goats were split into a calm control group and a stressed group.

The stressed goats faced a different challenge on each of four straight days: heat, a stress hormone dose, hoof care handling, and rain exposure. Their body temperature and breathing rate rose, and blood stress markers climbed. Genes in the udder tissue tied to stress response, inflammation, and antioxidant defense switched on more strongly. In the end the stressed goats gave less milk, and their milk carried more somatic cells, a sign of udder strain. The authors confirm that separate small stresses add up to a real production loss.
pmc-10706102:
Twelve authors chart food traits of bay scallops by shell hue and growth month in 2023. The shellfish holds high food and trade worth, yet hue-based food data stay thin. Harm marks, food parts, and taste parts were read month by month in the runs.

Harm counts sat under safe caps through growth in all hues. Month shifts beat hue shifts for food and taste parts in the reads. August gave best taste, while fall months gave top food worth. In fall, gold shells led on food parts and purple shells on taste.
pmc-10707602:
Bridget Bailey and co-authors survey how rural health care workers held up during the COVID-19 pandemic, in a 2023 paper. The team asked faculty, clinicians, and staff at a rural university about compassion fatigue, the wear of caring, and compassion satisfaction, its rewarding counterpart. They also asked which wellness resources workers used and which they wished existed. Four hundred six people answered in late 2020.

Fatigue ran high, satisfaction ran higher, and 42 percent screened positive for depression or anxiety. Few workers used the wellness resources already on offer. Their top wish, named by seven in ten, was simply time off, followed by on-site food trucks and support animals. Younger workers and those with depression or anxiety reported the worst fatigue, while older age and resilience protected satisfaction. The authors advise rural employers to guard time off, expand mental health care, and build resilience.
pmc-10707902:
Amy Barnett and co-authors feed iron-fortified lentils to teenage girls in Bangladesh and test their minds. Iron lack is rife in South Asia and dulls thinking. Their 2023 trial runs four months inside a larger community study. In all, 359 girls at rural clubs were split three ways: fortified lentils, plain lentils, or no supplied lentils. The lentil groups ate about 200 grams cooked, five days a week.

Five thinking tasks were run at the start and end. Blood marks of iron were tracked beside them. By the end, the fortified group beat both other groups on at least one score in nearly every task. The team reads the gain as iron at work, not lentils alone. School-age fortification gets a boost from the result.
pmc-10709302:
Daisuke Taniguchi and co-authors test a cell free airway patch in pigs in a 2023 study. Rebuilding damaged airways needs grafts that the body accepts, and stripped donor tissue is one hope. The team took left bronchi from stripped pig lungs and sewed them into windpipe windows in live pigs.

All pigs woke and lived to their set end points with no airway block. By one month the graft had knit into host tissue and grown a lining layer on its face. Immune marks in the graft matched calm tissue at two months. Strength dipped at one month but came back by two. The grafts look fit for patch repair trials.
pmc-10709402:
Tianyuan Gan and five co-authors present a 2023 paper on finding polyps in the colon with less hand labeling. Polyps are small growths that can turn into cancer, and doctors look for them during colonoscopy. Most smart tools need many images labeled by experts, which takes much time and cost.

Their method, called FPSiam, learns from unlabeled video first. A pyramid part joins fine local detail with broad scene features, and a twin network learns what colon images look like in general. That learned skill then moves to the polyp task. In tests on a large video set, the method beat other self-taught methods and beat transfer learning by a clear margin. It offers a cheaper path for clinics with few labeled images.
pmc-10709902:
David Boettiger and co-authors count the bill that age will bring to Saudi health care by 2030, in a study from 2023. The land's old share will near double in the span. Ten long ills ride that wave: heart, stroke, sugar, lung, kidney, mind, mood, joint, and two cancers.

Age and sex curves for each ill were run forth year by year. Care rates and per-soul costs from the press then turned counts to coin. What-ifs on spread, care reach, and cost test the sums. First reads show steep climbs for some ills, bowel cancer and stroke in the part of the head shown here. The purse moral: plan wards and funds now, ere the wave bills come due.
pmc-10711002:
Sungsoon Hwang and co-authors present a 2023 study of gene linked retinal decay in Korean patients. One gene, PROM1, can drive the slow loss of light sensing cells. The team set out to map the gene forms and eye traits of such cases at one Seoul center.

Charts of dystrophy patients tested between 2016 and 2023 were reviewed. Seven patients from five unrelated families carried a harmful PROM1 form, and all seven shared the same one. All showed decay in the central retina, and five had decay at the edges too. The span of decay varied much, even inside one family. Wide field scans caught mild edge decay that plain exams missed.
pmc-10711902:
Somalee Banerjee and co-authors measured what happened when a health system's computer records began prompting doctors to offer nicotine therapy to smokers in hospital. The prompts fired when a smoker was admitted and again at discharge, inside a large care system in northern California with over four million members. Hospital stays are a prime chance to help smokers quit.

The study used records from before and after the prompts began in 2015, comparing trends over time. It tracked whether therapy was ordered, whether patients filled it, and whether they later quit or returned to hospital. Built-in prompts cost little and reach every ward at once. The results show whether such quiet nudges change real outcomes, not just ordering habits.
pmc-10712102:
Lv and co-authors build a virus that delivers genes mainly to breast cancer cells. Their carrier is a changed AAV2 virus fitted with a targeting piece called a DARPin. The DARPin, named EC1, homes in on EpCAM, a marker found on many breast cancer cells.

The team tested how specific the carrier was and how well it fought tumors. Tests ran both in cell cultures and in living models. The goal is a treatment aimed at EpCAM-positive breast cancer that spares healthy tissue. Targeted delivery could cut side effects that come with broad cancer drugs.
pmc-10712302:
Oto Nakladal, Eliska Havrankova, and Vaclav Zumr test whether the liquid inside beetle traps skews counts of beetle diversity, in a study from 2023. Window traps are a standard way to sample beetles, and studies fill them with liquids such as beer, wine, or vinegar. If one liquid draws more beetles, studies that use unlike liquids may not be fairly compared.

Twenty four traps were set in sunny and shady spots, split across four liquids with plain water as the baseline. Over two summer months in 2021, close to thirty thousand invertebrates were caught, of which almost four thousand were beetles from 120 species. Counts of most groups were alike for beer and wine, and alike for vinegar and water. The liquid choice did shift some results, the authors warn.
pmc-10713302:
Tomoo Kishaba reports a randomized trial of prone positioning for COVID-19 pneumonia patients on regular wards in a 2023 paper. Lying face down improves oxygen in critically ill patients on ventilators, a proven rescue in intensive care. Whether awake ward patients with low oxygen benefit was the open question.

Patients were assigned by chance to prone positioning or usual care. Standard drug care, antivirals and anti-inflammatory agents, continued in both arms. Ward-level proning is cheap and needs no equipment, so a clear benefit would spread fast in future surges. The trial design gives a fair answer rather than the biased picture from uncontrolled ward reports early in the pandemic.
pmc-10714202:
Ong Kim Le, Viorel Chihaia, and Do Ngoc Son study a thin sheet material for use in breath tests for disease, in a paper from 2023. Breath can carry gases linked to liver cancer, but a sensor needs a sheet that reacts to those gases in a clear way. The team used computer models to test a sheet called germanene, in perfect form and with one or two missing atoms.

The models covered five gases found in the breath of patients. Sheets with gaps held the gases more strongly than the perfect sheet, and one gas, phenol, bound most strongly of all. The gases changed the energy gap of the sheets in clear ways. The authors find that the perfect sheet and the sheet with two gaps stay in a state fit for sensing.
pmc-10714502:
Valentina Rosolen and six co-authors measure how well COVID-19 vaccines worked in northeast Italy, in this twenty twenty-three study. People's differing response to the Green Pass rules could skew such measures, so the team set out to control that bias.

They used a test-negative design, comparing vaccine history in people who tested positive with matched people who tested negative. Records covered more than two hundred thousand cases and over eight hundred thousand controls across about a year. Extra checks probed how far rule-following gaps could move the result. The study gives a careful read on vaccine performance in real life.
pmc-10716002:
Hexiang Wang and co-authors build a 2023 deep learning score from CT scans to predict whether bladder cancer will return after surgery. Sorting patients by return risk is core to tailoring care: high-risk patients need closer watch and stronger therapy. A scan-based score that beats stage and grade could sharpen that sort a good deal.

The team enrolled 874 patients across four centres over 15 years, training the model on one centre and testing it on the rest. The model read three-phase contrast CT images and gave each patient a risk score. That score sorted return risk with a strong joint score in the test set, ahead of a clinic model and the standard staging system. Cut-off splits also parted survival curves for both return-free and overall survival.
pmc-10716402:
Nicola Thibault, Philippe Albouy, and Simon Grondin study how the brain times short and long gaps between sounds, in a 2023 paper. Behavior tests hint that gaps under and over about 1.2 seconds are handled in distinct ways. The brain basis for that split was unclear. The team used scalp recordings to watch the split happen.

Twenty people listened to a stream of tones with set gaps. Rare tones broke the pattern with shorter or longer gaps. Brain responses were read at the scalp and traced to sources. A slow wave tied to timing appeared only for longer gaps. Its sources sat in timing and motor areas. Short gaps were flagged earlier by a different signal. The results support two timing systems in the brain.
pmc-10716502:
Sheng proposes a framework for rebuilding microservice systems in cloud native settings, aimed at metaverse-style workloads. Large online platforms are split into many small services, and operators must balance delay, load, and cost while keeping the system secure and able to handle heavy traffic.

The paper sets up a multi-objective optimization with a defined fitness function and limits that filter for good splitting and deployment choices. It also redesigns the circuit breaker that throttles failing services, adds live checks of protocol settings, and tracks heartbeat signals between services. Experiments reported in the paper claim the framework eases bottlenecks in high-concurrency finance and securities scenarios.
pmc-10717102:
Xiwu Liu and co-authors built a aimed drug carrier in 2023 for a throat cancer that grows behind the nose. The carrier is a tiny DNA cage, a tetrahedron, tied to a short DNA strand that homes to a mark on the cancer cells. A classic cancer drug rides inside the cage. The team tested the loaded cage on cancer cells in dishes and on tumors grown in mice.

The cage homed to the cancer cells and to tumor tissue, and it spared other cells much of the drug's harm. Loaded at the best mix, it freed its drug over two days. In mice it found the grafted tumors, slowed their growth, and left healthy tissue near whole. The team calls it a safe, aimed route for this cancer.
pmc-10717202:
Daniela Cabral de Sousa and colleagues compare thinking problems in lupus and rheumatoid arthritis, hunting for blood biomarkers that explain them. Thinking gaps in both diseases vary widely and are poorly known. The one-time study took in fifty lupus patients, twenty-nine arthritis patients, and thirty-two healthy controls. It gauged disease activity, quality of life, and cognitive tests with oxidative and inflammatory markers in blood.

The biomarker patterns split by disease. In lupus, higher levels of the antioxidant glutathione tracked having no thinking problems. That points to oxidative balance as a shield. In rheumatoid arthritis, higher interleukin-6, an inflammatory signal, came with dysfunction. Two autoimmune diseases with similar burdens thus produce thinking problems by different routes, one oxidative, one inflammatory. Biomarker panels and treatments will likely need to be set disease by disease.
pmc-10717402:
Yang Wang, Xinyang Cao, Zhijie Xu, and Hai Fang set out a plan for a broad review of primary care research done by practice-based research networks. The networks link real clinics to research teams, and the authors want to map what they have produced from 1991 to 2023. The work follows a known framework for scoping reviews.

Under the plan, two reviewers will search three large databases, plus key journals and hundreds of related groups. They will screen each paper on their own, pull out data on eight points, and settle any clash by group talk. Charts and tables will then show patterns in output, topics, and methods over time.
pmc-10717502:
Jeongok Park and three co-authors sweep, in 2023 work, what is known of drip-rate slips in vein drug care. Vein drugs are a daily ward act, and wrong drip pace is a known harm root, yet the shelf of proof was unsorted. Twenty-two studies fed the sweep.

Slip roots sort three ways: the person, the build, and the house. Person roots span thin facts, weak acts, and wrong sums. The build root is the gear. House roots span breaks and noise, drills, thin staff, rules, and talk. Two of nine tried fixes cut slips. The team calls for fresh fix work as gear grows.
pmc-10719102:
Health studies often miss the very groups who carry the most illness, and Ameeta Retzer and co-authors built a toolkit to fix that gap, in work from twenty twenty-three. Groups left out can be rare in studies, heavy in care needs, or poorly reached by clinics. The toolkit came from a review of past methods plus a workshop of two dozen people.

Seven steps guide study teams, from naming the groups left out to setting fair share goals for the sample. Teams also plan how to handle outside blocks, how to check the final mix, and what legacy the study leaves. The authors argue fair samples build trust and make study results hold for the wider public, not just for easy-to-reach groups.
pmc-10722302:
William Coleman and Leah McCartney study nerve signals in earthworm muscle, in a 2023 paper. The worm's body wall muscle gets both go and stop inputs, which makes it a handy model for nerve work. Past work looked at stop signals acting after the nerve ending. The pair asked whether the chemical GABA also acts before the ending, to cut the signal at its source.

They loaded a glowing dye into the small packets that nerves use to send signals. With GABA present, the glow at the muscle junctions dropped by a clear amount. That drop means fewer packets were primed for release. The authors read the result as proof that GABA can brake the signal at the sending side as well. The finding adds a detail to how simple nerve circuits balance go and stop cues.
pmc-10725202:
Sanjula Singh and co-authors tested whether a simple brain care score predicts later dementia and stroke in a huge British cohort, in work published in 2023. The twenty one point score rewards habits and health choices that protect the brain. Data came from about four hundred thousand adults followed for a middle span of twelve and a half years.

A five point higher score went with much lower risk of both outcomes. The gain was largest in the youngest group for dementia, at about fifty nine percent lower risk. Stroke risk fell by about a third to a half across age groups. The authors say the score has clear clinical value, and they plan work on how to use it in care worldwide.
pmc-10728602:
Zhuge and co-authors ask parents what matters most when young children need sedation for dental work, in this 2023 study. The team used a choice experiment, offering parents bundles of options that varied on six features. Those features included fasting time, recovery time, how the drug is given, side effects, depth of sedation, and cost.

One hundred eighty-six parents completed the survey. Avoiding side effects mattered most by a wide margin, followed by keeping sedation light rather than deep. Parents also favored lower cost, shorter fasting and recovery, and inhaled delivery. Anxious parents weighed side effects and fasting even more heavily. The results give dentists a ranked list for family talks.
pmc-10729002:
Jia-jia Huang and colleagues test early heparin in cancer patients with sepsis. Their causal analysis from twenty twenty-three uses an intensive care database. Heparin thins blood and may also slow tumour spread. Its effect on survival in this exact group was unclear.

Over fifteen hundred patients with solid tumours and sepsis qualified. About half received early heparin treatment. Advanced models handled changing confounders over time. Intensive care deaths, clots, and hospital deaths were tracked. Several statistical approaches cross-checked the main result. Matching balanced the groups before outcome comparisons. The study design squeezes causal answers from routine data. Results can inform a proper randomised trial.
pmc-10729102:
Wei Wang and co-authors study how screen time, sleep, and mental health fit together for university students shut in by COVID-19 rules. Their 2023 study comes from Nanjing, where an airport outbreak in the summer of 2021 pushed campuses into closed management and online classes. The shift hit students' daily lives and mood.

A web survey gathered 1,070 valid replies. Set scales scored sleep quality, low mood, anxiety, and loneliness. More than half of the students showed signs of depression on the scale used. The team built models that adjust for side traits, then tested whether poor sleep sits in the middle of the path from long screen hours to poor mental health.
pmc-10730202:
Samira A. Hamed and colleagues published a 2023 laboratory study on protecting the gut lining from a harmful strain of E. coli linked to Crohn's disease. The invading bacteria break up the energy-producing networks inside gut cells, which weakens the barrier between the gut and the body. The team tested whether butyrate, a fatty acid made by helpful gut microbes, could prevent that damage.

In human gut organoids and a gut cell line, butyrate reduced the bacterial damage, preserved cell energy function, and changed how the bacteria themselves used fuel. A specific fatty acid receptor on the cells played a role. The findings support gut-made chemicals as possible therapy ingredients.
pmc-10733902:
Grammatikos, Svoliantopoulos, and Gizeli present a naked eye test for amplified DNA in saliva, in work from twenty twenty-three. LAMP is a simple molecular method that copies DNA at one temperature, ideal for point of care use. Reading its result in a crude sample like saliva, without instruments, is the hard part.

Gold nanoparticles capped with chitosan change color when amplified target is present. The particles were made by a green chemistry route. The single tube assay could visualize even a single target copy in saliva, the authors report. A color change readable by eye makes home or clinic testing far cheaper.
pmc-10734002:
Kristof Stagel, Laura Ielo, and Katharina Bica-Schröder present a continuous method for making carbamates, a useful class of chemicals, directly from carbon dioxide and amines. Older routes are slow and need harsher steps. Their route uses a single basic additive and runs the reaction in a flowing stream rather than in batches.

Flow chemistry lets the gas be added precisely and cuts reaction time sharply. Many different amines work in the scheme, which gives the products a wide range. Yields ran from moderate to high, and the products needed no column purification. The same setup can be adjusted to make a related ring-shaped family from three-membered starting rings. Greener chemistry gains a practical tool here.
pmc-10734302:
Roberta Campardelli and co-authors chase a reliable formula for emulsion droplet size in a 2023 engineering paper. Rotor-stator mixers whip oil into water across food, cosmetic, and drug production, and the average droplet size once the emulsion settles decides texture and shelf life, yet predictions stay shaky.

The team made oil-in-water emulsions with three oils, several mix ratios, and varied rotor speeds, then fitted a model built on dimensional analysis. Their correlation weighs viscous, inertial, and surface tension forces inside the turbulent regime the mixer creates. Checked against published models, the new formula held up well, offering process engineers a sturdier design rule.
pmc-10735402:
Shekinah Fashaw-Walters studies home health agencies that serve many Black patients yet still earn top quality scores. Such agencies are often assumed to give poor care, much like hospitals or nursing homes with the same patient mix. The study came out in twenty twenty-three.

Medicare home health gives nursing and therapy care to millions of older adults at home each year. The project mixes counts with close case work, using star ratings and a public Medicare data file. It picks out high quality agencies with high shares of Black patients, then studies three of them in depth to learn how they give care.
pmc-10735502:
Francesca Falzarano, Rachel Bloom, Megan McCarthy, and Francesco Osso ask why caregivers of people with dementia so rarely use the formal services meant to help them. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-three. In the United States, family caregivers carry the long-term care system on their backs. Services exist, yet referrals often fail to turn into use.

The team drew on a mixed-methods study of forty-six caregivers. Across every service type asked about, at least half the group reported no use. Barriers named included low trust, safety worries, rigid schedules, and cost. Spouses viewed services more dimly than adult children did. Heavier care loads, stronger early grief, and lower confidence all tracked with colder attitudes. The authors argue that fixing attitudes and trust is as vital as fixing supply.
pmc-10735602:
Fayron Epps and co-authors describe in 2023 a fully self-paced online program for dementia caregivers. Group training programs are proven to build caregiving skill and ease stress, yet many caregivers cannot attend live sessions because the person they care for needs constant presence. Their new version removes all live parts.

The program packs about sixteen hours into forty-six short interactive segments that caregivers open on their own schedule, with no classmates or live teacher. Twenty-nine caregivers finished the pilot and gave follow-up data. Caregiving mastery rose with a moderate to large effect, problem behaviors fell, and reactions to those behaviors softened. Depression, anxiety, and burden also eased modestly.
pmc-10735802: Jeong Eun Lee, Naomi Meinertz, and Tina Savla summarize a 2023 symposium on strength-based ways to help family caregivers. Caregiving is often framed only through strain and loss. The sessions instead highlight programs that build on what caregivers can do well. One session reports a person-centered course that cut depressive symptoms and raised confidence and emotion skills. Another shares early data from a live online program. The collection argues that support works better when it starts from caregiver strengths, not deficits alone.
pmc-10735902:
Margaret Avallone and co-authors describe training health workers to judge older adults' needs in this 2023 paper. Since 2019, a New Jersey program has worked with a nursing school and a support group at a low-cost housing site. Senior nursing students assess residents there to build skill and support aging at home.

Students worked in teams with social and community health workers and completed 92 resident assessments. The frame used covers what matters to the person, mind, medicines, and mobility, plus a fifth factor for complex need. On average residents had more than three risk factors. About nine in ten were classed as multi-complex and in need of services to stay at home.
pmc-10736202:
Maayan Agmon, Roy Tzemah-Shahar, and Tamar Shochat investigate the link between sleep and walking in this two thousand twenty-three study. Falls are a major danger for older adults, and people with sleep complaints face a much higher fall risk. Most earlier work studied older adults, so this team turned to community-dwelling midlife adults instead. They recruited just over one hundred participants with an average age near fifty-nine.

Gait was measured with a dual-task walking test using a mobility lab, while sleep was tracked by a week of actigraphy plus a standard sleep quality questionnaire. The researchers found that longer sleepers walked more slowly under the dual-task condition than shorter sleepers. The result hints that sleep and gait interact well before old age.
pmc-10736302:
Anna Rubtsova and seven co-authors study what blocks successful aging for older adults living with HIV, in a 2023 paper. Thanks to treatment, many people with HIV now reach old age. Yet aging well with the virus brings its own set of hurdles, and those hurdles may split by sex.

The team spoke at length with 31 adults aged 52 to 73 from sites in Atlanta, Brooklyn, and San Diego. Shared barriers spanned long-term illness, stigma, drug use, and thin resources. Men dwelt more on dread of old age and loneliness. Women stressed strain and the urge to give up.
pmc-10736502:
Ramraj Gautam, Karen Devereaux Melillo, Lisa Abdallah, and Patcharee Wangwun test whether talks with retired professors ease students' fear of aging, in a 2023 study. The work sits inside an age-friendly university drive that prizes learning across generations and drawing on a school's own retired staff. Teams of four or five undergraduates in a gerontology class held two hour-long video talks with emeriti professors.

Fifty-seven students took part, and thirty-one finished both the before and after surveys. After the talks, aging anxiety fell clearly, and hopes about their own aging rose. The authors read the result through a model that credits contact with positive older role models. Such simple sessions may soften age bias while students plan their careers.
pmc-10736602:
Denise Kropp and co-workers describe a team model that joins primary care with community services for older adults, in a 2023 paper. Health in old age depends heavily on social factors, so medical care alone is not enough. Their model brings aging agency case managers together with a care team.

The team, spanning nursing, social work, geriatric medicine, and pharmacy, meets weekly to plan care for complex cases. The meetings later grew to include remote agencies, a local health center, and a housing group. In an early set of cases the team found several medication issues per person. Falls, mood, and advance planning came up often.
pmc-10736702:
Amy Huang and co-authors wrote this 2023 review comparing guidelines on sedentary time for older adults. Most adults over 65 sit for more than 8.5 hours a day, a load tied to metabolic disease and falls. Many countries have issued guidance, but the advice had not been lined up side by side.

The team searched medical databases and grey literature for current guidelines in English. They found eight national and international sets and graded their quality with a standard tool. All rested on evidence rated low in quality and certainty. Terms for sitting time were used loosely and defined in clashing ways. Six sets advised cutting total sitting, one naming a limit under eight hours a day. Three suggested swapping sitting for light activity. The authors call for firmer ground under the advice.
pmc-10736802:
Emmanuel Garcia and Nicholas Reed link hearing loss to use of health care in two thousand twenty-three. They use a national study of older Medicare members living at home. Survey data were matched to claims records over six years. Hearing loss was based on aid use or trouble hearing in noise.

Each person with hearing loss was matched to a peer without it. The hearing loss group had more trips to the emergency room. They also spent more days in hospital over the six years. The count of hospital stays did not differ. The authors say aids or other help for hearing might cut use of care and its costs.
pmc-10736902:
Lun Li and co-authors study loneliness among Canadians over sixty-five who care for family. Their 2023 paper draws on over 6,600 older caregivers from a national aging study's second wave. Loneliness is a known risk of caregiving, yet it has drawn less study than burden or depression. The team asked which caregiving situations carry the most of it.

Three factors raised loneliness: caring for a spouse rather than another relative, caring more intensely, and caring for someone who lives elsewhere or in an institution rather than under the same roof. Two combinations stood out as the highest-risk groups: spouses caring intensely, and intense caregivers of someone in institutional care. The authors argue services should aim precisely there, since the loneliest caregivers are those whose loved one is both closest to them and, in the institutional case, physically out of reach.
pmc-10737002:
Chixiang Chen and co-authors build a claims-data method to find what shapes recovery at home after hip fracture in dementia patients, in this 2023 paper. Nearly 300,000 older Americans fracture a hip each year, and those with Alzheimer's or related dementia recover slowly. Patients value days spent at home, yet hospital quirks, uneven hospital sizes, and deaths can bias simple analyses.

Their approach uses unsupervised learning to handle those traps at once, and it behaved well in simulations. Applied to over sixteen thousand Medicare patients with dementia who fractured a hip in 2017 to 2019, it found clear signals. Older age, longer stays, more chronic conditions, and fewer home days before the break all meant fewer home days after. Older methods missed some effects entirely.
pmc-10737302:
Jing Wang, Bei Wu, and six co-authors study Chinese and Korean family caregivers of people with dementia. Their study, from twenty twenty-three, asks what these caregivers need most. It aims to adapt a proven support program from New York University for these two groups. The caregivers also live with more than one long-term health problem of their own.

The team spoke with fourteen Chinese and eleven Korean caregivers near New York City. Both groups said beliefs about family duty shape how they see dementia and care. The groups also differed in how they use family help and talk about self-care. The authors suggest phone and video tools can help caregivers link with support.
pmc-10737502:
Video visits boomed in rural clinics during the pandemic, yet older rural patients still sign on more slowly, often blocked by tech know-how. Revika Singh, Francesca Rosen, and Marquita Lewis-Thames set out to build a telehealth concierge for rural older cancer survivors, described in a 2023 report. Their design process puts the end users in charge through a community advisory board.

From mid-2022 the team found and contacted more than 30 community organizations across rural northern and central Illinois. Board members included a mental health professional, an older cancer survivor, and community members, oriented through in-person and virtual sessions. The board's task is to shape a navigation tool for survivors dealing with cancer-related distress. The report lays out the groundwork: who was recruited, how, and what the board will guide next.
pmc-10737602:
Sandra Zwakhalen, Silke Metzelthin, and Barbara Resnick introduce a symposium in 2023 on helping older adults stay active and able. As people age, function can decline and care needs grow. Nurses in homes, nursing homes, and hospitals often take over tasks that older people could still do, which can erode their remaining abilities.

The symposium presents studies from several countries and care settings that aim to change staff behavior. One trial tested a function focused care approach with over three hundred fifty patients. Another evaluated a program to support activity in Dutch nursing homes, with hundreds of staff and patients. A coaching program for people with dementia in primary care is also discussed.
pmc-10737702:
Jiawei Cao and Jialin Cui published this education study in 2023 on benevolent ageism, the kindly-seeming but patronizing bias toward older people. It is subtler than open prejudice and hard for students to spot in themselves. The authors tested a teaching approach in an entry-level gerontology class for healthcare majors. One class of 36 students got a semester of lectures, quizzes, videos, and group projects focused on the topic; a class of 43 got the regular course.

Both classes filled in an ageism questionnaire at the start and end of term. The groups began alike. By the end, the special class's benevolent ageism scores had fallen clearly, while the regular class's scores barely moved. The authors say the pedagogy looks useful for future healthcare workers. They add that randomized studies are needed to confirm the effect.
pmc-10737902:
Jeffrey Gregg and co-authors share in 2023 vet health plans to lift care for old vets with stacked body, mind, and mood ills. Old vets bear more calls than young vets or like age peers. Far homes and a dire lack of age care hands stack the bars.

Four plans take the stage. One builds a talk care for lung ill vets by screen. The next grows age mind care by screen for far homes. A third maps what helps or bars a team that steers ward exits and blocks re takes. The last rounds the set. Gains and reach form the shared tale.
pmc-10738002:
Benjamin Olivari and co-authors test how survey wording changes measured rates of self-reported memory decline in a 2023 study. Subjective cognitive decline can warn of future dementia, and a national survey module tracks it. Experts recently proposed simpler wording, but nobody knew how much the phrasing itself moves the numbers.

Over three thousand five hundred adults were randomly given either the old or the revised questions. Among adults generally, decline was reported by about nine percent with old wording and seventeen percent with new. Among those over forty-five, the new wording nearly doubled the old estimate, which matched prior national figures. Rates ran higher for poorer, less educated, and female respondents in both groups. The authors warn that trend lines break when questions change, however well meant the simplification.
pmc-10738102:
Carla Gomes da Rocha and seven co-authors published this study in 2023. It measures depressive symptoms in centenarians, people aged one hundred or more, during the COVID-19 pandemic. Almost nothing was known about mood at that extreme age, and lockdowns may have hit the very old hardest.

The Swiss study interviewed 171 centenarians, average age just under 102, plus family or care proxies, by phone between late 2020 and mid-2022. A short depression screen flagged about forty-four percent as possibly depressed, a higher share than in earlier studies of the very old. Women scored worse than men. Nursing home residents were more depressed than those living at home, despite similar health. The authors say mood screening should be routine in centenarian care, above all during crises that isolate them. They call for better support practices for this fast-growing age group.
pmc-10738702:
Hector Chavez and co-authors tested whether the placenta ages faster in a pregnancy illness marked by high blood pressure, in a study published in 2023. The placenta sits in a low oxygen setting early on, which can drive small changes in its genes over time.

The team read gene data from 84 placentas, from both healthy pregnancies and those with the illness. They counted rare gene changes per unit of DNA. In early onset cases, a higher count went with a shorter pregnancy. That group also carried a higher count than the other groups. The authors read this as a sign that the placenta in such cases ages ahead of schedule, which may help explain the illness.
pmc-10738802:
I-Ting Liu, a solo author, studies weak grip in older adults in a 2023 paper from Taiwan. Grip strength is a key sign of sarcopenia, the muscle loss that comes with aging and disease. Finding who sits at high risk could guide early help.

One hundred adults aged 65 or older at one hospital had a full geriatric check and a grip test between January 2022 and February 2023. Mood was screened with a short depression scale, and thinking with a short mental state quiz. Both low mood and impaired thinking linked to higher risk of poor muscle function. The two often travel together in old age, the author notes.
pmc-10739302:
Anasuya Guha and nine co-authors study inherited gene changes behind rare tumors of the head and neck in this 2023 paper. The tumors, called paragangliomas, are mostly benign. A gene named SDHD is the one most often mutated in families with the condition, yet the change can also appear when no family history is known, creating hidden familial cases.

The team analyzed one hundred five patients seen at two Czech centers between 2006 and 2021, and eighty were included in the final count. Only about twelve percent carried a germline SDHD change, lower than in many reports elsewhere. Roughly four in five of those carriers had no positive family history, and carriers more often had several tumors and were younger. One variant turned up in unrelated patients, though no founder effect was proven. The authors conclude the Czech mutation pattern differs from most countries studied.
pmc-10740502: Fengli Zhang and Michel Denis wrote a short 2023 editorial for a special issue. The issue covers small compounds made by microbes. It also covers compounds made when microbes meet a host. The note is brief and serves as a signpost, not a full research report. The editors say the issue holds thirteen papers. Authors come from more than ten countries. That spread hints at broad interest in these compounds for drugs, farming, and basic biology.
pmc-10740902:
Kostyuchenko and co-authors trace seed-cell genes in a small ring worm's growth. Seed line paths vary wide by kind and by growth stage. A held set of genes guards the seed line in most kinds. Those same genes mark cells that can form both flesh and seed. The team sought to learn how the worm sets its seed cells. They found 20 genes tied to seed and broad cell power. Gene kin span Vasa, Piwi, Nanos, Myc, and more clans.

Gene reads came from scan pools and clone work on worm bits. Dye tests showed where each gene acts in the worm. First seed cells seem to spring from small cells at two splits. Those splits hit the flesh-line lead cells in the young worm. Seed cells then clump, grow a bit, and walk to sex parts.
pmc-10741002:
Adina Fésüs and co-authors shared an audit in twenty twenty-three. It looks at how one Hungarian university hospital finds urinary tract infections. It looks at how the site picks the first antibiotic too. These infections are common. Staff often get the call wrong, and that wastes drugs. The team checked charts line by line. They used the European urology guidelines as the bar for both calls.

Of one hundred eighty-five patients, about forty-two percent did not meet the bar for the diagnosis. Some in that group were in fact misdiagnosed. Some had bacteria but no symptoms. That state needs no treatment most of the time. The label urosepsis, used at admission, often failed too. Symptoms and cultures did not back it up. The audit shows a wide gap at one internal medicine unit. What staff wrote down fell well short of the guideline bar.
pmc-10741402:
Qidi Shi and four co-authors probe, in a 2023 study, how the brain prepares a shot when sight or hearing is constrained. Light and noise both affect shooting performance, and trained shooters may show brain patterns unlike calm conditions under such strain. The team recorded electroencephalograph signals from 40 skilled marksmen during the preparation stage, under low light, noise interference, and a normal environment.

Average scores were 8.55 under normal conditions, 7.71 under visual restriction, and 8.50 under noise, so scores fell most in low light. Wave power in a slow band ran lower across frontal, side, and back head regions in noise than in the other two conditions. In low light, wave coupling between center, side, and back regions turned negative in a clear way. The authors say the patterns give a base for understanding how the brain copes with strain at the preparation stage.
pmc-10741602:
Male hormones help drive throat cancer spread, Cai and co-authors show in a 2023 study. The cancer type in view grows in the food pipe and strikes men far more than women. Past work showed the male hormone receptor can boost tumor growth. The new study asks if it can also switch on genes that aid spread.

One target gene was found that the receptor turns up with help from partner factors. That gene sped cell invasion in dishes and lymph node spread in animals. Blocking both the receptor and its partners cut invasion more than blocking either alone. The authors propose the gene as a marker and the pair as a drug target for this aggressive cancer.
pmc-10742002: Takehiro Uda wrote this short 2023 overview on brain imaging for surgery. The piece opens a journal section on imaging used in operations for brain tumors and epilepsy. Uda notes that surgeons must blend findings from many kinds of scans to make sound choices in the operating room. The hosted text gives only the opening lines, so the full scope of the section cannot be judged from it.
pmc-10742102: Katie Lovell, Lindsay Strowd, and Steven Feldman introduce a special issue from 2023 on skin care for children with psoriasis and atopic dermatitis. The editors give a broad look at where care for these two long-term skin diseases stands today. They point out the main problems doctors face when they treat young patients, and they note the recent steps forward that the papers in the issue cover in more detail.
pmc-10742402:
Sung Joon Park and co-authors published a 2023 study on a possible link between asthma and gum disease in Korean adults. Asthma is a long-term lung condition that narrows the airways. Periodontitis is a serious gum infection that can loosen teeth. Earlier hints suggested the two might travel together, but the evidence was mixed.

The team drew on a large Korean health study run from 2004 to 2016. They compared 2,521 adults with asthma against more than 130,000 without it. Gum disease was more common in the asthma group, at about thirteen percent versus seven percent. After adjusting for other factors, adults with asthma still had clearly higher odds of gum disease. The pattern held across age and sex groups. Oddly, the group whose asthma was well controlled showed the highest odds. The authors urge attention to oral health in asthma care.
pmc-10742602:
Dario Geißer and co-authors present a 2023 journal article questioning the standard kidney function estimate in older patients. The usual first-line test derives filtration rate from creatinine, but age can distort it. The team compared creatinine and cystatin C based estimates in 112 hospital patients over sixty, checking both against final case judgments.

The cystatin-based values ran about twenty percent lower on average, and in nearly half the cases they placed the patient in a worse kidney stage. In about a third of cases the downgrade matched the final diagnosis. The authors argue the creatinine test overstates kidney health in this age group and urge cystatin C first.
pmc-10742902:
Bojana Filipčev and co-authors design pasta spiked with wild garlic to test whether a tasty staple can carry extra health value, in this 2023 paper. Three forms of the plant went in: plain powder, an extract, and a protected encapsulated extract, each at three dose levels. The team then cooked the pasta and measured what survived: active compounds, antioxidant power, texture, color, and taste.

The additions lifted antioxidant activity several-fold and raised phenolics, flavonoids, and potassium in the cooked product. Cooking destroyed much of the flavonoid load, yet freed other phenolics from the dough. Powder and plain extract scored the strongest chemical gains. Encapsulation hurt cooking behavior. Tasters liked the powder version at low to middle doses best, marking it the practical winner.
pmc-10743002:
