Yujin Choi and co-authors ask whether early acupuncture helps Bell's palsy patients avoid a repeat attack, in a 2023 study from Korea. Bell's palsy weakens one side of the face, and steroids within three days are the standard care. Some past work hints that adding acupuncture early may help recovery.

The team mined national health insurance records for 45,986 adults treated with steroids from 2015 to 2017, then tracked them for at least three years. About 28,267 had acupuncture within a week of diagnosis. That group faced lower odds of the palsy returning, with an odds ratio of 0.81. The authors call for more research to confirm the benefit. Clinicians gain real-world evidence for a low-cost add-on.
pmc-10743102:
Jeong-Ah Kim and co-authors report a 2023 study of how nurses felt after training on patient deterioration, given face to face or on the web. The training used a simulation program built to sharpen how clinicians spot and act on signs that a patient is getting worse.

Ten focus groups drew nurses and managers from four sites. Nurses who were less at ease with tech liked the freedom of web learning and said it raised their confidence. Those in face-to-face groups prized live contact and feedback. The study asks which form best shifts daily practice, and for whom.
pmc-10743302:
Hyein Seo and co-authors scan DNA methylation, a chemical tagging of genes, in Korean adults with and without type 2 diabetes, in a 2023 study. Diabetes affects millions and runs partly through such tags, which can switch genes up or down without changing the code itself. Data came from a long-running Korean health cohort.

The scan found more than a hundred single sites and sixty-two regions where tags differed between groups. Several top sites sat in genes tied to sugar handling, and their tag levels tracked blood sugar measures closely. Some regions had been linked to diabetes processes before. The authors offer the sites as candidate markers and treatment leads for the Korean population and beyond.
pmc-10743402:
Researchers build a model to predict which gene changes cause a hearing disorder in this 2023 paper. The disorder, auditory neuropathy spectrum disorder, is tied to changes in the OTOF gene, which codes a protein called otoferlin that the inner ear needs.

The team gathered 270 known single amino acid changes in the gene and tested old prediction tools against a new model of their own. Their model uses a random forest fed with facts about the protein's shape and about how conserved each spot is across species. In cross checks it scored well on accuracy. Better prediction helps labs read sequencing results for patients with this hard to diagnose disorder.
pmc-10743602:
Avishay Edri and co-authors tested lab-grown natural killer cells, a type of immune cell, as a weapon against a cancer of the bone marrow. Killer cells strike fast and do not need the slow setup that other immune cells require. They are also easier to reshape with gene edits than the T cells used in many cell therapies.

The team grew donor killer cells with a vitamin-based method, removed a surface protein called CD38, and added a guided receptor that seeks that same protein on cancer cells. Removing the protein from the killer cells stops them from attacking each other. The design aims at stronger, safer attacks on the cancer. The work is part of a broad push to turn killer cells into ready-made cancer drugs.
pmc-10743702:
Giuseppe Fanciulli and co-authors, writing with the NIKE Group, review what predicts whether the chemotherapy drug streptozotocin will work against advanced pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors. The drug is a cornerstone treatment for these cancers, but responses vary widely from patient to patient. The team searched the literature and trial registries for studies that measured possible predictors.

Eleven studies yielded seventeen candidate factors. Thirteen of them held up statistically, spanning the patient's age and blood marker levels, the tumor's grade, growth index, and spread, and the treatment's place in the sequence of therapies. One gene's status in the tumor, MGMT, also mattered, as did how patients had answered earlier treatments. The authors offer the list as a practical guide for choosing who should get the drug.
pmc-10744302:
Elisa Da Silva and co-authors study how a gatekeeper protein controls whether the chemokine receptor CCR5 reaches the cell surface, in a 2023 paper. New receptors must escape the cell's internal factory to work. Transport vesicles carry them out of the endoplasmic reticulum. Escort proteins help some receptors leave, while gatekeepers hold others back. PRAF2 is one such gatekeeper.

It was known to retain part of another receptor through a tail motif. Screens suggested it also binds CCR5's tail, without that motif. CCR5 matters in immunity and as an HIV entry door. Surface levels decide how strongly cells respond. Cell biologists gain a trafficking rule with drug relevance. HIV research watches CCR5 regulation closely.
pmc-10744502:
Rina Buoy and co-authors present a leaner system for reading text in photos, in a 2023 paper. Systems that recognize scene text usually align image and language features with cross-attention, a step that costs heavy computation and slows things down on modest hardware. Their design drops cross-attention entirely while still learning an internal sense of language.

The system pairs a vision transformer front end with a transducer borrowed from speech recognition. In tests, it needed far fewer decoding operations and ran faster than attention-based rivals, while matching their accuracy. It also beat a simpler context-free baseline and held its own against recent leading methods. The authors target use in low-resource settings.
pmc-10744702:
Foundries throw away moulding sand once its alkali-phenolic binder is spent, unless heat can burn the binder off cleanly enough to reuse the grains. Mariusz Łucarz set out to find the right temperature for that thermal regeneration. He heated cured binders while tracking weight loss, in air and without it, and derived the temperature at which the polymer fully decomposes. Then he roasted spent sand at several temperatures to check the prediction.

Roasted samples were weighed, photographed under microscopes, and probed for the chemical makeup of their grain surfaces. From the comparisons he identifies the regeneration temperature that cleans the sand while limiting energy use, and lists the factors that decide whether the process yields a grain matrix worth reusing. The work turns a disposal problem into a settings question with an answer.
pmc-10745302:
Tak Kyu Oh, In-Ae Song, and Roland Dickerson ask whether how sepsis patients ate before falling ill predicts survival in a 2023 Korean study. Using a nationwide registry, they studied nearly two thousand five hundred adults who had routine health exams before a sepsis admission between 2018 and 2020. Nutrition was scored with a national lifestyle assessment tool.

About twenty seven percent died within ninety days and thirty four percent within a year. Each extra point on the nutrition score came with slightly lower odds of death at both time points, after adjusting for other factors. The effect per point is small, but the authors suggest good diet and eating habits before illness may protect sepsis patients.
pmc-10745402:
Yu-Dong Zheng and co-authors test, in a 2023 study, whether a helpful bacterium can settle in young Pacific oysters and shield them from a harmful one. The Pacific oyster is a major farmed species worldwide, and China leans on hatchery raised seed. Mass deaths in recent years threaten that supply, and vibrio disease is the most common problem in hatcheries and nurseries.

The team tagged the harmful strain with a green glowing protein and the helpful strain with a red one. That let them watch both strains colonize the larvae's digestive system. The harmful strain causes disease, while the helpful one was found in the same production setting. Tracking where each settles, and in what order, can guide probiotic use in hatcheries. A shield that works at the larval stage could cut the losses that plague seed production.
pmc-10745902:
Mieczysław Mąkosza and Michał Fedoryński celebrate chlorine as the quiet workhorse of organic chemistry. Their 2023 paper explains how one atom, by its charge and electron layout, plays many roles inside a molecule. It can leave as a chloride ion during swaps and eliminations, opening space for new partners.

The same atom helps pull protons off carbon and steadies the negative centers left behind. It also calms three kinds of reactive intermediates: carbenes, positive carbon centers, and radicals. Often a single chlorine speeds several steps of a sequence at once. Drawing on their own decades of work, the authors parade examples of each trick. Their case: few single substituents earn their keep in so many ways.
pmc-10746002:
Mengjiao Wang and co-authors published this study in 2023 on a model brain cell that can fire in more than one pattern at once. Their base is the Hindmarsh-Rose model, a set of equations for how neurons burst. They added a memristor, a part whose flow depends on past charge, to mimic how magnetic fields sway a real neuron. A mixed current, both fast and slow waves, drives the cell.

Under single and stacked drives, the model showed paired firing patterns living side by side. As the link strength of the new part changed, that doubleness could vanish, a rare twist the team flags. They then built an analog circuit that acts out the same math, and its traces matched the computer runs. The work may help labs probe how real nerve cells switch rhythms.
pmc-10746102:
Limei Guan and six co-authors published a marine microbiology study in twenty twenty-three cataloguing bacteria from South China Sea water and hunting for ones that fight crop fungi. Ocean microbes evolve unusual chemistry, making them a rich source of biocontrol candidates. The team sampled fifty-six sites across the sea.

Two hundred strains from seventy-two species were cultured, spanning three phyla, with Bacillus types dominant. Two Bacillus subtilis strains carrying antifungal genes stood out. In plate duels they suppressed rice blast and several other plant pathogens by up to ninety percent. Their culture broth also protected plant tissue in lesion tests. The screening pipeline shows how seawater can stock the search for gentler crop protection.
pmc-10747202:
The brain's cannabinoid receptor CB1 shapes appetite, mood, and pain, yet clean drugs that target it have been hard to find. Emanuele Criscuolo and co-authors go shopping in the medicine cabinet instead: they screen drugs already approved for other uses. Their 2023 study pairs computer docking against the receptor's shape with lab tests on the best matches.

The screen ranked approved compounds by how snugly they should fit the receptor, using two filters in a row. Shortlisted drugs then went into cell and biochemical assays to confirm they truly engage CB1 and to see what they do there. Several approved compounds showed promising action. The authors argue that repurposing in this way can cut years and cost from drug hunting, since safety data for these compounds already exist.
pmc-10747402:
Lorimar Robledo Gonzalez and co-authors review how gut bacteria help gut viruses survive heat and spread. Their 2023 review covers enteric viruses, a major cause of foodborne illness worldwide. These viruses start infection in the gut, amid dense bacterial crowds.

Fresh data show some viruses bind directly to bacteria. That binding can steady the virus particle and keep its infectivity intact. Such help may boost replication and disease in the host. The full mechanisms are still being mapped. The review sums what is known and weighs how the partnership shapes transmission. The authors frame it as a new paradigm for gut virus biology.
pmc-10747702:
Cells that lack a guard gene find a back road around iron death, report Malgorzata Adamiec-Organisciok and co-authors in work dated 2023. Ferroptosis is an iron-fed cell death from spoiled fats. The guard gene, GPX4, normally holds it in check. Colon cancer cells with the gene cut out should die fast under a death drug. They died less than the team first thought.

Fat spoilage marks and gene reads showed a spare shield at work. Two genes, FSP1 and PRDX1, ran high in the cut cells and held the death off. Death-path therapy must plan for such detours.
pmc-10747902:
Mi Deng and co-authors test in 2023 how patchy soil nutrients shape root growth and root enzyme activity in Fokienia hodginsii, a valued timber conifer. Past work screened growth traits and single fertilizers, but nutrient patchiness went unstudied. Roots that forage well in patchy soil could lift stand yield.

Ten seed lines grow in pots under patchy nitrogen, phosphorus, or potassium, against even-feed controls. Seedling height runs higher under even feeding than under any patch scheme. Root enzyme activity and growth differ by line and by patch type. Combined scoring sorts the lines for patch tolerance. The authors propose planting and feeding plans that match line strengths to soil patch patterns in managed forests.
pmc-10748102:
Jiongming Yang and co-authors ask how a warming climate will change where five kinds of floating water plants in the Hydrocharis group can live. Their 2023 study notes that water plants spread with ease along flows, so new warm zones could raise the risk of invasion. The team used six computer models to map where the climate suits each species now and in years ahead.

Three of the five species already suit wide areas and carry high invasion risk, while two suit much smaller zones. Under future climates, most species gain ground, and northern ones shift toward higher latitudes. High emission paths bring the largest shifts. The authors urge close watch and prompt reports on the high-risk species. Their maps give land and water managers a head start on control.
pmc-10749202:
Naphatsamon Uthailak and co-authors profile the small-molecule output of a pork worm in a 2023 study. The worm, Trichinella spiralis, sickens folk who eat raw pork. Drugs miss its muscle-stage young, so new marks and aims are sought. The team read molecule sets from adult worms and muscle young by mass tools. Cast-off goods of the young faced the same lens.

Each stage leaned on its own fuel path. Adults ran a build path; muscle young ran sugar burn. Cast-off sets held their own key paths. Six mark molecules stood out, two tied to host burn acts. The authors pitch the marks for tests and the paths as drug aims.
pmc-10750402:
Yuehang Yang and co-authors pool Chinese trials of mindfulness yoga for depression into a single statistical review, in a study from 2023. Yoga that pairs movement with mindful attention is widely offered for mood problems. Single trials are small, so a pooled estimate can say more about whether the practice truly helps.

The team searched four major databases for controlled trials published between 2000 and 2022. Twenty two studies with just over twenty two hundred patients passed their quality checks. The pooled analysis measured the average effect of the yoga programs on depressive symptoms across patient groups. The review also discusses how such a practice might work on the mind and body. Its findings give clinics in China a firmer base for offering yoga as part of care.
pmc-10750502:
Rodrigo Teixeira and co-authors catalog in this 2023 study the fleas riding wild mammals around Sorocaba, Brazil. Fleas bite many warm-blooded hosts, drain blood, and carry disease, yet wild hosts are rarely checked. From January 2021 to June 2023 the team collected fleas from wild animals at a zoo, some residents found infested at routine checks, others rescued from the wild.

Four flea species were pinned down, plus two more sorted only to genus. All hosts were mammals across eleven species in four orders, from carnivores to armadillos. The authors say such parasite surveys sharpen knowledge of where these agents live and which hosts they favor. Zoo vets now know which guests to check first.
pmc-10752002:
Zhao Na, Wei Wei, Yingfang Xu, Dong Li, Beili Yin, and Weiqun Gu review hormone therapy for bone protection after menopause in a 2023 paper. Use of the therapy fell over side effect worries. Its bone benefits are drawing fresh respect now. The review weighs fracture gains against real harms.

Therapy cuts fracture risk across bone density levels. Adding progestogens does not erase that benefit in studies. Gains may fade once treatment stops, evidence hints. Heart, clot, stroke, and cancer risks shadow the gains. Best candidates are newly menopausal women under sixty. Early menopause cases may justify longer protection. Personal risk checks should drive the choice.
pmc-10753502:
Hospitals lean on antibiotics heavily, and the pandemic years may have pushed use higher still. Six researchers mine administrative records from South Carolina hospitals between March 2020 and September 2022 in a 2023 study. They compare prescription patterns against patient traits, COVID status, and length of stay. The design is ecological, reading group-level patterns rather than individual charts.

Patients with COVID-19 had double the odds of receiving antimicrobials. Extra risk clustered in young adults, in Black and Hispanic patients with the virus, and in infected patients carrying two or more other conditions. The authors stop short of blaming any single cause. They call for wider studies across systems to test whether the pattern holds and to guide stewardship programs.
pmc-10753702:
Li Yan and five co-authors published a mining engineering study in twenty twenty-three on the coupled dance of gas, stress, and coal rock during methane drainage. Draining coalbed methane before mining prevents explosions, captures fuel, and cuts emissions, but the underground mechanics are tangled. The team built a mathematical model joining elasticity, seepage, and fluid mechanics.

The model links the stress field, coal deformation, and gas flow in one system. Its solutions matched analytical results, and physical similarity experiments in the laboratory confirmed the predictions. The authors present it as an improvement on older seepage theories, ready for use in outburst prevention and drainage design. Safer, better-planned boreholes are the practical payoff.
pmc-10753802:
Andreas Hulm and Christian Ochsenfeld (2023) speed up a simulation technique used to map how enzymes do their chemistry. Many enzyme reactions take several steps, so nobody can write down the reaction coordinate in advance. Path collective variables solve this by learning the route during the simulation itself, converging on the path of lowest free energy. The authors combine these adaptive paths with a powerful hybrid sampling algorithm that mixes metadynamics with an extended-system biasing force, prized for adapting fast when the path updates.

Two obstacles get new fixes. When the learned path jumps or shortcuts, the variables can tear; the authors add a stabilization algorithm for such discontinuities. Then they show that a statistical estimator, the multistate Bennett acceptance ratio, squeezes more convergence from the same data. The methods are demonstrated on the first step of a real enzyme's mechanism, a test with genuine chemical stakes.
pmc-10755702:
Soumyashree Jena and six co-authors report a 2023 chemistry study of a cobalt based system that adds one carbon atom to aldehydes. Aldehydes are common starting blocks in the lab. The products are a class of compounds prized as building blocks for larger molecules.

The system pairs cobalt with a boron part built into the same frame, and the two parts work as a team. The method runs in one pot and avoids the large additive loads, tight limits, and high heat of older routes. Early tests point to a cobalt carbon species as a key step. The products form with strong control over both shape and place of the new bond.
pmc-10756902:
Vijaykumar Muley wrote, in two thousand twenty-three, the lead piece for a set of works on gene use in brain ills and aging. The ills form a group of more than one hundred states in which nerve cells and their webs waste away. Why they start is not known.

Age is the chief risk. Genes, the wider world, and daily habits add to it. All of these act in part by shifts in gene expression, the cell's choice of which genes stay on or off. Some shifts come through epigenetic tags, small marks on DNA and its wrap. Some come through controls that start or stop a gene's read-out. The set Muley leads holds eight works, on data banks, such tags, cell death, body fuel use, and the gut-brain link. The hope is to find points where an ill could be slowed.
pmc-10757102:
Sha Liu and seven co-authors study blood markers in liver cancer patients in a 2023 paper. Simple ratios between immune cell types in the blood have been linked to outcomes in patients on immune therapy. The team tracked three such ratios, and how they changed during treatment, in over a hundred Chinese patients with primary liver cancer.

Patients whose disease was controlled had lower values on two of the ratios at the start. Cutoff values separated responders from non-responders for all three ratios. Patients below the cutoffs lived longer without their disease worsening, and two groups also lived longer overall. Low ratios also went with earlier stage and better general condition.
pmc-10761102:
Zhenhua Xu and co-authors tested whether carbon nanotubes could help rice seedlings cope with salty, alkali soil stress, in a study from 2023. Salt stress cuts growth, survival, and yield in rice. The team grew a rice variety in water culture and added the tiny tubes under set stress levels. They then tracked water uptake, leaf gas exchange, and sugar handling in the young plants.

Treated seedlings took up water better, above all through their roots. Leaf rates of food making rose, and the light-using system in the leaves worked more smoothly. The plants also held more green pigment and had higher rates for key enzymes. The authors read these gains as a sign that the tubes help rice keep growing when soil salts would slow it down.
pmc-10762702:
William Dean and Rengaraj Venkatesh offer, in a 2023 guide, what it takes to set up modern cataract surgery in places that have relied on older methods. The modern technique, called phaco, breaks the cloudy lens up with ultrasound and removes it through a tiny cut. Patients increasingly ask for it, since healing is faster and results better. Demand is sharpest for earlier, softer cataracts, where the manual method carries more risk.

The guide walks through the groundwork: machines and their upkeep, cassettes and fluids, a full shelf of lens implants, and measurement tools for choosing them. Stable power and backup retinal support need planning too. A Kenyan surgeon quoted in the piece reminds readers to keep manual skills sharp for hard cases and mid-surgery trouble. Training pathways, including simulators, round out the advice.
pmc-10763502:
Amalie von Barner Tvedegaard Heim and five colleagues sample shellfish along the Norwegian coast for a hospital superbug's relatives, in a 2023 study. Enterococcus faecium is a leading cause of drug-resistant hospital infections, and the sea might serve as its reservoir or highway. Bivalves, filter feeders that concentrate microbes, act as sentinels.

Enterococci turned up in most of 471 bivalve batches, though in low numbers, spanning ten species. Sequencing 148 of the target species showed high diversity dominated by non-clinical lineages. Resistance to at least one drug appeared in about forty percent of isolates, but none resisted the two last-line drugs. Only three isolates belonged to the hospital clan, and two of those clustered with human isolates. The authors conclude the marine niche mostly harbors harmless strains, while occasional overlap with clinical ones keeps the One Health question open.
pmc-10764202:
Aniruddha Sen and co-authors review a swelling signal in diabetic nerve damage in a 2023 paper. Diabetic peripheral neuropathy brings numbness, poor balance, and foot risk. The signal, TNF-alpha, has been proposed as a driver, but studies disagree.

The team gathered studies worldwide under standard review rules. Twenty-three papers entered the review and eleven the pooled analysis. Blood levels of the signal differed clearly between patients with nerve damage and controls in the pooled result. Wide variation among studies is noted as a caveat. The work supports a role for inflammation in this common diabetes complication.
pmc-10766602:
Da Eun Yoon and co-authors reported in 2023 on making base editing cleaner. Base editors change single DNA letters with great power, but they often cause unwanted insertions and deletions at the target site. Those indels are a real barrier for clinical use. The team set out to remove them while keeping the edits efficient.

Their fix swaps the nickase Cas9 in standard editors for dead Cas9, which cannot cut. They also added chromatin-modulating peptides to raise the conversion rate. In human cell lines and mouse primary myoblasts, the new setup gave accurate substitutions without the unwanted indels. It also showed fewer off-target effects at the DNA level than standard editors. The authors see it as a step toward safer gene-editing therapies.
pmc-10767002:
Geongoo Han and Shipra Vaishnava speak for the low-count germ kin that share our gut and skin. Their review appeared in twenty twenty-three. Most work reads the big packs and skips the rare, and lab beasts lack the wild mix. Yet rare kinds can be key stones that shape the whole pack and do set work for the host.

Low kinds of germs, fungi, old ones, and lone cells are summed for their play with the host. Shield growth, ill states, and pack shape in set spots all bear their mark. True host-germ grasp needs them in, the team hold.
pmc-10773802:
Jun Xing, Qianqian Han, Jiyang Liu, and Zhengzheng Yan build a reagent free sensor for a breast cancer mark, in work from 2023. CA15-3 levels in blood aid early screening and outlook calls for breast cancer. Aptamer sensors can catch the mark without labels if the signal probe stays fixed inside.

Twin layer silica channels on a cheap oxide glass base form the sensor body. Aptamers anchor on the outer face to grab the target mark from serum. A cobalt probe sits trapped inside channels by charge pull and push together. That fixed probe gives a stable signal across a huge range of mark levels. Spiked calf serum checks proved the sensor works in blood like fluid.
pmc-10783202:
Sandeep Khanna, Ranganathan Arunmozhi, and Chanan Goyal reviewed the literature in 2023 on neurodevelopmental treatment for children with cerebral palsy. That hands-on therapy is widely used in rehab care. The review asked what outcomes studies measure, and whether those measures match a world framework for function and disability.

The search covered three databases for English studies from 2000 to 2023. Fifty-four studies of the treatment in children with cerebral palsy were included. Forty-one found positive outcomes, while thirteen reached contradictory conclusions, in the counts reported. Readers get an honest balance sheet for a therapy used worldwide. Most reports are positive, a stubborn minority are not, and the field's measures are checked against children's daily lives.
pmc-10783602:
Muhammad Dawood and co-authors link the gene activity of breast tumors to what their tissue looks like under the microscope, in a 2023 study. Knowing a tumor's gene state guides treatment, but gene tests are costly and slow compared with routine slides. Predicting gene state from a slide image would be a cheap shortcut.

Genes switch on and off in coordinated groups, so the team first found clusters of genes that move together. A graph neural network then predicted each cluster's state from whole-slide images. A handful of cluster scores captured each patient's tumor state in a form doctors can read. The approach ties molecular type to visible tissue traits, which may help clinics without gene labs.
pmc-10790102:
Linda Sprague Martinez and co-authors examine how money arrangements shape community-engaged health research. Their 2023 paper studies efforts at two research-heavy universities to close the gap between research offices and community partners. How a partner is paid, the authors argue, sets the tone for shared decisions and ownership.

Subcontracting routes, they found, often slow or skew partnerships with community groups. Universities need clearer, simpler payment processes plus staff who can guide both sides through them. Without that support, engagement goals stall despite good intent. The paper speaks to administrators and researchers who want participatory work to move from slogan to practice.
pmc-10801102:
Maryam Mirahmad and three co-authors survey the ethical knots in clinical trials for osteoporosis, the bone-thinning disease. Their review appeared in twenty twenty-three. Hip fractures from weak bones are projected to soar by twenty fifty, above all where populations age.

Treatment options have multiplied since the first drug approval decades ago. Yet trial design raises hard questions: who should get a placebo when working drugs exist, and how long can risk be imposed? Safety worries shadow several drug classes. Rules from regulators shape how new therapies are proven. The authors walk through these tensions to promote trials that are both sound and fair. Their aim is research that patients can trust.
pmc-10804002:
Connor Richard Miller and co-authors warn that surveys may mismeasure the use of heated tobacco products, in a paper published in 2023. These products warm tobacco instead of burning it, and they sit beside vaping products on store shelves.

The authors argue that the two product classes look so alike that users may report the wrong one. Shifting ways of using cannabis add more confusion. Wrong answers could distort the data that health policy rests on. The paper suggests fixes, such as plain descriptions in surveys that separate the classes, and follow-up questions that probe past the first answer. Until checks are done, the authors urge care in reading survey results.
pmc-10806102:
Cystic fibrosis in North Africa is likely undercounted, Nada El Makhzen and co-authors review in a study the head dates to 2023. The catalog year says 2024, so the head's year is used. Cystic fibrosis is the most prevalent autosomal recessive disease globally, caused by variants in a chloride channel gene. Recent studies suggest higher global prevalence than previously thought, yet comprehensive data remain extremely scarce among African populations.

That scarcity creates an information gap in the African health care system. Underestimation of the disease among African children is likely, the authors argue, given the complexity of diagnosis without proper clinical and genetic investigation. The article reviews pathogenesis and prevalence across North African countries. It calls for specific genetic and epidemiological studies so patients can be identified early.
pmc-10806202:
Keiko Ihara and co-authors model motivation in a lever-press task with mice in a study published in 2023. The progressive ratio task measures goal drive by one breakpoint number. That single point hides how choices evolve during a session. The team built learning models that track every choice.

Four reinforcement learning models were compared on mouse behavior. Choices included rewarded presses, unrewarded presses, and magazine pokes. A perseverance model with choice traces fit best. It predicted shrinking reward error signals after empty pokes. Brain recordings of dopamine in the ventral striatum confirmed that pattern. A low drug dose raised poking without moving the breakpoint. The model captured that dissociation as well. The authors offer a richer barometer of motivation than breakpoint alone. Brain signal validation strengthens trust in the model.
pmc-10806802:
Camille Sautreuil and a team of co-authors study how drinking in pregnancy harms the unborn brain, in work published in twenty twenty-four. Past research showed that alcohol before birth weakens the placenta-brain link that guides blood vessel growth in the fetal brain. A placenta protein that helps vessels grow is part of that link.

The team focused on a partner protein found in the placenta and also in blood. They measured it in human placenta tissue and tested its role in vessel growth in the brain's outer layer. They also tracked support cells that settle near vessels. The work adds detail on how alcohol exposure may steer the fetal brain toward lasting harm.
pmc-10808502:
Melissa Cano and co-authors edit genes in a fast growing sea alga in a 2023 study. The alga thrives in salty warm water, which suits outdoor ponds. Dense growth wastes light when cells carry too much pigment. The team cut out the gene path for lutein, a yellow pigment.

Cells without lutein held less total pigment and a leaner light catching setup. They used low light more efficiently and grew slightly faster in dense culture. A green pigment partner proved essential, since its loss hurt growth. The findings support trimming pigments to raise biomass yield. That matters for algae grown for food and renewable fuels.
pmc-10811602:
Ece Turhan and Mohd Asgher introduce a journal collection on molecular priming, a way to vaccinate plants, in effect, against drought, heat, floods, and metal-tainted soils. Their 2024 editorial frames the stakes: such stresses stir up damaging oxygen byproducts in plant cells, slow growth, and cut crop yields worldwide just as food demand climbs.

Priming pre-treats plants with signals that wake their own defenses, lifting mineral uptake and antioxidant enzyme work before stress lands. The collection gathers four original studies and one review, all probing priming at the molecular level. Work cited in the issue shows, for one, that melatonin treatment helps barley bear water stress. The editors argue that priming, beside breeding and biotechnology, gives farmers a chemical-free-looking lever against a harsher climate.
pmc-10822702:
Kim wrote a history paper in twenty twenty-four on why the British biochemist Joseph Needham joined the international team that probed claims of bacterial warfare during the Korean War. Needham had spent four years in China during the Second World War as a science envoy, building close ties with Chinese scientists and officials.

Drawing on Needham's own records, Kim shows that a key motive was personal: in nineteen forty-four Needham had already looked into Japan's use of germ weapons. He also worked quietly to recruit fellow Cambridge professors to the team. Once appointed, he led much of the work himself, chairing expert talks, checking documents, and questioning witnesses. The evidence counters the view that the team merely rubber-stamped Chinese claims. Kim's account restores Needham's active hand in one of the Cold War's most disputed probes.
pmc-10822902:
Pengrui Tai and co-authors set out the play books and brain codes that let brain waves drive tools, in a review from 2023. A brain link rig reads waves a user makes by set tasks, then turns them to acts. The task book and the wave code are the two hinge parts of each rig, yet past print left their terms and build laws dim.

Main task books in use are walked through, from sight flash to thought move. Code kinds and their build laws get the same care. Next steps the team names: user first design, new task books past the stock set, firm wave grabs, and a join with smart code to lift read truth.
pmc-10823002:
Yani Su and six co-authors used genetics to test whether the age at which women first give birth changes their risk of esophageal disease. Observational links between childbearing and illness are easily confounded, so the team ran a Mendelian randomization study, using inherited variants tied to age at first birth as a natural experiment. Four conditions were examined: obstruction, varices, reflux, and cancer of the esophagus.

The main analysis found that a later first birth modestly lowers the risk of reflux and of esophageal cancer. No causal link appeared for obstruction or varices. The team repeated the test with eight statistical methods and ran sensitivity checks, which supported the two positive findings. Reported in 2023, the study adds genetic evidence that reproductive timing leaves a mark on the esophagus. It cannot say what drives the protection, and the cancer effect, while real, is small in absolute terms.
pmc-10826702:
Shalini Pandey and five co-authors report a fungus that makes a dark pigment, found in coal mine land in India. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-three. The team screened fungi from barren soil at a coal field site. Three of fourteen fungi made pigment, and one strain made the most by far.

Tests showed the pigment behaved like melanin, the dark pigment in skin and hair. It did not dissolve in water or common solvents, but it did dissolve in alkali. Gene tests named the fungus as a species of Thermothelomyces. The team then tuned heat, acidity, and trace foods to raise the yield. Output rose by about sixty-two percent under the best settings. Such pigments have uses in materials and health products.
pmc-10829102:
Halla Abdelbaki and co-authors published this study in 2023. It grows a catalyst from a plant extract and uses it to build a family of ring-shaped molecules called triazoles. Such rings appear in many drugs and farm chemicals, so cleaner ways to make them are in demand.

The team used an extract of the herb Artemisia campestris to form tiny beads of copper oxide with a flower-like shape. The plant juice both shaped the beads and kept them stable. With the beads as catalyst, the reaction yield jumped from twenty percent to over eighty-five percent. The authors tuned the amount of catalyst and the solvent mix, and reused the beads four times. The work shows a plant-based route to a recyclable catalyst for common chemical building blocks.
pmc-10835802:
Bahejiayinaer Tiemuerbieke, Jian-Ying Ma, and Wei Sun compare two desert shrubs as groundwater falls. Their study from twenty twenty-four works in the Gurbantunggut Desert. One shrub uses standard photosynthesis, the other a water-saving variant. Coexisting species survive drought by splitting strategies.

Three sites with different water table depths were sampled. Water sources, leaf function, and stored sugars were measured. Stem water status tracked stress across two growing seasons. The shrubs drew water and conserved it in different patterns. Those differences help explain how both persist together. Functional diversity itself is a survival strategy here. Desert restoration can copy such complementary pairings.
pmc-10842202:
James Howard and co-authors report in a study whose head gives 2023 as its year interim results from a long extension trial of a myasthenia drug. The illness weakens muscles through antibody attack at the nerve junction. The drug efgartigimod clears those antibodies by blocking their recycling route.

The open label extension ran up to three years across many centers worldwide. Dosing came in cycles of four weekly infusions, retimed by clinical judgment per patient. Of 151 who rolled over, 145 got at least one dose in the extension. Most, 84.8%, reported at least one side effect during the long run. Daily living and strength scores tracked benefit across the cycles given.
pmc-10859402:
Voorter and co-authors evaluate nineteen years of an international proficiency test for high-resolution HLA typing. Their paper reviews a scheme begun in 2004, when few European options existed for checking tissue typing accuracy. Participating laboratories receive DNA samples each year and report their typings of the immune genes that govern transplant matching.

The reference laboratory types each sample at high resolution, and results are judged against European standards. Over the years the scheme widened to more gene loci and finer levels of resolution. Methods shifted from Sanger sequencing toward next-generation sequencing across the field. Accuracy climbed with experience: nearly all samples have been typed correctly since 2017. The authors present the scheme as a quiet engine of quality in transplant medicine.
pmc-10860202:
Abhishek Mahajan and a large team of co-authors build an MRI scoring system for carotid body tumors in a study whose head reports 2023. These rare tumors grow at the fork of the neck artery, and surgery near the vessels and nerves is risky. The team reviewed scans for forty-four patients with fifty-one tumors treated between 2005 and 2020 and scored each tumor from zero to fifteen.

Low scores marked low surgical risk and high scores high risk. Their four-grade scheme uses traits such as distance from the skull base and contact angle with the artery. It predicted vessel and nerve injury patterns and offers an imaging-based rival to the standard surgical classification.
pmc-10871102:
Peyton Moore and co-authors review the genetics of myocardial bridging in a 2023 paper. In this birth anomaly, a heart artery dives into the heart muscle instead of lying on its surface. The muscle squeezes the artery with each beat. Many carriers never notice, but the squeezing can cause chest pain, heart attack, or sudden death in some.

Unlike most heart conditions, bridging has little molecular characterization. The review gathers what is known about genomic associations, hunting for inherited patterns that explain who gets symptoms. Such groundwork could one day flag at-risk carriers before an event. It also guides lab studies of how the anomaly forms during development of the coronary arteries.
pmc-10875302:
Weak bones in children are not just small adult osteoporosis, Leanne Ward stresses in this practical guide, published in 2023. Four differences shape care: telling fragility from playground bad luck, the many single-gene causes that surface young, the growing skeleton's power to rebuild itself, and targets that shift as children grow.

The guide walks clinicians through diagnosis and management step by step, from gene findings to when treatment should start. Early treatment, while growth plates stay open, beats late treatment for restoring bone shape. Ward also flags the field's biggest gap: nearly all drugs only slow bone loss, while bone-building agents are what children most need. The piece serves as a clinic-ready reference.
pmc-10882202:
Julie Duong and ten co-authors lay out a research protocol in 2023 for studying peer support among people with disability in Australia. One in six Australians lives with disability, and peer-led organizations promise support shaped by shared experience. The project itself is led by researchers who have that lived experience.

Over three years, three groups will be recruited through two peer groups in New South Wales: peers, peer leaders, and lived-experience researchers, with a focus on culturally diverse communities. Interviews, surveys, and focus groups will feed a thematic reading of the data through the researchers' own lens. The design treats taking part as method, not decoration.
pmc-10909102:
Mahdieh Salimi and Shima Rastegarpouyani checked a blood marker that may help predict outcomes for breast cancer patients, in a 2023 study. The marker is a chemical tag on a gene called ELF5, which normally helps hold tumors back. Such tags in free DNA floating in the blood can be sampled with a simple blood draw.

The team measured free DNA levels and the gene tag in 80 patients and in healthy controls. Free DNA ran much higher in patients, most of all in late-stage, aggressive, or spread disease. The gene tag showed up in 70 percent of patients, in both blood and tumor samples. Every patient whose cancer had reached the lymph nodes or distant sites carried the tag. The authors propose it as a noninvasive warning marker, with more study needed.
pmc-11114402:
Junji Yamaguchi and four co-authors present a case report from twenty twenty-three on delirium tied to Trousseau syndrome in a man with lung cancer. The syndrome makes the blood clot too much in cancer patients. The man, in his early sixties, was in hospital for the syndrome when delirium set in and grew worse. Three standard drugs failed to let him sleep.

A low dose of memantine was added next to perospirone. His mind signs eased step by step, and he slept four to five hours a night. He could then go home and restart his immune therapy for the cancer on schedule. The team calls this the first such case with this drug pair. More study is needed, they note.
pmc-11210602:
Claudia Haase reviews how couples handle emotion across adult life in a 2023 article. Close relationships stir strong feelings, and partners shape each other's moods in both directions. She sets out the key marks of this shared regulation: it moves over time, runs both ways, and can calm or inflame. She also weighs how it is measured, by self-report or by task performance.

A theory of aging holds that older people prize emotional meaning more as time feels short. Haase traces couple regulation from infancy through youth and midlife into late life. Her central claim is that regulation shifts from me to us with age. In late life it may grow more skilled, more central, and more tied to health and to how well a bond fares. She ends with ideas for new studies.
pmc-11389702:
Hassan Wafi Hussain Assad and co-authors wrote a 2023 article, in French, calling for stronger research training in health sciences across the Maghreb. Their piece takes its title from a doctor's prescription: a prescription for academic excellence. It opens with the arrival of global university rankings in 2003, which put research output in the spotlight.

Since then, a regional network has worked to train young health researchers in North Africa. The network joins health ministries, medical schools, journals, and teacher and student groups. About one hundred master classes have been held in cities across the region. One long-running project in Casablanca trains hospital interns in searching the literature and writing up studies. The authors present this shared training effort as the route to raising research quality across the Maghreb's health schools.
pmc-11535202:
Qinzheng Yang and co-authors work on, in a 2024 study, the accuracy of a rock crack gauge read from photos. The gauge, JRC, rates how rough a rock joint is, a key input for slope and tunnel work. Photo-based reads are fast but can drift with how the shots were taken. The team built a rig that picks camera spots on its own, by a search rule drawn from photo-build math. A plate with known points grounds each shot, and a move plan steers the camera round small rock samples. They shot 48 sets in the field with mixed settings.

From those sets they built a data set of shot traits and read error. Seven learning methods then built fix models for the gauge. Two of them cut the read error by a mean of about 86 percent. Bounds of the new path are set out as well.
pmc-11535302:
Niknam and five co-authors ask how blood pressure, awareness of the condition, and sticking to treatment relate to quality of life and mood. Their survey covered more than 7,000 Iranian adults, with a smaller group answering mood questions. The team split people by whether they knew they had high blood pressure and how faithfully they took their medicine.

Stronger commitment to treatment went with lower physical quality of life in both sexes, a puzzling pattern. Among women, commitment patterns linked to mental quality of life, anxiety, and stress in mixed ways. People unaware of their condition showed no deficits. The authors urge mental health checks as a routine part of blood pressure care.
pmc-11535402:
Muhammad Nour, Said Elsayed and Omar Mahmoud train machine learning to pick the cheaper directional drilling tool, in this 2024 Europe PMC paper. Directional wells are steered by one of two tools: rotary steerable systems, which clean holes well, or mud motors, which are versatile and cheaper to run. Choosing wrongly wastes money.

Using data from offset wells covering rock type, drilling performance, tripping and casing runs, their models predict section time and cost for each tool on a planned well. Gradient boosting gave the most accurate predictions in testing. No universal rule favored either tool; the best choice hinged on each well's conditions. The authors say the data-driven pick cuts bias and field costs.
pmc-11535502:
Cadmium, a toxic metal in soil, rides crops into the food chain and harms the people who eat them. Jun Yuan and twelve co-authors find a guard in the model plant Arabidopsis that cuts that ride at the root. Their 2024 study centres on a sensor protein in the root's cell walls.

When cadmium touches the root, the sensor builds up fast, by fresh making and by a block on its own disposal. It then tags a transporter that hauls cadmium in, marking that hauler for the cell's waste route. With fewer haulers at work, the plant takes in less of the metal. The pair forms a module the authors name for both parts. Crops bred with a stronger guard could keep more cadmium out of food.
pmc-11535702:
Qun Catherine Li and co-authors describe a hospital wide program that cut harm from care itself in a 2024 paper. Complications gained in hospital slow recovery and drain funds. The Australian service built a three pillar plan covering notes, coding, and clinical quality. A five year road map set shared goals across units.

Projects ran in short cycles with data checks and change support. Mean complication rates fell from the baseline years to the first program year. Lower rates then held through the next three years. The authors credit the whole system frame over single fix projects. Joint work across trades made gains stick, they argue, and the cycle tool proved handy.
pmc-11536602:
Hossein Bannazadeh Baghi and co-authors review how tiny regulatory molecules called microRNAs shape inflammation during viral infections, in a 2024 paper. Inflammation can clear a virus or turn deadly, and viruses themselves tamper with inflammatory pathways to escape immunity. MicroRNAs, short non-coding RNAs found across tissues, tune both the immune attack and the virus's progress.

The review gathers recent findings on which microRNAs rise or fall in infection and how that shifts the inflammatory response. Understanding these patterns, the authors argue, could sharpen diagnosis and open new ways to prevent or treat serious viral diseases. The piece maps a fast-moving field for researchers entering it.
pmc-11536802:
Hao Zhu and co-authors study sleep, diet, and metabolic syndrome in older adults in a paper from two thousand twenty-four. The survey covered residents over forty-five in a city in Anhui province, eastern China. Metabolic syndrome is a cluster of risks tied to heart disease and diabetes.

More than nine thousand people were included, and about thirteen percent had the syndrome. The team grouped sleep as short, normal, or long, and found three diet patterns from food surveys. Long sleep and fruit-milk or vegetable-cereal diets were tied to lower risk. A tuber-meat pattern was tied to higher risk. A decision tree ranked the vegetable-cereal pattern as the strongest factor and flagged five high-risk groups.
pmc-11536902:
Jiahao Cheng and co-authors identify a host protein that blocks a pig virus in a 2024 study. The virus causes severe diarrhoea in pigs and threatens farms worldwide. Proteins switched on by interferon, the body's alarm signal, can block viruses early, and the team tested one such protein against this virus.

Extra copies of the protein in gut cells cut virus growth, while removing it let the virus thrive. The protein sat on the surface of virus particles and bound one of their core proteins. Changes in the protein's tail end weakened its block, with a few spots mattering most. The findings point to a possible target for new antiviral drugs for pigs.
pmc-11538202:
Asmaa Ibrahim and five co-authors scale up production of an antibiotic in two thousand twenty-four. Cephalosporin C is made by a fungus, Acremonium chrysogenum, and feeds the widely used cephalosporin drug family. The team moved their strain from shake flasks to a laboratory fermenter.

They tuned the fermenter settings, settling on a small inoculum, set airflow, fast stirring, and an acidic controlled pH. Two measurement methods tracked the product amount. Output rose about three and a half times over the unoptimized run. Production also rose twice as fast in the first three days compared with flasks. The run yielded about one point six grams from four liters, showing fermenters beat flasks for scale.
pmc-11539502:
Yanhong Lan and co-authors catalogue the trihelix gene family in eggplant and track its stress responses. Their 2024 study finds thirty family members spread unevenly over twelve chromosomes. These transcription factors steer growth, hormone signals, and stress replies in plants.

Family members sort into six subfamilies, conserved across plant species, with kin sharing structure. Promoter regions carry switches tied to growth, hormones, and stress. Selection pressure reads as purifying, keeping the family stable. Four genes peak in roots, leaves, flowers, and fruit, one each. Most family genes answer cold, and two hormone signals, in lab tests. One gene jumps sharply under cold and is cloned for deeper work. The authors eye stress-hardy crop breeding.
pmc-11540102:
Xiaowei Fang and co-authors report a 2024 study of a foodborne germ that invades human cells. The germ, Listeria monocytogenes, causes serious disease in people and animals. A surface protein called InlB anchors to the germ's wall and helps it enter host cells. A sugar coating on the wall is needed to hold that anchor in place, at least for one strain group.

Several enzymes build that sugar coating, and one of them, GalE, is found in all strain groups. The team deleted the gene for GalE and watched what changed. Without it, the InlB anchor was impaired and the germ grew less able to cause disease. The result shows this shared enzyme is a key support for the germ's attack, and a possible target for control measures.
pmc-11545902:
Mircea and colleagues review in 2024 how spaceflight's radiation and weightlessness affect the heart and circulation. Space conditions change brain blood flow, venous return, and heart output, and can bring anemia and rhythm disturbances reported since early missions. Weightlessness slowly weakens heart muscle and alters its gene activity and calcium handling. Radiation adds long-term damage that may raise disease risk after missions end.

Knowing these changes helps crews adapt in flight and stay protected afterward. The review gathers the effects and the countermeasures proposed so far. It speaks to planning for longer missions beyond Earth orbit.
pmc-11547202:
Nuclear plants use steel-plate concrete walls that must hold under huge loads, and their grip depends on studs and tie bars buried in the concrete. Yeongun Kim and Byong Choi test how the concrete failure area around those anchors behaves. Their 2024 paper runs performance tests on full-scale wall pieces, from a lone stud up to stud-and-tie combinations.

Thicker walls and added tie bars change how the concrete breaks out around each anchor, and with it the wall's tensile strength. From the test results the authors draft a design rule for estimating that strength while counting the help tie bars give. The rule speaks to engineers sizing modular wall units for plants, where a weak anchor zone is not an option.
pmc-11547302:
Tianqing Li and co-authors tested adding nitrogen to a plasma arc welding process for super duplex stainless steel, in a 2024 study. The steel's strength depends on keeping two crystal phases, austenite and ferrite, in balance, and nitrogen helps hold that balance. Using the torch's focusing gas channel, they fed nitrogen into the arc and then into the molten pool.

With nitrogen, the weld metal's austenite share rose from about 22 to 40 percent. Its shape changed too, growing coarser plate-like forms, and the austenite grew harder while the ferrite softened slightly. The team maps how the gas reshapes the joint's structure and properties.
pmc-11568602:
Ji Min Kim and Sanghui Park study a diagnostic pitfall in bladder cancer surgery in this two thousand twenty-four paper. The cancer type is plasmacytoid urothelial carcinoma, a rare and aggressive form. During bladder removal, surgeons check the ureter cut edges with quick frozen sections. Tumor at the edge means more tissue must go. This cancer's cells can hide and mimic harmless ones, fooling the quick check.

The team reviewed cases from two thousand seventeen to two thousand twenty-three. They compared patients whose frozen margins read positive with those whose read negative. They also set frozen results against the final, slower sections. Fifteen patients had a large plasmacytoid share in their tumors. The paper maps where the quick test fails. Pathologists and urologic surgeons can use it to stay alert.
pmc-11569102:
Getting out of the house to meet others may be one of the simplest shields against frailty in old age. Sandra Mümken and co-authors test that idea in 2024 with survey data on more than thirteen thousand Europeans aged fifty and up. They tracked loneliness, low drive, social network size, and out of home activities across three survey waves.

Part of the harm from loneliness and low motivation reached later frailty through fewer outings. People who added outings between waves saw their frailty scores fall measurably by the final wave. The authors read out of home activity as a working part of prevention, not just a marker of health. They suggest programs should help older adults get out more, not only feel less lonely.
pmc-11569502:
Chao Han and co-authors ask, in 2024, whether platelet-rich plasma, widely used to speed wound healing, might also feed breast cancer growth. That worry limits its use in cancer patients. The team grew a human breast cancer cell line with the plasma in dishes, then injected it around mouse tumors and watched growth.

Instead of feeding the cancer, the plasma slowed it. Treated cells multiplied, migrated, and invaded less. Mouse tumors grew more slowly, with fewer dividing cells and more markers of cell death. The authors conclude the plasma inhibited both cell lines tested, though clinical meaning still needs study.
pmc-11571502:
Deniz Eroğul and co-authors test salt dips for keeping strawberries fresh after picking in a 2024 study. Much picked fruit rots before people can eat it, which wastes food. A calcium chloride dip is a cheap way to slow that loss.

Fruit of one type was dipped in salt mixes of two, four, or six percent. The berries then sat in cold storage for fifteen days. Every five days the team checked weight loss, rot, sweetness, acid, and breathing rate. They also tracked healthy plant compounds and vitamin C. The six percent dip gave the best scores on most counts. It best held back weight loss, rot, and quality fade across the storage span.
pmc-11574102:
Eleven authors led by Xuemei Yang study how soil locks away life-based matter across Inner Mongolia. Soils and desert sands from farm, forest, grass, and deep layers fed the tests. Life-based parts of soil, such as carbon and nitrogen from dead matter, can stay locked in stone or wash out to air and water. What tips that balance was the open point here.

Soils held more organic carbon and nitrogen than sands did. Sands and deep soils held more sulphur and stone-based carbon instead. Tight links tied sulphur to carbon and nitrogen across all samples. Soil acid level steered the lock: sour soils freed food that fed more lock-in, while sweet soils held complexes firm and freed less. The team reads pH as a key dial for soil carbon care in dry lands.
pmc-11574302:
Xiyuan Hu and a large team of co-authors test a compound against the most aggressive form of breast cancer, in two thousand twenty-four. That form lacks the usual drug targets and has a poor outlook. A cell protein that guards energy balance is often switched off in this cancer, which makes it a point of interest.

The compound, derived from a natural pigment family, slowed the cancer cells in dishes and in mice. It also pushed the cells into a programmed form of death. Protein scans showed it switched the energy guard back on. When the team knocked that guard out with gene editing, the compound's effect reversed, confirming the path.
pmc-11574402:
A heart-lung machine trick for a torn main vein is reported by Takaaki Maruhashi and co-authors in work dated 2024. Tears of the vein behind the liver are among the deadliest liver wounds. Packing is the usual first move, but open surgery can crash blood flow. The team first met the trick in a real case, a woman in her eighties whose heart had stopped.

On the machine, her liver bleed was blocked by a vessel plug. Raising machine flow then pulled blood away from the vein tear, and the leak stopped on scans. A dog model test backed the find. The team calls it a new, gentler option.
pmc-11574502:
Ted Fong, Kunjie Cui, and Paul Yip study gaming disorder in Chinese adolescents in this 2024 paper. Low self control is a known risk factor for problem gaming. A sense of meaning in life might blunt that risk. The team tested both factors and their interaction in one model.

The sample held 2,064 adolescents from five middle schools in Sichuan, surveyed in 2022. Students answered validated scales on self control, meaning, gaming symptoms, school commitment, and family function. Models checked that the scales worked the same for boys and girls. Meaning in life changed how strongly low self control linked to gaming symptoms. It also linked to school and family outcomes. The findings point to meaning building as a prevention angle.
pmc-11575002:
Waraporn Jumpato and co-authors survey black flies in Thailand in a 2024 study of a bird parasite. The parasite, in the genus Leucocytozoon, causes a disease in birds, including poultry, and black flies carry it from bird to bird. Little was known about how often the parasite turns up in these flies in Thailand.

The team caught flies at nine sites in the north and northeast and checked a sample with gene tests. They named the fly types by form and by DNA, and they matched parasite types to a known data bank. Their checks link parasite rates to fly numbers and to traits of the places where flies were caught.
pmc-11575202:
Wenbo Liu and ten co-authors examine the tiny vessels at the center of the eye in children who had retinopathy of prematurity, in a 2024 study. This disease of preterm infants can scar the retina. Modern drug treatment blocks vessel growth signals, but its long term marks need charting.

Scans covered 75 eyes from 44 children in four groups, including two drug treated groups, one healed without drugs, and healthy peers. The vessel free zone at the eye's center was smaller in all retinopathy groups. Central thickness ran higher except in one drug group. No clear difference separated the two drugs. Vessel measures linked to each other in tidy patterns. Follow-up imaging can track these quiet changes.
pmc-11576102:
Maria Ferreira and co-authors set out the traits of three carbon radicals that bear halogens, in a 2024 study. These short-lived species matter in atmospheric and combustion chemistry, but their shapes, spectra, and formation heats were not fully known. Where tests in the lab struggle, math steps in.

Several density functional methods were tested against composite ab initio models. Molecular shapes and vibration frequencies were worked out for each radical, and UV absorption spectra were derived from the shapes. Formation heats came out with stated uncertainties, two of them for the first time. The wider family with two to four halogens was compared, and closed-shell species got tighter values than the literature offered. The bromine radical's formation heat ran above zero, while fluorine's ran well below it. Kinetic modelers can add these species and trust them, and the test of methods against each other is a side gain.
pmc-11576602:
Christian Menschik and co-authors study everyday tech in homes for people with intellectual disabilities in a paper from two thousand twenty-four. Such residents risk being shut out of digital life when homes lack ways to use common devices. The team asked staff and managers what helps or blocks uptake.

They used a framework that tracks uptake through long-term use. Barriers showed up at many levels. Each person's speech and language skills shaped what could be used. Staff needed skills to back residents' use, and rules and funding were unclear. Speech support stood out as where tech adds clear value. The pandemic pushed some digital change. The authors call for set routines to back digital inclusion.
pmc-11577602:
Xia and five co-authors present a model predicting which circular RNAs affect drug sensitivity, in work from twenty twenty-four. Circular RNAs are ring shaped non coding RNAs. Recent studies tie some of them to how cancer cells respond to drugs.

Testing each RNA and drug pair in the lab is costly, so computation fills the gap. Their graph transformer model, called SGTCDA, is interpretable, showing its reasoning. The authors also argue that standard cross validation flatters such models, and they use a stricter assessment. Better validated predictions help labs spend wet lab time only on the most promising pairs.
pmc-11577902:
In a rare autoimmune disease that attacks blood vessels, many patients suffer destructive sinus inflammation that eats into facial bone, and no test predicts who. Marília Furquim and co-authors compare gene variants in the bone-control system: the RANKL signal and its decoy, osteoprotegerin. They studied ninety patients and 270 healthy controls, and also compared patients by bone damage.

Over half the patients showed facial bone erosion. Variant frequencies did not separate patients from controls overall. Within patients, though, one osteoprotegerin variant's double-copy form and a RANKL variant both tracked bone damage, as did longer disease duration. The authors suggest gene testing could one day flag patients at high risk of destructive sinus disease. They frame the study as groundwork for research into treatments aimed at this bone pathway.
pmc-11578402:
Muhammad Akhtar Abbas Khan wrote this 2024 analysis of why big foreign drug firms are leaving poorer lands, with Pakistan as the lens. Such firms brought new drugs and know-how, yet plant sales to local buyers have fanned debate. Local firms now hold about three quarters of the Pakistani market, up from less, while the giants' share has slid to about a quarter.

Khan names the squeeze: stiff local rivalry, mergers that stall plant growth, and joint ventures that feed the locals. Price freedom for non-essential drugs may lure the giants back, he notes. Holding ground will take fresh molecules and modern plants. The piece weighs what exits cost a health system in new treatments and jobs.
pmc-11583702:
Siebers and four co-authors interview family doctors about breast ultrasound in a study from two thousand twenty-four. Ultrasound is accurate enough that it could be the first test for women with a focal breast complaint, reserving other scans for unclear cases. Doctors who refer these patients had a say.

Sixteen Dutch general practitioners shared their routines and worries. Long waits for ultrasound topped the concerns, along with gaps in how results travel between radiologists, doctors, and patients. Shared decision-making mattered to them, as did patients drifting away after hospital results. Most welcomed an ultrasound-first path for its benefits. The authors list the practical hurdles, from workload to decentralized testing, that must be cleared first.
pmc-11585102:
Saskia Borsdorf and nine co-authors study how a sticky cell protein tunes a serotonin sensor in this twenty twenty-four paper. Serotonin helps set mood, and one of its receptors can pair up with other proteins. The team had found that this receptor binds CD44, a protein that helps cells cling and move.

Using light-based tests, they measured how eagerly the two bind, alone and paired. They then watched how pairing changed the receptor's signal output, with and without drugs that prod each partner. The results show CD44 acts as a dimmer for the receptor. Such tuning matters for how serotonin drugs may work in the brain.
pmc-11585202:
Mahboobeh Sheikh and co-authors compare an automated ultrasound AI tool with MRI for measuring the left heart chamber in weakened heart patients, in work from twenty twenty-four. MRI is the standard for heart size and pump fraction, but it is slow and costly. The AI tool reads 3D ultrasound and reports volumes on its own.

Thirty patients with dilated cardiomyopathy at a Tehran heart center had both scans within a day. The AI measures tracked MRI closely for chamber volumes, with strong reader agreement. The tool read small on chamber volumes and high on pump fraction and mass. Hand fixes to outlines improved the pump fraction calls. The authors deem it a fast, viable option.
pmc-11585602:
Zhenfeng Qiu and co-authors test how rock share and spread steady soil rock embankments in a 2024 paper. High fill road and rail banks oft mix soil with rock chunks. Their failure slides threaten the works built on them.

Static load model tests varied rock share and block placement. A slide face equation was built from share and spread, then checked by simulation. Below sixty percent rock, more rock lifted load skill and flattened slides. Past that mark, gains came slower as the fill packed dense. Blocks at crest or toe steadied banks, mid slope blocks hurt. Design rules fall out for bank builders.
pmc-11586402:
Eight authors, led by Yuteng Weng, name a switch that pushes stem cells toward bone in this 2024 paper. Bone repair starts when skeletal stem cells commit to a path, toward bone-making or cartilage-making cells. The steps just before that commitment were poorly understood.

The switch is a transcription factor called Zfp260. Its levels jump as stem cells turn into progenitors, the halfway stage. When it fails, cells stall at that stage and bone repair suffers. The factor keeps the DNA open at key spots and switches on Runx2, a master gene for bone, by building large enhancer complexes. A partner enzyme marks Zfp260 at three exact sites, and that marking is required for it to work. Mutating those sites breaks the switch, pointing to a finely tuned control step in early bone formation.
pmc-11586502:
Fruzsina Kotsis and colleagues reviewed surveillance for tumors in children with von Hippel-Lindau syndrome. Their 2024 paper focuses on pheochromocytomas and paragangliomas in young patients. Early detection prevents serious harm from these hormone-secreting tumors. German registry data supplied the cases for analysis. Seventy-five patients aged up to eighteen were included.

Most had a clinical tumor diagnosis before genetic testing. Over half joined a structured screening program in Freiburg. Follow-up ran for more than a decade on median. Screening paired yearly hormone checks with eye exams from age six. MRI scans of abdomen and nervous system began at age twelve. The paper weighs how current schedules perform in practice. Gaps in early detection guide its suggestions.
pmc-11588402:
Matthew Stanbrook presents a 2024 editorial on Canada's first steps toward national pharmacare. A new law, passed in October 2024, opens the door to universal public drug coverage. Its first concrete measures fund full coverage of diabetes medicines and supplies, plus contraceptives, with no cost to patients. The law also sets a one-year deadline for plans on a national drug list, bulk buying, and how a full program would run.

Stanbrook calls the step welcome but fragile: heavy on promises, light on substance, and exposed to political change. Without coverage, about one Canadian in twenty skips or stretches medicines for cost reasons, with far higher rates among the young, the poor, and the uninsured. That nonadherence feeds worse health and higher system costs. The editorial warns that Canadians still face deep uncertainty over whether guaranteed drug access will arrive.
pmc-11589202:
Longwen Li, Xiuhui Wang, and Wei Qi Yan teach a detector to pick out the small parts of trademark images in this 2024 paper. Trademark filings keep growing, and so do copycat disputes. Checking images by hand cannot keep pace, and the telling details are often tiny.

Their network builds on a transformer detector and adds two attention tools to the backbone, one that highlights where things are and one that reads the whole scene's context. A feature pyramid then boosts the fine detail that small elements need. On their test set the system reached about ninety-one percent accuracy, ahead of rival detectors. The authors present it as a practical aid for market regulators hunting infringing marks, where missing a small copied element can decide a case.
pmc-11589602:
Xiaoge Sun and co-authors review the gut-liver-brain axis, a three-way line of signals linking the digestive tract, the liver, and the brain. Their 2024 review builds on the known gut-brain link by adding the liver, the body's main processing plant for nutrients. Chemical messages made by gut microbes carry much of the traffic between these distant organs.

The review gathers what is known about how those messages shape energy use, immune activity, and the barriers that guard each organ, in animals and in humans. Gaps in the story remain, from how the pathway develops to how it fails in disease. The authors close by pointing to the studies most needed next.
pmc-11589702:
Yang Pengjin and co-authors published this study in 2024. It reads the pore space inside rock while the rock is being squeezed. Knowing live porosity helps judge stress and strength in deep engineering. The team crushed siltstone samples under three-way pressure while pinging them with ultrasound. Sound speed rose fast early on, then leveled as cracks shut. A new curve model captures that shape.

From sound speed, a corrected classic formula yields porosity moment by moment. Those values feed a compaction factor that tracks how cracks and pores close. A damage model then joins compaction with statistical cracking to predict the rock's response. The authors offer the chain as a live diagnostic for tunnels and mines. Sound, in their setup, becomes a stethoscope for buried stone.
pmc-11590402:
Meng Qin and co-authors link classroom conditions to how students' eyesight changes over a school year, in this 2024 study. In Shanghai's Fengxian District, forty-eight classrooms across eight high schools were measured for light, space, and board setup. Over a thousand students had their refraction checked in 2022 and again in 2023. A flexible statistical model hunted for links between room factors and eye drift.

Students' refractive error and astigmatism grew over the year, though plain visual sharpness held steady. No classroom met the standard gap between screen and front seat. Space per student, board height, and screen distance shaped sharpness changes; space also shaped refractive drift. Window area and board glare touched astigmatism. The authors compute a least-harm room profile and urge schools to meet national standards.
pmc-11590502:
Sen Huang and four co-authors link a stress sugar ratio to death after heart attack in a 2024 study. The ratio sets a patient's attack-time sugar against their long-run norm, and it calls bad outcomes with force. Past work found a U-shaped tie to harm, but its play in patients who also bear a faulty heart rhythm was not known.

The team drew more than 3,200 heart attack cases from a large care data bank. They split cases by rhythm fault and traced death risk across the ratio's range. Low-end risk drew a fresh look for its drivers. The study refines a cheap risk mark.
pmc-11590802:
Global health initiatives may change care quality, not just access, Irene Atuhairwe and co-authors set out to map in a 2024 protocol. Global initiatives have improved health care access worldwide. High maternal mortality, though, persists in low- and middle-income countries such as Uganda. Despite heavy investment, evidence on how these initiatives affect the quality of maternal health services is insufficient, and quality is what drives outcomes once women reach care.

Existing evidence focuses on outputs like facility deliveries and service use, which do not reflect quality. The protocol describes a scoping review to collate evidence on initiative effects on maternal care quality in Sub-Saharan Africa. It lays out questions, sources, and charting plans before the review runs. Readers get the blueprint.
pmc-11590902:
Ikko Sakamoto and co-authors show that the redox state inside muscle mitochondria decides whether stored glycogen can be broken down for fuel. Mitochondria and glycogen sit side by side in muscle, and mitochondria also set the redox tone during exercise. The link between that tone and glycogen use was not known. The team used mice whose muscle lacks SOD2, a key shield against superoxide inside mitochondria.

The mutant muscle piled up glycogen and the mice moved poorly. The enzyme that frees sugar from glycogen, muscle glycogen phosphorylase, was much less active. A superoxide-making drug had the same effect on normal muscle. Antioxidant treatment brought the enzyme's activity back and improved movement in the mutants. The control is thus a switch: too many reactive oxygen species turn the glycogen tap down, and clearing them turns it back up.
pmc-11593002:
Ivan Iliev and co-authors test in a 2024 study mistletoe extract paired with standard drugs against breast cancer cells. The extract, sold as Iscador Qu, has drawn decades of study as a companion therapy. Two cell lines anchor the tests, one slow to spread and one highly mobile.

Eleven approved drugs were paired with the extract across dose grids in the lab. On the mobile line, a docetaxel pairing cut the killing dose four fold. A cisplatin pairing backfired, raising that dose one and a half fold instead. On the slow line, an oxaliplatin pairing cut the dose 5.2 fold, the strongest gain. Two other pairings clashed on the slow line, a caution the authors flag.
pmc-11594102:
Cuihuan Zhao and co-authors build TPGPred, a learning tool that spots heat-loving proteins, in a 2024 paper. Thermophilic proteins keep working at temperatures that wreck ordinary proteins, which makes them prized for industry and basic research. Finding them by lab testing alone is slow, so a sharp computer screen helps.

The team trained a gradient boosting model on more than five thousand six hundred protein sequences, mixing several feature styles drawn from each sequence. They compared algorithms and feature blends to pick the best pairing. On a held-out test set of six hundred twenty-seven proteins, the model topped ninety-five percent accuracy with even stronger ranking scores. The tool gives biotechnologists a fast first pass over new sequences.
pmc-11595802:
Niantao Zhang and four co-authors wrote a 2024 study on judging fatigue life in steel catenary risers. A riser is a steel pipe that hangs in a curve from a sea platform to the seabed. Its welded joints face endless cycles of stress from waves and motion. Engineers must predict when those welds will crack.
