The team tested a full-scale riser weld two ways. The classic S-N curve method rates life by stress range against counted cycles. The fracture mechanics method tracks crack growth from real flaws. Test curves beat the standard design curve. The mechanics method, under a British engineering assessment code, gave sound estimates for full-scale welds. Early short-crack growth proved key to accuracy. Weld shape at the cap drove life, and grinding the weld still helped.
pmc-11596802:
Kirdaite and co-authors published a review in 2024 on joint injections for arthritis. Some joint diseases strike one joint, others strike a few or many. Cells in the joint lining drive much of the damage. Treating the joint from inside, by injection, can work with whole-body drugs.

The review sums up trials from the past decade on drugs injected into joints. New slow-release forms of steroids are one main line of work. Other trials target pain sensors in the joint, since pain comes from both swelling and worn cartilage. The authors also survey fresh targets, from cell surface marks to small RNA strands. They weigh gains and limits of each approach for doctors who treat sore joints.
pmc-11597502:
Hanlong Xin and co-authors study a gene signal in back muscle cells from girls with curved spines in a 2024 paper. The condition, called adolescent idiopathic scoliosis, has no clear single cause. Earlier work linked lower activity of the gene ESR1 on the concave side to the curve.

The team took muscle stem cells from both sides of the spine in 25 female patients. About half showed a strong left-right gap in gene activity. That group had worse curves, smaller concave-side muscle, and more fat inside that muscle. The size of the gap tracked with curve angle. The findings tie uneven muscle gene activity to how severe the curve becomes.
pmc-11599402:
Abhijeet Venkataraman and co-authors argue, in a 2024 perspective piece, that three fast-growing tools should be combined to study aging at the level of single cells. Aging brings cells that stop dividing yet refuse to die, and those cells release signals that age their neighbors. The immune system also weakens, which lets the cycle spread.

Engineered materials can mimic the cues around cells in an aging body. Tiny flow devices can copy the motion and cell mixing of real tissue. Spatial gene and protein mapping can show where aged cells sit and what they release. Used together, the authors say, these tools can model aging far better than any one alone.
pmc-11599602:
Two kinds of alpha rhythm coexist in the hearing cortex, Víctor López-Madrona and co-authors show in a 2024 study. Alpha oscillations there have been linked to attention and suppression of irrelevant information. Their anatomical organization and interaction with other processes, though, were unclear. The open question was whether alpha acts locally inside each neural source or comes from separate inhibitory sources that gate information across the network.

Intracerebral recordings from epilepsy patients were taken at rest and during tone listening. Source separation disentangled the neural generators. Sources were labeled oscillatory if they showed strong alpha at rest, and evoked if they responded to stimulation. The two kinds proved condition-specific and segregated in the auditory cortex. Readers get an anatomical answer to a gating debate.
pmc-11599902:
Ellelan Degife and a team of co-authors compare operations for infected heart valves with abscess in a 2024 paper. An abscess at the aortic root raises illness and death in valve infection, and whether to replace the root or spare it was unsettled. The team review all surgical cases of active aortic valve infection at one center over a decade.

About a third of patients had an abscess, and a quarter of those abscesses were missed on scans before surgery. Abscess strongly predicted death during the operation period. Five year survival was like between root sparing and root replacement repairs. The authors stress early detection and treatment.
pmc-11600602:
Seretis and a large team of colleagues wrote a commentary in twenty twenty-four on what to call cancers that arise from keratinocytes, the main cells of the skin's outer layer. A European consensus had proposed dropping the old term non-melanoma skin cancer in favor of keratinocyte cancer.

The authors agree the old term is vague and outdated, but they argue the new one should keep the word skin. Keratinocytes also line the mouth, nose, eyes, and other sites, and cancers there behave differently. Adding skin, making keratinocyte skin cancer, keeps the term exact. They note many dermatologists shared doubts about the shorter name for talks with patients.
pmc-11600802:
Brendan Kelly and co-authors review what is known about frailty in patients facing revision joint replacement, in a 2024 paper. Hip and knee replacements are among the most common operations in the United States, and as first-time replacements pile up, so do revisions, the harder operations that redo a failed joint. Projections see revision knee work growing by up to 70 percent between 2014 and 2030, with hip revisions growing even faster.

Revision surgery takes longer and fights bone loss, scar tissue, and distorted anatomy, so patients face higher risks than in first-time surgery. Frailty, the worn-down state of many older patients, compounds those risks. The review gathers how frailty is measured in this setting, how it predicts complications, and what teams can do before surgery to shore patients up. It frames frailty screening as a standard step in planning revision work.
pmc-11602102:
Older donor kidneys fail more often after transplant, and cell senescence, the worn-out state of aging cells, may be one reason rejection strikes. The authors combine bulk and single-cell gene data to test that link. They gather senescence-related genes from several databases, then use network analysis and machine learning to find the ones that predict rejection. Thirteen marker genes emerge. Rejection samples also split into two clusters with different senescence profiles and different graft survival.

Models built on the markers perform strongly: one diagnoses acute rejection without a biopsy at high accuracy, and another forecasts graft survival out to three years. Single-cell data fill in which cell types carry the senescence signal inside rejecting kidneys. The authors conclude that senescence sits close to the heart of rejection biology. They propose the marker genes as tools for earlier detection and for timing intervention to save grafts.
pmc-11602402:
Switching to a newer HIV drug stack raised body weight sharply in West African cohorts, and Thierry Tiendrebeogo and co-authors charted the climb, in work from twenty twenty-four. More than six thousand seven hundred patients with switch records were followed across three lands. Weight paths bent at the switch date in the model.

Yearly gain after the switch ran near three kilograms, clearly above the prior slope. Most had come from two older drug bases. A trial-style emulation checked big gain, set at a tenth of body weight in a year. The findings press clinics to pair the better drug with weight watch.
pmc-11602802:
Anderson Santos de Freitas and four colleagues published a soil study in two thousand twenty-four on bacteria in rice fields. Flooded rice farming covers most of world rice output and swings soil between wet and dry states. The team tracked bacterial communities in Brazilian rice soil through eleven drain-and-flood cycles.

The communities bounced back after each early disturbance, showing strong resilience. Over time, though, the steady swings wore that resilience down. Four distinct community states appeared across the cycles. Some bacterial groups faded while others grew, and predicted jobs shifted, with more nitrogen processing in dry phases. Diversity itself held up; the change came from swapping members. The authors link the pattern to sustainable rice soil care.
pmc-11603802:
Fanghua Liu and four co-authors present in 2024 a case of psoriasis treated with ixekizumab in a patient living with HIV. Psoriasis is a stubborn skin disease of red plaques and silvery scale. New biologic drugs have eased it for many, yet doctors worry about using them when HIV weakens the immune system.

Ixekizumab blocks interleukin 17, a signal protein that drives skin inflammation. The case tracks how the patient's skin responded and whether the drug stayed safe alongside HIV. Reports like this one help dermatologists weigh newer biologics for patients once steered away from them. Careful case evidence can widen treatment options where trial data are scarce.
pmc-11603902:
Eleonora Volpato and thirteen co-authors gather stories from patients with uncontrolled or severe asthma and their care staff in Italy, using narrative medicine. Inhaled therapy works, yet this hard form of asthma stays common. The study came out in twenty twenty-four.

A mixed method read drew themes, word choice, feeling, and story types from well over a hundred patients and dozens of staff. Patients had lived with the illness for years on average, with flares across recent months. The aim was to map how care quality, life quality, mind and social forces, and treatment sticking intertwine in daily life with severe asthma.
pmc-11604702:
Kazumasa Tanimoto, Yohei Hamada, and Ikuo Katayama tested whether drilling signals can reveal rock type changes underground in a 2024 study. They drilled mafic and ultramafic rocks from Oman and Japan in the lab, tracking torque and penetration rate. A water altered rock type, serpentinized peridotite, drilled about twice as fast as the others, wet or dry. The authors link the speed to weaker fracture strength after alteration.

They then compared lab readings with real scientific ocean drilling data, normalizing penetration rates for rotation and torque. The altered formation again drilled systematically faster than the gabbro layer, matching the lab pattern. The authors propose that live drilling parameters can flag rock transitions, such as serpentinite, during drilling. That would give geologists a cheap in place sensor for what the bit is passing through.
pmc-11605002:
Asma Al-Wasidi and four colleagues make magnetic copper ferrite particles that pull two harmful dyes out of water, in a twenty twenty-four study. The dyes, crystal violet and acid red 88, pollute water from factories. The team made the particles by a simple burn method using two fruit acids as fuel. The choice of fuel changed the particle size.

Best results came at set acidity levels and after eighty minutes of contact. The particles soaked up more than four hundred milligrams of dye per gram. Trials on real wastewater removed over ninety-five percent of both dyes. Since the particles are magnetic, they can be fished out with a magnet and reused. The authors present them as a cheap water cleanup tool.
pmc-11605602:
Kyoko Inai and co-authors test whether curcumin blocks brain tumor growth by disabling one enzyme activity. Their 2024 conference abstract concerns glioblastoma, the commonest malignant brain tumor, with a five-year survival near ten percent. The enzyme p300 helps switch genes on by adding acetyl groups, and its activity drives pancreatic cancer growth, but its role in this brain tumor was untested.

Curcumin inhibits that enzyme activity, while a close chemical cousin does not. Comparing the two compounds on a human glioblastoma cell line let the team isolate the enzyme's contribution to cell growth. A structure-activity design varied the molecule to find which parts carry the effect. The abstract reports the head-to-head comparison in tumor cells.
pmc-11606102:
Yi Ren and co-authors layer gene, chemical, and gut microbe data to find fresh markers of childhood obesity. Rising child obesity strains health worldwide, and simple cases hide tangled causes. Blood transcripts, blood metabolites, and stool microbes were profiled in the same children. Hundreds of genes and dozens of metabolites split the obese group from peers.

Immune-linked genes and paths stood out in the gene list. Lauric acid tracked body mass tightly and sorted obesity well on its own. A joint random forest using all three layers reached an accuracy score of 0.912. Fourteen indicators form the proposed marker set. Cross-layer links numbered 233 significant pairs, weaving the layers into one network.
pmc-11606202:
Claudia Gregoriano and a large team pool trial data on a blood guide for antibiotics in cancer, in work from 2024. Procalcitonin rises in bacterial infection and can signal when antibiotics may stop safely. Cancer patients were under studied for this guide despite high infection risk in care.

Close to eight hundred cancer patients came from fifteen randomized trials in the pool. Patients guided by the blood mark got notably fewer antibiotic days than usual care. Death rates at one month ran lower in the guided group, though the gap was not firm. Under age seventy, the death gap reached firm support in split checks. The authors back guided care as safe for this group.
pmc-11606302:
Cristian Ramos-Vera and seven co-authors adapt and validate a moral outrage scale for adults in Peru. Moral outrage is the felt response when a moral rule is broken. The study came out in twenty twenty-four.

Latin America has few such scales, despite wide inequality and social strain. Hundreds of Peruvians, mostly women in their twenties, took the scale. Two model types both fit a two part form, with a felt part and a thought part, and loadings were strong. The scale read the same across sexes. Its parts linked as hoped with authoritarian views and with sex, age, and class marks.
pmc-11606602:
Sophie Leclercq and co-authors profile blood chemistry in severe alcohol use disorder and after three weeks sober, in a 2024 study. Alcohol addiction remains hard to treat, partly because its biology is still sketchy. Blood carries thousands of small molecules reflecting diet, gut microbes, and body state — a rich place to hunt for clues and drug targets.

Ninety-six patients gave blood for untargeted chemical profiling. Patterns were tied to the psychological symptoms patients reported, and profiles before and after abstinence were compared to see what normalizes. Molecules that track mood or craving could become targets for medicines that support recovery. Chemistry that heals with sobriety also hints at what drinking breaks.
pmc-11607202:
Parminder Kaur and co-authors review long non-code RNAs as marks and targets in a fast T-cell blood cancer. The review appeared in 2024. The cancer strikes hard, and at least a fourth of cases come back. Came-back cases oft fare poor, so new care targets are in need.

Long RNAs shape how tumors grow and spread in many cancers. The review sorts how they are made and what they do in this cancer. Gene and RNA data on the disease are still thin, the authors note. That gap makes the RNA path more worth a close look. They may serve as find, fate, and care marks in time.
pmc-11607802:
Singh, Antonenko, Kocyła, and Krężel engineer a new variant of the enzyme butelase in a 2024 paper. Butelase is a plant enzyme prized for joining and labeling peptides and proteins with high precision. It is hard to produce and purify, which limits its use.

Two changes to key gatekeeping residues made the variant, called Butelase AY, more stable and easier to obtain in good yield. It labeled a small peptide, a globular protein, and a disordered protein with a fluorescent probe. It also handled substrates with unnatural amino acids and kept its target precision. The authors present it as a practical tool for protein engineering and synthetic biology.
pmc-11607902:
Ohsang Kwon and seven colleagues test whether simple mobility checks before spine surgery predict a common bending complication after it, in a 2024 paper. Proximal junctional kyphosis, a sharp curve above the fused segment, strikes many adults after deformity correction. The team reviewed 157 patients operated over two and a half years.

Before surgery each patient took three mobility tests: timed up-and-go, five sit-to-stands, and an alternate step test. A year later, about twenty-six percent had developed the complication. Of the three tests, only the sit-to-stand time separated the groups, with slower patients at higher risk. A cutoff near twenty-two seconds was suggested by the data. Adjusted analysis kept the test, age, and a disability score as significant predictors. The authors advise flagging slow risers for extra preventive effort during and after surgery.
pmc-11608002:
Nur Amelia Bachtiar and co-authors give clinical radiologists a short guide to MRI scans for stroke caused by a blocked vessel, with a stress on scans that need no injected dye. Such dyes can cost a lot and can harm people with weak kidneys or allergies.

The guide walks through the standard scan types and what each shows about where a stroke sits, how large it is, and how old it is. One scan type helps spot bleeding inside the damaged area. A further method can map blood flow in the brain with no dye at all, which can stand in for dye based vessel scans.
pmc-11608202:
Qiyuan Su and co-authors test a traditional Chinese medicine called Xuesanqi in mice with colitis in a 2024 study. Colitis inflames the colon, and the plant rhizome was expected to help by fixing gut microbe imbalance and calming signaling paths that drive inflammation.

Mice with induced colitis lost less weight, had less blood in stool, and kept longer colons with treatment. Gut microbe profiles moved back toward normal, and helpful short chain fatty acids rose. A key inflammatory signaling path settled, and proteins that seal the gut lining rose. The results support further study of the remedy.
pmc-11608502:
Huaiyong Zhang and nine co-authors fed an antioxidant supplement to heat-stressed chickens and saved their bones in a 2024 paper. Finisher broilers under chronic heat, seven hours a day at 34 degrees, built up reactive oxygen and lost tibia mass. The supplement, N-acetyl cysteine, feeds the body's own glutathione defense.

Gene profiling of shin bone showed heat switching on oxidation and inflammation programs. Two grams per kilogram of feed raised antioxidant defenses across gut, bone, and marrow, and damped the inflammatory pathway there. Bone-eating cells were suppressed while bone-cell genes rose. The supplemented birds kept denser, thicker-corticed tibias. Growth and gut microbes were unchanged. The authors trace a gut-to-bone route for heat damage.
pmc-11611702:
Mari Pesonen and co-authors survey Finns with long kidney ills on felt health and life cheer in a 2024 study. Such ills spread fast and oft hide till late, when harm is set in stone. Past work shows these patients grade life lower than the broad herd, the team notes.

A set-form poll of over five hundred patients forms the base of the work. Life cheer and felt health are the chief scores drawn from the forms. Group maths then sorts patients into kinds and ties kinds to past traits.
pmc-11611902:
Fengwen Cui and co-authors published a 2024 study comparing two ways to crack severe calcium in heart arteries. Calcified plaques resist stents; doctors must modify the rock before expanding the vessel. The standard is a step-up rotational atherectomy, a tiny burr that grinds calcium gradually. A newer rival, rota-tripsy, blends grinding with shockwave pulses that fracture calcium from within.

Clinical data on the newer method were thin, so the team mined records of 3,652 patients treated between 2021 and 2024. Cases were divided by technique and compared on procedural success and safety. Head-to-head evidence of this size helps operators choose per lesion rather than per habit. Calcium is where angioplasty goes to struggle, and each new tool must prove it on the hardest cases. The authors present the comparison as real-world evidence from the catheter lab's actual work.
pmc-11612002:
Xijie Hou and co-authors link daily movement to quality of life in older lung cancer patients on chemotherapy, in this 2024 study. Two hundred eight patients at two Chinese hospitals rated their activity and well-being. Most moved little: well over half fell in the low activity band, and only a handful reached the high band.

Moderate to high activity explained about a fifth of the spread in quality-of-life scores, which also tied to age, schooling, income, and where patients lived. The authors suggest tailored activity plans as part of care, matched to each patient's strength for safety.
pmc-11612502:
Greatness Olaitan, Wendy Lynch, and Jill Venton reviewed low-intensity focused ultrasound as a treatment for substance use disorder in a 2024 paper. Addiction care needs new tools, and sound focused deep in the brain can nudge circuits without surgery. The review gathers work in animals and humans on reward pathways.

Tuned sound appears to cut cravings and withdrawal strain, retune reward circuitry, and ease the body-sense and emotional sides of addiction. Settings like frequency, burst pattern, and intensity decide the balance between gain and safety. Results still vary between studies, and long-term effects are open. The authors call for joint work across fields to pin down parameters and mechanisms before the method can anchor care.
pmc-11612602:
Emily Morrow, Lyndsay Nelson, Melissa Duff, and Lindsay Mayberry present a 2024 paper on a phone tool for memory after chronic traumatic brain injury. Memory and learning loss are among the most deep and long harms of such injury. Yet rehab tends to stop at short clinic stays, in set rooms that do not match daily life.

Their tool pairs moment-by-moment checks with small helps, sent by phone as life goes on. That frame has served other long-term ills well. The paper tells how the tool was built for brain injury and how users found its ease of use in first tests.
pmc-11612702:
Donghoon Kang and co-authors run a drug trial for erosive gastritis, a sore and worn stomach lining, in a 2024 study. Doctors often use two drugs on their own: one shields the stomach lining, and one cuts acid. The trial tested whether using both drugs together beats the acid drug alone. It ran at many centers as a phase 4 study, the stage after a drug reaches the market.

The trial enrolled 260 patients whose gastritis was confirmed by a scope exam. Half took both drugs twice a day for two weeks, and half took the acid drug alone. Erosion improved in 62 percent of the combined group, against 49 percent with one drug. Both groups eased bleeding, redness, and symptoms at much the same rates. No drug-related side effects appeared. The authors conclude the pair works better for healing erosions.
pmc-11613402:
Hyder Mirghani and Ibrahim Albalawi compare two scar-free thyroid surgery routes on looks and pain. Their 2024 review pools studies of surgery through the mouth lining versus surgery through the areola. Both routes hide scars, a strong draw for thyroid patients, yet no past review had set them head to head.

Ten studies survive screening from hundreds of records across four databases. The mouth route wins on cosmetic outcome in the pooled sums. Pain scores after surgery show no clear gap between routes. Counts of central lymph nodes removed also match closely. The patient groups cover small cancers and other thyroid disease. The authors favor the mouth route where looks matter most, with pain a wash.
pmc-11613502:
Zhengyang Mei, Chenyi Cai, and Shulai Luo lead a team pooling trials of talk therapy for insomnia in teenagers. Their meta-analysis appeared in two thousand twenty-four. Cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia is the front-line treatment in adults. Whether it works as well in adolescents needed a pooled answer.

Eight randomized trials with nearly six hundred young participants were combined. After treatment, the therapy clearly improved overall insomnia severity. Teenagers also fell asleep faster and slept longer and more efficiently. Months later, the insomnia benefit was still detectable. Bias checks and sensitivity tests probed the pooled numbers for fragility. The authors conclude the therapy earns its place for sleepless teens. They note the small trial base as a limit. More and larger adolescent trials would firm up dosing and delivery choices.
pmc-11613702:
Xia Yang, Ning Zhou, and Jie Cao study how small airways may help form lymphoid follicles in COPD, in a 2024 paper. Those follicles are clusters of immune cells that grow in the lungs of some patients. Their formation process was not well understood.

The team compared lung tissue from patients with COPD, smokers, and non-smokers. Patients with follicles had worse lung function and stronger signs of a cell change process in airway lining cells. Smoke extract triggered the same change in lab-grown airway cells and raised a signal protein over time. Blocking the change lowered that protein, which suggests a causal chain.
pmc-11613802:
Imane Bensaghir and four colleagues report a woman with rheumatoid arthritis who developed lupus-like illness on a biologic drug, in a twenty twenty-four case report. The sixty-five-year-old took golimumab for her joint disease. She then developed sun sensitivity, tiredness, weak muscles, hair loss, mouth sores, and worse joint pain. Blood tests found high levels of antibodies against a cell protein called NuMA-1, at a strong titer, with no other such pattern.

Oral steroid treatment cleared her symptoms fully. The team believes the drug triggered the antibody response, a link not reported before. They urge close watching of patients on this drug who carry risk for autoimmune disease.
pmc-11614602:
Xiujin Zhang and three co-authors hunt for shared drug targets between high lung artery pressure and cancer in a 2024 study. The lung condition strains and swells the right side of the heart and kills many patients. Both diseases rewire cell metabolism in kindred ways, which hints at shared levers.

Using genetic data from over 289,000 people, the team tested whether any of 1,400 blood metabolites causally move the lung disease risk. Two fish-oil fats, DHA and EPA, were then tested in immune and cancer cell lines for calming oxidative stress and inflammation. The study also scanned tumor genomes and protein tags for patterns the metabolites might shift. Any fat that helps both fronts would be a cheap, safe lead.
pmc-11615002:
Zheng and nine colleagues map links between death anxiety and depression in men living with HIV in China in twenty twenty-four. Modern antivirals control physical symptoms well. Mental health and quality of life now need more attention. The team surveyed seven hundred one men in Jilin Province.

Network analysis treated each symptom as a node that can influence others. About eighteen percent may have had severe depression. Confusion about what follows death was the most central symptom. The strongest bridge joined rarely thinking of death with suicidal ideas. Thoughts of death also linked the two conditions most strongly. The authors suggest teaching accurate views of death and offering more counselling. Targeting bridge symptoms could ease both problems together.
pmc-11615302:
Ketki Patil and five co-authors test whether an HIV drug can fight an aggressive breast cancer in a 2024 paper. Triple negative breast cancer lacks the usual hormone and growth receptors, leaving few treatment options. Repurposed drugs can reach patients faster, and this drug is known to reach breast tissue, which drew the team's interest.

In lab tests the drug strongly curbed the growth of triple negative cells, while a kin drug had only weak effects. Treated cells showed more oxidative stress and cell death signals, plus shifts in key growth and matrix proteins. The authors propose the drug as a candidate for repurposing, alone or in combination, pending clinical proof.
pmc-11615702:
Brotzman and four co-authors report a survey study from twenty twenty-four on when older adults should stop colon cancer checks. Health rules say checks should stop at age seventy-five for most people. The gains from checks shrink for adults with more health problems and shorter lives. The team asked if adults with short or long expected lives accept that stop rule in the same way.

They used a large national survey of adults aged fifty and older from twenty eighteen. The final group held just over twelve hundred people with full answers. pmc-11618102:

pmc-11618402:

pmc-11618602:

pmc-11619102:

pmc-11621002:

pmc-11621802:

pmc-11622502:
Shahrbanoo Rezaee and four co-authors teach life skills to cut home harm and lift cure care in women with sugar ill met by mate harm. Their trial appeared in twenty twenty-four. pmc-11623802:

pmc-11624802:

pmc-11625202:

pmc-11625702:
Hongyu Gao, Liangyu Luo, and Jun Liu simulate back-tooth movement with clear aligners in a 2024 paper. pmc-11625802:
Ashley Griffin and co-authors test whether kidney injury during pregnancy leaves lasting damage in rats, in a 2024 paper. pmc-11625902:
Susilo, Setiawan, and Wibowo wrote a report in twenty twenty-four on a joint class for medical and pharmacy students in Indonesia. pmc-11626102:

pmc-11627102:

pmc-11627502:
Wanlin Dai and a large team review drugs that target epigenetics, in a 2024 paper. Epigenetics covers the systems that switch genes on and off without changing the DNA code itself. When those systems go wrong, they help drive many diseases, above all cancer.

pmc-11628302:

pmc-11629502:

pmc-11630502:

pmc-11630602:

pmc-11639802:

pmc-11640102:

pmc-11640302:

Kamila Krupa and co-authors review current treatments for the most common form of liver cancer, in a paper from 2024. Care for this cancer depends heavily on tumor stage and on how well the liver still works. Classic radiation and chemotherapy perform poorly against it, so the field built other options.

Early disease can be treated with a transplant. Approved procedures for more advanced cases include surgical removal, heat based destruction of the tumor, and chemotherapy delivered straight into its blood supply. Drug options now span targeted pills, immune therapies, and drugs that starve the tumor's vessels. Combinations of immune drugs with targeted or local therapy are under active study. The review lays out how doctors match these tools to each stage of disease.
pmc-11640802:
Takuya Henmi and co-authors test whether tiny parcels from aggressive colon cancer cells can stop the cancer spreading to the liver, in work published in 2024. Cancer cells that survive treatment can grow more dangerous and drive spread. The team built such a model by forcing colon cancer cells to overproduce a stemness gene called Nanog.

Mice were dosed with parcels from the altered cells three times a week for three weeks, then given the cancer cells. Two weeks later, the treated mice had far fewer liver colonies. The parcels boosted the eating activity of immune cells called macrophages and pushed them toward a tumour-fighting state. A scan of small RNAs in the parcels found nine that changed with the gene, with predicted targets tied to macrophage work. The findings suggest a vaccine-like use of cancer parcels.
pmc-11640902:
Maísa Lins and co-authors compare the tested questionnaires and tools that measure how well adults can cook. Home cooking tracks with healthier eating, but skill is hard to measure fairly across countries and cultures. Following standard review methods, the team searched five databases and screened over a thousand studies, keeping thirty-eight that used validated tools.

Eleven different instruments turned up. Some covered a wide range, from meal planning to techniques, and had been adapted across countries with success. One tool, the Cooking and Food Skill Confidence Questionnaire, stood out for its items, direct link to cooking skill, and ease of translation. The authors note wide variation among the scales, with some probing technique in depth and others mainly confidence and attitudes.
pmc-11641102:
Yaqiong Shi and co-authors tested in 2024 whether a plant compound helps maize seedlings survive drought from the roots up. A dose of the compound, 5-ALA, sped root growth in dry conditions: thicker, longer roots with more surface, plus better cleanup of harmful oxygen byproducts.

Gene activity scans found the compound switching on pathways for building amino acids and moving materials across cell membranes. Two maize lines answered in their own ways. A cheap seedling treatment that hardens roots could matter where rains fail early in the season, long before irrigation can rescue a crop.
pmc-11641302:
Argueta and co-authors study how a loose tail region shapes far-off active sites in the tautomerase superfamily. This protein group holds over 11,000 members in five families, with varied jobs. Most members remain unmapped in structure and function.

The team compared four enzymes against two well-studied ones using motion simulations. Each run lasted one microsecond and was repeated three times, for eighteen total. Wobble measures and correlation checks were matched with crystal structures. The tail's flex turned out to steer distant site residues. The findings aid how the whole family's catalytic work is read.
pmc-11641402:
Daniel González-Inostroz and co-authors link a lupus antibody and a signalling protein to thinking problems in a mouse model of lupus, in a 2024 paper. In human lupus, the immune system attacks the body, and brain involvement brings memory and thinking trouble. The protein osteopontin tracks disease activity, but its part in the brain side was unclear. The team used mice made lupus-like with an injection of pristane.

Seventy-six female mice were split among plain pristane, pristane plus a bacterial trigger, and control groups. The pristane group fared worse on behaviour tests of memory and spatial skill. Its blood carried more of the full-length protein and a cut fragment of it than controls did. Levels of a lupus antibody named in the title were weighed alongside. The work tests whether these blood markers could flag brain involvement early.
pmc-11641502:
Sarvin Salar and co-authors ask in 2024 what blocks sport and play for kids and teens with autism, by parent tale. This group tends to move less than peers. Which blocks lead the list had to be set by rank.

Three hundred seventy young folk aged eight to twenty form the set, drawn by lot. A home built form polls the blocks by kind. Folk to folk blocks came first, then pals and peers, then mind blocks third. Kin, thought, plan, town, and skill blocks fill ranks four through eight. The team ties the ranks to school and town plans that could lift play.
pmc-11641802:
Borros Arneth and Roberto Madeddu present a 2024 systematic review of genes and the immune system in multiple sclerosis. The disease damages the central nervous system and mixes genetic roots with environmental triggers. The authors gathered a decade of studies on the genetic and epigenetic paths into the illness, favoring genome-wide scans and immune-focused work.

Genes in the HLA class II region stand out as the strongest susceptibility signals. Epigenetic changes such as DNA methylation also steer disease progress through the immune system. The authors frame the findings as a map for future treatment design, since most current care already targets immune activity.
pmc-11641902:
Huiling Zhao and co-authors test a new foundation pile whose grooved, screw-like surface grips soil far better than a smooth cylinder. Screw-groove piles are precast, cheaper, and greener than many rivals. Their 2024 study loads model piles to failure and runs computer simulations to map how force travels down the shaft and where the soil takes it up.

The grooved pile's ultimate capacity came out 1.85 times the smooth pile's, and it used its material 2.85 times as efficiently. The grooves turn the shaft into a series of bearing points, enlisting a larger body of soil and raising skin friction along the way. Tuning matters: a wider inner groove radius lifts capacity but wastes material, and groove spacing has a sweet spot. Soil properties sway the result strongly, so design must be matched to the ground.
pmc-11642002:
Mohammad Iqbal Khan, Yassir Abbas, and Galal Fares test greener high-performance concrete mixes in a study from 2024. Cement making carries a heavy carbon cost. Swapping part of the cement for waste powders can cut that cost and use up industrial leftovers.

The base swap was ten percent silica fume. Extra powders included fly ash, limestone, and an ultrafine powder called MQ. Mixes used two, three, or four powders at varied levels. The team measured strength, chloride passage, and pore space under distinct curing regimes. MQ gave the best filling effect among the fine powders. The best blends stayed strong and dense. Such mixes point to durable concrete with far less cement.
pmc-11642102:
Heli Chauhan and co-authors examine, in 2024, how proteins that store dopamine interact in methamphetamine damage to the brain. Use of the drug is rising fast in the United States, and no approved medicine treats the disorder. One protective protein is known to fail in this damage, but its effect on dopamine storage was unknown.

In rats given binge doses of the drug, the team found two proteins interacting in the striatum for the first time, and the drug changed that interaction. Protein surveys showed rises in proteins tied to cell recycling and stress response. The results suggest dopamine neurons actively fight back in the first hours after a binge.
pmc-11642202:
Halszka Kamińska, Anna Rożnowska-Wójtowicz and Bożena Werner ask whether body mass affects heart recovery in children after a COVID-linked inflammatory syndrome, in this 2024 Europe PMC paper. The syndrome, PIMS-TS, can weaken the heart muscle. Their single-center study enrolled one hundred seventy children and checked heart function at discharge, six weeks and six months.

Advanced ultrasound measures sat within normal limits on average in all weight groups. But only normal-weight children showed clear improvement in left ventricle function between six weeks and six months. Underweight, overweight and obese children did not improve significantly on those measures. Weight status, the authors conclude, shapes the pace of cardiac recovery.
pmc-11642302:
Francesca Schillaci and co-authors examine a little-studied protein, ETNPPL, in the brain cells that die in Parkinson's disease. Those dopamine neurons carry a dark pigment, neuromelanin, which several studies tie to their decline. The team stained brain sections from six patients and six healthy controls and measured the protein's gene activity in the same tissue. In healthy brains, the protein sat closely with the pigment inside the neurons.

In Parkinson's samples the pattern broke down: the protein showed only weakly in the cell body and no longer matched the pigment. Its gene activity also ran lower in each patient than in controls. No signal appeared in the nucleus in either group. The authors suggest the protein supports normal dopamine neuron function, and that its loss of place may be part of the disease process.
pmc-11642402:
Whether invasion of a brain cover film forecasts lasting hormone excess is tested by the authors in work dated 2024. The tumors at hand grow in the pituitary gland and pour out growth hormone, a state called acromegaly. Film invasion is common in such tumors, but its link to this tumor type was unstudied. The team looked back at thirty-five patients cut at one hospital from 2017 to 2020.

Eleven cases showed film invasion. Their growth hormone levels at first check ran higher than the rest. A high level marked a tenfold risk of invasion. No other trait split the groups. Low levels of a growth marker at first check tied to cure at one year.
pmc-11642702:
Jingyu Zhang and co-authors tune a grout for tunnels in cold regions in a study from 2024. Grout fills and seals rock around tunnels, and its set stone must bear load for decades. Plain cement grout can crack and weaken in the cold.

Waterborne polyurethane was mixed into the cement to improve it. Orthogonal tests found the best recipe: a set water ratio plus small shares of cellulose, polyurethane, and a water reducer. Set stones were then hammered in dynamic tests at varied ages. Stone particle size drove the dynamic strength most. The tuned grout aims at safer, steadier tunnels in cold ground. Mines and rail tunnels in northern regions are the target users.
pmc-11643002:
Yon-Suk Kim, Jin-Hwa Jung, and Ki-Tae Kim test a rowan fruit extract against brain immune cell swelling in the lab, in work from twenty twenty-four. The plant is a traditional medicine across Korea, China, and Japan. Its fruit is known for antioxidant and anti-swelling traits elsewhere. Effects on brain immune cells had stayed largely unknown until now. Bacterial toxin triggers swelling in a standard microglia cell line.

Water extract beats alcohol extract at curbing excess nitric oxide output. Treated cells make less of two swelling enzymes and two swelling signals. Three linked switch paths in the cells are dialled down by the extract. A master swelling switch is also blocked from firing fully. Caffeic acid emerges as a lead active part of the extract. The fruit may hold promise for brain diseases tied to immune firing.
pmc-11643502:
Alexander Sirotkin and co-authors pit copper nanoparticles against a growth factor in ovarian cells. Their 2024 study cultures pig granulosa cells with each agent alone and both together. Copper particles are known to disturb ovary function, while betacellulin supports cell growth.

The particles entered the cells, cut every growth marker, raised every death marker, and boosted hormone release. The growth factor did the reverse on nearly every count. Added together, the factor blocked and even undid the particles' harm, while the particles blunted the factor's gains. The authors see a direct toxic effect of copper particles. They also see a protective role for the factor.
pmc-11643602:
Gloria Cubas-Basterrechea and co-authors link daily vegetables to metabolic health in older adults in this 2024 study. The group covered 264 people aged sixty-five to seventy-nine who lived at home. Metabolic syndrome, a cluster of risks for heart disease and diabetes, affected about forty percent of them.

Only a small share ate the advised two servings of vegetables a day. Those who did showed a clearly lower rate of the syndrome than those who ate few vegetables. After accounting for fruit, nuts, and social factors, low vegetable intake still stood as its own risk marker. The authors urge programs that help older people eat more vegetables.
pmc-11643702:
Qixin Leng and co-authors test a simple peptide carrier that delivers gene silencing RNA to solid tumors, in work from twenty twenty-four. The RNA, called siRNA, can switch off disease genes. Approved siRNA drugs so far reach only the liver, since carriers for other tissues tend to be complex.

Their linear peptide carrier holds a tumor targeting piece built right into its chain, so no extra link step is needed. In mice, vein injections silenced a marker gene in breast tumors by up to eighty percent in the best screens. A brief sound bath boosted the effect. The carrier also cut a cancer growth gene in a second tumor model. Simple synthesis aids clinical hopes.
pmc-11643802:
Konstantina Theodora Laina and co-authors tune, in a 2024 study, a two-energy method for pulling healing compounds out of medicinal plants. Ultrasound and microwaves each loosen plant material in their way. The team combined them to extract from oregano, rosemary, St John's wort, and chamomile with ethanol. They varied microwave power, ultrasound power, and time under a statistical design. Then they measured total phenolic content and antioxidant strength.

Every plant did better under the tuned combination. St John's wort led on phenolics and antioxidant power at moderate settings, reaching a fourteen and a half percent yield. Rosemary gave the largest yield overall, nearly a quarter of the plant mass. Oregano peaked at high power on both channels, and chamomile trailed on phenolics but still yielded well. The authors pitch the pairing as a faster, greener route to plant extracts.
pmc-11643902:
Elaheh Bayat and co-authors make the first glowing complex that joins a transition metal to melem, a ringed carbon-nitrogen compound. The complex pairs manganese chloride with melem and was made by heating the metal salt with melamine in a set ratio.

The solid forms a known crystal pattern and holds up well to heat, to a stated point. The team read its structure and traits with X-ray, infrared light, and heat based tests. Like runs with cobalt and iron salts gave two new kin complexes. The work shows how melamine acts at high heat with such salts, a path to new light based materials.
pmc-11644002:
Dereilo Belitibo and co-authors studied plant compounds from the roots of Dovyalis abyssinica in 2024 for antibacterial power. The plant is widely used in Ethiopia for human ailments, yet its chemistry was largely unexplored. The team separated the root extract and identified what came out.

Five compounds were isolated and confirmed by infrared, magnetic resonance, and mass spectra, most of them reported from this plant for the first time. Extracts and pure compounds were tested against six bacterial strains, including staph and gut germs. Computer docking then modeled how the compounds might bind bacterial targets, and a standard analysis predicted how the body would handle them. Readers get a first chemical and biological profile of a traditional remedy, with candidates for further drug work.
pmc-11644202:
Nielsen reviews the role of dietary magnesium in cardiovascular disease, in a review from twenty twenty-four. Twenty years of trials and population studies link low magnesium to heart risk. High blood pressure, calcium buildup in arteries, stroke, and heart failure all go with a shortage. Tests that drain the body of magnesium in a set way show the shortage shifts how the body works.

Taking extra magnesium undoes those shifts in the metabolic unit tests. The paths at work include inflammation, oxidative stress, lipid problems, and vessels that work poorly. Flaws in ion channels and in cell signals add more risk paths. Many people eat less magnesium each day than the amounts advised. Whole grains, pulses, and greens are the sources most often missed.
pmc-11644402:
Lignin, the tough polymer that stiffens wood, could replace oil as a source of carbon chemicals if it can be broken down cleanly. Lucie Lindenbeck and co-authors present a method for that breakdown in 2024, using electricity and a silver electrode in water.

Soda lignin was reduced in a mild water and sodium carbonate bath over five to twenty hours. The main small products were sodium salts of levulinate, acetate, and formate, alongside a spread of aromatic pieces that kept their rings. Chemical analysis confirmed the mix. The authors argue the route turns a waste stream into both building-block chemicals and reactive intermediates for a more circular economy.
pmc-11644502:
A team in Italy pilots a diet plan for stricturing Crohn's disease in a 2024 paper. More than half of Crohn's patients develop scarred, narrowed bowel that blocks flow. Muscle loss is common in the disease and tracks with worse outcomes, yet diet's role in scarring is little studied.

The pilot randomly split patients between a supplement plan and control care for twelve months. The plan added essential amino acids and a gut fatty acid salt. After a year, the diet group held more muscle mass and a higher muscle index than controls. Surgery was needed in four of ten controls but only one of ten in the diet group.
pmc-11645002:
María-Luisa Pinto-Salamanca and co-authors built chip hardware in 2024 that turns a skin like pressure sensor's readings into full three dimensional touch forces, fast enough for real time robot hands. Flat stress sensors alone report only pressing force; the sideways parts must be computed, and the math is heavy.

Their design exploits the sparsity of that math, the fact that most terms are zero, to shrink the chip's area, power draw, and memory. On a prototype chip platform, a ten by ten sensor grid produced force vectors in about fifty-nine milliseconds. Errors ran near thirteen percent for pressing force and eight percent for sideways force. The circuit needs no extra memory chips and uses a quarter of the computing parts of a dense design.
pmc-11645302:
Pauline Humphrey and co-authors shape in 2024 care recommendations for internal radiation therapy in advanced cervical cancer. Patient reports of the treatment vary widely, with some traumatic accounts. Draft recommendations come from an earlier interview study of patients.

Workshops with users and providers then vote, debate, and rank the drafts. Fifty one drafts enter, four new ones join, and wording tightens across rounds. A quarter of the final set earns top marks from every voter. The ranked list now guides kinder, clearer care for future patients. Users and providers sat in the same rooms for the ranking work.
pmc-11645902:
Wensi Ouyang and Guimei Guo wrote a letter from 2024 that questions a review of exercise therapy for worn knee cartilage. The review pooled trials to judge how well exercise eases pain and builds function and strength. The letter writers value the work but say its base has flaws that readers should know. They checked the review's own flow chart and counts with care.

They found the chart's numbers do not add up: the parts sum to more than the stated total. Seven extra studies also vanish from later counts. Two papers from the same center and period seem to cover overlapping patients, so counting both could bend the pooled result. The letter asks the team to verify the figures and re-run the pool if needed.
pmc-11646102:
Qiuyu Sun and co-authors review how the heart's fuel use goes wrong in failure in a 2024 article. A healthy heart burns mostly fat and glucose in its mitochondria to make the energy molecule ATP, with sugar splitting in the cell body adding a little. In failure, the mitochondrial route shrinks and the sugar-splitting route grows, yet total energy still falls short, weakening each squeeze.

One defect appears in every failure type: burning of the glucose-derived fuel pyruvate drops, even when its supply rises, wasting efficiency. Fat burning rises in some failure types and falls in others, and ketones step in as a backup fuel to varying degrees. The review maps these shifts by disease kind to guide metabolic therapies.
pmc-11646402:
Six authors wrote a study in two thousand twenty-four on internet dependence among university students. They ask how academic burnout interacts with depression and anxiety in this problem. Burnout could in theory either blunt or worsen the pull of the internet for students who feel low or tense.

The team surveyed students and kept seven hundred fifty-seven valid replies, with an average age near twenty-one. They found that anxious and low feelings linked to internet dependence both directly and through a lack of social support. Burnout changed the strength of that link. The authors frame the result as a model of what drives the habit and where support can help.
pmc-11646602:
A national surveillance team in the United Kingdom sequenced hepatitis C viruses that did not fit the common subtypes seen there. Hepatitis C comes in eight known genotypes and more than ninety subtypes, and rare forms matter because they can weaken the drugs meant to cure the infection. The team compared the odd samples against reference sequences to place them on the virus family tree.

Two samples from United Kingdom residents born in Pakistan and India proved to be new subtypes of genotype 8. A third, from a resident born in Guyana, sat so far from known types that it may mark a new genotype altogether. All three patients were cured with standard drug pairs despite resistance-linked changes in the virus. The work widens the known diversity of the virus and supports global efforts to eliminate it.
pmc-11646702:
Antonio Sirianni and co-authors studied in 2024 how coding languages spread together on GitHub, a shared coding platform. Technologies, like other innovations, spread in populations where related items are already present. The team borrowed the idea of relatedness from economics to model how languages help or compete with each other.

From how often languages appear together in projects, they scored each pair for working cohesion and for being interchangeable. From user histories, they measured how adopting one language predicts adopting or dropping another. Languages that work well together did tend to spread together. Evidence that interchangeable languages compete was weaker. The results support the broader idea that links between innovations shape their spread.
pmc-11646802:
Jiancheng Zhai and co-authors report a 2024 case of a rare kidney cancer, primary renal epithelioid angiosarcoma, in a man aged eighty-one. He had blood in his urine for a year before care. This cancer is very rare, often misread, and carries a poor outlook, so clear signs matter.

A scan showed a mass at the top of the left kidney with scattered calcium spots, plus spread to nearby lymph nodes and possible spread to the lung. Surgeons removed the kidney as a palliative step, and tissue study confirmed a malignant tumor with dead areas. Stains for three markers fit the diagnosis. The authors note that tissue staining can settle the call, and that the scattered calcium pattern on scans may help set this cancer apart from look alike kidney masses.
pmc-11647402:
Habeeb Tajudeen and three co-authors compare meat traits in three pig crossbreeds, with and without spent coffee grounds in the feed, in work from 2024. Fifty pigs from three hybrid lines were raised at a Korean university farm and measured for fat, acidity, colour, water holding and fatty acid makeup.

Breed mattered more than the supplement. The Berkshire and Woori crosses carried more fat, held water better and lost less drip than the commercial three-way cross, with richer unsaturated fat profiles. Coffee grounds at half a percent of feed did no harm to any measured trait. The authors judge the two alternative crosses close in meat quality and ahead on firmness and flavour traits.
pmc-11647502:
Xiaokai Zhang and co-authors built in 2024 a melt-away gel that carries a chemotherapy drug into liver tumors through their blood supply. The standard blocking treatment can starve vessels for good and stir up low oxygen, which dulls the immune response. Their gel mixes a temperature-sensitive base with iron oxide particles and the drug idarubicin.

In rats with liver tumors grown in place, the gel blocked vessels well and shrank disease. It also triggered a form of tumor cell death that alerts the immune system. Pairing that effect with an immune checkpoint drug looked promising in their tests. The authors say a degradable blocker can do double duty: deliver the drug and wake immunity. The work aims at better options for a deadly cancer.
pmc-11647602:
Sri Hari Raju Mulagapati and co-authors describe in 2024 a single lab test that checks many quality traits of viruses used in gene therapy. These viruses are a leading delivery platform, but making them is complex, and each batch must be checked for strength, purity, and how many virus shells carry a full gene load.

Their method runs samples through a size-sorting column watched by four detectors at once, sensing light in several ways. One run yields the gene dose, shell dose, purity, clumping, and the ratio of full to empty shells. Side-by-side tests showed results matching the separate standard assays for each trait. The authors stress that the method is fast, cheap, label-free, and needs little sample. It can serve development, release testing, and shelf-life checks alike.
pmc-11647802: Bouriche, Yvorra, and Gariboldi report an extremely rare coronary fistula case in a 2024 paper. A fistula is an abnormal channel between vessels, and one linking a coronary artery to a great vein is very unusual. The report follows the patient from the finding of the coronaro-cava fistula through to surgery, noting that such fistulas vary widely in anatomy and in how they present.
pmc-11647902:
Mary Foutz and eleven co-authors tune a family of molecules that make cells burn energy as heat. Such molecules, called mitochondrial uncouplers, short-circuit the cell's power plants so fuel is spent without being stored. A known uncoupler, BAM15, anchors the family. The team varied one ring position across a series of sister compounds and measured how strongly each raised the breathing rate of muscle cells. The best compound worked at low doses and lasted about two hours in the blood.

In mice fed into fatty liver disease, daily doses of the lead compound cut body weight and liver fat without raising body temperature. Even a very large single dose showed no ill effects in mice. The authors present the series as a candidate path toward drugs for obesity and fatty liver disease.
pmc-11648302:
Wang and coauthors test a hybrid surgery suite for brain bleeding. Fast, exact care is key when blood bursts in the brain. Hybrid suites blend open surgery tools with vessel therapy tools. Their value for grave bleed cases needs proof from real use.

The team tracked 103 bleed cases from 2019 to 2023. Cases held both burst bleeds and bleeds from trauma. Vessel scans guided which surgery each patient got. Scores of daily function were logged before and after care. The suite let teams switch methods without a move. Their aim was faster, safer care for mixed bleed cases.
pmc-11648802:
Posatorn Suwanpongsai and Kongkhet Riansuwan report a customized hip screw for a femoral neck nonunion with unusual anatomy, in a case report from 2024. The patient, an adult woman, first had her fracture fixed with screws and pins. About ten months later the bone had not united and the implant had loosened, so a valgus osteotomy with a dynamic hip screw was chosen.

Standard parts did not fit her femoral neck shape, so a custom lag screw was designed to match both her anatomy and a normal side plate. The part was cut on a computer-controlled machine. The nonunion and the osteotomy site then healed fully, with no complications reported in the case.
pmc-11648902:
Kamrunnahar Kanak and co-authors survey in 2024 microplastic pollution on the shores of three coastal islands of Bangladesh in the Bay of Bengal. Tiny plastic pieces under five millimeters pose physical and chemical hazards. The team took fifty four sediment samples from three beach zones on each island, from the debris line to the water's edge, and separated plastics with a salt solution.

Counts averaged from about one hundred seventy five to over two hundred sixty particles per kilogram, highest on Saint Martin's Island. Fibers were the most common shape, and one plastic type led the polymer counts. Surface study by microscope showed wear on particles. Readers get a baseline for a coast where such data were scarce.
pmc-11649202:
Lewkowitz and co-authors turn a proven talk-therapy program for preventing postpartum depression into a phone app, guided by the mothers it should serve. The in-person program halves new cases among low-income pregnant patients but needs trained staff. Draft app screens in English and Spanish carried therapy modules plus reminders, videos, and game-like rewards.

Twenty-five pregnant or new mothers on public insurance reviewed the drafts in interviews, half in Spanish. Their suggestions reshaped the screens, and each change was logged under a standard reporting framework. Recruiting stopped once three mothers in a row offered praise without new fixes. The authors present the refined design as ready for testing. They note the end users matched the group the app targets.
pmc-11649902:
A team led by Eva Beiner asks how felt stress and stress hormones line up in fibromyalgia, a long-term pain state, in a 2024 study. Ninety-nine patients and fifty pain-free adults gave samples and filled in a felt stress scale. The team also read two hormones in spit and hair, one for short-term strain and one for strain built up over time.

The patients felt far more stressed than the controls, and that felt stress rose with worse symptoms. The hormone levels, though, did not differ between the groups and did not track symptoms at all. Care, the authors argue, should aim at the stress patients feel, not at hormone gauges.
pmc-11650302:
Mathilde Richard and co-authors track tiny membrane sacs shed into the blood of women with metastatic breast cancer on a common drug combination, hoping the sacs reveal who is responding. Patients were classed as resistant, intermediate, or sensitive to the therapy. The team counted the vesicles and read their fat composition over the first months of treatment.

Vesicle counts swung widely during therapy, and an early rise went with faster progression. Counts stayed steady for a year in healthy women. The fat signature told more: sixteen fat species separated sensitive from resistant patients with about eighty-two percent accuracy within two months. That pattern appeared in vesicles but not in plain plasma, a point in favor of vesicle testing.
pmc-11651102:
Yu-Ling Han and co-authors profile in 2024 seven strains of a drug-proof, high-virulence lung bacterium from a Chinese hospital. The strains share near-twin plasmids that carry a key resistance gene. Such merged resistance and virulence traits pose a grave public threat with high death rates.

Whole-genome reads map the spread of resistance and virulence genes across the set. The resistance gene sits in the same mobile frame on all seven plasmids. A second resistance gene cluster appears in six of the seven plasmids. Lab mating tests probe how the plasmids pass between cells and spread the threat.
pmc-11651202:
Tsegaye Alemu and co-authors asked Ethiopians what blocks eye care in two thousand twenty-four. Vision loss is largely preventable with timely services. Two southern zones supplied the study communities. Adults joined deep interviews and group discussions. Sampling deliberately sought varied voices. Recordings were analyzed for recurring themes.

Barriers emerged at household and system levels. Distance, cost, and awareness all featured. Service trust and staffing shaped choices too. The zones had little prior research coverage. Findings give planners ground-level facts. Outreach can target the named obstacles directly. Similar rural regions share many of them.
pmc-11651702:
Samuel Bailin and a large team wrote a 2024 study on how fat under the skin relates to deeper belly fat in people with HIV. Heart and metabolic diseases are common in this group on modern therapy. Fat preferentially stored around the organs, visceral fat, is blamed, yet how the safer subcutaneous depot's cell programs track that risk was unclear.

Ninety-two participants on long-term therapy gave fat biopsies for gene sequencing, and 43 had single-cell sequencing. CT scans measured visceral fat volume. Higher visceral volume tracked with insulin resistance. Three cell types in subcutaneous fat, intermediate macrophages, myofibroblasts, and a marked fibroblast group, rose in share as visceral volume grew. The findings suggest the accessible fat depot mirrors the risky one. Biopsy of surface fat might flag metabolic risk.
pmc-11651902:
Juvenile hormone steers insect development, but Yoshitomo Kurogi and six co-authors find one of its adult targets had been overlooked. Using fruit flies carrying a glowing reporter that lights up where the hormone acts, they watched the seminal vesicle, part of the male reproductive tract, respond strongly. Giving a hormone analogue brightened the signal in its lining cells, while silencing the hormone's receptor gene dimmed it.

Hunting the genes switched on there, the team identified lactate dehydrogenase, a metabolic enzyme, as hormone-responsive in the vesicle lining. The finding suggests the hormone tunes energy metabolism in this organ. The authors say the work opens a new window on how insect reproduction is regulated in adult life.
pmc-11652502:
Gui Lu and colleagues published a 2024 study predicting recovery after a brain bleed. High blood pressure causes many such bleeds. Outcomes vary widely between patients. The team built a scoring chart from patient data. Scan features and blood markers fed the model.

Nearly one hundred fifty patients were studied. Discharge ability defined good versus poor outcome. Poor outcome patients had larger bleeds. Certain blood signals also ran higher in that group. Scan signs like irregular shape added information. The chart was checked for accuracy and usefulness. Such tools help families and doctors plan care early.
pmc-11653102:
Huaizhi Sun and six co-authors create Alzheimer's-like brain dysfunction in mice by combining a fatty diet with a diabetes drug, in a 2024 study. Metabolic disorder and brain decline travel together in people, and a faithful animal model is needed to test interventions. Neither insult alone reproduces the pairing reliably.

Mice on the combined regimen developed blood sugar turmoil plus impaired learning and memory. Their brains accumulated the amyloid precursor and altered tau protein that mark Alzheimer's disease, alongside raised inflammatory signals. Barrier proteins in brain vessels shifted, neurons were damaged, and the brain's support and immune cells overactivated. Insulin signaling proteins moved in the directions expected of resistance. The model compresses the human metabolism-to-dementia pathway into an experiment, giving drug hunters a testbed with both halves of the disease.
pmc-11653702:
Xingyu Jiang and co-authors trace in 2024 a protein chain that helps ovarian cancer resist platinum drugs. Platinum resistance drives relapse in this cancer, and stem-like tumor cells are a prime suspect. The team found a protein, SPC25, whose high levels track with poor outcomes. It acts as a scaffold, joining two partners into a three-part complex.

That complex switches on a growth pathway that keeps tumor cells stem-like. A decoy peptide that breaks the complex restored platinum's power in lab cells, in mice, and in patient-grown organoids. The authors propose the chain as a drug target. Blocking it may extend the useful life of platinum therapy.
pmc-11653802:
Cheng Li and co-authors reported a case in 2024 of a stubborn infection at a scar below a woman's navel, caused by a little known germ. The woman, aged 50, had a festering spot at the site of a keyhole surgery scar from nine years before.

The spot had burst at times over two years, leaking thick yellow pus. A lab grew the germ from the pus over three days and named it with a rapid test. One month of an oral drug, plus cleaning and draining the wound, helped at first. The infection came back six months later in a smaller form, and a silver based treatment cleared it within a week. The authors also review past reports of this germ.
pmc-11654002:
Samira Rabiei and co-authors explore poor nutrition in 2024 among young children in Iran. Malnutrition in children aged two to five can stunt growth and raise the risk of illness and death. The team used a national survey in eight provinces where food is hard to secure.

Over twenty-two hundred children were measured and their families questioned. About one in ten children were stunted, wasted, or underweight by standard scores. Stunting was more common in villages than in towns. A modeling method that maps linked causes showed that household wealth and schooling shaped nutrition most. Better-off homes had children with better scores on all three measures. The authors say policy must lift family resources to move child nutrition.
pmc-11654202:
Helia Ramezani, Hossein Sazegar, and Leila Rouhi built a plant-based drug carrier in this 2024 study. Their target is Pseudomonas aeruginosa, a bacterium that resists many drugs and forms stubborn biofilms. The drug payload is extract of Phyllanthus emblica, a medicinal plant known as amla.

The extract was packed into nanoparticles coated with chitosan over a casein core. The particles came out near 500 nanometers wide, trapped about three quarters of the extract, and stayed stable for 60 days in the cold. Tests then measured how the particles kill bacteria and block biofilm growth. Gene readings tracked three biofilm genes in treated bacteria. Safety checks on cells rounded out the lab work. The design aims to carry a plant compound past the defenses that make this germ so hard to treat.
pmc-11654302:
Yang, Song, Jin, and Peng explore security guards and bystander CPR in China, in work from twenty twenty-four. Cardiac arrest outside hospital is a major killer. A bystander who starts chest compressions can double survival, and guards are often first on scene in public places.

Fifteen guards from hospitals, housing areas, offices, and transit stations gave in depth interviews. Transcripts were coded by two researchers with both preset and emergent themes. Guards described the pull between duty and fear of blame or harm claims, summed up in the title quote. Naming those barriers is a first step to training and legal cover that help guards act.
pmc-11654402:
Mais Iflaifel and co-authors scope what is known about recruiting patients into mental health trials, a chronic weak point. Their review appeared in 2024. Trials in this field often miss their targets, delaying answers for vulnerable patients. Digital and online recruitment is the fashionable fix, promising speed and diversity, but the evidence is murky. The team examined 191 recent randomized trials from a national journals library and two leading psychiatry journals.

They summarized who the trials enrolled, by sex, ethnicity, and age, and cataloged the recruitment strategies in play. The scoping exercise maps where digital methods are actually used and where proof of benefit is missing. The authors frame it as groundwork for a fuller review that can tell trialists which recruitment spending is worth it.
pmc-11654702:
Kayla Kindig and co-authors reveal how zinc ions and acidity tune a human glycine receptor, in a 2024 study. Glycine receptors carry inhibitory signals that govern motor control and pain processing. The subtype they study sits in pain-sensing neurons of the spinal cord. Its failure is tied to chronic inflammatory pain, which makes it an attractive drug target. Many natural and foreign compounds tune its activity.

Using cryo-electron microscopy, they solve the full receptor's structure in several functional states. Acidic conditions cut the peak response to glycine. Zinc tunes the response in two directions depending on its concentration. The structures show where these effectors bind and capture the receptor in mid-change shapes. That detail can guide pain drug design aimed at this channel.
pmc-11655202:
Alejandro Sebiani-Calvo and co-authors review ways to edit crop genes without lab tissue culture in a 2024 paper. Gene editing can add prized traits to crops with great care. Yet most plant change methods need slow lab growth of tissue, which blocks many crops. Methods done in the living plant promise a faster path.

The review covers more than 250 papers and sorts the in-plant methods by strict rules. Rules include short time, few moves, simple steps, and no callus stage. The team tracks work that sent editing tools into crop plants this way. Wins are listed for nine crops, from rice and wheat to lemon and peanut. Model plants are left out, since past reviews covered them. The authors argue these methods can widen editing to more farms and crops.
pmc-11655302:
A nursing quality yardstick for aneurysm therapy in China is built by Hai-xia Yang and co-authors in work dated 2024. Care here threads a catheter into the brain to fix a weak vessel spot. The yardstick rests on a three-part quality frame: build, process, and outcome. Past work, talks, and two rounds of expert polls shaped the marks. Weight math set each mark's pull.

The final set holds three top marks, ten mid marks, and thirty-six fine ones. Expert trust scores ran high in both rounds. Ward teams gain a shared score sheet.
pmc-11655602:
Hyangpyo Kim and co-authors studied, in a 2024 paper, how Earth's magnetic shield shifts as solar wind reconnects with it. Two planned missions will watch the shield's edge glow in X-rays to read that process. Ground radar data can test what those missions should expect to see.

The team picked three cases where the space magnetic field turned while solar wind pressure held near steady. Radar maps gave the rate at which field lines merged on the day side. Standard models, fed with live solar wind data, gave the shield edge's place near noon. The merge rate rose as the edge moved closer to Earth, and fell as it moved out. It also rose when the solar wind coupled more strongly to the shield. The link aids planning for the new missions.
pmc-11655802:
Hongjie Tang and Changjiang Wei published a lung cancer cell study in two thousand twenty-four on a protein called DYNLL1. Lung adenocarcinoma is the most common lung cancer type. The team asked what this protein does in its cells and what controls it.

DYNLL1 was found at high levels in the cancer, and patients with more of it lived shorter lives. Silencing the protein slowed cell growth and pushed cells toward cycle arrest and death. A second protein, PRKN, normally tags DYNLL1 for destruction. Blocking PRKN undid the benefit of silencing, proving the pair work as a unit. The authors propose the pathway as a possible drug target.
pmc-11655902:
Maria De Bonis and others put out a methods match-up in 2024. They set two ways to predict brain age from scans side by side. Brain age signals health beyond age in years alone. Gaps can warn of early brain decline risk. One method extracts shape readings from MRI scans. The other feeds raw scans to deep learning. A many-site data set tested both ways fairly. Clarity tools showed what each model used. Feature methods and image methods were read apart.

Both paths did about as well on held-out sites. Each reached strong scores on outside testing. Shape traits offer direct body reasons on their own. Deep models needed heat maps for reading instead. Use in clinics depends on trust and openness too. Equal scores let users put clear outputs first.
pmc-11656002:
Deepak Gulwani and co-authors review how nanomedicine, drugs and imaging tools built at a tiny scale, could improve thyroid cancer care. Thyroid cancer is a common cancer of the hormone glands, and surgery, radiation, and standard drugs often give weak results. The review moves from general treatment toward care matched to each patient.

The authors survey nanoparticle systems that carry drugs straight to tumor cells and sharpen diagnosis. They weigh the gains shown in studies so far against safety and delivery problems. Clinicians and researchers get a map of where this fast-moving field may help most. It also notes where lab promise still falls short of proven benefit for patients in the clinic.
pmc-11656202:
Ramla Gary and co-authors present a 2024 imaging study using gold nanoparticles to sharpen pictures of a vessel enzyme in fish gills. The enzyme, eNOS, makes nitric oxide that relaxes blood vessels, and seeing exactly where it sits matters for physiology. Fluorescence staining can be dim and muddy in complex tissue.

Two suspensions of gold particles were compared: one held in a phosphate buffer, the other in citrate. The phosphate version spread evenly and stuck to tissue well, giving strong optical contrast of the enzyme. The citrate version clumped, and contrast fell. The lesson is mundane but decisive: the liquid a nanoparticle swims in shapes its imaging worth. The authors offer the tuned recipe for finer bioimaging of delicate tissues.
pmc-11656602:
Yuhui Zhang, Kunyun He, Bingjie Jin, and Jin Luan refine crude solder with electricity, in a study published in 2024. Standard refining wastes energy, pollutes, corrodes gear, and wastes current. Their bath uses methanesulfonic acid, a cleaner medium, and passes current through crude solder to plate out a pure tin-lead product.

They measured and modeled how well the bath conducts at varied tin levels, then tuned the process step by step. The best settings used a set current density, a mid-range tin and acid strength, close electrodes, and mild heat. Under those settings the cell ran at low voltage with over ninety-nine percent current efficiency. The fine solder came out over ninety-nine percent pure with a good finish. The authors present the route as a cleaner factory option.
pmc-11656902:
DianDian Jiang and co-authors interviewed lung cancer patients in South China about why they waited before seeking care, in a 2024 study. Patient delay stretches diagnosis and cuts survival, yet its inner reasons stay murky. Thirty patients described their paths in depth; waits ran from ninety to two hundred thirteen days.

Four themes emerged: the reasons for waiting, the triggers that finally pushed them to clinics, how they judged their own delay, and fixes they proposed. Dismissing symptoms as minor sat at the core. The interviews map the psychology of hesitation, giving clinics concrete points where outreach and education could shorten the wait.
pmc-11657002:
Jay Yoo, Khashayar Namdar, and Farzad Khalvati present, in a 2024 paper, a pipeline that outlines brain tumors in MR scans without hand-drawn training maps. Drawing those maps takes expert time and slows the building of diagnostic tools. Their method learns from a much cheaper label: whether a scan shows a tumor at all.

Two deep models train side by side. One chops the image into small patches called superpixels, and the other groups those patches into regions. A classifier trained on the cheap labels guides the pair toward the tumor and flags under-drawn areas. The patches end up hugging the tumor's edge. Scores on two standard measures beat rival weakly supervised methods, the authors report.
pmc-11657102:
Shasha Sun and co-authors test two cheap blood scores as survival gauges for liver cancer that cannot be cut out. Their 2024 study follows forty-nine patients on targeted pills plus immune therapy. One score ratios two white cell types, the other blends a blood protein with cell counts as a nutrition index.

Cut lines were set at two point four for the cell ratio and forty-one for the nutrition index. High cell ratio patients lived a median of seven months against nine for low. High nutrition patients lived twelve months against seven. The nutrition score and tumor spread held up as lone forecasters. The authors say both scores belong in pre-treatment talks.
pmc-11657502:
Matthew Savage leads an eight-author team profiling the health and habits of British university students, in a cohort study published in two thousand twenty-four. Student health is known to lag the general population's. Pandemic disruption and a more diverse student body made older data stale.

An online survey ran across three years, two thousand twenty-one to two thousand twenty-three. Three cohorts totaling 6,327 students reported movement, diet, lifestyle, and mental health. Body mass index was also recorded. Statistical comparisons looked for differences by gender and ethnicity. Trans and gender diverse students were part of the updated picture. The authors aim to give universities a current baseline for targeting wellbeing support where groups differ.
pmc-11657802:
