Debojyoty Bandyopadhyay and colleagues show a bitter melon compound starving head and neck cancer, in work from 2024. Cancers rewire metabolism to feed growth and dodge therapy, a core hallmark of the disease. Momordicine-I is a key active compound drawn from bitter melon plant tissue.

Treated cancer cells cut their sugar burning gene and protein levels across the board. Lactate build up fell, and broad chemistry maps confirmed the energy slowdown. Fat building enzymes also fell, while cell membrane fats shifted in shotgun reads. Cell power output dropped, self eating rose, and death signals fired in treated cells. Mouse tumours echoed the gene drops and shrank under the compound.
pmc-11658102:
Zurzycka and co-authors survey nurses, midwives, and students about searching online for private facts about patients. The internet holds much data on people who never grasp how exposed they are. The team used a custom survey with background questions and three case stories. Respondents judged the conduct in each story as well. The survey measured both how common such searches are and what drives them.

Most respondents, about 60%, admitted looking patients up online. Curiosity was not the only driver named. The study flags a quiet habit that sits uneasily with patient privacy. Training programs may need to address it head-on.
pmc-11658302:
Saeedeh Khadivi-Derakhshan and co-authors built an electrode sensor for a blood pressure drug in plasma, in this 2024 study. Measuring the drug in raw plasma is hard because the sample is complex. Their sensor coats a carbon electrode with a polymer film, platinum nanocubes, and a metal complex.

The probe read the drug across a wide range, down to a low limit in the tens of nanomoles. It proved selective, stable, and repeatable in checks. The reaction at the surface was governed by diffusion. Accuracy and precision tests passed well. The authors conclude the sensor suits routine drug analysis without sample pre-treatment.
pmc-11658402:
Ghader Mohammadnezhad and co-authors test whether guidance from a clinical pharmacist helps kidney patients follow their drug plans, in a study from 2024. People with long-term kidney disease often take many drugs. A service called medication therapy management has a pharmacist review the full plan with the patient.

One hundred patients took part and filled in surveys before and after the service. The surveys scored what patients knew, how they felt about their care, what they did in practice, and how well they stuck to their drugs. Scores for knowledge rose a great deal after the service. Attitude scores rose as well. The paper reports gains in self-care and drug use habits. The results support a larger role for pharmacists in kidney care.
pmc-11658902:
Anna Pogorzelska, Agnieszka Mielczarek, Piotr Regulski, Mike Lee, and Kazimierz Szopinski chart the nerve canal that wisdom-tooth roots can wrap around. Their 2024 study uses cone-beam CT scans, because pulling an impacted lower third molar without knowing where the inferior alveolar canal runs risks lasting numbness. The records covered 103 patients and 140 impacted teeth scanned in 2016 and 2017.

The commonest pattern was a tilted, two-rooted molar. Most often the canal passed below the roots while touching them, and the canal's cross-section was usually oval. Root count strongly predicted the canal threading between roots. Tilt type and root count did not vary by sex. Single-rooted and backward-tilted teeth grew commoner with age. The map guides safer extraction planning.
pmc-11661402:
Andrew Chan and co-authors review gadgets that track where older adults are inside their homes. Their 2024 systematic review serves remote health care for people aging in place in Canada. Knowing which room a person is in can flag frailty or memory loss early.

From nearly 2,000 papers, 36 on the tools and 10 on patient outcomes made the cut. Sensors could spot frailty but could not tell healthy minds from mild memory loss. Users took to the tools fairly well, most of all plain room sensors with no wearables. Room-level accuracy reached 92 percent in the best setups. The authors see promise but mixed proof of health gains so far.
pmc-11662902:
Jiajia Wang and co-authors test a teaching method for ultrasound trainees in a 2024 study. Residents must learn to zone the thyroid and neck lymph nodes by scan, a skill that blends anatomy with hand control. The trial joined a flipped classroom, where study comes before class, with a four step demonstration method.

Sixty six residents were split into two groups. The new method group scored higher on hands on skill and on clinical case tests than the classic teaching group. Trainees also reported stronger interest and less exam pressure. The authors back the combined method as a sound upgrade for standardized ultrasound training in residency programs.
pmc-11663602:
Raul Sanchez-Muñoz writes a 2024 commentary on how a gene network steers banana ripening, under a playful title about age and wisdom. For growers and shippers, overripe bananas are a real cost: peels lighten, flesh softens, and the finger tears more easily in handling and transport. The hormone ethylene drives ripening in such fruit, changing color outside and texture, sugar, and aroma inside.

The piece walks through a recent study that exposed bananas to ethylene and charted the changes over days. Cell wall proteins grew more active as color and texture shifted. Gene reading across two fruit zones hunted the switches in charge. Two named factors, NAP1 and MADS1, sit at the center of the network the study maps. Sanchez-Muñoz frames why nailing this control circuit matters for timing ripening on purpose.
pmc-11663702:
Alicja Kunkowska and Nicola Trozzi present a 2025 commentary on how plants space their lateral roots. Roots anchor the plant and draw water and food from the soil. Side roots that branch at even intervals explore the soil best and avoid competing with each other.

A known pathway sets that spacing: a peptide signal from neighbor cells is read by a receptor called RLK7, which switches on a factor that blocks new side roots nearby. How the receptor passes the signal inward was unknown. The commentary discusses a study in the same journal issue that found the missing partners. Proteins called CIKs work with the receptor to relay the signal. The finding completes a key circuit in root patterning.
pmc-11664002:
Kyle McGaughy and co-authors built a data set for tracking the full life cycle costs of food waste handling in the United States, in a 2024 paper. Their model pulls values from past studies and from government reports, above all from the national environment agency. Each value is paired with notes on its source and its limits. Users can run the model with default values or set their own.

The spreadsheet model covers five routes for waste food: gas-making digestion, two forms of composting, landfill burial, and burning. It also lets users add site-level choices, such as how gas from a landfill is used or how compost is treated. The data set is meant to feed full life cycle studies. Such studies weigh the total footprint of each route before a town or firm picks one.
pmc-11664402:
Mauricio Ferrao Blanco and co-authors hunt for a drug that fights joint damage in osteoarthritis, in this 2024 study. Two drivers of the disease are low-grade inflammation and a bone-forming process that goes astray in cartilage. The team mined public gene datasets and flagged a receptor called EPHA2 as tied to both processes.

Computer models predicted that switching the receptor on pushes cartilage cells toward inflammation and overgrowth. A drug that blocks the receptor then cut both effects in human cartilage cells. Given to mice with the disease, it slowed joint damage. The authors present their mixed pipeline as a route to disease-changing treatments.
pmc-11664502:
Pierce Pham, Oindrila Biswas, and Christian Hilty use soap-like micelles to let a super-sensitive NMR trick watch a protein grab its ligand, in a study from 2024. Parahydrogen polarization can amplify NMR signals hugely, but it runs in organic solvent where proteins cannot live. Reverse micelles split the difference: water droplets inside oil host the protein, while the polarization chemistry runs outside.

Iridium complexes in the oil phase reported on a ligand that crossed the boundary to meet the enzyme thiaminase inside. Signal boosts made the meeting visible. From the balance of bound and free ligand, they computed a dissociation constant near 40 micromolar. The authors offer the setup for other binding and enzyme questions that need the boost.
pmc-11666302:
George Gherlan and co-authors dissect three years of deaths from a hospital gut infection in a study from 2024. Clostridioides difficile is the top cause of hospital diarrhea worldwide. It also ranks among the deadliest hospital-acquired infections. Spotting who will fare worst is the clinical challenge.

Records covered every patient hospitalized from 2021 through 2023 at one center. Over a thousand carried the diagnosis. Ninety-seven patients, just under nine percent, died. Their traits were compared line by line with survivors'. Age, other illnesses, and infection marks likely separate the groups. Such profiles help wards triage attention before a routine infection turns fatal.
pmc-11666502:
Zhi Luo and co-authors probe how ammonia stress harms the black tiger shrimp, in this 2024 Europe PMC paper. Ammonia nitrogen is a major threat in aquaculture, cutting shrimp health and productivity. The team exposed Penaeus monodon to ammonia for twelve and ninety-six hours and checked stress markers, tissue damage and molecular changes.

Longer exposure badly damaged the hepatopancreas, the shrimp's main digestive and immune organ, with atrophy and deformation. Gene expression shifts touched cell death, immune defense and core metabolism, and metabolite profiling showed disturbed nucleotide turnover and weakened antioxidant defenses. The multi-omics picture offers biomarkers for monitoring ammonia risk on shrimp farms.
pmc-11667602:
Jae Eun Lee and five co-authors sorted citizens into types by willingness to join carbon neutrality activities. Public engagement decides whether climate pledges turn into daily practice, yet willingness varies widely. The team surveyed eight hundred residents of Cheongju, South Korea, about thirteen activities, from recycling to larger lifestyle changes, and used latent class analysis.

Three types emerged. An active group joins broadly, a second group takes part mainly in easy daily-life actions, and a passive group barely engages. Personal awareness mattered, but so did peer behavior: people join more when those around them do. The authors argue one-size campaigns waste this structure. Active citizens can be recruited as champions, the daily-life group nudged toward bigger steps, and the passive group reached through social proof rather than lectures. The typology is a planning tool for local climate policy.
pmc-11668602:
Yu Zhang and co-authors mine a national drug safety database for reports of neuroleptic malignant syndrome in this 2024 study. The syndrome is a rare but dangerous reaction to certain drugs, marked by fever and stiff muscles. The team used United States Food and Drug Administration reports filed from January 2004 to June 2024.

More than ten thousand reports named the syndrome. The drugs with the strongest links were mostly antipsychotics, followed by drugs for Parkinson's disease and depression. Reports were more common in males than in females. Among the strongest signals, the child group also included some calming and seizure drugs not seen in adults. The authors offer the list as a guide for safer prescribing.
pmc-11669002:
Shengbin Cui and Tamami Nakano ask whether body signals shape moral choices, in work from 2024. They focus on interoception, the brain's sense of inner states such as the heartbeat. Twenty-seven adults judged moral dilemmas while brain and heart signals were logged. The dilemmas varied by harm type and by how choices were framed.

A brain wave tied to heartbeats split choices framed by outcomes from choices framed by the act itself. The split held across dilemma types and showed at two time points. Checks ruled out plain heart artifacts as the cause. The team concludes the brain uses inner body data when it makes moral calls.
pmc-11669302:
A rare growth can choke a child's airway with no warning. The rush to clear it tests an anaesthesia team to the full. Amit Padvi and Namita Padvi report such a case from 2024. A five-year-old child came to emergency care in severe trouble. The child breathed with great strain, spoke with a hoarse voice, and made a harsh noise on each breath.

The growths are caused by a common virus. They sprout again and again in the airway. The child went at once to the operating room. There, the team cut the growths back to open the path. Sleep drugs in a blocked child's airway are a high-risk act. The tools and the growths share one narrow space. The report walks through each step and the care taken at each one.
pmc-11669502:
Fuyi Zhang and co-authors compare two scan methods for thyroid eye disease in a 2024 review. The illness can be active or quiet, and that call guides care. Two magnetic scan styles, T2 mapping and Dixon, each claim to grade that activity.

The team pooled seventeen studies with more than fourteen hundred people. They weighed how often each method caught active cases and ruled out quiet ones. T2 mapping showed fair catch rates and strong rule out rates in the pooled data. The review also probes why study results differed, which helps clinics judge which scan to trust for staging.
pmc-11669602:
Rui Tang and co-authors describe a step-by-step method to prepare a donor liver before transplant, in work from 2024. Bleeding during the operation is a major risk. Much of that risk comes from how the donor organ is trimmed and checked on a side table.

The team compared two groups from 2018 to 2020. One group of 43 patients got the older prep method. A group of 160 patients got the new fixed sequence. The new method took longer at the table but left fewer poorly cleaned arteries. Surgeons also rated the work in a follow-up survey. The authors argue that a fixed routine cuts bleeding after the liver is placed.
pmc-11669702:
Xiaochuan Chen and co-authors profile a chemical mark on RNA as a warning sign in nasopharyngeal cancer, in a 2024 paper. This cancer is common in Southeast Asia and China and often starts with no clear symptoms. The mark can reshape RNA and change how tumors grow, but its role here was unclear.

The team sequenced tumor and healthy tissue from a few patients, then joined large gene datasets from many more. They found many genes with altered marks, mostly tied to immune paths, and built a risk model from a shortlist of marked genes. Checks in other datasets backed the model. Immune and pathway study at bulk and single cell level rounded out the picture of how the mark tracks outcome.
pmc-11670202:
Deming Tong and co-authors report a hard case of bowel narrowing after rectal cancer surgery in a 2024 paper. A woman with rectal cancer also had a connective tissue disease, a family of immune disorders that can damage vessels and organs. Three months after surgery that removed the tumor and made a temporary opening, doctors tried to restore her bowel.

At that attempt they found the joined bowel narrowed for no clear reason, and the restoration failed. The authors place the case against past reports: the tissue disease can block intestinal vessels and inflame the gut, but such trouble after bowel surgery is rarely reported. They offer the case as a warning for teams planning restoration surgery in patients with this disease family.
pmc-11671302:
Shannon Argueta and co-authors program immune cells inside the body to fight solid tumors in a 2024 study. Cell therapies that equip T cells with tumor-targeting receptors work well in blood cancers but are costly, complex, and weak against solid tumors. Their approach instead delivers receptor instructions as mRNA in fat particles, aimed at myeloid cells, a different immune branch.

The receptor targets TROP2, a protein common on solid tumors, and it activates myeloid cells only when the full signaling partner is present. In dishes, treated monocytes killed tumor cells and released immune signals on contact with the target. In tumor-bearing mice and in monkeys, the particles expressed mainly in myeloid cells, and dosing shrank tumors in a mouse model.
pmc-11671402:
Chaoran Wang and co-authors review vagus nerve stimulation as a physical therapy for disorders of the brain and spinal cord. Their 2024 paper notes that these diseases often leave permanent damage and lack good treatments, despite their heavy toll. A device that pulses the long vagus nerve, running from brainstem to gut, offers a different lever.

Regulators in the United States have approved the therapy for epilepsy and depression. Trials and case work hint at gains in stroke recovery, disorders of consciousness, and Alzheimer's disease as well. Yet the reviewers stress how much stays unsettled: who benefits, how strongly, and by what mechanism. They gather the current clinical evidence and map the open questions that trials must answer next.
pmc-11671502:
Xi Liu and twelve co-authors used genetics to probe whether inflammation drives macular degeneration in a 2024 paper. Their method, Mendelian randomization, treats inherited variants as natural experiments, testing cause in both directions. They combined data on 91 inflammatory proteins from nearly 15,000 people with a large Finnish disease registry.

Sixteen inflammation markers first linked to the eye disease. After strict correction, higher levels of two proteins lowered risk, while a third raised it. Separate signals appeared for the wet and dry forms of the disease. The reverse direction also spoke: genetic liability to the disease raised one inflammatory marker. The authors read the pattern as evidence that specific immune pathways, not inflammation in general, shape the disease.
pmc-11671602:
Soon Sang Park and co-authors map aged cells in older tissues in work from 2024. Cells that have stopped dividing build up with age and can harm nearby tissue, but where they sit in normal organs was not clear.

The team found that fully aged cells marked by a key protein were rare in the main tissue and in support cells. They were far more common in immune cells. Aged T cells could trigger death and swelling in gut lining cells through a signaling path. The authors suggest that targeting immune aging may slow loss of function in older people.
pmc-11672702:
Daiana Capdevila and co-authors review how bacteria keep their metal house in order. Their 2024 paper names the whole craft metallostasis: sensing metal supply, reshaping the metal-using protein fleet, and routing metals to their posts. Metals serve as beams and sparks across that fleet, so supply must be just right. Bacteria sense it with both proteins and RNA switches.

The review sorts sensor families and the rules that set their pickiness, with an eye to borrowing those rules for built biology. Chaperones that hand metals to client proteins and rooms close the tour, plus gaps the field still owes.
pmc-11672802:
José Almeida-Bezerra and colleagues test phytol as an antibiotic helper against resistant germs, in work from 2024. Phytol is a plant alcohol found in essential oils with broad bio activity claims. Drug resistant bacteria urgently need helpers that restore old antibiotic power in treatment.

Bench dilution tests paired phytol with standard drugs against resistant strains. The plant compound slashed the drug dose needed against two resistant species sharply. Computer checks rated its body handling as low toxicity with friendly uptake traits. Docking runs showed real grip on two bacterial proteins, though below the drug rivals. The profile backs phytol as an adjuvant candidate worth animal testing.
pmc-11672902: Mario Maalouf, Adelaide Gaffney, Bridger Bell, and Robin Shaw examine a shortened form of connexin-43, a protein that builds channels between cells. The short form is made when the cell starts reading the protein's code partway through. The paper, from 2024, reviews what this isoform does and why it may matter. Connexins form channels that let cells pass signals to each other. A truncated version could change how those channels form or act. The record's evidence is brief, so the review's fine claims cannot be checked here.
pmc-11673002:
Shanshan Yang and four co-authors test a ginseng compound against udder barrier damage in cows in a 2024 paper. Subclinical mastitis quietly degrades milk quality worldwide. The blood-milk barrier leaks as the disease takes hold. Ginsenoside Rg1 is a plant antioxidant with anti-inflammatory fame.

In cells and animals, Rg1 eased the barrier breakdown. It curbed a stress-driven surge of self-eating in cells. That surge had been loosening the barrier's tight junctions. An inflammasome switch also quieted under the compound. A receptor called PPARγ emerged as its likely target. Turning that receptor on tamed the stress chain upstream. The axis offers a treatment target for dairy herds.
pmc-11673102:
Min-Kyeong Lee and six colleagues test a fatty acid that lightens skin pigmentation in laboratory cells, in a study from two thousand twenty-four. Melanin production sets the color of skin and hair and serves as a marker in a range of diseases. How fatty acids regulate that process was underexplored in past work.

A computer similarity screen first flagged 10(E)-pentadecenoic acid, which looked much like lipids known to work against pigment. In mouse melanoma cells goaded to make melanin, the compound cut melanin output and tyrosinase activity both, with no significant cell toxicity at the doses tested. Work on how it acts traced the effect in part to suppression of the MITF and tyrosinase axis, the master switch of pigmentation in the cell.
pmc-11673202:
Zhongjie Wang and five co-authors followed teens in two thousand twenty-four to see what shields them from bullying over time. More than fourteen hundred adolescents, average age near fourteen, were tracked for a year. Past work often lacked a time view and paid little mind to protective factors such as ties with teachers.

Bullying fell over the year, while feelings of control and teacher ties both rose. Feeling in control linked to less bullying, and teacher ties carried much of that effect. Growth in control also slowed bullying only through stronger teacher ties. Schools that build trust between teens and teachers may cut bullying at its roots.
pmc-11673502:
Fragile X syndrome brings learning problems, hyperactivity, and social fear, and its mouse model shows excess output from an enzyme called NADPH oxidase in the brain. Yolanda de Diego-Otero and co-authors tested apocynin, a drug that blocks that enzyme, as a treatment in this 2024 study. Mice got a daily oral dose for a long stretch, then faced behavior and learning tests plus lab checks.

Treated males grew calmer, and the higher dose also improved behavior and learning while calming free radical levels. Signs of oxidative damage fell, and protein signals tied to the enzyme dropped in set brain areas. The authors suggest that blocking this enzyme could open a new treatment path for Fragile X syndrome.
pmc-11674002:
Xiayi Wu and nine co-authors add fluorine to pig bone mineral to help new bone grow its own blood supply. Hydroxyapatite from bone resembles human mineral and encourages bone formation, but early implants vascularize too slowly, starving the repair. Fluoride ions are known to couple vessel growth with bone growth.

The fluorinated material kept the natural porous structure of cancellous bone and released fluoride in culture medium. Its extracts made endothelial cells form capillary-like tubes and raised vessel growth signals in marrow stem cells, with the lower fluorine level strongest. The partner signal from endothelial cells rose as well, showing the two cell types coordinating. In rabbit skull defects the material then supported vascularized bone growth in living tissue.
pmc-11674402:
Andrew Zalesky and co-authors review a 2024 question in brain science: can a person's wiring map predict how their brain areas work together? Deep networks have been trained to learn that link across the whole brain. The open issue is whether the outputs capture traits that are truly unique to each person.

The team rechecked past outputs for one thousand healthy adults with two strict tests. The outputs did beat group averages and null checks, so they hold real personal signal. But the edge was small, at about a tenth better than the group norm. The authors urge more modest claims and give tips for future work.
pmc-11674502:
Maebh Kenny-Jones and co-authors review how fear that cancer will return shapes patients' use of digital support and their grasp of health information, in a 2024 paper. Cancer services increasingly hand patients apps and websites to manage their care. Two fears hang over that shift: fear of recurrence and fear of progression. The review chased two questions through the literature, one on digital engagement and one on health literacy.

Only two papers spoke to the first question, and both suggested that stronger fear goes with weaker use of digital resources. Eight papers addressed the second, mostly finding stronger fear alongside lower health literacy, though one large, well-drawn study found no link. The authors warn that digital-by-default care may leave the most frightened patients behind, and they call for better studies.
pmc-11674602:
Peng Zhou and seven co-authors used genetics to ask whether statin drugs change the gut's microbial population, rather than merely traveling with other causes. Observational reports had linked long-term statin use to shifts in gut bacteria, but such links are easily confounded. The team ran a Mendelian randomization analysis on European data, using inherited variants as instruments for statin exposure and for the abundance of gut species.

Six causal links survived their checks. Statin use was tied to lower levels of five bacterial groups, including two Ruminococcaceae types and a Parabacteroides, and to higher levels of one, a Desulfovibrio. The tests found no sign of the statistical flaws that most often poison this method. The authors suggest the gut may be one route through which statins touch wider health, for better or worse. They propose watching microbial markers in patients on long-term statin therapy.
pmc-11674702:
Aysen Kutan Fenercioglu reviews how vitamin D calms inflammation and thereby supports health across many organs. Receptors for the vitamin sit in nearly all immune cells and in the linings of the gut, pancreas, lungs, and heart. Some immune cells can even make the active form of the vitamin themselves.

Once bound to its receptor, the vitamin steers genes that control immune signals. It lowers the output of pro-inflammatory messengers and raises anti-inflammatory ones. It also guides how immune cells grow and mature, and it blocks two pathways that switch inflammation on. The review gathers this biology into one account of why vitamin D status matters for inflammatory disease.
pmc-11674902:
Brody Andrews and co-authors study how caregivers help young people with mental health concerns stay connected to others in this 2024 paper. Young people in this group often lean on family for support while drifting away from friends. The team spoke with nine caregivers and studied what they do to keep social ties alive.

Three main tasks stood out from the talks. Caregivers learn the shape and quality of their young person's social world. They judge when the young person is ready to reach out again. They also coach social problem solving and build the young person's belief in their own skills. These tasks can pull in two directions at once, since support must not crowd out independence. The findings point to training and resources that back caregivers in this quiet work.
pmc-11675002:
A urine marker can flag prostate cancer, but body fluids hold many bits that foul a quick test. Thenmozhi Rajarathinam and co-authors built a hand-held sensor for that marker, in work from twenty twenty-four. The sensor reads current from an enzyme reaction and gives a result in under a minute. A phone-linked reader handles the data.

A three-part nano mix holds the enzyme steady and passes charge well. That build lets the sensor catch the marker at very low levels with sharp aim. Past tests of this kind were rare, since stray bits in urine and blood oxidize at the probe and blur the read. The team pitches the tool as a cheap, fast first screen for the cancer.
pmc-11675202:
Gaetana Affuso, Nicola Picone, and co-authors track kind acts, pal aid, and mind well feel in teens across four school years, in a 2024 study. Which way those three push each other in teen years was not yet split clean. A per teen change lens can part pool ties from true time leads.

Near six hundred first year teens fill forms once a year for four years. Pool ties link all three in plus ways at the group tier. Per teen, mind well feel calls kind acts one year on at each step. Kind acts and pal aid show no like lead in the per teen lens. Lift teen well feel to lift kind acts, they urge.
pmc-11675302:
People who survive cancer face stress, loss of control, and strained ties, all tied to basic mental needs. In 2024, Hyun-E Yeom and Jungmin Lee tested a Korean version of a scale that measures how well those needs are met or blocked. The scale covers three needs: autonomy, relatedness, and competence, each in both a met and a blocked form.

The study surveyed 367 cancer survivors living in the community. Tests confirmed the six-part structure of the scale and showed it lined up well with related measures. Scores were also steady and consistent within each part. The authors say the scale can guide care that supports self-care and quality of life.
pmc-11675602:
Yanyong Cao and co-authors catalog a family of plant gene switches in maize and test one member against drought in a 2024 paper. The trihelix family is unique to plants and shapes growth and stress responses. Drought is the top limit on maize yield, yet this family had not been mapped in maize.

The team found forty-six family genes spread unevenly across the ten maize chromosomes, falling into five subgroups. Many carry control elements tied to stress, and most changed activity under drought. One gene, when boosted in a model plant, gave stronger drought tolerance, with less oxidative damage and better photosynthesis. The catalog offers candidate markers for breeding hardier, higher-yielding maize.
pmc-11675802:
Jain, Paz, and Azem review the disease mutations that strike the TIM23 complex, the gatekeeper machine that pulls most proteins into mitochondria. Nearly all of the roughly 1,500 mitochondrial proteins are made outside the organelle and must be imported, and this complex handles about 60 percent of them. Broken parts cause mostly developmental and neurological diseases that begin early in life. The review asks whether some parts of the machine collect mutations more than others.

Two hotspots stand out. Among the core components, the gene for the Tim50 subunit seems especially prone to harmful changes. Among the motor subunits that drag proteins through, the genes for the chaperone mortalin and its regulators draw the most reports. The authors discuss what these clusters may reveal about how the machine works and where it is fragile. For geneticists reading a child's genome, the map helps judge which new variants deserve suspicion first.
pmc-11675902:
Roberta Teixeira de Oliveira and co-authors study in 2024 where Brazilian households buy their food, and what they buy, at each level of food insecurity. Not having enough food is a lasting problem in Brazil, with sharp gaps between regions. The team used a national budget survey of 57,920 households from 2017 and 2018.

Shops were grouped into supermarkets, small markets, street fairs and produce stores, and other sources. Foods were sorted into 12 groups, from rice and beans to sugary drinks. Supermarkets are the main food source across the country. In the North and North East, though, other sources play a larger role. The study maps how the shop mix and the food mix shift as insecurity grows. Such maps can guide aid and store policy toward the places and foods that poor households rely on.
pmc-11676002:
Antisense drugs are short strands of DNA-like material designed to bind a chosen RNA, and adding one locked nucleic acid unit makes the binding tighter. Elisa Tomita-Sudo and four co-authors ask whether that tightening can be predicted from the surrounding sequence. They measured the stability of DNA and RNA pairs carrying a single locked thymine unit in the DNA strand, across many sequences, and worked out the free energy change each one caused.

On average, the single change stabilized the pair by 1.5 kilocalories per mole. The size of the effect, though, depended on which bases sat nearby, so a single universal bonus value would mislead drug designers. The results point toward sequence-aware rules, similar to the nearest-neighbor parameters used for natural strands, for predicting how strongly a modified antisense drug will bind its target.
pmc-11676102:
Muhammad Faisal Amin and four co-authors tune a dye-based solar cell with a light-shy dye in its gel. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-four. The cell uses a polymer gel in place of a liquid to carry charge. The mix of polymer to liquid sets how well the cell works, so the team first finds the best ratio.

They then add an azopyridine dye that flips shape under ultraviolet light. The flip lets the gel take in heat from the light, which lifts how fast ions move. More dye raises the current the cell gives, in step with dose. Cell yield rises by about a tenth at the top dose.
pmc-11676202:
Isabella Pividori and co-authors measure stress hormones in hair in a 2024 case study from the pandemic. Mental distress during COVID-19 was studied a great deal. The body's stress hormones over the same span got far less attention, even though hair locks in a months long record of them.

Samples came from 200 healthcare workers and 161 patients with chronic illness or motor disability. The ratio of cortisol, a stress hormone, to a balancing hormone was the key measure of strain on the stress axis. Patients carried notably higher ratios than the workers. The gap hints that support during crises should reach chronic patients first.
pmc-11676302:
Yan Kim and co-authors ask whether stem cells from a sick liver still act like stem cells from a healthy one, in a study from 2024. These resident cells help hold liver tissue together and can aid repair. That matters because liver disease drives a large share of deaths worldwide. If sick-liver cells keep their core traits, they could seed new cell therapies.

The team drew cells from healthy-looking liver areas and from livers scarred by long-term swelling, scarring disease, and viral infection. A wide battery of tests compared the two sets. Marker proteins, growth, movement, and cell output all matched closely. Only a few immune-related switches differed between the groups. The authors conclude that even late-stage sick livers hold usable stem cells. Those cells could serve as raw stock for liver cell therapy.
pmc-11676402:
Zhonghang Ji, Yida Song, Mandi Gao, Qiong Zhang, and Yunqing Liu build a tiny absorber for K-band radio waves in this 2024 paper. Patterned metal surfaces can swallow microwaves almost fully, which serves sensing, imaging, and stealth. Their design packs an aperture plate, two rings, and two strips onto a thin circuit board with a metal back.

Across a wide slice of the K band, the surface absorbed over ninety percent of incoming waves for both wave polarizations. Tilting the wave changes the game: the device can switch between swallowing a broad band or picking single or multiple tones. Small size plus that flexibility suits crowded wireless gear.
pmc-11676802:
Myriam Heilani and co-authors report a 2024 study from Frankfurt on liver disease and a scan based test of liver stiffness. The test uses sound waves and comes in two forms. The team checked whether it could predict swollen veins in the food pipe and high pressure in liver blood flow.

The authors studied clinic patients over time and compared scan results with signs of high pressure. They also built a model that joins the scan with a blood count. For readers, the work shows how a painless scan might flag risk and cut the need for more invasive checks in some cases.
pmc-11677002:
Daria Cicha-Wojciechowicz, Natalia Drabińska, and Małgorzata Anna Majcher studied what shapes the aroma of mead in twenty twenty-four, with Yanping Qian also among the authors. Twelve model batches were made and matured for twelve months. The batches varied by honey type, wort heating, and fermentation method, spanning commercial yeast, wild fermentation, and a mold culture.

Smell-active compounds were charted with gas methods and a trained nose. Honey type drove the sensory profile, with clear aroma clusters for buckwheat, acacia, and linden honeys. A few compounds stood out as key odorants, tied to honey-like, malty, and fermented notes. Heating and fermentation choices shifted the aroma in measurable ways. The authors say the links they mapped can guide makers who want to tune mead quality on purpose rather than by luck.
pmc-11677102:
Gustavo Augusto Grossi-Oliveira and colleagues tested bone healing aids in rabbits in 2024. Dental implants in the upper jaw often need sinus lifting first. The team placed implants in lifted sinus spaces in forty rabbits. Four fillings were compared. They were plain blood clot, a cattle bone mineral, that mineral plus platelet-rich fibrin, and fibrin alone. Platelet-rich fibrin comes from the animal's own blood. Tissue checks ran at two set times after surgery.

Bone contact with implants rose over time in most groups. The mineral plus fibrin group led early on contact. It still led all groups at the later check. Its bone area share showed no such edge. The authors say pairing fibrin with the mineral aids implant bonding. That pairing may help patients who need sinus lifting. They note that proof on fibrin's wider effects remains thin. More clinical study should follow, they argue.
pmc-11677202:
Eugenio Graceffo and co-authors build a glowing reporter that reads gene splicing choices live in single cells in a 2024 paper. One gene, THRA, makes two versions of a thyroid hormone receptor. The first switches genes on; the second lacks the hormone grip and may brake the first, so their ratio steers development and metabolism.

No tool could watch that ratio inside living cells until now. Their plasmid reporter splices like the real gene and answers in two colors: red and green fluorescent proteins tag the two versions apart. Time-lapse imaging then counts each version cell by cell, even as conditions change. The authors aim the tool at mapping healthy tissue patterns, probing hormone resistance syndromes, and screening drugs that nudge the ratio toward health.
pmc-11677402:
Maryen Alberto Vazquez and five co-authors characterized a fibre-eating fungus in two thousand twenty-four, Curvularia kusanoi strain L7, as a candidate for turning plant waste into useful products. Plant cell walls resist breakdown, so fresh degrading strains are prized. They tracked its growth on varied media and its attack on raw wheat straw.

Infrared spectra showed clear drops in cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin signals as the fungus mineralized the straw. In fermentation on wheat and sugarcane bagasse, it poured out degrading enzymes, with top cellulase output on bagasse and top laccase on wheat. The authors back the strain for biomass conversion work.
pmc-11677502:
Sk Jahir Abbas and co-authors review site exact protein tagging by chemistry, simulation, and AI in a 2024 paper. Tagging a protein at one chosen site tracks its work in cells. The tag must not break the protein's native tasks.

The review spans direct chemistry on natural amino acids. Near driven methods tag by closeness to a guide part. Traceless labels swap or cut away after the tag lands. Computer models now foretell how a tag warps the fold. AI tools join the forecast stack for site picks. Exact tags open cleaner drug and probe builds.
pmc-11677702:
Lin Lu and Yalin Zhang survey a small genus of pine-feeding leafhoppers in China's Yunnan Province and add two species to science. Their 2024 paper revisits the genus Pinopona, recently moved into a new tribe slot based on fine head and leg traits. Careful anatomy separates its members: crown striping, short antennae, and the placement of the simple eyes all count.

The two new species come from Gongshan and Dali, and the paper illustrates both in detail. A checklist and a working key now cover every known species in the genus, letting other researchers name specimens without guesswork. The survey steadies a corner of leafhopper classification that had rested on few specimens.
pmc-11678002:
Ramon Cacabelos and co-authors review treatment options for Alzheimer disease, from the classic drugs to multi-target compounds, in a 2024 paper. The disease is a knot of hundreds of faulty genes, chemical marks on DNA, blood vessel changes, and life exposures, and it starts decades before symptoms. That long silent phase is where treatment should aim, the authors argue.

The classic drugs, which raise a brain messenger level, plus one drug, held the field from the 1990s until antibody therapies arrived in the 2020s. Meanwhile more than ten thousand compounds have been tested against some piece of the disease. Multi-target drugs try to hit several pieces at once, and over a thousand have been studied in models. The authors note one untried strategy: pairing drugs that act on DNA marks with multi-target agents. They point to biotechnology products with actions as an attractive, if not final, direction.
pmc-11678202:
Dan Dobrotă and five co-authors strengthen polymer resins with glass, hemp, and jute fibers while trying to use less material, in a two thousand twenty-four materials study. The design process follows TRIZ-ARIZ, a structured inventive problem-solving method aimed at sustainable composites.

Tensile tests gave jute the best strength, ahead of glass and then hemp. Reinforcing only the high-stress region matched full reinforcement almost exactly, cutting material use by up to sixty percent. Thermal analysis and microscopy showed glass composites most heat-stable and generally good fiber-matrix bonding, with voids weakening some samples. The authors argue natural fibers, especially jute, suit sustainable engineering.
pmc-11678302:
Fabian Barbieri leads a fourteen-author team validating a pacemaker sensor against laboratory sleep studies, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-four. Many implanted cardiac devices estimate sleep apnea from chest impedance. The feature has been used clinically for over a decade with surprisingly little accuracy data.

Two prospective trials, AIRLESS and UPGRADE, supplied the pooled data. Participants were heart failure patients qualifying for defibrillators or resynchronization devices. Each underwent gold-standard polysomnography for comparison. The analysis measured how well the device sensor detected apnea and graded its severity. Honest validation matters because treatment decisions may follow the device's readings. The paper fills an evidence gap for a widely deployed screening feature.
pmc-11678502:
Assunta Fabozzo and co-authors present a 2024 pilot study of nutrition screening in heart transplant patients. Poor nutrition is linked to worse results after heart surgery, yet clear scoring before transplant is limited. The team scored patients with the Malnutrition Universal Screening Tool, called MUST, at one center.

Records covered adults who had a heart transplant over a period of several years. Higher MUST scores were not tied to more major problems in the hospital or to early death. Higher scores were linked to higher risk of death during later follow-up. The authors treat the result as early evidence that simple screening may help flag patients who need closer long-term care.
pmc-11678602:
Maria Antonietta Dettori, Valeria Ugone, Davide Fabbri, and Paola Carta study how light reshapes a curry-linked compound, in a 2024 chemistry paper. The compound, dehydrozingerone, forms when curcumin breaks down. Under ultraviolet light, its shape can flip from one geometric form to the other.

The team shone UV light on the compound, on a doubled version of it, and on methylated variants of both. All produced flipped forms, with yields that depended on the solvent and the light's wavelength. The flipped plain compound and its dimer proved too unstable to purify. The methylated flipped forms, though, were isolated and fully mapped with magnetic and light-based methods, aided by computer models. The work adds detail on how light rewrites the shape, and likely the behavior, of curcumin-family molecules.
pmc-11678802:
Bogdan Cekic and co-authors tested a chestnut tannin feed product in a 2024 lamb study. Tannins are plant compounds that can aid gut health in farm animals, and this product is sold as a feed add-on. The team first mapped what is in the product, then asked how it shifts blood traits in fattening lambs.

Thirty lambs were split into three groups for 60 days. One group ate plain feed, and the other two got set doses of the tannin mix. Blood tests tracked protein, urea, and liver markers over the trial. The work is the first deep profile of this product, and it gives farmers data on dose and safety for lamb feed.
pmc-11678902:
The authors revisit how sodium hydroxide baths strip harmful chlorine from ancient bronzes, this time with numbers attached. Chloride buried in bronze rust drives ongoing corrosion, and removing it is a standard rescue step. Older samples made the process hard to measure, since their rust layers were messy and their chlorine content unknown. The team pressed samples with fixed chlorine amounts to get a clean test bed.

They found the bath works by converting cuprous chloride into a related hydroxychloride mineral. The catch is that the new layer swells, nearly doubling in thickness under one electric current setting. Measuring the bath liquid let them track removal over time and predict the endpoint. Plain baths removed only a few percent in a day, while a gentle current sped things up before gains reversed. The work gives conservators a clearer map of a routine treatment.
pmc-11679002:
Brain CT scans carry noise that reconstruction software can reduce, and Yusuke Inoue and co-authors compare two approaches: deep learning reconstruction and a hybrid iterative method. They rebuilt images of test phantoms and eleven patients' brains with the older standard method. They then used several strengths of each new method, across slice thicknesses from five millimetres down to a fraction of one.

Both new methods cut noise more as their strength rose. The deep learning method's gains grew on thinner slices, while the hybrid method barely cared about thickness. Object and tube current also shifted the deep learning results in ways the hybrid method avoided. Judged by eye, deep learning images looked better at thin slices but not at thick ones. The authors advise clinics to weigh slice, current, and subject when setting the deep learning strength.
pmc-11679102:
Haibin Liu, Yanglei Tang, and Huanjie Wang published this robotics paper in 2024. Robots find their place by matching new 3D scans of the world to maps they already hold. That matching step, called registration, can be slow or fail when the first guess is poor.

The authors present a method that first groups scan points into clusters, then splits the space into cells that adapt to each cluster's shape. This gives the matching step a better starting point and a wider reach. In tests, the method beat classic approaches on accuracy, speed, and how well it held up in hard cases. The work targets robots that must locate themselves fast and reliably.
pmc-11679802:
Dana Darwish and co-authors review inhaled drugs that put patients to sleep, and their uses beyond the operating room, in a 2024 paper. The review traces these drugs from early ether to modern agents. It also explains how they act on cell walls and on channels that carry signals in the body.

Later sections survey effects on the heart, lungs, liver, kidneys, and brain. Uses covered include care for stroke, bleeding effects in the brain, fits that will not stop, severe asthma, heart injury, and deep rest in intensive care. The authors also weigh the real limits of using the drugs outside surgery, such as gear and training needs. Readers get a broad map of where these old drugs may still help.
pmc-11679902:
Aneta Koronowicz and co-authors tested a medical nutrition mix on melanoma cells in a 2024 paper. Melanoma resists many standard chemotherapies fiercely. The mix, sold as food for special medical purposes, fed two cell lines. One line was primary tumor, the other a malignant spread line.

Doses ran over one to three days in the lab. A version without calcium caseinate was also tested. The full mix slowed growth of the malignant line only. Primary line cells kept growing as before. Selective effects like this invite deeper study of nutrition in cancer care.
pmc-11680102:
Franczak and co-authors ask if COVID bent the path of pox in kids at one ward. Pox here is chickenpox, a rife kid ill with skin spots. Ward logs held 350 kids past 18 years in the pool. Logs span 2018 to the end of 2023 at the ward base. The base is a kid, germ, and liver ward in the text. Counts of ward stays hit their low in the plague years.

Stays hit their high in 2023, past the plague span. Snags showed in 297 kids, 84.86 percent of the pool. Skin germ flare led snags at 168 kids, near half. Lung tract germs came next at 13.42 percent of kids. Post-plague, broad flare marks rose by a firm span. In 2023, some skin cases needed cuts for deep sores.
pmc-11683602:
Jose leads a team that screened mushroom compounds against a notorious cancer target by computer in a 2024 study, where the byline gives his full name as the first entry. The target, MYC, is overproduced in many cancers but has resisted drug design because of its loose structure. The team tested a family of triterpenes from fungi, using docking simulations, property predictions, and molecular dynamics.

Eight compounds passed the drug likeness filters, including several ganoderic acids from reishi type mushrooms. All eight docked favorably into the target. In motion simulations, four of them held on steadily and helped stabilize the protein's shape and energy. Binding energy calculations supported those four as the most promising. The authors present the work as a first computational case that this compound family deserves laboratory testing against MYC.
pmc-11687002:
Jéssica Martins and colleagues test chest ultrasound for lung disease in small primates, in work published in 2024. Lung ultrasound can speed early care for breathing problems in many settings. Primates serve as research models due to body likeness to humans, yet scan data for them were scarce.

Scans covered close to one hundred seventy marmosets kept under human care in Brazil. Four points on each chest side were scanned with a high frequency probe. About seventy animals showed some lung change on ultrasound. Many of those animals later died and had tissue checks after death. Half of checked tissues matched some form of lung disease, which supports scan use for early care.
pmc-11688002:
Xiaobin Min and co-authors report a rare case of a nerve disorder after brain surgery, in a 2024 paper. The disorder is Guillain-Barré syndrome, where the body's defense turns on nerves and weakens limbs. It most often follows infection, and cases after surgery for a brain bruise are rare.

A woman aged seventy nine had surgery, then lost strength in all limbs, with breathing failure and wide pupils. Tests of spinal fluid and blood pointed to the disorder, with a rare antibody type. She got antibody therapy and support care, and strength came back in days. She left care six weeks later with near full function.
pmc-11688902:
Deciding whether a medically fragile person can drive safely falls to driver rehabilitation specialists, who run fitness-to-drive evaluations. Anne Dickerson surveys 321 practicing specialists in this 2024 conference report to see whether their tool choices match the best research evidence.

Thinking tests with strong backing, like trail-making and clock drawing, are widely used, but other well-supported tools lag far behind. Meanwhile several weakly supported checks, including muscle strength and joint range, are used by nearly everyone. Dickerson also probes how road tests sway final judgments, and she discusses what the gaps mean for fair, evidence-based driving decisions.
pmc-11689002:
Anna Schwartz, Rachel Logue Cook, Courtney Vanderlaan, and Susan Brown wrote a 2024 study of a service learning program that pairs pre-health students with homebound older adults. The health workforce needs more people trained in care of older adults. Yet pre-health students rarely meet older patients during coursework.

In the program, called Hands and Health at Home, students were trained to lead hand exercises for older adults at home, twice a week for eight weeks. Forty students took part across three semesters. Before and after, they filled in scales on attitudes toward older adults and on coping confidence. Both scores rose clearly after the program. Students also rated the experience highly in feedback, saying they would join again.
pmc-11689102:
Iftekhar Amin and Syeda Jesmin link loneliness to self-reported memory decline in older Americans, in a 2024 study. Subjective cognitive decline, noticing one's own memory slipping, is an early warning flag health agencies want caught sooner. Whether feeling supported or isolated shapes that risk, and whether the pattern differs by sex, was unclear. The team mined a large national health survey.

Over thirty thousand respondents past sixty-five were analyzed. About one in ten reported confusion or memory loss. Weak support and strong isolation went with markedly higher odds of reporting decline, for both men and women. The tie was stronger in White and Black elders than in Hispanic elders. Strengthening social ties may be a lever against early decline.
pmc-11689202:
Ramraj Gautam, Linda Hollis, and Jennifer Mendez study how gerontology teaching can grow more global, in a 2024 paper. Gerontology is the study of aging, and the Academy for Gerontology in Higher Education supports its teaching, mostly within the United States. Yet aging is a worldwide concern, and educators in many countries rarely share materials. The study used the UN Decade of Healthy Aging as its frame.

The team recruited twenty-six educators from different countries through aging newsletters, online groups, and conference lists. They asked what international programs in aging education look like and where joint work could grow. The goal was practical: find partners, share teaching materials, and open more chances for students to learn about aging across borders.
pmc-11689302:
Andrew Huang and four co-authors build, in twenty twenty-four, a tool to predict six-month survival for older adults in assisted living. Death risk can guide who most needs timely end-of-life care. Few such tools exist for this setting. The team used health records linked to Medicare claims from twenty fifteen to twenty twenty-two.

More than thirty-one thousand residents from more than a thousand homes met the rules. Factors included age, health care use and cost, diagnoses, drugs, and tests of body and mind. The team picked final factors with both math and expert views. They then checked the tool's skill at sorting risk and at matching real rates.
pmc-11689402:
Anita Souza and Jenny Tsai frame a 2024 symposium on the health needs of older adults who lack stable housing. Adults over 50 are the fastest-growing group among people without homes, and many reach shelters with long-untreated illness plus the wear of years on the street.

One talk sorts shelter records to find hidden subgroups with shared needs. A second covers care given inside a low-barrier hotel shelter for guests with complex needs. A third reports what blocks mental health care for older adults in long-term supportive housing. Readers see both the scale of unmet need and field-tested ways that housing services can bring care to where people stay.
pmc-11689602:
Bernard Steinman, Scott Trudeau, and Maria Henke present a symposium on home modification services in this 2024 paper. Most older adults want to stay in their own homes as they age. Failing health and worn housing can block that wish. Changes such as grab bars and ramps help people stay safe and independent.

The session first sums up proof that such changes cut falls and delay moves into care homes. Three new studies then use national aging survey data to show when people install changes. They ask whether changes come before disability or only after crisis. A current service model closes the session, with lessons for how programs should reach people earlier.
pmc-11689802:
Maria Wirth, Markus Wettstein, and Klaus Rothermund follow how people's sense of time relates to life satisfaction across adulthood in a 2024 study. The young lean toward the future, building toward goals. Midlife tilts toward the present. In old age, letting go of unreachable goals and savoring the present and past is thought to protect well-being. Earlier studies gave mixed results, often measuring only one facet of time perspective or one age group.

This study tracks four facets over time: orientation to past, present, and future, and the sense of time as scarce or wide. It spans younger, middle-aged, and older adults, and links changes in outlook to changes in satisfaction. The design can show whether shifting with age is healthy, or whether satisfaction drives the shift. Time, the authors argue, is a developmental resource.
pmc-11689902:
Susan Hastings and co-authors read pain and sleep post hospital in older adults in a 2024 study. Six hundred eighteen veterans, mean age 70.6, took phone forms a month post discharge. Most were men; a fourth lived alone. Pain and sleep forms faced life grade, body work, and town range marks. Each mark set ran its own pooled math with ward marks in hand.

Pain load and sleep strain both tied to worse marks on all four fronts. Each held its tie sans the next. Readmits sat at 15 percent in the month. The authors urge care teams to treat pain and sleep as core post-ward aims, not side notes.
pmc-11690102:
Kelly McConnell, Jaime Gilliland, and Andrew Salner describe a project to develop support for anxiety in Latino caregivers of older adults with cancer, in a 2024 conference abstract. About two thirds of cancer caregivers in the United States care for an older adult. They give about thirty-three hours of care a week on average. More than a third report anxiety at a level that matters for health.

Talk therapy of a proven type is a first-line cure for anxiety, but it was built and tested mostly in white groups. Latino caregivers report high distress and low quality of life after a loved one's diagnosis, yet few programs are made for them. The project worked with stakeholders to build a program that fits their culture and needs. The goal is care that this large group can use.
pmc-11690202:
Gina Tucker-Roghi describes a project helping older adults speak up for age-friendly hospital care. Older patients face high risks of confusion states in hospital, lengthening stays and worsening outcomes. Simple steps — keeping the mind active, gentle movement, social contact, and good sleep habits — can prevent much harm, and personal knowledge of the patient helps staff use them. The project builds each participant a one-page life profile.

Occupational therapy students interview community-dwelling older adults and work with them to fill it with history, habits, routines, and preferences. If the person is later admitted to hospital, the profile goes with them so care teams know who they are. Feedback from one hundred eighty students over four years, and from the older adults, praised the project. Tucker-Roghi says it teaches students the worth of personal care while giving hospitals a tool for safer, kinder treatment.
pmc-11690402:
Claire Wang, Mengchi Li, and Junxin Li study music listening among older adults with mild memory loss. Their twenty twenty-four work sits inside a trial of personal music. Twenty-five people took part, with a mean age of sixty-eight. Each heard about thirty self-chosen songs for an hour a day, at least five days a week, for four weeks. The team tested music skill and taste at the start, then held talks after the program.

Most people already heard music with care for at least an hour a day. Close to half called music very key in their lives. Faith music was the top genre. Country, jazz, rock, and blues followed. Tempo and lyrics get close study in the talks.
pmc-11690502:
Allison Lindauer, Bryanna De Lima, and Elizabeth Eckstrom report on a training program from 2024 that helps research teams include older adults in studies. Many common health problems affect older people most, yet studies often leave them out. The team built a live online course and a set of tools to fix that gap.

The course ran for six sessions in the fall of 2022, and forty staff took part. A smaller group then tested the tools over the next few months. Surveys showed that staff liked the course, found the tips and tools useful, and planned to use what they learned. The most used tools were a guide for clear talk with older adults and a short check list for study plans.
pmc-11690602:
Madison Boudreaux and four co-authors study a screening tool that gauges how well patients can use remote health care, and ask if it widens gaps. Their study is from two thousand twenty-four.

Remote care has grown fast in the United States, most since the plague years. It can cut bars to care. But people with loss of sight, of hearing, or of thought may be left out, if their ease with the tools is not gauged well. The tool tests a person's skill, access, use, and ease with such tech. It was given to a hundred-plus patients at a front-line clinic over five months. The team matches groups by type of loss.
pmc-11690702:
Carla Hermann, a solo author, describes a study abroad course in a 2024 paper on aging and health care. Older people form a growing share of every country's population, and the United States is aging fast while growing more diverse. Every field of work will feel that shift, so training across majors matters.

A university in Indiana built a short interdisciplinary course abroad on health care and aging, open to students of any major. The paper reports what helped the course start and what blocked it. Other schools ran like courses before with a partner college abroad. The account gives planners a candid view of costs, partners, and student gains.
pmc-11690902:
Troy Andersen and six co-authors ask care workers what dementia training they actually need, in a study from 2024. Interviews covered 23 direct care workers, 7 supervisors and 8 administrators across assisted living facilities and personal care agencies. Burnout and turnover run high in this workforce, and poor dementia skills are part of the strain.

All three levels agreed on priorities: hands-on skills such as de-escalation, knowledge for tasks like bathing and distress, and clear paths to certification. Workers asked for training that is interactive, fits their shifts and answers problems in real time. Agencies complained that current topics feel academic and impractical. Flexible, setting-matched training is the shared demand.
pmc-11691002:
Kelly Cichy, Dakota Witzel, and Robert Stawski study how giving daily support to others couples with cognitive interference in a 2024 paper. To know that help is there when you need it is held to guard against stress. But handing help out has its own costs, which are read far less.

Data came from a national study of daily life, with day-by-day logs. On days when people gave more support, their minds were more apt to stick on the problems they had helped with. Worry and rumination rose with the giving. The pattern held both across days for one person and across people, on the whole.
pmc-11691202:
Blair Golden, Beth Fields, and Julia Berian present a set of talks on how hospitals can make family carers less unseen. Their piece, from two thousand twenty-four, grows out of a national plan to back family carers.

Carers give company, comfort, and help with discharge plans, yet teams often leave them out. The talks share a review that maps carer roles in hospital care, and a study of blocks that keep carers out of care for people with dementia. One talk sets out a free book for kin of very ill patients in deep care units. A last talk looks at how well staff teach carers and patients about sudden confusion.
pmc-11691502:
Sonja Rosen and co-authors describe a 2024 program at Cedars-Sinai, a large Los Angeles medical center, to screen older adults for social needs that affect health. Such needs can include food, housing, transport, and support at home. In 2021 the center built a system wide plan with a twelve part screener, a referral tool, community health workers, and links to local groups.

In the first two and a half years, staff screened older adults 97,757 times and found 30,245 unmet needs. A total of 411 older patients got help from a community health worker, and about six in ten were linked to aid. Older adults often needed a larger dose of support to succeed.
pmc-11692002:
Marielle Jensen-Battaglia and co-authors study how chronic illness shapes moves among older adults who struggle to move at home in a 2024 analysis. Staying in one's own home is a common goal, but trouble moving inside can block it. Earlier work with a national aging survey found that such trouble linked to moves into homes with fewer barriers or more household members.

The new analysis uses 25,490 person years from 5,894 people who moved 1,456 times. It asks whether cancer, heart attack or stroke, or dementia change the pattern. In raw models all three linked to moves into nursing or residential care. After adjustment, only dementia kept that link among people with no mobility trouble at the start.
pmc-11692202:
Laura Ginoux and Kirstie McAllum write in twenty twenty-four about teamwork in health and social care that goes past paid staff teams. Most views of teamwork focus on trained staff who share skills. Yet family care partners hold deep knowledge from daily life with the person they help. That knowledge is often left out of key choices.

Based on a review of past work, the authors set out a model of teamwork built on ties between people. They argue that care partners should sit on the team, not at its edge. Respect, trust, and care for the other person's world view help both sides blend skill types. The gain, they say, is better care for older adults and stronger teams.
pmc-11692302:
Junmin Park and Yeonjung Lee present a 2024 study from Korea on age bias and low mood. Respect for elders was a strong norm in Korean culture. Industrial change and new family forms have eroded that norm. Age discrimination can thus hit older adults hard. Social networks might soften that blow, as social capital theory suggests. They might also add stress of their own. The study tests which role networks play.

Formal networks count group and club activity. Informal networks count close personal ties. The team checks how each type changes the link between bias experience and depression. A buffer role would call for programs that build ties. A stress role would call for care in how networks are engaged. Policymakers for aging get evidence tuned to Korean culture rather than imported claims. The answer shapes whether network building is treatment or risk.
pmc-11692402:
Quinn Kennedy, Beatriz Hernandez, and Dorion Liston test, in a 2024 case study, whether eye movements can track brain health from home. The method, oculometrics, times and measures how the eyes follow a moving target, which reflects the state of the brain circuits behind perception and tracking. Their five-minute task runs on an ordinary home computer with a camera and produces ten scored measures rolled into one summary.

One 51-year-old woman took the task on 138 days over six months, noting anything that might sway her scores. Clean data landed on 111 days. Distractions in the room clearly dragged scores down, and poor sleep seemed to as well. Her scores improved over the first weeks, then leveled off. Seeing bad scores after bad nights even motivated her to fix her sleep. The authors call home monitoring feasible, with housekeeping caveats.
pmc-11692502:
Wan-Chen Hsu and co-authors study in 2024 how pandemic lockdowns affected loneliness, isolation, and thinking in retired people in Taiwan, and whether men and women fared unlike. Their survey, built by layered sampling, gathered more than a thousand retirees in their fifties to seventies in early 2023. Group talks added depth to the numbers.

About three in ten retirees felt lonely during the pandemic, and about a fifth of both men and women cut back on volunteering and group life. Score based models found no gender gap in loneliness or thinking test totals. Network analysis told a finer story: links among traits split by gender, with women's loneliness tied to a shape judgment task and men's thinking tied to volunteering. Elders in the group talks stressed how much community support carried them. The authors argue help should be shaped by gender specific patterns, not averages.
pmc-11692602:
Vanessa Young and co-authors present a 2024 study, part of the COMPADRE project, linking self-reported sleep quality to thinking skills in older Hispanic adults. Poor sleep has repeatedly travelled with worse cognition, but sleep quality has many parts, and a single score can hide which part matters. The team separated the strands.

Participants rated their sleep on a standard disturbance scale, plus measures of insomnia and plain dissatisfaction. They also reported their physical activity, and took cognitive tests. The analysis asks which sleep strand tracks with which mental skill, and whether being active softens the link. The focus on an understudied population sharpens what clinics can advise.
pmc-11692702:
Sarah Ashiqueali and co-authors move gut germs from long-lived dwarf mice into normal mice and watch the liver answer, in a 2024 study. Aging guts lose germ variety and stir inflammation, which feeds ills across the body. Ames dwarf mice, a mutant line, live far longer than their siblings and host a distinct gut mix. Stool swaps ran both ways between dwarfs and their normal littermates.

Dwarf stool reshaped the normal gut and reprogrammed which jobs the germ crowd performs, toward patterns tied to healthy aging. The liver's gene read shifted too, in a direction the team reads as better metabolic health. Three genes fell quiet: one tied to cell aging, and two to liver fat paths. The authors see a gut-liver axis that stool can steer. They pitch germ-targeted care as a route to longer health, with proof of the gears still to come.
pmc-11692902:
Wan Yun Chou and Su-I Hou examined how an older person's overall capacity relates to frailty, using a World Health Organization framework called ICOPE. The framework scores six domains: thinking, mobility, nutrition, vision, hearing, and mood. The pair studied 210 patients aged sixty-five and over on a geriatric ward in Taiwan in 2021, classing each person as robust, prefrail, or frail on a standard scale.

About 39 percent were prefrail and 29 percent frail. Loss of mobility and depressive symptoms were strongly tied to both states, and poor nutrition and hearing loss also raised frailty risk. The authors recommend routine ICOPE screening so problems are caught early, while noting their single-hospital sample limits how far the findings reach.
pmc-11693202:
Rose Lin and three co-authors report in twenty twenty-four on piano training for older adults with mild loss of thinking skill. Mood signs such as low mood often come with this loss. The team ran a twelve week course for seven older adults. Sessions mixed solo and group work, with short daily practice at home.

Talks with the group showed they found the course worth the effort. Daily practice gave shape to their days and a sense of purpose. Most went on to join a town piano class when the course ended. Peer support and kind, tuned help from teachers kept them going when new skills felt hard. The authors say piano work may lift mood and self trust, and larger trials should test long term gains.
pmc-11693302:
Courtney Gao and co-authors link marital status to vascular events in a diverse northern Manhattan group. Past studies tie marriage to heart and brain outcomes, with gaps by background. It is unclear if the pattern holds in mostly Hispanic groups.

The cohort followed adults aged forty and up who were stroke-free at entry. People were classed as married, single, widowed, or divorced or separated. Over long follow-up the team tracked stroke, heart attack, and death. Unmarried adults faced higher risk of any vascular event than married adults. They also faced higher risk of death from all causes. Subgroup patterns varied across the unmarried classes. The study adds long-term data from an under-studied population.
pmc-11693502:
Shuhan Liu and co-authors build a survival forecast for acute myeloid leukemia from gene whispers tied to an iron-driven cell death. This blood cancer moves fast and cures hard. Long non-coding RNAs steer cell fate, and ferroptosis, a rust-like death path, has joined the list of forces at play.

The team mines tumor data for RNAs linked to ferroptosis genes, then winnows them by survival ties. Ten RNAs anchor the final model, built through layered statistical sieves. The score sorts patients into risk bands whose survival curves split cleanly. Mutation maps and pathway scans add color: high-risk tumors lean on immune and cancer pathways. Immune cell mixes suggest high-risk patients may answer better to immunotherapy. The model gives doctors a molecular yardstick beside the classic clinical one.
pmc-11693802:
Breast cancer in men is rare enough that care rules are borrowed wholesale from women's medicine. Morteza Akbari, Hadi Nasiri, and Mojtaba Ziaee review the male disease in a 2024 paper. It makes up about one percent of male cancers and of all breast cancers. Most patients are in their fifties or older, and lumps are often first read as harmless gland growth.

Surgery leads care for contained cases, with radiation, drugs, and hormone therapy after. No large trials focus on men alone, so screening has no proven program. A team-based approach gives the best outcomes, the authors report. Risk factors from hormones to family history are covered. Follow-up care closes the survey.
pmc-11695102:
Aishwarya Pakhan and colleagues reported a giant skin growth case in two thousand twenty-four. The condition places mature fat cells inside skin layers. A young woman developed many brain-like surface nodules. They merged into a large plaque on her hip region. Growth continued over many months. Tissue study confirmed the classic form.

Treatment choices were discussed with the patient. Staged surgical removal promised the best appearance. The largest nodule came out under local numbing first. Remaining nodules followed months later under brief general anesthesia. Follow-up showed only a pale patch remaining. Early recognition prevents disfigurement in this rare condition. Wide lesions leave clinicians few options.
pmc-11696402:
Selvan Maruthasalamoorthy and Navamathavan Rangaswamy make a hollow sphere composite for supercapacitors in a 2024 study. Nickel pyrovanadate was grown as hollow nanospheres without any template, the solvent steering the shape. Blending in reduced graphene oxide at several loadings wrapped the spheres on conductive sheets. Diffraction confirmed the crystal and the carbon partner.

Charge storage ran through battery type redox reactions. More oxide surface met the electrolyte as the carbon share tuned the structure, lifting capacitance and stability. Solid state hybrid supercapacitors bridge batteries and capacitors for burst power jobs. A cheap, template free route to a high surface active material is exactly what scaling needs.
pmc-11696602:
Lucia Anettová and co-authors present a 2024 study on using lizards to track a parasitic worm. The rat lungworm is an emerging parasite that began in Southeast Asia and has spread through invasive rats and snails. On Tenerife it arrived over a decade ago, and the local lizard often carries its larvae.

The team caught lizards at nine sites across the island and sampled tail muscle with a painless shedding trick. A targeted DNA test found the worm in 31 of 129 samples. Infection rates varied by site, peaking near 64 percent in a humid spot. Because the lizard is the island's most common reptile, its infection map mirrors the worm's spread. Sentinel use of lizards could warn health officials cheaply.
pmc-11699402:
Testing CAR T cell therapy for acute myeloid leukemia needs mouse models that carry real patient tumors, not just cell lines. Mireia Mayoral Safont and eight co-authors lay out a step-by-step protocol in 2024 for building such a model that also glows for tracking.

The protocol covers how to insert a light-producing tag into patient-derived leukemia cells, grow them in mice, expand them, and enrich the tumor population. It then gives checks to run in dishes and in living mice before therapy tests begin. Because patient samples vary so much, the model keeps more of the disease's true complexity than cell lines do. The authors point to a companion study for the full worked example.
pmc-11700502:
Mazyad Alenezi and co-authors survey adults in the Qassim region of Saudi Arabia about tonsillectomy and immunity. Tonsils are immune tissue, and removing them eases repeated infections. Studies show no major harm to immunity or to risk of autoimmune disease, yet public misconceptions persist.

Nearly four hundred adults answered an online survey; about seventeen percent had had the operation. Over half believed the operation affects immunity, and over a third linked it to disease of the autoimmune kind. Health professionals were the top source of information, closely followed by social media and community talk. Schooling and occupation shaped awareness. The authors call for better public education on the evidence.
pmc-11700602:
Allison Baumhover and Stephanie L. Hansen wrote a 2025 article on the use of AI tools in animal science teaching. One author speaks as a teacher and the other as a new graduate student. Their topic is how staff and students can use these tools well and fairly.

Mixed messages about fair use and fear of job loss have made some users hold back. Hands-on use, by contrast, tended to shift views in a good way. The authors back open talk, clear rules, and care with these tools. They see AI as a partner to human skill, useful for tutoring, test design, and shared idea work.
pmc-11706302:
