Nick Li and nine co-authors studied arm vein clots linked to a common hospital line, in a 2024 paper. The line, a PICC, is threaded from the arm to feed patients or give drugs. It can trigger a clot in the upper arm veins. The team reviewed 168 surgical patients who received such a line over four years, and compared them with 136 medical patients from the same period.

Clots appeared in about one in twenty surgical patients, three times the rate in medical patients, even though the medical group was older and sicker. Most surgical patients had recent abdominal surgery. Cancer, a high burden of other illness, blocked bowels from cancer, and placing the line in the brachial vein each raised the risk. Standard blood-thinning prevention did not lower it. The authors urge care teams to weigh these risks when choosing lines for surgical patients.
pmc-11709402:
Katya T Numbers, Russell J Chander, Jason Chen, and Henry Brodaty untangle how mood symptoms, memory complaints, and test scores relate to later dementia. People may report memory slips long before tests show damage, and late-life mood or behavior changes can also warn of disease. Their 2025 study uses the Sydney Memory and Ageing Study, with seven hundred fifty-four older adults. It asks how complaints, symptoms, and measured cognition move together, and which pattern best forecasts who develops dementia.

Sorting these signals could sharpen early screening: whose complaint is benign worry, and whose is a first sign? The study's long follow-up in one community cohort is its strength. Results can guide clinics on which mix of self-report and testing deserves a closer look.
pmc-11709502:
Markley Oliveira and a large team test whether a blood marker of astrocyte reactivity links to hippocampal degeneration in vascular dementia, apart from amyloid pathology. Vascular dementia is the second most common dementia after Alzheimer disease, and white matter lesion burden drives its progression. The marker GFAP is known in Alzheimer research, but its role in vascular disease was poorly understood.

Data cover 796 participants from a research cohort and a memory clinic cohort. Groups split by amyloid status and white matter lesion status, with lesion values corrected for head size. The analysis ties GFAP levels to hippocampal volume loss in vascular cases. Such a marker could help separate vascular from Alzheimer driven decline in clinic samples.
pmc-11709602:
Angel Garcia De La Garza and co-authors compare two ways of asking older adults about their thinking in a 2025 study from the Einstein Aging Study. One way is a standard forty-item questionnaire asking people to recall changes over years. The other is a phone diary logging eighteen kinds of mental slips each day for two weeks.

The team used a Bayesian method to find shared and unique factors behind the two measures. They then tested which scores predicted who later developed mild cognitive impairment. Daily diaries capture life as lived, while recall forms lean on memory of memory itself. The study aims to sharpen early screening for cognitive decline.
pmc-11709802:
Jessica Britton and co-authors describe Agora in a 2025 paper, an open website that gathers evidence on possible drug targets for Alzheimer's disease. Promising targets are scattered across huge gene and protein data sets that many researchers cannot easily read.

The site lists over nine hundred fifty nominated targets from national research programs and the wider community. Each target page shows charts and plain summaries built from harmonized human data on genes, proteins, and metabolites. Interactive tools let non-specialists compare targets side by side. Recent updates add protein-level comparisons and links to lab resources. The aim is faster, shared judgment about which targets deserve trials.
pmc-11709902:
Pilar Rivero-Rios and co-authors present a 2025 conference abstract on the loss of dendritic spines in Alzheimer's disease. Spines are the tiny knobs where nerve cells receive signals, and their loss tracks memory decline more closely than amyloid does. The team studied how surface proteins recycle inside cultured hippocampal nerve cells.

Two recycling routes kept spine numbers up by returning distinct sets of proteins to the cell surface. Both routes need a signaling fat called PI3P to reach the synapse. That fat runs low in brain tissue from patients and from disease mouse models. The team argues that this shortage may help drive spine loss.
pmc-11710002:
Rosaleena Mohanty, Anna Marseglia, and Eric Westman untangle how different kinds of blood vessel damage in the brain relate to Alzheimer's disease. Vessel problems are now seen as key drivers of brain decline, but they come in many forms, from large strokes to tiny silent ones. Their 2025 paper asks which forms travel with Alzheimer's changes and which stand apart.

The study joined brain scans taken in life with postmortem exams for 77 people from a national Alzheimer's imaging project. Eight vessel markers were scored, including artery hardening, vessel amyloid, and old bleeds large and small. A statistical method compressed the markers into a few underlying dimensions. The team then checked those dimensions against plaques, tangles, and other coexisting pathologies. Their aim is a cleaner map of how vascular damage feeds, or merely accompanies, the loss of brain tissue in Alzheimer's disease.
pmc-11710102:
Tianjie Gu and co-authors check if gene marks on DNA in blood split by roots in Alzheimer disease, in a study from 2025. Such marks, called methylation, can switch genes up or down sans a change to the code. Past work hints the disease acts by unlike paths in unlike groups, but blood mark maps were thin.

The team read marks at near a million sites in 626 adults of European, African, and Hispanic roots, with and sans the disease. Marks that split sick from well ran in the hundreds per group. Yet the groups' lists did not meet: each root group had its own set. The team calls the work a first pass. A wider set may show shared marks, but care and tests may need group-wise maps.
pmc-11710202:
Adrian Oblak reports 2025 work on mouse models of late-onset Alzheimer's disease that lack the classic plaques and tangles. A large program breeds mice with human-like gene risk traits for the late form of the disease. Such mice should copy the human illness better than older gene-added models, which lean on rare early forms.

One model pairs two risk traits with a human form of the plaque protein, fed plain food or a high fat, high sugar diet. By 18 months, the rich-diet mice lost some nerve cells and showed more stray plaque protein and a blood sign of nerve harm. Gene and protein reads shifted in fat use and in cell links, and scans showed smaller brain areas. The mice also learned a touch task more slowly.
pmc-11710302:
Donald L Elbert presents a new computer pipeline, published in 2025, for turning brain scan data into working models of fluid flow in the brain. Fluids between and around brain cells carry proteins tied to nerve cell loss. Scans now show tissue in fine detail, but models of how those fluids move have lagged behind.

Elbert builds surface meshes from stacked electron microscope images, then solves flow and spread equations across the cells in each small block. The code runs on clusters of computers, with many blocks handled at once and flows matched at the borders. Test data from a public brain atlas showed clean fits between cells. The pipeline could help researchers study how harmful proteins move through brain tissue.
pmc-11710402:
Genes in the Alzheimer's brain switch on and off in coordinated groups, but which groups drive the disease and which merely react to it stays hard to prove. Pinghan Zhao and co-authors attack that sorting problem in a 2025 study with a cross-species trick. Gene groups found in human brain data are tested one by one in fruit flies carrying the disease's hallmark proteins.

Flies let the team flip hundreds of genes and watch whether brain decay sped or slowed. One group that rises in disease, rich in immune genes, proved to be a driver that worsens decay. A second group, tied to synapses and falling in disease, acted as a brake. The authors offer the sorted map as a guide to which networks drug hunters should push or protect.
pmc-11710502:
Hae Young Yi and co-authors probe a backup visual pathway in people with atypical Alzheimer's disease, using brain scans in a 2025 study. In these variants, language or vision falters first instead of memory. A side route that bypasses the main visual area may explain how emotion reading survives when back-brain regions shrink.

Seventeen patients and twenty-four healthy peers took structural and functional scans while viewing faces and scenes. At rest, patients showed weaker links from the pathway to vision areas, but during the task those links ran stronger than in controls. The authors suggest the pathway may step up to offset damage, though they call the work preliminary.
pmc-11710602:
Malaak Brubaker and co-authors present a 2025 study of a drug for unrest in people with dementia due to Alzheimer disease. Caregivers had named the acts that trouble them most, such as cursing, hitting, pacing, and asking for help again and again. The authors asked if the drug eased unrest in patients who showed those acts often.

They pooled data from two trials that lasted twelve weeks and used a fixed dose. In all, 610 patients took part, and scores came from a standard unrest scale. By week twelve, patients on the drug improved more than those on placebo in each group. Gains were seen from week eight in most groups.
pmc-11710702:
Isabel Castanho and co-authors report a 2025 study of why some people stay sharp despite Alzheimer type brain change. These resilient people meet the tissue signs of the disease after death but kept their wits in life. The team hunted for gene and cell signs that set them apart.

They joined many data types from a long study of aging and memory. Resilient donors sat between patients and controls in gene risk. In bulk tissue, just two genes differed from controls, and one rose in support cells of resilient brains. Some nerve cell groups were spared in resilient brains but lost in patients. The authors say these spared cells may hold clues for new treatments.
pmc-11710802:
Esteban Lucero and co-authors link higher dynein gene expression in a frontal brain region to lighter Alzheimer burden, in work from twenty twenty-five. Motor proteins haul cargo inside neurons and shape memory circuits. Past mouse work showed one motor can override amyloid harm to synapses. This study tests dynein motors in human brain data instead. Gene, pathology, and cognition records come from a large ageing study.

Hundreds of donors supply gene reads from the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex. Models adjust for age, sex, schooling, and post-mortem delay. In donors with Alzheimer disease, two dynein genes stand out. Higher expression of each predicts better cognition over time. Higher expression also predicts better scores at the last visit before death. Lower pathology burden tracks with the same high expression pattern. Motor support may buffer brains against amyloid damage.
pmc-11711802:
Murata, Iwasaki, and Shimizu review in 2024 the use of catheter ablation to treat a fast, faulty heart rhythm in patients with inflamed heart muscle. The illness stems from virus infection, drugs, vaccines, or immune attack, and its course varies widely. Tissue biopsy is the firm test for diagnosis and stage.

In the acute stage, drugs and support devices are the main care. Care for rhythm faults is not settled, though sudden death can occur. A table sums up past studies of ablation for this rhythm fault, mostly in the chronic stage. The review weighs how far ablation can help when drugs fall short.
pmc-11711902:
Natalie Leland and co-authors describe in 2025 how they built a large trial of dementia care in nursing homes without drug-based methods. Staff face hard daily work with residents who show strong behavior changes. Two known approaches stress either team training for all staff or expert help aimed at each new problem.

The trial compares those two approaches across many homes with help from the wider community. It tracks resident outcomes such as use of off-label calming drugs over the long term. It also asks staff and family carers how each approach felt in use. The design mixes counts with interviews to give a full picture.
pmc-11712302:
Yaolin Pei and co-authors study feeding choices among Chinese American dementia caregivers in a 2025 report. Tube feeding does not improve outcomes in advanced dementia, and guidelines advise against it. Yet earlier work found many Chinese American caregivers prefer it. The team began adapting a proven decision aid into Chinese.

They interviewed caregivers about how their families decide. Families thickened drinks, blended food, and made soups to prevent choking. Decisions were shared across the family, with harmony kept through prompt updates on the patient's health. The patient's own wishes mattered, though they were often unspoken. Translators proved key in talks with doctors. The authors use these findings to shape the adapted aid.
pmc-11712402:
Hao Yang, Jianping Jia and their co-authors use Mendelian randomization to test if diabetes drugs that block SGLT2 lower Alzheimer risk in 2025. People with type two diabetes face higher dementia risk, and these drugs show benefits beyond blood sugar control.

Gene-based proxies for drug action linked to lower risk of both diabetes and Alzheimer disease, for early and late onset forms alike. Among more than one hundred blood metabolites tested, citrate stood out as a possible middleman in the link. The authors say the gene evidence is strong but call for randomized trials to confirm the effect in patients.
pmc-11712502:
Catarina Tristão-Pereira and co-authors track brain and heart health together in midlife, in a 2025 report from the PESA study in Spain. Heart disease and dementia often appear together late in life. The team asked whether artery buildup and risk factors in midlife already track with brain change.

They followed about three hundred seventy adults with silent artery disease for near five years. Brain scans measured how well the cortex used sugar, a sign of brain activity. Lasting high heart risk went with a faster fall in that measure than low risk did. Blood markers were also tested for their role. The work supports early heart care as brain care.
pmc-11712602:
Stephanie Brown, Shahid Zaman, and John O'Brien scan a small brain hub in folks with Down traits to track Alzheimer wear, in a 2025 study. The hub makes the sole sleep switch chem in the brain. Poor sleep now counts as a risk mark for mind loss, so hub size may warn of wear.

Scans span more than three hundred fifty folks with Down traits plus kin checks. Hub size, set by skull share, shrinks in folks with mild loss or full mind loss. Small hubs track with worse thought scores in the checks. One front low sub part shrinks fast in clear Alzheimer cases. Sleep links may drive that fast wear.
pmc-11712702:
Yanbo Feng and eight co-authors mined tweets by dementia caregivers in 2025 to learn what weighs on them. Family caregivers post needs and worries in public, a rich record that surveys miss. Topic models can sort thousands of posts into themes, but standard versions blur the signal.

The team added two weighting schemes to a mixture topic model, tuned to lift rare but telling words. Four model variants were compared on the caregiver posts. Sharper topics mean support groups and services can aim at what caregivers actually discuss, from night wandering to money strain.
pmc-11712802:
Istikhar Ali and Aparajit Dey, two authors writing in 2025, explore daily life with dementia in India. Their study joins a large national aging survey that counts cases and risk factors. Numbers alone miss how the condition feels day to day across India's varied cultures.

Interviews and observation captured people aged sixty and over from many regions and income levels. Two themes stood out in the accounts. Emotional struggle marked efforts to adapt to modern settings and the toll of the illness. Social life also shifted, with many feeling pushed aside as behavior and thinking changed.
pmc-11712902:
Estela Benitez and co-authors link digital skill to phone use in older adults in a 2025 study. The set held 139 folk aged 60 to 90, mean 71.1. Forms read digital skill, phone stance marks, and use acts. Skill tied up with trust, ease, worth, and stance scores in the reads. Fear of tech tied down as skill rose. Pool math then set skill as the driver.

Skill called how oft phones saw use and how long folk had used them. App picks tied as well; app counts did not. The authors urge skill drills as the front door to tech for old folk.
pmc-11713002:
Sukhvir Kaur and Yogita Bansal design hybrid compounds that block two targets in Alzheimer's disease at once, in a 2025 study. Brain swelling helps drive the disease, and one swelling marker also feeds plaque growth. Blocking that marker plus the classic memory enzyme may beat single-target drugs. Four sets of hybrids joined a chromone head to an amine tail by chains of unlike length.

Docking picked sixteen best fits, and lab tests cut that to six strong enzyme blockers. One compound beat the rest on both targets. In mice with drug-induced memory loss, it restored memory in a dose-tied way at the top dose. Brain tissue then looked near normal. The authors back the chain length found as a design rule.
pmc-11713102:
Charles Chen and co-authors check antibody drugs against brain tissue itself in a 2025 Alzheimer's study. Trials of amyloid-clearing antibodies judge success by scans and spinal fluid, which measure the plaques only indirectly. This study used autopsy brains from a trial in dominantly inherited Alzheimer's disease, the rare genetic form. Ten trial cases, split between two antibodies and control arms, plus ten untreated observation cases, had plaque coverage measured across ten brain regions.

Direct tissue numbers can confirm or embarrass the biomarker story told during life. If a drug's scan signal says plaques fell while the tissue disagrees, dosing logic needs rethinking. Rare inherited cases offer the cleanest test bed because their disease course is so predictable.
pmc-11713302:
Brad F Boeve asks how trials for Lewy body dementia should measure whether a treatment helps, in a 2025 paper. Such trials need outcome scales that truly track the disease, yet no scale built for this illness captures its full course. Boeve notes that brain diseases mix memory loss with behavior, movement, and sleep problems. Borrowing scales made for other diseases is common but risky.

Scales built for Alzheimer's disease track early memory change, and scales from Parkinson's work track movement. Neither may show change well in Lewy body dementia, which spans all of those areas at once. Boeve reviews the limits of the borrowed tools and what trial planners should weigh when they pick one. He also reports work on a new scale built for this disease, meant for trials of drugs that aim to slow it.
pmc-11713402:
Konrad Talbot tests whether a class of diabetes drugs can ease insulin resistance in the Alzheimer's brain, in a 2025 study. Standard markers explain only about half of the spread in memory loss as the disease grows. A brain form of insulin resistance fills part of that gap. Its marker alone has tied to near half the spread in memory scores in older adults.

Talbot worked with donated tissue from the hippocampus, a memory hub, across healthy, mild impairment, and dementia cases. Insulin response in the tissue was weak in both impairment and dementia groups. Three drugs from the incretin class nearly restored that response in the mild groups. Only a dual-action drug helped the dementia tissue much. The study hints these drugs might aid the brain early, before dementia sets in.
pmc-11713602:
Cyprian Mostert wrote a 2025 policy paper arguing that African nations should reform their social pension programs. Old-age pensions are often paid late in life, after health has already failed. Mostert ties the timing of these payments to healthy brain aging. The paper draws on data from the World Bank, the World Health Organization, the United Nations, and other large bodies.

The numbers show a wide gap between total life span and years lived in good health. In sub-Saharan Africa, many people spend years in poor health before they qualify for a pension. Many men die before they ever receive one. Mostert proposes that payments begin when poor health starts, not at a fixed late age.
pmc-11713702:
A gene variant that may shield the brain from Alzheimer's harm is studied by Carello-Collar and co-authors in 2025. A rare variant in the reelin gene once delayed dementia by decades in one carrier, who had heavy plaque but little tau tangle growth. The team asks if common variants in the same gene protect in the usual form of the disease.

They study about two hundred adults, with and without memory loss, using brain scans for plaque and tangles plus gene tests. Early design and measures are set out in detail. If a shield effect holds, the gene path could guide new drugs that copy the body's own defense.
pmc-11713802:
Macedo and co-authors ask what blood tau marks really report in Alzheimer's disease in a 2025 study. Brain scans split tau harm into total load and spatial spread. Thinking loss tracks spread more than load. The team compares fluid tau forms against both scan measures in two cohorts totaling over seven hundred people.

Every fluid form tied to both spread and load. Across most brain maps, though, the tie to spread ran stronger. No region showed the reverse. The authors conclude that blood and spinal tau speak more to how far the disease has reached than to how much tau sits in one place. Trial designers may read the marks as spread gauges.
pmc-11713902:
Cyrus Ayubcha and co-authors use genetics to ask which blood proteins actually shape the brain and Alzheimer's risk. Proteins can be measured by the thousands now, but correlation is not cause. The team ran Mendelian randomization, using gene variants as natural experiments, across the two largest plasma proteomics efforts, each over thirty thousand people.

Dozens of proteins tied to brain imaging measures survived the screen, on both tissue structure and white matter wiring. Colocalization checks then separated likely causal signals from genetic hitchhikers. One example stood out: blood progranulin moved both Alzheimer's risk and the volume of the caudate. The authors offer the shortlist as leads for mechanism studies and drug hunting.
pmc-11714002:
Gill Livingston and a large team of co-authors totaled the share of dementia that could in principle be prevented, in a 2025 paper. Many risk factors for dementia are changeable over a life: schooling, hearing, blood pressure, smoking, and more. Each factor's share has been estimated before, but adding them up fairly is tricky because they overlap in the same people.

The authors put the evidence together into one population attributable fraction, the share of cases tied to all the changeable factors combined. A single honest number helps governments weigh dementia prevention against other health spending. It also sets a ceiling: even perfect action on every factor cannot pass that share.
pmc-11714302:
Oana Dumitrascu and co-authors present a 2025 study on amyloid plaques around eye blood vessels. The retina offers a window on brain decline. A laser scan can show vessel changes and amyloid, the protein that clumps in Alzheimer's disease. The team scanned 34 adults with normal or impaired thinking, plus brain imaging and standard tests.

Plaques hugged arteries more than veins across the group. In people with low test scores, plaques near second-order veins ran higher. Plaque counts in the smallest branches tracked smaller memory centers in the brain. They also tracked more white matter damage spots. The authors say retinal amyloid patterns mirror brain changes. Eye scans might one day flag decline without brain imaging.
pmc-11714502:
Margery Chen and eight co-authors build a lab test for a stray protein piece that could flag a hidden fault in Alzheimer's disease and a related illness, in a 2025 conference paper. The fault is the loss of TDP-43, a protein that quits the cell core in about half of cases of both illnesses. No test can now spot this loss in a living person.

When the protein fails, cells slip a wrong segment into other proteins, and one such host is called ACTL6B. The team made antibodies that bind only the stray piece. In lab cells the test fired only when TDP-43 was knocked down. It also lit up in patient brain tissue where the protein had left the core. The authors see a path toward a fluid test for patients.
pmc-11714602:
The full cost of Alzheimer's disease in the United States goes well past medical bills. A 2025 study by Amir Abbas Tahami Monfared and co-authors adds it up by disease stage. Their count joins direct health costs with unpaid care, lost work, and the harder-to-price loss of quality of life.

The team drew on a long national survey of older adults running from 1994 to 2018. They used a phone test of thinking to place people from mild impairment through disease stages. A side survey of one hundred patient-caregiver pairs measured quality of life, which was turned into money terms with a set value per healthy year. The study gives planners a stage-by-stage view of what the disease costs families and the country.
pmc-11714702:
Nicole Gatto and co-authors describe efforts to diversify the Adult Changes in Thought study cohort in a 2025 paper. The long-running Seattle cohort hunts dementia risk and protective factors in adults over sixty-five.

Historically the cohort was mostly non-Hispanic White. A new target seeks hundreds of enrollees from minoritized groups by 2026, lifting their share of the active sample. Steps included clearer recruitment materials, oversampling of target groups, and a second clinic in a diverse southeast Seattle area. Early rollout enrolled hundreds of new members in a year. New enrollees are compared with the wider health plan pool on age, sex, and deprivation. The work aims for dementia findings that fit all communities.
pmc-11714802:
Melissa Murray and Sara Dunlop describe an index that sorts Alzheimer disease cases by where their tangles sit in the brain, in work published in 2025. Tangle spread differs across patients and shapes their symptoms. The index was built from more than a thousand autopsied brains in a Florida cohort.

Cases with more cortical and less memory center tangles began symptoms younger and declined faster. They also more often showed non memory symptoms first. Scan data from a separate group matched the index, with lower scores tied to larger memory centers and higher tracer uptake. One subgroup had fewer active immune cells in cortex, which may help explain its higher tau load. The authors suggest care could be tailored by this pattern.
pmc-11714902:
Erika Meza studies whether gaining more education than ones parents boosts thinking skills in old age. Past work in rich countries links upward education paths to better late life cognition. Evidence from low and middle income countries is scarce, so Meza compares Mexico and South Africa, two nations with distinct education histories.

National samples of adults aged 50 and older come from harmonized aging studies in both countries. The analysis covers 1,031 adults whose parents had no formal education at all. About 58 percent are women. Regression models link first generation schooling to scores for orientation, executive function, language, memory, and global cognition. The cross country design tests whether the benefit holds across very distinct settings.
pmc-11715002:
People with mild cognitive impairment often make poor choices when the outcome of a choice is unsure. Mang Zhang and co-authors studied how the brains of such patients respond to feedback after a decision. They compared nineteen patients with twenty healthy adults of the same age. Both groups played two gambling-style tasks, one with known risks and one with unknown odds, while brain waves were recorded.

The patients showed weaker brain signals tied to reward and to attention after feedback. They also took longer to decide and adjusted their play less well. Feedback size and tone shifted the signals in both groups. The findings suggest that feedback processing itself is dulled in mild cognitive impairment, which may help explain risky choices in daily life.
pmc-11715102:
Ning Sun studies how education and marriage together shape cognition loss risk in older adults in China in a 2025 paper. The idea is that both reason and emotion support independent living in late life. Over a thousand older adults gave social data and took a standard mental state exam.

Low education paired with widowhood raised the risk of severe impairment in the oldest group. High education paired with marriage leveled the age-related risk in the data. The interaction matters more than either factor alone in Sun's account. Programs for aging populations may need to support learning and companionship together.
pmc-11715302:
Age tweaks in brain scan studies of the oldest old are weighed by Yi Lor and co-authors in work dated 2025. The LifeAfter90 study tracks adults aged ninety or more in north California. Brain zone sizes from scans were tied to change in two thinking skills over eight visits. Five ways to handle age in the sums were put head to head.

Two hundred nine people fed the study, most of them women with some college. Age at first test tied to zone sizes in mixed ways by zone. All five tweak ways left the zone-to-mind links much the same. Scan calls in the very old look robust to age handling.
pmc-11715602:
Shivani Suresh, Vanessa Raymont, and Sarah Bauermeister set out a plan in 2025 for a review of blood tests that could diagnose Alzheimer's disease at scale. The disease affects more than fifty million people, and its changes begin long before symptoms, yet current tests are costly or invasive.

The review will search five databases for human studies from the past five years in English. It will focus on three blood markers named in recent guidance from a national institute. Findings will be summed up in words, and pooled in a formal analysis if the data allow. The aim is to show which cheap tests are ready for wider use.
pmc-11715702:
Nik Lampe and Tara McKay study social ties and brain health among LGBTQ+ older adults in the United States in a 2025 paper. Lack of support and isolation are known risks for poor cognitive health. Older adults in this group report more isolation and less support than their peers in national surveys.

The team used first-wave data from a Vanderbilt study that recruited 1,256 adults aged 50 and older in four states during 2020 and 2021. Brain health was self-rated on a 15-item scale of memory and daily function problems. Tests then linked those scores to support for each person’s identity and to feelings of isolation from family, coworkers, and neighbors. The study isolates which ties matter most for this group.
pmc-11715802:
Eddy Roccati and co-authors tested in 2025 whether free university study in later life improves dementia risk factors and thinking skills. Most past work looked at schooling early in life. The team behind the ISLAND study argued that later study can still build cognitive reserve, even for people with little early schooling.

Their campus program, launched in 2019, offers free study in person or online to remove cost, place, and income barriers. After four years, campus participants were matched by age and gender with non-campus peers. The team compared change in risk factors, cognition scores, and a blood marker linked to Alzheimer disease. Readers get a rare long look at education as a late-life health tool, tested in a real program rather than a short lab course.
pmc-11715902:
Monica Zigman Suchsland and five co-authors ask how often Medicare wellness visits lead to a dementia related diagnosis in primary care, in this 2025 study. The yearly wellness visit gives family doctors a set chance to check the thinking of older patients. Care for memory problems is shifting toward these front line clinics, away from specialists alone.

Records came from fourteen clinics at the University of Washington covering more than forty thousand visits. Only about one percent of patients received a first diagnosis of impairment or dementia at a later visit. When a diagnosis came, it arrived a median of about nine months after the visit. Patients then averaged over three primary care visits a year. The long lag suggests visits alone are not catching problems early.
pmc-11716102:
Mahdieh Vahdatian and co-authors model the order in which Alzheimer's disease changes unfold in the brain, in a 2025 paper. The disease does not strike every region at once, and patients differ in their path. The team used an event-based model, which treats each change as a step in a sequence. They added maps of how brain regions connect, drawn from connectomics, to sharpen the sequence.

The data came from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative, spanning healthy adults and patients at several stages of impairment. Three kinds of brain scan tracked amyloid, tau, and sugar use across regions. The model placed early amyloid buildup in regions matching the brain's default mode network. Sugar use dropped earliest in many of the same areas. The authors say the approach could support earlier diagnosis and more personal treatment planning.
pmc-11716202:
Kasper Bormans and Sandra Zwakhalen report a drawing study from 2025 on how young children picture older people and dementia. The work asks whether hard times during the virus years, or warm contact with grandparents, can change those mental pictures. Children in Flanders and the Netherlands took part in drawing sessions held sixteen weeks apart.

In total, 848 drawings came from 106 children aged ten, split into three groups. One group drew after strict virus limits and made much smaller figures. A second group drew after good time with grandparents and people with dementia, and made larger, more social drawings. The third group showed little change. Readers learn that views of ageing can shift, and that contact may help shape them.
pmc-11716602:
Tim MacLeod reports lessons from a global program that planted early dementia screening in everyday clinics. The Davos Alzheimer's Collaborative program, launched in 2021, worked with seven health systems in six countries, from Brazil and Jamaica to Japan and Scotland. Its aim was to catch cognitive decline sooner by adding digital cognitive tests to primary care, with a blood test for amyloid offered when the screen raised concern.

Site leaders met monthly for two years to swap problems and fixes. Their shared hurdles spanned payment and purchasing rules, shortages of brain-health expertise and lab capacity, and the daily friction of training, blood draws, and shipping samples. Clinicians also needed support to use the tests and to explain blood results to patients. MacLeod stresses that teaching sites how the blood tests work, and where they fit in routine care, decided whether the tools could spread.
pmc-11716702:
Raphael Gabiazon and six co-authors published a study in 2025 on whether training people's confidence in their memory can itself improve memory. Older adults with mild impairment often lose faith in their recall, and low confidence may drag performance down further. The team built a six-week course aimed at rebuilding that confidence.

Twenty-eight volunteers were split evenly between the confidence course and a general education class. Both met weekly for ninety minutes in small groups. The researchers measured memory for linked items and tracked brain activity before and after. If belief alone lifts scores, clinics gain a cheap, drug-free tool to help patients hold on to daily skills.
pmc-11716802:
Cover, Vazquez and their co-authors follow neuronal, glutamate and blood flow changes in aging mice bred to model Alzheimer amyloid build-up in 2025. How early disease stages affect cortical health is still little known, though early action may matter most.

A small group of mice was imaged monthly from young age to one year, at rest and after a whisker puff stimulus. Light-based methods tracked activity across the whole brain and at cell level. Peak responses fell steadily and reached a clear drop by ten months. Signs of excitatory imbalance appeared in mid life, and glutamate clearance faltered briefly. Larger studies are planned.
pmc-11716902:
Ingo Kilimann and co-authors ask, in a 2025 study, whether drugs with anticholinergic effects shrink two brain regions tied to Alzheimer's disease. Such drugs are common in older care, and heavy use of them has been linked to worse thinking and higher dementia risk.

Data came from 787 people in a German study, ranging from healthy adults to people with dementia. Brain scans measured the basal forebrain and hippocampus, and drug exposure was scored by a standard burden scale. Overall, no clear link showed up. Only in people with mild self-reported decline did higher burden pair with smaller hippocampus size. The authors urge care with these drugs rather than alarm.
pmc-11721302:
Chenghui Wang and co-authors tied a gene fault to inherited vision loss in a 2024 study. The disease wears down nerve cells at the back of the eye, and faults in cell power parts are a known cause. Yet many of the parts at fault are still unknown, so gene hunts in sick families still matter.

The team found a change in the CRYAB gene in three Chinese families where the loss passed from parent to child. That gene makes a lens protein that also guards cell power parts and blocks cell death. Tests showed the changed protein is less stable, forms fewer clumps, and guards cells less well. It also binds a death-linked partner less, which helps explain the eye damage.
pmc-11728202:
Tomasz Jankowski and co-authors review ways to shield the palate after a gum graft. Their 2024 systematic review deals with free gingival grafts, where gum tissue is taken from the roof of the mouth. That donor wound is the main source of pain and bleeding after the operation.

Four databases were searched, and 38 full papers went into the final review. Most work tested platelet-rich fibrin, a gel made from the patient's own blood. It gave no clear gain in comfort or healing. Light therapy helped the wound close over but did not ease pain. The authors sort the shields by source: body-based, physical, or chemical, and note where proof is thin.
pmc-11728402:
Yili Wang, Dongbin Zhang, and Chen Zhang simulated a welding build process in a 2024 study. The process lays down a high-strength aluminum alloy, used in aircraft, by wire arc welding in a special cold transfer mode. It builds parts fast and cheaply, but no one had yet modeled its melt pool in full.

Their three-dimensional fluid model tracks how metal drops cross the arc and how the melt pool flows and sets. The drop pattern under this mode showed its own rhythm, distinct from plain arc modes. Pool flow maps help explain flaws such as pores. Builders can use the model to tune settings before burning real metal.
pmc-11728602:
Joon-Gyu Min, Young-Chul Kim, and Kwang-Il Kim study shellfish as carriers of a shrimp virus in a 2024 paper. White spot syndrome virus devastates shrimp farms worldwide. Filter-feeding shellfish share farm water and strain particles from it, so they might store and pass the virus. The team housed oysters, mussels, and clams with infected shrimp for two days.

All three shellfish took up the virus in gills and digestive glands, with glands holding more. Loads in tissue tracked the virus level in the water. Ground tissue from the shellfish killed healthy shrimp outright in infection tests, proving the stored virus stayed dangerous. After a week in clean water, virus levels in shellfish fell below detection. The authors call shellfish temporary reservoirs. They advise managing shellfish exposure on farms where the virus is present.
pmc-11729102:
Liqing Liu and seven co-authors published a 2024 study producing the receptor binding domain of the SARS-CoV-2 Delta variant as vaccine antigen material. This domain of the spike protein carries most of the spots neutralizing antibodies target, making it a favored vaccine ingredient. The team analyzed the protein's sequence traits, then engineered bacteria to produce it in single and doubled forms, and purified both.

Injected into mice, both forms provoked specific antibodies against themselves, showing solid immunogenicity. The authors present the bacterial production route as workable for this antigen. They suggest the results can support future coronavirus detection tools and vaccine development. The study is a methods-and-proof paper rather than a vaccine trial.
pmc-11731802:
Suhad Abdul-Huseen and Hazima Alabassi measure a signaling axis and two immune brake molecules in colon cancer patients after surgery and chemotherapy. Their 2024 study, run at a hospital in Ramadi, Iraq, compares 50 patients with 40 healthy controls. The axis pairs a receptor, CXCR4, with its partner signal, SDF-1, both tied to tumor spread.

Patients received four cycles of a standard drug pair after their tumors were removed. Blood tests showed the patients carried far lower levels of both axis parts than the controls. Gene activity for the two brakes, PD-1 and CTLA-4, also ran much lower in patients. The authors probe how these factors relate, hoping the pattern can guide diagnosis or treatment. All readings were taken after treatment, a limit on what the study can claim.
pmc-11733902:
Diego Santiago de Mendonça and nine co-authors map the shape variations of the sphenoid sinus, a hollow pocket deep in the skull, in this 2024 study. Surgeons pass through this sinus to reach the pituitary area, so its quirks matter for safety. The team read head scans to chart how the cavity expands and where vital structures sit inside its walls.

Scans from 320 adults were reviewed. The sinus reached backward under the skull base in most patients, and full internal walls dividing it were present in about ninety-one percent. As the cavity expanded more, the eye nerve and the main neck artery bulged into it more often, sometimes with paper thin coverings. Rates of each form varied widely across patients. The authors stress careful scan reading before any surgery through the nose.
pmc-11740202:
Mohammed Jamali, Suad Abdeen, and Thazhumpal Mathew measure vitamin D levels in healthy students at Kuwait University. Their cross-sectional study was published in twenty twenty-four. Sun-rich countries still show surprising deficiency, and young adults are seldom checked.

Two hundred and one medical and dental students gave blood and answered a survey. Eighty-five in each hundred fell below the deficiency line. Only about six in each hundred reached the optimal range. Deficiency hit men slightly harder than women. Students in the later, clinical years had notably higher levels than juniors. The authors urge awareness and screening on campus despite the desert sun.
pmc-11749902:
Hansraj Mangray and co-authors test, in 2023, whether videos plus home practice beat videos alone for teaching keyhole surgery stitching. Sixteen students watched a teaching video, then were timed tying a surgical knot after two weeks. They were then split into two groups for two more weeks of practice.

One group kept using only the video, while the other added a home simulation setup for hands-on practice. The combined group cut its median knot time to under thirty seconds, far ahead of the video-only group. Their tool movements also became cleaner, with less crossing and wasted motion. Skill, the authors argue, needs touch as well as sight.
pmc-11758502:
Jessica Seidelman and two co-authors tested a simple algorithm to cut needless blood cultures in heart and chest surgery patients at Duke University Hospital. Blood cultures hunt bloodstream infections, but ordering them too freely breeds false positives, extra antibiotics, and cost. Surgery step-down patients, fresh from operations and wired with devices, had never been the focus of such a rule. The algorithm went live in June 2023 across three units.

Nearly five thousand culture events were analyzed, about two thirds before the change. Culture rates fell by roughly a fifth after the algorithm arrived. Safety held steady: line infections, readmissions, and deaths showed no meaningful rise, though the death estimate was too imprecise to read much into. Reported in 2024, the study supports diagnostic stewardship in this complex group: fewer bottles drawn, no sign of harm, and a template other surgical units could adapt.
pmc-11760402:
Saurabh Kumar and Runki Saran test whether cleaning agents damage children's dental prostheses, in a 2024 study. The prostheses are made of polymethylmethacrylate, a plastic used for dentures and orthodontic appliances. Children wear such devices as space maintainers, habit breakers, and partial dentures. Regular disinfection protects the mouth and extends the device's life.

Chemical cleansers are the common cleaning route. Some agents, though, are known to alter the plastic's physical traits. The study checks how two widely used disinfectants change the surface of the material. Surface roughness and hardness matter for comfort and germ buildup. Findings help dentists pick cleansers that clean without harm. Parents also gain clearer care guidance for home use.
pmc-11769802:
Dakota Paine and co-authors watch the skin's first response to a virus-carrying tick in a 2025 study of Powassan virus. This tick-borne virus can cause brain inflammation, and it passes into the host during the earliest hours of feeding, while tick saliva is already reshaping local immunity.

The researchers biopsied bite sites one, three, and six hours after attachment of infected or uninfected ticks and sequenced the RNA there. Feeding alone rewired many skin genes within the first hours. The virus added little at first, but by six hours the site had swung toward a strongly inflammatory state. The timeline shows how quickly the battleground forms.
pmc-11770802:
Hamida Kwas and Sabrine Majdoub Fehri surveyed tobacco, alcohol, and drug use among high school students in Gabès, Tunisia, in 2024. Youth substance data guide prevention, and local numbers were scarce. A self-filled questionnaire went out in five schools in 2022.

Five hundred seven students, average age about sixteen, took part. About twenty-two percent smoked, many daily at around ten cigarettes a day, and nearly a third of smokers had started before age ten. E-cigarette use hit twelve percent, chewing tobacco nine, and hookah about fifteen. Alcohol use was near six percent and drug use near five, mostly cannabis. The authors urge school prevention programs built on these figures.
pmc-11786002:
Zahra Mahdavi and Ladan Hafezi measure a small hook of bone at the skull's base in Iranian women, hunting norms for a structure few studies touch. The pterygoid hamulus matters for throat and face diagnosis and can hide behind unexplained mouth pain. Cone-beam scans from 258 women aged twenty to forty supplied the data.

Right and left hooks averaged about five and a half millimeters long and two wide, with angles in the twenties of degrees. The sides disagreed on length, width, and one angle, so symmetry is not guaranteed. Slender was the commonest shape. Nothing shifted with age inside this range, a steady baseline for clinicians reading such scans.
pmc-11790602:
Yang and co-authors catalog the light-sensing gene family in Aikang58 wheat and track where each member acts. Phytochromes read red and far-red light and steer plant growth. Model plants have been studied deeply, but wheat got less attention. The team found eight family genes in this wheat variety. Gene shapes, shared blocks, and family trees all showed strong conservation. Comparisons stretched across wheat types, barley, rice, maize, quinoa, soybean, and Arabidopsis.

Shared chromosome blocks traced how the family evolved across crops. Activity data showed which genes answer light in which tissues. The catalog gives breeders targets for tuning light response. It also anchors wheat in the wider phytochrome story.
pmc-11794502:
Kala Kumar Bharani and co-authors trial ashwagandha root extract for gut health in elderly beagles, under full double-blind, placebo-controlled discipline. The herb is famed as an adaptogen that calms inflammation, and a healthy gut is central to aging well. Whether it moves gut measures in dogs was untested.

Their 2024 trial doses a dozen senior beagles daily for two months and tracks blood, stool, and microbiome panels. Treated dogs gained red cell counts and hemoglobin while two liver enzymes tied to strain fell clearly by day sixty. A gut-linked amino acid marker shifted too. The authors read the pattern as gentle systemic support, and call for larger trials to test the gut claim head-on.
pmc-11803202:
Margherita Cantelli and her co-authors present a 2024 systematic review on heat-altered stones in prehistoric archaeology. Such stones are common at ancient sites worldwide, yet researchers often overlook them. The team gathered seventy-three published records and charted where the stones appear, how old they are, what they are made of, and the food settings around them.

Heated stones show up from the Pleistocene onward, tied to cooking and other tasks among hunting, fishing, and gathering groups. They stay frequent through later periods, even as farming and pottery arrive. Studies from Africa, Oceania, Asia, and South America are notably scarce. Basic definitions for spotting such stones remain unsettled. The authors urge archaeologists and heritage managers to treat these stones as real evidence of ancient foodways before more is lost.
pmc-11808002:
A rice plant's leaves and grain husks need a clear sense of which side faces out, and Jun Tang and co-authors trace that polarity to a gene called DH2. Mutants lacking the gene, described in this 2024 study, grew leaves rolled toward their undersides and lemmas squeezed into rods. DH2 makes the ARGONAUTE 7 protein, which builds small silencing RNAs known as tasiR-ARFs. In the mutants those RNAs collapsed, and four target genes they normally restrain switched on in the wrong places.

Overexpressing DH2 rolled leaves the opposite way, confirming the gene's grip on polarity. The authors conclude the pathway polices the whole lemma rather than one side, a twist on how the same machinery works in the model plant Arabidopsis.
pmc-11810902:
Yosuke Sugiyama and co-authors measure in 2025 whether making music on a computer changes body chemistry. Software now lets beginners compose without deep training. The team ran short workshops and tracked two hormones: oxytocin, tied to bonding, and cortisol, tied to stress.

One workshop paired each person with a helper; the other had people compose in a group. In the paired format, oxytocin rose and cortisol held steady. In the group format, cortisol fell but oxytocin did not rise. The authors say the results hint that guided music-making can shift the body's social and stress signals, while noting that firmer trials are still needed.
pmc-11811502:
Palyanov and Palyanova present a method to store and study the genomes of the virus that caused the COVID-19 pandemic, all inside the memory of an ordinary computer. Around the world, labs collected about 16.8 million viral genomes, a mountain of data far too large for normal tools. Each genome is nearly thirty thousand letters long.

Their trick is to compare each genome with the first reference strain and store only the changes: single swaps, deletions, and insertions. That shrinks the full set by a factor of about fifteen hundred, to a few hundred megabytes. With the data held compactly in memory, patterns can be drawn and grouped quickly. The approach speeds the study of how the virus evolved.
pmc-11813802:
Podkolodnyy and three co-authors review the use of ontologies in handling big genetic data in a paper from 2024. Ontologies are structured vocabularies that let computers link facts across data sets. The field holds vast, mixed experimental data, and such structures can merge it, build large knowledge bases, and help explain the output of deep learning models.

The Gene Ontology knowledge base is presented as a success story, with causal models layered on term lists. A second example builds most of a large ontology by automated reasoning from reference sources. Two hybrid models that wire ontology structure into neural networks show how black box models can explain themselves.
pmc-11816102:
Helen Sharp and six co-authors give the first Indian evidence on how the pandemic affected preschool minds, in a 2024 study. World studies found little average effect on young children, but effects split sharply by prior hardship. Data from poorer countries were scarce, though their sharper inequalities could widen the split.

The team drew on a Bangalore birth cohort that followed children over time. Parents reported emotional and behavior problems at age two, before the pandemic, and again later. By stripping out normal age-related change, they could isolate the pandemic’s added effect. They then tested which COVID-linked hardships, such as income loss or illness, marked the children who fared worst. The work guides support toward the families hit hardest.
pmc-11827602:
Kothurkar and co-authors adapted a many-label imaging method to the zebrafish retina, in a study published in 2024. To understand a tissue, researchers need to see all its cell types at once. Standard staining can only show a few labels together, because the colors overlap. The method they used labels a sample in rounds, bleaching each round's glow before the next. Eleven antibodies were chained this way on one piece of tissue.

The full set lit up every major cell type of the retina at once. The team also made the method work alongside fish lines that glow on their own in set cells. Retinas are a favorite model for brain wiring and eye disease. A complete cellular map of one sample saves animals and aligns data perfectly. The adaptation opens the same trick to other fish tissues.
pmc-11835702:
Shuangling Yang and co-authors comment in 2025 on a study of how gut germs turn one hormone type into another. The source study found that body-made hydrogen gas lets gut germs strip a part from stress hormones to form sex-linked hormones. That path may shape health in women, the comment notes.

The writers trace the long path to this find, from old rat work in the late past to new lab tools. They set out what is still not known and where the field stands. Their aim is to frame how body gas and gut germs may jointly drive health in women.
pmc-11839502:
Jiajuan Wu and co-authors study a marked subset of killer T cells in lung cancer tissue, in a paper from 2024. The cancer in question is the non small cell type, the most common form of lung cancer. Immune checkpoint drugs are a main treatment for it, yet only a small share of patients answer well, so better markers of likely response are needed.

Tumor samples were split into central and non central regions. Flow based tests counted T cells carrying a marker called TIM3 and checked a second brake marker on their surface. The team then related those counts to how well patients answered immune therapy. A marker that sorts likely responders could help doctors aim the drugs at the patients most apt to gain from them.
pmc-11840402:
Hamin Lee and five co-authors profile a Korean cohort of atomic bomb survivors and their descendants. Their 2024 paper lays out the study's design and first data. Korean survivors of the 1945 bombs have been less studied than Japanese ones. Whether harm passes to children and grandchildren is a core question.

From 2020 to 2024, over two thousand five hundred people enrolled. Survivors numbered about eleven hundred, with over a thousand children and two hundred forty-two grandchildren. About seventy-two percent finished surveys and health exams. Exposure was checked against Red Cross records and Japanese handbooks. Illness counts rest on doctors' diagnoses as reported. These baseline data frame all future findings from the cohort.
pmc-11888702:
Sivan Priya and co-authors set out the rites and healing claims of Yajna in a 2024 paper. Yajna is a fire rite of selfless gifts, with herbs and goods cast to flame with chants. Health, in their frame, spans body, mind, and social weal.

Smoke from the rite is said to clear air germs and lift mood and fits. Past peoples built such rites to fight pestilence at many levels at once. The authors tie rite parts to each claimed gain in a set way. Wide vaccine drives can lag in a fast plague, so joint rites may back state work. Proof levels for each claim get a sober look.
pmc-11903402:
Susanne Kraske, Fanny Müller, and Vera Schellerer present a 2024 case report on a rare harm after penis surgery in a baby boy. The boy, seven months old, had surgery to fix a buried penis. After the operation, blood flow to the tip of the penis was cut off, a state called glans ischemia.

Doctors treated the boy with a blood thinner given through a vein. The wound seam opened fully, yet the tip healed on its own within four weeks. The authors also reviewed 43 years of past reports, from 1981 to 2023, on this harm after penis surgery in boys. They sum up how teams watch for it, treat it, and what results to expect. Early care can save the tissue.
pmc-11911202:
Luyao Li, Yupeng Niu, Fa Tian, and Bin Huang pair two lean neural networks to find and classify breast tumors in ultrasound scans automatically. Their study, published in 2024, targets a screening bottleneck in China, where manual ultrasound reading is slow and labor-heavy. One network outlines the tumor; a second, custom-built classifier names its type.

The outlining model scored 0.9702 accuracy with strong overlap against expert marks. The classifier beat standard networks overall, reaching 0.90 accuracy on normal cases though trailing slightly on benign and malignant ones. The authors argue the pairing reads scans fast and well enough to assist early diagnosis. Speed matters because early treatment drives survival in this cancer. The system is offered as an aid to, not a replacement for, sonographers.
pmc-11915102:
Tatiana Chernyshenko and colleagues update a meta-analysis comparing two liver cancer treatments that deliver chemotherapy through the artery feeding the tumour. One uses drug-eluting beads, the other the standard mix. Past pooled results conflicted, which prompted the update. Thirty-two studies with 4,367 patients were combined, covering tumour response, survival and complications.

The bead method won on every response grade. Overall survival ran about 3.5 months longer and time without spread about 3.1 months longer with beads. Complication rates were about the same in both groups. The authors read the bead route as a clear step up for patients fit for this therapy.
pmc-11922302:
Paul Conway and five co-authors survey the mental health of UK police who investigate child sexual abuse material. Their 2024 study covers 661 officers and staff in this grim specialty. Depression and anxiety ran far above general levels, while post-traumatic stress did not, a pattern that points away from simple exposure as the whole story.

What predicted suffering most was moral injury, above all the feeling of being betrayed by the institution itself. Exposure to the material and contact with victims also hurt, but measurably less. Feeling successful and supported protected strongly. Coping habits split the same way: self-blame, rumination, and withdrawal tracked with worse health, while positive refocusing, distraction, and social support tracked with better. The authors argue the remedy is largely organizational. Support and fairness inside the force may matter more than shielding staff from the material, which the job makes impossible.
pmc-11928302:
Badre Bakzaza and co-authors review studies of life quality among people with chronic disease in Africa, in a 2024 paper. Long term illness can erode physical health, mental health, and social ties. The team searched for African studies that measured those effects in a structured way.

They kept twenty three studies in English published between 2019 and late 2023. Across them, patients faced medical, mental, and social burdens that lowered their quality of life. The authors argue these patients should get priority when they seek care. They also call for stronger health systems in Africa, with better primary care and better trained staff. The review frames life quality as a core outcome, not an afterthought, in chronic care.
pmc-11967502:
A rare suspected case ties a man's sudden swallowing trouble to a parasite from raw seafood. Joonhee Han, Heung Up Kim, Sejin Kim, and Hyun Joo Song report the case in a 2023 paper. Their patient, sixty-six, ate abalone sashimi and woke unable to swallow well. Rash, itching, chest and belly pain, and diarrhea followed. He had suffered alike twice before after raw fish.

Scope images showed shallow sores and swelling in the mid food pipe. Scans found wall thickening plus a blocked small bowel with fluid. A blood marker for the parasite ran high, and the belly fluid held many white cells of one type. Swallowing eased after nine days. The team judged esophageal anisakiasis the likely cause.
pmc-11970502:
Saivarshini Magham and co-authors review a cell receptor as a drug target for Parkinson's disease. Their 2024 review notes that the disease ranks among the most common brain disorders and involves loss of dopamine in the brain. The receptor acts as a gate for inflammation in support cells of the brain.

When switched on in those cells, the receptor can drive release of inflammatory signals. Blocking it may thus protect nerve cells. The review covers the receptor's form, its signals, and its role in brain inflammation. It also surveys blocker designs, from small compounds to imaging tracers. The authors judge the target as promising, though its exact role and best use still need more work.
pmc-12094002:
Davie Muhamad, Nurul Manikam, and Ridho Syaiful link pre-surgery protein intake to wound infection after planned abdominal surgery. Their 2023 study follows 93 patients at a Jakarta hospital through thirty days after elective laparotomy. Infections at the surgical site are among the most common setbacks after such operations.

Week-long diet interviews split patients into adequate and inadequate protein groups. Infection risk runs over three times higher in the low protein group. Protein adequacy and blood albumin stand out as the strongest predictors in joint models. Surgery itself burns muscle protein through stress response, the authors note. Building reserves before the operation supports healing and immunity. The finding gives surgical teams a cheap, early lever against infection.
pmc-12094102:
Bad breath comes from sulfur gases made in the mouth, and mouthwash is the usual answer, but tablets would be easier to carry and use. The authors run a randomized, single-blind trial of breath products in 61 volunteers who meet the criteria for halitosis. One test arm measures instant effect: an effervescent tablet against a lozenge and a mouthwash. The other arm measures duration over two hours, setting the same tablet against two commercial probiotic products. Breath gases are measured directly at each point.

The effervescent tablet cuts the sulfur gases at once, matching the mouthwash and beating the lozenge. Two hours later, its effect still holds clearly, while both probiotic products have faded back to baseline. The authors conclude the tablet is a promising, portable alternative to mouthwash for fresh breath. They frame it as effective over a useful span and potentially safer for regular use.
pmc-12345202:
Mushroom-forming fungi make a wealth of terpenoids, compounds valued in food, medicine, and industry, yet these fungi are barely used as production hosts. Riccardo Iacovelli and co-authors review the push to engineer Agaricomycetes, the class that holds the true mushrooms, into terpenoid factories. The work appeared in 2024, per the text head.

Many of these species already serve the food sector, and their natural chemistry is rich and partly unique. The review covers recent genome work and the genetic tools now available for editing them. Better tools and growing methods, the authors argue, could turn mushrooms into sturdy cell factories. The payoff would reach food, biotech, and drug production.
pmc-1239902:
Sporns, Tononi, and Kotter propose mapping the human connectome, the full network of links inside the human brain. They argue that such a connection map would form an essential base for both basic and applied brain research. At the time they wrote, that wiring was still largely unknown.

Their paper lays out a structural picture: which brain parts connect to which, and how that web could be charted. Knowing the wiring should help explain how the brain works as a system, not just as separate regions. The connectome idea went on to shape large mapping projects worldwide.
pmc-12660402:
Li and eleven co-authors screen for a rare eye lymphoma with a routine blood test, in this two thousand twenty-five study. Primary vitreoretinal lymphoma is aggressive and often mistaken for other eye diseases, delaying treatment.

Their case-control study covered two hundred fifty-five patients and two hundred ninety-two controls. A random forest model using six complete blood count features reached strong accuracy, beating the eye-fluid biomarker doctors currently use. In a hospital population of over one hundred thousand people, the model flagged sixty-six as high risk and thirty-eight of them truly had the lymphoma, a sensitivity of ninety-five percent. A community cohort gave similar results. A web app turns the score into quick triage.
pmc-12661502:
Batteries that use a gel instead of a liquid are safer, and a rubber-like crystal material may make them conduct better when aligned the right way. Zakaria Siddiquee and co-authors tested that alignment effect in this 2025 paper. They compared gels whose internal order faced the electrodes with gels whose order ran alongside them.

With more added salt liquid, the face-on samples conducted better than the side-on ones. The best samples of both types reached strong conductivity at room heat and stayed stable across a wide voltage range. Face-on batteries also charged faster. The findings show that simply lining up the gel structure is a tuning knob for battery design, a cheap trick that needs no new chemistry.
pmc-12661602:
Min Kyung Park, Bada Kang, and their co-authors reviewed studies on indoor temperature and mental health in older adults living at home. Their 2025 review starts from a climate concern: swings between heat and cold are growing, and older people regulate body heat poorly and spend long hours indoors. That mix may put their mental health at risk.

The team searched seven databases in April 2024 with no limits on language or date. They gathered studies linking measured indoor temperature levels to mental health outcomes in community dwelling seniors. A standard quality tool from the National Institutes of Health graded each study's methods. The review pulls scattered findings into one account to guide housing fixes and policy for aging in place.
pmc-12661702:
Stephen Adesina and co-authors report a difficult fracture case from southwestern Nigeria in a 2025 article. A 40 year old man, the main earner for his family, was hit by a trailer truck while driving. He suffered fractures of both upper arm bones, a mild brain injury, and minor scrapes in the crash.

Plates fixed at a small private hospital failed, and both fractures failed to heal. Three months later he reached the authors facility with limited use of both arms but sound nerves and blood flow. The report follows the salvage strategy that followed. The authors use the case to show how poor transport infrastructure shapes injury patterns, how scarce resources strain fracture care, and how humanitarian groups can help.
pmc-12662202:
Rainfall over the Caribbean and nearby lands, the Atlantic Warm Pool region, is usually explained by sunshine: stronger summer sun, stronger rain. Hanying Li and co-authors challenge that view in 2025 with a precisely dated stalagmite record from Cuba spanning the last 129,000 years. They tie the region's wet and dry swings instead to the North Atlantic Subtropical High, the great pressure system over the ocean.

When high summer sun coincided with cooler surface waters in the tropical North Atlantic, the High grew stronger and pushed west, cutting rainfall across the Warm Pool. This coupling swelled the rainfall swings between about 130,000 and 60,000 years ago, when the sun's cycle was nearly twice as strong as later. Two sharp sun peaks, at 105,000 and 126,000 years ago, drove extreme dry events much like today's midsummer dry spells.
pmc-12663102:
Shiming Fan and co-authors test green tea's star compound against lung cell inflammation in a 2025 study. A bacterial toxin called lipopolysaccharide can inflame lung lining cells and help trigger acute respiratory distress, a dangerous flooding of the lungs. The tea compound, known as EGCG, is prized for calming inflammation, but its exact route was unclear.

Mouse lung cells were soaked in the compound for a day, then challenged with the toxin. A battery of gene, protein, and imaging tests traced the protection to one signaling chain running through a cell receptor and two relay proteins. Blocking or boosting parts of that chain moved the inflammation as predicted. Pinning the mechanism matters because a popular supplement only becomes a drug candidate once its target is known and dose can be reasoned about.
pmc-12663402:
Yuru Yang, Xiaotian Cheng, Yaonan He, Tingting Chen, Di Chen, and Andong Wang published this study in 2025. It investigates how compounds from a traditional Chinese medicinal herb, Scutellaria barbata, fight colorectal cancer. The herb has a folk reputation against tumors; the team wanted its receipts.

Seven diterpene compounds from the plant were tested, and one, BZL-5, stood out. Network pharmacology, a method that maps compounds onto the web of proteins they touch, predicted targets. The strongest binding was to HIF1A, a master switch for how cells handle low oxygen, placing the HIF-1 pathway at the center of the compound's action. Laboratory experiments checked the predicted mechanisms, which involve oxidative stress, inflammation, and programmed cell death. The authors frame the compound as a multi-target lead for colorectal cancer drug development. They stress the work is early and preclinical, a map for testing rather than a treatment.
pmc-12663602:
Justin Ziemba and co-authors tracked quality of life after a kidney stone surgery done through the skin in a 2025 paper. Adults having the operation for kidney or ureter stones joined the study and filled standard surveys. The surveys covered pain level, how much pain interfered with life, and how well patients could join social roles. They were taken before surgery and at four points in the month after.

Sixty two patients enrolled, though fewer answered at each later point. Pain level and pain interference jumped sharply on the first day after surgery, then eased over the month. The ability to join social roles did not drop in a meaningful way. By day seven, only pain interference was still clearly worse than before surgery. No patient trait predicted who would suffer most. The authors map the recovery curve so patients know what to expect.
pmc-12665202:
Ya-Hsin Li, Sin-Tong Lan, and Kuan-Ju Lai check whether gum disease tracks with pancreas cancer in Taiwan. Both diseases are growing more common, and past studies in other places gave mixed answers. Their 2025 study used a national health database that spans two decades.

More than four hundred thousand people with gum disease and matched peers without it were followed. Overall, gum disease did not link to higher cancer risk. Some groups stood apart, though: men, people past middle age, and those with low spend or frequent visits for gum care all showed higher risk. The authors urge good gum care for high-risk groups. They also call for more work on how body-wide swelling may link the two diseases.
pmc-12666202:
Qiang and a large team report a study from twenty twenty-five on lung vessel signs that may warn of fast decline. The patients have lung scarring tied to muscle swelling diseases. Some cases worsen very fast, and early warning signs are needed. The team used smart software to measure vessel traits on chest scans. They studied five hundred seventy-eight patients at one center first. A second center group then served to test their risk models.

Patients who worsened fast had wider lung vessels and more vessel bulk on scans. In two disease subgroups, vessel measures joined age as firm risk signs. The models held up well when tested at the second center. The authors say vessel checks on scans can help sort patients by risk.
pmc-12669602:
Amira Ben Gouider Trabelsi and four co-authors craft a new light-absorbing material from reduced graphene oxide layers. The superlattice hosts a polymer, poly(2-amino-1-mercaptobenzene), between its sheets. Bandgap can be set by changing the oxygen content of the sheets and the amount of polymer inside. That tunability promises wider use than plain graphene in photonic devices.

The test material showed broadband absorbance up to 690 nm, a fine crystalline size of 16 nm, and a bandgap of 1.86 eV. As a light-capturing device it reached a photocurrent density of 2.2 mA per square centimeter. Photoresponsivity peaked at 22.0 mA per watt across photon energies.
pmc-12679102:
Shen and co-authors track anxiety, depression, and quality of life in men before and after radical prostate surgery, in this 2025 study. Removing the prostate is a main treatment for prostate cancer, yet it can strain body and mind. The team followed 102 patients treated over about a year.

One month after surgery, quality of life scores rose sharply from their pre-surgery level. Anxiety and depression scores fell by roughly half over the same span. Pain ratings dropped steeply as well, and bladder leakage became less common. The results suggest that, for this group, successful surgery eased several burdens at once. The authors argue for watching mental health as part of routine follow-up.
pmc-12686502:
Kiara Lange and co-authors measure in 2025 enzyme activity released by corals and their partners under stress, as a window on reef nutrient cycling. The enzymes free carbon, nitrogen, and phosphorus from large molecules. They compared soft corals and stony corals under varied conditions, testing three enzymes tied to each nutrient in the surrounding seawater.

Mucus microbes alone showed low activity; whole coral systems were far more active. The nitrogen enzyme ran highest, then phosphorus, then carbon, suggesting nutrient limits. Heat and light stress shifted activity, with the phosphorus enzyme rising most. Soft corals showed much lower activity than stony corals overall.
pmc-12690402: Marchuk and co-authors report a 2025 case study on stubborn double vision in myasthenia gravis, a disease where the immune system weakens the link between nerves and muscles. The patient had isolated double vision that resisted many standard body-wide therapies. Injections of betamethasone beside the eye and under its surface membrane gave fast and lasting relief. The authors suggest targeted steroid delivery near the eye may spare patients heavier treatment, as long as eye specialists monitor them closely.
pmc-12690802:
Where older people go each day shapes their health and independence. Sapphire Lin and co-authors tracked 1,118 community-dwelling older adults in Singapore for two weeks. A phone app logged trips with precise locations. Participants noted what they did at each stop. The team tested whether a standard activity list captures real travel motives. They also asked which activities come with a larger life space, the area a person actually moves through.

The list fit the data well. Everyday errands were the most frequent trips. But trips for work and social life drove the largest life spaces. The authors suggest supporting those trips keeps older adults mobile and engaged.
pmc-12694202:
Wireless sensors watch rotating machines for early signs of failure, but their batteries are costly to maintain and bad for the environment. Vibration harvesters can power them instead, yet most designs ignore high frequency vibrations, which are weak but rich in machine health information. Worse, when two vibration sources shake a harvester, their waves can cancel each other. Weiqiang Mo and co-authors build a beam from a gradient metamaterial with a symmetric layout to solve both problems.

The beam traps waves in chosen frequency bands, a trick called rainbow trapping, and carries patches that turn bending into electricity. Simulations tuned the design, and bench tests confirmed it. The finished beam strengthened harvesting across several bands between one thousand and thirty-five hundred hertz, and lifted the harvested energy more than a hundred fold. The authors present it as a step toward sensors that power and sense at once.
pmc-12694802:
Sofia Pacheco-Forés and co-authors build a map that predicts strontium ratios across Mexico's Valley of Oaxaca, in this 2025 paper. Tooth ratios can reveal where ancient people grew up, but only against a solid baseline map. Such data were thin for much of Mesoamerica.

Plant samples from seventeen valley sites joined a continent-wide data bank, rock maps, and land data in a tree-based model. The map separates movers inside the valley from arrivals from farther off. Applied to burials at Monte Alban, it sharpens old migration reads by stating its own doubt. The authors stress local tuning for honest maps.
pmc-12695902:
Farshad Rahimi and Mahdieh Samadi present a control study from two thousand twenty-five on personalizing chemotherapy doses. The right dose differs per patient, and the body adds delays: a drug takes time to spread and to act. A dosing scheme that ignores those delays or the patient's own dynamics can overshoot into toxicity or undershoot the tumor.

Their framework learns online. A critic network estimates the long-term value of each dosing choice and guides real-time adjustments, with the delays explicitly built in. Simulations across varied patient profiles showed strong tumor suppression with toxicity kept in check. The scheme held up as delays and patient dynamics changed.
pmc-12696002:
To find which human genes a virus needs, labs often knock genes out one by one across the genome. Karen Cheng and co-authors build a safer screen for that hunt in a 2025 paper. Their screen uses a viral replicon, a stripped genome that copies itself but cannot spread as a full virus.

They first test the method on a dengue replicon that glows as it copies. The screen found known host needs and new ones that live-virus screens had missed.
