The team then ran the method on a chikungunya replicon and an Ebola one. Each virus called on its own set of host genes. The hits point to targets for host-based countermeasures.
pmc-12699802:
Jiyun Hwang and co-authors ask whether genes shape who gains most from lifestyle programs in mild memory loss in this 2025 study. Multi-part lifestyle plans can slow dementia, trials have shown. But who benefits most is still unclear. The team re-analyzed a Korean multi-domain program for people with mild cognitive impairment. They layered in two gene measures: a risk score for Alzheimer's and one famous risk gene's status. A standard thinking battery was the main outcome over twenty-four weeks.

Both program and control groups improved, the program arm more. The benefit grew as genetic risk rose. That flips a common guess that high risk means less hope. Targeting programs at high-risk patients could yield the most gain. The study is a second look at trial data, not a new trial. It argues genes may guide who gets intensive prevention first.
pmc-12700902:
Eleanor Mitchell and co-authors characterize in 2025 an odd receptor from the honey bee that answers to the wrong messengers. Nicotinic receptors are best known for fast signaling by acetylcholine in nerves and muscle. One bee subunit, tested alone in frog egg cells, broke that pattern sharply.

It responded far more strongly to dopamine and two related bee messengers than to acetylcholine itself, needing only tiny amounts of the first. Those amines also switched it on more fully. Computer motion models and tweaked receptor versions pointed to a missing double proline in one loop as a key cause of the dopamine strength. Family tree analysis across species adds an evolution angle. The study widens ideas about how this receptor family gained new jobs over time.
pmc-12703802:
Olga Sęczkowska and four co-authors report a training program in modern food risk assessment built around artisanal cheese in Poland and Spain. The fellow in training learned quantitative microbial risk assessment by doing each step, from naming hazards to estimating risk. The case germ was Listeria, which grows well in ready to eat cheese and poses a serious public health threat.

Lab work showed that heating milk at sixty degrees for nine minutes cut the germ by more than a million fold, in both cow and goat milk. Storing cheese above twenty-five degrees let the germ grow. Models built from the data fed an exercise estimating illness per serving. The program shows hands on training in action.
pmc-12703902:
Lu-Ran Wang, Dong-Xu Liu, Lei Yu, and Li Gao published this review in 2025 on vitamins and periodontitis, a long-lasting gum disease that harms the tissue and bone holding the teeth. The authors ask how vitamins A, C, D, E, and K act on the disease and which body targets they share. Their method was a literature review joined with computer-based network analysis and molecular docking tests.

The review finds that the vitamins calm inflammation and reduce oxidative stress, the cell damage caused by reactive oxygen. Vitamins D, K, and A also support bone growth cells and slow the cells that break bone down. The network analysis picked out shared targets tied to inflammation and bone pathways. Of the five, vitamins D and C had the strongest support for use alongside standard gum care.
pmc-12706002:
Thilo Schikorra and co-authors test a 3D-printed model of a child's abdomen for use with a new kind of CT scanner, in a 2025 study. Dose studies on real children are hard to justify, so a faithful dummy helps. The team printed the model from scan data of a five-year-old boy. They then scanned the model on a photon-counting CT unit, as they had the child.

Two scan settings were tried, each rebuilt with three software kernels. The team checked the brightness of eight body parts and the grain in the images. Organ and vessel values in the model matched the child's scan well. Fat and bone values drifted somewhat, and noise matched closely. Three experts rated the model's images high, though just under the real scan. The authors say such models can guide dose cuts ahead of time.
pmc-12706202:
Anna Qvarfordt and co-authors survey elite Para athletes about drug testing in a 2025 study. Anti-doping rules govern all top sport, but athletes with impairments can face extra hurdles: privacy strains, confusing procedures, and testing setups that ignore accessibility. Their side of the system was largely unrecorded.

An online questionnaire at major international events drew 109 athletes from twenty-five countries, spanning physical, visual, and intellectual impairment groups. The team summarized what athletes say works, what fails, and what should change. Giving the tested athletes a voice is a first step toward a fairer, more workable system for everyone it governs.
pmc-12706902:
Nur Nihal Türkel and co-authors validate a Turkish short form of a well-known questionnaire on time perspective. How people dwell on the past, present, and future shapes mood and behavior. The eighteen-item short form adds a subscale for gloomy views of the future. The team surveyed three hundred sixty-seven Turkish adults online and tested the structure three ways.

Six factors fit the data, matching the design, and most subscales scored reliably. The gloomy-future scale stood apart cleanly from its nearest neighbors. Mindfulness, measured alongside, carried part of the link between dark views of past or future and symptoms of depression and anxiety. The authors say the Turkish form is sound for research and clinics. They urge weaving time perspective and mindfulness into assessment and therapy together.
pmc-12707302:
Hao Li and co-authors trace a gene-splicing protein's role in heart failure after heart attack, in this 2025 paper. The protein, RBM25, edits how other genes are assembled. The team link it to a signal chain that can push heart cells toward death.

In rats with heart failure induced by tying a heart artery, raising the protein made the damaged area larger. Silencing it shrank the damage. Lab tests showed the protein causes a key gene to skip a segment, which strengthens a partner interaction and switches on the harmful chain. Death markers rose and fell with the protein, marking it as a drug target candidate.
pmc-12707602:
Gabriela Diniz Militão de Albuquerque and co-authors study newborn outcomes in 2025 after mothers in Brazil caught mosquito-borne viruses in pregnancy. Dengue, Zika, and chikungunya can all threaten newborn health, but the effects of infection near delivery, even without symptoms, are poorly mapped. The team studied women admitted with pregnancy problems in the northeast of the country.

Among 806 newborns, about one in six had an infected mother. Those babies were more often born early and more often developed sepsis, a severe body-wide infection. Babies of mothers with Zika showed about twice the sepsis rate of babies with uninfected mothers. The results argue for close watch of such newborns after birth.
pmc-12708302:
Anita Gupta and four co-authors measure hearing nerve signals in young adults in northern India in a study from 2025. The test records brainstem responses to sound and helps spot nerve faults and gauge hearing in people who cannot answer reliably. Responses vary with many factors, and sex may be one of them, yet data on adults just past their teens are scarce.

The team tested 120 healthy adults aged nineteen to twenty-five, seventy of them women. Several wave timings in both ears differed by sex, with women showing shorter times overall. The authors add local baseline data for clinics that read these tests in young adults.
pmc-12709702:
Sarah Rhodes and Ukachukwu Abaraogu comment in 2025 on the hard parts of reviewing behavior change interventions. Such programs aim to shift habits like activity, sitting, and eating across many settings and groups of people. Reviews try to judge both overall effect and which parts drive change in participants over time.

A standard taxonomy helps code the techniques inside each intervention, so staff can log what was done. The authors highlight method challenges that arise when reviews span complex, varied programs of this kind. Inconsistent coding and reporting can weaken conclusions and hide what works. They call for collaboration to build clear, consistent guidance, so reviews can better optimize behavior change programs.
pmc-12709802:
Florian Olde Heuvel and co-authors report a 2025 study of how a head injury stirs the spleen within hours. After brain injury, the whole body shows inflammation, and the spleen helps steer that response. Most past work measured signals in blood, not inside the organ itself. The team mapped early signals in the spleen of mice three hours after a moderate head injury.

A rare white blood cell, the basophil, rushed into the spleen fast. Signals from B cells and dendritic cells drew it in. Once there, the basophils switched those cells on through a messenger called IL-13 and boosted their protein output. The burst faded within three days. Alcohol blocked the basophil influx, which may matter for injured patients who have been drinking.
pmc-12710702:
Nam and co-authors build in 2025 tiny injectable pellets of cartilage grown from reprogrammed stem cells, aimed at worn knees. Cartilage barely heals itself, and cell therapy by open surgery is heavy going. Their pellets are sized as a minimal unit that a single joint injection can deliver.

Production followed clinical grade rules for safety and consistency. In animal models of joint wear, the pellets slowed cartilage breakdown and eased symptoms. Lab checks backed the tissue quality of the pellets. The team pitch the approach as a gentler route to cell based joint repair.
pmc-12711902:
Xiaohui Liu and a large team track how long natural hepatitis E protection lasts, in work from 2025. How well past infection guards against new infection in people was still unclear. A vaccine trial placebo group in China gave a rare long window to test that question cleanly.

More than seven thousand adults were followed for close to nine years in the study. People with antibodies at start had over half lower reinfection risk than those without. That edge held steady across the full follow up span without fading away. Higher starting antibody levels tracked with lower risk in a smooth dose pattern. Natural immunity blocked about seven in ten clear illness cases as well.
pmc-12712102:
Twu and nine co-authors map virus entry receptors in cattle tissues, in work from twenty twenty-five. Influenza A viruses and coronaviruses threaten many animal species, cattle included. Reports of SARS related infections and recent bird flu outbreaks in dairy cattle raise the stakes.

Where the receptors sit in the body decides which tissues a virus can infect. The team mapped influenza and coronavirus receptors across respiratory and intestinal lining tissue in beef cattle. An advanced image analysis tool gave spatial detail. Receptor maps help assess spillover risk and design surveillance for herds.
pmc-12714202:
Ambar Narwal and co-authors study how sim play shapes the way students write change in math forms. The study appeared in 2025. Sim work can build deep grasp in fields from physics to ecology. That grasp is oft cast in sign forms, and tests ask students to cast it with care.

Sixty-one undergrads were split into film sim, text sim, and no-sim groups. Both sim groups tweaked key values and watched a ball's path shift. The film group saw the ball move, while the text group read the shifts as set text. The text group then picked the right broad form for the change case more oft than both peers.
pmc-12715202:
Xi Lu and six co-authors formulate a chemical wash that undoes two kinds of damage in heavy oil wells, in this 2025 paper. Heavy oil deposits asphaltene in the rock and swells clays, choking flow. Lab experiments replayed the deposition process and measured how clay type and amount cut permeability.

From screens they picked a surfactant and an alcohol as the best viscosity-cutting pair, and an acid blend, hydrochloric with fluoroboric, that dissolved clays fastest. The final system mixes the four at a five-two-eight-twelve ratio. In sandpack tests it restored permeability after combined damage. Field use followed at fifty-six wells in the Shengli Oilfield: over ninety percent gained about thirty-five percent more oil output, while injection pressure fell by forty-two percent. The authors present the system as ready for wider heavy-oil deployment.
pmc-12716402:
Yanting Gong and co-authors built, in a 2025 study, an insect-scale robot that does many tricks with a single motor, by leaning on asymmetry. Tiny robots usually need one actuator per motion, which bloats their design. This one bends a hexagonal frame that is lopsided in both shape and mass.

The imbalance breeds nonlinear motion: the same drive signal can crawl the robot forward or backward, flip it upright, or slide it sideways, depending on input settings. A math model links those settings to behavior, guiding tuning. The robot coped with grit surfaces and landed safely after drops through posture shifts. An untethered version worked outdoors. The authors offer asymmetry itself as a design tool, turning a flaw into a gearbox.
pmc-12716502:
Chantal Backman and a large team of co-authors present a 2025 protocol for a scoping review of safety measurement in retirement homes. Residents are growing older and medically complex, while safety rules vary wildly by place. The review will map how harms of any kind are measured and monitored in these settings.

Four databases plus grey sources will be searched, with two step screening and charting. Homes with round the clock skilled nursing are out of scope. No ethics approval is needed for a literature study. Results are promised at conferences and in print, to steer better safety practice and sharper research questions.
pmc-12717202:
Samantha Maurotti and co-authors test whether pasta made from ancient grains can ease irritable bowel syndrome. Forty-two patients spent four weeks on a low-FODMAP diet, eating either ordinary gluten-free pasta or a functional pasta milled from emmer and rye flour. Symptom scores were recorded before and after. In parallel, the team applied an extract of the pasta to gut cells inflamed in the laboratory and watched markers of inflammation and oxidative stress.

The ancient-grain group improved far more: their symptom scores fell by 153 points on average against 83 in the control group, and 83 percent reached a meaningful improvement, against 35 percent. In the cell tests, the extract turned down two signalling pathways tied to inflammation. The authors see the pasta as a promising natural option for patients.
pmc-12717702:
Oliver Nguyen and nine co-authors present a 2025 scoping review on using electronic health records to cut low-value care in primary care. Low-value care means tests and treatments that do more cost than good. Record systems already help spread good practice; the team asked how they help retire bad practice instead. They gathered fifty studies and sorted the record-based tools into four types.

The types were alerts, order sets and preference lists, note templates, and team communication tools. Success rates varied widely, from about one study in six for communication tools to half for templates. Feedback audits and teaching sessions commonly supported the tools. Only some studies measured whether low-value care actually fell. The authors call the evidence promising but thin, and note that few projects used formal frameworks when designing their interventions.
pmc-12719502:
Wenjun Zhang, Tingting Li, and Fangyi Guo review the double-edged immune signal blocking mycoplasma vaccines, in this 2025 paper. Decades of work have failed to yield a vaccine against these wall-less bacteria, largely because vaccination can worsen the disease itself. The signal interleukin-17A guards mucosal surfaces, yet after vaccination it can flood the lungs with inflammatory cells and deepen injury.

Bacterial surface fats seem to trigger the harmful swing. Drawing on animal models and cell studies, the authors sketch vaccine designs that keep the signal's protection while dodging its pathology.
pmc-12720302:
Parisa Khaleghi and co-authors built a clear-box deep learning tool to detect depression from brain waves in 2025. Depression affects over 280 million people, and patients with brain disorders face extra risk from medicines. Standard diagnosis leans on subjective judgment, which varies between clinicians.

Their model trained on EEG records from 232 neurological patients and reached 98 percent accuracy. An explanation method, called SHAP, named the signals that drove each call. Ratios and band powers that clinicians know well ranked high. The tool fits standard EEG setups, which eases clinic uptake. The authors frame it as support for, not a swap for, clinical judgment.
pmc-12721402:
Jenna Randall and Nicole Kelp, two authors writing in 2025, survey tuberculosis knowledge in Colorado. The disease is rising even in low-incidence parts of the United States. What residents know and feel about it shapes how an outbreak would play out.

Two hundred twenty-five adults completed a survey built on a health belief model. Self-rated knowledge ran ahead of actual knowledge. People saw the disease as a global threat but felt little personal worry. Some said they would feel shame if infected. The authors urge clear public information plus stigma care to support care-seeking if cases climb.
pmc-12722402:
Amrollah Shamsi and co-authors counted single author review papers in medicine in 2025 and asked how that lone wolf pattern fits the rules of evidence based practice. Reviews that gather all studies on a question guide real treatment choices, yet guidelines call for teamwork to keep them honest.

Searching a major database for 2000 to 2023 turned up 2,504 such papers, and their number is climbing. They averaged forty-four citations each, and two thirds appeared in well ranked journals. A quarter of the authors had written more than one. Men wrote about sixty-five percent. The authors urge journals to enforce team authorship and clearer ethics rules for these reviews.
pmc-12722702:
Qian Luo and four colleagues published a rat study in two thousand twenty-five on a gut antibiotic that lifts mood. The gut-brain axis is suspected in depression, but the messengers are unclear. Rifaximin stays in the gut, making it a clean tool to test that link.

Chronically stressed rats showed anxious and depressive behaviour, weaker gut hormone cells, and less of a calming peptide, NPY, in colon and a brain control region. The antibiotic restored behaviour, gut cell function, and peptide levels, and rebalanced brain chemicals. Silencing the peptide in the brain erased the drug's benefit and lowered gut peptide too. The authors propose a peptide loop between colon and brain as the route.
pmc-12722802:
Fang and co-authors compared two ways of placing a long-term venous port in cancer patients, in a study published in 2025. The ports sit under the skin and give a durable line for chemotherapy. Placing one means piercing a vein with a needle, then cutting the skin to thread in a wire and the port. The order of those two steps varies by surgeon. The team asked whether cutting first or piercing first changes the complication rate.

Breast cancer patients at one hospital were assigned to one of the two methods. The team compared the length of the cut, healing, and problems such as infection or poor placement. Small steps in a routine procedure are worth testing, because ports are placed in huge numbers. A safer default order would quietly prevent many complications. The retrospective design reviews real practice rather than a staged trial.
pmc-12723902:
Ntelekwane George Khasapane and co-authors published this review in 2025 on drug-proof germs in Africa. The ESKAPE group names six germ types known for shrugging off many drugs. The team searched three data banks for studies from 2014 to 2024 on samples taken from people. They kept thirty-one studies for pooled counts.

Two germs led the counts: Staphylococcus aureus and Klebsiella pneumoniae. Resistance ran high against some common drugs, with near-total resistance in a few pairings. Two-thirds of tracked strains fought at least three drug classes at once. One resistance gene stood out as most common. Most African lands, the team notes, have no such data at all, so the map is patchy. They call for joined work across the continent to track these germs.
pmc-12727602:
Yanru Chen and co-authors pooled factors tied to oral frailty in older adults in a 2025 review. Oral frailty is the slow loss of mouth function with age, from weak chewing to dry mouth. It feeds poor nutrition and a chain of other harms, so early flags matter.

The team searched eight databases, Chinese and global, for observational studies up to April 2025. They pooled the factors that travel with oral frailty across those studies. The joined list gives clinics a check sheet for who to screen first. It also points to which factors care can change, such as tooth loss care and food support.
pmc-12727702:
Larissa Couto-Rosa and co-authors survey what Brazilian pharmacy students know about autism in a 2025 study. Thin knowledge among future pharmacists can shortchange autistic patients, and no Brazilian study had gauged it.

Near four hundred students answered an online set of forty nine knowledge and stigma items. Scores ran high across cause, signs, and care domains, and no student endorsed stigma. Students with an autistic family member scored best on care and signs. The authors say the results can steer how pharmacy courses polish training for a group that pharmacies serve daily.
pmc-12727802:
William Hopkins and co-authors gauge in 2025 how much of chimp brain size spread is born in the genes, and how it ties to mind and tool skill. Gene work can split born spread from life spread in such marks. Held chimps form the test group.

Whole brain and zone size marks show small to mid born shares. Side to side size gaps show weak born marks. Age cuts front zone size once kin ties are held. High mind scores tie to left lean in front zones. Tool apt chimps hold more front zone mass. No gene tie stands for skill.
pmc-12728002:
Yang Yu and co-authors explore brain activity in people with nerve pain after spinal cord injury, in this 2025 study. Such pain is common after injury and hard to judge by reports alone. The team used a light-based brain scan that tracks blood oxygen near the scalp. They hoped the scans would show clear brain marks of the pain state.

Three small groups took part: healthy adults, injured patients with nerve pain, and injured patients without it. Scans ran while subjects did motor tasks and while they rested. Patients with pain showed weaker links between brain areas and odd patterns of local activity. Their pain scores tracked closely with one resting link, and sleep scores tracked with motor-area signals. The authors suggest the scan could support more objective checks of this pain.
pmc-12728302:
Corrina Azarcon, Caroline Craven, and Jill Wells describe a rare case of a lung tumor spreading to two layers of the eye at once, in a 2025 report. Carcinoid tumors grow slowly, usually in the gut or lungs, and can spread despite their mild pace. Spread to the choroid, the eye's blood-rich layer, is not rare, but spread to the retina itself accounts for under one percent of eye metastases.

Their patient, a woman in her seventies, had lived fifteen years with a lung carcinoid and already had choroid tumors treated in both eyes. The report gives the first detailed multi-method imaging of paired retinal and choroidal deposits in such a patient, showing each lesion by photos, ultrasound, and cross-section scans.
pmc-12729102:
Elaine Lehane and nine co-authors reviewed how health students learn to support breastfeeding as a shared team skill, in a 2025 scoping review. Students mostly sat side by side rather than learning from each other, and the shared skills were seldom named as course goals. Tests of learning were rarely reported, and few studies tracked lasting change in practice.
pmc-12729202:
Xiaofeng Yang, Lei Ding, and Xin Ding study whether airway bacteria worsen respiratory syncytial virus disease in neonates. The virus is a leading cause of lower airway infection in infants under two years. A retrospective cohort at one childrens hospital covers cases from July 2017 to June 2024.

Presence of potentially pathogenic bacteria in virus positive babies links to more high fever, feeding difficulty, heart complications, and oxygen need. Oxygen therapy lasts longer and intensive care admission is more common when bacteria are present. Three species dominate detections, and one species shows a strong severity link in the data.
pmc-12729802:
Liu, Peng, Zhou, and Chen reply to critics of their study on Epstein-Barr virus encephalitis in this two thousand twenty-five letter. Commenters had questioned how the team decided which brain inflammation cases the common virus truly caused.

The authors agree that measuring viral load in spinal fluid, comparing it with blood levels, and checking for local antibody production would strengthen the diagnosis, but their retrospective data lacked those tests. They note there is still no gold standard for this diagnosis, and they explain the careful chart review behind the cases they counted. The exchange shows how medicine builds diagnostic criteria in public, one critique and reply at a time.
pmc-12729902:
Tzu Yi Ma and co-authors trace a dog's severe anemia to a spelling error in one gene, in a 2025 paper. Drugs against germs and against immune attack did not help, and scans and tests ruled out leftover infection, immune disease, and cancer.

pmc-12730402:
Yuqing Shi and four co-authors review metabolic disorders in vascular smooth muscle cells and their role in aortic aneurysms and dissections in a 2025 paper. These aortic faults can kill, and care still rests mostly on surgery, with few drugs that hit the root cause.

Smooth muscle cells in the vessel wall are central to how the disease starts and grows. The review covers their normal work, and how they switch type, die, and reshape the matrix around them. It then turns to how their energy use goes wrong, and what that means for new therapy.
pmc-12730602:
Brain-computer systems that read imagined movement can help people who cannot move, but weak signals break them outside the lab. Dong-Geun Lee and Seung-Bo Lee propose a sturdier classifier in a 2025 paper.

Votes from all slices are then blended into one call among four imagined actions: left hand, right hand, foot, or tongue. On two public contest data sets, the method beat simpler rivals. Accuracy at a low sampling rate matched that at a high rate, which matters for cheap portable gear in daily life.
pmc-12731102:

These tumors grow slowly compared with most cancers and can arise in the gut, the pancreas, or the lungs. Some pour out hormones that change how the body feels and eats.

The review gathers proof on how often weak nutrition and muscle loss occur in these patients. It weighs causes that include hormone effects, long term symptoms, body wide inflammation, and side effects of care. It also covers how doctors spot the problem and what steps may help. The aim is to give care teams a full picture in one place.
pmc-12731302:
Rudenko and coauthors study placenta changes in pregnant patients with COVID during pregnancy in detail. How COVID adds to placenta harm in preeclampsia was unclear. Preeclampsia is a grave pressure disorder in pregnancy for mothers. The team compared placentas across four patient groups in total.

Two groups had COVID in 2022, with and without preeclampsia. A 2019 group had preeclampsia without COVID infection at all. A control group had healthy pregnancies in 2019. Each study group held twenty placentas, controls held five. Tissue tests used markers for virus, vessels, and a receptor. Patterns split by infection and pressure status.
pmc-12731402:
Cemil Aktan and co-authors test whether chatbots can judge curved spines as well as surgeons in a 2025 study. Teen scoliosis surgery depends on a standard curve classification and on picking the right levels to fuse, both read from X rays.

Radiographs of 125 patients went to two expert surgeons and to four large multimodal models, asked the same fixed questions. The surgeons agreed with each other strongly, forming the reference. The models' own angle readings lacked a shared frame, so those were set aside. Agreement with the experts and repeatability a week later were scored instead. The paper asks how far such tools can be trusted in planning real operations.
pmc-12731702:
A team of chemists report new synthetic steroid compounds in this 2025 paper. Steroids such as testosterone and progesterone bind the androgen receptor, a switch that controls many body traits. Blockers of that switch treat prostate cancer and other conditions, so new candidates are in demand.

The team first used AI tools to predict which targets their new compounds would hit. They then tested the compounds in the lab for antiandrogenic activity, the power to block the androgen switch. The background notes that sex hormones also shape how the body answers viral infection and sugar change. That range of effects makes careful target checks vital before any use. The study joins computer prediction with bench tests to sort promising blockers from weak ones.
pmc-12731802:
Luiza Nechita and colleagues gave in 2025 a combined assessment of elite youth football players, joining body measures, physical tests, and lab markers in one machine learning analysis. One hundred players aged fourteen to eighteen were tested. Older players were heavier, limb asymmetry of about five percent was common, and lab markers stayed in normal ranges. Statistical tools pulled out hidden structural and metabolic patterns, and clustering found three adaptation types. A simple regression model predicted performance fairly well. The authors back combined monitoring to spot risk early and tailor training.
pmc-12732002:

Under the surface, the pair repaired the gut: friendlier microbes, less leaked bacterial toxin, calmer local inflammation, and stronger wall-sealing proteins. The authors read the benefit as a gut-first story, where a healed barrier cools body-wide inflammation and lets sugar control recover.
pmc-12732402:

The material, built from carbon and nitrogen sheets, reacts to light, kills microbes, and tolerates living tissue well. It has been studied for electronics and clean energy, but barely at all inside the mouth.

The review covers the material's two main structural forms, the leading ways to synthesize it, and the microscopy used to inspect its surface. It then surveys biological evidence: light-driven antimicrobial action and compatibility with cells, the traits a dental material needs. The authors are frank that dental research here is thin, with few systematic studies. That gap is the point: they map where this versatile material could serve dentistry, from antibacterial coatings to regenerative scaffolds, and call for the missing trials.
pmc-12732802:

Being shut out or dismissed in work and social settings drove the link most. Agreeing with some myth statements, oddly, tied to better ratings than staying undecided. pmc-12733002:

The study ran at a Romanian geriatrics institute from early 2024 to spring 2025. Three hundred fifty-nine patients over forty took part. Frailty parts, from grip weakness to weight loss, were measured in standard ways. Heart conditions, kidney function, and body measures were logged beside them. Most participants were aged sixty-five to seventy-nine. Mapping which frailty parts tie to heart traits can target help where it counts most.
pmc-12733102:

The herbal composition, called SLC, joins three herbs long used in Chinese medicine, each with antitumor reports.

The study asked how the formula inhibits this cancer type. It blocked mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation, the main energy pathway of the cancer cells, the title reports. Candidate active compounds within the mixture were identified. Starving tumor cells of energy is a known drug strategy; showing a traditional formula does it gives a basis for compound level development.
pmc-12733202:
Mngomezulu and co-authors map in 2025 a protein found across species, known for roles in making ribosomes and in hormone signals. Its roles are well known in mammals, but its spread and shape history across life were unclear. The team mined three large protein databases for copies of the protein.

They found 646 copies, all in one branch of complex life that spans fungi and animals. None turned up in bacteria, viruses, or plants. Most copies share two core domains and signs of hormone signal roles. Shape held up well despite low match in raw sequence. The map clarifies where this protein came from and how it changed.
pmc-12733302:
Vitor Luiz Silva and nine co-authors test how heat steps change a drink that joins a dark berry pulp with whey. Their study, from two thousand twenty-five, reads health marks, body traits, and taste.

The mix weds the berry's strong shield gains with whey's food worth. Nine heat plans were tried: three heat grades, each for three spans of time. Heat left the drink's body traits near as they were. Parts of its shield store did shift. Taste panels scored how well each form pleased. The aim is a heat plan that keeps the drink's gifts while it stays safe and liked.
pmc-12733402:
Adem Tuncer and co-authors track the body's stress response in 2025 around liver transplant surgery. They studied patients whose livers failed from hepatitis B, a virus that scars the liver over time. These patients got a new liver from a living donor, and the team compared them with the healthy donors.

Blood tests ran from before surgery to three days after. Before surgery, the patients had lower levels of key alarm signals than the donors. After the new liver went in, those signals surged and stayed high for days. Donor levels stayed flat through their smaller operation. The authors read the surge as the immune system waking back up as the new liver restores order.
pmc-12733802:

Good risk scores can shape a plan made for each sick person. The team sets out the tools that exist to guess risk. They then propose a clear follow up model for use at discharge. It covers folks with weak hearts and those with mild loss. The aim is best use of care funds and time.
pmc-12733902:
Jianmei Chen and co-authors hunt sugar genes in a 2025 study of sweet oranges. Sugar level decides an orange's taste and market value, yet the controls on sugar buildup during ripening are partly unknown. The team compared a standard navel orange with a high-sugar mutant of the same line.

Flesh sampled at two ripening stages yielded hundreds of genes whose activity differed between the lines. The changed genes clustered in sugar pathways, sugar transport, and hormone signaling. A network analysis grouped genes into modules, and one module tracked sugar content most tightly. Three candidate regulator genes emerged from that module, including two already tied to sugar handling. The authors offer the genes as targets for breeding sweeter fruit.
pmc-12734202:

pmc-12734302:

The framework can judge the fate of a new mutant gene, a new germ, or a species invading new ground. Xia works through its math history and gives an exact formula for the chance of extinction in a standard case. That formula is often missing from ecology texts, he notes. He also uses basic probability tools to clear up myths about human population patterns in the United States. The paper aims to put one classic tool back in daily use.
pmc-12734402:

Judged on pre-surgery data alone, the models were modest; fed the post-surgery course, they became sharp.

pmc-12734502:

Atom probe maps show longer holds grow bigger clusters and more pearlite-like ferrite share. Oddly, strength and stretch both rose together. The link gives steel makers a tuning knob for cast grades.
pmc-12734902:

pmc-12735202:

pmc-12735502:

pmc-12735702:

pmc-12736002:

pmc-12736102:

pmc-12736302:

pmc-12736802:

pmc-12736902:

pmc-12737202:

pmc-12737302:

pmc-12737602:

pmc-12737702:

pmc-12738702:

pmc-12739102:

pmc-12741102:

pmc-12742002:

pmc-12742102:

Traits of the trials were also weighed against how fully they used the set.
pmc-12742202:

pmc-12742302:

pmc-12742802:

pmc-12743402:

pmc-12743502:

The authors say trials with more people are needed before the method can be broadly advised.
pmc-12744302:

pmc-12744402:

pmc-12744602:

pmc-12744902:

pmc-12745402:

pmc-12747102:

pmc-12748002:

pmc-12748202:

pmc-12749202:

pmc-12749502:

pmc-12749802:

pmc-12749902:

pmc-12750002:

pmc-12750402:

pmc-12751302:

pmc-12751402:

pmc-12752002:

pmc-12752402:

pmc-12752902:

pmc-12753102:

pmc-12753402:

pmc-12753802:
Mohamed Mahmoud Samy and Aykut Fatih Güven size a hybrid solar and wind system for a Turkish campus, in this 2025 paper. Hybrid systems mix panels, turbines, and storage to smooth the gaps in sun and wind. Picking the right sizes is a hard search problem, so the team raced five modern metaheuristic algorithms on it.

The system pairs panels and turbines with both batteries and supercapacitors, tied to the grid. The goal was the lowest yearly cost at high renewable share, tested on real weather and load data. One algorithm, Hunger Games Search, won: a yearly cost near 603,538 dollars, energy at about 24 cents per kilowatt-hour against a grid price of 35, and an 80 percent renewable share. The authors add statistical checks so others can trust and repeat the comparison.
pmc-12754002:
Wei Wang and co-authors pool fifty studies to size growth retardation among Chinese children and teens in a 2025 review. The combined sample tops two and a half million young people drawn from eight databases. Stunting, the review finds, touches roughly one child in eighteen overall.

The burden concentrates in the youngest: toddlers under three show the highest rates, preschoolers next, and teenagers the lowest. Regional and study differences add texture beneath the headline. Early childhood is the window where nutrition programs matter most, the authors conclude. A national baseline now exists for tracking progress.
pmc-12754202:
Valenza and a large team of co-authors study, in a 2025 paper, breast surgery for patients whose cancer has spread but is creeping back only near the breast. These patients had first responded to drug treatment. The question was whether removing the breast tumor at that point lets them stay on the same drugs longer, rather than switching treatment lines early.

The cohort held fifty-nine patients treated at a European cancer institute. Most had hormone-sensitive or HER2-positive disease. Half went about fifteen months after surgery before the cancer moved again. Results were better for HER2-positive patients and for those whose first treatment stretch had lasted at least a year. The authors say selected patients can gain from the surgery.
pmc-12754602:
Matilde Massara and five co-authors follow smoking and compulsions in Parkinson's disease in a 2025 study. Smoking oddly protects against getting Parkinson's, yet may worsen its behavior symptoms. Impulsive compulsive behaviors trouble many patients. Earlier studies mixed treated and untreated patients, muddying the drug effects.

Their cohort held only newly diagnosed, untreated patients. One hundred sixty six patients and seventy nine controls were tracked five years. Former smokers made up part of each group. Among patients, twenty eight percent of former smokers showed a compulsive behavior. Only thirteen percent of never smokers did. Data came from a large public progression initiative. The contrast isolates smoking history before medication enters the picture. The authors urge behavior screening for patients with a smoking past.
pmc-12755002:
Kangnan He, Yunjie Ju, Ping Cheng, and Peng Xu report a trapped bowel hernia in a teen, in a case from 2025. Internal hernia through a birth defect in the bowel sheet is a rare cause of acute belly pain. Such cases are often found only during surgery, after scans raise doubt but not proof.

Surgery found a large bowel segment slipped through a defect behind the stomach outlet. Twisted bowel had died, so open surgery removed the dead part. Joining the ends saved the valve near the colon, and recovery went smoothly.
pmc-12755102:
Jintao Ao and nine co-authors present a 2025 systematic review on which spinal fracture patients fare badly when treated without surgery. Osteoporotic vertebral fractures are common in older adults and often managed conservatively, but some patients end with lasting pain, collapse, or deformity. The review gathered twenty-six studies with over four thousand patients, mostly women around seventy-three, all treated conservatively and followed for at least three months.

Age, a previous spine fracture, and steroid use predicted poor outcomes. On plain X-rays, fractures at the thoracolumbar junction, instability, middle-column injury, and certain shapes spelled trouble. MRI added warning signs: particular signal patterns and fatty wasting of the back muscles. The authors say all three lenses, clinical, X-ray, and MRI, can flag risk at first diagnosis. Early flagging lets doctors choose surgery or closer watching before decline sets in.
pmc-12755802:
Ben Long and co-authors test whether text reminders help heart failure patients fill their prescriptions and stay out of hospital. Their 2025 study looks back at patients who came to an emergency ward with heart failure as the main fault. Some replied to text nudges about their drugs, and some did not. Fill records were matched to each patient to see who in fact picked up their medicine.

Patients who engaged with the texts had higher odds of filling their drugs overall. They also had lower odds of a return hospital stay. The authors say an interactive text tool may lift fill rates across many patient groups and trim readmissions, though the design shows links, not proof of cause.
pmc-12756402:
Yuting Xiao and co-authors model how animal protein parts were gained and lost in a 2025 study. Proteins are built from domains, reusable blocks with their own shape and job. Rebuilding the ancestral stock of blocks shows how animal toolkits grew.

A birth-death-gain model runs over the animal family tree and today's domain census. Rates of birth, copying, and loss vary by both lineage and domain family. Clustering finds families whose rates rise and fall together through time. One strong pattern stands out in the results, the authors note. Evolution of parts, not just whole proteins, gains a firmer timeline here.
pmc-12757302:
Yun Tong and five co-authors review, in a 2025 paper, how treatment for lumbar disc herniation is changing. A disc that bulges out can press a nerve and cause low back pain and sciatica, a heavy burden worldwide. Care now spans drugs, physical therapy, and surgery from minimally invasive to open techniques, but the best path is still debated.

Emerging options get close looks. Platelet-rich plasma injections and bone marrow aspirate concentrate may slow disc degeneration and support repair. A drug method that dissolves the disc core, chemonucleolysis, is weighed too. The review also maps how artificial intelligence now helps in diagnosis, surgical planning, prognosis, and rehabilitation monitoring. Team care across fields is stressed. Open gaps include thin long-term evidence and care paths not yet fitted to each patient.
pmc-12759502:
Aline Muyle gives the treasurer's report for the Society for Molecular Biology and Evolution for the financial year 2024. The report covers the twelve months to the end of that year. In 2024 the society held its first annual meeting in Latin America, in Puerto Vallarta, Mexico, and drew on saved funds to back the step.

The year closed with a net shortfall of about 641,000 United States dollars. Total assets stood near 3.07 million dollars, most of it in an investment account, against small liabilities. The society's income rests on its two journals, whose shares are listed, one up and one down on the year before. The report also logs a late payment fix from the journals' publisher.
pmc-12764102:
Marie Decraecker and co-authors reported this 2025 study of a drug used for advanced pancreatic cancer. The drug, given in a fat-based carrier, is paired with two standard drugs. A past trial showed the mix helped patients live longer after earlier treatment. Trial patients, though, often differ from people seen in daily care, so the team checked results in real clinics.

The team followed 58 patients treated at three centers in France between 2020 and 2022. They tracked how long patients lived and how long the cancer stayed quiet. Treatment lasted a median of 3.6 months, and follow-up ran much longer. The study helps doctors judge what this drug mix can do for patients with poor outlooks outside strict trial rules.
pmc-12764202:
Shingles can leave lasting nerve pain called postherpetic neuralgia, and doctors would like to know in advance who is at risk. Bocheng Peng and Rui Min built a prediction chart for that risk from hospital records, reported in 2025.

The pair studied 650 shingles patients treated at one Wuhan hospital over seven years, and split them into a group used to build the model and a group used to check it. Age, the course of the illness, where the rash sat, pain scores, skin damage, and fever all raised the risk. Their chart combines those factors into a single score meant to flag high-risk patients early enough to act.
pmc-12764302:
Hongbo Peng, Zhenwei Xia, Yangyang Zhao, and Di Xie mine cell death genes for atrial fibrillation marks, in work from 2025. The erratic heart rhythm drives stroke, heart failure, and death worldwide at scale. Its molecular roots stay partly dark, so gene marks could sharpen early diagnosis.

Public gene reads fed network maps, cluster tools, and a twelve method learning pipeline. Four hub genes emerged and fed a chart plus a death path risk score. High scores came with heavy immune cell entry and skewed immune signals. Lab checks in paced heart cells confirmed the gene shifts seen in data. Blood cells from long term patients also showed two genes raised.
pmc-12765002:
Gennaro Auricchio and co-authors show in 2025 how Galton's board, the pegged device that sorts falling balls into a bell curve, can explain social patterns. Wealth shifts through countless small exchanges, and opinions drift through repeated contacts. They argue that many social outcomes grow from such repeated random events, just as the board's pattern does.

Reframing the board inside statistical mechanics, they generalize its mechanism to model varied social phenomena. The math captures a universal profile that emerges from simple repeated interactions. Their approach offers a compact physics-based lens on distributions in wealth, opinion, and similar quantities across society.
pmc-12765602:
Alan Villegas Meza and co-authors review hip microinstability in a 2025 article. The condition is a slight, painful shift of the ball of the hip in its socket, short of full dislocation. That shift breaks the suction seal of the rim cartilage and speeds wear. It overlaps with pinching syndromes and shallow sockets, so doctors often spot it late.

The review pulls together work from 2000 to 2025 on definitions, tests, scans, surgery, and outcomes. A four-part test plan sharpens diagnosis, with two stretch-and-rotate exam moves scoring best on their own and one prone test best for ruling the condition in. Scope surgery that saves the rim cartilage and fully closes the joint capsule lifts patient scores. The authors frame care around the seal, capsule, and a deep ligament.
pmc-12765902:
Preetanmol Singh and Varun Kalia write a letter about a trial of posture tape for neck pain in India. The trial tested tape meant to fix forward head posture in people with plain neck pain. It found less pain, less strain in one neck muscle, and more use of a shoulder muscle right after taping.

Singh and Kalia praise the use of firm measures, then raise three concerns. The trial had forty-two people but no prior plan for how many were needed. There was no fake tape group, so gains may reflect hope or the added exercise. Pain scores can also shift when people know they got the tape. Their letter shows readers how to weigh a neat result with care.
pmc-12768602:
Latorraca and co-authors present a 2025 project report on evidence support for Brazil's private health regulator. The agency, ANS, keeps the catalog of drugs, devices, and procedures that private plans must cover. New health technology arrives fast, so the catalog needs steady review. A São Paulo hospital team has supplied assessment reports since 2019.

Working with the agency and the health ministry, the project entered its third three-year phase in 2024. From 2019 to 2024 it produced ninety-seven technical reports and workshops. Those products feed decisions on what enters or leaves the coverage list. The report describes the model as a template for evidence-based regulation in middle-income health systems.
pmc-12768702:
Rasha Alshaikh and co-authors map how high risk medical devices win payment approval across Europe in a 2025 review. A new European rule on health technology assessment will change how such devices are judged. The team first needed a clear picture of how each land decides now.

They searched agency websites, major databases, and gray sources, and had national officials check what they found. Paths vary widely: some lands decide in one central body, others leave it to regions or hospitals. Use of head to head safety and effect proof is thin in several systems. The authors say this patchwork is the base the new rule must fit.
pmc-12768802:
Ofelia Noceti and Andrea Gimenez report lessons from a national workshop in Uruguay on the role of expert patients in judging new health tools, written in 2025. Patient input can widen the views that shape those judgments. The workshop was the first of its kind in the country.

Twenty-five people from seventeen patient groups took part, as patients or caregivers. They shared surveys and talks on key burdens, such as coping with illness, family strain, cost, and access to care. Group work set out the roles, skills, and training expert patients need. The aim was real input, not token presence.
pmc-12771002:
Ali Mohammed Alzahrani and co-authors revise the plant genus Verbascum in the Arabian Peninsula. Their paper from 2025 covers a genus in the figwort family. Such a revision sorts names, fixes type specimens, and maps where each species grows.

One species is newly described, and one is newly confirmed for the region flora. Seven names are set as new synonyms, and a small split genus is folded back into Verbascum. Varieties are also reshaped for two species.
pmc-12772602:
Michael Brownlow and eleven co-authors published a study in 2025 counting how often footballers head the ball across the English elite pathway. Heading is under scrutiny for its possible link to brain harm, yet solid counts by age and position were missing. The team coded match video from academy games up to the Premier League.

Across 687 matches they logged more than twenty-six thousand deliberate headers. Heading rates rose about thirteen percent with each age step, from the youngest academy boys to senior professionals. Central defenders headed the ball most, and long passes set up most headers. Accidental head clashes during heading were rare, under one percent of events. The counts give regulators a factual base for age-based heading rules.
pmc-12775502:
Shaoliang Zhu and nine colleagues present STD-Net, a neural network for finding and characterizing liver tumors in multiphasic scans. Multiphasic CT and MRI capture how lesions enhance over time, a signature radiologists use for diagnosis. Most networks flatten the phases into channels and lose that temporal story.

STD-Net instead decouples the problem: a shared three-dimensional encoder extracts anatomy, and a transformer module models the sequence of contrast patterns, like arterial brightening followed by washout. On three public datasets it beat leading baselines in segmentation overlap and classification accuracy. Gains were most stable for small or low-contrast lesions. The authors propose spatio-temporal decoupling as a general pattern for dynamic medical imaging.
pmc-12775602:
Chaisiri Chaichankul and five co-authors study a detail of spine surgery for age related curvature of the lower back, in this 2025 paper. In this condition a small side curve near the tailbone often throws the whole trunk off center. Surgeons have long corrected the main curve, but the twist of the key vertebra in the small curve has drawn less attention.

Records of 144 patients who had fusion surgery and at least two years of follow up were reviewed. The amount of twist correction at that vertebra tracked closely with how much the trunk's sideways balance improved. Links also appeared with the main curve angle and the tilt of two lower vertebrae. The tie ran strongest in one standard deformity type. The authors urge precise axial correction as a base for restoring balance.
pmc-12777402:

pmc-12780402:

Clearing the airways and staying in that pose are both hard. The team tested whether a scan-guided form of chest therapy could help more than standard care.

Ninety-two adults took part, and 87 were in the final count. The guided group gained more in blood oxygen by day five. They also stayed face down longer each day and felt more at ease. Fewer of them went on to need a breathing tube. Time in intensive care was much the same in both groups. Assessors did not know group status.
pmc-12780702:

For 20 days he played virtual reality exercise games for an hour a day, using store-bought gear.

pmc-12780802:

Researchers who presented projects to the board during its first year were surveyed about the feedback they received.

Eleven of thirteen researchers answered, and every one said the board influenced at least one aspect of their work. Study design, early planning activities, and implementation were the areas most often changed. Board members, for their part, valued seeing their input travel into real projects. The authors offer the experience as evidence that structured community engagement improves research aimed at rural health, rather than merely decorating it.
pmc-12782602:

Learners practice taking a focused history, building a list of possible causes for chest pain and breathlessness, and applying scoring rules that estimate clot likelihood. They also work through D-dimer testing, imaging choices, and treatments from blood thinners to clot-busting procedures. The authors aim to sharpen judgment where misdiagnosis is common.
pmc-12783102:

Disease was tied on with a thread around a molar for ten days after one local injection. Treated rats lost less jaw bone and kept more of its lattice, with milder inflammation. pmc-12783602:

The paper frames the tool as support for wider epilepsy management, not just detection.
pmc-12784902:

Escitalopram flies turned with far less scatter than controls: their choices were more alike from moment to moment. Tryptophan changed nothing significant. Only one dose of each was tested, and serotonin levels were never measured, so the authors read the result as a dose-specific behavior effect, not proof of a mechanism.
pmc-12785902:

pmc-12786202:

The question is whether the growth phase of the parent cells tunes what the parcels can do.
pmc-12786502:

pmc-12786702:

pmc-12786902:

pmc-12787702:

The review covers how these materials are designed and built. It then looks at how they stretch, bend, and break under hard loads. It also covers models and computer work that try to predict that behavior. The authors note a key gap: the link from small-scale design to large-scale strength is still not well mapped.
pmc-12788702:

The search covered medical databases from 1946 to March 2025, in English only. Ten studies passed the screen: cross-sectional work, case reports, and one experiment. Hints link class II bite faults to nearsightedness and jaw disorders to odd pupil and focus responses. Yet proof strength was rated very low. The authors urge better studies before clinics act on the link.
pmc-12790702:

Urinary scans cleared the bladder and urethra.

With no rear instability, the team chose a closed fix. Under anesthesia, both hips were bent, spread, and rolled out while hands pressed the joint home. Fluoroscopy watched the move land. Six weeks off his feet followed. Later scans held the fix with no new trouble.
pmc-12793802:

Open surgery and standard repairs were poor fits for her anatomy. The team used shock wave treatment inside the vessel to crack the calcium, with no stent left behind. The case shows a fresh option for very complex calcified disease.
pmc-12800102:

pmc-12800202:

The team maps a four-stage path from pit to snap. Galvanized bolts lasted over thirty days in drip zones untouched. Coating looks like a workable shield for wet roofs.
pmc-12801602:

Overall, lower doses showed no clear difference in total or major bleeding, though the studies varied a lot. When studies whose groups started uneven were set aside, lower doses cut both total and major bleeding clearly. There was no sign that lower doses let more clots through. The authors say dose cuts can be considered for light patients, but randomized trials are still needed.
pmc-12801902:

The authors read the result as a hint that a diet richer in branched-chain relative to aromatic amino acids goes with a healthier profile in overweight adults. They caution that one snapshot cannot prove cause, and they call for studies that follow people over time.
pmc-12802702:

A high score, six or more, lined up strongly with the presence of a PFO on bubble ultrasound testing. The link grew stronger for larger holes. Of twenty-eight patients picked for a closure procedure, twenty had it done, all with high scores and large holes. Low scores, in turn, pointed to strokes with a known cause.
pmc-12804002:

A set cutoff split patients into high and low groups, and the high group kept open ports for far less time. Adding the protein to a clinical model sharpened its warnings. The authors say the blood test could flag patients for closer watch.
pmc-12804802:
Xiaotang Xia, Zhihan Chen, and Yulin Xu shared a study in twenty twenty-five. They rebuilt a ruined Qing-Dynasty house in a computer. The house is the Dan Tao former residence. It sits in the Jingchu region of China. It is badly damaged. Its records are far from complete. The team fused many data streams to rebuild it digitally and log what makes its style its own.

The flow made up for sparse point clouds and lost papers. It gave a faithful three-dimensional restoration of the worn parts. It gave a way to spot Jingchu features at more than one scale. The authors offer it as a model others can move to at-risk buildings worldwide.
pmc-12805402:

pmc-12805602:
