The bowling action loads the spine brutally, and stress injuries of the lower back are the role's signature harm, worst in teenagers. Their 2025 systematic review sifts more than twenty-one thousand records down to thirty-seven studies on injury patterns and the body mechanics behind them.

Technique faults stood out. Shoulder counter-rotation past twenty-five degrees, sideways trunk bend, and a fairly straight front knee at landing all raised spinal and leg loads. Weak control of the pelvis and lower back raised stress injury risk by up to eighty-eight percent, while a flexible ankle that absorbs shock protected the back. The authors prescribe early movement screening, workload limits, and targeted core training, with rehab that rebuilds load gradually under long-term monitoring.
pmc-12808302:
Chi Chen and co-authors report a 2025 study of a crab that lives at shallow sea vents rich in sulfide and low in oxygen. The crab bears enzymes that detoxify sulfide, but how it shifts its energy use in that harsh home was less clear. The team compared it with a shore crab that lacks a vent home.

Vent crabs survived low oxygen better than shore crabs. Their blood lactate rose faster under low oxygen, a sign they switch fast to oxygen-free energy paths. Crabs returned to the vents switched the path off just as fast. Tests of oxygen-based paths rounded out the picture.
pmc-12808402:
Maryam Feiz-Arefi and five co-authors model how human error leads to severe maternal morbidity, the near-miss complications that audit obstetric care quality. Using case files from two Iranian universities plus expert interviews, they built a fault tree of basic events that can cascade into a severe outcome. Its probability was then estimated three ways, including fuzzy Bayesian networks with and without common-cause failures.

Three contributors dominated: delayed start of emergency resuscitation, poor management of obstetric hemorrhage, and weak team coordination. The final severe morbidity probability landed around two percent across methods, slightly lower when shared failure causes were modeled. Sensitivity analysis ranked each factor's influence, telling hospital managers which human factors to fix first.
pmc-12809602:
Jeff Clyde Corpuz writes a letter on what a large review of food sustainability policies at British universities can teach the Global South. The review found only about half of institutions had a public policy. Pledges most often covered communication, waste, and certification, and rarely covered research.

Corpuz argues that universities in poorer countries should publish clear targets tied to climate goals and local food needs. He urges them to link campus buying with research and teaching, support local crops and cuisines, and cut highly processed foods. He also warns that social aims like farm livelihoods and labor rights must not be left out.
pmc-12812602:
Lucia Cabrejos Hirashima and co-authors show that simple liver scarring scores, taken at hospital admission, flag COVID-19 patients headed for severe disease, in a study published in 2025. Earlier work hinted at the link, but mostly before the Omicron variant softened the illness.

The team reviewed 4,565 adults admitted between 2020 and 2024. High values on three scores built from routine blood tests each predicted death or organ support. A high FIB-4 score more than doubled the risk, and the pattern held in patients without known liver disease and across variant eras. The authors say these cheap scores can help sort patients early.
pmc-12812702:
Ryuma Shineha presents a paper whose head gives the year as 2025. The catalog lists it under 2026. The topic is cybernetic avatars: not only screen avatars, but robots and communication tech that extend a person's body, senses, and mind. Such avatars let several operators run many robot bodies together for large, complex work. Infrastructure for that shared operation is part of the concept. Because the idea is new, its ethical, legal, and social implications are under-discussed.

The paper maps those implications by borrowing from neighbor fields: robotic avatars, virtual worlds, social robots, telepresence, and human-robot interaction. Policy readers get a foresight survey before the technology hardens into norms. Avatar labor raises sharp questions about identity, liability, and who owns a remote body's actions. Early mapping gives regulators vocabulary while designs are still fluid.
pmc-12812902:
Jiuxu Chen and seven co-authors published a study in 2025 on teaching an AI to judge brain tumor grade from live microscope images during surgery. Some tumors fail to light up on standard scans, hiding malignant pockets that imaging misses. A confocal laser probe gives surgeons cell-level pictures in real time, but reading them is subjective, and single frames throw away the scanning motion experts rely on.

Their model reads whole image sequences, mimicking how a pathologist sweeps and judges. Trained on 105 sequences from sixteen patients, it reached about ninety-three percent accuracy at separating high-grade from low-grade tissue with its best feature extractor. Sequence-aware reading beat frame-by-frame classification across repeated splits. Live, objective grading could steer how much tissue a surgeon removes.
pmc-12813002:
Zijing Wang and co-authors build a score in a study published in 2025 that measures how mixed a colon tumor is inside. Tumors whose cells differ widely tend to evolve faster and dodge the immune system. Gene-level measures of that mix in colon cancer were incomplete, so the team built a score from RNA data across several large cohorts.

Patients with high scores lived markedly shorter lives, and high scores tracked deeper invasion and spread to nearby nodes. A nine-gene signature drawn from score-linked genes forecast survival steadily in training and outside cohorts. High and low groups also differed in immune cell mix and likely response to immune therapy. Lab tests confirmed key genes from the signature.
pmc-12815702:
Paul Bunker and Christina Brewster describe a training device that teaches dogs to find scents underwater, in a paper published in 2025. Search dogs already locate drowned bodies, whale waste, invasive fish, and spilled oil. Training is the hard part: real oil cannot be put into clean water for practice.

Their device releases target odor from the front of a boat without placing any material in the water. Dogs learn to search from the bow and signal when the scent reaches them. In October 2024 field tests, dogs trained this way detected petroleum compounds under water. The device opens safer practice for a range of water search work, from spills to conservation surveys.
pmc-12815802:
Paolo Manganotti and colleagues published a 2026 pilot study of shock wave treatment for drooling in Parkinson's disease. Excess saliva is a frequent, disabling problem in Parkinson's, usually treated with toxin injections into the salivary glands that can temporarily disturb swallowing. The team instead applied gentle focused shock waves to the glands.

Twelve patients with advanced Parkinson's or related conditions received two weekly sessions on both sides, guided by ultrasound. Symptoms and quality of life were checked repeatedly over the following weeks. As a noninvasive option, shock wave treatment could interest clinicians if this small early experience is confirmed in larger trials.
pmc-12816602:
Aigerim Ospanova and co-authors studied magnetic field sensing in 2025 for 3D printed Halbach arrays, magnet layouts that concentrate the field on one side and cancel it on the other. Such arrays serve many science and engineering uses. The team aimed for a cheap way to design, print, and check them.

They measured the field with a low-cost Hall-effect sensor, a device prized for accuracy, easy fitting, and low price. On the theory side, they derived the field from a magnetic potential under a standard approximation, expanded as a series. Printed arrays were then validated against those formulas. Readers get a budget route from design to measured field, which can put strong, one-sided magnets within reach of small labs and makers.
pmc-12817102:
Naif Alhamam and five co-authors present a 2025 study on platelet-rich plasma injections for a painful knee cartilage condition. In patellofemoral chondromalacia, cartilage behind the kneecap wears down, causing pain and weak function. The team reviewed records of 103 patients treated at a Saudi hospital and followed for six months. Pain and knee function scores were compared before and after treatment.

Pain scores fell sharply, from an average above six to near one on a ten-point scale. Function scores also rose clearly. Nearly every patient improved on both measures. Older patients gained the most function. Yet scans showed the cartilage grade itself unchanged in all patients over the six months. The authors read the treatment as strong symptom relief without structural repair. They support more research into this non-surgical option.
pmc-12817402:
Elizabeth Msoka and co-authors ask women in Tanzania in 2025 why breast cancer there is so often found late. Late diagnosis worsens outcomes, and many Tanzanian women reach care with advanced disease. Their qualitative study draws on deep interviews with patients at a cancer center in the Kilimanjaro region, split evenly between rural and urban women.

Most women in the group had stage three or four disease. Reasons sorted into three levels: the patient, the community, and the health system. On the patient level, misunderstanding of the disease led, with nearly every woman citing low knowledge of signs and symptoms. The study gives the late diagnosis problem a patient voice, naming what women themselves say delayed them. Such accounts can guide awareness work and service fixes aimed at earlier finding.
pmc-12817602:
Biao Tian and co-authors build a frailty score for newly diagnosed myeloma patients in this 2025 study. At least thirty percent of patients with this blood cancer are frail at diagnosis, and frailty cuts treatment tolerance and survival. Older scores, though, adapt poorly across mixed patient groups.

The team used records of 606 patients from one hospital, split into building and checking sets. They combined three statistical methods to pick five inputs. The inputs were age, a comorbidity index, daily function, disease stage, and a nutrition index. Their model sorted patients into fit, intermediate, and frail. It beat an older frailty model and the standard staging system at predicting survival and flagging early deaths. Frail patients also suffered more strong side effects at normal doses.
pmc-12817702:
Henning Bliddal and co-authors follow a knee injection over five years in a 2025 extension study. Knee osteoarthritis is common and painful, and standard injections such as steroids or hyaluronic acid tend to help only briefly, leaving patients with few lasting options.

Forty-nine participants received a single injection of polyacrylamide hydrogel into the knee. Thirty-five continued into yearly follow-up, and twenty-seven finished the full five years. Pain, stiffness, and physical function scores improved significantly from baseline and were tracked with standard questionnaires. Safety was watched through adverse events. The study tests whether one injection can give durable relief.
pmc-12819302:
Zhixia Liu and co-authors set out, in a 2026 trial protocol, a plan to test an AI health teaching system for stroke patients. People who survive a mild or moderate stroke often live with lasting limits and must manage their own health for years. Clinic-based care is costly and breaks up over time, and mood and behavior risks get missed. Their system, AI-HEALS, aims to give personal, long-term support.

Patients will be split by chance between standard care and standard care plus the system for three months. It runs through WeChat, China's most used social app. Features include an AI chat that takes voice or text questions, live tracking of body and behavior signs, personal reminders, and lessons made for stroke recovery. The trial will weigh body measures, risk awareness, and self-management habits.
pmc-12819402:
Soumyajit Roy and co-authors build a prediction tool for prostate cancer care in a 2025 paper. The setting is metastatic hormone-sensitive prostate cancer, treated with modern hormone-blocking drugs. A deep early drop in the PSA blood marker signals a good response, but doctors cannot tell in advance who will get one. The team trained a statistical model on patients from three large trials.

The locked model was then tested on patients from a fourth trial treated with a different drug of the same class. It sorted patients well: top-third predictions responded over ninety percent of the time, while bottom-third predictions responded under forty percent. The authors say that, pending prospective checks, such a tool could guide early treatment choices and spare poor candidates false hope.
pmc-12819602:
Guo leads a team building a rapid field test for an emerging tick-borne virus in a 2026 paper. Tacheng tick virus 1 causes feverish illness and had no established detection method. Their assay uses loop-mediated isothermal amplification, a technique needing no fancy lab gear.

Primers target the virus's nucleocapsid gene. The test detected vanishingly small amounts of target within an hour at a steady warm temperature. It ignored five related viruses completely. Positive samples turned visibly from purple to blue. Field tick samples matched the gold-standard lab test on every call. The authors pitch the assay for field and low-resource use. Cheap, fast screening could track the virus's spread.
pmc-12820302:
Xiang Shi, Hasrizal Abd Rahman, and Julia de Rezende improve how labs judge germ-killing chemicals in a 2025 study. DNA tests are the norm for counting microbes after a dose, but DNA lingers in dead cells, so live counts come out too high. A dye called PMA can block the dead cells' DNA.

The team dosed an oilfield microbe mix with two common biocides, then ran the standard DNA workflow with the dye added first. Live counts fell by at least tenfold against the no-dye read, a truer picture of the kill. The tweak suits energy sites that fight corrosion and fouling.
pmc-12820502:
Varun Rana, Blair Smith and Callum Leese surveyed Scottish GP trainees and trainers about learning from podcasts in 2025. Of 1,995 people invited, 219 replied, and about 70 percent already used medical education podcasts.

Nine in ten respondents saw podcasts as an effective way to learn in primary care. Most said podcasts had improved their knowledge, their confidence with patients and the care they give. Flexibility and easy access were the main attractions, while lack of personal time was the biggest barrier. Respondents wanted better quality assurance and better awareness of good shows. The authors ask for larger studies that test whether podcasts change knowledge and behaviour in practice.
pmc-12820902:
Raluca Badila and co-authors test in 2025 a blood mark that may forecast brain recovery after a cardiac arrest. Once the heart restarts, brain injury decides much of the outlook, and early forecasts are hard. The mark, a protein freed by hurt brain cells, was measured at one day and three days after the arrest in a Romanian hospital.

Of one hundred twenty patients in the final group, only twenty left the hospital alive. The protein ran far higher in patients with poor brain outcomes at both time points. Its accuracy in sorting outcomes was good. The authors argue the test, timed well, can support hard care talks with families.
pmc-12821202:
Bladder cancer that reaches the lymph nodes plays by rules written partly by its neighbourhood, and Ziwei Wang and co-authors charted that neighbourhood cell by cell. Combining single-cell and spatial gene profiling of matched samples, they built an atlas of thirty-two specimens spanning sixty-one cell subtypes, hundreds of control genes, and over a thousand verified cell-to-cell contacts.

Across different sites, tumour pressure bent distinct neighbourhoods toward a common shape. One fibroblast subtype stood out, marked by the gene PLXDC1. It crowded malignant tissue, predicted poor survival, and promoted blood-vessel growth while sitting beside a matching class of vessel cells. The authors nominate the pair as a targetable vascular niche feeding the cancer's spread.
pmc-12821302:
Langa, Netshapapame, and Goon explore why men avoid health services in a study from two thousand twenty-five. Their setting is the city of Mbombela in Mpumalanga Province, South Africa. They used in-depth interviews to hear men's own views on the barriers they face.

Twenty men aged eighteen to forty-nine were interviewed, and their answers were grouped into themes. Personal fears, anxiety, and stigma held many back. So did long waits and unfriendly treatment at facilities. Ideas about manhood also played a role, since seeking care can be seen as weakness. The authors suggest community programs, workplace health services, and support aimed at men to improve uptake and fairness in care.
pmc-12821802:
Ricardo Cortez Cardoso Penha and co-authors test whether DNA aging clocks forecast lung cancer in a 2025 paper. The clocks read chemical marks on DNA to estimate how old a body is inside. Smokers age faster on these clocks, and smoking also drives lung cancer. The team asks how much of the clock's warning is just smoking in disguise.

Four long-running cohorts in Australia, Sweden, Italy, and Norway supplied blood taken before any cancer appeared. Cases were matched to controls of the same age, sex, and smoking state. Clock scores were compared for how well they sorted future cases. Sorting the clock's signal from smoke itself matters before clinics can use it for screening.
pmc-12822002:
Rui Liu and a team including Xiang Luo show that helper immune cells aid recovery after spinal cord injury in mice by steering the cord's cleaner cells. Their study was published in twenty twenty-five. Spinal injury leaves lasting loss of feeling and movement, and clearing debris is a key early step toward repair.

Regulatory T cells flooded the injured cords of both patients and mice. The team found these cells push microglia, the cord's resident cleaners, to eat worn synapses. A signal pair, named the OPN-CD74 axis, carries the instruction. That cleanup supports working recovery of the injured cord. The work links an immune cell type to a precise housekeeping task, opening a possible treatment angle.
pmc-12822202:
Anastazja Szula and co-authors measure how time itself feels in borderline personality disorder in a 2025 study. Clinical writing describes these patients' inner time as frozen in the moment, yet hard measurement was missing. Fifty two inpatients faced a structured interview built to map temporal experience, against ninety eight healthy controls.

Patients scored higher across the board, above all on intrusive negative memories, flashbacks, a paralyzed sense of the present, and dread of the future. One clean statistical factor emerged under all the items: broken continuity of time. Disturbances also felt stronger than scores alone suggest. The authors propose temporal fragmentation as a core feature worth building into diagnosis and therapy.
pmc-12823602:
Rui Zhu and eight co-authors chart how cadmium pushes an esophageal cancer cell line toward worse behavior. Long-term cadmium exposure links to progression and drug resistance in this cancer, but the molecular path was murky. Gene-activity sequencing compared cadmium-treated cells with untreated ones. Network analyses across several RNA types and proteins screened for hub genes.

Enriched pathways included transport between nucleus and cell body, an iron-driven form of cell death, and cell aging. A network of competing RNAs joined three long non-coding RNAs with ten messenger RNAs. Mapping to drugs named an inhibitor of JAK3 as the most promising candidate. Candidate genes were checked in tumor cohorts and in 41 patient samples.
pmc-12825202:
Topçu Yenerçağ and Öztürk survey parents whose babies failed a first hearing screening test in Turkey. The national program refers these infants to centers for fuller hearing checks. A failed first test can worry parents, and their experience of the process matters. The study ran in Samsun Province with families screened during 2024.

Parents answered phone interviews about what they knew and how they felt. The team used standard scales for satisfaction and for state and trait anxiety. Satisfaction was scored on a five-point scale. The study aims to show where the screening program informs parents well. It also flags where better support could ease parental anxiety.
pmc-12826602:
Matthew Price and Francesca Pistollato argue in 2025 that Alzheimer's research should look past the amyloid plaque story. Plaques long dominated thinking about the disease, yet treatments aimed at them have disappointed. Infections, pollutants, and gut-brain signals may jointly fan the brain inflammation behind decline.

Cell dishes and lab mice capture that tangle poorly. The review champions lab-grown human brain models: mini-brain organoids and organ-on-chip devices. These systems reproduce plaque buildup, tau tangles, barrier leaks, and immune activation when challenged, and early gut-brain versions show gut signals reaching neural tissue. The authors see such models as the sharper tool for testing causes.
pmc-12827502:
Camila Medeiros da Silva Mazzeti, Cain Craig Truman Clark, and Bruna Paola Murino Rafacho wrote a 2026 editorial on new trends in handling obesity in primary care. Obesity is a complex, long-term condition shaped by social, economic, and cultural forces. Though it is widely called a global epidemic, it stays underdiagnosed and underfunded in health systems.

Care then arrives late, in pieces, and unevenly, which blunts its effect. The editors argue that primary care, with its easy access and long view of each patient, is the right base to break that cycle. It can join clinic care with community work, from prevention to steady follow-up.
pmc-12828002:
Cruz Velasco and Javier García de Abajo propose a new sensing method in a 2025 paper. Quantum sensors can beat classical limits, but they often need light states with many photons, which are hard to make and detect. The authors combine photons with free electrons to get past that barrier.

Their key step is a strong link between an electron beam and light guided in a waveguide. Each electron can emit or absorb many photons. By pairing beam splitters with two such interactions, phase changes in light can be sensed with far greater sensitivity. The authors back the claim with strict theory and say current technology can reach it.
pmc-12828902:
Łukasz Pulik, Beata Barszczak, Marcin Kowalski and Paweł Łęgosz wrote a 2025 review on cutting blood loss in total knee replacement for worn or inflamed joints. The operation works well but often bleeds heavily. The team distilled trials and reviews into a named protocol. Each letter of the name marks one proven step.

A clot-keeping drug gave the largest saving, plus fewer transfusions. Sealing the thigh bone canal and skipping drains also saved large amounts. Cold packs and knee elevation helped more modestly. Tourniquets cut bleeding during surgery but raised later loss. Shorter operations saved a little blood per minute. More study of long-term gains is urged.
pmc-12830602:
Serkan Eti, Fatih Karaman, Serhat Yuksel, Hasan Dincer, and Ipek Yaylali weigh in a 2025 paper what drives aircraft fuel burn with a new fuzzy decision method. Fuel is a top cost and a top climate load for airlines. Past studies split on which factors matter most, leaving planners without a ranking.

Their method, COWEB, scores every factor against the single best one to cut judge load. Three fuzzy logics layered together model expert doubt from several angles at once. Engine efficiency and technology top the ranking with a weight of 0.254. Pilot behavior and flight management follow close at 0.227 in the results. The weights held stable across the fuzzy layers in their checks.
pmc-12830702:
Zhe Bai and Damian Rouson taught a neural network to impersonate the aerosol physics inside a major climate model, so the slow calculations can be swapped for fast ones. Aerosols, tiny airborne particles, evolve through processes at scales too small for global grids, and the standard formulas eat computing time. Their surrogate, a dual-network design fed with location, time, and compressed summaries of the training data, learned from 9.8 million samples out of a global simulation.

The network reproduced the model's aerosol modes with high fidelity, even when pushed beyond its training conditions. The study also ranked which inputs the surrogate leans on, clarifying what drives its predictions. Timing tests on ordinary and graphics processors showed the emulation runs cheaply. The authors present the tool as a step toward climate simulations that keep detailed particle physics without paying its full price, a need that grows as models chase finer resolution.
pmc-12830802:
Mingfei Guo, Yaji Dai, and Xingxing Zhuang test a plant compound against diabetic kidney damage in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. The compound comes from Astragalus, a plant long used in herbal medicine. The team asks whether it protects the kidney by boosting a cleanup process inside kidney filter cells.

They used diabetic rats and mouse kidney cells grown in high sugar. The compound lowered blood sugar and protein loss in urine, and reduced kidney swelling in the rats. In cells, it restored the cleanup flow and raised the number of cleanup sacs. Further tests tied the effect to a chain of three proteins. Blocking the first link removed the benefit.
pmc-12830902:
Xin Chen, Liang He, and Yuhan Liu build a better tool for mining biomedical papers, in a 2025 paper. Many facts in medicine link two things across a whole document, not just one sentence, so software has to work at document level. Their system, called KnowFDI, blends the text around each fact with the document's structure and with outside knowledge about the things named.

The system reads with a pretrained language model, marks links between sentences with bridge points, and fuses views of the data through a two-stage attention step. Tested on two standard benchmarks, it beat prior methods overall and did especially well on links that span sentences. Removing parts of the design hurt the scores, which the authors take as proof that each source of information pulls its weight.
pmc-12831002:
Xinguo Zhang, Yitao Wang, and Tao Deng build a hybrid model that names human activities from wearable sensors in a 2025 paper. Their network stacks two rounds of multi-scale feature extraction and attention around a memory unit that reads sequences both ways. A wavelet method cleans the raw signals first. On their own collected dataset the model scored near ninety-seven percent accuracy, and it did similarly well on three public benchmark sets.

Ablation tests showed each part helps: the memory unit cut errors, the multi-scale blocks raised accuracy, and cleaning mattered. One classic wavelet beat rivals on signal quality and final score. Their self-collected sensor data matched benchmark quality, they report.
pmc-12831302:
Jinsheng Mai and co-authors reported in 2025 one case of a liver abscess treated with three guiding tools at once. Ultrasound alone can blur the edge of an abscess and nearby vessels. A dye that glows under special light and a three-dimensional rebuild can sharpen the view.

A man aged sixty-one came in with four days of fever and was found to have a pus-filled liver abscess from bacteria. After antibiotics, he had keyhole surgery to open and drain the abscess and remove the gallbladder. The combined guides located the abscess with precision. At three months he had no problems, and the authors present the mix as useful for like operations.
pmc-12831402:
Changlu Qin and co-authors build, in a 2025 study, fatty liver disease inside lab-grown human liver organoids, then use them to screen drugs. The disease is the world's most common chronic liver condition and lacks targeted medicines. Animal models take long to induce and differ from humans, while flat cell cultures stay too immature.

The team grew mature, polarized liver organoids from human stem cells. Flooding them with fatty acids recreated the disease's course in a dish. The organoids' proper orientation made the pathology realistic. Drug candidates could then be tested on human tissue that behaves like a liver. A faithful dish model shortens the search for the first real targeted therapy.
pmc-12836802:
Géraldine Deberdt and co-authors measure which parts of a weekend on-call shift actually cause stress for trainee general practitioners. Weekend cover is a known strain on young doctors, but the web of causes is usually guessed at. The team listed candidate stressors from the literature and group discussion, then drew a causal map for each factor before surveying trainees. That discipline keeps the statistics honest about what drives what.

Three stressors stood out with clear causal effects on stress levels. Interruptions that eat into rest time hurt. So did fear of making a work-related error, and a watchful, braced stance toward possible patient complaints. The authors note the pattern: the heavy load is emotional and psychological, not only a matter of hours or case counts. They urge preventive steps aimed at those pressure points for doctors in training.
pmc-12836902:
Hao-Ruei Mei and co-authors traced migraine drivers in mice in a 2025 study. Migraine strikes about fifteen percent of people worldwide, most of them women. The hormone prolactin had been tied to migraine-like pain in models using either dura stimulation or repeated stress, but where it acts was not pinned down.

The team followed the chain past prolactin in both mouse models. Immune cells called macrophages and an enzyme they use to make nitric oxide both proved key to the pain response. Blocking that enzyme path dulled the effect. The chain gives drug hunters fresh targets for a common ill.
pmc-12837002:
Cities are full of microbes that ride between hospitals, sewers, ambulances, and transit, carrying drug resistance with them. Suleiman Aminu and five co-authors mapped that hidden traffic in 2025 by rebuilding genomes from 767 public samples of city environments. Their pipeline yielded more than ten thousand draft genomes, grouped into about fifteen hundred species.

Each setting held a distinct mix, the team found. Hospital sewage was the richest and most mixed source, and blends in simulations flowed from it toward other sites. Hospital rooms stayed the most stable under mixing. Learning models could name a sample's source with high accuracy from its microbes alone. The authors offer the frame as a base for city wide germ watch.
pmc-12837902:
Rubén Martínez-Cuesta and six co-authors study how farm land use shapes the films of microbes on stream beds in 2025. Heavy farming can wash nutrients, soil, and sprays into streams. Those films drive nutrient cycles and help clean water, so shifts in their makeup may weaken them.

The team sampled young and mature films at five sites on two streams in Bavaria, Germany. One stream ran past cropland, grassland, and forest; the other flowed through land with no crops. Gene reads showed richer microbe mixes near heavy farm use. Land use also shaped which species thrived and pushed the mix toward set patterns over chance.
pmc-12838502:
Qiaojun Liu, Jian Shi, Ping Zhang, and Gaiyan Du survey what pregnant women who carry hepatitis B know about the virus in Taiyuan, China. Their study came out in 2025. Passing the virus from mother to child is the main route to chronic infection, so mothers' knowledge matters greatly.

More than two hundred women at five large hospitals answered a structured questionnaire. Nearly half had first learned of their infection during the current pregnancy. Most did not know their detailed antigen status, a marker of how infectious they are. Many wrongly believed the virus spreads through food. Doctors and the internet were the main information sources. Job type and urban or rural residence predicted knowledge scores, while years of education did not, which argues for education tailored to workplaces and places.
pmc-12840902:
Zheng Weng and co-authors map how cotton plants cope with salt in a 2025 study. Salt in soil cuts cotton yield and fiber quality around the world. The team dosed upland cotton with salt and read gene activity and small-molecule levels at set times. That paired read is called multiomics. It shows both the orders and the acts in the plant stress reply.

Near 34,000 genes changed their activity after salt. Hot paths spanned plant hormone signals, amino acid use, and starch and sugar use. The team also logged 6,292 small molecules, from fats to sugars, that shifted as stress wore on. Two paths stood out as joint hubs: a pump path for moving compounds and the starch and sugar path. Key genes in those hubs may guide breeds with stronger salt grit.
pmc-12841402:
Natalia Menshutina and co-authors study how to foam seaweed-based gels into airy scaffolds for tissue growth, in this 2025 paper. The material, alginate, is kind to living cells, and its pore pattern decides how well cells can move in. The team foamed alginate mixes under carbon dioxide pressure, then dried them with the same gas in a special state.

High pressure with a slow release gave an even network of mid-sized pores, while a fast release merged bubbles into giant holes. Cold, pulsed pressure, and a soap-like additive each tuned the pore pattern further. The authors map these links so makers can dial in a scaffold for medical use.
pmc-12843502:
Ali Palice, Omer Cicek, and Ayse Emre compared in 2025 two ways to open blocked heart arteries in patients with a type of heart attack plus kidney disease. One way threads a tube through the vessel, and the other is bypass surgery. Long-term proof in this high-risk group is thin.

The study tracked 150 patients with disease in several vessels. Long-term freedom from death, heart attack, or repeat opening was much alike in both groups. Repeat opening was more common after the tube method, while major bleeding was more common after surgery. Kidney severity did not change the pattern. The authors read the two paths as broadly equal over time, with different trade-offs.
pmc-12844202:
Huizhen Yang and co-authors test a system that sharpens blurred images without a sensor to measure the blur. Such systems bend a flexible mirror to undo the warping that air turbulence puts on light. A classic control method needs more and more rounds as turbulence grows, and it slows down badly.

The team built a lab rig with a light source, a sensor, a bendable mirror, and a camera to test a model-based version. Under strong turbulence, the model-based system kept a near steady speed and reached better final sharpness. The classic method needed far more rounds for the same job. The results support the model route for real-time fixes of large blur.
pmc-12846102:
Qingshan Li and six co-authors measure drug residues in animal manure and manure-based fertilizers, in a 2025 study from Shandong Province, China. Manure is a valuable soil amendment, but animals receive veterinary drugs that pass into their waste. Whether spreading that waste is safe for soil life was unclear. The team built a lab method to extract and measure seventeen common veterinary drugs in these materials.

Tetracycline antibiotics were the most common finds, with far higher levels in raw manure than in processed fertilizer. The method recovered between about seventy-three and one hundred nine percent of known amounts, showing it is trustworthy. Risk scores were then computed for soil organisms. The results help farmers and regulators judge when manure products are safe to spread.
pmc-12847702:
Brañas Casas and co-authors present a 2025 review on model organisms for POLG disorders, diseases of the mitochondrial DNA copying machine. Faults in the POLG gene family starve cells of energy and strike many organs, causing syndromes from liver-brain failure to creeping eye muscle paralysis. Five stand-in species carry the review. Yeast taught the basics of mitochondrial work.

Roundworms added many-celled context, and fruit flies exposed the nerve side. Mice showed whole-body effects in a mammal. Zebrafish, clear-bodied and easy to edit, now front drug screening. Each model's strengths are graded against the others. The authors chart how these creatures, together, carry findings from bench toward the clinic.
pmc-12848002:
Hong Wang and nine co-authors grew a paint-like coating that hides information in both flat patterns and three-dimensional shapes, in this 2025 paper. Counterfeiters copy labels, so security printing wants codes that answer differently to different tests. A coating that couples a two-dimensional response with a three-dimensional one would be harder to fake, but combining the two in one material has been a sticking point.

The team's trick is a self-growing film built from fluorine-rich monomers, a green fluorescent dye, and a light-switchable molecule woven into a pre-set 3D structure. Shining light flips the fluorescence from green toward red and back, while molecular interactions lock in the spatial pattern. The result is a surface whose flat colors and sculpted relief carry encrypted information, checkable at two levels. Coatings could tag medicines, documents, and luxury goods with fingerprints that grow themselves.
pmc-12848102:
Xinyue Mu and colleagues present a two thousand twenty-five study of cell-to-cell variation in engineered bacteria making a yellow pigment. Uneven production between cells wastes much of a batch's potential. Why output flickers across generations was unclear.

Microfluidic filming tracked pigment, its key enzyme, and growth in single cells over divisions. Over half of top producers slipped to middling output within two divisions. Most variation traced to noise in the enzyme itself. A mathematical model tested control designs. Linking enzyme production to nutrient access enriched top producers and multiplied yield several-fold in real tests.
pmc-12849402:
A face flickers with information about the mind, and Sara Ghafarfaraji reviews whether artificial intelligence can read it for diagnosis. From over seventeen hundred papers she kept thirty-six that used AI on faces, still or moving, to detect mental or neurological disorders, chiefly autism, depression, and anxiety. Reported accuracy ran from about eighty to nearly one hundred percent.

Populations, sample sizes, and inputs varied wildly, from photos to brain scans, which tempers the headline numbers. Quality checks were applied study by study. The field's promise is real, the review suggests, but the evidence needs the discipline that clinical tools demand before anyone diagnoses from a webcam.
pmc-12849602:
Qi Yanmeng, Li Yan, and Zhu Huadong studied deaths from a severe lung infection in a 2025 paper. Pneumocystis pneumonia strikes people with weakened immunity; cases in patients without HIV are rising as immune-suppressing drugs spread, and death rates are high. The team reviewed 165 severe cases treated at one Beijing hospital from 2019 to 2024.

Patients who died had lower platelet counts and lower albumin, a blood protein, and more often suffered shock or needed a breathing machine. Statistical modeling marked low albumin as a clear risk factor, along with older age. The study also split patients by drug regimen, comparing a standard antibiotic alone against two combination plans, to see which strategy served patients best.
pmc-12852802:
Katherine Davies, Stephen Welch, Brian Harcourt, Christina Spiropoulou and Jessica Spengler test how well three lab chemicals kill Ebola, Nipah and Lassa viruses in infected tissue. Tissues from animal studies often must leave high containment for tests that can only run at lower levels, so killing the virus first must be proven. Samples were cleaned after treatment so the chemicals would not fool the virus checks.

Formalin was tested from ten minutes to seven days, and two other reagents for one or ten minutes. All three pathogens were inactivated well, with at least a ten-thousand-fold drop in viral load. Reductions were measured across time points. The data back safe handling rules for research and outbreak work.
pmc-12853702:
Gui Qian and co-authors linked in 2025 a simple body measure, waist size adjusted for weight, to a warning syndrome for dementia in older Chinese adults. The syndrome pairs slow walking with memory complaints. Data came from a national aging survey wave in 2015, covering more than seven thousand people over sixty.

Each step up in the index raised the odds of the syndrome by about seventeen percent. The relation ran straight, with risk climbing past a clear threshold value. The pattern held across most subgroups. Because the index needs only a tape and a scale, the authors pitch it for early screening in clinics. They say flagging risk early can steer timely steps that protect aging brains.
pmc-12853802:
Aejin Lee and a large team test a nanofiber-protein complex as a diabetes treatment in mice, in a 2025 paper. Diabetes drugs target blood sugar, but harmful sugar byproducts called AGEs also drive complications. The team combined a binding protein with a small amino acid compound that forms nanofibers.

In fat cells, the complex boosted sugar uptake more than the protein alone. In obese diabetic mice treated for a month, it curbed overeating, weight, and excess insulin while improving tolerance. A key blood marker stayed near normal while other groups rose higher. Gene data suggested the complex opened liver filter cells for waste clearance, which the free compound blocked.
pmc-12854302:
Asadian and colleagues published in twenty twenty-five a qualitative study of why men smoke waterpipes on the coast of Bandar Abbas in southern Iran. Waterpipe use is common in the region, which ranks high nationally. The team interviewed seventy-six male smokers at a coastal waterpipe cafe. Interviews were in-depth and semi-structured, continuing until no new themes appeared. Content analysis extracted twelve categories of reasons. Physical and psychological factors were the most prominent categories named.

Easy access and abundant coastal supply ranked close behind. Family, friends, culture, unemployment, and despair all appeared among reasons. A positive attitude toward waterpipe use also sustained the habit. The authors call for preventive interventions at several levels. Health literacy and cultural reform are the long-term levers proposed. Short-term steps include banning beach sales of waterpipe and tobacco. Modern healthy entertainment options could compete with the cafes.
pmc-12857102:
Lim and co-authors set out the plan for a nurse-led frailty program in Singapore hospitals, in this 2025 protocol paper. Frail older patients face higher risks of poor outcomes while in hospital. Full geriatric assessment is advised for them, yet it usually needs specialist teams. Few hospital-wide models use frailty checks to pick out who should get that full review.

The program, called INFA, puts nurses in charge of screening older inpatients for geriatric syndromes and stepping in early. The paper lays out how the program will be rolled out and judged. It covers both whether the rollout works in daily ward life and whether patients fare better. The study aims to show a model other hospitals can copy.
pmc-12858902:
Natália Souza and twelve co-authors tested a simple prognostic score for brain hemorrhage outside its home setting. The eSAH score predicts how patients fare after a burst aneurysm using only age, coma scale, and the volume of blood seen on a scan. It had looked promising where it was developed, but scores often fail when they travel.

The team applied it to 472 patients from two large hospitals, one in the United States and one in Brazil. The score separated patients moderately well, with accuracy measures near 0.78 for poor functional outcome and 0.80 for death in hospital. Each extra point on the score a bit more than doubled the odds of a poor outcome. The authors also compared it with the standard neurosurgical grading scale. They conclude the score holds up across quite different health systems.
pmc-12859102:
Dawit Andualem Asrate, Fekerte Berhanu Tadle, and Yordanos Derseh Mihretie even out the airflow in industrial multi-tray dryers by optimizing fan placement, in a two thousand twenty-five food engineering paper. Uneven airflow leaves some trays under-dried and others scorched.

The framework couples computational fluid dynamics with sequential linear programming over a twenty-five-run experimental design for a thirty-two-tray dryer. A regression model linked fan positions to a uniformity index with strong fit. Trust-region methods collapsed the optimization from six hundred sixty-one iterations to as few as eight. The optimal layout reached seventy-six point five percent uniformity with minimal prediction error. The authors offer the approach for thermal process optimization broadly.
pmc-12859902:
Gilmar Ribeiro and a large team of co-authors investigate a Chagas disease outbreak in a dry rural area of Bahia, Brazil. Their study appeared in 2025. The inquiry began after a twelve-year-old child died. Suspicion fell on food or drink contaminated with the parasite's insect carriers. The team tested a family of five, plus animals and insects around the home.

Four of the five family members had acute Chagas disease. All had drunk juice from acerola fruit grown at home. Blood tests, parasite DNA checks, and insect gut analysis traced the route. The authors show how a shared homemade drink can carry the parasite when insects fall into the fruit. Their account guides health workers tracing oral outbreaks, now a known pattern in South America.
pmc-12860002:
Yingying Chai and co-authors published a 2025 systematic review and meta-analysis of breath tests for COPD, a lung disease that blocks the airways. Exhaled breath holds trace gases from the body, and their mixture shifts with disease. Two devices can read them: GC-MS, a laboratory instrument that sorts gases by mass, and an electronic nose that sniffs the mixture whole. Which device works better for this disease was not clear.

The team reviewed forty studies, with over two thousand patients and half that number of healthy people. A pooled analysis of eighteen studies found the markers separated patients from healthy people in over four of five calls, both ways. By device, the two were tied on hits. The electronic nose won on correct clear calls, where the laboratory instrument lagged far behind. The team presents the electronic nose as at least the equal of GC-MS.
pmc-12866202:
XiaoQian Che, QiuPing Chen, DongAn He, and LingLong Fan published a study in 2025 on heart risk in older patients. Their patients had an artery in the heart that was fully blocked. The team tested a blood score that mixes a swelling marker with a protein tied to nutrition.

The study followed 134 patients for about a year after they joined. About thirty-one in a hundred had a major heart event in that time. The mixed score forecast events better than either of its two parts alone. Low protein levels also raised risk on their own. Patients with high scores and low protein had the worst outcomes over two years. The authors say the cheap blood score can help flag patients who need closer watch.
pmc-12866302:
Yazan Al-Ajlouni and co-authors survey heroin stigma in Jordan in a 2025 study. Stigma blocks care and recovery, above all where faith and culture frame drug use as a moral fault. How traits like smoking or marriage shape that stigma in Jordan was little known.

An online survey in April 2024 drew nine hundred eight adults from across the country. Five items gauged stigma toward people who use heroin. Views ran strongly negative, with high fears of career harm, social rejection, and legal trouble. Non-smokers, married people, and retired people held firmer negative views than peers. The work maps where stigma sits hardest.
pmc-12866402:
Shoudi Hu and co-authors sort sleep types in midlife women in a 2025 study. The shift into menopause often wrecks sleep, with ripples for family life and health costs. The team asked whether women fall into distinct sleep profiles and what drives each one.

A survey in four Bengbu communities reached 281 women in late 2024. Scores came from a standard sleep index plus anxiety, mood, and coping scales. About a third met the bar for a sleep disorder. A latent profile method then split women into sleep types, and linked tests weighed which traits, from mood to coping style, sort women into each type.
pmc-12870902: Philippe Rola and co-authors wrote a short paper from 2025 on what a vein congestion score can signal about the heart's right side. The score, called VExUS, grades how backed-up the body's veins look on ultrasound. The authors argue it should alert the clinician to a mismatch between the right ventricle and the lung artery it pumps into. Finding the cause of an abnormal score with bedside ultrasound is the first step they urge.
pmc-12872902:
Alessandro El Motassime and others put out a 2026 review of robotic knee swap surgery. Robots help surgeons place man-made knee parts exactly. Most systems plan from medical scans taken beforehand. Newer systems work without those scans. The review asks whether scans are truly needed.

Imageless systems matched scanned systems on how well parts lined up. Patient results and how pleased they were also matched. Skipping scans cuts cost and radiation dose. Surgery room flow became simpler too. Surgeons faced a fair learning curve with the new method. The authors see imageless robots as a real option. Hospitals can choose based on means and training.
pmc-12876002:
Akib Al Mahir and co-authors use gene data and machine learning to study microbes living on plastic in a study whose text head gives the year as 2025. Plastic waste grows its own biofilm world, the plastisphere, and some residents can break plastic down. The team sampled ocean, surface water, and wastewater settings to compare these communities.

Wastewater films were the richest and most even, likely fed by heavy nutrients and constant microbe inflow. Each habitat favored its own set of possible plastic degraders. Network and forest models found steady partnerships between degraders and helper species that may trade nutrients or steady the film. The authors caution that species-level gene data cannot prove who degrades what, and they call for function tests and richer site data.
pmc-12885202:
Farshad Mohammadian Rasanan and co-authors trialed in 2025 flaxseed oil against a steroid cream for common psoriasis. Sixty patients with mild to moderate plaque disease were randomized, double-blind, to one of the two rubs. Each applied a thin layer twice daily for four weeks. Standard scores tracked skin severity and life quality before and after.

After a month, the flaxseed group had clearly lower severity scores than the steroid group. Their quality-of-life scores also improved more. No side effects appeared in the flaxseed group at all. The authors call the oil an effective complementary therapy for this condition. The result is notable because steroids are the usual first-line rub, with known long-term drawbacks. A cheap plant oil matching or beating them in a blinded trial invites larger confirmatory studies.
pmc-12890502:
David Strawn and a large team of co-authors study icotrokinra, a targeted oral peptide for moderate-to-severe psoriasis. Their 2025 paper reports early and sustained pharmacodynamic responses in a phase IIb study.

Icotrokinra is described as the first targeted oral peptide that binds the IL-23 receptor with high affinity to block IL-23 signaling precisely. In the FRONTIER-1 trial and its long-term extension, it gave high rates of complete skin clearance and durable control. This analysis looked at systemic and skin responses to the drug in trial participants. It also asked how those biological responses relate to clinical response, which can guide dosing and patient selection.
pmc-12907302:
Bruno Cessac and nine co-authors presented in 2025 a software platform for modeling the retina and the first stages of vision. Real eye experiments are slow and hard to vary, so a good model lets researchers test ideas on a computer first. Their platform, called Macular, builds a three-dimensional stack of layers, each layer a type of cell in the eye or visual brain.

Users feed in any video as input and can use ready-made cells and links or write their own with plain equations. The platform then writes and builds the needed code on its own and shows the layers at work. The goal is lab-style experiments run fully in software.
pmc-12907402:
A telepresence robot rolling through a hospital must dodge people who walk unpredictably, in corridors too tight for second chances. Heba Mohamed, Muhammad Nasir Khan, Fawad Naseer, Muhammad Tahir, and Mohsin Jamil couple two kinds of foresight for the job in this 2025 study. A small transformer forecasts where nearby people are heading, even through occlusions.

Those forecasts feed a learning controller as risk-aware occupancy signals, and a mathematical shield vetoes any move that breaches safety bounds. The system was tested over twenty-four hundred runs in a crowded corridor and a four-bed ward, against three rival schemes: a social-force planner, an attention-based learning policy, and predictive control. Success, collisions, clearance, and near misses decided the winner. Anticipation plus a hard shield, the authors argue, is the pairing hospital robots need.
pmc-12909502:
Megan Howard, Teni Davoudian, and Nicole Cirino try to define dysphoric milk ejection reflex. The condition brings a brief wave of sadness or agitation at milk letdown during nursing. The feelings pass within minutes, yet reports say up to a quarter of breastfeeding women know them. No official diagnosis exists, which stalls research.

The authors borrow the frame of premenstrual dysphoric disorder, a hormone-linked condition only lately classed in the diagnostic manual. Both troubles arrive on a predictable timer with mixed symptoms. Draft criteria for the milk reflex follow that template. The paper ends with research steps to sharpen the line against other causes of distress.
pmc-12912302:
Anna Katharina Eick and co-authors re-examine a suspected clock pathway in the fruit fly in a 2024 chronobiology paper. In mammals, the CREB protein family relays light signals into the master clock, and fly versions of these proteins were long assumed to do similar work in the insect clock.

The team disabled each fly Creb gene only in clock cells and watched behavior and clock-gene rhythms. Surprisingly, neither loss changed free-running activity rhythms, the period of clock neuron oscillations, or synchronization to light. The results challenge the idea of a conserved clock role for this pathway in flies. The authors call for fresh work on what these proteins do instead.
pmc-12931102:
Ameen Nasser and co-authors review how entering the heart through the wrist artery became cardiology's default route. Transradial access beat the older groin approach on bleeding, comfort, and outcomes, earning guideline endorsement. Technique keeps evolving, including entry farther down the radial artery near the hand.

The review synthesizes fifty peer-reviewed papers spanning trials, meta-analyses, registries, and expert consensus. It covers anatomy, left versus right wrist, radial versus femoral comparisons, and the newer distal variant. Gaps and controversies get their due alongside the wins. For trainees and practicing interventionists alike, it is a state-of-the-practice map of a craft where millimeters decide complications.
pmc-12952902:
Norton and nine co-authors study lack of steady food access among adults sent for lung tests, in a study from twenty twenty-five. Lack of food access hit over one in eight United States households in twenty twenty-three. It is tied to many long-term diseases, but its link to lung health was unclear. The team surveyed adults at a large health network in North Carolina.

Of over ten thousand adults screened, close to one in five reported food hardship. Those adults had weaker lung scores and more breathlessness. Among those with chronic lung disease, symptom burden was much higher with food hardship. The gap held for asthma patients as well. The team urges clinics to screen for food hardship as part of lung care.
pmc-12960602:
Hongyu Liu and co-authors review whether Chinese herbal medicines can protect failing kidneys by tending the cells' power plants, in a paper whose text dates it to 2025. Chronic kidney disease damages kidneys structurally and functionally, with heavy global toll. A recurring theme is mitochondrial quality control: the systems that keep mitochondria clean, balanced, and renewed. When they falter, through oxidative stress, faulty recycling, or bad dynamics, kidney disease advances.

Plant-based Chinese drugs, built from many compounds hitting many targets, look well suited to nudge those systems. The review gathers evidence on herbal ingredients and formulas that improve kidney outcomes by restoring mitochondrial control. It also weighs the gut microbes' role, since their products talk to mitochondria. The authors map a traditional pharmacopoeia onto a modern mechanism, hoping to speed drug development.
pmc-12991702:
Anuradha Khadilkar and co-authors scan the bones of 100 Indian patients with type 2 diabetes and compare them with healthy controls. Diabetes raises fracture risk even when bone density looks normal. Their tool, peripheral quantitative CT, looks past density to bone shape and inner structure.

Trabecular density ran low in men with diabetes. In both sexes, the outer and inner rims of bone sat closer in, a sign of cortical thinning. The bones were built weaker than density alone would suggest. The authors argue this imaging explains part of the extra fracture risk. It could help flag patients who need closer bone care.
pmc-13018402:
Shambhavi Soni, Himanshy Rai, Mohita Pandey, and Abhishek Mehta report, in a 2025 study from central India, how obesity affects pregnancy. Women with a body mass index above thirty face higher risks at every stage, from early pregnancy to after birth. The team studied eighty such women at a large hospital over one year.

They gathered data on health history, activity, diet, blood tests, and scans, then tracked outcomes for mother and baby. Obesity went with more diabetes in pregnancy, high blood pressure disorders, and anemia. Labour was more often long or early, cesarean births were more common, and problems after birth, such as heavy bleeding and wound infection, were notably higher. The authors call for joined-up care to cut these risks.
pmc-13037602:
Sophany Morm, Areerat Lunpha, Ruangyote Pilajun, and Anusorn Cherdthong swap cassava for concentrate in cattle feed in 2025. Cassava tops and fermented pulp are cheap local feeds in Thailand. How much concentrate they can replace without hurting digestion was the question.

Native cows ate full concentrate or mixes swapping in one-third or two-thirds cassava blend. The heavy swap cut intake and digestion of most nutrients. Protein digestion rose on both cassava diets, though. Key rumen acids fell on the heavy swap, and methane estimates dropped too. The authors conclude a one-third swap is safe, with more study needed for milking cows.
pmc-13080502:
Farms in Ethiopia mix trees with crops in home gardens and open parklands, but these systems are shrinking under land pressure and population growth. Admasu Moges, the sole author, surveys the woody plants in both systems across three districts of the North Shewa Zone. The study sampled 80 home gardens and 33 parklands and scored each species for diversity and importance.

The survey found 136 plant species from 58 families. Home gardens held far more kinds, 114 species, than parklands, with 79. One district, Tarmaber, led in both richness and diversity scores. About 61 percent of the species were native, while 38 percent were introduced. Moges warns that the rising share of introduced species could disturb local ecology. The study gives planners baseline data for protecting these farm forests.
pmc-13083602:
Rémi Amiraux and co-authors present a 2026 study on how food webs around one Arctic island run on different fuels in the north and south. Southampton Island sits in Hudson Bay, Nunavut, where ice algae and open-water plankton both feed the web. The team asked how depth and production supply split the island's ecosystems.

They measured chemical isotopes and marker compounds in 149 species, from invertebrates to marine mammals. The northern web sat over deeper water and leaned less on ice algae than on plankton. The southern web showed the opposite balance. Bottom-dwelling diversity also diverged between the coasts. Small-scale contrasts like these are often missed by pan-Arctic studies. Local knowledge matters as the ice season shrinks.
pmc-13084702:
Chrissy Baker and a large team test a blood test for leftover myeloma, in this 2026 paper. In multiple myeloma, minimal residual disease, the trace of cancer left after treatment, guides drug approval and care. The standard check needs repeated bone marrow biopsies, which hurt and can miss cancer hiding in other spots. A blood route could sample the whole body at once.

The team sequenced whole genomes from tumor samples, then hunted those exact changes in cell-free DNA floating in blood. They followed 25 patients with high-risk smoldering disease across 87 blood draws. Detection reached down to about one cancer fragment in ten thousand. Tumor fraction in blood predicted progression, and its changes over time warned of outcomes. The blood test agreed with marrow checks in about three quarters of samples and caught some the marrow missed.
pmc-13086002:
Nguyen Chi Thanh reviews a protective trick for cheap catalysts: seal the active metal inside carbon. Fuel cells and water splitters need catalysts for oxygen and hydrogen reactions, but platinum is dear and base metals corrode. Wrapping metal nanostructures in two-dimensional carbon layers promises the best of both: activity with armor.

The review surveys how these hybrids are made and structured, weighing each synthesis route's merits and faults to link structure with performance. The synergy is the selling point: more active sites, tunable electronics, and durability from the carbon shell. Applications span oxygen reduction and evolution and hydrogen evolution across fuel cells, metal-air batteries, and electrolysis. The author closes with the field's practical gaps and where development should head next.
pmc-13087102:
Mothers die not only from reaching care too late, but from care that stalls after they arrive — the third delay. Habtamu Wudu and Werkneh Minalu measured that stall in Ethiopia in this 2026 study. Government hospitals in the East Gojjam Zone were the setting. Five hundred twenty-five women who gave birth there were sampled systematically.

Interviews and observation checklists gathered the data over the last four months of 2023. The third delay is judged the deadliest of the delay stages in developing countries, the authors note. Yet it draws the least study at public hospitals. Knowing how often wards stall, and why, targets fixes inside the building rather than on the road.
pmc-13087502:
Julian Carlos Segura-Nuez and co-authors reported two missed elbow injuries in children, in a 2026 paper that also reviews past cases. The injury, a Jeffery type two fracture, is rare and can be missed when a child first comes in with a dislocated elbow. Few cases have been written up so far.

Both children, aged ten and eight, first came in with elbow pain after falls. The fractures were found three to four weeks later, and surgery followed at once. Both regained full bending and straightening, though some turning of the forearm stayed limited, with slow gains over time. The authors urge careful checks of X-rays for this injury in every child with an elbow dislocation.
pmc-13107602:
Zhang and co-authors present a 2026 study on new spine fractures after a bone cement procedure. Kyphoplasty fills a crushed vertebra with cement to ease pain from osteoporosis. Some patients soon crack another vertebra, though. The team reviewed 257 patients with single-level fractures treated at a Hainan hospital from 2021 to 2023.

Within a year, fifty-six patients suffered a new fracture. Data were split into training and check sets to build a scoring chart, called a nomogram. Screening plus regression picked the stand-alone risk factors. Chart accuracy was tested three ways, including how well scores match real rates. The tool flags high-risk patients for close watch and stronger prevention.
pmc-13114402:
Jingyi Yang and three co-authors compare two kinds of lab-grown brain tissue to see which better copies early human development. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-six. Tiny organ-like balls of cells, called organoids, let scientists watch the brain form, but single types cannot show how organs interact.

One model grows the brain alone. The other also grows the optic vesicle, the early eye bud, alongside it. Using stains and gene activity maps, the team found clear gaps between the two. The combined model formed eye-like structures and switched on a marker gene tied to the retina. Its gene patterns matched real early development more closely. The authors offer it as a stronger base for studying eye and brain growth together.
pmc-13116402:
Camilla Bo and co-authors report a wrecking wrist bone infection from a rare mold in a 2026 case report. The patient, aged sixty-eight, had received kidney and pancreas transplants, which blunt immune defenses. The mold grows slowly yet can eat deep into bone.

Drug therapy and repeat surgical cleaning gained control, but left a large gap in the wrist and forearm. Surgeons tried to save the hand with a bone and skin flap from the leg. The flap later died after fresh bacterial infection set in, and the forearm was amputated. The team stresses joint drug and surgical care, plus honest talks on salvage odds.
pmc-13120302:
Wipanan Jandang and co-authors scale up production of turmeric extract carriers in a study from two thousand twenty-six. The carriers are tiny lipid particles that hold curcuminoids, the active compounds in turmeric, which break down easily. Making them at factory scale with steady quality is a known challenge.

Using a quality-by-design approach, the team screened process settings with risk tools instead of running hundreds of trials. A two-step mixing process, first high-shear then high-pressure, was tuned for particle size and uniformity. The final one-hour process scaled from one hundred grams to five kilograms. The particles stayed in the target size range with high loading and stability, beating the single-step method.
pmc-13122002:
Abdellatif Bouayad, writing alone, reviews autoantibodies in Still's disease in a 2026 minireview. Still's disease is a rare, severe whole-body inflammatory disorder with spiking fevers, rash, and joint inflammation. Some patients make antibodies that neutralize IL-1RA, a natural brake on inflammation, but why they arise is unclear.

The review weighs host factors, such as certain immune gene types, and changes to the brake protein itself, including excess phosphate tagging. Detection is hard because lab assays vary, so combining methods is advised. For now, Bouayad argues, these antibodies are best read as a sign of immune dysregulation, meaning a misregulated immune system, rather than a proven direct driver.
pmc-13124502:
Xiaoli Fan and co-authors built in 2026 a system that reads emotions from body signals while people experience virtual reality scenes. Judging feelings from self-reports alone is unreliable. Their setup immersed twenty healthy volunteers in scenes designed to stir positive, neutral, or negative feelings. Brain waves, heart signals, and skin response were recorded together.

A deep learning model fused the three signal types, first compressing them and then learning their patterns over time. Careful validation kept training and test data strictly separate. Volunteers' own ratings confirmed the scenes worked. Signal features differed clearly across emotional states. The authors argue that combining several body channels beats any single one for objective emotion recognition.
pmc-13128402:
Liya Ai and Chikako Tanimoto trace how a shared identity forms among Pride parade participants in Japan. Their interview study was published in twenty twenty-six. Parades are protest and festival at once, and belonging is part of their power.

Thirty-six participants, most identifying as LGBT+, gave semi-structured interviews. Analysis followed constructivist grounded theory. Identity grew in four stages: joining the group, acting as a member, finding one's role, and finally universalizing the identity. Rainbow flags and chants cemented the acting stage. Roles split into core and supporting members. In the last stage, participants wanted the boundary itself dissolved, a paradox the theory embraces.
pmc-13128602:
Gan and five co-authors call sepsis ends from two blood marks with a deep net in this twenty twenty-six study. Sepsis kills fast, and ward teams need day-one risk sorts. One-mark tests miss much of that risk in sick folks at the door.

Inside, red cell spread span and blood bulk marks fed the net's build. Death-group folks showed both marks high in the first chart checks. The net hit high truth grades on two big care banks as well. Its curve grade beat each lone mark by a clear gap. The pair of marks could flag high-risk sick folks at triage.
pmc-13129502:
Kangyao Peng and co-authors design, in a study whose journal version is dated 2026, a test that can tell a vaccine strain of a pig pathogen from a wild one. The bacterium causes enzootic pneumonia in pigs, and live weakened vaccines protect well, but afterward nobody could tell vaccinated pigs from infected ones by testing. Their assay uses a quirk of an enzyme that only cuts when a probe matches the vaccine strain's sequence exactly, lighting up only for the two vaccine strains in use.

The test proved specific and sensitive, detecting as few as ten copies per microliter. Used on vaccinated piglets, it traced the vaccine strain's stay in the nose: first found three days after vaccination, peaking between days ten and seventeen. The authors present the assay as the missing monitoring tool for judging how well these vaccines take hold in real herds.
pmc-13133002:
Mirkamal Tolend and seven co-authors automate the first pass of literature screening for reviews. Their 2026 paper builds a Delphi-style panel out of five language models. Screening abstracts is a heavy burden in systematic reviews. The panel votes on each abstract's fit, round by round, until it agrees.

Panel labels train a simple ranking model that orders the rest and sends hard cases back up. The team tested the flow on three published psychiatry reviews. On an autism biomarker set, it caught ninety-seven percent of the papers humans had kept. It also saved over a third of the reading work at high recall. Such consensus tools could lighten review work without losing papers.
pmc-13133402:
Nada Al-Kadhi and three co-authors make and test nano-scale materials to pull zinc ions from water. Zinc pollution threatens ecosystems and health. Their materials blend barium compounds with carbon and were baked at two temperatures, giving two versions. Lab checks confirmed the crystal makeup of each and showed the hotter version grew larger crystals and coarser grains.

pmc-13135502:

pmc-13135602:

pmc-13136202:

pmc-13136502:

pmc-13136602:

pmc-13137202:

pmc-13138902:

pmc-13139602:
Raiane Ferreira Monteiro and colleagues combined quantum calculations with machine learning in 2026 to explain how sulfur poisons tiny metal catalysts. pmc-13141102:

The study gives a rare diet map for the oldest old.
pmc-13144802:

pmc-13144902:
Mergani Abdelwhab, Deirdre McCartan, and Barry Moynihan present a conference case of stroke in a man whose real diagnosis was a muscle disease, in a report published in 2026. pmc-13145002:
Judith Cendrero and co-authors report in 2026, in a conference summary, on a rescue method for strokes caused by clots in smaller brain vessels. pmc-13145202:
Monique Kilkenny and co-authors report a trial of a digital platform to prevent stroke in Australia in this 2026 abstract. pmc-13145402:

pmc-13145602:

Of those, 88 percent agreed with the deferred approach, citing the need for speed and the patient's lack of capacity. Just 3 percent disagreed, and 9 percent were neutral. pmc-13145702:
Cristina de Diego Alonso and Pablo Bellosta López present a study of mild stroke survivors in a 2026 abstract. Stroke is a top cause of long term disability worldwide. pmc-13145802:
Chen Chen and co-authors present a 2026 conference abstract on blood pressure care before hospital for brain bleeding strokes. pmc-13145902:

pmc-13146002:

pmc-13146102:

pmc-13146302:
Pol Camps-Renom and others told of a randomized trial in 2026. The HOPE trial studied blood pressure after stroke thrombectomy. Taking out a clot can restore brain blood flow. pmc-13146602:

pmc-13146702:

pmc-13146902:

pmc-13147002:

pmc-13150902:

pmc-13154902:

pmc-13155502:

pmc-13155602:

pmc-13155802:

pmc-13156302:

pmc-13156402:

pmc-13156802:

pmc-13157302:

pmc-13157502:

pmc-13157802:

pmc-13159602:

pmc-13162902:

pmc-13165202:

pmc-13166002:

pmc-13167302:
