pmc-13170602:
Guillermo Ceniza-Bordallo and co-authors review lasting pain after surgery in the young in a 2026 paper. Pain that stays past healing can shadow a child into adult life. Many pre-surgery traits have been named as risks, but findings clash and no review spanned childhood to young adulthood.

Searches of five databases to late 2025 found thirty studies on ages eight to twenty-two. Forty-four candidate traits appeared, yet only eight were reported alike enough to pool. Pain level before surgery stood out as the steadiest risk sign. Patchy reporting capped how firm the pooled calls could be. The team urge shared measures in future work.
pmc-13172602:
Raphael Ritti-Dias and Breno Farah review handgrip training as a way to lower high blood pressure. Their 2026 paper notes that heart and vessel disease killed 19.8 million people in 2022. High blood pressure is the top risk factor for that toll. About 1.28 billion people live with it. Gripping a device hard, without moving, can cut resting pressure.

Past work shows drops of about seven points on the top number and four on the lower, after eight to twelve weeks. Most studies used the same plan: four sets of two minute grips at thirty percent of max strength. Few tested other plans. A pooled review of thirty one trials is discussed. The authors map what is known about grip length, force, and sets, and where gaps remain.
pmc-13172902:
Yen Chen and Susan Murphy report early work in 2026 on a program to help people with systemic sclerosis who have problems with thinking and memory. Systemic sclerosis is a long-term disease that affects skin and organs.

The team held in-depth talks with fifteen people who live with the disease. Patients named trouble with short-term memory, focus, and speed of thought. They wanted flexible online sessions, more time to talk, and peer support. Tiredness, symptom swings, and lack of time were barriers. The team will use these views to shape a program that fits daily life.
pmc-13173102:
Lukas Caye and co-authors test a new pain drug built from a compound called agmatine. Their 2026 study seeks a safe drug for long term pain care. Rats were given the chance to press a lever to get the drug in a vein. How much they pressed showed if the drug was likely to be misused. The drug showed no such pull.

Mice with a nerve injury had lasting touch sensitivity in a hind paw. The drug eased that response when placed at the spinal cord. The team also recorded currents in nerve cells from spinal cord slices. Those cells carry pain signals. Watching how the drug changed the currents helps explain how it works at cell level. Results so far support more work on the drug.
pmc-13173202:
Silvia Karim and Erica Davis use a rare genetic syndrome to probe why some bodies store too much fat, in a 2026 conference abstract. Bardet-Biedl syndrome, an inherited fault of cell cilia, often brings severe obesity. Blame has centered on a brain pathway that controls appetite and energy use.

The team studies zebrafish that lack a working copy of one syndrome gene. They measure feeding, fat build-up, and a fish form of body mass index. They also track appetite and sugar-control genes in fed and fasted larvae. Early gene data show lower levels of the key appetite receptor and of leptin signals in the mutants, while feeding tests show no clear gap yet. The work links a rare syndrome to wider questions in metabolism.
pmc-13174402:
Sorting cancers into subtypes guides treatment, yet tumors profiled across several molecular layers resist tidy sorting because the data are huge, noisy, and mismatched. Hongyan Cao and twelve co-authors answer in 2026 with CEDR, a consensus subtyping method built on an ensemble of dimension-reduction tools.

Rather than trust one compression method, the framework blends linear and nonlinear ones, then clusters the squeezed data with robust methods and a probabilistic ensemble to settle on stable subtypes. A specially tuned estimator guards against outliers in the combined matrix. In simulations the method beat conventional pipelines repeatedly. The authors aim at subtypes steady enough to steer personal treatment choices.
pmc-13176202:
Qiang Hu and Yuanshui Sun review molecular PET imaging in gastric cancer immunotherapy. Gastric cancer is a major global burden, and immunotherapy now extends from advanced disease into surgical and conversion settings. Standard tissue markers do not capture how targets vary across lesions and over time, which limits patient selection.

Whole body PET can map target expression, stroma, and immune activity in all lesions at once. Tracers aimed at HER2, fibroblast activation, and granzyme B show promise for lesion profiling, early response checks, and prognosis. Imaging of PD-L1 rests mainly on preclinical data so far. Barriers include few prospective gastric specific cohorts and varied tracer designs and scan timing.
pmc-13177002:
Retired wind turbine blades resist recycling, being built to resist everything. Yingyue Teng and co-authors cooked them in a fixed-bed reactor and studied how an iron catalyst steers the breakdown products toward valuable chemicals. The catalyst did not change the order in which gases escaped, but it snipped side chains, freeing hydrogen and small molecules.

At five percent iron loading, hydrogen in the gas nearly doubled while carbon dioxide fell to a third, since the iron also shielded certain bonds. At fifteen percent, the liquid tar's phenol content hit forty percent, phenol being a saleable industrial feedstock. The authors present metal-catalysed pyrolysis as a dial for turning a landfill problem into a chemical harvest, tuned by catalyst dose.
pmc-13178402:
Vera Ferrari and co-authors found, in a 2026 experiment, that a crisp reminder strengthens memory more than a blurred one. Volunteers first viewed natural scenes, some emotional and some neutral. A short test then re-showed some scenes sharp and others blurred, mixed with new ones.

A week later, all old scenes returned sharp for a final test. Pictures tested before were recognized better than untested ones, and sharp-tested pictures gained the most. Feeling-rich scenes were remembered best overall, yet neutral scenes profited most from a crisp retest. Brain waves during the final test showed the classic old-new signal either way. The lesson: how clearly we revisit a memory shapes how well it survives. Retrieval is not neutral playback; its quality writes into the trace.
pmc-13179202:
Jorge Antonio Gonzaga Santos, Leiliane Oliveira dos Santos, and colleagues test whether charred sewage sludge can lock away heavy metals in a 2026 soil science study. The setting is a tropical clay soil contaminated with several metals at once. Biochar made from sewage sludge offers a double service: disposing of a waste and amending a poisoned soil, provided the metals stay immobilized rather than washing out.

Pyrolysis temperature turns out to govern how well the biochar holds the metals, a relationship the authors assess with several variables at once. Choosing the right charring temperature decides whether the remedy works or merely moves the pollution.
pmc-13179602:
Michael Knoke, Marcus Neudert, Thomas Zahnert, and Susen Lailach translate a quality-of-life questionnaire for chronic middle ear disease into German and test it. Their study was published in twenty twenty-six. The twelve-question tool was built in English, and German clinics lacked a checked version.

Seventy-nine patients facing middle ear surgery filled it in before surgery and six months after. Hearing tests ran alongside. Consistency was high at both visits, and repeat scores were steady. The form separated patients by disease state and answered to change after surgery. Some subtle shifts in how patients judge their health over time were also probed. The authors conclude the German version is fit for clinic and research use.
pmc-13180802:
Jian Zhang and eight co-authors test tangerine peel compounds in cigar tobacco curing in a 2026 study. Peel extracts are said to lift leaf flavor during the month long ferment, but the three lead compounds had never been tracked on their own. The team dosed curing leaves with each one and watched flavor gases and microbe crowds shift over thirty days.

A gas scan read one hundred fifty seven scent compounds in the leaves. Each compound steered the microbe crowd its own way and lifted flavor quality. One favored fruity esters, another piled up sweet ketones with a caramel tone. Gene based reads mapped which bacteria and fungi bloomed under each dose. The authors say peel dosing can tune cigar flavor by steering the ferment.
pmc-13181402:
Cong Li and ten co-authors report a gene edit that makes vegetable soybeans sweeter. Vegetable soybean, eaten as edamame, wins buyers with its sweet taste, and most of that sweetness is sucrose. In cereals, blocking starch production pushes carbon toward sugar instead: the maize gene Shrunken2 is the classic case, and its loss gave supersweet corn.

Writing as a letter to the editor, the team describes editing the soybean counterpart gene, GmSH2, with CRISPR/Cas9. The head of the paper sets out the logic: GmSH2 helps run starch building in the seed, so disrupting it should redirect carbon into soluble sugars. Earlier mapping studies had tied several regions to seed sugar, but few genes had been tested directly. The authors present the edit as a genetic strategy for breeding sweeter vegetable soybean varieties with better flavor.
pmc-13181802:
A large team in the United Kingdom and Ireland studies radiation after mastectomy in a 2026 paper. Radiation after breast removal lifts survival when lymph nodes hold cancer, yet its use with instant reconstruction is debated. The cohort study enrolled patients across many centers in 2016.

More than twenty-five hundred patients and twenty-six hundred breast procedures fed the study. About a third of each reconstruction type was advised to get radiation. Advice rose steeply with cancer stage, from a fifth in early node free cases to near nine in ten in advanced ones. Patients with implant only rebuilds were less apt to be advised radiation than those with no rebuild.
pmc-13183202:
The authors extract cancer-fighting sugars from a red seaweed in a 2026 study. Sulfated sugars from red algae draw interest for antioxidant and anticancer traits. The chosen seaweed is a rich source of them. Extraction, structure, and cell effects were all examined.

Ultrasound-assisted extraction was tuned for yield first. The product was mostly carbohydrate with modest sulfate content. One sugar dominated the composition of the chains. Standard assays confirmed strong radical-scavenging ability. Colon cancer cells and normal colon cells faced the extract. Staining and gene checks probed programmed cell death. Cancer cell death ran through reactive oxygen pathways. The title frames that oxygen stress as the killing mechanism. Normal cells provided the safety comparison in culture. The authors position the sugars as candidate anticancer agents. Further development would need animal testing.
pmc-13183602:
Anita Layton replaces hard-to-solve kidney models with trained neural networks in a 2026 paper. Models of kidney tubule transport are powerful but touchy: their equations are strongly nonlinear, need expert solvers, and often fail to converge. That fragility shuts out many researchers.

Layton trained networks on data from published models, varying transport settings and recording cell states like salt levels, voltages, and flows. The trained surrogate then predicted states for unseen settings quickly and accurately. It handled two tubule segments, modeled drug-like blocking of transporters, and could even infer hidden membrane traits from measurable data. Accuracy dipped when training on one sex and testing on the other. The paper frames surrogates as a sturdier front door to kidney modeling.
pmc-13185802:
Muneerah Alomar and co-authors build a solar evaporator that purifies water with sunlight in a 2026 paper. Sun-driven evaporation can desalinate off-grid, but designs trade off efficiency, easy making, and durability. Their device splits the jobs across layers so each can be tuned alone.

A cotton fabric coated with boron-dosed polypyrrole drinks in sunlight and turns it to heat. Foam beneath blocks heat loss, while a plain white cloth wicks water up a separate path. Under one sun of light, the device evaporated about 1.9 kilograms of water per square meter each hour at over ninety-two percent efficiency. The authors stress the build is scalable and low maintenance.
pmc-13185902:
Kunpeng Wu and co-authors study how activity and diet quality jointly relate to advanced heart-kidney-metabolic syndrome in older Americans. Their 2026 population study draws on a long-running national survey and exam program. Several thousand adults over sixty were included, about two fifths with the advanced syndrome.

Enough activity and a good diet score each tied separately to lower odds of the syndrome. Together they tied to roughly half the odds. The activity link bent with dose, while the diet link fell in a straight line. Body mass and a blood fat measure carried part of the associations. The message is that movement and food quality stack, which matters for prevention programs aimed at older adults.
pmc-13187702:
Howcroft and co-authors set out a plan for mapping how researchers define and measure empathy in health care robots and chatbots. Their 2026 paper is a protocol, a detailed plan written before the review itself is done. The team notes that the word empathy is used in loose and conflicting ways, which makes claims about caring machines hard to judge.

The planned review will search seven databases and screen papers with two reviewers and software help. For each study the team will record what the system is, how empathy is defined, what the system does that counts as empathic, and how that quality is scored. Early searches ran in January 2026, with the full work planned that year. The goal is a clear shared picture for future design.
pmc-13188102:
Museum shelves hold beasts that most students and scholars will never see in the flesh, and each year of loss makes those shelves count more. Constanza Delgado and co-authors set out in 2026 the first Chilean plan for turning a zoo collection into 3D digital form. Their base is a university museum in Chile.

The plan walks through each step: how to scan each beast, how to build its model, and where the snags lie. It then sets out how to build the shared store where the models will live. Free access to that store can back both study and class work. It can also feed facts into wild life policy while species loss mounts.
pmc-13189902:
Kristian Jones and co-authors set performance baselines for competitive golfers with disabilities in a 2026 study. Para golf sorts players into sport classes, yet no reference data existed for how far or straight each class actually hits. Such norms would help organizers run fair events.

One hundred forty-two golfers across four disability classes hit shots with three clubs while a radar launch monitor recorded club and ball data. Ability ranged widely both between and within classes. Sitting golfers carried the ball much shorter than others, with more variable distance but straighter flight. The visual class also showed higher distance scatter. Little else separated the groups. The authors offer the data set as a foundation for research and tournament design.
pmc-13190602:
Samuel Dummer and co-authors check, in a 2026 study, whether physical fitness tracks with cognitive function in people living with long COVID. The long tail of the illness often clouds memory and focus, which cuts quality of life. The team studied 34 adults who had been hospitalized for COVID-19 and had since recovered.

Each person took a detailed cognitive examination and a fitness test that gauges how much oxygen the body can use, known as VO2 max. Higher oxygen scores went hand in hand with higher total cognitive scores. The link ran strongest for memory. People who reported more physical activity in daily life also scored better on the cognitive test. The team backs exercise plans as part of rehabilitation for long COVID. They also urge wider efforts to keep former patients active.
pmc-13190802:
Carmen Klammer and co-authors issued in 2026 updated nutrition recommendations for people with diabetes, in a German-language guideline summary. Everyone with diabetes, they state, should get personal nutrition counseling and training from qualified professionals, matched to their diabetes type and treatment. The counseling stays patient-centered, built around real life and food preferences.

Goals for metabolism and weight are set jointly and realistically, to slow the disease and prevent late complications. Practical, food-based advice takes priority, with tools for portion sizes and balanced plates. Patients should learn to predict how meals move their blood sugar and to choose foods that soften the rise. Access to ongoing counseling is part of the standard. The summary distills the newest literature for daily practice.
pmc-13191302:
Jodie Schildkraut and co-authors warn that a key tuberculosis drug is losing its edge as germs learn to resist it, in a review from 2026. The drug anchors all standard plans for drug proof lung disease, next to two mates that cut deaths. World cases of the proof form ran near four hundred thousand in 2023, and most patients will soon get the anchor drug.

Pooled data put gained resistance on the drug at about two in a hundred treated cases. Risk runs higher for those who failed past care, took a kin drug, or hold a strain proof to a second drug. Loss of the anchor would force long, weak plans with worse harms and costs. The authors map the drivers and urge steps to slow the loss.
pmc-13191702:
Mohammad Rahman and five co-authors show that cheap, impure ingredients work as well as pristine ones in aluminum batteries, in a paper dated 2026. The electrolyte's key ingredient, aluminum chloride, sells in grades from ninety-eight percent pure to ultra-pure, at prices spanning two hundred-fold. Battery makers assumed purity matters.

The team built polymer electrolytes with six grades of the salt and measured everything that counts. Conductivity, stability range, and efficiency barely moved across grades. Capacity and energy density showed no clear link to purity either. Aluminum plating and stripping behaved the same throughout. The conclusion is liberating for a technology prized for cheapness: the costly purification step buys nothing, and dropping it cuts electrolyte cost directly.
pmc-13191902:
Antoine Azar and four co-authors report a small vaccine trial in healthy volunteers in a 2026 paper. A drug used for immune diseases lowers antibody levels by blocking their recycling. The open question was whether people on it can still answer a vaccine that does not rely on T cells.

Thirty-seven healthy adults were split into three groups. Two got the drug weekly for four weeks, with a pneumonia vaccine given either right before the drug course or two weeks after it; the third group got placebo. Antibody levels against all twenty-three vaccine strains rose after vaccination in every group, though individual responses varied. The team also tracked functional antibodies, B cell responses, and safety. The early-phase result suggests this antibody-lowering drug does not block this vaccine's effect, a reassuring signal for patients who need both.
pmc-13193902:
Muhammad Nadeem and co-authors survey the full armory bacteria use to defeat antibiotics. Bacteria reshape themselves with striking genetic ease, and resistance now rises steadily in hospitals. Their 2026 review catalogs the mechanisms. They include enzymes that chew the drug up, pumps that throw it out, and altered targets it can no longer grip. Other tricks are walls the drug cannot cross and detours around the pathways it blocks.

The genes for these tricks move fast. They arise by small mutations, assemble onto mobile elements, and jump between bacteria, so one transfer event can hand over resistance to many drugs at once. The review also looks ahead, at the hunt for new compounds aimed at fresh targets in bacterial structure and metabolism. The authors argue that understanding the genetic plumbing of resistance is the map drug hunters need, as the old arsenal thins.
pmc-13194002:
Zhiyu Liu, Chenchen Wei, Chongguo Zhang, and Zhaoxia Wang report a lung cancer case in a 2026 paper. An older patient had non small cell lung cancer with a gene change that first let a targeted drug work. His cancer also showed a high level of a marker that can hint at gains from immune drugs.

After six months, a spread of the cancer in one kidney grew while he felt no new pain. A biopsy proved the spread. Care switched to an immune drug plus standard chemo, and the tumor shrank. The calm state held for more than thirty four months. The authors say picks after drug failure should weigh the cause of failure, marker levels, and the patient's own state.
pmc-13194302:
Mario Cazzola, Clive Page, and Maria Matera review a frustrating drug target in airway disease in a 2026 paper. An innate immune signal drives inflammation in asthma and COPD. Its levels track neutrophil activity, flare frequency, and steroid resistance. Blocking it looked biologically obvious for years.

Trials of blockade and neutralization disappointed in most patients, though. Disease variety diluted the enrolled populations. No biomarker sorting guided who received the drugs. Backup inflammatory pathways compensated for the blocked one. Timing may also have missed the signal's active windows. The review catalogs these failure explanations carefully. New chances come from precision strategies instead. Enrichment by biomarker and upstream switch blocking lead the list. Combination targeting and airway-local delivery also feature. Trials should adapt designs to defined biological subgroups. The authors keep the target alive, with conditions.
pmc-13195502:
Rahul Muthalaly and colleagues characterized in 2026 new heart failure after ischemic stroke or transient ischemic attack, using UK Biobank data. More than four hundred thousand adults without prior heart failure were followed for nearly fourteen years. The team asked how often stroke survivors develop heart failure, what it means for survival, and what heart scans show.

Stroke survivors faced a much higher rate of heart failure admission than others, even after adjustment, and their heart failure risk topped their heart attack risk. Those who developed heart failure had weaker pumping and heavier heart muscle on scans, and a clearly higher death risk. The authors call for trials of preventive heart therapy in high-risk survivors.
pmc-13195702:
Health workers on big vaccination drives in Africa are often paid in cash, late, or not in full. Vincent Micheal Kiberu and co-authors studied the shift to digital pay for those workers in a 2026 paper. They covered eight countries in sub-Saharan Africa, four English-speaking and four French-speaking, including Uganda, Kenya, Nigeria, and Senegal.

The team paired a scoping review with deep interviews in each country during 2022. Digital pay is spreading fast on the back of wider phone coverage and helpful rules. Gains include faster, safer payment that workers can track. Barriers stood out too, among them weak networks, fees, and workers who lack accounts or phones. The authors frame the findings as a landscape map for governments that want campaign pay to arrive on time, a point tied to polio goals set for 2026.
pmc-13195802:
Jie He, Gang Yang, and Jianping Deng report a 2026 case where heart failure in a myeloma patient pointed to protein deposits stiffening the heart. The classic warning signs were missing. The seventy-four-year-old man had thickened heart walls and a sharply raised heart stress marker, but his heart tracings never showed the textbook low voltage.

Heart imaging showed a diffuse pattern typical of infiltration, while a bone scan added nothing useful in the setting of myeloma. The team settled on a working diagnosis of highly likely light-chain heart amyloidosis. Treatment aimed at the myeloma clone, plus careful fluid management, cut the stress marker by more than half. The heart's structure, though, stayed abnormal, underlining why early recognition matters.
pmc-13195902:
Laura Klempp and others surveyed medical PhD students in Germany in 2026. The survey asked who gets authorship credit. It also asked who merits that credit. World Vancouver rules define fair authorship. The study covered North Rhine-Westphalia students. That state has nine medical schools.

Knowing the rules was limited. Practice often fell short of guidance. Gender-related gaps also showed. Adviser gender pairing shaped felt practice. Students said rule spread was uneven. The authors call for stronger school frameworks. Regular teaching on credit ethics is needed. Clearer duty in supervision is also urged.
pmc-13196002:
Richard Mills and colleagues published a 2026 study of walking in idiopathic normal pressure hydrocephalus. In that condition, fluid builds up in the brain and walking becomes slow and unsteady. Standard timed walk tests may miss joint-level detail, so the team used full three-dimensional motion capture.

They compared 23 patients with 18 healthy adults of like age. Patients walked much slower, with shorter steps and wider steps. Joint tracking showed less motion at the pelvis, hip, knee, and ankle at key points in each step. A math model sorted patients from controls with high accuracy. The gait pattern could help doctors spot the condition in a more exact way.
pmc-13196102:
Bladder tumors defend themselves against the cell stress that chemotherapy tries to create, and a new drug pairing turns an enzyme into a stress generator inside the tumor. Yingying Xu and co-authors report that strategy in this 2026 study. The enzyme is hitched to a standard chemo drug so both arrive together.

Once inside, the enzyme produces a toxic byproduct that overwhelms the tumor antioxidant shields, a state the authors call carbonyl stress. That stress reshapes the tumor surroundings in ways that help the chemo drug work. Most past stress strategies relied on a single burst of reactive oxygen that the tumor quickly cleared. A self-feeding stress source could last longer. The work is at the lab stage, aimed at a cancer with stubborn relapse rates.
pmc-13197202:
Valeria Hirschler wrote a 2026 letter to the editor on Mauriac syndrome, a growth delay tied to long-term insulin shortage in diabetes. She responds to a case where an automated insulin delivery system, a pump guided by a sensor, aided a young patient over two and a half years.

Writing from Latin America, she notes that growth delay from poor insulin supply stays common there. Test strips, sensors, and pumps are scarce in public clinics, and many patients miss visits or doses. The reported patient, by contrast, kept all visits and stuck with care. She asks how much gain came from the device versus family effort and close staff support. Most likely, she argues, all parts worked together.
pmc-13197302:
Miguel López and colleagues present a 2026 model of the word fluency task. In that task, a person names as many words as they can in a class, such as clothing. Word lists reveal how the mind stores and finds words, shifting between tight clusters and new groups.

Their model treats each list as a walk across a word network, with added nodes for sudden jumps. New scoring tools check not just fit but how real the word links look. On 677 clothing lists, their BIGRAM-CN model made the most lifelike lists. It avoided overfitting, meaning it did not just memorize training lists. The tools can compare groups and thinking profiles.
pmc-13197402:
Ifani Pinto Nada and Stefano Bonacina design a recipe for translating messy cancer data into one shared format. Hospitals record cancer care in clashing styles, which blocks pooled research. The OMOP common data model is the field's standard answer, but cancer data, with their fine detail and free-text bulk, resist the move. The authors studied existing harmonization efforts and distilled their patterns and pain points.

Their process runs in five steps: initiation, requirement analysis, design planning, technical implementation, and maintenance. Experts reviewed and refined the draft along the way. Each step carries cancer-specific cautions, from source quality and tangled mapping to keeping the conversion alive as systems change. The authors offer the process as a reusable scaffold, so the next registry does not have to invent its own path into the shared model.
pmc-13198202:
Guizhi Liu and co-authors published this review in 2026. It asks whether fish-oil fats help the nutrition of people with pancreatic cancer. These patients often waste away, and standard feeding support frequently fails. The review pooled nine randomized trials of omega-3 supplements. Outcomes covered weight, lean mass, body mass index, and two blood proteins tied to nutrition.

The pooled result showed modest weight gain, but with low certainty and wide disagreement among trials. No clear effect appeared for lean mass, body mass index, or either blood protein. Most trials carried bias risks, and samples were small. The authors advise against routine use for now. They suggest case-by-case judgment, and call for larger, cleaner trials to find which patients, if any, truly benefit.
pmc-13198502:
Camila Suguiura Evangelista and colleagues checked mold toxins in dried tea herbs in a 2026 study. Mycotoxins are poisons made by molds that can taint plant goods. Dry herbs for tea are rarely screened, so the team validated a broad test and surveyed market samples.

Their method tracked fifteen toxins and related products at once. It passed accuracy and repeatability checks at three dose levels. Of ninety-one samples across thirty-three herb types, about a quarter held at least one toxin. Zearalenone appeared most often, then a fumonisin and two other toxins at low rates. Diet risk math for the two main toxins stayed far below daily safety limits. Tea drinkers face no clear concern from these herbs, they conclude.
pmc-13200002:
Qixin Wang and ten colleagues build a platform that predicts, from a single blood sample, how broadly a person's antibodies can neutralize many virus variants at once. For constantly evolving viruses, testing neutralization variant by variant is slow. Their system measures antibody binding across many receptor proteins simultaneously and layers in broader immune profiling.

Validated on the original SARS-CoV-2 spike and highly diverged Omicron sublineages, the platform found immune signatures predicting broad neutralization, differing between vaccine-only and hybrid immunity. Broad responses turned out to be woven through multi-type antibody networks rather than single markers. The authors propose the approach for rapidly gauging protection against newly emerged variants.
pmc-13200202:
Jiajun Wen and co-authors test a long acting numbing drug in a nerve block for knee replacement pain. Their trial from 2026 compares a fat wrapped form of the drug with a standard form and with no block. Pain care after knee surgery uses many drug types, and the value of this block is still debated.

Ninety patients were split evenly into three groups. Pain was scored at rest and in motion at one day, the main check, and at other times up to three days. The long acting group had clearly lower pain scores at one day than both other groups. Knee bend range, thigh strength, first walk time, and strong pain drug use were also tracked.
pmc-13200902:
Caroline Hénin and six colleagues report a lung cancer patient whose lung inflammation resisted standard care. The woman took osimertinib, a targeted drug for a gene-driven form of lung cancer. The drug inflamed her lungs, a known side effect. Steroids, the usual first fix, failed to settle it.

The patient was a sixty-seven-year-old woman with worsening breathlessness and a dry cough. Her cancer carried a gene change that the drug targets. The team turned to tocilizumab, a drug that blocks an immune signal, used here off label. She improved enough to leave the ventilator and the intensive care unit. The case adds a rescue option for a rare but dangerous drug reaction.
pmc-13201802:
Diabetic wounds often stall in inflammation, and a 2026 study led by Pengfei Wen describes a flexible device that senses the wound and treats it in a loop. The research article presents a dual-channel electrocatalytic system built around a palladium catalyst, microneedle arrays, and paired electrodes for nitric oxide sensing and hydrogen delivery.

Nitric oxide levels at the wound guide the system, which then produces hydrogen treatment on demand before sensing again. According to the authors, this single-cycle rhythm clears harmful reactive species, calms inflammation, and supports tissue regeneration. They report faster diabetic wound healing with good biocompatibility, pointing toward adaptive, feedback-controlled wound care.
pmc-13201902:
Most colorectal cancers resist immunotherapy, and a 2026 study by Limian Ling identifies a mitochondrial protein that may help unlock a response. The research article investigates PLSCR3, a protein of the inner mitochondrial membrane, and what happens to tumor immunity when it is missing.

Screening cancer cohort data singled out PLSCR3, and experiments in human and mouse tumor cells showed its loss damaged mitochondria. Leaked mitochondrial DNA then switched on the cGAS-STING immune alarm pathway, raising interferon signals and helping natural killer cells kill tumor cells. Mouse experiments extended the work to anti-PD-1 treatment, suggesting PLSCR3 as a possible target for resistant tumors.
pmc-13202102:
Lanlan Chen and two co-authors argued in 2026 that fatty liver disease labels should give way to trajectories. The umbrella term steatotic liver disease covers three labels set by alcohol dose and metabolic dysfunction. The middle label, MetALD, marks patients with both drivers. The authors say these are not fixed diagnoses but points on a moving spectrum, since drinking and metabolism shift over time.

One recent study found the middle and alcohol-led groups carried higher death and liver event risks than people without fatty liver. The purely metabolic group did not differ in that study, perhaps because simple fat alone is a weak disease signal. The piece lays out diagnosis using drinking measures and blood markers, plus risk tiers for care.
pmc-13202402:
Frailty may drain not just strength but the confidence to make plans about future care. Chi Hsien Huang and thirteen co-authors study 358 older adults receiving home health care in Taiwan in 2026, sorting them by frailty level from mild to very severe. They measure how sure each person feels about making decisions and how far each has engaged in advance care planning.

The group draws on a nationwide cohort's starting data. Advance directives, the written form of those plans, are counted alongside the confidence scores. Relations between frailty and planning in Asia have been little studied, the authors note. Their analysis tests whether the frailest patients are also the least ready to plan ahead.
pmc-13202502:
Karlee Fonteyne and co-authors asked young vapers what kind of phone help might aid them to quit, in this 2025 study. Vaping is common among youth and young adults, and stress, social pressure, and a lack of fit-for-youth tools make quitting hard. The team spoke with 12 young people who wanted to quit.

Four themes came from the talks. Social setting shapes each quit try, and success is not neat or final. Phone support could bridge private drive and social needs. Augmented reality, which layers digital cues on the real world, was seen as a way to make help feel personal. Ideas included cues tied to place, goals, and hard moments. The study aims to guide app design, not to test a finished tool.
pmc-13202702:
Vesna Homar and co-authors set out how bedside ultrasound should be taught to family doctors, in a 2026 position paper. The statement comes from the European academy for teachers in general practice. Point-of-care ultrasound is spreading in primary care, and training must keep pace across a doctor's whole career.

The academy advises weaving the skill through undergraduate study, specialty training, and later professional development, with teaching fitted to local systems. pmc-13203902:

pmc-13205002:

pmc-13208102:

pmc-13208902:

pmc-13209902:

pmc-13210102:

pmc-13211402:

pmc-13211502:

pmc-13211602:

pmc-13212402:

pmc-13213502:

pmc-13214702:

pmc-13215202:

pmc-13216102:

pmc-13218102:

pmc-13227102:

pmc-13227502:

pmc-13227602:

pmc-13227902:

pmc-13230302:
