Methylene blue colors factory waste water and resists natural breakdown, so cheap detection matters. The team grew neat nanotube arrays on titanium sheets, then ran current through them in a phosphate bath.

That step doped the tubes with a more conductive form of titanium and dressed the surface with phosphate. In acid, the dressed surface drew in the charged dye and piled it up for reading. Voltage scans showed how the pace of the reaction shifts with scan speed. The paired doping and coating sharpened the signal and kept readings steady, a model for tuned sensors.
pmc-13295002:
Yanhong Kang and colleagues map trial evidence on drug-free complementary therapies for knee osteoarthritis in a 2026 scoping review. The worn knee joint causes pain and disability for many adults, and hands-on or movement based options are widely used. Trials vary greatly in approach, comparison, and outcomes measured.

Searches of four databases for trials from 2016 to early 2026 gathered 53 randomised studies. Approaches ranged from acupuncture and manual therapy to exercise, mind-body programmes, and physical agents. Pain and physical function were measured most often, while quality of life and adherence appeared less consistently. The map shows a broad but uneven evidence base needing steadier designs.
pmc-13295102:
Ethan P Dudley, Brennen O Hunt, and Robert Valeris-Chacin test nose swabs for cattle immunity in a 2026 study. Mycoplasma bovis helps drive bovine respiratory disease, a costly feedlot problem. No checked test existed for measuring local antibodies at the nose surface where defences first meet the germ.

Stored swab washes came from 100 feedlot steers, half positive for the germ's DNA and half negative. A multi-target enzyme test was judged against DNA status and against a statistical model that estimates hidden antibody status. Two targets together reached high accuracy under the model, with strong agreement between operators. The approach offers a gentle way to track mucosal immunity in herds.
pmc-13295902:
Zeinab El Mawla and colleagues study, in 2026, a brain scan measure for predicting recovery after cardiac arrest. The grey-to-white matter ratio on early head scans reflects brain swelling, but hand measurement varies between readers and centres.

Records for 120 comatose patients with restored circulation were reviewed, using scans taken within a day. Higher ratios in every brain area tracked with better recovery at six months. An automated whole-brain measure performed best and predicted poor outcome on its own. The authors argue automation could make this early judgement more consistent across hospitals.
pmc-13296002:
Katerina Chavatza and colleagues ask, in 2026, whether keeping steroids during maintenance care prevents serious flare-ups in ANCA-associated vasculitis, a disease attacking small blood vessels. Records from three Greek centres covered 171 patients followed for a median of over seven years.

Steroid dose showed no link to lower risk of major relapse, while the drug rituximab did cut that risk. Higher steroid exposure instead tracked with more organ damage building up and more hospital admissions. Disease activity at diagnosis also raised relapse risk. The authors say the findings should inform long-term steroid decisions.
pmc-13296302:
Dana Patenaude, David McNaughton, and Rebecca DeLaMare report a 2026 study of video-based communication support for young children. The children were preschoolers with neurodevelopmental disabilities who watched a shared video alongside typically developing peers. Tappable hotspots on the video offered vocabulary the children could select to communicate.

All three children in the study used symbolic communication more often once the video displays were in place. Two showed very large gains and one showed a moderate gain. Peer interaction matters here, because shared activities give children reasons and chances to communicate. The authors suggest later work with less researcher help, plus checks on whether vocabulary itself grows through the activity.
pmc-13296802:
Monika Stefanska and co-authors profile, in 2026, immune cells inside mouse hearts during autoimmune myocarditis, an inflammation that can scar the heart into failure. Gene reading of over forty-six thousand heart cell nuclei at four time points mapped eighteen cell kinds and their chatter.

Resident macrophages dominated healthy hearts but collapsed when inflammation hit. Recruited macrophages flooded in, took over seventy percent of the group and stayed dominant into late remodelling, driving fiery signals and talking heavily with resting fibroblasts. Talks between cells peaked early, dipped, then rose again during repair. The authors pinpoint the macrophage handover as a driver worth targeting.
pmc-13297102:
Csaba Csutak and colleagues test whether CT texture can flag stroke patients likely to bleed after clot-busting treatment in a 2026 study. Bleeding into the brain is the feared complication of thrombolysis, and ordinary scans predict it poorly. Fifty treated patients from one centre were split by whether bleeding followed within a day.

Two texture measures of the infarcted area differed strongly between the groups. Their scores separated bleeders from non-bleeders with high accuracy in this small dataset. Such numbers could one day feed bleeding-risk models used before treatment. The authors label the work exploratory, citing the small sample, single centre, and lack of outside validation.
pmc-13297202:
Diren Beyoğlu and Jeffrey R. Idle review the two-way conversation between gut and lung microbes in a 2026 article. Gut bacteria ferment fibre into short-chain fatty acids and other products that travel to the lungs. Those molecules calm lung inflammation and support immune balance there.

Traffic also runs the other way, with lung microbes and their products able to disturb the gut. The review walks through asthma, chronic obstructive disease, cystic fibrosis, lung cancer, COVID-19, pneumonia, and tuberculosis. Diet, smoking, and vaping shape both microbial communities at once. The authors conclude that gut health forms a real part of lung health and disease.
pmc-13297302:
William García-Rodríguez and colleagues build graphene electrodes with a carbon dioxide laser for sensing histidine in fake sweat, in a 2026 study. Histidine is an amino acid whose levels in sweat can hint at health states. The electrodes were scribed onto plastic film, and planned test grids tuned laser speed, power, and line width.

The finished electrodes beat standard carbon electrodes in current tests, giving a far higher peak signal. They then sensed histidine in lab-made sweat with no added labels, with readings rising in a straight line across the tested range. Cheap, throwaway sensors of this kind could one day sit in wearables that track body chemistry during daily life.
pmc-13297402:
Yuan Shu and colleagues knit four fabrics modelled on bird feathers to keep older wearers comfortable outdoors, in a 2026 study. Feathers resist water, hold warmth, and let air pass, and each feather zone does so in its own way. The team copied down feathers, feather vanes, hooklets, and fluffy filaments into four knitted structures, then tested warmth, water resistance, airflow, and moisture handling.

Each structure led on a different measure. The first kept heat best, the second shed water and breathed best, and the fourth moved moisture vapour best. The third scored most balanced across all measures. Since older bodies heat and sweat unevenly by zone, the authors propose placing each fabric where its strength fits best.
pmc-13297502:
Daniela Taurino and a large team review whether a strong first drug regimen still lets lymphoma patients gather their own stem cells for transplant, in a 2026 single-centre study. The patients had aggressive B-cell lymphomas with high-risk traits, where standard results are often poor. The regimen, a dose-adjusted mix called R-DA-EPOCH, doubles as a platform for collecting stem cells from the blood.

Most patients gathered enough stem cells for the purpose. Transplant went ahead in over half the group, the grafts settled in predictably, and no death was tied to the transplant itself. The findings support the regimen as a workable first step for high-risk patients headed toward transplant.
pmc-13298302:
Qianqian Gao, Hongjie Pan, Yinglin Liu, and Naixi Chen simulate bank resolution choices when liquidity and credit risks interact, in a 2026 agent-based study. Their network holds banks, depositors, firms, and a central bank, letting plans play out over time. Resolution options included selling assets, expanding liabilities, granting debt relief, and extending debt maturities.

Selling assets helped at mid-level depreciation yet hurt when losses grew severe. Debt relief clearly made the whole system steadier, while extension helped only under certain liquidity settings and extension limits. Pairing debt relief with asset sales produced a positive synergy. The authors offer the results as guidance for joined, adaptive regulation.
pmc-13298502:
Doctors who treat brain aneurysms from inside the blood vessel often pick unlike plans for the same case. Sanjana R Salwi and her team show that spread in a 2026 survey. From June to September 2024, 108 doctors took case tales and named the fix they would choose.

Picks split hard by field of training. For burst cases, the scan group chose stent-aided coiling more than the brain and nerve groups did. Time in training, before or after flow tools came in, did not shift how often new tools were picked. Match scores were low, from 0.07 to 0.31 by type. The team call for work on why training steers these calls.
pmc-13298702:
Jakub Kwiatek and colleagues present a digitally planned implant case combining bone grafting and immediate restoration, in a 2026 case report. A patient needed ridge reconstruction plus implant therapy. Digital planning guided harvest of a bone cylinder from the same surgical site and its repositioning for augmentation, avoiding a second donor site.

A provisional crown shaped the soft tissue, and its profile was copied into a pre-designed final crown, streamlining delivery. Two years later, examinations showed stable hard and soft tissues without marginal bone loss or gum recession. The authors claim fewer stages and lower morbidity, while asking for larger prospective studies with cost analysis.
pmc-13299202:
Ndabereye Aubin Ndizeye and Makhutsisa Charlotte Mokoatle survey healthcare workers' trust in protective equipment during the COVID-19 years, in a 2026 study at a Johannesburg tertiary hospital. A structured survey took past accounts covering 2020 to 2022. Shortages forced reuse, while changing guidance bred confusion and falling confidence among staff.

Only a modest share believed the gear worked to prevent infection, and positive views tracked lower infection rates. Perception gaps across racial and occupational groups suggested risk communication missed some workers. The authors urge ongoing hands-on training for all staff groups, plus steady, fair supply tracked at ward level in poorer settings.
pmc-13299302:
Fatigue sits at the center of the symptom web for older people living with both hypertension and diabetes, find Xin Deng and co-authors in a 2026 network analysis. They surveyed 766 patients aged sixty and older in northern Xinjiang, China, mapping how their symptoms cluster and connect.

Fatigue was the most common complaint at 73.5% and also the most burdensome, ahead of dry mouth, pain, and dizziness. Symptoms grouped into three clusters spanning circulation and metabolism, endocrine and nerve effects, and general physical problems. Network statistics confirmed fatigue as the core node. The authors urge community nurses to screen for fatigue routinely and manage symptoms by cluster.
pmc-13299402:
Meryem Cansu Şahin, Ebru Başkaya, and Mihaela Tinca Udriștioiu compare workplace mobbing, gender role attitudes, and job satisfaction among radiation workers in Türkiye and Romania, in a 2026 cross-cultural study. Nearly two hundred healthcare staff completed three standard scales. Mobbing, meaning repeated hostile treatment at work, counts as a psychosocial hazard in radiology departments.

Job satisfaction fell as mobbing scores rose in both countries. Gender role attitudes linked to satisfaction and to mobbing only within the Romanian group, which shows culture shaping the pattern. The authors call for context-specific strategies tackling mobbing, gender perceptions, and work organisation to protect staff well-being.
pmc-13300002:
O Ventosa Blazquez and a large team map scar and slow-conduction zones in patients with dangerous ventricular rhythms after valve surgery, in a 2026 retrospective study. Seventeen ablation patients had heart scans defining scar and electrical mapping defining deceleration zones, then the two maps were compared segment by segment against valve positions.

Nearly every deceleration zone sat inside or beside scan-defined scar, mostly scar unrelated to heart attack. Zones clustered frequently around valve rings or prostheses, and most patients carried at least one such peri-valvular zone. The authors argue peri-valvular fibrosis forms an important rhythm substrate here, and mapping-guided ablation aimed there deserves larger prospective testing.
pmc-13300202:
Lycopene, the red pigment in tomatoes, gets a broad health audit in a 2026 review by Saleh A. Almatroodi and two colleagues. Drawing on cell and animal studies, the authors survey how the carotenoid acts on oxidative stress and inflammation, and where it might help across organ systems.

Reported benefits span protection for kidneys, liver, heart, and brain, plus roles against arthritis, obesity, and several cancers. The review also covers pairings with other compounds and nano-sized formulations meant to raise absorption. Poor water solubility and low uptake remain the main barriers, and the authors call for firmer dosing, safety, and interaction data from trials.
pmc-13300802:
Piotr Wróbel and co-authors run a randomized trial of socket preservation after tooth extraction in a 2026 dental study. Filling the empty socket with bone substitute aims to hold the ridge's shape for later implant work. Forty healthy patients were split into four groups by jaw site and material, receiving either human donor bone material or a bovine derived product, each sealed under a collagen membrane.

Imaging at one week and six months showed no significant difference between the materials in preserving ridge height or width. Both groups gained radiographic bone density over the healing period, with the bovine product ending significantly denser. Biopsies taken when implants were placed at six months went for microscopic analysis of the new bone. The authors conclude the materials tie on shape preservation, while the quality of the bone formed may still differ by material.
pmc-13300902:
Tianbo Kang and co-authors propose a mask refinement method for measuring tiny regular shapes under the microscope in a 2026 paper. Spheres, pores, and tubes in micro scenes are small, faint, and ragged edged, so ordinary segmentation outlines are too crude for precision measurement. Their framework starts with a segmentation pass boosted by adaptive super-resolution, then iterates, blending pixel evidence with the known geometry of the target to polish the outline toward a clean, continuous boundary.

On a sphere and tube assembly dataset, the method produced lower geometric errors on samples that could be fitted and raised the fitting success rate substantially. Removing either the dynamic super-resolution or the iterative refinement hurt performance, which the ablations read as proof both parts carry weight. The authors argue that baking geometric consistency into mask cleanup is the practical route to trustworthy micro measurement for assembly and quality control.
pmc-13301002:
Injecting treatment straight into a tumor can spark immune attack there and beyond, Vincent T Ma and colleagues survey in a 2026 review of intratumoral therapy for advanced melanoma. The field began with talimogene laherparepvec, a modified herpes virus that became the first oncolytic therapy approved for a solid tumor.

Newer viruses carry extra genetic tweaks, from fusogenic proteins to immune-stimulating payloads, aiming at stronger local killing and wider immune priming. Trials since 2010, alone and with checkpoint inhibitors, show better response rates and some lasting remissions even after checkpoint failure. Image-guided injection into deep lesions and use before surgery mark the newest directions, the authors note.
pmc-13301402:
T So and co-authors report stacking pulsed field energy on radiofrequency for ventricular tachycardia in a 2026 single center study. Eighteen patients treated between mid 2023 and late 2025 were split by whether operators added pulsed field deliveries, through a five spline catheter, after heat based work. Safety events and freedom from the rhythm over follow-up were the yardsticks.

Procedure and imaging times matched between the seven combined and eleven radiofrequency only cases. No pulsed field harm appeared: no blood breakdown, no clots, no coronary spasm, and no catheter injuries across a median of twenty-one applications per patient. The one heart block occurred in the radiofrequency group. Freedom from tachycardia at two years trended better with the combination, about eighty-six versus thirty-four percent, without reaching significance, though major cardiovascular events were fewer. The authors call the pairing safe and promising, with numbers too small for verdicts.
pmc-13302702:
A Saglietto and a multicentre team train, in a 2026 study, machine learning models to predict rhythm recurrence after pulsed field ablation for atrial fibrillation. Ablation slots are limited, so choosing patients most likely to benefit matters. Routine demographic, clinical, and ultrasound data from nineteen centres fed five candidate models.

The cohort held 1,688 patients, of whom about eighty-one percent stayed free of recurrence over roughly a year. A random forest performed best among the tested models, reaching moderate discrimination on unseen patients. Time between diagnosis and ablation was the single strongest predictor of recurrence, ahead of body mass index and upper-chamber size. The authors support model-guided selection to personalise who gets offered the procedure.
pmc-13302902:
Severe infection, autoimmunity, and inflammation mark whose thinking fades after long COVID, Iulia Elena Diaconu and colleagues track in a 2026 two-year study. Patients with neurological long COVID symptoms were split by baseline cognitive score, then matched on age, sex, and prior neurological illness, leaving fifty-four per group. Labs, vitamin levels, and brain imaging accompanied them over twenty-four months.

Among initially sharper patients, severe COVID, autoimmune disease, and a high neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio predicted decline. In the already-impaired group, diabetes joined autoimmunity and the same inflammation ratio, with stronger odds. Vitamin D levels tracked cognitive scores in both groups. The authors flag these factors as targets for early intervention trials.
pmc-13303202:
Signet ring cells in a stomach biopsy pointed at the wrong cancer, Amalia A. Sofianidi and colleagues warn in a 2026 case report. A fifty-two-year-old woman with metastatic lobular breast carcinoma, controlled since 2022 on hormone therapy and ribociclib, developed stomach pain and rising tumor markers. Biopsies showed diffuse adenocarcinoma with signet ring shapes and were first read as a new primary gastric cancer.

Expert review flipped the verdict: breast markers GATA3 and TRPS1 were positive, gut marker CDX2 negative, and E-cadherin lost, matching her breast tumor. Weekly paclitaxel followed. In lobular breast cancer patients, the authors insist, gastric signet ring findings demand a lineage panel before surgery is planned.
pmc-13303702:
Seong-Joon Kim, Sang-Jin Lee, and Sung-Deuk Choi report a 2026 field study of airborne volatile chemicals in small neighborhoods beside industrial complexes in Ulsan, South Korea. Such compounds are widely emitted and can harm health, yet tiny residential pockets near plants are rarely monitored.

Passive samplers at seven sites measured 59 compounds, with xylenes, toluene, and ethylbenzene most common. Levels rose near solvent-heavy industry, and pattern checks pointed to local sources within a few kilometers rather than distant drift. Only naphthalene passed a short-term non-cancer risk limit, while long-term risks stayed within accepted bounds.
pmc-13304402:
Yanyun Ru and colleagues build a computer method for tracking cracks in brittle solids in a 2026 engineering study. Sudden cracking threatens structures, and standard tools struggle to follow cracks that split and turn under fast loads.

Their peridynamics approach pairs a mesh-free solid model with an energy integral to compute crack-tip stress measures. Tests covered single and mixed crack types under still, slow, and fast loading, plus plates with holes that bend crack paths. Peak stress values under fast loads topped the still-load values, and crack branching was captured cleanly. Matches with theory and standard models confirmed accuracy.
pmc-13304702:
Tilek Kuanyshbekov and co-authors study membranes blending graphene oxide with a plant-based polymer in a 2026 materials report. Changing polymer share may tune strength, electric behavior, and moisture sensing in the same sheet.

Tests with infrared light, X-rays, microscopy, pulling, and electric meters tracked structure as polymer content rose. Layer gaps widened while crystal grains shrank, and sheets grew more even as polymer wrapped the flakes. Strength climbed a great deal, while dry electric resistance also rose. Wet air lowered resistance in a reversible way through water-assisted charge flow, suiting humidity sensors.
pmc-13305402:
Addisu Simachew Asgai leads a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis of bowel obstruction surgery outcomes in Ethiopia. Blocked bowel is a common surgical emergency, and results in low-resource hospitals vary widely between reports.

Twenty-one studies with 5,429 patients entered the pooled analysis. About one patient in four suffered a poor outcome, meaning complications or death in hospital, though rates swung widely by study. Arriving a day or more after symptoms began, staying over a week, and having bowel cut and rejoined each raised poor outcome odds. Earlier arrival and stronger ward care are urged.
pmc-13305502:
PingBo Zhang and DaWei Zhao share a 2026 case of breast cancer arising in both breasts at once with sharply different types. Paired cancers are uncommon, and mismatched biology between sides makes treatment planning genuinely hard.

A 51-year-old woman after menopause found a painless left breast lump, and scans flagged several spots on both sides needing checks. Both breasts were removed, and lab work proved two separate cancers: a triple-negative type with gland features on the right, and a mucus-rich hormone-linked type on the left. Tailored chemo and hormone care followed, and she stayed disease-free past thirty months.
pmc-13306002:
Larisa E. Botte reviewed methods for pulling fungal toxins out of complex samples in a 2026 survey of old and new techniques. Such toxins threaten food safety yet may also serve as farm pest controls, so clean separation matters for both aims.

Classic liquid extraction, cartridge cleanup and column methods suffer from weak selectivity, many steps and heavy solvent use in the authors' account. Newer ideas include designed crystals, pressurised fluid extraction, smart porous membranes and artificial intelligence guided by physical models. The review urges standard reporting so data can train prediction tools, moving isolation toward precise, greener practice.
pmc-13306102:
Faiza I. A. Abdella tested betanin, a natural pigment, on enzymes tied to obesity and diabetes in a 2026 lab and computer study. Red blood cells from humans were exposed to the compound to track sugar use and pathway switching.

Betanin slowed digestive enzymes more as dose rose, with half-blocking levels of 48.8 and 31.9 µg/mL for fat and starch enzymes in reported figures. Computer fits suggested tighter binding than two standard drugs used for comparison. The compound also switched on the energy sensor AMPK at low levels, supporting further checks as a metabolic aid.
pmc-13306502:
Riccardo Gaetano Cirrone reviewed how cheap light based water sensors are checked for truth in a 2026 scope review. Such tools could widen lake and stream watch, most of all for town led work, yet proof of truth is rare.

Forty studies were read for how they showed sense skill, truth, fine grain and repeat runs next to lab tools. Most gave sense limits, while full truth checks stayed thin and mixed across the set. The team gives a plan to make checks firm, so cheap tools can earn trust next to bench gear in the field.
pmc-13307602:
Giulia Russo and co-authors review in 2026 how to judge cat welfare in animal assisted services, where cats now join therapy, learning, and support work. A first broad search found no study that dealt squarely with welfare checks for cats in that setting, so they searched again by topic.

The wider search sorted known checks into health, behaviour, and body measures such as stress signals. No single check can capture welfare alone, so the authors favour a combined protocol that draws on all three fields. Vets, handlers, and researchers could use that mix to watch cats during sessions and to pull a cat out when strain shows.
pmc-13308302:
Lukas Trzebiatowski and co-authors review twenty-five years of studies in 2026 on how events during calving itself shape calf sickness and death on dairy farms. Four factor groups were covered: calving management, birth monitoring, induced birth, and difficult birth. Problems around birth echo through the calf's first weeks.

Every factor group influenced deaths immediately after birth in the gathered literature. Management quality and difficult birth also affected survival up to weaning. Good monitoring and preventing difficult births improved the calf's uptake of antibody-rich first milk. Morbidity fell when calving was managed properly across the board. The authors aim the synthesis at farmers who want healthier calves and at public reassurance. Birth is a short window with long consequences, and their review shows where attention pays off.
pmc-13308702:
Zheng Liu and co-authors recount in 2026 a rare case of bowel telescoping in an adult, caused by a lone Peutz-Jeghers polyp that mimicked colon cancer. The patient, a man aged 30 years, had a year of on and off belly pain and sickness, with no skin pigment marks and no family tale of polyps.

Scans showed the classic target sign, and a scope saw a large growth in the rising colon before surgery day. Direct checks during surgery found the true site in the end of the small bowel, which spared a needless colon cut. Gene reads found fresh changes in POLE and EXO1, and no change in the classic syndrome gene.
pmc-13309002:
Łukasz Lamch and colleagues build in 2026 a family of two-headed magnetic surfactants, soap-like compounds whose partner ions contain iron and answer to magnets. Three chain lengths were made and checked with several spectral methods. Heat traits, surface activity, and magnet response were set against simpler one-headed magnetic surfactants.

Cooling speed decided whether the compounds sat in uniform or layered phases, sometimes both side by side. Drops of their solutions changed shape inside a magnetic field, proving surface pull can be steered by magnets. Readings showed paramagnetic traits and a one-to-one ratio of surface cation to iron. Such switchable surface agents draw makers of smart materials, from steered foams to guided droplets. The authors present the double-headed design as widening what magnetic soaps can do.
pmc-13309202:
Brian Yu Chieh Cheng and co-authors report in 2026 neuroinvasive eastern equine encephalitis, a rare grave mosquito borne brain disease, in a healthy woman aged 56 years in Ontario. She came to urgent care in late July with four days of fever, headache, nausea, and vomiting, a week after mosquito bites at a lake.

Sent home as a plain virus case, she was found out cold three days later with a coma score of 3 and a fever of 39.5 degrees. Spinal fluid showed a white cell surge with high protein, and early scans could not split germ, herpes, or mosquito causes apart. Age over 50 years raises the risk of brain spread, and warm season growth may widen the map for this virus.
pmc-13309502:
Maha Kabil and co-authors introduce a virus that kills drug-resistant staph germs in a 2026 study of wound infection. The germ, MRSA, resists standard drugs and often infects chronic and surgical wounds. Viruses that infect bacteria, called phages, offer a targeted option when drugs fail.

Among 107 wound samples, near half grew MRSA. The new phage, taken from sewage, killed most tested MRSA strains and copied itself well while staying stable under body-like conditions. Its gene map showed no genes for dormancy, harm, or drug resistance. In infected mice, cream with the phage cut germ counts and sped wound closing, matching a phage-plus-drug mix. The authors propose it as a wound treatment candidate.
pmc-13309602:
Cornelia Westerberg and co-authors engineer small binding proteins that block an immune signal in a 2026 study. The signal pair CD40 and CD40L steers adaptive immunity and draws drug interest for autoimmune disease. Natural CD40L works as a three-part unit, so blockers shaped in threes may grip it best.

Binders found by directed evolution on a bacterial display platform were fused to collagen tail pieces that force three-part assembly. The triple forms gripped the target about 100-fold more tightly by apparent strength in lab tests and blocked signal-driven cell activity well. Heat stability and binding speed were also checked. The authors offer collagen tails as a general way to triple other binders.
pmc-13309902:
Karim Lakhdar and co-authors present a 2026 case of seizures as the first sign of high pressure inside the skull. The patient, a 41-year-old woman, had two weeks of severe headache before full-body seizures began. Her eye exam and brain scan pointed away from the usual seizure causes.

Eye checks showed swollen optic discs on both sides, and imaging showed an empty sella, a flattened pituitary space tied to raised skull pressure. A spinal tap measured pressure at 32 cm H2O with normal fluid makeup, matching idiopathic intracranial hypertension in the report. Hormone tests found one low pituitary signal. Two pressure-lowering drugs brought fast relief, pressure normalized, and seizures did not return.
pmc-13310102:
Seunghye Jang and colleagues tackle a materials flaw in 2026 that limits sodium-rich Prussian Blue, a cheap and promising sodium-ion battery cathode. Water lodged inside its crystal framework weakens performance, yet standard heat drying harms the material. The team instead drove out crystal water at room temperature by bubbling nitrogen through the synthesis mixture.

Surface analysis showed heating oxidised the surface, forming iron-oxygen bonds and leaving impurities behind. The room-temperature liquid route preserved the protective cyanide-terminated surface while still dehydrating the lattice. Electrochemical testing then compared the two preparations head to head. Sodium-ion batteries appeal because sodium is abundant and inexpensive compared with lithium. A gentler dehydration step could lift cathode stability without extra processing cost. The authors frame surface chemistry, not bulk composition, as the decisive lever for quality.
pmc-13310502:
Wu-lan Ao and co-authors review non-invasive brain stimulation for chronic insomnia in a 2026 article. Long-term insomnia dulls daytime function and raises mental and heart-metabolic risks. Talking therapy and drugs help many, yet access gaps, partial response, relapse, and side effects leave others searching.

Four stimulation routes are weighed: magnetic pulses, weak direct current, alternating current, and ear vagus nerve stimulation. Studies suggest gains in felt sleep quality and some measured sleep traits, but results vary widely by target, dose, schedule, and patient type. The authors argue for tailoring stimulation to patient profiles rather than one fixed recipe, a shift they call precision neuromodulation.
pmc-13310602:
Food Safety Commission of Japan presents a 2026 risk assessment of oxolinic acid, an antimicrobial used in crops and animals. The fifth edition adds fresh crop residue data, covering taro and broccoli among others, supplied by the Consumer Affairs Agency. Safe intake levels rest on how the chemical moves through bodies and where its harms begin.

Evidence spans fate in animals, humans, and plants, residues in crops and livestock foods, and toxicity tests from short-term to cancer and two-generation breeding studies. Main harms centered on slowed weight gain, testis and ovary changes in rats, and excitatory nerve signs. No fertility harm, birth defects, or meaningful gene damage appeared. The authors derive safe levels from the lowest no-harm dose found.
pmc-13310702:
Ji Li and co-authors report a 2026 case study and review on stomach surgery for adults with Prader-Willi syndrome and very severe obesity. The syndrome drives constant hunger, low energy use, and hard behavior issues, so weight loss care is complex. The team judged safety and weight change after sleeve surgery in this group.

One man aged 24 years had the operation after full team review, and his early recovery was smooth. Past studies show only modest weight loss, plus lasting needs for food checks, behavior support, and close follow up. The authors advise against routine use and urge careful case choice, with drug and breathing aids as added options.
pmc-13311202:
Huihui Sun and co-authors build a light edge model to spot wildlife and cut junk camera trap photos in a 2026 study. Remote cameras fire on wind and heat shifts, flooding scholars with empty frames and draining power. A single field ready model that filters fakes and names animals could run on the device itself.

Their WS-YOLO design adds wave based feature pulls, joint space and channel focus, and a loss that stresses hard border cases. Tests on four wildlife sets gave strong accuracy scores, led by tiger and park infrared sets. Running on a small Jetson board proved real time, low power field use.
pmc-13311302:
Md Fuad Al Fidah and co-authors examine a 2026 surveillance study of malnutrition in Bangladeshi teens who came to care with diarrhea. Growth faltering in the teen years can shape adult health.

Records covered 1597 patients aged 10 to 19 seen at a Dhaka hospital from 2012 to 2023. Stunting affected 29.6 percent and thinness 24.3 percent across the years in this group. Stunting fell from 40.8 percent in 2012 to 25.7 percent in 2023, while thinness edged up. Older age raised stunting odds, while a mother's schooling past primary level and richer households lowered them. Girls were less often thin.
pmc-13311702:
Ruben Mijnster and co-authors present the NISONE trial protocol in a 2026 article. The trial tests personal N-of-1 studies for people who quit statins over muscle symptoms, to sort true drug effects from nocebo effects.

The trial will enroll 249 patients with artery disease or inherited high cholesterol who stopped two or more statins. Two thirds get the personal study path: four blinded six-week rounds of statin or dummy pills, with symptoms logged in an app, then a feedback round. The rest get usual care. The goal is to restart statins safely where fear, not the drug, caused the symptoms.
pmc-13312002:
Yoseph M Habte and co-authors report the 2026 case of Chilaiditi sign found by chance in a healthy young woman during routine pre-travel screening. The sign, bowel looped between liver and diaphragm, can mimic a surgical emergency.

The 28-year-old had no symptoms, a normal exam, and normal labs. Her chest X-ray showed a gas-filled colon loop with fold markings under the right diaphragm and no free air. With the classic picture and no complaints, no further tests or treatment were done. The authors stress matching the image to the patient before rushing to procedures for what is often a harmless variant.
pmc-13313002:
Martin Milata and colleagues validate, in a 2026 multicenter study, a bedside sleep questionnaire against wrist actigraphy in hospital patients, and ask whether either can warn of delirium. Poor sleep is a known delirium risk, but general wards need a cheap way to spot it, and the Richards-Campbell questionnaire's agreement with objective recording was untested in this setting.

Across seven Czech institutions, 133 patients contributed 424 nights of paired questionnaire answers and MotionWatch recordings. Patients rated their sleep moderately good even when the recorder showed it badly broken. Only the questionnaire's sleep-depth item lined up meaningfully with the device, and the total score tracked objective sleep weakly. Subjective ratings did not predict delirium at all, while low measured sleep efficiency did, marking the wearable, not the form, as the useful risk signal.
pmc-13313202:
Weronika Pawlik leads a 2026 study that hunted through human RNAs for tracts of CAG repeats, the DNA pattern that grows too long in some brain diseases. Such tracts sit in many RNAs and have lengthened over evolution, and they may aid nerve cell work when kept at normal size.

The team found more than 600 human RNAs with at least 10 CAG repeats, coming from 58 places in the genome, with repeat length varying between people. Several round RNAs came from the ATXN7 locus, where repeat growth causes spinocerebellar ataxia type 7. One round RNA was traced in the cell fluid and in protein-making fractions, and was found in skin cells, blood, and cerebellum. Most striking, the team found a round RNA that carries a mutation, which may matter for how that ataxia unfolds.
pmc-13313302:
Zhongqin Huang reviews, in a 2026 article, the long-running question of whether gallbladder removal raises colorectal cancer risk. Huang argues the answer runs through gut microbes and a bile acid sensor called FXR. Gallbladder surgery is among the world's most common operations. Population patterns keep recurring. Cancers favor the proximal colon, risk runs higher in women, and incidence peaks five to fifteen years after surgery.

The mechanistic story centers on changed bile flow reshaping the gut community. Some protective bacteria shrink and others expand. Bile acid mixtures shift in ways that suppress FXR signaling. One 2025 study showed this suppression loosening FXR's restraint on a growth pathway and promoting tumors. An FXR-activating drug prevented the effect in animals, though toxicity limits its use in people. Huang proposes personal risk scoring from demographics, microbial signatures, and metabolic markers. That scoring would pair with gut-restricted drugs, probiotics, and Mediterranean-style eating.
pmc-13313802:
Haitham Elaadli and seven colleagues measure exposure to Chlamydia abortus, a bacterium that causes abortion in sheep and can pass to humans, in northern Egypt. They tested 196 sheep and 242 women with a history of abortion at an Alexandria hospital using antibody assays.

About twelve percent of sheep carried antibodies, with breed, governorate, breeding system, pregnancy status, and abortion history all shaping risk. Thirteen percent of the women showed recent-infection antibodies. Their risk clustered with rural residence, direct contact with sheep, and miscarriage history and timing. The authors present the first human seroprevalence data for the region and a One Health warning about occupational exposure around lambing.
pmc-13314002:
Ayad Nouri Diaa Alhakim, Dhurgham H. Al Haideri, and Abd-Alhadi Jaithom Marzok compare, in a 2026 study, two inhaled agents for the quality of heart tracings they allow in dogs. ECG recording demands a steady heart backdrop, and the anesthetic itself can distort the signal. Twenty healthy adult dogs were anesthetized with either isoflurane or sevoflurane under controlled conditions. Heart rate, conduction gaps, and rhythm stability were monitored continuously.

Sevoflurane produced the calmer tracing. It gave steadier ECGs, less waveform swing, and fewer rhythm-disturbing changes than the other agent, alongside a higher heart rate and shorter PR intervals. The QRS complex duration did not differ between groups, and waveform clarity favored sevoflurane throughout. Combined with its rapid induction and recovery, the authors recommend it as the preferred agent when dogs need anesthesia for cardiac assessment in clinic or laboratory.
pmc-13314202:
Hao Xie and a large team review MTA2, a gene-control protein, across diseases in a 2026 paper. MTA2 sits at the core of the Mi-2 chromatin remodeling complex and shapes gene activity through epigenetic control and many signal paths.

The review sets out the shape and molecular traits of MTA2, then traces its roles in cancer and beyond. Breast, gastric, and liver cancers get close focus, with weight on spread, drug resistance, and reshaping of the tumor setting. The authors weigh MTA2 as a sign for diagnosis and as a drug target, and they survey plans to block its control network. They close with the push for sharp, specific blockers of MTA2, which could turn a broad control protein into a precise point of care.
pmc-13314502:
Dongdong Zhang and co-workers report a 2026 case of an autoimmune brain and cord disorder with two rare twists. The disease, GFAP astrocytopathy, stems from antibodies against a cell protein and usually shows as brain and cord inflammation, often with clear brain scan changes.

Their patient was a 31-year-old woman with fever, headache, trouble passing urine, and signs of meningeal irritation. Her brain scan was clean, yet her spine scan showed patchy long lesions in the thoracic cord, standing alone. Spinal fluid held high pressure, extra cells, raised protein, and a share of 10 percent eosinophils on cell study, as stated in the report, a rare find in this disease. The case warns that a normal brain scan does not rule the disease out.
pmc-13315002:
Zong-Xia Yu and co-workers build the chromosome-level genome of a medicinal mint kin from high land, in a study put out in 2026. Mosla chinensis is a prized herb with few gene resources for sharp breeding.

The plant came from the Baiyunjian Reserve at 1611 meters above sea level, as stated in the report. Long-read and Hi-C methods yielded a genome of 444.26 Mb by their measure, with most reads anchored to 9 chromosomes at near-full accuracy. Repeats fill much of the genome, and a species own duplication event stands out. Chemical maps of tissues found flowers and leaves as hotspots for terpenes such as thymol and carvacrol, and gene reads pinned one synthase gene behind a key scent. The map speeds breeding of richer herb strains.
pmc-13315502:
Hamaad Ahmad Khan and the VOICE collaboration survey, in a 2026 national study, how ready British and Irish medical students feel for assisted dying law. With legislation advancing through the United Kingdom's parliament, today's students may be the first doctors practicing under it. Their questionnaire reached 896 students across the United Kingdom and Ireland in 2025, measuring ethical views, confidence, legal knowledge, and how much teaching their schools provide.

Support ran broad but shallow. Most students, 64.5 percent, believed assisted dying can be ethically justified, yet only 7.6 percent could correctly identify all the eligibility criteria, and nearly seventy percent reported minimal teaching on the subject. Teaching tracked with both greater confidence and stronger ethical agreement in the models. Students also worried about coercion and inequality in how such a law might operate. The authors conclude the future workforce endorses the principle while lacking the preparation, and they call for curricula before the law arrives.
pmc-13315602:
Tianxu Guo and co-authors study what happens when mice carry only one working copy of the Six1 gene, in a 2026 paper. The gene helps build the kidneys and lungs early in life. Mice with no working copy died at birth because their lungs were underdeveloped, so the team followed mice with one copy as they aged.

These mice kept flaws in their kidneys and lungs, and the flaws grew worse with age. Their tissues showed more markers of cell aging, more scarring, and a higher risk of lung fibrosis. Gene activity tests pointed to two switched-on pathways tied to inflammation, known as NF-κB and TNF. The authors link low Six1 levels to faster tissue aging through these routes.
pmc-13315802:
Leila Shokri introduces a question-and-answer feature in 2026 where STAR Protocols authors and board members share practical advice on CRISPR gene editing. Precise editing in cell lines and model organisms now shapes biology and clinical research, but success depends on solid protocols and good troubleshooting.

Experts answer common questions on editing strategy and fixes. On choosing guide RNAs, labs name tools such as sgRNAcas9, CRISPOR, CRISPR-P, and CRISPR-Local, plus annotation software for mapping guides and primers. Guides drawn from published genome-wide screens are another starting tip. The collected answers aim to help new and seasoned users avoid common pitfalls.
pmc-13315902:
Mengjie Xu and colleagues extracted polysaccharides in 2026 from fermented black beans using ultrasound plus a three-part deep eutectic solvent. The solvent mixed choline chloride, tartaric acid, and ethylene glycol, and tuning gave best results at 79 minutes, 35 percent water, and 65 degrees, yielding 115.37 milligrams per gram.

That yield was 4.8 times the hot-water method and 3.0 times ultrasound with water alone. The extract was rich in uronic acids, arabinose, and xylose, formed stable charged aggregates, and showed antioxidant action plus strong blocking of two sugar-breaking enzymes, with inhibition near 96.8 and 93.7 percent.
pmc-13316202:
Yuetong Chen and colleagues built copper nanoparticles in 2026 that push cancer cells into cuproptosis, a copper-driven death, to strengthen radiotherapy. Radiation often fails because tumors resist, making too few reactive oxygen species and too little DNA damage, and copper death offers a fresh lever.

Their platform uses a copper-doped ZIF-8 framework loaded with elesclomol, a copper carrier, to shuttle copper into mitochondria. That triggers excess reactive oxygen and mitochondrial failure, which team with radiation to shred DNA. Treated mice showed strong tumor shrinkage with little whole-body toxicity, in a first-of-its-kind pairing.
pmc-13316302:
Ifat Klein and a team of Israeli researchers published a 2026 pooled study on arm problems after breast cancer surgery, covering pain, stiffness, weak function, and swelling. Rather than blame surgery alone, they test how mood, sleep, habits, and health history add to the risk.

Data came from three forward-looking cohorts with 1,602 women checked up to 36 months after surgery, and harm appeared in 61 percent of them in the combined figures. Poor sleep nearly tripled the odds of problems, while distress, other illness, and chemotherapy also raised risk. More movement during recovery linked to better arms. The findings argue for screening and support that treat the whole person, not just the wound.
pmc-13317202:
Liyuan Ren and co-authors survey, in 2026, microbes living in the deep chlorophyll layer around an undersea mountain in the South China Sea. Seamounts may host rich microbial life because their shape stirs the water. The deep chlorophyll maximum is a layer where plant-like plankton gather below the surface.

Using gene sequencing for bacteria and protists in two size fractions, the team compared the Xianbei seamount with nearby coastal water. The seamount held richer large-fraction communities, linked to stronger chlorophyll signals. Flexible feeders and broad-ranging flagellates were enriched there, while interaction networks looked less clustered and less robust than coastal ones. Modelling suggested that chance processes shaped community assembly more than fixed rules, highlighting how seamount topography creates distinct microbial neighbourhoods.
pmc-13317402:
Asma Altaf Hussain Merchant and co-authors track mind health after heart bypass surgery in a 2026 study in Pakistan. The surgery saves lives in a land where heart ill runs high. Yet how mood and life joy run after it, in a lean-care land, was dim.

Patients at a large ward filled mood, worry, and life polls before surgery and at one and six months after. Scores were set in a line to see the true arc of heal. Such arcs can flag who sinks and when. Heart teams in like lands gain a local tale to plan mind care as part of chest care.
pmc-13317702:
Sangeeta Sahu and colleagues report, in 2026, a sulfur-rich polymer cathode that improves lithium-sulfur batteries. Such batteries promise very high energy storage, but an insulating layer of lithium sulfide coats the cathode and slows reactions. Controlling where that layer forms is a central challenge.

Their copolymer combines sulfur with a plant-derived unit carrying nitrogen and oxygen groups. Those groups attract dissolved lithium polysulfides and help redistribute them, guiding more even lithium sulfide growth. Magnetic resonance measurements showed faster lithium ion movement, and titration tests showed quicker reaction kinetics. Cells kept a high share of their starting capacity after 300 cycles at a demanding rate, with slow fade per cycle. The standard electrolyte was left unchanged.
pmc-13318702:
Ana Lourdes Oropesa and colleagues report a 2026 survey of veterinary students in Spain and Portugal. They measured self-rated knowledge of artificial intelligence, actual use, and attitudes. The survey ran during the 2023–2024 academic year. It drew 340 undergraduate and postgraduate students from public and private institutions.

Nine scaled questions fed composite scores on a 0 to 100 scale. Scores differed clearly between institutions. Students with any prior AI training scored higher on knowledge and use. Their attitudes were also more positive, with strong statistical support. Formal training was limited in many institutions, so most learning was informal. Daily social media use linked weakly to higher scores. The authors urge deliberate teaching of AI literacy in veterinary courses.
pmc-13318902:
Seyed Abdul Ahad Wadoodi and colleagues describe a 2026 case of late-onset vitamin K deficiency bleeding in a four-month-old boy. The preventable condition causes severe bleeding in early infancy. He arrived with fever, cough, and poor appetite. He had reportedly received vitamin K at birth by injection.

Sepsis with anaemia was suspected, and an antibiotic injection was given. A growing bruise with active bleeding then appeared at the injection site. Blood tests showed profound clotting failure, with INR above 4 in the reported results. His haemoglobin fell to 6.3 g/dL, and seizures followed. Scans found a subdural bleed with oxygen-related brain injury. Vitamin K, transfusion, and intensive care restored him. He left hospital after ten days without clear deficits.
pmc-13319302:
Huijung Kim and co-authors survey ways to shape graphene oxide surfaces for electric sensors in a 2026 review. The carbon sheet can be tuned in many ways and mixes well with water. That makes it a strong base for tests that pick up tiny traces of body chemicals, cells, and germs.

Five routes to change the surface are grouped and compared, from trimming its electric flow to adding metal grains or soft films. Each route is matched to uses such as finding proteins, gene bits, and whole germs. Work with live cells and small organ like cell groups is covered too, along with steps still needed before clinic use.
pmc-13320402:
Alexa Moschella and four co-authors reported a rare brain and skin disease case in 2026. A 26-year-old woman with ulcerative colitis, spine inflammation, and psoriasis arrived with three days of headache, nausea, vomiting, light sensitivity, and neck stiffness. Sweet syndrome is an inflammatory condition with fever and tender red skin bumps packed with neutrophils. When the same process hits the nervous system, it is called neuro-Sweet syndrome.

Her course stretched over weeks: a second visit for blurry vision, then a third with weakness and numbness on her right side. Skin lesions arrived late, which is part of what makes the case instructive. Recovery came only when the neutrophil skin disease itself was treated, the authors report.
pmc-13320502:
G. Mammone and colleagues weigh a jaw bone risk in a 2026 review of patient records. Some cancer drugs that slow bone breakdown can, in rare cases, kill jaw bone tissue. The question was whether adding blood vessel growth blockers, called VEGFR-TKIs, raises that risk further.

Records covered 233 people on both drug types and 986 people on bone drugs alone. Raw time to jaw harm looked shorter with both drugs, yet after checks for age, sex, smoking, and drug type the added drugs alone did not predict harm. Denosumab use and active smoking did. Among people on one bone drug class, the vessel blockers were tied to earlier harm, a split that needs care in clinic planning.
pmc-13320602:
Sahra Tasdelen and colleagues test how a fixing chemical changes human heart sac tissue in a 2026 lab study. Glutaraldehyde fixing is widely used to prepare pericardium for replacement heart valves, yet how dose and soaking time act together was not well mapped. The team varied both factors in a grid of conditions.

Tissue was treated at strengths from 0 to 2.5 percent for 5 to 90 minutes, then checked for collagen shape and stretch behaviour. Longer soaking made collagen fibres less wavy and more bundled. Dose and time interacted in a non simple way for stretch limits, while stress measures tracked each other closely. The results help valve makers tune fixing recipes.
pmc-13320702:
Kate H Marshall and colleagues survey, in 2026, how general practice serves Australian residential aged care homes, where residents have complex needs and care models vary widely. Family doctors, practice nurses and managers were asked about their models, satisfaction and plans to stay in this work.

The national survey ran in mid 2023 and drew 105 doctor responses plus smaller nurse and manager groups. Most doctors delivered care through unstructured arrangements rather than formal models. Just over half of doctors reported high satisfaction with their model, yet pay was the weakest element and most were dissatisfied with it. Satisfaction did not differ by model type. Younger and less experienced doctors were more likely to plan leaving aged care soon, prompting workforce warnings.
pmc-13321002:
Nicole Martinez and co-authors present a 2026 laboratory protocol for building cancer cell lines that resist treatment. Resistance and cross-resistance shorten how long cancer drugs keep working, yet shared in vitro methods for growing resistant models are scarce. The protocol covers human and mouse cell lines exposed to chemotherapy drugs and KRAS blockers.

Steps guide readers through growing, expanding, and keeping resistant cells under drug pressure. Later steps check that resistance is real, test whether it spills over to other drugs, and run a measured cell killing assay. The aim is a repeatable system for judging the resistance risks of new compounds before they move toward patients.
pmc-13321302:
José G. da Silva Filho and co-authors examine a lithium tungstate crystal under pressure in a 2026 study. The compound Li2W2O7 pairs stiff tungsten oxygen octahedra with a softer lithium network. The team combined lab measures with computer models to map structure, bonding, and vibration behaviour.

Model lattice values matched lab results within 5 percent, and charge analysis showed mostly ionic lithium bonds beside more covalent tungsten bonds. Lithium contacts dominated crystal packing at about 55.7 percent of surface contacts in the analysis. Under pressure up to 9.3 gigapascals, spectra shifted clearly between 6.3 and 7.5 gigapascals, signalling a structural change driven by octahedra tilting.
pmc-13321602:
Periyasamy Kuppusamy and co-authors gather pregnancy thyroid ranges by trimester from world and Indian studies, in a review from two thousand twenty-six. Wrong ranges risk wrong calls in pregnancy care. Forty-eight studies passed the screen from over one thousand found.

Top TSH bounds swung widely by trimester and by land. Free hormone ranges also spread across studies. Even inside India, ranges split by group. The authors insist each population set its own ranges from healthy, antibody-free women. One global chart will not do. Readers in lab medicine get a clear case for local norms in a common test.
pmc-13322502:
Yannick D. Höppner and a large team test whether antibody profiles can predict malaria infection outcomes in a 2026 study. Volunteers in a controlled human infection study gave blood before challenge with the PfSPZ parasite strain. The target was PfEMP1, a parasite surface protein that drives protection but varies widely and is hard to study.

Samples came from 25 people, malaria naive Europeans and lifelong exposed Africans. Every assay type showed that starting immune level and breadth strongly predicted how infection unfolded. Machine learning on the profiles found that a broad immune set, including against the most varied group B forms, marked lower risk. New parasite forms arising in the group escaped those starting defences.
pmc-13323302:
Ya-fei Cheng and co-authors describe anaesthesia care in children's heart transplants at one centre, in a 2026 descriptive study of 27 patients treated between May 2022 and October 2025. Ages ran from 6 months to 16 years, and dilated cardiomyopathy drove most cases.

All children had advanced heart failure, over half arrived on ECMO support, and bypass and cold ischaemia times were long on average in the reported figures. No major heart events struck during induction. After surgery about two fifths needed ECMO again, and 23 of 27 children were alive at follow-up. Brain injury from low oxygen was the leading major complication. The authors offer the series as real-world guidance for high-risk care.
pmc-13323502:
Emmanuel Nana Kwesi Ofori Darko, Zhanyong Qi and Zhiyuan Wang study generative AI use and teacher confidence in Ghana, in a 2026 mixed-methods study of K-12 educators. A survey reached 512 teachers across varied districts, followed by interviews with 20 teachers chosen for depth.

More frequent generative AI use correlated with higher teacher self-efficacy and instructional confidence in the survey results. Using the tools for lesson planning and for making differentiated materials predicted efficacy most strongly in layered models. Support from the institution and professional development shaped how far those gains went, and interviews added context on daily classroom use. The authors frame AI adoption as a belief-shaping change, not only a technical one.
pmc-13323802:
Anastasios Kollias and co-authors tested whether a handheld neck ultrasound adds value to standard heart risk scoring in middle-aged adults. Their 2026 study applied routine carotid ultrasonography with the SCORE2 model, which estimates ten-year cardiovascular risk from usual factors, to guide prevention decisions in a contemporary general population. The question was whether seeing plaque in the neck arteries would change who gets treated.

Carotid plaque reclassified risk upward beyond usual factors for decisions about lipid-lowering drugs, diabetes status, and blood pressure treatment. Among people not taking lipid-lowering drugs, a third had plaque and qualified to start a statin. Among those not on blood pressure drugs, about a third had plaque, with a quarter of that group hypertensive and eligible for therapy. Even among treated patients, most with plaque still had uncontrolled cholesterol. The authors argue that a quick scan can sharpen prevention choices.
pmc-13324202:
Fatemeh Dadashzadeh, Saeid Mehri, Alireza Mirzaei, and Aghil Habibi Soola study nursing leadership in Ardabil, Iran, in a 2026 paper. The leadership style examined, integral nursing leadership, draws on Wilber's integral framework and aims to align staff with shared goals. Four hundred fifty nurses from five university hospitals answered surveys between November 2024 and January 2025. A leadership scale was paired with single questions on job satisfaction and intent to leave.

Job satisfaction correlated strongly and negatively with the wish to leave, as expected. The study then measured how leadership scores tracked with both outcomes. Hospital systems everywhere struggle to keep nurses, so evidence that a leadership style holds staff has direct budget and care consequences.
pmc-13325902:
Nicolas Y. Jolivet and team combined FRET sensors with super-resolution microscopy to watch kinase activity at the nanoscale. Their 2026 paper presents BioSenSRRF, which pairs standard Förster resonance energy transfer sensors with super-resolution radial wobbles imaging. It needs no change to probes and runs on standard setups with open tools. Kinases control signals in tiny zones, but standard FRET sensors lack the spatial detail to map them.

Applied to Aurora kinase A, a regulator of cell-power work, the method revealed that cell-power activation and work are kept apart in zones containing ATP synthase. These zones depended on the kinase's chemical work and shifted under validated inhibitors. The cancer-linked F31I variant further boosted switching-on and ATP production on ATP synthase zones. The authors present BioSenSRRF as a widely open plan for picking apart how kinases organize in cells and drive body work and disease.
pmc-13326102:
Zhengyue Hong, Hengtao Li, and Yan Zhang present a database in 2026 for a rare class of bacterial proteins. These proteins carry an unusual building block that cells insert by re-reading a stop signal. That double duty makes the genes easy to miss or mislabel in genome records, above all in bacteria.

Their database, BSepDB, curates the genes and proteins in one place. Version one holds over 57,000 entries from 16,621 bacterial species, the largest set of its kind. Users can browse, search, run a match tool, and download data in bulk. Links to big genome banks help fix labels in large projects.
pmc-13326202:
Weipu Zou and three co-authors report a single case of fixing a faulty vein valve without destroying the vein. Their 2026 case study covers a sixty-year-old man with varicose veins and itching in his left leg. Scans confirmed that the top valve of his surface vein leaked, letting blood flow backward.

Guided by ultrasound, the team injected a gel filler around the outside of the valve to reshape it. Scans right after the shot showed the backward flow had stopped. At three months a brief leak had returned, and by twelve months the leak passed the normal limit again. No harm came from the procedure. The authors say the vein-saving trick works short term, but its lasting worth is unproven.
pmc-13326302:
Ephrem Kedir, Temesgen Teklu Alemayehu, and Mihiretu Tesfamriam Goshu present a study from twenty twenty-six on cesarean births at a hospital in southern Ethiopia. A cesarean late in labor, in the second stage, is hard surgery and risks more harm. The team matched outcomes for first stage and second stage cases among term women over six months in twenty twenty-four.

Just over two thirds had first stage surgery. Harm rates ran near a quarter for mothers and near a third for babies. Second stage surgery carried far higher odds of harm for both mother and baby. The team urges strong readiness for surgical snags and fast baby revival in late cases.
pmc-13327102:
Maria Milo and co-authors describe a 2026 case in which one heart clot caused two emergencies at once. A 41-year-old man with an earlier heart attack arrived with sudden numbness on his left side. Tests showed fresh heart muscle injury plus a new 10 mm clot at the tip of the left ventricle.

Brain imaging confirmed a large stroke at the back of the brain, and heart magnetic resonance imaging showed a second, fresh heart attack low in the back wall. The old front artery stent was blocked, while other stents stayed open, pointing to clot travel as the shared cause. Blood thinners were started and later scans showed no bleeding, showing how wide imaging can link separate events to one source.
pmc-13327402:
Omar Afroz, Raja Babu Ramawat, and Siddharth Sarkar examine drug price gaps in a 2026 cost study from India. They compared brand prices for essential psychiatric medicines on the national essential list with the low-cost generics sold under the Janaushadhi scheme. Price data came from a standard drug index and the scheme's own database.

Variation among brands ran from 20.8 percent for carbamazepine liquid up to 1604.4 percent for clonazepam 0.5 mg tablets, and median brand prices sat above the generic prices throughout. Escitalopram 10 mg showed the widest ratio, costing over seven times the generic version. Wide gaps like these can push poorer patients to skip doses, so the authors press for wider use of the cheap scheme.
pmc-13327802:
Yuichi Kato and co-authors test knee-watching cameras as a movement alarm during prostate radiotherapy in a 2026 study. Patients can shift without knowing it, and constant X-ray checks add dose, so surface guidance offers a gentler option. The team tracked knees as the watched region in 125 patients across 2,527 treatment sessions.

Movement of at least 4 mm showed up in 357 sessions, 14.1 percent of the total, grew more common late in sessions, and often hinted at a full bladder or urge to urinate. Bladder volume predicted both average shift and the share of large shifts. One patient's motion eased after a spoken prompt, showing the value of live detection for keeping dose on target.
pmc-13327902:
Tao Jian and colleagues uncover a scaffold protein that steers gut macrophages in colitis in a 2026 study. Macrophages drive both damage and repair in the inflamed bowel, but what sets their stance was unclear. Using a chemical colitis model in mice, the team focused on the protein AF6.

AF6 pushed macrophages toward the inflammatory M1 state by helping the JAK-STAT3 signal pair form, and removing AF6 from macrophages weakened that signal. Mice lacking AF6 in those cells fared better, and their macrophages made more IL-10, which switched on Wnt signals that grew gut lining in lab organoids. Blocking the AF6 axis could break the loop of inflammation and failed repair, the authors suggest.
pmc-13328402:
Luca Jokic and co-authors test overlooked light colors on basil photosynthesis in a 2026 study. Growers long assumed green light feeds plants poorly, based on old action spectra, and most trials still use just three standard wavelengths. The team measured fluorescence and gas exchange in basil under extra colors at strengths up to 5000 units on their irradiance scale.

Colors inside the supposed green gap gave the highest carbon dioxide uptake rates, ahead of deep blue and reddish light, a surprise against textbook ranking. Topping white light with shorter wavelengths worked best at a 25 percent share in the blends tried. Fine color tuning could raise yields in indoor farms, the authors suggest.
pmc-13328902:
Bushu Harna, Dinesh Sandal, and Shivali Arya review salvage hip replacement after failed thigh bone nails in a 2026 study. Nails are often used for breaks between the hip and shaft, but screws can cut out, slip back, or break, and bones may fail to heal. The group studied 59 patients who later had hip replacement.

Surgeons used either partial or full hip replacement, chosen for each patient. Removing old hardware and filling bone gaps made surgery hard. Problems after surgery included dislocation, deep vein clots, and new breaks near the implant. Average hip function at 24 months reached a Harris Hip Score of 79.2 in the reported follow-up. Careful choice and technique matter, the authors conclude.
pmc-13329502:
Jianguang Li and a large team test a plant tannin feed for broiler chickens in a 2026 trial. Tannic acids from Chinese gallnuts were added to feed as limits on antibiotic growth promoters grow. In total, 224 one-day-old male Ross 308 chicks were housed in 28 cages for a 35-day trial with four diets.

Diets were plain feed, plain feed plus one of two antibiotics, or plain feed plus the gallnut product. The gallnut diet improved feed conversion in early growth phases compared with plain feed in the reported results. Gut lining height rose and surface thickness fell, hinting at better uptake. Gut microbe diversity did not shift. The authors present the additive as a useful feed option.
pmc-13329902:
Lauren Fields and five co-authors map neuropeptide diversity in two newly sequenced crustacean genomes and link the signals to feeding. These small signal molecules run much of body function and behavior, but for many species they are still not well mapped, since genome notes are thin. The blue crab and the Jonah crab are widely used model organisms, and both now have new genomes.

A search of the genomes with a curated precursor database yields more than 23,000 candidate peptides across both genomes. Mass spectrometry confirms many and shows a wide range of forms, with new hormone isoforms and the first natalisin report in the Jonah crab. One precursor oddly encodes two distinct peptide families. A feeding test then shows shifts in levels, by tissue, in nerve centers and hormone release organs.
pmc-13330302:
Juanjuan Hu and co-authors describe newborn thyroid screening in Gansu, China, in a 2026 study. Congenital hypothyroidism stunts development if missed, and cases split into a passing form and a permanent form that needs lifelong care. Telling them apart early guides treatment.

The team reviewed over 757,000 newborns screened from 2019 to 2021 at the provincial center. Blood spot tests flagged babies for confirmatory checks, and 332 were confirmed with the condition. After treatment response tests, cases were classed as passing or permanent. The paper compares the two groups' clinical traits and hunts for risk factors that mark the permanent form.
pmc-13330802:
Daniel Schwarte and colleagues report two tin compounds and an unusual decay path in a 2026 crystal study. A 1 to 3 mix of isopropyltin iodide with pyridine N-oxide formed a previously unknown complex. Left in solvent over long storage, part of it broke down into a mixed tin(IV) and tin(II) salt, claimed as the first of its kind.

Both compounds are ionic, the authors report. Each holds an octahedral tin cation with three base molecules in a facial layout and two iodine atoms side by side. Balance comes from a lone iodide in the first salt and from a tri-iodide tin(II) anion in the second. That anion links into chains through weak tetrel bonds.
pmc-13331902:
Dragoș-Cătălin Vovea and Vasile Chiș built a 2026 machine learning model that predicts how long organic dye molecules keep glowing after excitation, a property called fluorescence lifetime. Measuring it in the lab is slow, so a fast estimate could speed screening for imaging probes, sensors, and light-based devices.

They trained tree-based models on molecule and solvent data from the Deep4Chem database, encoding structure with computed descriptors and fingerprints plus features for how molecule and solvent interact. LightGBM performed best, reaching a mean error of 0.8324 ns and an R² of 0.7523 under cluster-split cross-checks, with the weakest accuracy at very short and very long lifetimes where data are sparse. Checks against quantum calculations and fresh experiments supported the trends, and importance analysis pointed to quantum yield and molecular shape as leading drivers.
pmc-13332002:
Yasunori Matsuzaki and colleagues spent a decade testing virus shells meant to carry genes across the blood-brain barrier, and report the head-to-head results in marmosets in 2026. Gene delivery into the whole brain could help many brain diseases, but most engineered adeno-associated virus capsids were proven only in mice.

Using one shared protocol, the team gave eleven capsid variants, mostly derived from AAV9, plus plain AAV9 by vein injection and measured reporter glow across the whole brain. Most celebrated variants, including ones from their own screening, did no clearly better than AAV9 in the primates. One, VCAP-102, stood out with far stronger brain-wide expression, more vector copies in the cortex, and most marked cells being neurons. The authors offer the comparison as a benchmark and VCAP-102 as a leading candidate for whole-brain gene therapy.
pmc-13332402:
Patrick J Lao and a large team used three kinds of brain scan in a 2026 study to test whether inflammation sits between amyloid, tau, and tissue loss in Alzheimer's disease. Microglia, the brain's resident immune cells, can turn chronically hostile, and the team measured their density with a dedicated PET tracer.

The study covered 46 people, 21 thinking normally and 25 impaired, all scanned for amyloid, tau, microglia, and grey matter volume across 13 regions. In impaired participants, high microglia density overlapped with tau in 10 regions. That is more than with amyloid in 8 or shrinkage in 4. Statistical paths showed inflammation carrying part of tau's link to tissue loss. In people without amyloid, tau-linked damage still ran through inflammation. The authors suggest glial cells as a treatment target against tau-driven decline.
pmc-13333302:
Yu Liang and colleagues compare 2026 anti-CD20 therapies with steroids in IgA kidney disease with minimal change disease. In this combined disease, the efficacy of anti-CD20 antibodies and the profile of nephrin antibodies remain poorly understood. The retrospective cohort compared anti-CD20 antibodies, or combined short-course low-dose steroids, against full-dose prolonged steroids, and measured nephrin-antibody rate. Forty-five adult patients with the combined disease were studied.

Total remission rates for nephrotic syndrome were comparable between the antibody group and the steroid group. Notably, the antibody group achieved a longer relapse-free period after complete remission, a median of about thirty months versus about seventeen months. The antibody group also had significantly fewer total adverse events and return hospital stays. Nephrin antibodies in blood were detected in about thirty-one percent of patients tested.
pmc-13333402:
Magali de Sauvage and Jeffrey Patterson-Fortin describe a rare chemotherapy side effect in a 2026 case report: a painful vulvar reaction after a single cycle of treatment for rectal cancer. Mouth sores are a familiar cost of fluoropyrimidine drugs, but vulvar involvement is almost unheard of.

The 53-year-old woman had stage IIA rectal adenocarcinoma and was receiving modified FOLFOX-6 before surgery when the acute mucocutaneous reaction appeared. A low-strength steroid cream failed and pain grew, so care stepped up to a high-strength steroid cream, topical lidocaine, and vaginal estradiol. Timing and appearance pointed to a drug reaction, possibly a fixed drug eruption. The team then dropped the 5-fluorouracil bolus from later cycles while keeping the rest of the plan, and she finished all planned rounds with no return of the reaction. The authors say the tweak preserved treatment strength while preventing a repeat.
pmc-13333802:
Sujitha and Venkatasalam build a self-supervised system that spots defects in woven fabric without labeled examples of flaws. Factory inspection must catch small faults at high speed, and faulty samples are costly to gather. Older methods also lose fine texture detail, which causes missed defects and false alarms.

Their network, STDAN, splits each fabric image into a clean texture base and leftover anomaly cues. A generative module then magnifies hidden irregularities within the features, not the pixels. A contrastive training goal pulls normal textures together and pushes amplified defects apart. On public benchmarks, the system beat leading unsupervised and GAN-based rivals, above all on small, subtle defects.
pmc-13334002:
Feng-Ming Ou and co-authors designed a nine-speed bicycle hub with magnet-assisted shifting in a 2026 paper. The hub packs a planetary gear train inside the rear wheel. A rotary shifting mechanism changes ratios in a tight space. Permanent magnets help the shift snap cleanly.

Their method walks through structure, gear stages, tooth counts, and clutches. Four low gears, one direct gear, and four high gears result. Computer simulations confirmed the design works and holds together. Key performance numbers were checked analytically. Compact gearboxes for bikes and small machines could borrow the same design tricks.
pmc-13334402:
Diwakar Suresh and colleagues test 2026 whether aiming at AATF rewires the tumor surroundings and curbs liver cancer through MIR100HG-TGF-beta signals. Liver cancer, a leading cause of cancer death, has a dynamic and varied tumor surroundings driving progression and treatment resistance. The team earlier showed that cell-death-blocking gene factor AATF drives blood vessel growth in liver cancer, yet its role in the surroundings remained unstudied. A mouse model implanted human liver cancer cells into the liver.

Liver switching off was achieved by tail vein injection of adeno-associated virus 8 carrying mouse siAATF or siControl. Tissue, chemical, and molecular studies plus whole-genome gene readouts mapped to mouse and human genomes studied tumor and surroundings parts apart. Switching off AATF in the surroundings clearly reduced tumor growth versus controls and disrupted inflammation, immune response, blood vessel growth, and outer matrix reshaping.
pmc-13335202:
Na Su and co-authors built in 2026 a field test for a virus that bleeds Chinese rice-field eels to death on fish farms. The test marries two molecular tricks: a fast copy method that works at one temperature, and a CRISPR protein that flashes a signal only on the true target. Farms need answers on site, not after shipping samples away.

The assay detects as few as ten copies per microliter. It stayed silent against five other aquatic viruses and repeated within tight margins. On twenty-six farm samples it flagged six positives where the standard lab test found four. The authors call it sensitive, specific, and friendly enough for pond-side use. Early detection, they argue, is the cheapest defense against mass die-offs.
pmc-13335402:
Nur Aziemah Mohd Fauzi and co-authors checked the quality of health literacy questionnaires used with Asian schoolchildren in a 2026 full review. Many instruments exist, but weak measurement properties can make their scores meaningless.

Using PRISMA guidance, the team searched three sources for studies from 2013 to 2023 involving children aged 6 to 18 that graded measurement quality. Ten studies made the cut and were judged with the COSMIN checklist. Across 90 checklist items, only 25 rated very good, concentrated in structural validity, while internal consistency drew the most inadequate ratings and reliability the most doubtful ones. The patchy record tells schools and researchers to choose tools with care and to demand better proof before trusting scores.
pmc-13336002:
