Katarzyna Kuncewicz and colleagues present 2026 AI-designed cyclic peptides enabling controllable modulation of the CD28 immune checkpoint. Immune checkpoint treatments have transformed immune therapy but remain dominated by bio agents characterized by long receptor hold and limited drug control. Although multiple classes of immune-tuning drugs exist, synthetic types capable of directly targeting outside-cell immune checkpoint protein-protein contact points while enabling controllable immune modulation remain less explored.

The authors report an AI-guided strategy for discovering cyclic peptide blockers of the helper receptor CD28. The lead peptide, CIP-3, binds the CD28 outside-cell domain with tight binding and breaks CD28-ligand interactions. In primary human immune systems, CIP-3 blocks CD28-dependent T-cell firing without built-in agonist activity and exhibits rapid drug switch-off, enabling dose control of immune signals. In a T-cell transfer model of chronic colitis, CIP-3 confers dose-based defense.
pmc-13336102:
Michael Haug and co-authors unveiled the MyoRobot 3.0, a 2026 biomechatronics platform that measures single muscle fibers while watching them. Older rigs assumed a fiber keeps its shape during stretch, an assumption this device was built to test.

The system couples automated force measurement with a motorized optical setup that tracks the same fiber segment as it elongates. Stretching fibers to 40 percent strain thinned their diameter by about 13 to 15 percent, cutting cross-sectional area by roughly 27 percent and making uncorrected stress values systematically too low. Slow continuous stretch recordings revealed calcium-dependent stiffening that rapid step protocols missed entirely. The platform gives muscle physiologists a way to pair exact structure with function in one experiment.
pmc-13336502:
Wang Jun and co-authors trace in 2026 how a common cancer drug hurts the heart, and how a plant compound may stop it. The drug, doxorubicin, can damage heart muscle in a dose-linked way that caps its use. The team found the harm starts not in heart muscle cells but in the cells lining heart vessels.

Those lining cells sense the drug first and switch on an alarm path, they report. The alarm sets off a fire-like cell death and sheds vesicles that wreck power parts in nearby muscle cells, looping the harm. The plant compound blocks the alarm's core part directly, in a new way, guarding muscle cells at one remove. Aiming upstream at vessel cells may reshape how this heart harm is treated.
pmc-13336702:
Peng Liu and co-authors build a brain-mimicking gel for traumatic brain injury in a 2026 study. Low oxygen and inflammation drive much of the damage that follows the first impact. A danger signal called S100A8 fuels harmful talk between neurons and microglia, the brain's immune cells. Their gel, HPC@Gel, carries altered hemoglobin particles plus curcumin-based carbon dots.

In cell models the gel lowered S100A8 and calmed the neuron-microglia crosstalk; adding S100A8 back partly undid the benefit. In rats with a cortical injury, the gel eased low oxygen, cut inflammation, and supported nerve regrowth. Treated animals recovered better movement and thinking. Aiming at oxygen and immune signals together offers a fuller repair strategy.
pmc-13336802:
Take Hirooka, Zhaolin Liu, Ivan P Parkin, and Guanjie He review carbon cathodes for zinc-ion hybrid supercapacitors in a 2026 article. These water-based devices promise safe, cheap storage that blends battery-like energy with capacitor-like power and long life. The cathode largely sets performance, and porous carbons lead the field.

The review sorts recent cathode families, from activated and template-made carbons to framework-derived and biomass-derived ones. It weighs how pore shape, surface chemistry, and conductivity shape zinc storage. Added atoms and hybrid mixes get critical attention as routes to higher output. Gaps remain in pore control and in understanding how storage really works. The survey charts design rules for cheaper, safer grid and portable storage.
pmc-13337002:
Yu-E. Wang and co-authors build a self-fueling nanoplatform against colon cancer in a 2026 study. Their hollow manganese dioxide particles carry a lactate-burning enzyme and a light-sensitive dye, coated to home to tumor cells bearing CD44. Tumors hoard lactate, so burning it both starves them and reshapes their surroundings.

The enzyme turns lactate into pyruvate and hydrogen peroxide, which react with the carrier to release oxygen. Acid speeds the carrier's breakdown, freeing dye and manganese ions. Near-infrared light then drives dye-based heat and radical therapy while manganese sparks more radicals. The loop feeds itself, easing low oxygen as it attacks. Strong tumor suppression in animals supports metabolism-first cancer therapy.
pmc-13337402:
Haider H. Motlak, Mahmoud Elshal, and Marwa S. Serrya test a liver shield against a common drug's toxicity in a 2026 rat study. Methotrexate fights cancer and calms immunity, but dose-linked liver damage limits its use. The team induced injury with one injection and gave the NLRP3 blocker dapansutrile by mouth for seven days.

Methotrexate alone spiked liver enzymes, scarred tissue under the microscope, drained antioxidants, and fired inflammatory pathways that end in a fiery cell death called pyroptosis. It also stalled the liver's recycling system. Dapansutrile at both tested doses eased nearly every measure, damping oxidation, cytokines, and cell death while restoring recycling balance. The results nominate inflammasome blocking as a companion strategy for methotrexate users.
pmc-13337602:
Heinrich and co-authors grade PET scans for tumors that cause tumor-induced osteomalacia. These small phosphaturic tumors waste phosphate and soften bone. The study held 20 patients with suspected disease at one center. Scans targeted somatostatin receptors on tumor cells. Lab marks and clinical exams were tracked at follow-up visits.

Tumors were found in 12 patients, or 60 percent of the group. Those tumors were removed and confirmed by immunohistochemistry. Phosphate handling marks ran lower when tumors were found. FGF23 rise did not split the two groups clearly. Total lesion uptake tied inversely to phosphate recovery marks.
pmc-13337702:
Yun Zheng heads a 2026 search for better blood markers of rheumatoid arthritis. Lasting joint inflammation in this autoimmune disease slowly damages joints, and current markers lack accuracy. The team combined large gene datasets with single-cell data to find stronger candidates.

Machine learning and expression checks pointed to three genes: CD74, PGLYRP1, and TXN. Further work mapped their pathways, immune setting, and possible drug binding, using docking and motion simulations. Single-cell data showed which cell groups carried the signals. Tests on clinical samples with PCR, blotting, and tissue staining confirmed the pattern, supporting the three genes as candidate markers for diagnosis and study.
pmc-13337802:
Lynn A. Cialdella-Kam and co-authors evaluate a phone app for new Navy recruits in a 2026 study. Future Sailors in the Delayed Entry Program must build fitness and knowledge before basic training. The CoachMePlus app delivered general training, nutrition, and exercise modules with recruiter tracking.

A total of 92 recruits aged 18 to 28 enrolled, logging in about twice daily on average. Weight and body fat were checked monthly, and food logs were reviewed by a dietitian. Most recruits, 92.4 percent in the reported count, finished basic training. Knowledge of training and nutrition improved during the program, supporting app-guided preparation before service begins.
pmc-13338202:
Sandeep Jain and co-authors train learning models in a 2026 study to predict how two added metals change the strength of a high-entropy alloy. Such alloys mix many metals and are costly to test one mix at a time. The team varied the niobium and tantalum shares in a cobalt-based alloy.

Two models, a boosted tree type and a neighbor type, forecast with high accuracy. Clever ways of building new input features pushed accuracy still higher. For a fresh mix, the models drew a sound stress-strain curve, checked in tests. The plan could cut much trial-and-error lab work.
pmc-13340102:
Magdalena Harris and co-authors study crack pipe practice and lung harm in England. Their 2026 mixed-methods paper reports the baseline stage of a trial of safer inhalation equipment. Giving out gear for stimulant inhalation is banned under United Kingdom law, even as crack use rises across the country.

Seven hundred twenty-seven people who had smoked crack in the past month took the baseline survey, recruited through drug services and peer networks at six sites. Thirty-three also gave deep interviews. Over half used crack daily, and a minority also injected it. The authors place the survey numbers beside interview accounts of daily pipe practice. Their aim is to show how the equipment ban shapes risk on the ground.
pmc-13340202:
Chapter 11 of a reference work on fish lesions, published in 2026, covers the respiratory system. Wes Baumgartner leads a large author team describing how gills work and how they change in disease. Beyond moving oxygen and carbon dioxide, gills also clear nitrogen waste, balance salts, and guard against harmful agents in the water.

Readers learn how gill cells such as mucous and chloride cells adjust to shifts in gases, temperature, pH, and pollutants. Crucian carp show how gills can remodel when oxygen falls, while pollution can shrink the exchange surface through extra pavement cells and mucus. For pathologists, these responses help separate normal adaptation from damage.
pmc-13341502:
Pairing a black seed compound with standard chemotherapy rewires death pathways in colon cancer cells, in a 2026 study by Natalia Kurowska and colleagues. RKO cells received thymoquinone, 5-fluorouracil, or both for 24 hours before genome-wide expression profiling.

The combination reshaped networks for apoptosis, stress response, and proliferation without classic synergy in the math sense. Genes such as FAS and CYLD tied into stronger death signaling, while BIRC3 and EIF2AK3 marked adaptive, resistance-leaning responses. Validation by PCR and protein blotting backed the array data. Thymoquinone looks less like a direct killer and more like a context-dependent tuner of drug response.
pmc-13341602:
Why reinforcement learning struggles outside simulations is organized by Amar Ahmad and coauthors in their 2026 tutorial survey. Systems that beat humans at games still falter in the real world, and the authors blame four statistical limits rather than engineering gaps.

The four are sample inefficiency, nonstationarity as environments shift, partial observability that breaks the Markov assumption, and dimensionality that explodes exploration needs. Known lower bounds from theory are reviewed for each, plus mitigations like model-based methods, robust formulations, memory architectures, and hierarchies. Safety, explainability, and multi-agent issues are flagged as related but distinct concerns for deployment.
pmc-13342102:
A large team of researchers tests a blood method for spotting pregnancy risk in a paper from 2026. The risk is preeclampsia, a dangerous rise in blood pressure during pregnancy. Tiny bits of DNA float freely in a mother's blood, and their break patterns carry signals. The team built stable measures from those patterns using deep gene reading.

More than one thousand pregnant women took part in the study. The DNA measures alone separated women who later developed the illness from those who did not. Adding known risk factors made the models stronger still. Samples taken by week sixteen already worked well. The authors see a path to much earlier warning for mothers.
pmc-13343402:
Marta Goglia and co-authors open volume two of a research collection on proctology and colorectal surgery with a 2026 editorial. Colorectal care is shifting fast. Robotic and keyhole methods, dye-guided surgery, enhanced recovery paths, and precision cancer plans are all spreading. The editors frame the gathered studies within that change.

The studies span checks before surgery, new tools in the operating room, recovery care, cancer prediction, and hard cases. One highlighted study uses MRI markers in rectal cancer to flag aggressive features and tailor treatment tiers. Aging patients, frailty, and new tools such as immunotherapy and artificial intelligence raise complexity throughout. The editors cast modern colorectal care as personal, team-based, and guided by biology.
pmc-13343602:
Clare Nakubulwa, Deogratius Galagala, and Ivan Gidudu report a rare case of a severe skin reaction in a young child. Their case report, from twenty twenty-six, deals with toxic epidermal necrolysis. In this state, skin and moist linings peel off over a wide area after a drug. A one year old girl from east Uganda came in two days after a furosemide shot. The peel spread over her face, trunk, and limbs.

The peel covered sixty percent of her body surface. The team gave support care and she first got better. But her parents then left the hospital against medical advice. Readers learn how this rare drug reaction can hit a small child and how hard its care can be.
pmc-13344202:
Anna Marie Pacheco Young and colleagues tested perinatal quality drives in 2026 for reducing caesarean gaps in the United States. Racial and ethnic gaps exist in caesarean rates and reasons, prompting quality drives targeting drivers of inequity. Few studies had assessed whether those drives actually narrow gaps.

The look back cohort took in 3,629 first time mothers with full term, live born, singleton pregnancies in vertex position. They delivered at a large academic tertiary centre from October 2019 through December 2022. Caesarean rates and reasons before and after perinatal quality drives, aimed at more vaginal births and fairer care, were weighed. The study tests whether quality improvement can close equity gaps in childbirth.
pmc-13344602:
Sayan Gupta and co-authors describe a new synchrotron beamline built for X-ray footprinting of proteins. Their 2026 report covers design and first use at the Advanced Light Source. The method maps protein shape in solution by marking exposed side chains with radicals made by X-rays.

Marks are then read by mass tools, and changes between two protein states reveal shape shifts. The new line adds a fresh focusing mirror and an end station with automated sample handling. Dose is set with care using film measures. Two protein systems show off the line's power. A dedicated line ends years of shared, part-time access for users of this method in the United States.
pmc-13345802:
Ricardo Ortiz-Lozada and Pablo Salinas argue, in a 2026 commentary, that better stents alone will not fix coronary intervention outcomes in diabetes. Trial history shows each new design's edge fading against this biology. The authors urge unified care: best drug therapy and healthy habits wrapped around any device, rather than chasing innovation in hardware alone.
pmc-13346502:
Capela and co-authors study how cattle breeds handle heat stress in a 2026 paper. Heat harms cattle health and output, and breeds differ in tolerance. The team compared two tolerant local breeds with a sensitive dairy breed, sampling cows after summer and winter calving. They measured body temperatures, hair cortisol as a long-term stress marker, and blood heat shock proteins.

Heat shock proteins help cells survive stress, but their link to cortisol differed by breed. Some proteins rose with heat load only in the tolerant breeds. Others fell as both heat and cortisol rose, with the pattern flipping in one breed. The authors conclude that each breed shows its own response profile. Such profiles could guide breeding and care as summers grow hotter.
pmc-13346602:
A car's active suspension must react fast, yet delays in its commands and bumps it cannot foresee fight against smoothness. Pengfei Zhang and two co-authors design a controller in 2026 that watches the car through a special observer, guessing the hidden speeds and forces as they change. A gain that adapts on the fly does the steering.

One term in the design cancels the effect of the unknown delay, while another absorbs outside disturbance. Math proofs show every signal in the loop stays bounded, so the ride cannot spiral out of control. A worked example backs the design. The authors offer the method for suspensions that must stay steady despite late commands.
pmc-13347002:
Shunyu Yao, writing alone and listed for 2026, tackles fast spotting of hot spots in dry-type flexible cable terminals. Overheating faults raise failure risk, and the hot spots are small targets in busy aerial infrared images.

Yao defines four types of hot spots and builds an improved You Only Look Once model for the task. New blocks sharpen how the model shows key features and focus on small areas, while a lighter block cuts its size. The model beat its base version and other models in the same family. It met the speed need for real-time checks, the author reports.
pmc-13347802:
Kamilla R. Snyman, Jacques R. Snyman, and Angelique Coetzee compare iron products for treating low iron, in a prescribing review published in 2026. Iron drives oxygen carriage, DNA building, and energy flow, yet excess harms tissue. Shortage is the most common mineral lack, touching about 20 percent of people worldwide by the cited estimate.

Anaemia shares tied to iron lack are given for young children and women, noting that low iron without anaemia is even more common in clinic visits. The review weighs how well each iron complex works and how well patients tolerate it, aiming for patient-centred choices rather than habit picks when doctors write iron prescriptions.
pmc-13348402:
Muritala Issa Bale and colleagues report a draft genome for a drug-resistant staph strain from a caesarean wound in Nigeria, in an announcement from 2026. Strain MB02 was swabbed in July 2024 from a 32-year-old woman at a teaching hospital in Ogbomoso, grown on selective agar. Confirmed by stain and enzyme tests before sequencing, with disk tests showing wide drug resistance.

Surgical wounds after caesarean birth give skin staph an easy entry, and resistant strains can drive deep infection, wound opening, and body-wide spread in the risk picture given. The public draft supports tracking of resistance and harm genes for stewardship and outbreak watch in maternity care.
pmc-13349002:
Simon Londono and co-authors told in 2026 of an aortic dissection spotted at the bedside with suprasternal notch ultrasound in a 73-year-old man. Early spotting is vital since dissection can be elusive. Yet this ultrasound view remains little used in emergency departments.

The man, with hypertension, high cholesterol, smoking past, and a known aortic aneurysm, came in with two hours of severe left chest pain plus leg pain, numbness, and weakness. Checks found an odd slow pulse and an absent leg pulse, while a standard ultrasound view showed a dilated aortic root. The suprasternal view, done by an intern, clearly showed an intimal flap. CT confirmed a Stanford type A dissection needing urgent surgical transfer.
pmc-13349202:

This is a life-threatening syndrome of excess immune firing and cytokine storm. Secondary HLH most often follows malignancy, autoimmunity, or infection. Checks found liver inflammation, low blood counts, and an enlarged spleen. Testing confirmed acute cytomegalovirus infection, though at low viral levels. pmc-13349402:

Quality-controlled reads were aligned to the reference genome and analysed for pathway enrichment. pmc-13350002:

pmc-13350702:
Xinying Yu, Jian Chen, and Xiao Liu compare scope-based dissection with surgery for early stomach cancer of the signet-ring type in a 2026 multi-center study. pmc-13350802:
Yuxin He and Jian'an Wang wrote a 2026 editorial on electrosurgical leaflet modification during catheter aortic valve replacement. A feared complication is the new valve's frame or the old leaflet blocking a coronary artery, a risk growing as younger patients and repeat procedures become common.

pmc-13351402:

pmc-13351702:

pmc-13351902:

pmc-13352402:
Patrick G. Kelly and co-authors test how reliable fNIRS brain data are during a reasoning task in 2026. pmc-13352602:
Magavern and a team including Caulfield survey a British South Asian community on personalised prescribing in twenty twenty-six. Genetic testing can tailor drug choice and dose to each patient. pmc-13352802:
Min Zhang and co-authors review how Chinese law deals with violence against health workers, a risk they call a global job hazard. pmc-13352902:
Jiang and eight co-authors tested a training program for uneven leg strength in soldiers in twenty twenty-six. When one leg outperforms the other, injury risk rises. Integrated neuromuscular training blends strength, balance, and movement drills to correct such gaps.

pmc-13354802:

pmc-13355202:
Felice Crocetto and co-authors compared blood hormone and prostate test results in 2026 between 40 cancer-free African migrant men in Italy and 47 white controls. pmc-13355602:
Jean-Michel Halimi and Laurent Fauchier replied in 2026 to a letter questioning renal-risk guessing from high-feeling C-reactive protein in chronic kidney disease. pmc-13355802:
Omri Cohen and co-authors set kept gainst drawn vena cava nets in folks with vein clots. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-six. pmc-13356602:
Meng-Kan Chen and Chih-Cheng Wu replied in 2026 to a letter on causal interpretation in their haemodialysis blood pressure study. pmc-13357602:
Meshcheryakov and co-authors describe two swimming filaments from a salt-loving microbe, Haloarcula marismortui. Many archaea swim with rotating helical threads called archaella, about ten nanometers wide. Both filaments here carry an extra outer sheath, a trait not seen before in archaea.

pmc-13358502:
Jianxin Cai and co-authors report a 2026 study on blood signs of inflammation around lung cancer surgery. pmc-13358602:
Tongxin Li and co-authors present a 2026 study on predicting who will respond to immune therapy for throat cancer. pmc-13358702:
Winter and co-authors tested how much heat the leaves of a tropical mangrove tree can take, in a 2026 study. pmc-13359002:
Zein Kattih and co-authors review 25 years of lung transplants for sarcoidosis in a 2026 paper. Sarcoidosis can scar the lungs beyond repair, leaving transplant as the last option. Most patients had the most advanced stage of lung scarring, and nearly nine in ten also had high pressure in the lung arteries. pmc-13359502:
Maciej Gawęcki and co-authors scan the backs of eyes in a 2026 study of central serous chorioretinopathy. In this condition, fluid leaks under the retina and blurs central vision. pmc-13360002:
The journal Cells published a 2026 correction to a 2022 paper by Yair Romero and co-authors on lung fibroblasts from patients with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis. pmc-13360302:
Velizar Shivarov led a 2026 study of immune genes in a group of blood cancers called myeloproliferative neoplasms. In some patients these cancers are driven by faults in the CALR gene. pmc-13360802:

pmc-13361202:

pmc-13361702:

pmc-13362402:

pmc-13363102:

pmc-13363502:

pmc-13363902:

pmc-13364102:

pmc-13366802:

pmc-13368702:

pmc-13369702:

pmc-13371302:

pmc-13372202:

pmc-13373602:

pmc-13374202:

pmc-13376402:

pmc-13376602:

pmc-13377202:

pmc-13377702:

pmc-13380202:

pmc-13381902:

pmc-13382702:

pmc-13383402:

pmc-13383502:

pmc-13383902:

pmc-13385402:

pmc-13385802:

pmc-13386502:

pmc-13386902:

pmc-13387402:

pmc-13387702:

pmc-13387902:

pmc-13388002:

The automated settings improved motor scores by about seventy-six percent over no stimulation, statistically matching expert clinician settings and imaging-guided ones. pmc-13388702:
Tatiana A. pmc-13390402:
Padmavathy Krishna Kumar's team analysed India's rural and tribal public health capacity from 2011 to 2021 using Rural Health Statistics on sub-centres, primary health centres, and community health centres. pmc-13391002:

pmc-13391802:
Raakel Lintunen and Anselm Tamminen analyse, in 2026, whether a breast cancer diagnosis prompts women to quit smoking. Smoking raises breast cancer risk and worsens treatment outcomes, yet how quitting behaviour changes around diagnosis was not fully understood.

The retrospective study reviewed smoking status in more than six thousand consecutive patients treated from 2010 to 2022, focusing on the subgroup who smoked at diagnosis. Baseline questionnaires supplied smoking histories. The authors determine what share quit after diagnosis and which factors predicted quitting. pmc-13394102:
Vilja Vihtonen and others trace why induced births rose in Finland from 2005 to 2023 in a 2026 nation-wide birth file study. Induced birth aims to cut mother and baby harm, but gains for many common reasons are unsure, and rising rates tax health care.

All single, head-first births at or past 37 weeks went into the Finnish birth file across three spans. Shifts in mother traits, birth week, birth problems, and womb troubles were weighed, with induced births read apart. pmc-13394202:

pmc-13394802:
Kai T. Fox and colleagues review, in 2026, what cuff-based exercise may do to the brain paths that drive movement. Blood flow restriction pairs light loads with a cuff that partly blocks limb flow. pmc-13395502:
Kyu-Ho Yi and co-authors test, in 2026, filler shots that make collarbones stand out, a beauty trend in East Asia. pmc-13395902:

pmc-13396102:

pmc-13396302:

pmc-13396502:

pmc-13396602:

pmc-13396802:

pmc-13397102:

pmc-13397702:

pmc-13397802:

pmc-13398102:

pmc-13398502:

pmc-13399902:

pmc-13400102:

pmc-13400302:

pmc-13400602:

pmc-13400702:

pmc-13401302:

pmc-13401702:

pmc-13402102:

pmc-13402702:

pmc-13402802:

pmc-13403402:

pmc-13403602:

pmc-13403802:

pmc-13404202:

pmc-13404302:

pmc-13404402:

pmc-13404502:

pmc-13404702:

pmc-13406802:

pmc-13407402:

pmc-13407902:

pmc-13408602:

pmc-13408702:

pmc-13409102:

pmc-13410302:

pmc-13411102:

pmc-13411302:

pmc-13411902:

pmc-13412202:

pmc-13412302:

pmc-13412702:

pmc-13412902:

pmc-13413602:

The authors pitch the stator-free design for self-powered sensors.
pmc-13413702:

pmc-13414602:

pmc-13416202:

pmc-13416902:

pmc-13417002:
Araceli Sánchez-Ortiz and co-authors profile the scent chemicals given off by whole olives, in a 2026 study of cultivar differences and fruit damage. Lab tuning fixed the best heat, time, and sample size for trapping the volatiles. Varieties differed clearly in their scent profiles. Such fingerprints could help growers spot trouble early under a changing climate.
pmc-13418202:

pmc-13418602:

pmc-13418702:

pmc-13419302:

pmc-13420302:

pmc-13420702:

pmc-13421002:

pmc-13421202:

pmc-13421302:

pmc-13421502:

pmc-13421802:

pmc-13422702:

pmc-13423802:

pmc-13423902:

pmc-13424302:

pmc-13426402:

pmc-13427002:

pmc-13427402:

pmc-13427502:

pmc-13428002:

pmc-13429102:

pmc-13429802:

pmc-13429902:

pmc-13430202:

pmc-13430302:

Their motto, quoted from earlier statisticians, is that missing evidence is not evidence of missing harm.
pmc-13430702:

In lab dishes, cutting the gene back slowed growth and movement of cancer cells and raised cell death. The authors propose the gene as a marker for outlook and a possible drug target.
pmc-13431802:

pmc-13432202:

pmc-13432302:
Cancer patients who are lesbian, gay, bisexual, or transgender often meet care that misses their needs, and nurses deliver much of that care. Ya-Ching Wang and co-authors survey Taiwanese nurses about it in a 2026 cross-sectional study. The survey reached 608 nurses with cancer care experience through hospitals, associations, and foundations.

Nearly half had never cared for an LGBT cancer patient, a gap the authors link to confidence and training. The study measured care behaviors, the competencies behind them, and the nurses' own quality of life at work. It also asked what knowledge and skills nurses feel they lack. Working in a non-Western setting, the authors argue, exposes cultural factors that Western studies miss.
pmc-13433002:
Ammresh and colleagues refine how scientists divide a snake's backbone into regions, a question that shapes how body plans evolve. Snakes stretched the spine to hundreds of vertebrae, yet keep the regional pattern of limbed animals. Their 2026 study takes 3D scans of the columns of twelve elapid snakes. This family includes cobras and mambas. The team tests how sampling density and point schemes change which borders appear.

A model with four or five regions fit best. A short neck region spans the first few percent. A shape shift near a fifth lines up with heart position. A low back region closes the last five percent. Most lengthening happened in the chest region, which itself split into three modules. Skipping too many vertebrae erased the small regions. Sampling every two and a half percent of the column was the coarsest scheme still trustworthy.
pmc-13433802:
Mingyang Zhou and co-authors froze an RNA-tagging enzyme in 2026 with cold-scope cameras to show how it stamps a chemical mark on transfer RNA. The enzyme stands alone in its kind for this mark. Its misrule ties to cancer and to fast aging faults, yet how it grips RNA and fires stayed dim.

Frames show a twin build shaped like a heart, with the tag heart flanked by a twister part and an RNA grip part. Work with a helper protein pinned two key spots at the fire site and two charge patches that steer the RNA. Guide cuts in cells proved the fire work is a must: a fungus needed it for heat life, and mammal cells leaned on it in drug-driven aging.
pmc-13435402:
Yongliang Wang and coauthors test fitness and bone strength in 334 medical students in southwest China in 2026. Students aged 17 to 24 took six fitness tests and a heel bone scan. Han and minority students were both included, reflecting the region mix.

Men showed more overweight and more thin bones than women by the counts here. Students at normal weight scored fittest overall, in a curved pattern. Han and minority students did not differ on fitness or bone marks. Muscle strength best foretold bone strength in both sexes. Sit ups led for women, while pull ups led for men. Campus programs should build strength, not just cut weight.
pmc-13436002:
Hamza Sayadi and coauthors validate dosing math for dalbavancin, a long acting antibiotic, in 2026. Routine drug level data from 183 adults built a fresh model of how the drug moves through the body. A second group of thirty patients tested the model cold.

Kidney function and body weight drove drug clearance in the best model. Blending five prior models with two drug checks gave the sharpest forecasts. Repeat dose simulations held targets for three to seven weeks by patient type. A third timed dose restored cover for all groups. Long cures for bone and joint infections gain a dosing compass.
pmc-13436102:
Jorik Vergauwen's team compared diabetes care in 2026 across ten European countries using a cascade from diagnosis to treatment to control. Gaps persist even in wealthy nations, and population mix may explain part of the spread. The team drew on over eighteen thousand adults aged fifty and older from a European ageing survey. Diabetes was defined by report, medication, or blood sugar marker, and each cascade stage was tracked with adjusted models.

Prevalence ranged from thirteen percent in Denmark to thirty-seven percent in Spain and Greece, with up to forty percent undiagnosed, and only thirty-five to fifty percent of people with diabetes reached control. Belgium led across stages, while Greece treated and controlled well despite low diagnosis. Health systems get a cross-country scorecard that points first at finding undiagnosed cases.
pmc-13436602:
Boskabadi and co-authors compare schizophrenia patients in this 2026 cross-sectional study. They group patients by whether they have ever received long-acting injectable antipsychotics. These depot shots release medication over weeks. They bypass the daily pill adherence problem. The Iranian inpatient sample covered adults aged 18 to 65. All were diagnosed under standard psychiatric criteria.

Seventy patients entered the final analysis. Thirty-six had injectable experience, and 34 were treated only with oral medication. Symptom severity scores, global impression ratings, and lab markers did not differ between the groups at admission. The injectable group instead stood out historically. It had significantly longer illness duration and more previous hospitalizations. It also had much greater exposure to older first-generation antipsychotics at higher equivalent doses. The pattern suggests injectables reach patients later and sicker in this setting. The authors call for research on earlier versus delayed initiation.
pmc-13437202:
Thanh Duy Nguyen and Woojin Yi, writing in 2026, build on a review by Kim and colleagues about imaging in obesity care. Their letter argues the next task is not wider use of scans alone but shared rules for how scans confirm excess body fat. New guidance from a 2025 Lancet commission urges doctors to move beyond body mass index and back it with direct measures of fat.

Scans such as CT, MRI, and DXA can measure deep belly fat and fat stored in organs. Yet clinics still differ on body landmarks, single slice versus whole volume measures, tracing methods, and cutoff values. Imaging can also grade muscle amount and quality in the same pass, and weak, fatty muscle predicts poor outcomes after major surgery and in pancreatic cancer. The letter asks for standard capture, analysis, and reading rules so imaging can guide diagnosis and treatment fairly.
pmc-13437602:
Mengwei Yuan and colleagues measured mercury forms in semen to settle which kind actually tracks with poorer sperm? Their 2026 study collected paired semen and seminal plasma from 250 Hong Kong men aged twenty-six to sixty-three. The team split mercury into total, methyl, and inorganic forms, the last found by subtraction.

Most mercury in both fluids was inorganic, roughly two-thirds to seventy percent. Raw readings confused, since methylmercury alone rose with better semen quality. The story flipped once levels were scaled to sperm count: mercury riding with the sperm cells, in both forms, tied to worse shape and movement. The authors conclude placement matters more than total load. Mercury bound to sperm is the share that wounds them, while fluid levels mislead. They claim the first report of all three mercury forms in human semen, and urge fertility research to measure the element where it sits.
pmc-13439102:
Vanessa Neve and a large team map synapse-like links between brain cells and tanycytes, specialised glial cells of the hypothalamus, in research published in 2026. Tanycytes help tune hormone systems and body metabolism. Links shaped like synapses had been spotted on them before, yet their makeup and purpose stayed vague. The team set out to chart who connects to which tanycyte type and what those links do.

Counts showed many such links, built much like true synapses between neurons. Distinct tanycyte groups drew inputs from varied brain areas and answered to many chemical messengers. In mice, two groups of kisspeptin neurons, which drive the reproductive hormone axis, wired to separate tanycyte sets. Those routes shaped both steady levels and pulses of luteinising hormone, in patterns that differed by sex and brain region.
pmc-13439202:
Zijiang Yang's team exposed human dental pulp cells in 2026 to high glucose to see how sugar harms tooth pulp through recycling and energy pathways. Dental pulp cells were grown in control, low-glucose, and high-glucose conditions, then checked for viability, reactive oxygen, glutathione, ATP, and key autophagy and energy signals over four days. High glucose is a suspected stressor in diabetic dental disease, but pulp cell mechanisms were incompletely mapped.

High glucose raised a recycling-block marker, lowered a recycling driver, dampened AMPK signaling while raising mTOR signaling, and cut glutathione and ATP while raising reactive oxygen. The pattern points to stalled autophagy and disturbed mitochondrial balance in pulp cells under sugar stress. Dentists get a cellular mechanism linking diabetes to pulp vulnerability.
pmc-13439702:
Wyman and co-authors ask whether gene transcription itself mutates the human germline differently in males and females. Their 2026 paper starts from a puzzle: fathers pass on three to four times more new mutations than mothers, for reasons that remain largely unknown. The team combined gene expression data from germline cells with family pedigree records of brand-new mutations.

In females, mutation rates rose clearly with transcription levels in the fetal germline, in egg cells, and in ovary tissue. In males, no such link appeared in the fetal germline or adult testis overall. Looking stage by stage, expression in sperm stem cells was tied to more mutations, while expression in a later sperm-forming stage was tied to fewer. The authors conclude transcription raises mutation rates in females but has mixed, stage-dependent effects in males.
pmc-13439802:
El hassan Roussi's team evaluated nursing clinical placements in 2026 at two Moroccan public institutes, where placement quality shapes whether theory becomes practice. A sequential mixed-methods design surveyed 486 students with a validated learning environment scale, then interviewed twenty-six students, joining numbers and themes. Overall satisfaction ran low, with the weakest scores for ward manager leadership and the strongest, still modest, for nurse teacher role.

Hospital placements outscored primary care centers, and interviews blamed unsuitable environments, theory-practice gaps, weak supervision, and ineffective teacher roles. Nursing schools get a joined diagnosis for reform: placement sites, supervisors, and teacher roles need joint fixes. The two-institute scope limits national generalization.
pmc-13439902:
Rebecka O. Serpa's team tested L-DOPA in 2026 on iron release at the blood-brain barrier, a process disrupted in Parkinson disease. Brain iron excess fuels oxidative damage, yet how Parkinson drugs affect barrier iron handling was unclear. Human stem-cell-derived brain endothelial cells were used to measure iron efflux, retention, and iron-regulatory proteins under transferrin signals that normally tune release up or down.

L-DOPA strongly boosted iron release within one hour and sustained it for a day. It raised export under both iron-poor and iron-rich transferrin signals, while ferroportin fell as a likely compensatory response to depletion. Parkinson teams get a drug-effect warning: a mainstay therapy may itself shift brain iron balance. Clinical relevance needs patient-level confirmation.
pmc-13441402:
Wolfgang Uter and a large expert panel update the European Society of Contact Dermatitis guide on patch testing, publishing the 2026 update. Patch testing is the standard method for proving contact allergy in patients with allergic contact dermatitis and kindred delayed hypersensitivity conditions. Recommendations were agreed through a Delphi consensus process, where experts iterate toward shared positions. Sections pair short discussions with highlighted practical recommendations.

Coverage runs from materials and technique through test modifications, patient factors that bend results, and special groups including children, workers with job-linked skin allergy, and patients with drug eruptions. Testing substances patients bring from home gets its own guidance. Side effects of testing, final evaluation, and patient counselling close the clinical arc. The update ends with notes on training and electronic data collection for allergy tracking across Europe.
pmc-13441502:
Yuichi Hirata and colleagues describe threading two tools at once through a single delivery sheath to free a stuck bile duct stone, reporting a 2026 case. Their patient, a 75-year-old man with belly pain and liver test trouble, carried stones in the common bile duct, one wedged tight. A standard retrieval basket could not slip past the wedged stone and instead shoved it upward. The team switched approach mid-procedure.

A tapered delivery sheath was driven deep past the stone, its inner core removed, and a guidewire left reaching the liver ducts. Only the wire cage of a crushing basket then travelled up the same sheath beside the guidewire. That slim pairing reached the stone, which was removed endoscopically. Leftover fragments cleared smoothly with a balloon sweep. The authors present simultaneous two-device delivery as a way to keep duct access while still bringing crushing tools to bear.
pmc-13441702:
Zhiyuan Xu and colleagues test whether gut-made short-chain fatty acids can limit heart scarring after a heart attack, reporting mouse work in 2026. These fatty acids come from gut microbes and sway immune and metabolic behaviour. Male mice had a main heart artery tied off permanently, then received either mixed fatty acids by stomach tube from day one, a high-fibre diet that raises natural production, or neither. Blood and heart tissue were profiled at one and four weeks.

Heart attack scrambled fatty acid patterns, more clearly in blood than in heart muscle. Both interventions cut the collagen build-up that stiffens healing hearts, and both partly restored the energy stores that the attack had drained. Injury markers in blood also ran lower with treatment. A growth signal tied to scarring, by contrast, showed no clear difference. The authors link higher fatty acid availability to gentler post-attack repair.
pmc-13443202:
Juyeon Oh and colleagues report a 2026 pooled analysis asking which blood marker best tracks sudden drops in arterial oxygen in healthy volunteers. The team reanalyzed four controlled desaturation studies covering 48 volunteers and 1,194 arterial samples, as participants breathed low-oxygen gas to hold saturation between 70 and 100 percent.

Carboxyhemoglobin moved most across every saturation band and rose steadily as oxygen fell, while methemoglobin and lactate showed no reliable link. Korean volunteers showed larger carboxyhemoglobin rises than African volunteers, a pattern the authors flag as hypothesis-generating rather than settled. The marker looks promising for bedside oxygen tracking, pending tests in patients rather than volunteers.
pmc-13443602:
Yuze Ma and colleagues propose a 2026 control method for a maintenance robot arm mounted on armored vehicles, where vibration, tool changes, and unknown loads threaten steady motion. Their adaptive robust controller builds on the Udwadia-Kalaba dynamics framework and adds a leakage step that stops control gains from growing without bound under constant disturbance.

The leakage step also eases the gain once tracking errors settle, smoothing the transient response. Co-simulation in a multibody dynamics setting confirmed the design holds position reliably despite parameter uncertainty and outside disturbance. The method suits harsh field maintenance tasks, from underwater work to space station repair, pending tests on physical hardware.
pmc-13445202:
Hesamoddin Moradi and colleagues report a family of solid acid catalysts built inside tiny ordered pores, designed to speed two common reactions, in a 2026 chemistry study. The solids carry sulfonic acid groups, the active sites, on walls that mix silica with organic bridges. Some versions add plugs inside the channels, a change the team expected to keep reactants near the acid sites longer.

Four variants were made and compared with two known reference catalysts. The plugged version with ethyl bridges worked best, driving ester formation and the Biginelli reaction under mild conditions. It also kept its strength over repeated cycles of use. The authors credit the mix of bridges and plugs, which also helps push water, a reaction by-product, out of the pores.
pmc-13445502:
Sahil S. Telang and colleagues use a national database to ask whether the steroid dexamethasone, given around revision hip and knee replacement, links to fewer joint infections, in a 2026 study. The drug is common in first-time joint surgery, yet proof in the harder revision setting was thin. Patients were grouped by whether their surgeon used the drug often or rarely.

Records covered 35,222 adults who had clean revision surgery on both parts of a hip or knee between 2016 and 2023. Patients of high-use surgeons showed lower infection rates in the ninety days after surgery, for both hip and knee groups. Broader infection measures also ran lower. The authors back routine use of the drug in revision surgery, within a records-based design.
pmc-13446002:
Helena de Oliveira Santos and colleagues report a thirteen-year-old girl with a tangled vein growth in her hand, treated with a laser and a foam drug together, published in 2026. Such growths in the hand are hard to treat, given the tight anatomy and the hand's twin needs of function and appearance. Her lesion sat near the surface in a small area, which suited a gentle plan.

A long-pulse laser heated the vessels through the skin, while foam made from polidocanol closed them from inside. The paired method proved safe and worked well on her lesion. The authors present combined care as a low-invasion option for hand growths of this type, shaped to each lesion's site, depth, and spread rather than set by a fixed rule.
pmc-13446102:
Chang Liu and colleagues pair two nanoparticles into a combined attack on liver cancer, in a 2026 study. Liver tumors rouse the immune system weakly, and the scout cells that should train killer cells often stall in a tolerant state. Checkpoint drugs alone help only a share of patients.

One particle, spiked and guided by an antibody, carries a plant compound into tumor cells and kills them in a way that alerts immunity. The second wears the skin of mature scout cells and carries a signal that reprograms the faulty scouts. Together they curbed main tumor growth in models and built lasting guard against tumor return. Paired with a checkpoint drug, the dyad worked stronger still, a path the authors press for liver cancer care.
pmc-13446202:
Maria Grazia Fioriello and colleagues study the sense of smell in Niemann-Pick type C1 disease, a rare disorder of fat handling that wears the brain, in a 2026 study. Smell loss often comes early in brain diseases, so the nose may offer a window on the illness. The team used mice carrying the human gene fault most common in patients.

In mutant mice, the smell lining held fewer mature scent cells, more cell death, and more immune cell entry at both time points checked. Odor-driven nerve replies shrank, and the mice did worse on smell-guided tasks. In a human family, the child with the disease and both carrier parents each showed reduced smell of a distinct degree. The authors propose the smell lining as a sentinel for tracking the disease.
pmc-13446302:
Long Xu and colleagues test a blast of brief high heat in the roasting of dried tuna, asking whether it builds flavor faster than long, low roasting, in a 2026 food study. Roasting makes the taste and scent of dried fish, yet long heating can dull quality and stain color. Electronic noses and scent-separating machines profiled the result.

Heat-treated fish held more volatile scent compounds, and screening pulled out twenty-nine key aroma players. Taste chemistry jumped too: a savory nucleotide near doubled, while sweet and umami amino acids rose several-fold. The team credits the quick heat for driving scent-forming reactions and the taste gains together. The method offers dried fish makers a new lever for richer flavor in less time.
pmc-13447202:
Le Zhang and colleagues review inflammation in artery plaque disease and traditional Chinese medicine in 2026. Plaques grow through a mix of vessel lining damage, trapped fats, immune cell build-up and overactive signals, which can end in heart attack or stroke. Single-target drugs often fail to control such a web over the long term, the authors argue.

Herbal formulas act on many targets at once, which suits a multi-path process in principle. Evidence gathered here suggests such treatments can calm inflammatory signals, ease oxidative stress, protect the vessel lining and lower clot risk. Two major signal pathways recur throughout the account as shared control points. The review offers a framework for combining approaches and for modernising research on these traditional remedies, rather than proof from a single trial.
pmc-13447302:
S Meenakshi, N Raghunath and Amitabh Dwivedi test a structured ergonomics module for postgraduate dental students in a 2026 before-and-after study. Dentists work in cramped, lopsided postures during long procedures, building strain that can end in neck, shoulder and wrist disorders. Students who treat patients without assistance carry high risk early in their careers.

Thirty-six students across five clinical departments took a six-week course mixing talks, discussion, stretching routines and chairside setup advice. Unannounced photos graded working posture with a validated dental ergonomics scale at weeks two and six. Scores improved clearly in every department, and no dangerous postures remained at the final check. Knowledge gains were large, including recognition of carpal tunnel causes, prompting a call to embed such training from the start.
pmc-13447502:
Iouliani Koullourou and co-authors study borderline personality traits in the early teen years in a 2026 clinic-based analysis. Unstable close ties, identity trouble and poor emotion control define the borderline pattern, which often surfaces in the teen years. Insecure attachment to caregivers links to such traits in adults, and the ability to reflect on mental states may carry part of that link.

One hundred twelve young people aged eleven to fourteen at a community mental health service completed attachment, reflection and trait surveys. Both avoidant and ambivalent insecure styles raised the odds of high trait scores. Reflection partly explained the ambivalent path, while avoidant attachment also kept a strong direct link alongside a smaller indirect one. Distinct routes for each style suggest early help should be tailored rather than generic.
pmc-13448202:
Rye and co-authors compare the mitochondrial fingerprints of two rodent stress models. Their 2026 paper runs two models against each other. Stress-enhanced fear learning models post-traumatic stress. Chronic unpredictable stress models depression. Data-driven clustering sorted animals into susceptible, resilient, and depressive phenotypes, rather than assuming uniform effects. Mitochondrial energy machinery was measured across three brain regions alongside blood inflammation markers.

The hippocampus diverged by model: trauma-susceptible animals broadly upregulated their mitochondrial complexes, while depressive-model animals changed more narrowly. The amygdala converged, with vulnerable animals in both models raising the final energy complex. Within the prefrontal cortex the prelimbic subregion stood out, showing trauma-specific, phenotype-dependent changes that mark it as a candidate node for stress sensitisation. Blood levels of the inflammatory marker TNF-alpha also rose in a phenotype- and time-dependent way and tracked the regional mitochondrial changes.
pmc-13448502:
Schultz and colleagues compared two doses of bevacizumab, a drug that blocks blood vessel growth signals, for treating radiation necrosis, which is tissue death and swelling after brain radiation. Their 2026 retrospective review covers adults treated between 2021 and 2024 for primary brain tumors or brain metastases. The best dose for shrinking the swelling around damaged tissue has been unclear.

Schultz reviewed 104 patients, split almost evenly between a lower and a higher dose, each given a median of four treatments. Brain swelling responses favored the higher dose, with large swelling reductions more common in that group. The authors add a caution: the higher-dose group contained far more primary brain tumor patients, while the lower-dose group held more lung and breast cancer cases. tumor mix may explain part of the difference and dosing guidance needs cleaner comparisons.
pmc-13448702:
Xiankun Wu and co-authors describe in 2026 living bacteria reworked into an assembly line for chemical production inside oil-and-water emulsions. The team attached a light-driven catalyst to the surface of Escherichia coli cells that overproduce enzymes. The coated cells gather at droplet surfaces and hold the emulsion stable.

At those interfaces, combined chemical and enzyme steps ran up to 45 times faster than in ordinary two-phase mixtures. The system handled single, sequential, and one-pot cascades, including a gram-scale batch of benzoin. Because the surface link is reversible, either the living cells can be reused or the catalyst can be stripped off and fitted to fresh cells.
pmc-13448902:
Sébastien Renaut and eleven co-authors grouped lung tumors by gene activity to forecast patient outcomes, in a 2026 study. Five hundred fifteen early-stage tumors from one center were profiled. Survival links for smoking, grade, and stage were confirmed first. Unsupervised clustering then looked for natural tumor groups. Two groups fit best, not the three often reported.

Gene activity varied hugely across tumors, blurring the groups. Even so, cluster membership predicted survival beyond standard factors. Published gene signatures also predicted survival in this cohort. They did not beat plain pathologic staging overall. Within early-stage cases, though, clustering out-predicted staging. The authors back gene-based prognosis as a staging aid. Two broad tumor classes may be the honest reading. Larger multi-center checks should test that claim next.
pmc-13449302:
Aleef Daniel and colleagues explore in 2026 whether when Japanese women eat and sleep relates to premenstrual symptoms and period pain. They recruited 426 women, average age 33, through a mobile health app. Questionnaires captured first and last meal times, eating windows, wake and bed times, sleep length, chronotype, and the weekday-weekend mismatch known as social jetlag, alongside symptom scores.

Workday patterns tied mainly to eating-related premenstrual symptoms: a later first meal and earlier waking each came with stronger symptoms. Free days told a different story, where later last meals, longer eating windows, later waking, and longer sleep all tracked with worse period pain. Skipping breakfast more often meant stronger eating-related symptoms, and frequent nighttime snacking raised the odds of moderate-to-severe symptoms, with an odds ratio of 1.11. The authors frame daily timing as part of how social schedules press on the menstrual cycle.
pmc-13449502:
Zhen Li and coauthors surveyed hepatitis B patients in Qinghai Province, China, in 2026 to gauge what they know and do about their infection. Hepatitis B can lead to cirrhosis and liver cancer and can spread to others, so patient knowledge and habits matter for both personal health and public safety. The team wanted to find which patient traits went with better understanding and practice.

A validated questionnaire reached 263 patients at two public hospitals in June and July 2023. Just over half showed adequate knowledge, about three quarters held positive attitudes, and about two thirds reported good practices. Schooling level stood out among the factors linked to knowledge scores. Health educators can use the gaps to target teaching where it is most needed.
pmc-13449702:
Guangli Fan and colleagues profile in 2026 the gut microbes and blood chemistry of acute kidney injury patients together, hunting for early signals of a syndrome that is usually caught late. Sixteen patients were matched with sixteen healthy controls by age and sex. Stool underwent whole-metagenome sequencing while plasma went through detailed metabolite profiling, and the layers were integrated across gene, pathway, and module levels.

Sixty-five metabolites separated patients from controls, clustering in sugar and amino acid metabolism. Three stood out as candidate markers, led by maltol with a discrimination score of 0.961, and a three-metabolite panel chosen by machine learning scored 0.859. Patients' gut communities were less diverse and distinctly composed, with key short-chain fatty acid producers depleted. The authors frame the combined microbe-metabolite pattern as a map of the gut-kidney axis in this illness and a source of diagnostic leads.
pmc-13449802:
Daniel Ortuño-Sahagún and Lucrecia Carrera-Quintanar present in 2026 a research collection on dietary nutrients and bioactive compounds against neurodegenerative disease. Alzheimer and Parkinson diseases are climbing as people live longer, and no broadly effective drug yet alters their course. The editors frame food-derived molecules as easy-to-reach, multi-target candidates, since both share oxidative stress, chronic inflammation, failing mitochondria, lost synapses, and epigenetic drift, all pathways diet can touch.

The collection spans lab studies, pilot trials, reviews, and opinion pieces. Recurring themes include restoring antioxidant defenses, rebalancing inflammation, and protecting mitochondria and synapses. Plant polyphenols, sulfur compounds from foods like garlic, spices, and whole dietary patterns play leading roles. The editors keep a sober note throughout. Poor absorption and wide differences between individuals remain the field's central problems, and claims must clear them before dietary advice can harden into therapy.
pmc-13450002:
Sierra leads a team studying fatty donor livers in transplant recipients with steatotic liver disease, in a 2026 paper. Grafts with heavy fat have often shown acceptable survival. Grouping all fatty liver diseases together may hide key differences between them.

The team used a national United States registry covering a decade of adult transplants. Recipients were split by disease subtype. Those with metabolic dysfunction-associated disease who got very fatty grafts had worse early and long-term graft survival. The added risk was large and held after adjustment. No such link appeared for the alcohol-related subtypes. The authors argue that graft allocation should depend on disease type.
pmc-13450502:
Merle Egeborg and co-authors weigh in 2026 whether the path a surgeon takes to a child's back-of-brain tumor changes the risk of lost speech after surgery. That loss, part of cerebellar mutism syndrome, can also bring weak movement, slow thought, and mood change. One route cuts through the middle band of the cerebellum, called transvermian, while the other slips around it, called telovelar.

The review pooled 16 studies covering 1,369 young patients and found no clear gap in risk between the two routes. The pooled odds leaned toward more cases with the through-the-band route, yet the range around that figure crossed no effect. The authors conclude that choice of route alone does not explain which child loses speech.
pmc-13451302:
Jialiang He and colleagues designed an online art platform in 2026 that puts the gallery inside virtual reality scenes. The system combines exhibition, trading, and social features in one place. Its front end runs in the Unity 3D engine, with models built in 3ds Max, while the back end uses a Java SSM framework with a MySQL database. Front-end scenes and back-end management exchange data so visits and transactions stay connected.

The paper also tackles recommendations, since generic algorithms track changing tastes poorly on art platforms. The authors propose a graph-based recommendation approach for matching users with works. Platforms like this aim to give artists and small galleries a showroom that never closes and costs less than physical space. The design doubles as a case study in stitching immersive front ends to conventional enterprise back ends.
pmc-13451802:
Yusuke Shimizu and co-authors review in 2026 why cell therapy trials for limbs starved of blood give mixed results, and how patient state may explain the spread. Such trials enroll people with no path to vessel repair, a group whose health varies widely. The review sorts marks of body state, from blood tests of swelling and nutrition to fitness, smoking, and blood flow gauges.

Most marks forecast outcomes well, yet none has proof that it picks who gains most from the cells. The authors warn against reading after-the-fact subgroup hints as fact. They propose a trial frame that sorts patients into good, mid, and poor host-state bands before treatment, so future trials can test the marks head on.
pmc-13451902:
Vanessa Muhl and co-authors compare in 2026 the body clock hub of a day-active mouse with that of the standard night-active lab mouse. Both hubs look alike on coarse tests, which bred a view that they work the same. The team used long recordings from living tissue, light-based prods, and maps of cell timing in the hub of each species.

The day mouse hub ran a longer inner day and sat at a shifted phase under daily cues. Direct prods reset it in species-tied ways, with a strong mid-day delay absent in the lab mouse. Cell timing swept smoothly across the day hub yet jumped sharply in the night hub. Coarse likeness, the authors say, hides real gaps.
pmc-13452202:
Isaiah Patong and Pinky Larcelle Gas-ib write in 2026 a letter on what a Taiwan childbirth study means for training midwives. The study they cite prized trust, quick response, and whole-person care when frontline staff weigh invasive and gentle ways to track labor. The letter sets that beside a Philippine study of male midwives in Kalinga.

Male midwives there scored well across pregnancy, birth, and family planning care, despite lasting bias about men in the role. Skill, the letter argues, grows from training and patient rapport, not from sex. It urges schools to teach talk skills, culture-aware care, and gentle labor checks, so comfort and safety rise together for mothers.
pmc-13453002:
Charles Lu and others studied risk factors for acral melanoma in 2026, a rare but aggressive skin cancer on palms, soles, and nails. Unlike common melanoma, acral melanoma is not strongly tied to sun exposure, so its demographic and clinical risk factors were less clear. The team compared cases with two control groups at Boston centers.

A total of 2,115 patients were analyzed, with acral cases matched one to four to controls by follow-up time and dermatology care history. Acral patients were more often women and disproportionately Asian or Black than either control group. Links to leukemia and lymphoma, nonmelanoma skin cancer, and actinic keratoses also emerged. Clinicians gain risk profiles to guide earlier detection in groups where this cancer is often missed.
pmc-13453902:
Akiko Morimoto and co-authors study sleep that does not feel restful and how it links to self-rated health in middle-aged adults in Japan, in a paper from 2026. Waking unrefreshed is common in this age group. It has been tied to heart, metabolic, and mental health problems.

The team used a postal survey from 2020 in five cities in Osaka Prefecture. After missing replies were removed, just over eleven thousand adults aged forty to sixty-four were studied. People with unrefreshing sleep were about twice as likely to rate their physical health as poor. The same held for mental health. The link also showed up in people with no current illness. The authors argue that how sleep feels, not just how long it lasts, deserves attention.
pmc-13454102:
Quanzhou Lv and six co-authors probe how ultraviolet light changes the balance between pigment making and growth in melanoma cells from pet mice. In healthy skin, making melanin and dividing pull against each other. Their 2026 study exposes a mouse melanoma cell line to UV doses up to 2,880 joules per square metre, then measures both the dark pigment eumelanin and cell growth.

At low to moderate doses, pigment and growth rose together in a straight line link. At the highest dose that link broke down. A protein network analysis pointed to PIAS3, a regulator that touches two master switches of melanoma, as a possible hinge. The authors read UV as a double agent: it triggers pigment as a shield at mild doses while also feeding tumor growth, until overload breaks the pattern.
pmc-13454202:

pmc-13457002:

pmc-13457202:

pmc-13457702:

pmc-13458602:

pmc-13459202:

pmc-13461402:

pmc-13465502:

pmc-13465902:

pmc-13466402:

pmc-13466602:

pmc-13466902:

pmc-13467002:

pmc-13468002:

pmc-13468102:

pmc-13469302:

pmc-13469902:

pmc-13470002:

pmc-13470202:

pmc-13471002:

pmc-13471302:

pmc-13471402:
Peker and colleagues asked whether starting a hormone-blocking drug later in IVF stimulation harms results for women with polycystic ovary syndrome, a common hormone disorder. Their 2026 retrospective study compared 89 patients treated between 2017 and 2025, split by when the blocking drug began. The groups were similar in age and body mass index at the outset.

In the delayed group of 38 patients, injections started only once three follicles reached 17 mm, while the earlier group of 51 started at a single 14 mm follicle. The delayed group had higher estradiol, a hormone that rises with stimulation, when the blocker began, yet embryo outcomes did not suffer for it. Neither blastocyst numbers nor top-grade embryo rates tracked estradiol levels in the correlation analysis.
pmc-13471502:
Özbay and colleagues tested whether two inflammation scores from routine blood work can predict death in COVID-19 patients arriving at an emergency department. Their 2026 retrospective study analyzed 1,519 patients at a secondary-care hospital, comparing survivors with those who died across a panel of lab markers.

Mortality was high at 52.6% of the cohort, and nearly every inflammatory marker, from fibrinogen to ferritin, ran higher in patients who died. Yet the two headline scores fell short: neither the CRP-to-albumin ratio nor the systemic immune-inflammation index survived as an independent predictor in regression. Instead, blood urea nitrogen, creatinine, and the liver enzyme AST emerged as the independent mortality indicators, pointing to kidney and liver strain as the sharper warnings.
pmc-13471602:
Hama and co-authors pooled community studies of deprescribing, the planned cutting of inappropriate medicines, to see whether it trims drug burden and saves money outside hospitals. Their 2026 systematic review covered 27 studies published before April 20, 2025, with nine of them feeding the meta-analysis.

The pooled result showed a moderate but statistically significant drop in potentially inappropriate medications, though studies varied widely in design and population. Economic evaluations pointed the same way: one Irish analysis estimated that halving inappropriate anti-inflammatory drug use, a 49.8% reduction, could save up to €1,971 per person. Polypharmacy itself affects 26 to 40% of older adults, the authors note, which is why community-level programs matter.
pmc-13471802:
Xukun Dang leads a twenty two author effort in 2026 to set veterinary breakpoints for ceftiofur, a drug used against E. coli infections in dogs. Breakpoints are the lab thresholds that declare a bacterium susceptible or resistant. None existed for this drug in dogs, despite its use for urinary infections, especially in China. Missing thresholds hamper both prescribing and resistance surveillance.

Three cutoffs were derived from separate evidence streams. One came from the spread of resistance in collected isolates. One came from drug exposure modeling with Monte Carlo simulation. One came from a treatment trial in dogs with bladder infections. The proposed urinary breakpoints declare isolates susceptible at or below one microgram per milliliter. They declare isolates resistant at four or above, with matching disk test zones. The authors offer the values for standards adoption.
pmc-13472302:
Barathi Palani, Ľubica Cenknerová, and Martin Pumera build in 2026 a five metal framework material that stores ammonium ions for water based batteries. Ammonium batteries are cheap and safe, but their cathodes suffer low energy and fast fading. Their framework mixes cobalt, nickel, iron, manganese, and molybdenum nodes with an amino decorated linker, an entropy engineered design meant to spread stability across many metals.

The amino groups add polarity and hydrogen bonding sites that welcome ammonium, while molybdenum tightens the metal linker grip and slows dissolution. The cathode delivered a high reversible capacity at modest current and beat its non amino sibling. Capacity actually grew over thousands of cycles, reaching well past its starting value. A full cell with an organic anode kept most of its capacity after a thousand cycles.
pmc-13472802:
Lim and colleagues reported in 2026 new lab models for a brittle bone disease caused by variants in the MBTPS2 gene. Osteogenesis imperfecta makes bones fragile; most cases involve collagen genes, but MBTPS2 causes a rarer form. They grew stem cells from patient skin cells and guided them toward bone-forming cells, and built an image tool to inspect collagen fibres in cell cultures.

The stem cell route let them watch bone development step by step with the patient's own mutation. The image pipeline measured collagen misfolding and fibre organisation in two-dimensional cultures. Together, the models revealed differences in how this gene's variants disturb collagen compared with classic forms. The authors say the tools complement existing qualitative collagen checks. Understanding the distinct mechanism matters because treatment logic may differ by gene.
pmc-13474002:
Moxley, Chialvo, and Scott Chialvo published a 2026 gene model for a fruit fly's detox gene. The gene, Cyp6a14, belongs to a family that breaks down plant poisons and insecticides. Their subject was Drosophila cardini, a cousin of the classic lab fruit fly. Student researchers built the model under a genomics education partnership protocol.

The team placed the gene within the fly's published genome assembly. Neighboring genes matched the layout seen in the classic lab fly closely. Both flies carry the gene on the same DNA strand direction. The model joins a growing dataset on detox gene family evolution. Comparing layouts helps trace how fly lineages handle new plant toxins. Classroom researchers annotated the gene using a shared partnership protocol.
pmc-13474502:
Shi and colleagues trialled in 2026 an oral simulated tube feeding method against nasogastric feeding in acute pancreatitis. Sixty patients with moderately severe disease were randomised: thirty-one to the oral simulated method, twenty-nine to a nose-to-stomach tube. Feeding tolerance at twenty-four hours was the main outcome, in a non-inferiority design testing whether the new method is no worse.

The oral method's tolerance rate was about ninety-seven percent, versus about sixty-nine percent for tube feeding, comfortably non-inferior. Tolerance scores were also better, and bloating and nausea occurred less often. Hospital costs were significantly lower with the oral method: only about thirteen percent of its patients exceeded the cost threshold, versus about half of tube patients. Length of stay did not differ. The authors conclude the oral simulated method is a safe, cheaper alternative for these patients.
pmc-13474602:
Chi Dai and five colleagues described in 2026 a combined approach for front teeth that are both badly damaged on top and infected at the root tip. Root canal treatment alone cannot fix the gum line or the crown shape, so the team paired root-tip microsurgery with gum reshaping surgery in a single coordinated plan.

In two cases of remaining crowns with apical infection, microsurgery cleared infection and encouraged bone healing, while crown lengthening set a healthy gum contour and crown length. Final crowns were fitted after more than six months, and follow-up beyond a year found the teeth symptom-free, though X-rays showed incomplete healing. The approach offers a reference for saving similar complex front teeth.
pmc-13474802:
Taş and Güleryüz tested porcelain veneer designs in a 2026 lab study on teeth that have a cavity on the side facing the next tooth. They compared three setups on model front teeth: a sound tooth, a tooth first repaired with tooth-colored filling material, and a veneer built to cover the cavity directly in one piece. Each group held 12 teeth, giving 36 specimens whose fit and strength the team measured.

Fit was checked at 19 points on each tooth using silicone copies viewed under a microscope, and strength was tested by pushing until the veneer broke. The one-piece veneer left a clearly wider gap at the edge beside the cavity and a thicker cement layer inside that region of the tooth. Its breaking strength, however, matched the other groups and even averaged highest, so the authors call the design promising but unproven for real mouths.
pmc-13476302:
Paloma Casteleiro Costa and co-authors present a deep learning method in a 2026 paper that sharpens a special type of medical image. The imaging method reads how long glow lasts in tissue, which can flag disease without dyes. Its weak points are slow scans and noisy images, which force a trade off between speed and detail.

Their network rebuilds sharp images from scans taken with pixels five times larger, which speeds capture a great deal. Tests on tumor tissue from patients showed fine structure that the raw scans lost, with clear gains on standard quality scores. The method also needs much less time to run than rival approaches. Faster, sharper scans could help bring this imaging into real clinics.
pmc-13476402:
Charlotte Oris and co-authors test blood markers for concussion in rugby in 2026. Head injury checks in rugby lean on what players report, which can miss cases. Three blood proteins rise after brain injury and may add an objective check. The team followed a French elite rugby squad across two seasons.

Dozens of players gave samples under the head injury protocol when episodes occurred. The study weighs how well the markers track true concussion. It also tests whether they add value beyond the standard assessment. An objective blood check could protect players from returning to play too soon.
pmc-13477102:
Jialin Lu and co-authors test a pain control method for lung surgery in a randomized trial published in 2026. Patients had lung tissue removed through a single small cut with a camera-guided operation. Half received a nerve block between the ribs using a long-acting form of the numbing drug bupivacaine, and half received standard care with no such block.

The trial enrolled 199 patients. At 24 hours, the block group reported lower resting pain, with a median score of 2 against 3 in the control group. The block group also used less opioid pain medicine over two days and scored better on a recovery scale. Hospital stay and side effect rates were much the same in both groups. The authors note the trial cannot show the block beats other numbing methods.
pmc-13477602:
Ismail, a family physician, reflects in 2026 on grieving her own father's death while professionally guiding other families through loss. In the consultation room she had long delivered bad news with a practiced, steady hand, yet medical training gave her no immunity when the loss was hers. She describes oscillating between the daughter at the bedside and the doctor explaining his condition to the family.

She names the experience disenfranchised grief, a sorrow not openly acknowledged because professionals are expected to stay stoic and return to work. Focusing only on medical details became her defense, an intellectualization that postponed the emotional reality and added to her burden, alongside rescue fantasies about whether she had done enough as a doctor-daughter. She concludes that physicians are allowed to grieve, may need help themselves, and can turn anguish into personal growth and better patient care.
pmc-13478602:
Remil and colleagues turned discarded olive pits into activated carbon in 2026 and tested it for removing tartrazine, a yellow food dye, from water. The pits were soaked in phosphoric acid and heated to open a pore network, then the carbon's surface and chemistry were profiled with several instruments. Batch tests varied acidity, dye strength, carbon dose, time, and temperature to find the best cleanup conditions.

Cleanup peaked in strongly acidic water at pH 2, using a 40 milligram carbon dose against dye at 40 milligrams per liter over 24 hours. The top measured capacity reached 47.18 milligrams of dye per gram of carbon, and the uptake speed fit a standard second-order model with a fit score of 0.9996 in the analysis. Heat values showed the process releases heat and runs spontaneously, and the authors pitch the waste-derived carbon as a cheap option for dye-laden wastewater.
pmc-13479602:
Lafata and colleagues interviewed 12 experts in 2026 to identify which features of a care organization, not of individual doctors, shape cancer patient outcomes. The panel mixed organization theorists, cancer clinicians, and the people who build clinical data warehouses. They were asked which organization-level traits matter, and whether those traits could realistically be captured in existing data systems for research and improvement work.

Four feature families stood out: leadership structure and culture, quality monitoring processes, outside incentives, and the support services an organization provides its patients. Experts stressed deliberate attention to equity, noting the same features that lift quality also tend to lift fairness in who benefits from care. Some features are easy to pull from public records, while others resist extraction, so the authors say progress needs healthcare organizations themselves to share data as partners.
pmc-13479702:
Sara Moura and six co-authors engineer stem cells to heal bone better by blocking one small gene regulator, miR-195. Their 2026 study works with mesenchymal stem cells, repair cells used in advanced therapies whose results in patients have been uneven. Turning their healing power up is the goal.

Cells treated with the blocker showed gene patterns tied to movement, growth, and less cell aging, plus more of a bone density marker. Seeded on scaffolds and placed in mice, the cells spread faster than untreated ones. By four weeks the scaffolds held more collagen, more bone markers, and more and larger blood vessels. The authors back microRNA tuning as a way to strengthen cell therapies for bone defects.
pmc-13480202:
Jiahuan Li and co-authors present a 2026 field study of how soil microbes shape grassland plants on the steppe. The team tracked root fungi and root pathogens in thirteen grassland species, covering grasses and broader-leafed forbs, grown alone or in competition across overgrazed and restored soils. They then linked microbe levels to how strongly each species responded to its soil community.

Grass species tended to fare worse with their own soil microbes, while forbs tended to fare better. Forbs carried more friendly fungal partners in overgrazed soil, and stronger fungal ties matched stronger gains for them. Grasses carried more root pathogens, and heavier pathogen loads matched worse outcomes where grazing and solo growth combined. The split suggests that restoring steppe may call for different microbe strategies for grasses than for forbs.
pmc-13480402:
