Nay Htut and three colleagues report a 2026 study of adults whose sunken chest, called pectus excavatum, was repaired with the Nuss procedure. That operation lifts the sternum with a metal bar. The team tracked the thoracic Cobb angle, a measure of spinal curve, in 186 patients. All were treated at Taipei Tzu Chi Hospital between 2014 and 2024, and the review looked back over their records.

Chest X-rays showed the curve rising slightly one month after surgery. It then eased while the bar stayed in place. After bar removal the angle fell below its starting level, and every subgroup showed the same drop. The authors conclude the operation does not worsen spinal alignment. They note the gain itself was small.
pmc-13528002:
Franck Ale and seven colleagues reconstruct a measles epidemic in Yakusu Health Zone, Democratic Republic of the Congo, in a 2026 study. The outbreak ran from January 2018 to June 2019. A household survey covered 8,968 people. About fifteen percent reported having had measles. The team scaled the results to the whole zone.

They estimate roughly 22,000 true cases. Routine surveillance had caught only about twenty-eight percent of them. Among children under five, the attack rate was near forty-six percent. About five percent of young cases died within a month. Infants fared worst, and deaths kept coming after the standard cutoff. A reactive vaccine campaign arrived over a year into the outbreak. It mostly reached children who were already vaccinated. The authors stress faster response and better routine coverage.
pmc-13528102:
Lucas Martins and three colleagues link heart MRI signs with fingertip vessel damage in systemic sclerosis in a 2026 study. The disease scars skin and organs and harms small vessels. Forty patients had heart scans with a cold stress step. They also had nailfold vessel checks under a microscope. Heart involvement was judged by flow defects, strain, and scar patterns.

Twenty-two patients, fifty-five percent, showed heart involvement on MRI. Flow-related lesions appeared in about thirty-eight percent. Fibrosis-type lesions appeared in twenty percent. Patients with the late vessel pattern had more fluid around the heart. They also had more scar-type heart lesions. Fewer fingertip capillaries and more bare zones tracked with worse heart findings. The authors suggest the fingertip window mirrors the heart. Nail checks could flag who needs heart imaging most.
pmc-13528202:
Aakanksha Jha, Elizabeth R Lawlor and Cole A DeForest published this 2026 study building a gel that mimics the soft tissue where Ewing sarcoma, a childhood cancer, spreads. Flat cell cultures cannot reproduce the matrix signals tumours feel, and animal models cannot isolate matrix ingredients. Their hydrogel is built on a degradable polyethylene glycol network. It is decorated with binding peptides from collagen and fibronectin, plus a peptide from tenascin-C, a matrix protein enriched at metastatic sites.

Ewing sarcoma cells grown inside the gels changed their growth and cell state according to the matrix recipe. Adding the tenascin-C peptide drove tumour behaviours and shifted cells into states matching those produced by the native protein, validating the peptide as a stand-in. A built-in enzymatic release mechanism lets researchers recover the cells for assays. The authors offer the platform as a way to dissect how matrix composition steers metastasis.
pmc-13529802:
M. Aparicio and six colleagues compare three ways to teach medical students patient education in a 2026 study. Fifth and sixth year students all took the same theory lessons. One group then practiced with real patients in primary care. A second practiced with simulation in intensive care teaching. A third had no practice round. Knowledge tests and a judged practical exam measured the payoff.

Theory scores rose for everyone after the lessons. The simulation group topped the practical exam, scoring just over eight points. Real-patient practice came next, at about seven and a half points. The no-practice group trailed near seven points. Students also rated themselves higher than their teachers did. The authors crown theory plus simulation as the best mix. Simulated patients give safe, repeatable reps, they note. Self-confidence should be checked against outside judgment.
pmc-13530502:
Vu Thi Hoang Lan and colleagues tracked pregnancy care in Vietnam in a study published in two thousand twenty-six. Counting clinic visits alone can hide whether mothers actually received key checks. Using national survey data from three survey years, they built an index covering both visit numbers and the content of care.

Every measure improved over the decade, including skilled care and core services like blood pressure checks and blood and urine tests. Gaps by wealth, place, and ethnic group were also tracked over time. Health officials gain a fairer yardstick: progress counts only when mothers receive the full set of recommended services, not just appointments.
pmc-13530602:
Bryant and colleagues present in 2026, as conference poster 126, a prospective study of response shift after hip arthroscopy. Response shift is the phenomenon where patients' internal yardsticks move over time, so their later memory of how bad things were before surgery no longer matches what they reported then.

Fifty-six patients completed hip questionnaires before surgery and at one and two years, also re-rating their pre-surgery state from memory at each visit. Scores improved significantly at both time points. Yet meaningful response shift appeared in about half to three fifths of patients depending on the scale. Most often they remembered their earlier health as better than they had said, which shrank the measured size of the surgical benefit. Negative coping styles and adverse events predicted worse final scores, but nothing consistently predicted the size of the shift itself.
pmc-13530802:
Pengtao Shi and eight co-authors judge suture button fixation for syndesmotic instability that comes with chronic lateral ankle instability, in a study from twenty twenty-six. Instability of the distal tibiofibular syndesmosis often coexists with lateral ankle instability and delays healing. Suture button fixation is widely used, but its benefit here is in doubt. The team looked back at past cases.

Patients with an intact syndesmosis formed one group. Those with instability confirmed by arthroscopy got added suture button fixation. All patients had the same lateral ligament surgery and rehabilitation. Outcomes were tracked with standard ankle function, activity, and pain scores, plus range of motion. Of two hundred sixteen patients who fit, one hundred fifty-four finished follow-up. The follow-up ran over five years on average. The design lets midterm results for the added fixation be judged against ligament surgery alone.
pmc-13531202:
Julio Echarte-Morales and co-authors present a 2026 catheter replacement of a leaking mitral valve using a device built solely for that valve. The 77-year-old man had worsening breathlessness and fatigue from severe leakage and faced high surgical risk. His anatomy also suited the clipping alternative poorly.

CT planning mapped the route and guarded against blocking the outflow path after placement. The fully leg-delivered system crossed into the left atrium and seated a new valve, cutting leakage effectively. The case supports replacement as a real choice when repair geometry fails and surgery looms too risky.
pmc-13531302:
Abdellaoui and co-authors probe the light behavior of a new spinel nanopowder. Their 2026 study builds a zinc manganese aluminum oxide by a sol-gel burn route and confirms a single-phase tetragonal spinel form. Light reads across ultraviolet, visible, and near-infrared bands mark it as a semiconductor with a direct band gap. A low disorder energy hints at a clean crystal.

The powder bends light strongly while drinking almost none, and its losses at high frequency run tiny. A classic oscillator model fits its spread of refractive power. Gauged nonlinear replies run strong, which the team reads as promise for optical and electronic gear.
pmc-13531702:
Meimei Xu, Chenpeng Wang, and Xinying An map how long new drugs take to develop in China in a 2026 study. Fast access to new drugs matters for patients, and China has added fast-track review paths in recent years. The team tracked drugs cleared by the national drug agency from 2010 to 2025.

The study covered 232 new drugs, from standard chemicals to biologics and herbal drugs. The middle total time was just under seven years. Biologics were fastest, at about five years, and herbal drugs slowest, at over ten. Fast-track approval was linked to shorter times for cancer drugs. Review time at the last stage also fell sharply in later reform years.
pmc-13531802:
Maria Samuelsson and co-authors describe, in a 2026 study, how a caregiver support questionnaire was translated and adapted for Sweden, and pilot tested. The tool screens family caregivers of people with cancer for distress and unmet support needs. Moving such a tool across languages takes more than word for word translation, since phrases and care systems differ.

Professional translators did forward and back translation with the research team. Two expert panels, one of family members and one of health professionals, judged how clear and fitting the items were. Their feedback added five items to suit the Swedish context. The team then pilot tested the version's measurement traits in thirty adult Swedish family members of cancer patients, using classic test methods. The paper reports a careful adaptation process, with a small first check of how the tool behaves.
pmc-13531902:
Tom Eulenfeld and colleagues announce a 2026 update to AssayBLAST, a software tool that checks lab test designs on the computer before any bench work begins. Modern tests often hunt many targets at once, using short DNA pieces called primers and probes. If those pieces are flawed, the test fails and money is wasted.

Version two adds a check that paired pieces sit in the right direction and spacing for copying to work. It also predicts what the pieces will produce together, giving labs a benchmark before wet-lab trials. Its search settings now adjust on their own as databases grow, keeping speed and accuracy up. Tests against the older version back the gains. The update aims to cut failed designs and make complex tests more trustworthy.
pmc-13532002:
Zhiyin Wang and co-authors measure in 2026 a small RNA in blood cells of children newly diagnosed with immune platelet loss. Eighty-seven patients, split into severe and non-severe groups, plus 40 healthy controls gave samples for RNA measurement and T-cell subset counting by flow methods. The disease destroys platelets through misdirected immunity.

The RNA ran higher in patients than controls and higher still in severe cases. Helper cell balance tilted toward inflammatory types and away from regulatory cells, tracking the RNA level and platelet counts. A three-part combined score sorted severe cases with strong accuracy, pending prospective checks.
pmc-13532202:
Simon Roques and co-authors explore in 2026 what blocking methane production in dairy cow stomachs does to microbes and body chemistry together. Twelve cows received a methane inhibitor for six weeks while thirteen served as controls. Rumen microbe genes and activity were read alongside blood metabolite profiles from earlier work.

The overall microbe-to-body link proved moderate. A handful of quieted microbial pathways for sugar use, hydrogen handling, and protein building correlated with one-carbon metabolites in blood, alongside a dip in one bacterial order. The patterns raise fresh questions about hydrogen buildup when methane making stops.
pmc-13532302:
Leus and colleagues report a 2026 study comparing three ways to tell poultry E. coli strains apart, a key task in outbreak control. The team typed 200 isolates from four Dutch poultry farms. Two methods read the full genome, using Nanopore and Illumina sequencing. The third, the IR Biotyper, reads an infrared light fingerprint of each strain's surface chemistry.

Infrared grouping matched the genome-based grouping closely, with agreement scores in the high range, especially for type and core-genome clusters. Sequencing still gave the finest detail, but typing all 200 isolates took twelve to twenty-eight days, against a maximum of six days by infrared. The infrared route also costs less per strain. For farm outbreaks, where days matter, a fast fingerprint that agrees with genomes could guide action while sequencing confirms the details.
pmc-13532402:
Kotze, Murray, van der Horst, and Allsopp study how the Varroa mite affects male honeybees, in work from two thousand twenty-six. The mite harms bee groups and can cut the weight and life span of drones, the male bees. Less is known about how it affects drone sperm, though sperm health drives new bees.

They took drones of one Cape kind in South Africa and checked sperm traits with a computer-aided tool. Groups with few mites had sperm that swam much better and faster than groups with many mites. Weight, sperm counts, and life signs showed weak or no change. High mite loads also gave sperm with longer tails.
pmc-13532602:
William H Wu, Joanna K M Ng, and Joshua J X Li report in 2026 a rare case of clear cell sarcoma found in body fluids. The cancer is uncommon, grows in soft tissue, and can look much like melanoma or other cancers under the microscope. Their patient had spread to sputum plus fluid around the belly and heart.

Cell traits varied, and stains for pigment-linked marks gave mixed results across cases in past reports. Gene tests for a known fusion helped confirm the diagnosis. Readers learn why fluid samples from this cancer need cell study, stains, and gene proof together.
pmc-13533202:
Ivone Caroline and Lily Silva Ardiani present a case series in 2026 of eye inflammation after surgery that used an anti-adhesion gel. Drug caused eye inflammation is rare and often missed. Nine women developed inflammation in the front of both eyes after childbirth surgery or womb surgery where the gel, made of gelatine, chitosan, and poloxamer, had been used.

Symptoms began on the first or second day after surgery. Vision was mildly reduced, eye pressure stayed normal, and infection tests were negative. Steroid and pupil widening drops cleared the problem in all patients, with full vision restored. The authors warn surgeons and eye doctors to watch for this link and to counsel patients.
pmc-13533302:
Güven and colleagues scanned the retinas of children with accommodative esotropia, an inward eye turn driven by focusing effort, looking for blood vessel changes at the macula. The macula is the center of sharp vision. Their 2026 prospective study imaged 34 affected children and 35 healthy controls with a vessel-mapping scan. The patients were divided into the condition's three subtypes, adjusting for glasses prescription and eye length.

Güven found the superficial vessel layer unchanged, but deeper layers showed thinning of vessel density in the upper quadrant of the macula. The changes survived strict statistical correction in the choroidal layer for the high-convergence and partially accommodative subtypes. They also survived in the outer retina for the high-convergence subtype, while other apparent differences faded after correction. Because patterns differed by subtype, the authors suggest chronic focusing and convergence effort shapes retinal microcirculation, a hypothesis needing confirmation in larger groups.
pmc-13534202:
Sue-Yeon Song and Wei-Lin Chen study in 2026 how school tracks and parenting shape self-esteem from age 13 to 19 in South Korea. Status and pressure around school paths are strong there, yet family and school effects were rarely studied together. Data came from a national panel with 1,484 youth across three waves from 2010 to 2016.

Youth on some non-university paths reported lower self-esteem across all waves. Warm affection linked to higher self-esteem, while excess expectations and interference linked to lower scores. Parenting effects grew stronger for one technical path, pointing to school and family partnerships.
pmc-13535002:
Shun Zhou and co-authors review the tests for the inner ear's gravity sensors, the otolith organs. These small organs sense straight-line motion, and when they fail, people suffer vertigo, imbalance, and unstable gaze. The review walks through each modern test and what it can and cannot prove in the clinic.

Muscle-response tests remain the workhorse for the two otolith organs, and the tilted-visual test helps sort peripheral from central disease, now aided by phone apps and virtual reality headsets. A test of eye counter-rolling looks promising but lacks standards. Off-axis rotation serves motion sickness research, while devices that test acceleration perception are too unstable for routine care. The authors press for sharper, standardized otolith testing to guide treatment.
pmc-13535402:
The fluid that bathes a tumor may help the tumor hide from the immune system. Colin Laughlin and six co-authors studied that fluid in kidney cancer, using tumor samples and matched healthy kidney tissue from the same patients, in work reported in 2026.

The team measured more than two thousand small molecules in fluid from tumors and from healthy kidney tissue. They then grew immune cells in each fluid to see how the cells behaved. They report that the tumor fluid can suppress immune cells and can switch on G protein-coupled receptors, a large family of cell-surface sensors. The work frames this fluid as an active signal space, not just waste, in how kidney tumors resist immune attack.
pmc-13535502:
Priscila Chaverri and co-authors publish, in a 2026 paper, draft genomes of the reference strains of two fungi that cause scab on mango and avocado. These slow-growing fungi blight high-value fruit, yet genome resources for the group remain thin. The team tested five assembly routes and found a single-technology long-read build gave the most continuous result. Each genome came out near twenty-five million letters, in a handful of pieces, with near-complete gene coverage.

Each strain carries just over nine thousand predicted genes. Their enzyme kits for chewing plant walls are small, fitting a stealthy infection style. Both genomes hold large sets of secreted proteins, hundreds of proteases, and clusters that may make known fungal toxins. Many genes still lack any known function. The authors offer the assemblies as groundwork for studying how these fungi attack their hosts.
pmc-13537002:
Junkai Kou and co-authors measured the world burden of low-back pain blamed on smoking from 1990 to 2021, in a 2026 study. Back pain is the top cause of disability worldwide, and smoking speeds the wear of spinal discs. The team drew on a global disease database covering 204 countries.

Years lived with disability from this cause rose by nearly a third, reaching 8.67 million, driven by growth and aging in the world population. Yet rates per person fell by over a third, with men carrying the heavier load and risk peaking in the sixties. Rich countries improved fast, while some poorer regions worsened. The authors credit tobacco control and younger cohorts for the rate drops. They urge fairer control efforts in lower-income regions.
pmc-13537102:
Christian Tague and co-authors draw lessons from three countries certified malaria-free in 2025 for the African nations still fighting the disease, in a review from 2026. Malaria caused an estimated 263 million cases and 597,000 deaths in 2023, ninety-four percent of them in sub-Saharan Africa. Suriname, Timor-Leste, and Georgia each ended local transmission against that backdrop.

Drawing on World Health Organization and fund reports plus journal studies, the review finds shared roots of success: durable political commitment, sharp surveillance, community mobilization, and steady money. Tactics bent to place, from indigenous outreach and border control in the Amazon to the other national programs. The authors sort which ingredients might transfer south of the Sahara, and which were local.
pmc-13537902:
Na-Eun Kang and co-authors traced, in a 2026 study, how an RNA-binding protein helps head and neck tumors survive radiation. Such cancers are often treated with radiotherapy, yet resistant cells with stem-like traits regrow. The team bred a resistant line of tumor cells by dosing them again and again with radiation.

The survivors grew slower but showed far stronger stem cell behavior in sphere and colony tests. Among stem markers, Musashi-1 rose the most. Silencing it stripped the resistant cells of both stemness and radiation toughness, while forcing it into ordinary cells granted both. Gene profiles pointed to a hyperactive MAPK pathway, with the JNK branch driving the protein's rise. Blocking that branch, the authors suggest, could reopen resistant tumors to radiation.
pmc-13538202:
Achyudhan Kutuva and co-authors study a growth switch that helps the COVID virus copy itself in lung lining cells in a 2026 paper. The switch had been tied to coronavirus harm, but its exact hand in blunting early virus alarms was unsettled.

Human lung tissue tests show that blocking the switch with a drug cuts virus growth and lifts the alarm signal. A logic model of the cell's signal web, checked against dozens of past reads, backs that dual role. Thousands of tweaked model webs test how sturdy the claim is. The study marks the switch as a drug lead for lung infection.
pmc-13538402:
Jovana Periša and co-authors turn tomato waste into glowing carbon dots for copper sensing in a 2026 study. Stems and fruits served as separate carbon sources, with a nitrogen helper added to tune surface chemistry. The dots formed stable nanoscale clusters in water and glowed strongly under ultraviolet light, with brightness depending on excitation color. Detailed surface checks linked starting material to glow behavior.

Precursor choice shaped defect levels and surface groups, directly steering glow strength. Both dot types dimmed sharply when copper ions bound to surface groups, enabling detection at very low levels with slightly better sensitivity for stem dots. Surface oxygen and nitrogen groups drove the strong metal grip. The authors present farm waste conversion as a cheap, green route to useful sensors.
pmc-13538502:
Jan Jansen and colleagues released a large expert-labeled set of Antarctic seafloor photos. Published in 2026, the photo set pulls together images from 21 Antarctic research trips between 1985 and 2019. Seafloor photos offer cheap, gentle data on ocean life, yet steady labeled sets were rarely shared in public.

The set holds 52,491 place-tagged downward photos, of which 3,599 carry labels totaling 632,252 expert marks under a shared sea-life sorting scheme. Each mark's pixel spot is stored, so views can be tuned to a user's focus. The set serves studies of species spread, group patterns, change over time, and teaching programs to label sea life. Readers get a rare Southern Ocean baseline for guarding sea life and tracking change.
pmc-13538602:
Ximena Ruden and colleagues test a two-stage stress response in placental stem cells in a 2026 gene activity study. Stem cells first mount a cell-level survival program, then may shift to a development-linked program favoring the whole organism. Mouse placental stem cells faced strong salt stress. Gene activity was profiled from half an hour through a full day to watch for the same staged shift seen earlier in embryonic stem cells.

Early hours were dominated by building and metabolism genes typical of cell-level adaptation. Later hours swung toward development and differentiation pathways, matching activation of the second program. The authors read the pattern as evidence that the staged shift is a general feature of stressed developmental stem cells. Candidate markers are proposed for fertility care, miscarriage study, and regenerative medicine.
pmc-13539002:
James Colbert argues that artificial intelligence can restore human connection in medical care in a 2026 article. Doctors drown in paperwork while patients feel unheard, and trust between them keeps fraying. He defines connection through listening, eye contact, empathy, and shared choices.

Ambient tools that draft notes and sort inboxes could hand time back to clinicians. Agent-style systems may handle navigation tasks that now eat the visit. The author draws on published evidence and his own practice experience. He also names the risks plainly and lists safeguards for safe use. Deployed with oversight, he argues, these tools can free the attention that humane care requires rather than replacing it.
pmc-13540402:
Özkocaman and colleagues laid out in 2026 a practical guide to preventing and treating invasive fungal infections in blood cancer patients. Chemotherapy and stem cell transplants leave these patients with weak immune defenses. Such infections kill many patients, yet the right drug at the right time depends on each person's risk level. New targeted cancer drugs have added fresh twists, since several clash with standard antifungal medicines.

The guide sorts patients into high, middle, and low risk groups. High-risk patients, such as those starting treatment for acute leukemia, get mold-active preventive drugs, while low-risk patients get none. It gives dosing adjustments when antifungals meet drugs like venetoclax, and care pathways for cell therapy patients. Chest scans and fungal blood markers drive decisions on when to start, escalate, or operate.
pmc-13540902:
Siddharth Nahar and five colleagues present, in a 2026 software paper, a graphics-processor version of MitoGraph, a popular tool that traces mitochondrial networks in three-dimensional microscope images. New live-cell microscopes produce four-dimensional movies far too large for the original processor-bound program.

The rewrite pushes the heavy filtering maths onto graphics hardware and speeds up skeleton extraction. On yeast cells it ran up to eleven times faster, and on human lung organoid frames up to thirty times faster, with segmentation matching the original almost exactly. One organoid workload dropped from roughly five hundred hours to twenty. The authors offer the tool for large-scale studies of mitochondrial shape over time.
pmc-13541202:
Megha Uppin and co-authors report a 2026 study that sorts womb cancers by molecular type in a South Indian patient group. Womb cancer is the most common cancer of the female reproductive system, yet molecular data from Indian patients were thin. The team classed tumors into four groups using protein stains and gene checks. They also mapped changes in the POLE gene.

Most tumors were the common endometrioid kind. The four groups split unevenly, with the largest share showing no specific molecular profile. Gene checks found eleven POLE variants, six of them new to this patient group. Tumors with abnormal p53 acted most aggressively and needed drug therapy most often. The authors say pairing molecular tests with standard tissue study sharpens classing and outlook estimates.
pmc-13542102:
Qiaoyun Liu and colleagues propose a text classifier in a 2026 study. The tool sorts agricultural news with large language models. It needs no labelled training examples. Farm vocabulary is sparse, and annotation is scarce. Single-prompt methods judge from one angle only. That weakness drives the design.

The framework builds several prompts for each text. Each prompt views the text at a different level. Levels run from local terms to overall theme. A consistency check then compares decisions and confidence scores. Disputed items go to a second judgement round. Tests used French pest reports and a humanitarian news set. Accuracy beat the strongest rival by several points.
pmc-13542402:
Bo Wang and eight co-authors speed up cooling material discovery in a 2026 paper. Electrocaloric materials chill when voltage changes, a route to solid state cooling. Direct temperature measurements are rare and costly. Indirect estimates are plentiful but biased. Mixing the two data grades was the challenge.

Their learning framework fuses both grades with a co-kriging model. It learns how the grades correlate and where they disagree. Active learning then picks the most promising next experiments. The target ceramic family is barium titanate based. The search found a blend with strong cooling at minus seventy degrees. Its wide working span suits real devices. Lab checks tied the gain to a smeared phase transition. The recipe suits other sparse data material hunts.
pmc-13542702:
Cao and co-authors report a case of severe jaundice after routine gallbladder removal in a healthy 45-year-old man. Transient yellowing after abdominal surgery is known and is often blamed on stress inside the liver, usually in sicker patients. This man had no other health problems and his operation was smooth, with a normal duct check. Their report was published in 2026.

He returned two days later with very high bilirubin but clean scans. A scope procedure found no blockage or leak, and the jaundice then faded on its own. That procedure, though, triggered severe pancreas inflammation that needed several operations. The authors urge surgeons to weigh benign causes first, since the diagnostic scope itself carries real risk.
pmc-13543202:
Maria Denisa Statie and co-authors train a machine learning model to forecast jaw growth in untreated bite problems, in a 2026 study. The condition, class III malocclusion, pushes the lower jaw forward. Knowing how it will grow guides treatment timing. The team followed one hundred forty-four untreated subjects over time. Head X-rays were taken at several points. Sixteen landmarks were marked on each film as coordinates.

A graph neural network learned the growth patterns. Most of the sample trained the model, and the rest tested it. Short-term forecasts covered sixteen test subjects. Long-term forecasts covered thirteen. Most landmarks were predicted well. Points on the lower jaw proved hardest. Their average errors ran from about two to four and a half millimeters. The front and back jaw points strayed most. The authors say the model is accurate overall. Jaw points, though, need better handling before clinical trust.
pmc-13543602:
Rodrigo Sánchez-Jiménez's team turned the SCImago group's Integrity Risk Indicators into a working measurement system for universities in 2026. Instead of judging misconduct by one person, the framework asks how exposed an institution is to integrity risks. It looks at incentives, authorship patterns, citation dynamics, choice of publication venues, and transparency habits. The indicators are built from bibliometric data for institutions in the SCImago rankings.

The paper's advance is normalisation: each indicator is turned into a standard score centred on the global average, so unlike readings can share one scale and unusual outliers stand out by size. The authors insist the signals flag possible risk, never guilt. Read rightly, the system works like a smoke detector for research culture, helping universities strengthen their own defences rather than feeding another league table.
pmc-13543802:
Wong and co-authors present a 2026 analysis of cancer drug access across the Asia-Pacific region. The region bears about half of world cancer deaths, yet access lags in many countries. The team mined a 2023 global oncology survey for twenty Asia-Pacific nations. The World Health Organization's essential medicines list served as the yardstick.

Availability, patient out-of-pocket costs, and practical access were each graded. Richer nations in the region fare far better than poorer ones on most drugs. Case studies on immune therapy and oral targeted drugs show where the gaps bite hardest. The authors aim the findings at policy makers who set drug lists and prices across the region.
pmc-13544302:
Ming Yeh Lee and co-authors dissect what it would take to spread a successful youth diabetes program nationwide. The 4T Program starts children with new type 1 diabetes on glucose monitors early and watches their data remotely. Across three cohorts totaling four hundred fifty-one youths, the approach kept sugar control tight.

Using an implementation science lens, the team mapped the barriers the program faced and the strategies built to clear them. Clinician time topped the barrier list, answered by a decision-support tool that flags who needs attention and by steering monitoring toward those who benefit most. Family and clinic costs and stakeholder buy-in each got their own countermeasures. The blueprint now guides scaling through a national clinic network.
pmc-13544702:
Eladio Collado-Boira and co-authors report a single case of fingertip injury care in this 2026 paper. A 47 year old man cut off part of his right little fingertip with a kitchen slicer. Bone was exposed, but the nail bed was preserved. Care used a semi-occlusive dressing rather than surgery.

The dressing was changed weekly, and no antibiotics were given. Bone was covered by week four, and the fingertip pad was nearly rebuilt by week six. Six years later the man reported no pain and full motion. He had taken no sick leave and needed no second surgery. Minor losses in feeling and a small nail change remained. The case shows what careful conservative care can achieve.
pmc-13545002:
Neurologic diseases bring suffering that medicine cannot cure, only ease, yet training in that easing is patchy. Eileen Harrigan and co-authors survey the directors of neurology training programs across the United States. About one hundred eighteen responded. Most rated neuropalliative care education as important. Nearly all residency programs teach some palliative topics. Only two thirds of fellowships do.

What gets taught varies with each program's specialty focus. Directors named barriers plainly: too little time for trainees, and too few trained faculty to teach. The survey turns a vague worry, 'we should teach this better,' into a measured map. Programs know the need. What they lack, the authors argue, is the capacity and structure to meet it.
pmc-13547402:
Bisma Ali and colleagues benchmarked in 2026 three deep learning architectures for predicting how much life a lithium-ion battery has left and how its health fades. They used two public aging datasets from NASA and Oxford. Honest comparison is the point of the exercise, so every model received identical preparation and training. A strict leave-one-cell-out rule meant each model was always tested on battery cells it had never seen.

Sequence models, a convolutional variant, and a transformer variant were scored on errors across repeated runs, with extra statistics separating luck in training from true differences between cells. Performance swung with degradation complexity and cell-to-cell variety. The authors argue that rigorous cross-cell testing and reliability reporting matter more than any single leaderboard number.
pmc-13547602: Chang-Ju Kim opens the 2026 spring conference of the Korean Society of Exercise Rehabilitation in this editorial announcement. The meeting is set for a Saturday afternoon in June at Sangmyung University in Seoul. Two professors active in the United States were invited as guest speakers, and two newly appointed professors present their research, partly to celebrate their appointments. Thanks go to the host university's professors and graduate students who prepared the event. The gathering aims to spread new knowledge in exercise rehabilitation among the society's members.
pmc-13548602:
Yiyang Zhu, Changlin Zhai, and Jingjing Wang follow more than three thousand Chinese adults over time, in a 2026 cohort study. They ask how two blood markers, alone and together, relate to future heart and vessel disease. All participants had early-stage cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic syndrome, a clustering of risks gaining attention. One marker gauges inflammation, while the other summarizes fat-related risk in the blood over time.

During five years of follow-up, 495 participants developed cardiovascular disease. High inflammation scores raised risk by over a third, and high cumulative fat-index values raised it by about forty percent, each after full adjustment. People high on both markers faced roughly eighty percent greater risk than people low on both, with the combined pattern stronger in men. The authors propose tracking the pair together when judging risk in this syndrome's early stages.
pmc-13548702:
Yu Qi and colleagues expose a livestock bacterium to an antibiotic and read its genome, genes, and chemistry to learn how tolerance takes hold, in a 2026 multi-omics study. Pasteurella multocida, a common farm pathogen, was pressured with enrofloxacin, a fluoroquinolone drug. Tolerance, surviving without true resistance, is a suspected stepping stone to resistance, so the team compared the adapted strain with its parent.

The tolerant strain idled longer before growing, grew more slowly, formed less biofilm, and stretched into elongated shapes. A gene called dusB had been partly deleted and broken, and removing it deliberately reproduced the slow, tolerant style. A second regulator, cpxR, added tolerance when deleted, acting through ribosome-related genes, while the cell's central energy cycle switched on during adaptation. The authors name both genes as possible targets for blocking tolerance before it hardens into resistance.
pmc-13548902:
Bengt H. Gless and colleagues disarm Staphylococcus aureus by destroying its chemical chatter before the signal reaches the bacteria, in a 2026 study. Reporter strains confirmed the compounds shut the sensing system down across different staph types. Two chosen compounds then reduced skin infection by drug-resistant MRSA in mice. Because the strategy mops up signals rather than killing bacteria, it may press less toward resistance than antibiotics do. The authors see a path toward simple topical molecules for staph skin infections, with delivery methods still to be worked out.
pmc-13549302:
Jingwen Zhang and six colleagues review how acupuncture might treat depression through the gut-brain axis, in a paper from twenty twenty-six. Depression involves more than brain chemistry alone. Gut microbes, barrier damage, and low-grade inflammation all feature in patients. No earlier review had integrated the mechanisms of acupuncture across these systems.

Modern studies tie the classical practice to the vagus-adrenal axis and the endocannabinoid system. Inflammatory signaling pathways join the map. The multi-target character of acupuncture suits such a tangled system, the authors argue. They set out future therapy outlooks for testing the frame. The review offers clinicians a unified mechanistic picture.
pmc-13549802:
Kazunori Ohashi and colleagues build a dedicated test dummy, or phantom, for checking prostate MRI sequences, in a 2026 technical study. Diffusion-weighted imaging is central to spotting prostate cancer, yet gas in the rectum warps the images, and scanners vary. Their phantom mimics prostate tissue, tumor-like lesions, and rectal gas, letting six diffusion techniques be compared at two magnet strengths under identical conditions.

The team measured signal quality, warping artifacts, and geometric distortion against standard images, then had clinicians judge matching patient scans and technologists judge the phantom scans. Readers agreed strongly with each other on the phantom, and the artifact patterns seen in the dummy echoed those in real patients sequence by sequence. The authors offer the phantom as a reproducible stand-in for routine quality checks without scanning volunteers.
pmc-13550002:
Adding immune drugs to chemotherapy around the time of stomach cancer surgery is an emerging strategy, and a meta-analysis pooled the randomized trials to test its worth. Benefit measures and side effect rates were combined across trials. Single trials were too small to settle either the survival gain or the added risk. A careful synthesis guides surgeons and oncologists while the field waits for longer follow-up from the biggest trials.
pmc-13550602:
Wanling Zhang, with eleven colleagues, published a 2026 longitudinal study of how obsessive-compulsive symptoms and psychotic-like experiences develop together in young people. Data came from four waves of a large adolescent brain study with 7,451 participants.

Early links mostly reflected stable differences between children, although psychotic-like experiences predicted later rises in obsessive-compulsive symptoms from ages 12 to 13 within the same child. Intrusive thoughts and worry repeatedly bridged the two sets of symptoms, so the authors stress timing and symptom-level checks.
pmc-13550902:
Olga Sivell, with a large consortium of co-authors, published a 2026 genome assembly for Melanomya nana, a small black blow fly. The fly measures only 3 to 4.5 millimeters and belongs to the family Calliphoridae. Sequencing came from a single male specimen as part of the Darwin Tree of Life project, which builds reference genomes for species in Britain and Ireland.

The assembly presents two haplotypes, the two inherited copies of the genome, each near 1,400 megabases long. Nearly all of the first haplotype sits in five chromosome-scale pieces, while the second was assembled to scaffold level. A mitochondrial genome of 27.12 kilobases was also completed, giving researchers a full genetic reference for the species.
pmc-13551102:
Joanna Freeland and a large team of co-authors published this botany study in 2026. Later-generation hybrids look much like their parents, so field identification by eye is unreliable, and management suffers. Genetic testing works but is costly. They compared pollen and bracteole traits against genetic assignments for hundreds of plants. Pollen matched genetics for 96 percent of plants, and the bract trait for 95 percent, with later-generation hybrids causing most errors. The method works only on flowering plants, and one parent species may be undercounted from flower traits alone. Still, the authors offer it as a cheap tool for tracking the hybrid zone.
pmc-13551402:
Anton C. de Groot, with three colleagues, published a 2026 patch test study on Brazilian propolis. Propolis is a bee product used in health goods. It often triggers positive skin reactions in routine tests. The team had earlier found 98 chemicals in the test material. They built a test set from some of those chemicals and used it on 224 patients.

Forty-two patients in the group reacted to propolis itself. A few single chemicals drew reactions in small shares of patients. Benzyl acetate and one called δ-cadinene led that short list. Reactions occurred in propolis-positive and propolis-negative patients alike. No one chemical explained most reactions. The team presents the set as a step toward finding the true culprits.
pmc-13551802:
Hui-qi Kang, leading eight colleagues, published a 2026 cross-sectional study sorting fear of falling among older adults with sarcopenia into distinct profiles. The survey recruited 356 community-dwelling people aged 60 or older with sarcopenia between December 2023 and December 2024, using questionnaires on fall confidence, anxiety and depression, family function, and social support. Latent profile analysis searched for subgroups.

Four profiles appeared, from low fear in about a fifth of participants to severe fear in about a tenth, with the middle groups largest. A decision tree singled out physical activity level, family function score, and anxiety as the key classifiers in the reported model. Regression agreed that more active people clustered in lower-fear profiles, guiding tailored prevention programs.
pmc-13552002:
Satyam Singh and co-authors test, in a 2026 pilot study, a scope-based fix for reflux disease that ties off the stomach's top valve. Past case data hinted the method, PECC-b, is safe and works. This trial signed up patients who need daily acid drugs to hold their reflux. Of 130 screened, 40 had the fix and were tracked for three months. The group had a median age of 34, and three of four were men. The main gauge was a life quality score tied to reflux, read at the start and at three months.

That score fell from 22.8 to 12.0, a clear gain. In all, 85 percent of patients stopped acid drugs in full or in part. Acid time in the food pipe fell from a median of 28 percent to about 15 percent. Reflux counts and a joint score fell as well.
pmc-13552502:
Geneviève Baujat and co-authors measure the social and economic weight of a rare bone disease in France. Their 2026 paper studies fibrodysplasia ossificans progressiva, where soft tissue slowly turns to bone. They link a national rare disease registry with health system data. Records for 77 people with the disease were compared with 769 controls.

The disease rate came to about 1.4 cases per million people. Those with the disease had more other illnesses, more doctor visits, and more hospital stays than controls. Yearly health spending was more than ten times higher from a broad social view. Survival was clearly worse as well. The authors call for more awareness and for new interventions to cut these burdens on patients and families.
pmc-13552602:
Evgenia Gurevich leads a six-author team in a 2026 Israeli study linking a blood enzyme to kidney harm in sick children. The enzyme, alkaline phosphatase, was tracked in children aged up to eighteen with sepsis, a severe body-wide infection. Records came from four hospitals across more than two decades. The sepsis group held 701 records, set against matched children with fever alone.

Enzyme levels, adjusted for age and sex, sat lower in sepsis than in fever alone. They fell lower still in the near one quarter who developed acute kidney injury. Those children also stayed in hospital longer, a median of seven days against four. After other blood tests were weighed, low levels still pointed to kidney risk.
pmc-13553002:
Taiji Yoshimoto and co-authors report a hard case of removing a colon tumor through an endoscope, in a case report from 2026. The tumor sat in the sigmoid colon and measured 25 millimeters across. Two features made the work risky: the muscle layer pulled toward the cut, and a small pouch in the gut wall lay right under the tumor.

That pouch meant the muscle wall had a gap at that spot. During the cut, a small hole opened in the wall, but the team spotted it at once and closed it with endoscopic clips. They finished removing the tumor in one piece. Scans after the work showed only a small amount of free air, and the patient healed without surgery. The authors say prompt closure can save even very high-risk cases.
pmc-13553302:
Daniel Persaud and eleven colleagues build MAP-E, a self-run high-throughput platform for electrochemistry. Corrosion testing is slow, hands-on, and shaped by operator technique, which limits large, high-quality data for materials work. MAP-E pairs robotic liquid and sample handling with multi-channel voltage control. It extracts corrosion metrics with no human step.

Checks against an ASTM G61-analog benchmark showed steady results, with pitting potential varying by 75 mV across 32 runs. The team then used MAP-E to map pH-chloride stability maps for 304 stainless steel, guided by uncertainty-driven sampling on a Gaussian process model. The platform cuts operator input and speeds search of new settings.
pmc-13553502:
Nina Wawro and a large team develop a method for estimating usual dietary intake in the German National Cohort, NAKO. The blend adapts a known multiple source method so it runs fast on very large datasets. It matched the slow gold-standard approach with an agreement score of at least 0.97. Usual intake came out for 152,304 adults across 90 food groups and 124 food items. Simulations showed that more food lists sharpen each person's estimate. The team offers the blend as an efficient frame for dietary study at scale.
pmc-13553602:
Takuya Inouye and co-authors link mothers' fish intake to pregnancy blood pressure in a 2026 cohort study. High blood pressure disorders in pregnancy endanger mother and baby. Diet records covered fish and the balance of fatty acid families before and during pregnancy. The team then tracked who developed the disorders. Japan's high fish intake makes the cohort a strong natural test of the fish oil idea. Findings here can shape diet advice given at the very start of pregnancy care.
pmc-13553802:
Peter Ladlow and a large team gather expert consensus on force plate tests that screen soldiers before brutal training courses. Their survey study was published in twenty twenty-six. Better screening could flag injury risk and predict who passes.

Ten seasoned users of force plate technology answered an online survey. They picked the most valuable tests and measures to add to a pre-course battery. Candidates ranged from bodyweight jumps and rebound tests to single-joint strength holds. Readiness, injury risk, and course success were the three lenses for each pick. The consensus list gives military trainers a shared, evidence-led starting kit instead of each unit improvising its own screen.
pmc-13554102:
Gaddam Lakshmi and Perumalla Swetha present a 2026 defence system against phishing, the fake messages that trick people into giving up secrets. Crooks now use smart tools to craft fakes that look almost real. Their system reads wording, looks at page images, and checks hidden data all at once. Plain rules sit beside the learning parts, so choices rest on clear grounds as well as patterns.

Fake attack samples made by a diffusion tool hardened the system during training. A replay memory lets it keep learning as attack styles drift. A helper module names the features behind each warning, so analysts can follow the logic. Across public test sets the system scored high and beat rivals on new data by a clear margin.
pmc-13554202:
Poramaporn Luangprasert leads a nine-author team automating counts of lens cells tied to cataract in a 2026 study. Cells lining the lens help keep it clear, and their density may track cataract growth. Hand counting is slow and varies between counters. Their software learned to count these cells in microscope photos of lens capsules removed during surgery.

More than 43,000 cells were checked across twenty test images. The software matched expert consensus counts with accuracy above ninety-eight percent. Its error ran about half that seen between two human experts. Agreement scores also topped the human pair's marks. The authors offer the tool for fast, steady, repeatable density measures in clinic studies of cataract patients.
pmc-13554402:
Zhangshun Li and co-authors report a 2026 physics study on a superconductor film that can both tune and block terahertz waves. Such waves sit between microwaves and infrared light and may serve in fast future devices. Most materials force a trade among depth of tuning, speed, and shielding strength.

Their film, made of a copper-based compound that superconducts at high heat range, is just 43 nanometers thick. In its superconducting state it blocked terahertz waves far better than most known materials. The team also used the paired electron states in the film to switch the waves. One film doing both jobs could simplify future designs.
pmc-13554502:
Ke Liu and co-authors review a young drug strategy that destroys harmful proteins outside cells in a 2026 paper. The tools, called lysosome-targeting chimeras, grab a target protein and hitch it to a receptor that drags it inside the cell. There, the cell's waste system, the lysosome, breaks it down.

Standard degraders only reach proteins inside cells, so this route opens targets on the cell surface and in body fluids. Cousin strategies coax targets inward without a separate clearance receptor. The authors stress that entry alone does not prove real destruction. Their review sorts the designs, the proof each needs, and the gaps to close before such drugs can treat disease reliably.
pmc-13554802:
Robert J Heins, John Yazji, Philip Eber, and Stefanie Furlan report a rare tumour that floods the body with a hormone precursor and drives blood sugar down. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-six. The tumour is a neuroendocrine kind that sheds proinsulin, the form insulin is cut from. Insulin itself can read normal, which hides the cause.

A woman with spread cancer comes in with blocked bile flow and is found to have deep, silent low sugar in fasts. Proinsulin reads are very high. The lows come back in spite of steroids, sugar shots, and a raft of drugs. Even a strong sugar drip through a central line fails to hold her sugar. She moves to comfort care.
pmc-13556102:
Yannai DeJonghe and four colleagues surveyed care workers in 2026 about care left undone in nursing homes and the toll it may take on staff. Ageing populations and heavier workloads raise the risk that essential tasks slip, which earlier work tied to exhaustion in nurses. Their cross-sectional study drew survey data from 56 Belgian nursing homes collected in 2021, covering 1,054 nurses, assistants, and allied health staff.

Every domain of unfinished care linked to higher emotional exhaustion and depersonalisation, and to a weaker sense of personal accomplishment. Supportive management softened the link with depersonalisation, while unsupportive management appeared to sharpen the strain. The authors read the findings through a demands and resources lens. Tasks left undone act as a demand on staff. A good manager counts as a resource that can offset part of the damage.
pmc-13556302:
Yagiz Yedekci, Mehmet Fazıl Enkavi, and Ferah Yildiz present a medical physics study, published in 2026, on verifying radiation dose in cancer brachytherapy by watching it glow. In high dose rate brachytherapy a radioactive source sits inside the body, and steep dose gradients make checking the delivered dose hard. Their method images Cherenkov light, the faint glow charged particles make in water like material, boosted by a fluorescent dye.

Using a cobalt-60 source, whose photons carry more energy than the usual iridium source, the team calibrated glow brightness against absorbed dose in a custom printed phantom. Flat dose maps built from the glow were then checked against the treatment planning computer. The authors aim for real time, full field dose checks in the clinic.
pmc-13556402:
J Swainson and a large team review ketamine paired with talk therapy for depression in 2026. The drug effects are strong but short, often lasting only weeks. The review asks whether talk therapy can extend them.

Two broad routes are compared. One route helps patients work through the drug experience itself. The other runs standard therapy, such as cognitive behavioral therapy, alongside drug sessions. Studies of ketamine and esketamine are both covered. The team mapped what has been tried and what remains unclear. Readers get a clear map of a fast-growing field where practice is running ahead of proof.
pmc-13556502:
E Moon and co-authors study benzodiazepine combinations in anxiety care in 2026. Panic disorder and generalized anxiety disorder impair daily life heavily and cause deep distress. First-line drugs act slowly over weeks, so sedatives are often added early to bridge the gap.

In practice, more than one benzodiazepine may be prescribed at once for the same patient. Reasons include mixed anxiety profiles, poor sleep, and varied drug responses. These drugs carry risks of tolerance, dependence, misuse, and falls. Guidelines generally discourage such combinations in routine care. Readers learn the patterns the team found in real prescribing and why they matter for safety.
pmc-13556602:
G Maguire reviews drug treatment for stuttering in a 2026 conference abstract. Stuttering starts in childhood, affects over four percent of children, and persists in over one percent of adults. No drug has been approved for it by any regulator, and speech therapy gains often fade over time.

The review pulls together animal work, brain scans, and past drug trials. Drugs that block or partly stir dopamine D2 receptors helped in trials, with olanzapine the best studied and risperidone also showing gains. Two newer compounds need more study, and younger patients may respond better than older ones.
pmc-13556702:
T Youn and co-authors track side effects after starting long acting antipsychotic injections in 2026. Such injections help people with schizophrenia stay on treatment. Fear of side effects still sways whether patients accept and keep the shots. How side effects shift over time after the switch was poorly charted.

The team used a standard side effect rating scale filled out by patients. They looked for change points, the moments when burden starts to ease or speeds its fall. Knowing when relief tends to begin can help doctors counsel patients through the rough early weeks of a new regimen.
pmc-13556802: Violante presents a 2026 conference abstract on steering memory during sleep with a gentle brain stimulation method. Memory forms overnight as the deep memory hub talks with the thalamus and cortex in set rhythms, and wire studies found rhythm marks of good talk that track next day recall. The method sends two high tones that cross in the deep brain to nudge only that target. The group tests whether the nudge works only when timed to the brain's own replay bursts, and whether it shifts the rhythm marks of learning.
pmc-13556902:
Kasparek and Hribkova studied how clozapine acts on brain cells grown from patients who respond to it. Clozapine is the one drug that works when others fail in schizophrenia. How it works stays murky, and its mild grip on dopamine hints at other paths. Gene studies point toward glutamate, a key brain signal.

The team grew two cell types from reprogrammed cells of patients and healthy donors. One type mimics pyramid-shaped nerve cells, the other star-shaped support cells. They measured cell firing, calcium waves, and gene activity with and without the drug. Clozapine lifted the nerve cells' response to glutamate back toward healthy levels. Support cells were checked for a related chemical they supply. The work offers a lab window on the drug's hidden action.
pmc-13557902:
Tong Wu and Yun Jiang review how fat metabolism rewiring in tumour-associated macrophages drives resistance to immune checkpoint therapy in lung cancer. Their 2026 narrative review integrates mechanisms and possible counter-strategies.

Checkpoint drugs transformed non-small cell lung cancer care, yet many patients resist them, and response rates stay limited even in favourable marker groups. Macrophages inside tumours form a key part of the suppressive environment shielding cancers. Their lipid metabolism changes deeply affect their function and gene activity. The review explains how those changes promote immune suppression and therapy resistance. It then outlines therapeutic strategies aimed at the macrophage fat pathways to restore treatment sensitivity.
pmc-13558302:
Four authors review what broken-down chickpea protein could do in food and health. Chickpea hydrolysates and the peptides they release, made by enzymes or by digestion, are attracting interest as plant ingredients with side benefits. The team first mapped the wider field by network analysis of 5,728 records on plant protein hydrolysates. They then reviewed 72 studies on chickpea versions in depth, covering production, peptide makeup, and reported bioactivity.

The lab record looks broad: antioxidant, blood pressure lowering, anti-diabetic, anti-inflammatory, and fat-lowering effects all appear, mostly from test-tube, cell, and animal work. The path to products is blocked by messier problems: uneven methods, half-described peptides, little scale-up proof, and no human trials at all. The authors list standard methods and clinical tests as the needed next steps.
pmc-13558602:
Sushmita Kumari, Somnath Mandal, and Sajad Nabi Dar charted in 2026 two decades of land change in Saharsa District, Bihar, using satellite images from 2002 to 2023. The district sits on a flood-prone river fan in the Kosi Basin, where ecological stress was suspected but unmapped. The team classified land cover at four time points with a standard supervised method and built an ecological vulnerability index to locate stress hotspots.

Built-up land grew by about one hundred square kilometres while forest cover shrank by more than seventy. Vulnerability mapping showed ecological quality sliding from moderate toward poor and very poor, concentrated in the district's centre and southeast where clearing and building ran fastest. The authors urge sustainable land management, replanting, and flood-resilient town planning, and they suggest sharper imagery plus machine learning for the next assessment round.
pmc-13558702:
Darebe Yohannes and three colleagues redesigned in 2026 the animal-drawn tillage tools that Ethiopian smallholders use to furrow light wheat soils. The traditional maresha plough works, yet it is heavy and slow. Working in Misrak Bedawacho District, the team used pairs of oxen under real farm conditions. They built lighter multi-share tools with a shallower rake angle. Comparisons covered depth, pulling force, field capacity, and structural safety.

Working time for a quarter hectare fell from nearly seven hours to about two, and field capacity more than tripled, with efficiency approaching ninety-nine percent. Extra shares raised draft force slightly, while the pull stayed within what oxen can manage, and stress analysis kept every part inside safe limits. Treated soil also held moisture and shaped better for planting. The authors recommend local manufacture plus farmer training.
pmc-13558902:
Nitzan Letko Khait and co-authors combine stem cells with a slow release enzyme after stroke in rats in a 2026 study. Stroke is a leading cause of disability, and regrowing lost tissue stays hard. Neural progenitor cells grown from human induced stem cells are placed in the stroke cavity inside a gel. A redesigned enzyme is released slowly nearby.

The enzyme stays active long term and breaks down scar proteins that block growth, with no immune reaction seen. Each treatment alone improves movement by three weeks. Only the combined therapy keeps transplanted cells alive long term and helps them become neurons, they report.
pmc-13559102:
Lei Wang and four colleagues report a 2026 study that built a prediction model for refractory Mycoplasma pneumoniae pneumonia in children, the form that responds poorly to standard treatment. Their approach leans on measurable features from chest CT scans, combined with ordinary clinical and laboratory data. The records came from children first scanned between January 2019 and December 2021 across four hospitals.

The study group held 197 children, 60 with the refractory form and 137 with the general form. One hospital supplied the training set, while the other three formed an outside validation set. Four measures stood out as independent predictors: C-reactive protein, lactate dehydrogenase, the share of lung volume taken by lesions, and the share of ground-glass opacity. A nomogram built from them discriminated well in both sets. The authors offer the tool as an aid for earlier recognition and planning of care.
pmc-13559202:
Eleven authors test a local language model as a helper for prostate radiotherapy planning in this 2026 study. Planning such treatment takes many rounds of tuning and varies by operator, and a local model keeps patient data off outside servers.

Their agent, SAGE, was linked to a clinical planning system and tuned settings for seventeen past patients. Four versions were compared, mixing two model sizes with or without a memory tool, against the real clinical plans. Target coverage matched the clinical plans. The largest version with memory spared one sensitive organ better than the clinical plans. The study gives an early, careful check of AI help in a safety critical task.
pmc-13559402:
Gu and colleagues published a 2026 narrative review and policy analysis on lung nodule risk tools for people who never smoked. Screening rules were built around age, smoking history, and scan appearance, so never smokers rarely qualify for low dose CT screening. East Asian women face notable lung cancer risk despite never smoking, the authors stress.

Mapping guidelines, prediction models, and cohort studies, Gu found that smoking centred entry rules shut never smokers out of screening. Chinese and Taiwanese studies instead flagged local predictors such as family history, past tuberculosis, and chronic lung disease. A Taiwanese trial in never smokers found invasive cancers that scans could catch early. Models built on screening groups also lost accuracy in hospital patients, and delays in diagnosis cut survival chances.
pmc-13559802:
Rajaa El Azzouzi, Oumaima Boukhlouf, Bouchra Dani, and Malik Boulaadas report a 2026 case of optic nerve harm after a crash in a teen with diabetes. A blow can damage the optic nerve without touching the eye, a rare but grave outcome. Care choices range from high dose steroids to surgery to watchful waiting.

The patient was a 16 year old boy with poorly controlled type 1 diabetes after a road crash. On day three he lost vision in his right eye in a sudden drop. Scans showed cheek bone breaks with no eye damage, and a stretched optic nerve on MRI. Teams from eye, face surgery, hormone, and intensive care weighed the case jointly. The clash between saving sight and systemic risk drives the report.
pmc-13560302:
Laurens Léger and colleagues review blood microRNAs in depth as blood-marker leads for three inherited heart muscle diseases: hypertrophic, arrhythmogenic, and dilated cardiomyopathy. Their 2026 review searched electronic databases and applied strict filters, keeping only studies with healthy controls and proof the test separates sick from well. Nineteen papers survived for analysis.

One microRNA stood out as overexpressed in each disease across different studies: miR-29a-3p in hypertrophic disease, miR-185-5p in the arrhythmogenic form, and miR-454-3p in dilated disease. Beyond those leads, consistency crumbled. Attempts to tie microRNA levels to heart features or genetic background yielded no stable profiles between studies. The authors warn that sudden death can be these diseases' first symptom, which makes a blood test valuable, yet the field is not ready. Larger cohorts using shared methods must validate the candidates first.
pmc-13560402:
Musa Abbas Waziri and colleagues measure nontraumatic ileal perforation, a spontaneous hole in the small intestine causing obscure peritonitis, across three Ugandan hospitals. Their 2026 multicenter cross-sectional study uses a structured checklist on 149 consecutive gut perforation patients. The condition kills often and burdens low-income settings most, where hygiene and HIV shape its causes.

Typhoid fever caused the overwhelming majority of the perforations studied, about four in five cases. Most holes sat twenty to thirty-nine centimeters from the junction with the colon, measured half to one centimeter wide, and appeared singly on the antimesenteric border. Men, farmers, and rural residents carried the heaviest share. HIV-positive patients had far higher odds of this perforation type in the adjusted analysis. Using an open or closed pit latrine, rather than a flush toilet, also raised the odds sharply. The authors tie prevention to sanitation and typhoid control.
pmc-13560802:
Farah M. Babakurd and colleagues link the severity of anterior crossbite, where lower front teeth bite in front of the uppers, to appearance-based bullying in schoolchildren. Their 2026 cross-sectional study examines 2,080 children aged eight to twelve in Damascus public schools, sampled by clusters. Occlusion was scored with the ROMA Index, and bullying with a modified standard questionnaire.

Anterior crossbite appeared in 19.6 percent of the children, while 34.4 percent reported dental appearance bullying at victim frequency in the reported shares. Every form of crooked bite raised bullying likelihood, and crossbite did so most strongly. Crucially, bullying intensity climbed step by step with crossbite severity. Teasing and mockery dominated the abuse types, and playgrounds hosted most incidents regardless of dental group. The authors propose adding crossbite severity screening to school prevention programs for both oral and psychosocial health.
pmc-13561002:
Jin Xia and co-authors pair two antibody drugs as second line therapy for advanced throat cancer in a 2026 trial. Forty six patients whose esophageal cancer grew after first treatment received an immune checkpoint drug plus an antibody that blocks a growth receptor, at centers across China. About a third of tumors shrank, and over four fifths were at least held in check.

Median time before growth resumed was about nine months, and median survival about twelve and a half. Patients whose tumors amplified the growth receptor gene responded nearly twice as often and lived longer. Benefit appeared in both immune naive and immune treated patients.
pmc-13561402:
Anna Laizane and co-authors test online therapy for social anxiety in routine care across Finland in 2026, using team framing since the head byline is uneven. The program has seven sessions with therapist support. Past trials in set conditions showed such therapy works. Proof in daily care was weaker. The study uses registry data from 2019 to 2022.

More than two thousand patients were referred to the program. After filters, over sixteen hundred formed the main group. Scores on a social fear scale fell a lot by the end. Even dropouts gained, though less. About four in ten in the main group showed a firm gain. Among those who finished, near six in ten did. The shorter course may aid follow through.
pmc-13561802:
Inmaculada Márquez, Luis Lemus, and Mario Treviño probe how people intercept moving targets. Their 2026 study mixes advance planning with live feedback during movement. Normally the two blend so tightly that their shares cannot be split. The team froze the cursor just before contact on chosen trials, blocking late fixes.

Players moved a cursor to meet a falling target at its landing spot. With longer freezes, accuracy fell, as expected. But hands also lined up with the landing spot earlier, before the freeze began. Eyes showed no such shift. The pattern proves people lean harder on prediction when late correction is denied. Control, in short, redistributes toward planning.
pmc-13562002:
Parvez Amin Khan and co-authors build an AI system that works backwards for perovskite solar cells: give it target performance figures and it proposes device settings. Gains are hard because many device settings interact with efficiency in tangled ways. Training used 49,998 drift-diffusion simulations balanced across three main loss mechanisms.

A forward surrogate ensemble was checked under strict cross-validation, and its best model beat most rivals on the efficiency proxy. Series resistance and grain-boundary defects stood out as the top limits. A conditional variational autoencoder then generated candidate devices for target values. At the best guidance setting, hit rates beat random sampling by wide margins, and nearly all candidates were valid and new.
pmc-13562602:
Subhasri Biswas and co-authors show that the mitochondria a rat inherits steer how fast its ovaries age, in a 2026 paper. Ovarian aging ends fertility and shifts hormones body-wide, yet its inner drivers are murky. Mitochondrial DNA varies naturally between lineages, and the team asked whether that variation alone changes the ovary's clock.

Two rat cohorts with mixed nuclear genes but different mitochondrial types were compared. One type lost its primordial follicles faster and showed scarring, immune invasion, and giant fused cells in the ovary. Its mitochondria also breathed weaker, made less energy currency, and kept fewer genome copies, despite normal levels of the genome's caretaker protein. Inherited mitochondrial flavor, it seems, is destiny in part.
pmc-13563102:
Ting Xu and co-authors hunt, in a 2026 study, for a drug that can beat lung cancer cells that have learned to resist standard drugs. The target is EGFR, a growth switch that is mutated in many non-small cell lung cancers. Using the switch's shape, the team screened compounds in a computer and picked a lead, called XJ2-2. Lab tests checked it against two resistant mutant cell lines.

The compound slowed both mutant cell types at low doses. It binds the EGFR switch directly and shuts down its signals in cells and in animals. In mice carrying tumors, it shrank the tumor burden. No treatment-linked harm showed at any tested dose. With a fresh chemical shape and a taste for the mutant forms, XJ2-2 stands out as a lead for next-generation lung cancer drugs.
pmc-13563202:
Frans Irapanussa, Arif Prabowo, and Raden Praharsini report in 2026 a rare case of advanced womb prolapse in a woman who bore one child. Prolapse stems from weak pelvic floor support and can wreck daily life. Many births are the usual risk, so a one-birth case after menopause stands out.

The fifty eight-year-old had a two-year bulge that worsened and stuck out in recent months. Bladder emptying trouble and pain persisted after a support ring failed. Full womb removal by the vaginal route plus wall repair fixed the case. Recovery ran smooth with good pain control and no major bleeding.
pmc-13563302:
Sarri and co-authors set out in 2026 how a world society for drug outcome studies speaks up for public health. The field tracks how drugs work and harm in real crowds, a task grown harder by outbreak calls, gaps in drug access, and false claims about cures. Tight funds and world strain add to the load.

The society gives a world forum for shared methods and for talks on rules, teaching, and voice. It picks top issues, sets method standards, and joins public comment rounds on draft rules. It also trains new staff and builds team links across lands. The team argues that proof does not turn into policy on its own. Steady, aimed work is what bridges proof and action.
pmc-13563702:
Ahmed Emara and seven colleagues pool the trial evidence for orforglipron, a daily pill that mimics a gut hormone used against obesity and diabetes. Injected versions work but deter many patients, so an oral option could widen use. The 2026 review searched four databases to January 2026 and found three randomised trials with 2,505 adults who had both obesity and type 2 diabetes. Effects were pooled against placebo, split by dose, and graded for certainty with a standard framework.

Every outcome improved in a clean dose-response pattern. Extra weight loss over placebo ran from 2.43 percent at the 3 milligram dose to 7.80 percent at 24 milligrams. Long-term blood sugar fell by 0.80 to 1.67 percentage points across the dose range, and waistlines shrank significantly from 6 milligrams up. More people quit the drug over side effects, while serious harms matched placebo. With only three trials and some low-certainty ratings, the authors urge caution until bigger studies land.
pmc-13563902:
Hao Wang and twelve colleagues trace a self-feeding circuit in osteosarcoma, the bone cancer of teenagers, where sugar burning and gene switching keep switching each other on. The link is lactylation, a chemical tag built from lactate, the waste of glycolysis. Their 2026 study found these tags raised in tumour tissue over matched healthy tissue. Tag mapping showed the H3K9la mark sitting on the promoter of DHX9, a helicase, and proteomics found DHX9 carrying a lactyl tag at one spot, lysine 1024.

Cutting DHX9 slowed the cancer cells' growth, migration, and invasion, and shrank mouse tumours; adding it back did the reverse. Mutating the 1024 site so it cannot accept the tag broke the loop: glycolytic enzymes fell, lactate tags faded, and malignant behaviour ebbed. A tag-mimicking mutation restored the engine. The authors name the loop a metabolic-epigenetic interface and nominate that lysine as a target.
pmc-13564002:
Rihan Hai, Shanghuan Feng, and Yamei Wang tailor glue for flattened bamboo boards. Their 2026 study notes that stock wood glue wets bamboo poorly, since the grass is dense, slick, and hard for resin to cross. Four lab-made phenolic glues vary in chain length and thickness to find a better fit.

The new glues wet bamboo better than the shop resin and carry more reactive arms for hot pressing. Under a laser scope, the glue lines show deeper entry into the bamboo. Boards stuck with the new glues beat the shop boards on pull strength, dry and wet alike. Tuning chain length and thickness together is the design lesson.
pmc-13564102:
Chien-Chi Wu and co-authors present protein switches that turn a signal on when they bind a small molecule, in a research paper from 2026. Protein switches can detect drugs and other small targets, but past designs had weak signal range, poor reversibility, or fit only fluorescent readouts. A modular design would widen their use.

Their switch joins a labeling protein, a sensing protein, and a synthetic probe with a shielded tag. Binding shifts the shape and exposes the tag for readout. Signal gains reach more than a hundredfold, with fine sensitivity. The platform moved from one drug target to another, worked in fly brain tissue, and suited paper strip tests with gold particles.
pmc-13565002:
Qinghua Wang and co-authors probe what switches mandarin fish sperm on, in a 2026 study mixing lab physiology with gene and protein profiling. Freshwater fish sperm must swim fast on limited energy, and water saltiness is the trigger. Low saltiness below a threshold woke the sperm, while richer water kept them moving longer but started fewer.

Sodium and potassium media helped motion, while calcium suppressed activation except at very low levels. The profiling flagged a handful of genes and thirty-five proteins tied to ion signaling and energy production, with calcium and cAMP pathways standing out. The authors sketch a control network for sperm activation and suggest ways hatcheries can tune fertilization water.
pmc-13565102:
Ana Maria Hofer and co-authors link lifestyle to gum disease in Romanian patients in a 2026 study. Periodontitis, chronic gum inflammation, eats at the tissue holding teeth. Habits from smoking to diet may deepen the damage.

Two hundred four adults with confirmed disease in the northwest of the country answered a structured questionnaire. Clinicians probed pocket depth, attachment loss, and bleeding. Weight, activity, brushing, and diet items were modeled together against each clinical measure. Eating fish one to three times a week tied to shallower pockets after full adjustment. Sweets pointed the other way in the truncated record. The study supports counseling on habits beside the dental chair.
pmc-13565402:
Huang and co-authors review how nerves and immune cells drive inflammation together in skin and gut, in a 2026 narrative review. Skin and gut are both barrier organs with similar defenses, linked in a skin-gut axis. Nerve signals can spark or soothe immune attack in each. The review covers neurogenic skin diseases such as atopic dermatitis, psoriasis, and rosacea, then turns to gut inflammation from infection.

The gut's special nerve layout gets its own treatment. The authors then gather therapies that target the shared nerve-immune circuits of both organs. Clinical proof for such cross-talk treatments is still thin, and target precision is poor. Their framework aims to guide sharper anti-inflammatory strategies that act on nerves and immunity together.
