pmc-13565502:
Roberta Vella and a large team of co-authors published this 2026 study of the first robotic liver operations of one surgeon. Robotic removal of liver tumors is spreading fast, but how skill grows with case difficulty at mid-size centers is poorly charted. The team reviewed 58 straight cases from a single surgeon at such a center.

Most operations were minor resections, and only two rated expert-level hard on a standard score. Median blood loss was 100 milliliters, about one case in ten converted to open surgery, and no patient died within ninety days. Textbook outcomes, a bundle of ideal results, were met in 69 percent of cases by one definition. Running-total charts traced how results shifted from the earliest cases to the latest.
pmc-13565802:
Kathryn Coyne and co-authors take an early look at whether the balance of hormone receptors differs in the womb lining of women with endometriosis, in a 2026 paper. Endometriosis, where womb-like tissue grows outside the womb, often comes with resistance to the hormone progesterone. That hormone acts through two receptor forms, A and B, and their balance may shape the resistance. The team stained tissue samples to compare the forms in twenty women having laparoscopy, half with the disease.

In patients with endometriosis, total receptor staining ran high relative to the B form alone, both in the womb lining and in stray lesions. That pattern hints, indirectly, that the A form may dominate, though the study could not measure it directly. A modified form of the receptor showed no clear difference. The authors call the result preliminary and urge deeper work on receptor balance.
pmc-13566602:
Nicoleta Alina Mareș and co-authors studied why hysterectomy choices drift from a decision algorithm in Romania in 2026. Womb removal is common, and choosing the least invasive route raises care quality. A home-grown algorithm advises the route; practice often departs from it.

Nearly one thousand benign cases from two major centers over four years were reviewed. The algorithm guided about a third of cases; surgeon taste or local resources ruled the rest. Hospital stays averaged about seven days. In keyhole surgery, drifting from the algorithm did not lengthen stays. In open surgery it strongly did, nearly tripling the odds of a long stay. Non-clinical factors, the authors argue, steer many route choices.
pmc-13566702:
Jan Slosarz and eight co-authors look for the point where a cow's milk signals a body-wide shift, in a 2026 study. Farmers count somatic cells in milk to judge udder health, but the count where deeper changes kick in was fuzzy. The team studied 580 healthy Polish Holstein cows with no udder infection, split into four bands by cell count.

Below a count of two hundred thousand cells per milliliter, milk and blood markers barely moved. At or above that line, swelling signals rose, defense proteins shifted, and signs of oxidative strain and lower body weight grew, while milk yield fell. Breakpoints for a dozen markers all landed near that same line. The authors call it a zone of change, not a hard line for disease.
pmc-13567502:
Jiaxu Zhou and seven colleagues rank apple graft combinations by resistance to Valsa canker, a bark disease, in a 2026 paper. Orchards pair fruiting scions with rootstocks, and the pairing shapes vigor and disease fate. Fifteen combinations of three scions and five rootstocks grew under natural field infection.

The team measured growth, leaf photosynthesis, shoot anatomy, and mineral content, then correlated each with a disease index. One scion, Yueyanghong, led overall, and its pairing with Qingzhen No.2 rootstock combined the best graft compatibility with the strongest resistance profile. Two other pairings proved highly susceptible. Low disease tracked with faster photosynthesis, more potassium, thicker phloem, and denser shoot cells; iron, manganese, and zinc ran the other way. The authors propose their multi-trait index as a screening tool for growers choosing combinations.
pmc-13567602:
Catalin Cosma and co-authors track how nutrition-linked blood markers change after stomach removal surgery for stomach cancer. They followed 239 patients having part or all of the stomach removed, and checked blood values before surgery, at discharge, and three months later. Markers covered protein, cholesterol, immune cells, and a combined score.

All markers moved in a worse direction after surgery and hit their lowest point at discharge. By three months they had climbed back partway, but none reached the starting level. Full removal hit immune cell counts harder at discharge, though that gap closed by three months.
pmc-13568202:
Diana Castro Paupério and colleagues report, in a 2026 feasibility study at a Portuguese hospital, an automated digital tool that collects patient-reported outcomes for people awaiting heart and chest surgery. As part of a patient blood management program, 221 patients received scheduled questionnaires about health, pain, and mood over their care journey during 2024.

The two-stage digital journey was built in under two months, and patients completed about seventy-two percent of planned interactions. Mood screening flagged five severe and nine moderately severe depression cases for attention. Scores for general health and pain changed little by ninety days. The pilot shows automated outcome tracking can work inside a busy surgical pathway.
pmc-13569602:
Scott and co-authors studied a protein that may tip bone marrow stem cells toward fat instead of bone, in a paper published in 2026. As people age or gain weight, marrow fills with fat and fracture risk climbs. Stem cells in the marrow choose between making bone cells and fat cells, and the two fates trade off. A known master switch drives the fat fate. The protein studied here, a tagging enzyme, boosts that switch in fat tissue elsewhere in the body.

The team grew marrow stem cells from normal mice and from mice lacking the enzyme. They measured how well each set made bone or fat in the dish. They also compared bone shape in the two mouse lines. If the enzyme favors fat in marrow too, blocking it could protect bone. The study tests that idea at the cell and whole-bone level.
pmc-13569702:
Benjamin Wajsberg and colleagues tested a silk-and-hyaluronic-acid injection for voices weakened by incomplete vocal-fold closure. Glottic insufficiency, often from vocal-fold paralysis or age-related thinning, leaves voices breathy and weak and can cause swallowing trouble. Their retrospective study at one academic voice centre reviewed 33 patients who received 44 silk-HA injections between June 2022 and August 2025, mostly in the office.

About 86 percent reported at least minimal vocal improvement, and about 79 percent reported partial to significant improvement, matching plain hyaluronic acid in patients who had received both. Operative revisions were more frequent with silk-HA, though serious adverse events did not rise. The authors present silk-HA as a viable office-based option, with independent-centre evidence backing earlier claims.
pmc-13570202:
Renjie Liu, Tianyi Zhao, and Yadong Wang argue for one shared way to unmix tissue-level molecular data across all its forms. A tissue sample averages signals from many cell types, so a change may mean cells shifted in number or in state. Reading single cells directly solves this but is too costly and fragile for most stored clinical samples. Unmixing methods use small single-cell references to estimate the cell mix hidden in bulk data.

Most such methods were built for one data type at a time, while modern studies collect gene, protein, and metabolite data together. The authors set out what a universal unmixing method must handle to serve medical research across all three. Their piece frames the problem and the standards the field should meet.
pmc-13570302:
Lanlan Jiang, Yuxiao Huang, Shimin Zhang, and a team of co-authors test whether gum disease worsens diabetes by damaging the gut. The two conditions often appear together, and a leaky gut wall could be the bridge that lets inflammation spread from mouth to metabolism.

In mice with both conditions, the gut lining looked badly damaged under the microscope. Its sealing proteins and protective mucus fell, helpful immune cells shrank in number, and inflammatory signals rose. A known alarm pathway was switched on in the gut tissue. The doubly sick mice also ran higher blood sugar and insulin than mice with diabetes alone. The authors conclude that treating the mouth may matter for the body's sugar control.
pmc-13570502:
Josephine Ljungberg, a solo author, asks therapists what recovery from borderline personality disorder looks like, in a 2026 study. The therapy in view is dialectical behavior therapy, whose stated aim is to help clients build a life worth living. Yet how its therapists define recovery, and when it is enough to end treatment, was little studied. Ljungberg held deep interviews with eight such therapists and sorted the themes.

Therapists cast recovery as a move from suffering to a life of normal freedom. By the end of care, clients had stopped self-destructive acts and gained skills, which shifted how they saw themselves and let them build a stable life. Recovery and a life worth living feed each other, the therapists said. The study urges weaving client goals in early.
pmc-13570902:
Lingyu Mao and co-authors reviewed in 2026 how well a picosecond laser treats Becker's nevus, a benign patch of dark, sometimes hairy skin. Records covered forty-nine patients treated at one Chinese center from 2021 to 2025 with a 1064-nanometer Nd:YAG picosecond laser. Two skin doctors graded photos on a four-point gain scale. Half the group had hairy patches and half did not.

In the non-hairy group, more sessions clearly meant more gain. In the hairy group, session count did not track gain. Side effects were brief: pain, redness, swelling, and pigment shifts both ways. The team calls the laser a fair, well-tolerated option of modest power, and notes the single-center, no-control design as a limit.
pmc-13571202:
Concepcion Munoz-Sosa and co-authors test in 2026 whether dark mood carries the effect of angry brooding into bodily complaints. Aches with no clear cause burden many people and track with how emotions are handled. Their survey covered 507 adults, most of them women, with standard scales for body symptoms, negative affect, and anger rumination.

Brooding and dark mood each linked to more body symptoms in both sexes. When both were weighed together, brooding's link shrank in women and vanished in men. A mediation test found dark mood carried about sixty-two percent of brooding's total effect. The path points to mood work as a lever in care.
pmc-13571602:
Bruna Pereira Resende and co-authors probe how tuned atovaquone cousins block a key mitochondrial complex. Their twenty twenty-six study targets complex three of the cell power chain. Cancer cell mitochondria stay active and carry a strong negative charge, a handle for drug design.

A charged carrier group drags the drug into those mitochondria. Swapping ring groups, like adding fluorine-heavy ones, shifts electron spread and strength. The team links those redox and shape traits to how well each variant blocks the complex and slows cell growth. Smarter versions could hit tumor power supplies harder while sparing healthy cells, a long-sought balance in cancer drug craft.
pmc-13571702:
Lin Li and co-authors build in a 2026 paper a stir bar coated in biochar and cellulose gel for tracing bisphenols in canned food. The bar's spongy coat offers wide channels that speed uptake of target compounds. Both coat parts come from natural stock, and the build uses no organic solvent.

Home made bars beat shop bars on both speed and capacity in bench tests. Paired with a tandem mass method, the setup serves routine food safety checks. Extraction takes eight minutes, with detection floors in the low nanogram range. Solvent use in the extraction step drops to one milliliter per run. The authors claim the first use of this coat pair in stir bar work.
pmc-13571802:
López-Rodríguez Larissa and colleagues review, in a 2026 article with two new cases, what is known before birth about spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia congenita caused by the collagen gene COL2A1. This skeletal disorder affects the spine and bone ends. Published prenatal cases were gathered with a planned search, and two further cases from a referral center were described with later gene proof.

First detection ranged from eleven to twenty-eight weeks of pregnancy. Several families carried the condition, while others appeared sporadic, and extra imaging was often needed to clarify spine and bone hardening defects. No gene pattern foretold severity. Diagnosis before birth, the authors stress, needs imaging, genetic testing, and close teamwork together.
pmc-13572002:
Rui Chang and co-authors built a slow-release vitamin B12 carrier in a 2026 paper. The vitamin treats a childhood acid disorder but needs frequent shots. Swallowed doses absorb poorly and unevenly. Their carrier is a multivesicular liposome made by microfluidic mixing.

A sugar ring additive helped load the water-loving vitamin. The bubbles hold many inner chambers for a long release. Tests tracked how long levels stay up in the body. Higher and steadier uptake is the goal. Fewer injections would ease life for young patients and their families at home.
pmc-13572202:
Tian and four co-authors studied alarm signals in water fleas for this paper from twenty twenty-six. When predators kill prey, chemical cues warn the survivors, who often speed up growth and breeding. The team asked what happens when cues mix signals from two genetic lines at once. Two clonal lines of Daphnia served as the test system.

Pure cues triggered the classic adaptive switch in life history. Mixed cues instead caused chronic stress, stunting growth and breeding in line-specific ways. In long contests between the lines, the ranking flipped under mixed cues. The less stunted line rose, while the other was suppressed. The authors call the mixed signal a form of chemical interference that can preserve diversity.
pmc-13572402:
Jiachen Liu, with three colleagues, presents a 2026 computer framework for naming aircraft types in satellite and aerial images. Fine splits between look-alike planes matter for defence work, yet deep learning models rarely show why they choose a label. That gap limits trust when the stakes are high.

The framework, EC-AT, pairs transfer learning with checks on whether three explanation tools point at the same image zones. Eight plane types came from the MAR20 data set. Models that started from pre-trained weights, then had their last layers tuned, reached accuracy up to 99.9 percent. A new overlap score measured how well the three tools agreed. A trust scorecard then rated the whole setup on accuracy, logic, and clarity of display. The checks also flagged background clutter that can sway a call.
pmc-13572502:
Lais Takata Walter, with ten colleagues, details a 2026 study of nitric oxide in the wiring of the young rat retina. Nitric oxide is a gas that cells use as a signal. The team asked whether it shapes circuits through the retina's own waves of activity or through a route apart from those waves.

Work began at postnatal day 10, when the enzyme that makes the gas first appeared in two cell types and gas output was first detected. Blocking that enzyme left the timing and shape of stage III waves intact. Still, the network grew denser, with more links per cell. Gene levels for both chemical and electrical synapse parts fell, and their layered layout broke down. Cells grown in dishes grew longer fibres. The team reads the gas as a brake on wiring that acts apart from wave patterns.
pmc-13572902:
Azita Fathnezhad-Kazemi and Asal Rahbar Zeraati compare women's well-being across three groups in this 2026 study. Cosmetic surgery is growing worldwide, and women often seek it over body image worries. The team asked whether having surgery, wanting it, or neither lines up with different quality of life and mental health.

The study covered 375 women in Tabriz, Iran, split among past patients, candidates, and a comparison group. All filled in standard surveys on health, mood, body appreciation, and body image concern. Clear gaps appeared on every measure. Women who had surgery scored best on quality of life and mental health, and worried least about their bodies. Candidates scored lowest on body appreciation. The authors advise routine mental health checks and careful talks about motives before surgery.
pmc-13573002:
Boughattas and six co-authors present a report from twenty twenty-six on West Nile virus found in an aborted sheep fetus in Tunisia. Sheep abortions in Zaghouan prompt lab testing in September twenty twenty-five. One fetal sample tests positive for the virus by gene assay. Sequencing yields a near-complete viral genome from the sample. It falls in the lineage tied to local human brain infection cases. A marker motif on the envelope protein matches regional strains. The detection is the first of its kind in a sheep there.

The authors read it as proof the virus circulates locally. Animal and public health both face stakes, they stress. Surveillance of livestock losses gains a new signal.
pmc-13573302:
Jiahui Guo and co-authors review how BRCA-mutated cancers learn to resist PARP inhibitor drugs, and how to fight back, in a 2026 paper. Healthy BRCA genes run a DNA repair crew called homologous recombination. Tumors that lose it die when PARP, a second repair path, is blocked, a trap named synthetic lethality. Several such drugs are approved, yet resistance and side effects cap their long use.

The review sorts escape routes by how proven and how common each is in the clinic. It draws a firm line between combos for patients new to the drugs and moves saved for those already resistant. A biomarker map then links each escape form to the right sample, the right test, and a fitting counter-move. The authors aim the map at clearer trial design and sharper reading of patient data.
pmc-13573402:
Senem Askin Ekinci, with three colleagues, reports a 2026 mapping study of jaw fractures from CT scans. Knowing where jaw breaks cluster helps surgeons plan care and helps engineers design better plates. The team rebuilt fracture lines in three dimensions for a hospital cohort treated from 2018 to 2025.

The cohort held 158 patients, near two thirds men, with a mean age in the late thirties. In all, 239 fractures and 267 fracture lines were drawn. Breaks clustered behind the molars, at the jaw joint neck, at the canine socket, and near the chin hole. The angle and ramus zone broke most often, and assault was the top cause. Impacted wisdom teeth went with more angle breaks and fewer joint breaks. The heat maps show where the jaw is weakest in this group.
pmc-13573502:
Nicoline Mathiessen Andersen and co-authors ask whether new lung-test formulas change who can have lung cancer surgery. Their 2026 study notes that surgery is the main care for early lung cancer, and that lung tests help judge if a patient can bear it. Old European formulas set the bar that guides use now.

The team drew on the health records of 1,400 patients. They worked out each patient's lung scores under the old formulas and under two newer sets, one world-wide and one Danish. The world-wide set did not shift the share of patients who fell below key cut-offs. The Danish set did shift the share for one lung measure, which could change who is offered surgery.
pmc-13573602:
Xiao Xiao, Hongyu Zhao, and Zuoheng Wang present NDreamer, a tool for reading single-cell data without the noise that lab batches add. New sequencing tools yield huge cell data sets, but batch shifts and sparse counts can bend the results. The goal is to find gene shifts caused by a treatment or linked to a disease state.

NDreamer pairs a neural network that codes each cell in a compact form with a matching step that lines cells up fairly. Tests across platforms, organs, and species showed it beat older tools at cleaning batch noise. Used on an Alzheimer's disease set, it found gene patterns that split patients from healthy controls in ways that fit known biology.
pmc-13573702:
Shi and co-authors find a clock gene that drives spread in KRAS G12D pancreatic cancer. This KRAS type sits in about 40 percent of such cancers. It also carries the worst outlook of KRAS types. Data mining plus lab tests flagged ARNTL2 as a partner factor. ARNTL2 binds the SERPINE1 promoter and switches it on.

That axis drove shape change and spread in cells and mice. Rescue tests proved SERPINE1 was the needed link. Protein levels of both tracked together in patient samples. Joint levels split patients into distinct outlook groups. The axis also shifted reply to KRAS G12D drugs.
pmc-13573802:
Jinyang An and co-authors mapped in 2026 a scattered young field: tiny parcels called extracellular vesicles, shed by tissues other than bone, and their roles in osteoporosis. Such parcels might sway bone rebuilding, serve as blood markers, or carry drugs. The team sorted 114 studies by purpose and graded their evidence and maturity.

Most work is preclinical; only fourteen studies reached evidence in human participants, and none reached the clinic or industry stage. Claims often blur: proving a parcel matters is not proving its cargo or its source did. Human marker validation and dose tracking were rare. The authors offer the map as a discipline tool. They list the proofs the field must produce before any product talk.
pmc-13574502:
Yu-Hsuan Li, Junyi Wu and I Te Lee compared in 2026 two ways of priming thyroid cancer patients for radioactive iodine treatment, asking which is kinder to insulin control. One group of 47 got injections of lab-made thyroid-stimulating hormone; 29 others stopped their hormone pills to raise it naturally. Blood tests before and on treatment day fed a standard insulin resistance index.

The index fell in both groups, and the size of the fall did not differ clearly between them. In the injection group, patients whose triglycerides dropped most were far likelier to gain a large insulin benefit. The authors conclude the injection route eases insulin resistance about as well as withdrawal, without weeks of low thyroid symptoms. The fat link gives doctors a clue about who gains most. The study was observational, so the groups were not assigned by chance.
pmc-13574602:
Meng Wang and co-authors report a rare brain tumor in a ten-year-old girl that carried two gene mutations where one is the rule. Myxoid glioneuronal tumors, recognized only in the 2021 classification, grow in the brain's midline partition and usually alter a single growth receptor gene, PDGFRA. Hers also carried a pathogenic change in FGFR3.

The tumor was removed completely, and tissue study confirmed the diagnosis. The authors pair the case with a review of what is known about this young tumor type, including its generally gentle course and rare spread. A dual mutation in a brand-new category tests whether the standard story still holds, and argues for sequencing every case.
pmc-13574802:
Women with endometriosis often struggle to conceive, and their blood fats and metabolism may hold clues to who will succeed. Yanan Duan, Aiping Chen, and Yushuang Yao built a prediction model in 2026 from more than five thousand such women in the UK Biobank. They then checked it on a hospital cohort in Qingdao.

Metabolic and lipid measures were tested against later delivery in Britain and clinical pregnancy in China. A shrinkage method picked the strongest predictors, which were folded into a points-based nomogram, the paper chart doctors can read at a glance. Performance was graded in training, internal, and external sets. The authors offer the tool for counseling, with the external check as its main credential.
pmc-13574902:
Honoria Ocagli and co-authors pool the world's data on bad reactions to ultrasound contrast agents in a 2026 review. These microbubble agents sharpen ultrasound scans, and the review asks how often they harm, in adults and children alike.

Seventy four studies covered more than a million adults and thirty six thousand children. Severe sudden reactions were extremely rare: about six per hundred thousand adults and sixteen per hundred thousand children. Milder sudden reactions came to about one per thousand. Delayed reactions were vanishingly rare. No product stood out as riskier, and heart patients reacted at the same rate as everyone else. Reactions in pregnancy and emergency handling are also reviewed.
pmc-13575102:
Alexandra Rafeletou, Faezeh Fathi, Tatjana Kiseļova, Golnaz Taheri, and Arian Lundberg hunt quiet prostate cancers that will turn fast, in a 2026 paper. Low-risk labels rest on clinic scores that miss much of a tumor's true temper. The team fed gene, control-layer, and copy-change data from about 500 tumors into a network-shaped learning model. One gene stood out as a master switch of early aggression.

Tumors low in that switch carried more driver faults and showed predicted weakness to three drug families. A network rewiring score built on the switch tracked time without growth in the main cohort and return of a blood marker in two outside ones. The frame spots tumors in mid-turn, before they spread, the authors argue, when extra care may still change the ending.
pmc-13575202:
Zhenlong Zhao and co-authors teach a robot arm to thread cluttered space along paths that are short, cheap, and quick all at once. Those goals fight each other, and any path must also respect the arm's joint limits and motion dynamics. Their 2026 paper builds a planning framework around an evolutionary search steered by a reinforcement learning agent.

The learner, a tabular SARSA agent, watches the state of the search and picks which search behavior to deploy next. A hybrid crossover operator with gentle random kicks, nested inside a hierarchical neighborhood strategy, keeps the population of candidate paths refining without collapsing. Tests used a six-joint UR5 arm in scenes with one, three, and five obstacles. The method always found workable paths and earned the best composite scores, weighted toward dynamic stability, among five rival planners. Its joint motions also ran smoother.
pmc-13575402:
Elizabeth Dapre leads a 2026 report on how to draw South Asian women into diet trials for diabetes in pregnancy, and keep them taking part. Diabetes in pregnancy affects about one in five UK pregnancies at most, and South Asian women face roughly double the risk of white British women. A planned trial of an intermittent low-energy diet needed better recruitment.

Seventeen women in Greater Manchester who knew the condition personally or through family reviewed the study materials. Three priorities emerged: easing feelings of vulnerability and loss of control, making the trial easier to reach and join, and cutting the mental load from family duties and emotional strain. Contributors also named research fatigue and low trust. The feedback reshaped the trial design and recruitment plans.
pmc-13575502:
Emely Hoffman and co-authors delete a detox enzyme in mice and watch the liver and blood sugar pull in opposite directions. Their 2026 study knocks out glyoxalase 1, which clears the sugar byproduct methylglyoxal. On a sixteen-week diet rich in fat and sugar, the knockout mice were expected to fare worse across the board.

Instead, their livers stored notably less fat than normal mice on the same diet. Body fat tissue showed no such change, and the kidneys looked unharmed. Yet blood sugar control clearly worsened, with higher fasting glucose and poorer tolerance in tests. The authors read the split as a lesson in tradeoffs: one enzyme can guard sugar handling while its absence relieves the liver. The work refines where glyoxalase-targeted drugs might help or harm.
pmc-13576102:
Charles Ntalika and Eric Umar gather nurses' views on their ongoing training at Malawi's Zomba Central Hospital for a 2026 qualitative study. Ongoing training keeps nurses current, yet little was known about how programmes match daily needs in a low-resource hospital. Fifteen nurses were interviewed in depth.

Five themes came out of the talks. Nurses spot their own learning needs through practice, often with weak coordination from the hospital. Training was valued for knowledge, skill, and confidence, yet many sessions missed practical gaps and offered no mentoring afterwards. Facilitators often lacked teaching skill, according to participants. Time clashes, heavy workloads, and costs such as transport and mobile data blocked attendance. The authors call for training shaped around nurses' stated needs with follow-up support built in.
pmc-13576202:
Behnam Kiani Kalejahi and Mohammad Javad Rajabi retest a thyroid cancer diagnosis model under stricter rules in a 2026 study. Papillary thyroid carcinoma is the most common thyroid cancer, and diagnosis before surgery blends ultrasound images with needle biopsy cell samples. A recent paper reported near-perfect scores from classic methods on one random split of the data.

The pair held back 77 of 384 patients as an untouched test set and built a deep learning model joining both data types. On the held-out patients it scored 0.977 on the ranking accuracy measure, with sensitivity of 0.977 and specificity of 0.939 at the chosen cut-off. Its probability estimates were far better calibrated than a simpler baseline. It also beat the re-run classic methods on the same patients. The authors argue strict holdout testing gives a fairer picture.
pmc-13576302:
Michela Destito leads a 2026 study testing whether CT scan patterns can predict a key immunotherapy marker in lung cancer without a tissue sample. The marker, PD-L1, guides drug choice in non-small cell lung cancer, yet biopsy can miss tumour variety or be impossible. Radiomics turns scan texture into numbers a model can learn from.

Scans from 55 patients with confirmed cancer were analysed, and several learning models were trained with repeated cross-checks. A support vector machine did best, with median accuracy of 0.77 and a ranking score of 0.83 for spotting high PD-L1 levels. Texture features carried most of the signal, and adding clinical data did not help. The authors call the virtual biopsy idea feasible, as a partner or fallback for tissue testing.
pmc-13577202:
Coetzee and nine co-authors weigh mobile digital X-ray units for finding tuberculosis in South Africa in this 2026 paper. Chest imaging catches TB that symptom questions miss. A charity deployed nine units in four high burden districts between 2020 and 2022, in three forms: long term community vans, long term facility containers, and short term community vans. Over thirty-four thousand people were screened. A quarter had abnormal images, and 1,372 TB cases were found.

Long term vans won on every measure. Their positivity rate topped ten percent, and each case found cost under four hundred dollars in routine care terms. Short term vans screened crowds cheaply per person but cost over fourteen thousand dollars per case under charity led running. Staying power, not mobility alone, made the difference: a van that becomes a neighborhood fixture reaches the people symptom screening misses.
pmc-13578002:
Iris Mulder and four colleagues measure blood flow markers in eye tumours and other inner-eye lesions with MRI scans, in a 2026 exploratory study. Telling a uveal melanoma from a harmless mole or a benign blood vessel growth inside the eye can be hard. Perfusion imaging tracks how contrast washes through tissue, giving numbers that may separate the types.

Thirty-eight patients covering twelve diagnoses had 3 tesla dynamic scans. A standard model produced flow and leakage values, while simpler curve measures were taken for comparison. Blood vessel tumours showed by far the highest flow values. Melanomas sat above moles and metastases on the main measures. Simple and model-based numbers tracked each other well, and patterns matched a dye-based eye test. Small group sizes blocked firm comparisons between single diagnoses.
pmc-13578502:
Zora Arum and colleagues describe a meningioma program launched in September 2024 that joins treatment, research, and patient support under one roof. Meningioma, the most common primary brain tumor, leaves many patients with quality-of-life and thinking problems after diagnosis and treatment. The program combined a weekly tumor board, a multidisciplinary clinic, clinical trials, prospective registries, and a dedicated support group.

In its first fifteen months, the board discussed 602 cases and the clinic saw 142 patients in consultation. Twelve percent of board cases were offered trial enrollment and 84 percent were offered registry enrollment, while support-group members reported informational and emotional benefits. Consultation and treatment volumes rose sharply across departments, suggesting the model can streamline care for a complex tumor.
pmc-13578602:
Lihua Liu and co-authors surveyed psychiatric nurses in 2026 about a mild, early form of delirium that is easy to miss. They asked how nurses' knowledge, attitudes, and daily behavior around this condition hang together.

Scores showed positive links among all three: nurses who knew more tended to hold better attitudes and act more in line with good practice. Attitude carried a small part of the link between knowledge and behavior, about a fifth, while the direct link made up the rest. Knowledge itself was rated notably low, despite warm attitudes. Job title made no clear difference. The authors suggest prompts in health records and checklists at handover, plus more teaching.
pmc-13578702:
Zhang and a large team combine brain imaging with gene expression atlases in this 2026 study of Alzheimer's disease, focusing on the white matter hugging the cortex. They measured free water fraction, a diffusion MRI signal reflecting tissue disorganization, across 68 such regions in 194 patients with amyloid-confirmed Alzheimer's and 153 cognitively normal controls.

They then asked which of 15,633 genes, their expression mapped from the Allen Human Brain Atlas, track the regions where water accumulates. The linked genes clustered in lipid metabolism, neuron insulation, and synaptic signaling, and were expressed mainly in oligodendrocytes, the insulation-making cells, plus two neuron types. The enrichments replicated in two additional datasets. Mediation analysis added a functional twist: free water fraction partly carried the effect of the APOE4 risk gene on cognition, in a domain-specific pattern, positioning the imaging marker between genes and symptoms.
pmc-13579402:
Soha Elatrebi and co-authors argue that modern weight-loss drugs should be rethought as standard care after liver transplantation. Their 2026 review starts from a cruel pattern: the transplant saves a life, then obesity and metabolic disease move in, fed by the underlying illness and by immune-suppressing drugs. Fatty liver, kidney strain, and diabetes follow.

Drugs that mimic the gut hormones GLP-1 and GIP are already approved for long-term weight management. The authors weigh their fit for transplant recipients, whose drug balances are delicate. A plan that guards the new liver's metabolic health, they argue, is part of the transplant itself.
pmc-13579502:
Araújo and colleagues tested whether Brazilian green propolis, a resin bees make, can blunt the harm of a fatty diet in mice, in a study published in twenty twenty-six. Fatty diets drive weight gain, blood sugar trouble, and fatty liver disease in both mice and people.

Male mice ate a high-fat diet for twelve weeks, with some groups also getting plain propolis, a propolis extract, or an extract made from the leftover residue of oil production. All three forms cut weight gain and improved blood fats and sugar control. They also quieted genes that build fat in the liver, lowered inflammation, and eased liver fat buildup. A compound called artepillin C stood out in the extracts. The residue form is notable: a waste product performed like the premium forms, which could make treatment cheaper and greener.
pmc-13579802:
Annika Ericson and co-authors test, in a 2026 study, how well children with spastic cerebral palsy sense their knee's place. That sense, proprioception, steers how we move, yet leg reads in this group are rare. The study held 57 children with the ill, aged 6 to 18: 20 with one side hit, 37 with both. A sound group of 42 joined for clash. A 3D motion rig read the knee in a sit test with sight blocked. First, a tester lifted the leg to 45 degrees and the child held it. Then the child found that bend on their own and held it.

Errors split the groups in a flipped way: the one-side group erred more than the both-side group. Hold drift and wobble were read too.
pmc-13579902:
A fungal lung infection called pulmonary cryptococcosis turns deadlier when other infections ride along, but solid cohort evidence was thin. The authors of a 2026 study gather 454 patients, split between people living with HIV and those without it. They compare symptoms, scans, severity scores, and survival by co-infection status. Among patients without HIV, every death within a year came with a bacterial co-infection. Co-infected patients with HIV scored worse on severity measures.

One added infection stood out: a pneumonia found only in patients with HIV more than tripled the risk of death. Overall, patients with HIV faced eleven times the death risk of the others. The authors say co-infection checks should shape how these patients are triaged.
pmc-13581002:
Anna Coleman and co-authors describe how a Manchester research center built an inclusive research strategy, in a 2026 paper. Funders now require health research to include the full range of people it affects. The center and its clinical research facility co-produced the strategy with public contributors and partner teams. Workshops and one-to-one talks fed the drafting over several rounds.

Five principles anchor the strategy, from mapping inequality to building staff capacity and working with communities. A dedicated oversight board guards inclusive governance. Feedback stressed the value of shared production and the need to flatten power gaps between researchers and the public. The authors align the plan with national frameworks and build in review cycles. They offer the strategy as a model other centers can adapt.
pmc-13581202:
Godéré and colleagues test in twenty twenty-six a cheaper way to count microplastics inside giant clams for island nations with thin lab budgets. They stain clam tissue with a fluorescent dye that lights up plastic, photograph it across several light bands, and let a trained image model flag particles. Clams came from three French Polynesian islands, and counts were checked against a gold-standard spectroscopy method.

The model scored on par with human annotators. Gills held far more particles than gut tissue on every island. Spectroscopy showed the dye method overcounts, fooled by proteins and plant fibres, yet the pipeline still promises fast, standard screening. The real polymer mix pointed to fishing gear, farming, and household waste as sources.
pmc-13581302:
Sylvester Tumusiime and a team of co-authors recount turning a research health-record network into a disease surveillance engine. Their report appeared in twenty twenty-six. REACHnet held polished records from Louisiana and Texas health systems, while public health needed fresher, standardized feeds.

The rebuild repackaged those records into the MENDS format for chronic disease tracking. Health departments in both states, plus a national chronic disease association, gained access. Governance rules, privacy approvals, and plumbing all had to satisfy every partner at once. The paper itemizes the tools used and the snags hit along the way. Latency dropped while data quality held. The authors offer the playbook to other networks attempting the same jump.
pmc-13581702:
Patients increasingly ask chatbots about their cancer, and Wan and co-authors grade five leading language models on bladder cancer teaching. Twenty common patient questions went to each model on the same day in January 2026. Blinded pharmacists and specialists then scored the answers for clarity, usefulness, and quality. They also scored fit with the national treatment guideline, and readability formulas were checked too.

Three models, ChatGPT, DeepSeek, and Doubao, clearly beat the other two, and ChatGPT hewed closest to the guideline. No answer was harmful, though treatment answers ran hardest to read across the board. The authors back a careful, assistive role for the tools and note that education-specific scoring beats raw readability counts.
pmc-13581802:
Yi-Hua Liu and Bing Wei look for warning signs that endometrial cancer will return after surgery. They studied 368 patients treated at one center from 2019 to 2024, all of whom had surgery as their first treatment. Before surgery, each patient had blood tests, and the team checked whether three simple measures from those tests could flag a higher risk of the cancer coming back.

Over a median follow-up of thirty months, 32 patients saw their cancer return. Higher values of all three blood measures were tied to a higher chance of return, as were a later disease stage and deeper growth into the womb wall. The three measures added useful detail beyond the standard factors doctors already use. The authors caution that the cut-off values came from this one group and need testing in larger groups elsewhere.
pmc-13582202:
Mengxuan Tian and Sainyu Guo re-examined a huge pooled claim that exercise does almost nothing for memory, and found the claim hides a real effect, in a paper published in 2026. A sweeping review of reviews had put the average benefit near zero after correcting for publication bias. The authors suspected that lumping all memory types together had washed the signal out.

They re-sorted more than two thousand effect estimates from a public database and isolated those for verbal memory, the kind used for words and facts. The pooled effect came out about eight times larger than the blanket figure. Aerobic exercise gave the firmest gain, and bias checks found no clear distortion. The authors advise prescribing exercise by memory type, not by averages.
pmc-13582302:
Sourav Kumar Podder and co-authors weigh surgery against watchful care for ventral hernias in a huge records study of routine care. Their 2026 paper draws on a national database holding over 580,000 patients with the diagnosis. About one in seven had the hernia repaired.

Repair came with a clearly lower risk of bowel obstruction over time. No link appeared between surgery and later opioid misuse. Repaired patients used physical therapy far more often after care. Spine and pelvic floor problems ran slightly higher in the surgery group, while other gut and bladder outcomes barely differed. The authors say repair guards the bowel but does not cut functional complaints.
pmc-13582502:
Zengwei Kou, Yunsheng Liu, Wujie Qian, Sihan Zhang, Shulei Lou, and Da Shao present a 2026 map of the research field on antibody cures for Ebola. Antibody drugs became a mainstay after wins against the Zaire strain, yet the field's shape had no set chart. The team pulled 1,350 papers from three big stores, spanning 1990 to 2026. Count tools charted who writes, who teams with whom, and which themes wax and wane.

Output surged with outbreaks, above all the West African crisis of 2014 to 2016, then slid after 2020. Public search interest spiked anew with a 2026 outbreak of a strain with no licensed cure. Maps like this show funders where the field is deep and where it is thin.
pmc-13582602:
Mahmoud Ragab presents a smart model to track student grades in a 2026 study. Schools now mine student data to forecast marks and help learners do better in the next course. A sharp forecast can flag strugglers early and shape help to each student's needs.

Ragab's model pairs a deep network that attends to many points at once with a search method that tunes its weights. Scores are scaled to a set range before training. The aim is stronger forecasts, deeper engagement, and more personal learning paths. Readers see how the model's parts join to read student data.
pmc-13583102:
Matteo Jugovac and co-authors grow borophene, a one-atom-thick sheet of boron, and watch its electronic tune change with thickness. Borophene's behavior hinges on what it sits on and how many layers stack up. The team made single and double layers on a tungsten surface and read their band structures with electron microscopes and X-ray tools.

The single layer settled into an ordered pattern locked to the surface, with metallic states blended from sheet and substrate. The double layer kept long-range order but hid those blended states, showing bands of its own. The shift traces to the second layer rebuilding the structure and the layers acting on each other. The work maps a knob, thickness, for tuning this young material.
pmc-13583502:
Kwakye, Dzikowski, Wund, and Veeramah link gene activity to signs of selection in stickleback fish adapting to fresh water in twenty twenty-six. Genome scans find many adaptive gene variants, but tying them to traits is hard. The team instead asked whether genes whose activity differs between sea and fresh water fish sit in genome regions shaped by selection.

They read gene activity in brain and gill tissue from wild fish in one sea and two fresh water sites. The differing genes carried variants tied to fast adaptation and to genome divergence. Most such variants sat in gene control regions with mild predicted effects. Named genes pointed to calcium control in gills and fat use in brain.
pmc-13583602:
Sai Gao and five co-authors build, in 2026 work, silk microneedles that leave their tips in the skin to drip a psoriasis drug over days. The skin ill is a long flare driven by one flare signal, whose blocker is now shot through the whole body. Their patch's tips carry the drug; its base melts fast so the tips stay put.

Wet silk slowed the drip hard: most of the drug took two days to leave, against an hour unwetted. In cell tests the drip calmed fast scar close. In mice with a like skin ill, the patch eased scores, shrank spleens, and thinned the skin's overgrowth, while flare marks sank. Local, slow care is the aim.
pmc-13583702:
Sanam Shafaattalab and co-authors build a cellular NOT gate to guard nerves in prostate cancer therapy, in a 2026 paper. Therapies that target a prostate antigen can also hit healthy tissue that carries it, a recurring problem in solid tumor care. The antigen shows in the nervous system at levels that can top the prostate itself, and some drugs cause severe nerve harm.

Their gate uses an inhibitory receptor that switches the therapy cell off when it meets a second protein. That protein coats nerve support cells and is co expressed with the target in nerves. In lab tests the gated cells spared human nerve support cells while keeping their cancer task. The design aims to widen the safe use of such therapies.
pmc-13583802:
Luqman Munir and co-authors ask whether low oxygen across the body speeds the eye damage of diabetes. They matched over 92,000 patients with early diabetic eye disease, half with conditions that lower oxygen, such as anemia or sleep apnea, using a large health records network. Five years of outcomes were compared.

The low-oxygen group progressed to the severe, vessel-growing stage of eye disease more often, 4.2 against 2.6 percent. Bleeding, detachment, and blindness also ran higher, as did laser and surgery use. Anemia drove most of the effect. The authors suggest anemia checks could protect sight.
pmc-13583902:
One broken gene, SOD1, causes a fast and deadly form of ALS, the motor neuron disease. David Thompson and eight co-authors built a cleaner mouse model of it in 2026, replacing the mouse gene with the human one carrying the common North American mutation.

The engineered mice show little outward weakness, matching earlier knock-in models. Inside, though, gene and chemical profiling found wide disruption in sugar burning, the cell's main energy cycle, and fat handling. The authors read this as an early energy imbalance that arrives before muscle and nerve failure. They offer the model freely to labs hunting for treatment targets that act before symptoms start.
pmc-13584102:
Long opioid use drains a key glutamate transporter from star-shaped support cells in the brain's reward region, and that drain is tied to relapse. Woonyen Wong, Adil Shareef Mohammed, Wayne Childers, Magid Abou-Gharbia, and Youssef Sari test three lab-made compounds in mice kept on hydrocodone for this 2026 study. Two are antibiotic-free cousins of a known drug family; the third breaks the family mold entirely.

All three restored the transporter, called GLT-1, in the reward hub, and normalized a partner exchanger as well. The rescue ran through a chain of gene-control signals the team tracked in cell nuclei and fluid. Earlier work showed one compound also blunting opioid harm in the liver, widening the stakes. The results nominate the trio as addiction-treatment candidates that work without antibiotic side effects.
pmc-13584202:
Krasniqi and co-authors examine, in a 2026 study, whether calcium buildup on the heart's mitral valve ring raises the risk of heart valve infection. That infection, infective endocarditis, is dangerous, yet standard risk tools ignore such structural groundwork. The team drew on a Danish screening cohort whose members had chest scans that measured the calcium burden.

Nearly fifteen thousand people were followed, most of them men around age sixty-seven. Infection rates were low with no calcium and only slightly higher with mild buildup. With heavy buildup, the rate jumped about tenfold, and the ten-year risk rose to near two percent. Each added step of burden raised risk a little. Heavy buildup stayed linked to infection after known risk factors were counted, though the authors urge care since cases were few.
pmc-13584502:
Eigo Kawahara and colleagues use mice to show how a common bacterium can turn a viral lung infection far worse in this 2026 study. The virus is RSV, a leading cause of chest disease in babies, and the bacterium is a form of Haemophilus influenzae often found alongside it in severe cases. Whether the bacterium truly drives the harm, or merely shows up, was unknown.

Mice first caught RSV, then received live, ultraviolet-killed, or heat-killed bacteria into the windpipe. Only the live bacteria brought sharp weight loss, lung injury, and a flood of white cells and inflammatory signals. A signal called IL-6 tracked closely with how sick the mice became. Removing one T-cell type eased matters a little, which suggests those cells help the damage but cannot explain it alone.
pmc-13584802:
Tanvir Khaliq and Veerpal Kaur report a one-step way to make a natural alkaloid and its kin in a 2026 paper. The target, vasicinone, comes in left- and right-handed forms and shows wide biological activity. Past routes to it took more steps.

Their reaction joins two building blocks in a single step with a phosphorus reagent. Both handed forms were made in high yield and near-perfect purity, matching known values. The same step built many related ring systems, and one product led to a known drug lead against leishmania. A short, flexible route should help chemists explore this family for new drugs.
pmc-13585302:
Jingyi Hu and ten co-authors link a mild rise in a liver blood marker to worse outcomes in fatty liver disease, in a study from 2026. The marker often rises in this common liver condition, but what a mild rise means over time was unclear. The team tracked patterns, not just single readings.

They studied more than thirty thousand adults at two health systems. About one in ten had a marker that stayed mildly high. That group faced higher death risk and higher risk of major liver harm than peers whose marker stayed normal. Links were clearest in people at low or mid risk by a standard scar score.
pmc-13585802:
Yonatan Prat and co-authors ask general-purpose AI chatbots to read bladder scope images in a 2026 benchmarking study. Cystoscopy is the backbone of bladder cancer diagnosis, and reading its images varies with the reader. Specialist vision models exist but are hungry for data and hard to deploy; multimodal language models promise a lighter route.

Over seventeen hundred labeled public images were shown to four model sizes under three prompt styles, from direct questions to a carefully optimized script. The full-size and mini models with the optimized prompt led, sorting benign from malignant with accuracy in the high eighties. Confidence handling impressed more: when the top model was allowed to abstain on shaky reads, its confident subset scored near ninety-eight percent accuracy while covering about three fifths of images. Prompt craft helped, though not decisively. The authors frame triage, not replacement, as the near-term role.
pmc-13586002:
Eye vessel form in a form of early dementia is tied to brain drainage and small vessel harm by William Robert Kwapong and co-authors in work dated 2026. The disease is frontotemporal dementia, which wastes the front and side brain lobes. The team took eye photos and brain scans of thirty-four patients and the same count of healthy peers. They scored eye vessel branch density, brain drain marks, and vessel harm load.

Patients showed sparser eye vessels, weaker drain marks, and more vessel harm than peers. Sparser eye vessels also tracked worse thinking scores and harsher disease. The eye may thus give a cheap window on brain vessel health.
pmc-13586702:
Da Yeon Yoo and co-authors test a flower extract against the cell behavior behind eczema, in a 2026 study. The absolute oil of Paulownia tomentosa flowers, rich in thirteen identified compounds, went onto two lab cell types: a mast cell model and human skin cells. Doses stayed below toxic levels throughout.

The extract lowered two proteins that mast cells use to spill their contents. It also cut the release of histamine and a marker enzyme when the cells were provoked with an allergen setup. Skin cell barrier responses were tracked as well. A plant oil that calms both arms of the eczema reaction could seed gentler creams for sore skin.
pmc-13588002:
How a hybrid light catalyst turns carbon dioxide into carbon monoxide is traced by Dasom Kim and co-authors in work dated 2026. The hybrid pairs a titanium oxide base with a cobalt complex. It beats the plain base on both speed and pick of end goods. Why it picks carbon monoxide so well was not clear. The team joined voltage tests, theory sums, and fast light reads.

Sums show the gas binds the woken cobalt core more gladly than stray protons do, which cuts waste hydrogen. Light reads show fast electron flow from base to complex and a long-lived middle state. Both facts back the high pick rate.
pmc-13588102:
Ciara Sallowicz and co-authors set up a gentler fat-profiling workflow in a 2026 methods paper. Profiling lipids, the fats in tissue, usually runs at high flow, drinking solvent and needing more sample to catch rare species. A nano flow setup uses far less of both and sprays samples more efficiently.

On spiked cow liver extract, nano flow at a quarter of the usual load names far more lipids, and more of them at high quality, than high flow. Stray fragmentation drops by a fifth to a third. Detection reaches loads up to forty times lower. The authors present nano flow as a reliable discovery platform.
pmc-13589002:
Alessio Frisone and five colleagues review contrast ultrasound for sorting salivary gland lumps before surgery. Telling a harmless lump from a cancer in these glands is notoriously tricky, and contrast imaging adds a live view of the tiny vessels inside. Their 2026 systematic review gathered ten studies covering 663 lumps, the clear majority benign, all checked against tissue diagnosis afterward.

Cancers tended to light up unevenly with blurred edges and dead-looking dark patches. Their contrast also rushed in faster, peaked higher, and washed through with steeper curves than benign lumps showed. Blurred margins were a highly specific cancer sign, while uneven lighting was sensitive but less specific. Because study methods and cut-offs varied so much, the authors stopped short of pooled numbers and call the tool an adjunct, not a replacement for biopsy.
pmc-13589102:
Barsha and Miller-Kleinhenz chart in twenty twenty-six breast cancer rates by race, stage, and subtype in Mississippi, a high-burden state. Broad rates can hide sharp gaps between groups. They used the state cancer registry for women diagnosed over a ten-year span, split by Black and White race, stage at diagnosis, and tumour subtype.

Overall rates held steady over the decade. Black women had higher rates than White women, and more cancers found at later stages. Two aggressive subtypes were far more common in Black women in adjusted models. Rates of early-stage cancer rose in both groups. The authors call for watch systems and control plans that are split by group and aimed at fairness.
pmc-13589402:
Le-Chun Ou and co-authors map how gene messages are re-edited while the cornea heals in a 2026 paper. The cornea's surface must close fast after injury to restore sight. Genes can issue several versions, called isoforms, of one message, and those versions may do different jobs. Standard gene counts blur them together, so the team used long-read single-cell sequencing on monkey corneal tissue before injury and one and three days after.

They found wide isoform shifts that total gene levels hid. Genes for cell structure and stress response swapped versions while their overall output barely moved. Dozens of genes changed either their version mix or their version diversity over the repair days. Lab checks confirmed the timing and cell locations of key versions. The atlas is offered as a resource for future healing therapies.
pmc-13589502:
Vivek Behera leads a twelve-author team in a search for shared organizing principles across tumors, in a study from two thousand twenty-six. Tumor microenvironments mix cancer, immune, and support cells in bewildering variety. If a common architecture lies at the base of that mix was not known. The team set out to find one if it is there.

Spatial transcriptomics profiled 262 solid tumors, and it mapped gene activity in place. The team found these spaces split into discrete sub-regions of many cells, set in a hierarchy. They call these spatial groups. Pathologists and independent measurements confirmed the groups match real biological domains. To set tumors side by side through these groups gave a pan-tumor classification. Its dominant axis was spatial variation in immune biology. A small lung cancer cohort hinted the scheme ties to how well immunotherapy works.
pmc-13590002:
Kunlong Zhang and co-authors map brain immune cells after spinal cord injury in mice in a 2026 study. Nerve pain after such injury is disabling and hard to treat. Spinal immune cells are well studied in this pain, but cells in the motor cortex are not. Magnetic stimulation of the brain is one candidate therapy.

The team reads single nuclei from motor cortex tissue in sham, injured, and treated mice. Injury does not change overall cell mix, but microglia shift toward an inflammation state, they find. Stimulation links to a shift back toward a repair state. Lab checks and behavior tests on movement and pain support the map.
pmc-13590102:
Zhen Jia and co-authors track stressed Salmonella on chicken wings in a 2026 study. Food plants expose the germ to heat, cold, and acid, which may change how it grows later. That shift can bend shelf-life calls and risk sums.

Wings were stored at fridge, cool, and room heat, with germ states from fresh to thrice stressed. At cold levels the germ faded bit by bit, while at room heat it grew in full curves. Cold-stressed germs died slowest in the fridge, which hints at a built defense. Native wing bacteria were modeled for shelf-life forecasts. The work warns risk models to count pre-stress, not just dose.
pmc-13590302:
Keyi Zhu, Fei Gao, Junzhu Yue, Miaoxin Yang, Jingyang Wu, Ruyi Zhao, and Duo Li weigh diabetes and tooth decay in youth in a 2026 paper. Type 1 diabetes starts in childhood for many, and its links to cavities are debated. The team joins a pooled review with a gene based test of cause.

Across past studies, youth with the disease had more decayed, missing, or filled permanent teeth than peers. The gap was modest but steady across the pooled data. The gene test, which uses inherited variants as stand ins, found no sign the disease itself causes the decay. The authors read the link as real but likely driven by shared habits and care factors.
pmc-13590402:
Nidal Abu-Hamdeh and Mohammed Ajour build computer models of a drug process in this 2026 paper. They study how well a skin drug, clobetasol propionate, dissolves in carbon dioxide held under high pressure and heat, a state used in clean drug making.

Only heat and pressure were fed to the models as inputs. The team boosted three base models and tuned them with a search method named for fireflies. The best model matched the lab data very closely, well ahead of the weakest of the three. Such models can help makers pick process settings by screen test instead of by many costly lab runs.
pmc-13590502:
Sirion Aksornthong and six colleagues published a bone study in two thousand twenty-six on a blood disease that hardens bone. In myelofibrosis, the spleen swells and some bones thicken abnormally. A mouse model carrying a gene fault copies the disease, and the team asked whether spleen-made factors drive the bone change.

Removing the spleen in adult mice improved platelet counts but did not undo hardening in leg bones. It did prevent hardening in spine bones, though those bones then lost mass. Blood protein screening flagged a molecule called ICAM2, raised in the mutant mice and normalised after spleen removal. In cell tests, ICAM2 slowed the bone-eating cells that fuse to resorb bone.
pmc-13592302:
Christopher R B Swanson and three colleagues use enzymes, in 2026, to tag therapeutic DNA strands with radioactive hydrogen late in their making. Drug developers need such tags to track where a medicine travels in the body. Older chemistry demands costly radioactive building blocks, yields weak tags, and leaves much radioactive waste. Their platform borrows methyltransferase enzymes, which naturally add methyl groups to DNA with exact aim.

The enzymes tagged strands at preparative scale with sharp site control, reaching record tag strength for this class. Both stable heavy hydrogen and radioactive tritium versions were made. Swanson and the team expect the method to cut cost and waste by orders of magnitude and to spread to other drug types that need whole body tracking studies.
pmc-13593702:
Lidia Mendes de Aquino and a large team followed ninety-eight cow and calf pairs in a tropical beef herd for two years to track tick fever, a disease complex carried by ticks. Blood tests searched for three agents, one Anaplasma bacterium and two Babesia parasites, from birth until the males were slaughtered and the females had their first calves.

Passage from mother to calf before birth was found only for Anaplasma, in a small share of pairs. Yet by twenty days of age most calves already carried the agents' DNA, showing very early exposure, and antibody rates across the herd passed three quarters. Tick load was the one factor clearly tied to active infection. Clinical illness still broke out in animals of several ages despite widespread antibodies, which leads the authors to urge a rethink of tick fever control in tropical herds.
pmc-13593902:
Cartilage cushions our joints but heals poorly, since it has no blood supply and few cells. Silvia Todros and co-authors introduce a research collection on fixing cartilage in this 2026 editorial. The collection centers on new materials that mimic real cartilage and on the mechanics that any repair must match.

One study in the set mapped the surface and stiffness of a little-studied hip cartilage and turned the findings into design rules for grafts. Another built a robot-armed device to measure friction on curved joint surfaces and spot local defects. Other work weighs the strength of whole repaired tissue pieces. The editors argue that good repair must join knowledge of healthy and diseased tissue with materials built to restore function.
pmc-13594502:
Nurit Zusman, Martine Denise Freeman, and Caryn Scheinberg Andrews surveyed 260 Israeli healthcare workers. They asked about resilience, positive mood, and quality of life during a period that combined the pandemic's aftermath with active warfare. Their cross-sectional study used standard scales for bouncing back from hardship, for positive and negative feelings, and for quality of life.

Both resilience and positive mood predicted a better quality of life on their own. The two also interacted: positive mood mattered most for staff whose resilience ran low, easing the drawback, while among upbeat staff the resilience gap flattened. The authors advise managers to build positive feeling deliberately, through peer support and praise, aiming most at workers with thinner reserves. They also call for broad system-wide plans rather than resilience training alone. Long-term studies of effects on keeping staff are needed too.
pmc-13594702:
Jyoti Srivastava and Sanjay Premi reviewed in two thousand twenty-six how a chemical tag placed on proteins by nitric oxide may shape melanoma outcomes. Modern melanoma drugs can shrink tumors without lasting control. The tag, called S-nitrosylation, has been linked to drug resistance and to weaker immune attack on the tumor.

Blocking the tag in lab work raised stress signals on dying tumor cells and drew in immune cells. Still, proof that specific tagged sites control how visibly tumor cells die is missing. The authors propose a two-gate model to test next. Cancer researchers get a careful sorting of proven facts versus promising guesses.
pmc-13594902:
Tsuyoshi Okuhara and co-authors present a 2026 study of people in Japan whose pain has no clear medical cause. Such patients must work to be believed, in clinics and in daily life. The team read first-person illness stories from 16 adults in a national archive. Cases covered wide pain types, from fibromyalgia to pain with no name at all.

The stories show belief work that loops and wears down rather than wins trust. Tests rule the clinic, so felt pain that tests miss stays doubted. Few care options and firm role lines shrink shared choices. Patients then trim what they say, dress to look well, and hide strain, which starves doctors of facts. Four double binds frame the trap: each safe move also costs the patient. The study names why unexplained pain care so often stalls.
pmc-13595002:
Ying Ni Lin and five co-authors re-analyzed in 2026 two large trials of a weight-loss drug in people with sleep apnea and obesity. Losing weight eases apnea, but whether early loss predicts later gain was unclear. The team sorted four hundred sixty-nine trial members by how much weight they had lost at week twenty.

Those who had lost at least fifteen percent by then showed far greater apnea improvement at week fifty-two than those under five percent. The split held across the grouped bands. An early weigh-in, the authors suggest, can flag who is on track and who may need a change of plan.
pmc-13595102:
Drugs that release the brakes on the immune system can cause harm as well as good. In triple-negative breast cancer these checkpoint inhibitors now help many patients, but their side effects are hard to predict. Erin McGillivray, Savannah Kane, Armina Saadatkhah, and Kay Yeung review the search for warning markers. No approved test yet predicts toxicity. Candidates include blood counts, immune cell types, and signaling proteins.

Other leads involve gene activity patterns, inherited genetics, and gut microbes. Most evidence is early and comes from other cancers. The authors urge that future breast cancer trials build marker testing in from the start. Real-world multi-center checks are also needed before any marker guides care.
pmc-13595202:
Congenital syphilis, passed from mother to baby, has resurfaced in England even though nearly all pregnant women are screened. Helen Fifer and co-authors review sixty-seven cases from 2015 to 2024 in this 2026 national study to find where prevention slipped.

Babies showed enlarged organs, rashes, and bone changes, and thirteen were stillborn. Nearly half the mothers had screened negative and caught the infection during pregnancy itself. Other cases traced to late booking, unfinished treatment, or hard-to-reach lives, and some sick babies were first treated for sepsis without a syphilis test. The authors urge sharper vigilance and wider test use.
pmc-13596402:
Yuan Ren and colleagues published a 2026 study of how five common burdens of rheumatoid arthritis in older adults influence each other over time. They are pain, fatigue, anxiety and depression, poor sleep, and limits on daily function. One hundred seventy-seven patients were assessed in hospital and again one month after going home.

Network analysis mapped which symptoms sat at the center of the web at each point. Limits on function and fatigue mattered most at both times. Fatigue was also the only symptom that predicted later problems, worsening sleep afterward. The results suggest that treating fatigue early may protect several other parts of patients' lives.
pmc-13596902:
Yao Huang and co-authors test an ultra-fast form of radiation therapy against lung cancer that has spread to bone. The method, called FLASH, delivers the dose at about 94 gray per second, nearly a thousand times the usual rate. In mice with lung tumor cells planted in the shin bone, the team compared FLASH with standard radiation.

Both methods slowed tumor growth equally and eased the bone-eating damage, leaning on helper T cells of the immune system. FLASH went further: it curbed the cells that dissolve bone, reshaped the tumor's surroundings, and did less harm to the rest of the body. Its damage pattern also drained oxygen in a way that calmed an inflammation pathway and shifted a T cell subtype. The authors offer FLASH as a promising strategy for bone spread.
pmc-13597102:
Angélique Roquet and co-authors argue for culturally fit dementia care in Sub-Saharan Africa in this 2026 paper. Most people with dementia will soon live in poorer nations as populations age. Africa faces rising case counts with little screening or support in place.

The authors draw lessons from field research in West Africa. Dementia there is often read through spiritual lenses, which can bring stigma or abuse. A project comparing views in Togo, Morocco, and Switzerland found aging widely seen as a burden. Such beliefs delay recognition and care seeking. Western test tools fit poorly in these settings. The paper urges assessment shaped by local language and custom.
pmc-13597402:
Yuhui Yuan and eight co-authors report long-term results for a two-drug plan in patients with an immune disease that destroys blood platelets. Their 2026 study follows people whose illness resisted steroids or depended on them, and who had already failed the platelet-raising drug eltrombopag on its own. Adding the immune suppressant cyclosporine was the test.

Twenty-eight patients across several centers took both drugs, with responders staying on maintenance. Tracking ran to the start of 2026, a median of about thirty-two months. The authors chart how long responses lasted, how treatments failed, and what side effects appeared. The report aims to show whether the pairing gives durable control, beyond the short-term gains their earlier phase of the trial had found.
pmc-13598002:
Breast cancer growing in the belly wall leaves surgeons guessing where its lymph drains. The tissue sits far from the breast, along the old milk line. A glowing dye answered the question in a 2026 case report by Alessio Vinci and co-authors. Their patient was a 64 year old woman with a growing mass in that tissue.

The dye, injected around the tumor, lit a path to the armpit and none to the groin, live during surgery. The single sentinel node there proved clear, and a year on she remained free of disease. The authors say the tracer, standard in ordinary breast cancer, worked here for the first time on record.
pmc-13598202:
Lucía Arce Cubas and co-authors find that C4 plants already relax their sun protection faster than C3 plants. Their 2026 study measures nonphotochemical quenching, the leaf's way of venting excess light as heat, across plant pairs that share close ancestry but use different photosynthetic pathways.

Working within three genera that contain both types, they also drew on a meta-analysis of published data. They show the C4 species switch the protection off significantly faster when light drops. Blocking experiments traced the edge to the fast, energy-dependent part of quenching, tied to how C4 leaves manage acidity in their light-harvesting compartments under heavier energy demand. The sobering upshot for crop engineers: in C4 crops this particular speed-up, often proposed to raise yields, may already be built in.
pmc-13598302:
Yuhan Zheng and co-authors mine breast cancer data sets for long non coding RNAs that might flag patient outlook, in work from twenty twenty-six. These RNA strands do not build proteins but steer gene activity. The cancer often starts quietly and is caught late.

Network methods grouped the RNAs by how they move with immune cells and tumor traits. One chain stood out: a long RNA, a small RNA, and a target gene tied to survival. Lab checks found the long RNA and the target gene raised in breast cancer cells. The small RNA shifted in mixed directions across cell lines. Immune cell mixes also differed between tumor and control samples. The chain is proposed as a prognostic lead.
pmc-13598902:
Toma Shinkai, Koki Ogawa, Mohamed S. Injections are the only proven route today, and the team tested digestive enzymes, stomach-like fluid, and acidity one by one.

Pepsin, the stomach's protein-cutting enzyme, slashed the particles' protein-making ability and swelled their size, while amylase left them alone. Fat-cutting lipase at high concentration also damaged function, and rebuilding the particles around a lipid without the vulnerable chemical bonds blunted that damage, identifying the mechanism. Simulated gastric fluid crippled the particles, with the harm traced to extreme acidity near pH 1 rather than milder levels. The authors convert the findings into design rules for particles that might survive swallowing.
pmc-13599502:
Tomato plants in Canada and elsewhere face a stubborn disease called bacterial canker, for which growers have few good tools. Nasim Sedighian, Marie-Christine Groleau, and Eric Déziel report a 2026 search for helpful bacteria that can both feed growth and fight the disease.

The team screened more than 500 strains in the lab, then tested 32 of them on live plants. Three strains stood out. One slowed the start of disease by up to seven days and cut wilt scores sharply. Gene reads showed the best strains carry gene sets that likely make helpful compounds. The work points toward a living spray that could guard crops with less use of chemicals.
pmc-13599702:
Zainab Naaran and Amit Yashar published this 2026 study on how autistic adults search a visual scene and how much mental effort that search costs. Earlier work often found a search advantage in autism, but the effort behind it was unclear.

In one experiment, forty-eight autistic and forty-five non-autistic adults hunted for a colored target while their pupils were measured. Reaction times were similar, yet pupil responses were smaller in the autistic group, suggesting less effort. In a harder second task with brief, masked displays, autistic participants were more accurate. Both groups used recent trial history to guide attention, so the difference lay in how effort and accuracy shifted under pressure.
pmc-13600002:
Two immune drugs given together fight several cancers well, but the pair can badly inflame the liver. Severe liver injury struck 11 patients, about 14 percent, at a median of 38 days after the first dose.

A blood marker called KL-6, at or above 400 units before treatment, flagged risk strongly, with odds about thirteen times higher. Standard liver tests gave no such warning. Over half the severe cases resisted steroids or flared as doses tapered. A hidden virus, cytomegalovirus, had reawakened in half of those tested. pmc-13600102:

pmc-13649502:
Huan Zhou and Tiantian Zhang review how shifts in cell fuel use drive scarring in the lungs. In this disease, scar tissue builds up, stiffens the lungs, and slowly destroys their structure. No drug yet targets the disease itself with real success.

The review centers on how scar-forming cells rewire their use of sugar, fats, and amino acids. Those shifts feed the growth of the cells and the flood of tissue glue they pour out. Each shift is also a possible drug target. The authors gather the newest work on each fuel path. They weigh which targets look most ready for testing in patients. For a disease with few options, the fuel map offers fresh places to intervene.
pmc-13649702:
António Luís Vidinha Pereira and five colleagues weigh how Portugal's health system must adapt to one of the world's fastest aging populations. The national health service dates to 1979, an era when Portugal ranked among the youngest lands in Europe, and it focused on mother and child health. That focus no longer fits the country.

Care for older adults now centres on disease lists and deficits, and few staff hold deep training in old-age care in the community. The authors explore a World Health Organization approach called ICOPE, which screens for drops in core abilities and builds care around them. Their team is piloting the approach. They weigh its promise for joined-up primary care against time and staffing costs.
pmc-13649902:
Juliana Rachel Hoeper and co-authors weigh the costs of faster rheumatology diagnosis in Germany, in this 2026 paper. The Rheuma-VOR network was built to cut long waits for specialist verdicts in three joint diseases. Earlier diagnosis should start proper therapy sooner.

The study compared network patients with matched standard care records. Total savings reached about three point eight million euros, led by fewer hospital stays and lower drug bills. Far fewer patients needed costly biologic drugs. Quality of life held equal or better at lower cost per patient. The authors call the profile dominant: better value on both axes at once.
pmc-13650102:
Caterina Giorgio and co-authors review what a hit class of diabetes and weight drugs might do for skin disease, in a 2026 paper. The drugs act on a gut hormone signal, and the dual versions act on two signals at once. Beyond weight and blood sugar, they calm inflammation, reshape fat tissue, and help tissue repair, all of which matter to dermatology.

Evidence so far suggests benefit in psoriasis and in a painful sweat-gland disease, with hopeful signs for wound healing. The safety record on skin looks mostly good, though injection site reactions, allergy, hair loss, and rare immune rashes are reported.
