Outside the two lead conditions the data are thin and observational. The authors see the drugs as a new family of immune-metabolic treatments for skin practice.
pmc-13651602:
Ehsan Rahimi and five co-authors let machine learning read the scattered literature on micro- and nanorobots, the swimming devices being developed for drug delivery, sensing, imaging, and therapy inside the body. Reports in the field vary so wildly in setup and readouts that design lessons refuse to build up.

A dataset gathered from published systems was grouped by structure and correlation. Three descriptor kinds stood out: the setting of use, how drive and sensing couple, and the design intent. Trained models found learnable patterns in how drive methods are chosen. Forecasts of raw swimming speed carried over only somewhat, betraying deep shifts between materials, drive physics, body fluids, and lab protocols. The authors argue that the field's immediate gift from AI is a map of itself. It charts the design landscape, exposes reporting bias, and pushes all labs toward shared datasets that future forecasts can trust.
pmc-13651902:
Broken-heart syndrome, Takotsubo, stuns the heart after stress, but in a living animal the flood of body signals muddies what the heart muscle itself is doing. Amirali Nejat and ten co-authors isolate the organ in this 2026 paper. Rat hearts, kept beating on a perfusion rig, receive a controlled hormone dose. The dose triggers the full syndrome inside the heart alone.

Over six hours the treated hearts weakened in both squeeze and relaxation, while control hearts on plain solution did not. Ultrasound, an injury marker in the fluid, and tissue samples confirmed the picture, and statistical models teased apart the disease's features. With the body removed from the equation, researchers can now poke at the muscle's own machinery. The rig doubles as a test bench for candidate treatments.
pmc-13652102:
Bebiş and Gül test whether health lessons delivered over WhatsApp can teach women about skin cancer and sun protection. A nurse-led program sent structured, interactive education through the messaging app for twelve weeks. The trial used a Solomon four-group design, which includes groups with and without a pre-test to check that testing itself does not skew results.

A total of 152 women took part across the four groups. After the program, the taught groups scored clearly higher on skin cancer knowledge and sun protection behavior than the control groups, and no pre-test effect appeared. The authors present phone-based teaching as a cheap, scalable way to raise health literacy in the community.
pmc-13652402:
Lâamiri and co-authors report a rare case of a swallowed toothpick that pierced the upper small bowel. Swallowed toothpicks are uncommon but dangerous, since the sharp wood can pierce the gut and seed infection. Piercing of this bowel segment is rarer still.

Their patient was a 45-year-old man with general belly pain and vomiting. He had prior surgery for a burst appendix. A scan showed free air in the belly and a thin object crossing the bowel wall. Keyhole surgery found wide infection; the toothpick stuck through the bowel about seventy units past its start. Scar tissue forced open surgery, and the team removed the pick and repaired the hole. He went home on day four. The case credits scans for a find that is often missed.
pmc-13654102:
Huan Liu and co-authors study heart timing in people born with a two-leaflet aortic valve. Such a valve often comes with a widened aorta. Their 2026 study asks whether aorta width tracks with poor timing in how the left ventricle squeezes. Timing was read with real-time three-dimensional echocardiography, an ultrasound method that films the heart in 3D.

The study covered 79 patients with the valve condition and 40 people with normal valves. Aorta width was measured on CT scans and scaled to body size. Patients were split into widened and not widened groups by set cut-offs. The ultrasound gave timing spread across 16, 12, and 6 segments of the ventricle. The paper sets out how width and squeeze timing can be compared in this group.
pmc-13655402:
Jiyun Jang and co-authors compare skin gene activity across three itchy skin diseases to find what sets prurigo nodularis apart. Their 2026 study covers a chronic condition of hard nodules and relentless itch. Its molecular roots, above all the role of fibroblasts, stayed fuzzy.

Gene reads came from sore skin of eczema, atopic prurigo, and prurigo nodularis patients, plus healthy skin. Public single-cell data added cell-type detail. Prurigo nodularis stood out for a growth pathway switched on in fibroblasts. Nerve-linked cells rich in one marker seemed to talk strongly with those fibroblasts. Classic allergy signals ran weaker than in the other diseases. The authors name the nerve-fibroblast axis as a drug target lead.
pmc-13655802:
Yoshitaka Watanabe and Hirokazu Ikeda argue that liver upset in a childhood vessel-inflaming disease deserves more thought than it gets. Liver test changes are among the most common signs of the disease outside the heart. Yet they are usually mild and pass as the disease settles.

The main fear in this disease is damage to the heart's own arteries, which drives long-term risk. That focus leaves a basic question open: is liver upset just a shadow of body-wide inflammation, or a harm in its own right? The pair discuss a study in this issue that follows liver signs over time. They weigh when doctors should act on liver numbers rather than wait. Their piece asks for a clearer place for the liver in care plans.
pmc-13657602:
Taylor Schumann and co-authors study smoking and surgery risk in a 2026 paper. The surgery rebuilds damaged tissue with a flap of tissue moved from one body site to another. The flap needs good blood flow to survive and heal well. Smoking narrows blood vessels and weakens germ defense, so it may raise the risk of poor healing.

The team used a large national surgery database covering more than four thousand patients. About one in four patients smoked before surgery. After weighing other health factors, smokers had higher rates of deep wound infection and wound opening. Rates of flap loss and blood clots did not differ, a result that can guide talks before surgery.
pmc-13658302:
Sheridan Hoy profiles linerixibat, a new drug for the severe itching that comes with primary biliary cholangitis, a liver disease. The drug blocks the ileal bile acid transporter in the gut, cutting the recycling of bile acids that drives the itch. Developed by GSK, it won its first approval in the United States for this use. Becoming the first therapy approved there for cholestatic itching in this disease, with approval in the United Kingdom following.

Regulatory reviews were still running in Canada, China, and the European Union when the profile was written. As part of a first-approval series, the article traces the milestones of the drug's development, from its mechanism through the trials that supported licensing. Clinicians treating a symptom that ruins sleep and daily life for many patients get a compact account of where this option came from and where it stands.
pmc-13659002:
Raquel Ballarin and co-authors review whether vegetarian and vegan diets raise hip fracture risk in adults. Their twenty twenty-six review joins studies that compare plant-based eaters with meat eaters. Hip fracture is a major cause of hospital care, with high illness and death tolls.

Plant diets are growing in favor, yet past work links them to lower bone density. Six databases were searched for studies on the question. Two reviewers picked studies, graded bias risk, and pulled data in pairs. Hazard ratios with confidence ranges were pooled where studies allowed. The answer matters for diet guides aimed at older adults, whose bones already thin with age.
pmc-13660502:
Muhammad Bilal and co-authors pooled trials of a fast brain stimulation method for people with depressive illness, in a 2026 review. The method sends short magnetic pulse bursts to the scalp, with no surgery. The team asked whether real treatment beat sham treatment on suicidal thoughts, low mood, worry, and sleep.

Six trials met their rules. Real treatment cut suicidal thoughts by a clear margin over sham, and the edge held when one outlying trial was dropped from the pool. The pooled view, built under care rules for such reviews, helps doctors judge where this quick method fits among other care options.
pmc-13661702:
Anne-Cecilia van Marle and Evan Bowen describe, in a 2026 case report, a blood cancer that hid behind misleading cell shapes until gene testing named it. A man in Southern Africa came to a public clinic with growing fatigue. His blood showed many basophils and 21 percent blast cells, pointing at first to acute myeloid leukemia.

The marrow also held extra mast cells, raising a second candidate diagnosis. Sequencing settled it: a fusion involving the PDGFRA gene, marking a rare myeloid neoplasm already in blast phase. Odd granules in the cells, no rise in eosinophils, and slow turnaround for specialist tests in the public sector all delayed the answer. The stakes of the delay are high, because fusion driven cancers of this family often respond very well to targeted drugs. The case argues for molecular testing when morphology argues with itself.
pmc-13662702:
Young Joo Sun and co-authors build a three-dimensional test for gene variant harm in a 2026 paper. Doctors often meet gene changes whose effect is unknown, a problem in eye disease genes with many variants. Software predictors are strong but may lack data on how a change warps the protein or the symptoms it causes. The team combined both kinds of evidence.

Their framework pairs AI-built protein structures with clinical genomic records. Experts review the combined output in a human-in-the-loop setup. The test case was a retina gene tied to several distinct disease patterns. Forty-six known harmful variants were judged against a pool of unknown ones. The analysis found shape signatures that matched each clinical pattern, and a fresh patient group confirmed the approach.
pmc-13663802:
Casper Binding and co-authors count how heart-trace marks stack toward an unruly heart rhythm, in a study from 2026. The rhythm ill, atrial fibrillation, lifts stroke risk and hides till late. Heart traces bear known risk marks, but their joint weight in early catch was unproved.

The pool held near one and a half million souls with a trace on file. Five marks were scored: fast rest pace, a long gap twixt two waves, split waves, a bent wave tail, and a wide wave. Near six in ten bore at least one. Five-year rates of the rhythm ill and of stroke sat low with no marks and topped eight and seven in a hundred with all five. Stacked marks, the team shows, name a group wards should watch first.
pmc-13663902:
Liu and co-authors review a plan to shield T cells from oxidative harm so they can fight solid tumors better. Adoptive T cell therapy struggles in solid tumors, where the local setting suppresses immunity. A build-up of reactive oxygen species drives much of that resistance. Blanket antioxidant treatment lacks aim and can disturb normal signaling. The review instead maps how T cell types differ in their defenses.

Effector, memory, and regulatory T cells vary in fuel use, power plant behavior, and defense genes. Other immune cells in the tumor add to the suppressive web. The authors argue for boosting the antioxidant strength of the therapy cells themselves. Aim matters more than dose.
pmc-13665502:
Handan Özdemir and Sıddıka Ersoy ask whether inner spiritual strength tracks with how well kidney patients stick to hard care routines. Dialysis demands strict habits for years, and self-care sits at the heart of it. Their 2026 study surveyed 72 adults on long-term dialysis at one public hospital in Türkiye.

Spiritual strength linked strongly with both sticking to care and managing one's own health. The links held after the team weighed age, sex, time on dialysis, and other illnesses. Gains seemed to level off at the highest strength scores. The authors suggest that care plans weigh spiritual health beside reading skill, mood, and support. They call for wider, longer studies to learn which way the link runs.
pmc-13665602:
Macfadyen and a large team examine in twenty twenty-six why Australian canola growers rarely rely on helpful insects to control pests. Predators and parasitic wasps can cut pest damage, and integrated pest care prizes them. Yet their use is the hardest part of that approach to adopt at scale, the authors say.

Surveys of growers and advisors found few support practices in wide use, with selective sprays the most common. Growers also lacked clear knowledge of what gains to expect from each practice. Still, most wanted to manage helpful insects more actively. The authors list new tools built for this purpose and propose small steps, not whole-system leaps, toward wider use.
pmc-13666002:
Wen Xiao and seven colleagues published a molecular biology study in two thousand twenty-six on a famous noncoding RNA. Malat1 usually stays in the nucleus, shaping splicing and chromatin. In mouse neurons it slips into the cytoplasm and is translated into a tiny peptide called M1.

The team pinpointed an internal ribosome entry site that lets ribosomes start mid-message without the usual cap. Chemical probing revealed a three-loop structure matching a mouse B1 repetitive element. That segment alone pulled down ribosome parts and known entry-site helpers. Removing two helper proteins shut down peptide production. The authors call it a hidden functional unit inside a much-studied RNA.
pmc-13668302:
A rare liver disease slowly scars the bile ducts, and patients who fail the first drug need later options with solid proof. Marco Carbone and co-authors reviewed those later therapies in this 2026 paper. The disease is primary biliary cholangitis, and it can end in liver failure. The first-line drug helps many, but some respond poorly or cannot tolerate it.

The review searched major databases and trial listings through the autumn of 2025, plus recent conference reports. It gathered studies of approved and experimental second-line and later drugs. Results covered lab markers of disease activity, safety, and what patients themselves report about symptoms and life quality. Marker definitions differ between studies, which complicates comparisons. A single synthesis helps doctors weigh real trade-offs for patients out of first-line options.
pmc-13669802:
Moritz Schroll and four co-authors trace, in 2026 work, how chicory plants make a laughing gas that harms the climate. The gas feeds warming and eats at the ozone shield, yet world counts of it miss plant sources. The team grew chicory in clean labs and fed it marked forms of nitrogen to spot where the gas forms.

All plants let gas off in the dark, while lit shoots made less or took some in, which shows that light-driven work halts the flow. Roots fed nitrate made the gas by a reductive path, with nitric oxide as a mid-step. Shoots in the dark used a unlike path that roots did not. Past budgets and plant models miss these splits, the team says, and should now fold them in.
pmc-13670502:
He and co-authors test a leaf extract that eases drug-induced liver injury in mice by reshaping gut microbes. The leaves of Eucommia ulmoides are rich in flavonoids with liver-protective hints. Excess acetaminophen is a classic cause of acute liver damage. The team built that injury model in mice and dosed the extract. Liver function tests and tissue checks measured the damage. Gene sequencing mapped gut bacteria, and a targeted scan tracked bile acids.

Antibiotic arms tested whether microbes carry the benefit. Gut barrier strength was also checked. The extract calmed the disorder in microbe-driven bile acid handling. The work joins plant, microbe, and liver in one chain.
pmc-13671002:
Clarissa LeVasseur and eight co-authors track, in 2026 work, how neck joints next to a fused span move three years on. Lab bone work says fused spans push next joints harder, yet live reads at one year were mixed. Sixty-two patients were read before surgery and at one and three years, with pain-free peers as the mark.

A scan-track tool read joint moves in bend and twist. End-range growth proved firm only after two-level fusions. Mid-range growth rose after both kinds and topped peers. Shifts swung wide by patient. The team backs mid-range reads as the early flag of wear risk.
pmc-13672302:
Mareike Hülsemann, Christoph Löffler, and Anna-Lena Schubert recorded brain waves while 148 adults switched between tasks, hunting for the neural signature of cognitive flexibility. Flexibility lets people adapt when rules change, and it may underlie broader abilities. Three cued switching tasks covered parity judgments, global-local perception, and number-letter rules. Analysis combined time-frequency statistics with structural equation modeling. Switch trials were compared against repeat trials.

Two signatures stood out. A brief frontal theta increase was task-specific, reflecting control processes. A sustained alpha and beta suppression, seated further back, indexed general attentional processes from cue to target. Flexibility-related dynamics did not correlate with intelligence or working memory. The two-stage pattern fits existing switching models. The twenty twenty-six study separates what is special about each task from what switching always demands.
pmc-13674302: A correction notice amends the author list of the RDMkit article, a guide to a research data management toolkit for the life sciences. As first published, the list carried wrong affiliation details for some authors and misspelled the surname of Gil Poiares-Oliveira. The corrected list now stands in the article, and the authors apologize for any confusion the errors caused.
pmc-13675502:
Burkhard Bechinger and Evgeniy Salnikov review how fungal peptides sit in cell membranes in a 2026 paper. Peptaibols are short fungal peptides that can kill microbes, likely by acting on membranes. Their exact posture and grouping inside a membrane decide how they work.

Solid-state NMR studies used isotope-labeled peptides set into model membranes. A long member spans the membrane upright at some doses, while shorter ones lie flatter along the surface. Spinning-sample tests revealed clusters whose size grows with peptide dose. In bacteria-like membranes even the long peptide lay flat. The findings suggest more than one killing mechanism across the family.
pmc-13675802:
Yasaman Tavakoli and co-authors review a scoring tool for belly pain in pregnancy in this 2026 article. Appendicitis in pregnancy is hard to spot, since normal pregnancy signs can mask it. The score under review blends seven signs and lab values, such as pain site, fever, and white cell counts, into a twelve-point scale meant to rank how likely appendicitis is.

Pooling past studies, the authors found the score was right at a moderate level overall. It caught about seven in ten true cases and cleared about three in four healthy patients. Past single studies varied a lot, and some found far weaker clearing rates against scan results. The authors say the score can support, but not replace, imaging and surgical judgment, and they call for pregnancy-specific cut-off values.
pmc-13676102:
Gutierrez and co-authors mark out a distinct branch of a rare T-cell leukemia by one transcription factor, in a 2026 research letter. T-cell prolymphocytic leukemia is uncommon and aggressive, and standard chemotherapy rarely holds it for long. Sorting patients into biological subgroups is a first step toward smarter trials.

Tumors expressing GATA-3 formed their own subset, tied to skin involvement and to expression of CCR4, a homing receptor. The letter sets these cases against the standard diagnostic frame from the international study group. A marker that predicts skin disease and carries its own surface target could guide both monitoring and drug choice for this subgroup.
pmc-13676602:
Sandoval Villarreal and three co-authors wrote a review, published in 2026, on using mild electric pulses to guide stem cells toward heart cells. Stem cells from fat, bone, or other tissue can be pushed to act like heart muscle, and electric signals are one way to push them. Past lab studies used very different settings and measured success in different ways. The review gathers that scattered work into one picture.

The authors searched seven databases and kept 15 lab studies that fit their rules. Human cells were the most common source, and carbon-based parts most often delivered the pulses. Treated cells often changed shape and turned on early heart genes. The most used settings were one pulse per second and about two weeks of treatment. The authors stress that the wide mix of methods blocks firm claims, and they call for shared standards.
pmc-13676802:
Elgueta and co-authors give in 2026 an updated account of a worm infection in dogs that harms heart, lungs, blood, and nerves. The worm has spread past its old home ranges since 2000, which draws fresh focus to its control. Dogs show varied signs, which makes the infection easy to miss.

The classic test looks for worm larvae in dung, but blood and gene tests now aid the search. Once found, worm drugs and support care should start fast, matched to the dog's signs. The report also updates steps to prevent infection. Outcomes vary widely, and sudden death can occur, so early care matters.
pmc-13677202:
Qiaona Wang, Hongji Liu, and their co-authors tested a liquid metal lubricant on molybdenum surfaces across a wide heat range. Their 2026 study uses a gallium based alloy that flows like a liquid yet carries heat and current well, traits prized for harsh sliding parts. The test pair rubbed from room temperature to 300 degrees, in air and in argon.

In air, the lubricant cut disk wear by about ninety one to ninety nine percent against the dry pair. A gallium oxide rich film formed on the surface and did the protecting. In argon, the film peeled and flaked at high heat, and wear rose sharply. The contrast shows that oxygen in the air is a partner in the protection, not a bystander.
pmc-13678102:
Huo and five co-authors present a study from twenty twenty-six on a giant virus that infects a harmful water germ. The germ harms fish, livestock, and people, and slows fish farming. Viruses that infect germs offer a drug-free way to control such infections. The team isolated a new virus with a long tail and a many-sided head. It stayed active across wide heat and acid ranges. Its genome is large, with hundreds of predicted gene regions.

Family checks place the virus in a known virus family. Yet its genome matches known kin only weakly, at about three in ten parts. The team propose it as the first member of a new genus. They say it widens the known range of these viruses. It may also seed new germ control tools.
pmc-13678202:
Hyunwoo Yoo and Gail Rosen test ways to stretch scarce labels for DNA classification in a 2026 application note. Gene data is plentiful, but labels cost expert time, so semi-supervised learning trains on a few labeled cases plus many unlabeled ones. The catch is how to perturb DNA copies during training without breaking the biology that the labels rest on.

The pair tried twenty-five mixes of weak and strong changes, from flipping a strand to swapping codons, masking spots, and inserting or deleting letters. Gentle, shape-keeping changes worked best, while heavy masking or mutation hurt. Their winning recipe pairs short masked patches with a mild insertion-deletion rate. They share code and default settings for others to reuse.
pmc-13678502:
Rida Zameer and co-authors make a germ fighting composite the green way in a 2026 study. Lychee leaf extract served as the natural agent to form copper oxide particles, cutting harsh chemistry from the process. The particles were then spread over MXene, a layered material etched from a ceramic precursor. The hybrid was tested against microbes and nematodes.

Plant based synthesis doubles as reducer, stabilizer, and cap for the particles. Joining them to MXene aims to spread the active surface and hold the particles in place. Materials that kill crop nematodes and microbes without heavy chemical baggage suit farms under pressure to cut residues. The study reports a build route plus first activity checks.
pmc-13679002:
Merve Simsek and five co-authors compared two eye-muscle operations for children whose eyes drift outward, in a 2026 study. The condition, basic-type intermittent exotropia, is treated either by weakening both outer eye muscles or by weakening one outer muscle while shortening the inner one on the same eye. The team reviewed forty-eight children treated at their center.

Success rates one year after surgery were similar, about eighty-eight percent for the two-muscle operation and eighty-six percent for the combined one. Rates of perfect alignment and of needing another operation also matched. Depth perception improved after surgery in both groups and held at one year. A larger squint before surgery predicted lower odds of success.
pmc-13680302:
Gabriel dos Anjos Guimarães and co-authors measure tiny plastic bits in a lake in the central Amazon. Their paper from 2026 covers surface water and lake bed mud in the dry season. Tiny plastics are a growing worry in inland waters and may harm the life there.

Plastic bits were found in all sampled areas of Lake Canaçari. Counts in surface water ran up to one thousand per cubic meter, and counts in mud ran up to about three hundred per kilogram. Fishing areas and settled areas did not differ in a clear way. Most bits were blue fibers under a millimeter long. The most common plastic type was polyethylene, and blue and green pigments were also found.
pmc-13682602:
Marion David and co-authors build antibodies against a protein that helps tumors resist drugs meant to starve their blood supply, in a 2026 paper. Many cancers grow dense networks of blood and lymph vessels. Standard anti-growth drugs block one vessel signal, but tumors often escape by switching on a variant of that signal, called LVRF, which drives both vessel types.

The team made fully human antibodies that bind LVRF tightly and block its action. In lab tests the antibodies slowed cancer cell invasion and calmed vessel cells. In mice, they shrank kidney tumors that no longer answered the standard drug, and they pruned both blood and lymph vessels. In fish models, the spread of cancer cells fell as well. The authors propose LVRF as a fresh target for stubborn, vessel-rich tumors.
pmc-13682702:
Vincenzo Barbera and co-authors review how hormone problems in chronic kidney disease may touch the heart and blood vessels, in a 2026 paper. Failing kidneys often raise levels of prolactin, a hormone best known for milk production, and disturb the glands that govern sex hormones. In men, testosterone falls as kidney function declines. In women, monthly cycles break down and fertility ends early.

The review weighs lab findings that link these hormone shifts to vessel damage, clotting, and body changes against what patient studies actually show. Most patient evidence is observational, covers men more than women, and disagrees on prolactin. The authors treat the whole hormone-heart link as a working idea, not proven cause. They caution that measuring hormones in kidney patients is tricky, and they find no support for giving hormone-blocking drugs to patients who feel no symptoms.
pmc-13682802:
Simon Glimmann and eight colleagues compare liver cancers tied to hepatitis B and hepatitis D, in a 2026 study. Hepatitis D is the harshest form of viral hepatitis, yet its cancer profile is little known. The team reviewed patients at one center whose liver cancer grew from one virus or the other.

The sample held 162 patients, with about twice as many hepatitis B cases as D cases. At diagnosis, D-linked patients were younger, with worse liver function but smaller tumors. Their tumors less often invaded the main liver vein. Blood profiling of ninety-two inflammation signals split the groups cleanly. D-linked cancers carried a calmer, regulation-heavy immune pattern, while B-linked ones ran more inflammatory. Survival without events, though, matched between groups. The authors suggest future biomarkers and treatments may need to differ by virus.
pmc-13684602:
Laura Beebe, Lin Tian, and Loren Looger probe side effects of a calcium sensor inside cells in a 2026 paper. Fluorescent protein sensors report on cell chemistry from within, but their parts can tangle with the cell's own machinery. Checking that burden is now slow and ad hoc, which delays sensor design.

Working with the widely used GCaMP sensor, the team paired high content imaging with biochemical assays. Heavy sensor expression left a clear shape signature in a neuroblastoma cell line. A binding partner turned up in the cell skeleton, and cells lacking that structure shifted their shape profile as predicted. The dual method aims to flag problem sensor variants early in design.
pmc-13684802:
Montanez-Valverde and co-authors studied blood pressure among Hispanic and Latino adults in the United States, in a paper published in 2026. Race, as people report it, may not capture the mixed ancestry common in this population. The team asked how self-reported race and gene-based ancestry each relate to high blood pressure. They used data from a large community health study of Hispanic and Latino adults.

The study covered 10,586 unrelated adults. The team measured shares of West African, European, and Native American ancestry from genes. They then compared those shares, and self-reported race, with how common high blood pressure was. The results show that the two kinds of measures do not tell the same story. Each adds its own information about risk. The authors argue that health research should use both, rather than treating race as a stand-in for ancestry.
pmc-13685602:
Shanique Sterling-Lovy and seven co-authors ask whether replacing the pulmonary valve improves overall heart function in patients whose tetralogy of Fallot was repaired in childhood. A combined index of both ventricles' function predicts bad outcomes in this population, but its response to valve replacement was unknown. One hundred thirty-three patients had cardiac MRI within a year before and two years after their first valve replacement, compared against one hundred thirty-six controls.

Patients' index values ran well below controls', and nearly half were subnormal before surgery. After replacement, the mean index did not significantly change, while the right ventricle's own index fell. The study hunts pre-operative factors predicting severely depressed function afterward, complicating assumptions that valve replacement restores global function.
pmc-13688402:
Benoit Marteyn and eight colleagues compare two cancer drugs by watching immune cells fight fungus under a microscope. Both drugs block the BTK enzyme and are used for blood cancers. They also raise the risk of invasive Aspergillus infection, a known weakness of the class. The newer drug, zanubrutinib, is more selective, and patients on it seem to get fewer such infections.

Human neutrophils faced fungal material or living fungus with one drug or the other present. Both drugs blunted cell activation and slowed spore control. Live imaging split them: cells on ibrutinib stayed round, moved less, and ate fewer spores, while cells on zanubrutinib kept their shape and motion. The gap hints at off-target harm.
pmc-13689902:
Patrick Voorhoeve and co-authors show how fluorescent nanodiamonds can picture voltage and ion levels without wires or electrodes. The trick relies on nitrogen-vacancy centres inside the diamond, whose glow changes with the electrical state around them. Controlling that state in tiny particles had been hard. The team achieved reliable, reversible switching between a bright state and a dark state in particles under 30 nanometres wide, using surface oxidation and hydrogenation.

Layers of these particles on clear substrates then imaged applied voltages with a sensitivity reaching 16 millivolts, and tracked salt changes of under two percent per millimolar of sodium chloride. The method images ion gradients at microscope scale, all optically. The authors see it as a step toward fast, stable nanoscale voltage imaging.
pmc-1852402:
Hellemans, Mortier, De Paepe, and co-authors present qBase, a free program for handling real-time PCR data. PCR tests that track DNA growth are used to measure gene activity. Raw output from many samples and genes is hard to manage and easy to mishandle by hand.

qBase organises that data and automates the relative quantification step, which compares gene activity between samples. Automated, standard handling cuts errors and makes results easier to repeat. For labs running gene tests daily, shared software of this kind raised the reliability of reported changes in gene activity.
pmc-3412702:
Ye, Coulouris, Zaretskaya, and co-authors present Primer-BLAST, a tool to design target-specific primers for PCR. Primers are the short DNA pieces that start copying in a PCR test. Choosing them well is probably the single most important factor in whether the reaction works.

Specific copying requires primers that do not match other targets in the wrong orientation or at the wrong distance. Primer-BLAST checks candidate primers against sequence databases for such stray matches. The free tool saves labs from failed reactions and false results, and it is built into routine test design.
pmc-3965102:
Law, Knox, Djoumbou, and their team presented DrugBank version four in 2013. DrugBank is a free online database that holds deep detail on drugs, how they act, and what they target in the body. First described in 2006, it had grown fast as users asked for more.

The new release put fresh weight on drug metabolism, the way the body changes and clears a drug. Entries link a drug to its targets, enzymes, and chemical facts in one place. Doctors, chemists, and drug makers use that joined-up view to check safety, plan trials, and hunt for new uses of known drugs.
pmc-4029002:
Rosano and Ceccarelli reviewed in 2014 how to make proteins in the bacterium Escherichia coli. This microbe is one of the top choices for producing recombinant proteins, meaning proteins from genes placed into it on purpose. Its use as a living factory is well established and very common.

The review covers the many tools and protocols built for high-level production in this host. It also faces the hard parts, such as proteins that fold badly or form clumps. Clear guidance on strain choice, gene design, and growth conditions helps labs raise yields. Such proteins are used in research, medicine, and industry.
pmc-4383202:
Wan, Wang, Liu, and their co-authors tackled a common problem in meta-analysis in 2014. Reviews often need to pool the mean and standard deviation from similar clinical trials. Many trials, though, report only the median, the range, or the quartiles instead.

The authors give formulas to estimate the mean and spread from those reported values. Their methods were tested and compared so users can pick the best fit for each case. Without such estimates, many trials would be dropped from a review, wasting their evidence. The paper is a practical aid used by review teams across medicine.
pmc-4748402:
Atanasov, Waltenberger, Pferschy-Wenzig, and their colleagues reviewed plant-derived natural products in 2015. Medicinal plants have a long record as sources of molecules with therapeutic value. They still form an important pool for finding new drug leads today.

For some decades, industry focused mainly on libraries of synthetic compounds instead. The review covers both discovery of active plant products and the resupply problem, since a rare plant may not yield enough material. Solving supply through farming or synthesis decides whether a lead becomes a drug. The paper supports renewed investment in plant sources for future medicines.
pmc-5641502:
The GBD 2015 Neurological Disorders Collaborator Group published this large study in 2017. It measures how much illness, disability, and early death brain and nerve disorders caused around the world. The work covers global, regional, and national levels for the years from 1990 to 2015.

Readers get comparable figures for conditions such as stroke, dementia, epilepsy, and Parkinson disease across many countries and years. Health planners need numbers like these to decide where staff, beds, and money should go. The study shows that the share of disease linked to nerve disorders grew as populations aged, which makes planning harder.
pmc-6602502:
Stephan Greiner, Pascal Lehwark, and Ralph Bock presented OGDRAW version 1.3.1 in 2019. Chloroplast and mitochondrial genomes are small circles packed with genes. Drawing clear maps of them is a routine need as sequencing floods in.

OGDRAW turns genome annotation into publication-ready circular maps automatically. The update expands the toolkit and eases work on many genomes at once. Users can tune colors and layout without drawing by hand. Plant and organelle researchers use the maps in papers and teaching to show gene order at a glance. Maps can be exported in formats ready for journals, posters, and genome database pages.
pmc-6678302:
Laura Doyle and Matthew Wang gave an overview of extracellular vesicles in 2019. Cells release tiny vesicles, including exosomes, that carry markers of their state. Those parcels show up in blood and other fluids, which makes them tempting for tests.

Clinical use is held back by a lack of standard ways to isolate and measure vesicles. The authors review origins, contents, and the main separation methods, with the strengths of each. They stress reporting standards so studies can be compared. The overview helps newcomers avoid the field's common traps. Practical tables compare yield, purity, and cost across the main isolation methods.
pmc-7618802:
Al-Khatib and co-authors introduce a special issue, published in 2023, on trachoma, an eye infection that is the world's most common infectious cause of blindness. Past issues of the journal had tracked steady progress toward wiping out the disease. The editors say that progress continues. In April 2023, about 116 million people lived in areas still needing treatment and hygiene measures for this disease.

About 1.5 million people had the late, blinding stage, in which lashes turn inward and scar the eye. Both figures are far below those of 2002, down 92 percent and 80 percent. The issue gathers studies on the final push against the disease. The editors voice hope that the coming decade could be the last one for trachoma. Their message pairs that hope with a warning that the last cases are often the hardest to reach.
podmore-modern-spiritualism-1902:
Frank Podmore wrote the chief cool past of a faith in Modern Spiritualism, his two tome work of 1902. Podmore was the top doubt voice in the band that made such things its study. He knew the dark room from the in side. Here he tells the faith's tale from the Fox girls to his own day, fraud by fraud.

His tone is fair, dry, and oft wry. He grants some strange scraps, yet finds fraud at the root of most fame. All pasts of the theme since cite his work. It is the faith judged by its best foe.
recollections-of-the-private-life-of-nap: A plain-text publisher's header is the whole of the opening matter for the second volume of Constant's Private Life of Napoleon Bonaparte. It records the title, credits the work to Constant, and marks the language as English. Beyond those facts the pages at hand are blank of the work itself: no chapter heading, no table of contents, and no line of memoir appears. What this second part covers, and where its story picks up, cannot be told from what is printed here.
rhodes-last-will-testament-1902:
Cecil John Rhodes built a vast fortune in South African diamonds and gold, and he died in 1902 leaving a series of wills. Those wills set out how his money should be used after his death. Journalist W. T. Stead edited the wills for print that same year, adding long notes to explain them.

Readers find the actual terms Rhodes left behind, including money for scholarships and for grand plans in Africa. Stead's notes spell out the secret aims Rhodes attached to some gifts, aims later tied to the Round Table movement. Few books show so plainly how one rich man hoped to shape an empire from the grave.
richard-carvel-volume-02:
Winston Churchill's Richard Carvel continues in a second volume of five chapters, from Over the Wall to News from a Far Country. Under False Colours and The Red in the Carvel Blood stand between them, with A Festival and a Parting. The volume opens in Richard's voice, rueful over Dorothy Manners.

Dorothy, he says, treated him ill that spring, since she had tasted power at Carvel Hall. Suitors crowd her house, Dr. Courtenay and Will Fotheringay among them, while gentlemen call on her mother to see her. Richard, an awkward old playmate, gets scant attention. She teases him for knowing every twist of his nature, and bids him make her jealous instead.
rilke-buch-der-bilder-1902:
Das Buch der Bilder, The Book of Images, is Rainer Maria Rilke's early book of poems, published in German in 1902. The text here is the German original, since no English translation is in the public domain. Rilke was still in his twenties, fresh from Russia trips and deep study of art.

The poems picture saints, angels, lovers, beggars, and quiet rooms, each held in a tender, watchful gaze. Things in Rilke are never mere props; they seem to look back at the reader. His lines favor soft music over bold statement, and images over argument. The book stands at the source of modern German lyric poetry. Later came the sterner Elegies, but the seeds are here.
rob-roy-volume-02:
Sir Walter Scott's Rob Roy opens its second volume at chapter first, under a verse from Bürger about the dead riding fast. A picture of Helen MacGregor serves as frontispiece. The narrator, Frank, weighs two sorrows at once in the opening passage.

He grieves at parting from Miss Vernon, yet his father's troubles press on him too, with news of Mr. Tresham between them. Man can give only a fixed share of distress to each cause, he reflects, like a bankrupt's divided funds. His father's letter, not very distinct, bids him meet Owen at Glasgow, at the merchants MacVittie, MacFin and Company in the Gallowgate. Earlier letters seem to have miscarried or been intercepted.
run-to-earth-a-novel-pg9102: Run to Earth, a novel billed only as by the author of Lady Audley's Secret, Aurora Floyd, Ishmael, Vixen, and Wyllard's Weird. It opens with a picture of Honoria murmuring that she is in the power of a maniac. The contents list chapters headed Warned in a Dream, Done in the Darkness, and Disinherited. A fourth is headed Out of the Depths.
scheible-das-kloster-vol02:
Band two of Das Kloster, issued by editor Johann Scheible in 1845, gathers cells five through eight. Scheible's plan was bold for its time: rescue the cheap print of past ages before it rotted away. Whole texts went back into print under his Stuttgart imprint, in German, for any buyer to own.

Folk magic fills much of the space, from charms spoken over wounds to full spell books. Faust tales and Höllenzwänge, the hell-compelling grimoires, keep their full wording here. Chapbooks of popular story stand beside them without apology. Scholars still mine these pages when a lone copy elsewhere has crumbled or vanished.
scientific-phrenology-being-a-practical-: Pages shown here are for a work headed by its record title as a practical mental science from 1902. They consist of a publisher's list and press opinions. The opinions concern a related book by the same author. That related book, The Mental Functions of the Brain, is described as an investigation into their localisation and their manifestation in health and disease.
serapis-volume-02:
Georg Ebers wrote this historical novel of Alexandria; volume two opens at chapter five. Karnis has been long away from the boat, and young Dada frets through the wait with little Papias. When Karnis returns at sunset, she begs for the promised walk to see Alexandria.

Herse, her foster mother, forbids the trip until the next day. Dada bursts into tears, flings her distaff over the boat's side, and vows to run away. Karnis calms her by pleading his own deep weariness. Family warmth and a girl's restless spirit carry this middle volume's opening scenes.
serge-panine-volume-02: Volume two of Serge Panine, Georges Ohnet's French novel, stands behind these pages. Its English issue forms part of a series of Academy-crowned romances from France. Only the publisher's header appears here. The header repeats the title and Ohnet's name. It adds the series note and file data. Not one scene from this middle volume is shown. The tale's state at this point stays beyond fair statement from such thin front matter.
sketches-by-seymour-volume-02:
Robert Seymour's comic plates carry this second part of his sketches, opening at scene nine with verse. Two urchins, Tom and Bill, get hold of a pistol, powder, horn, and shot one day and set out on sport. A hare would crown their hopes, till Bill spots mother Tibbs's tabby cat instead.

Puss makes as good a mark as any bull's-eye, Bill argues, while the cat's mistress shrieks from above the wall. The shot leaves poor Tink finished and his mistress in a stew, while both boys flee. Cruel boy humor of the 1830s fills the plate's rhymed tale.
slave-narratives-a-folk-history-of-slave: Slave Narratives, a folk history of slavery in the United States from talks with former slaves, was typed from records made by the Federal Writers' Project in 1936-1938. The Library of Congress project put the set together, with photos, at Washington in 1941. One part is Volume IV, the Georgia Narratives, Part 1. Its list of those who spoke begins with Rachel Adams, Uncle Wash Allen, Hannah Austin, and Celestia Avery.
sombart-moderne-kapitalismus-vol1-1902:
Werner Sombart published the first volume of Modern Capitalism in German in 1902. Sombart, a German economist of the historical school, set out to explain how the modern economic system was born. The scale of the attempt, a full history of capitalism from its roots, matched the ambitions of its age.

Volume 1 traces the system's growth from medieval trade through the early crafts and the first great merchants. Sombart sorts economic life into stages and asks what spirit drives each one, the quiet craftsman against the bold entrepreneur. His answer gave later writers the phrase capitalist spirit to argue with. Weber, his younger rival, answered Sombart in famous essays of his own. The volume opens the most ambitious economic history of its time, and the argument it started has never fully closed.
sombart-moderne-kapitalismus-vol2-1902:
The second volume of Sombart's Modern Capitalism followed the first in 1902, completing the original design. Sombart had traced capitalism's birth in the opening volume; now the system stands full-grown. The German scholar's panorama widens to the whole industrial order of his day.

Volume 2 carries the tale into the industrial age: the factory system, the great firms and trusts, and the world market that bound them together. Sombart weighs the costs of the triumph, the uprooted crafts and crowded cities, beside the gains in wealth and power. His historical method piles up evidence where pure theory would argue. Economic history on the grandest scale ever attempted closes here, with capitalism triumphant and troubled at once. Later editions tripled the work, but the 1902 pair remains the statement that made his name.
strindberg-the-dream-play-1902:
August Strindberg wrote The Dream Play in 1902, here in Edwin Björkman's English translation for Western readers. The daughter of Indra descends to earth in the dream-drama that invented expressionist theatre for the modern stage. Strindberg's preface bids actors imitate the disjointed but seemingly logical shape of a dream in performance throughout.

Indra's daughter, as Agnes, marries, suffers, and watches human life repeat its pains in shifting scenes. An Officer waits for a singer who never comes, and a Lawyer wears mankind's grievances in his face. A castle grows from a dung heap, and a door with a cloverleaf hole guards life's secret. Humanity's refrain, men are to be pitied, tolls through scene changes that melt like thoughts in sleep. Björkman's version seeded the play's immense influence on theatre, film, and the modernist stage.
tales-and-novels-of-j-de-la-fontaine-vol:
Four verse tales fill the second volume of La Fontaine's Tales and Novels. They are The Cudgelled and Contented Cuckold, The Husband Confessor, The Cobbler, and The Peasant and His Angry Lord. A note from the producer points readers to a short list of bookmarks for sampling the author's ideas before making a whole meal of them.

The first tale follows a younger brother homeward from Rome. His travels have not improved him. He falls at once for a fair lady in a country town. He sees her safely home with gallant attention. Pardons from Rome he has in plenty; the virtues, the verse jokes, he left with His Holiness behind. La Fontaine's cuckolds, confessors, and craftsmen play out the old comedy of desire and deception in brisk rhymes.
tales-from-the-arabic-volume-02:
Payne's Tales from the Arabic continues in Volume the Second. A Delhi edition carries the printing, dated 1901. The Breslau text of the Thousand Nights and One Night goes on. Its frame is King Shah Bekht and his vizier Er Rehwan. It resumes from volume one.

Within that frame the contents list a pious woman accused of lewdness, a journeyman and a girl, and a weaver who became a physician by his wife's commandment. A run of sharper tales follows. Two sharpers cheat each his fellow in one. Sharpers deal with a money-changer and an ass in another. A sharper and the merchants come next. The hawk and the locust sit nested inside that tale. A king and his chamberlain's wife, an old woman and a draper's wife, and a foul-favored man with a fair wife keep the volume's world of tricks, lust, and sudden fortune turning.
the-adventures-of-ferdinand-count-fathom: Tobias Smollett wrote The Adventures of Ferdinand Count Fathom, and this second volume holds Part Two of the novel, with the author's preface and an opening essay by G. H. Maynadier of Harvard University. Chapter heads start at thirty-nine and trace fresh scenes of life, Renaldo's deepening distress as Fathom's plot thickens, the art of borrowing, and Monimia's honor guarded by a stroke of heaven.
the-antiquary-volume-02: Volume Two of The Antiquary by Sir Walter Scott is present only as cover and contents matter, with a second-volume title page and frontispiece named. Its chapters are counted in words from first to sixteenth and beyond, with no heads or summaries attached. No story text appears in these pages, so nothing of the novel's cast or course can be grounded from what is shown here.
the-arabian-nights-entertainments-volume: Contents pages list the second Aldine volume. Pickering and Chatto printed it at London in 1890. It has pictures by S. L. Wood, from Dr. Jonathan Scott's text. The volume centers on the little hunchback. A ring of tales surrounds him, told by a merchant, a purveyor, a physician, a tailor, and a barber. The barber's six brothers each get a story. Later come Aboulhassen Ali Ebn Ecar and Schemselnihar. Noor Ad Deen and the fair Persian close the list.
the-attache-or-sam-slick-in-england-volu: Volume two of Haliburton's Attaché repeats the front matter of the first. It has the motto and Slick's threat of the mitten for printed talk. It also has the author's London letter of July 3, 1843. That letter sends the attaché ahead to Edmund Hopkinson at Edgeworth. It pleads for indulgence of his eccentric ways. Its own contents then begin afresh, with The Nose of a Spy as chapter one and The Patron as chapter two.
the-bride-of-the-nile-volume-02:
Volume 2 of The Bride of the Nile, by Georg Ebers, opens at Chapter VI with a governor in deep unrest. Soul pangs and doubts of conscience drove him to buy a costly hanging as a gift. The dearer the gift, the stronger his hope of grace from the man who got it. He has cause to ask if he acted rightly.

Revenge is no Christian virtue, he knows, yet he could not let the Melchites' evil go unpaid when the chance to crush them came. His two bright young sons were murdered by them, and since that blow he has felt himself slowly dying. Greeks and Melchites were driven from Egypt in shame, some slain by crowds who hailed the Moslems as saviors. His revenge is complete, and now conscience lifts its voice.
the-burgomaster-s-wife-volume-02:
Volume 2 of The Burgomaster's Wife, by Georg Ebers, opens at Chapter VII in a spell of rain over Leyden. A second and third rainy day follow the first. White mists and grey fog hang over the meadows. The cold north-west wind drives heavy clouds together, and water in the canals grows turbid and rises toward the banks. Men and women hurry past each other, dripping and freezing, with no greeting.

Talk in the tap-rooms sounds anything but hopeful, and some men are heard calling resistance folly. Others demand aloud the desertion of the Prince of Orange and liberty. Three days have passed since Peter's departure, and the fourth nears noon. No message has reached his family. Maria, his wife, has put on her light-blue dress with Mechlin lace, for he must surely return today.
the-caxtons-a-family-picture-volume-02:
Part II of The Caxtons takes up the family tale again. Pisistratus, the son of the house, narrates his own youth in the first person. His father, a bookish scholar, presides over the household at the tale's center.

The chapter opens with the narrator at the head of his preparatory school at age twelve. His parents then look for a wider field for his studies. Love of study has come back to him in a keen, rival-driven form, and his father no longer tries to curb it. The father honors scholarship too much to block a son who might become a scholar.
the-celebrity-volume-02:
Volume 2 of Winston Churchill's novel opens at Chapter V, at the resort of Asquith. Its hero, the famed Mr. Charles Wrexell Allen, is known in the tale as the Celebrity. Society life by the northern lake frames this stretch of the story.

Knowing voices at Asquith find it small wonder that Allen is drawn to Irene Trevor. Lake breezes have brought color to her cheeks and spring to her step. Bit by bit it grows plain that Miss Trevor is gaining ground with the Celebrity, to the neglect of the other young women there. Word that he will lead the cotillon with her settles the matter for local gossips, and the narrator watches the match form.
the-confessions-of-jean-jacques-rousseau:
Book II of Jean Jacques Rousseau's Confessions stands here as volume II of the twelve-book set, privately printed for members of the Aldus Society at London in 1903. The book opens at the moment of the boy's flight from home and apprenticeship.

Rousseau contrasts two views of the same act. The moment when fear drove his flight seemed no more terrible than the moment of carrying it out seemed delightful. Yet reason draws a grim picture: a child leaving relations and resources midway through his training, before he could earn a living. Such a start runs toward misery and danger, toward vice, despair, snares, slavery, and death. How different, he says, was the idea he actually entertained, which was one of independence. Book II thus turns on the gap between a boy's dream of freedom and the hard world that waits for a runaway apprentice.
the-crisis-volume-02:
Volume 2 of Winston Churchill's The Crisis opens at Chapter VIII, Bellegarde. Miss Virginia Carvel comes down the steps in her riding habit while Ned waits in the street with the horses. She leaps into Vixen's saddle and canters off, neighbors waving from opened windows, to visit the Russell girls at their father's country place on Bellefontaine Road.

Her errand is to announce her hatred for a certain young Yankee upstart, a feeling she confided the day before to Anne Brinsmade and Eugenie Renault. At the Russells she finds a guest, Elise Saint Simon from New Orleans, and will not stay, pleading dinner at Bellegarde though it is only ten o'clock. Puss Russell presses her about a new young man in town as the chapter turns.
the-disowned-volume-02:
Volume two of Edward Bulwer Lytton's The Disowned begins at chapter eleven, with Clarence Linden settled in small lodgings at a house called Copperas Bower. His first morning there brings a thin, weak breakfast tea and sharp, funny talk from Mr. and Mrs. Copperas. Mr. Copperas works in stocks and loves a joke, while his wife prides herself on fine manners.

Clarence watches this odd household with dry amusement. The chapters mix social satire with the hero's slow rise in the world. Talk at the table hints at money, pride, and the schemes that will soon test him.
the-divine-comedy-by-dante-illustrated-h:
Cantos three and four fill part two of Hell in Dante's Vision, rendered into English verse by the Rev. H. F. Cary. At the gate of Hell, Dante reads the stern words that end with a call to leave all hope behind. Inside, he sees the souls who lost the good of the mind, and his guide steadies him for what lies ahead.

The part moves from the gate to the first circle. Dante meets crowds of the dead and learns how each soul is placed. Cary's blank verse keeps the scene grave and clear.
the-emperor-volume-02:
Volume two of Georg Ebers's The Emperor opens at chapter five, in the hall of the Muses at Lochias. Pontius the architect, back in good humour after a spat with the steward, calls the sculptor Pollux to supper. Pollux begs off: his mother has cooked cabbage and sausages, food of the gods, and his father has brought the bowl in.

Work for the emperor's visit drives the days, while Pollux jokes through his hunger. Clara Bell's rendering keeps Ebers's mix of craft talk, family warmth, and looming courts. Supper scenes ground the grand tale in daily bread.
the-history-of-don-quixote-volume-1-part:
Volume 1, Part 02 of Don Quixote comes from Cervantes, in Ormsby's English rendering. Chapter four tells of what happened to the knight when he left the inn. Day was dawning as Don Quixote rode out, so happy and gay at finding himself dubbed a knight that his joy seemed ready to burst his horse-girths.

On the road he recalls the advice of his host at the inn. The part continues the first sally begun in the earlier chapters, with the new knight fresh from his dubbing and full of delight. Cervantes keeps the tone light here, letting pride and pleasure carry a man who has no true idea of the road ahead.
the-honor-of-the-name-pg4002:
Emile Gaboriau wrote The Honor of the Name. Chapter one opens on the first Sunday of August 1815, at ten o'clock precisely, in the parish church at Sairmeuse. The sacristan sounds three strokes of the bell to warn the faithful that the priest is mounting the altar steps for high mass.

The church stands more than half full, and peasant women hurry in with shoes in hand, put on in reverence at the door. Most men stay outside to talk crops and news in the porch and yard, treating Sunday mass as a weekly market of talk. A sibling record in the library shows only the title page and contents for the same title.
the-innocents-abroad-volume-02:
Part 2 of Mark Twain's Innocents Abroad finds the travelers in France. The text comes from the 1869 first edition. Chapter XI opens the part. The party is getting foreignized rapidly, Twain says. Stone floors ring to the heel here. They kill all sentimental musing. Noiseless waiters hover like butterflies at the elbow. Ice comes made by artifice in bottles. One hardship stands beyond bearing. They must ring for soap at every wash.

He walks readers through the table d'hôte. Soup comes, then fish after a wait. Roast beef, peas, and lentils follow in turn. Snail patties and roast chicken arrive. Strawberry pie and ice cream close the meal. Wine stands with every course, this being France. His joke about Marseilles caps the chapter. Its people make hymns, vests, and soap for the world. They never sing, wear, or wash with them themselves.
the-inside-of-the-cup-volume-02:
Volume 2 of Winston Churchill's novel opens with chapter V. The rector has more food for thought here. Sunday after Sunday, Hodder surveys the same scene at St. John's. Winter light falls through stained windows. It colors the marble of the center aisle. The choir's voices echo among the arches. Certain landmarks fill the pews. Eldon Parr sits rigid in his empty pew. Everett Constable settles pompously into his own. His white-haired wife takes the far end. Their children once filled the space between.

Churchill catalogues the flock with malice. The Fergusons and the healthy Plimptons appear. Young Gordon Atterbury is forty-five and unmarried. His eyeglasses hang from a gold chain. The widowed Mrs. Larrabbee agitates any air she enters. Even prayer cannot settle her presence. Hodder feels her interest as almost personal. His discomfort hints at the crisis gathering below.
the-last-of-the-barons-volume-02:
Book Two, called the King Court, forms the portion in this record of Edward Bulwer Lytton novel of Earl Warwick. Young men ride along the Strand past half fortified mansions and merchants houses with orchards. They head for Marmaduke hostel in East Cheap.

Marmaduke Nevile, kinsman to a great minister, changes plain provincial dress for court finery sewn with seed pearls and gold fringe. The chapter shows London wealth and display under Edward IV. Private ambition enters a court famous for gorgeous dress and restless intrigue, display, and sudden shifts of favor among the great.
the-lerouge-case-pg3802:
Emile Gaboriau opens his detective novel on Thursday, March 6, 1862, shortly after Shrove Tuesday. Five women from La Jonchere village visit the police station at Bougival in France. Their neighbor, the Widow Lerouge, has not been seen for two days.

Knocks at her isolated cottage went unanswered, with shutters and door closed tight. The police commissioner resists at first, then sends gendarmes and a locksmith to force entry. Gaboriau builds one of the early modern detective novels from village alarm, careful police work, and a hidden family past. Village gossip gives the inquiry its first push.
the-lion-s-skin-pg2702: Rafael Sabatini's The Lion's Skin appears here with only a title page and a contents list, so the novel itself does not appear. The list runs to twenty-two chapters, four more than the contents shown for the companion record of the same title. Early chapters include The Fanatic, The Witness, and Moonshine, while the closing titles name The End of Lord Ostermore, Mr. Caryll's Identity, The Lion's Skin, and The Hunters.
the-memoirs-of-count-grammont-volume-02:
Volume 2 of Anthony Hamilton's Memoirs of Count Grammont, edited with notes by Sir Walter Scott, opens at Chapter Fourth, the Chevalier's arrival at the court of Turin. Hamilton argues that military glory is only half a hero's equipment, since love must give the finishing stroke. Fresh from the siege of Trino, Grammont and his companion Matta plan new sieges against the beauties and husbands of Turin.

Hamilton compares the pair to Amadis of Gaul and Don Galaor, then notes their real advantages. Unlike those silent knights of romance, Grammont and Matta are adepts at cards and dice. They are young, handsome, witty, and free with money, so Turin receives them warmly. The court, Hamilton says, was then the seat of gallantry and love. Readers get courtly intrigue told with open amusement at its heroes.
the-parisians-volume-02:
Volume 2 of Edward Bulwer-Lytton's The Parisians opens with Book II. Several weeks have passed, and the lime trees in the Tuileries are green. Graham Vane sits absorbed in thought at a writing table in a ground-floor apartment in the Rue d'Anjou. The narrator pauses to give his parentage and position.

Vane's father inherited a fair squire's estate and about half a million in investments, free of entail. A man of brilliant, irregular genius and princely generosity, he turned his hall into a ducal palace, then stood for the county and won early success in Parliament. The son's striking forehead marks him out in the Paris scenes that follow.
the-prince-of-india-or-why-constantinopl: Volume II of Lew. Wallace's The Prince of India, or Why Constantinople Fell, carries the same Longfellow verses as the first volume. The pages shown give the title page and contents, not the novel itself. The contents open at Book IV, The Palace of Blacherne, continued from the earlier volume. Chapters include The Princess Hears from the World and Lael Tells of Her Two Fathers. The Prince of India Preaches God to the Greeks stands at the centre. Later entries name The Imperial Cistern Gives Up Its Secret.
the-project-gutenberg-faq-2002:
Jim Tinsley's Project Gutenberg FAQ 2002 announces itself as a historical reference, not a current guide. Readers wanting up-to-date answers are sent to the project's site. A first answer tells questioners where to ask: the Volunteers' Board for production questions, the gutvol-d list for matters of general volunteer interest. Sections then cover Project Gutenberg itself, its publications, and more.

The opening questions ask what the project is, where it came from, and what it has achieved. They continue to who runs it, how many people take part, and how to help. Relations with Projekt Gutenberg-DE, Project Gutenberg of Australia, and Project Runeberg get their own question. The FAQ preserves the project's self-description at the start of the century.
the-red-lily-volume-02: Anatole France is named as author on the electronic edition header, which labels the text volume two and gives an April 2003 release. Here only that edition header and its general notices are present, so no part of the novel itself appears and nothing about its story can be told from these pages. A companion complete record in the set carries a biographical preface instead.
the-right-of-way-volume-02:
Gilbert Parker's second volume joins the story at chapter nine, where Jo Portugais runs a small raft downriver at night against the law of the river. Jo, a young man of many gifts who works as driver, woodsman, hunter, carpenter, or guide as whim takes him, has come alone from far upriver.

Contents for the volume promise old debts, a raised curtain, Rosalie's coming, Charley's adventuring, a mark in paper, a mission, a tailor's midnight foray, and a stolen cross. Habitual defiance of custom defines Jo at once. The volume listing overlaps the combined contents given in the complete record in the set.
the-story-of-my-life-volume-02:
Volume two of Georg Ebers's autobiography, translated by Mary J. Safford, opens at chapter six with his introduction to art among the neighbours of the Lennestrasse in Berlin. The Drakes of his sister's journal were a sculptor's family. Berlin owed splendid works of art to Drake. He was a warm friend of Ebers's mother. He welcomed the children into his studio. He gave them clay to shape.

Ebers watched statues, busts, and reliefs grow from rude clay and plaster casts turn into marble, while the calm master explained everything with unfailing patience. He credits those childhood hours for later characters in his novels: little Pennu in Uarda, Polykarp in Homo Sum, Pollux in The Emperor, and the cheery Alexander in Per Aspera.
the-thirty-years-war-volume-02:
Frederick Schiller opens Book Two of his History of the Thirty Years' War with Ferdinand's fateful resolution. That decision gave the war a new direction, a new scene, and new actors. What began as a Bohemian rebellion and the chastisement of rebels now spreads across Germany and then Europe. Schiller pauses to survey the balance between Roman Catholics and Protestants across the empire.

Catholics were more numerous and favoured by the constitution; Protestants held compact, populous territories, warlike princes, free towns, and command of the sea. Spain and Italy stood behind one side, Venice, Holland, and England behind the other. Schiller shows a continent balanced for catastrophe, then blames private interests for dissolving the Protestant union at the decisive moment.
the-wandering-jew-volume-02:
Volume two of Eugene Sue's Wandering Jew carries book two, opening with an interval titled The Wandering Jew's Sentence. Contents chapters move through an ajoupa, tattooing, a smuggler, the ruins of Tchandi, an ambuscade, a tempest, and a shipwreck. Paris draws nearer through Dagobert's wife, Agricola Baudoin, Adrienne at her toilet, and a closing interview.

The interval passage itself is printed after the contents. Its scene is a wild, rugged eminence of sandstone boulders, birch, and oak under a red western light left by the sun. Below lies a deep, fertile valley veiled in evening mist, with ripe corn gathered, church steeples rising, and a high-road running north to west. The hour of repose settles over the cottages.
thomson-bible-1808-vol-02:
The second volume of Charles Thomson's 1808 Bible carries the story from the first book of Kings through Esther. It then adds the wisdom books, from Job through the Song of Solomon. Thomson translated from the Greek Septuagint, and Jane Aitken printed the volumes at Philadelphia.

Readers meet Solomon's temple, the split of the kingdom, exile and return, and the court tale of Esther. Then the tone shifts to poetry: Job's debate, the Psalms in Greek order, Proverbs, and the Song. Because Thomson worked from Greek, names and lines often differ from the King James text. The volume shows the Bible as the Greek church read it.
tob-0102:
Abraham of Worms left an account of learning sacred magic from Abramelin, an Egyptian mage he met in his travels. Book one of the Sacred Magic of Abramelin tells that story. Abraham writes for his son, explaining why the true magic differs from the frauds and dark rites around him.

The prize is the Knowledge and Conversation of the Holy Guardian Angel, won through many months of prayer and a purified life. Book one sets out the journey, the teacher, and the rules of conduct. Few magical books demand so much of the reader. Later magicians, Crowley among them, treated the work as a summit.
tob-0202:
The Kybalion opens with a key line: as above, so below. The 1908 Hermetic classic teaches mental transmutation. That is, the art of changing one's inner state to change one's world. Seven rules, said to come down from Hermes of old Egypt, carry the whole teaching. The Three Initiates wrote for doers, not for scholars.

Mind, matching, rhythm, the pull of opposites, cause and effect: each rule is stated, then glossed, then put to use. The book is the New Thought world's most lasting handbook, still in print and still quoted. Its plain style is the point. Seven rules, meant to be used each day.
tob-10102:
Johann Arndt published True Christianity in the seventeenth century, in German as Vier Bücher vom wahren Christentum. His argument rebuked comfortable churchgoers: real Christianity is not attendance or correct doctrine alone. It is an inward transformation of the heart that changes how a person lives.

Arndt calls readers to repentance, prayer, humility, and daily practice of faith rather than mere profession. The book proved hugely popular, was carried by missionaries around the world, and shaped Protestant piety for generations. Its stern, searching tone still explains its influence: Arndt measured religion by fruit in ordinary conduct, not by labels.
tob-10402:
Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, spent much of his life fighting the teaching of Arius, who said Christ was a created being, not fully God. His discourses Against the Arians form his fullest defense of the Nicene faith. Enemies exiled him five times, yet he kept writing.

He argues from scripture that the Word is true God, of one being with the Father, and that only a divine savior can save mankind. The discourses mix close Bible reading with sharp attacks on his foes. They helped secure the doctrine of the Trinity in the church and remain a base text of early Christian theology.
tob-10802:
Charles Squire retold the myths of the British Islands, drawing on medieval Irish and Welsh sources. Cuchulain's heroics, the voyage of Bran, Arthur's court, and the old gods behind the tales all appear. Squire aimed at the general reader rather than the Celtic scholar.

Working as a storyteller with a scholar's conscience, he separates story from history where the evidence allows and admits where it does not. Gods become kings in some tales, heroes shrink or grow across versions, and Squire tracks the changes. V1 evidence calls the result the best single doorway into Celtic mythology; readers get narrative first, with learning carried lightly.
tob-14502:
Jalaluddin Rumi, the thirteenth-century Sufi master of Konya, composed the Masnavi, a vast poem in six books in Persian. He dictated it to a disciple over many years. Persian speakers have called it the Quran in Persian for its depth.

Story follows story: kings, fools, lovers, and animals act out lessons on the soul's longing for God. The opening song of the reed flute, cut from its reed bed, sets the theme of separation and return. Rumi breaks off tales to comment, joke, and pray. It is the most read poem in the Muslim world and a summit of Sufi teaching.
tob-3002:
Augustine of Hippo's Confessions, in E. B. Pusey's translation, trace his path from restless North African youth to Christian bishop. A stolen pear, a brilliant career in rhetoric, years with the Manichaeans, and a mother's prayers fill the early books. Conversion comes in a Milan garden, under a child's voice chanting take up and read.

Late have I loved thee, O Beauty ever ancient, ever new, runs his famous cry. The final books turn from story to memory, time, and Genesis, in thirteen books that effectively invented spiritual autobiography in Western literature. Pusey, an Oxford churchman, keeps the passion of the Latin in dignified English. The examined life starts here for many readers.
tob-4002:
Niccolò Machiavelli wrote The Prince in 1513 after his fall from Florentine politics cost him office, freedom, and nearly his health under torture. Addressed to a Medici ruler, the manual asks how new princes gain and keep power in a dangerous Italy of rival states and foreign armies. His answers shocked Christendom.

Power, Machiavelli argues, is kept by being feared rather than loved when both cannot be had, promises are tools to be judged by outcomes, and fortune favors the bold who act. He describes power as it is practiced, not as moralists said it should be. Five centuries of argument over his name began with these chapters.
tob-4102:
Kenneth James Saunders, scholar and missionary, translated the Dhammapada from the Pali under the title The Buddha's Way of Virtue. His 1919 edition carries introduction and notes for the general reader. The 423 verses of the original form the best-known summary of the Buddha's teaching.

Mind goes before all things, the opening verse declares; a trained mind brings happiness like a shadow that never leaves. Saunders renders the Pali with respect and a light touch. His notes explain terms from Buddhist practice for Western ears. Verified from the 1919 edition, the little book serves as a gentle, scholarly first step into Buddhist ethics.
tob-9102:
Melody rules the Sama Veda, the Veda of chants, in Griffith's translation verified from the 1919 scan. Its verses are mostly Rigvedic lines reset for singing at the soma sacrifice. Priests stretched and ornamented the words until the chant became an art of its own.

As a book of words, the Sama Veda is the shortest of the four Vedas. As a book of music, it is the root from which Indian classical singing claims descent. Griffith prints the verses in the order singers used them. Readers meet the Veda that exists to be heard, the liturgy behind the hymns found elsewhere.
travels-in-the-interior-of-africa-volume:
Volume two of Mungo Park's Travels in the Interior of Africa, in the 1887 Cassell edition, completes his account of the 1795-97 journey. Its introduction picks Park up where volume one left him. He had reached the Niger, then fallen sick, alone, and stripped of nearly everything.

The editor praises the tale as one of the most gripping in English travel writing. Park's good temper, courage, and kindness toward the people whose help kept him alive draw special notice. A half-starved man robbed in a forest still stops to admire a tiny moss, the introduction recalls. That eye for detail carries the homeward journey here.
trunko-watauga-democrat-1925-04-02:
A strange bulk fights the sea in the Watauga Democrat piece of April 2, 1925. The North Carolina paper reprints a tale from Margate, on the coast of South Africa, from the year past. There, guests watched a vast hairy beast fight two whales for hours. It looked like a polar bear grown huge. It then lay dead on the sand, lost ere it could be gauged for science.

Locals named the beast Trunko in lore since then. No proof of it was kept at all. The reprint is the root source of the whole tale. Its loss is the point.
uarda-a-romance-of-ancient-egypt-volume-:
Volume two of Georg Ebers's Uarda begins at chapter five, on the morning after Princess Bent-Anat knocked at the gate of the House of Seti. Dawn's freshness gives way to heat pouring from a cloudless sky. The limestone rocks of the Necropolis glare, and the air quivers as if over a flame.

Below, the harbor where boats cross from eastern Thebes crowds with barks waiting to return. Boatmen attached to priestly and noble houses rest, play at morra, and dispute eagerly. A vendor of food, drink, and cooling acids sets up under a sycamore. Ebers builds ancient Thebes from heat, dust, and the working riverfront before the plot resumes.
un-ga-res-president-george-w-bush-s-rema:
George W. Bush addressed the United Nations General Assembly on September 12, 2002, and turned the hall's attention to Iraq. A year after the September 11 attacks, he warned of a grave and gathering danger from Saddam Hussein's regime. The speech began the public march toward the invasion that came six months later.

Bush lists Iraq's breaches of past Council resolutions on arms and terror. He challenges the UN to enforce its own demands or risk fading into irrelevance. He pledges to work with the Council while reserving the right to act alone. The address frames the case that shaped a war.
un-sc-res-102:
Resolution 102 sets the terms for Japan to join the Statute of the International Court of Justice. The Council adopted it on 3 December 1953. The vote was ten to none. The Soviet Union abstained. Japan was not yet a UN member. So the Charter required the General Assembly to fix the terms. It would act on advice from the Council.

Japan would join once it filed a signed statement with the Secretary-General. The statement also had to be ratified under Japanese law. In it, Japan would accept the Statute in full. It would accept the duties in Article 94 of the Charter. It would also agree to pay a fair share of the Court's costs. The Assembly would set that share after talks with Japan.
un-sc-res-1302: Adopted by the Security Council and numbered 1302, this formal text is catalogued under the year 1995. Such texts can call for cease-fires, set up missions, impose duties, or settle points of UN procedure and membership.
