Its value lies in the primary wording: the decision as adopted, kept through the Wikisource transcription of the record. No summary replaces it; the record itself is the content of the entry.
un-sc-res-1402:
The second Palestinian uprising reached a grave point in March 2002. Suicide bombings had struck Israel. Israeli forces had attacked the headquarters of the President of the Palestinian Authority and moved into Palestinian cities. Resolution 1402 was adopted in March 2002, days after the two-state text, Resolution 1397.

The Council called on both parties to move at once to a meaningful cease-fire. Israeli troops were called on to withdraw from Palestinian cities, including Ramallah. Both sides had to work with the United States special envoy and others on the ground. Their first step was to carry out the Tenet security work plan in full. The Council also repeated the demand of Resolution 1397. All acts of violence had to end at once, including terror, provocation, incitement, and destruction.
un-sc-res-1502:
A bomb had destroyed the United Nations headquarters in Baghdad days before. On 26 August 2003 the Security Council spoke on the safety of aid and United Nations workers. It recalled the attack on the Iraq mission of 19 August. It voiced grave concern at violence against humanitarian staff in many places. Such attacks, it stressed, break the laws of war.

The Council condemns murder, abduction, hostage-taking, and attacks on aid convoys. It urges states to punish crimes against relief workers. It demands safe access for aid staff to all people in need. It also asks host countries to write stronger safety rules into their agreements with the United Nations.
un-sc-res-1602:
Burundi's operation was extended as elections neared on 31 May 2005. The Arusha Agreement's transition was moving toward its close. Burundians had approved a post-transition constitution in the referendum of 28 February 2005. On 15 May the president and the last rebel group's leader signed a Dar es Salaam declaration. They pledged an instant halt to fighting and a permanent ceasefire within a month.

The Council extended ONUB's mandate until 1 December 2005. All Burundian parties were called to work harder to make the elections a success. The Council looked forward to the Secretary-General's advice, due by mid-June, on the mission's future shape. He was to keep reporting on events as they unfolded. ONUB's work on a zero tolerance approach to abuse by its own staff was welcomed. The renewal carried the mission through the polls and the new government's birth.
un-sc-res-1702:
MINUSTAH was renewed behind an elected government on 15 August 2006. Haiti had completed a peaceful move to elected rule, with a new president and parliament. The government's program covered modernizing the state and creating wealth. A social relief program answered the country's urgent needs. The Secretary-General's report of 28 July set out the mission's next phase.

The Council extended MINUSTAH's mandate, as set by resolution 1542 (2004), for six months. The mission would keep a military part of up to 7,200 troops and a police part of up to 1,951 officers. Sixteen correction officers, seconded from member states, were authorized to help the prison service. Haiti's authorities were urged to finish the run-off legislative and local elections without delay. States were asked to supply well-qualified police. The Council restated its call for the mission to back the constitutional and political process and the rule of law.
un-sc-res-1902:
The Security Council adopted Resolution 1902 on Burundi on 17 December 2009. Burundi was preparing presidential and legislative elections for 2010. Rights abuses and limits on free assembly still drew concern. Youth groups tied to parties had clashed, and talks on justice for past crimes were under way.

The text extends the United Nations Integrated Office in Burundi, called BINUB, until 31 December 2010. The office should focus on the elections, fair rule, peace, and the return of former fighters. The government must create fair conditions for the 2010 vote. It should also keep fighting graft, set up an independent rights body, and avoid steps that could raise tensions again.
un-sc-res-2002:
Somalia and Eritrea are the subject of United Nations Security Council Resolution 2002, adopted on 29 July 2011. Drought and famine were gripping Somalia that summer. Armed groups blocked aid and taxed trade through ports they held. Weapons kept crossing borders in breach of two arms embargoes.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council widens who can face travel bans and asset freezes. Recruiting child soldiers now counts, as do attacks on schools, hospitals, and civilians. Blocking aid and stealing public funds also qualify for listing. Trade through Al-Shabaab ports may count as backing a listed group. The Monitoring Group gains twelve more months, and urgent aid payments are shielded from the freeze for a year.
un-sc-res-202:
Southern Rhodesia's drift toward a breakaway declaration met a warning on 6 May 1965. Elections under the rejected 1961 constitution were set for 7 May. The minority government was threatening a unilateral declaration of independence. The General Assembly and its special committee had long pressed Britain to free political prisoners and repeal repressive laws.

The Council noted Britain's stated terms for any grant of independence. It backed the majority view that Britain should call a constitutional conference of all parties. Britain and all member states were asked to refuse any unilateral declaration of independence. Britain had to act to prevent one from coming. No powers or armed forces were to pass to the Rhodesian government as it stood. The question stayed on the Council's agenda. The warning failed, and the Smith regime declared independence that November.
un-sc-res-2202:
Resolution 2202 gave the Security Council's backing to the Minsk agreements, the ceasefire deals meant to end fighting in eastern Ukraine. Rebels backed by Russia held parts of the Donetsk and Luhansk regions. The Council adopted the text days after the second Minsk deal was signed.

Inside, the members endorse the full package: a ceasefire, withdrawal of heavy weapons, local elections, and changes to Ukraine's constitution. They call on all sides to carry out every step. The resolution matters because it put the world's top security body behind a peace plan that both Ukraine and Russia had accepted.
un-sc-res-302: The library catalogues Resolution 302, a Security Council decision, under the year 1971. Voting in the Council requires support from its permanent members, so each adopted text marks a point of agreement. Readers will find the full wording here, taken from the English Wikisource transcription of the UN official record. The entry belongs to the library's DECLASSIFIED group of public official records.
un-sc-res-402: Preserved as Resolution 402, this Security Council text carries a 1981 date in the catalog record. A resolution may address a conflict, a court vacancy, a new member, or the running of the United Nations itself. Anyone studying UN practice can read the decision itself here, in the Wikisource transcription of the official record. The catalog places it in the DECLASSIFIED group of official public records.
un-sc-res-502:
Argentina's invasion of the Falkland Islands was met with a withdrawal order in April 1982. The Council's president had called on 1 April for both governments to shun force in the region. Reports then told of an invasion by Argentine forces on 2 April. The Council judged that a breach of the peace existed in the region of the islands.

The Council demanded an immediate end to hostilities. It demanded the immediate withdrawal of all Argentine forces from the Falkland Islands (Islas Malvinas). Argentina and the United Kingdom were called to seek a diplomatic answer to their differences. Both were told to respect the purposes and principles of the United Nations Charter in full. The text gave Britain the legal ground it stood on through the war that followed. Argentina did not withdraw, and the fighting ended only with its surrender in June.
un-sc-res-702: North and South Korea both sought United Nations seats in 1991. On 8 August 1991 the Security Council examined their applications separately. It recommended to the General Assembly that the Democratic People's Republic of Korea be admitted. It made the same recommendation for the Republic of Korea. The decision was taken without a vote. Both states joined that September. Their joint entry ended a long dispute over Korean representation.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci: Security Council resolution 102 was adopted on 3 December 1953, by 10 votes to none with one abstention. It recommends terms on which Japan could become a party to the Statute of the International Court of Justice, without joining the United Nations. Japan would deposit an instrument accepting the Statute and the obligations of Article 94 of the Charter. It would undertake to contribute an equitable share of the Court's expenses. The General Assembly would assess that share.

Iraq's oil-for-food programme gets another six months of life here, in a text passed on 8 June 2000. The programme let Iraq sell oil under United Nations control while wide sanctions stayed in force. The money paid for food, medicine, and other basic goods for Iraqi civilians.

Acting under Chapter VII of the Charter, the Council kept the rules first set in 1995 in force for 180 days from 9 June. Food, nutrition, and health kept first claim on the funds, with a fixed share set aside for the north of the country. The Council also pressed for fair sharing of goods in every part of Iraq and for stronger United Nations checks on the ground.

As Israeli tanks ringed the Palestinian leader's compound in Ramallah, the Council called for a ceasefire. On 29 March 2002, it adopted Resolution 1402. Fourteen members backed it and none opposed it. Syria took no part in the vote. The text voices grave concern at suicide bombings in Israel. It also cites the attack on the Palestinian Authority's headquarters.

Both parties must move at once to a real ceasefire. Israeli troops must pull out of Palestinian cities, Ramallah included. The text repeats the demand made in Resolution 1397 days before. All violence, terror, and wrecking must stop at once. It backs the envoys then working to restart the peace track.

A bomb at UN headquarters in Baghdad pushed aid worker safety onto the agenda in 2003. On 26 August, the Council adopted Resolution 1502 without dissent. The blast a week before killed the mission's chief. Twenty-one others died with him. The attack is named in the text itself.

The Council condemns in strong terms the violence aid staff now face. Murder, abduction, and attacks on convoys all count. States must make sure such crimes do not go unpunished. All parties must let aid workers reach people in need in safety. The text pledges steps of its own as well. Host states should adopt the safety pact's key guards. The text still anchors debate on aid worker safety.

Resolution 1602, adopted on 31 May 2005, extends the UN operation in Burundi as the country's transition nears its vote. Burundians had approved a post-transition constitution by referendum in February. In May, the sitting president and the leader of the last big rebel group, the Palipehutu-FNL, signed a declaration in Dar es Salaam moving toward a ceasefire. The Arusha peace agreement of 2000 was the framework everything rested on.

ONUB's mandate was extended for six months, to December 2005. The Council assured all Burundian parties of its determination to see the transition end successfully through free and fair elections. It also restated support for the Arusha process and called on the parties to honor their commitments in full.

Haiti's fresh start under an elected government is the backdrop for Resolution 1702, adopted on 15 August 2006. A new president and parliament had been chosen in a calm transfer of power. The UN Stabilization Mission in Haiti, MINUSTAH, was a key support. The government had approved a police reform plan and set social programs in motion, but gangs, weak courts, and crowded prisons still plagued the country.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council extends MINUSTAH until 15 February 2007. It sets the force at up to 7,200 troops and 1,951 police, plus 16 corrections officers to help fix the prison system. It asks MINUSTAH to shift its disarmament work toward a community violence reduction program with jobs for former gang members and at-risk youth. It also urges fast completion of run-off and local elections.

Burundi's integrated UN office is renewed by Resolution 1902, adopted on 17 December 2009. The Palipehutu-FNL had become a political party under the December 2008 agreements, an electoral commission and revised electoral code were in place, and elections were due in 2010. Continuing rights violations, curbs on opposition assembly and expression, and violence by party youth groups remained concerns.

The Council extends the mandate of the UN Integrated Office in Burundi, BINUB, until 31 December 2010. BINUB must focus on the electoral process, democratic governance, peace consolidation, reintegration, and gender issues, and be ready to give the electoral commission logistical support at key moments. The government is pressed to protect the commission's independence, finish the disarmament and reintegration strategy, set up an independent national human rights commission, and end impunity. A briefing on the elections is due in May 2010 and a full report in November 2010.

Somalia's targeted sanctions are sharpened and the monitors renewed in Resolution 2002, adopted on 29 July 2011. The Monitoring Group's July 2011 report documented embargo violations and revenue streams, drought and famine were worsening, and armed groups were obstructing humanitarian aid. The Council judged the designation criteria of Resolution 1844 (2008) needed reaffirming and strengthening.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council confirms the travel ban, asset freeze, and arms embargo reach those threatening the peace or the Djibouti process. They reach those violating the embargo, blocking humanitarian aid, recruiting children, or attacking civilians. Misappropriating transitional funds counts as a threat, and non-local commerce through Al-Shabaab-controlled ports counts as supporting a designated entity, so traders can be listed. It extends the Monitoring Group for twelve months with eight experts, tasked with investigating seaport operations raising revenue for Al-Shabaab. It exempts urgent humanitarian payments from the asset freeze for a year.

Southern Rhodesia's white rulers are pressed in Resolution 202, adopted on 6 May 1965 by seven votes to none with four abstentions. The General Assembly and its decolonization committee had repeatedly asked Britain, the colonial power, to free political prisoners, repeal repressive laws, and open political life. Two laws drew special dislike: the order law used to crush protest, and the land law that split farms and fields by race.

The Council endorsed those Assembly requests. It also flagged the danger in elections set for 7 May under a constitution most Rhodesians had rejected. The vote went ahead, the settler government won, and six months later it declared independence unilaterally, defying exactly the pressure this text applied.

Fighting in eastern Ukraine had caused heavy loss of life when diplomats reached a deal in Minsk in February 2015. Resolution 2202, adopted on 17 February 2015, endorses that deal. The Council said the crisis in the Donetsk and Luhansk regions could only be settled in a peaceful way.

The Council endorsed the Package of Measures signed in Minsk on 12 February 2015. All parties were called on to carry it out in full. The package is attached to the resolution. It ordered a cease-fire from 15 February and a pullback of heavy weapons to create wide safety zones. The OSCE would monitor the cease-fire. The package also covered talks on local elections, a special status for the area, and an amnesty law.

A special mission sent to investigate Portuguese attacks on Senegal reported back in 1971. Portugal had refused to cooperate with the mission. Resolution 302, adopted on 24 November 1971, is the Council's response to that report. It follows up Resolution 294, passed the previous July.

The Council thanked the mission and welcomed its proposals. It condemned once more the violence and destruction carried out since 1963. Portuguese forces from Guinea-Bissau had attacked Senegalese villages again and again. Portugal was criticized for refusing to help the mission, and it was told to act at once to respect Senegal's land and people. The Council also called on Portugal to honor, without delay, the right of the people of Guinea-Bissau to govern themselves and be free.

Lesotho, a small country entirely surrounded by South Africa, paid a price for a brave stand in 1976. South Africa had closed several border posts with Lesotho. The closures were meant to force Lesotho to recognize the Transkei. The Transkei was a so-called independent bantustan created under apartheid, and Lesotho refused to recognize it. Resolution 402 was adopted by consensus on 22 December 1976.

The Council praised Lesotho's refusal. It endorsed the General Assembly's call for all governments to deny the Transkei any recognition. South Africa's attempt at coercion was condemned, and it was told to reopen the border posts at once. The closures were causing Lesotho urgent economic harm. The Council therefore appealed to all states for immediate aid. United Nations agencies were asked to organize financial, technical, and material help for the country.

Resolution 502 was adopted in April 1982, right after Argentine armed forces invaded the Falkland Islands, called the Islas Malvinas in the text. The Council had already urged Argentina and the United Kingdom on 1 April to avoid using or threatening force in the area. Members said the invasion deeply disturbed them.

The Council rules that a breach of the peace exists in the region. It demands that fighting stop at once and that all Argentine forces leave the islands right away. It then calls on both governments to settle their differences through talks and to respect the UN Charter in full. The text became the Council's core legal statement on the opening of the Falklands War.

Two states share the Korean peninsula, but for decades neither sat at the UN. The Cold War kept both out. Each had a great-power backer blocking the other. That logjam broke in 1991. Resolution 702 passed without a vote on 8 August 1991. The Council had weighed each bid on its own.

The text backs both bids in turn. First comes North Korea, the Democratic People's Republic. Next comes South Korea, the Republic of Korea. The Assembly admitted both that September. The joint entry was a sign the Cold War was done. Rivals could now sit in the same hall. The door stayed open for talks, though the peninsula's split itself stayed firmly in place.
uslaw-cfr-t1-s426-102:
Section 426.102 of Title 1 of the Code of Federal Regulations sets out definitions for its part. It sits in Part 426, on the National Commission on Military, National, and Public Service. The definitions in part (a) of the Privacy Act, at 5 U.S.C. 552a(a), apply to the part. More terms are then defined for use in the part.

Business day means a calendar day other than a Saturday, Sunday, or legal public holiday. Chair means the Chair of the Commission or the person he or she names in that place. Commission means the National Commission itself. Commission system means a system of records kept by that body, as the text goes on to state. The text is drawn from the eCFR as of October 2026.
uslaw-cfr-t1-s426-202:
Section 426.202 of Title 1 of the Code of Federal Regulations covers proactive disclosures by a federal commission under freedom of information law. It sits in Part 426 of Title 1, for the National Commission on Military, National, and Public Service, in the electronic Code as of October 2026.

Records open for public inspection in electronic form may be reached through the Commission's website, named in the text. The Commission must keep its posted records and indices reviewed and updated on an ongoing basis. It has a public liaison who can help people find records of the Commission. Certain kinds of records must be open routinely on the website, without a formal request. Among them are any formal report issued by the Commission and testimonies and presentations, unless the records fall within an exemption listed in the Act.
uslaw-cfr-t1-s457-102: Section 457.102 of Title 1 of the Code of Federal Regulations states the application of a nondiscrimination part. The part applies to all programs or activities conducted by the agency. The agency is the National Capital Planning Commission. The part enforces nondiscrimination on the basis of handicap in its programs. The section sits near the head of Part 457 of Title 1. The hosted text comes from the electronic Code as of late October 2026, an unofficial compilation. One sentence gives the part its full reach.
uslaw-cfr-t1-s500-102: Section 500.102 of Title 1 of the Code of Federal Regulations states the reach of its part. It sits in Part 500, on the bar against bias based on handicap in programs run by the National Commission for Employment Policy. The rule is a single sentence. It states that the part applies to all programs or activities run by the agency. The text is drawn from the eCFR as of October 2026, an unofficial compilation. The official edition is the yearly Code of Federal Regulations.
uslaw-usc-t1-s102: Section 102 of Title 1 gives the exact wording for the resolving clause that opens each joint resolution. It belongs to the chapter that covers acts, resolutions, and the formalities of enactment. The clause is read as a resolution by the Senate and the House of Representatives of the United States of America, in Congress assembled. The hosted text gives the whole section in a single sentence.
uslaw-usc-t1-s202:
Section 202 of Title 1 orders the making of the tools that keep the Code current. There shall be prepared and published, under the supervision of the House Judiciary Committee, a set of works listed in the text. The first is a cumulative supplement to the Code of Laws of the United States for each session of Congress.

Each such supplement embraces the legislation of the sessions cumulatively. It also corrects errors in the current edition and in prior supplements. A parallel supplement is required for the Code of the District of Columbia, on the same plan. New editions of the Codes and Supplements follow in the list. The section sits in Chapter 3 of Title 1, beside the section that gives the Code its evidentiary force. The hosted Code text is current through Public Law 119-134, as published by the Office of the Law Revision Counsel.
uslaw-usc-t2-s1102: Section 1102 of Title 2 of the United States Code gives the definitions for the chapter on the John C. Stennis Center for Public Service Training and Development. It fixes the sense of three terms used in that chapter. Center means the Stennis Center set up under a later section of the chapter. Board means the Board of Trustees of that Center. Fund means the trust fund for the Center set out in a further named section.
uslaw-usc-t2-s1302:
Section 1302 of Title 2 of the United States Code lists laws that reach Congress staff. The list sits at the head of the accountability chapter for the branch. Each named law is to bind the legislative branch as the chapter sets. The Fair Labor Standards Act of 1938 is first in the list.

Title Seven of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 comes next in line. The Americans with Disabilities Act of 1990 is named after it. Age bias in jobs, family leave, and job safety acts are listed. Union ties for federal staff and a ban on lie tests are named. Plant closing notice and the Rehabilitation Act are in the list too. Veterans' job rights and a named part of Title 5 close the run.
uslaw-usc-t2-s1402:
Section 1402 of Title 2 tells a congressional employee how to start a dispute case. To commence a proceeding under the subchapter, a covered employee must file a claim with the Office. The employee must allege a violation of a law made applicable by the accountability scheme.

The Office may not accept a claim filed after the deadline the section sets. The claim must be made in writing, under oath or affirmation. It must describe the facts behind the claim and the violation alleged. It must identify the employing office said to have committed the violation, or where it occurred. It must be in the form the Office requires. The text adds that nothing in these rules limits an employee's ability to seek information from the Office. The section sits in Chapter 24 of Title 2, in the subchapter on dispute-resolution procedures.
uslaw-usc-t2-s1502:
Section 1502 of Title 2 of the United States Code gives definitions for the unfunded mandates reform chapter. Title 2 covers Congress, and this section sits at the head of that chapter in Title 2. The hosted text is the version current in twenty twenty six. Rather than restate terms, it borrows them from a budget chapter.

For purposes of the chapter, terms defined in a named section of the budget law carry those meanings here, the text states. One stated exception is flagged for a linked section. The term Director is then defined directly as the Director of the Congressional Budget Office. Shared terms keep mandate review and budget scoring speaking the same language.
uslaw-usc-t2-s1602:
Section 1602 of Title 2 defines the terms of the lobbying disclosure chapter. Agency carries the meaning given in the administrative procedure provision of Title 5 that the text cites. A client is any person or entity that employs or retains another person, for pay or other compensation, to conduct lobbying activities on its behalf.

A person whose own employees lobby for it is both a client and an employer of those employees. Where a coalition or association hires lobbyists, the client is the coalition or association, not its individual members. Covered executive branch official is then defined at length. The list starts with the President and the Vice President. It reaches officers and employees of the Executive Office of the President. It continues through the levels of the Executive Schedule, as the text goes on to detail. The section sits in Chapter 26 of Title 2.
uslaw-usc-t2-s1702:
Section 1702 of Title 2 of the United States Code sets the duties of the Librarian of Congress for sound recordings. Title 2 covers Congress, and this section sits in the chapter on sound recording preservation. Its subchapter creates the National Recording Registry. The hosted text is the version current in twenty twenty six.

For that registry the Librarian must set up criteria and procedures, the text states. Those rules govern how sound recordings may be placed in the registry. The aim is to mark recordings of lasting worth for the nation. Readers get the base duty from which the registry's selection process flows. Later parts build out the rest of the program.
uslaw-usc-t2-s1802: Section 1802 of Title 2 fixes the pay of the Architect of the Capitol by reference. The compensation of the Architect is at an annual rate equal to the annual rate of basic pay for level two of the Executive Schedule. That schedule is set under a provision of Title 5 named in the text. The section sits in Chapter 28 of Title 2, on the Architect of the Capitol. The hosted Code text is current through Public Law 119-134. Congress pegged the office's salary to the federal pay ladder.
uslaw-usc-t2-s1902:
Section 1902 of Title 2 of the United States Code sets the pay of the Chief of the Capitol Police. Title 2 covers Congress, and this section sits in the chapter on the Capitol Police, in the part on organization. The hosted text is the version current in twenty twenty six. It is a single sentence rule that ties one salary to another.

The annual rate of pay for the Chief is set equal to a named benchmark. That benchmark is the annual rate of basic pay for level two of the Executive Schedule. The schedule is set out in Title 5 for senior federal posts. By linking the two rates, the section lets the Chief's pay move with that schedule.
uslaw-usc-t2-s2002:
Section 2002 of Title 2 of the United States Code deals with the gain of buildings for a time of need. It sits in Chapter 30, on the work of the Capitol complex, in a part on the House. The rule stands even if a second law says the reverse. In order to meet a state of need, the Chief Administrative Officer of the House may gain buildings and plant. Those buildings are for the use of the House of Representatives.

The gain may be made if funds for the end are free for use. The ways of gain are named in the text. They are a lease, a buy, or a second form of pact that the officer holds to be fit. One such form is a pact of shared views with the head of an agency of the state.
uslaw-usc-t2-s2102:
Section 2102 of Title 2 states the duties of the Senate Commission on Art. The Commission is authorized and directed to take charge of the Senate's art. It must supervise, hold, place, protect, and make known all works of art, historical objects, and exhibits in its territory.

That territory is the Senate wing of the Capitol, the Senate office buildings, and all rooms, spaces, and corridors in them. The works covered are the property of the United States. In its judgment, the Commission may also accept works offered, given, or devised to the Senate, its committees, and its officers. Acceptance is for placement and exhibition in the same spaces. The Commission must prescribe regulations for the care, protection, and placement of the works. The section sits in Chapter 30 of Title 2, in the part on the Senate Commission on Art.
uslaw-usc-t2-s2202:
Section 2202 of Title 2 of the United States Code sets a high bar for naming any part of the Capitol Visitor Center. It sits in the general part of the Visitor Center chapter. As a rule, no part of the Center may be given a name or designation without set approvals.

The approval must come from at least three quarters of the Capitol Preservation Commission members of the Democratic party. It must also come from at least three quarters of the Commission members of the Republican party. The two party counts are kept apart, so each side must clear the bar on its own. One carve out is stated: rooms or spaces under the charge of the Senate or the House fall outside this rule.
uslaw-usc-t2-s302:
Section 302 of Title 2 is a one-line grant of rule-making power. The committee, it says, is authorized to prescribe such regulations as may be necessary. The regulations serve to carry out the purposes of the chapter.

The chapter in view is Chapter 10 of Title 2. It covers the classification of employees of the House of Representatives. The hosted Code text is published by the Office of the Law Revision Counsel. It is current through Public Law 119-134. Short as it is, the line does real work. It gives the committee in charge a legal basis for the detailed rules that a job classification system needs. Without such a grant, the standards in the chapter would have no machinery for their day-to-day application in the House.
uslaw-usc-t2-s4102:
Section 4102 of Title 2 of the United States Code covers the purchase of supplies for the Senate and the House of Representatives. It sits in Chapter 41, on officers of Congress and their work, in a general subchapter. The Code text is current through Public Law 119-134, as issued by the Office of the Law Revision Counsel.

The whole provision is a single sentence. It permits supplies for either chamber to be bought under one shared source: the schedule of contract items and prices kept by the Administrator of General Services. No other buying route is named in the section.
uslaw-usc-t2-s4302: Section 4302 of Title 2 of the United States Code sets a top pay rate. The post is Chief of Staff of the Joint Committee on Taxation. The section is a single short line of law on that cap. The top yearly rate for the post may not pass a set line. The line is the greater of two rates named in the text. One rate is a set sum of money stated in the line. The other is the rate in force under a Speaker's order.
uslaw-usc-t2-s4502:
Section 4502 of Title 2 covers funding for Members of Congress in the chapter on congressional pay and benefits. Starting with fiscal year 1983 and in each year after, it appropriates the sums needed for that purpose from Treasury funds not already set aside elsewhere. The amount follows two tests, what the law allows and what the President recommends for federal workers that year.

Funding under the section pays both member compensation and the related administrative expenses tied to it. A payment made under the section replaces any sums that built up in earlier years but were left unpaid. For this section, Member covers each Senator and each House member. It also covers the Resident Commissioner from Puerto Rico, the Delegates from the District of Columbia, Guam, the Virgin Islands, and American Samoa, and the Vice President.
uslaw-usc-t2-s4702:
Section 4702 of Title 2 of the United States Code covers notice of limits on work after leaving Congress. It sits in Chapter 47 of that title, on congressional ethics. Part (a) deals with notice of those limits. The duty arises after a Member of Congress or an elected officer of either House leaves office. It also arises when the work of a covered staff member ends.

The staff covered are those named in named parts of section 207(e) of Title 18. The Clerk of the House gives the notice, after talks with a further officer, as the text goes on to state. The text is current through Public Law 119-134, as issued by the Office of the Law Revision Counsel.
uslaw-usc-t2-s4902:
Section 4902 of Title 2 of the United States Code covers the John W. McCormack Residential Page School. It sits in Chapter 49 of that title, on congressional pages. Part (a) clears the building of a dormitory and classroom complex for the school. The site must be approved by two bodies acting jointly. They are the Senate Office Building Commission and the House Office Building Commission.

Plans for the complex are to be drawn up by or under the Architect of the Capitol. Those plans must be sent to both commissions and approved by them jointly. The part goes on with more terms for the project, as the text states. The text is current through Public Law 119-134, as issued by the Office of the Law Revision Counsel.
uslaw-usc-t2-s502:
Section 502 of Title 2 of the United States Code deals with Senate mail guidance. A Select Committee on Standards and Conduct holds the role here. It must give guidance, help, and advice on franked mail use. The aid comes as written views or as talks with the person.

The aid is for folk who hold the right to send franked mail. Members, Members-elect, and widows or widowers of such folk are named. Senate officials with the same right are in the class too. The panel must also write the rules for proper use of the right. A second part deals with claims of abuse of the mail right. It sets a probe, a notice, a hearing, and a ruling path.
uslaw-usc-t2-s5102:
Section 5102 of Title 2 of the United States Code lets the top three House leaders each hire one consultant. The Speaker, the Majority Leader, and the Minority Leader hold the power. Each may appoint a single consultant under the section.

The appointment may be temporary or intermittent, suiting expert help called in as needed. The consultant's pay is set by the leader who appoints him. A ceiling binds that pay by the day. The daily rate may not exceed the per diem equal of the highest yearly rate paid to standing committee staff. The section thus gives leadership offices a narrow channel to outside advice. One expert at a time, at a capped rate, is the measure of the grant.
uslaw-usc-t2-s5302:
Section 5302 of Title 2 states when a Member of the House is entitled to be paid. Each Member and Delegate, after taking and subscribing the required oath, is entitled to receive salary at the end of each month. The whole operative rule is that single sentence.

The section sits in Chapter 53 of Title 2, on Members of the House of Representatives. It falls in the subchapter on member pay. The hosted Code text is published by the Office of the Law Revision Counsel. It is current through Public Law 119-134. Two ideas are packed into the line. Pay follows the oath, so no salary runs before a member is sworn. And pay runs monthly, in arrears, at each month's end. The brevity of the text leaves no room for dispute about the basic timing of a member's pay.
uslaw-usc-t2-s5502:
Section 5502 of Title 2 of the United States Code covers House emergency operations positions. It sits in Chapter 55 of that title, on House officers and administration. Part (a) creates new posts with effect from fiscal year 2002 and each year after. Two added posts are created in each of three named House offices.

The three offices are the Office of the Clerk, the Office of the Chief Administrative Officer, and the Office of the Sergeant at Arms. Part (b) of the section takes up the duties of the staff named to those posts. The text is current through Public Law 119-134, as issued by the Office of the Law Revision Counsel.
uslaw-usc-t2-s5602: Section 5602 of Title 2 of the United States Code deals with the term of the Sergeant at Arms of the House. It sits in Chapter 55, on House officers, in a part on that office. A man duly chosen for the post and sworn is the subject. Such a man is to stay in the post till the man who is to take his place is chosen and sworn. The House keeps the right to take the post from him at any time.
uslaw-usc-t2-s602:
Section 602 of Title 2 of the United States Code sets the duties of the Congressional Budget Office. Its first duty is to aid the Budget Committees of both houses. The aid is facts that help them do the work in their charge. That work spans the budget, funds bills, and new spending bills.

Facts on tax gains and tax breaks are part of the same aid. Past and future tax takes, and shifts in tax flows, are covered too. The Office must also serve three more named committees on request. They are Appropriations, Ways and Means, and the Senate Finance Committee. Any facts that help those panels in their own fields must be given. Related facts the panels ask for fall in the same duty.
uslaw-usc-t2-s6102:
Section 6102 of Title 2 of the United States Code deals with grants for the costs of the heads of the Senate. It sits in Chapter 61, on the heads of the Senate, in a general part of the chapter. From the year of funds 1978, and each year from then on, a change is made. The grants for the costs of the Majority and Minority Leaders of the Senate are raised. They are raised to $40,000 in each year for each such head of the Senate.

A first bar deals with the grants of two more posts. From the year of funds 1983, the grants for the costs of the Majority and Minority Whips may not top $10,000 in a year for each Whip. A second bar deals with a span of time that starts on 3 January 1977.
uslaw-usc-t2-s6302:
Section 6302 of Title 2 of the United States Code deals with the wages of Senators. It sits in Chapter 63, on Senate members, in a part on the pay of members. The rule in chief deals with Senators named to fill a gap in the Senate. The wages of such a Senator start on the day of the naming. They run on till the man's heirs in the post are chosen and sworn in their place.

The text then adds rules for the men chosen to take the place of those named. If such a man is chosen in a break when the Senate is not in session, his wages start on the day after the poll. If he is chosen while the Senate sits, his wages start on the day he is sworn.
uslaw-usc-t2-s6502:
Section 6502 of Title 2 of the United States Code lets two Senate officers buy temporary help from private firms. The Secretary of the Senate and the Sergeant at Arms share the power. Their purchases are subject to regulations the Committee on Rules and Administration may set.

Each engagement of temporary help is capped in length. No single procurement of services may run longer than thirty days. The legal status of the workers is spelled out with care. A person performing such services is not an employee of the United States. He is not to be treated as one for any purpose during the work. The closing part of the section fixes its effective date. The design lets Senate offices meet short surges of work without swelling the federal payroll.
uslaw-usc-t2-s802:
Section 802 of Title 2 sets up the Congressional Award Program itself. The Board created by the prior section must establish and run the program. Its aim is to promote initiative, achievement, and excellence among youths. The fields named are public service, personal development, and physical and expedition fitness.

Medals are the awards under the program. They go to young people within the United States, aged fourteen through twenty-three. Exceptions to that age band are allowed if the Board prescribes them. A recipient must meet the standards of achievement the Board sets. The Board must set those standards, set ways to verify that a youth meets them, and designate the recipients. The section sits in Chapter 19 of Title 2. The hosted Code text is current through Public Law 119-134, as published by the Office of the Law Revision Counsel.
uslaw-usc-t2-s902:
Section 902 of Title 2 of the United States Code states the enforcement of pay as you go budget rules. It sits in the chapter on emergency powers to cut budget deficits. Its stated aim is to be sure that laws passed before October 1, 2002, that raise the deficit trigger an offsetting cut.

The cut, called a sequestration, falls not later than fifteen days after Congress ends a session. It is timed to match any cut under two sister sections of the title. The Office of Management and Budget works out the size of the deficit change. It adds its costings of direct spending and receipts laws, plus savings from past cuts under this scheme. The host text runs on into the full count method.
voltaire-philosophical-dictionary-1802:
Voltaire published his Dictionnaire philosophique in 1764, a pocket book of short articles meant to be carried and quoted. The London English edition of 1802, The Philosophical Dictionary, is the text here. He wrote many entries himself and shaped them all into an alphabet of the Enlightenment, from Abraham to Zoroaster.

Toleration, fanaticism, and superstition take the sharpest hits, while common sense gets the warmest praise. Each article is a small raid: a definition, a story, a sting in the tail. Voltaire meant the book to change the way his century thought, one entry at a time. It remains the most readable of his weapons, and the most quoted.
voyages-of-samuel-de-champlain-volume-02: Volume two of Samuel de Champlain's Voyages covers the years 1604 to 1610, in Charles Pomeroy Otis's rendering from the French, for the Prince Society. The Rev. Edmund F. Slafter edited the volume and wrote its memoir of Champlain, and twenty local maps appear as heliotype copies. Pages present here hold transcriber's notes, the title page, and the first lines of the preface only. That preface explains that two French poems of praise, printed with Champlain's 1613 edition, are left out here as having no historical worth. The voyages themselves are not shown.
what-will-he-do-with-it-volume-02:
Book two of Lord Lytton's What Will He Do With It? follows Lionel Haughton on a trip by rail and carriage. Lionel asks the way to Fawley Manor House, five miles off. The road runs through rough, empty country with wide commons and beech woods. No village, spire, or lodge comes in sight along the way.

Lytton contrasts this older, wilder England with the neat suburbs of his own day. Knights Templar or fleeing fighters of the Wars of the Roses might have ridden here, he muses. The quiet land shapes the minds of those who live in it, by his claim. Lionel rides toward Guy Darrell's house and a fateful meeting. The volume's mood turns grave and lonely.
works-of-john-bunyan-volume-02:
George Offor edited this second volume of John Bunyan's works, again covering experimental, doctrinal, and practical writings. Pages present here open with a treatise on the saints' knowledge of Christ's love. Offor's remarks say Bunyan left the piece ready for the press at his death. It first appeared in a folio gathering in 1692. Offor praises its depth and clear Christian thought.

Friends Ebenezer Chandler and John Wilson called the treatise excellent. It aims to help Christians grow in grace and win others over. Readers get mature Bunyan, writing on Christ's riches for believers. Devotion and doctrine stay tightly joined.
young-journal-of-discourses-vol02:
Liverpool printed Volume II of the Journal of Discourses in 1855, one more year of Utah sermons set in type. Brigham Young speaks often, joined by his counsellors, members of the Twelve, and other elders. Shorthand reporters caught the words as spoken, so the record keeps the rough edge of live preaching.

The talks mix high doctrine with farming, building, and conduct in a desert kingdom taking shape. Together the volumes form a year-by-year account of what the Saints heard from their pulpits. For students of the movement, few sources put them so close to the voices that led it.
young-theory-light-colours-1802:
Thomas Young, an English doctor and sage, read this Bakerian Lecture on light and hues across 1801 and 1802. Most men of his day held that light was a stream of tiny parts. Young held that light moves in waves, like sound through air.

His proof rests on the way light bands form when rays cross and mix. He showed the bands fit waves that add and cancel, not parts that fly straight. The wave view made a stuff called the ether seem a need, since waves must wave in something. The talk is still the root text of the wave view.
zicci-a-tale-volume-02:
Edward Bulwer-Lytton is named as author in the pages present here for this second book of the tale. Chapter ten opens on a mountain at night. Merton and his Italian guides reach the mules safely, then worry over missing Glyndon. Two forms approach through starlight. Zicci carries Glyndon, who was overcome by crater fumes. One more minute of vapour would have killed him, Zicci says.

The Italian guide trembles, claiming Zicci's face looked inhuman nights before. Zicci calmly notes his prophecy of the meeting came true. Rescue and dread arrive together. Readers get the tale's middle, with its start and end held in sibling records.
